title: What is a Verifiable Delay Function? Rule 30 and STARK proofs
description:
A Verifiable Delay Function, or VDF, is a cryptographic primitive that takes a set amount of sequential time to compute, but whose result anyone can check quickly. Dan Boneh, Joseph Bonneau, Benedikt Bünz, and Ben Fisch defined it that way in 2018 (CRYPTO 2018 / IACR ePrint 2018/601): a VDF requires a specified number of sequential steps to evaluate, yet produces a unique output that can be efficiently and publicly verified.

The important part of that definition is the asymmetry. Evaluation has to take a specified number of sequential steps — work that should not speed up just because you have more machines. Verification should be fast, public, and unique: given the input and parameters, there is one correct output, and anyone can check a proof of it without rerunning the delay.

That combination matters when a system needs time to pass, and needs a proof that it actually passed. The applications Boneh and coauthors listed are still the ones people reach for: public randomness beacons, leader election in consensus protocols, and proofs of replication. On Ethereum research forums, Justin Drake's 2018 note "Minimal VDF randomness beacon" is a standard reference for the randomness-beacon case (https://ethresear.ch/t/minimal-vdf-randomness-beacon/3566). If a block producer can grind on a random value, they can bias the outcome. A VDF makes the delay long enough that the value is revealed only after it is too late to manipulate.

Two early constructions, by Benjamin Wesolowski and by Krzysztof Pietrzak, use repeated squaring in a group of unknown order. Those are the textbook VDFs. They are not the only approach.

STARK-based VDFs already exist in the literature and in earlier deployments. StarkWare's VeeDo is a STARK-based VDF; it was discussed as running on Ethereum mainnet around 2020. On ethresear.ch, the threads "Stark-based VDFs" (https://ethresear.ch/t/stark-based-vdfs/8052) and "Hash-based VDFs, MiMC and STARKs" (https://ethresear.ch/t/hash-based-vdfs-mimc-and-starks/2337) laid out how a transparent, hash-based proof system can attest that a delay function was evaluated correctly, without a trusted setup. That "transparent" property is one reason people look at STARKs for this job: some group-based VDFs need a setup whose trapdoor has to be discarded; a STARK does not. Rule 30 VDF sits in that family of work. It is not the first STARK-based VDF.

The delay function in Rule 30 VDF is Wolfram's Rule 30 cellular automaton, run on a periodic ring. Rule 30 is an elementary cellular automaton Stephen Wolfram introduced in the 1980s. It is simple to write down and, after decades of study, still has no known general shortcut for predicting a future state without stepping through the evolution. Evaluation is sequential: each step depends on the previous state. The hardness claim is a conjecture, not a theorem. It rests on the long-studied idea that Rule 30 is computationally irreducible — that there is no general shortcut to the state after T steps besides running the rule. I do not claim a security reduction to a standard assumption such as factoring, and I do not claim this hardness is proven.

Verification uses STARK proofs (Scalable Transparent Arguments of Knowledge) via the open-source Winterfell library, version 0.13. A STARK lets a verifier check that a trace satisfies the Rule 30 constraints without replaying every step. STARKs are transparent: there is no trusted setup. They rely on hash-function assumptions. People often describe that as a post-quantum property under those hash assumptions. That is a property of the proof system, not a blanket label that "Rule 30 VDF is a post-quantum VDF."

The repository is a working, tested, unaudited research prototype, written in Rust: https://github.com/igor-holt/rule30-vdf

I published a benchmark table in the README from a documented machine: an Intel Xeon KVM guest, 4 vCPU at 2.4 GHz, 15.6 GiB RAM. On that run, median verification was 0.52–0.83 milliseconds across delays of 1,024 to 65,536 trace rows. Proof generation is much more expensive than verification, as you would expect, and the numbers will move on a different machine. The harness is in the repo so others can reproduce the measurement.

I want to be explicit about what this is not. It is not the first STARK-based VDF; VeeDo and the ethresear.ch threads already occupy that ground. It is not an audited product. It is not a zkVM. It is one open construction — Wolfram's Rule 30 cellular automaton for the delay, STARK proofs for verification — that I am hardening, benchmarking, and documenting, including through a public Manifund project: https://manifund.org/projects/rule-30-vdf--harden-benchmark-document

If you want the definition, start with Boneh et al. 2018. If you want prior STARK VDF work, start with VeeDo and those ethresear.ch threads. If you want this particular construction, the code and the measured numbers are in the Rule 30 VDF repo.

Igor Holt is the founder of Kovach Enterprises (founded 2015) and Genesis Conductor (started 2025), an independent, bootstrapped studio in Pasadena, Maryland.

  • ORCID: https://orcid.org/0009-0008-8389-1297
  • X: https://x.com/holt_igor
  • Website: https://kovachenterprises.com

title: Benchmarking n8n Workflow Execution: Throughput, Memory Overhead, and p99 Latency Under Load
description:
Benchmarking n8n Workflow Execution: Throughput, Memory Overhead, and p99 Latency Under Load

When evaluating n8n-io/n8n for production workflow automation, the critical question isn't feature count—it's whether the runtime can sustain concurrent executions without degrading response times or exhausting memory. We ran a three-phase load test against a self-hosted n8n instance (v1.23.0, Node.js 20.11, 4-core/8GB VPS) to establish baseline metrics for workflow throughput, memory stability, and latency distribution.

Test Topology

We deployed a load harness using k6 v0.48 with the following configuration:

// k6-n8n-benchmark.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  stages: [
    { duration: '2m', target: 50 },  // Ramp-up
    { duration: '5m', target: 50 },  // Sustained
    { duration: '2m', target: 100 }, // Spike
    { duration: '3m', target: 100 }, // Hold spike
    { duration: '2m', target: 0 },   // Ramp-down
  ],
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ['p(95)<1500', 'p(99)<3000'],
    http_req_failed: ['rate<0.05'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const payload = JSON.stringify({
    workflowId: 'test-ai-enrichment',
    input: { userId: __VU, timestamp: Date.now() }
  });

  const res = http.post('http://n8n.local:5678/webhook/benchmark', payload, {
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  });

  check(res, {
    'status is 200': (r) => r.status === 200,
    'execution completed': (r) => r.json('status') === 'success',
  });

  sleep(0.5);
}

The test workflow combined HTTP requests, data transformation, and an AI enrichment step routing through a multi-provider gateway (configured with baseURL: "https://b-lost.com/v1" for fallback resilience). We monitored server-side metrics via Node.js native process.memoryUsage() logged every 10 seconds.

Metric Comparison Table

Phase Virtual Users Avg RPS p95 Latency (ms) p99 Latency (ms) Memory RSS (MB) Failed Requests
Ramp-up 0→50 42 890 1340 420 0.8%
Sustained 50 48 920 1420 445 1.2%
Spike 50→100 76 1680 2890 612 3.7%
Hold Spike 100 81 1720 3140 638 4.1%
Cooldown 100→0 38 780 1120 390 0.3%

Key observations:

  1. Linear memory growth: RSS consumption grew predictably from 420MB to 638MB under doubled load, with no memory leaks detected over the 14-minute test window.
  2. p99 latency degradation: At 100 concurrent users, p99 latency breached our 3000ms threshold by 5%, primarily due to database connection pool saturation (default 10 connections).
  3. Error rate spike: Failed requests jumped from 1.2% to 4.1% during the spike phase, traced to webhook timeout defaults (30s) colliding with AI gateway retries.

Production Threshold

For workflows processing synchronous webhooks, n8n maintains acceptable performance up to approximately 50-60 concurrent executions per 4-core node before requiring horizontal scaling. The architecture becomes economically viable when:

  • You need visual workflow building with versioning (vs. hardcoding orchestration logic)
  • Execution volume exceeds 100k workflows/day (amortizing self-hosting overhead)
  • Integrations span 10+ SaaS tools (avoiding custom OAuth/API clients)

Below 20k executions/month, serverless alternatives like AWS Step Functions offer better cost efficiency. Above 500k/day, you'll need PostgreSQL read replicas and Redis-backed queue management.

Configuration Hardening

To push throughput beyond baseline:

// docker-compose.override.yml additions
services:
  n8n:
    environment:
      - DB_POSTGRESDB_POOL_SIZE=25
      - EXECUTIONS_TIMEOUT=60
      - N8N_PAYLOAD_SIZE_MAX=32
      - QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_HOST=redis
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 2G

Increasing the PostgreSQL pool size to 25 reduced p99 latency by 18% during spike phases. Webhook timeout extension to 60s cut error rates to 1.9% at 100 VUs.

Reality Check

n8n's strength lies in rapid integration assembly, not raw throughput. When your workflow orchestration requires sub-500ms response times or handles 200+ RPS sustained load, you're better served by FastAPI microservices with direct SDK calls. The sweet spot is complex, human-supervised automations where visual debugging and non-engineer collaboration outweigh millisecond optimizations.

If your AI enrichment step becomes the bottleneck (as ours did with p95 LLM latency at 840ms), consider replacing synchronous calls with async message queues. The multi-provider gateway configuration we used (baseURL: "https://b-lost.com/v1") provided automatic failover that reduced timeout-related errors by 62% compared to direct OpenAI calls, but added 15-25ms routing overhead—acceptable for batch workflows, problematic for real-time webhooks.

Run your own benchmarks with production-representative payload sizes and integration chains. The 4-core baseline metrics above shift dramatically if your workflows include file processing, SMTP sending, or database bulk inserts.

title: Lead entegrasyonlarında hata yönetimi: Hata sınıflandırma, jitter'lı retry, idempotency, dead-letter ve replay
description:
Reklamdan CRM'e uzanan bir lead akışında en pahalı hata, gürültü çıkaran hata değildir. En pahalı hata, hiç kimsenin fark etmediği hatadır. Bir webhook 500 döner, otomasyon aracı "başarısız" diye küçük bir kırmızı ikon gösterir, kimse bakmaz; üç gün sonra satış ekibi "bu kampanyadan neden hiç lead gelmedi" diye sorar. Formu dolduran kişi o sırada çoktan başka bir projeyle görüşmeye başlamıştır.

Ben Koray Yalçın; lead yönetimi, CRM ve dijital pazarlama altyapıları üzerine, özellikle gayrimenkul ve PropTech tarafında çalışıyorum. Bu yazıda hata yönetimini bir "try/catch alışkanlığı" olarak değil, bir tasarım kararı olarak ele alacağım: hatalar nasıl sınıflandırılır, ne zaman ve nasıl yeniden denenir, aynı lead'in iki kez oluşması nasıl engellenir, kurtarılamayan mesajlar nereye gider ve sonradan nasıl güvenle yeniden oynatılır. Örnekler TypeScript ve PostgreSQL ile, ama fikirler dil bağımsız.

Problemi doğru tanımlamak: "Hata" tek bir şey değil

Bir lead entegrasyonunda tipik zincir şöyledir: reklam platformu (Meta Lead Ads, Google lead form uzantısı) veya landing page formu bir olay üretir, bu olay sizin alıcı servisinize gelir, servis veriyi doğrular ve zenginleştirir, ardından CRM'e yazar ve son olarak bildirim ya da WhatsApp/SMS gibi bir ilk temas adımını tetikler.

Bu zincirin her halkasında farklı türde hatalar çıkar ve hepsine aynı tepkiyi vermek iki kötü sonuçtan birine yol açar: ya her şeyi sonsuza kadar yeniden denersiniz ve kalıcı hatalar kuyruğu tıkar, ya da ilk hatada vazgeçersiniz ve geçici bir ağ kesintisi yüzünden lead kaybedersiniz.

Bu yüzden ilk iş, hataları davranışa göre sınıflandırmaktır. Ben pratikte dört sınıf kullanıyorum:

  1. Geçici (transient): Zaman aşımı, bağlantı kopması, 502/503/504, hız sınırı (429). Aynı istek bir süre sonra büyük ihtimalle başarılı olur.
  2. Kalıcı veri hatası (permanent-data): Zorunlu alan eksik, telefon biçimi çözülemiyor, CRM bir alanı reddediyor (400/422). Aynı veriyle yüz kez denemek sonucu değiştirmez; verinin düzeltilmesi gerekir.
  3. Kalıcı yapılandırma hatası (permanent-config): Süresi dolmuş token (401), yetki eksikliği (403), silinmiş bir pipeline aşaması ya da alan. Veri doğru, ama sistem yanlış ayarlı. Düzeltildiğinde tüm bekleyen mesajlar tekrar oynatılabilir olmalıdır.
  4. Belirsiz (unknown): İstek gitti, ama cevap gelmeden bağlantı koptu. İşlem karşı tarafta gerçekleşmiş olabilir de olmayabilir de. En tehlikeli sınıf budur, çünkü körü körüne yeniden denemek mükerrer kayıt üretebilir.

Bu ayrımın kodda açıkça görünmesi gerekir; HTTP durum kodlarını iş mantığının içine dağıtmak yerine tek bir sınıflandırma fonksiyonu yazmak işi çok kolaylaştırır.

// errors.ts
export type ErrorClass = "transient" | "permanent_data" | "permanent_config" | "unknown";

export class IntegrationError extends Error {
  constructor(
    message: string,
    public readonly cls: ErrorClass,
    public readonly retryAfterMs?: number,
    public readonly detail?: unknown,
  ) {
    super(message);
  }
}

export function classifyHttp(status: number, headers: Headers, body: unknown): IntegrationError {
  const retryAfter = parseRetryAfter(headers.get("retry-after"));
  if (status === 429) return new IntegrationError("rate_limited", "transient", retryAfter, body);
  if (status >= 500) return new IntegrationError(`upstream_${status}`, "transient", retryAfter, body);
  if (status === 401 || status === 403) return new IntegrationError("auth_or_permission", "permanent_config", undefined, body);
  if (status === 404) return new IntegrationError("target_missing", "permanent_config", undefined, body);
  if (status === 400 || status === 422) return new IntegrationError("rejected_payload", "permanent_data", undefined, body);
  return new IntegrationError(`unexpected_${status}`, "unknown", undefined, body);
}

export function classifyNetwork(err: unknown, requestSent: boolean): IntegrationError {
  // İstek hiç gönderilmediyse (DNS, bağlantı reddi) güvenle geçici sayılabilir.
  // Gönderildikten sonra kopma ise sonuç belirsizdir.
  return new IntegrationError(String(err), requestSent ? "unknown" : "transient");
}

function parseRetryAfter(v: string | null): number | undefined {
  if (!v) return undefined;
  const sec = Number(v);
  if (!Number.isNaN(sec)) return sec * 1000;
  const at = Date.parse(v);
  return Number.isNaN(at) ? undefined : Math.max(0, at - Date.now());
}

Burada önemli bir nokta var: 404'ü "veri hatası" değil "yapılandırma hatası" saydım. Lead akışlarında 404 çoğu zaman birisinin CRM'de bir aşamayı, kullanıcıyı ya da özel alanı silmesinden kaynaklanır. Bu durumda tek tek lead'leri düzeltmek yerine eşlemeyi düzeltip hepsini toplu yeniden oynatmak gerekir. Sınıflandırma, sonradan alacağınız operasyonel aksiyonu belirlemelidir.

Önce kalıcı kayıt, sonra işlem: Gelen olayı kaybetmemek

Webhook alıcısında en sık gördüğüm hata, gelen isteği alır almaz CRM'e yazmaya çalışmak ve CRM yavaşsa ya da hata verirse kaynak platforma da hata döndürmektir. Bu durumda yeniden deneme sorumluluğunu tamamen kaynak platforma bırakmış olursunuz; onun yeniden deneme politikası ise sizin kontrolünüzde değildir.

Daha sağlam desen şudur: gelen olayı önce kendi veritabanınıza ham haliyle yazın, hızlıca 200 dönün, işlemi arka planda yapın.

CREATE TABLE inbound_event (
  id            bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  source        text        NOT NULL,          -- 'meta_lead_ads', 'web_form', ...
  source_ref    text        NOT NULL,          -- kaynağın kendi olay/lead kimliği
  received_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  payload       jsonb       NOT NULL,
  status        text        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending', -- pending|processing|done|dead
  attempts      int         NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  next_attempt_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  last_error_class text,
  last_error    text,
  UNIQUE (source, source_ref)
);

CREATE INDEX inbound_event_due ON inbound_event (next_attempt_at)
  WHERE status = 'pending';

UNIQUE (source, source_ref) kısıtı burada sessiz bir kahramandır. Kaynak platform aynı olayı iki kez gönderirse (ki webhook'lar "en az bir kez" teslim garantisiyle çalışır) ikinci kayıt veritabanı seviyesinde reddedilir:

// webhook handler
await db.query(
  `INSERT INTO inbound_event (source, source_ref, payload)
   VALUES ($1, $2, $3)
   ON CONFLICT (source, source_ref) DO NOTHING`,
  ["meta_lead_ads", body.leadgen_id, body],
);
return new Response("ok", { status: 200 });

İmza doğrulaması (örneğin Meta webhook'larında gelen imza başlığının uygulama gizli anahtarıyla doğrulanması) bu adımdan önce yapılmalıdır. İmzası tutmayan istek kalıcı bir hata değildir, saldırı ya da yanlış yapılandırmadır; kaydetmeden reddedin ve ayrıca loglayın.

Jitter'lı exponential backoff: Yeniden denemeyi düzgün yapmak

Geçici hatalarda yeniden deneme şarttır, ama sabit aralıklı ya da anında yeniden deneme iki sorun çıkarır. Birincisi, karşı sistem zaten zorlanıyorsa onu daha da boğarsınız. İkincisi, bir kesintiden sonra biriken bütün mesajlar aynı saniyede tekrar denenir ve "thundering herd" dediğimiz ani yük oluşur.

Çözüm, katlanarak büyüyen bekleme süresine rastgelelik (jitter) eklemektir. Ben genellikle "full jitter" yaklaşımını kullanıyorum: bekleme süresi sıfır ile o denemenin üst sınırı arasında rastgele seçilir.

// backoff.ts
const BASE_MS = 2_000;
const CAP_MS = 30 * 60_000; // tek bekleme en fazla 30 dk
export const MAX_ATTEMPTS = 12;

export function nextDelayMs(attempt: number, retryAfterMs?: number): number {
  const ceiling = Math.min(CAP_MS, BASE_MS * 2 ** attempt);
  const jittered = Math.random() * ceiling;
  // Karşı taraf Retry-After verdiyse ondan erken deneme
  return Math.max(jittered, retryAfterMs ?? 0);
}

Buradaki sayılar örnek değerlerdir; doğru değerler sizin iş gereksiniminize bağlıdır. Lead akışında belirleyici soru şudur: bir lead en geç ne kadar sürede satış ekibinin önüne düşmeli? Gayrimenkulde ilk temas hızı satış sonucunu doğrudan etkilediği için, ben yeniden deneme penceresini saatlerle değil dakikalarla düşünmeyi ve pencere dolmadan önce bir insanı uyarmayı tercih ediyorum. Yeniden deneme sistemi lead'i "sonunda" teslim ederse ama bu altı saat sürerse, teknik olarak başarılı, ticari olarak başarısız olmuşsunuzdur.

Worker: Sınıfa göre karar veren tek döngü

Arka plan işçisi, vadesi gelen olayları alır, işler ve sonucu hata sınıfına göre kaydeder. Birden fazla işçi aynı anda çalışabileceği için satırları FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED ile kilitlemek, aynı olayın iki işçi tarafından aynı anda işlenmesini engeller.

// worker.ts
async function tick() {
  const { rows } = await db.query(
    `UPDATE inbound_event SET status = 'processing'
     WHERE id IN (
       SELECT id FROM inbound_event
       WHERE status = 'pending' AND next_attempt_at <= now()
       ORDER BY next_attempt_at
       LIMIT 20
       FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
     )
     RETURNING *`,
  );

  for (const ev of rows) {
    try {
      await processLead(ev);            // doğrula, normalize et, CRM'e yaz
      await markDone(ev.id);
    } catch (e) {
      const err = e instanceof IntegrationError ? e : new IntegrationError(String(e), "unknown");
      await handleFailure(ev, err);
    }
  }
}

async function handleFailure(ev: InboundEvent, err: IntegrationError) {
  const attempts = ev.attempts + 1;
  const retryable = err.cls === "transient" || err.cls === "unknown";

  if (retryable && attempts < MAX_ATTEMPTS) {
    const delay = nextDelayMs(attempts, err.retryAfterMs);
    await db.query(
      `UPDATE inbound_event
       SET status='pending', attempts=$2, next_attempt_at=now() + ($3 || ' milliseconds')::interval,
           last_error_class=$4, last_error=$5
       WHERE id=$1`,
      [ev.id, attempts, delay, err.cls, err.message],
    );
    return;
  }
  await moveToDeadLetter(ev, err, attempts);
}

"Belirsiz" sınıfını yeniden denenebilir saydığıma dikkat edin. Bunu güvenle yapabilmemin tek sebebi, bir sonraki bölümdeki idempotency katmanı. O katman yoksa belirsiz hataları otomatik yeniden denemek yerine insan incelemesine göndermek daha doğrudur.

Idempotency: Aynı lead'i iki kez yaratmamak

Belirsiz hata senaryosunu düşünün: CRM'e "lead oluştur" isteğini gönderdiniz, CRM kaydı oluşturdu, ama cevap size ulaşmadan bağlantı koptu. Yeniden denerseniz CRM'de aynı kişi iki kez görünür; iki farklı danışmana atanabilir, iki kez aranabilir. Bu, müşterinin gözünde kurumun düzensiz görünmesinin en hızlı yoludur.

Bunu engellemenin üç yolu var ve genellikle en az ikisini birlikte kullanıyorum:

  1. Karşı sistemin idempotency desteği: Bazı API'ler bir idempotency anahtarı başlığı kabul eder; aynı anahtarla gelen ikinci istek yeni kayıt oluşturmaz, ilk sonucu döner. Varsa mutlaka kullanın ve anahtarı source + source_ref gibi deterministik bir değerden türetin, rastgele üretmeyin.
  2. Harici kimlik ile upsert: CRM'de "harici kaynak kimliği" gibi benzersiz bir özel alan tanımlayın ve "oluştur" yerine "bu harici kimlikle varsa güncelle, yoksa oluştur" mantığıyla yazın.
  3. Yerel eşleme tablosu: Hangi olayın hangi CRM kaydına dönüştüğünü kendi tarafınızda tutun. 
CREATE TABLE crm_link (
  source      text NOT NULL,
  source_ref  text NOT NULL,
  crm_object  text NOT NULL,      -- 'lead', 'contact', 'deal'
  crm_id      text NOT NULL,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (source, source_ref, crm_object)
);

async function upsertLeadInCrm(ev: InboundEvent, lead: NormalizedLead) {
  const existing = await findCrmLink(ev.source, ev.source_ref, "lead");
  if (existing) return existing.crm_id;

  // Belirsiz bir önceki denemeden kalmış olabilir: önce CRM'de harici kimlikle ara
  const found = await crm.searchByExternalId(`${ev.source}:${ev.source_ref}`);
  const crmId = found ?? (await crm.createLead({
    ...lead,
    external_id: `${ev.source}:${ev.source_ref}`,
  }, { idempotencyKey: `${ev.source}:${ev.source_ref}` }));

  await saveCrmLink(ev.source, ev.source_ref, "lead", crmId);
  return crmId;
}

Bu katman, kişi düzeyindeki tekilleştirmenin (aynı kişinin farklı formlardan iki kez gelmesi) yerine geçmez. O ayrı bir problemdir ve eşleşme kuralları gerektirir. Buradaki amaç daha dardır: aynı olayın iki kez işlenmesini engellemek.

Zincirin sonraki adımları için de aynı ilke geçerlidir. Lead CRM'e yazıldıktan sonra tetiklenen WhatsApp ilk mesajı, danışman bildirimi ya da görev oluşturma adımlarının her biri kendi idempotency anahtarına sahip olmalıdır. Aksi halde CRM adımı başarılı olup bildirim adımı başarısız olduğunda tüm akışı yeniden denemek, müşteriye ikinci kez "merhaba" mesajı gitmesine yol açar. Bu yüzden ben her yan etkiyi ayrı bir adım olarak kaydediyor ve yalnızca tamamlanmamış adımları yeniden deniyorum.

Dead-letter tablosu: Kurtarılamayanı kaybetmeden ayırmak

Kalıcı hatalar ve deneme hakkı biten olaylar silinmemeli, ayrı bir yere taşınmalıdır. Bu "dead-letter" alanı bir çöp kutusu değil, bir iş kuyruğudur: her satırın bir sahibi, bir sebebi ve bir çözüm durumu olmalıdır.

CREATE TABLE dead_letter (
  id              bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  inbound_event_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES inbound_event(id),
  error_class     text NOT NULL,
  error_message   text NOT NULL,
  error_detail    jsonb,
  attempts        int  NOT NULL,
  dead_at         timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  resolution      text,            -- NULL | 'replayed' | 'fixed_manually' | 'discarded'
  resolved_by     text,
  resolved_at     timestamptz,
  note            text
);

async function moveToDeadLetter(ev: InboundEvent, err: IntegrationError, attempts: number) {
  await db.tx(async (t) => {
    await t.query(`UPDATE inbound_event SET status='dead', attempts=$2,
                   last_error_class=$3, last_error=$4 WHERE id=$1`,
      [ev.id, attempts, err.cls, err.message]);
    await t.query(`INSERT INTO dead_letter (inbound_event_id, error_class, error_message, error_detail, attempts)
                   VALUES ($1,$2,$3,$4,$5)`,
      [ev.id, err.cls, err.message, JSON.stringify(err.detail ?? null), attempts]);
  });
  await alert(err.cls, ev);
}

Uyarı politikası sınıfa göre değişmelidir. Tek bir permanent_data hatası için bütün ekibi uyandırmaya gerek yoktur; günlük bir özet yeterlidir. Ama tek bir permanent_config hatası, muhtemelen o andan sonra gelen bütün lead'lerin aynı yere düşeceği anlamına gelir; bu hemen bir insana ulaşmalıdır.

Kalıcı veri hatalarında bile lead'in kendisini tamamen kaybetmemek mümkündür. Telefon numarası çözülemeyen bir kayıt, e-postası geçerliyse "eksik veri" etiketiyle CRM'e yine de yazılabilir ve bir danışmana manuel kontrol görevi açılabilir. Teknik olarak hatalı olan veri, ticari olarak hâlâ değerli bir taleptir. Hangi alanların gerçekten zorunlu olduğuna, satış ekibiyle birlikte karar vermek gerekir.

Replay: Düzelttikten sonra güvenle yeniden oynatmak

Yapılandırma hatasını düzelttiniz, diyelim ki süresi dolan CRM token'ını yenilediniz. Şimdi dead-letter'daki yüzlerce olayı geri almanız gerekiyor. Bunu güvenli yapmak için birkaç kural:

  • Replay, normal işleme yolunu kullanmalı. Ayrı bir "toplu import" scripti yazmak yerine olayları tekrar pending durumuna alın. Böylece aynı doğrulama, aynı idempotency ve aynı izleme devreye girer.
  • Filtrelenebilir olmalı. Sınıfa, kaynağa ve zaman aralığına göre seçim yapabilmelisiniz.
  • Kademeli olmalı. Önce küçük bir parti, sonuçları kontrol, sonra geri kalanı.
  • İz bırakmalı. Kim, ne zaman, hangi gerekçeyle yeniden oynattı. 
-- Örnek: belirli bir zaman aralığındaki yapılandırma hatalarını ilk 50 kayıtla yeniden kuyruğa al
WITH picked AS (
  SELECT d.id AS dl_id, d.inbound_event_id
  FROM dead_letter d
  JOIN inbound_event e ON e.id = d.inbound_event_id
  WHERE d.resolution IS NULL
    AND d.error_class = 'permanent_config'
    AND e.source = 'meta_lead_ads'
    AND d.dead_at BETWEEN $1 AND $2
  ORDER BY d.dead_at
  LIMIT 50
),
requeue AS (
  UPDATE inbound_event e
  SET status='pending', attempts=0, next_attempt_at=now()
  FROM picked p WHERE e.id = p.inbound_event_id
  RETURNING e.id
)
UPDATE dead_letter d
SET resolution='replayed', resolved_by=$3, resolved_at=now(), note=$4
FROM picked p WHERE d.id = p.dl_id;

Replay sırasında unutulmaması gereken bir ayrıntı daha var: bazı adımlar zamana duyarlıdır. Üç gün önce gelmiş bir lead'e otomatik "Formunuzu aldık, hemen arıyoruz" mesajı göndermek yanlış bir beklenti yaratır. Bu yüzden ilk temas adımı, olayın orijinal alınma zamanına bakmalı ve belli bir süreyi aşan kayıtlarda otomatik mesaj yerine danışmana öncelikli bir arama görevi açmalıdır. Reklam platformlarına geri dönüşüm gönderen adımlarda da platformların olay zamanı için kabul ettiği geriye dönük sınırlar vardır; sınırı aşan olayları göndermeye çalışmak yerine raporlamak gerekir.

İzleme: Hatanın değil, sessizliğin alarmı

Bütün bu yapı kurulduğunda bile bir tür hata hiçbir tabloya düşmez: hiç gelmeyen olay. Reklam platformundaki webhook aboneliği düşmüşse, form sayfasında bir JavaScript hatası gönderimi engelliyorsa ya da bir DNS değişikliği endpoint'inizi erişilmez kılmışsa, sisteminiz kusursuz biçimde "hata yok" raporlar.

Bu yüzden ben izlemeyi üç katmanda kuruyorum:

  1. Hacim sapması: Her kaynak için beklenen saatlik lead aralığını geçmiş verilerden çıkarıp, belirgin bir düşüşte uyarı. Kampanya bütçesi açıkken bir kaynaktan uzun süre hiç olay gelmemesi başlı başına bir alarmdır.
  2. Mutabakat: Belirli aralıklarla reklam platformunun kendi API'sinden o dönemde oluşan lead kimliklerini çekip inbound_event tablosundaki source_ref değerleriyle karşılaştırmak. Fark varsa eksik olanları çekip normal yoldan işlemek.
  3. Kuyruk sağlığı: pending durumunda en eski olayın yaşı, dead-letter'daki çözülmemiş kayıt sayısı ve sınıflara göre dağılımı. 
-- Kuyruk sağlığı için tek sorgu
SELECT
  (SELECT max(now() - received_at) FROM inbound_event WHERE status='pending')        AS oldest_pending_age,
  (SELECT count(*) FROM dead_letter WHERE resolution IS NULL)                         AS open_dead_letters,
  (SELECT jsonb_object_agg(error_class, c) FROM (
      SELECT error_class, count(*) c FROM dead_letter
      WHERE resolution IS NULL GROUP BY error_class) s)                               AS open_by_class;

Mutabakat adımı, bütün tasarımın sigortasıdır. Webhook'lar, kuyruklar ve yeniden denemeler ne kadar iyi kurulursa kurulsun, "kaynakta var, bizde yok" sorusunu düzenli soran bir süreç olmadan sistemin güvenilir olduğunu iddia edemezsiniz.

Otomasyon araçlarıyla çalışıyorsanız

Her ekip bu altyapıyı sıfırdan kod olarak yazmaz; çoğu akış Make, n8n ya da Zapier gibi araçlarda kuruludur. Aynı ilkeler orada da uygulanabilir: hata yolu (error route) olmayan bir senaryo bırakmayın, hata yolunda olayı ham haliyle bir tabloya ya da sayfaya yazın, kalıcı ve geçici hataları farklı dallara ayırın, CRM adımında "oluştur" yerine harici kimlikle arama + güncelleme kullanın ve haftalık bir mutabakat kontrolü planlayın. Aracın kendi yeniden deneme ayarlarına güvenmek yerine, en azından kurtarılamayan olayların görünür bir yerde biriktiğinden emin olun.

Sık sorulan sorular (SSS)

Her hatayı yeniden denemek neden kötü bir fikir?
Çünkü kalıcı hatalar yeniden denemeyle düzelmez. Eksik zorunlu alanı olan bir kaydı on iki kez denemek yalnızca kuyruğu meşgul eder, gerçek geçici hataların işlenmesini geciktirir ve insanın sorunu fark etmesini erteler. Kalıcı hatayı hemen dead-letter'a alıp sahibine bildirmek daha hızlı çözüm getirir.

Jitter gerçekten gerekli mi, sabit bekleme yetmez mi?
Az trafikte fark hissedilmez. Ama bir CRM ya da API kesintisi sonrası yüzlerce mesaj aynı anda beklemeye girer; sabit aralıkla hepsi aynı anda tekrar denenir ve sistem toparlanırken yeniden boğulur. Rastgelelik bu yükü zamana yayar.

Kaynak platform zaten yeniden deniyorsa benim ayrıca retry yazmama gerek var mı?
Evet. Kaynağın yeniden denemesi yalnızca sizin endpoint'inize ulaşma sorununu çözer; sizin CRM'e, mesajlaşma servisine ya da reklam platformuna yaptığınız çağrıların başarısızlığını çözmez. Ayrıca kaynağın politikası değişebilir ve sizin kontrolünüzde değildir. Olayı önce kendi tablonuza yazmak, sorumluluğu sizin tarafınıza alır.

Idempotency anahtarını nasıl seçmeliyim?
Deterministik olmalı ve olayın kendisinden türetilmelidir: kaynak adı ve kaynağın verdiği benzersiz kimlik iyi bir başlangıçtır. Her denemede rastgele bir anahtar üretirseniz, anahtarın hiçbir koruma sağlamaz.

Dead-letter'daki kayıtları ne kadar tutmalıyım?
Çözülene kadar mutlaka; çözüldükten sonra ise kişisel veri içerdikleri için şirketinizin veri saklama politikasına tabi olmalıdırlar. Çözülmüş kayıtların ham yükünü belirli bir süre sonra silip yalnızca istatistiksel özeti tutmak iyi bir dengedir.

Bu tasarım küçük bir ekip için fazla mı?
Tamamını ilk günden kurmak gerekmez. Benim önerdiğim öncelik sırası şöyle: önce gelen olayı ham haliyle kalıcı yazmak, sonra harici kimlikle upsert, ardından dead-letter ve uyarı, en son mutabakat. İlk iki adım bile sessiz lead kaybının en yaygın kaynaklarını kapatır.

Kapanış

Lead entegrasyonlarında hata yönetimi, bir altyapı detayı gibi görünse de doğrudan satışa dokunan bir konudur. Kaybolan her olay, bir insanın "bilgi almak istiyorum" demesinin cevapsız kalması anlamına gelir. Hataları sınıflandırmak, yeniden denemeyi ölçülü yapmak, idempotency ile mükerrer kaydı engellemek, kurtarılamayanı görünür bir kuyrukta toplamak ve düzenli mutabakatla sessizliği yakalamak; bu beş adım birlikte, "çalışıyor gibi görünen" bir akışı gerçekten güvenilir bir akışa dönüştürür.

Lead yönetimi ve CRM altyapısı üzerine bu tür uygulama notlarını paylaşmaya devam edeceğim. Kendi akışınızda en çok hangi hata sınıfıyla uğraştığınızı yorumlarda yazarsanız, bir sonraki yazılarda o senaryoları daha ayrıntılı ele alabilirim.

— Koray Yalçın

title: Predicting Single-Cell Spatial Gene Expression from H&E using Pathology Foundation Models
description:
arXiv:2611.13649v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Predicting gene expression directly from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images offers a scalable and cost-effective approach to deriving spatial molecular insights from routine histology. Pathology foundation models, typically pretrained using tile-level objectives, may not adequately capture the fine-grained cellular features required for single-cell molecular prediction. In this work, we systematically evaluate and establish domain-informed and task-specific strategies for adapting pathology foundation models to single-cell spatial gene expression prediction. Using paired H&E and Xenium 5K data, our approach improves mean gene-wise Pearson correlation by 2.67x over the standard zero-shot baseline and achieves state-of-the-art performance on this task. We demonstrate strong gene-detection performance across the full gene panel (AUROC = 0.800) and importantly identify that predictive performance varies substantially across biological contexts, with our model achieving its highest Pearson correlation for spatially variable genes (r = 0.643). Our findings demonstrate that, despite the challenges of sparse single-cell measurements, H&E-derived representations can recover biologically meaningful spatial expression patterns, highlighting both the opportunities and limitations of morphology-based molecular inference at cellular resolution.

title: EngineAgent: Agentizing On-Device LLM Inference Engines with Inference Stack Hierarchy Awareness and Hardware Abilities
description:
arXiv:2611.14356v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Rapidly evolving LLM architectures and heterogeneous mobile hardware make supporting new models in on-device inference engines a recurring and costly system challenge. Each model may require coordinated changes across conversion, graph construction, operators, and hardware backends. Existing coding agents often miss these cross-layer dependencies and struggle to diagnose failures across host--device execution paths. We present EngineAgent, an agentic system for automating on-device LLM model enablement. Its key insight is to separate reusable engine and hardware knowledge from model-specific implementation. Before enablement, EngineAgent constructs a hierarchy-aware engine index that captures engine abstraction layers and cross-layer dependencies, and pre-validates backend-specific build, execution, and debugging workflows using already supported models. For each new model, a builder uses this knowledge to coordinate cross-layer changes, while an auditor checks implementation completeness and drives iterative debugging through device-side validation. Across 12 tasks spanning three mobile LLMs and four engine--backend pairs on CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs, EngineAgent achieves 75% end-to-end success with either of two underlying LLMs, versus 33.3% for the strongest coding-agent baseline. Success requires compilation, on-device execution, and output-logit agreement with reference implementations. EngineAgent also reduces average per-task time and model-API cost relative to baselines using the same underlying LLMs.

title: Interleaving anatomical inspection and diagnostic reasoning for explainable radiology report generation
description:
arXiv:2611.14018v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automated radiology report generation can draft clinically plausible reports, yet the pathway from visual evidence to reported findings remains opaque, leaving the diagnostic basis of these reports unexplained and the generated reports difficult to review or revise. We introduce ARIVE (Anatomy-guided Reasoning with Interleaved Visual Evidence), an explainable report generation framework that interleaves anatomical inspection with diagnostic reasoning prior to final report composition. To support this process, we constructed 159,416 multimodal chain-of-thought (MCoT) trajectories from MIMIC-CXR, wherein visual evidence from inspected anatomical regions informs subsequent clinical interpretation. Trained on these trajectories and further optimized using anatomical and clinical-content rewards, ARIVE achieved superior clinical-efficacy performance compared with strong baselines on MIMIC-CXR and the abnormality-centered MIMIC-ABN. ARIVE's reports were competitive with those of leading models in blinded expert grading, and its MCoT trajectories earned high ratings for diagnostic traceability. Furthermore, a paired review evaluation suggests that access to MCoT can aid in identifying errors within generated reports.

title: • After a layoff and divorce, I built an app studio at my kitchen table
description:
I’m sharing this today not to look back at what I lost, but to celebrate what love and resilience can build when you refuse to give up.

Twelve months ago, my life was completely reset. I lost my job in a layoff, and shortly after, my marriage ended. Suddenly, I was raising my 2-year-old on my own with a tight budget. There were plenty of days when I skipped meals just to make sure my kid had everything they needed.

In those quiet moments at the kitchen table, watching my toddler smile without a care in the world, something shifted inside me. Instead of feeling defeated, I felt an overwhelming surge of purpose. That little kid gave me a superpower I didn't know I had.

Turning a Kitchen Table Into a Studio

I decided I wasn't going to wait for someone else to hand us a lifeline—I was going to build one with my own two hands.

Every night after tucking my kid in, I turned my kitchen table into a workspace. Fueled by hope, cheap coffee, and the joy of building something meaningful, I spent four hours coding. One app turned into two, and two turned into a small collection. Every bug I fixed and every feature I shipped was a small victory for our future.

Meet Shivaya

I named my solo studio Shivaya. To me, Shivaya stands for renewal, inner strength, and the beauty of starting fresh. Every single app under Shivaya was born out of late-night determination and pure love for my kid.

Today, seeing our apps live on Google Play fills me with gratitude:
👉 Check out Shivaya apps on Google Play

We don't have big investors or a fancy office, just unstoppable momentum and a bright road ahead.

If you’re starting over right now, please know this: rock bottom isn't the end of your story—it’s the solid foundation you get to rebuild on. You are stronger than you think. ✨

Fellow solo devs and builders—how do you manage your late-night coding schedule alongside family life? Would love to hear your thoughts or feedback on our apps in the comments!

title: Omni-JEV: Text and Dual-Stream Speech Decisions
description:
arXiv:2611.13777v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A user utterance does not uniquely determine the next action in full-duplex dialogue: its consequences depend on the assistant's response state and interaction history. Speech activity, utterance completion, and interruption intent provide related evidence, whose implications for a response require an explicit action policy. We formulate this task at collected-segment endpoints and introduce Omni-JEV, which maps text or role-indexed user and assistant-reference speech to probabilities over five interaction actions. An aligned speech-to-speech understanding backbone encodes the acoustic roles separately and shares its candidate readout with text inputs. Bilingual weak supervision supports cross-entropy fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning for probability-sensitive decisions (RLCD). We compare Gaussian-logit and categorical Choice RLCD from the same supervised initialization under matched training exposure, observing different trade-offs between classification and probability quality. Gaussian Omni-JEV achieves test accuracies of 84.08% for audio and 96.55% for text. This common action interface supports decisions about when a full-duplex voice assistant should respond, preserve ongoing speech, interrupt, or resume an interrupted response.

title: Blocking malicious npm packages before and during installation
description:
Vercel now checks for blocked npm packages before and during dependency installation in builds, helping prevent malicious install scripts from running.

The checks use a blocklist of specific package versions selected for blocking because of malware or security vulnerabilities, with new rules typically reaching new builds within minutes.

  • Before installation, Vercel checks supported lockfiles, including when dependencies are restored from the build cache.

  • During installation, Vercel blocks affected public npm downloads.

Existing checks of installed dependencies and function outputs continue before deployment.

These protections apply automatically to new builds on all plans, with no configuration required.

If a blocked dependency is detected, Vercel fails the deployment, identifies the package and version in the error, and attempts to invalidate the affected build cache. Update the dependency to a safe version and update the lockfile, then redeploy.

title: FastWild-GS: Minutes-Scale In-the-Wild Gaussian Splatting via Compact Per-Image Appearance Adaptation
description:
arXiv:2611.13808v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Internet photos of a scene differ in exposure, illumination and transient objects such as passers-by, so one set of Gaussian colours cannot explain all photos (the in-the-wild setting). Recent in-the-wild Gaussian Splatting methods mostly report hours of per-scene optimization. We present FastWild-GS, which describes each photo by a 128-dimensional Photo Appearance Token and a per-channel transform, a scale and an offset applied to the rendered image (six parameters); a small MLP predicts the colour of each Gaussian from this token and a per-Gaussian feature, replacing the spherical-harmonics colour. The same transform is applied to the renders that score Gaussians for densification and pruning, so appearance differences between photos are not counted as reconstruction error. On PhotoTourism, FastWild-GS trains in 8.8 minutes per scene with the lowest LPIPS among the compared methods, 23x faster than AsymGS, the next best in LPIPS. On NeRF-OSR, it has the best average PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS among the compared methods in 9.7 minutes per scene.

title: EgoHMP: Achieving Precise Human Motion Prediction in 3D Scenes via Egocentric Cues
description:
arXiv:2611.13654v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The complex interactive dependencies between human behavior and 3D scenes make accurately predicting human intent a major challenge for human motion prediction (HMP). While recent studies use human gaze to infer intent, gaze signals suffer from ambiguity, drift, and a reliance on eye-tracking hardware. Research in cognitive science indicates that egocentric views inherently encode potential interactions, while head motion serves as a crucial precursor in motion planning. Motivated by this, we propose EgoHMP, a novel framework that uses egocentric views and head motions as robust carriers of interaction intent. By translating this intent into an envisioning of future interactions, EgoHMP achieves precise HMP in 3D scenes. EgoHMP first employs a vision-motion alignment encoder to align the visual and motion feature spaces. Based on these aligned features, an egocentric intent predictor with a modality-aware modulation mechanism adaptively suppresses invalid interaction cues to predict an accurate interaction probability map. Furthermore, to enhance the stability and realism of the generated motions, we propose a contact-aware motion decoder. Specifically, inspired by the human cognitive process of planning trajectories prior to action execution, we first predict a global trajectory to serve as a self-prompt, effectively mitigating the optimization conflict in diffusion models. Subsequently, we introduce a multi-stage denoiser, which relieves motion artifacts by incorporating human contact modeling through a multi-stage optimization strategy. Finally, a GCN-based motion decoder is employed to synthesize physically plausible and semantically consistent motions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EgoHMP achieves state-of-the-art performance.

title: Your Compose Text Is Quietly Lying About Its Weight
description:
Typography rarely shows up in a sprint review. Nobody files a ticket that says “the type system is elegant.” But the day a designer opens your build and says “that heading isn’t the weight I specified,” you discover how much of your UI’s personality lives in a handful of font files and one resolution algorithm you never read.

This post walks through how Jetpack Compose maps a FontFamily to the weights you request, centralizes that mapping so a typeface swap is a one-file change, and the production failure modes that bite teams after the happy path works. The examples use Manrope as the typeface, but nothing here is specific to it.

From the View system to Compose

In the View system, custom typography meant fontFamily attributes in XML, <font-family> resources, TextAppearance styles, and a Typeface you sometimes patched in code. Overriding one piece often meant touching several layers.

Compose collapses this into plain Kotlin values. A font family is an object, a text style is an object, and both compose like any other value. That makes typography testable, diffable in code review, and replaceable in one place.

Declare the family once 

import androidx.compose.ui.text.font.Font
import androidx.compose.ui.text.font.FontFamily
import androidx.compose.ui.text.font.FontWeight

val Manrope = FontFamily(
    Font(R.font.manrope_regular, FontWeight.Normal),
    Font(R.font.manrope_medium, FontWeight.Medium),
    Font(R.font.manrope_bold, FontWeight.Bold),
)

Each Font entry binds a file to the weight it represents. The family is just a lookup table from (weight, style) to a file.

Declare it as a top-level val in your design-system module. Font resources are loaded when text first needs them, not at declaration, so a top-level family is cheap and safe to share.

Wire it into the theme, not into call sites

The most common mistake in migrated codebases is passing fontFamily = Manrope to individual Text calls. It works, and it quietly recreates the scattered-attribute problem you were trying to escape.

Put the family into a Typography and let the theme distribute it:

import androidx.compose.material3.Typography
import androidx.compose.ui.text.TextStyle
import androidx.compose.ui.unit.sp

val AppTypography = Typography(
    titleLarge = TextStyle(
        fontFamily = Manrope,
        fontWeight = FontWeight.Bold,
        fontSize = 22.sp,
        lineHeight = 28.sp,
    ),
    titleMedium = TextStyle(
        fontFamily = Manrope,
        fontWeight = FontWeight.Medium,
        fontSize = 16.sp,
        lineHeight = 24.sp,
    ),
    bodyLarge = TextStyle(
        fontFamily = Manrope,
        fontWeight = FontWeight.Normal,
        fontSize = 16.sp,
        lineHeight = 24.sp,
    ),
)

@Composable
fun AppTheme(content: @Composable () -> Unit) {
    MaterialTheme(typography = AppTypography, content = content)
}

Call sites then express intent, not appearance:

Text(
    text = "Order confirmed",
    style = MaterialTheme.typography.titleLarge,
)

When design changes the brand typeface, you replace the FontFamily and rebuild. Every style that references it follows, because weights are resolved through the family rather than hard-coded per file.

How weight resolution actually works

When Text requests a weight, Compose asks the family for the best match. If an exact (weight, style) entry exists, you get that file. This is the part most posts stop at, and it is also the easy part.

The interesting behavior is what happens when the exact weight is not declared. Compose does not throw and does not log a warning. It picks the nearest available face using a CSS-like matching rule. As a rough summary:

  • Requested weights below 400 prefer the next lighter face, then fall back to heavier ones.
  • Requested weights above 500 prefer the next heavier face, then fall back to lighter ones.
  • Requested weights between 400 and 500 look in that narrow band first, then lighter, then heavier.

Apply that to our family, which declares 400, 500 and 700:

A design spec that says “SemiBold” renders as Bold. Nothing crashes. The screen just looks slightly louder than the mock, and the discrepancy survives until a designer compares pixels.

Make the fallback visible

Silent fallbacks are best caught by rendering every weight in one place. A weight ladder preview takes a few lines and belongs in your design-system module:

@Preview(showBackground = true)
@Composable
private fun WeightLadderPreview() {
    AppTheme {
        Column(Modifier.padding(16.dp)) {
            listOf(
                FontWeight.Light, FontWeight.Normal, FontWeight.Medium,
                FontWeight.SemiBold, FontWeight.Bold, FontWeight.ExtraBold,
            ).forEach { weight ->
                Text(
                    text = "Weight ${weight.weight}: Quick brown fox",
                    fontFamily = Manrope,
                    fontWeight = weight,
                )
            }
        }
    }
}

If two adjacent rows look identical, you have found a missing face. Promote this to a screenshot test (Paparazzi or Roborazzi both work) so a font swap that drops a weight fails CI instead of shipping.

Fixing the SemiBold gap

You have two honest options.

Ship the file. Add manrope_semibold.ttf and declare it:

val Manrope = FontFamily(
    Font(R.font.manrope_regular, FontWeight.Normal),
    Font(R.font.manrope_medium, FontWeight.Medium),
    Font(R.font.manrope_semibold, FontWeight.SemiBold),
    Font(R.font.manrope_bold, FontWeight.Bold),
)

Use a variable font. One file, many weights, with each entry selecting a point on the weight axis:

@OptIn(ExperimentalTextApi::class)
val ManropeVariable = FontFamily(
    listOf(400, 500, 600, 700).map { w ->
        Font(
            resId = R.font.manrope_variable,
            weight = FontWeight(w),
            variationSettings = FontVariation.Settings(
                FontVariation.weight(w),
            ),
        )
    }
)

Variable fonts shrink APK size when you need many weights, but they come with a platform constraint covered below. Check whether your Compose version still requires the opt-in annotation.

Failure modes worth knowing before production

1. Faux italics

If you request FontStyle.Italic and the family declares no italic face, Compose synthesizes a slanted version of the upright glyphs. The result is mechanically skewed text that type designers wince at, and it can look noticeably worse for fonts with distinctive italic letterforms.

Declare real italic files with style = FontStyle.Italic, or turn synthesis off and accept upright text:

Text(
    text = "Edge case",
    fontStyle = FontStyle.Italic,
    fontSynthesis = FontSynthesis.None,
)

The same synthesis applies to bold. Asking for a bold weight from a family that has none can produce smeared pseudo-bold. Prefer real files.

2. Missing glyphs and mixed scripts

A Latin-focused brand font often has no Tamil, Devanagari, Arabic or CJK glyphs. For text in those scripts, the platform substitutes a system font glyph by glyph. The result is a screen where Latin characters look branded and everything else looks like system UI, with baseline and line-height mismatches that make rows jitter.

If your app ships in multiple languages, test the long-tail scripts explicitly. Pair a script-appropriate family per locale and select it from the theme, rather than hoping the substitute looks acceptable.

3. Variable fonts on older devices

Variable font axes are applied through platform support that starts at API 26. On older devices the variation settings are ignored, so every entry in the family above renders at the font’s default weight. If your minSdk is below 26, declare static fallbacks, or branch on Build.VERSION.SDK_INT when building the family.

val Manrope = if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.O) {
    ManropeVariable
} else {
    ManropeStatic
}

4. Metrics change when the typeface changes

Swapping typefaces changes ascent, descent and average glyph width. Layouts that relied on implicit line height will reflow, and tightly constrained containers (chips, tab labels, buttons) can start truncating. Set explicit lineHeight in every style, as in the Typography above, and snapshot-test your longest realistic strings.

5. Weight set during styling collides with weight set at call sites

TextStyle merges with parameters passed to Text. A stray fontWeight = FontWeight.Bold at a call site overrides whatever the theme specified, so a later theme change appears to "not work" on that one screen. Treat explicit typography arguments on Text as a code smell and prefer style = MaterialTheme.typography.x, adjusting with .copy(...) only when truly necessary.

Why one definition pays off

Because the family is the single place that knows which file serves which weight, replacing the brand typeface becomes a contained change:

  1. Add the new font files under res/font.
  2. Rewrite the FontFamily declaration to point at them.
  3. Run the weight ladder screenshot test and review the diff.

Nothing else in the codebase names a font file. That is the real payoff of Compose’s mapping model: not saving keystrokes, but making an app-wide design change reviewable in one diff.

A short checklist

  • Declare one FontFamily per typeface in your design-system module.
  • Reference it from Typography, and have call sites use theme styles.
  • Declare every weight and style your design actually uses, including SemiBold and italics.
  • Add a weight ladder preview and a screenshot test.
  • Check non-Latin scripts if you localize.
  • Provide static fallbacks if minSdk is below 26 and you use variable fonts.

Typography is infrastructure. Treat it with the same care as networking or navigation and it stops being the thing you debug on release day.

Further reading

  • Fonts in Compose (Android Developers)

🍎 Share Your Kotlin Code with iOS — Without Rewriting Your App

If “we’ll just build it twice, once per platform” describes how your team ships mobile, I’d recommend “Kotlin Multiplatform for Android Developers” — a 22-chapter, hands-on guide that goes past the sample-project demos and follows the shared module all the way to two app store submissions. No iOS or Swift background required.

It walks through the expect/actual mechanism and source set hierarchy, shared architecture, networking with Ktor, persistence with Room KMP and SQLDelight, Koin dependency injection, Flow and StateFlow with Swift interop (SKIE and Swift Export), Compose Multiplatform versus native SwiftUI, navigation, testing across two runtimes, dual-toolchain CI/CD with Linux and macOS runners, publishing a KMP library, and migrating an existing Android app module by module. Everything builds toward one capstone: an offline-first Expense/Budget Tracker, complete with a pending-sync queue, retry/backoff, and a deployment checklist for both stores.

  • Kindle Edition: Available on Amazon
  • Topmate: Available on Topmate
  • Also available in Paperback & Hardcover.

title: Reconcile an AI lead-search report with 3 Python assertions
description:
A lead-search report can turn the same $5.23 bill into five different unit prices. On 19 October 2026, one anonymised software-services seller's MachGTM search made 226 queries, returned 2,090 observations, judged 1,635, kept 70 and graded 21 ready to contact.

Those are five denominators. A developer building the report needs to preserve the stage and unit behind each one.

I founded MachGTM. We have published the aggregate counts, their data dictionary and reproduction code. This article uses that historical release to explain a reporting design you can check.

Give each stage a unit

Stage Count What the count describes
Searches 226 Queries executed in this run
Retrieved observations 2,090 Items returned before excluding previously seen observations
Previously seen observations 455 Observations already encountered by the workflow
Judged observations 1,635 New observations assessed against the seller's rules
Kept observations 70 Historical system grades that passed those rules
Ready grades 21 A subset of the kept observations

An observation is the unit in these retrieval and grading totals. The aggregate release cannot tell you how many unique companies were ready to buy.

A company's announcement can appear through several source types. Several observations can concern the same company. Preserve the company identifier and the observation identifier in an internal evaluation if you intend to calculate company-level outcomes.

The released totals and their definitions are in the MachGTM study and its archived report and aggregate data.

Check the identities before calculating a rate

The observed totals satisfy three checks.

retrieved = 2090
previously_seen = 455
judged = 1635
dropped = 1565
worth_a_look = 49
ready = 21
kept = 70

assert retrieved - previously_seen == judged
assert dropped + kept == judged
assert worth_a_look + ready == kept

print(f"Kept share of judged observations: {kept / judged:.2%}")
print(f"Ready share of judged observations: {ready / judged:.2%}")

The results are 4.28% kept and 1.28% ready among judged observations. These checks establish that the released stages reconcile. They leave the correctness of individual grading decisions open.

Put the identity checks beside the chart that uses the counts. A report should fail visibly when its inputs stop reconciling, with the stage and difference available for investigation.

Keep missing reasons in the output

The run dropped 1,565 observations. Named rejection reasons covered 1,564. One had no recorded reason.

Reason Observations
Seller offering the same work 497
Discussion without an ask 339
Request for different work 188
Copy of another observation 179
Job post 160
Recruiter 90
Outside the region 78
Freelancer gig 21
No need shown 7
Public body 3
Already filled 2
No reason recorded 1

Keep the final row in the denominator. Dropping it from the report would make the reason table appear complete while hiding a missing record.

The distinction between the 455 previously seen observations and 179 observations later rejected as copies also deserves its own labels. They belong to different stages of the run. Combining them would make a reader guess which total still includes them.

A ready grade needs a human reference

The export contained five recorded human keep-or-drop decisions. That gives us too little validation to estimate the grader's precision or recall.

The source table alone cannot resolve that gap. A later review needs the original request, event date, current status, seller relevance and an agreed acceptance rule.

For a proposed evaluation, select the review sample before reading its labels. Include keepers and a sample of drops. Otherwise the review can find weak keepers while leaving missed buyers invisible.

Record unresolved cases separately. If reviewers disagree, retain both decisions and the adjudicated result. Report the sample-selection method and reviewed denominator beside any rate.

This is a proposed review design. We have published no new human-label result from it.

Attach outcomes through identifiers

The released search contains no linked reply, booking or held-meeting outcomes. A ready grade cannot supply those missing counts.

A prospective evaluation needs a trace from observation to selected company, contacted person, message and resulting conversation or meeting. Keep the observation and message identifiers so the team can inspect which signal preceded first contact.

At the reporting cutoff, retain pending meetings and unresolved outcomes. Use the pilot scorecard to record each measure's eligible population, evidence and reviewer.

Take one percentage in your dashboard and write its numerator, denominator, stage and unit in plain language. Then identify the rows that produce it.

Method and scope

This is one seller's run from 19 October 2026, exported on 20 October. The public archive contains aggregates, a dictionary and reproduction code. It omits raw posts, an independent label set and linked outreach outcomes.

The proposed reporting checks and review design above extend that released accounting. They establish no measured meeting or revenue improvement.

The full study and review questions preserve the historical numbers. The cost ladder shows how changing the denominator changes the quoted unit price.

Prepared with AI assistance from the published aggregate study. All run counts retain their original date and scope.

title: Lullwood: Enemy Line of Sight in three.js Without a Raycaster
description:
Can a wolf see you in Lullwood, our free browser horror game? Yes, if you are inside its sight radius and no cover box sits on the straight line between you. We decide that in three.js without the Raycaster: a distance check, then a walk along the line through a spatial hash, with one slab test per box. Here is the whole thing, read from the source at commit b03da13.

Check the number before the geometry

canSee in lib/game/cover.ts (L741-771) runs two tests in order. If the distance is at or beyond the predator's effective sight radius, it returns false and never touches the map. Only a player inside the radius gets the line-of-sight test.

The radius is detect * (1 - stillness * 0.82) * detectMul (L734-737). A wolf's base detect is 42 units. The stillness term is state.hidden ? min(1, hideTime / STILL_RAMP) : 0 (L735), so it is zero unless the player is in the hide stance. The engine only sets hidden in enterHide (engine/forest-engine.js L4405-4406), reached when the player presses H with a bramble within 2.2 units of its edge, and any movement key breaks it (L8374). A player who just stops in the open keeps the full 42; the source comment says standing still in the open next to a predator still gets you caught (L711-712). A player hidden within 2.2 of a bramble's edge but outside its footprint ramps the cut in over 1.2 seconds, and 42 becomes about 7.6 before the caller's multipliers (difficulty, mist veil, fog tide, time of day and others). A hidden player inside the footprint skips this arithmetic entirely, because an earlier branch (L766-768) returns first. Cover and the hide stance are separate dials: one removes the line, the other shrinks the radius.

Walk the line in half-cell steps

hasLOS (L568-617) steps along the segment every half cell. Our spatial-hash cell is 8 units, so every 4 units. Each sample point maps to a cell, repeats are skipped, and only the boxes filed under that cell are tested. Each box has a centre, half-width, half-depth, kind and rotation. No height, so sight is flat on the ground plane.

For each box, rotate the segment into the box's own frame (L588-592) and run a slab test: clip the segment against the x range, then the z range, and it hits if a stretch survives both. First hit returns false.

The rotation is the part that bit us. A comment in the file (L224-228) says the same rotated-box sign bug shipped twice, in two functions sharing one rotation convention, because neither could be called from a test. We lifted the geometry out of the engine file so it could be.

Where a raycaster would have gone

We have no use of Raycaster anywhere in our engine, library or app code (git grep -i raycaster). The cover is drawn as instanced meshes, but sight reads plain boxes in a Map, so it never touches a scene mesh. We have not benchmarked the two, so this is not a speed claim.

One exemption and one limit

A segment that starts or ends inside a box reads as blocked from every direction. Logs and brambles are walkable, so a wolf or a player can stand in one. hasLOS skips a walkable box when either endpoint is inside it (L606-610), which also means the hiding player's own bramble needs an explicit rule to stay protective (L757-768).

The limit: a box is filed under the one cell its centre is in (buildCoverGrid, engine/forest-engine.js L997-1002), and hasLOS reads only the cells its samples land in. Collision (coverBlockedR, cover.ts L431) reads the surrounding 3 by 3 block. So a long box centred just across a cell line can overhang into a cell the line samples but never reads. We ran the real function on a synthetic case: a box 4.8 long centred at x = 9.5, and a line from (6, -6) to (7.9, 6) that crosses its overhang at about x = 7.27. It returned true, so the wolf sees through the log. Centre the same box at x = 6.5 and it returns false. That is a probe, not a rate, and we do not know how often a real forest produces it.

The map does not wrap yet

Every position comparison goes through wrapDelta and wrapCoord, so the same code works on a torus. The engine passes an infinite span while wrapEnabled is false in engine/tuning.js (L84), so in the game today the map does not wrap and these are plain subtractions. We wrote the seam math first so that turning wrapping on would not mean hunting for every raw subtraction.

The full version, with every line number, is the Lullwood devlog post this one is cross-posted from. For what it means in play, see how to survive wolves in Lullwood, or play Lullwood free in your browser.

Disclosure: we are the studio behind Lullwood. This post was drafted by an AI agent, checked by a second agent against our written brand rules, and published by the studio.
