title: How to Migrate From Webflow to Shopify Without Losing SEO
description:
Moving platforms changes every URL, template, and tag on your site. Here's the process I use so the rankings you've already earned come with you.

Most SEO losses after a migration aren't caused by the new platform. Shopify is perfectly capable of ranking. They're caused by three avoidable things: old URLs that lead nowhere, titles and content that quietly change in transit, and nobody checking the results after launch.

The principle behind everything below is simple. Search engines need to find every important old page, land on its closest new equivalent, and find the same content and signals when they arrive. A migration that does that keeps most of what it had. One that doesn't spends months recovering.

On a Webflow-to-Shopify migration for a motorcycle brand, I audited the Webflow storefront first and then built the product import with Matrixify. This is the process I follow, in five phases: baseline, map, build, launch, monitor.

First: Does the Whole Site Need to Move?

Before planning redirects, check whether a full migration is actually the right call. Many brands keep Webflow for the marketing site, the blog, and the landing pages, and move only the store to Shopify.

That changes the SEO plan significantly. Your blog and brand pages stay put, and the redirects only need to cover commerce URLs: products, categories, and anything tied to the cart. Less moves, so less can go wrong. If your marketing content ranks well and your problem is store functionality, this split is worth considering. It's the kind of architecture I cover under Webflow development alongside the Shopify build.

If you are moving everything, the rest of this post applies in full.

Phase 1: Baseline Everything Before You Touch Anything

You can't tell whether a migration worked without a record of what you had. Capture this before any build work begins:

A full crawl of the Webflow site. Use Screaming Frog or a similar crawler. Export every URL with its status code, title tag, meta description, H1, canonical, and indexability. This spreadsheet becomes the source of truth for everything that follows. Don't rely on the Webflow designer's page list, because it won't show you everything search engines have indexed.

Search Console data. Export top pages and top queries. Search Console only keeps around sixteen months of data, so export it now rather than after launch.

Analytics by landing page. Pull organic sessions and revenue by landing page from GA4. This tells you which pages actually earn money, which is not always the same as which pages get traffic.

Backlinks. Export the pages on your site that have external links pointing at them (Search Console's links report is free, and paid tools show more). These URLs must redirect precisely, because they carry authority from other sites.

Existing Webflow redirects. Copy out everything in Webflow's 301 redirect settings. Redirects that live in Webflow stop working the moment your domain points at Shopify, so every one has to be rebuilt.

Custom code. Note everything in Webflow's head and footer code: analytics, ad pixels, schema markup, verification tags. None of it carries over automatically.

Then rank your pages. Anything with organic traffic, revenue, or backlinks is tier one. These get hand-checked at launch. Everything else is tier two.

One more thing worth doing at this stage: audit the conversion flow of the existing store. A migration is the cheapest moment to fix leaks you'd otherwise carry across to the new platform. A CRO and website audit done before the build means the new store launches better than the old one, not merely equal to it.

Phase 2: Map the URLs

This is the phase that decides most of the outcome. Webflow and Shopify structure their URLs differently, so a large share of your pages will change address.

Typical patterns look like this, though your crawl is the source of truth because Webflow setups vary:

Page type Typical Webflow URL Shopify URL
Homepage / /
Product /product/slug /products/handle
Category /category/slug /collections/handle
Blog post /blog/slug /blogs/blog-handle/slug
Static page /about /pages/about

Shopify's prefixes (/products/, /collections/, /pages/, /blogs/) are fixed. You can't remove them, so every one of these URLs needs a redirect.

Keep slugs identical to handles wherever you can. If the Webflow product slug is carbon-slip-on-exhaust, make the Shopify handle carbon-slip-on-exhaust. The mapping becomes mechanical, and mechanical means fewer mistakes.

Build the redirect map in a spreadsheet. Columns: old URL, new URL, page type, priority tier, notes. Shopify redirects are exact-path matches and, in the built-in tool, there are no wildcards. You can't write "send everything under /product/ to /products/" as one rule. Generate the full list with a spreadsheet formula instead. If you need pattern-based rules, redirect apps support them.

Import in bulk. Shopify accepts a CSV with two columns, "Redirect from" and "Redirect to", using relative paths that start with a slash. Matrixify can also import redirects as part of the same migration job. Check the current redirect limit for your plan against the size of your list, because standard plans have a cap.

Redirect to the closest equivalent, not the homepage. When a product won't exist on the new store, send it to the most relevant collection or a similar product. Mass redirects to the homepage can be treated by Google as soft 404s, and the visitor who arrives gets nothing useful anyway.

Flatten chains. If an old Webflow redirect sends A to B, and B is now being redirected to C, update A to go straight to C. Chains slow things down and leak authority.

Remember images. Image files on Webflow's CDN can't be redirected to Shopify's CDN. If images bring you search traffic, expect some movement. Keep file names descriptive and alt text intact on the new store to give those images the best chance.

Phase 3: Build for SEO Parity

The goal on the new store is parity first, improvement second. Rebuild what's ranking before you try to make it better.

Match titles, descriptions, and H1s. Take them straight from the baseline crawl. In Shopify, each product, collection, page, and blog post has its own search engine listing fields. If you're using Matrixify for the product import, SEO title and description can be imported in the same sheet instead of being typed in by hand.

Migrate the catalogue deliberately. Webflow lets you export products as CSV from the Ecommerce panel. Map that export to Shopify's structure, with particular attention to variants and options, which Webflow and Shopify model differently. Shopify's native importer handles simple catalogues. Matrixify handles complex ones, including metafields. Check the plan limits against your catalogue size, because the free tier only covers a small number of items per file.

Move the blog and pages. Export Webflow CMS collections as CSV, then import them into Shopify blogs and pages. Preserve publish dates and slugs. Blog URLs will change shape because of the /blogs/ prefix, so they need redirects like everything else.

Rebuild structured data. Shopify themes include product schema out of the box, but Webflow custom code won't carry over. Test product pages in Google's Rich Results Test, and re-add any Article, FAQ, or Organization schema you were using.

Re-implement tracking. Recreate analytics, conversion tracking, and ad pixels deliberately, and test that they fire. Missing tracking after launch makes every later comparison unreliable.

Update internal links. Links inside your content that point to old URLs should be rewritten to the new ones. Redirects work, but internal links that rely on redirects waste crawl budget and slow pages down.

Check the theme's speed on staging. Premium themes plus a pile of apps is how many Shopify stores end up slower than the Webflow site they replaced. Test Core Web Vitals before launch, not after.

Resist changing everything at once. If rankings matter, don't rewrite all copy, restructure all URLs, and redesign every template on the same day you switch platforms. Migrate like-for-like first, then iterate. If you are redesigning, keep the content and headings of your top-ranking pages as close to the original as you can.

Phase 4: The Launch Checklist

Before the cutover:

  • Import the full redirect list before pointing the domain, so redirects are live the moment traffic arrives
  • Lower your DNS TTL a day or two ahead so the change propagates quickly
  • Pick a low-traffic window, avoid launching just before a peak sales period, and don't launch when no one can monitor it
  • Freeze content changes on the Webflow site during the migration window, so nothing new needs redirecting at the last minute

At the cutover:

  • Update DNS using the values shown in Shopify's domain settings, and confirm HTTPS works on both the root domain and www
  • Set the primary domain so one version of the URL is canonical
  • Remove the storefront password. A password-protected store can't be crawled, and leaving it on after launch is one of the most damaging mistakes on this list

Immediately after:

  • Crawl your tier-one URLs from the redirect map and confirm each returns a 301 to a page that returns a 200, with no chains
  • Submit the new sitemap (/sitemap.xml) in Search Console
  • If the domain name has stayed the same, you don't need Search Console's change-of-address tool. That's only for moving to a different domain
  • Keep the Webflow project as a backup until you're confident the redirects are working. Don't delete anything yet

Phase 5: Monitor for the First 90 Days

Launch isn't the finish line. Most recoverable problems get found in the first few weeks, and only if someone is looking.

Daily in the first week:

  • Search Console's page indexing report, for new 404s, redirect errors, and pages excluded unexpectedly
  • Crawl errors on tier-one URLs
  • GA4 organic landing pages compared against your baseline

Weekly after that:

  • Clicks and impressions for top pages and queries, compared against your pre-migration export
  • Rankings for your priority keywords
  • A fresh crawl to catch redirect chains, broken internal links, and canonical problems

When you find a 404 that had traffic or backlinks, add the redirect immediately and note it for the next review.

Some movement in rankings in the weeks after a migration is normal while search engines reprocess the site. What matters is the pattern. A sustained drop on pages you redirected correctly points to something else: changed titles, thinner content, slower pages, or weaker internal linking. Compare against the baseline and investigate those first.

The Mistakes I See Most Often

If you only take a short list from this post, take this one:

  • Redirecting everything to the homepage instead of mapping page by page
  • Leaving the storefront password on after launch
  • Forgetting the blog, or forgetting that blog URLs change
  • Ignoring old Webflow redirects, which then break or form chains
  • Rewriting titles and content during the move, so you can't tell what caused any drop
  • Losing tracking and structured data because it lived in Webflow custom code
  • Launching with no baseline to compare against
  • Deleting the old site before the redirects are verified

Every one of these is preventable with the spreadsheet from Phase 1 and the crawl from Phase 4.

The Principle Underneath

A migration is a data problem more than a design problem. Everything that earned you rankings, the URLs, the titles, the content, the links pointing in, has to arrive intact at the other end. The store you're moving to can be better than the one you're leaving. But it can only inherit the old one's search performance if you treat the move as something to be mapped, built, verified, and monitored, rather than something that happens on launch day.

If you're planning a move from Webflow and want it handled with the SEO work built in, I do Shopify development and migrations through Webko, and I offer a free three-page mockup so you can see the new design before committing to anything.

I'm a freelance web designer and developer specializing in Shopify web design and Webflow development for e-commerce brands globally. I run Webko, a web design studio focused on high-converting e-commerce storefronts.

Connect with me on LinkedIn or explore my work on GitHub.

title: Continuous-Time Set-Transformers for Asynchronous WiFi-IMU Indoor Localization
description:
arXiv:2611.13057v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Indoor localization commonly combines WiFi received signal strength indicator (RSSI) fingerprints with inertial measurements. However, these sensor streams are sampled asynchronously at different rates; therefore, observations rarely align in time and may be missing or stale. Most existing methods resample the data onto a shared clock and process each modality using a separate branch. We instead present a continuous-time transformer that represents observations as an unordered set of timestamped tokens. Each token encodes its measurement, modality, and elapsed time since acquisition. A single attention block jointly fuses information across modalities and time, avoiding both resampling and modality-specific branches while remaining invariant to token order. During training, we randomly mask entire modalities and individual observations, enabling the model to operate under missing or outdated inputs. We validate the modality-specific encoders on their respective benchmarks and evaluate the fused model on both simulated and real datasets, including a crosssession dataset collected on unseen days. The proposed approach improves upon an open WiFi fingerprinting baseline under cross-session drift, remains competitive with learned fusion and dead-reckoning baselines, and degrades gracefully as observations become missing or stale. These results suggest that a single continuoustime transformer provides a practical framework for indoor localization from asynchronous sensors.

title: Amazon EKS Auto Mode now supports security groups for Pods
description:
Amazon EKS Auto Mode now supports security groups for Pods, letting you apply dedicated Amazon EC2 security group rules to individual Pods. Different workloads on the same node can carry different security groups, giving your Pods network-level segmentation without creating separate node pools for each application.

Security groups for Pods extends your existing AWS network controls to the Pod level, so your Pods can reach resources such as Amazon RDS and Amazon ElastiCache databases that authorize connections by security group under the same rules the rest of your VPC uses. You define which Pods receive which security groups with a SecurityGroupPolicy resource, and Pods not matched by a policy keep using their node’s security groups.

Security groups for Pods is included as part of EKS Auto Mode at no additional charge and is available on clusters running Kubernetes version 1.36 or later, in all AWS Regions where EKS Auto Mode is supported. To learn more, see Security groups for Pods in the Amazon EKS User Guide and the Amazon EKS Auto Mode product page.

title: Kimi K3.1 Pro and Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed are available now in AI Gateway
description:
Kimi K3.1 Pro from Moonshot AI is now available on AI Gateway, along with Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed, a faster version for interactive use.

K3.1 Pro is the first model in Moonshot's K3.1 series. It builds on Kimi K3 with improvements in coding, 3D modeling, financial analysis, and agentic tasks, and keeps the 1M-token context window and image input.

For coding, K3.1 Pro handles work ranging from small fixes in an existing codebase to building a full project, including long agent runs with many steps. It builds front-end pages and interactive scenes with stronger typography and animation than earlier Kimi models. In finance, it can carry a task from start to finish, such as building a linked financial model with adjustable assumptions and scenarios, or writing research grounded in source documents. K3.1 Pro makes fewer factual errors than earlier Kimi models on difficult prompts.

Moonshot AI plans to release the model weights by November 4: support for more providers will follow.

title: Unified Optimization of Traffic Signal and Lane Channelization for an Isolated Intersection Using Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.13599v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Optimizing traffic signal control has been a long-lasting critical issue in traffic engineering, and a number of robust methodologies have emerged to solve the problem so far. On the other hand, the road design for lane channelization is a static problem that is difficult to solve jointly with the real-time traffic signal control. If traffic volume does not vary, it is possible that both problems can be solved in an integrated manner as a single static optimization problem. Recently, researchers have devised a mixed integer linear problem (MILP) to jointly determine the traffic signal and road width designs. However, this joint optimization problem must be solved repeatedly whenever the traffic flow pattern varies. Solving the MILP may also take impractical computing time as the problem size gets larger. We present a robust methodology for solving the joint optimization problem using reinforcement learning (RL) on a real-time basis. Abrupt changes in lane markings with an incompatible signal phase can jeopardize drivers. To sidestep such a dangerous action change, we train a model with human feedback to filter infeasible action transitions in a rule-based manner. We devised a deep Q-network that can accommodate joint actions for traffic signal and lane marking plans. To ensure the implementation of the proposed operation, a variable sign for lane markings is necessary at each stop line of an intersection. The experimental results confirm that the proposed methodology enhances the intersection performance by increasing throughput.

title: FERN: Cross-Benchmark Table Retrieval for Text-to-SQL with Frozen Retrievers and Learned Ranking
description:
arXiv:2611.14477v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Text-to-SQL systems over large pooled catalogs must first retrieve the tables a question needs. We compare against the published table recall of RASL, which uses Claude 3.5 models to extract keywords and select tables, on pooled BIRD, Spider, and Fiben catalogs. FERN (Feature-Engineered Ranking with No generative LLM) instead fuses three frozen retrievers into 100 candidates, describes each with up to 120 features, and reorders them with LightGBM rankers fitted once on BIRD's training questions. On Spider, where it was not fitted, its candidate pool alone reaches RASL's published recall at fifteen tables (98.0), and the ranker raises the share of questions with every gold table in the top five (complete@5) from 83.9% to 95.6%. At five tables, FERN's recall is within one point of RASL's on Spider (96.7 vs 97.0) and on BIRD with its evidence hints (96.6 vs 97.5), and 8.2 points below on BIRD without them (89.3). On 121 real BEAVER questions, without BEAVER fitting, its recall at fifteen (82.1) falls between two BEAVER-trained retrievers (80.8, 84.5), but its complete@15 is below both (49.6 vs 54.5 and 62.0). On Fiben, it falls far short at fifteen tables (54.2 vs 69.2, different question sets), although its recall at fifty is numerically close to RASL's question-only retrieval result (80.7 vs 79.4). On BIRD dev with evidence, non-retrieval features raise complete@5 by 7.7 points over retrieval signals alone. On BIRD dev, median latency is 208 ms per question on one A100, without hosted model calls.

title: Agent Benchmarks Stop Ranking Before They Run Out of Tasks
description:
arXiv:2611.13541v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Data-science and ML-engineering agents are evaluated on benchmarks such as MLE-bench, ALE-Bench, SWE-fficiency and AlgoTune, whose tasks yield a quantity (a Kaggle metric, contest score or speedup). When one stops separating the best models, the usual remedy is a harder version. Re-scoring released runs of eight benchmarks, including SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench for breadth, we find much of this saturation lies in the measurement, not the tasks. Most agent benchmarks reduce a run to one pass/fail bit, which fails in two ways. It is too coarse: neighbouring top-ten agents on SWE-bench Verified differ by less than its tests' errors, and correcting them reorders neighbours no more than deleting a random sixth of each agent's passes. It is capped at the reference: ALE-Bench's top ten, separated by contest score, tie when graded against the median human, although nearly half the runs beat that human. On fixed tasks, a higher bar only moves the problem; graded credit fixes it. We derive a clipped log-ratio score with dated anchors and cost as a separate axis. In a Terminal-Bench re-run, pass/fail-tied models differ over tenfold on the quantity the tests discard.

title: StatPrompt-LLM: A Lightweight Statistical Refinement for Foundation-Style Time-Series Forecasting
description:
arXiv:2611.12974v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Time-series forecasting has recently seen a paradigm shift with the introduction of foundation-style models that adapt large pretrained language architectures to sequential data. However, effectively exposing fundamental temporal structures, such as trend, scale, and temporal dependence, to these models remains an open challenge, particularly when the available observations are limited. In this paper, we conduct an exploratory empirical study across different generations of forecasting architectures and propose StatPrompt-LLM, a lightweight statistical refinement of Time-LLM. StatPrompt-LLM augments the existing Time-LLM prompting mechanism with dataset-level statistical information and introduces a zero-initialised autoregressive bypass as a complementary linear forecasting pathway. We evaluate our framework on electricity and meteorological time-series benchmarks, including ETTh1, ETTh2, and Weather, under full-prefix and reduced-prefix configurations. Under the 10% reduced-prefix configuration, StatPrompt-LLM achieved lower in-sample prediction errors than Time-LLM, with unweighted average relative reductions across datasets of 40.2% in MSE and 21.4% in MAE. Full-prefix results were more dataset-dependent. Ablation analyses revealed relatively modest and dataset-dependent changes when selected additional statistical descriptor groups were masked within the combined architecture. Computational profiling indicated additional model parameters and runtime overhead relative to Time-LLM.

title: F3-AGI v4.0: Bioenergetically-Gated Active Inference, Metaplastic Preconditioning, and Residual Program Synthesis for Sample-Efficient Abstract Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.13325v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Few-shot abstract reasoning on ARC-AGI requires inducing algorithmic transformations from 2 to 5 demonstration pairs without task-specific pretraining. Because few-shot demonstrations under-constrain the hypothesis space, program synthesis suffers from the Rashomon effect (predictive multiplicity): heuristic search finds spurious programs with low training error that fail on test inputs, while unconstrained library growth degrades latency. We introduce F3-AGI v4.0, a CPU-native neuro-symbolic and active inference architecture comprising three mechanisms: (1) F3-Metabolic-Optim, combining mistake-gated plasticity, Fisher-EMA preconditioning, and virtual ATP gating; (2) Adaptive Complexity-Guided Program Synthesis (AACR) with a Cycle-3 ResidualPatchSynthesizer and smallest-pair early rejection; and (3) a 512D L2-normalized random projection driving Expected Free Energy (EFE) exploration with dead-signature pruning. Across three empirical studies: (i) on a synthetic 5-task class-incremental stream without replay, F3-Metabolic-Optim achieves 91.67% final accuracy with 9.17% forgetting, skipping 93.47% of updates, cutting L1 plasticity cost by 65.7%, and running 2.19x faster than EWC; (ii) on the 400-task ARC-AGI-1 public evaluation set (offline CPU, zero LLM calls), F3-AGI v4.0 solves 57/400 tasks (14.25% pass@2; 56/400 pass@1) with a mean latency of 1.62 s/task, decomposed into 19/50 (38.00%, 1.19 s/task, a 42.5x paired speedup over Horizon 2) on the 50-task calibration slice and 38/350 (10.86%) on the 350 strictly uninspected hold-out tasks (with 7 autonomous Cycle-3 patch solutions); and (iii) in a local 5-game (15-level) ARC-AGI-3-inspired interactive suite, our agent completes 15/15 levels with 89.44% level-weighted RHAE (90.72% unweighted).

title: Program-Aided Patchable Skill Evolution
description:
arXiv:2611.14019v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agent skills have emerged as an effective means of enabling LLM agents to solve complex, interactive tasks by encoding reusable knowledge without modifying model parameters. Recent approaches further improve skill adaptation by distilling reusable experience from agent execution trajectories and evolving skills based on downstream task feedback. However, existing methods primarily represent skills as natural language documents, intertwining procedural logic with descriptive knowledge and making skills difficult to maintain and evolve. To address this limitation, we propose PASE (Program-Aided Patchable Skill Evolution), a program-aided framework that iteratively evolves skills by associating them with executable programs. Unlike prior approaches that encode trajectory-derived experience primarily in natural language, PASE separates reusable procedural logic into editable programs, enabling targeted updates to executable components while reducing the need to repeatedly revise natural language skills. Extensive experiments across diverse models and benchmarks demonstrate that PASE consistently outperforms all baselines, by achieving over 2.8% improvements. Further analyses show that PASE exhibits greater evolutionary stability and generalisation capability, highlighting the critical role of programmatic knowledge in skill evolution. We will release all data and code via GitHub.

title: Building kakemono: A Wallpaper Manager That Comes With Me to Any OS
description:
TL;DR

  • kakemono is a wallpaper manager for macOS, Linux and Windows. A small daemon downloads wallpapers from Wallhaven, Unsplash, Reddit, Bing, NASA's Astronomy Picture of the Day, or your own folders, and changes the wallpaper on a timer
  • One Rust binary is both the daemon and the command-line tool. A Tauri app adds a tray icon, a thumbnail picker and a settings window
  • It started as a macOS-only Go app. I rewrote it in Rust so it keeps working if I ever move to Linux or Windows
  • The code is public at github.com/RielJ/kakemono, and v0.1.0 has installers for all three systems

The demo turns on a Wallhaven search in Settings, opens the picker, and clicks a thumbnail. The new wallpaper is set before the Settings window closes.

How it started

Linux has Variety. It's a plain little app that does one job well. You give it a list of sources, it downloads images in the background, and every half hour your desktop changes. If you liked the last one, you step back to it. If you hated it, you trash it.

I wanted that on my Mac, so I wrote wallpaperd: a Go daemon with a command-line client, six image sources, and a Unix socket. I wired it into sketchybar, so my menu bar showed the current wallpaper and had next and previous buttons. I used it every day.

The code had a weak spot, though. It set the wallpaper by running osascript and asking System Events, which needs the Automation permission. It checked for dark mode by running defaults read. Everything that touched the desktop went through another program, and every one of those programs exists only on macOS.

I keep thinking about moving to Linux one day. If I do, I want my wallpaper setup to come with me, and I'd like it on a Windows machine too. So I asked my coding agent whether I should rewrite the app in Rust.

Its first answer was no. The app sleeps 99.9% of the time, Go handles timers and sockets well, and nobody would notice the speed difference. That's fair. But I didn't care about speed. I cared about two things: no dependence on other apps, and one codebase for three operating systems. With those goals, Rust and Tauri made sense, and the rewrite began.

I also needed a new name. wallpaperd is very close to wpaperd, an existing Rust wallpaper daemon for Wayland. A kakemono is a Japanese hanging scroll, a picture on the wall that people swap out with the seasons. That's close enough to what the app does.

What it does

  • Sources. Wallhaven and Unsplash searches, a subreddit, Bing's daily images, NASA's APOD archive back to 1995, and local folders. You can add the same type more than once, for example two Wallhaven searches.
  • Rotation. By default the wallpaper changes every 30 minutes. A background downloader fetches one new image every 10 minutes and keeps the download folder under 500 MB, oldest files first. It never deletes favorites.
  • History, favorites and trash. kakemono prev goes back. favorite copies the current image to a favorites folder. trash moves it out and sets the next one, and the picker can undo that.
  • Light and dark. When the system switches theme, kakemono can set a new wallpaper and prefer images that suit the theme.
  • Filters. The settings copy Variety's "When possible, use images that..." section: landscape only, or at least 80% of the screen resolution.

The picker is a strip of thumbnails along one edge of the screen. It has five tabs: Sources, Downloaded, Local, Favorites and Cache. The Sources tab shows previews from your online sources without downloading anything. A click downloads the full image and sets it. Every action has a key, so I rarely touch the mouse.

The settings window lists the sources in one table. You turn each one on or off, and "Use Only These" limits rotation to the ones you selected.

How it's built

There are two programs. kakemono is the daemon and the CLI in one binary. kakemono-ui is the Tauri app. Both talk to the daemon in newline-delimited JSON over a Unix socket, or a named pipe on Windows. That means you can script it with nc or jq, and my sketchybar plugin still works.

kakemono next ────┐
tray, picker, ────┼──▶ socket (named pipe on Windows) ──▶ daemon
settings          │                                        │
sketchybar ───────┘                                        ├─ sources: download images
                                                           ├─ engine: rotation, history, cache
                                                           └─ platform: set the wallpaper

The Rust workspace has eight crates: protocol, config, engine, sources, platform, fs, cli and ui. Only platform knows which OS it's on.

Setting the wallpaper is the part that differs most between systems:

  • On macOS, kakemono calls NSWorkspace setDesktopImageURL:forScreen: through objc2, once for each screen. No osascript, and no Automation permission. One catch: macOS has no API that sets every Space, so only the current Space on each screen changes.
  • On Windows, it uses the IDesktopWallpaper COM interface from the windows crate.
  • Linux has no single API, so kakemono detects the session. It checks for a desktop environment (GNOME, KDE, XFCE and others), then for a wallpaper daemon that's already running (swww, hyprpaper), then the compositor (Hyprland, Sway, niri), then X11 tools like feh. That covers 17 backends. kakemono detect tells you which one it picked and why. If yours isn't covered, you can set your own command.

The tools:

Part Tools
Daemon and CLI Rust, tokio, clap, reqwest with rustls, serde, tracing
Native APIs objc2 (macOS), windows-rs (Windows), zbus for D-Bus (Linux)
App Tauri 2, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, Vite
Tests cargo test, insta snapshots, Vitest, Testing Library
CI and releases GitHub Actions on macOS, Linux and Windows, Docker, QEMU

How I built it

I built kakemono with coding agents in Pi. First, four models each wrote a plan, and I merged the best parts into one. Next, I wrote short contracts for the pieces that crates share: the config format, the platform API and the source interface. Then subagents built slices against those contracts in parallel, each in its own git worktree, which I wrote about in my pi-git-worktrees post. The rewrite took 152 commits over two days.

Three things kept the rewrite honest:

  1. Golden fixtures from the Go app. Before writing any Rust, I recorded what the Go daemon sent and received on its socket, and how it read its config. The Rust tests replay those recordings, so the new daemon had to answer the way the old one did.
  2. Lots of tests. There are 1,422 Rust tests and 392 frontend tests. The source tests replay recorded HTTP responses, so they never hit Wallhaven or Reddit.
  3. Testing on systems I don't own. GitHub Actions tests every push on macOS, Linux and Windows. I also wanted to catch failures before pushing, so the Linux checks run locally in Docker. The Windows checks run in a Windows 11 ARM virtual machine on my M4 MacBook, through QEMU and Apple's Hypervisor framework. A script installs Windows from an answer file with no clicks, runs the same tests CI runs, and shuts the VM down.

One surprise came at the end. I downloaded the first release on my other laptop, and macOS said the app "is damaged and can't be opened". It wasn't damaged. The app isn't signed with an Apple Developer ID, so macOS blocks it when it's downloaded from the internet. The fix is one command, and it's in the install steps below.

How to use it

Download the installer for your system from the Releases page.

macOS. Open the .dmg (aarch64 for Apple silicon, x64 for Intel) and drag kakemono to Applications. Because the build isn't signed, clear the quarantine flag before you open it:

xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/kakemono.app

Linux. Install the .deb or .rpm, or run the AppImage:

sudo apt install ./kakemono_0.1.0_amd64.deb      # Debian, Ubuntu
sudo dnf install ./kakemono-0.1.0-1.x86_64.rpm   # Fedora

Windows. Run the .msi or the -setup.exe. When SmartScreen warns about an unknown publisher, click More info, then Run anyway.

Open the app. It starts the daemon and puts an icon in the menu bar, tray or notification area. From there you can open Settings, add a source, and open the picker.

If you prefer the terminal:

kakemono service install   # start the daemon at login
kakemono next              # set a new wallpaper now
kakemono prev              # go back to the previous one
kakemono favorite          # keep this one
kakemono trash             # never show this one again
kakemono pause             # stop rotating; `kakemono resume` starts again

Sources live in ~/.config/kakemono/config.toml, one [[sources]] table each:

[daemon]
interval = "30m"

[[sources]]
id = "wh-nature"
type = "wallhaven"
location = "nature"

[[sources]]
id = "pictures"
type = "folder"
location = "~/Pictures/Wallpapers"

On Linux, run kakemono detect once to see which backend it picked. If the wallpaper doesn't change, kakemono doctor prints the session, the command it would run, and what the daemon is doing.

The README has every command and config key. If you try it and something breaks on your desktop, please open an issue.

RielJ / kakemono

Rotating wallpapers from Bing, APOD, Reddit, Unsplash, Wallhaven and local folders, with a tray picker. macOS, Linux and Windows.

kakemono

kakemono is a wallpaper manager for macOS, Linux, and Windows. A small daemon downloads wallpapers from Bing, Wallhaven, Unsplash, Reddit, NASA APOD, or your own folders, and changes the wallpaper on a timer. It keeps a history you can step back through, saves favorites, and can prefer dark images in dark mode and light images in light mode.

The kakemono binary is both the daemon and the command-line client. The kakemono app adds a menu-bar (tray) icon, a thumbnail picker for browsing and setting wallpapers, and a settings window.

Install

Prebuilt downloads are on the Releases page. Each release has two kinds of file:

  • The app (kakemono_<version>_<arch>.dmg, .deb, .rpm, .AppImage, .msi, or -setup.exe). It contains the kakemono binary too, so most people need only this.
  • The command-line tool alone (kakemono-<version>-<target>.tar.gz, or .zip on Windows), for servers and window managers where…

title: EarthRecord: From Pixels to Land Change with Multimodal Agents over Four Decades of Satellite Imagery
description:
arXiv:2611.12934v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While multimodal agents now carry out complex data analysis with tools, their ability to turn decades of satellite imagery into reliable land-change analysis, crucial for Earth observation science, remains unmeasured. Existing benchmarks fall short: they pose questions on curated images or give agents preprocessed inputs, leaving out the raw multi-sensor archives where such analysis begins. We introduce EarthRecord, a benchmark built on the raw record of 56 sites: four decades of Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2 data, with cloud masking and cross-sensor harmonization left to the agent. It poses 238 land-change questions across ten analysis tasks, scored against withheld references from global products, agreement among methods, and visual interpretation. Two controls test what answers rest on: the closed book removes the record, and instrument pairs alter one satellite's data while nothing changes on the ground. Evaluations of twelve multimodal agents reveal that leading agents complete most analyses end to end but falter when an answer requires mapping from imagery. Further analysis shows that the record moves answers from prior knowledge to the pixels but not yet to the real change on the ground: when one satellite's data are altered, half of the right answers follow the alteration. EarthRecord thus provides a principled platform for measuring and advancing agents from pixels to land change.

title: The deletion cookie that forgot Secure — a teardown of 230 Java files in 46 seconds
description:
Most security scans end with a long list and no clear answer to "so what do I fix first?"

This teardown is from a real run — the sample scan we publish so builders can see exactly what a check looks like before they buy one. No client code was involved. The targets were two public Java codebases, scanned as-is:

  • MyBatis JPetStore-6 — a real online-store web app: 46 Java files, 7,628 lines
  • Spark (perwendel/spark) — a Java web framework: 184 Java files, 21,272 lines

Total: 230 files, 28,900 lines, about 46 seconds of instrument time. The instrument was Semgrep 1.140.0 with a frozen set of OWASP-category rules for Java — SQL injection, XSS, command injection, path traversal, weak crypto, weak randomness, insecure cookies, and others. It reads Java source only; anything living in XML mappers or config is outside its sight, and we say so in the report.

Findings issued: 16. Every one was read in context and dispositioned.

What actually broke

One real fix, low severity — and it's the kind of bug almost nobody writes on purpose:

Spark, Response.java:314 — the cookie that deletes a cookie was built without the Secure flag.

Spark's normal cookie path does this right. Its deletion path didn't carry the same flag. A deletion cookie should carry the same protections as the cookie it replaces. Otherwise you have one code path that respects your cookie policy and a second, quieter path that doesn't.

The fix is one line. The lesson is bigger:

Check every path that sets a cookie — create, update, and delete. Frameworks and apps usually secure the happy path. The cleanup path is where the flag gets dropped.

If you ship anything with session cookies, grep for every cookie construction in your codebase today — not just the login handler.

What held — and why we report it anyway

JPetStore-6: 1 finding, not a defect. A ThreadLocalRandom call in the Maven wrapper downloader names a temporary file during a build-tool download. It protects nothing, so weak randomness there is not a security problem. Counted, explained, no fix recommended.

Spark, Response.java:292: not a defect. This is the correct normal cookie method. It calls setSecure(secured) from its own parameter. A pattern scanner can't see that the flag is parameterized, so it fired anyway. We note it so a reader can see why a hit was dismissed, not just that it was.

The noise, counted in the open

  • 4 × SQL injection (CWE-89) in Spark's route dispatcher — false positives. The lines are route-dispatch calls like Routes.execute(...). The file contains no SQL at all. The rule's sink pattern binds on a generic execute(...) shape. That's a known collision class.
  • 8 × insecure cookie in test code. Mock verifications asserting that a cookie method was called. They set no cookies. Counted here, excluded from the fix list.
  • 1 × weak randomness in example code. new Random() minting an ID in a bundled example app. Fine in a demo. It would be a real problem if that pattern were copied into production — predictable IDs are guessable IDs.

Tally: 1 real fix (low), 1 informational, 14 not-a-defect — each with the reason printed beside it.

On the labeled benchmark corpus where this same rule set was calibrated, its measured precision was 0.7169. In plain terms: even a decent scanner will hand you hits that don't survive reading. The reading is the service.

What a builder can use from this

  1. Audit cookie deletion as well as cookie creation. Same flags, every path.
  2. Don't let example-code randomness reach production. new Random() for IDs, tokens, or filenames that matter is a defect; for a throwaway temp name, it isn't. Context decides.
  3. Demand dispositions, not just counts. "16 findings" means nothing until each one is marked real, informational, or not-a-defect with a reason. If a report won't show its dismissals, you can't trust its fixes.

If you want this kind of check on your own app before launch, the intake is at verify.novitasnexus.com — verify@novitasnexus.com if you prefer email.

title: PhyRubric: Rubric-Grounded Diagnostic Evaluation of Physical Commonsense in Text-to-Video Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.13576v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As text-to-video (T2V) models are increasingly positioned as world simulators, it is essential to evaluate whether their videos conform to physical commonsense. However, existing benchmarks rely on annotators who rate each video with a single score based on intuition, yielding ratings that are subjective and do not tell which physical principle is violated. We introduce PhyRubric, a rubric-grounded diagnostic framework for evaluating physical commonsense in T2V generation. For each caption, PhyRubric constructs a caption-specific rubric before any video is seen, decomposing the caption into semantic and physical items, and derives scores from item-level verdicts grounded in timestamped evidence. We instantiate this framework as PhyRubric-Bench, which spans 34 categories across five physical domains, and scale it up to PhyRubric-Train with 3,788 videos, on which we fine-tune the open-source PhyRubric-Judge. Empirical results across ten T2V models show that physical commonsense remains far from solved, and that PhyRubric-Judge correlates more closely with human judgments than existing open-source judges while matching the frontier proprietary Gemini 4 Argon. Further analysis provides actionable insights for T2V models.

title: JAX-WAVE: A Differentiable Physics-Supervised Framework for Inverse Wave Design in Heterogeneous Media
description:
arXiv:2611.13826v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Designing a prescribed wave field in a heterogeneous medium requires an initial pressure distribution that compensates for the medium's propagation response. Repeated numerical inversion solves this task afresh for each target and environment. We introduce JAX-WAVE for amortized inverse wave design: a shared neural network maps desired terminal fields and known wave-speed maps directly to bounded initial pressures. Training through a differentiable finite-difference time-domain solver uses the physical design objective without requiring optimized control labels. Linear propagation and symmetric pressure bounds imply an exact sign-reversal relation for the regularized optimum. A shared-weight projection enforces this relation, preserves feasibility, and satisfies an exact identity for the paired-sign objective. We characterize the discrete propagator and its weighted adjoint to connect learning, numerical inversion, and optimality assessment. On an independent confirmation set, three trained models achieve unseen-material errors of 25.24% for geometric targets and 4.77% for reachable targets. Matched-capacity comparisons show improved reconstruction with the sign parameterization. Within a 5 ms median online budget, the learned map reduces mean error by 45% relative to accelerated numerical inversion on the heterogeneous benchmark; longer numerical solves recover greater accuracy. The results establish a reusable inverse-design procedure and show how its accuracy and computational value depend on target structure and query workload.

title: Recurrent Modular Structure in Spiking Neural Network Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.14262v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Biological neural circuits are both modular and recurrent, with dense communities sparsely linked to one another. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) for reinforcement learning are usually feed-forward, and it is unclear how to obtain functional modules in a recurrent SNN or what they buy. In this work, we introduce a class of spiking networks, called Community Recurrent SNNs (CoRe SNNs): recurrent networks partitioned into communities with fixed roles. A controller community receives the stimulus, each action has its own community, and latent communities carry internal state. Spiking activity is then a walk between communities, and the action is the community the walk reaches. All learning is local and three-factor, and the recurrent communities are closer to cortical microcircuits than a feed-forward actor. We compare three regimes for obtaining the communities: dynamic modularity, in which a new learning rule we introduce, Map-STDP, encourages modular structure during learning; partial modularity, in which a stochastic block model (SBM) initialization enforces it partly; and full modularity, in which sealing enforces it fully. On CartPole, across three spiking neuron models, Map-STDP improves learning over the same network without it matches full modularity (sealed communities) on two of the three models, and makes the observed spike walk more compressible. Replacing the feed-forward actor of a TD-STDP actor-critic with recurrent action communities improves on the feed-forward network on CartPole and LunarLander, and matches it on Acrobot. How strongly to enforce modularity depends on the task: full modularity helps most on Acrobot, while on LunarLander the dynamic, partial and full regimes perform alike. Overall, these recurrent modular networks can match or even improve upon feed-forward approaches, with improvements in bio-plausibility and energy efficiency.

title: Test-Time Compute vs More Parameters: Where the Inference Budget Actually Goes
description:
Two roads lead to a smarter answer. a larger trained model front-loads the work into training, so every inference is a single forward pass through a heavy network. test-time compute keeps the model smaller and spends extra tokens thinking, searching or verifying at inference. The pitch for the second road is that you pay only when the problem is hard. The catch is that you pay in wall-clock latency and in fleet size, and those costs land on the exact requests you most want to serve quickly.

Test-time compute trades a flat, predictable serving cost for one that scales with problem difficulty, and the fleet must be sized for the worst case.

Part One: What is actually being compared

These two options are usually presented as alternative implementations of one capability. They are better read as two different answers to the question of where uncertainty is allowed to live. test-time compute absorbs it in one place, a larger trained model in another, and a comparison that measures only the average outcome misses precisely the reason a team would accept the extra complexity of either one in reasoning-model serving economics.

There is an accounting asymmetry worth making explicit. test-time compute tends to put expenditure into capital, where it is spread over years and needs an approval process; a larger trained model keeps it in operations, where it is easy to approve and difficult to cap. Finance and engineering usually prefer opposite sides of that line, so the decision is often settled by the budgeting calendar rather than by a measurement in reasoning-model serving economics.

Part Two: The arithmetic that decides it

The arithmetic hinges on how often problems are hard. Suppose a verification or search loop multiplies inference compute by eight on the difficult tenth of requests. If the smaller model plus the loop still costs less per correct answer than the large model on those hard requests, the loop wins. But the same loop, applied indiscriminately to easy requests, multiplies the fleet you must provision by the same factor, because the machines are busy thinking on queries that a big model would have answered in one pass.

What actually decides the outcome is the slowest link in the chain, not the fastest. test-time compute improves one step, but if the surrounding steps still dominate the total, the improvement barely moves the wall clock. This is the recurring disappointment in reasoning-model serving economics: a component-level win that is real, reproducible and almost invisible to the user because it was applied to the wrong term in the sum.

Deployment changes what gets measured. After test-time compute goes in, the metric people optimise tends to shift toward predictability; after a larger trained model, toward unit price. That shift is why two teams can look at the same production data and reach opposite conclusions about which option won, and why an evaluation should record the metric before the trial rather than after it.

Part Three: Where the simple model breaks

Latency is where the model and the loop disagree about what matters. a larger trained model answers in one bounded pass, so tail latency is predictable. test-time compute can run until it is confident, which means a hard query may take seconds to minutes, and a user who asked a simple question next to a hard one shares the same queue and the same delay. A product that promised speed can quietly become a product that is fast on average and slow when it matters.

A verification loop that multiplies inference compute eightfold on the hard tenth of requests can win per-answer but forces an eightfold fleet on every query it touches.

Part Four: The cost that arrives later

There is a deployment asymmetry. a larger trained model is one artifact to host, version and cache; a single serving path serves everyone. test-time compute needs a controller that decides how much budget each query earns, a verifier that can judge answers, and a way to cap runaway loops. That controller is itself a system that must be tuned, monitored and occasionally overridden, which is a standing operational cost the single large model does not carry.

Adoption is unlikely to be a single flip. The first movers are the cases where the deciding variable is most extreme, the middle of the market follows once tooling and reference designs exist, and the long tail stays with a larger trained model until the cost of switching falls below the cost of maintaining an exception. A reasonable reading of the next several years is coexistence with a slowly moving boundary rather than a replacement event.

Part Five: What this changes outside the engineering team

For a person asking a tax question at midnight, the difference is whether the answer arrives before they give up. A thinking loop that is confident and fast feels magical; one that ruminates on a trivial question feels broken. The daily-life version of this trade is a help desk that either answers immediately or makes you wait while it consults three manuals, and users remember the waits far longer than the wins.

There is a mundane public-facing consequence as well: reliability and predictability are what people actually notice. A household, a commuter or a small shop does not experience an architecture, only whether a screen updates, a bill arrives on time or a service works after two years. Those are the terms in which the eventual judgement will be made.

A fair trial holds answer quality fixed and measures cost per correct answer and tail latency at a realistic mix of easy and hard queries, with the loop budget capped. A comparison that reports accuracy without the fleet multiplier and the latency tail is half a result.

A market sizing sanity check

If reasoning models move from a research curiosity to a default tier by 2030, the market for test-time controllers, verifiers and budget-aware routers is plausibly $3B to $10B annually. The low end assumes the loop stays inside a few dominant model APIs; the high end assumes a distinct orchestration layer is sold across clouds and on-premises fleets. The driver is not model size but the fraction of queries that are worth thinking about.

Treat the numbers as a scale model. They are built to show where the curves cross and which term dominates, and they deliberately round the inputs that vary most between deployments. The ranking is robust to those rounds; the exact threshold is not.

The comparison that matters

The comparison that matters is between a flat cost you can plan and a difficulty-weighted cost you must cap. Test-time compute wins on hard problems where the loop beats a bigger model; a larger trained model wins on easy and latency-sensitive traffic where predictability is the product. Real fleets will run both and route between them.

A change in regulation, in the supply of a single component, or in the tariff a site faces could invalidate the ranking overnight. The comparison is a snapshot of prices and constraints in reasoning-model serving economics, not a property of the technologies, and anyone reusing it in a different year should re-run the threshold rather than reuse the conclusion.

Run both and route: a larger model for easy, latency-sensitive traffic and a thinking loop for hard problems, with the loop budget hard-capped.

title: The Database Scaling Ladder: Fix a Slow Database in the Right Order
description:
Indexes, then cache, then read replicas, then a bigger machine, and sharding only at the top

Say the order page of an online store starts taking a few seconds to load. Someone looks at the Cloud SQL dashboard, sees CPU near the top, and says, "Let's shard." That is usually the most expensive answer to the question.

The problem

A slow database has many possible causes, and each fix costs a different amount of effort and money. Jump to the top fix too early and you pay for a sharding project when a missing index was the real issue. Stay too long at the bottom and you keep tuning queries while a single primary has truly run out of room.

I think of it as a ladder. Climb one rung at a time, cheapest first, and only go up when the current rung stops helping.

The solution: five rungs

Rung 1: indexes and queries

First, confirm the real cause. A query that scans a whole table because a column is not indexed will be slow on any machine size.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

-- if it shows a full table scan:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_created ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC);

This costs almost nothing and is the first thing I check.

Rung 2: cache

Many reads ask for the same thing again and again: a product's details, a category list. A Memorystore (Redis) cache in front of Cloud SQL answers those repeated reads in memory, and the database only sees misses. Every key gets a TTL, and when the data changes, the app updates Cloud SQL and then deletes the key. The database stays the source of truth.

Rung 3: read replicas

If reads are still heavy after caching, read replicas take read-only queries off the primary. Writes still go to the primary. The catch is replication lag: a replica can be slightly behind, so a user who just placed an order might not see it on a replica for a moment. Reads that must be fresh, like "show the order I just placed", should go to the primary.

Rung 4: scale up (vertical scaling)

Now give the same instance a bigger machine. For example, going from 2 vCPU and 8 GB RAM to 8 vCPU and 32 GB RAM. The data, instance name and connection address stay the same. Only the machine type changes.

How I would do it:

  1. Confirm the cause again. A bad query needs a fix, not a bigger machine.
  2. Pick an off-peak time and tell the team.
  3. Take an on-demand backup.
  4. Edit the instance and choose the new machine type.
  5. The instance restarts, connections drop briefly, and the app reconnects.
  6. Watch CPU, memory and latency while the cache warms up again.

A few details matter here. A machine type change needs a restart, so there is brief downtime (HA setups can shorten it; check the current docs for your edition). Growing the disk does not need a restart and can happen automatically. Shrinking a disk has limited support. Read replicas should be resized too, so they keep up with the primary. And a primary does not resize itself: you do it, or you automate it from monitoring.

Rung 5: shard

Stop scaling up when the largest machine type is reached, when cost grows faster than the gain, or when the single primary is still the write bottleneck. Replicas help reads, not writes. That is when sharding makes sense: spread users across several databases so writes are spread too.

Trade-offs and limits

  • Measure before climbing. Query insights and slow query logs tell you which rung you are actually on. Guessing is how teams end up sharding an unindexed table.
  • Retries are part of scaling up. The restart is only a short blip if the app retries connections. Without retries, it looks like an outage.
  • Caching brings staleness. It needs a clear rule for invalidation and a TTL as a safety net. Some reads, like payment amounts or stock at checkout, should never come from cache.
  • Replicas bring lag. I would route read-after-write paths to the primary on purpose, not by accident.
  • Sharding is a project, not a setting. It needs a routing layer, a migration plan and a new answer for cross-shard reports. That is exactly why it sits at the top.

Takeaway

Check queries and indexes before touching infrastructure.

Cache and replicas scale reads; a bigger machine buys time for everything.

Shard only when one primary can no longer take the writes.

title: Towards Scalable Network-Based Interventions for HIV Treatment and Prevention via R2C-Agent
description:
arXiv:2611.13312v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) remains a pressing public health challenge worldwide. Targeting limited HIV prevention and treatment resources effectively with network-based algorithms is a long-standing problem with a rich history at AAMAS and other computational venues. However, optimizing targeted biomedical interventions for minimizing spread of HIV often requires observability of the contact network of HIV transmission risk behavior among individuals, which is prohibitively expensive to collect at scale. Peer referral networks, i.e., networks collected through a recursive peer referral process, are an alternative network class often used to study HIV in hidden populations that can be collected digitally at scale, but they deviate from the underlying contact network: referrals can follow non-risk social ties and participants accept only one referral, hiding contacts among already-recruited individuals. In this work, we first formalize the novel problem of planning network-based interventions to minimize HIV spread in the hidden contact network while observing only the peer referral network. Second, we implement R2C-Agent, a decision making agent for interventions that is designed around our new conditional graph diffusion model called Referral-to-Contact Diffusion (R2C-Diff). R2C-Diff positions the peer referral process as incremental corruption of the underlying contact network and learns to reverse it. R2C-Agent plans its interventions over contact networks sampled from R2C-Diff, so its decisions account for uncertainty about the hidden contact network. Finally, we conduct simulated experiments using real-world HIV network data that demonstrate that R2C-Agent empirically plans more effective interventions than baselines from interdisciplinary literature and highlight key tradeoffs and assumptions driving performance.

title: TimeOmni-o1: Bidirectionally Coupling Time Series Foundation Models and LLMs for Multimodal Reasoning and Forecasting
description:
arXiv:2611.12902v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Time series from real-world systems are often accompanied by text, such as a report on an event that affects them. Two common tasks on these series are understanding, e.g., answering questions about a series, and forecasting its future values. Both tasks require reasoning over the series and the text together. Moreover, understanding outputs text while forecasting outputs a time series, so serving both requires a model that reads and generates both modalities. Large language models (LLMs) read time series as digit tokens and handle long series poorly. Time series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast well from large-scale pretraining but typically neither read nor generate text. Time series language models add a time series modality to the LLM but forecast on the LLM side, leaving the TSFM's pretrained forecasting ability unused. We present TimeOmni-o1, which couples a pretrained TSFM and an LLM bidirectionally. In one direction, the TSFM encodes the series in compressed form for the LLM, which reasons over it together with the text. In the other, the LLM's reasoning is fed back into the TSFM, which produces the forecast conditioned on it. One model architecture thus reads and generates both series and text, reasons in text, and draws on the TSFM's pretrained forecasting ability. To train it, we build MMTR, a multimodal time series reasoning dataset with annotated reasoning traces, covering both tasks across 12 domains with 500k+ samples. On MMTR, TimeOmni-o1 outperforms existing models on both understanding and forecasting across most domains, as well as the LLM and the TSFM inside it when used individually. The gains carry over to three open benchmarks, where it outperforms the dedicated time series models.

title: Antalia-2 Mini: A 7.6-million-parameter Turkish text-to-speech model trained entirely on synthetic speech
description:
arXiv:2611.13811v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Antalia-2 Mini is a single-voice Turkish text-to-speech model with 7,620,931 parameters. It reads characters and produces 48 kHz audio at 41 times real time on an Apple M5 laptop CPU (2 threads). Its training audio came only from VoxCPM2 (the teacher), about 300 times larger, cloning one synthetic clip; automatic checks kept about 1,790 h. Fine-tuning the vocoder on the acoustic model's own mel spectrograms cut the word error rate (WER) of Whisper's transcripts from a mean of 3.89% to 1.75% at adjacent pre-release checkpoints. The teacher corrupts the start of a clip when the first word begins with \"o, the student learned this, and a spoken prefix we cut from the output hides it. On the 495-sentence Freya-TR-Eval benchmark, where we tuned settings, version 1.0.1 has WER 1.09% and character error rate 0.22% on our public harness. A paired bootstrap cannot distinguish these from EMA Lightning, an 8.6M Turkish model, which scores higher on full-band UTMOS, an English-trained quality proxy. No human listening test exists. Weights, inference code and the benchmark harness are public under Apache-2.0; training code and data are not.

title: Rethinking Evaluation for Video Capsule Endoscopy: Validation Protocol, Source-Video Diversity, and Cross-Dataset Shift
description:
arXiv:2611.13245v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automated video capsule endoscopy (VCE) classification remains challenging due to severe class imbalance, limited source-video diversity, and variations in image appearance across datasets. Although deep learning models have demonstrated promising performance on established benchmarks, their reliability under different validation protocols and external dataset shift remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we introduce DMSNet, a deformable adaptive multi-scale edge-guided attention network integrating adaptive multi-scale feature fusion, deformable lesion refinement, edge-guided attention, and sparse feature selection. We benchmark DMSNet against 18 representative convolutional, transformer-based, and pretrained vision architectures on Kvasir-Capsule under random frame-level and source-video-disjoint validation protocols. We further identify source-video overlap between the original training and test splits and evaluate model performance on both the complete test set and a source-video-disjoint subset. Under random frame-level validation, DMSNet achieves an MCC of 0.442 $\pm$ 0.020 on complete test set and 0.456 $\pm$ 0.037 on the source-video-disjoint subset. On the external CV2024 dataset, ConvNeXt-Tiny achieves the highest MCC of 0.207, while performance degrades substantially across architectures relative to in-domain evaluation. We further investigate source-video diversity using a per-class cap of 200 training frames. With the total training-set size held fixed, increasing the maximum source-video coverage from four to eight improves MCC for 17 of 19 evaluated architectures. Overall, these findings demonstrate that model rankings and classification performance depend substantially on evaluation protocol, training-source diversity, and cross-dataset shift, emphasizing the need for source-aware validation and rigorous external evaluation of VCE classification systems.

title: Stop trusting file extensions: validating uploads by content (with ffmpeg)
description:
A user of my free tool uploaded a recording named voice.m4a and got "This doesn't look like a real .m4a file." The file was fine. It was a WebM/Opus recording that had been saved with an .m4a extension. My upload check was wrong, not the user.

This is a short write-up of what I changed, and why file extensions are the wrong thing to trust.

The bug

My converter (Node + ffmpeg) checked the first bytes of an upload against the file's extension:

// before: decide by extension, then check one signature
case "m4a":
  return head.slice(4, 8).toString() === "ftyp";

Real files are renamed all the time: WebM saved as .m4a, an MP3 named .wav, a screen recording shared as .mp4. ffmpeg itself does not care about the extension and detects the format from the content, so my stricter check only rejected good files.

The fix: sniff the content, accept any known media container 

export function isKnownMedia(head: Uint8Array): boolean {
  const ascii = (s: string, at = 0) => [...s].every((c, i) => head[at + i] === c.charCodeAt(0));
  if (head.length < 8) return false;
  // ISO base media (MP4, M4A, MOV, 3GP, HEIC): size + box type
  if (["ftyp", "moov", "mdat", "free", "skip", "wide"].some((t) => ascii(t, 4))) return true;
  if (ascii("ID3") || ascii("RIFF") || ascii("OggS") || ascii("fLaC")) return true;
  if (head[0] === 0x1a && head[1] === 0x45 && head[2] === 0xdf && head[3] === 0xa3) return true; // Matroska/WebM
  if (head[0] === 0xff && (head[1] & 0xe0) === 0xe0) return true; // MP3/ADTS frame sync
  return false;
}

Only binary signatures match. Plain text never does.

Why not just accept everything?

Because ffmpeg is more powerful than it looks. A text file can be an HLS playlist (#EXTM3U) or a concat script (ffconcat version 1.0) that points at other files or URLs. If you hand a user's text file to ffmpeg, it may read local files or fetch remote ones for them. Two cheap defences:

  1. Reject text. The signature check above never matches a playlist, because it starts with printable characters.
  2. Restrict protocols. Pass -protocol_whitelist file before -i, so even a crafted input cannot reach the network. 
await run("ffmpeg", ["-y", "-hide_banner", "-loglevel", "error", "-protocol_whitelist", "file", "-i", input, "-vn", "-map", "0:a:0", out]);

Test with real files, not just unit tests

The unit tests were green and the bug still shipped, because I never fed it a real renamed file. I now generate a matrix of real files with ffmpeg (AAC, Opus, MP3 with an ID3 tag, FLAC, WAV, HEVC MOV, VP9 WebM, and each one with the "wrong" extension), upload them to the running service and check the output. It found two more gaps (a tool that rejected audio files in a video tool) within minutes.

Takeaways

  • Decide by content, not by name. Let the real decoder be the final judge.
  • Allow-list binary signatures; never let text reach tools that interpret text (ffmpeg, ImageMagick, LibreOffice).
  • Restrict what the tool may touch (-protocol_whitelist, no network, size caps, per-IP rate limits).
  • Keep original filenames only for display, and keep Unicode letters in them (I used /[^\p{L}\p{N}._\- ]+/gu), or users with Urdu or Arabic file names get underscores.

I use this in a free converter site with audio, video, PDF and image tools: saveanyreel.com. Bug reports with the file type that failed are very welcome.

title: Do Language Models Feel the Sentiment? Investigating Emotion Vectors
description:
arXiv:2611.13744v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Emotion vectors are directions in a language model's internal representations that are associated with emotional concepts. Prior work shows that these vectors can influence model behavior, but their role in sentiment classification remains unclear. This study investigates emotion directions in Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. Eight directions extracted from GoEmotions are evaluated through sentiment probing, activation interventions, and supervised correction. Emotion-only probes achieve 88.66% and 90.70% accuracy on binary TweetEval. In exploratory matched-ablation experiments, raw emotion-space removal causes 2.39 and 1.10 percentage points more accuracy loss than matched isotropic random-subspace removal for 0.5B and 3B, respectively. All four TweetEval raw and denoised effects are significant after Holm adjustment across eight comparisons. An exploratory SST-2 extension shows smaller raw excess losses of 0.66 and 0.57 points, with no effects surviving Holm adjustment. Frozen sentiment-correction classifiers are also tested on 20,000 Amazon Polarity reviews. Emotion-based correction improves accuracy over uncorrected Qwen, but does not consistently outperform margin-only baselines. These results distinguish sentiment information available in model representations, the effects of changing those representations, and their practical value for classification. They do not establish a uniquely emotional mechanism.
