title: Your UI should tell you what's going on
description:
I opened a budget app last month to check one number, how much I had left to spend, and I could not find it. The balance was on one screen, the spending was on another, and the budget was a third screen with a tiny progress bar I had to squint at. I knew the data was in there somewhere, the app had it, it just was not showing me. I closed it and did the math in my head instead, which is the exact moment a UI has failed at its job.

I keep coming back to a line from Ben Halpern's post, ask more of your UI. The idea is simple: a UI should act like an instrument panel, showing you what is going on, live, instead of hiding the state behind taps and menus. A car dashboard does not make you open a menu to see your speed. It is just there, all the time, because the whole point of the dashboard is to tell you where you stand.

I built a little budget tracker to try the idea out, nothing fancy, just a panel that shows the four things I actually check. Balance, spent this month against the budget, the next bill coming up, and whether the data is synced. Every number updates the moment something changes, so the panel is always current. Here is the version the demo below runs, with buttons to add an expense and watch the numbers move.

Try it: a budget panel that talks back
Try it live on nayemalam.com.

the quiet UI vs the panel

The quiet version of this app is the one I opened last month. It has the same data, but it shows you almost none of it. You tap through three screens to assemble the picture yourself, and by the time you have, you have forgotten why you opened the app. The panel version puts the four numbers on one screen and keeps them current. Nothing about it is clever, and that is the point. The clever part would be hiding the numbers behind a gesture.

The pattern shows up everywhere once you start looking for it. A form that tells you the password is too short while you type, instead of after you submit. A file upload that shows progress and a real error message, instead of a spinner that just keeps spinning. A settings page that says when it last synced, instead of leaving you to wonder whether your change saved. In every case, the fix is the same: surface the state, keep it live, and let the user see it without asking.

the cost is real, and small

The objection I hear is that showing more state means more code, and more code means more bugs. That is fair, and it is also mostly wrong at this scale. The budget panel is a handful of useState calls and a progress bar. The state already exists in the app, it is the same state the quiet version hides. The work is not computing the numbers, it is deciding to render them. The extra code is a few lines of JSX, and the payoff is that the user stops doing mental math to fill in the blanks.

Where I draw the line is noise. An instrument panel is not a firehose. A car dashboard shows speed, fuel, and warnings, not the raw sensor feed. The budget panel shows four numbers, not every transaction since 2019. The test I use is whether the number changes a decision. Balance changes whether I buy something. Spent-against-budget changes whether I cook tonight. Sync status changes whether I trust the numbers at all. If a number would not change a decision, it does not earn a spot on the panel.

What I took away from building the panel is that showing state is a design choice, not a feature. The data was always there. The quiet app had it and hid it. The panel just decided the user is allowed to see it. I check the budget app more now, not because I enjoy budgeting, but because opening it answers the question in one glance instead of three taps. A UI exists to tell you what is going on, and the ones that do it well feel less like software and more like a dashboard you can trust.

Originally posted on nayemalam.com/blog.

title: DroneSegEdit: Adapting Pretrained Generative Editors for UAV Segmentation with Language-Grounded Verification
description:
arXiv:2611.13890v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent work has shown that pretrained image generators can support diverse visual tasks. Yet directly applying them to language-guided unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) segmentation exposes a key limitation: a plausible mask may correspond to the wrong instance among small and repeated objects. We call this mismatch between mask rendering and expression-level target selection the Grounding-Rendering Gap. We present DroneSegEdit, which combines RGB proposal rendering with language-grounded, proposal-constrained verification to select supported foreground while retaining rendered geometry. DroneSegEdit adapts the open-weight LongCat-Image-Edit model using task-specific LoRA and fixed color-to-label decoding. For referring segmentation, a Language-Grounded Spatial Verifier (LGSV) reads hierarchical states from the frozen multimodal large language model backbone to derive expression-conditioned spatial evidence, which is mapped back to the rendered proposal without introducing foreground outside it. On RIS-LAD, DroneSegEdit reaches a new state of the art at 52.78 mIoU, 7.16 points above the previous best. It remains competitive overall on UAVid-RIS and VDD-RIS, with its clearest class-wise gains on compact, application-relevant categories, notably vehicles and humans. A separate verifier-free experiment extends the RGB interface to full-scene parsing: a task-specific adapter jointly renders all classes from one task-level instruction without enumerating class names or palette colors.

title: Beyond Proxy Metrics: MLLMs as Human Surrogates for Explainable AI Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2611.13926v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) has expanded into a broad and impactful research area, but the fundamental question of how best to evaluate explanation techniques has proven frustratingly elusive. Methodologies typically revolve around either proxy metrics which tell us little about the utility of an explanation, or human evaluation which---while generally considered the gold standard---is expensive, difficult to scale, and challenging to reproduce. In this paper, we investigate if Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can act as surrogate human participants to automate the evaluation of XAI. To do this, we first propose a ``purpose-grounded'' evaluation framework with metrics applicable to both MLLMs and human users alike. Then, we offer some conceptual insights as to why and when we can trust these models to automate this process. Lastly, we conduct extensive empirical testing across five purpose-grounded areas such as model improvement and fourteen popular MLLMs. Results indicate that all models trend positively, but OpenAI and Qwen models generally show higher alignment compared to other variants, which would be the recommended choices in practice. We expect our insights not to replace user testing, but rather to help XAI researchers complement their current evaluation methodologies and move the field away from heavy reliance on proxy metrics for measuring explanation utility.

title: Sending GCash-Style Payment Reminders for a Small PH Reseller Shop (Node.js, No Database)
description:
Small social media resellers in the Philippines often run everything from Messenger and a spreadsheet. The thing that slips most? Following up on unpaid orders. Here's a tiny Node.js script that reads a CSV of pending orders and drafts polite reminder messages you can paste into chat. No database, no server.

The CSV 

order_id,customer,service,amount_php,created_at,paid
1042,Ana,TikTok views 5k,250,2026-11-09,no
1043,Mark,FB page likes 1k,180,2026-11-10,yes
1044,Joy,IG followers 1k,320,2026-11-08,no

The script 

import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";

const rows = readFileSync("orders.csv", "utf8").trim().split("\n").slice(1)
  .map(l => l.split(","))
  .map(([order_id, customer, service, amount_php, created_at, paid]) =>
    ({ order_id, customer, service, amount: Number(amount_php), created_at, paid }));

const daysAgo = d => Math.floor((Date.now() - new Date(d + "T00:00:00+08:00")) / 864e5);
const peso = n => "₱" + n.toLocaleString("en-PH");

for (const o of rows.filter(r => r.paid === "no")) {
  const age = daysAgo(o.created_at);
  const tone = age >= 3 ? "Just a gentle follow-up po" : "Hi po";
  console.log(`${o.customer}: ${tone}! Your order #${o.order_id} (${o.service}) is ${peso(o.amount)}. ` +
              `Let me know once sent so I can start it right away. Salamat!`);
}

Note the +08:00 offset. Philippine time is UTC+8, and getting this wrong makes "3 days ago" off by a day around midnight.

Why not auto-send?

Because platform messaging rules change and bulk automated DMs can get a page restricted. Drafting messages and sending them by hand keeps you safe and still saves 90% of the time.

Keep money in integers

If you start doing math on totals, store centavos as integers rather than floats. 250.00 becomes 25000. Fewer rounding surprises.

For the business side of running social media services for Filipino customers, this overview of SMM in the Philippines is a useful primer. BoostingPH is one PH panel with peso pricing if you need a supplier to plug into this workflow.

title: Figma vs Sketch in 2026: Which One Actually Fits Your Team?
description:
Picking between Figma and Sketch looks simple until you count everyone on your team, not just the designers.

title: ACH Return Codes Explained: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Each
description:
ACH Return Codes Explained: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Each

ACH Return Codes Explained: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Each

When an ACH transfer fails, you don't get a generic "payment declined" message. Instead, the National Automated Clearing House Association (Nacha) assigns a specific return code—a two-character alphanumeric that tells you exactly why the transfer bounced. Understanding these codes is critical for building robust payout systems that can recover gracefully or route to fallback rails.

This guide covers the most common ACH return codes, what triggers them, and the right developer response for each.

The Big Three: R01, R03, and R10

R01: Insufficient Funds

What it means: The receiver's account doesn't have enough money to cover the debit.

When it fires: During the debit entry processing phase, typically 1–2 business days after the ACH originates.

How to handle it:

  • Log the return with timestamp and amount.
  • Flag the receiver's account as temporarily insolvent.
  • Retry after 2–3 business days (funds may have arrived).
  • If it's a recurring payout (payroll, gig work), notify the receiver and pause future attempts until they confirm account status. 
if (achReturn.code === 'R01') {
  await db.updates.flagAccount({
    accountId: receiver.id,
    status: 'insufficient_funds',
    retryAfter: addDays(new Date(), 3)
  });

  await notificationService.send({
    userId: receiver.id,
    type: 'payout_failed_insufficient_funds',
    amount: achReturn.amount
  });
}

R03: No Account / Unable to Locate Account

What it means: The bank can't find an account matching the routing number and account number you provided.

When it fires: Usually during pre-debit validation, but can occur during settlement if the account was closed between submission and processing.

How to handle it:

  • This is a permanent failure—don't retry the same account.
  • Request account re-verification from the user (new routing + account number).
  • Route to an alternate rail (RTP, Visa Direct) if available and approved.
  • Log for compliance and dispute resolution. 
if (achReturn.code === 'R03') {
  await db.updates.markAccountInvalid({
    accountId: receiver.id,
    reason: 'account_not_found'
  });

  // Trigger re-verification flow
  await verificationService.requestBankDetailsUpdate(receiver.id);

  // Check if RTP is available as fallback
  if (receiver.rtpEligible) {
    return await routeToRTP(payout);
  }
}

R10: Unauthorized / Customer Initiated Reversal

What it means: The account holder (or their bank) disputes the debit and requests a reversal.

When it fires: Typically 10–60 days after the original ACH entry, often triggered by the receiver claiming they didn't authorize the transfer.

How to handle it:

  • This is a chargeback scenario. Document the original authorization (consent form, timestamp, IP).
  • Respond to the dispute through your ACH provider's chargeback process.
  • Flag the receiver's account as high-risk or suspend future payouts pending investigation.
  • If it's a one-time mistake, allow re-authorization; if it's a pattern, escalate to compliance. 
if (achReturn.code === 'R10') {
  await db.disputes.create({
    achReturnId: achReturn.id,
    amount: achReturn.amount,
    status: 'open',
    requiredAction: 'provide_proof_of_authorization'
  });

  await accountService.updateRiskProfile(receiver.id, { riskLevel: 'high' });
}

Other Common Codes: Quick Reference

Code Meaning Retry? Action
R04 Invalid routing number No Re-verify bank details
R05 Unauthorized user / account closed by institution No Request new account
R07 Authorization revoked by customer No Investigate & document
R08 Payment stopped by customer No Check receiver communication
R09 Uncollected funds Yes Retry after 3–5 days
R16 Account frozen / legal hold No Escalate to compliance
R20 Non-transaction account No Require valid checking/savings account
R29 Corporate customer advises not authorized No Verify original consent

Integration Pattern: Decode and Decide

async function handleAchReturn(returnEvent) {
  const { code, amount, receiverId, originalTraceId } = returnEvent;

  const isRet

---

The [ACH Return Codes API](https://rapidapi.com/payoutrail-ach-return-codes/api/ach-return-codes-api?utm_source=nichestream&utm_medium=devto&utm_campaign=payoutrail-ach-returns) returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.*

title: Monitoring One Channel Is Not Communication Control: Causal Evidence for Adaptive Reallocation of Joint Message--Route Codes
description:
arXiv:2611.12959v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Monitoring a visible channel can change how learned agents communicate without removing why communication is useful. We test this distinction in an end-to-end game where a sender and receiver learn a discrete protocol and route policy without communication supervision. In two independent 20-seed batches, 20/20 and 19/20 protocols form. Online partial coverage increases shadow-route share over no monitoring by .701 [.574,.826] and .575 [.412,.737], while task accuracy remains .905/.913 and signed frozen message contribution remains .592/.563. Complete coverage removes most selective migration without removing communication. Frozen interventions, including a fresh pre-outcome confirmation, show that route is semantic: joint message--route shuffling changes .668 of receiver predictions and route alone retains .388 accuracy versus .25 chance. A corrected explicit-silence cost makes 18/20 policies fully silent and lowers mean sending to .050, but its strict complete-suppression gate fails because two seeds retain communication. Failed semantic-evasion and operational gates further bound the result. The evidence supports adaptive reallocation of a joint message--route code under partial monitoring, not open-world route discovery, emergent encryption, or a universal defense.

title: RBLA+: Efficient Rank-Specific LoRA Adapter Extraction for Federated Fine-Tuning with Heterogeneous Clients
description:
arXiv:2611.12961v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Federated fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces communication and computational overhead by training and exchanging compact trainable LoRA factors. Clients may use different LoRA ranks to meet adapter communication budgets and accommodate different local adaptation needs. The server must process these differences during aggregation and construct adapters at each client's rank for local training. We distinguish pre-aggregation alignment, which handles factor dimensions and scaling conventions before aggregation and rank-specific LoRA adapter extraction, which constructs client-sized pairs from the aggregated global model. Two common approaches to rank-specific extraction are direct rank truncation and Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of the dense update. Direct prefix truncation keeps the leading columns of one aggregated factor and the corresponding rows of the other. It is cheap but can increase reconstruction error. The dense SVD approach first forms the product of aggregated LoRA factors. It then decomposes this matrix and retains the leading singular components to construct adapters at the target rank. This gives the optimal rank-constrained approximation in Frobenius norm but incurs significant computational overhead. To address this trade-off, we propose RBLA+ as an extension of RBLA. It uses established compact QR/core-SVD decomposition to minimize Frobenius error for the extracted LoRA update without forming the dense update. It also accounts for client and server scaling conventions during upload and broadcast. Across vision and language tasks, RBLA+ improves accuracy over RBLA in multiple heterogeneous settings. In CPU benchmarks with synthetic adapters, RBLA+ has lower extraction time than the dense partial-SVD baseline. RBLA+ preserves each client's prescribed adapter size and per-round communication payload.

title: Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available on Vercel
description:
Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available for builds and Vercel Functions.

This release includes:

  • HTTP/2 by default for built-in fetch (Undici 8) lets multiple requests share a connection with servers that support it. This can reduce latency when your functions call APIs or databases over HTTP.

  • Temporal API offers an alternative to Date with immutable values and built-in time zone and calendar support.

  • V8 version 14.6, the updated JavaScript engine, adds features such as Map.prototype.getOrInsert() to retrieve an existing value or insert a default when a key is missing.

Using Node.js 26

Node.js 26 is the default for all new projects.

  • Automatic upgrades: If engines.node in your existing project’s package.json allows 26, such as >=20, your Node.js builds on Vercel will use 26 on the next deployment.

  • Manual upgrades: Set engines.node to 26.x in your project's package.json and redeploy.

  • Prebuilt deployments: Use Vercel CLI version 65.8.0 or later to deploy Node.js 26 Functions.

  • HTTP/1.1 in Functions: To keep HTTP/1.1, set the VERCEL_FETCH_DISABLE_H2 environment variable to 1 and redeploy.

Minor and patch updates to Node.js 26 roll out automatically for builds and Vercel Functions.

Read the Node.js version documentation to learn more.

title: IntentTwin: Deconfounding Candidate Support and the Oracle-to-Deployment Gap in Offline Web Behavior Prediction
description:
arXiv:2611.12918v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Offline web-behavior benchmarks frequently insert the demonstrated action into a finite candidate set and then measure reranking. We show that this protocol can create a candidate-support confound: when the target is outside training support while all distractors are sampled from that support, support membership identifies the gold action without modeling behavior. We formalize this effect with support-identifiability rate (SIR), construct support-balanced candidate sets, and evaluate a target-free dual-path proposer that combines support retrieval with open-vocabulary DOM/LM proposals. On filtered OPeRA (4,282/469/992 train/dev/test steps), the original protocol has SIR 1.0000 on target-OOV rows and a support-only rule reaches 1.0000 OOV Exact@1. Support balancing reduces SIR to 0.0000; the strongest conditional reranker obtains 0.7214 overall Exact@1, 0.7988 on IV rows, and 0.5668 on OOV rows. The target-free dual-path system reaches Proposal Recall@16 0.6915 and end-to-end Exact@1 0.5212, compared with oracle conditional Exact@1 0.7450. On Mind2Web, the same audit yields SIR 0.2380 and an oracle-to-proposal gap of 0.2125. A 200-row semantic audit labels 0.7150 of exact-key OOV targets as semantically novel, 0.2450 as locator/string variation, and 0.0400 as ambiguous (Cohen's $\kappa=0.8173$). These measurements show why support composition must be controlled alongside candidate accuracy when offline results are used to reason about deployment.

title: Your SaaS Says “Saved”? Refresh the Page.
description:
A client of ours vibe-coded their product with AI tools and brought it to a demo. The forms worked, the screens looked finished, and the app said Saved after every action. During that demo it turned out the data had never been stored.

Nothing on the screen hinted at it. From the user's side it looks like this. You type a task, press Save, the task appears in the list, the input clears, and a small green "Saved" shows up under the form. Then you refresh the page and the task is gone, because the server never stored it.

The task appears with a Saved message, then disappears after a page refresh

A false success state is a screen that tells the user an action worked before the server confirmed it, or after the server refused it. This article grew out of that demo. When I review a save flow now, I don't take the green message as proof. I create the record through the UI, reload the page, read the record back through the authenticated API, try the same ID as a different user, and then break the request on purpose to see what the UI says.

To show all four, I built a small React app with an Express API, SQLite and Playwright, then broke it in three different ways. The results surprised me a little. A server that answered 201 and wrote nothing passed the test for failed saves, and a server that leaked tasks between users passed both persistence tests. Every bug got past at least one check, so a single test was never enough.

People write these bugs by hand too. With AI-built features the risk is higher, because an agent can produce a whole flow in minutes and it's easy to accept code you haven't read line by line.

The handler that lies

This is the broken path in the React app. It runs inside the form's submit handler.

setTasks((rows) => [...rows, { id: crypto.randomUUID(), title }]);
setStatus("Saved");
setTitle("");

fetch("/api/tasks", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify({ title }),
}).catch(() => {});

React adds the row right away, the API answers 503 and writes nothing, and the UI never looks at the answer.

Two things go wrong here. Saved appears before the request finishes, and the code never checks the HTTP status. As MDN explains, fetch() resolves on a 503 the same way it resolves on a 200, so the .catch() fires only for network errors and the 503 goes by unnoticed.

Showing a pending task right away is a fair design choice. The trouble starts when that pending row gets the word Saved, because at that moment the app is confirming something it never checked.

For this small app I picked a simpler contract. The text stays in the input while the request is in flight, the row appears after the server confirms the write, and if confirmation fails, the input keeps the text and an error message shows up.

Give every test its own account

The tests use cookie sessions. A page fixture creates a fresh user for each test and deletes that user's records afterwards. The /__test/* endpoints exist only when TEST_MODE=1 is set and skip real login, so they have no place in a deployed app. In your own project, use seeded test accounts and your real login flow.

import { test as base, expect, Page } from "@playwright/test";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const test = base.extend({
  page: async ({ page }, use) => {
    await page.request.post("/__test/session");
    await use(page);
    await page.request.delete("/__test/session");
  },
});

I create a new user per test because a new browser context gives you fresh cookies and storage, and that's all it gives you. Two tests logged in as the same user still write to the same rows on the server. Playwright's authentication guide makes the same point and recommends separate accounts for tests that change server state.

The shared save function starts listening for the POST response before it clicks, so a fast reply can't slip past it.

async function saveTask(page: Page, title: string) {
  await page.goto("/tasks");
  await page.getByLabel("Task name").fill(title);
  const pending = page.waitForResponse(
    (r) =>
      new URL(r.url()).pathname === "/api/tasks" &&
      r.request().method() === "POST",
  );
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Save", exact: true }).click();
  const response = await pending;
  await expect(page.getByRole("status")).toHaveText("Saved");
  return response;
}

Test 1. Reload the page 

test("saved task survives reload", async ({ page }) => {
  const title = `Release check ${randomUUID()}`;
  await saveTask(page, title);
  await expect(page.getByRole("list", { name: "Tasks" })).toContainText(title);
  await page.reload();
  await expect(page.getByRole("list", { name: "Tasks" })).toContainText(title);
});

With the broken handler, the first assertion passes because the task lives in React state. After the reload the app asks the API for the list, the API returns what it stored, and the task isn't there. This is the same thing the client saw in the demo, caught by a test in a few seconds.

A passing reload test proves less than it seems. An app can rebuild its list from localStorage, IndexedDB, a service worker or an HTTP cache, and then the task survives a refresh with no database row behind it. In this demo the list always comes from the API, responses send Cache-Control: no-store, and the Playwright config blocks service workers. Even so, I want to hear from the server itself.

Test 2. Read the record back through the API

The POST response carries the new record's ID. I use it for a separate authenticated GET and compare the fields I meant to save.

test("saved task is readable through the authenticated API", async ({
  page,
}) => {
  const title = `API check ${randomUUID()}`;
  const write = await saveTask(page, title);
  expect(write.status()).toBe(201);
  const created = await write.json();
  const read = await page.request.get(`/api/tasks/${created.id}`);
  expect(read.status()).toBe(200);
  expect(await read.json()).toEqual({ id: created.id, title });
});

page.request shares cookies with the browser context (see APIRequestContext), so this GET runs as the same user who filled in the form. If your app uses bearer tokens, set the Authorization header yourself. There's no mocked response anywhere in the persistence tests, they talk to the real local API.

The fake201 server mode shows why this test exists. It answers 201 with a believable ID and skips the insert. The status assertion passes, the follow-up GET returns 404, and the test fails.

In this app the GET reads from SQLite. In your architecture it might read a cache or a replica, so check where the read path goes before you call this a persistence test. Async APIs need a different assertion too. A 202 says the server accepted the work and nothing more, so follow the operation ID and poll for the completed state with a timeout.

Test 3. Request the same ID as another user

A record can be saved perfectly and still be readable by the wrong person. This test seeds a private task, checks that its owner can read it, then logs in a second user in a separate browser context and asks for that task by its ID.


test("another user cannot read a known task ID", async ({ page, browser }) => {
  const seed = await page.request.post("/__test/seed", {
    data: { title: `Private ${randomUUID()}` },
  });
  const task = await seed.json();
  expect((await page.request.get(`/api/tasks/${task.id}`)).status()).toBe(200);
  const outsider = await browser.newContext({
    baseURL: "http://127.0.0.1:4173",
  });
  try {
    await outsider.request.post("/__test/session");
    const forbidden = await outsider.request.get(`/api/tasks/${task.id}`);
    expect(forbidden.status()).toBe(404);
    const list = await outsider.request.get("/api/tasks");
    expect(await list.json()).toEqual([]);
  } finally {
    await outsider.request.delete("/__test/session");
    await outsider.close();
  }
});

This API answers 404 for a task the caller doesn't own. If your contract says 403, assert 403. A redirect to the login page, a 500, or a loose !response.ok() check would let a real problem pass here. The owner read at the start is a positive control, because if the task was never created, a 404 for the second user would prove nothing.

The fixed lookup filters by both the ID and the logged-in owner, and req.user comes from the server's session store, never from the request body.

const task = db
  .prepare("SELECT id, title FROM tasks WHERE id = ? AND owner = ?")
  .get(req.params.id, req.user);

A workspace product has real roles, and a teammate may be allowed to see the record. There I'd test someone from another tenant, a read-only member, a member who was removed, and the write endpoints as well as the reads.

Test 4. Make the failed save visible

This one checks what the user sees when the save fails. It intercepts only the POST, answers with a controlled 503, and lets the GET go through to the real server.


test("rejected save keeps the draft and never says Saved", async ({ page }) => {
  const title = `Rejected ${randomUUID()}`;
  await page.route("**/api/tasks", async (route) => {
    if (route.request().method() === "POST")
      await route.fulfill({
        status: 503,
        contentType: "application/json",
        body: '{"error":"Write rejected"}',
      });
    else await route.continue();
  });
  await page.goto("/tasks");
  await page.getByLabel("Task name").fill(title);
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Save", exact: true }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole("alert")).toHaveText(
    "Save was not confirmed. Your draft is still here.",
  );
  await expect(page.getByRole("status")).toBeEmpty();
  await expect(page.getByLabel("Task name")).toHaveValue(title);
  await expect(page.getByRole("list", { name: "Tasks" })).not.toContainText(
    title,
  );
});

This mock tests the frontend's error handling and tells you nothing about the database, so I keep it apart from the real-server tests.

The fixed handler checks the status before it adds the row or clears the draft.

setSaving(true);
setError("");
setStatus("");

try {
  const response = await fetch("/api/tasks", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ title }),
  });

  if (!response.ok) throw Error("Save was not confirmed.");

  const task = await response.json();
  setTasks((rows) => [...rows, task]);
  setTitle("");
  setStatus("Saved");
} catch {
  setError("Save was not confirmed. Your draft is still here.");
} finally {
  setSaving(false);
}

A rejected save and a lost response are two different situations. The network can drop after the server has already committed the write, and then the client has no way of knowing what happened. So the message says the save wasn't confirmed, which is true in both cases. Keeping the draft is safe, and resending it blindly can create a duplicate, so before I add automatic retries to a real create flow, I give each operation a stable idempotency key and deduplicate on the server.

What the tests caught

I ran the same five tests against all four modes in Chromium, with two workers and retries turned off. The fifth test, not shown above, checks that an anonymous request can't list tasks.

Playwright HTML report with the failed reload test in broken mode

Run it yourself

The companion project has the React app, the server, the tests, the Playwright config and a lockfile. I tested it on Node 24, React 19.2.0 and Playwright 1.56.1. From the saved-demo folder on Linux or macOS, these commands run the fixed version.

npm ci
npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
npm test

To see the bugs, run each mode on its own. These runs are supposed to exit with failures.

MODE=broken npm test
MODE=fake201 npm test
MODE=leaky npm test

In CI, give every job a throwaway database and keep test auth state out of git. The project has a CI workflow for the fixed mode, and the numbers in the table above come from my local run.

Where I'd start in a bigger app

In a real product I wouldn't try to test every form at once. I'd pick the save flow where a lost record costs the most and add one real-server create-and-read test, one access test with a specific expected status, and one controlled failure test.

If an AI agent built the feature, you can hand it this prompt and then review the tests it writes. Replace the parts in square brackets with your own names.

Write Playwright tests for the [create task] flow in this app.

1. Create a [task] through the UI, reload the page, and assert it is still in the [Tasks] list.
2. Take the ID from the POST response, GET [/api/tasks/:id] with the same session, and assert status 200 and the saved fields.
3. Log in a second user in a new browser context, request the same ID, and assert [404].
4. Make the POST return 503 with page.route, then assert that "Saved" never appears, the draft stays in the input, and an error is shown.

Give every test its own user account. Do not mock the API in tests 1 to 3.

Four green tests don't make an app production-ready. They do show whether one specific Saved message holds up after a reload, an API read, a second user and a failed request. Before your next demo, save one record and read it back as the person who will need it tomorrow.

What's the strangest fake success you've seen in an AI-built app? Tell me in the comments.

Frequently asked questions

Why does a task disappear after refreshing an AI-built app?

The frontend may have updated local state even though the write failed, or the reload may query a different account or data source. Look at the POST response and the GET that follows it. A disappearing record on its own doesn't tell you which cause you have.

How do I test database persistence with Playwright?

Create the record through the UI, then read it back by ID through an authenticated API request and compare the stored fields. Confirm that the endpoint reads the database you care about, since a refresh test can pass on browser-stored data.

How do I test data isolation between SaaS accounts?

Create a record for its owner and confirm the owner can read it. Then log in a second user in a separate browser context, request the same ID, and assert the documented denial status. Extend the test to write endpoints and to the tenant roles your product has.

Can I mock API calls in a persistence test?

Mock a failed response when you test how the UI reacts to failure. Use the real write and read endpoints when you check saved state, because a mocked create response passes even when the backend is completely broken.

title: What Is React? Explained Simply for Beginners
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

React is a free JavaScript library for building user interfaces, the parts of a website or app that people actually see and click. Instead of writing one giant page of code, you build small reusable pieces called components, like buttons, cards, menus and forms, and React puts them together on the screen. You describe what the screen should look like, and React updates it automatically when your data changes. That simple idea is why React powers so many modern websites, from small blogs to huge social networks.

A Short History: Where Did React Come From?

React was created by Meta, the company behind Facebook and Instagram. Engineers there were struggling to keep a fast-growing interface in sync, and updating everything by hand was slow and full of bugs. React was released in 2013, and other developers quickly adopted it.

Today React is open source, so anyone can use it for free. A huge community builds tools and tutorials around it, so when you get stuck, someone has almost certainly solved the same problem before.

The Big Idea: Components

Think of a page like Lego bricks. A header is one brick, a product card another, a footer another. In React, each brick is a component: a small JavaScript function that returns markup for that piece.

Components are reusable. Build a Button once and use it ten times with different text and colours. Build a ProductCard once and show fifty products without copying fifty blocks of HTML. Change the component in one place, and every copy updates.

If this idea is new to you, our guide to React components, props and state walks through it slowly with more examples, so keep that open in another tab while you practise.

Your First React Component

Here is a tiny but complete React component. It shows a greeting and a button that counts how many times you click it:

import { useState } from 'react';

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  return (
    <div>
      <h2>Hello from React!</h2>
      <p>You clicked {count} times.</p>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>
        Click me
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

export default Counter;

The function returns markup that looks like HTML. The {count} part inserts a JavaScript value into that markup. When you click the button, setCount changes the value, and React redraws just that piece with the new number. You never wrote code to find and rewrite the paragraph by hand.

That strange HTML-inside-JavaScript syntax has a name: JSX. JSX lets you write markup inside your JavaScript files, which feels odd for about a day and then feels completely natural. Under the hood, tools convert JSX into regular JavaScript before the browser runs it.

The official React documentation (react.dev) — the Quick Start page creates a first component in a few lines.

Props and State: Passing Data and Remembering Things

Two words you will hear every day in React are props and state. Props are inputs passed from a parent component to a child, like passing ingredients to a chef. A ProductCard might receive a name, a price and an image as props, and simply display them. Props flow one way, from parent to child, which makes data easy to follow.

State is data a component remembers and can change: whether a menu is open, what a user typed, or the click count above. When state changes, React re-renders the component. Props are given to a component; state is owned by it.

The best way to learn both is by building. The official tutorial at react.dev/learn teaches components, props and state step by step with interactive examples you can edit in the browser, so you see results instantly without installing anything.

Declarative UI: Describe the Result, Not the Steps

React uses a declarative style. Declarative means you describe what the interface should look like for a given state, instead of listing every step to change it. Compare these two approaches for a loading spinner. In plain JavaScript you might write: find the spinner element, show it, find the button, disable it, and later remember to reverse all of that. In React you write something like: if loading is true, show the spinner and disable the button.

Your code becomes a description of the screen at any moment, rather than a diary of changes. That makes interfaces easier to predict and debug: when something looks wrong, you check the state, because the screen is simply a reflection of it.

What Is the Virtual DOM?

You will often hear that React is fast because of the virtual DOM. Here is the plain version. The DOM is the browser's live model of your page. Changing it directly, again and again, can be slow. React keeps a lightweight copy of the page structure in memory, called the virtual DOM.

When state changes, React updates this copy, compares it with the previous copy, and applies only the smallest real changes to the actual page. If one price on a page of fifty products changes, React updates that one price instead of rebuilding the whole list.

React vs Plain JavaScript

React is still JavaScript, so why not skip it? For tiny pages, plain JavaScript is perfectly fine. As an app grows, though, keeping the screen and the data in sync by hand becomes painful. This table sums up the difference:

Feature Plain JavaScript React
Building the UI You create and update elements manually You build reusable components
Updating the screen You find elements and change them yourself React updates the screen when state changes
Reusing code Copy and paste, or custom functions Components are reused by design
Code organisation Can get messy in large apps Each component keeps its markup and logic together
Learning curve Nothing extra to learn Needs JSX, props, state and hooks
Best for Small pages and simple effects Interactive apps with lots of changing data

Neither side wins everywhere. React earns its place when an interface has many moving parts that depend on shared, changing data.

Where Is React Used?

React runs parts of Facebook, Instagram and countless dashboards, shops and streaming sites. Companies like it because it is fast, well supported and easy to hire for.

React also reaches beyond the browser. React Native uses the same component ideas to build real mobile apps for Android and iOS, so learning React opens a door to app development too. Frameworks such as Next.js build on top of React, adding routing, server rendering and better search engine support for public websites. You can explore what the library offers on the homepage at react.dev, which links to the docs, the blog and the community resources.

Who Should Learn React, and What Comes First?

Learn React if you want to build modern web apps, apply for front-end jobs, or create projects like dashboards and online stores. Job listings ask for React constantly.

But do not start with React on day one. First learn HTML, CSS and JavaScript, especially functions, arrays, objects and methods like map and filter. Weak JavaScript makes React feel twice as hard. Our step-by-step beginner roadmap for learning React lays out the order to follow, week by week.

A good first project is a to-do list, a weather app using a free API, or a small shop page with a working cart. Keep projects small and finish them. Finishing beats perfect, every single time.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is React a language or a framework?

React is a JavaScript library, not a language and, strictly speaking, not a full framework. It focuses on the user interface. You add other tools for routing, data fetching and styling as your app needs them, or use a framework like Next.js that bundles those choices for you.

Is React hard for beginners?

React is beginner-friendly if your JavaScript basics are ready. JSX and state take a few days to feel normal. Most confusion comes from shaky JavaScript, not from React itself, so strengthen functions, arrays and objects first and React will click much faster.

Is React free to use?

Yes. React is completely free and open source under the MIT licence. You can use it for personal projects, client work and commercial products without paying anything, and the official documentation and community resources are free as well.

Can I build mobile apps with React?

Yes, through React Native. It uses React components and JavaScript to build genuine Android and iOS apps from one codebase. The concepts you learn for the web, like components, props and state, transfer directly, which makes it a popular next step after web React.

Conclusion

React is a JavaScript library for building interfaces from small, reusable components. You describe what the screen should look like, keep changing data in state, pass data down with props, and let React update the page efficiently for you. Learn HTML, CSS and JavaScript first, then build tiny projects one at a time. Start small today, and the components will soon start making sense.

title: Kova: A Macro-Free PostgreSQL & SQLite ORM for Rust (Flat AST Types, Native Binary JSONB & FTS5)
description:
Over the past few months, I’ve been building Kova, a relational query builder and ORM for Rust targeting PostgreSQL and SQLite.

When working with databases in Rust, we usually have to pick between three compromises:

  1. Heavy runtime abstractions (ActiveModel / object graphs) that hide SQL behind session trackers and invite N+1 queries.
  2. Deeply nested generic tuple trees where every joined table and selected column is encoded into the return type, great until a 5-table join produces 200 lines of compiler errors and explodes compile times.
  3. Procedural query macros, which require a live database or offline schema cache just to run cargo check, and quickly turn into string stitching when you need dynamic filters.

I wanted something closer to how we actually write Rust and SQL: if you know SQL, you already know Kova.

  • Macro-free queries & zero trait imports: Apart from #[derive(Model)] (or FromRow, Cte) on your structs, there are no query macros and no use kova::prelude::*. Every operator lives as an inherent method on columns and AST nodes.
  • Flat, constant-width typestate: Kova checks SQL validity at the method call boundary and immediately erases phantom type markers (EraseX) inside the AST. Query builders have a fixed generic width, meaning fast compile times and readable error messages (powered by #[diagnostic::on_unimplemented]).

edvong / kova

A macro-free, modern PostgreSQL and SQLite ORM for Rust with native binary JSONB and FTS5

Kova

In production, the traditional ORM is an architectural lie. It turns domain logic into an unreadable mess far worse than raw SQL, while choking the database with implicit queries and lock contention.

Industry veterans blame the object-relational impedance mismatch; modern developers claim Rust’s strictness makes ORMs impossible. Both excuses are an intellectual cop-out. Mapping flat rows to native structs has zero inherent friction. Rust’s compiler didn't create these problems—it simply exposed the rot. The true culprit is a data layer built on three bankrupt design dogmas:

1. The "Object Graph" Delusion Mainstream ORMs peddle a fantasy: that you can pretend the relational database doesn't exist, treat physical tables as a network of in-memory pointers, and hot-swap database engines at runtime behind a single watered-down dialect. Sustaining that illusion requires bloating the framework with lazy loading, session caches, units of work, and dirty checking. Half a century of battle-tested relational…

View on GitHub

Here is a quick tour of the four core design ideas behind Kova.

1. Macro-Free Query DSL & Zero prelude::* Imports

Let’s start with a basic schema (User and Order). You only import the structs and SQL functions you actually use, no wildcard trait imports needed.

use kova::{Model, Options, Result};
use kova::dsl::func::{Count, Sum, Wildcard};

#[derive(Model)]
pub struct User {
    #[kova(auto)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub name: String,
    pub bio: Option<String>,
    pub balance: f64,
    pub is_active: bool,
}

#[derive(Model)]
pub struct Order {
    #[kova(auto)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub user_id: i32,
    pub amount: f64,
    pub is_active: bool,
}

async fn run_queries() -> Result<()> {
    let client = Options::from("host=127.0.0.1 user=postgres dbname=app")
        .max_size(16)
        .build()?;

    // 1. Batch insert & RETURNING
    // Empty slices short-circuit safely; large slices exceeding wire limits
    // (PG: 65,535 / SQLite: 32,766 params) are automatically chunked.
    let new_users = [
        User { id: 0, name: "Alice".into(), bio: Some("Architect".into()), balance: 1000.0, is_active: true },
        User { id: 0, name: "Bob".into(), bio: None, balance: 200.0, is_active: true },
    ];
    let ids = client
        .insert(&new_users[..])
        .returning(User::id)
        .execute_in::<i32>()
        .await?;

    // 2. Ergonomic filtering with "&", "|", "!"
    // `User::bio` is `Option<String>`, yet accepts `&str` directly.
    // `User::balance` is `f64`, yet accepts `i16` via lossless widening.
    let active_users: Vec<User> = client
        .select::<User>()
        .filter(User::is_active.eq(true) & User::bio.eq("Architect") & User::balance.ge(100_i16))
        .load()
        .await?;

    // 3. Joins, aggregations, and positional tuple extraction
    let stats = client
        .select::<User>()
        .inner_join::<Order>(Order::user_id.eq(User::id))
        .columns((User::id, User::name, Sum(Order::amount), Count(Wildcard)))
        .filter(User::is_active.eq(true) & !User::name.like("%bot%"))
        .group_by((User::id, User::name))
        .having(Sum(Order::amount).gt(50.0))
        .order_by(Sum(Order::amount).desc())
        .limit(10)
        .load_in::<(i32, String, f64, i64)>()
        .await?;

    Ok(())
}

At the same time, Kova’s fixed-width typestate machine and capability traits catch invalid SQL at compile time without nested generic types:

// ❌ Compile error: UPDATE is in `Unset` state without `.set()`; `.execute()` doesn't exist yet.
client.update::<User>().filter(User::id.eq(1)).execute().await;

// ❌ Compile error: `on_conflict` requires `.do_nothing()` or `.update(...)` before executing.
client.insert(&new_users[0]).on_conflict(User::id).execute().await;

// ❌ Compile error: Aggregate functions do not implement `CanGroup`.
client.select::<User>().group_by(Sum(Order::amount));

// ❌ Compile error: Non-nullable `User::name` rejects `Option`, preventing null pollution.
client.select::<User>().filter(User::name.eq(Some("Alice")));

// ❌ Compile error: Lossy narrowing from `i64` to `i32` is blocked.
client.select::<User>().filter(User::id.eq(100_i64));

2. Single-Query Nested Views via Native Binary JSONB

A common reason people reach for heavy ORMs is to load nested data, for example, fetching a Post along with its Author and a Vec<CommentDto>, where each comment also includes its commenter.

Instead of firing $N+1$ queries or trying to fold flat LEFT JOIN rows in memory, Kova leans on the database's native JSON/JSONB aggregation. The database builds the tree in C, and Kova deserializes it in a single query and a single round-trip:

use kova::{FromRow, Model};
use serde::Deserialize;

#[derive(FromRow)]
pub struct PostView {
    pub id: i32,
    pub title: String,
    pub content: String,
    pub author: Author,
    pub comments: Vec<CommentDto>,
}

#[derive(Deserialize, FromRow)]
pub struct CommentDto {
    pub id: i32,
    pub content: String,
    pub commenter: Author,
}

#[derive(Deserialize)]
pub struct Author {
    pub id: i32,
    pub name: String,
}

On PostgreSQL, Kova uses JsonbBuildObject and JsonbAgg (automatically wrapping jsonb_agg in coalesce(..., '[]'::jsonb) so posts with zero comments decode cleanly into vec![] instead of failing on SQL NULL):

use kova::dsl::func::{JsonbAgg, JsonbBuildObject};
use kova::query::Select;

let views = pg_client
    .select::<Post>()
    .columns((
        Post::id,
        Post::title,
        Post::content,
        JsonbBuildObject((User::id, User::name)).alias(PostView::author),
        Select::from::<Comment>()
            .columns(JsonbAgg(JsonbBuildObject((
                Comment::id,
                Comment::content,
                JsonbBuildObject((User::id, User::name)).alias(CommentDto::commenter),
            ))))
            .inner_join::<User>(Comment::user_id.eq(User::id))
            .filter(Comment::post_id.eq(Post::id))
            .alias(PostView::comments),
    ))
    .inner_join::<User>(Post::author_id.eq(User::id))
    .load_as::<PostView>()
    .await?;

On SQLite (3.45+), you can assemble payloads using binary JsonbObject and JsonbGroupArray, converting to text via Json(...) only at the outer projection edge:

use kova::dsl::func::{Json, JsonObject, JsonbGroupArray, JsonbObject};
use kova::query::Select;

let views = sqlite_client
    .select::<Post>()
    .columns((
        Post::id,
        Post::title,
        Post::content,
        Json(JsonbObject((User::id, User::name))).alias(PostView::author),
        Select::from::<Comment>()
            .columns(Json(JsonbGroupArray(JsonbObject((
                Comment::id,
                Comment::content,
                JsonObject((User::id, User::name)).alias(CommentDto::commenter),
            )))))
            .inner_join::<User>(Comment::user_id.eq(User::id))
            .filter(Comment::post_id.eq(Post::id))
            .alias(PostView::comments),
    ))
    .inner_join::<User>(Post::author_id.eq(User::id))
    .load_as::<PostView>()?;

3. Respecting Physical Boundaries: Async PostgreSQL, Sync SQLite

Many libraries try to unify all databases behind an async trait. That makes sense for PostgreSQL, which communicates over a network socket, yielding the task while waiting on TCP I/O is exactly what async/await is for.

SQLite, however, is an in-process C library reading memory pages or local disk directly on the calling thread, often finishing in microseconds. Wrapping SQLite in an async interface means boxing closures, shipping them across threads via spawn_blocking, and waking an executor, overhead that often takes longer than the query itself.

Kova respects the physical boundary of each engine:

  • PostgreSQL (features = ["rustls"]) is natively async, backed by tokio-postgres, deadpool-postgres, and automatic per-connection prepared statement caching (prepare_typed_cached).
  • SQLite (features = ["sqlite"]) is natively synchronous, backed by rusqlite, statement caching (prepare_cached), zero-copy ValueRef slice borrowing, and a lightweight built-in LIFO connection pool that opens connections outside the mutex lock.

Aside from .await, the query DSL is identical across both engines, while each engine exposes its own native superpowers, like PostgreSQL's JSONB operator chains (->, ->>, @>, ?|), 1D arrays, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, and set-returning functions (Unnest, GenerateSeries), or SQLite's FTS5 full-text search with bm25(), highlight(), and snippet():

// SQLite FTS5 full-text search with BM25 scoring & contextual snippets
let hits = sqlite_client
    .select::<Post>()
    .columns((
        Post::title,
        Post::content.highlight(1, "<b>", "</b>"),
        Post::content.snippet(1, "[", "]", "...", 10),
    ))
    .filter(Post::content.matches("Rust AND SQL"))
    .order_by(Post::content.bm25().weights([10.0, 2.5]).asc())
    .load_in::<(String, String, String)>()?;

4. Solving Cargo Workspace Orphan Rules with Codec<X>

If you've ever built a multi-crate Rust workspace, you've probably wanted a pure models crate shared across services, containing types like uuid::Uuid, url::Url, chrono::DateTime<Utc>, or custom domain structs like Decimal and ProductSpec.

With traditional ORMs, Rust's Orphan Rules (E0117) get in the way: you can't implement the ORM's Encode/Decode traits for Uuid in your service crate because both the trait and the type are foreign. You're forced to either rely on hardcoded feature flags inside the ORM crate, or wrap every field in a DbUuid(Uuid) newtype inside your models crate.

Kova solves this by parameterizing its codec and capability traits over a context type X:

// 1. In your standalone `models` crate:
// Zero database driver dependencies, zero newtype wrappers.
#[derive(Model)]
pub struct Product {
    pub id: Uuid,
    pub price: Decimal,
    pub vendor_url: Url,
    pub specs: ProductSpec,
    pub created_at: DateTime<Utc>,
}

#[derive(Model)] generates an implementation generic over X. Then, in your downstream service crate, you define a local marker pub struct AppCodec;. Because AppCodec is local to your crate, you can implement zero-copy codecs, SQL capabilities (CanMath, CanString, CanPgJsonb), and cross-type compatibility rules for any external or domain type:

// 2. In your downstream `app-service` crate:
pub struct AppCodec;

impl<'a, 'b: 'a> Encode<'a, AppCodec> for &'b Uuid {
    fn encode(self) -> Result<Value<'a>> {
        // Zero-copy 16-byte slice borrow directly from Uuid
        Ok(Value::Blob(Cow::Borrowed(self.as_bytes())))
    }
}
// (+ Encode for Uuid, Decode for Uuid, and `decode_column!(AppCodec, Uuid, ...);`)

// Grant SQL capabilities & cross-type parameter rules under AppCodec:
impl CanMath<AppCodec> for Decimal {}
impl Compatible<Static<Decimal>, AppCodec> for Static<i64> {}

impl CanString<AppCodec> for Url {}
impl<'a> Compatible<Static<Url>, AppCodec> for Static<&'a str> {}

impl CanPgJsonb<AppCodec> for ProductSpec {}

Bind AppCodec to your client (a zero-cost phantom marker swap), and your custom types behave just like built-in primitives:

let client = base_client.codec::<AppCodec>();

client
    .update::<Product>()
    .set((
        Product::price.increment(500_i64),            // Increment Decimal directly by i64
        Product::vendor_url.set("https://apple.com"), // Pass &str directly to a Url column
        Product::specs.set(&new_specs),               // Write ProductSpec as JSONB
    ))
    .filter(
        Product::id.eq(&target_uuid)                  // Zero-copy 16-byte slice bind
            & Product::vendor_url.ilike("https://%")  // Call ILIKE directly on a Url column
            & Product::specs.json_path_text("warranty").eq("2_years")
    )
    .execute()
    .await?;

Explore More on GitHub

This post only scratches the surface. If you're curious about:

  • Compile-time TypeId table tags (.tag::<Buyer>()) for self-joins and correlated subqueries without string aliases,
  • Window functions (OVER, PARTITION BY, Lag/Lead, frame bounds) and CTEs (#[derive(Cte)]),
  • Closure-driven transactions with Higher-Rank Trait Bounds (HRTBs) that statically prevent transaction handles from escaping,
  • Or the deeper architectural trade-offs behind EraseX and tuple polymorphism,

check out the full documentation and test suite in the repository:

edvong / kova

A macro-free, modern PostgreSQL and SQLite ORM for Rust with native binary JSONB and FTS5

Kova

In production, the traditional ORM is an architectural lie. It turns domain logic into an unreadable mess far worse than raw SQL, while choking the database with implicit queries and lock contention.

Industry veterans blame the object-relational impedance mismatch; modern developers claim Rust’s strictness makes ORMs impossible. Both excuses are an intellectual cop-out. Mapping flat rows to native structs has zero inherent friction. Rust’s compiler didn't create these problems—it simply exposed the rot. The true culprit is a data layer built on three bankrupt design dogmas:

1. The "Object Graph" Delusion Mainstream ORMs peddle a fantasy: that you can pretend the relational database doesn't exist, treat physical tables as a network of in-memory pointers, and hot-swap database engines at runtime behind a single watered-down dialect. Sustaining that illusion requires bloating the framework with lazy loading, session caches, units of work, and dirty checking. Half a century of battle-tested relational…

title: When Covariance Is Not Enough: Kernel-Based Regularization for Single-Cell Counterfactuals
description:
arXiv:2611.13748v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Counterfactual editing of single cells, predicting how an observed cell would look had one factor been different, enables in-silico screening where experiments are infeasible, but is useful only if the edit is faithful to the individual and not merely to the condition. Concept bottleneck generative models make the effects of interventions interpretable by decomposing a cell's representation into known and unknown factors. Previous work uses a linear cross-covariance penalty to disentangle known and unknown dimensions. We demonstrate that this first-order criterion does not fully separate information when non-linear interactions are present. We first demonstrate the inadequacy of linear cross-factor penalization with simulation experiments with controlled edits and known non-linear covariate effects. We then demonstrate that adding a nonlinear kernel criterion, the normalized Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion, is able to recover the true intervention effects on simulation data. Finally, we apply the non-linear concept bottleneck model to a complex single-cell RNA-seq dataset and find that it improves the ability to generate counterfactual expression profiles of cells under different tissue environments.
