title: CroCoMAE: Cross-modal self-supervised collaborative representation learning for SAR-optical remote sensing data
description:
arXiv:2611.14124v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Remote sensing increasingly captures the Earth's surface through complementary sensors such as SAR and optical, yet ground-truth annotations remain scarce, limiting supervised approaches. Self-supervised learning (SSL) addresses the label scarcity, and cross-modal SSL further exploits the complementarity between co-located sensors, but existing cross-modal frameworks align modalities mostly through global image-level representations or treat them as largely redundant, leaving their fine-grained complementary structure underexploited. We propose CroCoMAE, a cross-modal SSL framework for SAR-optical remote sensing that unifies contrastive learning and masked image modeling within a ViT-based architecture, operating at two complementary levels. At the image level, an intra-modality contrastive loss on the class token yields globally discriminative, augmentation-invariant representations. At the patch level, masked image modeling drives fine-grained per-modality representations, while a cross-modal contrastive objective aligns a shared subspace across SAR and optical patch tokens, leaving the complementary subspace unconstrained to retain modality-specific information. On two SAR-optical benchmarks covering scene classification and semantic segmentation, CroCoMAE improves over uni-modal SSL baselines and outperforms state-of-the-art cross-modal frameworks in most configurations, with gains in both single-modality and multi-modal evaluation across varying label regimes and the largest improvements on semantic segmentation.

title: What If Your AI App Didn’t Need All Those Services?
description:
Originally published on Harper. I’m Senior Manager of GTM at Harper.

The first generation of AI applications has largely been built by adding systems. Start with an application and a database, then add an LLM. Add a vector database for semantic retrieval, an embedding service to populate it, a search engine for exact retrieval, a cache to control latency and cost, and an agent framework to coordinate everything. Background jobs, queues, schedulers, and observability often follow.

Each of those technologies may be excellent at what it does. The architectural problem is what happens between them. Every boundary introduces another network call, another credential, another deployment, another place for state to become inconsistent, and another system a team has to understand and operate.

As AI moves from experimentation into production applications, that complexity matters more. Intelligent applications increasingly need data, search, business logic, models, permissions, and application state within the same interaction. When each capability lives in a different system, even a relatively simple request can become a distributed-systems problem.

There is another way to think about the AI stack: instead of adding more infrastructure around the application, move more of those capabilities into the application runtime itself.

A common assembled AI stack

The individual technologies may all be excellent. The architectural cost comes from everything between them: network calls, credentials, duplicated state, synchronization, deployments, and operational ownership.

AI applications are becoming a loop

Strip away the terminology and many AI applications perform some version of the same process: find the right information, understand what it means, decide what should happen, take an action, and learn from the result.

A support application might retrieve account history and relevant documentation, interpret what a customer is asking, classify the request, trigger the appropriate workflow, and record the outcome. A commerce application might retrieve products and customer context, understand shopper intent, decide which experience to present, respond, and use the result to improve what happens next.

Today, those steps are often distributed across different technologies. Full-text search finds exact words. Vector search retrieves information based on semantic similarity. A model interprets the request. An orchestration framework determines which tools to call. Application code applies the business rules, while databases and caches maintain the state required throughout the process.

The result works, but the application spends a surprising amount of its time and money (infrastructure) moving context between systems.

What if more of that happened inside the runtime?

Harper has always approached application architecture from the opposite direction. Instead of treating the database, application server, cache, messaging layer, and APIs as separate systems by default, Harper brings those capabilities into a single process on a multi-threaded unified runtime.

Over the last several releases, that same architectural philosophy has increasingly extended into AI. This is the more important story behind Harper 5.0 through 5.3. The individual features matter, but together they point toward a different model for building AI-enabled applications.

The goal is not to create another AI framework or to replace the models developers already want to use. It is to reduce the amount of infrastructure required around those models.

The AI application on Harper

The model can still live elsewhere. What changes is everything around it. Retrieval, state, application logic, permissions, decisions, and orchestration can operate within the same runtime.

That distinction is important. The argument is not that every model should somehow run inside Harper. The opportunity is to collapse much of the infrastructure surrounding the model, so the application can reach its data, retrieval capabilities, business logic, and AI services without traversing a long chain of systems.

The pieces have been coming together

This direction did not appear suddenly in Harper 5.3. The architecture has been developing over several releases.

Harper 5.0 established much of the foundation. Harper became fully open source at the core, expanded its storage capabilities, and continued the move toward a runtime where data and application logic can operate together. For AI applications, that smaller surface is significant because both developers and agents have fewer infrastructure boundaries to understand.

Harper 5.1 made AI a direct capability of the runtime. Applications gained a common interface for generating text and embeddings across model providers. Embeddings could be generated automatically as data was written. Harper added a built-in MCP server so AI clients could discover and invoke application operations directly, and model-driven applications could execute tool-calling loops without introducing another orchestration service solely to connect those pieces.

Harper 5.2 focused heavily on making these architectures practical at production scale. Vector retrieval became more efficient, application-level filtering could participate directly in retrieval, and capabilities such as scheduling, secrets management, caching, and routing continued moving closer to the application itself.

With 5.3, two additional pieces make the broader direction easier to see: native full-text search and model-assisted decisions.

The releases matter less as isolated feature lists than as a progression: more of the intelligent application can operate within the runtime.

Search is not one problem

Vector search has become closely associated with AI because it can find information based on meaning rather than exact wording. That makes it particularly useful for retrieval-augmented generation and other applications where a user's language may not exactly match the underlying content.

But semantic similarity is not the answer to every search problem. Sometimes the exact words matter. A query for a product number, policy name, error message, contractual term, or specific phrase may be better served by full-text search.

Modern AI applications often need both. A useful way to think about the distinction is that full-text search helps an application find the words, while vector search helps it find the meaning. Harper can now perform both alongside the data and application logic they serve.

Find the words. Find the meaning. Apply judgment.

From generating answers to making controlled decisions

Most conversations about AI applications begin with generation: send a model some context and ask it to produce text. But many production workflows do not actually need another paragraph of generated language. They need a judgment.

Should this support request go to billing, refunds, or engineering? Does this new product belong in one category or another? Is this alert a duplicate, something worth investigating, or noise? In each case, the possible actions are already known. The application needs the model to help choose among them.

This pattern has recently gained more attention through Jev and other decision-model approaches. Jev is a useful reference because it makes the distinction easy to see: instead of asking a model to freely generate an answer, give it a bounded set of possibilities and ask it to judge which one best fits the input.

The underlying pattern, however, is broader than Jev or any one specialized model. Small inference models have performed classification and ranking tasks for years, and modern language models can perform the same kind of bounded judgment alongside their generative capabilities. What changes is how easily that judgment can become a first-class part of application logic.

Harper 5.3 exposes that pattern directly through models.decide().

An application provides the context and defines the allowed answers. Harper asks the configured model to evaluate those choices and returns both the selected value and a score for each permitted alternative. For example, an incoming request might be evaluated against billing, refund, or bug.

The important part is not simply that the model chooses billing. The application also receives information about the alternatives, which gives it something concrete to act on. A strong result might continue through an automated workflow. An uncertain result might be sent for human review. A separate “none of these” score can indicate that the choices themselves may not adequately describe the request.

The model contributes judgment, but the application retains control over what the possible actions are and what happens after the judgment is made.

That makes decisioning a useful middle ground between traditional deterministic software and open-ended generation. Business rules can continue handling the situations where the answer is known precisely. Generation can handle tasks where new language or content is required. Decision models handle the increasingly important space between them: situations where software knows the available actions but needs contextual judgment to choose among them.

And because models.decide() is an interface rather than a Jev-specific feature, the underlying model can change. A highly optimized decision model such as Jev could sit behind it. A local model could serve the decision. A general-purpose LLM could do the same job. The application's decision contract does not have to change with the model.

Harper can also persist those decisions and associate them with later outcomes. That creates a path toward evaluating how different models behave on an organization's actual workloads and establishing automation thresholds based on observed results rather than assuming that a model score corresponds directly to real-world accuracy.

From model input to application decision

Jev helped bring attention to decision models, but the broader pattern is more important: applications can ask models for bounded judgments without handing control of the workflow to the model.

Search finds evidence. Decisions turn it into action.

This is where the retrieval and decision capabilities start to fit together. Full-text search can retrieve information when the exact words matter. Vector search can retrieve information based on meaning. The resulting context can then inform a bounded decision about what the application should do next.

The model does not have to invent the workflow. It does not need authority over the application. It helps evaluate the evidence within a set of choices the application already understands.

That is a subtle difference, but potentially an important one as AI moves deeper into production systems. Search helps the application find the evidence. Decision models help interpret it. Application logic remains responsible for what happens next.

Fewer systems changes more than the architecture diagram

Infrastructure consolidation is often described in operational terms: fewer services, fewer vendors, and fewer things to deploy. Those benefits are real, but intelligent applications make the implications larger.

AI interactions frequently require context from several sources before the application can do anything useful. When data, retrieval, application logic, permissions, model access, and workflow coordination all sit behind separate service boundaries, that context constantly moves across the network. Each transition introduces latency, consumes resources, expands the security surface, and creates another potential failure point.

Bringing more of those capabilities together changes the economics of the request itself. Less data has to cross service boundaries, fewer systems need to coordinate the same operation, and fewer infrastructure components need to scale independently.

The fastest network call is still the one an application never needs to make.

This is not about replacing the model

Models are evolving rapidly, and organizations should be able to choose the providers and models that fit their requirements. Harper's architecture is designed around that assumption.

The model is a configurable capability used by the application. The application owns its data, state, permissions, business logic, allowed actions, and operational behavior. Models contribute generation, interpretation, or judgment where those capabilities are useful.

That separation also makes the architecture less dependent on any particular model provider. As models improve or organizations change providers, the surrounding application does not necessarily need to be redesigned with them.

The AI stack may be starting to consolidate

New technology categories often expand before they consolidate. The first generation of a new architecture naturally produces specialized systems for every emerging problem because those problems need to be solved quickly.

AI followed that pattern. Teams assembled databases, vector stores, search engines, embedding pipelines, agent frameworks, model gateways, caches, queues, schedulers, and application servers into increasingly capable systems.

The next phase may look different. Search does not necessarily need to be separated from the data being searched. Embeddings do not necessarily require a standalone pipeline. Agent tools do not necessarily need a separate gateway. Model access does not necessarily belong in custom integration code across every application. And model-assisted decisions do not necessarily need to occur somewhere outside the application responsible for acting on them.

Harper 5.3 is another step in that direction.

As AI becomes part of ordinary application behavior, the infrastructure supporting it can become part of the application runtime too.

The future of the AI stack may not be a bigger stack at all. It may be a more unified runtime.

title: SaaS Subscriber Delivery: Simple Queue Retries, Backoff, and DLQ Isolation
description:
For an edtech shipment-update fan-out, use at-least-once delivery with idempotent subscriber sends, a small retry budget, exponential backoff with jitter, and a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for exhausted jobs. That is the least complex policy that keeps a temporary downstream failure from becoming either a lost notification or an infinite retry loop.

The important choice is the unit of work. Create one immutable job per subscriber, not one job for the whole shipment audience. A worker can then acknowledge successful subscribers independently while delaying only the failed ones. The shipment event carries a stable ID; each child job adds the subscriber ID and channel. A unique delivery key ties those values together, so a redelivery can be recognized without pretending the queue provides exactly-once effects.

Split the fan-out early.

How should a simple SaaS queue retry failed background jobs with exponential backoff?

Start with failure classification. A timeout, a connection reset, or an HTTP 429 can be transient, so the job may be tried again after a delay. A malformed destination or a rejected payload is terminal and should move directly to the DLQ. Authentication failures deserve their own operational alert: repeatedly sending the same request with unchanged credentials adds load but does not change the outcome. The exact classification depends on the subscriber channel, and I'm not sure a provider's generic error category is sufficient until its documented status codes have been exercised in an eval fixture.

Keep the retry policy deliberately small: count every delivery attempt, cap the count, calculate a delay, and record the decision. For attempt number n, a useful baseline is min(cap, base * 2 ** (n - 1)). Add jitter so a cohort of jobs that failed together does not wake together. This is a policy recommendation, not a promise about the timing precision of a particular queue. Delayed delivery means "eligible after this time"; workers, queue load, and scheduler resolution can make actual execution later.

The DLQ is part of the normal control flow. AWS's SQS documentation describes a redrive policy whose maxReceiveCount controls when a source-queue message moves to a dead-letter queue. It also warns that a DLQ can break strict ordering, which matters if subscriber updates must be observed in sequence. The general lesson travels well: pick a retry budget from the business deadline, and don't attach a DLQ mechanically when reordering would violate the job's contract.

For shipment updates, ordering is often better expressed in application data. Include a monotonically increasing shipment version, let the subscriber-side delivery record reject an older version, and make the message useful on its own. Then a delayed "packed" update cannot overwrite a newer "shipped" state. This turns queue order from a hidden assumption into something an eval can verify.

A runnable Python retry decision before the worker grows complicated

I like to make the policy a pure function first — notebook-sized, deterministic under a seeded random generator, and cheap to evaluate across thousands of generated cases. The queue adapter can stay boring. The example below models decisions without depending on a commercial SDK; wire publish to the queue already used by the application.

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass, replace
from enum import Enum
import hashlib
import json
import random
from typing import Protocol


class Action(str, Enum):
    ACK = "ack"
    RETRY = "retry"
    DEAD_LETTER = "dead_letter"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ShipmentJob:
    shipment_id: str
    shipment_version: int
    subscriber_id: str
    channel: str
    attempt: int = 1

    @property
    def delivery_key(self) -> str:
        raw = (
            f"{self.shipment_id}:{self.shipment_version}:"
            f"{self.subscriber_id}:{self.channel}"
        )
        return hashlib.sha256(raw.encode()).hexdigest()


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Outcome:
    action: Action
    delay_seconds: float = 0.0
    reason: str = ""


class Queue(Protocol):
    def publish(
        self, queue_name: str, body: str, delay_seconds: float = 0.0
    ) -> None: ...


def retry_delay(
    attempt: int,
    rng: random.Random,
    base_seconds: float = 5.0,
    cap_seconds: float = 300.0,
) -> float:
    exponential = min(cap_seconds, base_seconds * (2 ** (attempt - 1)))
    return rng.uniform(0.0, exponential)


def decide(
    job: ShipmentJob,
    status_code: int,
    rng: random.Random,
    max_attempts: int = 6,
) -> Outcome:
    if 200 <= status_code < 300:
        return Outcome(Action.ACK)

    retryable = status_code == 429 or status_code >= 500
    if not retryable:
        return Outcome(Action.DEAD_LETTER, reason=f"terminal:{status_code}")

    if job.attempt >= max_attempts:
        return Outcome(Action.DEAD_LETTER, reason="attempts_exhausted")

    return Outcome(
        Action.RETRY,
        delay_seconds=retry_delay(job.attempt, rng),
        reason=f"transient:{status_code}",
    )


def finish_attempt(
    queue: Queue, job: ShipmentJob, outcome: Outcome
) -> None:
    if outcome.action is Action.ACK:
        return

    envelope = {
        "job": job.__dict__,
        "delivery_key": job.delivery_key,
        "reason": outcome.reason,
    }
    if outcome.action is Action.RETRY:
        next_job = replace(job, attempt=job.attempt + 1)
        envelope["job"] = next_job.__dict__
        queue.publish(
            "shipment-delivery",
            json.dumps(envelope),
            delay_seconds=outcome.delay_seconds,
        )
        return

    queue.publish(
        "shipment-delivery-dlq",
        json.dumps(envelope),
    )

The worker still needs an atomic boundary around its effect. Before contacting an external notification channel, reserve the delivery key in durable storage; after success, mark it complete. If the process stops between the external effect and that final write, the same job may be observed again. There is no generic transaction across a queue, a database, and somebody else's API, so the receiving operation should accept an idempotency key when possible. If it does not, define duplicate notification as an explicit product risk rather than hiding it behind an "exactly once" label.

One detail is easy to miss in the example: republishing a delayed retry and acknowledging the current message must be coordinated. A queue with native retry delay can own that transition. With a generic adapter, persist an outbox entry in the same transaction as the local attempt record, publish the outbox asynchronously, and acknowledge only after the durable handoff. Don't acknowledge first. A process stop in that gap loses the retry.

The code treats 5xx as retryable because it models a generic downstream HTTP service, not because every endpoint has the same semantics. A 501, for example, usually won't improve through repetition. Production classification should be an allowlist derived from the downstream contract, while the broad rule above is kept compact for the policy walkthrough.

Delivery guarantees are a product decision, not a queue checkbox

The right guarantee is the one the subscriber can observe. At-most-once delivery avoids duplicates but may lose an update after a worker failure. At-least-once delivery accepts redelivery and requires idempotent effects. Exactly-once processing is sometimes available inside a bounded system, yet the end-to-end claim becomes much harder once the job calls an external channel. For a shipment notification, at-least-once plus a stable delivery key is usually the honest contract. Consider the awkward boundary: the worker sends a version-8 “shipped” message, the channel accepts it, and the worker stops before acknowledging its queue job. The queue is correct to deliver the job again because it cannot observe the channel's side effect. On the second attempt, the same delivery key lets the channel or the application's delivery ledger suppress another visible notification. If version 7 arrives afterward, the stored shipment version rejects it as stale. These are two different protections — deduplication handles the same event twice, while version comparison handles distinct events arriving out of order — and an eval suite should exercise both.

Name that boundary.

Concern Policy Eval assertion
Temporary throttling Retry with jittered backoff A 429 schedules one later attempt
Invalid destination Dead-letter immediately A terminal 4xx consumes no retry budget
Worker redelivery Reuse the delivery key The visible effect is recorded once
Stale shipment state Compare shipment versions Version 7 cannot replace version 8
Exhausted attempts Preserve the final envelope in the DLQ The reason and original identifiers remain inspectable

A fixed six-attempt budget in sample code is not a universal default. Work backward from the useful delivery window. With a 300-second delay cap, a job may remain retryable long after an update has stopped being useful, especially when queue time is added. Conversely, a subscriber integration with a documented hour-long maintenance window may need a longer budget or a separate recovery workflow. Your mileage may vary — the deadline, not a fashionable attempt count, should settle it.

This is also where prompt-cost awareness helps, even though the worker itself is ordinary infrastructure. If a later stage generates personalized notification copy with a model, do not regenerate it on every transport retry. Store the approved rendered payload or a content hash with the job and retry only the delivery side effect. Otherwise a transient channel error quietly multiplies model calls and makes eval results hard to reproduce.

The catch is that a DLQ is not suitable as long-term business storage, and a retry queue is not a scheduler for every kind of future work. Keep authoritative shipment state in the application database. Use the queue to move bounded work, use the DLQ to isolate jobs requiring inspection or redrive, and use a scheduler when an action is intentionally planned far in the future. If strict ordering across all updates is mandatory, stick with a single ordered stream per shipment or subscriber and accept the throughput and head-of-line-blocking trade-off.

Operate the policy with evals, budgets, and deliberate redrive

Before deployment, build a failure matrix rather than testing only the happy path. Feed the pure decision function success, throttling, terminal rejection, the last permitted attempt, and an old shipment version. Seed randomness in tests and assert delay bounds instead of a single sampled value. Then run an integration test that stops a worker after the external effect but before acknowledgement. That uncomfortable case is where duplicate behavior becomes visible.

Watch attempt count, job age, scheduled delay, terminal reason, and DLQ depth as separate signals. Averages blur the exact failure mode: a low average attempt count can coexist with a small cohort trapped at the cap. Trace one delivery key across the original job and every retry, but avoid putting subscriber contact details into queue names, metric labels, or logs. High-cardinality identifiers belong in traces or structured logs with suitable access controls.

Redrive needs a gate. First correct the terminal condition or update the payload under an auditable rule; next replay a small sample; then compare success rate, duplicate suppression, latency, and downstream throttling against the predeclared eval thresholds. Bulk replaying an untouched DLQ merely recreates the failure burst. AWS also recommends setting DLQ retention longer than source-queue retention, because message age and retention behavior affect how long operators have to investigate.

Keep the runbook short enough to use under pressure. It should state who owns each terminal reason, how to pause a redrive, what evidence permits replay, and how old a shipment update may be before it is discarded. Review retry constants beside product deadlines during deployment, verify that alarms cover job age as well as queue depth, and rehearse one rollback. Done. The queue library can change later; these observable contracts should not.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/

title: Building in the Cloud: A Practical Guide to IaaS Architecture Using DigitalOcean
description:
If you’ve ever built a web application, you’ve likely faced the classic architectural fork in the road: Do you pay upfront CapEx for physical hardware, deploy to a opinionated Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS), or provision your own virtual environment from scratch?

For developers who want raw control, root access, and cost transparency without managing physical server racks or datacenter cooling, Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) is the sweet spot.

In this article, we’ll break down what IaaS actually brings to the table, how it fits into the modern cloud ecosystem, and walk through a step-by-step case study of architecting a scalable production stack on DigitalOcean.
What is IaaS, Really?
At its core, IaaS is a cloud model where you rent bare-metal computing resources abstracted over the internet. Instead of buying physical hardware, your provider delivers three core primitives on demand:

Compute: Virtual Machines (VMs) or instances with configurable vCPUs and RAM.
Storage: Block storage (attached SSD/NVMe volumes) and S3-compatible Object Storage.
Networking: Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs), software-defined firewalls, load balancers, and floating/reserved IPs.

By shifting from CapEx (buying servers upfront) to OpEx (paying hourly/monthly for active usage), you scale infrastructure alongside real user demand.

Architectural Layer
PaaS Managed Scope
IaaS Managed Scope
Application Layer
Developer code & configurations
Complete OS, runtimes, & libraries
Platform & Middleware
Managed runtimes, framework tuning, auto-patching
Manual distro updates, kernel flags, custom packages
Infrastructure Base
Virtual instances, scaling triggers, base security
Full hypervisor isolation, raw CPU/RAM allocation
Physical Facilities
Datacenter power, cooling, bare hardware
Datacenter power, cooling, physical network links

The Cloud Spectrum: IaaS vs. PaaS vs. SaaS
To understand where IaaS sits, look at the division of responsibility:

SaaS (Software as a Service): Fully managed applications (e.g., GitHub, Notion, Gmail). You manage data and access.
PaaS (Platform as a Service): You deploy application code; the platform manages runtimes, OS updates, and underlying servers (e.g., Vercel, Heroku, Railway). You manage code and configuration.
IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): You get a clean virtual slate. You select the Linux distro, tune the web server kernel, harden firewalls, and orchestrate scaling. You manage almost everything except the physical hypervisor.
Case Study: Scaling a High-Traffic App on DigitalOcean
Let’s examine a real-world scenario. Imagine you're building a REST/GraphQL API or content backend experiencing rapid traffic growth. A single basic instance is no longer cutting it during peak hours.

Rather than diving straight into the overwhelming complexity of hyperscalers like AWS or GCP, you opt for a clean, developer-focused IaaS architecture on DigitalOcean.
Phase 1: The Monolithic Starter Node
In early production, everything runs on a single Droplet (DigitalOcean's moniker for a VM):

OS: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS
Stack: Nginx reverse proxy, Node.js API process (managed by PM2), and a local PostgreSQL instance.

While cost-effective, this setup carries a glaring Single Point of Failure (SPOF). If PostgreSQL consumes all system memory or Nginx hits a worker connection limit, your entire platform drops offline.
Phase 2: Decoupling into a Scalable IaaS Architecture
To make the application resilient and production-ready, we separate compute, database, and asset storage using isolated IaaS building blocks:

Component
Resource Type
Function in Architecture
Traffic Ingress
Managed Load Balancer
SSL/TLS termination, round-robin HTTP balancing
Compute Nodes
Dual App Droplets
Stateless API workers running Node.js + Nginx
Internal Network
Isolated VPC (10.116.0.0/20)
Private non-routable communication between nodes
Data Persistence
Managed PostgreSQL Cluster
Dedicated database instance with automatic failover
Media Assets
DigitalOcean Spaces (CDN)
S3-compatible object storage with global edge caching

Here is how the infrastructure pieces fit together:

Network Isolation (VPC): We provision a private Virtual Private Cloud network (10.116.0.0/20). Backend Droplets communicate with the database via internal IPs, keeping backend transit isolated from public routing tables.
Horizontal Compute Scaling: We spin up multiple worker Droplets with identical runtime environments. A managed Load Balancer sits at the perimeter, terminating SSL/TLS and distributing HTTP requests across healthy nodes via round-robin.
Database Offloading: We move PostgreSQL off the app nodes into a managed database node (or a dedicated database Droplet with attached Block Storage), preventing disk I/O contention with API processes.
Object Storage for Media Assets: Instead of writing user uploads directly to ephemeral node disks, uploads stream to DigitalOcean Spaces (S3-compatible object storage), integrated with a built-in CDN edge for rapid global distribution.
Why Developers Choose IaaS Over PaaS
While managing your own OS requires active maintenance—patching CVEs, configuring ufw, and setting up monitoring—the trade-offs are well worth it for growing projects:

Granular System Access: You hold root privileges (sudo). If your stack requires custom kernel flags, eBPF telemetry, custom C libraries, or optimized Nginx directives, you aren't restricted by platform sandboxes.
Cost Predictability: Serverless or PaaS billing can surprise you when request volumes spike. IaaS provides transparent hourly and monthly billing per instance, making runway forecasting straightforward.
Elimination of Vendor Lock-In: Because your application runs on standard Linux environments using standard configuration scripts (Ansible, Docker, Terraform), migrating from DigitalOcean to Linode, Hetzner, or AWS requires changing host IP definitions—not rewriting code.
Wrapping Up
Infrastructure as a Service remains the foundation of modern cloud engineering. Whether you're running light workloads on developer-first clouds or building complex container fleets on custom VMs, mastering IaaS gives you full authority over performance, security, and cost.

Over to you: How are you handling server provisioning in your current stack? Are you team PaaS for speed, or team IaaS for control? Let's talk in the comments!

title: I built Aegis — a personal cyber defense platform that checks links, emails, files and passwords before they hurt you
description:
Most people don't get hacked by nation-state attacks. They get hacked by a fake link in a text message, a convincing "verify your account" email, a malware attachment disguised as an invoice, or a password that already leaked in someone else's data breach.

So I built Aegis — one place where a non-technical person can check each of those things before it hurts them, built to the same security standard it checks for.

🔗 Live demo: https://aegis-cyber-defense-platform.onrender.com (free hosting — first load after idle can take ~ a minute)
💻 Code: https://github.com/Manoj-2424150118/aegis-cyber-defense-platform

What it does

Smart Scan is the front door: paste anything — a link, an email, a suspicious message — and Aegis detects what it is and routes it to the right analyser automatically.

Underneath are 10 tools, each answering a question a worried user actually asks:

  1. URL Analyser — "Is this link safe?" IP-instead-of-domain, look-alike domains, brand names hidden in paths, shorteners, credential bait.
  2. Email Analyser — "Is this email really from my bank?" SPF/DKIM/DMARC authentication, display-name mismatches, pressure language, and every link inside re-scored.
  3. File Scanner — "Is this attachment dangerous?" Content-vs-extension mismatches, double extensions like invoice.pdf.exe, hidden code. Files are examined in memory only — never opened, never run, never saved.
  4. Password Lab — offline guess-time estimation, common/repetitive pattern detection, secure generation.
  5. Breach Check — k-anonymity lookup: only the first five characters of the password's hash ever leave the machine.
  6. Secret Scanner — finds leaked API keys and credentials hiding in text and code.
  7. Encrypted Vault — AES-256-GCM with keys derived via Argon2id; the server stores only scrambled data, and tampering is detected automatically.
  8. Website Audit — any site graded A–F on HTTPS enforcement, security headers and cookie safety.
  9. Scam Message Checker — recognises Indian scam scripts: fake "digital arrest" threats, KYC/account-block warnings, OTP harvesting, Telegram task scams.
  10. Domain & TLS Checker — live grading of a domain's email-auth records, plus a real handshake to verify a site's certificate.

The part most tools skip: the fix

Every finding in every report ends with a Suggested Fix — concrete next steps written for the person holding the report. A test enforces that no finding can ship without one. A report should end the problem, not just name it.

Since v2.0, a detection-engine "Signal" layer sits across the analysers, and public Trends show what people are actually checking.

How it protects itself

A security tool has to survive its own audit:

  • The website-audit feature could once have been tricked into fetching internal network addresses (SSRF). It now resolves every target first, refuses private/internal addresses, and re-checks every redirect.
  • Uploads are read in capped chunks and rejected exactly at the 10 MB limit — no memory-exhaustion via huge files.
  • Login responses are timing-equalised with generic errors, so attackers can't enumerate real accounts. Accounts lock after repeated failures; login is rate-limited.
  • Auth is Argon2id + JWT, and the platform ships the same strict security headers its own audit module grades other sites on. Aegis's self-audit score: 100, grade A.

Testing is evidence, not decoration

186 automated tests, all passing, with CI and CodeQL green on every push. The canonical reference scores never drift between releases: the reference phishing link scores 85, the phishing email 100, the disguised program 40 — in every battery, on every version. A scripted QA battery (functional checks, attack suite, fuzzing, load) runs in a sandbox before deployment and against the live site after it.

Stack

FastAPI (Python) back end, React + TypeScript front end, single Docker container, Neon Postgres for storage (accounts and vault items survive redeploys — proven by test).

Honest limits

  • The demo runs on free hosting, which sleeps when idle — the first load can take about a minute. The code is identical to what a paid deployment would run.
  • The checkers use explained heuristics, not magic. They can over- or under-flag at the margins — which is exactly why every finding shows its reasoning, so the user can judge.

I'm Manoj Kumar Sharma, a cybersecurity & software professional (MCA, Manipal University Jaipur) based in Jaipur, India. I also run Scam Decoded, where I break down real Indian scams in short videos.

If you try Aegis, I'd genuinely like to hear what it got right — and what it missed.

title: IIT Patna at "ICPR 2026 TVRID Competition on Privacy-Preserving Person Re-Identification from Top-View RGB-Depth Camera"
description:
arXiv:2611.12960v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Privacy-aware person re-identification (Re-ID) from top-view cameras replaces frontal appearance with anthropometric shape, while depth sensing further reduces color-based identity cues. The ICPR 2026 TVRID competition evaluates this setting using 86 identities captured by four synchronized Intel RealSense D455 cameras with RGB and Depth streams across flat, ascent, descent, and oblique viewpoints. Performance is measured using mAP and CMC@1 across within-camera in/out, ascent-descent, and flat-oblique scenarios. The competition had 147 registered participants and 33 final submissions. Three teams from IIT Patna participated: 'abhinavkumar03' and 'sjkdgfhl_' ranked 5th and 7th among 31 ranked participants, and 'vivek katuri' reached 77.67% CMC@1 / 85.20% mAP on the RGB track. This paper presents the methods of the two top-10 teams. Methodology 1 (abhinavkumar03) achieves 93.51% mAP and 90.42% CMC@1 on Depth, ranking 4th of 28, while Methodology 2 (sjkdgfhl_) reaches 99.63%/99.35% on RGB and 86.26%/80.34% on Depth. Both substantially outperform the 57.19% track-average Depth mAP, with Methodology 1 yielding a 7.3-point gain over Methodology 2. These results demonstrate the importance of depth representation and supervision for privacy-preserving Re-ID.

title: Your DePIN Provider Can Change the Rules by Vote
description:
Akash stakers approved Prop 346 on November 2. It passed with 97.27% of the votes cast, turnout was 69.5% of bonded stake (about twice the quorum), and AKT will relaunch on Solana as an SPL token.

Sector overviews went out of date within days. This rundown of 12 DePIN projects, published November 6, already lists Akash as a Cosmos project moving to Solana, next to Render, io.net, Helium and Grass, which are there already. I keep it open when I can't remember which DePIN network runs on which chain and how each one pays its operators.

If you deploy on Akash, the vote itself changes less than the headlines suggest.

What the vote actually authorized

Prop 346 approves the plan and the token. SPL AKT launches after two independent audits of the token and the portal, which the team expected to take two to three weeks. The ticker stays the same, the token uses 6 decimals, and total supply doesn't change. The portal swaps AKT 1:1, works in one direction only, and stays open for two years.

The marketplace stays on akashnet-2 for now. Moving it needs a separate cutover proposal. Before that vote, marketplace audits have to pass, a provider testnet has to run for at least six weeks with 25 or more operators, and a 14-day community rehearsal has to finish with zero blockers. No date is set. After cutover, existing leases keep running for 90 days before the old chain halts.

So for deployers, nothing changes this month. The cutover vote is the one to watch.

Where it gets less comfortable

Staking rewards and inflation on the old chain end at cutover. What replaces them isn't settled yet. The team says new staking mechanisms will be announced before cutover, and the emissions curve for provider and treasury incentives still has to be published. If your team stakes AKT, migrating starts a 21-day unbonding inside the same portal transaction, and on a Cosmos chain unbonding tokens don't earn rewards.

Akash is open about what it gives up: its own consensus, native IBC connections and live slashing, which isn't available on Solana yet. AKT sitting on Osmosis or other IBC chains has to come back to akashnet-2 before it can migrate. The project's own security warning is about phishing, and it says there is exactly one official portal domain. Two years is a long time for lookalike sites to work.

The one-way part makes me a little uneasy. I get why a migration is built that way. I'd still read the audit reports before moving anything I couldn't afford to lose.

The case for the move is mostly cost. Akash estimates fees for its whole marketplace at about 0.075 SOL a day and says a marketplace operation would cost about 9x less than on an EVM layer 2 on a quiet day, and about 300x less under load. It also stops maintaining its own forks of cosmos-sdk and CometBFT. For a small core team, I suspect that's the bigger saving.

Helium already went through this

Helium moved to Solana in 2023. This year's change went deeper into the economics.

HIP-149 went live on July 29 and retired Proof-of-Coverage on Mobile and IoT, so hotspots now earn from the data they transfer. Read the Mobile floor and cap carefully, because they aren't fixed dollar amounts. The floor is 0.5x the payer rate and the cap is 3x. With the payer rate cut from $0.50 to about $0.10 per GB, that works out to $0.05 and $0.30. If the rate changes, the band moves with it.

The same vote approved about 141 million new HNT over 36 months. The tokens go into a multisig vault run by Nova Labs, which uses them for carrier expansion, grants and operating costs. Hotspot rewards don't get any of it. Effective max supply rises from about 206 million to about 347 million HNT. Sarson Funds closed its HNT position in June, while the proposal was still being discussed, citing the dilution and the sale of Helium Mobile to Noble Mobile. Their point was that liking the network and liking the token had stopped being the same trade.

If you built a dashboard or earnings estimate on Helium, the payer rate is now an input you have to track, and coverage numbers are history.

Filecoin tried putting the rule in code

Filecoin Onchain Cloud went live on mainnet on March 26. Data sits with two independent providers, proofs are checked onchain every 24 hours, and payments halt automatically when the proofs stop. Launch coverage put the price at $2.50 per TiB a month. Of the three designs, this is the one I'd find easiest to depend on, because I can verify the condition I care about myself.

Demand is the open question. At launch the network held 49.41 TiB across 478 datasets, with 81 payer wallets connected. The same week, FIL traded around $0.83, close to its all-time low, and a day of network fees came to about $1,950.

What I'm doing with this

Nothing clever. For every DePIN network I depend on, I keep the governance page bookmarked next to the docs and write down which inputs a vote can change: payer rates, reward rules, sometimes the chain itself. For Akash, the next item on that list is the cutover proposal.

title: Seeing the Small: Deformable Duality Mamba for Retinal Lesion Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2611.13514v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) lesions vary widely in shape, and microaneurysms (MAs) span only a few pixels. We hypothesize that modeling the spatial organization of lesion regions, with global context and shape-adaptive scanning, improves the segmentation of such small and irregular lesions. To test this, we propose D$^2$Mamba, which couples non-causal state space duality with deformable Mamba scanning. We evaluate it with five-fold cross-validation on the DDR dataset, comparing against representative segmentation baselines under an identical training protocol, and conduct ablations on each component. D$^2$Mamba achieved the best overall performance, with 33.87% mIoU, 2.99 percentage points above the strongest baseline. The largest gain appeared on MAs, the smallest and most easily missed lesions, where Dice improved by 10.06 percentage points. These results confirm our hypothesis that spatially adaptive state space modeling benefits tiny-lesion segmentation. Code and pretrained weights are available at https://github.com/PUREPANEL1/D2Mamba.

title: The Interface Questions That Matter in a Disposable-Inbox Workflow
description:
The last mile of many sign-up flows is not the password form. It is the short window in which a person must receive a verification code or confirmation link, extract it, and return to the original tab before the moment passes. When that window is clumsy, users blame "email." From a product-design point of view, the inbox is doing a specialized job: complete a short-lived message task with as little extra identity as possible.

This article is a UX-engineering review lens, not a source-code analysis and not a hands-on benchmark. I am treating the disposable-inbox workflow as a public interface problem. The questions below can be asked of any similar tool, including one you are designing yourself.

The job is not "own an email account"

A conventional mailbox is organized around ownership: authentication, long-term storage, search, folders, and a stable identity. A disposable inbox is organized around a shorter job.

Typical tasks look like this:

  • obtain an address quickly enough to paste into a form;
  • wait for one message without wondering whether the page is stuck;
  • copy a code or open a link without hunting through a heavy template;
  • sometimes download a ticket, document, or image before the mailbox is gone;
  • recover when a site rejects a well-known disposable domain;
  • leave the session without implying that the address will be waiting next year.

If you evaluate the interface with Gmail-shaped expectations, you will over-weight features that do not serve the job, and under-weight the states that actually cause drop-off. The useful review question is not "how complete is this email client?" It is "how clearly does this interface carry a person from address, to message, to done?"

States worth testing at the interface layer

The following are test questions, not claims about any private implementation. If you cannot observe an answer in the public UI, mark it as unknown rather than inferred.

First address. Is an address visible when the page becomes usable, without a second registration or a recovery email? If the first paint shows a placeholder, is it obvious whether the address is ready to copy or still being prepared?

Copy. Can the address be copied in one deliberate action? After copying, is there a brief confirmation? Failure here looks minor in a screenshot and expensive in a form that clears itself on blur.

Waiting. While a verification message is in transit, does the inbox communicate that it can receive mail in real time, and is a manual refresh available when the person does not want to rely on automatic updates alone? The waiting state should not look like an empty, possibly broken list.

Reading. When a message arrives, can the person open it and still see enough context to know it is the expected sender? If the product surfaces a verification code from supported messages, does the original message remain available so the code is not a naked number with no context?

Attachments. If a legitimate sender includes a ticket, document, or image, is a download path visible, and is it clear that this has to happen before the mailbox expires?

Domain choice. If a site rejects the first address, can the person switch among available domains without starting a completely unrelated product journey? Does the interface avoid promising that every sender will accept the next domain? Availability can change, and some sites block disposable mail as a matter of policy.

History and lifetime. If recently used addresses can be listed on the same device while they remain valid, does the UI present this as local convenience rather than as cloud backup or permanent recovery? Can the person review remaining lifetime for an active inbox?

Multiple inboxes. If more than one inbox can be active, is switching among them obvious, or can a code arrive somewhere the person is not currently looking?

These questions already form a practical QA sketch. You can turn each one into an expected observation, an ambiguous observation, or a missing observation. That is more honest than a feature matrix filled with guesses.

Rejection and delay are part of the happy path

In many products, a rejected email domain is treated as an error state, complete with red text and a sense that the user did something wrong. In a disposable-inbox workflow, rejection is a normal branch. Sites maintain blocklists. Domain availability changes. A person who came only for a one-time code needs a calm way to try another available domain, or to decide that this particular site should receive a permanent address instead.

Delay is equally normal. A review should not invent a delivery-time promise the interface does not make. The testable question is whether the waiting state remains truthful: new mail can appear as it is received, refresh is available, and the person is not scolded for waiting.

There is also a classification fork that the UI cannot solve alone, but can avoid making worse. If someone uses a short-lived inbox for a purchase or a recovery-dependent account, the later failure will look like a product defect. Interface copy that reminds people to keep those accounts on a permanent inbox is not decoration. It is a safeguard around the job the tool is actually good at.

A public example of the pattern

After the job and the test questions are clear, it helps to look at a public page that presents this workflow in the open, as a product surface rather than as a private architecture.

TempMail.ai offers a free disposable email address with a real-time inbox and no sign-up step, which matches the "do not create a second account in order to avoid creating an account" constraint. I am not treating that as a measured ranking, only as a visible example of the pattern under discussion.

The Temporary Email Generator page describes the same loop in three steps: copy the address already displayed, use it for a replaceable sign-up, and read the incoming mail. The page also states interface-level capabilities that map cleanly onto the questions above: codes can be surfaced from supported messages while the original remains available; supported attachments can be downloaded before expiry; domains can be switched when a sender rejects the first address; local history may list recent addresses on the same device while they remain valid, without promising permanent recovery; and the inbox can show remaining lifetime, refresh delivery, and switch among inboxes.

Public view of the Temporary Email Generator product page (verified official screenshot, not a personal test result).

Those statements are useful because they are bounded. They tell a reviewer what to look for, and they do not require access to source code.

What a UI review should refuse to claim

A review should keep the security story modest. Using a short-lived address more often can reduce how widely a long-term inbox is stored, but that is not the same as disappearing from a network, and a clean inbox interface cannot certify that a website is safe to use.

A review should also refuse several other overclaims:

  • that every sender will accept a disposable domain;
  • that local device history is a backup strategy;
  • that unseen delivery speed or lifetime numbers are known because a marketing phrase sounded confident;
  • that a public UI reveals how mail is stored, routed, or secured internally.

If you are designing a similar system, the most transferable deliverable from this article is not a vendor preference. It is the question list. Walk a first-time user from a blank tab to a copied code, note every moment of uncertainty, and treat those moments as the actual product surface. The inbox that wins a disposable task is the one that makes the short path obvious, and the limits equally obvious.

title: Free stand-ins for Calibri, Segoe UI and Helvetica, measured, and the CSS that stops the jump
description:
Calibri, Segoe UI and Helvetica turn up in a lot of mockups, and none of them can ship as a web font. Calibri and Segoe UI come with Windows: you can use them on that computer, but their licence doesn't let you put the font file on a website. Helvetica is sold by Linotype and comes with macOS.

So the stack becomes font-family: "Segoe UI", sans-serif, and on a phone or a Mac the visitor gets whatever the fallback is, with different line breaks.

We build FontKind, a site that measures free fonts letter by letter. For the Windows fonts we measured which free fonts come closest, then checked in a browser what it takes to swap one for the other without the page moving. The short version: there are two kinds of "alternative", and they fix different problems.

Looks like it vs. sets like it

"Which free font looks like Calibri?" and "which free font sets text exactly like Calibri?" have different answers.

Carlito is drawn to Calibri's exact widths and heights. Swap one for the other and no line moves. But it's by Łukasz Dziedzic, who drew Lato, and our model scores Lato as its closest font with a full 100: it's Lato's design fitted to Calibri's metrics. Against Calibri itself it scores only 56 out of 100, because its k, O and 9 are drawn differently.

Asap Condensed scores 93. It looks closer, but it's 9% narrower, so every paragraph rewraps.

So, before you pick a replacement, decide which problem you have:

  • The layout must not change (a document template, a UI built around Calibri's widths): use the metric twin.
  • You want the look: use the closest shape, and fix the size difference in CSS (below).

How we measure, briefly: widths are the average advance width of the 26 lowercase letters, read from the font file. Likeness comes from an image model (Meta's DINOv3) comparing 62 letters and figures of each font, an a with an a, a g with a g, scored 0 to 100. Details are on our methodology page.

What we measured

You designed with Same widths (metric twin) Closest look, measured How it differs
Calibri Carlito Asap Condensed (93) 9% narrower, x-height 12% taller
Segoe UI none TASA Explorer (84) 7% wider
Sarabun (82) nearly identical proportions
Tahoma none DejaVu Sans (88) 15% wider, 12% lighter
Trebuchet MS none Merriweather Sans (80) 9% wider, x-height 7% taller
Microsoft Sans Serif none Miedinger (86) nearly identical proportions
Helvetica Arimo, via Arial not measured

Helvetica is the odd one out: we have no licensed copy, so we haven't measured it. Arimo is drawn to Arial's widths, and Arial shares Helvetica's widths, so Arimo is the twin to reach for. For the look, Inter, Roboto and IBM Plex Sans are in the same class.

Each measured page lists 24 free fonts, closest first, with the differences named.

Checking it in a browser

Numbers from a catalogue are one thing, so we loaded the pairs in headless Chromium, the Windows font from the system and the free one from Google Fonts, and measured the average width of a–z with canvas measureText:

Pair Average width, in em
Calibri / Carlito 0.4559 / 0.4559
Arial / Arimo 0.4895 / 0.4895
Segoe UI / TASA Explorer 0.4933 / 0.5265, 6.7% wider
Trebuchet MS / Merriweather Sans 0.5006 / 0.5472, 9.3% wider

The twins match to the fourth decimal. The look-alikes are off by about what the catalogue says.

Then one paragraph at 18px in a 380px column. TASA Explorer sets it in 6 lines, 132px tall. Segoe UI as the fallback sets it in 5 lines, 120px. That difference is the jump people see when the web font arrives.

The CSS

A metric twin needs nothing 

body {
  font-family: Calibri, Carlito, sans-serif;
}

Self-host Carlito (it's under the SIL Open Font License). Windows visitors with Calibri get the original, everyone else gets Carlito, and the line breaks are the same. Same idea for Helvetica, Arial, Arimo.

A look-alike needs a described fallback

When the web font only looks like the system font, give the browser a fallback face scaled to the web font's widths:

@font-face {
  font-family: "Segoe UI fallback";
  src: local("Segoe UI");
  size-adjust: 106.7%;
  ascent-override: 88.1%;
  descent-override: 24.4%;
  line-gap-override: 0%;
}

body {
  font-family: "TASA Explorer", "Segoe UI fallback", sans-serif;
}

With it, the fallback sets the same paragraph in 6 lines and 132px, exactly like TASA Explorer. The swap no longer moves anything.

Where the numbers come from:

  • size-adjust is the web font's average width over the fallback's: 0.5265 / 0.4933 = 106.7%.
  • ascent-override and descent-override are the web font's ascent and descent in em, divided by that size-adjust, because the overrides apply to the already scaled font.
  • line-gap-override is the web font's line gap, divided the same way. TASA Explorer has none.

You can get the first three in the browser console of any page that loads the web font:

function metrics(family) {
  const ctx = document.createElement('canvas').getContext('2d');
  ctx.font = `100px "${family}"`;
  let width = 0;
  for (const ch of 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz') width += ctx.measureText(ch).width;
  const box = ctx.measureText('H');
  return {
    avg: width / 26 / 100,
    ascent: box.fontBoundingBoxAscent / 100,
    descent: box.fontBoundingBoxDescent / 100,
  };
}

await document.fonts.load('100px "TASA Explorer"');
const web = metrics('TASA Explorer');
const fallback = metrics('Segoe UI');
const size = web.avg / fallback.avg;

console.log({
  sizeAdjust: `${(size * 100).toFixed(1)}%`,
  ascentOverride: `${((web.ascent / size) * 100).toFixed(1)}%`,
  descentOverride: `${((web.descent / size) * 100).toFixed(1)}%`,
});

Canvas doesn't expose the line gap. If the web font has one, read hhea.lineGap / unitsPerEm from the file, or set line-height explicitly and skip the question.

A few things to know:

  • local("Segoe UI") only exists on Windows. Add one fallback face per system font you expect (Segoe UI on Windows, Helvetica Neue on macOS, Roboto on Android) and list them in order.
  • If you use next/font, it already builds a fallback like this for you, from Arial or Times New Roman. The method is the same; a closer fallback just needs less scaling.
  • Chrome, Edge and Firefox support all four descriptors. Safari added size-adjust in version 17; check caniuse for the three overrides before you rely on them there.

Where to find the rest

Every font on FontKind with a "measured" label lists its 24 closest free fonts with the differences spelled out, and the compare tool puts up to six side by side in your own words. If there's a system or paid font you'd like measured against the free catalogue, say so in the comments.

title: Rotating mTLS Certificates Across Clouds Without Dropping Connections
description:
Mutual TLS fails in a particular way during rotation. The new certificate is valid, the old one has not expired yet, and traffic still breaks — because the two sides of a connection stopped trusting each other at different moments. In a single cloud that gap is usually minutes. Across clouds, where each platform has its own certificate authority, its own distribution mechanism, and its own reload behaviour, the gap can stretch to hours if nobody designed for it.

The problem is rarely cryptography. It is sequencing.

Two rotations, not one

Every mTLS rotation is actually two separate changes. First, what a service presents: its leaf certificate and key. Second, what a service trusts: the bundle of issuing roots it will accept from peers.

Those two changes must happen in opposite orders depending on direction, and they cannot safely happen at the same time. If a service starts presenting a certificate from a new authority before its peers trust that authority, peers reject it. If a service stops trusting the old authority before peers have stopped presenting certificates from it, it rejects them.

The safe sequence is always the same: widen trust first, wait until the wider trust bundle has actually reached every workload, then change what workloads present, wait again, and only then narrow trust back down. Skipping the waiting steps is where most rotation incidents come from.

Trust bundles do not propagate instantly, and they do not propagate the same way

Each cloud delivers trust material differently. One platform may push a new bundle when a workload restarts. Another may mount it as a file that a sidecar polls. A third may require a deployment to pick it up at all.

That means "the bundle was updated" is three different statements in a three-cloud estate, each true at a different time. A rotation plan that records a single timestamp for the whole estate is recording something that never happened.

Track propagation per platform, and verify it from the workload's point of view — what roots does this running process accept right now — rather than from the control plane's point of view. Control planes report intent. Workloads enforce reality, and they enforce the old reality until the new material is loaded and the process has actually re-read it. Some servers cache the bundle for the lifetime of a connection listener, so a file update alone changes nothing until a reload or a graceful restart.

Long-lived connections hide the change, then expose it all at once

Existing connections are usually not re-authenticated when certificates rotate. A connection established under the old trust keeps working, which makes early testing look reassuring — and misleading.

The break appears later, all at once, when connections churn: a deployment, a load balancer draining a node, a network blip that forces reconnects. Suddenly many clients reconnect under the new rules at the same moment, and any trust mismatch that was latent becomes an outage. This is also why rotation incidents often appear to be caused by an unrelated deploy hours later.

Plan for that. Rotate during a window where forced reconnects can be tested deliberately, in stages — reconnect a small slice of clients first and watch handshake failures before widening. A handshake failure rate, broken down by presenting authority and trusting side, is the signal that tells you which half of the sequence went wrong.

Short-lived certificates reduce one risk and raise another

Automated issuance with lifetimes measured in hours or days makes a missed rotation less catastrophic, because there is no single annual cliff edge, and it limits how long a compromised key stays useful. It also means issuance becomes a production dependency: if the issuer or the distribution path in one cloud stalls, workloads there start failing authentication as their certificates expire, with very little slack.

If certificates are short-lived, monitor time-to-expiry the way latency is monitored — as a distribution, not an average, and alerted well before the shortest lifetime in the estate. And test the issuer-outage case explicitly: what happens in each cloud when no new certificate can be issued for twice the normal renewal interval?

A rotation sequence that survives contact with three clouds

  1. Inventory every issuing authority in the estate and which workloads present and trust each one. Unknown authorities found in trust bundles are a finding in themselves.
  2. Publish the new authority into trust bundles everywhere, alongside the old one. Verify, from inside running workloads on each platform, that both are accepted.
  3. Force a controlled reconnect for a small slice of traffic and confirm handshakes succeed in both directions.
  4. Start presenting certificates from the new authority, platform by platform, watching handshake failures by authority pair.
  5. Wait until no workload still presents from the old authority — verified from observed handshakes, not from deployment status.
  6. Remove the old authority from trust bundles, again platform by platform, with the same workload-level verification.
  7. Record the measured propagation time for each platform. The next rotation plan should be built from those numbers, not from assumptions.

None of this needs a particular product. It needs the rotation to be treated as a distributed-systems change that happens to involve certificates, with the same staging, observation, and rollback discipline as a schema migration.

Teams that run these estates day to day — including the work described at CloudVerg around VergShield zero-trust controls and VergMesh private connectivity — tend to keep the trust inventory in the same place as the network design, so a new authority or a new cloud cannot be added without both being updated together. However the estate is built, the principle holds: widen trust, prove it arrived, then change what is presented — never the other way round.

title: HandsOnAid: Building and Evaluating an Offline First-Aid Assistant for Emergency Response Scenarios
description:
arXiv:2611.14059v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Emergencies can occur where there is no phone signal and no ambulance nearby. A small language model on a phone can be helpful in such situations, but its advice needs to be safe and accurate. We built HandsOnAid, a 4-bit Gemma 2B model fine-tuned with QLoRA on FirstAidQA dataset, a corpus of 5,550 first-aid question-answer pairs. We compared seven configurations, including the base, 4-bit and 8-bit fine-tuned models, and versions with a length floor, safety gate, or retrieval. We used a 41-pair question-answer bank with medically reviewed references that followed ANZCOR guidelines, and a strict 0-5 score rubric, with twelve safety overrides. Four frontier LLM judges (GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, DeepSeek V4 Pro, GLM-5.3) blindly scored every answer, with 45 hidden controls used to check judge reliability. Fine-tuning improved the mean score by +1.08 over the base model to 2.34. The best configuration scored 2.51 out of 5 which was the fine-tuned 4-bit model with retrieval. A medical professional also conducted a blind evaluation of 40 answers across the base, the 4-bit fine-tuned, and the retrieval configurations, and the scores were similar to the LLM judges' average scores. A keyword audit found limited coverage of several details of ANZCOR guidelines in the training corpus, that are required by the rubric, which suggests that missing information in the training data could be a cause of the low scores. On a smartphone device (Pixel 7 Pro) with six CPU threads and no network connection, the 4-bit fine-tuned model produced its first displayable text in 6.86 seconds and a complete answer in 14.88 seconds on average over ten questions.

title: From Bias to Positionality: A critical grammar for Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.14079v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bias has become a default lens for understanding what machine learning systems do and how we should relate to them. Bias is at root a deviation from a standard; in decision making systems we can supply a standard from outside: a law, a protected attribute, a benchmark, a statistical property. However, even there, biased is often used as a shorthand, without stating what the position taken is - a silent ``relative to''. In a general use of language models, nothing supplies the standard: there is no decision to audit and no counterfactual output, so the shorthand fails. We argue that positionality -- the located, articulated, owned and contestable position from which anything is said -- is the better grammar for the question these models now force: who is speaking, from where? Against the vendors' answer of nowhere and the seductive possibility of everywhere, we argue that when a model is taken as-if speaking, it speaks from somewhere, and this means positionality can describe models, and the way they are believed beyond their warrant, even though they are not accountable speakers. A model's positionality is laminar -- laid down across corpus, tuning, system prompt, application and the live conversation. We separate three sets of factors: the positionality of a model's creators, the behaviour they intend for it, and the behaviour it enacts, and situate current work within this matrix. This lets us highlight what each stratum inherits from the one below, with ruptures and collapses where that inheritance is disavowed. We then return to where models speak from, and discuss the implications for how models are made, read and held accountable.

title: Your input Handler Is Firing on Half a Character, and You Cannot Reproduce It
description:
A report comes in saying the search box "goes mad" while they type, or that the form will not accept their name, or that the character counter is wrong. You open the page, type the same thing, and everything is fine.

They are using an input method editor. You are not.

What a composition session is

An IME is how you type a language with more characters than keys. You type several keystrokes, the system shows a provisional string, and at some point you commit it and the real text lands. Japanese, Chinese and Korean most obviously, but the same machinery covers something far more common than that, which I will come back to.

The W3C UI Events specification calls this a composition session, and describes it as "one compositionstart event, one or more compositionupdate events" and "one compositionend event".

So far so reasonable. The part that breaks code is what happens inside the session.

Your input listener fires on the provisional text

Section 3.6.6 of the spec is titled "Input Events During Composition", and it sets the order: for each update, beforeinput, then compositionupdate, then input.

So input fires repeatedly, during the session, carrying text the user has not committed and in many cases would not recognise as anything they typed.

And then the sting, from the same section:

Since there are no DOM updates associated with the compositionend event, beforeinput and input events should not be sent at that time.

Read that twice if you have ever written field.addEventListener('input', validate). Your handler runs several times on provisional fragments, and then does not run at the moment the user finishes.

The practical results are all the ones in that bug report. A validator rejecting a half-formed string. A character counter counting the wrong thing. A search-as-you-type sending a request per keystroke of a word that does not exist yet. An autosave storing a fragment.

The flag that fixes it

Both InputEvent and KeyboardEvent carry isComposing, defined as:

true if the input event occurs as part of a composition session,

and, completing the sentence, "i.e., after a compositionstart event and before the corresponding compositionend event." Its uninitialized value "MUST be false", so on ordinary typing it is simply false and costs you nothing.

field.addEventListener('input', (e) => {
  if (e.isComposing) return          // provisional text, not a value yet
  handle(field.value)
})

// and because no input event arrives at the end of a session:
field.addEventListener('compositionend', () => handle(field.value))

Two listeners. The second one is the half people leave out, and leaving it out means an IME user's committed text is never processed at all.

The advice you will find, and why it is wrong

Search this problem and you will be told to check for keyCode === 229.

That does appear in the specification. It appears in section 7.3.1, under a heading that says, in the document's own words, "This section is non-normative", in a legacy appendix describing one historical model. The same document says plainly:

Authors SHOULD use the key attribute instead of the charCode and keyCode attributes.

It also notes that keyCode's values "are not normatively defined in this specification". So the famous number is not a rule, it is a description of what some implementations used to do. isComposing is the attribute that is actually specified for this, and it is on the event you are already handling.

One more correction while here: it is often said that key events stop during composition. The spec says the opposite. "During the composition session, keydown and keyup events MUST still be sent," and those events "MUST have the isComposing attribute set to true".

Why this is not only a CJK problem

Here is the line that should widen your idea of who is affected. The spec describes isComposing on the input event as true when the event is dispatched

during a dead key sequence or while an input method editor is active

Dead keys. A French, Czech, or Vietnamese layout, or a US-International layout, produces accented characters by a dead key followed by a letter. That is a composition session too. Anybody typing é, ñ, ô or ü can hit the same code path, on the same keyboard hardware you have.

Which is the honest reason this survives so long in so many codebases. It is not exotic. It is simply invisible from a machine configured the way yours is, and the people who hit it describe it in the only words available to them: it does not work when I type my name.

That sentence contains the entire bug and explains none of it, and no amount of re-reading the ticket will get you to a dead key.

Specification quotes are from the W3C UI Events Working Draft of 21 February 2026, which asks to be cited as a work in progress.

title: Bootstrapped On-Policy Distillation
description:
arXiv:2611.13680v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language models by distilling teacher predictions on student-generated trajectories, while on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) removes the need for an external teacher by using a reference-conditioned copy of the model as the teacher. Despite its great early improvements, we find that OPSD does not remain consistently effective under continued training and can eventually suffer substantial performance degradation. We study this training behavior and link the degradation to a growing mismatch between the evolving reference-free student and the frozen privileged teacher. In the early stage of OPSD, the privileged teacher remains closely aligned with the student and provides useful guidance for improving the student's generation trajectories. However, as training progresses, the growing distributional mismatch between the privileged teacher and reference-free student can cause the teacher to provide misleading supervision, ultimately degrading student performance. This phenomenon motivates us to first leverage privileged reference supervision to acquire useful knowledge and then transfer it to a fresh student. We introduce Bootstrapped On-Policy Distillation (BOPD), a two-stage framework that first uses OPSD to internalize task-relevant information from reference-conditioned supervision into an intermediate model, and then distills this reference-free intermediate model into a fresh copy of the initial model. Experiments across models show that BOPD improves mathematical reasoning and code generation beyond both the initial models and the constructed OPSD teachers. These results suggest that privileged reference supervision can be more effectively exploited by first transferring its task-relevant signal into a task-adapted model and then distilling from that model without reference conditioning.

title: Off-policy Learning with Excursion Policies
description:
arXiv:2611.13275v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Off-policy reinforcement learning (RL) tries to learn the value of a target policy while data comes from a different behavior policy. This often requires trading off bias for variance or stability. One way to trade these off is to linearly interpolate between the behavior and target policies, but this represents only one point in a broader space of interpolation mechanisms. We introduce excursion policies--a structured alternative where the agent follows the target policy for a multi-step "excursion" before reverting to the behavior policy. We derive dynamic programming results for these policies, establishing the theoretical basis for their use in RL. We further develop provably sound off-policy temporal-difference (TD) algorithms for excursion value estimation. We find that excursion policies provide an efficiency-stability trade-off comparable to mixture policies in continuous control benchmarks, and our analysis illustrates conceptual differences in their behavior.
