title: Java 方法的使用：定义、传参、重载与递归
description:
1. 方法是什么，怎样定义和调用

方法就是把完成某个功能的代码放在一起，起一个名字，需要时通过这个名字调用。 同一段逻辑可以反复使用，也能把复杂任务拆成几个更容易理解的小任务。

理解一个方法，先看三件事：接收什么数据（参数）、完成什么操作（方法体）、交回什么结果（返回值）。 方法也可以没有参数，或者没有返回值。

1.1 从一个完整程序入手 

public class MethodDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("调用前");
        int result = add(10, 20);
        System.out.println("调用后，结果为：" + result);
    }

    public static int add(int x, int y) {
        System.out.println("正在计算");
        return x + y;
    }
}

输出：

调用前
正在计算
调用后，结果为：30

add 的定义可以这样读：

部分 含义
public static 修饰符，本章先按这个固定写法使用，具体含义后续学习
int 返回值类型，表示方法交回一个 int 结果
add 方法名，通常使用小驼峰命名，如 isLeapYear
int x, int y 参数列表，表示调用时需要提供两个整数
{ ... } 方法体，调用时要执行的代码
return x + y; 把计算结果交回调用处，并结束本次方法调用

一般格式为：

public static 返回值类型 方法名(参数类型 形参名, 参数类型 形参名, ...) {
    方法体
}
  • 没有参数时，括号写成 ()；有多个参数时，用逗号分隔，每个参数都要写类型。
  • 没有返回值时，返回值类型写 void。
  • 本章的方法写在类的 {} 内，与 main 并列，不能把方法直接定义在另一个方法内部。
  • 同一个类中，方法写在 main 前面或后面都可以，不需要在调用前另写一条声明。

1.2 一次调用到底怎样执行

对上面的 int result = add(10, 20);：

  1. 把 10 和 20 分别传给 x、y。
  2. 进入 add，输出“正在计算”。此时 main 等待这次调用完成。
  3. 执行 return x + y;，得到 30，结束本次 add 调用。
  4. 回到原调用位置，相当于完成 int result = 30;。
  5. main 继续执行下一条语句。

定义方法不会自动执行方法体，调用才会执行；方法结束后，会回到调用处继续执行。 同一个方法可以被多次调用，每次使用这次传入的数据重新执行。

2. 返回值：把结果交回去，不是打印出来

2.1 返回、接收、打印是三件事

假设 add 只负责计算，不包含打印语句：

public static int add(int x, int y) {
    return x + y;
}

下面的语句放在同一个类的 main 中：

add(1, 2);                       // 执行计算，但丢弃返回值，不会输出
int result = add(1, 2);           // 用变量保存返回值
System.out.println(result);      // 输出 3
System.out.println(add(3, 4));    // 直接输出返回值 7
int twice = add(1, 2) * 2;        // 返回值参与运算，twice 为 6

有返回值不代表一定要用变量接收，但不使用它，就得不到这次计算的后续用途。 是否输出，取决于有没有执行打印语句。

例如，求 1 + 2 + ... + n 后再乘以 2：

public static int getSum(int n) {
    return (1 + n) * n / 2;
}

在 main 中调用 int result = getSum(10) * 2;，先得到 55，再计算出 110。

2.2 返回值类型必须兼容

方法返回的数据，要能赋给声明的返回值类型；接收结果的变量，也要能保存这个结果。

int a = add(1, 2);       // 正确
double b = add(1, 2);    // 正确：int 可以自动转换为 double

因此，“类型匹配”不等于必须逐字相同。反过来，不能把一个 double 返回值直接赋给 int 变量。

返回值也可以是布尔值。例如判断闰年：

public static boolean isLeapYear(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

条件表达式本身就是 true 或 false，可以直接返回。调用 System.out.println(isLeapYear(2024)); 会输出 true。

执行到 return 就会结束本次方法调用，不会继续向后执行。 对本章这些有返回值的方法，要保证每条可能正常结束的分支都能返回结果，不能只在某个 if 分支中返回，其他情况却没有返回值。

2.3 不需要交回结果时，用 void 

public static void print(int x, int y) {
    System.out.println("x = " + x + "，y = " + y);
}

在 main 中：

print(10, 20);                 // 正确：直接调用
// int result = print(10, 20); // 错误：void 方法没有值可以赋给变量

void 不表示“返回 0”，而是不返回任何值。这种方法可以执行到末尾结束，也可以使用不带值的 return; 提前结束。

选择返回值时，问自己：调用者是否还要使用计算结果？需要就返回；如果任务只是打印内容，不需要交回结果，就可以用 void。

3. 参数传递：形参拿到的是实参值的副本

3.1 分清形参和实参 

public static int add(int x, int y) { // x、y 是形参
    return x + y;
}

调用 add(a, 20) 时，a 和 20 是实参。

  • 形参：定义方法时写的变量，用来接收传入的数据。
  • 实参：调用方法时实际提供的值，可以是常量、变量或表达式。
  • 调用时按位置传递：第一个实参给第一个形参，第二个给第二个，依此类推。
  • 实参与形参的个数、顺序和类型要匹配；类型允许合法的自动转换。

例如，只有 getSum(int n) 时，getSum(10) 合法，而 getSum(10.9) 会编译失败，因为 double 不能直接传给 int 形参。

形参不要求与调用处的变量同名。add(a, b) 中的 a、b 与方法里的 x、y 是不同变量。

3.2 为什么 swap(a, b) 交换不了 a、b 

public class SwapDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int a = 10;
        int b = 20;
        swap(a, b);
        System.out.println("a = " + a + "，b = " + b);
    }

    public static void swap(int x, int y) {
        int temp = x;
        x = y;
        y = temp;
        System.out.println("x = " + x + "，y = " + y);
    }
}

输出：

x = 20，y = 10
a = 10，b = 20

执行过程：

阶段 main 中的变量 swap 中的变量
调用时复制值 a = 10，b = 20 x = 10，y = 20
交换形参后 a = 10，b = 20 x = 20，y = 10
调用结束后 a = 10，b = 20 本次调用中的局部变量不再使用

Java 始终按值传递参数。 对这里的 int 来说，复制的是整数值，x、y 不是 a、b 的别名，所以交换的是副本。

本章先掌握基本类型参数的这个结论；借助类和对象处理类似需求的方法，留到相应章节。

4. 用方法拆分任务：计算阶乘之和

计算 1! + 2! + 3! + 4! + 5!，可以拆成两个职责：

  • factorial(n)：只负责求一个数的阶乘。
  • main：依次调用，再把结果相加。 
public class FactorialSumDemo {
    public static int factorial(int n) {
        int result = 1;
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            result *= i;
        }
        return result;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int sum = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
            sum += factorial(i);
        }
        System.out.println(sum); // 153
    }
}

五次调用依次返回 1、2、6、24、120，相加得到 153。每次进入 factorial，都会重新创建并初始化自己的 result，不会沿用上一次的值。

这样写是把内部循环封装进方法，使任务更清楚；并没有消除内部循环，也没有自动减少运算次数。

5. 方法重载：同一个名字，接收不同参数

5.1 为什么需要重载

两个整数相加、两个小数相加、三个小数相加，做的都是“相加”，没必要分别起三个名字。可以使用同一个方法名，通过参数列表区分。

public class OverloadDemo {
    public static int add(int x, int y) {
        return x + y;
    }

    public static double add(double x, double y) {
        return x + y;
    }

    public static double add(double x, double y, double z) {
        return x + y + z;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(add(1, 2));           // 3
        System.out.println(add(1.5, 2.5));       // 4.0
        System.out.println(add(1.5, 2.5, 3.5));  // 7.5
    }
}

本章在同一个类中判断重载：方法名相同，参数列表不同。 编译器根据调用处的参数个数和类型等信息，确定调用哪个方法。

5.2 怎样才算“参数列表不同”

下面只比较方法名和参数类型，省略方法体：

变化 示例 能否构成重载
参数个数不同 add(int, int) 与 add(int, int, int) 能
参数类型不同 add(int, int) 与 add(double, double) 能
参数类型的排列顺序不同 add(int, double) 与 add(double, int) 能
只改变形参名字 add(int x, int y) 与 add(int a, int b) 不能
只改变返回值类型 int add(int, int) 与 double add(int, int) 不能

前三种差异满足一种即可，并不是要求同时满足。把两个 int 形参换个位置，类型序列仍是 (int, int)，也不能构成重载。

返回值类型不参与重载的区分。 例如 double result = add(1, 2);，在上例中调用的仍是 add(int, int)，然后把返回的 int 转换成 double，不会因为左边是 double 就选择小数版本。

5.3 方法签名与字节码中的描述符

对于本章的普通方法，方法签名可以理解为“方法名 + 参数类型列表”，不包括形参名字和返回值类型。例如 add(int, int) 与 add(double, double) 的签名不同，所以可以重载。参见 Java 语言规范：方法签名。

编译后，.class 字节码中还会使用方法描述符记录参数类型和返回值类型。它与源代码层面的方法签名不是同一概念，也不是把方法名改成一个长名字。

可使用 JDK 自带的 javap 查看。先编译，再进入 .class 所在目录执行：

javac OverloadDemo.java
javap -v OverloadDemo.class

描述符的格式是 (参数类型)返回值类型。例如：

方法 描述符 读法
int add(int x, int y) (II)I 接收两个 int，返回 int
double add(double x, double y) (DD)D 接收两个 double，返回 double
void main(String[] args) ([Ljava/lang/String;)V 接收 String 数组，没有返回值

描述符中的符号：

符号 含义
V void，用于返回值位置
Z boolean
B byte
C char
S short
I int
J long
F float
D double
[ 数组，一个 [ 表示一维，如 [I 表示 int[]
L类的内部名; 类类型，如 Ljava/lang/String; 表示 String

数组可以先理解为存放一组同类型数据的结构；这里的类名使用 / 分隔包名，记住 String 对应的写法即可，具体用法后续学习。

描述符包含返回值类型，并不意味着 Java 源代码允许仅凭返回值类型重载。 这两层规则要分开理解。参见 Java 虚拟机规范：方法描述符。

6. 递归：把问题交给规模更小的自己

6.1 递归的两个关键条件

一个方法在执行过程中调用自身，就是递归。 它适合把原问题转化成“规模更小、解法相同”的子问题。

写递归前，先回答：

  1. 什么时候直接得到答案，不再调用自己？ 这是递归出口。
  2. 怎样把问题缩小，并利用子问题的结果？ 每次调用都要向出口靠近。

只有出口但永远到不了出口，也不能正确结束。

6.2 递归求阶乘

对正整数 n：

  • 1! = 1，作为出口。
  • n! = n × (n - 1)!，把求 n! 转化为求 (n - 1)!。 
public static int factor(int n) {
    if (n == 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return n * factor(n - 1);
}

调用 factor(5) 得到 120。这个版本的输入要求是 n >= 1，不能传入 0 或负数，否则 n - 1 会不断远离出口；示例还要求结果不超出 int 范围。

6.3 重点：递进去之后，还要逐层返回

以 factor(4) 为例：

向下调用：
factor(4) 等待 4 * factor(3)
factor(3) 等待 3 * factor(2)
factor(2) 等待 2 * factor(1)
factor(1) 返回 1，停止继续调用

向上返回：
factor(2) 得到 1，计算 2 * 1，返回 2
factor(3) 得到 2，计算 3 * 2，返回 6
factor(4) 得到 6，计算 4 * 6，返回 24

return n * factor(n - 1); 不是遇到 return 就立刻跳走，而是先算出它后面的表达式，再把结果返回。因此，必须等待 factor(n - 1) 完成，才能乘以本层的 n。

每一层调用都有自己的 n。进入 factor(3) 不会把上一层的 n = 4 改成 3。

可以加入输出，观察进入和返回的顺序：

public static int factorTrace(int n) {
    System.out.println("进入：" + n);
    if (n == 1) {
        System.out.println("返回：1");
        return 1;
    }
    int result = n * factorTrace(n - 1);
    System.out.println("返回：" + result);
    return result;
}

调用 factorTrace(3) 的输出：

进入：3
进入：2
进入：1
返回：1
返回：2
返回：6

6.4 调用栈为什么能记住每一层

每次方法调用都会建立一个栈帧，保存这次调用的参数、局部变量、执行位置等信息；这些尚未结束的调用组成调用栈。

可以把它想成一叠记录纸：调用新方法时放上一张，方法返回时取走最上面一张，继续处理下面那张。因而，最后进入的方法先返回。

在最深处，调用关系是 main → factor(4) → factor(3) → factor(2) → factor(1)。factor(1) 返回后，恢复的是 factor(2)，不会直接跳过中间几层回到 main。在 IDEA 调试时，可以通过调用栈查看这些层次。

7. 递归练习：从拆分规律写出代码

以下方法都写在类中，在 main 中调用。示例使用非负整数或正整数，具体范围见各题；计算结果需在 int 能表示的范围内。

7.1 按顺序打印一个非负整数的每一位

对 1234，num / 10 得到前面的 123，num % 10 得到最后一位 4。要从左到右打印，就先处理前面的部分，再打印当前最后一位。

public static void printDigits(int num) {
    if (num > 9) {
        printDigits(num / 10);
    }
    System.out.println(num % 10);
}

调用 printDigits(1234)，会分四行输出 1、2、3、4。

printDigits(1234)：先处理 123，等它结束再打印 4
printDigits(123) ：先处理 12，等它结束再打印 3
printDigits(12)  ：先处理 1，等它结束再打印 2
printDigits(1)   ：不再递归，直接打印 1

返回时依次打印 2、3、4。递归调用之前的代码在向下调用时执行，之后的代码在返回后执行。 如果把打印放到递归调用前，就会先打印末位，顺序变为 4、3、2、1。

这里没有显式写 return 作为出口：当 num <= 9 时，跳过递归调用，打印后方法自然结束。输入 0 也会正确打印 0。

7.2 求 1 + 2 + ... + n

输入要求 n >= 1。设结果为 sumTo(n)：

  • 出口：sumTo(1) = 1。
  • 拆分：sumTo(n) = n + sumTo(n - 1)。 
public static int sumTo(int n) {
    if (n == 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return n + sumTo(n - 1);
}

sumTo(10) 返回 55。它和递归求阶乘的结构相同，只是把乘法换成了加法。

7.3 求一个非负整数的各位数字之和

对 1729，把问题拆成“最后一位 9 + 前面 172 的各位数字之和”。剩下一位数时，直接返回这个数。

public static int digitSum(int num) {
    if (num < 10) {
        return num;
    }
    return num % 10 + digitSum(num / 10);
}

digitSum(1729)
= 9 + digitSum(172)
= 9 + 2 + digitSum(17)
= 9 + 2 + 7 + digitSum(1)
= 9 + 2 + 7 + 1
= 19

注意两类题的区别：求 1 到 n 的和，每次用 n - 1；处理一个整数的各位数字，每次用 num / 10 去掉最后一位。

7.4 求斐波那契数列第 n 项

本题从第 1 项开始计数：1，1，2，3，5，8，13，...。前两项为 1，从第三项起，每项等于前两项之和，输入要求 n >= 1。

public static int fib(int n) {
    if (n == 1 || n == 2) {
        return 1;
    }
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}

例如 fib(6) 返回 8。

这个写法简洁，但会重复计算相同的子问题。

fib(5)
├── fib(4)
│   ├── fib(3)
│   └── fib(2)
└── fib(3)       ← 同一个 fib(3) 又算了一次

输入越大，重复计算越严重。计算一次 fib(40) 会得到 102334155，其中 fib(3) 会被调用 39088169 次。

若要统计次数，可以在类中、方法外定义 public static int count = 0;，并在 fib 的出口判断之后、递归调用之前加入：

if (n == 3) {
    count++;
}

count 是静态成员变量，这里只需理解为各次调用共同使用的计数器；每次重新统计前将其设为 0，调用结束后打印它。不能在 fib 内定义一个普通局部变量 count = 0 代替，因为每层调用都会有自己独立的计数。

本题可以用循环避免重复计算，只保留前两项：

public static int fibLoop(int n) {
    if (n == 1 || n == 2) {
        return 1;
    }
    int last2 = 1; // 当前要计算的项的前两项
    int last1 = 1; // 当前要计算的项的前一项
    int current = 0;
    for (int i = 3; i <= n; i++) {
        current = last2 + last1;
        last2 = last1;
        last1 = current;
    }
    return current;
}

每次先算出新的一项，再把“前两项、前一项”向后移动：

本次计算 更新前 last2 更新前 last1 current
第 3 项 1 1 2
第 4 项 1 2 3
第 5 项 2 3 5
第 6 项 3 5 8

递归适合表达问题的拆分关系，但不代表一定更高效。判断时既要看能否到达出口，也要看是否反复计算相同的子问题。

title: Neural Network-Assisted CLEAN for Efficient Multipath Parameter Estimation in MIMO Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.13298v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: High-resolution multipath estimation in wideband multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) channels requires repeated searches over angle of arrival, angle of departure, and propagation distance. This paper presents neural network-assisted CLEAN (NN-CLEAN), which replaces the multidimensional search at each extraction step with a multi-head classifier while retaining least-squares (LS) estimation of the complex path gain, parametric reconstruction, and residual cancellation. The same classifier is applied to successive residuals, allowing the extraction depth to vary without changing its output structure. With the number of iterations prescribed by the reference multipath-component (MPC) count, off-grid synthetic tests show that NN-CLEAN slightly exceeds grid-search CLEAN (GS-CLEAN) in path accuracy for one and two MPCs, although its accuracy declines more rapidly at larger path counts. For complete three-MPC extraction at a batch size of eight, NN-CLEAN achieves an approximately $27\times$ speedup and a $52$-fold reduction in peak GPU memory relative to GS-CLEAN. Applied without retraining to two-MPC line-of-sight (LOS) and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) Sionna ray-tracing channels within a coded MIMO link, NN-CLEAN substantially reduces channel-reconstruction mean-squared error (MSE) and bit error rate (BER) relative to interpolated LS channel estimation. GS-CLEAN retains an accuracy advantage on these channels, indicating the estimation cost associated with the computational savings.

title: UNDERSTANDING IaaS THROUGH AMAZON EC2: A BEGINNER'S GUIDE
description:
Understanding Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): A Case Study of Amazon EC2

Introduction

Technology has changed the way individuals and organizations store data, run applications, and manage their computing resources. In the past, organizations had to purchase physical servers, storage devices, and networking equipment to operate their IT systems. This required significant financial investment, maintenance, and technical expertise.

Cloud computing provides an alternative by allowing organizations to access computing resources over the internet. One of its major service models is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS).

This article explains IaaS, how it works, its benefits and challenges, using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), a service offered by Amazon Web Services (AWS), as a case study.

What is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?

Infrastructure as a Service is a cloud computing model in which a cloud provider offers computing resources such as virtual servers, storage, and networking over the internet.

Instead of purchasing and maintaining physical hardware, customers rent these resources from a cloud provider and use them according to their needs.

IaaS gives customers control over important computing resources, including their operating systems, applications, and data, while the provider manages the underlying physical infrastructure.

Case Study: Amazon EC2

Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is a computing service provided by AWS. It allows users to create and manage virtual servers called instances in the cloud.

These instances provide computing capacity without requiring customers to own physical servers.

For example, imagine a small business in Cameroon that wants to develop and host its own website. Traditionally, the business would need to purchase a physical server, install an operating system, provide storage, and maintain the equipment.

With Amazon EC2, the business can rent a virtual server, install its preferred operating system, configure the necessary software, and host its website through the internet.

This demonstrates how IaaS makes computing infrastructure available without requiring customers to purchase the physical equipment.

How Amazon EC2 Works

Amazon EC2 operates by providing virtual computing resources through AWS’s cloud infrastructure.

The process involves the following steps:

  1. Creating an AWS account: The user creates an account and accesses the AWS Management Console.

  2. Selecting a virtual server: The user chooses an EC2 instance with suitable computing resources, such as processor capacity and memory.

  3. Selecting an operating system: The user selects an operating system, such as Linux or Windows, using an Amazon Machine Image (AMI).

  4. Configuring security and networking: The user configures network access and security settings to control communication with the virtual server.

  5. Launching the instance: AWS provisions the virtual server, making it available for the user to access and manage.

  6. Installing and running applications: The user can install software, host websites, store and process data, or run other applications.

Major Features of Amazon EC2

Amazon EC2 provides several features that make it useful for individuals and organizations.

  1. Virtual servers: EC2 allows users to create virtual machines without purchasing physical servers.

  2. Scalability: Users can increase or decrease their computing capacity depending on their requirements.

  3. Flexible pricing: Users can choose different purchasing options, including On-Demand Instances, where they pay for the computing capacity they use.

  4. Storage: EC2 works with Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS), which provides persistent storage volumes for virtual servers.

  5. Security: EC2 provides security groups, which act as virtual firewalls to control incoming and outgoing network traffic.

  6. Networking: Users can configure networking resources and control how their virtual servers communicate with other systems.

Benefits of Using Amazon EC2 as an IaaS Solution

Amazon EC2 offers several advantages:

  • Reduced hardware costs: Organizations do not need to purchase expensive physical servers before deploying applications.
  • Flexibility: Users can select computing resources that suit their workloads.
  • Scalability: Computing resources can be adjusted as demand changes.
  • Accessibility: Virtual servers can be accessed and managed remotely through the internet.
  • Faster deployment: Users can provision virtual servers without waiting to purchase and install physical hardware.
  • Resource management: Organizations can monitor and manage their computing resources according to their requirements.

Challenges of Using Amazon EC2

Despite its advantages, Amazon EC2 also has some challenges.

  1. Internet dependency: Accessing and managing cloud resources generally requires a reliable internet connection.

  2. Security responsibilities: Although AWS provides security tools, customers must properly configure their operating systems, access permissions, applications, and data protection measures.

  3. Cost management: Poor resource management can result in unexpected expenses, especially when users leave unnecessary resources running.

  4. Technical knowledge: Users need some technical understanding to configure, secure, and maintain their virtual servers.

Conclusion

Infrastructure as a Service has transformed how individuals and organizations obtain and manage computing resources. Through services such as Amazon EC2, users can access virtual servers, storage, and networking without purchasing and maintaining their own physical infrastructure.

Amazon EC2 demonstrates how virtualization, scalability, flexible resource allocation, and cloud-based infrastructure work together to make IaaS possible.

As organizations continue to adopt cloud computing, IaaS remains an important solution for reducing hardware investments, improving flexibility, and supporting the development and deployment of modern applications.

References

  1. Amazon Web Services. What is Amazon EC2? https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/concepts.html
  2. Amazon Web Services. Amazon EC2 Security Groups. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-security-groups.html
  3. Amazon Web Services. Amazon EC2 Pricing. https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/pricing/

title: Five Users Is a Stop Rule, Not a Sample Size
description:
Every front-end team has inherited some version of this: "we don't need real usability data, Nielsen said five users is enough." The recommendation is real. The way it gets quoted into standups is not. Five users is a stopping rule for problem discovery. It is not a sample size for anything you want to measure, and the difference is arithmetic you can implement in about twenty lines.


Conceptual AI-generated cover for this article, composited with the unchanged official Design Den Solutions logo. The logo artwork itself is not AI-generated.

The model behind the number

Jakob Nielsen's original claim (Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users, NN/g, 18 March 2000) is a coverage model, not a headcount heuristic:

P(n) = 1 - (1 - L)^n
  • n = testers in the round
  • L = the proportion of the total problem set that one tester finds
  • P = cumulative proportion of the problem set found after n testers

Nielsen used L = 0.31, which lands at ~85% at n = 5. He was explicit that this is a cost/benefit stopping point, not a completeness claim: "The best results come from testing no more than 5 users," and in the same article, "You need to test with at least 15 users to discover all the usability problems." His 2012 restatement (How Many Test Users in a Usability Study?) keeps "test 5 users in a qualitative usability study" and gives the reason not to inflate n: "ROI drops like a stone with a bigger N."

const coverage = (L, n) => 1 - (1 - L) ** n;

for (let n = 1; n <= 8; n++) {
  const prev = n === 1 ? 0 : coverage(0.31, n - 1);
  console.log(
    `n=${n}  total=${(coverage(0.31, n) * 100).toFixed(1)}%  ` +
    `this tester adds ${((coverage(0.31, n) - prev) * 100).toFixed(1)} pts`
  );
}
// n=1 total=31.0% this tester adds 31.0 pts
// n=3 total=67.1% this tester adds 14.8 pts
// n=5 total=84.4% this tester adds  7.0 pts
// n=8 total=94.9% this tester adds  2.3 pts

That marginal column is the entire argument. Tester five returns roughly a fifth of tester one's yield. The model assumes equal findability across problems, which is false in practice: a label nobody clicks is nearly invisible to every tester, while a broken button is found by the first person who touches it. So L is not measurable before the round, and 85% is a planning figure, not a guarantee. At L = 0.20, five testers cover 67.2%; at L = 0.15, 55.6%.

Implement the stop rule, not the magic number

The useful engineering artefact is a uniqueness curve over the problems you have actually logged:

function shouldStop(problemLog, testersNeeded = 2) {
  const firstSeen = new Map();
  problemLog.forEach((p, i) => { if (!firstSeen.has(p.id)) firstSeen.set(p.id, i); });

  const newPerTester = Array.from({ length: problemLog.length }, (_, t) =>
    [...firstSeen.values()].filter((i) => i === t).length
  );

  const tail = newPerTester.slice(-testersNeeded);
  return {
    newPerTester,
    stop: tail.every((x) => x === 0),
    reason: `last ${testersNeeded} testers surfaced ${tail.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)} new problem classes`
  };
}

"Stop" is not "five reached". It is "the last two testers produced no problem class you had not already recorded". On a checkout flow with one obvious blocker, that can happen at three. On a genuinely untested dashboard, it may not happen until seven. Five is the expected cost of a round, not the exit condition.

What five people cannot tell you

This is where teams write a number into a deck that the data cannot carry.

Three of five testers abandon the enquiry form. Someone reports "60% of users fail the form". Five is not a survey; the correct statement is an interval.

function wilson(k, n, z = 1.96) {
  const p = k / n, d = 1 + (z * z) / n;
  const c = (p + (z * z) / (2 * n)) / d;
  const h = (z * Math.sqrt((p * (1 - p)) / n + (z * z) / (4 * n * n))) / d;
  return [Math.max(0, c - h), Math.min(1, c + h)];
}

wilson(3, 5);   // [0.23, 0.88]  -> "23% to 88%"
wilson(12, 20); // [0.39, 0.78]

A 65-point-wide interval is not a conversion finding. To hold ±10 points around a 60% success rate you need n = z²p(1−p)/e² ≈ 93. If the goal is a rate — task success, completion time, benchmark against a competitor — that is a quantitative study with a different budget, and no amount of qualitative rounds substitutes for it.

Two more things five users will not do:

  • Prove the redesign worked. Before/after on five people each is anecdote with a delta.
  • Establish accessibility conformance. WCAG is a standard you audit against, not a headcount. Contrast under SC 1.4.3 is 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text, computed from relative luminance. Five sighted testers will not tell you whether your orange-on-white passes, and neither will fifty.

And one that is easy to get wrong: five per study is not five per audience. The NN/g guidance is "you'll need close to 5 users per group". Split across two personas, each group gets 2.5 people and the model's single-population assumption no longer applies.

Rounds beat bigger N

A second round of five after the fixes is not a repeat of the first. It runs against a changed interface, so it can surface problems the first round structurally could not reach — the flow you just unblocked, the copy you just rewrote, the regression you just shipped. One round of ten would find 97.6% of the problems that existed at the start, and 0% of the ones created by your fixes. Iteration is the point; Nielsen's own phrasing is to "plan for a lot of iterations".

Make each session produce a bug, not a vibe

Instrument the same fields every time so the round aggregates:

{
  "task": "find out whether installation is included",
  "tester": "T3",
  "completed": false,
  "helpRequested": true,
  "timeOnTaskSec": 143,
  "firstClick": ".pricing-card",
  "quote": "I can't tell if they fit it or just sell it",
  "problemIds": ["pricing-scope-ambiguous"],
  "severity": "serious"
}

Severity rubric that survives review: blocker = cannot complete without help; serious = completes with visible struggle or a wrong assumption; cosmetic = preference, no task impact. Then write the finding the way you would write a defect: task, page or selector, observed action, user's stated goal, consequence. pricing-scope-ambiguous with two testers and a quote is actionable. "Users find pricing confusing" is not.

Two operational constraints worth putting in the test script before you invite anyone:

  1. Consent and data. Record only with explicit consent, store the minimum, and never let a tester enter real personal data, make a payment, or fire a live enquiry into your own production system. Use a staging environment or stop at the boundary.
  2. Recruit for the actual population. Colleagues share your mental model and will silently repair your copy for you. Five strangers beat five teammates every time.

The honest summary

Five users is the cheapest round that reliably produces a ranked fix list, because the marginal yield collapses right after it. Use it to decide what to build next. Do not use it to report a percentage, to certify accessibility, or to claim a lift. Those are different studies, and the arithmetic above will tell you the sample size you actually need before you promise anyone a number.

References

  • Nielsen, J. Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users. Nielsen Norman Group, 18 Mar 2000.
  • Nielsen, J. How Many Test Users in a Usability Study? Nielsen Norman Group, 3 Jun 2012.
  • W3C, Understanding SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), WCAG 2.2.

All percentages come from the discovery model and the code shown above, which was executed before publishing; no client data or user metrics are represented.

title: Enterprise DSPM Rollout Framework: Timeline, Resource Allocation, and Effort Estimation for Vendor Evaluation and Budgeting
description:
Foundational Discovery and Governance Alignment

Enterprise Data Security Posture Management (DSPM) solutions are frequently marketed as turnkey integrations: a single API credential dropped into a cloud tenant promises a fully populated, classified asset inventory within forty-eight hours. Production realities directly contradict this vendor narrative. When a scanner hooks into a multi-petabyte cloud estate spanning heterogeneous environments (such as AWS S3, Azure Blob, and distributed SaaS repositories like Salesforce and SharePoint), unmanaged ingestion pipelines saturate immediately. Unconstrained parallel metadata extraction triggers HTTP 429 throttling errors via cloud provider token-bucket algorithms, exhausts thread pool memory allocations, and causes worker nodes to crash under payload saturation.

Achieving structural viability requires treating this initial phase as a rigorous systems architecture engineering challenge rather than an administrative checkbox. When security, data engineering, and GRC teams fail to establish explicit data estate boundaries prior to deployment, the scanning engine executes unstructured operations, generating systemic resource contention across three distinct technical vectors:

  • Exponential Regular Expression Backtracking: In the absence of granular classification profiles, scanner worker threads execute overly broad regex patterns against binary payloads or massive log files. Nested quantifiers within these unoptimized patterns trigger catastrophic backtracking in the parsing engine, locking CPU cores, thread-starving worker processes, and artificially inflating latency metrics across production storage accounts.
  • Divergent Permission Inheritance Paradigms: On-premises file shares, object storage buckets, and identity providers evaluate Access Control Lists (ACLs) and IAM policies through fundamentally incompatible mechanical models. If GRC teams fail to reconcile these trust boundaries before execution, the DSPM engine miscalculates actual exposure paths. This generates high volumes of false positives, misinterpreting assets as publicly exposed due to permissive root-level inheritance that is structurally overridden by explicit bucket or service-control policies.
  • Metadata Store Write-Queue Saturation: Ingesting millions of object headers, ACL matrices, and schema definitions floods the DSPM’s backing graph or relational database. Without scoped discovery boundaries, transactional write volumes outpace database index update capacity, causing cascading transaction timeouts, index fragmentation, and complete interface unresponsiveness during initial sweeps.

True time-to-value necessitates calibrating the ingestion engine directly against network bandwidth limits, IOPS ceilings, and API rate-limiting thresholds. Enterprise-scale deployment demands a dedicated sixty-to-ninety-day window of iterative boundary scoping and regex optimization before any actionable, low-noise risk intelligence can be reliably surfaced.

Platform Integration and Initial Scans

Enterprise software vendors routinely market Data Security Posture Management (DSPM) deployment as a frictionless 48-hour administrative exercise: drop in a cross-account IAM role, configure service principals, and let the discovery engine map the data estate. Operationally, this abstraction collapses under the weight of heterogeneous enterprise cloud architecture. Realizing a reliable return on investment requires reframing DSPM not as a plug-and-play utility, but as a foundational component of a structured 12-to-18-month rollout that demands deliberate, cross-functional resource allocation across visibility, classification, and remediation phases. When uncalibrated connectors execute parallelized metadata extraction across petabyte-scale storage tiers without architectural bounds, they trigger severe mechanical failures that stall time-to-value.

The primary point of operational friction lies in ingestion mechanics and cloud-native API rate limiting. Unconstrained parallel requests directed at object stores—such as AWS S3 or Azure Blob storage—systematically exhaust token-bucket rate-limiting algorithms, returning recurring HTTP 429 throttling errors. As internal retry queues swell exponentially, worker threads lock system memory allocations while awaiting socket acknowledgments. This cascade precipitates thread-pool exhaustion, destabilizing runtime workers and ultimately crashing the core scanning gateway daemon.

Furthermore, naive regex scanning against unindexed unstructured data introduces severe compute bottlenecks. When broad regular expressions featuring nested quantifiers parse massive log files or binary payloads, the scanning engine enters catastrophic backtracking. CPU core execution threads lock at 100 percent utilization as the matching algorithm cycles through exponential permutations, starving other worker processes and inflating storage I/O latency across connected production workloads.

Complex permission inheritance models compound these discovery failures. Mechanical discrepancies between cloud-native Access Control Lists (ACLs) and hierarchical Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies frequently confound automated scanners. When a root-level inheritance rule is overridden by an explicit service-control policy or boundary condition, the DSPM engine misinterprets the resulting access boundary, generating a high volume of false-positive exposure alerts that overwhelm compliance teams.

To bypass these structural failure vectors, engineering teams must abandon turnkey assumptions and institutionalize rigorous mechanical boundaries during the initial visibility phase (Months 1 through 3):

  • Data Estate Boundary Scoping: Isolate high-churn operational buckets from cold storage archives to prevent metadata store write-queue saturation. Unscoped ingestion of object headers and ACL matrices floods backing graph or relational databases, causing transactional write volumes to outpace index update capacity, resulting in transaction timeouts and index fragmentation.
  • Engine Calibration: Rate-limit ingestion threads directly against backing network bandwidth ceilings, cloud provider IOPS limits, and explicit API rate-limiting thresholds to prevent downstream resource starvation.
  • Regex Optimization: Strip nested quantifiers and anchor search patterns to prevent CPU core locking and thread starvation during deep content inspection.

Without budgeting for this mandatory calibration period and its cross-functional governance overhead, organizations face chronically stalled discovery phases, inflated cloud egress and storage costs, and a data inventory riddled with noise rather than actionable risk intelligence.

Risk Triage and Policy Tuning

Once initial visibility and classification engines stabilize, the operational bottleneck shifts inexorably to triage. Although enterprise security vendors market automated risk scoring as a frictionless turnkey capability, raw alert volume inevitably overwhelms security operations centers (SOCs) unless underlying permission evaluation mechanics are systematically tuned.

The primary driver of high-noise triage queues is permission inheritance divergence. Multi-tenant cloud platforms rarely rely on a monolithic access model; instead, they enforce authorization through a compounding hierarchy of legacy Access Control Lists (ACLs), granular Identity and Access Management (IAM) trust policies, and organizational Service Control Policies (SCPs). When a DSPM engine evaluates a storage bucket's public-read ACL in isolation without parsing the overriding structural denial enforced by a parent SCP, it registers a false-positive critical exposure on an operationally secure asset. This compounding evaluation gap floods the SOC triage pipeline with phantom vulnerabilities, eroding analyst trust and depleting engineering bandwidth.

To neutralize this architectural friction and establish a resilient triage framework, security engineering teams must operationalize four core controls:

  • Filter False Positives via Policy Correlation: Execute graph-based policy simulation against raw findings. Cross-referencing raw asset states with calculated effective permissions suppresses phantom alerts generated by rule precedence and implicit denials.
  • Automate Data Owner Mapping: Codify accountability by programmatically parsing resource tags, Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) state files, and IAM assume-role trust relationships. Mapping discovered data stores directly to internal business units eliminates the manual overhead of identifying orphan assets.
  • Prioritize Exposures by Blast Radius: Rank risk scores through compounding threat vectors—correlating data classification sensitivity (e.g., PII, PHI, financial records) with active exposure vectors, such as public internet route-ability and unencrypted at-rest states—to prevent alert fatigue.
  • Establish Remediation Workflows: Integrate verified findings directly into developer ticketing pipelines via API webhooks. Enforce automated remediation scripts for low-risk misconfigurations while embedding mandatory manual review gates for production data stores housing regulated assets.

Omitting this rigorous tuning phase degrades the DSPM platform from an enterprise risk-reduction instrument into an expensive, high-noise dashboard. In such environments, analyst burnout and alert fatigue inevitably combine to bury genuine exposures beneath thousands of false alarms.

Operationalization and Continuous Monitoring: Sustaining Posture Without Analyst Burnout

Vendors routinely market Data Security Posture Management (DSPM) as a plug-and-play solution capable of achieving steady-state operation within 48 hours. In reality, moving past the initial 12-to-18-month rollout into continuous monitoring exposes a fundamental engineering friction: cloud infrastructure is never static. Ephemeral serverless functions, automated Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) deployments, and continuous developer data mutations constantly rewrite storage boundaries, which outpaces static inventory mechanisms. Without a disciplined operational framework, continuous scanning engines inevitably overwhelm internal security teams with stale alerts and high-noise false positives.

Transitioning from Triage to Continuous Cadence

To prevent operational fatigue and maintain an accurate data posture, organizations must shift from reactive alert triage to a structured, automated governance cadence. This requires integrating DSPM telemetry directly into existing CI/CD pipelines and enforcing strict feedback loops between data owners and security operations.

title: The Shape of a Program: Path Signatures for Trace-to-Program Induction
description:
arXiv:2611.13005v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Synthesizing programs from execution traces is a fundamental challenge in algorithmic interpretability and the reverse engineering of complex systems. We bring a rough-path-theoretic perspective to program induction, treating execution traces as high-dimensional rough paths and encoding them with the path signature transform, a tool from stochastic analysis whose expectation provably characterizes the distribution of traces a program induces. On three program-induction domains, Karel, List, and RASP, our log-signature trace encoder outperforms LSTM, Transformer, and Fourier baselines in almost every setting, with its largest margins when training data is scarce. We further observe that the trace-to-program pipeline is naturally contractive: it often produces valid programs that are shorter than the ground truth. We turn this into a bootstrapping procedure that exposes redundancy in the ground-truth supervision without any external oracle, which we demonstrate on redundancy-injected versions of our datasets. Finally, the log-signature encoder induces a markedly more interpretable latent geometry than the baselines, in which the nearest neighbors of every state lie on its own execution trace.

title: Cognitive Mapping of Learning by Thinking Mechanisms in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.14382v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly exhibit capabilities that resemble human Learning by Thinking (LbT), the acquisition of new insight through internal processes such as explanation and reasoning, without new external input. A systematic account of the cognitive mechanisms behind these capabilities, and of their limits, remains underdeveloped. This paper proposes a Cognitive LbT Framework that maps four mechanisms (Reflective Reasoning, Synthetic Memory Formation, Internal Simulation, and Conceptual Self-Organization) onto computational processes in LLMs. Drawing on representative methods, including chain-of-thought prompting, self-consistency, self-reflection, Tree-of-Thoughts search, Self-Instruct, and self-taught reasoning, the analysis argues that selected methods can functionally approximate aspects of these mechanisms and can improve performance on some tasks without additional labeled examples, although this does not always constitute durable learning in model parameters. For example, Self-Instruct generated approximately 52,000 instructions from 175 seed tasks and reported a 33% absolute improvement on Super-NaturalInstructions (Y. Wang et al., 2023). The same mechanisms also produce characteristic failures, including hallucination diffusion, model collapse, concept drift, and high computational cost. These failures are not isolated technical defects but follow from four structural asymmetries between LLMs and human cognition: the identity of generator and monitor, closed learning loops without external grounding, symbolic rather than sensorimotor simulation, and the cost of inference-time computation. The framework yields testable propositions about when LbT in LLMs should succeed or fail and offers a structured basis for designing more reliable autonomous learning systems.

title: AdjointFlow: Accelerating Scientific Inverse Problems with Physics-Based Transport
description:
arXiv:2611.13389v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Inverse problems are ubiquitous across scientific applications ranging from seismic imaging to astrophysics to nondestructive testing, yet classical solvers often struggle with nonconvexity and repeated evaluations of expensive physical models. Diffusion models can amortize this computation offline, but largely data-driven conditional models underutilize known physics and suffer from ill-conditioned transport maps when the target distribution is concentrated. Plug-and-play (PnP) methods explicitly leverage the physical model to guide a learned prior, improving data consistency but reintroducing costly iterative computations. We instead propose AdjointFlow, a framework built on stochastic interpolants that injects the known physics into the generative transport itself. We design a data-dependent, adjoint-based initialization to reduce transport distance to the target, modify the transport velocity to remain regular as the endpoint distributions concentrate, and parameterize the network to build the initialization directly into the learned velocity. Together, these enable accurate reconstruction at substantially lower cost than generative models starting from Gaussian noise. Experiments on inverse scattering, seismic imaging, and black hole imaging show that AdjointFlow consistently produces more accurate reconstructions than conditional diffusion models while being up to five orders of magnitude faster at inference than PnP methods. Optional inference-time refinement that queries the physical model can further improve data consistency, matching or exceeding the accuracy of PnP methods without retraining.

title: Java 类和对象（一）
description:
1. 从“完成哪些步骤”到“让哪个对象做什么”

面向过程关注完成一件事需要哪些步骤；面向对象关注由哪些对象参与、每个对象负责什么，以及对象之间如何配合。

例如洗衣服：

  • 面向过程：依次考虑加水、浸泡、搓洗、漂洗、拧干等步骤。
  • 面向对象：把洗衣机看作一个对象，给它放入衣物、设置时间并启动，由洗衣机完成内部的洗涤过程。

面向对象不是没有步骤，而是把相关数据和操作组织到对象中。两者都是解决问题的思路，没有绝对的优劣。

Java 支持面向对象编程，简称 OOP（Object-Oriented Programming）。

2. 类、对象与成员

2.1 类描述“有什么”和“能做什么”

类是一种自定义类型，用来描述一类对象共同具有的属性和行为。

例如描述宠物狗：

要描述的内容 Java 中的表示 例子
属性：有什么数据 成员变量，也叫字段 名字、颜色
行为：能做什么 成员方法 叫、摇尾巴

使用 class 定义类：

public class PetDog {
    public String name;
    public String color;

    public void bark() {
        System.out.println(name + "：汪汪汪！");
    }

    public void wag() {
        System.out.println(name + "：摇尾巴！");
    }
}
  • 成员变量定义在类中、方法外；方法内部声明的变量是局部变量。
  • 类名使用大驼峰，例如 PetDog、WashMachine；变量名和方法名通常使用小驼峰。
  • 本章的成员统一使用 public，表示允许外部访问；访问权限的完整规则后续再学。
  • 上面的成员方法不加 static，需要通过具体对象调用。

通常一个源文件放一个类。上面的 public 类必须保存在 PetDog.java 中；如果修改类名，文件名也要同步修改，使用开发工具的重命名功能更稳妥。

2.2 类是模板，对象是具体实例

PetDog 描述宠物狗有哪些数据、能做哪些事；“阿黄”和“赛虎”则是根据这个类创建出的两个具体对象。

可以把类理解成房屋设计图，把对象理解成按图建造的房屋：一张设计图能建多套房屋，一个类也能创建多个对象。 每个对象都有自己的实例成员变量。

定义类只是定义类型，不等于已经创建了这个类的对象。

3. 创建对象并访问成员

3.1 用 new 实例化对象

通过类创建对象的过程叫实例化。

PetDog dog = new PetDog();

这条语句可以拆开理解：

部分 含义
PetDog 变量的类型
dog 引用变量，用来引用对象
new PetDog() 创建并初始化一个 PetDog 对象
= 将新对象的引用赋给 dog

引用变量不是对象本身。 可以把引用暂时理解成“找到对象的线索”。

PetDog dog;        // 只声明局部引用变量，没有创建对象，也还不能读取它
dog = new PetDog(); // 创建对象，把引用赋给 dog

3.2 用 . 访问成员

访问格式：

引用.成员变量
引用.成员方法(实参)

将下面的代码保存为 Main.java，与前面的 PetDog.java 放在同一目录：

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        PetDog dog1 = new PetDog();
        dog1.name = "阿黄";
        dog1.color = "黄色";

        PetDog dog2 = new PetDog();
        dog2.name = "赛虎";
        dog2.color = "黑色";

        dog1.bark();
        dog2.wag();

        dog1.color = "白色";
        System.out.println(dog2.color);
    }
}

输出：

阿黄：汪汪汪！
赛虎：摇尾巴！
黑色

两次 new 创建了两个对象，修改 dog1 所引用对象的颜色，不会改变另一个对象的颜色。

3.3 null 不是“空对象” 

PetDog dog = null;

这表示 dog 没有引用任何对象，不是创建了一个内容为空的对象。此时不能通过 dog 访问实例成员，否则会出现空指针异常。

一个引用变量在同一时刻只能引用一个对象，或者为 null；它不能同时指向多个对象。

4. this：当前对象的引用

4.1 为什么 year = year 没有修改成员变量？

假设日期类有成员变量 year，方法也有同名参数：

public void setDate(int year, int month, int day) {
    year = year;
    month = month;
    day = day;
}

这里的参数遮蔽了同名成员变量，year = year 的左右两边都指向参数，相当于把参数赋给它自己，对象中的成员变量没有变化。

解决办法是用 this.成员变量 明确指出对象中的字段：

public class Date {
    public int year;
    public int month;
    public int day;

    public void setDate(int year, int month, int day) {
        this.year = year;
        this.month = month;
        this.day = day;
    }

    public void printDate() {
        System.out.println(this.year + "-" + this.month + "-" + this.day);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Date d1 = new Date();
        Date d2 = new Date();

        d1.setDate(2021, 6, 9);
        d2.setDate(2022, 7, 10);

        d1.printDate();
        d2.printDate();
    }
}

输出：

2021-6-9
2022-7-10

以 this.year = year 为例：

  • 左边 this.year：当前对象的成员变量。
  • 右边 year：本次调用传入的参数。

4.2 谁调用方法，this 就引用谁

  • 执行 d1.setDate(...) 时，方法里的 this 引用 d1 所引用的对象。
  • 执行 d2.setDate(...) 时，方法里的 this 引用 d2 所引用的对象。

所以，同一个成员方法能够处理不同对象的数据。调用时不需要额外传入 this，Java 会隐式提供当前对象的引用；也不要在普通参数列表里手动添加所谓的 this 参数。

在没有同名局部变量或参数遮蔽时，访问当前对象的成员可以省略 this。例如上面 printDate() 中的 this.year 可以简写成 year。

记住以下用法与限制：

写法或规则 含义
this.成员变量 访问当前对象的成员变量
this.成员方法(实参) 调用当前对象的成员方法
this 的类型 在本例中是 Date 类型
不能写 this = ... 不能让 this 改为引用另一个对象
static 方法中不能使用 this 静态方法不依附于某一个对象，没有当前对象

main 是 static 方法，因此需要先创建对象，再通过引用访问实例成员。this 也能用于构造方法，下面会用到。

5. 对象中的数据如何初始化？

5.1 成员变量有默认值，局部变量不能照搬

局部变量必须在读取前被赋值：

int a;
// System.out.println(a); // 编译错误：变量 a 可能尚未初始化

但对象的成员变量会自动获得默认值：

成员变量类型 默认值
byte、short、int 0
long 0L
float 0.0f
double 0.0d
char '\u0000'，不是字符 '0'，也不是空格
boolean false
引用类型，如 String、数组、自定义类 null

使用上一节中尚未定义构造方法的 Date 类：

Date d = new Date();
d.printDate(); // 0-0-0

d 这个局部变量已被赋予对象引用，而对象中的三个 int 字段获得了默认值 0。

注意：String 字段的默认值是 null，不是空字符串 ""；日期字段默认为 0，也不代表这个日期有实际意义。

5.2 就地初始化：声明字段时直接赋值 

public class Date {
    public int year = 1900;
    public int month = 1;
    public int day = 1;
}

此时执行 new Date()，得到的日期数据是 1900、1、1。

这种方式适合为对象设置统一的初始数据。如果希望创建不同日期的对象时直接传入不同的年月日，就需要构造方法。

5.3 构造方法：创建对象时完成初始化

构造方法也叫构造器，用来在创建对象时执行初始化操作。

public class Date {
    public int year;
    public int month;
    public int day;

    public Date(int year, int month, int day) {
        this.year = year;
        this.month = month;
        this.day = day;
    }

    public void printDate() {
        System.out.println(year + "-" + month + "-" + day);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Date d = new Date(2021, 6, 9);
        d.printDate(); // 2021-6-9
    }
}

执行 new Date(2021, 6, 9) 时，会调用参数匹配的构造方法。这样，对象创建完成时就已有需要的数据，不必再单独调用 setDate()。

构造方法的两个关键语法要求：

  1. 名字必须与类名完全相同。
  2. 没有返回值类型，连 void 也不能写。 
public Date() { }      // 构造方法
public void Date() { } // 普通方法，不是构造方法

构造方法随对象创建而调用，不能写成 d.Date(...)，也不能在对象创建完成后再次调用它来重新初始化对象。后续若要修改日期，可以调用普通的 setDate() 方法。

本章使用 public 构造方法；private 构造方法属于后续特殊用法，此处不展开。

5.4 默认构造方法：什么情况下会自动生成？

只有一个类没有声明任何构造方法时，编译器才会提供默认的无参构造方法。

类中自己写了什么 是否自动提供默认无参构造方法 能否使用 new Date()
没写任何构造方法 是 可以
只写了有参构造方法 否 不可以
自己写了无参构造方法 否 可以，调用自己写的那个

例如，5.3 节的 Date 只有三个参数的构造方法：

Date d1 = new Date(2021, 6, 9); // 正确
// Date d2 = new Date();       // 编译错误：没有匹配的无参构造方法

解决办法是传入所需参数，或者自己补写无参构造方法。这是编译错误，不是运行后才发现的问题。

另外，成员变量的默认值不依赖编译器生成的默认构造方法。即使自己写了构造方法，字段也会先获得默认值。

5.5 构造方法重载与 this(...)

一个类可以提供多个参数列表不同的构造方法，让对象有不同的创建方式：

public class Date {
    public int year;
    public int month;
    public int day;

    public Date() {
        this(1900, 1, 1);
    }

    public Date(int year, int month, int day) {
        this.year = year;
        this.month = month;
        this.day = day;
    }

    public void printDate() {
        System.out.println(year + "-" + month + "-" + day);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Date d1 = new Date();
        Date d2 = new Date(2021, 6, 9);
        d1.printDate(); // 1900-1-1
        d2.printDate(); // 2021-6-9
    }
}

这两个构造方法构成重载。new Date() 进入无参构造方法后，this(1900, 1, 1) 会调用本类的三个参数构造方法，复用赋值代码。

执行顺序：

new Date()
    → 进入无参构造方法
    → this(1900, 1, 1) 调用三参数构造方法
    → 给当前对象的 year、month、day 赋值
    → 返回无参构造方法，继续执行剩余语句
    → 对象初始化完成

整个过程只创建了一个对象。所以，不能简单理解成“创建一个对象时只可能执行一个构造方法”；多个构造方法可以通过 this(...) 配合完成同一个对象的初始化。

沿用本章课件的语法规则，this(...)：

  • 只能在构造方法中使用，并放在第一条语句。
  • 调用的是本类其他构造方法，不会新建对象。
  • 不能直接或间接形成循环调用。

下面的片段会编译失败，因为两个构造方法互相调用：

public Date() {
    this(1900, 1, 1);
}

public Date(int year, int month, int day) {
    this();
}

不要混淆：this.year 是访问字段，this.printDate() 是调用普通成员方法，this(...) 是调用本类构造方法。

5.6 把初始化顺序串起来

对本章这种普通类，只看当前对象的实例字段，顺序是：

默认初始化 → 就地初始化 → 构造方法中的赋值。

public class Date {
    public int year = 1900;
    public int month = 1;
    public int day = 1;

    public Date(int year, int month, int day) {
        System.out.println(this.year + "-" + this.month + "-" + this.day);
        this.year = year;
        this.month = month;
        this.day = day;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Date d = new Date(2021, 6, 9);
        System.out.println(d.year + "-" + d.month + "-" + d.day);
    }
}

输出：

1900-1-1
2021-6-9

字段的变化过程：

阶段 year month day
默认初始化 0 0 0
就地初始化后 1900 1 1
构造方法赋值后 2021 6 9

传入参数不等于自动给字段赋值。 如果把构造方法体留空，即使写了 new Date(2021, 6, 9)，字段仍然是就地初始化得到的 1900、1、1。必须通过 this.year = year 等语句把参数保存到对象中。

6. 打印对象：toString()

直接打印自定义对象的引用：

System.out.println(person);

如果没有自定义 toString()，通常会看到类似内容：

Person@1b6d3586

默认格式是 类的全限定名 + @ + 哈希码的十六进制表示。全限定名包含类所属的包名；没有包名时就是类名。后面的数字不应直接当作对象的内存地址，也不需要背下来。

如果希望打印对象的属性，就在类中重写 toString()：

public class Person {
    public String name;
    public String gender;
    public int age;

    public Person(String name, String gender, int age) {
        this.name = name;
        this.gender = gender;
        this.age = age;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "[" + name + "," + gender + "," + age + "]";
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Person person = new Person("Jim", "男", 18);
        System.out.println(person);
    }
}

输出：

[Jim,男,18]

这里先掌握三点即可：

  • Java 的 Object 类提供了默认的 toString()；这里的“重写”可以先理解为，为当前类重新提供对象转成字符串的实现，继承与重写的完整规则后续再学。
  • @Override 是一个标记，让编译器检查是否正确重写了已有方法。
  • toString() 要返回字符串，不能改成 void，也不要只在里面打印而不返回。打印非空对象引用时，println 会使用它返回的字符串。

7. 用本章练习检查易错点

7.1 判断下面的说法

说法 判断与原因
一个类只能实例化一个对象 错。一个类可以创建多个对象
一个引用可以同时指向多个对象 错。一个引用变量在同一时刻只能引用一个对象，或为 null
Person p = null; 表示引用指向一个空对象 错。null 表示没有引用任何对象
类中没写构造方法，就不会有构造方法 错。此时编译器会提供默认无参构造方法

7.2 创建对象时，参数必须匹配构造方法

如果 Person 类只提供了下面这个构造方法：

public Person(String name, int age) {
    this.name = name;
    this.age = age;
}

那么：

// Person p1 = new Person();           // 错：没有无参构造方法
// Person p2 = new Person("zhangfei"); // 错：没有只接收 String 的构造方法
Person p3 = new Person("lisi", 9);     // 正确

最直接的修改方式是按已有构造方法传参：

Person p1 = new Person("zhangsan", 10);
Person p2 = new Person("zhangfei", 10);
Person p3 = new Person("lisi", 9);

如果确实需要无参或单参数的创建方式，则应补写对应的构造方法。不能指望先用不存在的构造方法创建对象，再通过赋值补救。

title: Mobile AI Factory: Building Specialized Language Models for Your Mobile Device
description:
arXiv:2611.13509v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Small language models (SLMs) running on mobile devices can keep user data private and work without connectivity. But they perform well only when fine-tuned for the target task and sized for the target device, a process that today requires repeated expert tuning. We present {\it Mobile AI Factory}, an agentic system that builds a fine-tuned, quantized SLM for a given task and phone. Given a task specification and a target phone, an orchestrator LLM chooses whether to tune hyperparameters, mine real data, or generate synthetic examples, while fixed rules roll back changes that hurt accuracy. The factory searches from small to large models across base models and quantizations, adapts its accuracy goal as it searches, and uses real measurements of the target phone across inference engines and backends. We evaluate Mobile AI Factory on ten tasks and four Android phones. On an unseen testset, its on-device models outperform two five-shot frontier models on five tasks, by up to 0.34, and match them on three more. Its search comes within 0.03 of exhaustively training all 27 model variants on an entity extraction task, while using 19$\times$ less GPU time. Phone measurements also matter: the best configuration changes across phones. Without phone measurements, Claude Opus 5.5, given the full hardware and model specifications, misses the app's requirements in 25\% of easy and moderate cases and in 60\% of hard ones. Code is available at: https://github.com/evanly-gh/SLM_Factory.

title: Fermat ProbCover: Coverage-Based Active Learning on Fermat Distance Graphs
description:
arXiv:2611.13448v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Active learning aims to reduce annotation cost by selecting the most informative examples for labeling. In the low-budget regime, where uncertainty-based methods often fail, coverage-based active learning methods such as ProbCover have been shown to be effective. However, these methods typically rely on Euclidean distance, which may not adequately capture the underlying geometry of data. In this article, we propose PC-Fermat, a coverage-based active learning method that replaces Euclidean coverage neighborhoods with neighborhoods defined by a Fermat distance, i.e., a data-adaptive distance that reflects the underlying distribution of the data points. To facilitate computation, we construct a weighted Euclidean neighborhood graph and use a truncated shortest-path algorithm to compute the Fermat coverage graph. We also establish sufficient conditions under which this construction exactly preserves the Fermat coverage computed on the complete graph. Finally, we evaluate PC-Fermat on eight classification datasets across varying labeling budgets, with particular emphasis on the very low-budget regime. Our experimental results demonstrate that PC-Fermat outperforms several existing active learning methods on the majority of the datasets.

title: AutoScaffold: AI-Guided Scaffolding for Reinforcement Learning of Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.14515v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) produces rich training experience, yet outcome rewards reduce each attempt to a single number and leave most of this information unused. Training-time scaffolds, such as strategies or hints added to the prompt during training, offer a natural way to turn this information into guidance, but their design and adaptation are largely left to humans and tailored to specific domains. We introduce AutoScaffold, a unified AI-for-AI framework that turns a student's training experience into adaptive scaffolds, with minimal domain-specific information and no human intervention during training. A frozen teacher periodically examines this experience, diagnoses bottlenecks, and designs scaffolds in two forms: (i) strategies shared across a class of tasks and (ii) hints for individual hard tasks, adjusting the content and amount of support as the student learns. The scaffolds are removed at evaluation. We apply the same framework to ALFWorld, search-based QA, mathematical reasoning, and GPU kernel generation. When evaluated without scaffolds, students trained with AutoScaffold outperform those trained with the corresponding RL baselines in all four domains, with gains of 7.2 points in ALFWorld success and 4.0 points in average QA exact match. On GPU kernel generation, AutoScaffold increases the fraction of tasks with a correct kernel that runs faster than the PyTorch reference by up to 5.0 points. On math, our student surpasses QuestA's reported accuracy using approximately one-third as many student training steps. Analyses show that the teacher identifies a different failure in each task class and shifts its scaffolds from step-by-step workflows to targeted fixes as the student improves, and that its revised scaffolds help the student learn more than keeping the previous scaffold or using no scaffold.

title: AI Alignment Is Neither Solvable nor Sufficient
description:
arXiv:2611.13167v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Humans and AI systems increasingly act within the same social and economic environments. Alignment, the goal of ensuring that AI systems act in accordance with human values, is widely regarded as a central challenge for ensuring that AI benefits society while avoiding harm. We argue that this endeavor is misguided. First, alignment is not well defined, as it presumes a sufficiently stable and identifiable set of human intentions or values. Second, where a concrete notion of alignment can be specified, it is not solvable. Third, where alignment appears solvable, solving it would not necessarily mitigate the negative consequences of AI. A key reason is that alignment is typically framed as a property of individual AI systems, while the resulting hybrid societies of humans and machines are complex systems shaped by interactions and feedback loops. Emergent risks, and not only those posed by individual misaligned systems, are therefore likely to become a major source of harm. We conclude that AI safety is an ongoing challenge and not a problem that can be solved once and for all by verifying a particular model property.

title: Catch It Where It Happens: Real Time Error Correction During LLM Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.13107v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly trusted with mathematical, scientific and engineering work, yet their mistakes are often confidently written and hard to spot. A single wrong step tends to propagate, making the model waste inference tokens following a false premise. Existing safeguards either check only the final answer and restart from scratch, or rely on a verifier LLM that competes for GPU capacity and slows down response time. We propose online, deterministic verification: many kinds of reasoning steps can be validated by code, so a step can be verified in real time, as it is written, without any model call or GPU use. Whenever a check fails, we point out the mistake and let the model continue from the same spot. We demonstrate this approach on symbolic mathematics, where derivations already contain explicit expressions that a computer algebra system can check in milliseconds. Tested on the ASyMoB benchmark with three open-weights models, our online validation improves accuracy by 1.4-5.6 percentage points, corresponding to a 1.8-14.9% net reduction in incorrect answers, while increasing token usage by only 6-7%. Because the verifier is independent of the model, the approach complements progress in LLMs rather than competing with it: every new model can benefit immediately, and the benefit grows as deterministic checkers extend to more kinds of reasoning steps.

title: What a "song for dad" form taught me about asking users for input
description:
I build SongUp AI, an AI song maker. People type a few lines about someone, pick a voice and a mood, and get a song back. One of the most common reasons to open it is a gift for a parent, and the "song for dad" flow has taught me more about input design than any dashboard I have built. These are the notes I wish I had before writing the first form.

Adjectives are the wrong question

The first version of the gift form had a box that said, more or less, "Describe him". People answered with adjectives: kind, funny, hard-working, the best. A language model can write a verse from that, and the verse is fine, and it fits every father on earth. Nobody cries at "you were always there for me".

What works is the opposite of a description: small true details. So the prompts now ask for things like:

  • one thing he always says,
  • one thing he fixed, built or drove you to,
  • what you never say to him out loud.

The last one does most of the work. It is also the on-screen hook of the short video we made for the page: "Write what you never say out loud". A question that is slightly uncomfortable to answer gives you the line the whole song hangs on.

The general lesson for any generative product: the quality of the output is capped by how specific the input is, and users do not volunteer specifics unless the form asks for them one at a time.

Names are the hardest field

A gift song has one word that must be right: the name. Text models spell it fine; singing voices do not always pronounce it the way the family does, and "Dad" itself is Papa, Baba, Abba, Appa or Tata depending on the house. We sing in 76 languages, so this comes up daily.

Two things helped. First, treating the name as its own piece of input instead of something buried in a paragraph. Second, a pronunciation hint: a place to write the name the way it sounds. It is a tiny field, and it removed a class of "the song is lovely but that is not his name" messages.

If your product reads user text aloud, in any voice, give names their own handling early. It is cheaper than apologising later.

Long input needs a decision, not a silent cut

People who write to their fathers write a lot. Some paste a full page. A song has a length, so something has to give. Quietly trimming the text is the worst option: the user notices the missing verse, which is always the one that mattered.

Now, when the lyrics run past roughly 1,700 characters, the Create step asks what to do: split it into parts, shorten it, or go ahead anyway. One extra question, asked only when needed, and the choice stays with the person who wrote the words.

Let people hear it before the price matters

The piece of the flow I would defend hardest is the order: you hear the first 30 seconds of your own lyrics, sung, before paying anything. One full song is then $2.99.

For a gift this matters more than usual. The buyer is not judging audio quality in the abstract; they are checking one thing, "does this sound like it is about my dad?" No landing page copy answers that. Thirty seconds of their own words does. It also keeps us honest: if the preview is not good, nobody has paid for it.

What I would tell another builder

  1. Ask for facts, not opinions. "What does he always say?" beats "Describe him".
  2. Find the one field that must be right (for us, the name) and give it its own input and its own check.
  3. When input does not fit, ask; never cut silently.
  4. Put the proof before the price.

None of this is specific to music. It applies to any tool where a model turns a few lines from a person into something that is supposed to feel personal.

If you want to see the flow as a user would, it is here: a song for dad, in your own words.

title: Building World Models from Intrinsic Motivation
description:
arXiv:2611.13113v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In the absence of extrinsic rewards or task supervision, human behavior is guided by intrinsic motivation---neural signals that drive curiosity, creativity, play, and other essential facets of intelligence. Intrinsic motivation plays an important developmental role in building robust world models that enable generalization and adaptation. Yet existing studies leave open how a broad range of intrinsic motivations interacts with world-model representation learning to support downstream control. This limits our understanding of which intrinsically collected experiences build reusable models. To address these gaps, we integrate 24 intrinsic objectives, including established methods and explicit variants spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency, into a common model-based reinforcement learning framework. We evaluate the world models they build through zero-shot, few-shot, and multi-task control in locomotion, manipulation, and open-ended gaming environments, using three representation-learning strategies: observation reconstruction, latent prediction, and redundancy reduction. Curiosity-driven exploration with observation reconstruction yields the strongest aggregate family profile, although the best individual pairing depends on the experiment. In compositional vision-based tasks, intrinsic motivation derived from both episodic and lifelong novelty---providing a complementary memory to the world model's generic recurrent state---achieves the best zero-shot transfer and few-shot adaptation. These findings motivate designing intrinsic motivation and representation learning jointly. Our results demonstrate world models as a powerful tool for measuring the quality of intrinsically motivated experience, and positions intrinsic motivation as a key ingredient for building world models autonomously.

title: MuJoCo for Developers: A Practical Guide to Google DeepMind's Physics Engine
description:
If you have trained a reinforcement learning agent to walk, looked at a robotics paper, or used Gymnasium's HalfCheetah or Humanoid environments, you have already used MuJoCo, possibly without knowing it.

MuJoCo (short for Multi-Joint dynamics with Contact) is an open-source physics engine maintained by Google DeepMind. It is built for fast and accurate simulation of articulated bodies (robots, animals, humans, mechanisms) interacting with their environment through contact.

This guide covers what a developer actually needs to know to get productive with it: how to install it, how its data model works, how to run and visualize a simulation, and where the sharp edges are.

Why MuJoCo matters

A few things make MuJoCo stand out from game physics engines and other robotics simulators:

  • Accuracy over spectacle. It is designed for model-based control, optimization and research, where you need physics you can trust, not just physics that looks right.
  • Speed. The core is written in C, uses preallocated memory, and avoids allocations during simulation. Stepping a model millions of times is normal.
  • Contact handling. Contacts are solved with a convex optimization formulation, which makes it stable for grasping, walking and other contact-rich tasks.
  • Free and open source. It is licensed under Apache 2.0, so you can use it in commercial and research projects.
  • A large ecosystem. Gymnasium, dm_control, MuJoCo Playground, MuJoCo Menagerie and many robotics frameworks are built on top of it.

Installation

For most developers, Python is the starting point. The PyPI package ships with a copy of the MuJoCo library, so there is nothing else to download.

pip install mujoco

Check that it works:

python -c "import mujoco; print(mujoco.__version__)"

A few practical notes:

  • The current README lists Python 3.11 or newer for the bindings.
  • Prebuilt binaries exist for Linux (x86-64 and AArch64), Windows (x86-64) and macOS (universal).
  • Linux wheels target manylinux2014.
  • If you want the C library directly, download a release from the GitHub releases page. Building from main is possible, but the tip of main can be unstable.

The two core objects: MjModel and MjData

This is the single most important concept to understand. MuJoCo splits a simulation into two structures:

Object What it holds Changes during simulation?
MjModel The description of the world: bodies, joints, masses, geometry, actuators, timestep, solver options No (treat it as constant)
MjData The current state and everything computed from it: positions, velocities, controls, forces, contacts, time Yes

You build one MjModel, then create one or more MjData objects from it. Because the state lives entirely in MjData, you can run many independent simulations of the same model in parallel just by creating more MjData instances.

The most-used fields in MjData:

  • data.qpos – generalized positions (joint angles, free-body positions and orientations)
  • data.qvel – generalized velocities
  • data.ctrl – control inputs for actuators (this is what your policy or controller writes to)
  • data.time – simulation time
  • data.xpos, data.xquat – global positions and orientations of bodies
  • data.contact, data.ncon – active contacts

Describing a world with MJCF

Models are usually written in MJCF, MuJoCo's XML format. URDF files (common in ROS) can also be loaded, but MJCF exposes the full feature set.

Here is a minimal scene: a floor, a light, and a box that falls onto the floor.

<mujoco model="falling_box">
  <option timestep="0.002" gravity="0 0 -9.81"/>

  <worldbody>
    <light pos="0 0 3" dir="0 0 -1"/>
    <geom name="floor" type="plane" size="2 2 0.1" rgba="0.8 0.8 0.8 1"/>

    <body name="box" pos="0 0 1">
      <freejoint/>
      <geom type="box" size="0.1 0.1 0.1" rgba="0.2 0.4 0.8 1" mass="1"/>
    </body>
  </worldbody>
</mujoco>

Key MJCF building blocks:

  • worldbody is the root of the kinematic tree.
  • body elements nest inside each other to form a tree (a robot arm is a chain of nested bodies).
  • joint defines how a body moves relative to its parent (hinge, slide, ball, or freejoint for a body that moves freely in 3D).
  • geom defines shape for collision and rendering, and contributes mass and inertia.
  • actuator defines motors, position servos and other force generators that you drive through data.ctrl.
  • sensor defines measurements (joint positions, touch, IMU readings and so on) written to data.sensordata.

Your first simulation in Python 

import mujoco

XML = """
<mujoco>
  <worldbody>
    <light pos="0 0 3" dir="0 0 -1"/>
    <geom type="plane" size="2 2 0.1"/>
    <body name="box" pos="0 0 1">
      <freejoint/>
      <geom type="box" size="0.1 0.1 0.1" mass="1"/>
    </body>
  </worldbody>
</mujoco>
"""

model = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_string(XML)
data = mujoco.MjData(model)

# Simulate 2 seconds of physics
while data.time < 2.0:
    mujoco.mj_step(model, data)

print("Time:", data.time)
print("Box height:", data.body("box").xpos[2])

What is happening:

  1. from_xml_string compiles the XML into an MjModel. Use from_xml_path for files.
  2. MjData(model) allocates state for that model.
  3. mj_step advances the simulation by one timestep (model.opt.timestep).
  4. data.body("box") is named access, which saves you from tracking integer indices.

Two other functions you will use constantly:

  • mujoco.mj_resetData(model, data) resets the state to its initial values.
  • mujoco.mj_forward(model, data) computes all derived quantities (positions, contacts, sensor values) for the current state without advancing time. Call it after you manually set qpos or qvel.

Controlling a robot

Actuators turn values in data.ctrl into forces. Here is a single pendulum with a motor at the hinge:

import mujoco
import numpy as np

XML = """
<mujoco>
  <option timestep="0.002"/>
  <worldbody>
    <body name="pole" pos="0 0 1">
      <joint name="hinge" type="hinge" axis="0 1 0" damping="0.1"/>
      <geom type="capsule" fromto="0 0 0 0 0 -0.5" size="0.03" mass="1"/>
    </body>
  </worldbody>
  <actuator>
    <motor name="torque" joint="hinge" gear="1" ctrlrange="-5 5"/>
  </actuator>
</mujoco>
"""

model = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_string(XML)
data = mujoco.MjData(model)

target = np.pi / 4  # 45 degrees
kp, kd = 20.0, 2.0

for _ in range(2000):
    angle = data.joint("hinge").qpos[0]
    velocity = data.joint("hinge").qvel[0]
    data.ctrl[0] = kp * (target - angle) - kd * velocity  # simple PD controller
    mujoco.mj_step(model, data)

print(f"Final angle: {np.degrees(data.joint('hinge').qpos[0]):.1f} degrees")

The pattern is always the same: read state from data, compute a control, write it to data.ctrl, call mj_step. A reinforcement learning environment is this loop with a reward function around it.

Visualizing

Interactive viewer

The quickest way to inspect any model file is the built-in viewer:

python -m mujoco.viewer --mjcf=path/to/model.xml

To watch your own simulation loop, use the passive viewer. It runs your code and renders alongside it:

import time
import mujoco
import mujoco.viewer

model = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_path("model.xml")
data = mujoco.MjData(model)

with mujoco.viewer.launch_passive(model, data) as viewer:
    while viewer.is_running():
        step_start = time.time()
        mujoco.mj_step(model, data)
        viewer.sync()
        # Keep roughly real-time
        time.sleep(max(0, model.opt.timestep - (time.time() - step_start)))

On macOS, launch_passive must be run with mjpython (installed with the package) instead of python, because macOS requires GUI work on the main thread.

Offscreen rendering

For datasets, videos or vision-based policies, render to NumPy arrays:

renderer = mujoco.Renderer(model, height=480, width=640)

mujoco.mj_forward(model, data)
renderer.update_scene(data)
pixels = renderer.render()  # shape (480, 640, 3), dtype uint8

On a headless Linux server, set the rendering backend before importing MuJoCo, for example MUJOCO_GL=egl (GPU) or MUJOCO_GL=osmesa (software).

Editing models in code with MjSpec

Writing XML by hand gets tedious when you need to generate variations (different terrain, randomized objects, procedurally built robots). MjSpec lets you build and modify models programmatically and then compile them:

import mujoco

spec = mujoco.MjSpec()
spec.worldbody.add_geom(
    type=mujoco.mjtGeom.mjGEOM_PLANE, size=[2, 2, 0.1]
)

for i in range(3):
    body = spec.worldbody.add_body(name=f"ball_{i}", pos=[i * 0.3, 0, 1 + i * 0.5])
    body.add_freejoint()
    body.add_geom(type=mujoco.mjtGeom.mjGEOM_SPHERE, size=[0.1, 0, 0])

model = spec.compile()
data = mujoco.MjData(model)

You can also load an existing XML with mujoco.MjSpec.from_file(...), change it, recompile, and even export it back to XML with spec.to_xml(). The official Model Editing notebook walks through this in depth.

Scaling up: MJX and MuJoCo Warp

Modern robot learning often needs thousands of simulations in parallel. MuJoCo offers two GPU-oriented options alongside the standard C engine:

  • MJX (MuJoCo XLA) reimplements MuJoCo in JAX. You get jit compilation, vmap for batching thousands of environments, and automatic differentiation through the physics step. It runs on GPU and TPU.
  • MuJoCo Warp is a GPU implementation built on NVIDIA Warp, developed with NVIDIA and officially released in MuJoCo 3.5.0. It targets high throughput on NVIDIA GPUs, especially for contact-heavy scenes.

A minimal MJX example:

import jax
import mujoco
from mujoco import mjx

model = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_path("model.xml")
mjx_model = mjx.put_model(model)

@jax.vmap
def batched_step(qpos):
    d = mjx.make_data(mjx_model).replace(qpos=qpos)
    return mjx.step(mjx_model, d)

step = jax.jit(batched_step)
qpos_batch = jax.numpy.zeros((4096, model.nq))
result = step(qpos_batch)  # 4096 simulations in one call

A rule of thumb: use the standard C engine for single simulations, debugging and CPU work; use MJX if you live in the JAX ecosystem or need gradients; use MuJoCo Warp for maximum GPU throughput. Not every feature is supported in every backend, so check the MJX and Warp docs for your model's features.

The ecosystem around MuJoCo

You rarely need to start from scratch:

  • MuJoCo Menagerie – a curated collection of high-quality robot models (arms, quadrupeds, humanoids, hands) ready to load.
  • MuJoCo Playground – GPU-accelerated environments and training pipelines for locomotion and manipulation, including sim-to-real work.
  • Gymnasium – the standard RL benchmark environments (Ant, Hopper, Humanoid and others) use MuJoCo.
  • dm_control – DeepMind's control suite, including PyMJCF for composing models in Python.
  • Bindings in other languages – first-party C#/Unity and JavaScript/WebAssembly bindings, plus community bindings for Rust, Julia, Swift, Java and MATLAB Simulink.
  • Converters – tools exist for OpenSim, SDFormat, OBJ meshes and Onshape CAD assemblies to MJCF.

Things developers should know before going deep

1. Pin your version. MuJoCo releases roughly every month and uses a modified form of Semantic Versioning (introduced in 3.5.0). Physics fixes between releases can change simulation results. If you publish benchmarks or train long-running policies, pin the exact version in requirements.txt and record it with your results.

2. Do not use mujoco-py. Many older tutorials use mujoco-py, the legacy OpenAI wrapper. It is unmaintained. Use the official mujoco package instead.

3. Timestep matters. The default timestep is 0.002 seconds. Making it larger speeds things up but can make contact-heavy scenes unstable. If objects jitter, explode or pass through each other, reduce the timestep before changing anything else.

4. Generalized coordinates are not always obvious. qpos and qvel have different sizes when a model contains free or ball joints, because orientation is stored as a quaternion (4 values in qpos) but angular velocity has 3 values in qvel. Use model.nq and model.nv, and use named access (data.joint("name")) instead of hardcoding indices.

5. Call mj_forward after editing state. If you set qpos manually and then read body positions or sensor values without stepping, they will be stale until you call mj_forward.

6. Reuse MjData for performance. Allocating new MjData objects in a hot loop is wasteful. Reset with mj_resetData instead. For batches of CPU rollouts, look at the multithreaded rollout module.

A good learning path is: run the introductory notebook, load a robot from Menagerie in the viewer, write a small control loop for it, and then wrap that loop in a Gymnasium environment. From there, MJX or MuJoCo Warp are the natural next step if you need to train at scale.

title: One Trajectory, Two Requirements: Accuracy and Local Stability in Euler Sampling for Flow Matching Policies
description:
arXiv:2611.13311v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Flow matching robot policies commonly use a fixed Euler step count selected from offline accuracy sweeps. At inference time, however, each policy input (visual observation, robot state, and language instruction) together with a source-noise draw defines a different ODE trajectory and sequence of local Jacobians. We ask whether a step count that accurately follows the nominal noise-to-action trajectory can still be too coarse for strongly contracting directions around it. An exact two-coordinate system and a controlled augmentation of six trained flow models show that trajectory accuracy and local Euler stability can impose different step requirements even when the original learned transport is unchanged. We then study a frozen $\pi_{0.5}$-LIBERO checkpoint without modifying its weights or action dynamics. Across 30 policy inputs from 10 LIBERO-10 tasks, the Jacobian exhibits strong contracting directions near the action endpoint, yet no sampled mode violates the Euler non-expansion condition. On five of those inputs, accuracy sweeps require 4--9 Euler steps at 5% terminal error and 87--112 at 1%. These five paired cases are therefore consistent with accuracy-limited rather than stability-limited sampling under this local criterion, while the controlled experiments show why endpoint accuracy alone cannot rule out a separate stability requirement.
