title: Amazon ElastiCache Serverless now supports vector, full-text and hybrid searches plus aggregations
description:
Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey now supports vector, full-text, and hybrid search, along with aggregations. Applications searching live data often face a hard trade-off between latency and recall, along with delays before updates become searchable. With search on ElastiCache Serverless, applications can search data with latency as low as microseconds at up to 99% recall for vector search, while serving billions of queries per day. Updates are searchable in as little as microseconds, as soon as writes complete.

Search on ElastiCache Serverless is ideal for latency-sensitive applications with unpredictable traffic and for teams that want to get started with search quickly. You can combine search types in a single query, tune recall as needed, and analyze results with server-side aggregations. Developers can give every agent, session, or task its own datastore for memory and context retrieval, so agents can experiment, fail, and retry without touching production or each other. Each datastore is ready in seconds, reachable over a public endpoint with no network setup, and billed only for what it uses, with zero infrastructure to manage. Applications can also power product discovery, recommendation systems, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

Search is available on ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey in all commercial AWS Regions, AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud Region on ElastiCache version 9 for Valkey. Valkey is the most permissive open source and vendor-neutral alternative to Redis and the recommended engine for ElastiCache. To get started, create a new serverless cache or upgrade an existing one to Valkey 9 using the AWS Management Console, AWS SDK, or AWS CLI. To learn more, see the ElastiCache documentation. For pricing, see the ElastiCache pricing page.

title: Tabular Foundation Models in Financial Predictions
description:
arXiv:2611.13550v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This technical note introduces tabular foundation models (TFMs) to accounting research and evaluates their performance in one common benchmark task: predicting firms' next-year earnings changes. TFMs produce numeric predictions and learn in context, without post-release training or tuning, making them natural and easy to use for forecasting. The TFMs we study are pretrained on synthetic tabular data, so they avoid look-ahead bias from memorizing firms' outcomes. We compare Google Research's TabFM with a fine-tuned open-weight large language model developed in recent accounting research and with several tree-based models. TabFM is more accurate than all comparison models. It is also faster and less computationally intensive than the large language model. Several tree-based specifications produce predictions more quickly than TabFM, so choosing between them involves a trade-off between accuracy and speed. We conclude that TFMs have promise as a new tool for forecasting in accounting and finance. However, our evaluation is based on a single benchmark task, and no class of models is likely to dominate in all settings.

title: Fintech Cleanup Sweeps: Webhook Queue Rate Limits, Delayed Retries, and a DLQ
description:
The trade-off that settles this is not price per message. It's whether the queue hands you delayed jobs, per-destination rate limiting, and a DLQ you don't have to rebuild in application code — pick the one whose retry semantics you can make idempotent cheaply, because retry amplification, not the invoice, is what gets a periodic cleanup paged at 03:00.

Everything below is that one decision, taken apart.

Cleanup that outlives the HTTP request

The job is unglamorous. A fintech ledger carries card authorization holds that expire on a schedule; once a hold passes its expiry, the money has to be released in the ledger and the merchant has to be told over a webhook so their own reconciliation lines up. US and EU tenants live in separate regions for residency reasons, so it is two sweeps with two queues, not one global one. Every merchant endpoint publishes a limit — 5 requests per second is a normal number — and some of them enforce it with a hard 429 rather than a queue of their own. So the sweep is not "release N rows"; it is "release N rows at a pace someone else controls, exactly once, in two jurisdictions, without a human watching."

Running that inside an HTTP handler is the original sin.

The shape of that failure is always the same: someone wires the sweep to an admin endpoint, the gateway cuts the connection at its 60-second limit, the caller (or the load balancer, or an impatient operator) retries, and now two sweeps walk the same rows. Half the holds get released twice, the merchant gets two webhooks with different payload ids, and their reconciliation opens a ticket that lands back on you. Missed jobs are annoying. Duplicate deliveries are the ones that generate finance-side work, and they are the reason the idempotency question outranks the pricing question in this design.

The trigger is not the reliability boundary either. Scheduled CI triggers are convenient — GitHub's own documentation says scheduled workflows can be delayed during periods of high load, so treat the tick as a hint, not a guarantee. Whatever fires the sweep, the sweep itself has to be safe to run twice, late, or concurrently with its own previous run.

What a rate-limited sweep actually costs

Per-message pricing is the smallest line in this system, and reasoning about it first is how teams end up with a cheap queue and an expensive on-call rotation.

Do the arithmetic on amplification instead. Take 50,000 expired holds in a nightly window, a 2% slice of destinations answering 429, and a worker that retries five times on a fixed one-second backoff with no jitter: that slice turns 1,000 deliveries into 6,000 requests, all aimed at the endpoints that were already asking you to slow down, all in the same second because fixed backoff synchronizes retries. The queue charge for those extra messages is rounding error. The costs that actually show up are the merchant's rate limiter escalating to longer bans, your egress and log volume (per-attempt structured logs are what you need in a postmortem, and they are billed per line), and the engineer who has to decide at 03:00 whether the DLQ contains 400 poison payloads or one broken endpoint.

There is a deployment cost too. A queue with server-side pacing means the limit is a config value you can change without a deploy; a queue without it means the limiter lives in your worker, and every limit change is a code change, a rollout, and a chance to get it wrong under pressure.

Should a rate-limited webhook queue own delayed jobs, retries, and the DLQ?

Compare the candidates on where each mechanism lives, not on the sticker. Caps and defaults move, so I re-read these pages before I commit a design to them.

Option Delayed jobs Pacing per destination Failure landing zone
Amazon SQS (standard) DelaySeconds up to 15 minutes consumer-side; you write the limiter redrive policy to a DLQ after maxReceiveCount
RabbitMQ / CloudAMQP delayed-message-exchange plugin, or TTL plus dead-letter routing consumer-side, via prefetch and your own token bucket dead-letter exchange; quorum queues add a delivery-limit
Google Cloud Tasks scheduleTime up to 30 days out queue-level: max dispatches per second and max concurrent dispatches retry config only — no dead-letter queue, so you record the terminal failure yourself
Upstash QStash delay on publish, HTTP push model per-endpoint controls, no long-lived consumers inspectable DLQ you can re-publish from

Read that table as four different answers to one question: who holds the pacing state. Cloud Tasks puts it in the queue and gives you nothing to catch terminal failures; SQS and RabbitMQ put it in your worker and give you a real landing zone for poison messages. Neither arrangement is wrong. But the one you choose decides how much of the next section you have to build yourself, and that is the real bill.

For a two-region sweep the practical constraint is usually duller than any feature matrix: a queue you can run in both us-east and eu-central with the same worker binary, so the EU deployment isn't a fork of the US one.

Idempotency keys make redelivery boring

At-least-once delivery is the contract every one of these systems actually offers. The design goal is not zero duplicates in flight — it is that a duplicate does nothing the second time.

That starts before the queue. The sweep plans work and hands out keys; it never releases a hold itself.

// sweep.go — the sweep only plans work. Nothing is released in here.
type Hold struct {
    ID        string
    AccountID string
    Region    string // "us" or "eu": separate queues, same binary
    ExpiresAt time.Time
}

// Stable across every redelivery: no attempt counter, no run id, no wall clock.
func idemKey(h Hold) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte("hold.released|" + h.ID + "|" + h.ExpiresAt.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339)))
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

func planSweep(ctx context.Context, db *sql.DB, q Queue, now time.Time) (int, error) {
    tx, err := db.BeginTx(ctx, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    defer tx.Rollback()

    rows, err := tx.QueryContext(ctx, `
        SELECT id, account_id, region, expires_at
          FROM auth_holds
         WHERE state = 'active' AND expires_at < $1
         ORDER BY expires_at
         LIMIT 500
           FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, now)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    defer rows.Close()

    n := 0
    for rows.Next() {
        var h Hold
        if err := rows.Scan(&h.ID, &h.AccountID, &h.Region, &h.ExpiresAt); err != nil {
            return n, err
        }
        // Spread the batch instead of firing 500 messages at one endpoint.
        delay := time.Duration(n/25) * time.Second
        if err := q.Enqueue(ctx, h.Region, Message{Key: idemKey(h), HoldID: h.ID}, delay); err != nil {
            return n, err
        }
        n++
    }
    if err := rows.Err(); err != nil {
        return n, err
    }
    return n, tx.Commit()
}

Enqueue-then-commit is a dual write, and I left it that way on purpose: if the process dies between the last Enqueue and Commit, the next tick re-plans the same holds and the queue receives the same keys again. That's survivable precisely because each key comes from the hold and its expiry rather than from the run. A transactional outbox removes the dual write entirely and is the better shape once the sweep matters enough to justify the extra table — the reason to know both is that the key discipline is what makes either one safe.

The worker side does one attempt and reports one of three outcomes. Retry policy is data, not if statements scattered through delivery code.

// worker.go — one attempt, three outcomes. The queue decides what happens next.
type Outcome int

const (
    Done Outcome = iota
    RetryLater
    DeadLetter
)

func attempt(ctx context.Context, d Delivery, lim *rate.Limiter, secret []byte, hc *http.Client) (Outcome, time.Duration, error) {
    if err := lim.Wait(ctx); err != nil { // one bucket per endpoint, never one global bucket
        return RetryLater, 5 * time.Second, err
    }

    ts := strconv.FormatInt(time.Now().Unix(), 10)
    mac := hmac.New(sha256.New, secret) // HMAC-SHA256, RFC 2104
    mac.Write([]byte(ts))
    mac.Write([]byte("."))
    mac.Write(d.Body)

    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, d.Endpoint, bytes.NewReader(d.Body))
    if err != nil {
        return DeadLetter, 0, err // a malformed endpoint will not get better on attempt 4
    }
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", d.Key)
    req.Header.Set("X-Hold-Signature", ts+"."+hex.EncodeToString(mac.Sum(nil)))

    resp, err := hc.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return RetryLater, backoff(d.Attempt), err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body) // drain, so the connection gets reused

    switch {
    case resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests:
        // The receiver's own limiter outranks ours.
        return RetryLater, retryAfter(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), backoff(d.Attempt)), nil
    case resp.StatusCode >= 500:
        return RetryLater, backoff(d.Attempt), nil
    case resp.StatusCode >= 400:
        return DeadLetter, 0, fmt.Errorf("rejected: %d", resp.StatusCode)
    default:
        return Done, 0, nil
    }
}

Three details in there carry most of the reliability. backoff must include jitter, or every retry from a batch lands in the same millisecond and re-triggers the limit that caused it. Retry-After is a documented HTTP header and receivers that send it are telling you the exact answer — honouring it is cheaper than guessing. And the Idempotency-Key header only helps if the receiver stores it; when a merchant ignores it, the fallback is that your own release step writes to a ledger table with a unique constraint on the key, so the second delivery is a no-op insert and the webhook is just noise.

Testing this is less work than it sounds. A fake endpoint that returns 429 for the first two calls, then 200, then 500 forever, exercises every branch above in a unit test, and a counter of distinct Idempotency-Key values versus total requests is the single metric worth alerting on. If that ratio drifts above 1.0 in normal operation, your retry policy is louder than your idempotency guarantees.

Where this advice stops working

The catch is scale in the other direction. If the sweep touches a few hundred rows in one region and no external endpoint is rate limiting you, a queue is a second system to operate for no benefit — a cron-triggered job with an advisory lock, a LIMIT clause, and an in-process limiter is honestly fine, and it is less to page on.

Ordering is the other boundary. Standard queues are not suitable when releases for one account must land in order; that pushes you toward FIFO-style grouping or an ordered log, and both cost throughput. If the cleanup grows human approvals, compensation steps, or multi-day waits, a message queue isn't the right tool at all — that's workflow-engine territory, and bolting state machines onto retry policies is how the state machine ends up in your DLQ.

I'm not sure there's a universal answer on where the limiter belongs. Queue-side pacing has fewer moving parts, worker-side pacing gives you finer control per destination and works identically in both regions; your mileage may vary with how many endpoints you deliver to. What doesn't vary is the ordering of the decision: settle idempotency first, then retry policy, then the DLQ, and only then look at what any of it costs per million messages.

Sources

  • Amazon SQS delay queues — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-delay-queues.html
  • Amazon SQS dead-letter queues — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html
  • RabbitMQ quorum queues: delivery-limit and dead lettering — https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/quorum-queues
  • Google Cloud Tasks queue configuration: rate limits and retry — https://cloud.google.com/tasks/docs/configuring-queues
  • Upstash QStash documentation — https://upstash.com/docs/qstash
  • RFC 2104: HMAC keyed-hashing for message authentication — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104
  • RFC 9110 section 9.2.2: idempotent methods — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-9.2.2
  • GitHub Actions: events that trigger workflows (schedule) — https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows
  • MDN: Retry-After header — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Retry-After

title: Bits or permutations? Spending a fixed inference budget on weight precision or on option-order averaging in small local language models
description:
arXiv:2611.14413v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Local language models can save memory by storing weights in fewer bits, and they can reduce sensitivity to the order of answer options by averaging a few reorderings. We ask whether the first makes the second worse, and which is the cheaper way to spend a fixed budget. On Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B with simulated round-to-nearest weight quantization (8, 6, 4 and 3 bits, fp16 reference), read from the logits of the letters A to D on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MMLU and HellaSwag (300 items each), 6 bits lose no accuracy against fp16 (they score +1.8 (+1.0 to +2.5) and +0.9 (+0.3 to +1.5) points higher, which we do not explain), and 8 bits change it by -0.7 (-1.1 to -0.3) and -0.4 (-0.7 to -0.2) points. At 4 bits the answer-slot skew rises from 0.15 to 0.53 (0.6B) and from 0.07 to 0.12 (1.7B); Gaussian noise at the same weight SNR gives 0.15 and 0.37 (two draws) and 0.19 (one draw), so the control is inconclusive on whether rounding adds slot skew beyond equal-power noise. Flip rates rise but stay below an accuracy-matched baseline of independent uniform errors. Averaging four cyclic orders recovers +12.6 points at 4 bits for 0.6B (+5.3 at fp16). We price bits and passes in one machine-independent unit, weight bytes read times passes. In cost-matched pairs, extra orders beat extra bits only when the weights have 6 or more bits, and the decision table reduces to: use 6-bit weights and spend the rest of the budget on up to four orders, one pass each. Everything is simulated on two small models with the simplest quantizer; a title-level search found no earlier study of quantization together with option order.

title: Prompt2Echo (P2Echo): Text-Prompted Multi-View Echocardiography Segmentation with One Model
description:
arXiv:2611.13425v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automated segmentation in multi-view echocardiography is essential for comprehensive cardiac assessment, yet remains challenging due to substantial anatomical and appearance variability across standard acoustic windows. In this paper, we present P2Echo, a unified framework capable of segmenting diverse cardiac structures across multiple standard echocardiographic views using a single model controlled by structured view-aware text prompts. Unlike recent foundation model adaptations that rely on implicit latent priors, P2Echo explicitly conditions the segmentation process via a novel Dynamic Image-Text Alignment (DyITA) module. DyITA integrates a differentiable routing mechanism and token differential operators to dynamically modulate decoder features according to the requested view and target structure. This allows the network to adaptively switch its processing pathways for different views without architectural changes. Extensive experiments on a large-scale internal dataset (seen during training) and held-out evaluation on three external datasets demonstrate that P2Echo matches or exceeds both view-specific specialists and state-of-the-art universal models at a fraction of their computational cost, offering an efficient, controllable solution for multi-plane cardiac analysis. Code is available at: https://github.com/moeinheidari7829/P2Echo.

title: FastAPI Fundamentals & Dependency Injection: Explained from Absolute Zero ⚡
description:
⚡ FastAPI Fundamentals & Dependency Injection: Let's Learn from ZERO!

Ever wondered how FastAPI receives requests, validates data, calls your Python functions, connects to databases, handles authentication, and organizes a real-world backend? 🤔

In this post we'll learn it all from scratch, with simple examples, real-life analogies, Python code, and folder structures. No prior backend knowledge needed! 🚀

1. 🤔 What exactly is FastAPI?

Imagine you're building Instagram. Your app has:

  • ⚛️ A React frontend
  • 🐍 A Python FastAPI backend
  • 🐘 A PostgreSQL database

A user clicks the Like button. What happens?

⚛️ Frontend (React)
   User clicks Like
        │  HTTP request
        ▼
⚡ Backend (FastAPI)
   Receives request, validates data, executes logic
        │  Database query
        ▼
🐘 PostgreSQL Database
   Stores the like information
        │
        ▼
⚡ FastAPI returns a response
   200 OK → { "message": "Post liked successfully" }

📌 FastAPI is a modern Python web framework used to build APIs. An API (Application Programming Interface) lets two software applications communicate.

FastAPI helps us:

  1. 🛣️ Create API endpoints
  2. 📥 Receive data from frontend applications
  3. ✔️ Validate incoming data
  4. 🧠 Execute business logic
  5. 🗄️ Communicate with databases
  6. 📤 Return responses in JSON
  7. 📖 Automatically generate API documentation 
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/")
def home():
    return {"message": "Hello World"}
  • from fastapi import FastAPI imports the FastAPI class
  • app = FastAPI() creates our application
  • @app.get("/") creates a GET endpoint at the root URL
  • def home() is the Python function that handles the request
  • return sends the response back to the client

Visit http://127.0.0.1:8000/ and you get:

{
  "message": "Hello World"
}

That's your first FastAPI endpoint! 🎉

2. 📬 Understanding API Parameters

When a frontend calls a backend, it often needs to send information:

  • Which post should we retrieve?
  • Which page of posts should we show?
  • What data should we save?
  • Which user is making the request?

FastAPI has three parameter types you need to know:

  1. 🛤️ Path parameters
  2. ❓ Query parameters
  3. 📦 Body parameters

2.1 🛤️ Path parameters

Values passed directly inside the URL path. You have 100 posts and want post number 25:

GET /posts/25

Here 25 is the path parameter, because it's part of the URL path itself.

from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/posts/{post_id}")
def get_post(post_id: int):
    return {
        "post_id": post_id,
        "message": "Post retrieved",
    }
  • {post_id} is a dynamic placeholder
  • The actual value comes from the URL
  • FastAPI extracts it and passes it to your function

When you request GET /posts/25, FastAPI internally calls:

get_post(post_id=25)

Response:

{
  "post_id": 25,
  "message": "Post retrieved"
}

Notice we wrote post_id: int. What if somebody sends GET /posts/hello? FastAPI automatically validates the value. Since "hello" can't become an integer, it returns a validation error (HTTP 422). You don't write that validation yourself! ✨

Real-life examples: /users/10, /posts/25, /comments/100, /products/500.

🧠 Path parameters generally identify a particular resource.

2.2 ❓ Query parameters

Extra values passed after a ? in the URL. Want only 10 of your 100 posts?

GET /posts?limit=10
GET /posts?limit=10&skip=20
  • /posts = endpoint
  • ? = start of query parameters
  • limit=10 = a query parameter
  • & separates multiple query parameters 
@app.get("/posts")
def get_posts(limit: int = 10, skip: int = 0):
    return {
        "limit": limit,
        "skip": skip,
    }

limit: int = 10 means limit should be an integer, and if the user doesn't provide it, use 10. Same idea for skip, defaulting to 0.

Request Response
GET /posts {"limit": 10, "skip": 0}
GET /posts?limit=5 {"limit": 5, "skip": 0}
GET /posts?limit=20&skip=40 {"limit": 20, "skip": 40}

Real-life uses:

Query parameter Purpose
?limit=10 Get 10 records
?page=2 Get page 2
?search=deepika Search for something
?sort=latest Sort by latest
?category=technology Filter by category

In a social feed, query parameters are perfect for pagination, filtering and searching, like GET /feed?limit=10&cursor=abc123.

2.3 📦 Body parameters (request body)

A user wants to create a new post and must send a caption, image URL and location. That data usually goes in the request body:

POST /posts

{
  "caption": "Beautiful evening!",
  "image_url": "https://example.com/image.jpg",
  "location": "Bengaluru"
}

from pydantic import BaseModel


class PostCreate(BaseModel):
    caption: str
    image_url: str
    location: str


@app.post("/posts")
def create_post(post: PostCreate):
    return {
        "message": "Post created",
        "caption": post.caption,
    }
  • PostCreate is a Pydantic model
  • post: PostCreate tells FastAPI to expect request-body data matching that model
  • post.caption and post.image_url access the values

2.4 ⚖️ Path vs Query vs Body

Type Role Example Question it answers
🛤️ Path Identifies which resource GET /posts/25 Which post? Post 25
❓ Query Controls how we retrieve GET /posts?limit=10 How many posts? 10
📦 Body Carries data to create/update POST /posts + {"caption": "My new post"} What do we save? The caption

🧠 Quick rule: Path = which resource? · Query = how should we retrieve it? · Body = what data are we sending?

3. ✔️ Pydantic Models: Request and Response Schemas

Imagine your frontend sends:

{
  "username": "deepika",
  "age": "twenty",
  "email": "not-an-email"
}

Age is a string instead of an integer, and the email isn't valid. Should your backend blindly accept that? Obviously not! We need a way to validate incoming data. Enter Pydantic.

3.1 🛂 What is Pydantic?

📌 Pydantic is a Python library for data validation and parsing. It checks whether incoming data follows the structure and rules we've defined.

Think of it as an airport security checkpoint ✈️: before passengers enter, their details are checked. Before request data reaches your business logic, Pydantic validates it.

3.2 🏗️ Creating a Pydantic model 

from pydantic import BaseModel


class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    username: str
    age: int
    email: str

BaseModel is Pydantic's base class. We inherit from it to create a model.

Field Expected type
username String
age Integer
email String

3.3 ✅ Valid data arrives 

{
  "username": "deepika",
  "age": 22,
  "email": "deepika@example.com"
}

Pydantic validates it, creates a Python model object, and you access user.username, user.age, user.email.

3.4 ❌ Invalid data arrives 

{
  "username": "deepika",
  "age": "hello",
  "email": "deepika@example.com"
}

"hello" can't become an integer, so FastAPI automatically returns:

{
  "detail": [
    {
      "type": "int_parsing",
      "loc": ["body", "age"],
      "msg": "Input should be a valid integer"
    }
  ]
}

💡 FastAPI handles this request-validation error automatically. You don't write manual if checks for every field.

3.5 📏 Validation rules 

from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, Field


class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    username: str = Field(min_length=3, max_length=20)
    age: int = Field(ge=18, le=100)
    email: EmailStr
  • min_length=3: username needs at least 3 characters
  • max_length=20: username can't exceed 20 characters
  • ge=18: age must be greater than or equal to 18
  • le=100: age must be less than or equal to 100
  • EmailStr: validates email format

📝 EmailStr requires the optional email-validator package.

3.6 🕳️ Optional fields and defaults 

class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    username: str
    age: int
    bio: str | None = None
  • str | None means the value can be a string or absent/null
  • = None provides a default value

3.7 🔄 Request schemas vs Response schemas

🎯 A VERY important distinction in real backends!

A user creates an account and sends:

{
  "username": "deepika",
  "email": "deepika@example.com",
  "password": "secret123"
}

That's a request schema. But should we return the password? Absolutely not! 🙅 We return:

{
  "id": 101,
  "username": "deepika",
  "email": "deepika@example.com"
}

That's a response schema.

from pydantic import BaseModel


# Incoming data
class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: str
    password: str


# Outgoing data
class UserResponse(BaseModel):
    id: int
    username: str
    email: str

Connect them in FastAPI:

@app.post("/users", response_model=UserResponse)
def create_user(user: UserCreate):
    return {
        "id": 101,
        "username": user.username,
        "email": user.email,
        "password": user.password,
    }

Even though the function returns a dict containing the password, the response_model filters the output to the fields in UserResponse. The client never sees the password. 🔐

Why separate request and response schemas?

  1. ✔️ Validate incoming data
  2. 🎛️ Control outgoing data
  3. 🔒 Prevent sensitive information from being exposed
  4. 📜 Maintain a clear API contract
  5. 🧹 Make code easier to maintain

Common naming conventions:

Model Purpose
UserCreate Incoming user creation data
UserUpdate Incoming user update data
UserResponse Outgoing user data
PostCreate Incoming post creation data
PostResponse Outgoing post data
LoginRequest Login credentials

4. 💉 Dependency Injection (DI): The MOST Important Concept!

Don't worry about the big name. Let's use a simple example.

4.1 🚨 First, the problem

Whenever a user views their feed, your backend needs a database:

def get_feed():
    db = connect_to_database()
    posts = db.get_posts()
    return posts

Now imagine 20 endpoints needing database access. Would you write db = connect_to_database() inside all 20 functions? That causes:

  1. 🔁 Repeated code
  2. 😩 Hard to maintain
  3. 🧪 Hard to test
  4. 🔌 Hard to manage database connections

What if one function provided the database connection whenever another function needed it? That's the basic idea of Dependency Injection.

4.2 🧩 What is a dependency?

📌 A dependency is something a function or class needs to do its work.

def get_feed(db):
    posts = db.get_posts()
    return posts

Here db is a dependency, because get_feed() depends on it. Other examples:

  • 🗄️ Database session
  • 👤 Authenticated user
  • ⚙️ Configuration settings
  • 📝 Logger
  • 🌍 External API client
  • ⚡ Cache connection

4.3 💉 What is Dependency Injection?

📌 Dependency Injection means: instead of creating everything a function needs by itself, we provide those things from outside.

❌ Without DI:

def get_feed():
    db = connect_to_database()
    return db.get_posts()

The function creates its own dependency.

✅ With DI:

def get_feed(db):
    return db.get_posts()

The dependency is provided from outside. This is more flexible. For example, during testing you can pass in a fake database instead of the real one. 🧪

4.4 🎯 What is Depends() in FastAPI?

FastAPI has a built-in function, Depends(), to declare dependencies:

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI

app = FastAPI()


def get_database():
    return "Database connection"


@app.get("/posts")
def get_posts(db=Depends(get_database)):
    return {
        "database": db,
        "message": "Posts retrieved",
    }

get_database() is our dependency provider. Now the interesting part:

def get_posts(db=Depends(get_database)):

Depends(get_database) tells FastAPI: "Before executing get_posts(), run get_database() and inject its result into the db parameter."

Client sends GET /posts
        ▼
FastAPI sees Depends(get_database)
        ▼
Executes get_database()
        ▼
Injects the returned value into db
        ▼
Executes get_posts(db)
        ▼
Response returned

You never manually call get_database() inside get_posts(). FastAPI resolves it for you. That's the beauty of Depends()! ✨

4.5 🗄️ A practical example: database dependency

With PostgreSQL and SQLAlchemy, we create a database session provider:

from app.database import SessionLocal


def get_db():
    db = SessionLocal()
    try:
        yield db
    finally:
        db.close()
  • db = SessionLocal() creates a new database session (a temporary working connection to the database)
  • yield db hands the session to the function that requested it
  • finally: db.close() closes the session after the request finishes, even if an exception occurs

🤔 Why yield instead of return? A generator dependency lets FastAPI run cleanup code after the request completes.

Now use it in an endpoint:

from fastapi import Depends
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session


@app.get("/posts")
def get_posts(db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
    posts = db.query(Post).all()
    return posts
  • db: Session is the expected SQLAlchemy session type
  • Depends(get_db) tells FastAPI how to provide it
  • db.query(Post).all() retrieves all Post records

We never created the session manually. FastAPI manages its lifecycle through the dependency.

📝 This is a simplified synchronous SQLAlchemy example. Async SQLAlchemy uses an async session and an async dependency.

4.6 🔐 DI for authentication

A user wants to create a post. Before allowing it we check: Is the user logged in? Is their token valid? Which user is this? Create a dependency:

def get_current_user():
    # Validate access token
    # Find user in database
    # Return authenticated user
    return current_user

Then use it:

@app.post("/posts")
def create_post(current_user=Depends(get_current_user)):
    return {
        "message": "Post created",
        "user": current_user.username,
    }

What happens:

  1. The client sends a request
  2. FastAPI sees Depends(get_current_user)
  3. It runs the authentication dependency
  4. The dependency validates the user's identity
  5. It returns the authenticated user
  6. FastAPI injects that user into current_user
  7. The endpoint executes

If authentication fails, the dependency can raise an HTTP 401 or 403, and the endpoint won't run normally. With 15 endpoints needing authentication, you reuse the same dependency instead of repeating token logic 15 times. ♻️

5. 🔄 Inversion of Control (IoC)

You understand DI, so IoC is easier now.

5.1 🤔 What is IoC?

📌 Inversion of Control means transferring the responsibility of managing something from your code to an external framework or system.

❌ Without IoC, you decide when to create the session, how to pass it, and when to close it:

def get_posts():
    db = create_database_session()
    try:
        return db.get_posts()
    finally:
        db.close()

✅ With IoC using FastAPI:

def get_posts(db=Depends(get_db)):
    return db.get_posts()

FastAPI manages dependency resolution and the cleanup lifecycle for the request. You simply declare what you need. Control has shifted from your endpoint to the framework. That's Inversion of Control. 🎛️

5.2 🔗 Relationship between IoC and DI

Concept Meaning
IoC The general principle of handing over control
DI A technique used to implement IoC
Depends() FastAPI's mechanism for declaring dependencies 
Inversion of Control (IoC)   → the general design principle
        ▼
Dependency Injection (DI)    → a way to achieve IoC
        ▼
FastAPI Depends()            → a built-in dependency mechanism

🎤 Interview-ready explanation

"Inversion of Control is a design principle where the responsibility of managing dependencies is transferred from our application code to the framework. In FastAPI, we achieve this using Dependency Injection through Depends(). For example, instead of manually creating database sessions inside every route, we declare Depends(get_db), and FastAPI resolves and manages the dependency."

6. 🗂️ APIRouter: Organizing API Endpoints

As your app grows, you might write everything in one file:

from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/users")
def get_users():
    pass


@app.post("/users")
def create_user():
    pass


@app.get("/posts")
def get_posts():
    pass


@app.post("/posts")
def create_post():
    pass


@app.get("/comments")
def get_comments():
    pass

Imagine 100 endpoints in one file! 😵 We need to split them by responsibility. That's APIRouter.

6.1 🤔 What is APIRouter?

📌 APIRouter is a FastAPI class that organizes related endpoints into separate modules.

Think of dividing a company into departments: the user department handles users, the post department handles posts, the comment department handles comments, the auth department handles authentication.

6.2 📁 Recommended folder structure 

backend/
└── app/
    ├── api/
    │   ├── users.py       # User endpoints
    │   ├── posts.py       # Post endpoints
    │   └── comments.py    # Comment endpoints
    └── main.py            # Main application

6.3 🛠️ Creating a router

users.py:

from fastapi import APIRouter

router = APIRouter()


@router.get("/")
def get_users():
    return {"message": "All users"}


@router.get("/{user_id}")
def get_user(user_id: int):
    return {"user_id": user_id}


@router.post("/")
def create_user():
    return {"message": "User created"}

router = APIRouter() creates a separate router. Instead of @app.get("/") we write @router.get("/"), because these endpoints belong to the router, not directly to the main app.

6.4 🔌 Connecting the router to the main app

main.py:

from fastapi import FastAPI

from app.api import users

app = FastAPI()

app.include_router(
    users.router,
    prefix="/users",
    tags=["Users"],
)
  • include_router() registers the router with the main app
  • prefix="/users" means every endpoint in that router starts with /users
  • tags=["Users"] groups these endpoints under a Users section in Swagger docs
Router endpoint Final endpoint
@router.get("/") GET /users/
@router.get("/{user_id}") GET /users/{user_id}
@router.post("/") POST /users/

6.5 ✅ Why use APIRouter?

  1. 🧩 Modularity: separate related endpoints
  2. 🛠️ Maintainability: easier to modify code
  3. ♻️ Reusability: routers can be included in different apps
  4. 📖 Readability: easier for developers to understand
  5. 📈 Scalability: suitable for large backends

⚠️ Important: APIRouter does not create a separate server or application. It organizes routes inside one FastAPI application.

7. 📖 Automatic Interactive Documentation: Swagger UI and ReDoc

One of FastAPI's coolest features! You create 50 endpoints. How will your frontend developer know which endpoints exist, which methods they support, what parameters and request body they need, and what they return? You could write docs manually, but FastAPI generates them automatically! 🪄

7.1 🧪 Swagger UI

An interactive interface to explore and test your API. After starting your app, visit:

http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs

You can:

  1. View all endpoints
  2. Expand an endpoint
  3. See required parameters
  4. Enter request data
  5. Click Try it out
  6. Click Execute
  7. View the response and HTTP status code

You can test your backend without writing any frontend code! 🎉

7.2 📚 ReDoc

Another automatically generated documentation interface:

http://127.0.0.1:8000/redoc

It presents your API in a more reference-oriented, organized layout.

7.3 ⚖️ Swagger UI vs ReDoc

Feature Swagger UI ReDoc
URL /docs /redoc
Interactive testing Yes Primarily documentation-focused
API exploration Yes Yes
Layout Interactive interface Reference-style documentation
Generated automatically Yes Yes

Both are generated from FastAPI's OpenAPI schema.

7.4 📜 What is OpenAPI?

📌 OpenAPI is a standard specification that describes your API: available endpoints, HTTP methods, request parameters, request body schemas, response schemas and authentication requirements.

FastAPI generates it automatically at:

http://127.0.0.1:8000/openapi.json

Swagger UI and ReDoc read this schema to display the docs.

7.5 🪄 How does FastAPI generate docs automatically? 

@app.get("/posts/{post_id}")
def get_post(post_id: int):
    return {"post_id": post_id}

FastAPI understands the HTTP method (GET), the endpoint (/posts/{post_id}), the parameter name (post_id) and its type (integer). Likewise:

class PostCreate(BaseModel):
    caption: str
    image_url: str

FastAPI understands the request-body structure, and:

@app.post("/posts", response_model=PostResponse)

tells it the expected response schema. It collects all this into OpenAPI docs. That's why type hints and Pydantic models matter so much in FastAPI. 💡

8. 🎯 Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

SRP is one of the five SOLID principles of object-oriented design. Let's focus on just this one.

8.1 🤔 What is SRP?

📌 A function, class, or module should have one clear responsibility, or one reason to change.

Think of a restaurant 🍽️: the chef prepares food, the cashier handles payments, the waiter takes orders, the manager manages operations. If one person did everything, it'd be chaos. Similarly, we shouldn't put all backend responsibilities into one function.

8.2 ❌ The problem: without SRP 

@app.post("/posts")
def create_post(post: PostCreate):
    # Validate user
    # Connect to database
    # Check image URL
    # Create post in database
    # Send notification
    # Return response
    return {"message": "Post created"}

This function handles too many responsibilities:

  1. Receiving the HTTP request
  2. Validating user permissions
  3. Handling database operations
  4. Executing post creation logic
  5. Sending notifications
  6. Returning the HTTP response

Change notification logic? Modify this function. Change database logic? Modify it again. It becomes hard to maintain. 😩

8.3 ✅ Applying SRP: separate responsibilities 

🛣️ Router Layer      posts.py             Receives HTTP requests, reads parameters, calls services, returns responses
        ▼
🧠 Service Layer      post_service.py      Contains business logic and rules
        ▼
📚 Repository Layer   post_repository.py   Handles database operations (insert, update, retrieve)
        ▼
🗄️ Database           Stores application data

A. Router layer (posts.py)

@router.post("/")
def create_post(
    post: PostCreate,
    db: Session = Depends(get_db),
):
    return post_service.create_post(db, post)

Its job: receive the request, get the request data, obtain the database dependency, call the service, return the result. It doesn't need to know the internal business rules.

B. Service layer (post_service.py)

def create_post(db, post):
    if not post.caption:
        raise ValueError("Caption is required")

    return post_repository.create(db, post)

Its job: implement business rules, decide what should happen, coordinate the required operations (like checking whether a user is allowed to create a post).

C. Repository layer (post_repository.py)

def create(db, post):
    new_post = Post(caption=post.caption)

    db.add(new_post)
    db.commit()
    db.refresh(new_post)

    return new_post

Its job: talk to the database (insert, retrieve, update, delete).

Why is this better? If your database changes, you modify the repository layer without rewriting all your HTTP endpoints. If business rules change, you update the service layer. The app becomes easier to maintain and test. 🧪

📝 These layers are an architectural choice, not a mandatory FastAPI requirement. Small apps can have fewer layers. The key is to avoid mixing unrelated responsibilities.

9. 🧵 Putting Everything Together: A Real FastAPI Example

Let's build a mini Instagram backend with an endpoint to create posts.

backend/
└── app/
    ├── api/
    │   └── posts.py              # Routes
    ├── schemas/
    │   └── post.py               # Pydantic models
    ├── services/
    │   └── post_service.py       # Business logic
    ├── repositories/
    │   └── post_repository.py    # Database operations
    └── main.py                   # Application entry point

Step 1: create Pydantic schemas (schemas/post.py)

from pydantic import BaseModel


class PostCreate(BaseModel):
    caption: str


class PostResponse(BaseModel):
    id: int
    caption: str

Step 2: create the repository (repositories/post_repository.py)

def create_post(db, caption):
    new_post = {
        "id": 1,
        "caption": caption,
    }
    return new_post

📝 A simplified repository using a dictionary instead of a real SQLAlchemy database.

Step 3: create the service (services/post_service.py)

from app.repositories import post_repository


def create_post(db, post):
    return post_repository.create_post(db, post.caption)

Step 4: create the router (api/posts.py)

from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends

from app.schemas.post import PostCreate, PostResponse
from app.services import post_service

router = APIRouter()


def get_db():
    return "Database session"


@router.post("/", response_model=PostResponse)
def create_post(
    post: PostCreate,
    db=Depends(get_db),
):
    return post_service.create_post(db, post)

Step 5: connect the router (main.py)

from fastapi import FastAPI

from app.api import posts

app = FastAPI()

app.include_router(
    posts.router,
    prefix="/posts",
    tags=["Posts"],
)

Start the server:

uvicorn app.main:app --reload

Visit http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs, find POST /posts/, and send:

{
  "caption": "My first post!"
}

Expected response:

{
  "id": 1,
  "caption": "My first post!"
}

9.1 🔍 What happened internally?

  1. 🌐 Frontend sends the request: POST /posts/ with JSON data
  2. 🛣️ FastAPI identifies the route: it finds the matching endpoint in the posts router
  3. ✔️ Pydantic validates request data: checks that the caption is a string
  4. 💉 Dependency Injection happens: FastAPI sees Depends(get_db) and resolves the database dependency
  5. 🧠 Router calls the service: post_service.create_post(db, post)
  6. 📚 Service calls the repository: the repository performs the database operation
  7. 📤 Response model validates output: FastAPI uses PostResponse to validate and serialize the response
  8. 🔙 Response goes back to the frontend as JSON

This is how everything you've learned works together in a real backend. 🎯

10. 📋 Quick Revision: Everything at a Glance

Concept What it does Example
FastAPI Python framework for APIs FastAPI()
Path parameter Identifies a resource /posts/10
Query parameter Filters or controls retrieval ?limit=10
Body parameter Sends structured data JSON request body
Pydantic Validates and parses data BaseModel
Request schema Defines incoming data PostCreate
Response schema Defines outgoing data PostResponse

11. 🎤 Interview Questions

1. What is FastAPI?
A modern Python web framework used to build APIs. It supports automatic request validation, dependency injection, asynchronous programming and automatic API documentation.

2. What's the difference between path and query parameters?
Path parameters identify a particular resource, whereas query parameters provide additional filtering, sorting or pagination information.

3. What is Pydantic?
A Python data validation library. It validates incoming data based on the types and rules defined in our models.

4. Why do we need separate request and response schemas?
Request schemas validate incoming data, while response schemas control the structure of outgoing data and prevent unwanted fields, such as passwords, from being exposed.

5. What is Dependency Injection?
A technique where required objects or services are provided to a function from outside instead of the function creating them internally.

6. What is Depends() in FastAPI?
FastAPI's built-in mechanism for declaring dependencies. FastAPI resolves them and injects their results into endpoint functions.

7. What is Inversion of Control?
A design principle where control over certain operations is transferred from application code to a framework or external component. FastAPI implements this through dependency injection.

8. What is APIRouter?
It organizes related API endpoints into separate modules, making large applications modular and maintainable.

9. What's the difference between Swagger UI and ReDoc?
Swagger UI provides an interactive interface for exploring and testing APIs. ReDoc provides a documentation-focused interface.

10. What is SRP?
The Single Responsibility Principle says a component should have one clear responsibility. In FastAPI, we apply it by separating route handling, business logic and database operations.

12. 🧪 Test Yourself!

Try these before peeking at the answers! ❤️

  1. You want to retrieve post number 50 using /posts/50. What type of parameter is 50?

    • A) Query parameter
    • B) Path parameter
    • C) Body parameter

  2. Which library validates incoming request data using BaseModel?

    • A) SQLAlchemy
    • B) Uvicorn
    • C) Pydantic

  3. What does Depends(get_db) do?

    • A) Deletes the database
    • B) Asks FastAPI to provide a database dependency
    • C) Creates a new API endpoint

  4. Which component organizes related API endpoints?

    • A) APIRouter
    • B) BaseModel
    • C) ReDoc

  5. Where can you interactively test your FastAPI endpoints by default?

    • A) /redoc
    • B) /openapi.json
    • C) /docs

  6. Which layer should contain business logic?

    • A) Router
    • B) Service
    • C) Frontend

👀 Click to reveal answers
  1. B: 50 is part of the URL path, so it's a path parameter
  2. C: Pydantic validates data using BaseModel
  3. B: It asks FastAPI to resolve and inject the get_db dependency
  4. A: APIRouter groups related endpoints
  5. C: /docs opens Swagger UI for interactive testing
  6. B: The service layer holds business logic

13. 🧭 What to Remember in Your Own Backend

When you open your own FastAPI project, try to identify:

  • 🛣️ api/: where are the routes?
  • ✔️ schemas/: what request and response structures are defined?
  • 🧠 services/: where is the business logic?
  • 📚 repositories/: where are database operations performed?
  • 💉 Depends(): how are dependencies provided?
  • 🗂️ APIRouter: how are endpoints grouped?
  • 🚪 main.py: where are routers registered and the app created?

Once you can spot these in real code, you'll understand how a professional FastAPI backend is structured instead of just memorizing definitions.

🚀 What's Next?

Pick one endpoint and trace its complete flow: frontend request → router → dependency → service → repository → database → response. That's far more valuable than memorizing 50 definitions. 💡

If this post helped you, drop a ❤️ or 🦄 and share it with a friend learning FastAPI. Happy coding! 👩‍💻✨

title: Keep Failed Collections Out of Your AI Search Mention Denominator
description:
Your brand disappeared from a report. Did the AI answer omit it, or did the collection fail? If both situations become the same zero, the report can send an editor to fix the wrong thing.

Summary

Store completed answers, explicit no-answer outcomes, and collection errors as different states. This local Python example uses synthetic records and shows which denominator each rate uses. Prepared with AI assistance for TheLogic.

Contents

  1. Define the three states
  2. Calculate one clearly named rate
  3. Inspect the report before comparing runs
  4. FAQ

Define the three states

Here, answer means a completed answer string is present, no_answer means the collection completed and recorded an explicit absence of an answer, and error means the observation failed. A valid answer can still contain no brand mention. This schema is a local reporting convention, not an OpenAI response format.

A missing brand name and a failed observation need different labels.

Calculate one clearly named rate

Use the code below to keep the counts visible. The mention rate is defined only over answer rows. Report no-answer results and errors alongside it so readers can see coverage.

def summarize(rows):
    counts = dict(answer=0, no_answer=0, error=0, mentioned=0)
    for row in rows:
        state = row['state']
        if state not in {'answer', 'no_answer', 'error'}:
            raise ValueError('Unknown state')
        if state == 'answer':
            if not isinstance(row.get('answer'), str) or not row['answer'].strip():
                raise ValueError('An answer row needs nonempty text')
            if type(row.get('mentioned')) is not bool:
                raise ValueError('mentioned must be a boolean')
            counts['mentioned'] += int(row['mentioned'])
        counts[state] += 1
    rate = counts['mentioned'] / counts['answer'] if counts['answer'] else None
    return counts, rate

rows = [
    dict(state='answer', answer='Example with brand', mentioned=True),
    dict(state='answer', answer='Another answer', mentioned=False),
    dict(state='answer', answer='Third answer', mentioned=False),
    dict(state='no_answer'),
    dict(state='error'),
]
counts, rate = summarize(rows)
assert counts == dict(answer=3, no_answer=1, error=1, mentioned=1)
assert rate == 1 / 3
assert summarize([])[1] is None
try:
    summarize([dict(state='unknown')])
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError('Unknown states must fail')
print(counts, rate)

Five attempts produce three answer rows, one explicit no-answer outcome, and one error. One mention divided by three answer rows is 33.3%. These are synthetic examples, not a customer result.

State Included in mention-rate denominator Also report
answer Yes Mentioned or not mentioned
no_answer No, by this definition Count of completed no-answer outcomes
error No Count and reason if available

Inspect the report before comparing runs

Keep the same question set, platform, search setting, and period when comparing runs. A smaller error count can change how many answer rows you have. Show both counts and rates before interpreting a difference. TheLogic's public GEO methodology distinguishes collected observations and their source records.

FAQ

Is this the only correct denominator
No. You can define a rate over all completed observations, but name the denominator and keep failure counts visible.

Can no_answer be inferred from an empty answer field
Only if your collector guarantees that meaning. Otherwise use an error or unknown state until it is classified.

Does the script query an AI service
It summarizes local records and makes no network requests.

title: A Concept-Based Interpretable Framework for Clinical Text-based Prediction via Token-Concept Attention without Concept Supervision
description:
arXiv:2611.13564v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Objective: Concept-based interpretation has emerged as a promising approach for explaining blackbox models using human-understandable, high-level concepts. However, most existing methods require annotated concept labels to train the model to identify concepts in the input, and obtaining such annotations in clinical text is often expensive. This study aims to enable concept-based interpretation for language models without concept supervision on clinical prediction tasks. Methods: We propose a novel framework that enables concept-based interpretation without concept supervision through a tailored cross-attention bottleneck. Clinical text and the text descriptions of medical concepts are first tokenized and embedded by a pretrained language model. A cross-attention module then estimates the presence of each concept for each text token, producing concept relevance scores that capture how concepts are involved throughout the note. These scores are pooled and used in a linear prediction layer to model clinical outcomes in an interpretable manner. Results: The performance of the proposed framework was compared against blackbox models across two tasks: chest trauma severity stratification using a private dataset and an in-hospital mortality prediction task using the publicly available MIMIC-III dataset. The proposed framework achieved AUROC values within 0.02 of the corresponding blackbox models. The framework also enabled cohort- and patient-level interpretation, capturing the overall concept importance across the cohort and patient-specific concept contributions. Conclusion: Our proposed framework realizes concept-based interpretation without requiring ground-truth concept presence labels. It improves the transparency of clinical text predictions while maintaining strong performance in clinical prediction tasks.

title: Dependable Long-Horizon LLM Agents: A Trajectory-Centered Empirical Study of Where Errors Enter and Which Controls Reach Them
description:
arXiv:2611.13254v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When an LLM agent fails part-way through a long task, the usual analysis records a symptom: a failure-mode label, or the agent and step judged responsible. It does not say where the error entered, which state carried it to the symptom, whether anything in the trajectory contradicted it, or which control could have caught it. We define an episode record that ties a candidate fault to its origin, propagation, detection, response and consequence, located by operational phase and state domain, and that names the control families whose observation and reach cover it. We turned the record into a written annotation protocol and applied it to 95 failed runs of six multi-agent systems from the public Who&When and MAD corpora, reading each trajectory in full. Faults enter early (median at 0.18 of the run), mostly as wrong decisions or fabrications over task state, and in 37 of 88 Who&When runs before the step the corpus' human labels mark as decisive. In 72% of failed runs the trajectory already contained evidence against the error before the failure; in 88% of those no agent acted on it. Something flagged a deviation in 31% of runs, but no response removed the deviated state. Independent judges reading the unused evidence, task contracts fixed at admission, and re-checking beliefs against the environment reach most episodes; restoring the agent's own state would have sufficed in 35 of 95 runs. A text scan of the raw corpus also shows that 45% of the hand-crafted Who&When failures ended with a provider content-filter crash after which the harness emitted a final answer no agent produced, a failure class that neither symptom taxonomies nor responsible-agent labels represent. Protocol, records and scripts are included.

title: Thermodynamics of words
description:
arXiv:2611.14039v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We introduce the word thermalization hypothesis according to which in a literary work there are effective interactions between words that drive them to thermalization where their word frequency distribution is the same as for the phenomenon of Rayleigh-Jeans (RJ) thermalization and condensation. In this concept, the different words play a role of classical oscillators (particles) and their word frequencies, or related tokens, are analogous to certain filling factors over energy state levels. The thermalization process is characterized by the conservation of total system energy, or total number of words/tokens, and total probability norm, or total number of different words. We apply this approach to analyze 16 literary works, including Bible, complete works of Shakespeare, and data from American National Corpus. We show that for these cases the effective system energy is very low and thus there is the RJ condensation phenomenon with a big fraction of total probability concentrated at the lowest energy states corresponding to a big fraction of rare words appearing only once or twice in the whole text. Such a RJ condensation is observed for light propagation in multimode optical fibers and other physical systems. We relate the thermalization of words to the recently proposed wealth thermalization for households in world countries. The economy concepts of Lorenz and Pareto curves, and also Zipf curves, are applied to the word frequency distributions of the selected 16 cases and it is shown that the thermalization theory gives a strikingly good description of real data.

title: Multifidelity Operator Inference for Non-intrusive Model Reduction under Data Scarcity
description:
arXiv:2611.13624v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many-query analyses, in which a computational model is repeatedly evaluated, play an important role in uncertainty quantification and optimization for engineering design. However, many-query analyses can be prohibitively expensive when considering high-fidelity numerical models, especially those governed by partial differential equations (PDEs). Surrogate modeling replaces costly simulations with cheap approximations, enabling practical uncertainty quantification and design workflows. Machine learning (ML) approaches to surrogate modeling have gained significant traction in the development of surrogate models due to their non-intrusive nature; they do not require access to the underlying simulation code. The Operator Inference (OpInf) approach, in particular, fits reduced operators to state and corresponding time derivative data. However, high-fidelity training data is scarce due to limited computational budgets, and OpInf models trained on such scarce data often exhibit high variance, a critical liability in high-risk engineering design. We propose Multifidelity Operator Inference (MF-OpInf), which reduces this variance by supplementing scarce high-fidelity snapshots with abundant low-fidelity data drawn from coarser discretizations of the same problem. MF-OpInf handles data across varying fidelity levels by utilizing a multifidelity linear regression framework to estimate the reduced operators. Numerical experiments on model PDE problems demonstrate that MF-OpInf predicts PDE solution fields with higher accuracy compared to the high-fidelity-only OpInf with the same computational budget.

title: What are the best Paperspace alternatives in 2026?
description:
The best Paperspace alternatives in 2026 are Nodus for training runs that have outgrown a notebook, RunPod for cheap per-second GPU pods, and Kaggle Notebooks for students who need a free GPU. Nodus lists the NVIDIA H100 at $2.60 per GPU-hour on its pricing page, against $5.95 on Paperspace, and restores your latest checkpoint on a replacement machine when one is lost. Stay on Paperspace if its $8 or $39 monthly plan already gives you free notebook GPUs that cover your hours.

We build Nodus, so read this list with that in mind. Every fact about another company links to its own pricing page or docs, and each sum is written out so you can redo it with today's prices.

What does Paperspace offer and charge today?

Paperspace is now part of DigitalOcean, and its notebooks still exist. DigitalOcean's Paperspace docs list four products: Notebooks (a browser Jupyter IDE), Deployments, Workflows and Machines, which are Linux virtual machines with GPU options. The Notebooks, Deployments and Workflows products and the subscription plans still carry the Gradient name, per DigitalOcean's documentation index.

Two prices stack up. A Gradient subscription plan is Free, Pro at $8 per month or Growth at $39 per month, and each one includes a set of free notebook machines. Paid machines then bill by the hour: an A100-80G is $3.18/hr, an A6000 $1.89/hr and an H100 $5.95/hr, and an H100 x 8 machine is $47.60/hr, all from DigitalOcean's Paperspace pricing page.

The free machines come with limits. Per the Machines features page, they shut down after at most six hours, notebooks idle for an hour shut down, and only one notebook can use a free machine at a time. On the Free plan, free machines are always public.

H100s take a request. The H100 reference says they run only in the NY2 region and need approval from support, and the Machines limits page says requests typically take 1 to 2 business days.

How do the Paperspace alternatives compare?

They split along one line: a notebook you sit in, or a run that finishes without you. Paperspace and Kaggle are built around the first. RunPod gives you a GPU pod and leaves the run to you, and Nodus runs a command or training job to completion.

Platform What you get Free option A100 80 GB per hour H100 per GPU-hour If the machine is lost
Paperspace Notebooks and virtual machines Free plan with an M4000 notebook GPU $3.18 $5.95 Not stated in the docs we read
Nodus Jobs, Workspaces with JupyterLab, TrainingJobs None; prepaid credit $1.090 $2.600 (H100 SXM) Latest checkpoint restored on a replacement machine
RunPod GPU pods billed per second Not listed on the pricing page $1.79 Secure, from $1.39 Community (A100 SXM) $3.99 Secure, from $2.69 Community (H100 SXM) Not stated on the pricing page
Kaggle Notebooks P100 or 2 x T4, 12-hour sessions Not listed Not listed Not stated; sessions end at 12 hours

Prices checked November 11, 2026: Paperspace pricing, Nodus pricing, RunPod pricing and Kaggle Notebooks docs. Nodus lists GPU rates and CPU-plus-memory rates as separate lines; Paperspace lists one hourly price per machine.

If you are leaving Paperspace for a plain virtual machine at its parent company, our DigitalOcean GPU Droplet alternatives post covers that comparison. For pods, our RunPod alternatives guide goes deeper on RunPod's two clouds.

What does it cost to turn a notebook into a training run?

On listed rates, the same run costs less than half as much on Nodus as on a paid Paperspace machine. We priced two runs a notebook user typically graduates to, using each company's public pricing page on November 11, 2026, GPU compute only.

The first is a 10-hour fine-tune on one A100 80 GB. Paperspace's A100-80G at $3.18/hr comes to $31.80. RunPod's A100 SXM is $17.90 on Secure Cloud at $1.79/hr and from $13.90 on Community Cloud at $1.39/hr. Nodus at $1.090/hr comes to $10.90, which is $20.90 or 66% less than Paperspace.


For a single-GPU fine-tune, a paid Paperspace A100 costs about three times the Nodus rate.

The second is a bigger run: 8 x H100 for 10 hours, or 80 GPU-hours. Paperspace's H100 x 8 machine at $47.60/hr comes to $476.00. RunPod is $319.20 on Secure Cloud at $3.99 per GPU-hour and from $215.20 on Community Cloud at $2.69. Nodus at $2.60 comes to $208.00, which is $268.00 or 56% less than Paperspace.


At list prices, 80 H100 GPU-hours cost $268.00 less on Nodus than on a Paperspace H100 x 8 machine.

Two caveats keep this fair. Nodus adds CPU and memory lines on top of the GPU rate, so run nodus run --dry-run and compare that estimate, not this table. RunPod's Community rates are "from" prices, so your pod may cost more.

When is a Paperspace plan cheaper than paying by the hour?

A Paperspace plan wins once your free-machine hours pass a break-even point. Pro costs $8 a month and includes a free A4000 notebook machine. Growth costs $39 a month and includes free A6000 and A100-80G machines, per the free machines table on the Paperspace pricing page.

Divide the plan price by the Nodus rate for the same card. Against the RTX A4000 at $0.173/hr, Pro pays for itself after 46.2 hours a month ($8 / $0.173). Growth breaks even after 35.8 hours of A100 80 GB at $1.090/hr ($39 / $1.090), or 117.1 hours of RTX A6000 at $0.333/hr ($39 / $0.333). Counting Nodus CPU and memory lines would make each break-even come sooner.


If you live in an A100 notebook more than about 36 hours a month, the $39 Growth plan is the better deal.

The catch is that free sessions are capped. Each one stops after at most six hours, and the paperspace.com pricing page describes faster free GPUs as "based on availability".

So here is the decision rule we use. Interactive notebook hours belong on a Paperspace plan. Any run longer than six hours, or one that must finish by morning, belongs on a platform that bills only for the run and restarts it after a lost machine.

Where is Paperspace still the better choice?

Paperspace is better for cheap, steady notebook time. A student on the Free plan gets a free M4000 GPU and 5 GB of storage for $0. Nodus has no equivalent: our credits docs say the public starter offer has ended and new accounts add prepaid credit first.

It is also the simpler bill if you want a monthly ceiling. Plans and storage on the pricing page have a maximum monthly price, after which they stop charging for the cycle. Paperspace Machines come with free unlimited bandwidth, per the Machines features page, and compute billing stops when you power a machine off.

Pick Paperspace too if your work is mostly in a notebook and fits a six-hour session, or if your team already shares projects and datasets there. Moving costs you setup time, and the savings only show up once you run long jobs.

Which Paperspace alternative is best for students?

For a student with no budget, Kaggle Notebooks is the strongest free option we found. The Kaggle Notebooks docs offer a free NVIDIA Tesla P100 or two T4 GPUs, 12-hour sessions and 20 GB of auto-saved output. Kaggle says free GPU availability is limited, so you may wait in a queue at busy times.

Paperspace's Free plan is the second free option, with shorter six-hour sessions and public notebooks. Once a class project needs an A100 or H100 for a few hours, paying by the hour beats a monthly plan. Three hours on a Nodus A100 80 GB at $1.090/hr is $3.27, against $39 for a month of Growth.

How do you move a Paperspace notebook to Nodus?

Start a Workspace, which is the closest Nodus match to a Paperspace notebook. Per the Workspaces guide, it is a GPU or CPU machine with JupyterLab, browser VS Code and SSH. Its /home/nodus directory is saved whenever it stops, and by default it stops after an hour idle.

$ pip install nodus-compute
$ nodus login
$ nodus create workspace lab --gpu H100

Upload your notebook and data to the home directory and develop as you did on Paperspace. When the code is ready for a long run, send it out as a Job instead of leaving a notebook open overnight:

$ nodus run --from workspace/lab -- python train.py

The Job runs on a saved copy of your Workspace home, so you can stop the Workspace while it trains. To survive a lost machine, write model, optimizer and step files under /nodus/state and load them on start, as the checkpoints guide shows; our post on resuming training after spot preemption walks through a full loop.

FAQ

Is Paperspace still available in 2026?

Yes. DigitalOcean's Paperspace docs still document Notebooks, Deployments, Workflows and Machines, and its pricing page was updated in July 2026. Windows templates were retired for new users in July 2024, so new accounts get Linux machines.

Can I connect my Paperspace account to Nodus?

No. Paperspace is not one of the providers on the Nodus cloud accounts page. DigitalOcean is, but that connection covers CPU and GPU Droplets, not Paperspace Machines or Notebooks.

Does Paperspace have multi-GPU machines?

Yes. The pricing page lists 8-GPU machines of the A6000, V100-32G, A100, A100-80G and H100, and the H100 x 8 at $47.60/hr is exactly 8 times the single-GPU rate. DigitalOcean's H100 reference says the H100 x 8 supports NVLink and the H100 x 1 does not.

Is Nodus a good fit if I only use notebooks?

Only if you also run long jobs. Without a free tier, Nodus suits people who pay for compute anyway and want runs that finish; a free Kaggle or Paperspace notebook is cheaper for occasional exploration.
