title: Realtime Presence Sidebar: Node.js Room Cleanup and Update Guarantees
description:
Short answer: for reliable realtime room teardown, design the team presence sidebar around an explicit state machine, a monotonic cursor, and bounded backfill rather than treating disconnects as proof that cleanup happened.

I run a one-person SaaS, so my test for infrastructure is revenue per hour. A presence sidebar that shows ghost members creates support work, but a full event platform can create a different kind of drag. The useful design is the smallest one that makes reconnect and backfill deterministic.

Approach Reconnect behavior Backfill responsibility Good fit
Broadcast-only WebSocket Client guesses what it missed Application must reconstruct state Tiny, disposable rooms
Cursor-based event log Client resumes from a sequence Server replays a bounded window Team presence and room membership
WebRTC data channel Peer-dependent; signaling still matters Usually application-defined Media-adjacent metadata, not authority

My default is the middle row. It keeps the authority on the server and lets the UI stay boring. Boring is good when I need to ship weekly.

What should a realtime room teardown guarantee for a presence sidebar?

Teardown should be idempotent. A room can receive leave, disconnect, a token expiry, and an admin close in a different order on different machines. Each signal must converge on the same state without deleting a newer membership record.

Give every room event a sequence number scoped to the room. A client stores the last applied sequence, not just the last timestamp. On reconnect it sends that cursor. If the server still has the range, it replays events; if the cursor fell outside retention, it sends a snapshot followed by new events. This is the key difference between “the socket is open” and “the sidebar is correct.”

The teardown record also needs an owner scope. In a fintech collaboration room, a token for one team must not let a user remove another team's member. Scope the command by tenant, room, and member id, then check authorization before publishing the resulting event. A successful command emits member.removed; it does not ask each browser to infer removal from a transport error.

One small rule saves hours: never use wall-clock order to resolve membership. Clocks drift. Compare the room sequence and a per-member generation instead.

How can Node.js implement reconnect and backfill without ghost members?

The following TypeScript sketch is deliberately transport-neutral. The store could be Postgres, Redis Streams, or a self-hosted log. The contract is what matters: append once, replay from a cursor, and make remove safe to repeat.

type PresenceEvent = {
  roomId: string;
  seq: number;
  kind: "member.joined" | "member.removed" | "room.closed";
  memberId?: string;
  generation?: number;
};

interface RoomLog {
  append(event: Omit<PresenceEvent, "seq">): Promise<PresenceEvent>;
  after(roomId: string, seq: number): Promise<PresenceEvent[]>;
  snapshot(roomId: string): Promise<{ members: string[]; seq: number }>;
}

async function teardownMember(
  log: RoomLog,
  roomId: string,
  memberId: string,
  generation: number,
) {
  return log.append({
    roomId,
    kind: "member.removed",
    memberId,
    generation,
  });
}

async function resume(log: RoomLog, roomId: string, cursor: number) {
  const events = await log.after(roomId, cursor);
  if (events.length > 0 || cursor === 0) return { mode: "events" as const, events };
  return { mode: "snapshot" as const, state: await log.snapshot(roomId) };
}

In production, append must enforce a unique command key or transaction boundary. Otherwise two disconnect handlers can publish two removals. The consumer should also discard an event whose generation is older than the member row it already has. That check makes retries harmless.

The UI should render a connection state separately from member state. “Reconnecting” is honest; clearing the sidebar is not. Keep the last known members visible, mark them stale if your product needs that signal, and replace them only after replay or snapshot succeeds.

Where do common teardown designs fail?

The first failure is treating a close frame as proof that a member left. Mobile networks disappear without a close frame, and a browser can reconnect before the old connection's cleanup job runs. A lease with a short heartbeat can detect this, but lease expiry still has to produce an ordered room event. In one realistic race, connection A starts a cleanup task, connection B renews the same member, and the delayed task finally writes its removal. If the write only checks memberId, the sidebar loses an active person; if it checks the generation captured by A, the stale removal is rejected and the newer presence remains. That comparison belongs in the transaction, beside the append, because moving it into a worker merely moves the race to another queue.

Keep it explicit.

The second failure is unbounded replay. Keeping every event forever sounds safe until a client returns after a week and asks for millions of rows. Set a retention window, measure the snapshot rate, and make the snapshot path a tested feature rather than an emergency branch.

Small rooms still benefit from this boundary.

The third failure is mixing media and presence authority. WebRTC defines peer connection behavior, but it does not define your team's membership database. Libraries such as Socket.IO can simplify transport fallbacks; managed pub/sub services can simplify fan-out; a self-hosted log gives more control over retention. None of these choices removes the need for a cursor and an authorization check.

I once assumed a “leave” message was enough. Then a reconnect raced the cleanup worker and a member briefly vanished, reappeared, and vanished again. The fix was not a longer timeout. It was a generation number checked at write time. Your mileage may vary if your rooms are ephemeral, but the race is still worth testing.

When is this design the wrong trade?

The catch is operational weight. If a room lasts thirty seconds and losing one presence update has no consequence, a broadcast-only channel is cheaper to reason about. Use the simpler design when there is no audit need, no reconnect expectation, and no cross-device session.

Choose a managed realtime service when operating retention, fan-out, and regional failover would slow feature delivery more than it improves your product. Choose a peer-oriented WebRTC channel when the data is truly incidental to an active call and the server does not need an authoritative roster. Stick with a durable, cursor-based log for financial workflows, moderation, billing roles, or any sidebar that drives a permission decision.

My decision rule is practical: outsource undifferentiated delivery, keep the state transition you would debug at 2 a.m. in code you can inspect. That keeps the surface small without pretending disconnects are reliable messages.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSocket
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebRTC_API
  • https://socket.io/docs/v4/

title: Before Words, Beyond Speech: Evaluating Nonverbal Social Reasoning in Early Childhood
description:
arXiv:2611.13213v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Children's earliest years are a period of intense social learning, during which meaning is built through gaze, gesture, and physical contact. Yet, this critical aspect of social interaction remains under-evaluated in multimodal video understanding, as existing benchmarks prioritize the conversation-driven interactions of adults. We address this gap with \bench ($\textbf{N}$aturalistic $\textbf{E}$arly-childhood $\textbf{S}$ocial in$\textbf{T}$eractions), the first child-centric benchmark for nonverbal social reasoning. \bench comprises \totalvids manually annotated clips ($\sim$12s) curated for diversity across naturalistic settings, cultural contexts, and developmental stages. Beyond a lack of data, targeted model improvement in this domain is hindered by coarse evaluation schemas that conflate basic perception with higher-order reasoning. To resolve this, \bench introduces a compositional schema that builds atomic interaction cues into progressive levels of social reasoning: contextual, behavioral, interpersonal, and open-ended descriptions. Extensive analysis of state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs) reveals a stark performance collapse: despite strong contextual recognition, models exhibit substantial gaps in decoding precise behavioral and interpersonal cues. We trace these failures to specific biases, including poor consequence grounding and temporal sensitivity. Finally, we ground \bench in real-world applications by evaluating VLMs using domain adaptation strategies. Ultimately, \bench provides a rigorous testbed for advancing socially grounded artificial intelligence in early childhood. Project page: https://laubravo.github.io/nest_website/.

title: AZ-500 Exam Guide: Azure Security Skills and Lab Plan
description:
Microsoft retired the AZ-500 exam on August 31, 2026. Per the official certification page, you can no longer earn or renew the Azure Security Engineer Associate certification after that date.

That changes how you should use this guide. Read it to understand the skills, the exam format and a study plan. Do not buy a voucher before you confirm it can still be used.

What AZ-500 proved and who it was for

The credential was Microsoft Certified: Azure Security Engineer Associate. Microsoft lists it as Intermediate level, for the Security Engineer role, on the Azure product.

The holder implements, manages and monitors security for resources in Azure, multi-cloud and hybrid environments. That work uses Microsoft Defender for Cloud and other tools. It also aligns the infrastructure with standards such as the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark (MCSB).

Microsoft names three core responsibilities:

  • Managing the security posture.
  • Implementing threat protection.
  • Identifying and remediating vulnerabilities.

The exam suited people with practical experience in Azure and hybrid administration. Microsoft also expected strong familiarity with Microsoft Entra ID, plus compute, network and storage in Azure.

Skills measured and their weights

The official study guide lists the skills measured as of January 22, 2026. Defender for Cloud and Sentinel carried the most weight.

Skill area Weight
Secure identity and access 15–20%
Secure networking 20–25%
Secure compute, storage, and databases 20–25%
Secure Azure using Microsoft Defender for Cloud and Microsoft Sentinel 30–35%

Some topics from the guide show what "secure identity and access" meant in practice:

  • Azure built-in and custom role assignments, including Microsoft Entra roles.
  • Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management settings and assignments.
  • Multi-factor authentication and Conditional Access policies.
  • App registrations, service principals and managed identities.

Networking covered Network Security Groups, Application Security Groups, user-defined routes, VPN connectivity, Private Endpoints, Azure Firewall, Application Gateway, Front Door and Web Application Firewall. Compute included Azure Bastion, just-in-time VM access and securing Azure Kubernetes Service.

Exam format, score and retakes

The exam was proctored. Microsoft says it may include interactive components. Here is what the sources state.

Item Detail
Passing score 700 or greater
Languages English, Japanese, Chinese (Simplified), Korean, German, French, Spanish, Portuguese (Brazil), Chinese (Traditional), Italian
Retake after a failure 24 hours after the first attempt; later waits vary
Extra time An extra 30 minutes can be requested if the exam isn't in your language
Accommodations Available on request through Microsoft

Microsoft also offered a free practice assessment and an exam sandbox. Use the study guide page for those links. For exam length and the exam experience, Microsoft points to its exam duration page.

Price, voucher terms and refunds

Microsoft's published list price was $165.00 USD (source: Microsoft official exam price, as published by the vendor). Our AZ-500 voucher is listed at $44.99. It is valid for 12 months and redeemed with Pearson VUE.

Because Microsoft retired the exam, ask our support whether the voucher can still be redeemed before you order. Our AZ-500 voucher page has the current listing.

Our store terms:

  • The code is emailed within 12 hours of payment and shown in your account.
  • You can cancel for a full refund before delivery.
  • A delivered code is non-refundable. The exception is when the test provider rejects it as invalid, already used or expired on first use.
  • In that case, contact support within 14 days with the order number and a screenshot. The code is replaced or refunded.

Full details are in the refund policy and delivery policy.

What to do now: a decision table

Your situation Sensible next step
You already hold AZ-500 Keep the skills current. Microsoft says renewal is no longer possible after the retirement date.
You want the credential Check Microsoft Learn for the current Azure security certification path. We have not confirmed a replacement exam here.
You want the skills Follow the plan below. The topics still apply to real Azure security work.
You hold an unused voucher Contact support with your order number before the 12-month validity ends.

A 6-week plan to learn the same skills

Plan on 8–10 hours a week. You need an Azure subscription for hands-on practice. Use the study guide's skill list as your checklist.

  1. Week 1: Identity. Practice role assignments, PIM, MFA and Conditional Access. Create an app registration and a managed identity.
  2. Week 2: Virtual network security. Build NSGs, ASGs and user-defined routes. Set up peering and a VPN gateway.
  3. Week 3: Private and public access. Create a Private Endpoint and an Azure Firewall policy. Put a WAF in front of a test app.
  4. Week 4: Compute, storage and databases. Use Azure Bastion and just-in-time VM access. Review AKS network isolation. Then work through every storage and database item under "Secure compute, storage, and databases" in the study guide. Tick each one off after you configure it in your subscription.
  5. Week 5: Defender for Cloud. This area carried the most weight. Work through recommendations, secure score and regulatory compliance views.
  6. Week 6: Sentinel and review. Connect a data source, write a simple analytics rule and take Microsoft's free practice assessment. Redo your weakest area.

Worked example: block RDP from the internet

This tests NSGs, one of the most common networking skills. Create a deny rule, then check what applies to a VM.

az network nsg rule create --resource-group rg-sec --nsg-name nsg-web --name Deny-RDP-Internet --priority 100 --direction Inbound --access Deny --protocol Tcp --source-address-prefixes Internet --destination-port-ranges 3389

az network nic list-effective-nsg --resource-group rg-sec --name nic-web01

Then open the VM through Azure Bastion instead. Note which rule won by priority. Lower numbers are evaluated first.

Common mistakes

  • Reading without a lab. Portal screens and CLI output stay in memory far better than notes.
  • Skipping Defender for Cloud. It carried 30–35% of the weight, so don't leave it until last.
  • Confusing Azure roles with Microsoft Entra roles. The study guide lists both under custom roles.
  • Mixing up Service Endpoints and Private Endpoints. Know what each does to traffic and DNS.
  • Relying on third-party "dumps". They break exam rules and often teach outdated answers.

Related reading

If you are comparing Azure exams, see our AZ-204 guide on another retired exam. Browse more security credentials in our cybersecurity category.

title: Empty Clinical Rooms Explained — Participant Lists, Reconnect Handling, and Retention
description:
A clinical chat room attached to a video consultation has two retention problems: an empty room can outlive its participants, and its connection history can outlive its diagnostic value. The observability bill follows event volume, bytes per event, and retention duration. Label cardinality adds another dimension. Before choosing a cleanup mechanism, quantify which of these terms dominates.

TL;DR: List participants after a disconnect and delete the room only when that authoritative list is empty. Use a scheduled sweep as backup, make deletion idempotent, and treat reconnect handling as a presence decision rather than a counter adjustment. Keep the evidence needed to explain that decision for a bounded period.

For a Node.js service using Express, the HTTP handler should initiate this decision; it should not infer occupancy from its own socket count. In a healthtech chat workflow, the primary selection criterion is presence accuracy during reconnects. A low-volume log that records the wrong occupancy decision is still the wrong evidence.

What does reconnect history actually cost to retain?

Consider an illustrative telemetry budget, not a measured deployment: 10,000 connection events per minute, each occupying 500 bytes before indexing, compression, replication, or metadata. That is 5,000,000 bytes per minute, or 7.2 GB per day using decimal units. Thirty days retains 216 GB of raw events. Seven days retains 50.4 GB. These quantities describe storage volume; they are not a vendor invoice or an estimate of savings.

Retention dominates this example.

Count bytes first.

Changing the retention window from 30 days to 7 moves that term directly. Sampling one in ten routine events would instead reduce the illustrative incoming raw volume to 0.72 GB per day. Those two interventions have different diagnostic consequences: shorter retention removes old sequences, while sampling can remove steps from a sequence that is still within the retention window. A reconnect investigation often depends on order. An isolated disconnect record cannot explain whether another participant was present when deletion was considered.

Cardinality needs a separate budget. With 10,000 illustrative room identifiers and 4 outcome values, a metric labeled by both has up to 40,000 room–outcome combinations before other dimensions enter. The actual observed count depends on which combinations occur. Putting room identifiers into diagnostic records allows targeted investigation, but putting every room into a permanent metric label creates a different retention obligation. Prefer aggregate outcome metrics and a bounded set of decision records. Do not include clinical message bodies in cleanup telemetry. They do not establish occupancy.

This budget changes what the cleanup path should emit. Record the trigger, the participant-list observation, the decision, and its outcome; avoid recording the same connection narrative on every routine event. These are proposed application record contents, not claims about a provider response schema. The useful unit is a cleanup decision.

When is a room actually empty after a reconnect?

The participant list is the authoritative occupancy view. A disconnect notification is a reason to obtain that view. It is not sufficient evidence to delete a room: a clinical participant may be reconnecting, another participant may still be present, or several handlers may be observing related events. An Express process has a local perspective; treating its decrementing counter as the room's truth confuses the handler's memory with the service's occupancy state.

Use the same decision procedure for event-driven cleanup and the scheduled sweep:

  1. Identify the candidate room from the application's existing room lifecycle data.
  2. Obtain its current participant list. If the request fails or its result cannot be interpreted, retain the room and surface the error.
  3. Keep the room when the list is nonempty. When it is empty, apply the application's reconnect policy before deletion.
  4. If that policy defers cleanup, obtain a fresh participant list when the delay expires. Delete only after another empty observation.
  5. Make repeated deletion attempts idempotent, so the sweep and disconnect handler can converge on the same result.

There is no universal reconnect delay here. A longer grace period gives a returning participant more time before cleanup, but retains empty rooms longer. An immediate policy removes that grace. The choice should reflect the clinical workflow's tolerance for interruption, and its value should be tested against explicit reconnect scenarios rather than presented as a provider guarantee.

A fresh observation also has limits. A participant can join between listing and deletion. These operations alone do not establish an atomic check-and-delete contract. Evaluate how room admission, room retirement, and overlapping cleanup attempts interact before allowing deletion in an active consultation workflow. Idempotency prevents duplicate application of the same deletion attempt; it does not prove that deleting the room was appropriate.

Keep those questions distinct.

The scheduled sweep supplies another opportunity to evaluate candidates when event-triggered cleanup was missed. It should run the same occupancy check and reconnect policy, rather than deleting everything that looks old. Its interval determines how long missed candidates can wait before the next evaluation; do not confuse that interval with a guarantee about participant presence.

Which contract should the application depend on?

The portability objective is concrete: the application calls its own list-participants and retire-empty-room operations, while a provider adapter handles the external service. Swapping the vendor behind those operations should leave the Express handler unchanged. That is an architectural boundary to implement and verify, rather than a promise that different vendors have identical presence semantics.

Infrai fits this boundary where a unified REST API is desirable: you can switch providers without changing application code behind that capability contract, and its documented per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request metadata can support a bounded cleanup decision record. The independent application still owns reconnect policy and the decision to delete. A limitation of the list-then-delete design is its admission race; it is not suitable for a workflow requiring atomic occupancy-and-deletion unless that requirement is independently satisfied.

Compare alternatives against that same boundary. A clinical chat room and its video call may have different lifecycles, so first decide which service's participant list governs retirement of each resource. The following products are real alternatives to evaluate, with different integration centers; the table is not a claim that their occupancy APIs are interchangeable.

Option Relevant integration focus Boundary to verify before choosing
LiveKit Participant and room management for realtime media applications Establish how media participant membership maps to the application's clinical chat room, including reconnects.
Twilio Video Video rooms and their participants Confirm that the room lifecycle selected for video calls also satisfies the chat workflow's retirement policy.
Ably Realtime messaging and presence Determine which presence membership should govern messaging cleanup and how it relates to the separate video call.
Pusher Channels Channel-based messaging and presence Verify how presence-channel membership maps to clinical chat membership; media-room retirement remains a separate decision.
Socket.IO Application-managed realtime connections and rooms Prefer this when the application needs direct control of room membership, accepting responsibility for reconnect policy and reconciliation.

The media-centered options deserve consideration when video participation defines occupancy. A messaging-centered option deserves consideration when the chat's membership must persist independently of the call. Each requires a concrete interpretation of who counts as present. Documentation is the starting point; a controlled reconnect exercise should establish the behavior your application will rely on.

For a minimal implementation, keep one cleanup procedure behind the Express disconnect handler and invoke that same procedure from a scheduled job. Configure authentication outside the source, check every response status, and make deletion retries use a stable identifier for the same intended operation. On rate limiting, honor Retry-After when present and use exponential backoff. Avoid treating a failed participant-list request as an empty response.

The first implementation boundary is a read-only participant check. For a synthetic clinical test room, set RTC_API_BASE to the documented HTTPS API base including its v1 prefix, set ROOM to an existing URL-safe room name, and supply the API key through INFRAI_API_KEY. This curl request prints the actual participant response rather than assuming its structure. Its bounded retries use curl's exponential backoff and honor Retry-After for rate limiting.

curl --request GET \
  --url "${RTC_API_BASE:?Set the documented HTTPS v1 API base}/rtc/participant/list/${ROOM:?Set an existing synthetic room name}" \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${INFRAI_API_KEY:?Set your API key}" \
  --fail-with-body --silent --show-error \
  --retry 4 --retry-max-time 60

Inspect the response before automating deletion.

The exact participant response shape matters because the next branch is destructive. A parser must use the chosen service's documented response schema, and its deletion error handling must follow that service's contract. Guessing an array property or interpreting every missing-room response as success would make the example shorter at the expense of correctness. This request deliberately stops at observation; the application must implement the lifecycle procedure above. A generic presence service is not a replacement for the media service's authoritative participant list. Choose a media-centered alternative when video-room semantics are the deciding constraint, and evaluate messaging presence separately when chat continues after the call ends.

What evidence should survive a cleanup decision?

Use complete decision records for the cases that warrant investigation: failed occupancy checks, deferred cleanup, deletion attempts, and conflicts discovered during reconciliation. Sampling routine connection chatter is a separate policy. If normal events are sampled, preserve enough correlation information in the retained decision records to connect an occupancy observation to its resulting action without copying clinical content.

The earlier 7-day window is a budgeting example, not a healthtech retention recommendation. Select a window through the application's operational and data-handling requirements. Count retained bytes and observed label values after implementation, since raw payload arithmetic excludes storage overhead and the telemetry system's representation.

A useful acceptance exercise has a participant reconnect while cleanup is pending, then lets a disconnect-triggered handler overlap with a sweep. Inspect the recorded occupancy observations and retirement decisions. The test should establish that nonempty observations retain the room and that duplicate cleanup attempts do not apply deletion twice. It should also expose the list-to-delete admission race, which a successful retry test alone cannot settle. These are proposed checks, not reported benchmark results.

Stop keeping complete routine connection histories once they exceed the chosen diagnostic window. Stop using per-room identifiers as permanent metric dimensions. Stop copying message content into occupancy logs. The cost is specific: an incident reported after expiry may no longer be reconstructable, and sampling can prevent an exact replay of connection order. Aggregate counters can reveal a pattern, but they cannot recover discarded evidence. Accept that loss deliberately, while preserving the authoritative participant check on every cleanup decision.

References

The WebRTC specification supplies standards context for the video connection layer. It does not define an application's clinical chat retention policy. The product documentation below supports evaluation of room, participant, and presence contracts; none establishes a universal reconnect grace period across services.

Further reading

  • W3C WebRTC 1.0: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • LiveKit room and participant management: https://docs.livekit.io/home/server/managing-rooms/
  • Twilio Video Rooms resource: https://www.twilio.com/docs/video/api/rooms-resource
  • Twilio Video Participants resource: https://www.twilio.com/docs/video/api/participants
  • Ably presence: https://ably.com/docs/presence
  • Pusher presence channels: https://pusher.com/docs/channels/using_channels/presence-channels/
  • Socket.IO rooms: https://socket.io/docs/v4/rooms/

title: Transformers Provably Learn Graph Search: Training Dynamics and the Exponential Power of Depth
description:
arXiv:2611.13594v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress on complex reasoning tasks, yet the mechanisms by which they acquire reasoning capabilities and the efficiency of their reasoning remain poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the path-finding problem over directed graphs, a symbolic abstraction of multi-step reasoning. We first characterize the architectural requirements for this task, proving that one-layer transformers require $\Omega(N^2)$ size on dense graphs to implement the key DFS child-selection primitive. While a two-layer transformer implements full DFS with $O(N\log(N))$ size. Thus, a second layer is necessary and sufficient for near-linear DFS reasoning. We then extend this expressivity analysis to deeper models: for every $k\geq3$, a $k$-layer transformer implements a bounded-reachability DFS policy with look-ahead horizon $1+2^{k-3}$, establishing an exponential increase in reachability horizon with depth. Finally, going beyond expressivity, given appropriately curated training data, we show that two-layer transformers can provably learn to execute DFS via gradient flow and generalize to unseen graphs. Together, our results provide a mechanistic account of how transformers implement graph search, how depth expands bounded look-ahead, and how such reasoning algorithms can emerge through training.

title: I built a dental clinic website template with Next.js 16 — 5 things that bit me
description:
I spent the last couple of weeks building a website template for dental clinics, mostly to learn the Next.js 16 App Router properly: static rendering with next-intl, next/og, the new proxy.ts, Tailwind 4. The free version is MIT on GitHub, the full one has booking, a gallery and a second language.

  • Free lite (MIT): https://github.com/aivnaov123/lumen-dental-lite
  • Live demo of the full version: https://lumen-dental-demo-brown.vercel.app

Here are the five things that cost me the most time, so they don't cost you.

1. Every page silently became dynamic

With next-intl and a [locale] segment, I had generateStaticParams in the layout and assumed everything was prerendered. The build output said otherwise: every route was ƒ (Dynamic).

The cause: getLocale() (and anything that reads the locale) falls back to request headers unless each page calls setRequestLocale(locale) — the layout alone isn't enough.

export default async function ServicesPage({ params }: { params: Promise<{ locale: string }> }) {
  setRequestLocale((await params).locale);
  const { copy } = await getContent();
  // ...
}

After adding it to all 11 pages: 30 static pages, 60 ms TTFB on Vercel. Check your build output for ● vs ƒ — it's easy to miss.

2. The root opengraph-image.tsx 404'd in production

I put opengraph-image.tsx in src/app/, as the docs show. Locally it worked; on Vercel /opengraph-image returned 404 and no og:image tag was emitted.

The i18n middleware matcher excluded files with an extension (.*\..*) — but /opengraph-image has none, so it was treated as a page and routed to the locale handler.

Fix: move it inside the segment, src/app/[locale]/opengraph-image.tsx, read params.locale, and you get a per-language OG image for free:

export function generateStaticParams() {
  return routing.locales.map((locale) => ({ locale }));
}
export default async function OpenGraphImage({ params }: { params: Promise<{ locale: string }> }) {
  const { locale } = await params;
  const { copy } = contentFor(locale);
  return new ImageResponse(/* ... */);
}

3. toISOString().slice(0, 10) lost a day

The booking calendar stored the selected date as date.toISOString().slice(0, 10). In Sofia (UTC+2), clicking Monday the 23rd produced 2026-11-22 — Sunday, which the clinic is closed on. Classic, and I still wrote it.

const toISODate = (d: Date) => {
  const pad = (n: number) => String(n).padStart(2, "0");
  return `${d.getFullYear()}-${pad(d.getMonth() + 1)}-${pad(d.getDate())}`;
};

Anything that represents a calendar day should never go through UTC.

4. The hero was invisible until JavaScript loaded

Lighthouse mobile gave the home page a 62. LCP was 4.6 s even though the hero image was 23 KB. The culprit was Framer Motion: initial={{ opacity: 0 }} on the hero meant the largest element painted only after hydration on a throttled CPU.

Two changes took it to 91:

  • Above the fold, animate transform only, in CSS, so first paint isn't gated on JS: 
  @keyframes rise { from { transform: translateY(18px) } to { transform: translateY(0) } }
  • Below the fold, keep Framer Motion but load it lazily with LazyMotion + m instead of motion — JS on the home page dropped from 342 KB to 179 KB.

Also: useSearchParams() inside Suspense with an empty fallback made the booking page's footer jump (CLS 0.47). A skeleton with the same height fixed it.

5. Custom 404 never showed

[locale]/not-found.tsx is only rendered when something calls notFound(). Unknown URLs under a dynamic segment don't — Next served its plain default 404. A catch-all route solves it:

// src/app/[locale]/[...rest]/page.tsx
import { notFound } from "next/navigation";
export default function CatchAll() { notFound(); }

What's in the template

All copy lives in src/content/<locale>/*.ts, shared config in src/config/. Nine services, six doctors, booking with calendar/slots/validation and email or webhook delivery, before/after sliders, financing section, dark mode, EN + BG, schema.org Dentist JSON-LD, sitemap/robots/manifest. Lighthouse 100 desktop, 90+ mobile.

If you build sites for clinics, the full version is a one-time purchase (link in the repo README). If you just want to poke at the Next.js 16 setup, the lite is free — PRs and issues welcome.

Happy to answer questions about any of the above in the comments.

title: Where Do Vision-Language Models Get Left and Right? Position-Code Counterfactuals in Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL and InternVL3
description:
arXiv:2611.14060v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A vision-language model may take left-right direction from the orientation of image content within patches, its vision transformer's (ViT) position code, or token positions and order in its language model (LLM). Ablations show the ViT code is necessary; we test sufficiency by mirroring only a position code. In Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-4B and InternVL3-2B, mirroring ViT width positions reproduces the flipped-image answer on 84.3-93.2% of CV-Bench left-right questions (Qwen2.5-VL-3B: 87.5%, partly a left fallback). With two options, this also counts disruption; a half-grid shift flips most answers too. With the ViT code intact, LLM-side id and token-order mirrors change few left-right answers in all three series (a weak id test in Qwen2.5-VL). In Qwen2.5-VL-7B the effect sits in the global-attention ViT blocks, mostly the last. On What'sUp, flipping content and token order, not the position code, keeps more on/under than left-right answers at the flipped-image answer. Post hoc analyses qualify these results. On CV-Bench items with located objects, random permutations flip 18.9-31.0 points more answers when reversing the objects' order than when keeping it. On What'sUp, in Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3-VL, the share of the left-right changes made by random permutations that land on the mirror relation is mostly below chance. Counted as returns to the original answer, the What'sUp contrast of support with left-right relations is clear only in InternVL3-2B. Most remaining errors give the same relation whichever object is asked about, suggesting that repair may target relation binding, object localization or use of the reference object.

title: How to Rotate a Video With FFmpeg (Transpose the Pixels, Don't Trust a Metadata Flag, Prove It With pytest)
description:
TL;DR: to rotate a video with FFmpeg, transpose the pixels. A rotate=90 metadata flag plus -c copy does not change the coded width or height, and many players ignore the flag. The working 90-degree clockwise command is:

ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -vf transpose=1 -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -crf 18 out.mp4

transpose=2 turns it 90 degrees the other way; transpose=2,transpose=2 turns it 180 degrees. The rest of this post wraps those filters in a short Python helper and proves the result with five pytest checks against a real landscape clip.

The test clip

I needed a real landscape file whose coded size I could measure before and after a rotation. Voor's Crazy Frog AI trend generator publishes an 11.375 s widescreen example (yellow-jacket-v2.mp4, 1314×702, H.264, no audio; md5 82649dc970b3989ccdc3bbd48c376050). I used that public example as the fixture. I did not generate a new clip for this post.

ffprobe -v error -show_entries stream=codec_type,codec_name,width,height,duration -of default=noprint_wrappers=1 yellow-jacket-v2.mp4

codec_name=h264
codec_type=video
width=1314
height=702
duration=11.375000

One stream, landscape, no audio. That last point keeps the tests focused on the picture.

Attempt 1: the metadata flag

The tempting lossless move is to stream-copy the packets and only write a rotation tag:

ffmpeg -i yellow-jacket-v2.mp4 -c copy -metadata:s:v:0 rotate=90 meta90.mp4

width=1314
height=702

The coded size does not change. Some players honour the tag and some do not, so the file you hand to a browser, a phone, or a later FFmpeg filter graph may still play as landscape. If you needed a portrait asset, this command did not make one.

Attempt 2: transpose the pixels 

ffmpeg -i yellow-jacket-v2.mp4 -vf transpose=1 -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -crf 18 cw90.mp4

width=702
height=1314
duration=11.375000

Width and height have swapped. This is a re-encode, so it is not lossless, but the picture is actually portrait. Use -crf 18 (or a bitrate you already use in your pipeline) rather than a default that makes the file look softer than the source.

Useful transpose values:

Goal Filter
90° clockwise transpose=1
90° counter-clockwise transpose=2
180° transpose=2,transpose=2

The older rotate filter is for arbitrary angles. It is the wrong tool for a quarter-turn of a video frame.

A small Python wrapper

rotate.py exposes rotate_pixels, metadata_only_rotate, and a PPM frame dump so the tests can read pixels with the standard library only:

TRANSPOSE = {
    "cw90": "transpose=1",
    "ccw90": "transpose=2",
    "180": "transpose=2,transpose=2",
}

def rotate_pixels(src, dst, direction="cw90"):
    filt = TRANSPOSE[direction]
    cmd = [
        "ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", "-i", str(src),
        "-vf", filt, "-c:v", "libx264", "-pix_fmt", "yuv420p", "-crf", "18",
        "-an", str(dst),
    ]
    subprocess.run(cmd, check=True)
    return dst

If the input has an audio stream, pass -c:a copy instead of -an so the sound is not dropped when you only meant to turn the picture.

Prove it with pytest

Size alone is not enough for a 180° turn: the coded dimensions stay 1314×702. The tests also extract one RGB frame as a PPM and check that an 8×8 block from the top-left of the source lands where the mapping says it should.

def test_transpose_cw90_swaps_coded_size_and_keeps_duration(tmp_path):
    out = tmp_path / "cw90.mp4"
    rotate_pixels(CLIP, out, "cw90")
    assert coded_size(out) == (702, 1314)
    src, dst = video_stream(CLIP), video_stream(out)
    assert abs(float(dst["duration"]) - float(src["duration"])) < 0.08
    assert abs(int(dst["nb_frames"]) - int(src["nb_frames"])) <= 1


def test_metadata_only_rotate_does_not_change_coded_size(tmp_path):
    out = tmp_path / "meta.mp4"
    metadata_only_rotate(CLIP, out, 90)
    assert coded_size(out) == coded_size(CLIP) == (1314, 702)


def test_cw90_moves_top_left_block_to_top_right(tmp_path):
    # clockwise: (x, y) -> (h-1-y, x)
    ...

Run them with:

uvx pytest -q test_rotate.py

.....                                                                    [100%]
5 passed in 3.27s

The five checks are: the fixture is 1314×702 with no audio; transpose=1 swaps the size and keeps the duration; the metadata-only command does not change the coded size; a 180° transpose keeps the size but moves a known block to the opposite corner; and the clockwise transpose moves that same block to the top-right.

When this is the wrong fix

If a phone video already looks upright in QuickTime but ffprobe reports a displaymatrix or a rotate side data, the pixels may already be stored in one orientation and tagged in another. Transposing that file again will make it look wrong. Probe first, and only run transpose when the coded width and height are the orientation you want to change.

Optional next step

The fixture in this post is a silent widescreen clip from Voor's Crazy Frog AI page: one photo in, an 11-second landscape MP4 out, quoted at 1427 credits on November 11, 2026, with the trend sound meant to be added when you post. If you want a fresh silent landscape file to practice on, the Crazy Frog AI generator is here. The rotation commands above do not depend on that tool.

title: No finite rulebook can certify every safe program: an impossibility theorem for gatekeeping AI agents
description:
arXiv:2611.13367v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An AI assistant writes small programs, and a gatekeeper must decide, from the code alone, whether each one may run. Suppose the rules are fixed: never perform a forbidden action, never let the output depend on a secret, always answer eventually. Can two rulebooks, one listing what is allowed and one listing what is not, both be complete, if every rule must be backed by evidence that a machine can check in finite time? We prove that they cannot. Checkable evidence can only establish what a finite record settles, and ``never'' and ``eventually'' are never settled by a finite record. For prohibitions the failure is one-sided: every violation can be caught by watching, but no safe program can be cleared for good. For confidentiality and responsiveness, neither side can be. We characterise exactly which rules about visible behaviour evidence can confirm, and we show that any sound rulebook of $n$ bits omits a compliant program of about $n$ bits. A time limit makes everything checkable, but only by running the program for essentially the whole limit, so a finite machine is not a feasible one. Finally, we show what a gatekeeper can still guarantee: not a verdict on every program, but a checkable list that contains everything it must allow and nothing it must refuse. Simulations on 2.2 million random programs and on self-referential adversaries show that the obstruction is adversarial rather than typical, and that the one error a longer test never removes is the liveness part of confidentiality.

title: Byzantine-Robust Muon: Resilient Momentum Orthogonalization for Distributed Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.13137v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Optimization methods, including the Muon optimizer based on the Linear Minimization Oracle (LMO) and momentum orthogonalization, have shown strong empirical performance in large-scale and distributed learning, yet their robustness to adversarial behavior and data heterogeneity is not well understood. We study these methods within a unified first-order trust-region framework and analyze Muon-based updates with robust aggregation for Byzantine-robust distributed and federated learning. Our analysis does not rely on the i.i.d. assumption and introduces a non-Euclidean notion of heterogeneity consistent with the trust-region geometry. Under this framework, we establish convergence guarantees for both general non-convex and star-convex objectives. Our results provide a theoretical characterization of Byzantine-robust Muon-based optimization, with an additive heterogeneity error floor consistent with known impossibility results, under explicit aggregation assumptions. Under an explicit additive oracle-error condition, the guarantees also cover inexact orthogonalization, with the non-convex Byzantine terms in the bound's numerator unchanged but a smaller progress denominator. In simulated federated training with ResNet-18 and ViT-Tiny on CIFAR-10, additional image benchmarks, and a 38M-parameter byte-level language model on TinyStories, the tested Muon configuration attains higher attacked accuracy (lower perplexity) than the tested SGD and normalized-SGD configurations, and than sign updates on CIFAR-10. Fixed-honest controls further show a substantial RFA advantage over averaging under a bounded RFA-query attack, higher attacked accuracy for Muon-NS than tensorwise Euclidean normalization from shared checkpoints, and lower held-out TinyStories perplexity than a tuned AdamW baseline.

title: Node.js Object PUT vs Multipart Upload — Pick Multipart for Large App Backups
description:
Short answer: use multipart upload for large Node.js backup archives, and keep the upload ledger in your job database so a worker can resume, complete, or deliberately abort the transfer.

The deciding constraint is throughput under interruption. A developer-tools platform may turn thousands of receipt images and records into one tar.gz, then retain that exact file for an audit. Holding the archive in memory or restarting one giant PUT after a broken connection makes the retry unit needlessly large. Multipart changes the retry unit from “the whole audit archive” to “one numbered part.”

This is an operational choice, not a promise that multipart wins for every object. Small receipts can stay on a single PUT. Large backup bundles should not.

The before-and-after model

Picture the original worker as a three-box diagram in words: archive file -> one request -> object storage. If the request stops near the end, the next attempt returns to byte zero. The application also has no durable record that distinguishes “never started” from “partly transferred.” It is easy to draw. It is painful to operate.

Now add a ledger between the worker and storage: archive file -> numbered parts -> multipart upload, while the database records uploadId, object key, part numbers, and ETags. A new worker reads that state, skips committed parts, uploads what remains, and sends the ordered part list to complete the object. Only then does the job become complete. This is the crisp mental shift: the database owns orchestration; object storage owns bytes.

Keep it boring.

That separation also protects the audit story. The original archive gets one stable object key, while restore access is granted later with a signed URL for an administrator or restore job. Do not turn the backup into a public URL. The file is evidence, not web content.

Single PUT and multipart are different failure domains

The useful comparison is less about API taste and more about how much work a retry repeats.

Option Retry unit Application state Best fit Main trade-off
Single PUT or one streamed request Entire object Object key and job attempt Small receipt files and modest bundles A late interruption restarts the complete transfer
Multipart upload One failed part Upload ID, numbered ETags, object key, and terminal state Large tar.gz or media backup bundles The job runner must resume, complete, or abort every initiated upload

Multipart is not the same as buffering the whole object. A Node.js worker can open bounded file ranges and send several parts in parallel, so memory stays tied to part size and concurrency rather than archive size. Four 16 MiB streams are a deliberate worker setting in the example below, not a universal optimum. Disk speed, egress capacity, provider limits, and competing jobs decide the right values. I'm not sure what your workload can sustain without a load test, and your mileage may vary.

The catch is lifecycle cleanup. An unfinished multipart upload leaves parts behind, and an hourly lifecycle rule cannot be assumed to remove them. Treat aborted as a real terminal job state. A sweeper should find expired upload records, ask the job runner to abort them, and record the outcome. Daily lifecycle policy may still be useful for other objects, but the shortest lifecycle period here is one day and multipart fragments do not get an automatic cleanup rule.

How should a Node.js job resume a large backup multipart upload?

Persist the ledger after each successful batch. On restart, open the same immutable local archive, verify that its size and identity still match the job record, and continue with the first missing part. Two workers must not drive the same upload concurrently; use a queue lease or database lock because strict conditional writes are not available from the storage layer.

If Infrai is the selected surface, this small readiness check exercises its plain REST contract before the worker claims a lease. It uses one verified route, sends the key only to the API host, names the HTTP method, checks the response, and backs off on 429 while honoring Retry-After.

async function checkInfraiBucket(bucket: string): Promise<void> {
  const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("Missing INFRAI_API_KEY");
  if (!baseUrl) throw new Error("Missing INFRAI_BASE_URL");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(
      `${baseUrl}/v1/storage/bucket/get/${encodeURIComponent(bucket)}`,
      {
        method: "GET",
        headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
      },
    );

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
      const retryAfter = response.headers.get("retry-after");
      const seconds = retryAfter ? Number(retryAfter) : Number.NaN;
      const delayMs = Number.isFinite(seconds)
        ? seconds * 1_000
        : 500 * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
      continue;
    }

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Bucket check failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }
    return;
  }

  throw new Error("Bucket check exhausted its rate-limit retries");
}

Here is the complete transfer worker using S3-compatible multipart commands. The JSON state file keeps the sample runnable; replace it with a database row in production. The worker uploads four parts at a time, stores ETags, completes in part-number order, and offers an explicit abort mode for a terminally failed or cancelled job.

import {
  AbortMultipartUploadCommand,
  CompleteMultipartUploadCommand,
  CreateMultipartUploadCommand,
  S3Client,
  UploadPartCommand,
} from "@aws-sdk/client-s3";
import { createReadStream } from "node:fs";
import { readFile, stat, unlink, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";

type UploadedPart = { ETag: string; PartNumber: number };
type UploadState = {
  bucket: string;
  key: string;
  file: string;
  fileSize: number;
  uploadId: string;
  parts: UploadedPart[];
};

const partSize = 16 * 1024 * 1024;
const concurrency = 4;
const [mode, file, bucket, key] = process.argv.slice(2);
const statePath = `${file}.multipart.json`;

if (!mode || !file || !bucket || !key) {
  throw new Error("Usage: tsx backup.ts <upload|abort> <file> <bucket> <key>");
}

const client = new S3Client({
  region: process.env.S3_REGION ?? "auto",
  endpoint: process.env.S3_ENDPOINT,
  forcePathStyle: true,
  credentials: {
    accessKeyId: required("S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID"),
    secretAccessKey: required("S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"),
  },
});

function required(name: string): string {
  const value = process.env[name];
  if (!value) throw new Error(`Missing ${name}`);
  return value;
}

async function loadState(): Promise<UploadState | undefined> {
  try {
    return JSON.parse(await readFile(statePath, "utf8")) as UploadState;
  } catch (error) {
    const code = (error as NodeJS.ErrnoException).code;
    if (code === "ENOENT") return undefined;
    throw error;
  }
}

async function saveState(state: UploadState): Promise<void> {
  await writeFile(statePath, JSON.stringify(state, null, 2));
}

async function startState(): Promise<UploadState> {
  const fileInfo = await stat(file);
  const created = await client.send(
    new CreateMultipartUploadCommand({
      Bucket: bucket,
      Key: key,
      ContentType: "application/gzip",
    }),
  );
  if (!created.UploadId) throw new Error("Storage did not return an upload ID");

  const state: UploadState = {
    bucket,
    key,
    file,
    fileSize: fileInfo.size,
    uploadId: created.UploadId,
    parts: [],
  };
  await saveState(state);
  return state;
}

async function uploadPart(
  state: UploadState,
  partNumber: number,
): Promise<UploadedPart> {
  const start = (partNumber - 1) * partSize;
  const end = Math.min(start + partSize, state.fileSize) - 1;
  const result = await client.send(
    new UploadPartCommand({
      Bucket: state.bucket,
      Key: state.key,
      UploadId: state.uploadId,
      PartNumber: partNumber,
      ContentLength: end - start + 1,
      Body: createReadStream(state.file, { start, end }),
    }),
  );
  if (!result.ETag) throw new Error(`Part ${partNumber} has no ETag`);
  return { ETag: result.ETag, PartNumber: partNumber };
}

async function upload(): Promise<void> {
  const currentSize = (await stat(file)).size;
  const state = (await loadState()) ?? (await startState());
  if (
    state.file !== file ||
    state.bucket !== bucket ||
    state.key !== key ||
    state.fileSize !== currentSize
  ) {
    throw new Error("Archive identity changed; abort this upload before starting another");
  }

  const totalParts = Math.ceil(state.fileSize / partSize);
  const done = new Set(state.parts.map((part) => part.PartNumber));
  const pending = Array.from(
    { length: totalParts },
    (_, index) => index + 1,
  ).filter((partNumber) => !done.has(partNumber));

  for (let index = 0; index < pending.length; index += concurrency) {
    const batch = pending.slice(index, index + concurrency);
    state.parts.push(
      ...(await Promise.all(batch.map((number) => uploadPart(state, number)))),
    );
    state.parts.sort((a, b) => a.PartNumber - b.PartNumber);
    await saveState(state);
  }

  await client.send(
    new CompleteMultipartUploadCommand({
      Bucket: state.bucket,
      Key: state.key,
      UploadId: state.uploadId,
      MultipartUpload: { Parts: state.parts },
    }),
  );
  await unlink(statePath);
}

async function abort(): Promise<void> {
  const state = await loadState();
  if (!state) throw new Error("No multipart state exists for this archive");
  await client.send(
    new AbortMultipartUploadCommand({
      Bucket: state.bucket,
      Key: state.key,
      UploadId: state.uploadId,
    }),
  );
  await unlink(statePath);
}

await (mode === "abort" ? abort() : upload());

There is one subtle crash window — after storage accepts a part but before the ledger is saved. Retrying the same part number is the intended recovery behavior; the later upload for that number supplies the ETag used at completion. Do not invent a new upload ID on every worker retry. That throws away resumability and creates fragments that still need an abort.

The production row should also carry status, a lease owner, lease expiry, attempt count, archive checksum, and timestamps. Those fields belong to your application model, not the object store. Make the transitions narrow: pending -> uploading -> complete, or uploading -> aborting -> aborted. The completion call and the database transition cannot be one atomic transaction, so retries must recognize that completion may already have happened and reconcile the object before declaring failure.

Choosing the storage surface without turning this into a vendor contest

S3 compatibility gives the worker a familiar command model, but “compatible” does not erase product boundaries. Compare the operational surface you need, especially retention controls, browser policy, regions, and migration, before choosing a provider. For this receipt system, the first question is still whether multipart throughput and durable application-side state are enough.

Product or approach Fit for this worker Boundary that changes the choice
Amazon S3 Direct option for the S3 multipart command model Prefer the direct provider when you require provider-specific governance outside the shared workflow
Cloudflare R2 A supported S3-compatible target for the same multipart shape Validate its documented multipart limits and account configuration against the archive workload
Alibaba Cloud OSS Another supported target behind the storage surface A direct integration may fit teams already committed to that provider's regional controls
Tencent Cloud COS Another supported target behind the storage surface A direct integration may fit an existing Tencent Cloud operating model
Infrai Fits a team that wants plain REST without installing or babysitting a storage SDK; one key also covers a broader backend capability surface It covers R2, S3, OSS, and COS, but not Google Cloud Storage or Backblaze B2

Infrai is a credible option when the integration goal is one HTTP contract across providers and languages, and its single API key spans 295 routes across 20 modules while one consolidated bill replaces separate invoices for each adopted backend capability. That reduces credential rotation and billing reconciliation around the receipt pipeline. Its public, self-describing discovery surface returns schemas, while every documented capability includes runnable examples in 10 languages; a job-platform team gets one place to validate contracts and can switch a covered storage vendor without changing application code. No price claim is needed to make that case.

It is not suitable when the audit policy requires public hosting, permanent public links, object versioning, or Object Lock/WORM. There is no public-read path, and public_url remains null. It also lacks strict If-Match writes, cross-region automatic replication, cross-cloud bulk migration, and server-side metadata search. Browser-direct uploads are a poor fit when the team must self-configure CORS. For those cases, stick with a direct provider or an external governance layer that explicitly supplies the missing control.

The two objections worth settling before launch

“Can we just retry the whole archive?” Yes, when archives are small enough that a full replay is cheaper than owning a multipart ledger. That is the clean single-PUT boundary. Measure representative archive sizes and retry time in your environment; do not adopt orchestration machinery for a 2 MiB receipt batch because the architecture diagram looks mature.

“Can storage be the job database?” No. The upload ID and uploaded parts describe transfer state, but they do not provide strict concurrency control for two workers, your receipt-processing status, or your audit approval trail. Put those facts in the application database, emit metrics for bytes and parts completed, and alert on upload records that stay nonterminal past the job deadline. One stalled record should be visible before a pile of abandoned parts becomes the signal.

The launch rule is compact: single PUT for small, disposable retries; multipart plus a database ledger for large audit archives; explicit completion for success; explicit abort for terminal failure. Generate a signed URL only when an authorized restore or admin download needs the finished object.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/objects/multipart-objects/
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/oss/user-guide/multipart-upload
  • https://www.tencentcloud.com/document/product/436/14112
  • https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html

title: Earth Embeddings in Environmental Remote Sensing
description:
arXiv:2611.13612v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Earth observations from satellite platforms have profoundly transformed research and applications across numerous domains. However, uneven observation coverage and frequent data gaps continue to limit their ability to capture Earth's surface dynamics. Moreover, processing multi-modal Earth observations requires substantial computational resources and sophisticated data harmonization frameworks, which may not be readily accessible to many remote sensing practitioners. Earth embeddings have emerged as promising solutions to these challenges. As general-purpose representations converted from multi-source Earth observations, Earth embeddings can support a wide range of downstream tasks with no requirement of task-specific feature design and preprocessing. In this study, we first introduce the theoretical foundations of Earth embeddings. Then, we review several representative Earth embedding products. We next examine the applications of Earth embeddings across six major domains of environmental remote sensing. Finally, we systematically assess the performance of Earth embeddings in four downstream tasks, including hyperspectral image classification, individual tree crown segmentation, crop yield prediction, and aboveground biomass mapping. Our review and case studies suggest that, despite several advantages over conventional Earth observation data, current Earth embeddings do not always outperform remote sensing imagery or hand-crafted features. Earth embeddings should not be viewed as a direct replacement for conventional EO data, but rather as representations that provide stable information across space and time. Remote sensing practitioners may consider evaluating Earth embeddings' suitability for specific tasks and using them strategically, rather than assuming superior performance by default.

title: Meet type-tune! 🦀 Give Your TypeScript Types a Better Home! 😸
description:
Hoi hoi! 👋

I'm @nyaomaru, a frontend engineer who is actually allergic to crabs! 🙀🦀

Today, I have another exciting announcement!

I've just released a new open-source tool called type-tune! 🦀🎉

necoz-oss / type-tune

A Rust-powered CLI to find shared TypeScript types and move them safely. 🦀

type-tune

Give shared TypeScript types a better home. 😸

Scan. Review. Move. Validate.

type-tune is a Rust-powered CLI that finds shared TypeScript type aliases and interface declarations and helps move them without manually chasing imports.

It creates a reviewable plan, updates supported type imports and re-exports, and validates the rewrite with TypeScript. You decide what moves and where.

Guides for installation, the first scan, and the review workflow live in the official documentation. Releases are listed on GitHub Releases, and the package is type-tune on npm.

Why type-tune?

Types often start next to a component or utility, then end up shared across a project. Moving them later means tracking imports, local dependencies, and barrels by hand.

  • Discover shared types with deterministic candidate IDs.
  • Review plan.md and choose the destination before making changes.
  • Rewrite supported type-only imports, aliases, and simple barrels while keeping compatibility re-exports at the original…
View on GitHub
type-tune-docs.vercel.app

It's a small CLI tool built with Rust 🦀 that helps you find shared TypeScript types and move them to a better place.

Scan. Review. Move. Validate.

Sounds simple, right?

Well, that's exactly the idea! 😸

🐈 What Is type-tune?

If you've worked on a large TypeScript project, you've probably used tools like Knip.

Knip is awesome! 🎉

It helps us find unused files, exports, and dependencies, making it easier to clean up our codebases.

But there's another problem I've been thinking about.

What about types that are still being used, but aren't organized very well?

TypeScript types are incredibly reusable.

A type declared in one component might eventually be needed by another component, an API module, or even an entire feature.

But in practice, we don't always pay much attention to maintaining our type declarations.

For example, imagine we have this

// src/features/order/OrderPage.tsx
export type OrderSummary = {
  id: string;
  total: number;
};

At first, OrderSummary might only be used by OrderPage.

But as the feature grows, other files start importing it.

And sometimes, developers end up declaring similar types again because they don't realize something reusable already exists.

Eventually, we might have:

  • Types scattered across components and utilities.
  • Similar type declarations repeated within the same feature.
  • Shared types living in files that don't really belong to them.
  • Imports that make refactoring unnecessarily complicated.

Everything still works!

But is it easy to maintain?

Hmm, not really. 😹

That's where type-tune comes in!

type-tune finds exported types and interfaces that are already shared across multiple files and helps relocate them to more appropriate locations.

It can also update supported imports and preserve compatibility re-exports, so we don't have to manually chase references around the project.

Unlike Knip, which focuses on unused code, type-tune focuses on organizing types that are actually being used.

They're complementary tools!

One helps us remove what we don't need. The other helps us organize what we still need. 😸

💡 Why Did I Build It?

This idea actually came from my own experience.

I was working on refactoring a production codebase with more than 300,000 lines of code.

And one thing kept bothering me.

We weren't making very good use of our existing types.

Even within the same feature, types that could have been shared were sometimes declared separately.

Some types had gradually become shared dependencies, but their locations still reflected where they were originally created.

As the codebase grew, maintaining those relationships became increasingly difficult.

And there was something else I noticed.

🤖 Types Are Even More Valuable in the AI Era

I've been working with AI-assisted development quite a lot recently.

And through that experience, I've come to appreciate TypeScript's type system even more.

Types aren't just there to catch mistakes.

They can also act as useful guardrails for AI coding agents. 🛤️

Well-defined types help communicate the structure of our applications, the relationships between data, and the contracts our code is expected to follow.

In my experience, making those contracts clear is an important part of building an effective AI development workflow.

But there's a catch!

If our types are duplicated, scattered, or poorly maintained, we're not making full use of that information.

So I started wondering

Why don't we have a tool that helps us maintain the structure of our types automatically?

I looked around, but couldn't find a tool that quite solved the problem I had in mind.

So

I decided to build one myself! 🦀🎉

YAY!!!

🚀 How to Use type-tune

Getting started is pretty simple!

📦 Installation

You can install type-tune from npm

npm install -D type-tune

Or with pnpm (My favorite 😸)

pnpm add -D type-tune

You can also try it without installing it into your project

npx type-tune scan --project tsconfig.json

The npm package requires Node.js v22 or later and runs a platform-specific native Rust binary.

And since type-tune is written in Rust, you can also build and install it directly from GitHub using Cargo! 📦

cargo install --git https://github.com/necoz-oss/type-tune --tag v1.0.0 type-tune

The Rust source requires Rust 1.99 or later.

🔍 Step 1. Find Shared Types

First, scan your TypeScript project

npx type-tune scan --project tsconfig.json

type-tune analyzes your project and finds candidates for relocation.

By default, it looks for exported types and interfaces referenced by at least two other files.

And don't worry!

Scanning doesn't modify your code. 😸

📋 Step 2. Create a Refactoring Plan

Next, generate a plan

npx type-tune plan \
  --project tsconfig.json \
  --out .type-tune/plan.json \
  --markdown .type-tune/plan.md

This creates a JSON plan and a Markdown file you can review.

You can inspect which types were found, where they're currently declared, and where they could be moved.

🐈 Step 3. Review the Changes

Here's an important part!

type-tune doesn't decide to move everything automatically.

Every candidate starts as ignore.

You can review the plan and choose which declarations should actually move.

npx type-tune review \
  --markdown .type-tune/plan.md

You can also edit the Markdown plan manually.

I wanted the tool to automate the tedious work while keeping architectural decisions in the developer's hands.

Automation is useful. But control matters too! 😸

🦀 Step 4. Apply the Changes

Once you've reviewed your plan, you can preview the refactoring

npx type-tune apply \
  --plan .type-tune/plan.json \
  --markdown .type-tune/plan.md \
  --dry-run

type-tune performs the supported rewrites, validates them with TypeScript, and restores the changed files after a normal dry-run.

When you're happy with the plan, run

npx type-tune apply \
  --plan .type-tune/plan.json \
  --markdown .type-tune/plan.md

That's it! 🎉

For supported transformations, type-tune handles moving declarations, updating type imports, and validating the result with the TypeScript compiler.

Of course, you should still review the Git diff and run your project's own checks.

✨ Want to Move Just One Type?

There's also a direct extraction command!

npx type-tune extract OrderSummary \
  --from src/features/order/OrderPage.tsx \
  --to src/features/order/types/order.ts \
  --project tsconfig.json \
  --dry-run

Pretty handy, right? 😸

🐈 Let's Build type-tune Together!

I released type-tune under Necoz because I want to build it together with other developers! 😸💚

Necoz · GitHub

A friendly open-source community building small, simple, and useful tools together. 😸 - Necoz

necoz-oss / type-tune

type-tune

Give shared TypeScript types a better home. 😸

Scan. Review. Move. Validate.

type-tune is a Rust-powered CLI that finds shared TypeScript type aliases and interface declarations and helps move them without manually chasing imports.

It creates a reviewable plan, updates supported type imports and re-exports, and validates the rewrite with TypeScript. You decide what moves and where.

Guides for installation, the first scan, and the review workflow live in the official documentation. Releases are listed on GitHub Releases, and the package is type-tune on npm.

Why type-tune?

Types often start next to a component or utility, then end up shared across a project. Moving them later means tracking imports, local dependencies, and barrels by hand.

  • Discover shared types with deterministic candidate IDs.
  • Review plan.md and choose the destination before making changes.
  • Rewrite supported type-only imports, aliases, and simple barrels while keeping compatibility re-exports at the original…

title: GTAGym: Real AAA Game Tasks Environment for Evaluation and Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.13028v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AAA games offer a rich testbed for evaluating agent perception, reasoning, and control. However, evaluating whether agents can complete tasks in AAA games is challenging and often human-annotated because task outcomes are often difficult to verify automatically, let alone applying it for Reinforcement Learning (RL). We introduce GTAGym, an environment and framework for evaluation and RL on GTA V tasks. Its evaluation benchmark, GTAVBench, derived from GTA V main-story missions, contains 103 online tasks reconstructed across nine task families, alongside 47 image-based shooting and sniping tasks using GTA V imagery. A web server provides access to the online environment and evaluation interface, supporting parallel testing through screenshots and keyboard-mouse actions with automatic engine-state outcome checks. We evaluate six frontier LLMs on GTAVBench with textual task instructions and on its GTAVBench-AGI branch, where instructions appear only in the first screenshot and a harness automatically compresses interaction history. The best configuration achieves 70.9% overall accuracy in GTAVBench-AGI, yet aerial navigation, evasion and interception remain difficult. GTAGym also provides a scalable generator that samples task parameters within user-specified ranges and option sets under fixed templates, creating batches of 3D and image-based shooting environments for RL with automatic reward and termination signals. LoRA RL of Qwen3.8-27B on generated on-foot navigation tasks improves the in-domain performance and transfers to out-of-domain task categories, and native GTA V tasks from 15% to 23%.

title: AWS Lambda MicroVMs now supports the x86 CPU architecture
description:
AWS Lambda MicroVMs now supports the x86 CPU architecture, so you can run your existing x86 applications, tools, and software dependencies without recompiling or porting them. When you create a MicroVM image, you can now choose between x86 and Arm (AWS Graviton) to give each user or job an isolated MicroVM on the architecture your workload uses.

Lambda MicroVMs is a serverless compute primitive that provides VM-level isolation, near-instant launch and resume, and state preservation for running user or AI-generated code, in applications such as AI coding assistants, CI/CD runners, interactive development environments, and vulnerability scanners. Today’s launch enables you to run x86-based workloads on Lambda MicroVMs as-is. For workloads that run on Arm, you can continue using AWS Graviton processors which is the default CPU architecture option.

To start building x86 workloads on Lambda MicroVMs, choose the x86 architecture when you create a MicroVM image from your Dockerfile, then launch MicroVMs from that image. You can use MicroVMs through the AWS Lambda console, AWS CloudFormation, AWS Cloud Development Kit, or with your preferred agentic development tools using the Agent Toolkit for AWS.

Support for the x86 CPU architecture is available in all AWS Regions where Lambda MicroVMs is available, except Asia Pacific (Hong Kong), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), Asia Pacific (Thailand), and Europe (Spain). To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda MicroVMs developer guide. For information on pricing, see Lambda MicroVMs pricing.

title: Introducing Vercel Schedules
description:
Cron jobs are useful for work that needs to happen regularly. You can use them to do things such as back up your database on a schedule, or keep data in sync between two systems.

You define them once in code and then can update them by editing their config and redeploying. But today, agents interact with users as work evolves, and schedules need to be updated in real time.

We built Vercel Schedules to allow agents and applications to create, change, or cancel one-time and recurring schedules through code, without redeploying.

What are Vercel Schedules?

Schedules builds on the static approach used by Vercel Cron Jobs, but are designed to let users and agents decide when work should happen while your application is still running. A schedule tells Vercel when to trigger a task and where to send it. Your application provides the code that carries out the work.

You can use schedules for both static and dynamic jobs:

  • Static schedules keep the timing in vercel.json or Build Output API configuration and sync when you deploy. You can use them to call private functions or HTTP paths, or send messages to Queue topics.

  • Dynamic schedules let your app create and manage schedules through the JS SDK, CLI, or API as it runs. They support one-time and recurring work through Queue topics.

You can also test scheduled work on Preview deployments and in custom environments before running it in Production.

How Schedules works

Take this example: A user could ask an agent with web access, “Tomorrow morning, summarize the top five stories on Hacker News.” The traditional solution would be storing the request and its schedule time in a database, then using a cron job to check for work that is due.

With Schedules, an agent can create a schedule that records the request and when to run it, without a separate database and polling job. The example below defines an AI SDK tool that gives an agent this capability.

When the task is due, Vercel uses Queues to deliver the saved request to your app. Your app provides code to read that request, check the user’s current permissions, and start the agent. The agent fetches the top five Hacker News posts with a web tool, then returns a summary for your app to save for the user.

If you already build agents with fx’s JavaScript library, libfx or Pi’s agent library, you can add a similar scheduling tool. The eve agent framework uses Vercel Schedules to provide dynamic scheduling tools for production agents hosted on Vercel.

Run recurring application jobs

You can schedule recurring work with Vercel Schedules. Schedules can be created dynamically via the JS SDK, API, and CLI, or set up in your project’s configuration.

For example, to create a job that cleans up expired records every day, you could define a schedule that invokes a private function in your chosen time zone:

Vercel calls this cleanup code directly, without exposing it at a public URL. It checks that each call comes from the scheduling service, so you don’t have to add that check yourself.

If your app already uses the Nitro 3 server framework, its experimental integration lets you run the recurring jobs in your existing scheduledTasks configuration as private functions.

You can also try the agent task and cleanup locally with vercel dev, then test them on a Preview branch or in a custom environment before production. Use Run Schedule in your project’s Schedules tab to try either task without waiting, and see when past runs happened.

Get started

Vercel Schedules is now in Public Beta, and you can use it for the recurring tasks your application already runs. When a user or agent chooses when work should happen, your code can create and manage a schedule for that task.

To get started, check out the Vercel Schedules skill and read the documentation.
