title: ZoomGain: Mining Global-to-Zoom Perception Gaps for Fine-Grained Visual Supervision
description:
arXiv:2611.14076v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fine-grained visual perception requires Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to locate and interpret subtle evidence within complex scenes. Constructing supervision for this ability is challenging: questions must have correct, unambiguous answers that depend on actual fine-grained visual details rather than coarse cues or language priors. Verifying these properties makes manual annotation labor-intensive and automatic generation difficult for models that themselves struggle with fine-grained perception. Yet the same models can often recognize such details once the region is zoomed in. We exploit this global-to-zoom perception gap and introduce ZoomGain, a data construction pipeline that constructs questions about the full image from visual information gained only by zooming in. It verifies each answer on the zoomed view with multiple models, ensures that each question remains unambiguous in the full image and cannot be answered from language priors, and specifically generates high-quality distractors for multiple-choice questions. With this pipeline and human-only screening (no manual QA editing), we build ZoomGainBench, a 1,000-question bilingual benchmark on which the best of 28 VLMs achieves only 61.08. Failure analysis reveals that models favor a particular type of distractor when answering multiple-choice questions incorrectly. Beyond evaluation, training on just 9K ZoomGain samples substantially improves the visual perception capabilities of our 4B/9B models, enabling them to outperform several hundred-billion-parameter models across various perception benchmarks. The trained 9B model achieves SoTA performance on several benchmarks, such as 90.25 on HR-Bench 4K. These results establish global-to-zoom perception gaps as a practical basis for scaling fine-grained visual supervision for both evaluation and training. Our code is available at https://github.com/inclusionAI/ZoomGain.

title: MADSNet: A Multi-Scale Axial-Attentive Dense Spiking Network for Spike Camera Image Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2611.12980v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spike cameras encode dynamic scenes into high-temporal-resolution binary spike streams for efficient high-speed vision. Although spiking neural networks (SNNs) can process such signals with sparse and accumulate-only computation, existing SNN-based reconstruction methods are typically shallow and still lag behind ANN-based models in reconstruction fidelity. This paper proposes MADSNet, a Multi-scale Axial-attentive Dense Spiking Network for spike camera image reconstruction. MADSNet adopts a hierarchical spiking encoder--decoder, where a multi-scale spike stem extracts early features, axial spike attention captures long-range dependencies, a dense spiking bottleneck enhances feature reuse, and a spike-to-continuous decoder reconstructs continuous intensity images from spike-domain representations. Experiments on gray-scale and color spike reconstruction show that MADSNet outperforms SSIR by 4.3 dB PSNR and Spk2ImgNet by 1.94 dB on SREDS. Compared with Spk2ImgNet, it achieves about 15$\times$ lower latency and uses only about 1/40 of the estimated energy, demonstrating that carefully designed SNN architectures can improve reconstruction quality while preserving computational efficiency.

title: Fintech Mail Cutovers — Safe DNS Record Writer Evidence for Incident Response
description:
Restore company mail routing with a safe DNS record writer: read the zone's current state, compare it with the intended MX set, skip a matching set, and verify every attempted mutation. Consider an illustrative page that says a fintech company's mail cutover is still unverified. The responder sees a successful change request in the dashboard, but the incident record contains no observation of the resulting MX set. What page fired, and what evidence would let someone close it?

Short answer: A safe DNS record writer uses read, compare, conditional write, and read back; a no-op skips the write, while an uncertain outcome triggers another read before any retry. Choose customer-owned or platform-owned zones by who can authorize and coordinate changes. Preserve that ownership boundary throughout the operation.

The earlier signal should have been an unresolved difference between approved intent and observed configuration, attached to a named zone owner. A dashboard's completed task cannot supply that evidence by itself. This is a proposed incident-response design, not a report of a production outage, and its alert thresholds are policy choices to test against the team's delivery requirements.

What should a safe DNS record writer read before changing mail routing?

Start the investigation with the evidence that the writer actually collected. An accepted mutation, an observed record set, and a completed mail cutover answer different questions. Treating them as one green status makes it difficult to tell the responder whether to inspect permissions, concurrent edits, configuration, or the mail delivery path. The useful incident artifact ties together the approved intent, the state read before the attempt, the mutation outcome, and the state observed afterward.

Keep those separate.

For a concrete example, use the reserved example domain treasury.example as the fintech company's mail domain. Its approved target is an MX set containing preference 10 with exchange inbound.mail.example. and preference 20 with exchange backup.mail.example.. These are illustrative values, not a provider's configuration instructions. The actual target must come from the mail provider's instructions and the company's approved change. The writer must compare the complete intended set, including the TTL chosen for this change, rather than decide that the job is done because one desired exchange appears somewhere in the response.

The instrumentation change is to record a reconciliation result independently of the request result. In this design, each run records a change identifier, ownership mode, intent identifier, pre-write revision, attempt status, and verification status. A successful no-op is observable too: it means a fresh read matched the approved target and no mutation was necessary. An unresolved read is an error, never an empty record set.

That distinction matters during a page. If the initial read failed, the responder has no basis for a replacement. If the write returned an error but the next read matches, the responder has evidence of the desired control-plane state, even though the request's outcome was ambiguous. Neither result establishes that a real message has reached a mailbox.

Ownership determines who can resolve the difference

For a customer-owned zone, make the customer's authority explicit in the change record: which zone, which mail domain, which MX set, and which approved intent the writer may apply. If the writer lacks that authority, the useful output is an actionable handoff to the customer, with the expected set and the observed difference. Repeated automated attempts cannot repair missing authorization.

For a platform-owned zone, make the platform's coordination responsibility explicit instead. All participating writers need a way to detect stale observations or serialize mutations for the affected record set. Central ownership makes that coordination easier to arrange organizationally, but it doesn't make a read followed by a write atomic. An administrative console, another automation job, and an emergency change can still produce conflicting intent.

The trade-off is operational control. Customer ownership preserves the customer's change authority and introduces a handoff when the platform cannot act; platform ownership lets the platform coordinate the change directly and makes the platform responsible for that coordination. Choose based on who must approve the change and who can respond when it stalls. Request volume and unit pricing don't settle that question.

Don't broaden an MX correction into a replacement of the whole zone.

In this design the mutation boundary is one explicitly selected MX set, so unrelated records stay outside the operation. Mail authentication also needs its own review: RFC 7489 describes DMARC evaluation in relation to SPF and DKIM alignment. An observed MX match is therefore a deliberately narrow verification result, not proof that the company's entire mail configuration is correct.

Make the writer return evidence, including on a no-op

The following Go example expresses the safety contract behind a Node.js read-compare-write implementation. The language is incidental to the sequence: await a fresh read, compare canonical sets, conditionally replace, and read again. A Node.js implementation needs the same error boundaries and coordination guarantees.

This is adapter code, not a claim that every DNS API exposes a conditional replacement operation. ReadMX must return the complete selected set, a revision covering that set, and an error on incomplete or failed reads. ReplaceMX must atomically reject a stale revision without modifying anything; an adapter that cannot provide that guarantee must reject the operation or use a coordination mechanism whose scope covers the relevant writers. A second client-side comparison cannot manufacture that guarantee.

Here the adapter canonicalizes exchange names, sorts the set, and rejects duplicates before returning it. The approved target passes through the same validation. Consequently the comparison below is an exact comparison of validated canonical data, not an assumption about the ordering of an arbitrary API response. The caller supplies an authorized zone and owner name, a nonempty validated target, and a context with a deadline. This snippet uses the standard library's slices package, requiring Go 1.21 or later.

package mailchange

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "slices"
)

type MX struct {
    Preference uint16
    Exchange   string
}

type Set struct {
    TTL     uint32
    Records []MX
}

type Snapshot struct {
    Revision string
    Set      Set
}

type Zone interface {
    ReadMX(context.Context, string, string) (Snapshot, error)
    ReplaceMX(context.Context, string, string, string, Set) error
}

type Result struct {
    Attempted bool
    Verified  bool
    Before    Snapshot
    After     Snapshot
    WriteErr  error
}

func equal(a, b Set) bool {
    return a.TTL == b.TTL && slices.Equal(a.Records, b.Records)
}

func Reconcile(ctx context.Context, z Zone, zone, owner string,
    want Set) (Result, error) {
    var result Result
    before, err := z.ReadMX(ctx, zone, owner)
    if err != nil {
        return result, fmt.Errorf("read before change: %w", err)
    }
    result.Before = before
    if equal(before.Set, want) {
        result.After = before
        result.Verified = true
        return result, nil
    }

    result.Attempted = true
    result.WriteErr = z.ReplaceMX(ctx, zone, owner, before.Revision, want)
    after, err := z.ReadMX(ctx, zone, owner)
    if err != nil {
        return result, fmt.Errorf("read after attempt: %w", err)
    }
    result.After = after
    result.Verified = equal(after.Set, want)
    if result.Verified {
        return result, nil
    }
    if result.WriteErr != nil {
        return result, fmt.Errorf("target unverified after attempt: %w",
            result.WriteErr)
    }
    return result, fmt.Errorf("observed MX set differs from target")
}

Attempted is intentionally precise. It says a mutation was attempted; it doesn't claim that this invocation caused the observed state. A concurrent actor could have applied the same target. Keep WriteErr in the incident evidence even when read-back succeeds, because a verified target and a clean request history are different observations.

The no-op branch is short because its evidence already exists. It performs a fresh read, compares the full selected set, and returns without writing. That avoids making an unnecessary mutation the price of proving that the configuration is already correct.

A read-back through the management interface verifies what that interface reports. Resolver observations and an appropriate mail delivery check belong to subsequent verification stages, with their own outcomes. Give them distinct names in the incident record so the dashboard cannot quietly substitute one for another.

Reconstruct the failure before authorizing another attempt

The most dangerous recovery instruction is an unconditional retry of the old payload. In this design a retry starts a new reconciliation against fresh state and current approved intent. If the preceding attempt took effect, the new run can finish as a no-op. If another authorized actor changed the set, the responder must resolve the competing intent before overwriting it. A revision conflict is evidence to investigate, not permission to discard the revision check.

Rollback deserves the same treatment. Store the pre-change snapshot as evidence, but require fresh authorization and a fresh conditional comparison before restoring it; a saved snapshot doesn't prove that restoring it is still appropriate after another change. This adds work during response. It also prevents an old recovery action from automatically becoming the newest conflicting writer.

Before deployment, exercise the boundaries that would otherwise confuse the responder:

  • Start with an already matching set and assert that no write occurs.
  • Introduce a concurrent edit between read and replace and require rejection.
  • Simulate a request error after the target has been applied and require read-back to settle the observed state.
  • Fail the read-back and require an unresolved verification result, with no blind second mutation.

These tests evaluate the adapter contract and the recovery policy, not just whether a function returned nil. If the original context has expired, preserve that unresolved result; schedule a separate observation under a fresh bounded context rather than pretending the failed read verified anything.

The team also needs an owner for each unresolved result. A customer-owned zone may require customer action; a platform-owned zone may require an internal response. Record that routing alongside the evidence, avoiding mailbox contents or credentials in operational logs.

A page needs someone.

Close the page on evidence, and tune the noise budget

Define the paging threshold around a mismatch that remains unresolved beyond an explicitly chosen verification window, and separately identify failures that prevent any observation. Pick the window from the cutover's delivery requirements and the verification stages being monitored. No universal duration follows from the reconciliation algorithm.

The false-positive cost is concrete: a threshold that treats every intermediate mismatch as an incident can summon a responder who has no useful action beyond waiting for the next observation. A threshold that allows indefinite uncertainty leaves a failed cutover without an owner. Preserve the intermediate results, group repeated observations by approved change, and page when the evidence calls for a decision that someone can actually make.

Close the configuration portion when the intended MX set is observed, and close the broader cutover only when its separately defined delivery checks pass. Keep the ownership handoff visible throughout. That gives the next responder a defensible stopping point and makes the alert explain what still needs action.

References

RFC 7489 supplies the mail-authentication context for keeping MX verification separate from DMARC evaluation. The Go package reference documents the comparison primitive used in the example. The reconciliation contract and alert policy above are proposed engineering choices.

  • RFC 7489, Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7489
  • Go standard library, slices: https://pkg.go.dev/slices

Further reading

  • https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7489
  • https://pkg.go.dev/slices

title: When to Start Denoising? Adaptive Denoising Entry for Generative Video Compression
description:
arXiv:2611.13620v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative video compression offers a promising solution for compressing and reconstructing videos under extremely low bitrate constraints, among which the diffusion-based solutions still achieve the best performance by providing the powerful generative latent prior. However, their effectiveness critically depends on when the compressed latent is introduced into the diffusion process, which directly governs the trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and perceptual realism. To address this limitation, we identify denoising start-timestep selection as a key factor governing this trade-off and formulate it as a geometric optimization problem. Based on this formulation, we propose a novel adaptive diffusion entry method for generative video compression (ADE-GVC), the first timestep-aware generative video compression framework, featuring a lightweight predictor that estimates an adaptive denoising start point from the compressed latent. A temporal adapter further extracts compression-aware conditions and injects them into a pretrained video diffusion model, enabling the reconstruction of videos with both high fidelity and realism. More importantly, we observe a strong quantitative relationship between the predicted timesteps and the distortion between the original and compressed latents, providing empirical support for our optimization formulation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ADE-GVC achieves the state-of-the-art performance on perceptual metrics and substantially improves reconstruction realism over existing generative video compression methods. Notably, our ADE-GVC achieves an average bitrate savings of 40.99\% (on DISTS) and 95.24\% (on PSNR) compared to the latest open-source baseline GLC-Video.

title: Breakdown of Autoregressive Multi-Step Reasoning Under Concentrated vs. Diffuse Attention Head Dropout
description:
arXiv:2611.14209v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: During extended wakefulness, mammalian neocortical networks experience localized periods of transient neuronal silence termed off-states. Here, we examine how analogous spatiotemporally concentrated disruptions affect sequential reasoning in autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs). Evaluating 250 paired derivations on the GSM8K benchmark across two 8B models (Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct), we contrast clustered bursts of attention head masking against budget-matched diffuse i.i.d. dropout. Concentrated bursts induce substantial reasoning degradation: at onset parameter $\mathcal{B}=0.10$ (scheduling $\sim 5.7\%$ of vulnerable head-token volume), Qwen3-8B accuracy drops from $91.2\%$ under diffuse noise to $78.8\%$ under burst dropout ($\Delta = -12.4$ percentage points [pp], exact McNemar $p = 5.5 \times 10^{-6}$), while LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct drops from $84.0\%$ to $76.8\%$ ($\Delta = -7.2$ pp, $p = 0.0198$). Conversely, dispersing the identical cumulative budget uniformly across generation steps via stratified quintile matching yields substantially milder degradation (retaining $91.2\%$ in Qwen and $84.0\%$ in LLaMA). In an exploratory factorial dissociation ($N=100$), single-step dropout density is associated with an acute drop in a single schedule draw ($-10.0$ pp on Qwen, $p_{\text{holm}} = 0.0425$), while multi-token continuity exhibits an inconclusive compounding trend ($-7.0$ pp, $p_{\text{holm}} = 0.1892$). Error analysis reveals that Qwen failures reflect derivation errors within formatted responses (conditional accuracy drop of $-11.4$ pp), whereas in LLaMA $22.2\%$ of discordant losses lack a final answer format line (conditional gap narrows to $-5.0$ pp). These findings demonstrate that autoregressive reasoning chains are particularly vulnerable to concentrated structural disruptions, providing empirical benchmarks for fault tolerance in transformer architectures.

title: Beyond Passive Imitation: On-Policy Mid-Training Distillation for Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.13855v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Continual pre-training (CPT) adapts large language models (LLMs) to specialized domains, yet its standard next-token prediction (NTP) objective treats every corpus token as a fixed target, regardless of its utility to the current model. In a controlled study on the same 1B-token mathematical corpus, we observe sharply different outcomes across base models: NTP improves Llama-3.2-3B's performance on mathematical benchmarks but substantially degrades Qwen3-1.7B-Base's performance, indicating that, under a fixed training recipe, the same training sequences can have model-dependent effects. To address this problem, we introduce On-Policy Mid-Training Distillation (OPMD), which reformulates mid-training from offline text imitation into active, query-driven knowledge acquisition. At selected anchor positions, OPMD samples trajectories from the evolving student policy and applies dense token-level reverse-KL rewards from a frozen teacher, training the model on states it actually visits rather than only on ground-truth prefixes. This on-policy objective reduces the training-generation mismatch of teacher-forced NTP. On MATH-500 and Minerva, OPMD improves the Qwen student over its base performance and outperforms the evaluated NTP baseline, which degrades on both benchmarks. OPMD integrates into CPT pipelines without added inference-time overhead and offers a model-aware alternative to passive domain adaptation.

title: Static, Finally: Moving Android Code from Companion Objects to Companion Blocks
description:
For a decade, every Android codebase written in Kotlin has carried the same quiet tax. You want a factory function, a constant, a TAG, a newInstance() for a Fragment, and the language answers with a nested singleton called Companion. It works, it is idiomatic, and it leaks into places you never planned for: Java call sites, reflection, ProGuard rules, bytecode size.

Kotlin 2.5.0-Beta1 introduces an experimental alternative: companion blocks and companion extensions. JetBrains describes the feature in The Companions to Come, and the full design lives in KEEP-0449. This article is the Android engineer’s view: what changes, what to try first, and, more importantly, how an adoption goes wrong.

Status note. The feature is experimental. Snippets below follow the syntax shown in the announcement, so pin your toolchain and re-check against the KEEP before copying anything into production. Where I am reasoning from the design rather than quoting it, I say so.

1. The problem a companion object solves, and the one it creates

A companion object is a real object. That is its strength (it can implement interfaces, be passed around as a value) and its cost (the compiler must materialize a class and a holder for it).

Here is the pattern most Android modules contain today:

data class Money(val minorUnits: Long, val currency: Currency) {

    operator fun plus(other: Money): Money {
        require(currency == other.currency) { "Currency mismatch: $currency vs ${other.currency}" }
        return copy(minorUnits = minorUnits + other.minorUnits)
    }

    companion object {
        fun zero(currency: Currency) = Money(0L, currency)

        fun fromMajor(major: BigDecimal, currency: Currency): Money =
            Money(major.movePointRight(currency.defaultFractionDigits).longValueExact(), currency)
    }
}

On the JVM this produces a Money class, a nested Money$Companion class, and a static field on Money that holds the singleton. Kotlin callers never notice. Java callers, reflection-based libraries, and shrinker configurations do.

2. What the new syntax looks like

The block form is deliberately a near-copy of the old one. The keyword object disappears:

data class Money(val minorUnits: Long, val currency: Currency) {

    companion {
        fun zero(currency: Currency) = Money(0L, currency)

        fun fromMajor(major: BigDecimal, currency: Currency): Money =
            Money(major.movePointRight(currency.defaultFractionDigits).longValueExact(), currency)
    }
}

Call sites in Kotlin are unchanged: Money.zero(usd). What changed is the compilation strategy. According to the announcement, companion blocks compile to static members on platforms like the JVM, instead of members of a hidden singleton class.

Extensions: adding members to types you do not own

The second feature is the one Android developers will notice first. A companion extension attaches a type-level member to any class or interface, including Java classes and types without a companion:

import android.net.Uri

companion fun Uri.forRoute(route: String, query: Map<String, String> = emptyMap()): Uri =
    Uri.Builder()
        .scheme("shopapp")
        .authority("app")
        .appendPath(route)
        .apply { query.forEach { (k, v) -> appendQueryParameter(k, v) } }
        .build()

// call site
val link = Uri.forRoute("cart", mapOf("promo" to "DIWALI"))

Uri.Builder percent-encodes path segments and query parameters for you, so callers never hand-escape values. A Map parameter also avoids the array allocation a vararg of pairs creates on every call, which matters if routing code runs on a hot path.

Until now the same idea meant a top-level function with an awkward name (uriForRoute(...)) that no one could discover through autocomplete on Uri.. Here the function reads as if the platform class had always shipped it.

3. Opting in, and who you lock out

Two compiler flags control the feature:

  • -Xcompanion-blocks enables blocks.
  • -Xcompanion-blocks-and-extensions enables both blocks and extensions.

In a Gradle build, apply them narrowly, through a convention plugin rather than ad hoc per module:

// build-logic: AndroidAppConventionPlugin.kt (sketch)
class AndroidAppConventionPlugin : Plugin<Project> {
    override fun apply(target: Project) = with(target) {
        extensions.configure<KotlinAndroidProjectExtension> {
            compilerOptions {
                freeCompilerArgs.addAll("-Xcompanion-blocks-and-extensions")
            }
        }
    }
}

The reach of each flag is the part that bites. Per the announcement, turning on extensions makes the compiler emit pre-release binaries, so a library that uses companion extensions cannot be consumed as a dependency until the feature stabilizes. Exposing plain blocks from a library is allowed, but anyone consuming those blocks must also enable the blocks feature.

The practical reading: extensions belong in leaf application modules for now. Blocks can reach library code, but only if you control, or can coordinate with, every consumer.

4. Keep, migrate, or extend: a decision path

JetBrains is explicit that nobody has to migrate. Companion objects remain a guaranteed part of the language, and a handful of use cases only they serve. The clearest one: a companion that must implement an interface, because it compiles to a full class.

fun interface ScreenFactory<S : Screen> {
    fun create(args: Bundle): S
}

class CheckoutScreen(private val cartId: String) : Screen {

    // Must stay an object: it is passed around as a ScreenFactory value.
    companion object : ScreenFactory<CheckoutScreen> {
        override fun create(args: Bundle) =
            CheckoutScreen(requireNotNull(args.getString("cartId")) { "cartId missing" })
    }
}

// somewhere in navigation setup
registry.register("checkout", CheckoutScreen)   // the companion as a value

A companion { } block has no instance to hand over, so this registration style cannot move. Everything else (constants, factories, newInstance helpers) is a candidate.

The announcement describes mechanical migration as deleting the object keyword in most cases, followed by a recompile of the module and everything that depends on it.

5. Failure modes: how this goes wrong in a real app

The syntax migration is trivial. The consequences are not. These are the places I would expect trouble, grouped along the build-to-runtime pipeline. Items marked inferred come from reasoning about the design, not from the announcement, so verify them against your own build.

Failure 1: the silent binary break in a published library

The announcement states that the migrated project and everything depending on it must be recompiled. For an app module that is a non-event. For an AAR you publish, it means existing consumers compiled against Money.Companion.zero(...) will fail when they pick up the new artifact. Treat a migration in public API as a binary-breaking change: bump the major version, or leave that library on companion objects.

Failure 2: Java callers that stop compiling (inferred)

If any Java in your codebase, or in a downstream app, calls the member through the singleton accessor, that route is tied to the old shape:

// Before: works because Companion is a real field holding a real object
Money zero = Money.Companion.zero(usd);

Since blocks compile to static members, I expect the Java form to become a plain static call, Money.zero(usd). Search the repository for .Companion. before flipping anything. It also means that @JvmStatic on these members likely becomes redundant. Confirm in the KEEP rather than assuming.

Failure 3: reflection that expects a companion instance

Anything that discovers type-level functionality by asking Kotlin reflection for the companion will find nothing after migration:

import kotlin.reflect.full.companionObjectInstance

fun <T : Any> KClass<T>.findFactory(): ScreenFactory<T>? =
    @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")
    companionObjectInstance as? ScreenFactory<T>

For classes converted to blocks, companionObjectInstance returns null, and the code above quietly falls back to whatever default you wrote. Plugin systems, custom DI glue, and serialization helpers are the usual suspects. Grep for companionObject and companionObjectInstance, and write a unit test that asserts the lookup still succeeds for each registered type.

Failure 4: R8 and ProGuard rules written for a class that no longer exists (inferred)

Keep rules aimed at **$Companion classes silently match nothing once the nested class is gone. The build stays green; the failure arrives in release builds as a stripped or renamed member that reflection or JNI still expects. After migrating, diff the R8 usage.txt and seeds.txt outputs for the affected classes, and rewrite the rule against the outer class's static members.

Failure 5: tooling that has not caught up

The announcement is candid here: other ecosystem tools may not support blocks yet, and JetBrains is working with the major players. For an Android project that list is long: annotation processors, KSP-based code generators, lint rules, IDE inspections. Do not discover this on your main branch. Spend a day on a throwaway branch with the flag on and the full CI matrix running.

Failure 6: a flag that leaks into a library

The cheapest way to reproduce the pre-release problem is to enable the extensions flag in a convention plugin that every module shares. A guard in the build prevents it:

// root build.gradle.kts (sketch)
import org.jetbrains.kotlin.gradle.tasks.KotlinCompilationTask

subprojects {
    plugins.withId("maven-publish") {
        // afterEvaluate so flags added by convention plugins are already visible
        afterEvaluate {
            tasks.withType<KotlinCompilationTask<*>>().configureEach {
                val flags = compilerOptions.freeCompilerArgs.get()
                check("-Xcompanion-blocks-and-extensions" !in flags) {
                    "$path publishes artifacts; companion extensions would produce pre-release binaries."
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

Two details matter here. First, the check runs when Gradle configures the compile tasks, so a bad flag fails the build before any compilation starts, rather than midway through execution as a doFirst block would. Second, matching on KotlinCompilationTask<*> instead of the narrower KotlinCompile also covers Android variant and multiplatform compile tasks, which a KotlinCompile-only match can miss depending on your Kotlin Gradle plugin version. Treat the snippet as a starting point and test it against your own AGP and KGP combination, including with the configuration cache on.

Failing at configuration time is far cheaper than failing in a consumer’s sync a week later.

6. A rollout plan I would actually run

  1. Canary branch. Enable -Xcompanion-blocks in one app module, convert a single class, run unit tests, instrumentation tests, and a release build with R8.
  2. Grep before you edit. Search for .Companion., companionObject, and $Companion across Kotlin, Java, and keep-rule files.
  3. Convert leaf utilities first. Constants and pure factories, with no interface implementations and no reflection consumers.
  4. Leave interface-bearing companions alone. They are first-class citizens, not legacy.
  5. Add extensions last, and only in apps. Start with platform types where the readability win is obvious, such as Uri, Bundle, and Intent helpers.
  6. Gate libraries. Add the publishing guard above before any teammate touches a shared convention plugin.

7. Where this leaves Android and Multiplatform

For pure Android work, the benefit is cleaner bytecode and a more natural Java story. For Kotlin Multiplatform, the announcement points to a larger payoff: because blocks compile like platform statics, an expected companion block member can be actualized by a Java class with static members. That removes a long-standing wrinkle at the Android boundary. The KEEP has the exact rules, and I would read it in full before designing a shared API around it.

My position: adopt blocks for new application code once your toolchain passes the canary branch; defer extensions in anything you publish; and never migrate a companion just because you can. The old companion object is not deprecated and not going away. The new form is a sharper tool, not a replacement.

Sources

  • The Companions to Come, JetBrains Kotlin Blog
  • KEEP-0449: Companion blocks and extensions

title: Advancing Mass-Conserving Deep Learning for Distributed Hydrologic Modeling: A Case Study in a Snow-Dominated Watershed
description:
arXiv:2611.13346v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent progress in physics-aware deep learning (DL) has embedded mass conservation within Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) architecture for hydrologic modeling, improving physical consistency and enabling diagnostics of internal states. However, existing mass-conserving neural networks are primarily developed in lumped formulations. Consequently, previous studies provide only fragmented and often indirect evidence of when and why imposed physical constraints may lead to unrealistic hydrologic behavior. To address this limitation, we propose Physics-Enhanced Conservation-Augmented Net (PECAN), a mass-conserving convolutional LSTM-based framework for distributed hydrologic modeling and diagnosing structural limitations of physics-aware DL models. PECAN is implemented in two variants: (1) PECAN-MC with a strict precipitation-based conservation constraint and (2) PECAN-MCR with a relaxed conservation constraint allowing additional water inputs beyond precipitation. Both variants are trained solely on gauge streamflow and evaluated in a snow-dominated watershed in Colorado. We benchmark PECAN against lumped DL baselines and the distributed process-based Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) model. Results show that PECAN achieves competitive outlet streamflow simulation accuracy while producing spatially explicit latent states for interpretation. Comparisons with reference soil moisture indicate that PECAN cell states resemble meaningful temporal soil moisture dynamics. However, analyses also reveal that PECAN misrepresents snow processes by prematurely removing winter snow water storage from the system rather than retaining it for spring release. PECAN demonstrates accurate streamflow simulation at gauges and shows diagnostic potential to expose structural limitations in hydrologic process representation, thereby informing future physics-aware neural network development for hydrology.

title: Mixed Signals: Weight-Space Programming for EEG and ECG
description:
arXiv:2611.13758v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Weight-space programming allows language models to read a trained neural network's weights and edit them. This opens the door to ``training'' by reasoning rather than through gradient descent. Prior work has demonstrated its functionality and promise for game-playing networks and fixing specific failures in language models, even extending to diffusion models. In this work, we present its applicability to models trained on biosignal data, specifically EEG and ECG data. We show that frontier models are not only able to debug specific faults planted in biosignal-based models without being told what these faults are, but are even capable of writing all the weights of a network from scratch, given only the architecture, the task, and a minimal set of training subjects. In particular, in one set of experiments, a language model was able to match standard gradient-descent training using $6\times$ fewer training subjects, through reasoning alone and without any gradient descent step. Networks written by Claude Opus 5.5 also scored higher than classic hand-crafted EEG pipelines (alpha band power, and common spatial patterns with linear discriminant analysis) when built from the same 5 subjects. We also highlight some of the limitations, which include the inability of language models to improve already well-trained classification models, and their incapacity to reliably recognize, from the weights alone, the task a network was trained on. Overall, our results indicate that weight-space programming can be useful for small networks, such as those deployed on edge devices and wearables, but the concept still requires further investigation before it can be used in practice.

title: LandslideFM: A Foundation Model Towards Unified Landslide Perception and Understanding
description:
arXiv:2611.12936v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Intelligent landslide detection is essential for disaster prevention. However, existing models primarily focus on isolated visual tasks, require extensive labeled data, and lack deep analytical and scene-understanding capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose LandslideFM, the first unified foundation model that connects visual perception tasks with contextual interpretation of landslides. Specifically, LandslideFM adapts to multiple visual tasks via a Source-Agreement Graduated Trust semi-supervised learning framework that leverages limited labeled data alongside abundant unlabeled data. Furthermore, predicted landslide regions provide explicit spatial guidance to a Vision-Language Model adapted through parameter-efficient fine-tuning, enabling comprehensive landslide reasoning. To support training and evaluation in this domain, we also present LandslideVL, the first benchmark for intelligent landslide analysis, combining visual imagery and newly introduced textual prompts. Comprehensive experiments across public datasets and LandslideVL demonstrate that LandslideFM achieves superior quantitative and qualitative performance. Most importantly, LandslideFM surpasses general-purpose VLMs in specialized landslide reasoning and scene analysis. Our code is released at https://github.com/wangshanwen001/LandslideFM.

title: Amazon S3 Tables now support S3 server access logging
description:
Amazon S3 Tables now support server access logging, providing you detailed records of the requests made to your table buckets. You can now track table operations, namespace management, and data access to support security audits, access analysis, and cost attribution. Log delivery is available at no additional cost, and you pay only for the storage of the log files.

When you enable server access logging on a table bucket, S3 delivers logs for requests to all tables and namespaces in that bucket to a general purpose bucket in the same account and Region. Each record captures the requester, operation, table name, namespace, response status, and request timing, using the same space-delimited format as S3 server access logs for general purpose buckets. This lets you reuse your existing log analysis workflows to query S3 Table logs with any query engine of your choice such as Amazon Athena and DuckDB.

Server access logging for S3 Tables is available in all AWS Regions where S3 Tables are available. You can enable it using the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or AWS CloudFormation. To learn more, visit the S3 Tables overview page and S3 Tables server access logging in the Amazon S3 User Guide.

title: RB-LDC: Redundancy-Balanced Latent Coding for Noise-Robust Diffusion Latents
description:
arXiv:2611.13955v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Latent diffusion models decode approximately correct latents, making decoder sensitivity to perturbations relevant to image quality. After whitening, forward diffusion corrupts every direction at the same signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), despite unequal decoder sensitivities. We study an invertible linear layer between the encoder and diffusion process that shifts each direction's log-SNR. Its linear minimum mean-square-error (LMMSE) recovery risk has an exact spectral expression for any whitened latent distribution. Under an energy budget and a floor ensuring invertibility, minimizing decoder-sensitivity-weighted LMMSE risk integrated over the diffusion schedule yields a unique optimal allocation. The layer aligns with the decoder's expected pullback metric and equalizes marginal risk reduction across directions, computed by a deterministic spectral solver. At large budgets, the allocation follows a power law in sensitivity whose exponent is determined by the low-SNR tail of the loss weighting: one half for noise prediction and two thirds for data prediction under the cosine schedule, with a crossover on truncated schedules. We instantiate this principle as RB-LDC using Jacobian-based sensitivity estimates. On ImageNet at 256 x 256 resolution with SD-VAE and VA-VAE, trained RB-LDC improves reconstruction from noisy latents over budget-matched isotropic coding in all four metrics and five coding configurations, averaged over 15 SNRs and three pipeline seeds. It reduces average perturbed FID by 17.1 for VA-VAE block-local coding while preserving clean reconstruction. We also report intermediate SNRs where perturbed FID worsens. With a frozen diffusion model, RB-LDC yields lower FID point estimates in all 12 tested combinations of sampling progress and channel SNR under corruption during sampling.

title: Trajectory-Regularized Distribution Distillation for One-Step Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.12978v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Distilling flow matching models for one-step generation generally follows two paradigms. Trajectory alignment supervises the student with the teacher's probability flow ODE, but its performance degrades under very small sampling budgets. Distribution matching directly optimizes the generated distribution, but estimating its reverse Kullback-Leibler gradient typically requires a separate network to track the evolving student score. We propose trajectory-regularized distribution distillation (TRD), which combines distribution-level and trajectory-level supervision through a momentum-mixture policy predicted in a single student forward pass. This policy serves simultaneously as a one-step generator, an estimator of the student's marginal velocity that removes the need for a second trainable network in distribution matching, and a closed-form time-dependent velocity field supervised along the teacher ODE trajectory. Experiments on SANA-1.6B and Stable Diffusion 3.5 show that TRD outperforms representative consistency and distribution matching baselines in generation quality and training efficiency for both one-step and few-step generation, with a trade-off in sample diversity.

title: Tailwind CSS RTL in Next.js: logical utilities, the rtl: variant and what must never flip
description:
We ship every Next.js template in English and Arabic, with a real right-to-left layout. After doing that across every website and dashboard we sell, the whole approach fits in one sentence:

Set dir on <html>, write spacing and position with logical utilities (ms-4, not ml-4), and keep the rtl: variant for the few things logical properties cannot express.

This post is the practical version of that sentence, with code from real projects. Every class below was checked against Tailwind CSS 4.3.

1. Put dir on <html>, on the server

Logical properties read the element's direction, the rtl: variant looks for it, and screen readers use lang to pick a voice. Put both on <html>, not on a wrapper: dialogs, menus and toasts usually render in a portal under <body> and only inherit a direction set above them.

With next-intl and the App Router, let app/[locale]/layout.tsx render <html>:

// src/config/i18n.ts
export const directionOf = (locale: string): "rtl" | "ltr" =>
  locale === "ar" ? "rtl" : "ltr";

// src/app/[locale]/layout.tsx (trimmed)
export default async function LocaleLayout({ children, params }: {
  children: React.ReactNode;
  params: Promise<{ locale: string }>;
}) {
  const { locale } = await params;
  if (!hasLocale(routing.locales, locale)) notFound();
  setRequestLocale(locale);
  const messages = await getMessages();

  return (
    <html lang={locale} dir={directionOf(locale)} suppressHydrationWarning>
      <body>
        <NextIntlClientProvider messages={messages}>{children}</NextIntlClientProvider>
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}

Do not set dir in a useEffect. The server HTML then arrives left to right, paints that way, and flips after hydration: a visible jump on every Arabic page load.

2. Logical utilities do most of the work

ml-4 is margin-left in both languages. ms-4 is margin-inline-start: the left in English, the right in Arabic. One class, both directions.

Physical Logical CSS
ml-4 / mr-4 ms-4 / me-4 margin-inline-start / -end
pl-4 / pr-4 ps-4 / pe-4 padding-inline-start / -end
left-0 / right-0 inset-s-0 / inset-e-0 (or start-0 / end-0) inset-inline-start / -end
text-left text-start text-align: start
border-l border-s border-inline-start-width
rounded-l-lg rounded-s-lg the two start corners

Tailwind CSS 4.2 added inset-s-* and inset-e-* and deprecated start-* and end-*. The old names still compile to the same property, so existing code is fine.

What already flips without a new class: flex and grid rows, justify-start / justify-end, mx-*, px-*, and in Tailwind CSS 4 also space-x-* and divide-x. So never add flex-row-reverse "for Arabic": the row already reversed when the direction changed, and reversing it again puts it back in English order.

An input with an icon shows the pattern in one component:

<div className="relative">
  <span className="pointer-events-none absolute start-4 top-1/2 -translate-y-1/2">
    {startIcon}
  </span>
  <input className="h-12 ps-11" {...props} />
</div>

Icon at start-4, text padded with ps-11. In Arabic both move to the right with no override.

Physical utilities are still right when the thing is physical: left-1/2 -translate-x-1/2 centres in both directions, and a before/after photo slider keeps "before" on the left in every language. Decide per element, and leave a comment so nobody "fixes" it later.

3. The rtl: variant, for what logical properties cannot express

Transforms, gradients, transform origins, keyframes and icon meaning have no logical version. That is what rtl: and ltr: are for. In Tailwind CSS 4.3 they compile like this:

.rtl\:-scale-x-100:where(:dir(rtl), [dir="rtl"], [dir="rtl"] *) {
  --tw-scale-x: calc(100% * -1);
  scale: var(--tw-scale-x) var(--tw-scale-y);
}

The :where() adds no specificity, and the selector matches the element's own direction, a dir="rtl" attribute, or any ancestor with dir="rtl". Keep that last part in mind (see the catch below).

Direction icons:

// Mirror a "next" arrow in Arabic
<IconArrowRight aria-hidden className="h-5 w-5 rtl:-scale-x-100" />

Prefer -scale-x-100 (a true mirror) over rotate-180, which also turns the icon upside down. Flip arrows, chevrons and "view all" links. Do not flip play buttons, media progress bars, clocks or logos.

translate-x is physical, so anything that slides off screen needs a variant:

// A mobile menu that slides in from the inline start
<div className={cn(
  "absolute top-0 start-0 h-full w-64 rounded-e-xl transition-transform",
  isOpen ? "translate-x-0" : "ltr:-translate-x-full rtl:translate-x-full",
)} />

Gradients have no logical direction in Tailwind CSS 4.3:

<div className="absolute inset-0 bg-linear-to-r from-black/85 to-transparent rtl:bg-linear-to-l" />

Transform origin too: a progress bar should grow from the side the text starts on, ltr:origin-left rtl:origin-right.

Keyboard arrows are behaviour. In tabs or a slider, the right arrow key should move towards the next item on screen, which is to the left in Arabic:

const isRtl = useLocale() === "ar";
const forward = isRtl ? "ArrowLeft" : "ArrowRight";

The catch: rtl: still matches inside a dir="ltr" island

Because rtl: matches any dir="rtl" ancestor, it still applies inside a dir="ltr" element on an Arabic page. When you need the element's own direction, use an arbitrary variant on the :dir() pseudo-class:

<IconChevronRight className="[&:dir(rtl)]:-scale-x-100" />

4. What must never flip

Mixed runs of digits and punctuation take the direction of the Arabic around them, so phone numbers, prices and counters like 3 / 12 can come out scrambled. Isolate them.

Latin digits in Arabic: ask for them explicitly, because the region decides otherwise:

new Intl.NumberFormat("ar-SA").format(1248.6);           // "١٬٢٤٨٫٦"
new Intl.NumberFormat("ar-SA-u-nu-latn").format(1248.6); // "1,248.6"

Prices:

<bdi dir="ltr" className="tabular-nums">{formatPrice(price, currency)}</bdi>

Phone, email, URLs: typed and shown left to right, but aligned with the Arabic form:

<Input type="tel" dir="ltr" className="rtl:text-end" {...register("phone")} />
<a href={`mailto:${email}`} dir="ltr">{email}</a>

Text written by users can be either language, so let the browser decide: <p dir="auto">{review.body}</p>.

Code blocks and Latin logos stay dir="ltr". Photos are never mirrored.

5. Arabic type: font, line height, letter spacing

Many Latin UI fonts have no Arabic glyphs, so load one font per script with next/font and switch under [dir="rtl"], Arabic first so Latin words inside Arabic text fall through to your Latin font:

[dir="rtl"] body {
  font-family: var(--font-arabic), var(--font-inter), system-ui, sans-serif;
  letter-spacing: 0;
}
  • Line height: a leading-[1.1] display heading can clip Arabic ascenders and diacritics. Open it up in Arabic only: leading-[1.1] rtl:leading-[1.4].
  • Letter spacing: Arabic is a connected script, and tracking makes it look broken. Reset it with rtl:tracking-normal.
  • Uppercase does nothing in Arabic, so an eyebrow label that relies on caps needs weight or colour instead.

6. A short RTL test pass

Run it on every page in Arabic, light and dark, phone and desktop:

  1. View source (not the inspector): <html lang="ar" dir="rtl"> is in the server HTML, and nothing flips after load.
  2. Sidebar, logo and main action sit on the right. Nothing is reversed twice.
  3. Drawers, menus and toasts open from the correct side, portals included.
  4. Arrows point the right way; play buttons and clocks do not flip.
  5. Phone, email and code fields type left to right.
  6. Prices, phone numbers and counters read in the right order.
  7. The Arabic font actually loads, headings do not clip, no Arabic letter spacing.
  8. Arrow keys in tabs and sliders follow the screen.

Then search for physical classes and decide on each hit:

grep -rnE --include='*.tsx' \
  '(^|[^a-z0-9-])-?(ml|mr|pl|pr|left|right)-([0-9]|\[|\(|px|auto|full)|(^|[^a-z0-9-])(rounded|border)-(l|r|tl|tr|bl|br)([^a-z0-9]|-|$)|(^|[^a-z0-9-])(text|float)-(left|right)([^a-z0-9-]|$)' \
  src

On our apps it returns between 2 and 10 lines per app (centred elements, symmetric pairs, a physical slider, lines that already carry an rtl: override). Short enough to read every line, which is the point.

The full guide, with the next-intl routing and proxy setup, charts and time axes, unicode-bidi, self-hosted Arabic fonts and an FAQ, is on our blog: Tailwind CSS RTL Guide: Logical Properties and the rtl: Variant.

If you would rather start from code where this is already done: our Next.js templates ship in English and Arabic with full RTL. title: Learning from First Discrepancies with Joint Reset and Pilot Guarantees
description:
arXiv:2611.13913v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A run that stops at its first wrong decision shows the queries and their correct labels up to and including that decision, and nothing after it. We study how many such runs are needed for learning. Each run tests a hypothesis, the pilot, chosen beforehand from a fixed binary class of VC dimension at most $d$, on a fresh record of at most $D$ queries drawn from one unknown distribution that does not depend on the pilot. The terminal information of a record is shown only if the pilot makes no discrepancy, and a bounded loss, fixed in advance, is attached to the position where a hypothesis stops. If the discrepancy probabilities of members of the class have infimum at most $f$ and their risks have infimum at most $r$, one learner uses $\widetilde O((d+1)[D(f+\varepsilon)+r]/\varepsilon^2)$ runs and $\widetilde O(D(1+f/\varepsilon))$ distinct pilots on every history. It returns a member of the class and an interval of width at most $\varepsilon$ containing, with probability at least $1-\delta$, both the output's risk and the optimal risk. We also treat unknown ceilings and expected costs. Lower bounds for finite classes show that each order is necessary in the worst case, possibly on different instances, at positive dimension, small accuracy and fixed confidence. The learner enumerates label patterns of the class on displayed queries, possibly in exponential time; the results, under standard measurability conditions, concern statistical resources only. The proof combines a gain computable from stopped displays, exponential weights, a sparse depth-robust graph and a harmonic-mean bound.
