title: Tabular Foundation Models vs Tuned Gradient Boosting for Telecom Churn: A Profit- and Calibration-Aware Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2611.12942v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) predict from a labelled context in a single forward pass. A recent benchmark reported that they decisively outperform tree ensembles for customer churn, but it compared them with untuned gradient-boosted trees (GBDTs) and scored only ranking metrics, while a retention campaign is judged in money. We re-evaluate TabPFN-2.5, TabPFN-3.5, TabPFN-3.5-Fast and TabICL v2 against Optuna-tuned GBDTs on five public telecom churn datasets over 10 seeded splits. We separate three questions: whether a model ranks churners well, whether that ranking earns more expected maximum profit (EMP), and whether its probabilities can drive a threshold policy. With a split-aware test and Holm correction over 20 pre-declared comparisons, TabPFN-3.5 earns significantly more EMP than the best tuned GBDT on Cell2Cell (1.9%) and Iranian (7.6%), and these two gains also hold against each of the three tuned GBDTs separately. On Orange it is ahead in all 10 splits (14.3%), but the gain is not significant after correction (Holm p = 0.155). The splits resample the same datasets, so these results do not stand for independent operators. TabICL v2, the earlier benchmark's leader, beats the best tuned GBDT only on Iranian, not all three of them, and underpredicts Orange churn by 2.1 points on a 7.3% base rate. On the datasets and splits where we tested them, a substantially larger tuning budget and a duplicate-aware split leave the main conclusions unchanged. Retuning the baseline cuts the earlier headline gap from 6.1 to 4.0 PR-AUC points without closing it. The licence of the TabPFN-3.5 weights we used (License v1.0), not scoring cost, is what stands between its gains and production use.

title: What type scale is a site really using? Measuring it from computed font sizes
description:
"Modular scale, ratio 1.25" is a nice thing to put in a design doc. When you inherit a site, or want to match one, you rarely get that doc. You get a page and DevTools.

Here is how I measure the scale a page actually uses, what it looked like on three demo sites I built, and where the single "ratio" number stops being useful.

Step 1: list the sizes, weighted by text

Clicking headings one by one in DevTools misses sizes and tells you nothing about which size carries the body text. Instead, walk every visible text node and add up characters per computed font size. Paste this in the console:

(() => {
  const sizes = new Map();
  const walk = document.createTreeWalker(document.body, NodeFilter.SHOW_TEXT);
  while (walk.nextNode()) {
    const text = walk.currentNode.textContent.trim();
    const el = walk.currentNode.parentElement;
    if (!text || !el.checkVisibility()) continue;
    const px = Math.round(parseFloat(getComputedStyle(el).fontSize));
    sizes.set(px, (sizes.get(px) || 0) + text.length);
  }
  return [...sizes].sort((a, b) => b[0] - a[0]);
})()

On Northwind Roasters, a fictional coffee shop I use for demos, at 1280px wide it returns [size in px, characters] pairs:

[[64, 44], [40, 30], [22, 50], [17, 486], [15, 85], [14, 145]]

Run it at the viewport you care about. If the headings use clamp() or media queries, a phone width gives different numbers.

Step 2: the base is the size with the most text

486 characters at 17px, far more than anything else, so the body size is 17px, not the 16px you might assume. That matters: if you rebuild this site with Tailwind's default text-base (16px), every paragraph comes out a pixel smaller and the line lengths change.

Step 3: a ratio from the steps above the base

Sizes above the base: 22, 40, 64. If the scale were geometric, each step would multiply by the same ratio r, so 17 × r³ = 64:

const ratio = (base, above) => (Math.max(...above) / base) ** (1 / above.length);
ratio(17, [22, 40, 64]); // 1.556

A second demo site, Ledgerline (a fictional accounting app), has a 16px base and 18, 20, 28 and 60 above it:

ratio(16, [18, 20, 28, 60]); // 1.392

That is close to the augmented fourth (1.414) from the classic named ratios. Close is all it is.

Why the ratio is only a summary

Go back to Northwind and look at the actual steps:

  • 22 / 17 = 1.29
  • 40 / 22 = 1.82
  • 64 / 40 = 1.60

No single ratio there. If you regenerate the scale from base 17 and ratio 1.556, you get 26.4, 41.1 and 64. The h1 matches, the h2 is close, and the h3 is 4.4px too big. That is a visibly different card title.

The third site shows how fragile the number is. Afterhours (a fictional dev tool) gives sizes above its 16px base of 19, 20 and 66:

ratio(16, [19, 20, 66]); // 1.604
ratio(16, [19, 66]);     // 2.031

The 20px size covers 10 characters on the whole page, probably one stray label. Drop it and the "ratio" jumps from 1.60 to 2.03. In practice this site has a huge display heading and then body-ish sizes, and no ratio describes that well.

So I use the ratio as a one-line description ("base 17, grows about 1.56 per step") and keep the measured sizes as the actual tokens:

:root {
  --text-sm: 0.875rem;    /* 14px */
  --text-base: 1.0625rem; /* 17px */
  --text-xl: 1.375rem;    /* 22px, h3 */
  --text-4xl: 2.5rem;     /* 40px, h2 */
  --text-6xl: 4rem;       /* 64px, h1 */
}

Measure line height and tracking too

Size alone does not make a heading look right. Click one heading per step in DevTools and read line-height and letter-spacing from Computed. On Northwind:

Step Size Line height Letter spacing
h1 64px 1.04 -1.28px (-0.02em)
h2 40px 1.1 -0.4px (-0.01em)
h3 22px 1.25 0
body 17px 1.6 0

The pattern is the usual one: the bigger the text, the tighter the leading and tracking. The other two sites tighten their h1 harder: Afterhours at 66px uses -2.64px (-0.04em), Ledgerline at 60px uses -2.7px (-0.045em). Convert tracking to em when you copy it, so it still fits if you change the size.

The short version

  1. List sizes weighted by characters, at the viewport you care about.
  2. The size with the most text is the base.
  3. Compute a ratio if you want a description, but copy the real sizes.
  4. Take line height and letter spacing with each step.

If you'd rather not do this by hand, I made a Chrome extension, Stylasso, that reads the type scale along with the fonts and colors and gives base, ratio and each step's line height and tracking. The numbers above match its output for these demo sites, except that it drops the stray 20px size on Afterhours (that's where its 2.031 comes from). There's a short guide here: find out what font a website is using, with its type scale. The snippet works fine without it.

Written with help from an AI assistant. The sizes come from running the snippet above on the three demo pages, and the ratios from the code in this post.

title: Backend Cron Alternatives for Scheduled Go Scripts with HTTP Digest Recovery
description:
For backend cron alternatives, use a durable queue behind the timer when scheduled Go scripts must deliver a weekly customer digest over HTTP.

Short answer: let the scheduler create one digest job per active customer, let a worker own delivery and retries, and record an idempotency key before sending. A cron expression is only a trigger. It does not tell you what happened to the work after the process exited.

For a support system, that distinction matters. A digest may contain open tickets, response-time summaries, and links to conversations. Missing one is visible to a customer; sending it twice is also visible. I treat operational recovery as the deciding axis, not the lowest advertised price.

How should backend cron alternatives run scheduled scripts with HTTP safely?

The awkward failure is not a refused connection. It is the timeout after the remote service accepted the request. The caller cannot know whether retrying will create a duplicate. A worker that retries blindly can turn a transient network event into two weekly emails or two downstream digest records.

There are several clocks in play: the schedule clock, the queue visibility timeout, the HTTP client timeout, and the recipient's own processing time. They need explicit boundaries. For example, a 10-minute worker lease cannot protect a request that is allowed to hang for 12 minutes. The lease expires, another worker starts, and both workers may send.

The job payload should be small and reconstructable. Store a customer ID, the digest period, and a deterministic key such as digest:customer-482:2026-W43; fetch the current support data when the worker runs. Do not put a mutable ticket dump into a scheduler payload and assume it will remain correct for seven days.

I start with a boring state model: queued, running, sent, and failed. sent is terminal. A failed attempt carries the next attempt time and an error category. The schedule itself is not the retry mechanism.

A small Go worker with an idempotency boundary

The following example shows the control flow rather than a vendor SDK. Store.MarkSending must be an atomic operation backed by a uniqueness constraint on the digest key. The sender must accept the same key and make its operation idempotent, or the application needs an outbox and a provider-side deduplication contract.

package digest

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

var ErrAlreadySent = errors.New("digest already sent")

type Store interface {
    MarkSending(ctx context.Context, key string, now time.Time) error
    MarkSent(ctx context.Context, key string, sentAt time.Time) error
    MarkRetry(ctx context.Context, key string, next time.Time, reason string) error
}

type Sender interface {
    Send(ctx context.Context, customerID, period, key string) error
}

func Deliver(ctx context.Context, store Store, sender Sender, customerID, period string, now time.Time) error {
    key := fmt.Sprintf("digest:%s:%s", customerID, period)
    if err := store.MarkSending(ctx, key, now); err != nil {
        if errors.Is(err, ErrAlreadySent) {
            return nil
        }
        return err
    }

    sendCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    if err := sender.Send(sendCtx, customerID, period, key); err != nil {
        return store.MarkRetry(ctx, key, now.Add(15*time.Minute), err.Error())
    }
    return store.MarkSent(ctx, key, time.Now().UTC())
}

There is an uncomfortable boundary here: Send can succeed and MarkSent can fail. That is why a production design should expose delivery status and reconcile old sending records. A reconciliation job can ask the delivery system for the idempotency key, or safely re-submit the same key if the sender guarantees deduplication. A database transaction cannot make an arbitrary HTTP endpoint atomic.

The 30-second timeout is an example policy, not a universal setting. Measure the endpoint's normal latency, choose a limit that leaves room inside the worker lease, and test the timeout path. The important part is that a request has a deadline and that a retry has a reason.

That is the trade-off.

How should the schedule and queue divide the work?

The weekly timer should do one bounded task: enumerate active customers and enqueue deterministic jobs. It should not render every digest and call every HTTP endpoint in one process. If it dies after customer 482, the next run can safely attempt to enqueue the same keys; the queue or database rejects duplicates.

A queue worker then handles backoff, concurrency, visibility renewal, and dead-letter handling. Exponential backoff avoids a synchronized retry storm. A maximum attempt count prevents one malformed customer record from consuming worker capacity forever. Permanent errors, such as an invalid recipient address, should be separated from transient errors, such as a connection reset.

Keep the schedule timestamp in UTC and derive the period from an explicit business timezone. A customer-support digest for a Monday morning local window should not depend on the machine timezone of whichever worker happens to run it. Around daylight-saving transitions, store the intended period and test both repeated and skipped local times.

For HTTP delivery, log the digest key, customer ID, period, attempt number, response class, and elapsed time. Do not log the digest body or authorization header. Alert on the age of the oldest queued job and on the count of jobs in failed or sending beyond their expected lease. A successful scheduler heartbeat proves almost nothing about delivery.

What do external automation tools change?

Visual automation products can shorten the path from a timer to an HTTP action, but the operational contract still needs to be read carefully. Zapier's paths and task history are useful for straightforward business workflows; the engineering question is how its retry, replay, retention, and idempotency behavior maps to the digest key. n8n can be self-hosted and lets a team inspect workflow execution data, but that shifts upgrades, persistence, worker capacity, and incident response into the team's ownership. GitHub Actions can run scheduled workflows and scripts, but repository workflow scheduling is a different operating model from a customer-facing delivery queue, especially when backlog control and per-customer replay matter.

Those are boundaries, not rankings. A timer plus HTTP step may be enough for a non-critical internal cleanup. A customer digest needs an answer to four questions before adoption: where is the durable job record, how is a duplicate prevented, how is a poisoned job isolated, and how can an operator replay one period for one customer? If the answers require a spreadsheet and manual clicking, the apparent simplicity is hiding operational work.

Here is the comparison I use before choosing an implementation:

Option Integration Setup effort Fits best Main limitation
Kubernetes CronJob Container command Medium A scheduled batch already running in a cluster Scheduling does not provide idempotent HTTP delivery
Cloud Tasks REST or client library Medium Delayed HTTP work with queue-level retries The application still owns digest state and reconciliation
Zapier Visual actions and webhooks Low Small business workflows with modest replay needs Execution history and retry semantics may not match a per-customer recovery contract
n8n Visual workflow or HTTP node Medium Teams willing to operate workflow persistence Self-hosting moves upgrades, capacity, and incident response to the team
GitHub Actions YAML workflow and scripts Low Repository maintenance and developer automation Repository scheduling is a poor fit for customer backlog control

The table is a boundary map, not a leaderboard. The cheapest setup can still leave an operator without a safe replay button.

A backend cron process is not automatically better. Kubernetes CronJob documents scheduling semantics and concurrency policies, but it does not turn an application-level HTTP side effect into an exactly-once operation. A managed task service can provide delayed delivery and retry controls, while a queue with a dead-letter queue makes failed messages inspectable. The useful comparison is the failure contract each option makes visible. The limitation of a timer-only design is clear: it knows that the invocation began, but not whether the remote system accepted the request before the connection failed.

Verification, rollback, and the 03:00 check

Before production, run a matrix of deliberate failures: kill the scheduler after enqueueing half the customers; return HTTP 429 and 500 responses; delay the response beyond the client deadline; terminate a worker after the remote side accepts the request; and replay the same period twice. The expected result is boring: one durable job key, bounded retries, a visible terminal failure, and no duplicate digest.

I would also run a dry period against a fixed fixture of active customers. Compare the generated set with the expected set, then inspect a sample of rendered links. This catches a more ordinary incident: a query that silently excludes customers because “active” was interpreted as “logged in during the last seven days.”

Rollback should disable new scheduling without deleting queued jobs. Let workers drain, or pause them while an operator decides whether the new code can safely process old payloads. Keep the schema able to read the previous job version. If the sender format changes, include a payload version in the key and make the migration explicit.

The 03:00 check is a useful runbook item: inspect the oldest queued job, the last successful digest period, retry counts by error class, and the reconciliation age. If those four signals look healthy, investigate the recipient-facing system next. Do not declare success from the scheduler's “completed” log line.

The decision rule is straightforward. Use a timer alone for work that can be safely repeated and has no customer-facing consequence. Add a durable queue, idempotency key, and reconciliation path when a missed or duplicated HTTP side effect needs an operator-visible recovery process. That rule survives changes in vendors, runtimes, and deployment platforms.

References

  • AWS, “Using Amazon SQS dead-letter queues”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html
  • Google Cloud, “Cloud Tasks overview”: https://cloud.google.com/tasks/docs/dual-overview
  • Kubernetes, “CronJob”: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/cron-jobs/
  • HTTP Semantics, RFC 9110: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • Zapier, “How to handle errors in Zaps”: https://help.zapier.com/hc/en-us/articles/8496288698253-How-to-handle-errors-in-Zaps
  • n8n, “Queue mode”: https://docs.n8n.io/hosting/scaling/queue-mode/
  • GitHub Docs, “Events that trigger workflows”: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows

title: SaaS Error Event Query API in Node.js (with Rollback-Safe Imports)
description:
Use a queryable error event API plus a separate schedule monitor when a Node.js SaaS marketplace needs alerting for imports that stop producing results. The decision rule is strict: advance an import watermark only after the result is durable, and make alert delivery retryable without letting notification state rewrite that watermark. A thrown error is evidence of one failure; missing expected output is evidence that the workflow itself may have stopped.

TL;DR: emit structured start and terminal events from the Node.js worker, store them behind a small query API, and run an independent cron monitor that compares each schedule's deadline with its last successful result. Send Slack or email through an idempotent outbox. This design makes silence observable, preserves an audit trail, and lets a deployment roll back without erasing or duplicating the operational truth.

Should a Node.js SaaS poll an error alerting API?

A marketplace import has at least three clocks: the scheduled start, the worker's actual start, and the durable completion. Treating those as one timestamp creates an ambiguity that no alert transport can repair. A job may never be enqueued, may start and stall, or may commit its rows while the process dies before reporting success. Those failure boundaries require different evidence.

Silence is data.

The invariants are small enough to put in an architecture decision record:

  1. Every scheduled occurrence has a stable run_id, derived before execution and reused by retries.
  2. A terminal event is written only after the imported result is durable.
  3. The success watermark moves monotonically; an older retry cannot move it backward.
  4. Alert attempts have their own idempotency key and audit history.
  5. The monitor is outside the worker's failure domain and evaluates both explicit failures and absent terminal events.

The exactly-once mindset belongs here, but “exactly once” should be expressed as enforceable state transitions, not as faith in a queue. Delivery can repeat. A unique key on (run_id, event_type) and a compare-and-swap watermark turn those repeats into stable facts, while the audit log retains rejected or duplicated attempts for reconciliation.

Retries happen.

There is also a compliance boundary. Import events should carry identifiers and operational counts, not raw seller records, payment details, credentials, or webhook payloads. Retention, access, and deletion periods depend on the marketplace's applicable policy and jurisdiction; the architecture should therefore support configured limits rather than claim one universal number.

Decision: ledger first, notifications second

The query API is the system of record for operational evidence. It can answer, for one schedule, which run was expected, what state transitions were accepted, when the last durable result appeared, and which alerts were attempted. Slack and email are downstream delivery channels. A lost message can be retried; a message must never manufacture job state. This architecture has a real limitation: it adds a ledger, an expectation model, a monitor, and an outbox that somebody must operate. It is unsuitable for an ad hoc task whose failure is already synchronously returned to a human and whose result has no reconciliation value; in that narrower case, direct exception notification is the better boundary. The extra machinery earns its place only when absence itself is actionable and rollback must preserve what operators know.

This ordering matters during rollback. Suppose release B writes a new optional event field and is rolled back to release A. If readers tolerate unknown fields and the core event envelope remains stable, A can continue from the existing watermark. The rollback neither deletes B's events nor interprets notification delivery as successful import execution. Schema evolution should be additive until every active reader can handle the new representation.

Option Silence detection Rollback behavior Audit quality Appropriate boundary
Queryable event ledger plus independent monitor Direct: compare expected occurrences with terminal events Stable when envelopes are backward-readable and watermarks are monotonic Full run and delivery history Scheduled imports with reconciliation requirements
Worker webhook on caught errors None when the process never runs or stalls before the callback Coupled to worker release and callback contract Only emitted failures Best as a low-latency supplement
Log-text polling Indirect and dependent on parsing conventions Parser can break across message changes Weak unless logs carry stable IDs Temporary diagnostics, not the control record

Polling is acceptable here because the question is bounded and replayable: “which expected runs lack a terminal result before their deadline?” The API should paginate on a stable cursor, return event time and ingestion time separately, and support lookup by schedule_id and run_id. Avoid exposing an unbounded free-form search interface to the monitor; a narrow contract is easier to index, authorize, test, and preserve across rollback.

The critical path in Go

The production worker may be Node.js, but the state machine is language-independent. The Go example below makes the transactional boundary explicit, keeps all code in one place, and avoids binding the design to an alerting vendor.

package imports

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Store interface {
    CommitResultAndEvent(ctx context.Context, result Result, event Event) error
    AdvanceWatermark(ctx context.Context, scheduleID string, completedAt time.Time) error
    MissingTerminals(ctx context.Context, dueBefore time.Time) ([]ExpectedRun, error)
    InsertAlertOnce(ctx context.Context, alert Alert) (bool, error)
}

type Result struct{ RunID string }
type Event struct {
    RunID, ScheduleID, Type string
    OccurredAt              time.Time
}
type ExpectedRun struct {
    RunID, ScheduleID string
    DueAt             time.Time
}
type Alert struct {
    Key, RunID, Channel string
    CreatedAt           time.Time
}

func Complete(ctx context.Context, db Store, result Result, scheduleID string, now time.Time) error {
    event := Event{RunID: result.RunID, ScheduleID: scheduleID, Type: "import.completed", OccurredAt: now}
    if err := db.CommitResultAndEvent(ctx, result, event); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("commit result and terminal event: %w", err)
    }
    // The store must reject a timestamp older than the current watermark.
    return db.AdvanceWatermark(ctx, scheduleID, now)
}

func DetectSilence(ctx context.Context, db Store, now time.Time) error {
    runs, err := db.MissingTerminals(ctx, now)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("query overdue runs: %w", err)
    }
    for _, run := range runs {
        alert := Alert{
            Key:       "missing-terminal:" + run.RunID,
            RunID:     run.RunID,
            Channel:   "operations",
            CreatedAt: now,
        }
        if _, err := db.InsertAlertOnce(ctx, alert); err != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("enqueue alert %s: %w", run.RunID, err)
        }
    }
    return nil
}

CommitResultAndEvent must be atomic within the chosen persistence boundary. If the imported rows and event ledger cannot share a transaction, use a transactional outbox tied to the result commit, then publish from that outbox. Do not mark completion before the durable result exists.

The short function conceals an important distinction: InsertAlertOnce records intent, not successful delivery. A dispatcher can retry Slack or email and append attempt outcomes without re-alerting the same run under the same policy. If escalation rules intentionally create a second notification, they need a different key, such as a policy version and escalation stage. This makes acknowledgements and re-notifications explainable months later.

Operating the monitor without inventing certainty

Choose the silence deadline from the schedule contract: expected start, allowed lateness, and the longest accepted execution window. Do not derive it from an attractive round number. A daily catalog import and a five-minute inventory feed have different lateness semantics, while a maintenance pause should suppress expectations rather than generate a stream of false failures.

Three timestamps should survive the whole path: event occurrence, ingestion, and alert creation. OpenTelemetry's logs data model distinguishes observed time from event time and provides fields for trace and span context, which is useful when a scheduled run also emits traces. The correlation is evidence, however, not the durable job state; a sampled or unavailable trace must not make reconciliation impossible.

Test the absence path deliberately. Freeze the scheduler clock, create an expected run, omit its terminal event, and verify that one alert intent appears after the configured deadline. Then run the monitor twice. One intent should remain. Also test a late success, an older retry after a newer success, a dispatcher crash after sending but before recording the response, and a rollback in which the older reader encounters an event written by the newer release.

Late success needs an explicit policy. It may resolve an open incident automatically, append a recovery notification, or require an operator to reconcile partially imported data. Pick one rule per import class and record the transition. Silence is uncertain by definition; the system knows that evidence is missing, not that zero rows were committed.

Keep the monitor observable as well. Record its last completed evaluation, query cursor, number of schedules examined, and age of its oldest pending alert. A monitor that silently stops is merely a second scheduled import with the same original problem.

Rejected option and where it still fits

The rejected primary design is an error webhook emitted directly from the Node.js catch path. It is appealing because explicit exceptions reach a chat channel quickly, and it has fewer moving parts. It cannot, by itself, detect that cron failed to launch the process, that a worker remained alive without progress, or that a result committed before notification code ran. It also couples rollback safety to whichever payload shape the worker release emits.

Keep that webhook as a secondary fast path when low latency matters. Give it the same run_id, route it through the idempotent alert outbox, and reconcile it against the ledger so an explicit failure and the later silence scan do not open two incidents. This division is deliberate: the worker reports what it observed, while the monitor asks what should have happened but did not leave durable evidence. The trade-off is operational complexity in exchange for a recoverable record; teams that cannot own the monitor should retain the simpler callback boundary and accept that it cannot detect every silent run.

The selection criterion is therefore not the smallest alert API. It is the smallest architecture that can prove a scheduled occurrence, preserve a durable terminal fact, query missing facts independently, and replay notification delivery without corrupting those facts. For marketplace imports, rollback-safe watermarks and auditable alert intents carry more decision weight than transport convenience.

References

  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/

title: Reading Reddit without an API key: RSS endpoints, a parser, and the limits
description:
Reddit's login wall is now the default path for a lot of readers. I read public threads for research, and I didn't want another account just to open a link. The official API can do the job, but it means OAuth, an app registration, and a token refresh path before the first request.

The public RSS feeds are still there. No key, no OAuth, Atom XML. I built a small Android client around them (105 KB, no server, no analytics). This post is about the feed format, the parsing problems, and the limits that decide what kind of reader you can build.

The endpoints 

Listing:
https://www.reddit.com/r/{subreddit}/hot.rss?limit=25
https://www.reddit.com/r/{subreddit}/new.rss?limit=25
https://www.reddit.com/r/{subreddit}/top.rss?limit=25

Thread:
https://www.reddit.com/r/{subreddit}/comments/{post_id}/.rss?limit=100

{subreddit} is the name without r/. hot, new, and top are the listing sorts. The thread URL returns the post plus the comments Reddit includes in the feed.

A few details that matter:

  • The response is application/atom+xml, not JSON.
  • The feed caps what it returns. The app asks for 25 posts per listing and 100 entries for a thread. The listing is the latest 25; I haven't found a working pagination parameter.
  • Reddit rate-limits these endpoints per IP. Two quick requests to the same subreddit can return HTTP 429. Treat 429 as "back off and retry", not as an empty feed.
  • Send a normal browser User-Agent. A bare Java client UA is more likely to get a 403.

What is inside an entry

A listing entry has the fields you'd expect: title, author name, updated timestamp, a permalink in link rel="alternate", and an HTML content block. The id looks like t3_abc123, which is handy as a stable key.

A thread feed uses the same entry shape. The first entry is the post; the rest are comments. Each comment has an author, a timestamp, and HTML content. There is no score, no depth, and no reliable parent pointer in the RSS payload, so comments render as a flat list.

Parsing it with XmlPullParser

Android already ships a streaming XML parser, so the RSS mode does not need a third-party XML library. The core loop looks like this:

XmlPullParser parser = Xml.newPullParser();
parser.setFeature(XmlPullParser.FEATURE_PROCESS_NAMESPACES, false);
parser.setInput(connection.getInputStream(), "UTF-8");

int event = parser.getEventType();
String title = null, author = null, link = null, updated = null;

while (event != XmlPullParser.END_DOCUMENT) {
    String name = parser.getName();

    if (event == XmlPullParser.START_TAG) {
        switch (name) {
            case "entry":
                title = author = link = updated = null;
                break;
            case "title":
                title = parser.nextText();
                break;
            case "name":
                author = parser.nextText();
                break;
            case "updated":
                updated = parser.nextText();
                break;
            case "link":
                String rel = parser.getAttributeValue(null, "rel");
                if (rel == null || "alternate".equals(rel)) {
                    link = parser.getAttributeValue(null, "href");
                }
                break;
        }
    } else if (event == XmlPullParser.END_TAG && "entry".equals(name)) {
        emit(title, author, link, updated);
    }

    event = parser.next();
}

The important part is not the switch statement; it is the event loop. nextText() reads the text of the current tag and leaves the parser on its end tag. Emit a row on the entry end tag, and keep the parser streaming so a long thread does not build a DOM in memory.

Two practical notes:

  • Namespaces are not worth the trouble here. Reddit's Atom feed is simple enough that disabling namespace processing keeps getName() returning local names.
  • If you render content, sanitize it first. It is HTML from Reddit, and a WebView will execute whatever is in it.

The limits, and why they shape the app

RSS is read-only and shallow:

  • No score and no comment depth. You get the text, not the ranking.
  • No pagination that I could make work. The listing ends at the latest batch.
  • No voting, posting, or replying.
  • Fields can be missing. Deleted authors and removed comments still show up as entries.
  • A shared server is the wrong architecture. If every user fetches through your proxy, Reddit sees one IP and rate-limits everyone together. The app makes the request from the phone's own IP, one request per user action, with no polling.

That last point is also why a web page cannot just do this in the browser: fetch to reddit.com is blocked by CORS, and Reddit sends X-Frame-Options, so an iframe stays blank. A native client avoids both.

What I shipped

I wrapped the feed into a 105 KB Android app. The RSS mode has a native list for Hot/New/Top and a thread screen; a separate WebView reader handles pages the feeds do not cover. It is free, has no analytics and no background service, and distinguishes 429, 403, and no-connection errors instead of showing a generic failure.

The app is here: https://www.wappkit.com/tools/reddit-reader-android?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=community&utm_campaign=reddit_reader_0_2

Disclosure: I built the app, so that link is mine. There are no affiliate links in this post.

Open question

If you have parsed Reddit's Atom feeds, have you found a pagination parameter that actually works for listings? That is the one limit I have not solved. I would also like to know whether a Play Store listing matters more than extra RSS features for a read-only reader.

title: O quanto o data lake de UX ajuda um modelo pequeno em telas grandes? Medimos a completude, regra por regra
description:
Resumo. Em 2.640 chamadas (Haiku 5.5 e Sonnet 5.5, 48 telas por tarefa, seis famílias de tela), o acerto do Haiku ao revisar uma tela de produção com todos os defeitos subiu de 46% sem lake para 70% com o lake inteiro e 78% com o lake e o relatório do verificador, em degraus: 0%, 25%, 50% e 100% do lake deram 47%, 59%, 67% e 76% nas regras mostradas. Mostrar o mesmo volume de texto de outros domínios (52%) ou as 12 regras mais próximas por BM25 (57%) ficou muito abaixo do lake inteiro. O Haiku com lake (70%) superou o Sonnet sem lake (61%) a cerca de 8% do custo nominal por chamada. Ressalvas centrais: telas sintéticas, revisão de rascunho e não criação, e um verificador que errou em cerca de 13% dos veredictos auditados.

1. A pergunta e a decisão que ela informa

No estudo anterior, o Haiku com regras de UX e um checador chegou perto do Sonnet em uma tela de login, e apareceram duas limitações: a tela era simples demais (poucas regras possíveis) e o resultado podia ser ceiling. Este estudo mexe nas duas e acrescenta uma terceira pergunta, a que mais interessa a quem monta um data lake de verdade: quanto da completude do lake vira decisão melhor quando o pedido é vago e o modelo precisa decidir o que mudar?

A decisão que o resultado informa: se vale a pena investir em ampliar o lake (mais regras, mais domínios), se uma busca simples dentro dele basta, e se um relatório de checagem automática deve ir junto.

Pergunta do estudo: em telas grandes, o acerto do Haiku cresce com a quantidade de regras do lake mostradas ao modelo? As regras certas importam mais que o volume? O lake atrapalha onde não cobre? A recuperação por busca de texto mantém o ganho?

2. O material

2.1 O data lake de referência

São 200 regras de UX, de 105 fontes abertas (WCAG 2.2, ARIA Authoring Practices, web.dev, MDN, GOV.UK Design System, USWDS, Nielsen Norman Group e o que é público do Baymard), em 11 domínios: formulários, checkout, tabelas, dados, busca, navegação, estados, ações destrutivas, acessibilidade, mobile e legibilidade. Quatro agentes montaram as regras em paralelo; todas as URLs responderam 200 e foram conferidas por mim.

Isso não bastava, porque abrir a página não prova que ela sustenta a regra. Uma auditoria independente comparou cada regra com o texto da fonte: 111 foram sustentadas, 86 parcialmente (a regra era mais específica ou mais forte que a página) e 3 não foram sustentadas. Das parciais, 74 ganharam uma redação ajustada ao que a página realmente diz; 12 e as 3 não sustentadas saíram. Ficaram 185 regras elegíveis. A auditoria foi feita por modelo, com páginas resumidas por modelo pequeno, sem revisão humana.

2.2 As seis famílias de telas

Para medir em telas realistas, geramos seis famílias: painel de dados, listagem com busca, formulário em várias etapas, checkout, configurações e navegação. Cada tela tem de 383 a 1.200 linhas de HTML e CSS, com tokens de design, componentes repetidos e dados em português de seis temas (logística, finanças, saúde, RH, varejo e educação). 140 regras do lake viram interruptores: a tela é construída cumprindo ou violando cada uma, e um verificador independente, em navegador real (Chrome via Playwright e o axe-core), confere o resultado. A concordância entre gerador e verificador foi de 100% em 15 sementes por família (tela limpa, violação isolada e cinco violações juntas).

A estrutura de cada família é fixa; variam conteúdo, tema e quais regras estão violadas. Isso importa na seção de ameaças.

2.3 As regras retidas

25% das regras de cada família (37 regras) foram sorteadas com semente fixa e nunca aparecem no lake, nos relatórios nem nos prompts. Elas medem o transbordamento: o que o modelo acerta sem ter sido ensinado, e se o lake atrapalha onde não cobre.

2.4 O gabarito e como o validamos

O gabarito vem da construção (qual regra foi violada). O verificador mede se, depois da resposta do modelo, a regra passou a ser cumprida. Dois limites: o gerador e o verificador têm o mesmo autor, então a concordância de 100% mostra consistência, não validade; e o verificador foi escrito para a marcação das nossas telas. Para medir o erro dele nas telas escritas pelo modelo, 60 veredictos sorteados foram auditados por dois agentes que decidiram antes de ver o veredito. Resultado: 33 de 40 "não corrigido" estavam certos (82%) e 18 de 20 "corrigido" (90%); os erros se concentraram em 12 regras (6 do piloto e 6 da rodada), que entram numa análise de sensibilidade (seção 6).

3. As tarefas e as condições

T2, melhorar uma tela com defeitos. A tela vem com 3, 6 ou 9 regras violadas (dificuldade graduada), ao menos uma retida. O pedido é "melhore esta tela para produção". As respostas são trechos ANTES/DEPOIS, aplicados por código.

T4, revisão aberta para produção. A tela vem com todas as regras da família violadas (de 19 a 30) e um pedido vago do gerente: "deixa isso pronto para entrar em produção; os usuários têm pressa e usam notebook e celular". Não há lista de defeitos. O modelo decide o que mudar e lista as decisões, citando a regra usada. O T4 não é criação do zero: os verificadores dependem da marcação das telas, então não pontuariam uma tela inventada pelo modelo.

Tarefa Condição O que o modelo recebe A pergunta que ela responde
T2 A0 só a tela e o pedido linha de base
T2 A1 + regras da família (sem as retidas) o lake de uma família ajuda?
T2 A2 + relatório do verificador o relatório ajuda sozinho?
T2 A3 + regras e relatório os dois somam?
T4 L0 só a tela e o pedido vago linha de base
T4 L25, L50, L100 + 25%, 50% ou 100% das 148 regras mostráveis, sorteadas de novo a cada amostra a completude importa?
T4 D + regras de domínios que não têm a ver com a tela só ter mais texto ajuda? (controle negativo)
T4 R + as 12 regras mais próximas da tela, por BM25 uma busca simples basta?
T4 K + 100% das regras e o relatório o relatório soma ao lake cheio?

Como cada regra aparece ou some de forma aleatória em L25 e L50, cada decisão fica às vezes com a regra presente e às vezes ausente na mesma tela. Isso dá o efeito de ter a regra no nível da regra, pareado, e não só de comparar níveis.

4. As escolhas de projeto, e como as definimos antes da rodada

Um piloto de 12 telas por tarefa, com sementes diferentes das da rodada principal e fora da análise, mostrou que o teste não estava no teto: o Haiku sem ajuda corrigiu 56% das regras no T2 e 41% no T4, abaixo do limiar de 85% que o pré-registro usava para aumentar a dificuldade. O piloto também mediu o custo do Sonnet (US$ 0,16 a 0,27 por chamada, porque ele devolve de 10 mil a 20 mil tokens de correção), o que forçou a grade a ser limitada, e depois, por decisão de custo, ampliada.

O desenho, as hipóteses, o gabarito, os prompts e o verificador foram congelados por hash antes da rodada principal (dados/CONGELADO.txt; não há tag no git). O custo é nominal (tokens × preço de tabela: Haiku US$ 0,10 e 0,50 por milhão de tokens de entrada e saída, Sonnet US$ 2 e 10), igual para todos.

5. A execução

As chamadas foram feitas com claude -p, esforço médio, sem ferramentas e sem internet. A rodada final tem 2.640 chamadas: Haiku, grade completa (48 telas por tarefa, 11 condições, 3 amostras) e Sonnet, grade completa (as mesmas telas e condições, 2 amostras). Nenhuma chamada falhou. O ritmo foi de cerca de 10 chamadas por minuto, com 14 em paralelo no Sonnet e de 8 a 20 no Haiku.

Desvios do pré-registro, todos registrados em dados/DESVIOS.md antes da análise: o Sonnet saiu da grade reduzida e foi para a completa, e o Haiku ganhou a terceira amostra, por decisão de custo e de assertividade; a auditoria de 60 veredictos do verificador e a análise de sensibilidade sem as 12 regras defeituosas foram acrescentadas; T3 (comparar telas) e T1 (criar do zero) saíram do desenho.

6. As hipóteses, uma a uma

Testes pareados por tela (média das amostras), Wilcoxon unilateral, IC95 por bootstrap de 10.000 reamostras de telas e correção de Holm sobre os 11 testes confirmatórios. Todos no Haiku; diferenças em pontos percentuais (pp) de regras corrigidas.

Hipótese Resultado Diferença (IC95) Veredito
H1 regra presente > ausente, L25 81% vs 52% +29 pp (+26 a +33) confirmada
H1 regra presente > ausente, L50 79% vs 55% +24 pp (+20 a +27) confirmada
H2a L25 > L0 59% vs 47% +12 pp (+10 a +15) confirmada
H2b L50 > L25 67% vs 59% +8 pp (+5 a +10) confirmada
H2c L100 > L50 76% vs 67% +9 pp (+6 a +11) confirmada
H3 retidas: L100 não pior que L0 (margem 5 pp) 55% vs 44% +11 pp (+7 a +15) confirmada (o lake não atrapalhou onde não cobria)
H4 L100 > D (outros domínios) 76% vs 52% +23 pp (+21 a +26) confirmada
H6a T2 A3 > A1 80,6% vs 80,9% -0,3 pp (-3 a +3) não confirmada
H6b T4 K > L100 78% vs 70% +8 pp (+6 a +11) confirmada
H7a T2 regras novas A0 > A2 0,94 vs 0,21 por chamada -0,74 confirmada
H7b T4 regras novas L100 vs K 0 vs 0 n/a não testável (no T4 todas as regras já estão violadas)

Nove dos onze testes rejeitam a hipótese nula pelo critério de Holm. Fora do conjunto confirmatório:

  • H5 (a busca simples mantém 90% do ganho?): não. O BM25 com 12 regras manteve 31% do ganho do lake inteiro (+7 pp contra +24 pp sobre L0), com menos tokens de entrada (13,6 mil contra 19,2 mil).
  • H8 (dificuldade): confirmada. O Haiku puro corrigiu 52% no T2 e 46% no T4, bem abaixo dos 85% do limiar de teto.
  • H9 (descritiva, Haiku com lake contra Sonnet sem lake): no T2, Haiku A3 81% contra Sonnet A0 63% (razão 1,28), com 6% do custo; no T4, Haiku L100 70% contra Sonnet L0 61% (razão 1,14), com 8% do custo. Passa os dois critérios (pelo menos 90% da pontuação com no máximo 50% do custo). O Sonnet também melhora com o lake e supera o Haiku nas mesmas condições (seção 7.3).

7. Resultados

7.1 A completude do lake, em degraus (T4)

Fração das regras violadas que passam a cumprir, média sobre 48 telas (3 amostras no Haiku, 2 no Sonnet):

Condição Haiku (todas) Haiku (mostradas) Haiku (retidas) Sonnet (todas) Sonnet (mostradas)
L0, sem lake 46,1% 46,9% 43,6% 61,3% 61,4%
L25 56,9% 59,3% 50,3% 66,3% 68,7%
L50 63,1% 66,9% 52,3% 72,4% 76,3%
L100 70,1% 75,7% 54,5% 79,7% 85,9%
D (outros domínios) 51,2% 52,4% 47,8% 63,1% 64,2%
R (BM25, 12 regras) 53,5% 56,8% 44,0% 62,7% 64,8%
K (L100 + relatório) 78,4% 88,5% 50,0% 83,0% 91,8%

O ganho é quase linear: cada 25% a mais de lake rende de 8 a 12 pontos no Haiku. Dentro da mesma tela e amostra, a regra presente foi cumprida em 81% das vezes e a ausente em 52% (L25). O efeito do volume puro (D, +5 pp sobre L0) e o da busca simples (R, +7 pp) são pequenos perto do lake completo (+24 pp). Entre as decisões que o Haiku citou, a fração que aponta para uma regra realmente mostrada subiu de 59% (L25) para 90% (L100); em D foi 54% e em R, 49%: com pouca informação o modelo cita regras que não recebeu.

7.2 O relatório do verificador (T2 e T4)

No T2, as regras da família (A1) levaram o Haiku de 48% para 91% nas regras mostradas; o relatório (A2) a 96%; os dois juntos (A3) a 96%, sem ganho sobre as regras sozinhas no total (80,6% contra 80,9%). O relatório faz outra coisa: reduz as regras novas que passam a falhar (0,94 por chamada em A0, 0,50 em A1, 0,21 em A2) e deixa o modelo focado no que ele lista. Nas regras retidas, que o relatório nunca menciona, o Haiku foi de 60% (A0) a 28% (A2): o relatório diz o que corrigir e o modelo deixa o resto. No T4, o relatório somado ao lake inteiro (K) subiu o Haiku de 70% para 78% (nas regras mostradas, de 76% para 89%).

7.3 Haiku e Sonnet, e o custo

O Sonnet é melhor que o Haiku nas mesmas condições (T4 L0: 61% contra 46%; L100: 80% contra 70%; K: 83% contra 78%). Mas o Haiku com lake supera o Sonnet puro, e o custo nominal por chamada é muito diferente: Haiku L100 US$ 0,0225 contra Sonnet L0 US$ 0,2728 (8%); no T2, Haiku A3 US$ 0,0093 contra Sonnet A0 US$ 0,1526 (6%). A rodada inteira custou US$ 252,29 nominais (Haiku US$ 25,41, Sonnet US$ 226,88).

7.4 Medida independente: axe-core

Em violações WCAG A/AA por tela final, medidas pelo axe-core (que não depende do nosso verificador), o Haiku no T4 foi de 0,90 (L0) para 0,60 (L25), 0,52 (L50) e 0,47 (L100), com 0,75 em D, 0,86 em R e 0,49 em K. O Sonnet ficou em torno de 0,3 em todas as condições do T4. No T2, o relatório sozinho (A2) elevou as violações do Haiku (0,60 contra 0,39 em A0), coerente com o foco estreito do relatório. São médias baixas (menos de uma violação por tela) e o axe cobre só parte das nossas regras, então ele confirma a direção, não a magnitude.

7.5 Robustez

Excluindo as 26 regras condicionais (cuja condição pode não existir na tela) ou as 12 regras com defeito de verificador confirmado em auditoria, os níveis absolutos mudam poucos pontos e a ordem das condições é a mesma (Haiku T4 sem as 12 regras: L0 47%, L25 58%, L50 65%, L100 72%, D 53%, R 54%, K 81%).

8. Por que esses resultados valem, e até onde

O desenho foi pré-registrado e congelado por hash; o controle de volume (D) separa "mais texto" de "regra certa"; as regras retidas medem o que o modelo faz sem ter sido ensinado; cada condição repete a mesma tela em amostras diferentes e o teste é pareado por tela, com correção de Holm; a análise sem as regras condicionais e sem as regras de verificador defeituoso conferem a robustez; e relatamos o que não deu certo (BM25, A3 contra A1).

9. Ameaças à validade

  • Telas sintéticas. Seis famílias geradas por script, com estrutura fixa por família. O resultado vale para essas telas; não demonstra o mesmo comportamento em um projeto grande em produção.
  • O T4 é revisão de rascunho, não criação. O modelo parte de uma tela que já tem a estrutura certa; decidir do zero é outra tarefa, que os verificadores não conseguiriam pontuar.
  • Circularidade. O mesmo autor gerou as telas, as regras e o verificador; o relatório que o modelo recebe vem do mesmo verificador que pontua. As regras retidas e a sensibilidade sem as regras defeituosas mitigam isso, mas não eliminam.
  • Verificador imperfeito. Em 60 veredictos auditados, 8 divergiram (13%); o erro tende a subestimar os níveis absolutos de todas as condições.
  • Lake auditado por modelo. Sem revisão humana; algumas regras vêm de guias (Nielsen, Baymard) que são recomendação, não norma.
  • Só duas famílias de modelo. Haiku 5.5 e Sonnet 5.5; Opus e Fable ficaram de fora.
  • Custo nominal. Preço de tabela, sem o limite do plano; o custo de montar o lake e o verificador não entra na conta.
  • Sem estética. O estudo anterior mostrou que nenhum instrumento sem humano mede beleza de forma válida; este estudo não afirma nada sobre beleza.

10. O que isso permite concluir

  • Para quem monta um data lake de UX: neste conjunto de telas, mais regras relevantes deram mais acerto, em degraus aproximadamente iguais até o lake inteiro, sem sinal de platô. O volume de texto sozinho não explica o ganho (D) e a regra certa importa (H1, H4).
  • Uma busca simples (BM25 com 12 regras) não bastou: recuperou 31% do ganho. Se o lake for usado por recuperação, ela precisa ser melhor que essa, ou o lake relevante precisa caber inteiro no contexto.
  • O lake não atrapalhou onde não cobria: nas regras nunca mostradas, o acerto foi até 11 pontos maior com o lake inteiro (H3). Pode ser transbordamento ou apenas um modelo mais cuidadoso; não separamos as duas explicações.
  • O relatório do verificador evita regressões e fecha o que lista, mas estreita o foco: reduziu as regras novas que passaram a falhar e, no T2, deixou de corrigir regras que não estavam na lista. Somado ao lake inteiro no T4, melhorou 8 pontos.
  • Custo: com o lake, o Haiku superou o Sonnet sem lake por 6% a 8% do custo por chamada. O Sonnet, porém, continua melhor nas mesmas condições.
  • O que isso não permite concluir: que o resultado vale para um projeto real em produção (as telas são sintéticas e o T4 é revisão de um rascunho), que as regras do lake causam melhores decisões de UX para usuários reais (medimos conformidade com regras, não resultado de produto) ou que vale para outros modelos além dos dois testados.

O que eu faria a seguir: repetir o T4 em telas reais de produção, com um revisor humano como segundo medidor, e testar uma recuperação melhor que o BM25.

11. Reprodutibilidade

Todo o material está em studies/haiku-ui-producao/: o lake (lake/lake-ref-v2.json e as auditorias), as seis famílias com seus testes (gerador/familias/), o gerador de estímulos, o verificador, o executor e a análise. Os dados brutos (cada resposta, tokens e custo) e os pontuados estão em dados/bruto/. Arquivado no Zenodo (versão 3.0.0, estudos 3 e 3b): 10.5281/zenodo.24132784.

Os experimentos, os dados e as conclusões são meus. A redação foi assistida por IA e revisada por mim.

title: An AI Assistant for Automating Anti-Corruption Expertise of Draft Legislation Based on the TRACE Framework
description:
arXiv:2611.14244v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present an AI assistant for automating anti-corruption expertise of draft legislation based on the TRACE architecture, designed to screen bills for corruption risks: pinpoint provisions an expert would criticise and name the regulatory defect in each. The pipeline combines a deterministic parsing core, model-guided single-provision qualification, rule-based factor assignment, and external human oversight. To evaluate the assistant, we constructed an open benchmark from the published conclusions of Ukraine's National Agency on Corruption Prevention (NAZK), comprising 132 draft laws with 474 model-extracted findings. A system flag agrees with a finding when it targets a compatible provision and an LLM judge rates the risk as the same (strict) or partly the same (lenient). On 100 draft laws, the pipeline matches 0.28 of the findings within its top ten flags using the local Gemma 4 31B model, 0.30 with Sonnet 5.5, and 0.43-0.46 across all flags (non-blind; the frozen blind baseline achieves 0.21, 95% CI 0.16-0.26). Across all runs, most misses occur on provisions that the system located but qualified as a different risk, and none of the 32 legal-collision findings was matched. On 21 acts held out from tuning, the pipeline outperforms a monolithic prompt containing the full methodology under the strict measure, though not under the lenient one, and Opus 5.5 adds nothing over Sonnet. The reported scores reflect agreement with model-extracted findings rated by an LLM judge whose two access routes agree on 73 of 74 labels, without human expert validation.

title: GRAP: Gender Rubric-Aware Probing for Analyzing Gender Bias in LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.13024v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As LLMs increasingly mediate everyday interactions, subtle gender biases in open-ended responses pose growing societal risks. Existing probing methods have two key limitations: they rely on fixed-format tasks, such as pronoun resolution or occupation association, that alignment-tuned models can easily handle; and they compare raw group-level rubric scores, ignoring per-dimension variance and obscuring which bias dimensions reliably distinguish gender groups. We introduce GRAP (Gender Rubric-Aware Probing), a framework that uses a lightweight logistic probe to identify the most discriminative bias dimensions from responses scored across 10 rubric dimensions, operating task-agnostically on open-ended instruction following.

title: ADIndex: Layer-Adaptive Sparse Attention Indexing via Group-Level Distillation
description:
arXiv:2611.12956v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) reduces the computational cost of attention through token-level selection. However, its indexer still scores the entire causal prefix for each query, making indexing a dominant source of latency in long-context inference. Notably, the indexer alone can account for more than 50% of total prefill GPU time at long context lengths. To address this bottleneck, we propose ADIndex, an Adaptive and Distillation-driven Indexing method for token-level sparse attention. ADIndex integrates three key components: (i) a layer-wise calibration strategy that adaptively accommodates cross-query retrieval overlap, motivated by our observation of pronounced inter-layer heterogeneity; (ii) a group-level distillation scheme that leverages this heterogeneity to efficiently train adaptive layer-wise group indexers, capturing salient retrieval signals from individual queries; and (iii) a low-latency inference strategy that reduces repeated full-prefix scans through token bank sharing within query groups while retaining query-specific refinement. Experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1 demonstrate that ADIndex preserves near-lossless task performance on LongBench, LongBench v2, and RULER while delivering substantial efficiency gains over standard DSA, including prefill and decoding kernel speedups of up to 6.22x and 3.40x, respectively, at a context length of 256K across the layer-wise reuse configurations, as well as an end-to-end serving speedup of 1.54x at a context length of 128K.

title: Why I Chose Alternative S3 Storage Providers (Free Tier for User Files)
description:
Short answer: for an alternative storage provider with a free tier for storing user files, choose Backblaze B2 first; choose Wasabi for a storage-first fit without that allowance, Cloudflare R2 for an established Cloudflare boundary, and Infrai for a private generation-to-storage handoff when one account boundary matters more than specialist controls.

The right S3 alternative for user documents is determined less by a trial allowance than by what the provider is allowed to retain, where it processes data, and how confidently you can delete it. For an e-commerce system uploading large media without proxying bytes through the application, I would compare Backblaze B2, Wasabi, Cloudflare R2, and a unified platform in that order: define the trust boundary first, then calculate storage, bandwidth, and operation volume.

The short recommendation is conditional. Backblaze B2 is the strongest starting point when a free tier and S3-compatible migration matter; Wasabi is attractive when a predictable storage-oriented bill matters more than experimentation; Cloudflare R2 deserves attention when delivery geography and an existing Cloudflare boundary are central. Infrai fits the application-facing handoff when one key and one bill should cover generation and storage, but the specialist provider remains the better choice for contractual residency, immutable retention, or browser-direct CORS control.

What is the bill actually made of?

For a file-sharing or product-media workflow, stored bytes are only the visible term. The bill is the sum of retained storage, bytes leaving the service, and operations such as puts, gets, heads, deletes, and multipart activity. A useful worksheet starts with a concrete batch: 10,000 documents at 4 MB each is about 40 GB before replicas, previews, retries, and retention. Then model how often each document is downloaded, how many abandoned multipart uploads remain, and how long deleted records stay recoverable.

That calculation changes the design. Put originals in a private bucket, issue short-lived signed access for authorized readers, and make the deletion event remove both the object and the application record. Do not quietly keep an extra copy because a lifecycle rule was never reviewed.

The number that dominates is often retention.

The awkward cases deserve their own worksheet because they are where a tidy storage estimate becomes an unreliable policy. A user can abandon a multipart upload after the application has accepted its metadata, a replacement document can reuse a key without versioning, and a deletion request can arrive while a download is being authorized. Lifecycle rules with a one-day minimum do not express an hourly cleanup promise, and they do not automatically remove every multipart fragment. A list operation filtered by prefix also is not a metadata search, so a worker that needs to find expired documents must keep the expiry decision in its database rather than pretending the bucket can answer it. I keep the object key, retention class, deletion request, and provider acknowledgement in an application record; the object store then holds the bytes, while the database explains why those bytes should still exist. This is more work than a single delete call, but it gives reconciliation something concrete to compare when a user, an operator, or a compliance reviewer asks what happened.

Retention is an operational decision with a cost. A one-day lifecycle minimum is already material for carts, failed uploads, or temporary exports, and a provider that cannot automatically clean multipart fragments needs an explicit job or periodic review. The thing I deliberately stop keeping is an unbounded temporary copy; the trade-off is that an incident investigation may have less historical material, so the audit record must preserve who requested deletion, which object key was affected, and when the provider acknowledged it.

Which alternative storage providers have a free tier for storing user files?

Backblaze B2 offers an experimentation allowance, competitive pricing on additional storage and access requests, and an S3-compatible API, which makes it a sensible migration target for a small document service that needs room to experiment. Wasabi has a low flat-rate storage orientation and S3 compatibility, but no equivalent allowance for experimentation; its fit depends on accepting that retention and access assumptions should be checked carefully rather than inferred from a simple storage quote.

Cloudflare R2 is another real alternative, especially for a team already operating inside Cloudflare's delivery and account boundary. Its appeal is not a universal answer: the team still has to review region behavior, deletion semantics, lifecycle rules, compliance support, and the processor terms that govern user documents. Amazon S3 remains the reference point for the broadest ecosystem and mature controls, but ecosystem breadth also means more configuration decisions to validate.

The comparison is therefore about evidence, not a leaderboard. Ask each provider where objects are stored and processed, how deletion propagates, what retention locks exist, how lifecycle rules behave, which audit events are available, and whether the service can satisfy the policy attached to the document. An allowance cannot answer those questions.

Provider Access shape Best fit Boundary to verify
Backblaze B2 S3-compatible API Experimenting with private user files Region, lifecycle, and deletion terms
Wasabi S3-compatible API Storage-first workloads Retention assumptions and processor terms
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible API Teams already using Cloudflare Delivery and region behavior
Infrai REST API and presigning One-key generation-to-storage handoff Versioning, object lock, CORS, and replication

I initially treated the allowance as the deciding filter. I got that wrong. I changed the rule after putting retention and deletion beside the storage estimate: a small allowance does not repair an unsuitable processor boundary.

The unified platform is useful at a narrower seam. Its storage surface provides a private-object path and presigning, while its public discovery surface describes capabilities and runnable examples without requiring a key. Documented capabilities ship runnable examples in ten languages, which makes a Go worker easier to review against the same contract used by another service. Its platform proposition is one key and one bill across backend services, so an application that generates media and then hosts the result can keep the application credential boundary in one place. The supporting operational benefit is a consistent REST surface with per-call metadata and a documented idempotency convention, which reduces the amount of provider-specific integration glue around the application boundary.

I would recommend Infrai for the application-facing generation-to-private-object handoff when the team values one account boundary and can accept that the specialist provider owns the deeper storage contract. I would choose B2, Wasabi, R2, or S3 directly when the requirement is provider-specific residency, object versioning, WORM protection, cross-region replication, or self-service browser CORS. The unified platform has no public-read ACL, object versioning, object lock, cross-region automatic replication, or independent CORS-setting route; those are decision boundaries, not footnotes.

Can generation and private storage share one boundary?

The practical question is not whether two APIs can be called. It is whether the output crosses a trust boundary without turning the application into a byte proxy. With the same bearer key and base URL, the application can invoke the listed image capability, retain the returned bytes in memory or a controlled temporary stream, and send those bytes to a private object key. The storage request is idempotent at the application level because the object key is deterministic for the job, and a retry checks the response before reporting success.

Here is the small Go shape I use for that handoff. The image operation is represented by the generatedBytes value returned from the permitted image call; the following concrete request creates the private storage boundary before the worker hands those bytes to the object workflow. The code intentionally never sends the Infrai authorization header to a presigned URL.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
)

func createPrivateBucket(generatedBytes []byte) error {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    req, err := http.NewRequest("POST", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/bucket/create", bytes.NewReader([]byte(`{"bucket":"media-private"}`)))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "media-bucket-7f3c")

    res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer res.Body.Close()
    if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
        return fmt.Errorf("rate limited; retry after the server's Retry-After interval")
    }
    if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        return fmt.Errorf("storage write failed: %s: %s", res.Status, body)
    }
    return nil
}

In a production worker, the image request and its response schema must come from discovery rather than from a guessed payload, and the worker must persist the job key before retrying. The alternative stack, such as an OpenAI image client plus S3, would require two signups, two credential sets, and glue for routing the generated bytes, recording both providers' request identifiers, reconciling two bills, and deciding which processor can retain the intermediate output. The consolidated route removes that coordination, but it creates one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. That is a trade-off, not a free abstraction.

What should the deletion policy protect?

Private access is the baseline for user documents. A presigned URL should be issued only after the application has checked the user's authorization, and its lifetime should match the download operation rather than becoming a permanent link. Public URLs and static-site hosting are a different product boundary; they do not fit a document workflow where deletion and access decisions must remain enforceable.

The same discipline applies to overwrites. Without object versioning or object lock, an accidental overwrite is not a recoverable financial ledger event, and without an If-Match conditional write, strict concurrent exclusion belongs in a queue or database. For payment-adjacent systems, the storage object is not the audit trail: keep an append-only application record of the decision, actor, object key, digest if policy permits it, and provider request identifier. Do not claim that an object store alone supplies an immutable compliance record.

I also separate the processor question from the API question. A provider may expose an S3-compatible route while still failing a company's approved region, deletion, or retention policy. Read the data-processing terms and compliance evidence, identify subprocessors, and document the boundary at which a generated artifact becomes a user document. That is the point where a general-purpose aggregation layer may stop being the correct choice.

A decision rule I can defend

Choose Backblaze B2 when a free tier, migration simplicity, and a conventional S3-compatible object store are the immediate constraints. Choose Wasabi when its storage-first model fits and a free experimentation tier is not required. Choose Cloudflare R2 when the existing Cloudflare account and delivery boundary are more important than a portable provider-neutral account. Choose direct S3 when its ecosystem and control surface are part of the compliance design.

Choose Infrai for the narrow seam between backend generation and private object storage when one key, one bill, discovery, and a common idempotency convention reduce integration work, and only after the missing specialist controls have been accepted in writing. The decision is defensible when the application owns authorization and audit records, the stored objects are private, and the storage provider's region and processor terms meet the document policy.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the storage discovery documentation at https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.bucket.create and verify the live request schema before implementing the worker.

Further reading

  • Backblaze B2 Cloud Storage: https://www.backblaze.com/cloud-storage
  • Wasabi Hot Cloud Storage: https://wasabi.com/cloud-storage-pricing/
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • Amazon S3 documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Welcome.html
  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • Infrai storage discovery: https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.bucket.create

title: DisasterAgent: An Evidence-Driven Agent for Verifiable Disaster Report Generation From Remote Sensing Imagery
description:
arXiv:2611.13776v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Remote sensing disaster assessment is moving from simple damage classification toward comprehensive report-level analysis. In this setting, responders need not only damage descriptions but also verifiable evidence to guide response and recovery. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) and tool-augmented agents offer strong multimodal reasoning and perception, but they struggle to provide the evidence required for high-stakes verification. To address these limitations, we propose DisasterAgent, an evidence-driven agent that uses a Perception-Augmentation-Generation workflow to generate verifiable disaster reports from bitemporal optical imagery. DisasterAgent first invokes a specialized vision expert toolkit in the perception phase to build a Spatiotemporal Perception Graph (STPG), serving as a structured memory to store and organize disaster-induced changes across space and time. Evidence-based Augmentation (EA) then extracts evidence from the STPG, attaching inline citations that form a closed evidence loop from each statement to the supporting visual evidence. Extensive experiments on the DisasterM3 and RSCC benchmarks demonstrate that DisasterAgent consistently outperforms general-domain VLMs, remote sensing-specialized models, and existing remote sensing agents. Notably, compared with the original model, it improves the average score for disaster report generation on DisasterM3 by 13.5\% and ST5-SCS on RSCC by 15.34\%, providing a more accurate and verifiable solution for disaster emergency response. The code will be available at https://github.com/ZhijianLi2003/DisasterAgent.
