title: Do AI Agents need Preventive Care? An Epidemiologic Cohort Design for Agentic AI
description:
arXiv:2611.13333v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As AI agents increasingly perform tasks autonomously across sectors, including healthcare and biomedical research, understanding how their behaviors develop and influence outcomes over time becomes increasingly important. Existing evaluations largely focus on model capabilities and performance on predefined tasks. Here, we propose an epidemiologic cohort design for studying agentic AI, drawing on principles established in human population studies. The framework treats individual agents as members of a cohort, their underlying model as genetic makeup, accumulated work as their time scale, and naturally occurring behaviors as exposures that may influence subsequent outcomes. By following agents longitudinally, this approach enables investigation of behavioral determinants of adverse events, estimation of their potential preventable burden under causal assumptions, and characterization of behavioral changes over an agent's work life. We illustrate the design through two prospective observational cohorts examining curiosity and probing as a safety question, and data checking and analytical accuracy as a reliability question. Together, the framework and illustrative studies provide a generalizable blueprint for designing epidemiologic cohorts of AI agents.

title: I Broke My Own Firestore Rules in Production Once. Now the Emulator Catches It First.
description:
The deploy that taught me the lesson

I changed one line in my Firestore security rules. It looked safe — I was tightening a read rule on a collection so only the owning tenant could read its documents. I deployed it, moved on, and found out later that a legitimate read path had started failing. Nothing dramatic broke in a way that paged me. It just quietly stopped working for a real user flow, and I only caught it because I happened to test that flow by hand afterward.

That is the worst kind of bug: a security change that fails closed in the wrong place, silently, with no test to catch it. I had unit tests for my API. I had tests for my scoring logic. I had no tests for the rules that decide who can read and write my data. The rules were the one layer I was editing by feel and verifying by hope.

So I fixed it the boring way: I put my Firestore rules under test in CI, using the Firebase Emulator Suite, and made the deploy pipeline refuse to ship rules that fail those tests. This is the setup I run now, what it caught, and where it still has gaps.

Why rules deserve tests like code

Firestore security rules look like configuration, but they are authorization logic. A single allow read: if line is an access-control decision, and access-control decisions are exactly the kind of thing that should never ship untested. Three properties of rules make this worse than ordinary code:

  1. They fail silently in production. A wrong rule does not throw an exception in your logs. It returns a permission-denied to a client, and unless you are watching for that specific error, you find out from a user.
  2. They are easy to get subtly wrong. request.auth != null is not the same as "this user owns this document." resource.data.tenantId == request.auth.token.tenantId only works if the custom claim is actually set, and if the claim is missing the comparison fails in a direction you need to think about — does it fail open or fail closed?
  3. They change with the data model. Add a field, rename a collection, change how tenancy is represented, and a rule that was correct last month is wrong now. The rule file and the app code drift apart unless something checks them together.

My stack is Firebase Auth with custom claims for tenancy, a FastAPI backend that enforces the same tenant check in middleware, and Firestore as the store. The backend middleware is tested. The rules were not. That asymmetry was the bug.

The setup: emulator + rules unit tests

The Firebase Emulator Suite ships a rules testing library, @firebase/rules-unit-testing, that lets you spin up a Firestore emulator, load your rules file, and make reads and writes as authenticated or unauthenticated users with specific claims. The tests run in Node, against the emulator — no production project involved, no real data at risk.

First, the rules file itself. Here is a simplified version of the shape I test — a multi-tenant collection where each document carries a tenantId, and access requires a matching custom claim:

rules_version = '2';
service cloud.firestore {
  match /databases/{database}/documents {
    match /readinessReports/{reportId} {
      allow read: if isSignedIn()
        && request.auth.token.tenantId == resource.data.tenantId;
      allow create: if isSignedIn()
        && request.auth.token.tenantId == request.resource.data.tenantId;
      allow update, delete: if false;
    }
    function isSignedIn() {
      return request.auth != null;
    }
  }
}

Two deliberate choices in there. Updates and deletes are denied outright — reports are append-only, and any correction goes through a new report, so the rules enforce that invariant rather than trusting the client. And the tenant check reads the claim from the token, not from a field the client supplies — a client can claim anything in a request body, but it cannot forge a custom claim.

Then the test file. The pattern is: initialize the emulator with the rules, create an authenticated context with a given set of claims, and assert that the operations you expect to succeed do, and the ones you expect to fail do:

import { initializeTestEnvironment, assertSucceeds, assertFails } from "@firebase/rules-unit-testing";
import { doc, getDoc, setDoc } from "firebase/firestore";
import { readFileSync } from "fs";

let testEnv;

beforeAll(async () => {
  testEnv = await initializeTestEnvironment({
    projectId: "rules-test-project",
    firestore: {
      rules: readFileSync("firestore.rules", "utf8"),
      host: "127.0.0.1",
      port: 8080,
    },
  });
});

afterAll(async () => { await testEnv.cleanup(); });
beforeEach(async () => { await testEnv.clearFirestore(); });

test("owner tenant can read its own report", async () => {
  const alice = testEnv.authenticatedContext("alice", { tenantId: "tenant-a" });
  await testEnv.withSecurityRulesDisabled(async (ctx) => {
    await setDoc(doc(ctx.firestore(), "readinessReports/r1"),
      { tenantId: "tenant-a", status: "READY" });
  });
  await assertSucceeds(getDoc(doc(alice.firestore(), "readinessReports/r1")));
});

test("other tenant cannot read it", async () => {
  const bob = testEnv.authenticatedContext("bob", { tenantId: "tenant-b" });
  await testEnv.withSecurityRulesDisabled(async (ctx) => {
    await setDoc(doc(ctx.firestore(), "readinessReports/r1"),
      { tenantId: "tenant-a", status: "READY" });
  });
  await assertFails(getDoc(doc(bob.firestore(), "readinessReports/r1")));
});

test("unauthenticated reads fail", async () => {
  const anon = testEnv.unauthenticatedContext();
  await assertFails(getDoc(doc(anon.firestore(), "readinessReports/r1")));
});

test("a user with no tenant claim cannot read anything", async () => {
  const noClaim = testEnv.authenticatedContext("mallory", {});
  await assertFails(getDoc(doc(noClaim.firestore(), "readinessReports/r1")));
});

The last test is the one I care most about. A user who is authenticated but has no tenantId claim is the exact case that fails in a confusing direction if you write the rule carelessly: request.auth.token.tenantId is null, the comparison is false, and the read is denied. That is fail-closed, which is what I want — but I want it fail-closed because I tested it, not because I assumed it. The test pins the behavior down so a future rule edit cannot quietly flip it. Fixtures are seeded with rules disabled, so test setup never depends on the rules being correct — a broken rule cannot make a test pass vacuously by failing to create the fixture.

Wiring it into CI

Tests that only run on my laptop are a suggestion. The rules tests run in CI on every pull request that touches firestore.rules, the test file, or the Firebase config. The CI job is small:

- name: Install Firebase CLI
  run: npm install -g firebase-tools
- name: Install dependencies
  run: npm ci
- name: Start emulators and run rules tests
  run: firebase emulators:exec --only firestore "npm run test:rules"

firebase emulators:exec starts the emulator, runs the command, and shuts it down — no background-process juggling in CI, no port left listening. The job takes well under a minute for my rule set, which is the whole reason there is no excuse for skipping it.

The second half of the wiring is the deploy gate. The deploy step for Firestore rules runs only if the rules tests passed in the same pipeline. It is easy to end up with a deploy script that runs firebase deploy --only firestore:rules from a laptop on a Friday afternoon, bypassing CI entirely. I removed that path: rules deploy from CI only, on merge to main, after the tests pass.

What it has actually caught

Since I set this up, the tests have caught three kinds of mistakes, all of them mine:

  • A claim propagation assumption. I added a new collection and wrote its rule assuming the custom claim would be present on every authenticated user. The no-claim test failed, because a freshly registered user does not get the claim until a backend step assigns it. The rule was correct; my mental model of when claims exist was wrong. I fixed the onboarding flow, not the rule — and I only knew which one was wrong because the test isolated the rule.
  • A write-path tenant check I forgot. I added a create rule that checked the claim against the document being created, then refactored the data model so the tenant lived on a parent document instead. The create test started failing because request.resource.data.tenantId no longer existed on the new document shape. The old rule would have denied every legitimate create — fail-closed, but broken for real users.
  • An over-broad read I introduced while debugging. I temporarily loosened a read rule to allow read: if request.auth != null while chasing a different bug, intending to tighten it back. The cross-tenant test failed immediately in CI. Without the test, that line could have shipped and stayed.

None of these were exotic. All three were the kind of edit you make quickly, confidently, and wrong.

Where the setup still has gaps

Honesty requires saying what this does not cover.

First, rules tests verify the rules, not the backend. My FastAPI middleware does its own tenant check, and the rules and the middleware can disagree. I test them separately, and I do not have a single test that exercises the full path through the API to Firestore with the rules loaded. That end-to-end check is the next thing to build.

Second, the emulator is not production. The rules language is the same, but emulator behavior around edge cases — timestamps, request.time, certain functions — can differ subtly from production evaluation. The tests catch logic errors, not platform quirks. A staging deploy with a smoke test of the real read paths is still necessary.

Third, custom claims take time to propagate. A claim set by the backend is not instantly visible in every token — the user needs a token refresh. My tests use contexts with claims already set, so they never exercise the propagation delay. In production, a user who was just assigned to a tenant can hit a permission-denied until their token refreshes, and that looks identical to a rules bug. I handle it by forcing a token refresh after tenant assignment, but the test suite does not prove that path works.

The pattern is still worth it. It moved Firestore rules from "edited by feel" to "changed with a failing test first," the standard I already held everywhere else in the codebase. The rules were the exception because they looked like config. They are not config. They are the authorization boundary for the data, and they deserve the same discipline as any other security code.

Takeaways

  • Firestore rules are authorization logic. Test them like code, not like config.
  • Use the Firebase Emulator Suite and @firebase/rules-unit-testing: seed fixtures with rules disabled, then assert both the allows and the denies.
  • Always test the cross-tenant deny, the unauthenticated deny, and the authenticated-but-no-claim case — that last one pins down fail-closed behavior.
  • Run rules tests in CI on every change to the rules, and deploy rules from CI only, after the tests pass.
  • Expect the tests to catch your own wrong assumptions, not just typos — the claim-propagation mistake was a wrong mental model, and only the test showed it.
  • Know the gaps: rules tests do not cover backend middleware agreement, emulator-versus-production quirks, or claim propagation delay. Test those paths separately.

title: An Interpretable Stylometric Framework for Early Chinese Buddhist Translator Styles: A Case Study on the Attribution of Disputed Works of An Shigao
description:
arXiv:2611.13636v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Attributing early Chinese Buddhist translations requires evidence that scholars can trace back to the texts. We develop an interpretable stylometric framework that uses features defined or reviewed by Buddhist philologists, including function characters, sentence formulas, sentence-final characters, sentence length, and part-of-speech n-grams. We construct stylistic profiles from 31 authenticated translations by seven translators from the Eastern Han through the Western Jin, then compare eight disputed texts with An Shigao's profile. Two texts, T1557 and T0101, show the strongest stylistic similarity to the authenticated An Shigao corpus, with scores of 0.783 and 0.687, respectively. The attributions agree with those reported by a published BERT-based approach on the same set of disputed texts. The framework requires no task-specific training and allows scholars to inspect which linguistic features support each proposed attribution.

title: Reasoning-Aware Relational Representation Learning for Open-Vocabulary Scene Graph Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.13496v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Open-Vocabulary Scene Graph Generation (OV-SGG) requires models to recognize visual relationships beyond the training vocabulary, yet existing methods often rely on dataset-specific object--predicate co-occurrence patterns. Under long-tailed distributions and noisy object localization, such reliance leads to biased, entangled relation representations, limiting both rare-relation recognition and generalization to unseen predicates. To address these challenges, we propose RaRe, a reasoning-aware relational representation learning framework that transforms MLLM-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) rationales into structured relation embeddings. Rather than using CoT only as an intermediate reasoning trace for final prediction, RaRe directly optimizes the rationale-derived representation space to improve inter-relation discriminability. Specifically, RaRe first aligns rationale embeddings with textualized relation descriptions through self-supervised contrastive learning, and then refines rationale generation with a specificity-oriented reinforcement learning objective that encourages semantically object-pair-specific relational evidence. Experiments on VG150 and PSG demonstrate improved category-balanced recognition over existing baselines, while the additional gains from learning vary across datasets and proposal settings. Code available at: https://artanic30.github.io/project_pages/RaRe.

title: 🚀 New React Challenge: Nested Comments
description:
Flattening a comment thread into a single array works until you need to reply to a reply. Then you're faking depth with parent ids, and every edit or delete means rebuilding the whole list. A recursive tree keeps the shape of the conversation and lets you update just the branch that changed.

🧩 Overview

Build a threaded comments UI: render a recursive thread, then reply, edit, collapse, and delete nodes while every update returns a new tree instead of mutating the seed.

👉 https://www.reactchallenges.com/challenges/nested-comments

✅ Requirements

  • Render the full thread from initialComments, with replies nested inside their parent.
  • Each comment shows its author and text, and exposes reply, edit, and delete controls.
  • Comments with replies get a collapse control with aria-expanded that hides or shows only their replies.
  • Replying opens a form, appends a trimmed reply authored by "You", and closes it. Empty or whitespace-only text is rejected and the form stays open.
  • Editing opens a prefilled editor, saves a trimmed update to that comment only, or cancels to restore the original text.
  • Deleting removes the comment and its entire subtree, leaving siblings intact.
  • Deleting every comment renders an empty state.
  • All updates are immutable: neither the seed tree nor any replies array is mutated.

💡 Notes

The core idea is a recursive tree update. Map the current level, recurse into replies when the target isn't the current node, and rebuild only the nodes on that path:

function updateComment(
  comments: Comment[],
  id: string,
  update: (comment: Comment) => Comment,
): Comment[] {
  return comments.map((comment) =>
    comment.id === id
      ? update(comment)
      : { ...comment, replies: updateComment(comment.replies, id, update) },
  );
}

Reply and edit both reuse it: one callback appends a reply, the other returns { ...comment, text }.

Collapse is UI state, not tree data. Keep the collapsed ids in a Set and let rendering hide the replies, so the branch still exists in the tree.

Delete is the same walk with filter instead of map, which removes the whole subtree in one pass.

🧪 Tests

  1. renders all seed comments with replies nested under their parent
  2. shows the author and text of every comment
  3. collapses a comment's replies and keeps the comment visible
  4. expands a collapsed comment again
  5. opens the reply form under the correct comment
  6. adds a reply with the author You and closes the form
  7. rejects an empty or whitespace-only reply and keeps the form open
  8. prefills the editor with the current comment text
  9. saves an edited comment and closes the editor
  10. cancels an edit and restores the original text
  11. deletes a comment and its replies, keeping siblings intact
  12. shows the empty state when every comment is deleted
  13. never mutates the imported seed tree

Once you can update a nested comment thread immutably, you can apply the same helper to file explorers, menus, org charts, and nested settings. That's the skill this challenge gives you: thinking in trees instead of flat lists.

🔥 Start the Challenge Now

title: Partition, Refine, and Detect: Preserving Novel Category Capacity in Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.12976v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) expects the model trained on base classes to recognize both base and novel classes at inference. Typical methods rely on CLIP-style vision-language embeddings, yet the learned space is often biased toward base categories, with limited effective capacity preserved for novel concepts. Such a base-dominated representation can compress novel semantics, leading to semantic collapse and mis-calibrated confidence at inference. To address this issue, we present PR-OVD, a partition-and-refine framework that explicitly reserves capacity for novel categories and strengthens category separation, while being seamlessly integrated into different detector architectures. Specifically, PR-OVD first performs coarse partitioning to build global divisions for base, novel, and an explicit background partition in both visual and textual modalities, preventing object-irrelevant embeddings from leaking into category-specific representations. It then applies category-level refinement within each partition to sharpen decision boundaries and alleviate the lack of fine-grained region-level pretraining in CLIP. To further provide reliable visual anchors for novel categories, we design a cognitively inspired Structure Prompt (SP) that encodes both egocentric attributes and allocentric context, facilitating stable partition-and-refine learning. Extensive experiments on two OVD benchmarks show that PR-OVD delivers an average 6.5\% proportional improvement on novel categories over the state-of-the-art methods. Notably, PR-OVD also benefits other open-vocabulary tasks, including segmentation and classification, further confirming its effectiveness and generality.

title: The Case for AI-Enabled Gate Monitoring as Farm Security in the UK: A PRISMA-Guided Review of the Evidence on Rural Crime, Livestock Predation and Farm Access
description:
arXiv:2611.13933v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Farm security in the UK rests on thinner evidence than its cost suggests. We ran a PRISMA guided review: twelve searches of Web of Science and Scopus on 2nd -4th November 2026 returned 1,183 records (761 unique), and grey-literature and hand-searches added 35 assessed sources. We synthesised 96 database records and 24 grey sources narratively. UK peer-reviewed evidence is small (16 records), and the main UK survey of crime and farmer mental health has 80 responses. Cost estimates rest on insurer claims: NFU Mutual put UK rural crime at {\pounds}41.5 million in 2025, with livestock theft up almost 30% to about {\pounds}4.5 million and dog attacks on livestock costing {\pounds}1.95 million. The Home Office states that agricultural crime cannot be separately identified in its central data. We found no independent evaluation of cameras, sensors, trackers or marking; light and sound deterrents lost effect within one to five months in a systematic review of anti-predator interventions; and no study examined how often farm gates are left open or what follows. Camera-trap AI papers report accuracy on ecological datasets, none at a farm gate in the records we found, and in one comparison machine learning detected 41% of wildlife against 81% for analysts. We argue, as an inference from these gaps and not as a demonstrated effect, that continuous gate-level AI-mediated monitoring, as implemented in Fieldmark AI, would be highly beneficial for UK farm security. It would create the farm-level, time-stamped record that no official source holds, verify events that periodic human checks miss, resolve whether foxes, dogs or people were responsible, and give every other security measure something to be tested against. No study has yet shown that it reduces loss, and we set out the evaluation needed to show it.

title: Bookmark Managers Are Graveyards: Why I Built a Single-Binary Go + SQLite Action Engine
description:
You save 200 interesting links. You open maybe four. The rest rot in a folder called "Later".

Like most developers, I have self-hosted or used almost every read-it-later and bookmark tool out there. They are all great at saving links—and terrible at helping you do anything with them.

The missing piece wasn't another bookmark folder. It was an action engine that sits between messy daily capture and your clean knowledge base or task board.

So I built Sparkkeep (v0.1.0, AGPL-3.0): a single-binary, self-hosted capture, AI triage, and deterministic deep-research engine.

BurlacuAndrei / sparkkeep

Self-hosted capture & AI action engine. Turn links, notes, and chat messages into triaged execution boards, cited research dossiers, and Obsidian/Notion notes.

Sparkkeep

Capture anything. Triage it with AI. Ship what matters.

Sparkkeep is a self-hosted action engine for the ideas you keep collecting and never execute. Share a link, a note, a voice memo, or a screenshot — it scrapes it, filters the noise, synthesizes an actionable brief, and puts it on a board you actually work from.

One binary. One SQLite file. No Postgres, no Redis, no cloud account.



Bookmark managers are graveyards

You save 200 interesting links. You open maybe four. The rest rot in a folder called "later".

Sparkkeep is not a bookmark manager. It is an action engine:

Capture ──► Noise Gate ──► AI Triage ──► Horizon Routing ──► Execution Board ──► Research ──► Digest ──► Shipped
  1. Capture from Telegram, Discord, Slack, the browser extension, a webhook, or a plain note with no URL at all.
  2. Filter engagement bait and spam before it reaches your inbox.
  3. Synthesize…
View on GitHub

The Pipeline: From Messy Capture to Shipped Work 

Capture ──► Noise Gate ──► AI Triage ──► Horizon Routing ──► Execution Board ──► Research ──► Digest ──► Shipped
  1. Capture from anywhere: Send a URL, voice memo, screenshot, or raw URL-less note via a two-way Telegram bot, Discord embeds/buttons, Slack Block Kit, the Chrome/Firefox Web Clipper, or a universal webhook.
  2. Filter the noise: A fast noise gate scores and filters engagement bait before it clutters your inbox.
  3. Synthesize an actionable brief (100% BYOK / Local LLM friendly): Using Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, OpenAI, or DeepSeek, Sparkkeep extracts a TL;DR, why it matters, and a concrete checklist of next steps.
  4. Swipeable Triage Deck & Execution Board: Burn through your unreviewed inbox with 1 / 2 / 3 / Esc, route cards into Now / Next / Later, and execute from a widescreen board with a Focus Spotlight and 7-day Execution Pulse.

Why Deterministic Research Playbooks Beat Unbounded Agent Loops

When I tried wiring autonomous ReAct agents to research saved technical topics, two things happened:

  1. Small local models (7B–14B) got stuck in repetitive search loops.
  2. Cloud API models burned unpredictable token budgets and still hallucinated citations.

Instead of open-ended loops, Sparkkeep ships with Playbook Studio—a bounded, visual step sequencer with a 5-Pillar Research Health Linter, token cost estimator, zero-cost dry runs, and SearXNG web search integration.

Every research run produces a cited Research Dossier with a clear Pursue / Watch / Skip verdict:

Knowledge Sinks, Not a Walled Garden

Sparkkeep is the staging and research desk in front of your permanent notes. When a card moves into active work (To-Do, In Progress, Done) or completes deep research, Sparkkeep automatically exports it idempotently to:

  • Obsidian (clean Markdown + YAML frontmatter mirrored directly to your vault)
  • Notion (auto-provisioned database properties + rich Notion blocks)
  • Joplin (Self-Hosted Joplin Server or Desktop Web Clipper API)
  • Authenticated Outbox RSS & 1-click intents for Logseq, Things 3, Todoist, and GitHub Issues

And at the end of the week, the Intelligence Digest synthesizes your shipped wins, flags stale bottlenecks, and prepares your next focus items:

Under the Hood: One Binary, One SQLite File (<30 MB RAM)

I wanted Sparkkeep to run effortlessly on a Raspberry Pi, home NAS, or €5 VPS without maintaining Postgres, Redis, or Meilisearch containers:

  • Go 1.26 Standard Library HTTP
  • Pure-Go SQLite (modernc.org/sqlite, zero CGO) in WAL mode with FTS5 full-text search
  • React 19 + TypeScript + Vite compiled into internal/web/dist and embedded into the Go binary via //go:embed
  • 6 UI Languages out of the box: English, Romanian, Spanish, Portuguese (Brasil), French, and German

Try It in 10 Seconds (Includes a 1-Click Demo Library) 

docker run -d \
  --name sparkkeep \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  -v sparkkeep_data:/data \
  ghcr.io/burlacuandrei/sparkkeep:latest

Open http://localhost:8080. The first-run setup wizard includes a 1-click Demo Library so you can explore the Execution Board, Triage Deck, Playbook Studio, and Research Dossiers before connecting an AI provider.

Support & Feedback

If Sparkkeep looks useful for your workflow:

title: Pydantic v2 Deep Dive & Custom Validators: Explained from Absolute Zero 🛡️
description:
🛡️ Pydantic v2 Deep Dive & Custom Validators: Let's Learn from ZERO!

Almost every API you build needs to validate incoming data, reject invalid values, convert data into Python objects, and control what goes back to the frontend. In FastAPI, Pydantic does all of that. 🚀

No Pydantic knowledge is assumed. We'll connect every concept to a React + FastAPI social-feed backend so you see how it works in a real project, not just as definitions.

1. 🤔 What problem does Pydantic solve?

Your React frontend sends this to your FastAPI backend:

{
  "username": "deepika",
  "age": 22,
  "email": "deepika@gmail.com"
}

But what if it accidentally sends this?

{
  "username": 12345,
  "age": "twenty-two",
  "email": "not-an-email"
}
  • ❌ Username is a number instead of a string
  • ❌ Age is text instead of a number
  • ❌ Email is not a valid email address

Should your backend blindly accept it? Absolutely not! 🙅

📌 Pydantic is a Python library for data validation, parsing, and serialization using Python type annotations. In simple words: it checks whether data follows the structure and rules you defined.

Think of Pydantic as a security checkpoint ✈️ at the entrance of your backend:

  • ✅ Correct data → allowed through
  • ❌ Incorrect data → validation error
  • 🔄 Data needing conversion → converted when the rules permit

🤝 Why do we need it in FastAPI?

FastAPI integrates directly with Pydantic. When a request reaches an endpoint, FastAPI can use a Pydantic model to:

  1. Read incoming JSON
  2. Validate its fields
  3. Convert compatible values into Python types when allowed
  4. Give your endpoint a validated Python object
  5. Generate API documentation automatically
  6. Validate and serialize outgoing responses

2. 🏗️ What is a Pydantic model?

First, a normal Python class:

class User:
    def __init__(self, username, age):
        self.username = username
        self.age = age


user = User("deepika", 22)

print(user.username)  # deepika
print(user.age)       # 22

But Python doesn't validate the types here:

user = User(12345, "twenty-two")  # Python happily creates this 😬

Now with Pydantic:

pip install pydantic

from pydantic import BaseModel


class User(BaseModel):
    username: str
    age: int


user = User(username="deepika", age=22)

print(user)

username='deepika' age=22
  • BaseModel is the main Pydantic class that provides validation and serialization
  • username: str and age: int are type annotations. They tell Pydantic what to expect

Now try User(username=12345, age="twenty-two") and Pydantic raises a ValidationError. 💥

📌 A Pydantic model is a Python class that inherits from BaseModel and defines the expected structure and validation rules of data.

Incoming Python data / JSON
        ▼
Pydantic BaseModel   → checks fields, types and validation rules
        ├── ✅ Valid data   → Python model object
        └── ❌ Invalid data → ValidationError

3. 🆕 Pydantic v2: What's New and Important?

Pydantic has two major versions: v1 (older API) and v2 (newer implementation, faster, with updated APIs). Focus on v2.

Pydantic v1 Pydantic v2
@validator @field_validator
@root_validator @model_validator
.dict() .model_dump()
.json() .model_dump_json()
.parse_obj() .model_validate()
.schema() .model_json_schema()
.copy() .model_copy() 
user.dict()          # old
user.model_dump()    # new ✅

💡 In new projects, learn and use the v2 APIs.

4. 🎚️ Required Fields, Optional Fields and Defaults

Not every field in an API request is mandatory. In a registration API, username, email and password are required, but a profile bio might be optional.

from pydantic import BaseModel


class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: str
    password: str
    bio: str | None = None
  • username: str → required
  • bio: str | None = None → can be a string, can be None, and defaults to None if omitted 
user = UserCreate(
    username="deepika",
    email="deepika@gmail.com",
    password="secret123",
)

print(user.bio)  # None

⚠️ Optional vs default value (a classic interview question!) 

class User(BaseModel):
    bio: str | None        # value may be None, but the field is STILL REQUIRED

class User(BaseModel):
    bio: str | None = None  # the user can omit it ✅

In the first version, the caller must explicitly supply bio, even if the value is None.

🧮 Default values 

class User(BaseModel):
    username: str
    is_active: bool = True
    followers_count: int = 0

🏭 Default factories

Need a new list for every object?

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class User(BaseModel):
    username: str
    interests: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)

Field(default_factory=list) creates a fresh empty list whenever a default is needed, so objects never accidentally share the same mutable list. You can also use it for timestamps:

from datetime import datetime, timezone

created_at: datetime = Field(
    default_factory=lambda: datetime.now(timezone.utc)
)

Each object gets its own creation timestamp. ⏱️

5. 📏 Field(): Adding Validation Constraints

Imagine someone sends {"username": "", "age": -10}. Technically the username is a string and the age is an integer, but the values make no sense! We need extra rules. That's what Field() is for.

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class User(BaseModel):
    username: str = Field(min_length=3, max_length=20)
    age: int = Field(ge=18, le=100)

🔤 String constraints

Constraint Meaning
min_length=3 Minimum 3 characters
max_length=20 Maximum 20 characters
pattern="..." Must match a regular expression 
username: str = Field(
    min_length=3,
    max_length=20,
    pattern=r"^[a-zA-Z0-9_]+$",
)

This means 3 to 20 characters, using only letters, numbers and underscores.

🔢 Numeric constraints

Constraint Meaning
gt=0 Greater than zero
ge=18 Greater than or equal to 18
lt=100 Less than 100
le=100 Less than or equal to 100
multiple_of=5 Must be divisible by 5 
price: float = Field(gt=0)        # must be greater than zero
age: int = Field(ge=18, le=100)   # between 18 and 100, inclusive

📚 Collection constraints 

tags: list[str] = Field(min_length=1, max_length=5)

The list needs at least 1 item and at most 5. Because of list[str], Pydantic also checks that every item is a string.

🧠 Remember: Field() defines declarative constraints. Validators define custom logic. min_length=3 is a constraint, but "username must not contain a prohibited word" needs custom code.

6. 🧪 What are Custom Validators?

In your social-feed registration API you want to enforce:

  1. Username must not contain spaces
  2. Email must be lowercase
  3. Username must not contain offensive words

Field() can't express all of that. We need Python logic.

📌 A custom validator is a function you write to check whether a value (or a whole model) satisfies your application's rules.

Pydantic v2 gives you two decorators:

  • @field_validator: validates one field
  • @model_validator: validates the whole model

7. 🎯 @field_validator: Validating Individual Fields 

from pydantic import BaseModel, field_validator


class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    username: str

    @field_validator("username")
    @classmethod
    def validate_username(cls, value):
        if " " in value:
            raise ValueError("Username cannot contain spaces")

        return value

Line by line:

  • @field_validator("username") → "run this function when validating the username field"
  • @classmethod → in Pydantic v2, field validators generally take cls as the first parameter
  • def validate_username(cls, value) → value is the value being validated (e.g. "deepika")
  • if " " in value → our check
  • raise ValueError(...) → rejects the value. Pydantic catches it and produces a structured ValidationError
  • return value → allows the value to continue. A field validator must return the value it wants Pydantic to use

You can validate several fields with one validator:

@field_validator("username", "display_name")
@classmethod
def validate_names(cls, value):
    return value.strip()

Testing it:

UserCreate(username="deepika")          # ✅ works
UserCreate(username="deepika rao")      # ❌ ValidationError

💡 raise ValueError() rejects the input. return value lets the validated value continue.

8. 🔀 Field Validator Modes: Before, After, Plain, Wrap

@field_validator supports four modes:

Mode When does it run?
before Before Pydantic's normal type validation
after After normal type validation
plain Replaces normal validation
wrap Wraps normal validation and controls when it runs

🅰️ before: clean raw input

The frontend sends " deepika " and you want to strip the spaces first:

from pydantic import BaseModel, field_validator


class User(BaseModel):
    username: str

    @field_validator("username", mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def clean_username(cls, value):
        if isinstance(value, str):
            return value.strip()

        return value

Incoming value: "   deepika   "
        ▼
Before validator → strip() removes extra spaces
        ▼
Pydantic type validation → checks the result is a string
        ▼
Final value: "deepika"

Why isinstance(value, str)? Because before validation, Pydantic hasn't checked the input yet. It could be a string, integer, list or anything. A before validator must be ready for raw input.

Use before to clean, normalize or preprocess incoming data.

🅱️ after: check validated values 

class User(BaseModel):
    age: int

    @field_validator("age", mode="after")
    @classmethod
    def validate_age(cls, value):
        if value < 18:
            raise ValueError("User must be at least 18")

        return value

For User(age="22"), in default (non-strict) mode Pydantic converts "22" to 22 first, and then your validator receives 22 and checks the business rule.

Use after for values that have already passed type validation. It's the easiest and safest mode for beginners. ✅

🅲 plain: take full control

A plain validator replaces Pydantic's normal validation:

from pydantic import BaseModel, field_validator


class Product(BaseModel):
    quantity: int

    @field_validator("quantity", mode="plain")
    @classmethod
    def validate_quantity(cls, value):
        if isinstance(value, int) and value > 0:
            return value

        raise ValueError("Quantity must be a positive integer")

Even though the field says quantity: int, Pydantic won't run its normal integer validation after this. Your function is responsible for checking the input. Use plain only when you deliberately want to replace normal validation.

🅳 wrap: advanced control

A wrap validator receives the incoming value and a handler that runs Pydantic's normal validation. You can run logic before it, after it, or catch errors:

from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidatorFunctionWrapHandler, field_validator


class Product(BaseModel):
    quantity: int

    @field_validator("quantity", mode="wrap")
    @classmethod
    def validate_quantity(cls, value, handler: ValidatorFunctionWrapHandler):
        print("Before normal validation")

        result = handler(value)

        print("After normal validation")

        return result

For Product(quantity="10"):

Before normal validation
        ▼
handler(value) → Pydantic validates and converts "10" to 10
        ▼
After normal validation
        ▼
Return result

If the input is invalid, the handler raises a validation error, which you can catch to implement fallback behavior.

📊 All four modes at a glance

Mode Idea Example
before Preprocess first, then normal validation Remove extra spaces
after Normal validation first, then custom logic Age must be at least 18
plain Custom validator replaces normal validation Implement your own full validation
wrap Custom logic controls normal validation Intercept errors, fallback behavior

💡 Recommendation: become very comfortable with before and after first, then learn plain and wrap.

9. 🧩 @model_validator: Validating Multiple Fields Together

A registration form has password and confirm_password:

{
  "password": "hello123",
  "confirm_password": "hello456"
}

Individually both are valid strings. Together they violate a rule: they must match. A field validator can't conveniently solve this. Use @model_validator, which validates the entire model.

from pydantic import BaseModel, model_validator


class UserRegister(BaseModel):
    username: str
    password: str
    confirm_password: str

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def check_passwords(self):
        if self.password != self.confirm_password:
            raise ValueError("Passwords do not match")

        return self
  • @field_validator("username") validates one specific field
  • @model_validator(mode="after") validates the complete model
  • An after model validator receives the complete model instance, so you access self.password and self.confirm_password
  • return self returns the validated model instance

⏪ before model validators

A before model validator runs before field validation and receives the raw input:

from typing import Any

from pydantic import BaseModel, model_validator


class User(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: str

    @model_validator(mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def preprocess_data(cls, data: Any):
        if isinstance(data, dict):
            data = data.copy()

            if "user_name" in data and "username" not in data:
                data["username"] = data.pop("user_name")

        return data

If someone sends {"user_name": "deepika", "email": "deepika@gmail.com"}, the validator turns it into {"username": "deepika", ...} and then normal field validation happens. Notice we copy the dictionary instead of modifying the original input.

📊 Model validator modes

Mode Behavior
before Receives raw input before field validation
after Receives the validated model instance
wrap Can control and wrap the entire model validation process

📝 Unlike field validators, model validators don't have a plain mode.

⚔️ Field validator vs model validator

Feature Field validator Model validator
Main purpose Validate individual fields Validate relationships between fields
Decorator @field_validator @model_validator
Example Username cannot contain spaces Passwords must match
Can access whole model? Not directly in the normal way Yes, in after mode
Modes before, after, plain, wrap before, after, wrap

10. ℹ️ ValidationInfo: Accessing Other Field Values

Sometimes you validate one field based on another. For example, reject a display_name identical to the username:

from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationInfo, field_validator


class User(BaseModel):
    username: str
    display_name: str

    @field_validator("display_name")
    @classmethod
    def validate_display_name(cls, value, info: ValidationInfo):
        username = info.data.get("username")

        if username and value == username:
            raise ValueError("Display name cannot equal username")

        return value

info.data contains the previously validated fields.

⚠️ Field validation normally follows the order in which fields are declared. Here username comes before display_name, so its validated value is available. Reverse the order and username might not be available yet. For relationships between several fields, model_validator(mode="after") is often clearer.

11. 🌍 Custom Validation: A Real-World Example

Registration rules for your social-feed app:

  1. Username has 3 to 20 characters
  2. Username cannot contain spaces
  3. Email must be lowercase
  4. Age must be at least 18
  5. Password has at least 8 characters
  6. Confirm password must match password 
from pydantic import (
    BaseModel,
    Field,
    field_validator,
    model_validator,
)


class UserRegister(BaseModel):
    username: str = Field(min_length=3, max_length=20)
    email: str
    age: int = Field(ge=18)
    password: str = Field(min_length=8)
    confirm_password: str

    @field_validator("username")
    @classmethod
    def validate_username(cls, value):
        if " " in value:
            raise ValueError("Username cannot contain spaces")

        return value.strip()

    @field_validator("email")
    @classmethod
    def validate_email(cls, value):
        value = value.strip().lower()

        if "@" not in value:
            raise ValueError("Invalid email")

        return value

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def validate_passwords(self):
        if self.password != self.confirm_password:
            raise ValueError("Passwords do not match")

        return self

📝 This uses a simple email check to demonstrate custom logic. For production-grade email validation, use EmailStr with the email-validator package. And never store plain-text passwords. Hash them with an algorithm such as Argon2id.

🧭 Where should validation happen?

Not every business rule belongs in Pydantic:

Rule Best place
Username must be a string Pydantic
Username length must be 3 to 20 Pydantic
Password confirmation must match Pydantic
Email must have valid format Pydantic
Username already exists in database Service / database
User has permission to delete a post Authorization / service layer
Post belongs to the logged-in user Service / database

Pydantic is for validating data structure and input rules. It shouldn't become responsible for database operations, authorization, or application workflows.

12. 🔄 Request Schemas vs Response Schemas

🚨 EXTREMELY IMPORTANT for FastAPI projects!

A user registers and the frontend sends:

{
  "username": "deepika",
  "email": "deepika@gmail.com",
  "password": "secret123"
}

Your database stores:

id username email password_hash
1 deepika deepika@gmail.com $argon2id$...

Should the backend send that complete record back to React? Never! You must never expose password hashes to the frontend. That's why we separate request and response schemas.

🅰️ Request schema

What the client is allowed or expected to send:

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    username: str = Field(min_length=3, max_length=20)
    email: str
    password: str = Field(min_length=8)

🅱️ Response schema

What the backend is allowed to return:

from pydantic import BaseModel


class UserResponse(BaseModel):
    id: int
    username: str
    email: str

Notice there's no password field. That's intentional. 🔐

🤔 Why separate them? 

Frontend → Backend:   UserCreate     (username, email, password)
        ▼
Backend processes and stores data
        ▼
Database:             id, username, email, password_hash
        ▼
Backend selects safe output fields
        ▼
Backend → Frontend:   UserResponse   (id, username, email)  ✅ no password hash

This gives you security, clear API contracts, better maintainability, independent validation for input and output, and control over exposed fields.

📚 Other common schema types 

class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: str
    password: str


class UserUpdate(BaseModel):
    username: str | None = None
    bio: str | None = None


class UserResponse(BaseModel):
    id: int
    username: str
    email: str
    bio: str | None = None


class UserLogin(BaseModel):
    email: str
    password: str
Schema Responsibility
UserCreate New user registration
UserUpdate Updating profile details
UserResponse Returning safe user information
UserLogin Accepting login credentials

🧠 A database model and a Pydantic schema are not the same thing. A SQLAlchemy model represents database structure and behavior. A Pydantic model represents the structure and validation of data entering or leaving your API.

13. ⚡ FastAPI response_model: How Does It Work?

response_model tells FastAPI which schema should describe and validate the endpoint's output.

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()


class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    username: str
    password: str


class UserResponse(BaseModel):
    id: int
    username: str


@app.post("/users", response_model=UserResponse)
def create_user(user: UserCreate):
    return {
        "id": 1,
        "username": user.username,
        "password": user.password,
    }

The function returns a dict with the password, but UserResponse only has id and username. FastAPI validates the returned data against UserResponse and serializes the response according to it. The extra password field is not included in the normal serialized response:

{
  "id": 1,
  "username": "deepika"
}

✅ Why is response_model useful?

  1. Validates outgoing response data
  2. Serializes data into the expected representation
  3. Filters fields that aren't part of the response schema
  4. Generates accurate API documentation
  5. Establishes a clear contract for the frontend

🚨 Security warning: don't rely on response filtering as your only security measure. Never pass secrets into response construction unnecessarily. Build safe response data explicitly and keep sensitive fields out of API-facing schemas.

🆚 Request body vs response_model 

@app.post("/users", response_model=UserResponse)
def create_user(user: UserCreate):
    ...
  • user: UserCreate → defines the incoming request body
  • response_model=UserResponse → defines the outgoing response

🎛️ More response_model options 

@app.get(
    "/users/{user_id}",
    response_model=UserResponse,
    response_model_exclude_unset=True,
)
Option Meaning
response_model_exclude_unset=True Excludes fields not explicitly set
response_model_exclude_none=True Excludes fields whose value is None
response_model_exclude_defaults=True Excludes values equal to their defaults
response_model_include={...} Includes selected fields
response_model_exclude={...} Excludes selected fields

💡 Prefer creating a dedicated response schema over relying heavily on include/exclude tricks.

14. 📤 Serialization: Python Objects → JSON 

user = UserResponse(
    id=1,
    username="deepika",
    email="deepika@gmail.com",
)

This is a Python object, but React expects JSON. Converting it is serialization.

📌 Serialization means converting a Python object or structured data into a format that can be transmitted, stored, or consumed elsewhere.

🅰️ model_dump(): model → Python dict 

user_data = user.model_dump()
print(user_data)

{"id": 1, "username": "deepika", "email": "deepika@gmail.com"}

It produces a Python dictionary, not a JSON string.

🅱️ model_dump_json(): model → JSON string 

print(user.model_dump_json())

{"id":1,"username":"deepika","email":"deepika@gmail.com"}

🅲 model_validate(): Python data → validated model 

user_data = {
    "id": 1,
    "username": "deepika",
    "email": "deepika@gmail.com",
}

user = UserResponse.model_validate(user_data)

🅳 model_validate_json(): JSON text → validated model 

user_json = """
{
    "id": 1,
    "username": "deepika",
    "email": "deepika@gmail.com"
}
"""

user = UserResponse.model_validate_json(user_json)

📊 Quick comparison

Method Purpose
model_dump() Model → Python dictionary
model_dump_json() Model → JSON string
model_validate() Python data → validated model
model_validate_json() JSON string/bytes → validated model
model_copy() Create a copy of a model
model_json_schema() Generate JSON Schema

🎛️ Serialization options 

user.model_dump(exclude={"email"})
# {"id": 1, "username": "deepika"}

user.model_dump(exclude_none=True)    # skip fields whose value is None
user.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)   # skip fields not explicitly supplied/set

⚠️ exclude_unset and exclude_defaults are different. A field explicitly provided with its default value is still considered set.

15. 🏷️ Aliasing: Different Names in Python and JSON

Your Python backend uses snake_case (created_at), but your React frontend uses camelCase (createdAt). Both mean the same thing. Do you rewrite your Python codebase in camelCase? No! Use aliases.

📌 An alias is an alternative name for a field, used when validating input or serializing output.

🅰️ Basic alias 

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class Post(BaseModel):
    created_at: str = Field(alias="createdAt")


post = Post(createdAt="2026-11-11")

print(post.created_at)  # 2026-11-11

Python still uses created_at, but incoming data used createdAt.

🅱️ alias vs validation_alias vs serialization_alias

Property Purpose
alias Alias for both validation and serialization
validation_alias Alternative name when accepting input
serialization_alias Alternative name when producing output

validation_alias: the frontend sends {"userName": "deepika"} but your field is username:

class User(BaseModel):
    username: str = Field(validation_alias="userName")

serialization_alias: you want created_at to appear as createdAt in outgoing JSON:

class Post(BaseModel):
    created_at: str = Field(serialization_alias="createdAt")


post = Post(created_at="2026-11-11")

print(post.model_dump(by_alias=True))
# {"createdAt": "2026-11-11"}

print(post.model_dump())
# {"created_at": "2026-11-11"}

by_alias=True tells Pydantic to use the serialization alias instead of the Python field name.

🅲 Different input and output names 

class User(BaseModel):
    username: str = Field(
        validation_alias="userName",
        serialization_alias="displayName",
    )


user = User(userName="deepika")

print(user.model_dump(by_alias=True))
# {"displayName": "deepika"}

Incoming JSON  →  userName
Python model   →  username
Outgoing JSON  →  displayName

🅳 Alias generators

With 50 fields (created_at, updated_at, first_name, ...) you don't want to write each alias by hand:

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict
from pydantic.alias_generators import to_camel


class User(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(
        alias_generator=to_camel,
        validate_by_alias=True,
        validate_by_name=True,
    )

    first_name: str
    last_name: str
    created_at: str
Python field Alias
first_name firstName
last_name lastName
created_at createdAt 
user.model_dump(by_alias=True)
# {"firstName": "Deepika", "lastName": "Rao", "createdAt": "2026-11-11"}

📝 validate_by_name and validate_by_alias are the granular settings in newer Pydantic v2 releases. Older v2 examples commonly use populate_by_name=True.

16. ⚙️ ConfigDict: Configuring Pydantic Models

Sometimes you want rules for the entire model: should extra fields be allowed? Should strings be auto-stripped? Should strict validation be on? Can the model be built from object attributes? Pydantic v2 uses ConfigDict:

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict


class User(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(
        extra="forbid",
        str_strip_whitespace=True,
    )

    username: str
    email: str

🚫 Understanding extra

The frontend sends:

{
  "username": "deepika",
  "email": "deepika@gmail.com",
  "admin": true
}

But the model defines only username and email. What should happen?

Setting Behavior
extra="ignore" Ignore extra fields (default)
extra="forbid" Reject extra fields
extra="allow" Allow extra fields and retain them

For registration APIs, extra="forbid" is useful when you want unexpected input rejected rather than silently ignored.

🔧 Other useful settings 

model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True)

Strict mode prevents many automatic type conversions. For example, an int field generally won't accept "22" in strict Python-object validation.

model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)

This lets Pydantic read data from object attributes, which is handy with ORM objects (more on this in section 21).

17. 🪆 Nested Pydantic Models

Real API responses are rarely flat. A post contains an ID, caption, author info and comments. Instead of one giant model, create smaller models and nest them:

from pydantic import BaseModel


class UserResponse(BaseModel):
    id: int
    username: str


class CommentResponse(BaseModel):
    id: int
    content: str
    author: UserResponse


class PostResponse(BaseModel):
    id: int
    caption: str
    author: UserResponse
    comments: list[CommentResponse]

Example response:

{
  "id": 101,
  "caption": "My first post!",
  "author": { "id": 1, "username": "deepika" },
  "comments": [
    {
      "id": 10,
      "content": "Beautiful!",
      "author": { "id": 2, "username": "sneha" }
    }
  ]
}

Pydantic validates the post, the author inside the post, every comment in the list, and the author inside each comment. This is nested model validation. 🎯

18. 🎨 Enums and Literal Values

A post's visibility should only be public, private or followers. You don't want the frontend sending "secret_everyone". Use an Enum:

from enum import Enum

from pydantic import BaseModel


class Visibility(str, Enum):
    PUBLIC = "public"
    PRIVATE = "private"
    FOLLOWERS = "followers"


class PostCreate(BaseModel):
    caption: str
    visibility: Visibility

PostCreate(caption="Hello", visibility="public")     # ✅
PostCreate(caption="Hello", visibility="everyone")   # ❌ rejected

For a small fixed set of strings you can use Literal:

from typing import Literal


class PostCreate(BaseModel):
    visibility: Literal["public", "private", "followers"]

19. 🚨 Pydantic Validation Errors 

from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError


class User(BaseModel):
    username: str
    age: int


try:
    user = User(username="deepika", age="hello")
except ValidationError as error:
    print(error)

error.errors() returns structured information:

  • type: type of validation failure
  • loc: location of the invalid field
  • msg: human-readable message
  • input: the invalid input
  • sometimes ctx: additional error context

⚡ What happens in FastAPI? 

@app.post("/users")
def create_user(user: UserCreate):
    return user

If the frontend sends invalid JSON data, FastAPI normally returns HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity:

{
  "detail": [
    {
      "type": "greater_than_equal",
      "loc": ["body", "age"],
      "msg": "Input should be greater than or equal to 18"
    }
  ]
}

The exact structure depends on the failure. The important distinction:

  • ❌ Request validation failure → normally HTTP 422
  • 💥 Invalid data returned by your endpoint that violates response_model → server-side response validation failure, normally HTTP 500

Why 500? Because the server failed to produce the response promised by its own API contract.

20. 📦 EmailStr, HttpUrl and Other Built-in Types 

from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, HttpUrl


class User(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: EmailStr
    profile_url: HttpUrl

To use EmailStr, install the email validation dependency:

pip install "pydantic[email]"
Type Purpose
EmailStr Email validation
HttpUrl HTTP/HTTPS URL validation
AnyUrl General URL validation
IPvAnyAddress IPv4 or IPv6 address validation
PositiveInt Integer greater than zero
NonNegativeInt Integer greater than or equal to zero
PositiveFloat Positive floating-point number 
from pydantic import BaseModel, PositiveInt


class Post(BaseModel):
    id: PositiveInt
    likes_count: int = 0

💡 You don't need a custom validator for every simple rule. Use Pydantic's built-in types whenever they fit.

21. 🔌 from_attributes: Connecting Pydantic with SQLAlchemy

Especially important for a FastAPI + PostgreSQL project. Your SQLAlchemy model is a Python object with attributes (id, username, email), but a Pydantic model normally expects data. How can Pydantic read the SQLAlchemy object's attributes?

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict


class UserResponse(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)

    id: int
    username: str
    email: str

response = UserResponse.model_validate(user_object)

Pydantic reads user_object.id, user_object.username, user_object.email and creates a validated Pydantic object.

🐘 PostgreSQL        → stored user record
        ▼
🗄️ SQLAlchemy ORM    → Python database object
        ▼
✔️ Pydantic model_validate()   (from_attributes=True)
        ▼
📤 UserResponse      → validated response object
        ▼
JSON response → ⚛️ React frontend

📌 from_attributes=True does not execute database queries. SQLAlchemy retrieves the object, and Pydantic reads its attributes.

backend/
│

│   │

Folder / file Responsibility

schemas/user.py

from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, Field


class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    username: str = Field(min_length=3, max_length=20)
    email: EmailStr
    password: str = Field(min_length=8)


class UserResponse(BaseModel):
    id: int
    username: str
    email: EmailStr

api/routes/users.py

from fastapi import APIRouter

from app.schemas.user import UserCreate, UserResponse

router = APIRouter()


@router.post("/users", response_model=UserResponse)
def create_user(user: UserCreate):
    # Call service layer here

    return {
        "id": 1,
        "username": user.username,
        "email": user.email,
    }

Your route doesn't contain every validation rule. Pydantic schemas handle data validation, while services handle business logic.

🔍 What happens when the frontend calls this API?

  1. React sends JSON
  2. FastAPI receives the request
  3. FastAPI validates the body using UserCreate
  4. If validation fails, FastAPI returns a 422 error
  5. If it succeeds, the endpoint receives a UserCreate object
  6. The endpoint calls the service layer
  7. The service performs application logic and database operations
  8. The endpoint returns data
  9. FastAPI validates and serializes it using UserResponse
  10. React receives JSON

23. 🧪 Testing Pydantic Validators with pytest

Knowing how to write validators is good. Knowing how to test them is better.

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator


class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    username: str = Field(min_length=3, max_length=20)

    @field_validator("username")
    @classmethod
    def validate_username(cls, value):
        if " " in value:
            raise ValueError("Spaces are not allowed")

        return value

tests/test_user_schema.py:

import pytest
from pydantic import ValidationError


def test_valid_username():
    user = UserCreate(username="deepika")

    assert user.username == "deepika"


def test_username_with_spaces():
    with pytest.raises(ValidationError):
        UserCreate(username="deepika rao")


def test_username_too_short():
    with pytest.raises(ValidationError):
        UserCreate(username="ab")

pytest.raises(ValidationError) means "we expect this code to raise a validation error." If it does, the test passes. If the code unexpectedly accepts invalid data, the test fails.

What to test:

  • ✅ Valid input
  • ❌ Missing required fields
  • ❌ Incorrect types
  • 📏 Minimum and maximum constraints
  • 🧪 Custom validator failures
  • 🧩 Cross-field validation
  • 🏷️ Serialization and aliases

24. 🚀 Important Advanced Concepts

🅰️ Strict validation

By default, Pydantic tries to convert compatible values:

class User(BaseModel):
    age: int


User(age="22")   # "22" is converted into 22

To reject conversions:

class User(BaseModel):
    age: int = Field(strict=True)   # "22" is now rejected

Or for the whole model: model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True).

🅱️ Computed fields

Include a value calculated from other fields:

from pydantic import BaseModel, computed_field


class User(BaseModel):
    first_name: str
    last_name: str

    @computed_field
    @property
    def full_name(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.first_name} {self.last_name}"


user = User(first_name="Deepika", last_name="Rao")

print(user.full_name)  # Deepika Rao

user.model_dump() includes full_name in the serialized output.

🅲 JSON Schema 

print(User.model_json_schema())

JSON Schema describes field names, types, required fields, constraints and descriptions. FastAPI uses this to generate the OpenAPI docs that power Swagger UI and ReDoc.

🅳 Custom error types 

from pydantic_core import PydanticCustomError

raise PydanticCustomError(
    "username_taken",
    "Username '{username}' is already taken",
    {"username": "deepika"},
)

Useful when you want a specific, machine-readable validation error type.

🅴 Validation context 

User.model_validate(
    {"username": "deepika"},
    context={"allowed_usernames": ["deepika", "sneha"]},
)

A validator can read this through info.context, which helps with dynamic rules. But rules requiring database queries should usually stay in your service layer.

26. 🎤 Common Interview Questions

1. What is Pydantic?
A Python library for data validation, parsing and serialization based on type annotations.

2. What's the difference between BaseModel and a normal Python class?
A normal class stores whatever you pass without checking types. A BaseModel validates (and where allowed, converts) data against its annotations and constraints, and provides serialization methods.

3. What's the difference between field_validator and model_validator?
field_validator validates individual fields. model_validator validates the whole model, so it can check relationships between fields, such as password and confirm password.

4. What's the difference between before and after validators?
before runs before Pydantic's type validation and receives raw input, which suits cleaning and normalizing. after runs after type validation and receives the already validated value, which suits business rules.

5. Why do we separate request and response schemas?
Request schemas validate what clients send. Response schemas control what the API returns, preventing sensitive fields such as password hashes from being exposed, and giving the frontend a clear contract.

6. What does response_model do in FastAPI?
It tells FastAPI which schema describes and validates the output. FastAPI validates and serializes the returned data against it, filters fields not in the schema, and documents the response in OpenAPI.

7. What is serialization?
Converting a Python object or model into a format that can be transmitted or stored, such as a dictionary (model_dump()) or a JSON string (model_dump_json()).

8. What's the difference between alias and serialization_alias?
alias applies to both validation (input) and serialization (output). serialization_alias only changes the field name in outgoing data, used with by_alias=True.

9. What is from_attributes=True?
A ConfigDict setting that lets Pydantic read values from object attributes, such as SQLAlchemy ORM objects, when using model_validate().

10. What's the difference between ValidationError and HTTP 422?
ValidationError is the Pydantic exception raised when validation fails. HTTP 422 is the response FastAPI sends to the client when request validation fails. A response-validation failure in your own endpoint is usually a server error (500).

27. 🏋️ Practical Exercises

Try these in a separate Python file:

  1. Create a Product model with name, price and quantity. Price must be greater than zero
  2. Create a username field_validator that removes extra spaces
  3. Create an email validator that converts emails to lowercase
  4. Create a registration model with password and confirm_password. Reject mismatches
  5. Create UserCreate and UserResponse schemas. Never expose the password in the response
  6. Create a Post model with a nested UserResponse author and a list of comments
  7. Use validation_alias and serialization_alias to convert username into userName on input and displayName on output
  8. Create a FastAPI POST endpoint using a request schema and response_model
  9. Enable extra="forbid" and test what happens when an unknown field is submitted
  10. Write pytest tests for valid and invalid usernames

28. 🏁 What to Remember

  1. 🏗️ Pydantic models define the structure of API data
  2. 📏 Field constraints enforce basic rules such as minimum lengths and positive numbers
  3. 🧪 Custom validators enforce additional input rules
  4. 📥 Request schemas define what the frontend can send
  5. 📤 Response schemas define what the backend returns
  6. 🔄 Serialization converts Python model data into dictionaries or JSON
  7. 🏷️ Aliases let Python and JavaScript follow different naming conventions
  8. ⚡ FastAPI integrates all of this into the request-response lifecycle
  9. 🗄️ SQLAlchemy handles database persistence; Pydantic handles API data validation and serialization
  10. 🧠 Services handle business logic that shouldn't live inside your schemas

🎯 One important architectural lesson: Pydantic validates whether data is structurally and semantically acceptable. It does not replace database constraints, authentication, authorization, or business logic.

🚀 What's Next?

Implement these concepts in a mini registration and post-creation API: write the schemas, add validators, wire up response_model, and cover it all with pytest. 💡

If this post helped you, drop a ❤️ or 🦄 and share it with a friend learning FastAPI. Happy coding! 👩‍💻✨

title: MMDM: Measuring Massive Multitask Decision Making
description:
arXiv:2611.14309v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: System-1 Decision Models directly make structured probabilistic decisions over query-specified options given a state in a single forward pass, without autoregressively generating reasoning trajectories or textual responses. Recent evaluations cover diverse tasks but often rely on existing benchmarks, where prior exposure to test material can obscure generalization. Moreover, real-world decision making often involves long contexts, large option spaces, and complex logical dependencies, challenges that existing benchmarks do not adequately capture together. Thus, we introduce MMDM (Massive Multitask Decision Making), a benchmark of 5,448 high-quality questions across 16 task categories, combining newly constructed tasks with source-grounded recompositions and rewrites for single-select, multi-select, and soft-label decision making in fresh contexts. It covers realistic scenarios such as agent state tracking, tool and skill selection, preference judgments, and rubric scoring, with option spaces ranging from 2 to 1,024 and inputs extending to 64,817 tokens. With MMDM, we conduct a comprehensive quantitative evaluation of 28 decision models, showing that many perform well on common knowledge yet struggle with interdependent options, constrained decisions, and multi-select tasks. For example, Perplexity Decider-V1.2 reaches 78.75% Hard Single-select Accuracy on world knowledge, but only 53.95% on option logic and 47.95% on constraint planning, while the best Hard Multi-select Accuracy across all models is 36.81%. These results highlight joint reasoning, constraint-aware selection, and complete multi-select recovery as key priorities for decision model development, with MMDM providing a testbed for measuring this progress.

title: CURRENT: A Recurrent Neural Network for Concurrent Spatial and Temporal Super-Resolution of 4D Flow MRI
description:
arXiv:2611.14058v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Objective: To improve the spatial and temporal resolution of aortic 4D flow MRI through a unified deep learning framework for post-acquisition super-resolution (SR) of reconstructed velocity vector fields.
  Methods: We propose CURRENT, a recurrent neural network that performs spatial and temporal SR with a single network architecture. Supervised training was conducted using paired low- and high-resolution datasets generated by embedding computational fluid dynamics simulations of aortic flow into in vivo thoracic MRI backgrounds, followed by controlled spatial and temporal downsampling. CURRENT was evaluated for two-fold spatial and temporal SR against 4DFlowNet and for two-fold spatiotemporal SR against sequential spatial and temporal SR pipelines based on 4DFlowNet. Image-based and k-space-based quantitative metrics were considered and conventional interpolation were used as baselines. In addition, the impact of CURRENT's spatiotemporal SR on physics-informed relative pressure estimation was assessed. Finally, the ability of CURRENT to generalize from synthetic training data to in vivo acquisitions was investigated.
  Results: CURRENT achieved superior spatial SR performance and comparable temporal SR performance to dedicated 4DFlowNet models while providing a unified solution for both tasks. Simultaneous spatiotemporal SR using CURRENT yielded more accurate relative pressure estimates than either spatial or temporal SR alone and outperformed sequential 4DFlowNet-based spatial and temporal SR approaches. Furthermore, the proposed model demonstrated promising generalization to in vivo 4D flow MRI data despite being trained exclusively on synthetic datasets.
  Conclusion: CURRENT provides a unified framework for spatial and temporal SR of 4D flow MRI. The proposed approach has the potential to enhance physics-based analysis and broaden the applicability of accelerated 4D flow MRI.

title: The more UX rules Haiku sees, the better it decides: but simple search is not enough
description:
The simple version of the study "How much does a UX data lake help a small model on big screens?". For the full method and every number, read the technical article. Here is what it means if you want to use it tomorrow.

In one sentence

When the request is vague ("get this ready for production"), Haiku (the small model) fixed 46% of the issues with no rules, 70% with the whole set of 148 UX rules and 78% with the rules plus a verifier's report. With the rules, it beat Sonnet (the larger model) without rules (61%) at about 8% of the cost per call.

What we did

We built 6 kinds of big screen (dashboard, listing, form, checkout, settings and navigation, 383 to 1,200 lines) and a data lake of 200 UX rules from open sources (WCAG, GOV.UK, web.dev, Nielsen Norman and others), checked one by one against the source. On each screen we deliberately broke 3 to 30 rules. Then we asked Haiku and Sonnet to fix them, showing 0%, 25%, 50% or 100% of the rules, and measured with a verifier in a real browser how many rules came to be met. That was 2,640 calls, and the hypotheses were written and frozen before running.

What we found

  1. Every extra 25% of rules gave 8 to 12 more points of accuracy on Haiku (47%, 59%, 67% and 76% on the rules shown). In practice: expanding the lake is worth it, and there is no sign it has reached its end.
  2. It is not just text volume. Giving the same amount of rules from other subjects only raised accuracy from 47% to 52%. The right rule is what matters.
  3. The lake helped even where it did not cover. On rules the model never saw, accuracy was up to 11 points higher with the full lake: the model became more careful overall.
  4. The verifier report avoids breaking what was already right. It cut the rules that started failing from 0.94 to 0.21 per screen, and added to the full lake it raised accuracy from 70% to 78% (and from 76% to 89% on the rules shown).
  5. Better and cheaper. Haiku with rules beat Sonnet without rules (70% against 61%) at US$ 0.0225 per call against US$ 0.2728, about 8% of the cost. On fixing screens with known defects, Haiku with rules reached 81% (against 63% for Sonnet without rules) at 6% of the cost.
  6. More rules, better-grounded decisions. The share of Haiku's decisions citing a rule it actually received rose from 59% (25% of the lake) to 90% (full lake).

What the study proved

We wrote the questions before running, and those that matter most to someone using the lake were confirmed, with statistical correction for multiple comparisons:

  • Completeness improves the decision: 25%, 50% and 100% of the lake each gave higher accuracy than the previous step.
  • The right rule matters more than volume: the full lake (76% on the rules shown) stayed far above the same amount of rules from other subjects (52%).
  • The lake does not hurt where it does not cover, and the verifier report adds to the full lake and reduces regressions.
  • Cost: the small model with the lake beats the larger model without it, at 6% to 8% of the cost per call.

Some things we tested did not work or did not apply (for example, how much of the lake simple search recovers). They are in section 6 of the technical article.

Caveats

  • The screens are synthetic (six kinds, script-generated) and the task is reviewing a draft, not creating from scratch. That does not prove the same behavior in a large production project.
  • We measured rule compliance, not whether the end user ended up better off.
  • The verifier was wrong on about 13% of audited verdicts, and the lake was audited by a model, without human review.
  • We tested only two models and nothing about aesthetics.

Want the data and method? Read the technical article.

The experiments, the data and the conclusions are mine. The writing was AI-assisted and reviewed by me.
