title: Cloudflare Offers 1,500 Connections. Your Database Needs a Budget.
description:
Cloudflare raised Hyperdrive’s limits on November 11: Workers Paid customers can configure up to 1,500 origin database connections per configuration, up from 100, and create up to 100 configurations per account, up from 25. The useful question is how much connection capacity your database can spare across all those configurations. The new maximum is a choice, not a throughput result.

This article was generated with AI assistance from public sources. The capacity example below is illustrative and does not describe a measured deployment.

The change gives larger workloads more room. It also gives a small application more room to overwhelm its own origin if every team sizes its pool independently. Start the decision at the database, with a budget shared by every caller.

One workflow can have several competing callers

The TMC Price Intelligence case study describes a delivered 2023–2025 engagement that connected supplier emails and attachments to structured pricing records, reviewable reports, quotes, and invoice workflows. Processing cost and operational usability were part of the work.

That is a useful workload shape for discussing capacity. Imports can arrive in batches while a person is trying to prepare a quote. A reporting task may run at the same time. Faster attachment processing has limited value if the person using the resulting records cannot get a responsive screen.

The public case study does not specify Hyperdrive or a relational connection-pool design. Consider the following as a proposed architecture exercise for a similar pricing system using a relational origin.

Suppose that database has a connection ceiling of 120. A first planning pass allocates 35 connections to an import path, 25 to interactive work, and 10 to reporting. That totals 70, leaving 50 for other clients and headroom.

Those numbers are invented. They are a starting allocation to investigate, not recommended settings or a claim that 70 connections will perform well. CPU, memory, query plans, and locks could constrain this fictional system long before it reaches 120.

The important artifact is the complete list of callers. Include direct application connections, scheduled jobs, administration tools, and any other pooling service. Two teams each staying below the database maximum can still exhaust it together.

The pool setting leaves room for surprises

Cloudflare’s pool tuning guide says to account for multiple configurations pointing at the same database. It also describes the origin connection limit as soft: network failures can lead Hyperdrive to establish additional connections for availability. Cloudflare recommends setting it below the origin’s limit.

So the budget needs a margin. A pool setting of 120 against an origin ceiling of 120 leaves no planned room for another client or a temporary overshoot. Treat the allocation as an operating plan that needs observation.

A separate reporting configuration can make ownership and tuning clearer, but it does not create more capacity in the shared database. Record which origin each configuration reaches. Give every allocation an owner who can explain when its workload runs and what happens when it waits.

That last question matters for the pricing example. It may be acceptable for a historical report to finish later. A staff member preparing a current quote may need a much shorter wait. Those priorities should influence application concurrency and scheduling as well as pool sizes.

Count how long a connection stays occupied

Hyperdrive uses transaction pooling: the connection is assigned for the transaction and returned when the transaction completes. That makes transaction boundaries an engineering decision worth reviewing before raising the ceiling.

In the proposed import path, avoid opening a transaction and holding it while an external model interprets an attachment. Prepare the candidate data first. Then use a short transaction to perform the database checks and writes that need to stay atomic. If preparation used an earlier database snapshot, recheck the relevant version or constraint before committing.

A rough occupancy calculation helps explain the stakes. At a steady 20 transactions per second, an average connection-holding time of two seconds implies about 40 occupied connections on average. At 0.05 seconds, it implies about one. This arithmetic ignores bursts and contention; it is not a sizing benchmark.

Both cases process the same count of transactions. The time spent holding a scarce connection changes the load. More available connections may help genuine parallel database work; they do little to justify holding a transaction during unrelated waiting.

Run the mixed workload before raising the number

For a staging exercise, replay synthetic imports while someone follows the quote-preparation path and a report runs. Observe transaction duration, pool wait, database load, failures, and time to finish the interactive task. Keep completed import throughput alongside those measures.

Increase one allocation at a time. If imports speed up while the quote screen stalls, the result gives you a scheduling or resource-sharing problem to solve. If the database is healthy and connection waiting dominates, a larger pool may be useful.

Cloudflare’s higher ceiling expands the configurations you can try. Choose the setting with evidence from the whole workflow, including the person who needs to use the data while the import is still running.

title: One-Sided Expert-Parallel All-to-All for Mixture-of-Experts Inference over NVLink
description:
arXiv:2611.13188v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Expert parallelism (EP) shards the experts of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layer across GPUs, so every MoE layer requires two all-to-all communications, namely dispatch and combine. Compared with training, inference processes relatively few tokens per GPU at a time, and at small batch sizes fixed costs that do not grow with the number of tokens, rather than data movement, dominate the latency. We present NVLinkOneSided, a one-sided EP all-to-all for GPUs within a single NVLink domain. Each source rank pushes its tokens, without first exchanging metadata, into rank-major buffers on the target GPUs, and the grouped GEMMs read them in place instead of from a per-expert copy. We provide two protocols for the synchronization that the communication requires, namely Fence and Sentinel, for high-throughput and low-latency scenarios respectively. On Blackwell GPUs, NVLinkOneSided completes dispatch and combine 1.2-3.0$\times$ faster than DeepEP, with the largest speedups at small batch sizes. The resulting MoE layer is up to 2.4$\times$ faster than DeepEP with DeepGEMM. It even outperforms the fused DeepGEMM MegaMoE at up to 128 tokens per GPU, making it still competitive for decoding. We expose NVLinkOneSided through a modular interface, so that it is agnostic to the activation quantization format, decoupled from the MoE compute backend and easy to integrate into inference frameworks.

title: Deep Personalization: Continuous Context Observation for Local Proactive Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.13457v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As AI agents become increasingly capable, users must still recognize when and how to ask for help, leaving many opportunities for useful support unrealized. Proactive agents hold the promise to close this gap, but effective proactivity requires understanding users' real-time activities and personalizing intervention timing so that assistance is offered when it is likely to be helpful rather than disruptive. We introduce deep personalization, a closed-loop process that connects continuous context observation with continual agent adaptation: an agent observes user activity, selectively retains long-term context, and adapts intervention decisions from implicit feedback. We initiate deep personalization in Coco, a proactive desktop agent, by having a separate Observer Agent that monitors desktop activity, maintains compact long-term user modeling context, and learns when assistance is desirable from implicit signals such as engagement, dismissal, explicit requests, and repeated work patterns. We further develop efficient on-device strategies to enable the Observer Agent to run on local AI compute platforms without streaming raw activity data off-device. For evaluation at scale without collecting sensitive real-user activity, we introduce a data-synthesis pipeline that transforms existing computer-use trajectories into OSWorld-Persona, a benchmark with persona-conditioned intervention labels. On OSWorld-Persona, deep personalization improves macro F1 across three model backbones from 0.12-0.19 under direct prompting to 0.35-0.48 after adaptation, a 2.4-3.0x relative gain. In a week-long user study, we observe that Coco improves its macro-averaged F1 score from 0.199 to 0.515. These results suggest that on-device deep personalization can make proactive agents more timely and increasingly aligned with each user's everyday work.

title: Margin-Guided Token Credit for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
description:
arXiv:2611.14015v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, a language model is rewarded for a correct final answer, and GRPO passes that reward to every token of the solution in equal measure. We instead place the credit where the model hesitated, in a method we call MCPO (Margin-Credit Policy Optimization). We measure hesitation by the top-2 margin $M=p_1-p_2$ of the policy's next-token distribution, map it to a score with two fixed thresholds, and spread each solution's advantage over its tokens so that the mean stays unchanged. The margin is read from a forward pass the trainer already performs, so the method needs no extra model evaluation and no batch statistics. We train MiniCPM5-2B-Base with LoRA for 200 steps on 2,048 DAPO-Math problems and evaluate on six competition-math benchmarks. MCPO beats an unmodified GRPO baseline for all five data seeds, by 6.55 points of macro avg@32 on average (95\% CI $[4.1, 9.0]$), and a Qwen3-4B-Base replication improves for all three seeds ($+4.75$). The gain is largest on problems that GRPO solves only some of the time and grows with $k$ in pass@$k$, reaching 13.8 points at pass@32. MCPO models also write two to three times longer answers, and runs that write longer score higher; our experiments do not separate the two effects.

title: Durable BlobStore Deletion Across Reopen and Index Loss
description:
AI disclosure: This article was produced through fully autonomous authorship by an AI agent using public sources and the reproducible artifacts linked below.

Affiliation: Thyn develops Telys, and this article was prepared by the team behind the fix. The comparison uses public packages and artifacts, but it is not independent third-party validation.

Deleting a key is not durable if reopening the store can make its value readable again. In telys 0.1.14, BlobStore could do exactly that after an ordinary put, delete, sync, close, and reopen. The live index said the key was gone, but the append-only slab still contained its payload without a deletion marker. Recovery could therefore reconstruct a value that the user had deleted.

Telys 0.1.15 changes the on-disk representation to preserve deletion history. This article walks through a credential-free reproduction of the baseline failure and the fix. Every count below comes from the published evidence, not from a benchmark or an inferred result.

Why a deleted key could return

A legacy TELYBB01 store has an append-only data.slab, an index.json snapshot, and sometimes an index.log mutation log. A put appends the key, metadata, and payload to the slab. In 0.1.14, however, a deletion only removed the key from the current index. The slab had no tombstone recording that deletion.

The first scenario reduces the problem to these operations in a fresh store:

store.put("last", b"durable-payload", {"revision": 1})
store.delete("last")
assert len(store) == 0
store.sync()
store.close()

reopened = BlobStore(path)
print(len(reopened), reopened.keys())
reopened.close()

Before sync(), both versions report zero keys, and the mutation log contains both the put and delete. After 0.1.14 syncs and closes, the snapshot correctly contains an empty records object and the log is absent. But reopening can recover by scanning the slab. Without a tombstone, that scan sees only the original put and resurrects last.

Version 0.1.15 uses TELYBB02, which can append a deletion tombstone to the slab. Recovery then encounters the deletion as part of the store’s history rather than relying solely on the latest snapshot.

Run the standalone reproduction

Download the standalone Python script or inspect the captured evidence JSON. After downloading the script to the path shown below, run exactly:

python3 /path/to/telys-blobstore-durable-deletes.py --output evidence.json

Use CPython 3.12.11 to match the recorded run. The captured host was macOS 27.0.1 on arm64, with sysconfig platform macosx-15.0-arm64. The script downloads each wheel from PyPI, verifies its size and SHA-256 against PyPI metadata, and checks that the installed blob.py matches the wheel. Each version runs in a fresh temporary virtual environment with isolated pip installation and a Python -I worker. Temporary environments, wheels, and stores are removed afterward.

This is a test of the pure Python SDK’s BlobStore. The runner loads telys/blob.py directly without executing telys/__init__.py. It installs with --no-deps because this module uses the standard library. No Telys runtime, runtime discovery, Mojo, login, credentials, or private artifacts are involved. Consequently, this is not a test of the full SDK or its optional NumPy, cryptography, and runtime integrations.

Public releases and fix provenance

The compared artifacts are public:

  • 0.1.14: PyPI release and telys-0.1.14-py3-none-any.whl, SHA-256 eed2191771235861d7d5b56f66fde6c205fa104ef254dfc86b48bf2aef383a98.
  • 0.1.15: PyPI release and telys-0.1.15-py3-none-any.whl, SHA-256 a13aca3993f034ad53163b8a7ac98e1fcc3be050a12e5f0c4cc8ad89050f498a.

The fix is public in thyn-ai/telys PR #209, merged at source commit 87dacc288760ce3315913296e9d817bf48f7e40c. The v0.1.15 release resolves to release commit 8c0714a4893b797cc8e28fee308167b310ac4db3. The script verifies package bytes, not GitHub provenance; those public PR, release, and commit records provide the separate source trail.

The four scenarios and exact results

1. Put, delete the last key, sync, close, reopen

Immediately after deletion, both versions have 0 keys. After reopening, 0.1.14 has 1 key, last; get("last") returns the 15-byte payload durable-payload with metadata {"revision": 1}. Version 0.1.15 has 0 keys, an empty key list, and get("last") raises KeyError("last"). The deletion now survives an ordinary reopen.

2. The same history followed by snapshot loss

This scenario repeats the first history, reopens and closes once, then removes index.json. Before removal, index.log is absent, so there is no mutation log left to explain the deletion. After snapshot loss, 0.1.14 again exposes 1 key, last, with durable-payload. Version 0.1.15 exposes 0 keys, and the get raises KeyError("last"). Its slab tombstone preserves the deletion even when neither index file remains.

3. Valid legacy migration followed by snapshot loss

The constructed TELYBB01 fixture contains 4 slab records: live=live-v1, overwritten=old-value, deleted=delete-me, and overwritten=new-value. Its valid snapshot contains only 2 keys, live and overwritten, representing the earlier deletion; no log exists.

On first open, both versions report those 2 keys, and deleted is absent. Version 0.1.14 leaves the slab as TELYBB01. Version 0.1.15 migrates it to TELYBB02, using the valid snapshot to materialize the missing deletion history. After index.json is removed, 0.1.14 reconstructs 3 keys: deleted, live, and overwritten. Version 0.1.15 reconstructs 2 keys: live and overwritten; deleted raises KeyError("deleted"). In both versions, overwritten still resolves to new-value, not the superseded payload.

4. Ambiguous legacy history without a snapshot or log

The fourth scenario uses the same 4-record legacy fixture but removes its snapshot before the first open. Version 0.1.14 opens and exposes 3 keys, including the supposedly deleted key. Version 0.1.15 does not open a store or expose any keys. It fails closed with BlobStoreError:

cannot recover a legacy TELYBB01 slab with records but no valid index snapshot; historical deletions are ambiguous

That refusal is necessary because the remaining records cannot reveal which keys a lost snapshot had deleted. Guessing would risk resurrection.

Compatibility and limits

The new tombstone is durable history, but it is also a format change. New TELYBB02 stores are not readable by old readers: 0.1.14 rejects the new magic rather than silently appending deletion-unaware records. Valid legacy stores can migrate; ambiguous legacy history fails closed instead of offering availability at the cost of uncertain deletion semantics.

The evidence has a deliberately narrow envelope:

  • It covers only the recorded CPython 3.12.11, macOS, arm64 environment, not other operating systems or architectures.
  • Legacy stores are deterministic, constructed fixtures based on the public formats, not captured production datasets.
  • Removing a snapshot after an orderly close models index loss. It does not simulate power loss, kernel crashes, or partial writes, and it does not prove hardware fsync behavior.
  • There is no NFS, multiwriter, concurrency, or performance benchmark. No throughput or latency claim follows from these results.
  • The direct, dependency-free BlobStore test does not validate the full SDK, optional runtime, or Mojo integrations.

Within that envelope, the four scenarios establish a specific correctness result: 0.1.15 preserves tested deletions across reopen and snapshot loss, migrates valid legacy history, and refuses recovery when deletion history cannot be known.

title: Semantic Chains: From Reachable Facts to Justified Answers
description:
arXiv:2611.14252v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How can the facts that justify an answer be found from a question and presented as a sequence of connected statements? This paper models a context as a graph of logical facts and takes as given which expressions represent each fact. A parent fact can express a relation among its subfacts, and a preserving edge allows the content of a subfact to be recovered within a full representation of its parent. Suppose a root fact justifies the full answer and a path of preserving edges leads from that root to a fact that designates an object shared by the question and the answer. Under the conditions of the model, a search starting from the objects in the question reaches the root and covers every fact in the selected expansion. The root then admits a text that forms a single link connecting the question to the full answer and justifying it. For chains with several links, the paper gives a complete enumeration of candidate orders within the stated class and specifies when the link texts jointly preserve the justification and support every transition.

title: Megrez: A Knowledge-Guided Agent for Formal Mathematics over MK Set Theory
description:
arXiv:2611.13613v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: General-purpose coding agents equipped with proof-assistant tools have shown strong performance on standalone competition problems, yet cumulative textbook formalization inside a low-resource mathematical library still faces three obstacles: aligning textbook concepts with library declarations, keeping long-horizon search synchronized with live proof states, and integrating locally verified proofs reliably into a growing codebase. We present Megrez, a knowledge-guided formalization agent for Rocq libraries built on Morse--Kelley (MK) set theory. Megrez coordinates a general coding agent through three mechanisms: (1) a source-rebuildable knowledge graph merging formal declarations, compiler references, and curated metadata to support retrieval via Chinese aliases, concept clusters, proof dependencies, and multi-lane full-text ranking; (2) a feedback-driven 1--5 tactic short-burst proving loop paired with a goal-local branch ledger and exponential-interval structured reflection; and (3) a three-check acceptance pipeline (statement fidelity, axiom auditing, and full builds) coupled with a multi-corpus Provider stack and a candidate-bound recoverable batch state machine. Deployment and evaluation on a point-set topology corpus demonstrate effective cross-chapter formalization and scalable premise retrieval.

title: khammoon: From a Linguistic Guideline to a Thai Morpheme Segmenter
description:
arXiv:2611.13012v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Thai is written without spaces between words, making segmentation a foundational step in most Thai NLP pipelines. Existing tools primarily reproduce the word-level conventions of corpora such as BEST; however, because the notion of a "word" in Thai lacks a unified linguistic consensus, these conventions struggle with productive compounding, leading to arbitrary boundaries and ambiguity in downstream representations. Instead, we propose operating at the morphological level, focusing on khammoon, the smallest atomic unit that carries meaning. Segmenting at the morphemic level provides an explicit, consistent morphological representation that eliminates compounding ambiguity. Crucially, this representation benefits downstream learning: models trained on morphemes perform on par with or exceed word-level baselines across part-of-speech tagging, named-entity recognition, and sentiment classification, demonstrating that linguistic consistency improves representation quality without downstream performance penalty. To operationalize this representation, we translate linguistic principles into a formal decision guideline with near-perfect human agreement ($\kappa \approx 0.99$), scale annotation with an LLM, and correct systematic errors with human labels. Finally, we train khammoon, a lightweight 1M-parameter convolutional BiLSTM segmenter designed for efficient CPU inference, achieving a boundary F1 of 0.992 on out-of-domain text. The guideline, datasets, model, and library are all publicly released.

title: Reinforcement Learning based control of Cancer Chemotherapy treatments
description:
arXiv:2611.12940v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement Learning has achieved tremendous success in recent years. Extending its scope from the traditional complex games such as Atari, Go, Pokeman, and Chess, reinforcement learning has caught researchers' attention on modelling real-life scenarios. Personalized medicine and the dynamic treatment regimen are two such preliminary research fields; researchers are focusing their mindsets currently. Estimating the optimal dynamic treatment regimens from the observational real clinical data is being popularized among the researchers, widening its scope towards more advanced versions of reinforcement learning algorithms.
  This research is about a research study that focused on reinforcement learning techniques that have been approached in the context of cancer chemotherapy treatments. Primarily this thesis addresses the result of the study by means of the state-of-the-art on reinforcement learning techniques used in generating the optimal policy for sequential treatments, including the existing online reinforcement learning approaches. Thereby a simulation for cancer chemotherapy via traditional Q-learning would be presented. Secondly, the study will extend towards using offline reinforcement learning in the optimal policy generation. Thus, the proposed solution follows a data-driven approach, which works on the real human colon cancer clinical data.
  The novelty of the proposed solution resides in the implementation of an offline reinforcement learning approach by means of a model-based architecture using the conservative Q-learning and the model-based offline policy optimization algorithm. As per the experimental results and the evaluations, it was revealed that the proposed Chemo RL model caters well the problem of cancer chemotherapy treatment scheduling and serves as a supportive model for the junior oncologists in deciding their treatment decisions.

title: I Built an Open-Source Tool to Test What Happens When MCP Servers Fail
description:
I've been spending a lot of time exploring MCP servers and AI agents lately.

One thing that caught my attention: we spend a lot of time testing whether tools work, but what about when they don't?

What happens when an MCP tool crashes? When it receives invalid arguments? When a protected endpoint receives an unauthorized request?

And more importantly, does the server actually report those failures correctly?

That's what led me to build MCP Verdict.

The problem

Imagine an MCP tool fails internally but returns something like this:

{
  "isError": false,
  "content": [
    {
      "type": "text",
      "text": "Operation failed"
    }
  ]
}

The message says the operation failed, but the MCP response reports success.

That inconsistency can cause problems for clients and agents relying on the tool's result.

And it's exactly the kind of behavior that's worth testing before deploying an MCP server.

Introducing MCP Verdict

MCP Verdict is an open-source Python CLI that lets developers define expected MCP server behavior and check what actually happens.

Instead of writing separate scripts for every failure scenario, you describe your expectations in YAML.

For example:

server:
  command:
    - python
    - examples/basic_stdio/server.py

tool:
  name: ping
  arguments: {}

expected: success

Then run:

mcp-verdict check --config verdict.yaml

MCP Verdict connects to the server, executes the tool, and checks whether the actual result matches your expectation.

What it supports

The first release includes:

  • STDIO and Streamable HTTP — Test real MCP servers using the official Python SDK.
  • Tool outcome checks — Verify success and expected tool errors using MCP's isError field.
  • HTTP security checks — Test selected authentication and authorization responses, including HTTP 401 and 403.
  • YAML configuration — Define repeatable checks with configurable timeouts.
  • JSON reporting — Generate structured results for automated workflows.
  • CI-friendly exit codes — Distinguish PASS, FAIL, and execution ERROR.

Testing incorrect error reporting

Here's another example.

Suppose a tool is expected to return an MCP tool error, but instead reports success.

MCP Verdict can detect that mismatch:

known-failure: FAIL: Expected tool_error, observed success
Summary: 0 passed, 1 failed

This is the behavior I find most interesting: testing not just whether an MCP tool works, but whether it fails correctly.

Try it

MCP Verdict v0.1.0 is now available on PyPI.

Requires Python 3.11 or 3.12.

pip install mcp-verdict

Verify the installation:

mcp-verdict --help

For runnable examples, clone the repository:

git clone https://github.com/kuruash/mcp-verdict.git
cd mcp-verdict
mcp-verdict check --config examples/basic_stdio/verdict.yaml

The repository also includes calculator, intentional error-handling, and local HTTP security examples.

What I learned

Building this made me appreciate how much work goes into handling the unhappy paths of software.

Connecting to a server is one thing. Handling timeouts, unexpected disconnects, malformed responses, authentication failures, and cleanup reliably is a different challenge.

I also learned a lot about Python packaging, GitHub Actions, testing with real subprocesses, and publishing through PyPI Trusted Publishing.

There's still plenty to improve. MCP Verdict isn't a comprehensive MCP security scanner, and it doesn't attempt to audit arbitrary OAuth/JWT implementations.

For now, the goal is simple: make failure scenarios reproducible and help developers catch regressions.

I'd love some feedback

If you're building or maintaining MCP servers, I'd love to know:

What's the most frustrating failure scenario you've encountered while testing an MCP server?

I'm especially interested in edge cases that MCP Verdict doesn't handle yet.

GitHub: https://github.com/kuruash/mcp-verdict

PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/mcp-verdict/

Issues, feedback, and contributions are welcome!

title: ChipOmni: A General-Purpose AI Agent for Electronic Design Automation
description:
arXiv:2611.13020v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Electronic design automation (EDA) workflows remain highly fragmented, requiring engineers to coordinate heterogeneous representations, specialised software tools, and iterative verification across multiple design stages. Although large language models have brought more general reasoning and code-generation capabilities to EDA, many existing approaches remain focused on isolated tasks and struggle to plan, verify, and repair designs autonomously within executable engineering environments. Here we introduce ChipOmni, a knowledge-enhanced, context-evolving AI agent framework for EDA. ChipOmni integrates multimodal understanding, dynamic planning, multi-agent collaboration, and verification-driven tool interaction into a unified autonomous system. By continually incorporating feedback from external engineering tools, the framework maintains an evolving task context, integrates domain knowledge, and iteratively refines intermediate designs. Across benchmarks for analog circuit, RTL, testbench, and formal-assertion generation, ChipOmni improves multiple task-specific measures over the evaluated baselines and solves all 30 AnalogCoder-Pro tasks. In a long-horizon case study, ChipOmni advances a natural-language RISC-V specification through three design levels to a micro-SoC GDSII layout that passes physical sign-off, without human intervention after initialization. Together, these results show that ChipOmni can coordinate verification-driven design across heterogeneous tasks and sustain long-horizon engineering workflows, advancing a shift from fragmented, tool-centred processes towards agent-centred, closed-loop systems.

title: Joint Quantization and Dynamic Partitioning for Context-Aware Edge Vision Transformers
description:
arXiv:2611.14196v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deploying vision transformer models across connected and automated vehicles (CAVs) requires joint management of computation and Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) communication. Static split-inference methods use fixed partition points and cannot adapt to time-varying link bandwidth, processing load, and concurrent multi-stream traffic. This paper proposes an edge orchestration framework that jointly selects model partition points, per-layer quantization bitwidths, and execution placement across heterogeneous vehicular compute nodes. The joint partitioning and mixed-precision allocation problem is formulated as a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP) that minimizes compute and communication energy subject to end-to-end latency and task-quality constraints. The framework is evaluated on Jetson Orin Nano (8~GB), Jetson Orin NX (16~GB), and Jetson AGX Orin (32~GB) nodes using OPV2V-driven multi-stream workloads with $K \in \{2,4,6,8\}$. Across the evaluated configurations, the proposed formulation reduces V2V communication energy by $33.3$--$36.0\%$ relative to a Uniform INT8 split. At $K=8$, end-to-end task completion latency is reduced by $34.0\%$ on the Orin Nano and $33.1\%$ on the Orin NX relative to the same baseline, while limiting the reduction in 3D detection accuracy to $3.1$--$4.1$ percentage points in $\mathrm{mAP}_{50}$ relative to FP16 execution.

title: Towards Reliable VLM Judges: State-Conditional Invariance and Presentation-Aware Diagnostics
description:
arXiv:2611.13596v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as automated judges for multimodal and embodied tasks, yet aggregate accuracy or consistency alone does not reveal whether a judge changes its verdict for the right reason. We propose State-Conditional Invariance (SCI), a reliability principle requiring a judge to remain stable under semantics-preserving changes in presentation while responding to causal interventions that change the task outcome. We instantiate SCI in GridWM-Judge, a simulator-grounded diagnostic benchmark built from deterministic MiniGrid trajectories with aligned Full, evidence-removal, and counterfactual variants, plus presentation and representation probes. Across five diagnostic tasks, GridWM-Judge tests local perception, action-conditioned transitions, presentation stability, representation exchangeability, and Full-CF causal discrimination. Our diagnostic evaluations reveal heterogeneous failure modes, including sensitivity to evidence presentation and encoding, low activation on successful trajectories, and weak paired counterfactual discrimination. Perception-controlled analyses further indicate that visual grounding and objective recovery are substantial, model-dependent bottlenecks. These results motivate jointly reporting correctness, presentation stability, and causal sensitivity instead of relying on a single score.

title: Property Import Feature Flags: 2026 Trade-offs Between Free Tools and Paid Control
description:
Short answer: choose free tools when the team can operate and restore the control plane; choose paid control when delegated operations are worth the dependency, but in either case persist each flag decision beside the import run so rollback evidence survives.

A flag system is suitable for scheduled property imports only when its decision is observable and its rollback is boring. The useful comparison is not a free-versus-paid feature checklist; it is the boundary between a control plane that can be restored and an application path that can explain what happened.

For a property-management SaaS, I would require four invariants: an import run has a durable identity, every flag decision is attributable to a version and subject, an empty result is distinguishable from a successful empty dataset, and disabling a rollout cannot erase the evidence needed for reconciliation. Those rules matter more than the billing model.

What must remain true when an import goes quiet

A nightly lease or unit import can stop producing records while the scheduler itself continues to report success. A flag may have disabled the fetch, selected an empty tenant scope, or routed the worker to a new parser. The alert should describe that boundary rather than merely say that a process is alive.

The import record is therefore the primary object, and flag evaluation is an input to it. Store an immutable run ID, tenant ID, source cursor or watermark, flag-set version, evaluation reason, start time, finish time, record count, and terminal status. Do not put raw lease data into a flag context just to make a diagnostic query convenient. Logging guidance from OWASP treats sensitive data handling as a design concern, and property data deserves the same restraint.

A useful status model has more than success and failure:

  • completed_nonempty: records were accepted.
  • completed_empty: the source validly returned no records.
  • skipped_by_flag: the control intentionally prevented work.
  • failed_after_start: the worker began and could not finish.
  • missing_heartbeat: no terminal record arrived within the schedule's expectation.

The alert policy can then ask a precise question: did a run cross its expected completion window without a terminal status, or did it complete empty when the tenant's normal contract says that is suspicious? That is a rollback decision, not a dashboard decoration.

How do free tools and paid feature flags compare for rollback?

There are two broad choices: operate the flag evaluation and storage yourself, or use a managed control plane while keeping run evidence in your own system. Both can work. The deciding question is what remains available during a bad deployment, a control-plane outage, or a mistaken flag update.

Decision boundary Self-hosted flag service Managed flag service
Evaluation during control-plane loss Requires a tested local cache or embedded snapshot Requires a tested SDK cache or snapshot policy
Rollback authority Internal operators own storage, access, and procedure Provider supplies the control surface; the team owns its emergency path
Audit evidence Team must retain change records and evaluation metadata Team must export or independently persist the evidence it needs
Operational burden Patching, capacity, backups, and access controls are internal work Service operations are delegated, while integration and policy remain internal
Exit test Restore the snapshot and replay decisions locally Prove the application can run from a known-good snapshot without live calls

This is not a ranking. A small team may reasonably delegate control-plane operations, while a regulated environment may prefer tighter ownership of the storage and restore procedure. The non-negotiable part is the same: a flag lookup must not be the only copy of the decision that affected a financial or operational record.

The free-versus-paid distinction usually changes who carries operational work and which managed capabilities are available; it does not remove the need for local evidence. A self-hosted deployment can still fail its rollback test. A paid service can still leave an import unexplained if the application records only the final row count. The limitation of the self-hosted choice is operational ownership; the limitation of the managed choice is dependency on its availability and export boundary. Neither option is a fit for a team unwilling to test restoration.

How should a worker record a flag decision?

Keep the critical path small. Evaluate once for a run, persist the result before doing source work, and emit a structured completion event after the terminal state is known. The example uses generic interfaces so the rollback behavior is visible without binding the design to a product.

package importer

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Decision struct {
    Enabled bool
    Version string
    Reason  string
}

type Run struct {
    ID          string
    TenantID    string
    FlagVersion string
    FlagReason  string
    Status      string
    RecordCount int
    StartedAt   time.Time
    FinishedAt  time.Time
}

type Flags interface {
    Evaluate(ctx context.Context, tenantID, key string) (Decision, error)
}

type Runs interface {
    Create(ctx context.Context, run Run) error
    Finish(ctx context.Context, run Run) error
}

func Import(ctx context.Context, flags Flags, runs Runs, tenantID string, now time.Time) error {
    decision, err := flags.Evaluate(ctx, tenantID, "property-import-v2")
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("evaluate import flag: %w", err)
    }

    run := Run{
        ID:          newRunID(),
        TenantID:    tenantID,
        FlagVersion: decision.Version,
        FlagReason:  decision.Reason,
        StartedAt:   now,
        Status:      "started",
    }
    if err := runs.Create(ctx, run); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("create import run: %w", err)
    }

    if !decision.Enabled {
        run.Status = "skipped_by_flag"
        run.FinishedAt = time.Now().UTC()
        return runs.Finish(ctx, run)
    }

    count, err := fetchAndPersist(ctx, tenantID, run.ID)
    if err != nil {
        run.Status = "failed_after_start"
        run.FinishedAt = time.Now().UTC()
        _ = runs.Finish(ctx, run)
        return fmt.Errorf("import run %s: %w", run.ID, err)
    }

    run.RecordCount = count
    run.Status = "completed_nonempty"
    if count == 0 {
        run.Status = "completed_empty"
    }
    run.FinishedAt = time.Now().UTC()
    return runs.Finish(ctx, run)
}

The persistence boundary is deliberate. If the worker crashes after creating started but before finishing, a separate watchdog can classify the run as missing a heartbeat after the schedule-specific deadline. If it crashes after writing imported rows, the run ID and idempotency key let reconciliation distinguish a retry from a second business event. Exactly-once processing is an aspiration at the orchestration layer; the durable key and idempotent writes are what make retries safe.

The example uses a simple newRunID and generic storage methods because the important contract is the ordering. In production, make the run creation and the import's idempotency record compatible with the database transaction model. Do not claim completion when only the scheduler callback completed.

What should the alert contain?

An alert for a silent import should be actionable without exposing tenant records. Include the tenant identifier or an approved surrogate, schedule name, run ID, last terminal status, expected deadline, flag key, flag-set version, evaluation reason, and a link to the audit record. Exclude access tokens, source payloads, lease terms, and full property addresses. OpenTelemetry describes logs as a signal that can carry structured attributes and correlate with other telemetry; use that correlation to join the run, worker trace, and alert without copying sensitive business data into every event.

A useful event might look like this:

{
  "event": "property_import_terminal",
  "run_id": "run_01JEXAMPLE",
  "tenant_ref": "tenant_742",
  "status": "completed_empty",
  "record_count": 0,
  "flag_key": "property-import-v2",
  "flag_version": "cfg-18",
  "flag_reason": "tenant_allowlist",
  "trace_id": "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736"
}

The exact attribute names are less important than stable semantics and a retention policy. Audit trails should answer who changed the control, what version was evaluated, which run consumed it, and what terminal result followed. They should not become a second source database.

Why not let the scheduler own the truth?

A scheduler heartbeat is a valid signal for worker liveness, but it is a poor substitute for import completion. The scheduler can enqueue a job successfully while the job is blocked on a flag, waiting on an upstream source, or failing before it writes its terminal record. Treating enqueue success as business success creates a false green path that rollback cannot repair.

The rejected design is a single dashboard metric such as imports_completed_total, with a flag state inspected only during an incident. It is cheap to start and useful for a low-risk prototype, but it loses the decision version and cannot tell an empty result from a skipped run. It becomes valid when the job has no tenant-specific consequences, the source is naturally idempotent, and the team has accepted that post-hoc explanation is unnecessary. Property imports usually do not meet that bar.

Test the failure boundaries, not only the happy path: restore an old flag snapshot, kill a worker after Create, deliver the same source page twice, return a valid empty source response, and revoke control-plane connectivity. Each test should leave a predictable run state and a reconciliation record. The rollback is complete only when the next import can be evaluated from the known-good state and the previous decision remains auditable.

The practical comparison is therefore architectural. Choose the control-plane arrangement that your team can restore, observe, and explain; then keep import evidence independent enough that a flag change cannot rewrite history.

References

  • OpenTelemetry, “Logs: Concepts”: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • OWASP, “Logging Cheat Sheet”: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html

title: Personalized Affective Perception via Continual Learning in Human-Agent Negotiation
description:
arXiv:2611.14247v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-interested intelligent agents that negotiate with humans should interpret nonverbal expressions and adapt their behavior accordingly. However, generic facial-affect models degrade across individuals and contexts, creating a generalization gap. We introduce an affect-adaptive negotiation strategy that incorporates Continual Learning with Imagination for Facial Expression Recognition (CLIFER) to personalize valence-arousal perception in real time. Differential feedback converts changes in valence-arousal direction and intensity into adjustments of the agent's target utility. An asynchronous architecture updates CLIFER in the background during live interaction. In a counterbalanced within-subject study in which 66 participants negotiated with a humanoid robot, the CL-enabled agent achieved significantly higher individual utility and elicited higher participant concession rates than the FaceChannel baseline. The CL condition yielded significantly higher mean arousal estimates, alongside a broader output range. Participant utility and Nash distance did not change significantly between conditions. These outcomes support the practical value of coupling continual affective personalization with differential feedback for real-time negotiation.

title: Go Archive Previews — 4 Copy Boundaries for Images and PDF Viewers
description:
Use cached page images for the media archive's result lists and an embedded PDF viewer for document detail, with the archive team owning the presentation template and the deletion policy for every derivative.

TL;DR: Converting a page to an image gives a fast, cacheable, lossy preview; embedding a PDF viewer preserves the document more faithfully but puts a heavier rendering path in front of the reader. Neither choice establishes where a scanned document may be processed or how long its copies may survive. Decide those boundaries before sending an unpublished source document anywhere.

What page fired when the archive became searchable?

Start a postmortem with that question. A green conversion dashboard is poor evidence that a newsroom can safely retrieve a scanned source document, inspect its original page, and subsequently remove the document and its derivatives when required. The useful signals belong to the reader's task: an unavailable detail document, a thumbnail that represents the wrong revision, or an old preview still accessible after withdrawal. These are proposed checks, not a report of an observed incident.

Count the copies.

For this workflow, treat the scan, searchable OCR text, page image, and search-index entry as four distinct artifacts. The number describes the proposed design, not a provider limit. A successful OCR operation doesn't prove that an image preview has been invalidated; a refreshed thumbnail doesn't prove that an old text extract has disappeared from search. Each artifact needs a document revision and an accountable owner, because deletion crosses more boundaries than generation.

The primary ownership decision is who controls the archive's display template: the list card, page selection, caption, access check, and link to the authoritative document. Keep that template in the archive application. A conversion service can supply a derivative without becoming the owner of the newsroom's presentation rules, and an embedded viewer can display the source without defining which excerpts belong in search results.

For teams that can approve an external processor, try Infrai for the storage-to-page-conversion handoff, because its public, self-describing discovery surface supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples without requiring a key just to inspect the contract. Its storage and document-processing capabilities also share one API key, removing a second credential integration from that particular seam. That is a concrete reason to evaluate it; region, retention, deletion, and the downstream processor still need approval before a source scan enters the workflow.

Should you convert a page to an image or embed a PDF viewer?

A list of search results should not initialize a PDF renderer for every thumbnail. Render page images ahead of retrieval, cache them, and invalidate them with the document revision. Reserve the PDF viewer for the detail page, where a reader has actually chosen a document and the extra rendering work has a purpose. Desktop browsers often provide native PDF viewing, so assess that existing path before adding another viewer dependency.

Images lose information.

A page image is a visual derivative, not searchable OCR text and not the authoritative PDF. The archive should retain the relationship between all three, rather than treating an attractive thumbnail as proof that a scanned name, caption, or page has become searchable. Verification must separately inspect OCR output and the detail document. No preview architecture can establish OCR accuracy merely by displaying a page.

Candidate Where to evaluate it Ownership and trust question that decides the fit
Native browser PDF viewer Detail-page inspection of the original PDF Can the archive authorize access to the source and accept the browser's viewer presentation? Native desktop support can avoid another renderer dependency.
AWS S3 plus Cloudinary Separate storage and image-delivery components Can the team own the handoff, keep the archive template independent, and approve both processing boundaries? Validate the required PDF-to-image behavior before selection.
AWS S3 plus imgix A separate storage and image-serving arrangement Does its documented source and PDF support fit the archive, and can the team reconcile its URL authorization with the storage access policy?
Infrai Storage access followed by document conversion through one API Can the approved boundary include the selected processor, while the archive retains template, revision, and derivative-lifecycle ownership?

There are also document-focused alternatives worth evaluating rather than pretending an image-serving stack covers the whole job. Gotenberg belongs on the shortlist when the team wants to operate its own document-conversion service and accept responsibility for its processing boundary. WeasyPrint is a candidate for a team-owned HTML/CSS-to-PDF presentation template; evaluate it for generated archive cover sheets rather than assuming it supplies scanned-page OCR. DocRaptor is a hosted document-generation alternative when the team prefers a service relationship for template rendering and can approve that external processor. None should be selected for this scanned-document preview workflow without separately verifying the required input formats, OCR path, and deletion terms. Template generation and preview conversion are different acceptance tests.

These are architectural candidates, not a claim that every option supplies interchangeable OCR, document rendering, or retention controls. Cloudinary and imgix deserve their own document-format evaluation; S3 is the storage component in the alternative stacks, not an OCR engine. A specialist OCR provider is the better choice when searchable extraction quality or required processing terms decide acceptance, and a direct provider arrangement is preferable when the necessary contractual boundary can only be established there.

The separate S3-plus-Cloudinary or S3-plus-imgix design involves two service relationships, two credential configurations, and application glue connecting a private source to the image-processing side. The work includes deciding who signs which URL, where expiration is checked, and how a document revision revokes its descendants. A shared API key reduces that integration work; it does not remove the underlying data-processing relationships. The combined approach means one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface.

Put authorization ahead of the conversion handoff

Before implementation, write the processing record in terms that a responder can use: permitted region, processor identity, retention for source and derivatives, deletion responsibility, and the evidence that closes a deletion request. Discovery can describe capabilities and expose region and vendor information; that information must be reconciled with the actual service agreement and deployment configuration. An API description is not a retention commitment.

Keep source objects private or signed-only. A presigned URL should grant only the access needed for the operation, and its lifetime must fit both the processing window and the archive's exposure policy. Do not forward the API bearer credential to that returned URL. Treat it as a separate bearer capability, avoid logging it, and distinguish expiration of access from deletion of the object.

The following Go program demonstrates the narrow handoff: request a storage presign, select the signed URL from that response, and place it into a document-conversion request. Both authenticated requests use the same base URL and key. It deliberately accepts request documents and a response JSON pointer from the operator, because the selected capability's discovered schemas determine the actual parameter names; guessing a convenient field name is a bad way to build a runbook.

Save it as main.go. Set INFRAI_API_KEY, ARCHIVE_BUCKET, and ARCHIVE_KEY; prepare presign.json and convert.json against the discovered schemas. In the conversion request, put the literal string SIGNED_URL_FROM_STORAGE at the schema-defined input location. Run go run main.go presign.json convert.json /the/actual/url/member, replacing the final argument with the JSON pointer to the signed URL in the documented response. Those filenames are local operator inputs, not an asserted API schema.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

func must(err error) {
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

func request(client *http.Client, key, path string, body []byte, id string) []byte {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, baseURL+path, bytes.NewReader(body))
        must(err)
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", id)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        must(err)
        data, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 8<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        must(err)
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if wait := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            } else if until, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
                if wait := time.Until(until); wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("API status %d; inspect the response securely", resp.StatusCode))
        }
        return data
    }
    panic("retry limit reached")
}

func readJSON(name string) any {
    data, err := os.ReadFile(name)
    must(err)
    var value any
    must(json.Unmarshal(data, &value))
    return value
}

func replace(value any, signed string) (any, int) {
    count := 0
    switch v := value.(type) {
    case string:
        if v == "SIGNED_URL_FROM_STORAGE" {
            return signed, 1
        }
    case []any:
        for i := range v {
            var n int
            v[i], n = replace(v[i], signed)
            count += n
        }
    case map[string]any:
        for k := range v {
            var n int
            v[k], n = replace(v[k], signed)
            count += n
        }
    }
    return value, count
}

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 4 {
        panic("usage: go run main.go presign.json convert.json /response/json/pointer")
    }
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    bucket, object := os.Getenv("ARCHIVE_BUCKET"), os.Getenv("ARCHIVE_KEY")
    if key == "" || bucket == "" || object == "" {
        panic("set INFRAI_API_KEY, ARCHIVE_BUCKET, and ARCHIVE_KEY")
    }
    pointer := os.Args[3]
    if !strings.HasPrefix(pointer, "/") {
        panic("use a nonempty JSON pointer")
    }
    presign := readJSON(os.Args[1])
    conversion := readJSON(os.Args[2])
    body, err := json.Marshal(presign)
    must(err)
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 60 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(_ *http.Request, _ []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    runID := strconv.FormatInt(time.Now().UnixNano(), 10)
    path := "/storage/object/presign/" + url.PathEscape(bucket) + "/" + url.PathEscape(object)
    data := request(client, key, path, body, runID+"-presign")
    var selected any
    must(json.Unmarshal(data, &selected))
    for _, segment := range strings.Split(pointer[1:], "/") {
        segment = strings.ReplaceAll(strings.ReplaceAll(segment, "~1", "/"), "~0", "~")
        switch node := selected.(type) {
        case map[string]any:
            selected = node[segment]
        case []any:
            index, err := strconv.Atoi(segment)
            must(err)
            if index < 0 || index >= len(node) {
                panic("JSON pointer index out of range")
            }
            selected = node[index]
        default:
            panic("JSON pointer does not resolve")
        }
    }
    signed, ok := selected.(string)
    if !ok {
        panic("selected response member must be a URL string")
    }
    parsed, err := url.Parse(signed)
    must(err)
    if parsed.Scheme != "https" || parsed.Host == "" {
        panic("expected an HTTPS presigned URL")
    }
    conversion, count := replace(conversion, signed)
    if count != 1 {
        panic("conversion input must contain exactly one signed URL marker")
    }
    body, err = json.Marshal(conversion)
    must(err)
    _ = request(client, key, "/pdf/convert", body, runID+"-convert")
    fmt.Println("Conversion request accepted; verify completion against its documented response.")
}

This program does not download the signed URL, so it never sends the API authorization header to the storage destination. It retries rate limits with exponential delay and honors a longer Retry-After, while keeping the same idempotency key for each request's retries. The key covers retries within this invocation; a production worker should persist its operation identity across restarts, tied to the document revision and transformation, rather than generating a fresh identity on redelivery.

There is a deliberate observability trade-off here: response bodies may contain sensitive data, so failures report the status rather than echoing a document URL into terminal logs. In production, retain the real error response in an approved restricted diagnostic path and surface a safe correlation reference to the responder. Also validate conversion completion and output against the discovered response contract; an accepted request alone is not evidence of a usable thumbnail.

Verify the reader's path, then rehearse withdrawal

Use a synthetic scan with a harmless archive caption, such as “Harbor desk, page 2,” to test the complete path before approving real material. Confirm that OCR makes the caption retrievable, that the result card uses the intended document revision, and that opening detail displays the original PDF. Inspect network activity: a list should fetch preview images rather than initialize a PDF renderer for every row. These are acceptance checks, not performance measurements.

Then replace that scan.

The new revision must invalidate the old preview and search entry under the archive's policy. Exercise withdrawal separately: stop new access, remove the index entry and derivatives, perform source deletion through the approved storage process, and collect the processor-side evidence required by the retention agreement. A signed URL expiring during this rehearsal proves only that one access token expired. It does not demonstrate that a conversion copy, cached image, or OCR extract was deleted.

The page should fire on a reader-visible breach of the intended behavior, with enough context to distinguish authorization failure, conversion failure, stale revision, and missing source. Avoid dumping document contents into alerts. A dashboard that says “jobs completed” cannot settle any of those questions.

Roll back without widening access

If image conversion fails the acceptance checks, disable thumbnail publication and show a neutral placeholder while preserving authorized access to document detail. Keep the previous template version available for rollback, but never use that rollback to restore a withdrawn scan or its derivatives.

If the processing boundary itself is unacceptable, stop sending new documents and use the approved specialist or local processing path; changing the preview component cannot repair a retention agreement. Keep ownership of the archive template and lifecycle record with the archive team, because that is what makes a provider change possible without guessing which copies remain.

References

  • ISO PDF specification
  • Amazon S3 presigned URL documentation
  • Cloudinary image transformation documentation
  • imgix rendering API documentation
  • Gotenberg documentation
  • WeasyPrint documentation
  • DocRaptor documentation

If this storage-to-conversion boundary fits your archive, inspect the schemas and runnable examples in the Infrai documentation before sending a source document.

title: Multimodal Judges Flag, Humans Decide: A Review-and-Edit Framework for AI-Generated Product Video Ads
description:
arXiv:2611.13178v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative pipelines can now turn every product page of an e-commerce catalog into a short video ad, but deciding whether such an ad is usable is not one good-or-bad call. We describe how we operationalized the review and editing of these ads so that both can keep pace with generation: reviewers go through each ad scene by scene and answer six questions, on the product, scene quality, pronunciation, script, sound and captions; judges built from vision-language, speech and language models file each finding under the matching question, and reviewers accept or reject each finding and add what the judges missed. Each confirmed issue then opens an edit tool matched to it. The questions and the routing from a finding to its fix do not depend on the models that generate the ad. Across 120 ads from our pipeline, reviewed with judge findings on screen, reviewers marked the product wrong on 60% of scenes, and script, caption or sound problems on under 10% each. On 60 of these ads, they marked the product wrong on 58% of scenes, far more than the 26% marked by two reviewers who later saw the ads with the judges hidden; one reviewer who saw the ads both ways marked 57% with judge findings and 19% without. On 120 blind-labeled scenes, a product judge that watches the clip with the catalog photos reached AUC 0.84, while video-quality and photo-similarity scores were close to chance. We tune the judges for recall: the product judge catches nearly all defects but also flags many clean scenes, so reviewers decide; together, the judges widen what reviewers mark and reviewers add what the judges miss. Without judge findings, one reviewer's marking faded over a session. We release a review-portal template and our review data (120 ads and 562 scenes with judge findings and human marks, plus 120 blind-labeled scenes with baseline scores) at https://github.com/anoubhav/ad-review-and-edit.

title: Off-target posterior mass: A training-free diagnostic for fine-tuning spoken language diarization probes
description:
arXiv:2611.13430v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Spoken Language Diarization (SLD) models provide frame-level language information of a speech recording. SLD modeling pipeline includes feature extraction from pre-trained speech models followed by clustering. Fine-tuning pre-trained speech models has shown performance gains for SLD with its magnitude being dataset dependent. Off-target Posterior Mass (OTPM), computed based on posterior language identification probabilities is proposed as a diagnostic metric to forecast performance gains from SLD fine-tuning. OTPM obtains positive correlation with probe gains, 0.56 on unseen synthetic bilingual data and 0.23 on real-world corpora. These results indicate promising potential of OTPM as a diagnostic metric for SLD.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks: Methods, Frameworks, and Perspectives
description:
arXiv:2611.13868v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep neural networks underpin fundamental tasks in a wide range of signal domains, such as image, audio, and language processing. However, their internal mechanisms are notably difficult to interpret. Internal activations are structured signals transformed across layers that may encode a multitude of interdependent relationships, as individual neurons frequently represent multiple underlying concepts. Mechanistic interpretability aims to uncover the internal mechanisms of neural networks by identifying components whose activations are causally responsible for specific behaviors. In such a context, this article provides an overview of advances in mechanistic interpretability for the analysis of causal inference in deep neural networks.

title: SLIC: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning Small LMs for Multi-Turn Analog Circuit Optimization
description:
arXiv:2611.13452v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Analog integrated circuit (IC) design is a multi-turn, simulator-grounded engineering task that demands iterative reasoning over coupled performance tradeoffs, yet proprietary process design kits (PDKs) make hosted large language model workflows difficult to deploy in practical design settings. We present SLIC (Small LM Iterating on Circuits), a reinforcement fine-tuning framework that trains a 4B-scale, locally deployable language model for closed-loop analog circuit optimization. SLIC pairs structured circuit representations with discretized relative-update actions, domain- and success-gated multiobjective rewards, and Reward-Guided Rollout Steering (RGRS), which turns per-step simulator feedback into signals for both policy learning and online rollout construction in this sparse, highly constrained domain. We further release an open, goal-conditioned benchmark of 41 amplifier topologies with standardized protocols for in-distribution validation, held-out topology evaluation, and cross-technology-node transfer. Trained solely with open source 65 nm CMOS predictive technology models (PTM), SLIC-Random achieves 87.1% in-distribution four-specification Pass@1 within eight turns, surpassing the 763B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Think by 48.5 percentage points. Beyond the training distribution, SLIC-Softmax reaches 72.6% Pass@1 on held-out topologies, and the trained policies consistently transfer across five unseen technology nodes without additional fine-tuning. This transfer extends to a commercial TSMC 65 nm CMOS PDK, where SLIC-Random achieves 49.9% held-out-topology Pass@1, demonstrating practical deployment through local inference without transmitting proprietary data to external LLM services. Performance further scales with test-time simulator interactions, reaching up to 83.2% held-out-topology Pass@1 at a 32-turn budget.

title: Auditable Human-Agent Teams for Autonomous X-ray Experimentation
description:
arXiv:2611.12933v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Closed-loop autonomous experimentation can accelerate scientific discovery, but implementation effort limits accessibility. Agentic systems may lower this barrier, although sustained operation on physical instruments remains largely unexplored. Here, using coding-agent infrastructure grounded in validated scientific methods, we demonstrate autonomous synchrotron X-ray experiments on nanoparticle superlattices under evolving, human-defined objectives. Complete human-agent and agent-agent transcripts enable an audit that reconstructs decision provenance and characterizes the division of cognitive labor. Across three experiments, 61-67% of messages involved interpretation or judgment, while the share of methodological and scientific contributions increased from 46% in the setup-focused first experiment to 56-61% in later experiments. Provenance showed that 59-68% of error corrections involved multiple participants and that about half of all decisions incorporated the input of another participant. These results may guide design principles for multi-agent scientific systems and inform future agent harnesses, model training, and accessible autonomous experimentation.
