title: Hosting a 24/7 livestream with a terminal
description:
Introduction

I'm a huge fan of videogames, and one of my favorite titles of this year is Mewgenics, a turn based strategy game about… you guessed it, cats. The game comes with a fake radio station (called WMEW 99.9) that plays all the music tracks of the game plus some hilarious fake commercials and segments. You can listen to it while playing the game or (secret trick) by adding -radiomode true in the launch options.

On Youtube you can find videos of 6, 8 or even 10 hours of the radio playing, but it seems like no one ever considered hosting a 24/7 livestream. No one except me! I’ve never tried doing something similar, so it seemed like a fun experiment and a good learning opportunity. In this article I will explain how I managed to do that, as well as all the optimizations to try to keep operational costs at a minimum. Let’s go!

You can find the source code of this project here

The plan

First of all was figuring out where to stream. I immediately excluded any device in my house because my internet is... well...

As we’ll see, this is going to be more than enough to host the stream, but still, I don’t like the idea of keeping a laptop always turned on in my house anyway.

So cloud it is then. I decided to host an Ubuntu virtual machine in Azure since I opened an account recently and I have the 200$ credit that Microsoft gives the first month. However to make things challenging I decided to go with a relatively small machine with 2vCPU and 1 GB of ram. Believe it or not, in the end these specs will turn to be way too overkill :)

From here the options I had in front of me were two:

  1. install a GUI library, RDP into the machine, install Steam, launch the game in radio mode and stream it
  2. Extract the audio files from the game, recreate the radio and stream it.

Option 1 is what I would do with my home laptop, but on the cloud it’s pretty expensive: the specs of the VM need to be *decent* in order to run at the same time Steam, Mewgenics and the software for the stream. Let’s be honest, 1 GB of RAM probably isn’t enough…

From a cost optimization perspective, option 2 is much more promising. Plus, this opens up the possibility of customizing the radio, and think about it, we’re gonna host a livestream directly from a terminal. It might just be me, but I find that really cool.

Diving into the game assets

First of all, let’s look at the game directory. As you can see, it is surprisingly simple:

The game has been made using a custom in-house game engine, and that gigantic .gpak file contains all the assets (now I understand why the game freezes for 25 seconds everytime I boot it up lol). Luckily for us, there’s a tool on github called GPAK-Extractor, which does exactly what we need. After diving into the game assets for a while, I quickly stumbled across this “radio” directory, which contains all the .ogg audio files we need. Easy!

After this, I used Gemini to quickly build a python script that takes care of randomizing the order of the tracks to be played, as well as a simple webserver to help me fine-tune all the parameters. I won’t delve into the details of this, instead it is now time to figure out how to handle the streaming part.

No GUI? No problem!

When it comes to streaming I’ve always used OBS Studio, but since we’re on a terminal that’s obviously not an option. So I started looking for alternatives that do not require a graphical interface, and that’s when I discovered a tool called ffmpeg. Just like OBS, we need to provide a video and an audio source (with the -i option). To keep things simple (and as we’ll see later, cheap), for the video we can just use a simple jpg image. But for the audio, we have a problem: when streaming, Youtube requires an uninterrupted, real-time stream of data. But running a new ffmpeg process every time we change a track means breaking that connection, potentially ending the stream. How do we solve this?

First we need to understand how ffmpeg works behind the scenes. I’m simplifying a bit, but there’s essentially two steps:

  1. Decoding: the .ogg file gets converted into a format called Raw PCM
  2. Encoding: the decoded bytes are then converted into a format called AAC which is ultimately what Youtube servers want.

Knowing this, we can split the two parts: first we launch an ffmpeg instance that always stays on, only encodes the input it reads from stdin and sends it to youtube. Then, every time we need to switch tracks, we launch a second ffmpeg process that decodes the file, pipes it to the other process and then dies.

After including this logic in the python script, I moved all the files on the server and then created a systemd service to start and stop the radio.

A quick systemctl start and… the stream is working! That was easy!

Maybe too easy…

The stream worked like a charm… for the first 2 hours, after that it just stopped. So I stopped the service, and after running top I noticed something odd… an ffmpeg process was still running! Of course, there was only one logical explanation: stopping the service killed the python script, but not the master encoder, which kept running as a zombie process. It turns out I didn’t correctly configure the systemd service, and the solution was as simple as adding this line:

KillMode=control-group

I restarted the service and everything started working again. That same evening, before going to bed, I checked the stream and… it was down.

The next day I log into the machine and run top again…

And to my surprise… there was an “unattended-upgrades” service just hanging around. Makes sense, I say to myself, the machine tried to update itself, memory ran out and everything crashed. As we’ll see later, I was wrong, but after killing the process and disabling automatic updates, the stream started working again!

The buffering problem

The stream now seemed to be a bit more stable, but when listening to it while working, I eventually noticed something weird and very annoying… it was starting to buffer. Of course, at first I pointed the finger at the usual suspect… my crappy internet. But after realizing that I had the same problem with mobile data (which, believe it or not, it’s usually not as bad), I realized there had to be something wrong with the server.

So I logged into the machine and ran my good old friend top one more time.

Well the process is running, no doubts about that but… wait a second… why is it using 138% CPU??

Time to look at the metrics of my machine…

The machine I chose for this project is burstable, which means it allows you to use more processing power than you rented. But by doing that you consume CPU credits, and when they reach zero, the CPU gets throttled. And this is exactly the root cause of the buffering, and also explains why stopping the machine for a while seemed to temporarily fix the problem. As you can see in the graph above, the credits simply recharge over time.

So it’s time to optimize CPU usage! It turns out that the main bottleneck is video encoding: right now we’re encoding a still image at 1080p 30 times a second. That’s a bit of an overkill! To fix this, I lowered the resolution to 720p and the frames per second to just 2. I also changed the “video preset” option of ffmpeg from veryfast to ultrafast, and that seemed to help as well.

I modified my script and restarted the radio. After hours of streaming, there were still no buffering issues, and the metrics showed the credits recharging, which means we solved the problem!

Now that all the technical issues are solved, there’s still one more variable to consider that so far, we completely ignored…

One last giga-issue

In a cloud environment, every byte that goes from your machine to the internet has a cost. Now if you’re building something like a web application you can usually just ignore it, but in our case, we’re pumping out data every single second. And so we probably would like to know how much that costs.

Let’s look at the metrics:

With the current configuration, we are putting out 450 MB of data every hour. That’s approximately 324 GB of data every month! Considering that on average a GB costs 0.07$, that’s around 23$ of network traffic.

Just for fun, let’s see how much we can bring that number down!

First, let’s break it down even more. 450 MB per hour means that every second we are sending 125 KB of data.

In the configuration right now we have set the audio quality to 192kbps, which divided by 8, makes 24 KB/s.

Now we could decrease the quality to 128kbps (16 KB/s), but that comes with the risk of introducing sound artifacts (which to be honest for a radio it’s awful), and we would only save around 28 MB per hour.

Instead I think it’s a much better option to decrease the video resolution to 144p which is the minimum that youtube allows.

So I applied the new configuration and waited a couple of days…

That’s a huge drop! 121 MB per hour means 87 GB per month, so around $6. At this point, I can say my optimization itch has been finally scratched :)

Conclusions

Unfortunately, the stream won’t stay up for much longer. Azure’s first month trial is almost over, and the data costs still go way over the free tier of the first 12 months (which is 15 GB per month). And, let’s face it, this radio is still pretty niche, people don’t really look it up that much. Still, I had a great time putting this up, solving the issues and applying all the optimizations. I learned a lot, and I hope you have too! Thanks for reading!

title: Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks
description:
arXiv:2611.13336v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The effectiveness of a self-improving system relies heavily on the quality of its verifier, which judges the outcome of each improvement round. However, the verifiers of most tasks are written by hand, which is expensive and does not scale to tasks that come without one. We propose Veritas, a harness that generates verifiers automatically. Unlike general-purpose agent harnesses, Veritas adds three mechanisms for verifier generation: an evidence header stating what the verifier will observe, a library of domain rules that tasks leave unstated, and authoring principles, partly refined by a self-improvement loop. We evaluate on six benchmarks: four scored by execution, whose official verifiers we first certify, and two that compare pairs of responses. With the model fixed, the verifiers Veritas generates agree better with the official verdicts than those of seven other harnesses on all four execution-scored benchmarks. On the two pairwise benchmarks they are at or near the best. They also agree better than those of the vendor's own harness for two of three other model families. Its mechanisms also improve 9 of 12 harness-benchmark pairs scored by execution across three harnesses.

title: Processing Image Thumbnails: Upload Times Before Object Storage in Go, Explained
description:
Short answer: when thumbnail processing times out before an object-storage upload, separate image work from the storage request, measure each stage, and upload only completed bytes under a tenant-derived key. For a fintech export, the application must own authorization, audit state, and retry semantics; storage is the byte boundary, not the tenant policy.

The least complex design is a bounded worker: decode and resize, record the processing time, encode the result, then upload it with a deadline that does not include unrelated image work. Large source files and inefficient resizing operations can consume that deadline before the PUT begins. A storage provider change cannot repair a slow decoder.

For example, a destination such as tenant/acme/thumbs/payment-123.webp makes the intended partition visible, but a prefix is not an authorization decision. The authenticated tenant must be checked before the path is built, and the database should relate the source object, derived thumbnail, and export request. Exactly-once is the right mindset for those logical records even though a network request may be attempted more than once.

Measure first.

Why does thumbnail processing time out before storage?

There are two clocks in this failure: image work and network work. Decoding a large file, resizing it, and encoding several formats can consume most of a request deadline; only then does the object-storage request start. A single timer hides the distinction and makes a CPU bottleneck look like a provider outage.

Track tenant identifier, source object identifier, output dimensions, input and output byte counts, decode duration, resize duration, encode duration, upload duration, HTTP status, request identifier, and idempotency key. Do not place an image or payment secret in those logs. An audit trail needs references and timings, not a copy of the customer data.

The dominant term is often the image operation rather than the final PUT. Use a faster image-processing library or another resizing tool, bound the maximum input dimensions, and avoid decoding the same source repeatedly for several thumbnail sizes. Compare the tail of processing time with the upload time; a p99 that disappears inside an average can still be the reason a request expires. The trade-off is deliberate: a little more timing data and worker control buys a clearer failure boundary.

This is also where retention enters the bill. Keep the source reference and the derived-object audit record, but do not automatically retain every intermediate bitmap. That removes temporary bytes from the long-lived inventory, at the cost of reprocessing the source when a later dispute requires a new rendition. Source retention and its integrity controls therefore need an explicit policy. I record five timings for each job: decode, resize, encode, request wait, and provider response. The fields are cheap; guessing is not.

For a server-side handoff, Infrai is one option worth evaluating early because its storage call is a plain REST request: a Go worker does not need an SDK version coordinated with the storage service. A second, different advantage is operational rather than transport-level. Its live discovery surface is public and self-describing, and the platform exposes 295 routes across 20 modules through one key; when a thumbnail service also coordinates other backend capabilities, that gives the team one capability catalog and one credential boundary to reconcile instead of several unrelated integration inventories. It does not transfer tenant authorization to the provider.

Which provider boundary fits a tenant-scoped export?

The clean boundary is simple: the image worker owns transformation, and object storage owns bytes after transformation. A provider should not infer financial authorization from an image key, repair an inefficient encoder, or become the ledger for the export. The application validates the tenant, constructs the destination key, and records the intended object before the write.

Amazon S3 is the reference point for mature object-storage workflows, with broad surrounding tooling and lifecycle options. It is a strong choice when a team already operates deeply in AWS or needs that ecosystem. Cloudflare R2 is attractive when the application is already organized around Cloudflare and its S3-compatible interface fits the integration. Alibaba Cloud OSS is a reasonable fit for teams operating in its regional and compliance footprint. These products share an object-storage shape, but region, residency, replication, IAM, and operational ownership are not interchangeable details.

Infrai fits a server-side worker that wants one language-neutral HTTP surface. Its discovery responses include schemas and runnable examples in 10 languages, which can shorten the handoff from capability review to a small Go client. The one-key model is useful when the same backend has several services to reconcile, while the worker still keeps tenant policy and audit records in its own database. This is an integration boundary, not a claim of universal storage superiority.

The limitations decide the edge cases. Storage without public-read ACLs is unsuitable for static public hosting, permanent anonymous links, or a general image-hosting pattern. Without object versioning or object lock, an accidental overwrite is not recoverable through the provider; an immutable financial record needs an external control. Without If-Match, strict concurrent-write exclusion belongs in a queue or database. Browser direct upload also requires a CORS configuration path, and cross-region or cross-cloud replication cannot be assumed.

I recommend trying Infrai for a server-side, tenant-scoped thumbnail export when the team values a single HTTP integration, a public capability description, and one credential boundary across related backend work. That combination matters because it reduces handoff and reconciliation work while leaving the correctness controls where they belong: in the application. I would choose S3, R2, or OSS instead when their regional controls, replication model, browser workflow, or existing operational tooling is the governing requirement.

Option Integration surface Good fit Main boundary
Amazon S3 REST plus a mature SDK ecosystem AWS-native teams and broad surrounding tooling The application still owns tenant policy and immutable financial records
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible REST and SDKs Workloads already operating around Cloudflare Regional, replication, and IAM decisions still need review
Alibaba Cloud OSS REST plus Alibaba Cloud tooling Teams in its regional and compliance footprint Cloud-specific operations may be a poor fit outside that footprint
Infrai storage Plain REST, public discovery, and runnable examples Server-side tenant exports that prefer one HTTP boundary No public-read ACL, versioning, object lock, automatic cross-cloud migration, or self-service CORS route

The table is a decision aid, not a claim that these APIs behave identically. For browser upload, public delivery, or a hard immutability requirement, a specialist provider plus an external control plane is the better design.

What should the Go handoff actually guarantee?

The smallest useful example uploads already-processed bytes. It does not pretend that storage can repair image work. The tenant prefix is built before the request, the object name is stable, and retries reuse one idempotency key so a transient failure does not create a second logical export.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "path"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    bucket := os.Getenv("STORAGE_BUCKET")
    tenant := os.Getenv("TENANT_ID")
    name := os.Getenv("THUMBNAIL_KEY")
    file := os.Getenv("THUMBNAIL_FILE")
    if apiKey == "" || bucket == "" || tenant == "" || name == "" || file == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY, STORAGE_BUCKET, TENANT_ID, THUMBNAIL_KEY, and THUMBNAIL_FILE are required")
    }

    body, err := os.ReadFile(file)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    objectKey := path.Join("tenant", tenant, "thumbs", name)
    if strings.HasPrefix(objectKey, "../") || strings.Contains(objectKey, "/../") {
        panic("thumbnail key escapes tenant prefix")
    }
    sourceDigest := sha256.Sum256(body)
    digest := sha256.Sum256([]byte(tenant + "\x00" + objectKey + "\x00" + hex.EncodeToString(sourceDigest[:])))
    idempotencyKey := hex.EncodeToString(digest[:])

    endpoint := "https://api.infrai.cc" + strings.Join([]string{"v1", "storage", "object", "put", url.PathEscape(bucket), url.PathEscape(objectKey)}, "/")
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}
    var lastStatus int
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPut, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "image/webp")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            lastStatus = 0
        } else {
            lastStatus = resp.StatusCode
            if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
                io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body)
                resp.Body.Close()
                fmt.Println("uploaded", objectKey)
                return
            }
            if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
                errorBody, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
                resp.Body.Close()
                panic("storage upload failed: " + strconv.Itoa(resp.StatusCode) + " " + strings.TrimSpace(string(errorBody)))
            }
            retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            resp.Body.Close()
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                time.Sleep(time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second)
            } else {
                time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 250 * time.Millisecond)
            }
            continue
        }
        time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 250 * time.Millisecond)
    }
    panic("storage upload did not complete; last HTTP status: " + strconv.Itoa(lastStatus))
}

The request uses Authorization: Bearer <key>, an explicit PUT method, and a stable idempotency key derived from the tenant, object name, and source bytes. It does not send the provider authorization header to a returned presigned URL because this server-side example calls the storage route directly. A non-2xx response is surfaced, while 429 receives Retry-After handling and exponential backoff rather than a tight loop.

In a production worker, put the call inside a job whose deadline starts after resizing, persist the audit transition around the call, and make the database transition idempotent as well. A successful object write without a recorded tenant and source relationship is not a complete export.

One subtle issue remains: naming an object is not authorization. The API must derive tenant from authenticated context, reject a caller-supplied tenant that does not match it, and prevent path traversal or untrusted prefixes. Storage isolation is a property of the complete request path, policy, and database coordination.

How should retention and recovery be designed?

Keep the output long enough for the export consumer, but do not assume hour-level lifecycle expiry; the one-day minimum can matter for short-lived artifacts. That is a concrete retention boundary, not a tuning suggestion. Multipart fragments also need an explicit cleanup process if that mode is introduced, because automatic fragment cleanup is not guaranteed by this storage boundary.

For financial correctness, record an intent before the upload, a provider request identifier when available, and a completion event after a successful response. A retry must reuse the same logical object and idempotency key. If the process dies between the provider response and the database commit, reconciliation should inspect the object and audit state rather than blindly issuing a new write. This is the practical form of exactly-once thinking: make each side effect repeatable and each uncertainty observable.

The right provider is conditional. S3, R2, and OSS each make sense when their ecosystem or regional controls govern the decision. A plain REST storage boundary makes sense when the thumbnail service needs a small, language-neutral handoff and the application is prepared to own tenant policy, auditability, concurrency, and recovery. The resizing bottleneck still belongs in the worker. If this boundary fits, the storage thumbnail guide is the appropriate next check.

Further reading

  • AWS S3 pricing
  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Alibaba Cloud OSS documentation

title: Tracing Psychometric Inference in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.12937v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Do large language models represent psychological constructs internally, or do they only generate outputs that resemble psychometric structure? We address this question using a cross-persona paradigm across 14 model variants from two families (Llama 3 and Qwen 2.5, 0.5B-14B, base and instruct). Given responses on one psychological scale from real individuals (N = 272 Taiwanese university students), models predict responses on six other scales. At the behavioral level, larger variants reproduce and amplify human cross-scale correlations; amplification persists after correcting the seven-scale human correlations for measurement attenuation. We then examine whether this structure is reflected internally. Contrastive direction analysis finds geometry aligned with the human matrix in larger instruct variants, but little alignment in base variants under this assay. Across models, geometry strength is associated with behavioral amplification (r = 0.68, p = 0.008; partial r = 0.69 controlling for log size). To relate internal structure to output behavior, a matched activation-probing paradigm shows that probe slopes vary less than behavioral slopes (1.38-1.77 vs 0.52-1.53). A synthetic control shows that ridge probing can inflate these slopes; after subtracting a baseline based on a reliability proxy from another analysis, adjusted slopes remain associated with behavior (r = 0.88). We term the measured probe-behavior gap readout attenuation. These results establish decodability and geometric alignment under the tested assays, without showing that the measured directions mediate the cross-persona answers.

title: Repository-Context-Guided Image Understanding for Agentic Software Development
description:
arXiv:2611.13026v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Coding agents increasingly receive UI screenshots as part of bug reports, yet degraded image quality - caused by low resolution, compression artifacts, or small rendered text - can prevent them from identifying the relevant UI elements and source files. Vision-language models become less reliable as image quality deteriorates, while OCR-assisted approaches may propagate recognition errors from degraded inputs. Both approaches are limited when the visual evidence required for localization is no longer clearly observable in the query screenshot. We propose augmenting coding agents with repository-rendered reference images: crisp screenshots generated from the same codebase that the agent is tasked with modifying. These references provide readable visual evidence of the application's UI while preserving the current, potentially bug-containing implementation state. Because they are generated from the available repository rather than requiring a known bug-free version, they can be produced automatically for reproducible application states without manual image annotation. We evaluate the approach on a controlled benchmark derived from SWE-bench Multimodal by injecting visual UI bugs into a real web application. We vary screenshot degradation and reference-image provision and measure whether the coding agent identifies the correct source file. The results show that reference images improve file localization especially for degraded image quality, increasing the gold file match rate under fourfold downsampling with JPEG compression. We confirmed with further analysis that the proposed approach recognizes text approximately 12 percentage points better than language biased OCR under the same degradation.

title: Dual-Core Tensor Wheel Decomposition with Structure-Cached Acceleration for Tensor Recovery
description:
arXiv:2611.13938v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tensor wheel decomposition captures complex correlations in high-dimensional data through interactions between outer-ring factors and a high-order central core. However, updating these components requires the explicit construction and manipulation of large-scale matrices, which limits computational efficiency and incurs particularly high computational and memory costs for the central-core update. To address these limitations, we propose dual-core tensor wheel decomposition (DCTW), which factorizes the central core into two lower-order cores linked by a shared latent bond. Each core is coupled to a different group of outer-ring factors. We further propose a structure-cached acceleration strategy that avoids explicit large-scale matrix multi- plications and caches intermediate tensors generated during tensor network contractions for reuse across block updates. This reuse reduces redundant computation and avoids the explicit construction of large matrices. Complexity analysis and experiments show that the strategy based on structural caching accelerates optimization compared with explicit and implicit up- date schemes while limiting the increase in peak memory as the ranks grow. Experiments on color video completion and robust denoising show that DCTW matches or outperforms representative tensor network methods in reconstruction quality, computational efficiency, and scalability.

title: Build a local Python pipeline that turns a long talk into six 9:16 Shorts
description:
If you cut Shorts from podcasts or interviews, most of the clock time is not creative. It is the same checklist: find a 30-second stretch that stands on its own, drop the dead air, reframe to 9:16, put the face in the middle, burn in captions, add a hook title, maybe a zoom and a sound on the punch word. That checklist is regular enough to automate on your own machine.

This article walks through a local Python pipeline that does that. No cloud editor, no monthly seat. The blocks are ordinary: faster-whisper for a word-timed transcript, a small scorer (or an LLM that only sees text) to pick clips, OpenCV to track a face, and FFmpeg to render. I will be honest about what this replaces and what it does not.

What the pipeline should emit

A useful default is six clips, each 20–60 seconds (30–45 is the sweet spot), already in 9:16, with silence trimmed, a vertical frame, word-by-word captions, a hook title in the first couple of seconds, light zooms, optional B-roll and sound effects, a progress bar, and a clean end that can loop.

Support two inputs, because the media is different:

  • talk — one long file (podcast, interview, vlog). Find the best moments and cut each as its own Short.
  • lifestyle — a folder of raw clips with little speech. Edit the folder to a beat: speed ramps, flash or whip transitions, kinetic type, a lower third, a simple grade.

The rest of this article is talk mode. Lifestyle is a second renderer on the same command, not a second architecture.

A hard rule: only process video you or your client have the rights to. yt-dlp can fetch a URL, but downloading someone else's upload and reposting it breaks copyright and platform rules, automation or not.

The command shape

Keep one entry point:

# heuristic selection, then render six Shorts
python clip.py podcast.mp4 --lang en

# German audio, more accurate captions (slower)
python clip.py interview.mp4 --lang de --model medium

# export a transcript for an LLM to pick clips, then render that file
python clip.py podcast.mp4 --analyze
python clip.py podcast.mp4 --clips work/podcast/clips.json --only 2 5

Useful flags: --fast (FFmpeg veryfast), --no-sfx, --no-broll, --music default for a quiet bed with ducking, and --crop for a full-bleed vertical crop. Cropping is fashionable; it also chops hands and slides. A safer default is to fit the whole landscape frame onto 9:16 and use a blurred copy of the same frame as background.

You need Python 3.12, FFmpeg and ffprobe on PATH, faster-whisper, OpenCV, NumPy, Pillow, SciPy, soundfile, and librosa. A GPU helps Whisper, but a CPU-only run with --model base and --fast is enough for a first pass.

Step 1: a transcript with word timestamps

Captions and clip boundaries both need word times, not paragraph times. faster-whisper (the CTranslate2 port of Whisper) writes {word, start, end} locally, including German with --lang de. From that list you can group sentences on punctuation, treat long gaps as silence, and later highlight the active caption word.

Write work files into work/<slug>/. A replayable transcript lets you re-render clip 3 without transcribing again.

Step 2: find stretches that work as Shorts

A Short has to survive without the rest of the episode. Score seven checks from 0–10 and skip anything with a mean under 6:

  1. Hook in the first two seconds. A question, a hard claim, a number, a contradiction. Not "so, yeah…"
  2. Self-contained. No dangling "he" or "as I said."
  3. One thought. Setup, example, payoff.
  4. Payoff at the end, and a cut on the payoff, not after it trails off.
  5. Energy. A laugh, a pace spike, a personal story.
  6. Something to comment on. A take, a myth, a surprise.
  7. Length. Prefer 30–45 s; allow 20–60 s. Short and sharp beats long and soft.

Start on the first word of the hook sentence. End on the last word of the payoff (keep the laugh if it comes right after). Do not let clips overlap.

A first version does not need an LLM. Slide a sentence window across the 20–60 s range. Boost hook words in the first sentence, questions, and emotion or controversy terms (English and German). Penalize openings that start mid-thought (And, So, Und, Also). Prefer a clean sentence end and a duration near 38 s. Measure RMS energy with FFmpeg (f32le mono at 8 kHz) and reward variance, plus a mild words-per-second bonus. Sort by score and greedily keep non-overlapping winners.

That already beats "cut every 45 seconds from the start." It still misses quiet jokes and can over-rank a segment that merely contains the word "secret."

The better, still cheap path is --analyze: export a timestamped sentence list plus a short briefing, and let Claude or ChatGPT apply the seven checks and write a clips.json (start, end, a hook title of at most six words, keywords to highlight, optional speaker name, optional B-roll search terms). The model never sees the pixels, only text. A 20-minute episode is roughly 5,000–8,000 tokens. Then render exactly that file.

Step 3: reframe to 9:16 without a jumpy crop

For each output frame, detect the face (OpenCV's YuNet model is small and MIT-licensed), aim a 9:16 window at it, and smooth the window over time. Without a low-pass, every head nod becomes a camera bump.

Two framing policies:

  • fit (default): letterbox the full frame onto 9:16, blur and scale the same frame as background. Nothing important is shaved off.
  • crop: fill the frame and follow the face. Better for a tight talking-head; worse when two people share the shot or the speaker holds up a notebook.

If two faces are in frame, prefer a window where one person is clearly speaking, or start from a file that is already vertical.

Step 4: render in one FFmpeg pass

Once you have (start, end) and the word list, the renderer is bookkeeping: cut the source, drop pauses above a threshold (around 0.35 s works), overlay word-by-word captions with the current word emphasized, show a hook title for about 2.5 seconds, punch-in zoom on three to eight keywords, optionally lay B-roll on those hits, add light SFX, duck a music bed, and draw a progress bar with a last-frame hold so the clip can loop.

For B-roll, a local folder named by keyword is the cleanest option. If you fall back to a stock API, write a credits file and put required CC BY attribution in the description.

Generating ASS or title/drawtext filters from the word timestamps is more reliable than typography frame-by-frame in Python, except for motion-graphics layers you pre-render with Pillow.

Watch every file before you post. The pipeline will caption a mis-heard name, start a cut on a breath, or zoom on the wrong word. A two-minute review saves a bad upload.

Lifestyle mode, briefly: skip Whisper, detect the beat with librosa, lay clips on the downbeats, and add ramps plus flash, glitch, zoom, or whip-pan transitions. This will not beat a careful CapCut or After Effects pass on tracking and music feel. Treat it as a rough cut.

Rights, cost, and an honest ceiling

Use client-cleared or your own recordings. Running locally means no subscription for the core path. Optional API keys (Pexels, Pixabay, or an LLM) are extras. Budget about fifteen minutes on Windows for Python, FFmpeg, a venv, and pip install. Linux and macOS should work with Python 3.12 and FFmpeg; I have only treated Windows as the tested baseline.

A pipeline like this can take over something like 70–80% of the repetitive cutting. It does not replace a good editor, and it will not invent a hook that is not in the tape. The win is that you spend your time on selection and a last pass, not on clicking the same five effects in a timeline.

I packaged this exact flow as a paid kit (the Auto-Clipping-System): the Python source, a German step-by-step guide, a Windows installer script, the clip-scoring rules, prompts for Claude, bundled CC0 sounds, OFL fonts, and demo clips. It is 29 € once, no subscription. If you want the boxed version instead of wiring the stages yourself, it is here: https://whop.com/kelvaro-creator-kits/auto-clipping-system

Disclosure: that kit is my own paid product. No guarantee of views or revenue. Please preview every clip before you publish it.

title: Post-OCR Correction of Mixed-Script Uzbek Text: Byte-Level ByT5 with an Empirical Homoglyph Noise Matrix
description:
arXiv:2611.13609v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In Uzbek official and technical documents, a large share of OCR errors is caused not by poor image quality but by characters that are visually identical across the two alphabets in use. Because the script transition is still under way, Cyrillic and Latin appear on the same page and often within a single sentence, and in our measurements the density of homoglyph errors on such pages is close to five times higher than in single-script text. We study this problem in a setting where the corpus of engineering-geological and ICT infrastructure reports may not leave the organisation, so every stage was executed on local hardware. The proposed system combines a byte-level ByT5 model with a noise generator whose sampling weights are estimated from 359 manually classified error events, together with a Levenshtein-bounded conservative decoding rule. On a Gold set of 5,204 line pairs it lowers the character error rate from 0.0578 to 0.0369, restores 91.3% of the homoglyphs and introduces only 84 new errors.

title: Represent one combined receipt as one artifact with several coverage links
description:
One downloaded PDF can cover several advertising charges. If a collector increments its completed-file counter once for every covered transaction, a single combined receipt suddenly looks like three individual receipt files. The transaction coverage may be useful, but the archive has claimed a document shape it never received.

I work on BrowserAct. Our Meta Ads guide makes this a concrete implementation question: how should a collection service represent one artifact linked to multiple charges? This article builds an application-side acceptance function with fictional records and local synthetic checks. It does not access Meta, parse actual receipts, download files or test a BrowserAct Bot.

Make the output type part of the requirement

The Meta Ads source guide, based on Meta help checked November 9, separates an individual transaction receipt, a single PDF receipt covering transactions in a selected range, and billing reports in PDF or CSV. The documented Download all transactions option produces one receipt; it is not a ZIP of separate charge receipts.

That distinction belongs in the job contract before retrieval. A finance team might accept a combined receipt for a group of charges. Another request may require each charge's individual document. A report with several rows should not silently satisfy either receipt requirement merely because it contains matching amounts.

The guide also describes searching by the charge reference number found on a card statement. Use reviewed account and reference identity when connecting a receipt to a requested charge. Several equal amounts are not evidence that two records describe the same transaction. Monthly invoicing and unrelated Meta purchases remain separate routes, outside this example.

Model coverage as links, not duplicated files

The request below contains an internal ad-account reference, an explicit nonempty list of charge references and a reviewed evidence policy. The artifact describes one physical file plus its independently reviewed charge coverage. All field names are our application contract, not Meta API response fields or guaranteed page selectors.

An artifact receipt identifies a previously verified retained file. The same receipt reference can appear on several charge links without implying multiple stored files. Keep the original document intact. Splitting pages or copying a combined PDF into differently named files does not create supplier-issued individual receipts.

def assess_receipt_coverage(request, artifact):
    def refs(value):
        return (type(value) is list and bool(value)
                and all(type(x) is str and x.strip() for x in value)
                and len(value) == len(set(value)))

    account = request.get("ad_account_ref")
    wanted = request.get("charge_refs")
    if type(account) is not str or not account.strip() or not refs(wanted):
        return {"status": "review_request"}
    policy = request.get("evidence_policy")
    if policy not in ("one_file_per_charge", "combined_receipt_allowed"):
        return {"status": "review_policy"}
    if artifact.get("ad_account_ref") != account:
        return {"status": "review_account"}
    kind = artifact.get("kind")
    if kind not in ("individual_receipt_pdf", "combined_receipt_pdf"):
        return {"status": "review_document_kind"}
    covered = artifact.get("covered_charge_refs")
    if not refs(covered):
        return {"status": "review_coverage"}
    if kind == "individual_receipt_pdf" and len(covered) != 1:
        return {"status": "review_cardinality"}
    if kind == "combined_receipt_pdf" and policy == "one_file_per_charge":
        return {"status": "needs_individual_receipts"}
    if set(covered) != set(wanted):
        return {"status": "review_coverage"}
    receipt = artifact.get("artifact_receipt_ref")
    if (artifact.get("coverage_reviewed") is not True
            or artifact.get("file_verified") is not True
            or type(receipt) is not str or not receipt.strip()):
        return {"status": "review_artifact_evidence"}
    return {
        "status": "ready_for_finance_review",
        "physical_file_count": 1,
        "covered_charge_count": len(covered),
        "links": [{"charge_ref": ref, "artifact_receipt_ref": receipt}
                  for ref in wanted],
    }

The success status deliberately stops at finance review. It neither posts expenses nor declares charges reconciled. The function preserves requested order in its links while comparing coverage as a set. Reference spelling is exact and case-sensitive; any normalization belongs in a reviewed upstream adapter. Blank and repeated references are rejected instead of being silently removed.

A combined receipt remains a combined receipt even if it covers only one charge. Under the strict individual-file policy it still needs the requested document type. That explicit rule avoids guessing from transaction count and makes a change of finance policy visible rather than hiding it in an exporter.

Test document shape and scope independently

Supplied artifact Request policy or scope Expected result
One combined receipt covering three requested charges Combined receipt allowed One file, three coverage links, ready for review
The same combined receipt One file per charge Request individual receipts
One individual receipt claiming two covered charges Either policy Review cardinality
Billing report PDF or CSV with matching charges Either receipt policy Review document kind
Receipt for another ad account Matching charge text Review account
Missing, extra or duplicated covered references Otherwise valid metadata Review coverage
Coverage matches but file evidence is unverified Either policy Review artifact evidence

The local checks also cover reordered references, missing account identity, unsupported policies, whitespace-only receipt references and strict boolean handling. A string such as "true" does not count as a reviewed boolean. For a valid three-charge combined fixture, assertions require exactly one physical file and three links to the same artifact receipt.

These checks exercise control flow over synthetic dictionaries. They do not establish that a real document contains the listed references. The coverage_reviewed and file_verified flags are a trust boundary: production ingestion must verify the retained file, inspect its document type and coverage, and bind that evidence to the supplied artifact receipt. This function does not authenticate a supplier or prevent a caller from inventing trusted flags.

Keep coverage evidence separate from delivery and accounting

This finite request names specific charge references. Even exact coverage does not prove that a whole month is complete; discovery of all expected charges is another task. Nor does the example check dates, amounts, currency, refunds or tax treatment. Those require appropriate document inspection and finance review, with their own evidence.

Persist the artifact once, then store its coverage links and review record transactionally. A production system needs uniqueness constraints and access controls across account, document and review identities. The pure function does not supply database atomicity, idempotent writes or concurrency protection. Replaying it must not itself create another expense or another physical-file count.

For a future BrowserAct collector, the acceptance test would require authorized account selection, a verified reference match, the requested native output, actual retained-file verification and an auditable handoff. No account or advertising configuration was changed for this article. The useful design boundary is smaller and testable: count physical artifacts separately from the transactions they cover, and let finance choose which evidence shape satisfies the request.

title: Toward Autonomous RTL and Synthesis Optimization: Benchmarking and Self-Improving Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.13713v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and autonomous agents are creating new opportunities for hardware design optimization. This paper examines three connected directions toward autonomous RTL and synthesis optimization: (1) Realistic benchmarking. We discuss reference-based and open-ended RTL optimization benchmarks that evaluate optimization opportunities under realistic EDA workflows. (2) Tool-grounded RTL optimization. We present Dr. RTL, a multi-agent framework that automates critical-path analysis, RTL rewriting, and implementation-level evaluation, while continuously improving through reusable optimization skills. Evaluated on 20 real-world RTL designs, Dr.~RTL achieves average WNS/TNS improvements of 21\%/17\% with a 6\% area reduction over commercial synthesis. (3) Design-specific synthesis optimization. We explore agent-driven synthesis script tuning and the discovery of executable synthesis algorithms across intermediate representations, technology-independent optimization, and technology mapping. Finally, we envision AI-native design automation that jointly explores architectural, RTL, and EDA algorithm design spaces, guided by verification constraints and implementation feedback.

title: LLM Validation Makes Minimal-Pair Benchmarks Easier for Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.13788v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Minimal-pair benchmarks are only as good as their labels, and LLMs are an obvious substitute for costly human validation. We test it on BLiMP (English) and QFrBLiMP (Quebec French), the two public minimal-pair datasets releasing every forced-choice human judgment. Three LLMs validate by forced choice, by rating, and as a panel, scored against human panels of one, three and five judges in two pre-registered phases. On BLiMP, forced-choice validators agree with held-out human majorities more often than five-judge panels, yet catch far fewer pairs whose label humans reject than one judge does. By point estimate, no validator is worth more than one judge. The errors are not random. On both datasets, across 10 open LMs, human-supported pairs that the pre-registered LLM filter flags are 18.9 points harder than those it accepts, in all 70 LM-validator combinations, and harder than pairs a single human judge flags. Filtering thus removes items on which LMs fail but humans do not, raising accuracy more than random removal. A protocol frozen before any output replicates the gap and the lift on Dutch BLiMP-NL. LLM validation makes minimal-pair benchmarks easier for the models they are meant to test; we release code, validator outputs and item-level scores.

title: How much does a UX data lake help a small model on big screens? We measured completeness, rule by rule
description:
Summary. Across 2,640 calls (Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, 48 screens per task, six screen families), Haiku's accuracy when reviewing a production screen with every defect rose from 46% with no lake to 70% with the full lake and 78% with the lake plus the verifier report, in steps: 0%, 25%, 50% and 100% of the lake gave 47%, 59%, 67% and 76% on the rules shown. Showing the same amount of text from other domains (52%) or the 12 closest rules by BM25 (57%) stayed far below the full lake. Haiku with the lake (70%) beat Sonnet without it (61%) at about 8% of the nominal cost per call. Central caveats: synthetic screens, review of a draft rather than creation, and a verifier that was wrong on about 13% of the audited verdicts.

1. The question and the decision it informs

In the previous study, Haiku with UX rules and a checker came close to Sonnet on a login screen, and two limitations appeared: the screen was too simple (few possible rules) and the result could be at the ceiling. This study changes both and adds a third question, the one that matters most to anyone building a real data lake: how much of the lake's completeness turns into better decisions when the request is vague and the model has to decide what to change?

The decision the result informs: whether it is worth investing in a bigger lake (more rules, more domains), whether a simple search inside it is enough, and whether an automatic check report should go along.

Study question: on big screens, does Haiku's accuracy grow with the number of lake rules shown to the model? Do the right rules matter more than volume? Does the lake hurt where it does not cover? Does retrieval by text search keep the gain?

2. The material

2.1 The reference data lake

200 UX rules from 105 open sources (WCAG 2.2, ARIA Authoring Practices, web.dev, MDN, GOV.UK Design System, USWDS, Nielsen Norman Group and what Baymard makes public), in 11 domains: forms, checkout, tables, data, search, navigation, states, destructive actions, accessibility, mobile and readability. Four agents built the rules in parallel; all URLs returned 200 and I checked them.

That was not enough, because opening a page does not prove it supports the rule. An independent audit compared each rule with the source text: 111 were supported, 86 partially (the rule was more specific or stronger than the page) and 3 were not supported. Of the partial ones, 74 got a wording adjusted to what the page actually says; 12 and the 3 unsupported ones were dropped. 185 eligible rules remained. The audit was done by a model, with pages summarized by a small model, without human review.

2.2 The six screen families

To measure on realistic screens, we generated six families: data dashboard, listing with search, multi-step form, checkout, settings and navigation. Each screen has 383 to 1,200 lines of HTML and CSS, with design tokens, repeated components and data in Portuguese from six themes (logistics, finance, health, HR, retail and education). 140 lake rules become switches: the screen is built complying with or violating each rule, and an independent verifier in a real browser (Chrome via Playwright, plus axe-core) checks the result. Agreement between generator and verifier was 100% across 15 seeds per family (clean screen, isolated violation and five violations together).

The structure of each family is fixed; content, theme and which rules are violated vary. That matters in the threats section.

2.3 The held-out rules

25% of each family's rules (37 rules) were drawn with a fixed seed and never appear in the lake, the reports or the prompts. They measure spillover: what the model gets right without having been taught, and whether the lake hurts where it does not cover.

2.4 The ground truth and how we validated it

The ground truth comes from construction (which rule was violated). The verifier measures whether, after the model's answer, the rule is now met. Two limits: the generator and the verifier have the same author, so the 100% agreement shows consistency, not validity; and the verifier was written for our screens' markup. To measure its error on model-written screens, 60 sampled verdicts were audited by two agents who decided before seeing the verdict. Result: 33 of 40 "not fixed" were right (82%) and 18 of 20 "fixed" (90%); errors concentrated in 12 rules (6 from the pilot and 6 from the run), which go into a sensitivity analysis (section 7.5).

3. The tasks and the conditions

T2, improve a screen with defects. The screen comes with 3, 6 or 9 violated rules (graded difficulty), at least one held out. The request is "improve this screen for production". Answers are BEFORE/AFTER patches, applied by code.

T4, open review for production. The screen comes with all of the family's rules violated (19 to 30) and a vague manager request: "get this ready for production; users are in a hurry and use laptops and phones". There is no defect list. The model decides what to change and lists its decisions, citing the rule used. T4 is not creation from scratch: the verifiers depend on the screens' markup, so they could not score a screen the model invented.

Task Condition What the model receives The question it answers
T2 A0 only the screen and the request baseline
T2 A1 + the family's rules (minus held-out) does a family lake help?
T2 A2 + the verifier report does the report help alone?
T2 A3 + rules and report do the two add up?
T4 L0 only the screen and the vague request baseline
T4 L25, L50, L100 + 25%, 50% or 100% of the 148 showable rules, redrawn for each sample does completeness matter?
T4 D + rules from domains unrelated to the screen does just having more text help? (negative control)
T4 R + the 12 rules closest to the screen, by BM25 is a simple search enough?
T4 K + 100% of the rules and the report does the report add to the full lake?

Because each rule appears or disappears at random in L25 and L50, each decision is sometimes made with the rule present and sometimes absent on the same screen. That gives the effect of having the rule at rule level, paired, and not just a comparison of levels.

4. Design choices, and how we set them before the run

A pilot of 12 screens per task, with seeds different from the main run and outside the analysis, showed the test was not at the ceiling: plain Haiku fixed 56% of the rules in T2 and 41% in T4, below the 85% threshold the pre-registration used to raise difficulty. The pilot also measured Sonnet's cost (US$ 0.16 to 0.27 per call, because it returns 10 to 20 thousand tokens of fixes), which forced the grid to be limited, and later, by cost decision, expanded.

The design, hypotheses, ground truth, prompts and verifier were frozen by hash before the main run (dados/CONGELADO.txt; there is no git tag). Cost is nominal (tokens × list price: Haiku US$ 0.10 and 0.50 per million input and output tokens, Sonnet US$ 2 and 10), the same for everyone.

5. The execution

Calls were made with claude -p, medium effort, no tools and no internet. The final run has 2,640 calls: Haiku, full grid (48 screens per task, 11 conditions, 3 samples) and Sonnet, full grid (same screens and conditions, 2 samples). No call failed. The pace was about 10 calls per minute, with 14 in parallel on Sonnet and 8 to 20 on Haiku.

Deviations from the pre-registration, all recorded in dados/DESVIOS.md before the analysis: Sonnet moved from the reduced grid to the full one, and Haiku got a third sample, by cost and accuracy decision; the audit of 60 verifier verdicts and the sensitivity analysis without the 12 defective rules were added; T3 (compare screens) and T1 (create from scratch) left the design.

6. The hypotheses, one by one

Paired tests by screen (mean of samples), one-sided Wilcoxon, 95% CI by bootstrap of 10,000 screen resamples and Holm correction over the 11 confirmatory tests. All on Haiku; differences in percentage points (pp) of rules fixed.

Hypothesis Result Difference (95% CI) Verdict
H1 rule present > absent, L25 81% vs 52% +29 pp (+26 to +33) confirmed
H1 rule present > absent, L50 79% vs 55% +24 pp (+20 to +27) confirmed
H2a L25 > L0 59% vs 47% +12 pp (+10 to +15) confirmed
H2b L50 > L25 67% vs 59% +8 pp (+5 to +10) confirmed
H2c L100 > L50 76% vs 67% +9 pp (+6 to +11) confirmed
H3 held-out: L100 not worse than L0 (5 pp margin) 55% vs 44% +11 pp (+7 to +15) confirmed (the lake did not hurt where it did not cover)
H4 L100 > D (other domains) 76% vs 52% +23 pp (+21 to +26) confirmed
H6a T2 A3 > A1 80.6% vs 80.9% -0.3 pp (-3 to +3) not confirmed
H6b T4 K > L100 78% vs 70% +8 pp (+6 to +11) confirmed
H7a T2 new failures A0 > A2 0.94 vs 0.21 per call -0.74 confirmed
H7b T4 new failures L100 vs K 0 vs 0 n/a not testable (in T4 every rule is already violated)

Nine of the eleven tests reject the null hypothesis under Holm's criterion. Outside the confirmatory set:

  • H5 (does simple search keep 90% of the gain?): no. BM25 with 12 rules kept 31% of the full lake's gain (+7 pp against +24 pp over L0), with fewer input tokens (13.6 thousand against 19.2 thousand).
  • H8 (difficulty): confirmed. Plain Haiku fixed 52% in T2 and 46% in T4, well below the 85% ceiling threshold.
  • H9 (descriptive, Haiku with lake against Sonnet without lake): in T2, Haiku A3 81% against Sonnet A0 63% (ratio 1.28), at 6% of the cost; in T4, Haiku L100 70% against Sonnet L0 61% (ratio 1.14), at 8% of the cost. It passes both criteria (at least 90% of the score at no more than 50% of the cost). Sonnet also improves with the lake and beats Haiku under the same conditions (section 7.3).

7. Results

7.1 Lake completeness, in steps (T4)

Fraction of violated rules that come to be met, mean over 48 screens (3 samples on Haiku, 2 on Sonnet):

Condition Haiku (all) Haiku (shown) Haiku (held-out) Sonnet (all) Sonnet (shown)
L0, no lake 46.1% 46.9% 43.6% 61.3% 61.4%
L25 56.9% 59.3% 50.3% 66.3% 68.7%
L50 63.1% 66.9% 52.3% 72.4% 76.3%
L100 70.1% 75.7% 54.5% 79.7% 85.9%
D (other domains) 51.2% 52.4% 47.8% 63.1% 64.2%
R (BM25, 12 rules) 53.5% 56.8% 44.0% 62.7% 64.8%
K (L100 + report) 78.4% 88.5% 50.0% 83.0% 91.8%

The gain is almost linear: each extra 25% of the lake yields 8 to 12 points on Haiku. On the same screen and sample, the present rule was met 81% of the time and the absent one 52% (L25). The effect of pure volume (D, +5 pp over L0) and of simple search (R, +7 pp) are small next to the full lake (+24 pp). Among the decisions Haiku cited, the fraction pointing to a rule actually shown rose from 59% (L25) to 90% (L100); in D it was 54% and in R, 49%: with little information the model cites rules it did not receive.

7.2 The verifier report (T2 and T4)

In T2, the family's rules (A1) took Haiku from 48% to 91% on the shown rules; the report (A2) to 96%; both together (A3) to 96%, with no gain over the rules alone in total (80.6% against 80.9%). The report does something else: it reduces new rules that start failing (0.94 per call in A0, 0.50 in A1, 0.21 in A2) and keeps the model focused on what it lists. On the held-out rules, which the report never mentions, Haiku went from 60% (A0) to 28% (A2): the report says what to fix and the model leaves the rest. In T4, adding the report to the full lake (K) raised Haiku from 70% to 78% (on shown rules, from 76% to 89%).

7.3 Haiku and Sonnet, and the cost

Sonnet is better than Haiku under the same conditions (T4 L0: 61% against 46%; L100: 80% against 70%; K: 83% against 78%). But Haiku with the lake beats plain Sonnet, and the nominal cost per call is very different: Haiku L100 US$ 0.0225 against Sonnet L0 US$ 0.2728 (8%); in T2, Haiku A3 US$ 0.0093 against Sonnet A0 US$ 0.1526 (6%). The whole run cost US$ 252.29 nominal (Haiku US$ 25.41, Sonnet US$ 226.88).

7.4 Independent measure: axe-core

In WCAG A/AA violations per final screen, measured by axe-core (which does not depend on our verifier), Haiku in T4 went from 0.90 (L0) to 0.60 (L25), 0.52 (L50) and 0.47 (L100), with 0.75 in D, 0.86 in R and 0.49 in K. Sonnet stayed around 0.3 in every T4 condition. In T2, the report alone (A2) raised Haiku's violations (0.60 against 0.39 in A0), consistent with the report's narrow focus. These are low averages (under one violation per screen) and axe covers only part of our rules, so it confirms the direction, not the magnitude.

7.5 Robustness

Excluding the 26 conditional rules (whose condition may not exist on the screen) or the 12 rules with a verifier defect confirmed in the audit, absolute levels move a few points and the order of conditions is the same (Haiku T4 without the 12 rules: L0 47%, L25 58%, L50 65%, L100 72%, D 53%, R 54%, K 81%).

8. Why these results hold, and how far

The design was pre-registered and frozen by hash; the volume control (D) separates "more text" from "the right rule"; the held-out rules measure what the model does without having been taught; each condition repeats the same screen across samples and the test is paired by screen, with Holm correction; the analysis without conditional rules and without defective-verifier rules checks robustness; and we report what did not work (BM25, A3 against A1).

9. Threats to validity

  • Synthetic screens. Six script-generated families, with a fixed structure per family. The result holds for these screens; it does not demonstrate the same behavior in a large production project.
  • T4 is draft review, not creation. The model starts from a screen that already has the right structure; deciding from scratch is another task, which the verifiers could not score.
  • Circularity. The same author generated the screens, the rules and the verifier; the report the model receives comes from the same verifier that scores. The held-out rules and the sensitivity without the defective rules mitigate this, but do not eliminate it.
  • Imperfect verifier. In 60 audited verdicts, 8 diverged (13%); the error tends to understate the absolute levels of every condition.
  • Model-audited lake. No human review; some rules come from guides (Nielsen, Baymard) that are recommendation, not standard.
  • Only two model families. Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5; Opus and Fable were left out.
  • Nominal cost. List price, without plan limits; the cost of building the lake and the verifier is not counted.
  • No aesthetics. The previous study showed that no human-free instrument measures beauty validly; this study claims nothing about beauty.

10. What this lets us conclude

  • For anyone building a UX data lake: on this set of screens, more relevant rules gave more accuracy, in roughly equal steps up to the full lake, with no sign of a plateau. Text volume alone does not explain the gain (D) and the right rule matters (H1, H4).
  • A simple search (BM25 with 12 rules) was not enough: it recovered 31% of the gain. If the lake is used through retrieval, retrieval has to beat that, or the relevant lake has to fit whole in the context.
  • The lake did not hurt where it did not cover: on never-shown rules, accuracy was up to 11 points higher with the full lake (H3). It may be spillover or just a more careful model; we did not separate the two explanations.
  • The verifier report prevents regressions and closes what it lists, but narrows focus: it reduced new failures and, in T2, left unfixed the rules that were not on the list. Added to the full lake in T4, it improved 8 points.
  • Cost: with the lake, Haiku beat Sonnet without it at 6% to 8% of the cost per call. Sonnet, however, is still better under the same conditions.
  • What this does not let us conclude: that the result holds for a real production project (the screens are synthetic and T4 is draft review), that the lake's rules cause better UX decisions for real users (we measured rule compliance, not product outcome) or that it holds for models beyond the two tested.

What I would do next: repeat T4 on real production screens, with a human reviewer as a second measure, and test a retrieval better than BM25.

11. Reproducibility

All the material is in studies/haiku-ui-producao/: the lake (lake/lake-ref-v2.json and the audits), the six families with their tests (gerador/familias/), the stimulus generator, the verifier, the executor and the analysis. The raw data (every answer, tokens and cost) and the scored data are in dados/bruto/. Archived on Zenodo (version 3.0.0, studies 3 and 3b): 10.5281/zenodo.24132784.

The experiments, the data and the conclusions are mine. The writing was AI-assisted and reviewed by me.

title: The BRIDGE dataset: paired brightfield whole-slide images of prostate core-needle biopsies in paraffin, after deparaffinization and H&E staining
description:
arXiv:2611.13883v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Computational approaches are increasingly being explored to streamline histopathology workflows, including label-free methods that aim to reduce reliance on chemical staining. Among these, deep learning-based label-free virtual staining uses images of unstained tissue to computationally generate stained images. Despite growing interest, model development and validation remain constrained by the scarcity of paired, clinically annotated whole-slide imaging datasets. We present BRIDGE, a dataset of prostate core-needle biopsies collected at the Prof. Franciszek Lukaszczyk Oncology Centre in Bydgoszcz, Poland. The dataset comprises 869 glass slides from 169 patients, each digitized sequentially after sectioning, deparaffinization, and hematoxylin and eosin staining, yielding in total 2607 whole-slide images. The dataset supports the development and external validation of label-free virtual staining, virtual unstaining, image-registration and segmentation methods. Each slide is accompanied by a Gleason score, enabling downstream analyses of cancer classification and grading concordance. The stained images can be used independently for color normalization and cross-scanner robustness studies. All images are de-identified, distributed in their native scanner format and will be available through the BioImage Archive.
