title: Market-Conditioned JEPA: Learning from Unpredictable Market Shocks
description:
arXiv:2611.13572v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Much of the variation in financial time series is driven by market-wide shocks that cannot be predicted from an asset's own history. Per-asset self-supervised learning treats this variation as irreducible noise. Under a latent factor model, we show that conditioning prediction on the realized market factor makes the asset's market exposure necessary for optimal prediction, while reducing the noise against which the asset-specific component is learned. Building on this insight, we introduce Market-Conditioned JEPA (MC-JEPA), a joint-embedding predictive architecture for financial time series. During training, we construct a leave-one-out market condition for each asset from the future target embeddings of other assets and incorporate it through factor loadings derived from the asset's own representation. On 11 years of minute-level Chinese A-share data, MC-JEPA improves over per-asset JEPA across nine targets spanning returns, market exposure, risk, and liquidity, with the strongest and most statistically significant gains in exposure, risk, and liquidity. It achieves the best RankIC on all liquidity targets and on return horizons from two hours to five days, outperforming time-series foundation models and self-supervised baselines, and delivers the best portfolio performance in a historical backtest. Ablations show that the return and exposure gains require the condition to be aligned with the realized market movement. After restoring the volatility scale removed by normalization, the predictor's factor loadings rank stocks by market beta nearly as well as a supervised probe, without labels. A synthetic factor-model study with known parameters shows that conditioning improves the recovery of both market exposure and the asset-specific component.

title: An ensemble of graph generative models for assisted history matching of the Brugge field case
description:
arXiv:2611.12927v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Assisted history matching remains non-unique because many geological realisations can reproduce equivalent production responses with substantial differences between individual well matches. This ambiguity increases when a field comprises several depositional settings and modelling strategies. The paper applied a graph autoencoder approach to history matching of a benchmark Brugge field that comprises different depositional zones. Each stratigraphic zone is modelled with its dedicated generative model that comprises a joint latent space for optimisation history matching loops. Graph-based generators operate directly on the active cells of the corner-point grid, so its irregular geometry is handled without conversion to a regular lattice. The optimisation search in the 160-dimensional joint latent space is done with the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy. The multi-component objective function includes static well data mismatch, dynamic production mismatch, and a geological realism penalty based on the Decoder induced latent metric. Latent space diagnostics with topological data analysis are applied prior to history matching to test whether one generator is sufficient or whether a multiple generator formulation is required. The results show that the zone-based formulation gives coherent latent spaces, preserves the main porosity and permeability relations that vary from one zone to another, and supports history matching while keeping the solutions within the learned geological manifold. The matched models reproduce field oil and water production within the prior uncertainty range and provide a comparable well-level match to previously published Brugge studies based on Ensemble Kalman Filter, Particle Swarm Optimisation with principal component analysis of parameterisation, and Multiple Kernel Learning with Particle Swarm Optimisation.

title: Serving a heavy model without blowing up the server bill
description:
An AI model is heavy and hungry. Served carelessly, it blows up response times and the server bill. On an audio-analysis SaaS that I designed and shipped solo, it had to stay fast, secure and economically viable.

The hosting decision. I served the model on a server I run, with NGINX and automatic file cleanup, rather than on usage-billed infrastructure. It means more deployment work, but the bill no longer follows the number of analyses. It can be forecast.

On the code side, two rules matter for a service like this.

1. Load the model once, at startup. Not on every request. With FastAPI, that's what the lifespan parameter is for. The application doesn't receive requests until startup is finished.

from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from fastapi import FastAPI

models = {}

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    models["main"] = load_model()  # slow: done once
    yield
    models.clear()

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)

The old way, on_event, is deprecated.

2. Don't block the server during a computation. An async def function that computes for a long time blocks the whole application. A def function is run by FastAPI in a thread pool.

@app.post("/analyze")
def analyze(file: UploadFile):  # def: runs in a thread pool
    return models["main"].predict(file)

That's how the model runs in production on this SaaS.

Amine Affif, full-stack developer in Paris. amineaffif.com

title: ARE-bench: Benchmarking Agents' Research Ability in Real-World Researcher Sessions and Workspaces
description:
arXiv:2611.14364v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Research agents achieve increasingly strong benchmark scores, yet these scores do not necessarily translate into reliable delivery in ongoing research projects. Many research-agent benchmarks emphasize standalone tasks and relatively self-contained workflows in clean or curated workspaces. However, researchers ask agents to complete one step within an ongoing project, where requests depend on earlier session decisions and workspaces contain unfinished files, outdated versions, and failed attempts. We introduce ARE-bench to evaluate whether research agents advance ongoing projects while respecting prior decisions and existing workspace state, grounded in real session context and in-progress workspaces. ARE-bench includes 75 tasks built on agent sessions and full workspaces from recruited researchers' own projects, spanning seven research stages, 33 requirements, and 150 sub-requirements, with 1,173 binary checklist items in total. Each task is anchored at a real user request, preserves its requirements, and summarizes the earlier requests still in effect as background. The complete workspace is replayed to that boundary without cleanup, preserving artifacts from earlier turns. Each checklist is compiled from an intent-aligned rubric and credits any valid solution. Across seven frontier models, the strongest passes every checklist item on only 66.2% of tasks, and Design and Execution rank among the hardest stages for every model. Three models pass about 69% of tasks when only delivery contracts and general norms are checked, but just 28.4% to 40.0% once historical and material or workspace requirements are also checked. Evaluating delivery without these contextual requirements can therefore overestimate research agents and mask differences between them.

title: Three systems, three numbers: write a metric contract before you put an AI agent on your CRM and ERP
description:
A sales manager asks for one number. The CRM says 100 sold. The ERP says 80 invoiced. Somebody's spreadsheet says 120. None of them has to be wrong: each system records a different moment of the same sale, entered by different people at different times.

This is the normal state of many mid-sized companies that run Salesforce next to a separate ERP and glue them together with spreadsheets. It is also exactly the setup where teams now want to add an AI agent that "answers questions about the business". If you do that without fixing the definitions first, the agent inherits the same argument and picks one of the three numbers for you.

This post shows a small, practical artifact that helps before any agent work: a metric contract.

Why the numbers disagree

Take "sales this month". In a Salesforce org alone there are already two valid answers:

-- Won opportunities closed this month
SELECT SUM(Amount) FROM Opportunity
WHERE IsWon = true AND CloseDate = THIS_MONTH

-- Activated orders effective this month
SELECT SUM(TotalAmount) FROM Order
WHERE Status = 'Activated' AND EffectiveDate = THIS_MONTH

Both queries are correct SOQL and they can return different totals on the same day. "Invoiced" lives in the ERP and has its own date logic. The spreadsheet usually mixes all of them plus manual corrections. Three sources, three numbers, one meeting to decide which one wins.

The metric contract

A metric contract is a short, versioned file that says, for each number leadership asks about, exactly where it comes from and who owns it. YAML is enough:

metric: sales_this_month
question: "How much did we sell this month?"
definition: "Sum of activated orders by effective date"
source_of_truth: salesforce
object: Order
filter: "Status = 'Activated' AND EffectiveDate = THIS_MONTH"
amount_field: TotalAmount
owner: sales_operations
not_this: ["won opportunities", "invoices issued"]
reconciles_with:
  - metric: invoiced_this_month
    expected_gap: "orders activated but not yet invoiced"
---
metric: invoiced_this_month
question: "How much did we invoice this month?"
definition: "Sum of posted invoices by invoice date"
source_of_truth: erp
owner: finance

The values above are an example of the format, not a real company's setup. What matters is that every metric has exactly one source of truth, one owner, and an explicit list of what it is not.

What changes for the agent

With a contract in place, an agent that answers "how much did we sell?" has a single query to run and a documented gap to explain when the invoiced number is lower. Without it, the agent has three sources that disagree and no rule for choosing.

A few practical rules that follow:

  • Give the agent the contract as context, not just database access.
  • If a metric needs a spreadsheet to compute, the contract should say so. That row is a candidate for removal, not for automation.
  • Review the contract when a process changes, the same way you review code.

When a single data source removes the problem

The contract reduces arguments, but it does not remove the reconciliation work when sales, invoicing and inventory live in separate databases. That is why we build EGA Futura ERP natively on Salesforce: sales, invoicing, inventory, purchasing, treasury and accounting share the same database as the CRM, so the "sold" and "invoiced" metrics in the contract point to the same place. If you are earlier in the journey, the contract is still the cheapest first step.

I wrote the business side of this, in Spanish, as the typical day of a manager reconciling Salesforce, the ERP and Excel.

Juan Manuel Garrido, founder of EGA Futura and co-founder of Vantegrate.

title: Investigating Composite Modeling in Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization for Scientific Design
description:
arXiv:2611.13565v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scientific design often requires balancing competing objectives that are expensive to evaluate through experiments or simulations. Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) addresses this challenge by using probabilistic models to guide the selection of promising designs. In many applications, tunable inputs map to observable intermediate responses, which are then combined through known functions to compute the final objectives. Prior work on Bayesian optimization of composite functions shows that learning from these intermediate responses, which we call Composite modeling, can substantially improve sampling efficiency in single-objective optimization, compared to methods that condition only on black-box observations of the objective function. The benefits of Composite modeling in MOBO, however, remain understudied. In this work, we study the benefits of Composite modeling in MOBO and investigate the factors driving variation in its gains. We first establish single-objective conditions under which intermediate observations provide no additional predictive information beyond objective values, where composite and black box methods use the same warped Gaussian process prior. Controlled numerical experiments with versions of four MOBO methods across eight synthetic and application-inspired scientific-design benchmarks examine how these conditions relate to optimization gains in the multi-objective setting, where the black box approach models the objective functions with a standard multi-output Gaussian process. Both investigations support the claim that composite modeling tends to help more when the function mapping intermediate responses to final objectives is non-bijective and non-affine.

title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.14320v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. To address this, we introduce WikiTrace, an evidence-linked memory system designed to let agents check each lesson against its original trajectory. Specifically, motivated by the finding that a trajectory often still holds the evidence needed to catch an erroneous lesson, WikiTrace stores each lesson as a concise insight linked to a summary of why its trajectory succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory itself. Then, on a new task, the agent starts from all insights and, whenever one lacks details needed to act, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed task, descends through its links with terminal tools to fill in missing details or correct the insight before acting. We validate WikiTrace on five agentic benchmarks, showing that it consistently outperforms existing memory approaches and a baseline given the same insights alone, while also reducing memory-induced degradation. Our code is available at https://github.com/yukyeongleee/wikitrace

title: Branch-and-Commit for Frozen RL Agents: When and Where to Spend Test-Time Compute
description:
arXiv:2611.13003v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning agents are often deployed with policies that cannot be retrained or modified. In digital environments whose states can be copied and resumed, an operator has another option: sample several continuations from the current state, evaluate them, and continue from the endpoint of the selected branch. We call this procedure branch-and-commit. We study when it improves return, what produces the improvement, and where its computational budget should be spent. Across four environments, two frozen policies, five continuation verifiers, and a model-free selection rule, we find that the benefit of branching depends on dispersion: the difference between the best candidate return and the mean candidate return. Branching provides no benefit in low-dispersion settings, while increasing return by 12.8% in our main Craftax-Medium setting. Most of this gain comes not from selecting better actions, but from selecting among different stochastic realizations of the same action. Several competent verifiers achieve similar episode returns, suggesting that verifier quality is not the main constraint at our operating budget. Instead, computation is better allocated to states where useful dispersion is likely. On held-out seeds, gating branching using predicted dispersion retains 69% of the improvement from uniform branching while using 48% as many branching calls. These results characterize when branch-and-commit is useful and clarify what its gains represent.

title: I screenshot five embedded wallet sign-ups every week
description:
Vendor docs describe login methods and pricing. They rarely show the screens a person actually clicks through. I wanted that, so I built KYC Flows: a free site with side-by-side screenshots of Privy, Dynamic, thirdweb, MetaMask Embedded, Crossmint, and one KYC vendor, Didit.

I re-shoot the flows every week from test accounts. No real IDs. As of the November 9, 2026 update, the four wallet logins were recaptured and had not changed, so those pictures still date to November 2. Didit's intro and a new consent screen are from November 9.

I have not timed any of these paths. The compare pages still say "Not measured yet" for time to a first wallet.

What the first screen asks for

Each lab uses a default or sandbox client, and the methods you turn on will change the first screen. Here is what the captures show.

Privy. This lab offers email only. The address is submitted from that first screen.

Dynamic. The sandbox shows an email field, then MetaMask, Coinbase, and WalletConnect.

MetaMask Embedded. The default modal offers email or phone, MetaMask, and other wallets.

thirdweb. This client asks for an email address.

Crossmint. The sign-in sheet offers Google, or an email with Submit on the same row, plus a "Secured by Crossmint" line.

Those first screens already disagree. Privy and thirdweb, in these clients, start with email. Dynamic and MetaMask Embedded put external wallets on the first screen. Crossmint puts Google next to the email field.

How far each walk got

I only finished two of the wallet paths.

On Privy, the lab path was email, a one-time code, a screen that says it is creating the wallet, then an all-set screen that says the account is secured. MFA did not appear. That is four captured screens of the five the page lists. The extra security check is still pending.

On Dynamic, the path was email, a code, then a signed-in widget. A separate wallet-creation screen did not appear, and the extra-details and extra-check screens also did not show up. The site counts that as email, code, then a signed-in widget. Three screens captured of five listed.

thirdweb stops on the code screen after the email step. MetaMask Embedded stops on a screen that says "Verify your Email account to continue." I did not enter those codes, so no wallet was reached. Crossmint is a login sheet, the email filled in, then a six-digit code screen. That code was not entered either, so no wallet was created.

If a vendor page lists four or five sign-up steps, some of those boxes are still empty, or only described in the docs. The honest count is the screens I actually captured, and whether I reached a wallet.

Didit added a consent step

Didit is the only KYC vendor on the site. It does not create a wallet. I added it because a wallet flow often grows a verification step, and because Didit publishes prices in the open.

The November 9 re-shoot caught a new intro layout: scan an ID, take a selfie, and continue on another device. After that intro sits a new required screen titled "Before we take your selfie."

The screen says face geometry comes from the selfie and the ID photo, plus a short liveness video. It says KYC Flows and Didit have that data, it is not sold, and it is deleted when no longer needed, never later than 12 months after the last verification. The checkbox is required before "Agree and continue."

The document screens after that are still the November 2 captures. The face steps are not on the site, because they need a real ID, and I do not submit one. Nine of twelve listed screens are captured. Didit's intro says the check takes about a minute. That is their claim, not a time I measured.

Crossmint's public wallet price, as of November 9

The same changelog notes that Crossmint's login screens did not change. Its public wallet price, recorded on November 9 from Crossmint's pricing page, is free for 5,000 monthly active wallets, then $0.01 per wallet. Custom pricing starts at $0.01. The site lists onramps and checkout as separate, per-transaction products, not part of the login price.

For contrast, thirdweb's published shape is 1,000 wallet MAUs free, then from $0.015, plus a platform plan starting at $99. Those are snapshots of public pages, not quotes.

What I would not read into this

The modal an app shows is a configuration. Privy's lab is email only. Dynamic's sandbox shows wallets on the first screen. MetaMask Embedded's default modal is not the same as a custom button that skips the picker. Times are not measured. Some walks stop on the code screen.

The screens, the public prices, and the weekly changelog are on kycflows.com. I built this. If a screen or a cited price changes, I recapture it the following week.

title: IaaS Explained: A Beginner's Guide Using Amazon EC2 as a Case Study
description:
By Samuel Andong, Cloud Computing student
When I started my cloud computing course, I kept hearing three terms: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS. This article explains the first one, Infrastructure as a Service, in simple language. It then looks at Amazon EC2 as a real case study.
What is IaaS?
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) is a cloud model where a provider rents you computing resources over the internet. These resources are virtual servers, storage, and networking. You do not buy or maintain any physical hardware. You create what you need in minutes, and you pay for what you use.
Think of renting an empty building. The owner looks after the land, the walls, the electricity and the security guards. You decide what goes inside, how to arrange it, and who comes in.
IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS
The main difference is who manages what.
Model
You manage
The provider manages
Example
IaaS
Operating system, runtime, apps, data
Servers, storage, networking, virtualization
Amazon EC2, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure
PaaS
Your app and data
Everything below the app, including the OS
Cloudflare Workers, Railway
SaaS
Only your own use of it
The whole application
Gmail, Google Docs
IaaS gives you the most control, but also the most responsibility. If you rent a server, you must install updates, secure it and set it up yourself.
Key characteristics of IaaS
• On-demand: you can create or delete a server in minutes.
• Pay as you go: you are billed for usage, not for owning hardware.
• Scalable: you can add more servers when traffic grows and remove them when it drops.
• Full control: you choose the operating system, software and network rules.
• Global: you can place servers in data centers around the world.
Case study: Amazon EC2
Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) is the IaaS service from Amazon Web Services (AWS). It lets you rent virtual machines, called instances, and it is one of the best-known IaaS products in the world.
The main building blocks
• Instances: the virtual servers. You pick a type based on CPU, memory and cost. Some are small for tests, and others are large for heavy workloads.
• AMI (Amazon Machine Image): a template that holds the operating system and software. You pick an AMI, such as Ubuntu or Windows, when you launch a server.
• EBS (Elastic Block Store): storage disks that attach to your instance, like a hard drive.
• VPC and security groups: your private network and the firewall rules that decide which traffic can reach your server, for example port 80 for web traffic and port 22 for SSH.
• Key pairs: a secure login method, so you connect with a private key file instead of a password.
• Regions and Availability Zones: AWS has data centers in many parts of the world. You choose where your server runs, and you can spread servers across zones for reliability.
How you pay
EC2 offers several pricing options:
• On-Demand: pay per use with no commitment. This is best for beginners and short projects.
• Reserved or savings plans: commit to a period of usage for a lower price.
• Spot instances: use spare capacity at a large discount, with the risk that AWS may take it back.
AWS has offered a free tier for new accounts. Always check the current terms and set a billing alert so you are not surprised by a bill.
Scaling
Auto Scaling can add EC2 instances when traffic rises and remove them when it falls. A load balancer spreads visitors across the servers. This is how a busy website can survive a sudden spike without crashing.
Comparison: Amazon EC2 vs Oracle Cloud Infrastructure
Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) is another major IaaS provider. It offers the same core idea as EC2, which is virtual servers, storage and networking on demand, but it uses different names for many things.
Feature
Amazon EC2 (AWS)
Oracle Cloud Infrastructure
Virtual server
Instance
Compute instance
Server sizes
Instance types
Shapes
OS templates
AMI
Images
Disk storage
EBS
Block Volume
Private network
VPC
VCN (Virtual Cloud Network)
Firewall rules
Security groups
Security lists and network security groups
Organizing resources
Accounts and tags
Compartments
Server login
Key pair
SSH key pair
Free option
Free tier for new accounts
Always Free resources and a trial credit
The terms differ, but the workflow is almost the same: pick an image, choose a server size, set the network rules, add an SSH key and launch. Once you understand one IaaS provider, learning another is mostly learning its vocabulary. Free offers and limits change often, so check each provider's current terms before you sign up.
Example: hosting a website on EC2
Here is the typical flow for putting a small website online on IaaS:

  1. Create an AWS account and choose a region.
  2. Launch an instance and select an Ubuntu AMI.
  3. Create a key pair and download the private key.
  4. Set the security group to allow SSH (port 22) from your own IP and HTTP (port 80) from anywhere.
  5. Connect with SSH, install a web server such as Nginx, and copy your files to it.
  6. Open the instance's public address in a browser to see the site. Compare this with a PaaS platform. On a platform like Cloudflare, I connected my GitHub repository and the platform published my site. With IaaS, I would have to create the server, install the web server and secure it myself. That is more work, but it gives me full control. Benefits of IaaS • No upfront hardware cost • Fast setup and easy experimentation • Flexible scaling up and down • Full control of the operating system and software • Reliable infrastructure run by experts Challenges of IaaS • More responsibility: you handle patches, security settings and backups. • Cost surprises: a forgotten running server keeps charging you. • Skills needed: you need to understand servers, networking and security. • Vendor lock-in: moving to another provider can take effort. When should you choose IaaS? Choose IaaS when you need full control, custom software, or special network settings. Choose PaaS when you just want to deploy code quickly, and SaaS when you only need a ready-made tool. Conclusion IaaS is the foundation of cloud computing. It gives you virtual servers, storage and networks on demand, with control over everything above the hardware. Amazon EC2 shows how this works in practice: you choose a server, set up the network, install your software and pay for what you use. For a student, IaaS is a great way to learn how real systems run, as long as you secure your servers and watch your costs. References • AWS documentation: What is Amazon EC2? (docs.aws.amazon.com) • AWS Pricing for EC2 (aws.amazon.com/ec2/pricing) • NIST definition of cloud computing, Special Publication 800-145

title: Train High, Ship Low: Efficient LoRA Synchronization for Distributed On-Policy Post-Training
description:
arXiv:2611.13306v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Transmitting LoRA adapters to rollout workers can bottleneck distributed on-policy post-training over bandwidth-constrained networks. Lowering the training rank may limit the capacity a workload needs, while adaptive optimizer updates are difficult to compress. Rollout workers can instead reconstruct updates from gradients by maintaining replicated optimizer states. We introduce HiLo, a compressor-agnostic framework that replaces parameter transmission with compressed gradient dissemination and local optimizer replay. By applying the same decoded gradients, the learner and workers maintain consistent policy states at the same version under reproducible execution. We further develop Spar, a budget-aware gradient compressor that combines spectral truncation, adaptive rank allocation and error feedback to decouple training rank from communication cost. Experiments across on-policy distillation and reward-guided post-training show that HiLo with Spar maintains learning quality close to full synchronization while transmitting as little as 1.6% of the adapter bytes, and accelerates end-to-end updates by up to $2.2\times$ under bandwidth constraints.

title: 1 of 41 Cold Emails Bounced. That's 2.4% or 1.9%, Depending on What You Divide By
description:
On Nov 9 I sent 41 first emails for cold outreach for Posting Dude, a backlink service I run. A day later my sending tool said 40 were delivered and 1 bounced.

1 in 41 is 2.4%. My pause line is 2%. So I should stop, right?

Except that batch wasn't the whole stream. Counting every first email I'd sent in that sequence so far, it was 1 bounce in 53. That's 1.9%. Under the line.

Same bounce, two answers. Here is how I decided, the small script I now run before any follow-up goes out, and the two DNS cases that would have bounced if I hadn't looked.

Why bother before the follow-up

Follow-ups are where a dirty list hurts twice. A bounced address in step 1 is one bad send. Leave it in the sequence and it bounces again on day 4, and again on day 11. Google's sender guidelines literally say to "automatically unsubscribe recipients who have multiple bounced messages" (Google's email sender guidelines). Mailbox providers keep score, and repeat bounces are the cheapest way to lose it.

So the check runs the day after the first batch, before day 4.

The 5 steps

1. Send the first email to a small batch. 41 people, not the whole list. If the list is bad, you find out on 41 addresses instead of 400.

2. A day later, pull the delivery status of every message. Not "sent". Sent only means your tool accepted it. You want delivered / bounced per address, from your sending tool's API or export. Mine gave 40 delivered, 1 bounced.

3. Divide by first emails only. Follow-ups go to people who already received mail from you, so they barely bounce (mine: 0). If you put them in the denominator your rate looks better than your list really is. Batch: 1/41 = 2.4%. Stream: 1/53 = 1.9%.

4. Set the pause line before you look. Mine is 2%, decided before the first send. Under it, keep going. Over it, stop and clean the list before anything else goes out. Deciding after you see the number is how 2.4% turns into "basically 2".

5. Never follow up a bounced address. Pull it out of the sequence the same day, so day-4 only goes to inboxes that actually took mail.

So which number won?

Both, for different decisions.

  • Stream-wide (1.9%) decides whether the sequence keeps running. It was under the line, so day-4 follow-ups stay scheduled for Nov 13.
  • Batch (2.4%) decides how fast I grow. That batch was over the line, so the next batch stayed at about 40 instead of going up. I only raise it if the next batch comes back with 1 bounce or fewer.

The one bounce was a role inbox (a support@ address), and it's suppressed now. Also, to be clear about results: zero human replies so far. One auto-ticket reply, which doesn't count. A clean list doesn't make people answer; it just stops you from burning the domain while you find out.

The script

No dependencies, Node 18+. Feed it a CSV export: email,step,status,code, where step is first or followup and code is the SMTP enhanced status code if your tool gives one.

// node bounce-check.mjs sends.csv [pauseLine=0.02]
// sends.csv columns: email,step,status,code   (step = first | followup)
import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";

const [file, pauseArg = "0.02"] = process.argv.slice(2);
const pauseLine = Number(pauseArg);
const rows = readFileSync(file, "utf8").trim().split("\n").slice(1)
  .map((l) => { const [email, step, status, code = ""] = l.split(",").map((s) => s.trim());
    return { email: email.toLowerCase(), step, status: status.toLowerCase(), code }; });

const firsts = rows.filter((r) => r.step === "first");
const bounced = (r) => r.status === "bounced";
const hard = (r) => bounced(r) && !r.code.startsWith("4"); // 5.x.x or no code = treat as permanent
const firstBounces = firsts.filter(bounced);
const rate = firstBounces.length / firsts.length;

console.log(`first emails: ${firsts.length}, delivered: ${firsts.filter((r) => r.status === "delivered").length}, bounced: ${firstBounces.length}`);
console.log(`bounce rate vs first emails: ${(rate * 100).toFixed(1)}%  (pause line ${(pauseLine * 100).toFixed(1)}%)`);
console.log(rate > pauseLine ? "STOP: over the pause line. Clean the list before anything else goes out." : "OK: under the pause line.");

// never follow up an address that bounced hard, anywhere in the stream
const dead = new Set(rows.filter(hard).map((r) => r.email));
const soft = new Set(rows.filter((r) => bounced(r) && !hard(r)).map((r) => r.email));

async function mx(domain) {
  const res = await fetch(`https://dns.google/resolve?name=${domain}&type=MX`).then((r) => r.json());
  if (res.Status === 3) return "NXDOMAIN (domain doesn't exist)";
  const recs = (res.Answer || []).filter((a) => a.type === 15).map((a) => a.data);
  if (recs.length === 0) return "no MX (mail falls back to the A record, risky)";
  if (recs.length === 1 && /^0 \.$/.test(recs[0])) return "null MX (domain says it takes no mail)";
  return "ok";
}

const due = firsts.filter((r) => r.status === "delivered" && !dead.has(r.email));
const keep = [];
for (const r of due) {
  const verdict = await mx(r.email.split("@")[1]);
  if (verdict === "ok") keep.push(r.email); else console.log(`skip ${r.email}: ${verdict}`);
}
for (const e of soft) console.log(`hold ${e}: soft bounce (4.x.x), retry later, don't sequence it yet`);
for (const e of dead) console.log(`suppress ${e}: hard bounce`);
writeFileSync("followups.csv", "email\n" + keep.join("\n") + "\n");
console.log(`follow-ups due: ${keep.length} -> followups.csv`);

I used Google's DNS-over-HTTPS endpoint because the box I run this on intercepts plain DNS. If yours doesn't, dns.promises.resolveMx works too.

Run against a made-up 7-row file (fake people, real domains), today:

first emails: 7, delivered: 5, bounced: 2
bounce rate vs first emails: 28.6%  (pause line 2.0%)
STOP: over the pause line. Clean the list before anything else goes out.
skip cara@example.com: null MX (domain says it takes no mail)
skip dev@no-such-domain-2026-11-11.com: NXDOMAIN (domain doesn't exist)
hold eli@outlook.com: soft bounce (4.x.x), retry later, don't sequence it yet
suppress support@shop.example: hard bounce
follow-ups due: 3 -> followups.csv

The parts that are easy to get wrong

Hard vs soft. RFC 3463 splits delivery failures into 4.x.x ("persistent transient failure", a full mailbox, a server that's down) and 5.x.x ("permanent failure", not likely to work if you resend). Suppress 5.x.x for good. Hold 4.x.x and retry later, but don't let it ride the sequence on autopilot. If your tool gives no code, treat it as hard. Guessing soft is how dead addresses get three emails.

"Delivered" doesn't mean the domain takes mail now. Some status APIs report what happened at send time. A day later a startup can be gone. That's why the script re-checks MX right before follow-ups.

Null MX. example.com publishes an MX record of 0 . today. That's RFC 7505's "null MX": the domain is telling you it accepts no mail at all. A naive check that only asks "is there an MX record?" passes it. The script catches it.

No MX at all. Mail then falls back to the domain's A/AAAA record. Sometimes that works, often it's a web server that won't take mail. I skip these for cold follow-ups; you might not.

If you'd rather eyeball one domain than run a script, the free email DNS checker on Uno (a directory I run) shows MX, SPF and DMARC with a plain verdict, including "this domain can't receive mail". And before any of this, your own sending domain needs SPF, DKIM and DMARC set up, which I wrote up in this SPF/DKIM/DMARC check before a launch email. The longer playbook on picking who to email in the first place is in how to send cold emails to your first B2B customers.

What I'd tell myself a week ago

  • Pick the pause line before the first send, and write it down.
  • Bounce rate is per first email. Keep follow-ups out of the denominator.
  • Look at both the batch and the stream. They answer different questions.
  • One bounce in 41 isn't a crisis. One bounce you email three times is a habit.

What pause line do you use for cold email, and do you count it per batch or per sequence? I picked 2% mostly by gut and I'd like to hear where other people landed.

title: Agent Architecture Cost-Success Trade-offs: A Controlled Evaluation across Enterprise-Style SOPs
description:
arXiv:2611.12953v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Enterprises increasingly use large language model agents to execute standard operating procedures (SOPs): long, branching, tool-intensive workflows. Yet there is little controlled evidence for choosing among competing agentic architectures. Holding the model, tasks, and tools fixed and varying only the architecture, we compare four designs (a function-calling single agent, a skill-augmented agent, centralized multi-agent orchestration, and a triage swarm; eight arms) across 13 enterprise SOPs, and introduce a skill-definition quality rubric to build matched high and low-quality skill corpora. Three takeaways emerge. (1)~\textbf{There is no universal best architecture; the right choice is SOP-dependent.} On a given SOP, task success ranges from under $10\%$ on the hardest to near $100\%$ on the easiest; no architecture is statistically separable in aggregate, and added structure only plausibly pays off on complex, branching SOPs (a directional, not yet significant, trend). (2)~\textbf{Added architecture cost must be justified by a task-success gain.} Every coordinated arm (multi-agent or skill-augmented) spends $1.4$--$4.7\times$ the tokens and $2.6$--$5.8\times$ the latency of the single agent for gains that are usually small and rarely significant, making the single agent the efficient default; high-quality skills do lift success (to $73.1\%$ from $67.4\%$) while degraded skills fall below it. (3)~\textbf{Implementation quality outweighs the single- versus multi-agent choice.} A plausible multi-agent implementation loses to the single agent, yet a targeted redesign of it becomes the only arm to significantly beat the baseline ($75.6\%$ vs.\ $67.4\%$).

title: Optimizing Document Lookup: Making Atlas Search and Vector Search Up to 5x Faster
description:
Sometimes the biggest performance gains come not from making core operations faster, but from eliminating unnecessary work surrounding them. That is exactly what we discovered while optimizing document lookup in MongoDB Atlas Search and Vector Search. By removing redundant query planning and execution overhead, we made search queries up to 5x faster without changing the underlying search algorithms.

When you run a $search or $vectorSearch query in MongoDB, two key stages work together to deliver the results. First, mongot, MongoDB's search process powered by Apache Lucene, executes the search query to identify and rank the most relevant documents. Then, mongod joins the search results with the corresponding BSON documents from the underlying collection using their _ids. The resulting documents can be further processed by additional aggregation pipeline stages before being returned to the application. Figure 1 illustrates this two-stage process:

Figure 1. Search execution in mongot and document materialization in mongod.

This second stage, known as document materialization, is handled by an internal aggregation stage called $_internalSearchIdLookup. While search execution has been extensively optimized, we discovered that document lookup had become a significant performance bottleneck. For every matching document, the stage repeatedly constructed a new query plan and acquired collection resources, introducing substantial overhead for queries returning hundreds or thousands of results. In our profiling, approximately 30% of mongod CPU time was spent on query planning and collection acquisition, rather than retrieving documents.

To address this, we redesigned the document lookup execution path to eliminate redundant query planning, reuse execution plans, and amortize resource acquisition across multiple lookups. The result: up to 4.9x faster $search queries, 5.5x faster $vectorSearch queries, and approximately 2.75x higher throughput under concurrency.

These optimizations shipped in MongoDB 9.0, are enabled by default, and require no application changes. In this post, we'll explore how we identified the bottleneck, redesigned the execution path, and achieved these performance improvements.

The hidden cost of repeated query planning

Looking up a document by its _id is typically a fast operation in MongoDB, thanks to its efficient _id index. However, the original $_internalSearchIdLookup implementation constructed and executed a new aggregation sub-pipeline for every document returned by mongot, even though only the _id value changed:

For each document, MongoDB parsed the query, optimized the pipeline, constructed an execution plan, acquired collection resources, attached a cursor, executed the lookup, and released resources.

The problem was not the indexed document retrieval, but the repeated preparation work surrounding it. Even though the query structure was identical across lookups, MongoDB rebuilt the execution plan and reacquired collection resources for every document instead of reusing them. This overhead accumulated linearly with the number of results. For example, a search query returning 1,000 documents could trigger 1,000 separate cycles of query planning, collection acquisition, and resource cleanup. As result sets grew, the repeated preparation work became a substantial contributor to end-to-end search latency. Figure 2 illustrates this repeated execution overhead.

Figure 2. Repeated query planning and resource acquisition for each document lookup.

To quantify this overhead, we profiled representative Vector Search workloads. The results revealed that approximately 30% of mongod CPU time was spent on query plan construction and collection acquisition, rather than retrieving documents. This confirmed that the bottleneck was not primarily the underlying document reads, but the redundant work surrounding them.

Redesigning the document lookup execution path

To eliminate redundant lookup overhead, we redesigned $_internalSearchIdLookup around two key optimizations: reusing parameterized execution plans and batching document lookups to minimize resource acquisition overhead. Together, these changes allow MongoDB to retrieve thousands of documents without repeatedly rebuilding query plans or acquiring collection resources.

1. Reusing a parameterized SBE execution plan

The first major optimization was introducing SbeSingleDocumentLookupExecutor, built on MongoDB's Slot-Based Execution (SBE) engine. The key observation was simple: every document lookup follows the same query structure, and only the _id value changes. Instead of constructing a new execution plan for each document, the optimized executor builds the lookup plan once, caches it, and reuses it by rebinding the _id parameter for subsequent lookups.

For example, when retrieving 1,000 documents, the original implementation could construct 1,000 separate query plans. With the optimized executor, all 1,000 lookups can reuse a single parameterized plan.

This eliminates redundant query parsing, optimization, and plan construction, significantly reducing per-document execution overhead.

2. Batching document lookups to reuse collection resources

While plan reuse eliminates repeated query planning, acquiring and releasing collection resources for every document can still introduce substantial overhead. To address this, we introduced a reusable BatchedEnrichmentStage that buffers incoming search results and processes them within a shared resource scope. Instead of independently acquiring and releasing collection resources for every document, the optimized execution path reuses collection resources across multiple lookups within a batch, amortizing the acquisition and cleanup costs. For example, with 1,000 documents and a batch size of 100, collection resources can be acquired just 10 times instead of 1,000 times, i.e., once per batch rather than once per document. Although the number of document lookups still grows linearly with the result set size, batching significantly reduces the repeated resource management overhead.

Combined with SBE plan caching, this allows thousands of document lookups to share both an execution plan and collection resources, substantially reducing CPU overhead. The result is a more efficient document lookup architecture: build the execution plan once, reuse it across documents, and minimize repeated resource acquisition.

Figure 3 illustrates how the optimized approach eliminates redundant work by reusing execution plans and collection resources across document lookups.

Figure 3. Original per-document lookup vs. optimized batched lookup with shared execution plans.

Performance results: End-to-end latency and throughput

As shown in Figure 4, both Atlas Search ($search) and Atlas Vector Search ($vectorSearch) achieved substantial reductions in end-to-end query latency across all evaluated result-set sizes (100, 1,000, and 10,000 documents). At 10,000 results, median latency dropped from approximately 2.6 seconds to 527 milliseconds for Atlas Search (4.9× faster) and from 3.1 seconds to 561 milliseconds for Atlas Vector Search (5.5× faster).

An important pattern emerges: the larger the result set, the greater the speedup. This is consistent with the underlying optimization. While search execution still incurs its own costs, eliminating repeated query planning and resource acquisition overhead becomes increasingly valuable as more documents are materialized.

Figure 4. End-to-end query latency improvements for Atlas Search and Atlas Vector Search in MongoDB 9.0.

Higher throughput under concurrency

Lower latency is only part of the story. We also evaluated performance under concurrent query execution. With 16 concurrent clients running a $search workload, the optimized implementation delivered:

  • Approximately 2.75x higher throughput

  • Approximately 3x lower median latency

These results demonstrate that the optimization does more than accelerate individual queries. By eliminating repeated query planning and resource acquisition, it reduces unnecessary CPU work per document lookup, allowing mongod to process more concurrent search requests with the same execution resources. The approximately 30% CPU overhead identified in our earlier profiling and the nearly 80% latency reduction observed in our benchmarks represent different measurements and workloads, rather than directly proportional improvements.

Real-world customer impact

To understand the potential impact on real-world workloads, we analyzed 163.8 million Atlas Vector Search executions across 610 customer clusters over 90 days. The analysis shows that larger result-set limits are used across a meaningful portion of the customer fleet. At least 40% of clusters execute queries with limits between 21 and 50, and at least 17% execute queries with limits above 100.

These workloads are particularly well-positioned to benefit from the document lookup optimizations, as eliminating repeated query planning and resource acquisition becomes increasingly valuable when more documents are retrieved.

Importantly, these improvements require no application changes. The optimized document lookup path is enabled by default in MongoDB 9.0.7. Applications do not need to rewrite queries, rebuild search indexes, or adopt new syntax. Existing $search and $vectorSearch pipelines can automatically benefit when running on supported configurations.

Faster search, without the extra work

This optimization began with a surprising observation: a simple _id lookup was spending a significant portion of its CPU budget preparing to execute rather than retrieving data. By replacing repeated aggregation planning with lightweight execution, introducing reusable batching infrastructure, and caching parameterized SBE plans, we removed a major source of overhead from Atlas Search and Vector Search. The result is up to 5.5× faster end-to-end queries in our benchmarks, along with substantial throughput improvements under concurrency.

More broadly, this work illustrates an important database engineering principle: sometimes the biggest performance gains come not from making the core operation faster, but from eliminating the unnecessary work surrounding it. This effort was made possible through collaboration across MongoDB's Atlas Search Query, Query Execution, Query Integration, and Server Triage & Release teams.

title: GroundCascade: Selective Second Opinions for GUI Grounding
description:
arXiv:2611.13177v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) grounding maps a screenshot and a natural-language instruction to the screen location where an agent should act. Zoomed views can reveal small targets but may lose the context needed to identify them. We introduce GroundCascade, a training-free controller that uses agreement between a grounder's full-screen and zoomed predictions to decide when to consult a complementary model. It selects between zoomed predictions while preserving corroborated full-screen locations. An optional Finalizer predicts from an unmarked joint crop when disagreement remains (Full); omitting it yields the two-stage Selective variant. GroundCascade reaches 85.33% on ScreenSpot-Pro with Indeed-UI-32B/8B/32B and 88.43% on the visible-target OSWorld-G-Refined subset with Qwen3.6-27B/3.8-27B/3.8-27B, gains of 2.66 and 2.35 percentage points over the stronger standalone two-pass grounder. On UI-Vision, GroundCascade reaches 72.20% category-balanced accuracy, with Selective slightly higher at 72.28%. Across these three evaluations, GroundCascade in Full mode uses 2.42-2.73 calls per request, 31-39% fewer than unconditionally acquiring both models' two-pass predictions. At matched second-model call budgets, selective acquisition gains 1.52-2.56 points over standalone Two-pass, compared with 0.22-0.69 points from stratified random acquisition. GroundCascade leads the official ScreenSpot-Pro leaderboard and exceeds reported GUI-specialist comparisons on OSWorld-G-Refined and UI-Vision, subject to differences in external evaluation protocols.

title: 100% annotation agreement can mean one labelled record out of twelve
description:
A single percentage can make two annotation files look more complete than they are. Suppose you have two JSON files that both label the same texts, and a short script reports 100% agreement. The bundled partial-agreement example constructs exactly this case: only one of twelve records is labelled by both sides, and that one record matches, so conditional agreement is 100% while both-labelled coverage is 1/12. The percentage says nothing about the state of the other eleven records.

Annotation, checkpoints, and agreement

Annotation means assigning a text one label from a small set. A checkpoint is the annotation tool's JSON snapshot: an ordered record list plus a state for each record. Given two checkpoints that cover the same records, a reviewer first wants the places where they disagree, then the places where someone has not finished.

Conditional agreement counts only records both sides labelled: same labels divided by both-labelled records. The default example lays out the boundaries of that number. Four records are labelled by both sides, two of those match, agreement is 50%, and coverage is about 33.3%. The six comparison states contain two records each: same_label, different_label, both_abstained, one_abstained, both_unlabelled, and one_unlabelled.

When neither side labelled anything, the metric has no denominator. The no-labels example has zero both-labelled records; JSON stores label_agreement as null, and the page displays N/A, not 0%.

My tool first verifies that both checkpoints carry the same record list, taxonomy, and order. A missing record, changed text, different group, or reordered taxonomy rejects the pair. The tool does not compare only the overlapping records, join after normalizing text, or silently remap labels. An unknown group stays null instead of gaining an invented group.

This screenshot is from the actual running Hugging Face page with bundled synthetic data. It shows 12 records, 4 labelled by both roles, 50% conditional agreement, and 2/4 same labels. Agreement is not accuracy, and A/B are not verified independent people. The pinned method notes and the live Space provide the same details.

same_label is not a claim about whole files

A matching label means one record has the same label state in both annotations. The partial-agreement pair uses two checkpoints with the same content digest, so identical_checkpoint is true, yet both-labelled coverage is still one record, item-01. The default pair uses different A and B files; item-01 and item-07 have matching labels and count as same_label anyway. A record-level match cannot grow into a claim that the two complete files are the same, and it cannot represent the whole list as undisputed.

Each final decision starts unresolved, including records where both labels match. The page does not merge automatically and has no bulk accept. A reviewer can choose any existing label, abstain, or reopen a result as unresolved. A and B are file roles. They may come from the same person or the same checkpoint, and identical inputs receive an explicit warning. The original two annotation sets remain inside the exported review, while manual decisions live in a separate layer.

Each real change increments the revision; saving the identical decision again does not. The limit is 1e9. Undo restores the last 20 real changes without erasing provenance or rewriting the source text. Notes are limited to 2,000 UTF-16 code units and must contain valid Unicode scalar values. Emoji and other astral characters use two code units each. An unresolved decision must have an empty note.

What saving and restoring cost

The page keeps current work in browser memory only. There is no autosave, account, or server copy. Typing in the form is not recording. For that form edit to enter a snapshot, press Record decision first. Preparing a download captures the decisions recorded at that revision, and the page cannot confirm where the browser saved the file. Reopen as unresolved and Undo last change also update decisions and the revision when a real change occurs; they act on recorded state and do not carry unrecorded form text with them.

Restoring a review reads the complete file, recomputes digests, shows a preview, and then waits for explicit confirmation. A malformed file is rejected while active work stays in place. Swapping A and B invalidates the old binding. A saved review is self-contained and can restore the pair it originally carried after preview.

The snapshot contains both complete original checkpoints, all source text, both annotation sets, the comparison matrix, notes, and every manual decision, so I have to check its contents before sharing. Browser-local processing describes the computation path; it is not a privacy or secrecy guarantee. SHA-256 checks consistency and can be recalculated after content changes, so it does not authenticate the source. Duplicate JSON keys follow JSON.parse last-key semantics rather than strict duplicate-key rejection. BOM, invalid UTF-8, and invalid Unicode scalars are rejected.

Reproducing on the complete package

Start by copying the full public package into a fresh directory. cli.mjs loads review.mjs and vendor/queue.mjs, so two demo JSON files alone will not run. Once the complete package is in place, execute:

node cli.mjs demo-a.json demo-b.json NEW-review.json

The terminal prints the comparison object: total is 12, each of the six buckets is 2, both_labelled is 4, label_agreement is 0.5, both_labelled_coverage is 0.3333333333333333, and identical_checkpoint is false. Inside NEW-review.json, all 12 decisions are unresolved, including the demo items with matching labels, item-01 and item-07. Both source checkpoints are kept in full. The command creates its output exclusively, so it fails when NEW-review.json already exists instead of overwriting it.

Direct links: live Space, direct app, and pinned source commit aa1c89b.

Written by Renchao Wu. English original.

title: Precision on Demand: Escalating Weight Bits at Uncertain Decoding Steps in a Small Local Model
description:
arXiv:2611.14418v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Local decoding usually fixes one weight precision for the whole generation. We study a different allocation: store 8-bit weights, decode with their top 4 bits, and redo a step at 8 bits only when the low-precision output distribution looks uncertain (entropy above a threshold or a small top-two margin). Quantization is simulated, the model is Qwen3-0.6B, and the benchmark is GSM8K. Cost is counted in weight bytes read per token. On 36724 replayed steps the entropy of the low pass ranks argmax flips with AUC 0.93. At a 15% escalation budget it catches 78% of flips and the margin gate 94%, against the 15% expected for a random gate of equal rate (a computed expectation, not a run). In 150 live problems all-high scores 64.0% and all-low 55.3% (McNemar p=0.053). An entropy gate with a 16% escalation rate scores 62.7% at 0.87 of the all-high weight bytes. Its paired difference is -1.3 (-8.0 to +5.3) points to all-high and +7.3 (+0.0 to +14.7) points to all-low (p=0.080), so the live data do not separate the gate from either end. Verified speculation reaches zero KL at similar bytes in the same cost model. A live random control, a thinking-mode phase rule, a second model and live KL were not run.

title: Multimodal Road Closure Mapping via Cross-Modal Graph Attention
description:
arXiv:2611.13192v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate and timely identification of road closures is critical for large-scale navigation and logistics systems, yet remains challenging due to the need to jointly reason over visual evidence, spatial context, and road network topology. Existing approaches either rely on manual map updates or focus on detecting closure-related objects without resolving which road segment is affected. In this work, we introduce a unified multimodal and multitask framework that jointly performs road closure classification (no, partial, complete) and road segment association within a single learning architecture. Our model integrates graph-structured map data, satellite imagery augmented with projected street-level detections, and street-view images using modality-specific encoders and cross-modal transformer attention, enabling explicit reasoning over visual cues and network topology. Evaluated on nearly 20K real-world scenarios collected from a large-scale commercial vehicle fleet, our approach achieves 72.7% closure classification accuracy and 60% road segment association accuracy, outperforming frontier vision-language models by over 28 percentage points on closure classification while being over 4,000x smaller and 100x faster at inference. Extensive ablations demonstrate the importance of cross-modal attention, edge-aware pooling, and graph message passing for accurate geospatial reasoning. This work establishes the first benchmark for joint road closure classification and segment-level attribution, and shows that task-specific architectural inductive biases substantially outperform general-purpose multimodal models for structured geospatial understanding.

title: Trust, but verify, audit and attribute: a human-in-the-loop framework for checking AI-produced research results
description:
arXiv:2611.13042v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems now produce research results in bulk: in October 2026 a single laboratory released more than 700 AI-generated mathematics manuscripts, only part of them with machine-checked proofs. Such volumes will be checked mostly by AI agents that call specialised software. A passing check certifies only the artefact that was checked. For proofs translated into the proof assistant Lean, it has been shown that this artefact may state something other than the author's text, and that deciding whether a translation is faithful is undecidable in general. The human researcher therefore stays in the loop, and human and AI contributions must be recorded. We propose a domain-independent, human-in-the-loop framework for checking AI-produced results. Validated, agent-usable tools with different grounds of trust check the results; a fidelity audit asks whether each check addressed the claim as stated; the human decides at fixed points; and a dialog report attributes the work to the human and to the AI. We describe two automatic implementations of the tool layer, for mathematics (Wolfram Language, MATLAB, Lean) and statistics (Python and R), and run the mathematical one on a two-claim example. An ambiguous claim was split into two readings, one refuted and one proved.

title: I built a manga translator app with Kotlin Multiplatform, and cut the cost per page from $0.05 to under half a cent
description:
I'm a solo developer, and for the past months I've been building Mangit: an iOS and Android app that translates manga, manhwa and comic pages. You take a photo or screenshot of a page, and the app puts the translation back inside the speech bubbles, so you read the page like it was lettered in your language.

Here's how it's built and what I learned.

The pipeline

Every page goes through five steps:

  1. Detect the speech bubbles and text regions
  2. Read the text (OCR)
  3. Translate it, with the source language detected automatically
  4. Erase the original lettering (inpainting) without damaging the art
  5. Typeset the translation back into the same bubble, fitting the font size to the space

Steps 4 and 5 are where most of the work went. A translation that's correct but overflows the bubble, or leaves ghost strokes of the original text, feels broken to readers.

The stack

  • Kotlin Multiplatform + Compose Multiplatform for one shared UI and logic layer on iOS and Android
  • Koin for DI, Ktor for networking, Room for the local library, RevenueCat for subscriptions
  • Firebase Cloud Functions (Node.js) as the backend that orchestrates the AI calls
  • A self-hosted processing pipeline on Modal for the detection / erase / typeset work

Sharing the UI across both platforms is what makes it realistic to ship this alone. The platform-specific parts are small: image picking, file access, and a couple of expect/actual abstractions.

Cost was the real problem

The first version sent every page to a large image model. The output was good, but it cost about $0.05 per page. Manga readers don't translate one page: they translate whole chapters. At that price a free tier is impossible and even paid users can lose you money.

So I built a "lite" pipeline: smaller specialised models for each step instead of one big model, plus my own typesetting. It now runs at roughly $0.001 to $0.004 per page, with the big model kept as a fallback. That's what lets the app have a real free tier.

Lessons from going multilingual

The app translates into 30+ languages. The hardest bugs weren't in the translation but in rendering: a font that covers Latin scripts happily renders Thai, Arabic or Hindi as empty boxes, or nothing at all. If you typeset text yourself, test every script you support with real pages, not just English.

Try it

  • iOS: https://apps.apple.com/app/mangit/id6756326988?pt=126724485&ct=devto&mt=8
  • Android: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.measify.mangit&referrer=utm_source%3Ddevto

It's free to try (3 pages to start, then 3 free pages every week). I'd love feedback, especially from anyone who has worked on text detection, inpainting or typesetting, or on Compose Multiplatform at this scale.
