title: Type 257 Characters of Anything. You're In.
description:
How two sensible decisions, made four years apart in two different projects, turned into a password bypass on Alpine Linux. And why the same bug is probably hiding in your code.

On November 4, 2026, a researcher named Özgün Kültekin reported a bug to the OpenSSH project.

The next day, OpenSSH shipped an emergency release.

That almost never happens. OpenSSH is one of the most carefully reviewed pieces of software on the internet. It runs on nearly every Linux server you have ever touched. Its maintainers do not rush.

But this time, Damien Miller, one of OpenSSH's lead developers, told anyone running the affected setup to turn off password logins or disable SSH immediately.

The bug now has a name, *sshole, and a number, CVE-2026-123158.

Here is what it does, in one sentence:

On an affected Alpine Linux server, an account that has no password at all will accept any password between 257 and 1024 characters long.

Not a correct password. Any password.

A string of 300 letter A's works.

Wait, How Is That Even Possible?

The honest answer is the most interesting part of this story.

Nobody wrote a bad line of code.

No one was careless. No one skipped a review. Every piece involved made a reasonable decision for a good reason.

The bug only exists where those decisions meet.

To understand it, you need three small pieces of history. They happened in 2012, 2012 again, and 2016.

Decision One: musl Makes Failure Safe (2012)

Most Linux systems use a C library called glibc.

Alpine Linux uses a smaller one called musl. That is part of why Alpine images are so tiny, and why so many Docker images and cloud VMs are built on it.

Both libraries provide a function called crypt(). It takes a password and a salt, and returns the hashed form that gets stored in /etc/shadow.

In August 2012, musl changed what crypt() does when it fails.

Instead of returning NULL, it started returning the string "*".

That was a sensible safety choice. Plenty of old code calls crypt() and never checks for errors. If it got NULL, that code could crash. If it gets "*", it simply sees a hash that will never match a real password. Login fails. Nothing breaks.

A few weeks later, musl added a second protection. Its SHA-256 and SHA-512 code started rejecting passwords longer than 256 bytes. Without that limit, an attacker could send a giant password and make the server burn CPU hashing it.

Also sensible.

So from late 2012, on musl:

A password longer than 256 bytes makes crypt() fail. And a failed crypt() returns "*".

Hold on to that.

Decision Two: Linux Marks "No Password" With the Same Character

On Linux, /etc/shadow stores one line per account.

When an account has no password, the password field often holds a single character:

alpine:*:20000:0:99999:7:::

That * means "nothing will ever match this." It is how you create a user who can only log in with an SSH key.

On Alpine, root itself ships as root:*.

You can probably see where this is going.

Decision Three: OpenSSH Fixes a Timing Leak (2016)

In 2016, OpenSSH fixed a different security problem, CVE-2016-6210.

Attackers had noticed that sshd answered faster for accounts with no real password hash. By timing the response, they could tell which usernames existed on a server.

The fix was smart. When the target account has no real hash, sshd now hashes the attempt anyway, borrowing the salt from another account on the system. Every login takes about the same time. The timing leak disappears.

Again, a reasonable decision.

Now Put Them Together

Here is a simplified version of what sshd does when it checks a password without PAM. This is an illustration of the logic, not the real OpenSSH source:

/* Simplified illustration. Not the actual OpenSSH source. */

char *stored  = shadow_entry->password;     /* "*" for a key-only account      */
char *attempt_hash = crypt(attempt, salt);  /* salt borrowed from another user */

if (strcmp(attempt_hash, stored) == 0) {
    return AUTH_SUCCESS;
}
return AUTH_FAILURE;

Now send a 300-character password to a key-only account on Alpine:

  1. The account's stored field is "*".
  2. sshd borrows a real salt from another account, so crypt() runs a SHA-512 hash.
  3. musl's SHA-512 code sees a password over 256 bytes and refuses it.
  4. crypt() fails, and musl returns "*".
  5. sshd compares "*" with "*".
  6. They match. Login succeeds.

The error value and the "no password" marker were the same string. Nobody planned that. It just happened, across two projects and four years.

The upper limit of 1024 comes from sshd itself, which caps password length at that size.

Who Is Actually Exposed

This is where the story gets calmer, and where a lot of headlines got it wrong.

According to Alpine's advisory, a host is exploitable only when all four of these are true:

  1. sshd checks passwords without PAM. Alpine's default openssh-server package is built this way. The openssh-server-pam package is affected only if you set UsePAM no.
  2. PasswordAuthentication is yes. That is OpenSSH's default.
  3. An account that can log in has * as its password field. For example, a key-only user, or the alpine user on official cloud images.
  4. At least one other account has a real $5$ or $6$ password hash. sshd needs that salt to borrow. One such account is enough to expose every passwordless account on the host.

So, what does that mean for a typical backend team?

Environment Status
Ubuntu, Debian, RHEL, Fedora, macOS ✅ Not affected (glibc, PAM, or both)
Alpine Docker containers that do not run sshd ✅ Not affected, per Alpine. Your FROM alpine API service is fine.
Alpine VMs and servers running sshd with password logins on ⚠️ Affected. Patch today.
Official Alpine tiny-cloud images, 3.18.11 through 3.24.3 ⚠️ Special attention (see below)
Embedded devices on musl with OpenSSH (Buildroot, Yocto, OpenWrt) ⚠️ May be affected. OpenWrt's default SSH server, Dropbear, is not.

About those tiny-cloud images: they create an alpine user with no password and passwordless doas. They are safe on first boot, because no account has a password hash yet. But the moment anyone sets a password on any account, an attacker can log in as alpine and become root.

What about root directly? OpenSSH's default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password blocks password logins to root, even though root has * on Alpine. That helps, until the attacker lands on another account that can become root.

The Part That Should Change How You Think About Patching

Kültekin did not find this by reading code line by line.

According to his write-up, he used AI agents to run about 17,600 unusual login attempts against sshd builds for glibc and musl, with and without PAM, using malformed hashes and oversized passwords.

The bug had been sitting there since 2016.

A decade of human review did not catch it. A systematic, machine-driven sweep of weird inputs did.

This is not a one-off. When OpenSSH released version 10.6 in October, the announcement said the team had been receiving a large number of security reports from AI models or made with AI help. It also said that bugs found by AI tools were later being found again, independently, by different researchers.

The team's conclusion was blunt. If friendly researchers can find these bugs with AI, attackers who never report anything probably can too. So OpenSSH would release fixes faster instead of batching them.

That is the real headline for backend engineers.

The time between "a bug exists" and "someone can find it" is shrinking. Long-lived assumptions like "nobody would ever try a 300-character password" are exactly what automated testing is good at breaking.

What to Do on Monday

These steps come from Alpine's advisory and the published guidance. Run them as root on each host, or inside any container that runs sshd.

Step 1: Find out if a host meets the conditions 

# Is sshd running on musl?
cat /etc/alpine-release 2>/dev/null || ldd "$(command -v sshd)" | grep -i musl

# Which openssh-server package is installed?
apk info -v 2>/dev/null | grep '^openssh-server'

# What is sshd actually using right now?
sshd -T | grep -Ei '^(usepam|passwordauthentication|permitrootlogin) '

# Accounts with no password
awk -F: '$2=="*" {print $1}' /etc/shadow

# Accounts with a real $5$ or $6$ hash
awk -F: '$2 ~ /^\$[56]\$/ {print $1}' /etc/shadow

How to read the output:

  • If the first command prints nothing, sshd is not on musl. You are not affected.
  • If sshd -T shows passwordauthentication yes and either usepam no or no usepam line at all, the host is exposed until it runs the fixed package.
  • If both awk commands print names, the accounts from the first list are the ones an attacker could log in as.

One catch: sshd -T shows global settings. A Match block in your config can turn password logins back on for some users or addresses. Read the config file too.

Step 2: Patch, and actually restart sshd 

apk upgrade -U -a
apk info -v | grep '^openssh'
rc-service sshd restart

That last line matters more than it looks.

Upgrading the package does not replace the sshd process that is already running. Until you restart it, the old, vulnerable code is still the one answering on port 22.

Alpine backported the fix to every branch from 3.16 to edge. Stable branches keep their older OpenSSH version number and carry a patch, so do not go looking for "10.6" on 3.22. Compare your package version against Alpine's advisory table instead.

Step 3: If you cannot patch today, turn off password logins

Before you do this, confirm that SSH key login works, and keep your current session open until a new login succeeds.

mkdir -p /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d
echo 'PasswordAuthentication no' > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-no-passwords.conf
sshd -t && rc-service sshd restart
sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication
# expected output: passwordauthentication no

Alpine reads drop-in files from 3.19 onward. On older releases, change the setting in /etc/ssh/sshd_config directly, including inside any Match blocks.

Honestly, if nobody on your team needs password logins over SSH, leave them off after you patch. Key-only SSH would have made this entire bug irrelevant.

Step 4: Check whether anyone already got in

A successful attack leaves a normal-looking log line. The giveaway is who it names.

grep 'sshd.*Accepted password for' /var/log/messages*
awk -F: '$2=="*" {print $1}' /etc/shadow
grep doas /var/log/messages*

An Accepted password for line naming alpine, root, or any key-only user cannot happen legitimately. Those accounts have no password.

Check your central log store too, because local logs can be wiped after a break-in.

As of November 5, no attacks had been reported, and the CVE was not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. But the bug has existed since 2016. "No reports" is not the same as "nobody used it."

If you find a suspicious login you cannot explain, Alpine's advice is to treat the machine as compromised. Rebuild it rather than cleaning it, and rotate any secrets it held.

Step 5: Stop it from coming back in your images

If any of your Dockerfiles install an SSH server, you want to know about it. A quick check you can add to CI:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Flag any Dockerfile that installs an OpenSSH server.
# Most application containers should never run sshd.

matches=$(grep -rniE 'apk add.*openssh(-server)?|apt(-get)? install.*openssh-server' \
  --include='Dockerfile*' . || true)

if [ -n "$matches" ]; then
  echo "Found images that install an SSH server:"
  echo "$matches"
  exit 1
fi

If a container really needs remote access, there are usually better options than sshd inside the image, such as kubectl exec or your platform's own session tooling. If an image truly must run sshd, rebuild it on the fixed package and set PasswordAuthentication no in the image itself.

The Bug That Is Probably in Your Own Code

It is easy to read this as "an OpenSSH problem" and move on.

Please don't.

The pattern behind *sshole is one of the most common mistakes in backend code: an error value that looks like real data.

Here is a version of it that could easily exist in an API service today. This is a made-up example, written to show the pattern:

import hashlib

def hash_api_key(raw_key: str) -> str:
    # Guard against huge inputs.
    if len(raw_key) > 256:
        return ""                     # failure looks like a normal value
    return hashlib.sha256(raw_key.encode()).hexdigest()

def is_valid(raw_key: str, stored_hash: str) -> bool:
    # stored_hash is "" for revoked keys
    return hash_api_key(raw_key) == stored_hash

Every piece looks reasonable on its own.

Limiting input length is good. Marking revoked keys with an empty string feels tidy.

But send a 300-character key against a revoked entry, and "" == "" returns True.

Same shape as *sshole. Two sensible choices, one shared value, one open door.

Here is a safer version:

import hashlib
import hmac

class KeyTooLong(ValueError):
    pass

def hash_api_key(raw_key: str) -> str:
    if len(raw_key) > 256:
        raise KeyTooLong("API key exceeds 256 characters")   # fail loudly
    return hashlib.sha256(raw_key.encode()).hexdigest()

def is_valid(raw_key: str, stored_hash: str | None) -> bool:
    # A missing or malformed stored value can never be a match.
    if not stored_hash or len(stored_hash) != 64:
        return False
    try:
        candidate = hash_api_key(raw_key)
    except KeyTooLong:
        return False
    return hmac.compare_digest(candidate, stored_hash)

Three habits made the difference:

  1. Errors are exceptions, not values. A failure should never be something that can be compared to stored data.
  2. Check the stored side too. A valid hash has a known shape. Anything else is an automatic "no." This is essentially what the OpenSSH fix does: sshd now refuses a match when the stored field is shorter than four characters.
  3. Compare secrets with a constant-time function. hmac.compare_digest avoids leaking information through timing, which was the very problem OpenSSH was solving back in 2016.

If you want a quick exercise for your team this week, search your codebase for every place that compares a computed hash, token, or signature against a stored value. For each one, ask a single question:

"What does this function return when it fails, and could that ever equal what is stored?"

Whose Bug Was It, Anyway?

The projects do not fully agree, and that is worth noticing.

OpenSSH's release notes describe the fix as a workaround for a root cause outside sshd.

musl's maintainer, Rich Felker, says it is not a musl bug but an erroneous use of crypt() by the caller. He also said he expects musl to change the behaviour in its next release cycle anyway.

Both positions are defensible. That is exactly the point.

When a bug lives in the seam between two components, each side can reasonably say the other one owns it. Meanwhile, the door stays open for whoever finds it first.

As a backend engineer or tech lead, you will rarely be the person writing the C library or the SSH daemon. But you are almost always the person who decides how they fit together. Which base image. Which defaults. Which accounts exist. Whether password logins are even on.

That seam is your job.

The Takeaway

*sshole was not a failure of skill. It was a failure of assumptions.

Nobody assumed anyone would send a 300-character password. Nobody assumed an error string and a shadow file entry would ever be compared. Nobody assumed a 2016 timing fix would meet a 2012 safety choice.

AI-driven testing is now very good at exactly one thing: trying the inputs nobody assumed.

So the question for your team is not "are we running Alpine?"

It is this:

"Where in our system do two sensible decisions meet, and has anyone ever tested what happens at the edge?"

Go find that seam before someone else does.

What's the scariest "two sensible decisions" seam you've found in your own stack? Tell me in the comments 👇

If this was useful, follow me here for more stories from the backend trenches, and subscribe to The Backend Tech Lead on Substack for weekly blueprints.

title: Multimodal Abstention That Preserves Acquired Correct Answers
description:
arXiv:2611.14311v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adding abstention to a task-adapted multimodal model can discard correct answers, including capabilities acquired during adaptation. We formulate abstention repair as maximizing correct abstention on unanswerable questions under a budget on newly lost correct answers. We propose ReFrain (Regression-Free Abstention), which combines a linear probe on first-token logits, threshold calibration on held-out image clusters, and a deterministic veto that replaces rejected outputs with the displayed "none of the above" option while preserving all other responses. "Regression-free" denotes zero loss on the calibration set at the zero-budget target. All abstention methods in our main comparison start from the same answering-SFT checkpoint; we separately track lost correct answers, repaired errors, and retained SFT gains. On Qwen2.5-VL-3B, ReFrain at zero budget retains all 57 SFT-gained answers with no losses and improves correct abstention by 7.30 percentage points. At a 0.5% calibration budget, it reaches 74.05% correct abstention with 8 losses and retains 55 gains; CLIP-UP EmbLoRA reaches 64.65% with 62 losses, 41 repairs, and 40 retained gains. The same probe at its default threshold loses 298 correct answers. With models and thresholds frozen, confirmation on 228 independent question clusters yields 66.05% correct abstention and no losses at the 0.5% point, exceeding EmbLoRA by 32.72 percentage points. Ordinary refusal SFT achieves higher correct abstention at greater regression cost. Code and reproduction materials: https://github.com/ModeLiberaL/ReFrain.

title: Predictive Surprise as Self-Grounding Concept Bottleneck for Interpretable Time Series
description:
arXiv:2611.12955v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Time-series classifiers deployed in risk-sensitive domains must be (1) accurate, (2) interpretable, and (3) able to abstain when evidence is weak. Existing methods do not deliver all 3 at once, and the obstacle is structural, rather than logistical. Meaningful temporal patterns cannot be defined without knowing segment boundaries, yet meaningful boundaries cannot be placed without knowing which patterns to expect. Existing approaches break this circularity by using fixed windows or expert-annotated vocabularies, thereby sacrificing at least one of the 3 properties. We introduce ConceptTime, which closes the loop through a single self-supervised signal. A frozen probabilistic forecaster predicts a distribution over the next observation at every timestep of the sequence. We call the mismatch between its prediction and the realized signal the predictive surprise. This signal both locates segment boundaries and characterizes each resulting segment through the forecaster. Segments are thus grounded by how they behaved relative to expectation, not by what they look like. These summaries cluster into a vocabulary of dynamical regimes that we call concepts. A lightweight head classifies from the concept sequence, and the distance to the nearest concept yields reliability by design. Across 17 public benchmarks, ConceptTime is competitive with state-of-the-art black-box accuracy, beats every interpretable baseline, and retains near-98% accuracy on Epilepsy with 1% of labels. It further remains competitive with softmax, prototype-distance, and SHAP/TimeX/TimeX++ on OOD detection and deletion faithfulness, without a single annotation, language model call, or domain expert. Code is available at: https://github.com/Sachithx/ConceptTime.git.

title: NestJS Request Lifecycle & SOLID Design Principles
description:
1. Introduction

NestJS provides a structured request-handling mechanism that processes incoming HTTP requests through different components before returning responses to clients.

These components include Middleware, Guards, Interceptors, Pipes and Exception Filters.

Apart from request handling, NestJS applications benefit from software design principles such as the Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) and Single Responsibility Principle (SRP).

These principles help developers build applications that are maintainable, reusable and loosely coupled.

In this blog, we will understand the NestJS request lifecycle and important SOLID design principles using practical backend examples.

2. NestJS Request Lifecycle

What is the Request Lifecycle?

The request lifecycle describes the sequence of operations performed when an HTTP request enters a NestJS application and a response is returned to the client.

For example, when a user requests an Instagram profile:

GET /users/101

The request passes through different stages before the application sends the response.

Request Lifecycle Flow

Client Request → Middleware → Guards → Interceptors → Pipes → Controller → Service → Response

Main stages

  1. Middleware: Executes operations before the route handler pipeline.
  2. Guards: Determines whether the request is allowed to access a route.
  3. Interceptors: Executes logic before and after the route handler.
  4. Pipes: Validates and transforms incoming arguments.
  5. Controller: Handles the HTTP request.
  6. Service: Executes business logic.
  7. Exception Filters: Handle exceptions and generate appropriate error responses.

Exception filters are not a normal step in every successful request. They handle exceptions when they occur.

3. Middleware

What is Middleware?

Middleware is a function that executes during the request-response cycle before the route handler is executed.

It has access to the request object, response object and the next middleware function.

Why do we use Middleware?

  • Logging incoming requests.
  • Tracking request information.
  • Adding request metadata.
  • Processing certain headers.
  • Implementing general request-processing operations.

Example 

import {
  Injectable,
  NestMiddleware
} from '@nestjs/common';

import {
  Request,
  Response,
  NextFunction
} from 'express';

@Injectable()
export class LoggerMiddleware
implements NestMiddleware {

  use(
    req: Request,
    res: Response,
    next: NextFunction
  ) {
    console.log(
      `${req.method} ${req.originalUrl}`
    );

    next();
  }
}

Understanding the code

  • NestMiddleware: Interface used to define NestJS middleware.
  • use(): Executes when a request reaches the middleware.
  • req: Contains incoming request information.
  • res: Represents the HTTP response.
  • next(): Passes control to the next middleware or request-processing stage.

For example, if a user sends:

GET /users/101

The middleware logs:

GET /users/101

4. Guards

What are Guards?

Guards are components used to determine whether a request is allowed to access a particular route.

They are commonly used for authentication and authorization.

Why do we use Guards?

Consider an Instagram application.

Suppose a user wants to access a protected profile endpoint.

GET /users/profile

Before allowing access, the application checks whether the user has an authenticated session.

Example 

import {
  Injectable,
  CanActivate,
  ExecutionContext
} from '@nestjs/common';

@Injectable()
export class AuthGuard implements CanActivate {

  canActivate(context: ExecutionContext): boolean {

    const request = context
      .switchToHttp()
      .getRequest();

    return !!request.session?.userId;
  }
}

Understanding the code

  • CanActivate: Interface implemented by guards.
  • ExecutionContext: Provides information about the current request and handler.
  • switchToHttp(): Accesses the HTTP request context.
  • getRequest(): Retrieves the request object.
  • canActivate(): Returns whether access is allowed.

If the user has a valid session containing userId, access is granted.

Otherwise, access is denied.

Applying the Guard 

@UseGuards(AuthGuard)
@Get('profile')
getProfile() {
  return 'User profile';
}

The guard checks the request before the controller handler executes.

5. Interceptors

What are Interceptors?

Interceptors are components that execute logic before and after a route handler.

They can intercept the execution of a request and process its result.

Why do we use Interceptors?

  • Logging execution time.
  • Transforming response data.
  • Implementing caching.
  • Monitoring application performance.
  • Handling common response-processing logic.

Example 

import {
  Injectable,
  NestInterceptor,
  ExecutionContext,
  CallHandler
} from '@nestjs/common';

import { Observable, tap } from 'rxjs';

@Injectable()
export class LoggingInterceptor
implements NestInterceptor {

  intercept(
    context: ExecutionContext,
    next: CallHandler
  ): Observable<any> {

    console.log('Before request handler');

    const startTime = Date.now();

    return next.handle().pipe(
      tap(() => {
        console.log(
          `Execution time: ${Date.now() - startTime}ms`
        );
      })
    );
  }
}

Understanding the code

  • NestInterceptor: Interface used to create interceptors.
  • intercept(): Executes before the route handler.
  • next.handle(): Passes execution to the next stage and returns an Observable.
  • tap(): Performs a side effect when the response data is emitted.

An interceptor can perform operations before and after the controller handler.

6. Pipes

What are Pipes?

Pipes are components used to validate or transform incoming data before it reaches the controller method.

Why do we use Pipes?

  • Validating request parameters.
  • Converting data types.
  • Transforming incoming values.
  • Preventing invalid input from reaching business logic.

Example: ParseIntPipe 

import {
  Controller,
  Get,
  Param,
  ParseIntPipe
} from '@nestjs/common';

@Controller('users')
export class UsersController {

  @Get(':id')
  getUser(
    @Param('id', ParseIntPipe) id: number
  ) {
    return {
      userId: id
    };
  }
}

Understanding the code

Suppose the frontend sends:

GET /users/101

The URL parameter initially comes as a string.

ParseIntPipe converts it into a number.

If the incoming value is not a valid integer, NestJS returns a validation error.

Other Common Pipes

  • ValidationPipe
  • ParseIntPipe
  • ParseBoolPipe
  • ParseUUIDPipe
  • DefaultValuePipe

7. Exception Filters

What are Exception Filters?

Exception Filters are components used to handle exceptions and customize the error responses returned to clients.

They help manage errors in a consistent way.

Why do we use Exception Filters?

  • Handling application errors.
  • Returning appropriate HTTP status codes.
  • Customizing error messages.
  • Centralizing error-handling logic.

Example 

throw new NotFoundException('User not found');

If a requested user does not exist, NestJS can return:

{
  "statusCode": 404,
  "message": "User not found",
  "error": "Not Found"
}

Common HTTP Exceptions

Exception HTTP Status
BadRequestException 400
UnauthorizedException 401
ForbiddenException 403
NotFoundException 404
ConflictException 409
InternalServerErrorException 500

NestJS provides built-in exception handling. Custom exception filters can be implemented when specific error formatting or handling is required.

8. Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

What is DIP?

The Dependency Inversion Principle is one of the five SOLID design principles.

It states that high-level modules should not depend directly on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions.

In simple terms, business logic should depend on a contract rather than a specific implementation.

Without DIP

Consider a service that directly creates a PostgreSQL database object.

class PostgreSQLDatabase {

  saveUser() {
    console.log('User saved');
  }
}

class UsersService {

  private database = new PostgreSQLDatabase();

  createUser() {
    this.database.saveUser();
  }
}

Here, UsersService is tightly coupled to PostgreSQLDatabase.

If we want to change the database implementation, the service may need modification.

Applying DIP

First, define an abstraction.

interface UserRepository {
  saveUser(): void;
}

Then create an implementation.

class PostgreSQLDatabase
implements UserRepository {

  saveUser() {
    console.log('User saved in PostgreSQL');
  }
}

Now the service depends on the abstraction.

class UsersService {

  constructor(
    private database: UserRepository
  ) {}

  createUser() {
    this.database.saveUser();
  }
}

Now UsersService does not directly depend on PostgreSQLDatabase.

Benefits of DIP

  1. Reduces tight coupling.
  2. Improves flexibility.
  3. Makes unit testing easier.
  4. Supports replacing implementations.
  5. Improves maintainability.

In NestJS, dependency injection tokens and provider configurations can be used to inject different implementations of an abstraction.

9. Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

What is SRP?

The Single Responsibility Principle is another important SOLID design principle.

It states that a class should have one responsibility and one reason to change.

Without SRP

Consider a class that handles multiple responsibilities.

class UserManager {

  createUser() {}

  deleteUser() {}

  sendEmail() {}

  generateReport() {}

  connectDatabase() {}

}

This class manages users, sends emails, generates reports and connects to the database.

This makes the class difficult to maintain.

Applying SRP

Separate the responsibilities into different classes.

class UsersService {
  createUser() {}
  deleteUser() {}
}

class EmailService {
  sendEmail() {}
}

class ReportService {
  generateReport() {}
}

class DatabaseService {
  connectDatabase() {}
}

Now every class has a clearly defined responsibility.

SRP in a NestJS Application

Class Responsibility
UsersController Handle user HTTP requests
UsersService User business logic
PostsController Handle post HTTP requests
PostsService Post business logic
AuthService Authentication operations
PrismaService Database connectivity

Benefits of SRP

  1. Improves code readability.
  2. Makes debugging easier.
  3. Reduces complexity.
  4. Improves code reusability.
  5. Makes testing easier.

10. Practical Application in an Instagram Backend

Consider an Instagram-style backend built using NestJS, Prisma and PostgreSQL.

When a user requests their profile:

GET /users/profile

The application may perform the following operations:

  1. Middleware logs the incoming request.
  2. AuthGuard checks the authenticated session.
  3. An interceptor records request execution time.
  4. Pipes validate incoming parameters when required.
  5. UsersController receives the request.
  6. UsersService executes the business logic.
  7. PrismaService communicates with PostgreSQL.
  8. The response is returned to the frontend.

If an exception occurs, NestJS exception handling returns an appropriate error response.

DIP helps separate the business logic from specific database implementations, while SRP ensures that each class has a clear responsibility.

11. Difference Between Middleware, Guards, Interceptors, Pipes and Filters

Component Main Responsibility
Middleware Processes incoming requests
Guards Controls access to routes
Interceptors Processes execution before and after handlers
Pipes Validates and transforms input
Exception Filters Handles exceptions

These components work together to create a structured request-processing mechanism.

12. Conclusion

NestJS provides several components to manage HTTP requests and application behavior effectively.

Middleware handles incoming request processing, Guards manage route access, Interceptors process execution and responses, Pipes validate and transform input, and Exception Filters handle errors.

Along with these components, SOLID principles such as DIP and SRP help developers write loosely coupled, maintainable and reusable code.

Understanding these concepts is important for developing scalable backend applications using NestJS.

title: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.14493v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Deploying LLM-based analytics agents in enterprise settings requires evaluation frameworks that can reliably detect failures across complex, multi-tool workflows. We present a three-phase comparative study of three evaluation frameworks, each representing a distinct evaluation paradigm (trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics), applied to two analytics agents in a controlled research setting using frozen execution traces. Phase 1 quantifies evaluation harness stability through repeated measurements, finding that 97% of configurations meet the stability threshold and that stability patterns are agent-independent. Phase 2 measures known risk detection on 72 ground-truth test cases, where the trace-based framework achieves the best precision-recall balance (F1=0.90) while text-only evaluation matches on recall but generates 5x more false alarms. Phase 3 evaluates unknown risk discovery, uncovering 24 novel failures with zero overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming. Our results demonstrate that (1) the information available to the evaluation harness determines evaluation quality, (2) functional and security evaluation are complementary, and (3) LLM-based evaluation harnesses surface subtle errors that human reviewers miss. We recommend a two-framework strategy: trace-based evaluation for functional assessment and adversarial red-teaming for security validation.

title: Bringing Docker Parity to GitLab Runner's Kubernetes Executor: Logging the Helper Image in CI Job Logs
description:
A deep dive into executor observability, helper image resolution, configuration expansion, and CI trace logging in Go.

GitLab Runner uses helper images to perform several internal operations during CI job execution, including source retrieval, cache handling, and artifact management.

When running jobs through the Kubernetes executor, the helper image is particularly important because it runs as part of the job's execution infrastructure.

However, there was an observability gap: when users configured a custom helper_image, the Kubernetes executor did not expose the selected helper image directly in the CI job trace.

This made debugging container image configuration more difficult than necessary.

I addressed this behavior in GitLab Runner Merge Request !7778, resolving Issue #2387.

This article explores the underlying problem, the difference between runner debug logging and job trace logging, the implementation, configuration edge cases, and the regression tests added to verify the behavior.

1. Understanding the GitLab Runner Helper Image

Before looking at the implementation, it is useful to understand the role of the helper image in GitLab Runner.

GitLab Runner uses a helper image to execute internal operations required by CI jobs.

Depending on the executor and job configuration, these operations can include:

  • Cloning and fetching the project repository.
  • Downloading job artifacts.
  • Uploading job artifacts.
  • Restoring caches.
  • Uploading caches.

The helper image is separate from the primary job image configured through .gitlab-ci.yml.

For example:

build:
  image: golang:1.25

  script:
    - go build ./...

Here, golang:1.25 is the job image.

The helper image is managed by GitLab Runner and is used for internal job preparation and execution operations.

1.1 Why custom helper images are used

Organizations running self-managed GitLab Runner installations may need to override the default helper image.

Common reasons include:

  • Pulling images from an internal container registry.
  • Operating in restricted or air-gapped environments.
  • Using a controlled image distribution process.
  • Maintaining consistency with internal infrastructure requirements.
  • Avoiding direct dependencies on public container registries.

GitLab Runner provides the helper_image configuration option for this purpose.

A Kubernetes executor configuration might look like:

[[runners]]
  executor = "kubernetes"

  [runners.kubernetes]
    helper_image = "registry.internal.example.com/gitlab/runner-helper:v1.0.0"

When a custom helper image is configured, knowing exactly which image the executor selected becomes important for troubleshooting.

2. The Observability Gap

The issue addressed in this contribution was a difference in logging behavior between GitLab Runner's Docker and Kubernetes executors.

2.1 Existing Docker executor behavior

The Docker executor already displayed the selected helper image in the CI job output.

For example:

Using helper image: registry.gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab-runner/gitlab-runner-helper:x86_64-<revision>

When a custom helper image was configured, the log also indicated that the image had been overridden and showed the default image information.

This made the selected image visible to developers directly from the job trace.

2.2 Existing Kubernetes executor behavior

The Kubernetes executor followed a different logging path.

Inside:

executors/kubernetes/kubernetes.go

the prepareInfrastructure method used s.BuildLogger.Debugln(...) to report the selected helper image.

The relevant implementation was:

if imageNameFromConfig := s.ExpandValue(
    s.Config.Kubernetes.HelperImage,
); imageNameFromConfig != "" {

    s.BuildLogger.Debugln(fmt.Sprintf(
        "Using helper image: %s (overridden, default would be %s:%s)",
        imageNameFromConfig,
        s.helperImageInfo.Name,
        s.helperImageInfo.Tag,
    ))
} else {
    s.BuildLogger.Debugln(fmt.Sprintf(
        "Using helper image: %s:%s",
        s.helperImageInfo.Name,
        s.helperImageInfo.Tag,
    ))
}

At first glance, the image information appeared to be logged correctly.

However, the important distinction was the logging destination.

BuildLogger.Debugln writes to the runner's internal debug logging mechanism rather than the regular CI job trace.

Consequently, developers inspecting their job output could not see which helper image was selected.

This was an observability inconsistency between the executors.

3. Understanding the Logging Boundary

The central part of this issue was not helper image resolution itself.

It was understanding where the log message was being written.

GitLab Runner has different logging paths for different audiences.

Logging mechanism Intended visibility
Runner internal debug logging Runner operators and administrators
Build/job trace logging Developers and CI job users

The Kubernetes executor was sending useful configuration information to the wrong logging destination.

3.1 Why BuildLogger.Debugln was insufficient

The original implementation used:

s.BuildLogger.Debugln("Using helper image: ...")

This is appropriate when information is intended for internal debug diagnostics.

However, the selected helper image is also operationally relevant to the CI job itself.

A developer debugging an image pull failure should not need access to the runner host's internal logs just to identify the image configured for the job.

Even enabling:

variables:
  CI_DEBUG_TRACE: "true"

did not solve the underlying issue of logging through the wrong output mechanism.

The problem was the destination of the message, not simply the verbosity level.

3.2 The desired behavior

The Kubernetes executor should provide the same useful visibility as the Docker executor.

The selected helper image should appear directly in the job trace:

Using helper image: registry.internal.example.com/gitlab/runner-helper:v1.0.0

For overridden configurations, the output should also identify the override and its default image information.

The objective was to improve observability without changing helper image selection or execution behavior.

4. Implementing the Fix

The implementation was made in:

executors/kubernetes/kubernetes.go

Specifically, the prepareInfrastructure method was updated.

The important change was replacing:

s.BuildLogger.Debugln(...)

with:

s.BuildLogger.Println(...)

The updated implementation:

if s.Config.Kubernetes.HelperImage != "" {
    s.BuildLogger.Println(fmt.Sprintf(
        "Using helper image: %s (overridden, default would be %s)",
        s.getHelperImage(),
        s.helperImageInfo,
    ))
} else {
    s.BuildLogger.Println(fmt.Sprintf(
        "Using helper image: %s",
        s.helperImageInfo,
    ))
}

4.1 Why use BuildLogger.Println?

The regular Println method writes the message to the CI job trace.

This makes the helper image visible to the people who actually need the information while investigating a job.

The change does not alter:

  • Which helper image is selected.
  • How the helper image is configured.
  • How the Kubernetes executor creates its infrastructure.
  • How containers are pulled or executed.

It changes the visibility of the selected configuration.

This is an important distinction: the fix improves observability without modifying the underlying execution semantics.

4.2 Reusing existing helper image resolution

The implementation uses:

s.getHelperImage()

for the configured override.

This avoids duplicating helper image resolution logic inside the logging statement.

The default helper image information is obtained through:

s.helperImageInfo

Reusing these existing values keeps the logging implementation aligned with the executor's established image configuration behavior.

It also avoids introducing a separate image-resolution path purely for diagnostic output.

5. An Important Edge Case: Environment Variable Expansion

One of the more interesting details in this change is how the configured helper image is checked.

GitLab Runner supports variable expansion in configuration values.

For example:

[runners.kubernetes]
  helper_image = "$CUSTOM_HELPER_IMAGE"

At runtime, the configured value is expanded using:

s.ExpandValue(...)

Consider the following scenario:

Configured value: $UNSET_PROBE_VAR
Expanded value:   ""

The original implementation checked the expanded value:

if imageNameFromConfig := s.ExpandValue(
    s.Config.Kubernetes.HelperImage,
); imageNameFromConfig != "" {
    // Override logging
}

This creates an ambiguity.

The configured value is non-empty, meaning the user explicitly configured an override.

However, the expanded value is empty because the referenced environment variable is unset.

Checking only the expanded value makes the code treat this configuration as though no override had been configured.

5.1 Checking the original configuration

The updated implementation instead checks:

if s.Config.Kubernetes.HelperImage != "" {

This distinguishes between two different states:

Configuration state Original value Expanded value
No override configured Empty Empty
Valid literal override Non-empty Non-empty
Variable-based override Non-empty Depends on environment
Unset variable override Non-empty Empty

This distinction is important because configuration intent and runtime expansion are not necessarily equivalent.

The logging path should be able to identify that an override was configured even if its expansion produces an empty value.

In that scenario, the output can expose the unresolved configuration rather than silently presenting it as an ordinary default configuration.

This makes debugging configuration problems considerably more straightforward.

6. Regression Testing

A logging change can appear trivial, but testing its output is important because the behavior depends on both configuration and the logging destination.

I added a dedicated test:

TestPrepare_HelperImageLogging

Location:

executors/kubernetes/kubernetes_test.go

The test covers three important scenarios.

6.1 Default helper image configuration

The first case verifies the behavior when no custom helper image is configured.

Expected behavior:

Using helper image: <default-helper-image>

The job trace should contain the default helper image information.

6.2 Custom helper image override

The second case configures:

custom.registry.io/custom-helper:v1.0.0

Expected behavior:

Using helper image: custom.registry.io/custom-helper:v1.0.0 (overridden, default would be <default-helper-image>)

This verifies that the override is visible and that the default image information is also retained in the log.

6.3 Unset environment variable

The third case uses:

$UNSET_PROBE_VAR

The variable is intentionally unset.

This verifies the important distinction between checking the configured value and checking its expanded result.

The test ensures that a non-empty configured override is still identified as an override even when its runtime expansion is empty.

6.4 Running the test

The focused test can be executed with:

go test -v ./executors/kubernetes \
  -run '^TestPrepare_HelperImageLogging$'

This provides a targeted way to validate the behavior without running the entire GitLab Runner test suite.

The test exercises the preparation path and verifies the resulting helper-image log output for the different configuration states.

7. Why This Change Matters Beyond Logging

The implementation is small, but the underlying engineering concern is broader.

In distributed CI infrastructure, observability is part of the user-facing behavior.

When a CI job fails because a helper image cannot be pulled, developers need enough information to understand what the runner attempted to use.

Without that information, debugging may require:

  1. Identifying which runner processed the job.
  2. Accessing the runner host or its internal logs.
  3. Inspecting the runner configuration.
  4. Resolving any configured environment variables.
  5. Determining the actual image selected at runtime.

Exposing the selected image in the job trace removes an unnecessary diagnostic step.

7.1 Executor parity

GitLab Runner supports multiple executors, each with its own infrastructure implementation.

Users should not have to lose useful diagnostic information simply because their jobs run on Kubernetes instead of Docker.

Matching the Docker executor's helper-image visibility makes the experience more consistent.

7.2 Better debugging in restricted environments

This is especially useful for organizations using private registries.

When an image pull fails, knowing the exact configured image and whether an override was applied helps narrow down possible causes:

  • Incorrect registry hostname.
  • Incorrect image name or tag.
  • Missing image availability.
  • Configuration expansion problems.
  • Registry authentication or access issues.

The log does not solve all these problems, but it provides a useful starting point.

7.3 Observability without changing execution

A good diagnostic improvement should avoid changing the system behavior it is trying to explain.

This implementation keeps image resolution and infrastructure preparation intact while making the selected configuration visible through the appropriate logging interface.

8. Final Implementation Summary

The contribution can be summarized as follows:

Area Before After
Logging method BuildLogger.Debugln BuildLogger.Println
Log destination Internal runner debug logs CI job trace
Default image visibility Not visible in regular job output Visible
Override visibility Not visible in regular job output Visible
Override detection Based on expanded value Based on configured value
Regression coverage No dedicated coverage for these cases Dedicated preparation test

The core implementation involved three decisions:

  1. Use the CI job trace logging method instead of internal debug logging.
  2. Reuse existing helper image resolution information.
  3. Detect an override using the original configuration value rather than its expanded value.

Together, these changes address the observability gap without introducing a new image-selection mechanism.

9. Conclusion

This contribution addressed a small but meaningful inconsistency in GitLab Runner.

The Kubernetes executor already knew which helper image it was using, but the information was written to internal debug logs instead of the CI job trace.

By switching to BuildLogger.Println, reusing the existing helper image information, and checking the original configuration value, the implementation makes helper image selection visible to CI job users.

The regression tests cover the default configuration, a custom registry override, and an override referencing an unset environment variable.

The broader engineering lesson is that observability is not only about collecting logs. It is also about delivering the right diagnostic information to the right audience, at the right point in the execution lifecycle.

This was a focused improvement to GitLab Runner's Kubernetes executor that brings its helper-image logging behavior closer to the Docker executor.

References and Implementation

  • Merge Request: GitLab Runner !7778
  • Issue: GitLab Runner #2387
  • Implementation: executors/kubernetes/kubernetes.go
  • Regression Tests: executors/kubernetes/kubernetes_test.go
  • Test: TestPrepare_HelperImageLogging

title: When Should Agents Remember? Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution for LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.14326v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon, verifier-rich environments, but current self-improvement mechanisms often write episode-derived lessons directly into memory, making local success an unreliable signal for reusable and safe knowledge. This paper addresses the core question of when an experience-derived behavioral update should be admitted into persistent agent state. We propose Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution (FGSE), a verifier-grounded framework that represents each candidate lesson as a structured hypothesis with an explicit precondition, behavior change, expected effect, and verifier. FGSE applies the hypothesis only in a temporary state, tests it on target-transfer, falsification, and archived-regression probes, and then commits, refines, or rejects it according to measured gain and risk. Across web, app, tool-use, and long-term memory benchmarks, FGSE achieves strong task performance, including 39.8 WebArena success rate, 78.8 AppWorld average completion, and 0.724/0.487 Pass$^1$ on $\tau$-Retail/$\tau$-Airline, while reducing falsification failures to 5.0%, regression damage to 1.3%, and harmful committed updates to 3.6%. These results suggest that testing memory updates as hypotheses supports more reliable long-term adaptation.

title: Stillpoint: a two-minute breathing retreat that learns your rhythm
description:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge

What I Built

Stillpoint is a two-minute, camera-only breathing retreat. It measures your natural breathing
rate through a webcam, then guides you into a slower rhythm that starts from where you already are.

Most breathing apps ask you to match a fixed pace. Stillpoint does the opposite: it spends 32
seconds quietly learning your rhythm, then eases the guide toward a calmer 10-second breath without
ever making a slow breather go faster. An orb grows and settles with the pace, live pulse and
breathing values appear as they become reliable, and the landscape subtly responds to your
expression if you enable that optional setting.

There is no wearable, no account, no recording, and no upload. The whole experience is designed
around a simple constraint: the camera frames should never leave the machine.

Demo

Watch the 2-minute demo (MP4)

Release page: https://github.com/pham-canh/stillpoint/releases/tag/demo-v1

The demo shows a live session on a Linux x64 machine with a USB camera: the local camera preview,
live SmartSpectra pulse and breathing readings (HRV when the signal is ready), validation hints, the
adaptive pacer, and the summary. The app is shown running locally, which is the intended deployment.
The recording uses a 70-second shortened session via SETTLE_MS / SESSION_MS; the default is 32
seconds of settling plus 90 seconds of guided breathing.

Code

https://github.com/pham-canh/stillpoint

Setup:

git clone https://github.com/pham-canh/stillpoint.git
cd stillpoint
npm install
cp .env.example .env   # add SMARTSPECTRA_API_KEY
npm start
# open http://127.0.0.1:4317

Requirements and platform notes are in the README. The SmartSpectra Node SDK ships native
binaries, so the app runs on macOS Apple Silicon, Linux x64/arm64, and Windows x64; Intel Macs are
not supported by the SDK. The UI still loads on unsupported platforms, and a local video can drive
the same pipeline through DEMO_VIDEO for testing.

How It Responds to Human Signals

Stillpoint uses three live SmartSpectra signals by default — pulse rate, breathing rate, and
HRV — plus expression when the optional scene setting is enabled. It requests only those
four metrics, not traces, landmarks, blinking, or talking.

The integration path:

  1. The local Node process opens the camera with the SDK's native useCamera(CameraSelection.byId(id), { width: 1280, height: 720, fps: 30 }) path. Frames stay inside that process; there is no browser-to-server frame hop and no browser camera prompt in the default mode.
  2. The SDK emits metric buffers. decodeMetrics reads metrics.breathing.rate.at(-1), metrics.cardio.pulseRate.at(-1), metrics.cardio.hrv.at(-1), and, when enabled, metrics.face.expression.at(-1).
  3. The SDK's videoOutput event provides a processed frame. The server downsamples it to a 320×240 RGBA preview and sends it to the browser over the loopback control WebSocket, so the person can check framing without a second camera consumer.
  4. The server pushes deduplicated samples to the browser over Server-Sent Events. The optional CAPTURE_MODE=frames fallback keeps the original browser getUserMedia → 640×480 RGBA → useCustomInput() / sendFrame() path for machines where the server cannot access a camera.

How the experience reacts:

  • Breathing rate becomes the starting pace. After a 32-second settle, the pacer begins at the measured period, clamped to 6–12 seconds. It eases toward 10 seconds by 750 ms per breath. If your measured rhythm is slower than 10 seconds, it stays there.
  • The orb is the guide. Inhale takes 40% of the cycle and exhale 60%. The orb's radius, the landscape's mist, and the reflection on the lake all follow the same breath value.
  • Pulse drives subtle ripples. Reliable pulse samples add heartbeat ripples to the lake, so the scene feels connected to the measurement without turning the session into a dashboard.
  • HRV is shown, not scored. RMSSD appears when confidence is high enough; there is no gamification.
  • Expression is optional art direction. If enabled, the strongest expression label blends the scene palette. Turning it off removes the expression metric from the SDK request entirely.
  • Validation hints are actionable. "Face not centered", "too dark", "chest not visible", and similar SDK hints appear on the preview, then fade back to the resting instruction.

The app uses live SDK readings in the default camera mode. The DEMO_VIDEO option uses the same
pipeline with useFile() and is intended for tests and recordings, not as the primary experience.

Prize Categories

Entering both:

  • Most Creative or Delightful Use — a webcam becomes a quiet, responsive landscape rather than a vitals dashboard. The adaptive pacer starts from the person instead of a preset, and the optional expression palette makes the same two minutes look different for different people.
  • Best Thoughtful Real-World Use — a low-friction two-minute microbreak for desk workers, students, and caregivers. No wearable, no account, no streak, no score. The session is short enough to repeat, and the privacy design removes the main reason people avoid camera-based tools.

Consent and Data Handling

Consent. The camera is not opened until the person ticks an explicit consent checkbox and
presses Begin. In the default native mode the local Stillpoint process opens the camera at that
point; the browser does not request camera access, so there is no extra browser prompt. Expression
analysis is optional and off by default; it can be enabled before starting.

Frames. Video only, never audio. In the default mode the local Node process opens the camera at
up to 1280×720 and the SDK processes frames in memory. A downsampled 320×240 RGBA preview is sent to
the page over a loopback WebSocket. Frames are not recorded, written to disk, cached, logged, or
uploaded. The live preview is local and can be hidden. The CAPTURE_MODE=frames fallback uses
browser capture and a loopback frame WebSocket instead.

Measurements. Pulse, breathing, HRV, and optional expression are computed locally by the
SmartSpectra SDK running natively in the Node process. Derived values are held in memory for the
session, shown in the interface, and discarded when the session ends. Stillpoint does not persist
them.

Network and third parties. Stillpoint does not send frames or measurements to Presage. The
SmartSpectra SDK authenticates the API key, verifies the subscription, and may obtain its model or
update files from Presage; those requests do not include Stillpoint's frames or measurements.
Stillpoint has no accounts, analytics, ads, or tracking, and uses no optional AI service. The SDK
telemetry option is explicitly disabled (enableTelemetry: false). The page loads no external
scripts, fonts, or images.

Retention and deletion. There is no stored data to retain or delete. Stopping the session,
pressing Escape, hiding the tab, disconnecting, or finishing normally releases the camera, closes the
sockets, and releases the in-memory session state. Closing the tab clears the rest.

Security. The server binds to 127.0.0.1, origin-checks WebSocket and control requests, and sets
a strict Content Security Policy. The intended URL is http://127.0.0.1:4317.

Demo video. The recording was made separately, with the participant's consent, outside the app's
data path. Stillpoint itself does not record the session. If the optional DEMO_VIDEO setting is
used, it reads a local clip chosen by the operator; that clip is not uploaded.

Full details: https://github.com/pham-canh/stillpoint/blob/main/PRIVACY.md and the in-app /privacy page.

Wellness only. SmartSpectra metrics are not FDA-cleared and are not a diagnosis or treatment.
Stillpoint does not provide medical advice, make medical decisions, or monitor anyone covertly.

title: Give Haiku the UX rules and a checker, not just the request
description:
The simple version of the "Haiku with a UX kit" study. For the full method and every number, read the technical article. Here is what it means if you want to use it tomorrow.

In one sentence

When Haiku (the small model) gets open-source UX rules and a simple piece of code that checks the screen, it creates and improves login screens at the level of Sonnet (the larger model) working alone, for about 10% of the cost per task. For comparing two screens, the code did not help. And we could not measure aesthetics reliably without a person.

What we did

We picked one small screen, the login screen, and built three tasks: create the screen from scratch, improve a screen with hidden defects, and compare two screens by reading their code. To help Haiku we built:

  • a data lake of 30 rules (contrast, labels on fields, button size, a password-recovery link and others), all taken from open sources (WCAG, web.dev, Material Design), none from memory;
  • a small code checker, with no browser, that reads the HTML and CSS, says which rules fail and lists the real differences between two screens.

We ran 2,244 tasks with Haiku and Sonnet, each 3 times, with no failures in the end. Before running, we wrote the hypotheses and the criteria.

What we found

1. The rules in the prompt already change a lot. When creating a screen, Haiku alone met 74% of the rules; with the rules in the prompt, 99%. When improving a screen with defects, 75% rose to 89% with the rules alone, and to 97% with the checker report.

2. The checker helps with improving and creating, and helps the small model more. The gain was larger for Haiku than for Sonnet in creating and in improving. Sonnet alone already improves a screen well (94%) and even got worse when given the rules alone (81%).

3. The combination costs a tenth. On average per task, Haiku with rules and checker cost US$ 0.0022 and Sonnet alone US$ 0.0210, with Haiku's accuracy at 1.07 times Sonnet's.

4. An independent tool confirmed part of it. We ran the created screens through axe-core, an accessibility checker that neither our checker nor our prompts know: violations fell from 0.50 per screen (Haiku alone) to 0.03 (with rules and checker).

5. Comparing two screens needed no help. Given the code of both screens, Haiku and Sonnet already get about 93%, and the checker report made it slightly worse (to about 90%), mainly on CSS changes. Neither model invented a difference where there was none.

What the hypotheses meant

Before running, we fixed the hypotheses and how much of a result would be enough. Of the confirmatory comparisons, 7 of 12 passed the multiple-testing correction:

  • Creating and improving with rules and checker: yes, well above the baseline.
  • The checker helps Haiku more than Sonnet: yes in creating and improving; no in comparing.
  • The checker is worth more than just a second self-critique pass (creating): yes by our rules, but axe-core did not see that difference.
  • The checker reduces false alarms when comparing: could not be tested, because nobody made mistakes on those pairs.
  • The main criterion (Haiku with the combination reaches 90% of Sonnet at up to half the cost): supported, but only against Sonnet. Opus was left out of the study because of cost.

What did not work, and what to be careful about

  • Aesthetics: no instrument without a human passed validation. We tested a model trained on design ratings (UIClip), a set of code-based measures and a Fable pairwise judge against real A/B tests. Fable got 55.6% right (we needed 60%) and changed its answer when we swapped the order of the screens in 4 out of 10 cases. So this study says nothing about beauty.

  • The yardstick is the rules. Creating and improving are scored by the same 30 rules we helped the model meet. axe-core softens this for creating, but not for improving. Read it as "Haiku meets the rules it is given", not as "Haiku does good UX".
  • One screen, script-generated screens, no Opus, no real browser in the checker. We do not know whether it holds for real screens.

The recipe

  1. Pick one small screen and list the rules that matter, from open sources only (WCAG, official guides), never from memory.
  2. Put the rules in the small model's prompt. That alone solves a good part of creating.
  3. Write a minimal checker (reading HTML and CSS is enough for many rules) and hand its report to the model, asking for fixes as patches.
  4. Measure with a tool the model and the checker do not know, such as axe-core, and be wary of scoring with the same rules you handed over.
  5. Do not measure aesthetics without a person. If you have no designer, say you did not measure it.

All the code, stimuli and raw data are in the study repository, so you can check or repeat it.

The experiments, data and conclusions are mine. The writing was AI-assisted and reviewed by me.
