title: De una app de tareas a Azure: .NET 10, Cosmos DB, Terraform y GitHub Actions
description:
Una lista de tareas es un buen punto de partida para practicar NoSQL y automatización. El problema es sencillo de comprobar: creo una tarea en el navegador, la marco como hecha y vuelvo a abrir la aplicación. Si el estado se conserva, puedo seguir el recorrido desde la interfaz hasta la base de datos y comprobar qué parte del despliegue permite que todo funcione en Azure.

Esta es la experiencia del equipo para la Actividad Grupal 01 de Base de Datos II en la Universidad Privada de Tacna. El código está disponible en el repositorio público del proyecto.

1. De la interfaz a un documento en Cosmos DB

La interfaz vive en wwwroot. Desde ahí, el navegador usa la API de ASP.NET Core (.NET 10) para crear, listar, completar y eliminar tareas. La aplicación agrupa las rutas bajo /api/tareas, y TareasRepo concentra el acceso a Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL mediante el SDK de .NET.

Cada tarea se representa como un documento. Este ejemplo ilustra los campos del modelo:

{
  "id": "53316b1d-b681-41cd-8b37-079be264189f",
  "titulo": "Revisar el despliegue",
  "hecha": false,
  "fecha": "2026-10-24T03:31:05Z"
}

El contenedor tareas de la base tareasdb usa /id como clave de partición. Eso permite que el repositorio busque una tarea con su identificador y su clave de partición en una lectura puntual. La lista completa se consulta aparte, ordenada por fecha descendente. Así, la operación de abrir una tarea y la de listar todas tienen recorridos distintos en el código.

2. Terraform prepara Azure y GitHub Actions publica la aplicación

La automatización está separada en dos flujos dentro de .github/workflows:

Flujo Qué hace Cuándo se ejecuta
infra.yml Inicializa y valida Terraform, y aplica la configuración de infra/main.tf. Esta define los recursos de Cosmos DB y Azure App Service. Al enviar a main cambios en infra/ o en el propio flujo. También admite ejecución manual.
deploy.yml Prepara .NET 10, genera el paquete Release con dotnet publish, inicia sesión en Azure, despliega en App Service y consulta /health. Al enviar a main cambios en src/ o en el propio flujo. También admite ejecución manual.

En una primera instalación, la infraestructura debe estar lista antes de publicar el código. Después, un cambio en la aplicación puede lanzar su propio despliegue. El estado de Terraform se configura en Azure Storage. GitHub Actions obtiene las credenciales de Azure desde los secretos del repositorio, y Terraform configura la conexión a Cosmos DB en App Service.

Las ejecuciones de GitHub Actions y las capturas del repositorio documentan ambas etapas.

3. Comprobación en la nube

La aplicación se publicó en Azure App Service. En las evidencias del despliegue se ve cómo se crea una tarea, se marca como completada y se elimina. La respuesta de /api/tareas permite revisar los documentos devueltos por la API. La ruta /health devuelve el estado de la aplicación, la base utilizada y el número de tareas que se pudieron leer.

La URL corresponde al despliegue documentado. Durante la preparación de este artículo no pude verificar que la instancia siguiera respondiendo. Las capturas y el video conservan el resultado de la prueba en Azure.

Video del equipo

Yerry Maycol Tarqui Collatupa muestra la construcción, la automatización y la prueba de la app en 4 minutos y 35 segundos.

title: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): Understanding Cloud Infrastructure Through the AWS Case Study
description:
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): Understanding Cloud Infrastructure Through the Amazon Web Services (AWS) Case Study

Tags: "cloud" "iaas" "aws" "technology" "beginners"

Introduction

Imagine starting a company that wants to provide online services to thousands or even millions of customers. You would need powerful computers, storage devices, networking equipment, cooling systems, and a team to maintain everything. Purchasing and managing all this infrastructure can be expensive and time-consuming.

Fortunately, cloud computing has introduced a more flexible approach known as Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS).

Infrastructure as a Service allows individuals and organizations to rent computing resources over the internet instead of purchasing and maintaining physical hardware themselves.

In this article, we will explore what IaaS means, how it works, its major benefits and challenges, and how Amazon Web Services (AWS), particularly Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2), demonstrates this technology in practice. We will also examine Netflix as a real-world case study.

  1. What Is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?

Infrastructure as a Service is a cloud computing model that provides users with essential computing resources such as virtual servers, storage, processing power, and networking through the internet.

According to the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), IaaS allows consumers to provision processing, storage, networks, and other computing resources while maintaining control over their operating systems and deployed applications.

In simple terms, instead of buying a physical server and keeping it in an office, a business can rent a virtual server from a cloud provider and access it whenever necessary.

Some popular IaaS providers include:

  • Amazon Web Services (AWS).
  • Microsoft Azure.
  • Google Cloud Platform (GCP).
  • Oracle Cloud Infrastructure.
  1. How Does IaaS Work?

IaaS works through virtualization and cloud infrastructure.

A cloud provider owns and maintains large data centres containing physical servers, storage devices, and networking equipment. Through virtualization, these physical resources can be divided into multiple virtual computing environments.

Customers access these resources through a web-based dashboard or application programming interfaces (APIs).

The process generally works as follows:

  1. A customer creates an account with an IaaS provider.
  2. The customer selects the required computing resources.
  3. A virtual machine or server is created.
  4. The customer installs an operating system and necessary applications.
  5. The customer manages and uses the resources remotely.
  6. The customer pays according to the resources and usage selected.

This arrangement gives organizations the ability to increase or decrease their computing resources depending on demand.

  1. Key Features of Infrastructure as a Service

a. Virtualization

Virtualization allows physical computing resources to be divided into multiple virtual machines. Each virtual machine can operate independently and run its own operating system and applications.

b. Scalability

Organizations can increase or decrease computing resources depending on their requirements. For example, an online shopping platform can increase its server capacity during a major sales promotion.

c. On-demand resources

Users can request computing resources whenever they need them without purchasing additional physical equipment.

d. Pay-as-you-go pricing

Most IaaS providers offer usage-based pricing. Customers pay for the resources they consume, although pricing arrangements vary between services.

e. Remote accessibility

Resources can be managed through the internet, allowing administrators and developers to work from different locations.

f. Storage and networking

IaaS providers offer storage and networking services that allow organizations to store information, connect systems, and manage communication between applications.

  1. Case Study: Amazon Web Services (AWS)

Amazon Web Services is one of the major cloud computing providers in the world. It offers a wide range of cloud services that enable individuals, startups, educational institutions, and large organizations to build and operate applications.

One of its important infrastructure services is Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2).

Amazon EC2 provides virtual servers known as instances. Customers can select the computing capacity they require, configure their servers, install software, and manage their applications.

For example, a company developing a student management system can use Amazon EC2 to host its application instead of purchasing a physical server.

The company can select an appropriate virtual server, install its preferred operating system, configure its application, and make the system accessible to authorized users over the internet.

Important AWS infrastructure services

Amazon EC2: Provides virtual computing capacity for running applications and operating systems.

Amazon S3: Provides scalable object storage for files, images, backups, and other data.

Amazon VPC: Allows users to create logically isolated virtual networks within AWS.

Elastic Load Balancing: Distributes incoming application traffic across multiple targets to support availability and performance.

AWS Auto Scaling: Helps automatically adjust computing capacity according to defined demand and scaling policies.

Together, these services demonstrate how cloud infrastructure can support modern applications.

  1. Real-World Case Study: How Netflix Uses AWS

Netflix is one of the world's most recognized online entertainment and video-streaming platforms. It provides movies, documentaries, television series, and other entertainment content to millions of subscribers around the world.

Providing uninterrupted streaming services requires substantial computing resources, storage capacity, networking, and the ability to respond to changing user demand.

Netflix uses Amazon Web Services to support its infrastructure needs.

How AWS supports Netflix

  1. Computing resources

Netflix uses AWS computing infrastructure to support its applications and services. Amazon EC2 provides scalable computing capacity that helps Netflix run workloads and respond to changing demand.

  1. Scalability

The number of people watching Netflix can change significantly depending on the time of day, popular releases, and special events.

AWS provides Netflix with infrastructure that can scale to meet changing capacity requirements.

  1. Storage and data management

Netflix requires substantial infrastructure to manage information and support its services. AWS provides storage and database capabilities that contribute to its cloud environment.

  1. Global infrastructure

AWS operates infrastructure across multiple geographical regions. This gives Netflix access to computing resources in different locations to support its worldwide operations.

  1. Flexibility and innovation

Using cloud infrastructure allows Netflix to concentrate on improving its services and developing new features without having to build and maintain every physical computing resource itself.

What can we learn from Netflix?

Netflix demonstrates that IaaS is not only useful for small businesses. Large organizations can also use cloud infrastructure to support complex systems and changing workloads.

Its AWS experience illustrates the importance of scalability, flexibility, infrastructure management, and reliability in modern computing.

  1. Advantages of Infrastructure as a Service

IaaS provides several benefits to businesses and individuals.

Cost reduction: Organizations do not need to purchase expensive physical servers and networking equipment before starting their operations.

Scalability: Computing resources can be increased or reduced depending on demand.

Flexibility: Users can choose operating systems, applications, and computing configurations that suit their needs.

Faster deployment: Virtual servers can be provisioned much faster than purchasing and installing physical infrastructure.

Accessibility: Cloud infrastructure can be accessed remotely through authorized internet connections.

Business continuity: Cloud storage, backup arrangements, and geographically distributed infrastructure can support disaster recovery and service continuity when properly configured.

  1. Challenges of Infrastructure as a Service

Although IaaS provides many advantages, it also presents challenges.

Security risks: Poor configurations, weak passwords, and inadequate access controls can expose cloud resources to security threats.

Internet dependency: Accessing cloud infrastructure requires reliable network connectivity.

Cost management: Uncontrolled resource usage can result in unexpected expenses.

Technical knowledge: Users need knowledge of operating systems, networking, cloud security, and server administration to manage their infrastructure effectively.

Vendor dependency: Organizations may find it difficult to migrate applications and data between cloud providers because of differences in technologies and configurations.

  1. Understanding the Shared Responsibility Model

An important aspect of IaaS is that responsibility is shared between the cloud provider and the customer.

The cloud provider is generally responsible for maintaining the physical data centres, servers, networking hardware, and virtualization infrastructure.

The customer is generally responsible for managing the operating system, installed applications, access permissions, data, and security configurations within their environment.

This means that using AWS does not automatically guarantee that an application is secure. Customers must also configure and manage their resources properly.

  1. IaaS Compared with PaaS and SaaS

Cloud computing has three major service models.

Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): Provides computing infrastructure such as virtual machines, storage, and networking. Users have considerable control over their operating systems and applications.

Platform as a Service (PaaS): Provides an environment for developing, testing, and deploying applications without requiring users to manage the underlying infrastructure.

Software as a Service (SaaS): Provides ready-to-use software applications over the internet. Users generally access the application through a web browser or mobile application.

For example:

  • IaaS: Amazon EC2.
  • PaaS: Google App Engine.
  • SaaS: Google Workspace.

The major difference is the level of control and responsibility given to the customer.

  1. Conclusion

Infrastructure as a Service has transformed the way individuals and organizations access and manage computing resources. By providing virtual servers, storage, networking, and processing capacity over the internet, IaaS reduces the need for businesses to purchase and maintain expensive physical infrastructure.

Amazon Web Services provides a practical example of how IaaS works through services such as Amazon EC2. Its use by Netflix demonstrates how cloud infrastructure can support large-scale applications, changing workloads, and global operations.

As technology continues to develop, Infrastructure as a Service will remain an important part of modern computing, helping organizations become more flexible, scalable, and efficient.

Understanding IaaS is therefore essential for students, developers, IT professionals, and businesses interested in the future of cloud computing.

References

  1. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). (2011). The NIST definition of cloud computing (Special Publication 800-145). https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-145

  2. Amazon Web Services. What is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)? https://aws.amazon.com/what-is/iaas/

  3. Amazon Web Services. What is Amazon EC2? https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/concepts.html

  4. Amazon Web Services. Netflix on AWS: Case Studies and Innovator Stories. https://aws.amazon.com/solutions/case-studies/innovators/netflix/

title: Multimodal Graph Learning: A Survey of Models, Benchmarks, and Frontiers
description:
arXiv:2611.12990v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal attributed graphs (MAGs), in which nodes carry text, images, and other modalities while edges encode relations among entities, underlie e-commerce, social media, content platforms, and creative applications. Learning on MAGs has developed along two complementary lines: graph-centric methods redesign how modalities are fused, propagated, and connected within message passing, while foundation-model-centric methods pretrain transferable multimodal graph encoders or bring graph context into multimodal large language models for prediction and generation. In parallel, several benchmarks have appeared with different datasets and evaluation protocols. This survey takes an algorithm-centric and evaluation-grounded view of the field and makes three contributions. Modeling: we introduce a unified message-passing formulation and organize methods into five integration levels (feature, propagation, topology, learning, and foundation model), covering discriminative and graph-conditioned generative models; within this formulation we derive representative methods as special cases, compare their assumptions, expressiveness, and cost, and identify cross-modal sensitivity as a property that separates otherwise similar architectures. Datasets and evaluation: we review recent benchmarks, summarize their datasets and metrics, define model-independent descriptors (label homophily, average degree, clustering, and edge provenance), and map each evaluation protocol to the baselines it uses. Frontiers: we connect multimodal graph learning to AI agents, covering the multimodal graphs that agents perceive and remember and graph engineering, the practice of organizing agent workflows as explicit graphs; we then discuss open problems, concrete efforts for the community, and research directions, including when graph structure helps in the presence of strong multimodal foundation models.

title: Figma handoff checklist: what developers need from designers
description:
Moving a design from Figma into code should feel like a smooth transition, but it often turns into a frustrating guessing game. Designers hand over a clean file, developers start building, and immediately the questions begin. What happens when this button is hovered? How does this card look on an iPad? Where are the actual image files?

When design files lack structure, projects slow down, budgets stretch, and the final product starts drifting away from the original vision. You end up wasting hours in meetings clearing up details that should have been obvious in the layout.

Whether you are working with my team on a Figma to Next.js build or partnering with any other developer, establishing a solid handoff routine saves everyone time. Here is a practical checklist of what developers actually need from designers to build pixel-perfect, responsive websites without the constant back-and-forth.

Organized components and variants

In modern web development, websites are built using reusable pieces rather than static pages. If a designer hands over a file with fifty separate button frames that all look slightly different, a developer cannot easily tell which one is the master component. It creates massive amounts of redundant code and inconsistent user interfaces.

A proper design file uses master components with clear variants for different styles and properties. If a button has primary, secondary, and ghost styles, those should live inside a single component set rather than scattered across the artboard. This mirrors how React and Next.js developers build user interfaces using props and reusable modules.

Clean component structures also make future updates much easier. When a brand color changes or a border radius gets updated, editing the master component propagates that change everywhere. Developers appreciate seeing explicit component states mapped out clearly in the design file.

  • Use master components for repeating elements like cards, buttons, form fields, and navigation bars.
  • Group variations such as hover, active, disabled, and loading states inside the component properties.
  • Avoid detached instances or unlinked copies that look like components but lack systemic rules.

Clear interactive and responsive states

Static screens only tell half the story of a modern website. Users interact with buttons, hover over cards, type into input fields, and trigger error messages. If these states are missing from the design file, developers have to invent them on the fly, which rarely matches what the designer intended.

Designers should explicitly show what happens during interaction. What does a submit button look like when clicked? How does an error message display when a form field is left blank? Providing these extra frames eliminates guesswork during coding.

Responsive behavior across screen sizes needs the same level of clarity. Instead of assuming a desktop layout simply shrinks down for mobile, designers should define how multi-column grids collapse, when text sizes scale down, and how navigation menus transform into mobile hamburger drawers.

  • Design hover, focus, and active states for all clickable elements.
  • Provide explicit error, success, and loading states for forms and interactive widgets.
  • Include distinct layout frames for mobile, tablet, and desktop viewports rather than relying on automatic scaling.

Design tokens for colors, typography, and spacing

Consistency is what separates a professional website from a messy collection of web pages. When designers use arbitrary font sizes like 15px, 17px, and 18px across different pages, or use slight variations of a brand blue hex code, it creates visual clutter and bloats the codebase.

Design tokens act as a single source of truth for design decisions. They define a strict system for colors, typography scales, border radii, shadows, and spacing increments. When these tokens are clearly documented in Figma, developers can translate them directly into configuration files like Tailwind CSS.

Using a consistent spacing scale, such as increments of four or eight pixels, ensures that margins and paddings look harmonious throughout the site. It also speeds up development because engineers do not have to inspect every single padding value manually.

  • Establish a defined color palette with descriptive names like primary, background, and muted rather than raw hex codes.
  • Use a typographic scale that limits font sizes to a deliberate set of options.
  • Stick to a consistent spacing grid for margins, padding, and layout gutters.

Proper asset preparation and export readiness

One of the most common bottlenecks in a web project is waiting for image and icon assets. If icons are embedded as flattened bitmap graphics or complex vector paths with thousands of stray points, they cannot be used effectively on the web.

Developers need vector assets exported as clean SVG files that can scale infinitely without losing quality. Raster images like photographs should be supplied in high resolutions so they can be optimized and converted into modern formats like WebP or AVIF for fast loading times.

Organizing these assets into dedicated pages or sections within Figma prevents developers from hunting through old artboards to find the right logo or illustration. Naming layers logically, such as icon-search or logo-header, makes exporting a quick, automated process.

  • Export all icons as clean, optimized SVG files.
  • Provide high-resolution source images for photography and illustration.
  • Use clear, logical naming conventions for all layers and asset frames.

Practical takeaways for your next handoff

A successful design handoff is not about delivering a massive document; it is about clear communication and structured systems. When designers and developers speak the same language around components, tokens, and responsive behavior, projects move forward without unnecessary friction.

Before sending your next design file over for development, take a quick pass to clean up unused artboards, check your component states, and verify your color and typography systems. Taking ten minutes to organize your file saves hours of clarifying questions down the road.

Want help with this? See my Figma → React / Next.js service, or send me your site for a free review.

title: Evaluating Compositional Generalization in Transformers: The Role of Composition Equivalence and Module Coverage
description:
arXiv:2611.13498v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Compositional generalization is an important form of out-of-distribution generalization, defined as the ability to train on some combinations of modules (e.g., functions such as sort, filter) and then generalize to unseen combinations. Despite substantial empirical work evaluating compositional generalization in transformers, findings have been inconsistent because evaluations were often conducted on a limited set of train-test splits, defined in an ad hoc manner. Through a systematic evaluation, we identify two key aspects of the train-test distribution that strongly affect performance: composition equivalence and module coverage. We show that the apparent performance of direct models (trained only on final outputs) results primarily from exploiting composition equivalences, meaning different sequences of modules that reduce to identical end-to-end functions. When benchmarks eliminate these equivalences, performance drops significantly, showing their inability to generalize to compositions of known modules that produce novel end-to-end functions. We further demonstrate that performance degrades monotonically as module coverage shifts increase (when modules appear in different contexts between train and test), affecting both direct and step-by-step models (trained on intermediate and final outputs). These findings have concrete implications for benchmark design: benchmarks that include compositional equivalences can lead to significant overestimation of the generalization abilities of direct models, and benchmarks that include both module coverage violations and compositional equivalences can exacerbate shortcut learning. As a case study, we demonstrate the role of compositional equivalence on the generalization performance of the pre-trained model Llama3-8B on the code-output prediction task in the coding benchmark LiveCodeBench.

title: Prediction-Powered LLM Ranking with Adaptively Collected Human Feedback
description:
arXiv:2611.13186v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ranking large language models (LLMs) through human evaluations is essential for downstream decision-making. Because human feedback is expensive, evaluation platforms often collect it adaptively, prioritizing informative model comparisons using previously observed feedback. To further improve precision with limited human feedback, evaluators can draw on abundant unrated responses and relatively inexpensive LLM judges; however, judge bias and adaptive dependence challenge standard i.i.d. inference frameworks. We propose Prediction-Powered Ranking (PP-Rank), a framework that combines LLM-judge predictions with human feedback to improve precision while providing valid inference under adaptive sampling. Data-driven prediction weights minimize the asymptotic covariance trace within the proposed class. In theory, we establish asymptotic normality for general evaluation targets and simultaneous ranking inference. A joint martingale analysis handles dependence between adaptive human feedback and auxiliary data. We further derive a rule for reducing exploration that prioritizes lower-cost comparisons while matching a conservative variance bound, and characterize allocation limits for regular $\sqrt{T}$-rate estimation of pairwise means. Semi-synthetic experiments on UltraFeedback-Extended show improvements over human-only baselines in score estimation, confidence interval width, and ranking certification. Synthetic experiments demonstrate robustness to judge quality and adaptive allocation, while showing that PP-Rank can substantially reduce evaluation costs without sacrificing precision.

title: TreeAgent: Structure-Aware Memory Agent for Processing Long Hierarchical Data
description:
arXiv:2611.13946v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Practical Web applications increasingly require agents to interpret long conversations or documents. For inputs exceeding the context windows of large language models (LLMs), memory agents process segments sequentially and retain past information in bounded memory. However, they typically divide inputs into flat token segments without preserving structure or hierarchy, causing three limitations for structured data such as API responses or HTML documents. First, fixed-length segmentation can split fields of the same record, breaking their relationships. Second, segments lack hierarchical information, obscuring their structural context and positions. Third, successive memory updates may discard details of earlier sibling records needed for reasoning on later segments. To address these limitations, we propose TreeAgent, a structure-aware agent that uses the input hierarchy to guide both segment-wise context processing and access to past information. Specifically, TreeAgent constructs segments from complete subtrees and groups of adjacent sibling subtrees to preserve local structural relationships. We provide theoretical guarantees on segment counts to guide token budget selection toward matching the segment count of fixed-length segmentation. We further attach structural paths to the segments for the agent to identify their ancestors and hierarchical positions. We also introduce residual memory links from the segments of low-level children to the segments of high-level parents, enabling direct information flows beyond successive memory updates. We evaluate TreeAgent with four representative memory agents on eight retrieval and aggregation tasks. The inputs are derived from real-world application data in JSON, HTML, YAML, and JavaScript and range from 8K to 1M tokens. TreeAgent improves the average score across the four datasets for all four agents, with 3.61% performance gain on average.

title: GigaEdge Spench: An SDK for Practical Streaming Speech Enhancement
description:
arXiv:2611.13243v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present GigaEdge Spench, an open-source SDK for streaming speech enhancement on CPU servers, mobile devices, and in browsers. Applications can build enhancement channels from neural denoising, normalization and dynamics blocks, sample-rate conversion, and acoustic echo cancellation where supported. These stages can be combined, while normalization can also run without a neural model. The release includes an 8 kHz INT8 denoiser and discriminative and hybrid 48 kHz FP32 models. A shared C++ core supports ONNX Runtime and TensorFlow Lite through native interfaces, Android and iOS SDKs, and WebAssembly integration. Independent stream contexts share model resources, and consecutive frames from one stream can be processed in a single inference call. We evaluate the released models on EARS-WHAM v2 and compare their quality and processing costs with RNNoise and DPDFNet2. All tested native and Web configurations process files faster than real time, although larger chunks require more time to collect input. We also measure how many streams a shared model can process on a CPU. Our contribution is a configurable deployment system and an experimental study of how model choice, chunk size, and execution environment affect its use. All reported SDK timing uses ONNX Runtime. Index Terms: speech enhancement, streaming inference, cross-platform deployment, temporal frame grouping, computational efficiency
