title: Dark Matters: VAE-Aware HDR Encoding for SDR-to-HDR Video Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2611.13504v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: SDR-to-HDR reconstruction is an ill-posed problem in which clipped highlights, crushed shadows, and quantization artifacts must be recovered while preserving the original content. Latent diffusion models provide powerful generative priors for restoring missing detail, but their effectiveness is constrained by how HDR signals pass through the pretrained VAE. We find that common log-like encodings suppress low-luminance chromatic differences before generation, producing a dark-side collapse in the frozen-VAE latent. We introduce EquivFlow, a compact, invertible exposure-equivariant encoding that maps exposure changes to additive shifts while retaining a scale-independent chromatic component, without modifying the VAE. Encoding-level tests across pretrained image and video VAEs show that its exposure structure and deep-dark chroma transport persist across the tested hosts. Integrated into SDR-to-HDR video diffusion, EquivFlow delivers consistent chromatic-fidelity gains across the tested settings while retaining competitive reconstruction fidelity.

title: Sharp Sample Complexity of KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.13480v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: KL-regularized reinforcement learning, the objective behind maximum-entropy RL and RL from human feedback, is variational inference in the graphical model of "control as inference": the regularized optimal policy is a posterior over trajectories, and the suboptimality of a policy is $\beta$ times a KL divergence between path measures. However, it is not known how many samples it takes to learn this posterior, even with a generative model. Earlier $1/\epsilon$ guarantees scale with $H^5$ in the effective horizon $H$, and no lower bound for MDPs depends on the temperature $\beta$. In this work, we show that for a discounted MDP with $K$ state-action pairs, the plug-in estimator finds a policy that is $\epsilon$-optimal from every initial state with $\widetilde{O}(KH^3/(\epsilon\max\{\epsilon,\beta\}) + KH)$ samples, and that no algorithm, even one that chooses where to sample, can do with fewer when $\epsilon \lesssim \min\{H, H^2/\beta\}$. For $\epsilon < \beta$ this is a $1/\epsilon$ rate with the same horizon dependence as unregularized RL. We also find the exact asymptotic constant of the plug-in estimator, a Fisher-weighted variance of the estimated soft Q-function. The estimator is locally asymptotically minimax among methods that sample every pair equally often, and we give the allocation of samples that is optimal among adaptive designs. Simulations on small MDPs match the rates and the constants.

title: SpecValley: Aggregation as Spectral Valley in Dense Heterophilic Graphs
description:
arXiv:2611.14176v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Node classification in heterophilic graphs remains an open problem: aggregating over neighbourhoods can damp precisely the part of the signal that carries the labels. The field has answered with ever more expressive propagation operators, leaving the aggregation step that precedes them fixed by degree normalisation. However, degree normalisation acts as a spectral valley in its own right, attenuating a fixed middle band whose position at lambda equal 1 is set by the normalisation rather than by the data, exactly where the eigenvalues of dense graphs accumulate. We therefore begin with the representations rather than the propagation, in two stages: a learnable aggregation followed by an ordinary spectral filter. The first, SpecValley learns the position, sharpness and flank gains of the valley for every graph. We show formally how the aggregation operator and downstream filter interact. We establish that the response 1 minus lambda of degree normalisation vanishes exactly at that accumulation point. A spectral energy budget shows that what aggregation removes from a band, no linear spectral filter can recover. Crowding alone says nothing about the benefit. That is decided by how much label energy the valley removes, which we measure for every graph. SpecValley achieves strong results across heterophilic benchmarks, and a controlled ablation over aggregation operators and downstream filters attributes the gain to aggregation rather than the filter.

title: Cache-Busting Static Assets with ?v=: So Visitors Actually Get the Fix
description:
The most embarrassing bug report I ever got went like this: I fixed a bug, deployed it, tested it myself, and the visitor still saw the broken version. The new file was on the server. My own browser showed the fix. Then I talked the visitor through clearing their cache, and suddenly everything worked.

The bug was never in my code. It was in the browser cache, and it taught me the cheapest lesson in web performance: browsers remember your files far longer than you expect, and you have to give them a reason to forget.

Why the browser holds on so tightly

When a browser downloads style.css or app.js, it keeps a copy. The next time it needs that file, it checks its cache first. If the server sent a far-future Cache-Control header like max-age=31536000, the browser may not even ask the server whether the file changed. It just serves the old copy, silently, for a year.

That is exactly what you want for performance. A returning visitor should not re-download files that have not changed. The problem starts the day you do change one. The URL is identical, the filename is identical, and the browser has no way of knowing the contents are different. Your fix is live on the server and invisible to everyone who visited before.

The ?v= trick

The fix is almost embarrassingly simple: change the URL when the file changes. Browsers cache by URL, so a different URL means a fresh download. I append a version query string to every static asset:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/style.css?v=20261106">
<script src="/js/app.js?v=20261106"></script>

The ?v=20261106 part means nothing to the server. It serves the same file and ignores the query string. But to the browser, /css/style.css?v=20261106 and /css/style.css?v=20261105 are two different resources. The day I ship a change, I bump the number, and every visitor fetches the new file on their next visit.

Bumping the version by hand is a trap

I did this by hand at first: edit the file, remember to bump the number in every page that references it, deploy, and hope I did not miss one. I missed one, of course. The homepage got the new script, a tool page kept the old one, and I spent an evening debugging a bug that only existed on one page.

So I stopped trusting my memory and let PHP do it. On a plain PHP site with no build step, filemtime() gives you the file's last-modified time for free:

function asset($path) {
    $full = __DIR__ . '/' . ltrim($path, '/');
    $v = file_exists($full) ? filemtime($full) : time();
    return $path . '?v=' . $v;
}

Then every reference becomes <?= asset('/js/app.js') ?>, and the version bumps itself the moment the file changes on disk. No deploy checklist, nothing to forget. The timestamp is a Unix epoch, so it looks ugly in the HTML source, but nobody reads query strings for beauty.

One catch: filemtime() reads the disk on every request. For a handful of assets on shared hosting that is cheap enough to ignore, but if you serve dozens of files per page, write the version into a small config file and regenerate it at deploy time instead. Same idea, one less disk read.

Where it does not work

The trick is not perfect. Some older proxies and a few CDNs ignore query strings when deciding what to cache, and can serve the stale file anyway. The big CDNs handle it correctly today, but if your caching layer is unusual, filename versioning (app.20261106.js) is the bulletproof version of the same idea. It is also more work on a site with no build step, which is why I stayed with ?v=.

The other edge is the service worker. I run a network-first service worker on my downloader site, ramrom.io, and it caches pages and assets too. A cache-busted URL helps there as well, because the worker keys its cache by URL just like the browser does — but if the worker itself is stale, it can keep serving old responses no matter what the URL says. That is a separate problem, and it is why I version the service worker file as well.

The habit that stuck

Cache-busting is not a clever technique. It is a habit: never ship a changed static file under the same URL. The version can be a date, a timestamp, or a hash of the file contents — the format does not matter. What matters is that it changes when the file changes, and that the change happens automatically, because the one time you forget to bump it by hand is the one time a visitor reports a bug you already fixed.

These days I do not think about it at all. The helper writes the version, the browser fetches the new file, and the bug reports that used to say "it still looks broken" have quietly stopped coming. That silence is the whole point.

title: INTENT: Out-of-Sample, Out-of-Time, and Cold-Start Evaluation on User Event Sequences
description:
arXiv:2611.13069v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Banks now train foundation models on ordered sequences of customer events such as transactions, app sessions, and authorizations. Deployed, such a model predicts forward in time, often for customers and merchants absent from training, yet each is evaluated on private data, so no two can be compared. Public benchmarks for such sequences rarely test a period the model has not seen; recommendation studies usually hold out each user's last events instead. We present INTENT (INTEraction, Novelty, and Transfer evaluation for next-action prediction), a public benchmark that scores a model in seven cells defined by whether the user, the period, and the target item appeared in training. An audit of 59 public dataset families retains five datasets; the most common defect is the lack of a calendar timestamp that orders events. No date lies within the time span of all five datasets, so each is split at its own cutoff, chosen by one rule fixed before any model is evaluated. Summed over the datasets, every cell holds at least 111,769 users. In reference results the cell determines the best model: a transformer leads on seen items after the cutoff but scores zero on new items, a variant that embeds item metadata helps mainly on MicroLens, and repeating the user's last item leads on new items in four of five datasets. This parameter-free control also shows that on three datasets most of the score lost after the cutoff reflects changed behavior rather than the model. The pipeline, the cutoff rule, and the per-cell user counts are publicly available.

title: React Query Showed the Wrong User's Data — Here's How to Reproduce and Fix It
description:
A React dashboard can display the wrong user's data even when the API is returning the correct response.

One of the easiest ways to introduce this bug is by using a query key that doesn't account for the current user.

Consider this:

const { data } = useQuery({
  queryKey: ["orders"],
  queryFn: () => fetchOrders(userId),
});

It looks perfectly reasonable.

But there's a problem.

The query function depends on userId, while the cache key doesn't.

If Alice's orders are already cached and the application switches to Bob, both users can end up sharing the same cache entry.

Depending on the query's freshness settings, Bob's dashboard could display Alice's previously cached orders.

I wanted to break down why this happens because it's the kind of issue that's easy to overlook when testing with only one account.

We'll reproduce it in a small React application, fix the query key, and then look at what changes when authentication, logout, and multiple SaaS workspaces are involved.

Alice logs in and opens her orders page. Everything looks fine.

She logs out, and Bob logs in using the same browser.

But Bob sees something unexpected.

Alice's orders are still showing on his dashboard.

You check the backend. The API works. The database queries are correct. Your authorization checks appear to be doing their job.

So why is Bob seeing Alice's data?

The issue might be hiding in one line of React Query code:

queryKey: ["orders"]

That looks harmless, doesn't it?

But when the data depends on the authenticated user, this query key doesn't tell TanStack Query whose orders it's caching.

Let's reproduce the issue, understand why it happens, and fix it properly.

We'll also look at a few related problems that are easy to miss in production: switching workspaces, logging out, and displaying previous data while a new request loads.

1. The bug starts with a perfectly normal-looking query

Consider a React component that fetches the current user's orders.

import { useQuery } from "@tanstack/react-query";

function Orders({ userId }) {
  const { data, isPending } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ["orders"],
    queryFn: () => fetchOrders(userId),
  });

  if (isPending) {
    return <p>Loading orders...</p>;
  }

  return <OrdersTable orders={data} />;
}

At first glance, there's nothing unusual here.

We have a query key, a query function, and a loading state.

The problem is that fetchOrders() depends on userId, but the query key doesn't.

Let's say Alice has these orders:

[
  { "id": 101, "product": "MacBook Pro" },
  { "id": 102, "product": "Keyboard" }
]

And Bob has these:

[
  { "id": 201, "product": "Monitor" },
  { "id": 202, "product": "Mouse" }
]

Our React component requests different data depending on the user.

But TanStack Query sees this:

Alice → ["orders"]

Bob   → ["orders"]

It's the same cache key.

TanStack Query doesn't automatically inspect the variables inside your query function to identify the data.

It relies on the query key you provide.

If two requests use the same key, they're treated as requests for the same cached query.

And that's where things can go wrong.

2. Let's reproduce the problem

Instead of stopping at the explanation, let's create a small React application where you can see the bug yourself.

We'll use Vite and TanStack Query.

No backend or database is required for this demonstration.

The data is mocked so we can focus entirely on caching behavior. We're simulating account switching, not implementing real authentication.

Step 1: Create the project

Run:

npm create vite@latest react-query-cache-demo -- --template react

cd react-query-cache-demo

npm install

npm install @tanstack/react-query

npm run dev

Step 2: Configure QueryClient

Open src/main.jsx and replace its contents with:

import React from "react";
import ReactDOM from "react-dom/client";

import {
  QueryClient,
  QueryClientProvider,
} from "@tanstack/react-query";

import App from "./App.jsx";

const queryClient = new QueryClient();

ReactDOM.createRoot(
  document.getElementById("root")
).render(
  <React.StrictMode>
    <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>
      <App />
    </QueryClientProvider>
  </React.StrictMode>
);

Step 3: Create the demo

Now replace src/App.jsx with:

import { useState } from "react";
import { useQuery } from "@tanstack/react-query";

const ordersDatabase = {
  alice: [
    { id: 101, product: "MacBook Pro" },
    { id: 102, product: "Keyboard" },
  ],
  bob: [
    { id: 201, product: "Monitor" },
    { id: 202, product: "Mouse" },
  ],
};

async function fetchOrders(userId) {
  // Simulate network latency
  await new Promise((resolve) =>
    setTimeout(resolve, 500)
  );

  return ordersDatabase[userId];
}

export default function App() {
  const [userId, setUserId] = useState("alice");
  const [fixed, setFixed] = useState(false);

  const {
    data: orders = [],
    isPending,
  } = useQuery({
    queryKey: fixed
      ? ["orders", userId]
      : ["orders"],

    queryFn: () => fetchOrders(userId),

    // Keep cached data fresh for this demo
    staleTime: Infinity,
  });

  return (
    <div style={{ padding: 24 }}>
      <h1>Orders Dashboard</h1>

      <p>
        Logged in as: <strong>{userId}</strong>
      </p>

      <button onClick={() => setUserId("alice")}>
        Switch to Alice
      </button>

      <button onClick={() => setUserId("bob")}>
        Switch to Bob
      </button>

      <hr />

      <label>
        <input
          type="checkbox"
          checked={fixed}
          onChange={(event) =>
            setFixed(event.target.checked)
          }
        />
        Use correct query key
      </label>

      <h2>Orders</h2>

      {isPending ? (
        <p>Loading...</p>
      ) : (
        <ul>
          {orders.map((order) => (
            <li key={order.id}>
              #{order.id} - {order.product}
            </li>
          ))}
        </ul>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

Step 4: See what happens

Open the application.

Initially, Alice is selected.

Wait for her orders to load.

You should see:

Logged in as: alice

Orders:
#101 - MacBook Pro
#102 - Keyboard

Now click Switch to Bob without enabling the checkbox.

You might expect Bob's orders to appear.

But the screen still shows:

Logged in as: bob

Orders:
#101 - MacBook Pro
#102 - Keyboard

That's the bug.

We're displaying Alice's cached orders while the interface says Bob is the current user.

Why does this happen?

Our query key hasn't changed:

queryKey: ["orders"]

We also deliberately configured:

staleTime: Infinity

This tells TanStack Query to consider the cached data fresh indefinitely, unless it is manually invalidated.

Because the cache key remains unchanged and the data is considered fresh, changing userId doesn't trigger a new query.

This setting makes the problem easy to reproduce.

With the default stale-time configuration, you may see different refetching behavior depending on when the query mounts or is invalidated. But the underlying problem remains: two different datasets are sharing one cache identity.

3. Fixing it with the correct query key

The fix is straightforward.

Instead of:

const { data } = useQuery({
  queryKey: ["orders"],
  queryFn: () => fetchOrders(userId),
});

Use:

const { data } = useQuery({
  queryKey: ["orders", userId],
  queryFn: () => fetchOrders(userId),
});

Now the cache keys are different:

Alice → ["orders", "alice"]

Bob   → ["orders", "bob"]

TanStack Query can distinguish the two datasets.

Go back to the demo and enable Use correct query key.

Switch between Alice and Bob again.

The orders should now match the selected account.

When you switch back to Alice, her previously fetched data can be retrieved from her own cache entry.

That's exactly the behavior we want.

Here's the principle I follow:

If a variable changes which data your query returns, it probably belongs in the query key.

Not every variable needs to be part of the key. But variables that determine the identity of the requested data do.

4. The same mistake becomes more complicated in multi-tenant SaaS applications

Now imagine a more realistic application.

You're working on a SaaS platform where a single account can belong to multiple organizations.

For example:

Alice
  |
  |-- Company A
  |     |-- Orders
  |     |-- Customers
  |
  |-- Company B
        |-- Orders
        |-- Customers

Alice can switch between Company A and Company B without logging out.

You might already be using this query key:

queryKey: ["orders", userId]

It separates Alice's data from Bob's.

But it doesn't separate Company A's orders from Company B's.

Both organizations still share the same key for Alice.

A better key would be:

queryKey: [
  "orders",
  userId,
  organizationId,
]

And what if the orders table has filters?

Suppose users can filter by order status, search terms, or pages.

Those variables also affect the result.

queryKey: [
  "orders",
  userId,
  organizationId,
  {
    status,
    page,
    search,
  },
]

Now each dataset has its own cache identity.

For example:

["orders", "alice", "company-a", { page: 1 }]

["orders", "alice", "company-b", { page: 1 }]

["orders", "bob", "company-b", { page: 1 }]

One important detail: don't include access tokens, passwords, or other secrets in query keys.

Use stable, non-secret identifiers.

And remember that cache scoping is not authorization. Even if a user manipulates a query key, the backend must independently check permissions.

5. How I'd structure the query in a real application

For a workspace-based SaaS application, I prefer keeping the query logic inside a reusable hook.

Something like this:

import { useQuery } from "@tanstack/react-query";

async function fetchWorkspaceOrders({
  workspaceId,
  status,
  page,
  signal,
}) {
  const params = new URLSearchParams({
    status,
    page: String(page),
  });

  const response = await fetch(
    `/api/workspaces/${encodeURIComponent(workspaceId)}/orders?${params}`,
    {
      credentials: "include",
      signal,
    }
  );

  if (response.status === 401) {
    throw new Error("Authentication required");
  }

  if (response.status === 403) {
    throw new Error("Access denied");
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error("Failed to fetch orders");
  }

  return response.json();
}

export function useWorkspaceOrders({
  userId,
  workspaceId,
  status = "all",
  page = 1,
}) {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: [
      "orders",
      userId,
      workspaceId,
      { status, page },
    ],

    queryFn: ({ signal }) =>
      fetchWorkspaceOrders({
        workspaceId,
        status,
        page,
        signal,
      }),

    enabled: Boolean(userId && workspaceId),
  });
}

There are a few details worth understanding.

The query key describes the data. It includes the account, workspace, and filters that determine the response.

The enabled option prevents automatic fetching until the required identifiers are available. It doesn't remove cached data or enforce access control.

The query function uses the supplied AbortSignal. This allows obsolete requests to be cancelled when TanStack Query cancels the query.

HTTP errors are handled explicitly. The browser's fetch() function doesn't automatically reject a promise for responses such as 403 or 500.

For this example, I'm assuming the backend uses cookie-based authentication. If your application uses bearer tokens or another mechanism, the request implementation will be different.

The query key should still reflect the authenticated data context.

6. Don't forget what happens on logout

Correct query keys solve an important problem, but I wouldn't stop there.

Consider a shared computer.

Alice logs in, opens her dashboard, and logs out.

Then Bob logs in using the same browser tab.

If both sessions use the same QueryClient, Alice's previously fetched data can remain in its in-memory cache even after her session ends.

Correctly scoped keys help prevent the new session from accidentally requesting Alice's cached data.

But for private information, I generally prefer clearing the previous session's cached state when the authentication boundary changes.

TanStack Query provides:

queryClient.clear();

This clears both the query cache and mutation cache associated with that client.

You can also cancel active queries:

await queryClient.cancelQueries();

But the order of operations matters.

A safer logout strategy

The application should immediately stop displaying authenticated screens when logout begins.

Then it should coordinate request cancellation, cache cleanup, and session revocation.

Here's a simplified example:

async function handleLogout() {
  // The application must stop rendering private screens.
  setAuthStatus("signing-out");

  // Cancel active queries.
  await queryClient.cancelQueries();

  // Clear in-memory query and mutation caches.
  queryClient.clear();

  // Revoke the authenticated session on the server.
  const response = await fetch("/api/logout", {
    method: "POST",
    credentials: "include",
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    // Keep private screens hidden and provide
    // a way to retry or recover from this error.
    setAuthStatus("logout-error");
    return;
  }

  setAuthStatus("signed-out");
}

This assumes your application uses authStatus to stop rendering all protected components when the value isn't an authenticated state.

It's an example of the sequence, not a complete authentication implementation.

A few things are important here:

  • Clearing React Query's cache doesn't revoke a server session.
  • Cancelling a query doesn't undo a request the server has already processed.
  • An unsuccessful logout request must not be presented as successful server-side logout.
  • If you're persisting queries to browser storage, that persisted data must be handled separately.
  • Other caches, global stores, service workers, and open browser tabs may also need attention.

For applications with sensitive information, the full authentication lifecycle deserves its own design and testing.

A cache clear is useful, but it isn't a complete security solution.

7. Another mistake: showing previous data during account switches

There's another subtle situation worth understanding.

TanStack Query supports showing previous query data while the next result loads.

For example:

import {
  keepPreviousData,
  useQuery,
} from "@tanstack/react-query";

const { data } = useQuery({
  queryKey: ["products", page],
  queryFn: () => fetchProducts(page),
  placeholderData: keepPreviousData,
});

This is often useful for pagination.

Instead of briefly displaying an empty table whenever the page changes, you can keep showing the previous page until the new result arrives.

That's a good experience for many interfaces.

But imagine using the same approach when switching between private workspaces.

Even with correctly scoped query keys, previous-data placeholders can temporarily display information belonging to the previous workspace.

The query cache entries may be isolated correctly, while the component still renders the previous result as placeholder data.

These are different behaviors.

For public product listings, this might be harmless.

For customer invoices, medical records, financial reports, or private business dashboards, it could be unacceptable.

A smoother loading experience isn't always the correct loading experience.

When the authenticated user or tenant changes, I generally prefer a loading or empty state over showing data from the previous context.

8. Is this actually a security vulnerability?

It's important to be precise here.

A wrong query key can cause the frontend to display data fetched under a previous authenticated context.

That can create a confidentiality problem, especially on shared devices or when sensitive information remains visible after switching accounts.

But this doesn't automatically mean the backend has an authorization vulnerability.

Consider two different scenarios.

Scenario A: Client-side cache isolation failure

Alice is authorized to access Company A.

The backend correctly returns Company A's orders.

Later, the frontend switches to Company B but mistakenly displays the previously cached Company A orders.

The UI has displayed inappropriate cached data.

That doesn't necessarily mean the server authorized an invalid request.

Scenario B: Broken backend authorization

Alice requests:

GET /api/workspaces/company-b/orders

Even though she doesn't have permission to access Company B.

The server returns Company B's private orders anyway.

That's a backend authorization failure.

Correcting React Query keys won't fix it.

The backend must verify that the authenticated user has access to the requested resource, regardless of what the frontend sends.

In a multi-tenant application, I would treat both areas seriously:

Frontend isolation: Make sure cached data is associated with the correct user and tenant.

Backend authorization: Enforce resource access permissions on every protected request.

Neither replaces the other.

9. Let's add a test for the cache behavior

It's easy to assume a bug is fixed because switching users appears to work manually.

I'd also want a small automated test that verifies how the cache behaves.

Install Vitest:

npm install -D vitest

Create src/query-cache.test.js:

import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";
import { QueryClient } from "@tanstack/react-query";

const orders = {
  alice: ["Alice Order"],
  bob: ["Bob Order"],
};

describe("React Query cache isolation", () => {
  it("demonstrates the shared-key mistake", async () => {
    const client = new QueryClient();

    const aliceOrders = await client.fetchQuery({
      queryKey: ["orders"],
      queryFn: async () => orders.alice,
      staleTime: Infinity,
    });

    const bobOrders = await client.fetchQuery({
      queryKey: ["orders"],
      queryFn: async () => orders.bob,
      staleTime: Infinity,
    });

    expect(aliceOrders).toEqual(["Alice Order"]);

    // Bob receives the cached result for Alice.
    expect(bobOrders).toEqual(["Alice Order"]);

    client.clear();
  });

  it("keeps each user's orders separate", async () => {
    const client = new QueryClient();

    const aliceOrders = await client.fetchQuery({
      queryKey: ["orders", "alice"],
      queryFn: async () => orders.alice,
    });

    const bobOrders = await client.fetchQuery({
      queryKey: ["orders", "bob"],
      queryFn: async () => orders.bob,
    });

    expect(aliceOrders).toEqual(["Alice Order"]);
    expect(bobOrders).toEqual(["Bob Order"]);

    client.clear();
  });
});

Run:

npx vitest run

Notice that the first test deliberately expects the wrong result.

It's a regression demonstration: it confirms that the same fresh cache key is being reused.

The second test verifies that distinct keys keep the data separate.

This doesn't replace UI-level or authentication testing. In a production application, I'd also test account switching while requests are in progress, logout behavior, tenant authorization, and persisted cache cleanup.

10. My checklist before shipping a multi-tenant dashboard

When reviewing a React Query implementation, these are the cases I'd verify:

Scenario Expected behavior
Alice opens her orders Alice's orders appear
Alice switches to Bob in the demo Bob's orders appear with a different key
A user switches organizations Only the selected organization's orders appear
Filters or pagination change The query uses the correct cache identity
A user logs out Protected screens stop rendering and cached session data is cleaned up
An old request resolves after logout Its result doesn't reappear in the new session's private UI
An unauthorized workspace is requested The server rejects access
Previous-data placeholders are enabled Private data isn't shown across authentication or tenant boundaries

One detail I find especially important is testing with more than one account.

An application can look completely correct during development when you always test with the same user and workspace.

Context-switching bugs often become visible only when you deliberately switch accounts, organizations, or permissions.

Final thoughts

TanStack Query makes it much easier to manage server state in React applications.

Caching, refetching, request deduplication, loading states, and error handling are all valuable features.

But caching introduces a responsibility that we shouldn't overlook.

The cache needs to know what makes one dataset different from another.

Sometimes that difference is a product ID.

Sometimes it's a page number or filter.

And in SaaS applications, it might be the current user, organization, or workspace.

This small change:

// Too generic for user-specific data
queryKey: ["orders"]

to:

// Separates users and workspaces
queryKey: ["orders", userId, workspaceId]

can prevent a surprisingly confusing class of bugs.

But the bigger lesson isn't simply to add more identifiers to every query key.

It's to think carefully about data ownership, cache lifetime, authentication boundaries, and what the user is actually allowed to see.

A working API doesn't guarantee that the interface is displaying the right data.

That's something worth testing before calling a feature production-ready.

How do you handle React Query caching when users log out or switch workspaces? Do you clear the cache, use user-scoped query keys, or combine both approaches?

I'd be interested to hear how others handle this in production.

Further reading

  • TanStack Query — Query Keys
  • TanStack Query — Query Cancellation
  • TanStack Query — Placeholder Query Data
  • TanStack Query — QueryClient API

title: You Are What You Read: Indian Political News Media Bias Dataset for Hindi Language
description:
arXiv:2611.13686v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Media bias understanding and detection remains an under-researched problem for Indian context, specifically for Indic languages, such as, Hindi, which is widely spoken in India. In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive, multi-annotator, explainable dataset consisting of 448 unique articles from four leading Indian news agencies publishing in Hindi. We focus on Hindi, the most spoken and an official language of India. The study of media bias is particularly relevant in the Indian context due to the country's linguistic diversity and large population, where the same event is often reported by multiple news agencies in different languages, thereby introducing scope for bias. The dataset comprises Hindi political news articles annotated by 14 experts and classified into four bias categories - selection bias, framing bias, clickbait bias and omission bias - when an article is identified as biased or unbiased. For each biased article, annotators also provide a textual explanation, enabling future semi-automated approaches to incorporate explainability when language models reason over the dataset. Cohen's Kappa scores were 0.81 for simple bias/no-bias classification reflecting strong inter-annotator agreement. For the multi-label task, the Cohen's Kappa values are 0.89, 0.75, 0.81, and 0.79 for clickbait, selection, framing, and omission biases, respectively, resulting in an average Kappa of 0.80, which also reflects strong agreement.

title: I moved two Electron apps to Tauri. The installer went from 198MB to 5.6MB.
description:
GitHub: https://github.com/ESeungJun/smash · https://github.com/ESeungJun/poketmon_idle

I've built a handful of desktop apps this year, and most of them are Electron apps. Every installer ended up over 100MB. Smash!, an app that tidies my Downloads folder, was 114MB. A desktop pet that grows while I focus was 198MB. Then I built a weather widget with Tauri, and it came out at 17MB, 3D assets included. (I wrote this with help from Claude and checked every number myself.)

So I moved two of the Electron apps to Tauri, which means Rust on the native side. I did it together with Claude Code. This post covers how I picked the order, and what I did so the people already using these apps wouldn't notice anything except a smaller download.

The numbers

On the Mac, the pet app went from 198.7MB to 5.6MB, and Smash went from 114MB to 6.2MB. Smash used to ship separate builds for Apple silicon and Intel. Now it's one universal build at 6.2MB. On Windows, the installers went from 92.8MB to 2.0MB and from 115MB to 2.2MB.

I could only compare memory for Smash. The Electron version used 244MB across 8 processes. The Tauri version uses 88MB.

That 88MB needs a note. Tauri draws the UI with the system WebKit on macOS, and WebKit runs in its own processes outside the app. My first measurement only counted the app process and gave me 48MB. That felt like cheating, so the number above adds the three WebKit processes that started with it.

Which app first

Before touching any code, I went through my Electron apps one by one. "Port it to Rust" sounds like a big rewrite. In practice, the UI (HTML or React) stays almost the same, and you rewrite the Electron main process, the Node part, in Rust.

So I counted how big each main process was and which Electron features it used.

The pet app's main process was only 494 lines, and everything it used (tray, transparent window, always-on-top) has a Tauri equivalent. Smash was bigger, with 1,816 lines plus an MCP server. DroidLens, an Android dev tool of mine, has over 5,000 lines to rewrite, and install size matters less for a dev tool. I put it on hold.

I also wrote down what I expected to get: smaller installers, less memory, faster startup. I didn't expect features to get faster just because of Rust. My apps were never slow because of JavaScript. The cost I accepted was that each OS now uses its own webview (WebKit on macOS, WebView2 on Windows), so the UI can look slightly different per OS.

The plan was simple. Port the smallest app, measure, and only move on to Smash if the numbers held up. I'd rather pick the next app from a measured number than from an estimate.

Goals

I used three goals to make decisions along the way.

The first one mattered most. A smaller installer is nice, but if updating wipes your rules or quietly breaks your Claude setup, it's a step back.

Keep the UI, match the boundary

I barely touched the UI code in either app.

In Electron, the UI talks to the main process through an object like window.electronAPI or window.tidy. I wrote one small file that builds the same object on top of Tauri commands. The UI calls the same functions and gets the same values back, so it doesn't need to know whether Electron or Rust is on the other side.

For the pet app, all 38 React components stayed as they were. The 494-line main process became 720 lines of Rust, and the installer dropped from 198.7MB to 5.6MB. That was enough to move on to Smash.

Smash, MCP server included

Smash had more to port: the rule engine, the folder watcher, trash handling, history, the Claude integration, and an MCP server. I started after midnight and shipped 2.0.0 around noon the same day. The Rust side is 3,841 lines, tests included.

The MCP server is the biggest change. You can register Smash as an MCP server in Claude Code or Claude Desktop and say "tidy my Downloads". In the Electron version, the server ran by starting the bundled Electron binary as if it were Node. Now it's the app binary with --mcp, and Node isn't involved at all.

That created a problem, though. Anyone on 1.x had Claude configured with the old Electron path. The moment they updated, that path would disappear, and Claude would silently lose Smash.

So the first time 2.0 starts, it looks for Claude config files and rewrites any old Smash entry to point at the new binary. That covers ~/.claude.json, the Claude Desktop config, and per-profile config folders. It leaves places where Smash isn't registered alone, and it skips the rewrite when the app runs from a temporary path, like straight from the disk image.

What the tests didn't catch

I ported the existing tests for the rule engine and file moves to Rust, and all 21 pass. A few things still slipped past them.

My edit reshuffled the user's Claude config. When I first built the registration fix, a review showed that reading and rewriting the JSON sorted every key alphabetically. It still worked. But ~/.claude.json holds a person's whole Claude Code setup, and changing one entry shouldn't reorder the entire file. I switched to keeping the original key order. Then I compared three real config files on my machine before and after, and only the smash entry had changed.

The nag banner lost the folder name. When auto-tidy runs, Smash shows a banner like "Tidied 3 files in Downloads". After the port, I dropped a real file into the folder and got "Tidied 1 file in" with no folder name. The watcher was passing a path where it should have passed the folder's ID, and no test looked at that value. I fixed it and made the test check the ID.

Building only in CI made me find errors late. At first this Mac had no Rust, so every build ran on GitHub Actions. That meant waiting over ten minutes to learn about a single compile error. (Not my proudest afternoon.) I installed Rust locally, and now I build and test on my machine first. CI only does the things I can't do here, like the Windows build.

The first two only showed up with the installed app, my real config files and real files. So after porting, I left the installed app running for over 40 seconds, measured memory, and talked to the MCP server directly before calling it done.

No more manual downloads

Neither app had auto-update in its Electron days. Every release meant downloading again.

Both apps now check 15 seconds after launch and every 6 hours after that. When there's a new version, they download it in the background and add "Install new version and restart" to the tray menu. They only install when you click it. That rule comes from the pet app: it's a focus timer, and it shouldn't restart in the middle of your focus session.

I checked that a test build actually updated itself to the real 2.0.0. In 2.1.0 I also added the current version and a "Check for updates" button to the settings screen.

What's left

  • On Windows, I've only confirmed that the installer builds. I haven't run it on a real Windows machine yet, and WebView2 may render the UI a little differently.
  • Next in line is Claudy, a desktop pet that shows what my Claude sessions are doing. Its main process is 2,799 lines. With numbers like these, I think it's worth doing.

What I learned

  • Size and memory dropped a lot. Feature speed didn't change in any way I could feel, which is what I expected.
  • The Rust rewrite wasn't the hard part. Carrying over settings, history and Claude registrations without breaking anything took more care.
  • Porting the smallest app first and measuring it made the next decision easy.

If one of these apps sounds useful, a star on GitHub would make my day.

  • Smash: https://github.com/ESeungJun/smash
  • Pokémon Idle: https://github.com/ESeungJun/poketmon_idle
  • LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/승준-이-53707a328/

title: How a Privacy-First Online Image Editor Works Without Uploading Your Photos (WebAssembly + On-Device AI)
description:
Most online image editors follow the same pattern. You pick a file, the browser uploads it, a server processes it, and a result comes back. It is simple to build, and it quietly means every photo you edit passes through someone else's infrastructure.

Browsers no longer need that arrangement. With WebAssembly, the Canvas API, and models that run on the client, the work of a photo editor, background remover, and image converter can happen on the device in front of you.

Akhouri Systems built APIC, a free browser-based editor, around that constraint. This article documents how a privacy-first online image editor is put together when nothing is uploaded, which trade-offs come with that design, and what users can reasonably expect from it.

Why "no upload" is an architecture decision, not a slogan

Privacy claims are cheap. Architecture is harder to fake.

When image processing happens on a server, privacy depends on policy: retention windows, access controls, and trust. When processing happens on the device, the image never leaves the browser tab, so there is nothing to retain and nothing to leak in transit.

That changes a few things for anyone building or choosing an online photo editor:

  • Sensitive images stay local. ID photos, product prototypes, client work, family pictures.
  • There is no upload queue. Speed depends on the user's hardware, not on server load.
  • Large files are no longer a bandwidth problem. A 40 MB photo does not need to travel anywhere.
  • Offline use becomes possible. After the first load, much of the tooling does not need a connection.

The cost is that the client has to do real work. The rest of this article is about how that work gets done.

The building blocks of a browser-based image editor

1. Canvas for live editing

Filters, brightness, contrast, saturation, blur, rotation, and flipping are all operations on pixel data, and the Canvas API handles them well. Because the work is local, sliders update the preview live with no round trip.

For more demanding color work, the same approach scales up. APIC's advanced panel includes a live histogram with shadow and highlight clipping indicators, RGB curves, an 8-band HSL mixer, three-way color grading, clarity, and grain. It can also export a 33×33×33 3D LUT as a .cube file, so a grade built in the browser can be reused in tools such as DaVinci Resolve, Premiere, or Photoshop.

One honest limitation: spatial effects like clarity, sharpening, vignette, and grain are not purely color transforms, so they cannot be baked into a LUT. The export covers the color-only parts of the grade.

2. WebAssembly for the heavy lifting

JavaScript alone is not the right tool for neural-network inference on a full-resolution photo. WebAssembly gives near-native execution inside the browser sandbox, which is what makes on-device AI practical. Every AI feature below runs this way.

3. Model caching so the cost is paid once

On-device AI has a real first-run cost: the model has to be downloaded. A well-behaved implementation downloads it once, caches it in the browser, and reuses it afterward.

For background removal, APIC offers three tiers so users can match the model to their device:

Tier First download Best for
Light about 5 MB Phones and quick cut-outs
Fast about 44 MB Everyday use
Maximum about 176 MB Highest accuracy, multi-pass, desktop-class hardware

After the first run, the model loads from cache, and nothing is sent to a server at any point. If a download fails, the app retries automatically and surfaces a retry button rather than failing silently.

On-device AI background removal

Background removal is a segmentation problem: classify every pixel as subject or not, then turn that mask into transparency. Doing this locally means the full-resolution original stays in memory on the user's device.

Two details matter for quality:

  • Edge refinement. Raw masks tend to leave hard or jagged boundaries. A refinement pass smooths them.
  • Color-fringe removal. Pixels at the edge often carry color from the old background. Removing that spill is the difference between a cut-out that looks pasted on and one that looks natural.

For output, keep transparency by exporting to PNG or WebP. JPEG has no alpha channel, so it will flatten the result.

Removing objects with on-device inpainting

Object removal is a different problem from background removal. You paint over what you want gone, such as a stray person, a sign, or a blemish, and a model fills the region so it blends with its surroundings.

APIC uses two engines, which illustrates a useful design pattern, graceful degradation:

  • MI-GAN (about 28 MB) is lightweight enough to run on phones.
  • LaMa, a large Fourier-convolution inpainting network (about 208 MB), gives the most accurate fills for big or complex areas, and is intended for desktop-class devices.

If a model cannot load, the tool steps down automatically: Ultra, then MI-GAN, then a quick patch fill. Only the area around the brush is processed, and the fill is color-matched and re-grained to match the original photo, which avoids the telltale "too clean" patch.

A practical tip that applies to any inpainting tool: paint slightly outside the object, so shadows and reflections are covered too.

Compressing an image to an exact file size

A common real-world task is hitting an upload limit: "under 200 KB" for a form, "under 1 MB" for a CMS. Guessing a quality slider is tedious.

A better approach is to search across quality levels and keep the highest one that fits the target. APIC's compress image online tool works this way. If the target is impossible at any quality, it reduces the dimensions as a fallback and reports the actual resulting size rather than pretending it hit the number.

Resizing without the muddy look

A single large downscale is a classic source of soft, blurry results. Resampling in several half-size steps preserves more detail, and every pixel is recomputed at full quality. The tool leaves the image uncropped and unstretched unless you deliberately change the aspect ratio. You can specify exact pixels or a percentage, with an aspect-ratio lock.

Converting formats: PNG, JPG, WebP, BMP, ICO, PDF

Format conversion is where most people start. The practical rules of thumb:

  • PNG: lossless, supports transparency. Best after background removal.
  • JPEG: small files, no transparency. Best for photos.
  • WebP: small files and transparency. A strong default for the web.
  • BMP: uncompressed.
  • ICO: app and favicon icons.
  • PDF: a single-page document from an image.

All six conversions run locally, so converting a private document scan does not involve a third party.

Social media sizes without the guesswork

Every platform has its own dimensions for profile pictures, banners, covers, posts, and stories, and they change. APIC's Social tab holds exact-size presets for 15 networks, including Instagram, YouTube, Facebook, X, TikTok, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Snapchat, Threads, Bluesky, Discord, Twitch, and Spotify.

Two features make this more useful than a list of numbers: safe-zone guides that show where a platform crops or covers your image, and ZIP export so you can download every size for a network at once.

Batch processing and an offline desktop version

Single-image tools only go so far. A batch studio takes many images through background removal, resizing, compression, and conversion in one pass and returns one ZIP, again processed entirely on the device.

For people who want no browser involved at all, there is also a Windows desktop build that runs fully offline with the edit, convert, and compress tools.

A note on accounts and what data is involved

Being specific here matters, because "no upload" can be misread. The editing tools work without an account. Signing in with Google is optional, and it uses your name, email, and photo for the account. The images themselves are not uploaded.
We request you to signing in APIC even when it is optional because it will help us to send you guys update emails.

Frequently asked questions

What is a privacy-first online image editor?
It is an editor that processes images on your own device instead of sending them to a server. Editing, conversion, compression, resizing, and AI features all run in the browser.

Can AI background removal run without uploading the photo?
Yes. A segmentation model can run in the browser through WebAssembly. The model downloads once, is cached, and processes the image locally.

Is there a free online photo editor that keeps images on-device?
APIC is one. It is free, has no paid tiers, and runs its tools locally.

How do I compress an image to a specific size in KB?
Use a compressor that searches for the highest quality under your target size, such as the Compress tool in APIC.

Which format keeps a transparent background?
PNG and WebP. JPEG does not support transparency.

Does it work on phones?
Yes. Lighter model tiers exist specifically for phones, with heavier ones recommended for desktop hardware.

Where to try it

If you want to see these techniques in practice, APIC is a free online photo editor, background remover, and image converter that runs in your browser, with no uploads of your images.

We are interested in how other engineers approach on-device processing. Which tasks have you moved from the server to the client, and what held you back? Share your experience in the comments.

About Akhouri Systems: we build software with privacy and performance as design constraints. Follow our dev.to organization for more engineering write-ups.

title: Preserving Cultural Records: A Large-Scale Benchmark and Visual-Prior Routing Network for Ancient Book Image Restoration
description:
arXiv:2611.13010v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ancient books preserve invaluable cultural heritage, yet their images often suffer from complex degradations caused by long-term ageing, environmental exposure, and physical damage. Existing ancient book image restoration benchmarks are limited in scale and rely on simplified degradation simulations, which cannot fully represent real-world degradation patterns and restrict the generalization ability of restoration models. To address these challenges, we introduce AncBench, a large-scale synthetic paired benchmark containing 100K aligned clean-degraded image pairs. AncBench models realistic composite degradations through a comprehensive degradation pipeline that considers material ageing, paper texture variation, blur, staining, water-induced geometric distortion, and local occlusion. Furthermore, we propose AncRestore, a degradation-aware visual-prior routing network for ancient book image restoration. AncRestore first learns degradation representations from degraded images and then dynamically selects and integrates suitable visual priors according to different degradation characteristics. Guided by these degradation cues, a dynamic routing mechanism combines expert-wise and region-wise routing strategies adaptively adjusts the contribution of these priors across different regions, enabling the model to recover both global appearance and local text details. Extensive experiments show that AncRestore effectively suppresses composite degradations while preserving text structures and enhancing restoration quality against other methods, highlighting its application potential for intelligent ancient book image restoration in cultural heritage preservation.

title: Personal account or work account? A 610 KB Windows taskbar widget for Claude Code and Codex
description:
Personal account or work account? If you pay for Claude or ChatGPT yourself and your company gives you a seat, you know the feeling: you open the CLI, start a long task, and only later realize which account just spent its quota. Maybe it was your employer's.

I kept hitting this, so I built CCT (claude-codex-taskbar): a small strip on the Windows 11 / 10 taskbar that answers three questions at a glance:

  1. Which account am I on? A short label of your choice (P, W, Me, Work…) sits right before the Claude and Codex gauges.
  2. How much is left? The 5-hour and weekly limits of the account that is logged in right now, for Claude Code and for Codex, refreshed every 2 minutes. Hover for reset times.
  3. Can I switch without /logout and /login? Yes: right-click the strip → Claude account → pick one. Claude Code uses it on its next request, with no restart.

Three rules I did not want to break

  • free forever: MIT, no paid tier, no account, no "pro" version.
  • tiny always: one native .exe of about < 1MB, written in Rust on raw Win32 + Direct2D. No runtime, no installer, no admin rights, about 15 MB of RAM, and zero telemetry.
  • 3 clicks away: switching accounts is right-click, menu, pick. And it is always a click by you: CCT never switches on its own.

A few things I learned building it

Don't touch the tokens. CCT reuses the login the official claude and codex CLIs already saved, read-only. It never refreshes a token itself, so it never fights the CLI over the login. The one exception is the account switcher, and even then it writes only when you click, under Claude Code's own lock files, atomically, after backing up the outgoing login. Saved logins are encrypted with Windows DPAPI for your Windows user.

Never show 0% for an error. A gauge that says 0% because a request failed is worse than no gauge. When CCT can't read a value it shows — and puts the reason in the tooltip ("Codex login expired — run codex login").

Fallbacks matter more than the happy path. When the Codex usage endpoint fails, CCT asks the installed codex CLI, and as a last resort it reads the newest limit the CLI wrote in its own session logs, if that window has not reset yet.

Idle cost is a feature. A taskbar widget runs all day. Repainting only when something changed, keeping the Direct2D resources between frames and caching the taskbar lookup cut idle CPU by about 40% in v0.4.2.

Try it

  • Download: latest release, extract, run claude-codex-taskbar.exe.
  • Guides: check Claude Code usage on Windows · check Codex limits · switch Claude Code accounts
  • Source and issues: github.com/chiarorosa/claude-codex-taskbar. Testers on unusual setups (multi-monitor, high DPI, auto-hide taskbar) are very welcome.

CCT is an independent project, not affiliated with Anthropic or OpenAI.

title: Adaptive Residual Quantization for Memory-Efficient Temporal Action Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2611.13262v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Temporal action segmentation (TAS) is commonly trained on large banks of pre-extracted frame features, but storing and replaying those features becomes a practical bottleneck for long-form video, especially in incremental TAS where past-task data must remain available to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. Recent TAS replay and condensation methods reduce this burden, but they rely on dense frame-wise annotations and allocate storage through fixed segment-level structures, limiting their flexibility for long procedural videos whose frame complexity varies substantially over time. We introduce Adaptive Residual-Quantized Variational AutoEncoder (ARQ-VAE), a compact and label-free memory representation for TAS features that learns a discrete residual quantization of frame-level video features and then adaptively truncates the residual chain on a per-frame basis, retaining only the residual prefix that best reconstructs each frame feature. This yields a practical compact feature memory that does not depend on frame-wise labels and can therefore support multiple TAS settings with the same stored representation, while a lightweight fine-tuning stage further improves reconstruction quality for the truncated codes that are actually retained. Across standard TAS benchmarks, ARQ-VAE achieves a substantially improved storage-performance trade-off over prior replay and condensation baselines. On Breakfast, our final representation reduces training-set storage from 28 GB for the original I3D feature bank to 10 MB while retaining strong downstream segmentation performance; with ASFormer, it achieves 71.5 Edit and 51.2 F1@50 in the supervised setting. We further show that the same label-free memory remains effective for incremental and unsupervised TAS. We position ARQ-VAE as a practical memory representation for TAS and a promising direction for broader dataset condensation applications.

title: Why vLLM and SGLang might not be the best option to run AI agents
description:
vLLM and SGLang are great inference engines. If you serve chat or batch jobs, use them. But AI agents are a different workload, and I wanted to see how well these engines handle it. So I measured it.

How an agent talks to the model

A coding agent works in turns:

  1. It sends the whole conversation to the model.
  2. The model answers with a tool call (run a command, edit a file).
  3. The agent runs the tool, appends the result, and sends the whole conversation again.

In the traces I used, a median session has about 60 turns and grows to tens of thousands of tokens. Every turn re-sends everything before it.

To answer a turn, the engine needs the KV cache for the full history. If the cache from the last turn is still in GPU memory, only the new tokens need computing. If it was evicted while the agent was running its tool, the engine computes the whole history again.

What vLLM and SGLang do between turns

Both engines have a prefix cache: blocks from earlier requests stay in memory and get reused if the next prompt starts the same way. But they don't know that a request belongs to an agent that will come back in half a second.

  • vLLM 0.33.0 accepts a session_id on chat requests, but it's only used as metadata for KV cache events. There's no pinning and no time-to-live. When memory runs out, blocks are evicted least recently used first.
  • SGLang 0.5.23 has real sessions (/open_session, /close_session), but its OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint only forwards the session_id, not the session parameters. The mode that keeps a session's KV pinned (--enable-streaming-session) is off by default and needs the /generate API. Eviction is LRU by default, with options like TLRU.

So under load, while one agent waits on its tool, other agents' requests push its history out of memory. When it comes back, the engine pays for that history again.

The test

I wrote a small serving engine in Rust (about 1,700 lines) that keeps each agent's session in GPU memory between turns, shares the common prompt start (system prompt, tool definitions) across sessions, and only admits new sessions when the ones already running still fit. I compared it with vLLM and SGLang:

  • Workload: 24 real coding-agent sessions from the SWE-rebench-OpenHands dataset (791 turns), all running at once.
  • Same conditions for every engine: Qwen3-8B, one NVIDIA L40S, and the same KV cache size (173,200 tokens).
  • Tool time: a fixed wait between turns of 0.5 s, 5 s or 60 s. Measured coding-agent tool calls have a median gap of about 0.42 s, so 0.5 s is the realistic one.
  • Two runs per configuration. I wrote down before each run what result would count as a pass.

Results

Total time for all 24 sessions with a 0.5 s tool wait (lower is better):

Engine Run 1 Run 2 History recomputed First token (median)
vLLM 0.33.0 2264 s 2222 s 55% 28.6 s
SGLang 0.5.23 (LRU) 2013 s 2048 s 51% 35.0 s
SGLang 0.5.23 (TLRU) 2067 s 2024 s 52% 36.3 s
Rust session engine 1506 s 1586 s 8-16% 4.5 s

More than half of all the prompt tokens vLLM and SGLang processed were history they had already computed once and then evicted. Keeping sessions in memory cut that to 8-16% and made the whole run 1.31x faster than SGLang and 1.45x faster than vLLM. The first token came about 5x sooner.

The gain shrinks as tools get slower:

Tool wait vs best baseline vs vLLM
0.5 s 1.31x faster 1.45x faster
5 s 1.13x faster 1.24x faster
60 s about the same about the same

With a 60 s wait, few agents need the GPU at the same time, so there's less memory pressure and every engine does about as well. My engine was also slower to the first token there.

What this doesn't mean

  • vLLM and SGLang aren't slow. Token for token, they're faster than my engine: its decoding is 15-21% slower per token than vLLM. The gain comes only from not recomputing history.
  • The idea isn't new. InferCept, Pensieve and Continuum, among others, already proposed keeping agent KV caches alive across tool calls. What I added is a measurement against the current versions of both engines on real agent traces.
  • It's one setup. One model, one GPU, one load level, fixed tool waits. I didn't test CPU offload (LMCache, SGLang HiCache) or SGLang's streaming sessions, which might close part of the gap.
  • Not everything worked. Three of my pinning policies lost to vLLM with 60 s waits. Pinning sessions for too long blocks memory other agents could use. The paper lists them all.

So should you switch?

Probably not yet. My engine is a research prototype, and the right fix is for vLLM and SGLang to learn about agent sessions. Both projects have open proposals for exactly that: vLLM PR #38514 and RFC #37003, and SGLang RFC #24656.

But if you run many agents on your own GPUs, check how much of your prompt traffic is recomputed history. Both engines can report cached tokens per request (--enable-prompt-tokens-details in vLLM, --enable-cache-report in SGLang). If it's over half, like in my test, you're paying for the same tokens twice.

Code and paper

Everything is open: the engine, the replay client, the raw results and the scripts that produce every number above.

  • Code: https://github.com/Nahuel990/agent-session-engine
  • Paper: When Does Keeping Agent Sessions in GPU Memory Pay Off? A Rust Serving Engine and a Replay Study on Real Agent Traces (in the repo under paper/)

title: The Third Cloud Breaks Your Peering Model: Transitive Routing and the Hub Decision
description:
Two clouds are easy to connect. A pair of private links, a handful of route tables, and traffic flows both ways. The design fits on a whiteboard and it works — until a third cloud arrives, usually through an acquisition, a GPU region that only exists on one provider, or a SaaS workload that had to live somewhere specific.

That is the moment most multi-cloud networks quietly break. Not with an outage, but with a diagram that stops matching reality.

Peering is not transitive, and that is the whole problem

In most cloud networks, peering is deliberately non-transitive. If network A is peered with network B, and B is peered with network C, A cannot reach C through B. Each provider enforces this for good reasons — isolation, billing boundaries, and failure containment — but it means a full mesh is the only way to keep direct connectivity as the estate grows.

The maths turns against the design quickly. Two networks need one connection. Three need three. Four need six. Five need ten. Every new connection is not just a link: it is route tables on both sides, firewall rules on both sides, health checks, and a new place where a prefix can be advertised incorrectly.

Worse, the mesh hides an assumption. Teams start treating "connected" as a property of the estate, when it is actually a property of each pair. A service that works from cloud one to cloud two may have no path at all from cloud one to cloud three, and the failure looks like an application bug — timeouts, retries, partial results — rather than what it is: there was never a route.

What a hub actually changes

A hub-and-spoke design replaces the mesh with a transit point. Each cloud network connects once, to the hub, and the hub forwards between spokes under explicit policy. Adding a fourth or fifth cloud becomes one new spoke instead of a new connection to every existing network.

That simplification is real, but it is not free. Three trade-offs arrive with it, and a useful design names all three up front.

First, latency. Traffic between two spokes now crosses the hub, so placement matters. A hub in the wrong region turns a short cross-cloud hop into a long detour, and for chatty service-to-service calls or GPU checkpoint traffic that detour is paid on every request.

Second, blast radius. The hub is now on the path for everything. If it fails, fails over badly, or receives a bad route advertisement, spokes lose each other at the same time. The mesh failed one pair at a time; the hub can fail all pairs at once. That argues for a hub that is itself redundant across zones, with route advertisements validated before they are accepted, not after traffic has already shifted.

Third, cost shape. Mesh costs grow with the number of pairs. Hub costs grow with the volume that crosses the hub, including traffic that previously went direct. Neither shape is always cheaper — the right comparison is measured traffic between specific spokes, not the total estate size.

Three ways teams build the transit layer

Cloud-native transit services attach directly to one provider's networking model. They are the fastest to adopt inside that provider and handle route propagation natively, but each provider's version stops at its own boundary, so a three-cloud estate often ends up with three hubs that then need connecting to each other — the mesh problem, one level up.

Self-managed routing, usually virtual appliances or open-source routers in a dedicated transit network, works the same way in every cloud and gives full control over route policy and filtering. The cost is operational: patching, high availability, and performance testing become the team's job, and throughput limits are discovered in production unless they are load-tested deliberately.

Managed overlay fabrics build a private backbone between clouds and present one routing and policy model across all of them. They trade some provider-native visibility for consistency: the same route policy, the same segmentation, and the same troubleshooting view in every cloud. For estates where different platform teams own different clouds, that consistency is often the deciding factor, because most cross-cloud incidents are really disagreements between three locally-correct configurations.

None of these is the correct answer in general. The useful question is narrower: where should route policy live so that exactly one place can be checked when two clouds cannot talk?

Route policy is the design, the links are not

Whether the transit is native, self-managed, or an overlay, the failures that matter are almost always policy failures: a spoke advertising a default route it should never advertise, overlapping prefixes arriving at the hub from two spokes at once, or summarisation that hides a more specific route a workload depends on.

A hub design that survives growth therefore keeps a few disciplines from the start:

  1. One source of truth for which prefixes each spoke owns, validated at the hub before advertisement is accepted.
  2. No spoke may advertise a default route or another spoke's prefixes. Reject, alert, and log it when one tries.
  3. Summarise only where the underlying addressing plan guarantees no workload needs a hidden, more specific route.
  4. Test spoke isolation deliberately: a new spoke should reach only what policy grants it on day one, not everything the hub can route to.
  5. Record measured latency and loss per spoke pair through the hub, so the detour cost is known from data rather than discovered from application complaints.

Addressing discipline decided early pays for all of this. If each cloud and each region receives a distinct, non-overlapping block from a single plan, hub routing stays simple. If prefixes were picked independently per cloud, the hub inherits that collision problem as well, and no transit product fixes addressing after the fact.

When to stay with the mesh

A hub is not mandatory at three networks. If traffic between the third cloud and the other two is small, one-directional, or served well by a single private API endpoint, a full transit layer may be more machinery than the estate needs. The signal to move is not the cloud count alone. It is when route tables are being edited in several places to add one service, when nobody can answer which path traffic between two clouds actually takes, or when a new region takes longer to connect than the workload took to build.

At that point the peering model has already broken — the hub decision is just acknowledging it and choosing where the complexity will live instead of letting it spread across every pair.

Teams that operate these estates day to day — including the work described at CloudVerg around VergMesh private multi-cloud connectivity and VergForge network design — tend to treat the transit decision as an addressing and policy decision first and a product decision second. However the estate is built, the principle holds: make routing transitive on purpose, in one governed place, or accept that every new cloud multiplies the work and the failure modes of all the clouds already there.

title: User-Friendly Mobile App UX Design – Best Practice & Process
description:
Mobile applications have become a key part of everyday life. People now rely on them for shopping, banking, communication and entertainment. But despite having the right features in place, the overall user experience is key to ensure an application is successful.

To ensure your mobile application is easy to use, the design should be intuitive, easy to understand, fast, and accessible for a wide range of users. If users face difficulties finding features or completing simple tasks within your application then it is more likely that they will leave.

Therefore, focusing on making your mobile application user-friendly is important.

What Is Mobile App UX Design?

User Experience (UX) design for mobile applications ensures that users can interact with your application and achieve their goals easily.

UX design includes researching your users’ expectations, how information is presented, navigation design, wireframing and testing how users interact with your application.

UI design focuses on the look of your application including colours, fonts, icons and layout. Whereas UX design focuses on ensuring users can achieve their goals throughout the entire experience.

Both are important to creating an effective mobile application.

Why Is User-Friendly Mobile App Design Important?

Having a well-designed mobile application has many benefits.

Improved User Engagement
By making navigation and interfaces easy to understand, users will engage with your application and try out features.

Improved User Retention

If users can easily complete tasks then they will return to your application.

Improved Conversion Rates

By optimising the user journey, users can easily complete tasks such as signing up, purchasing products, booking appointments and filling out forms.

Improved Accessibility

An accessible application allows those with varying ability levels to use your application easily.

Improved Brand Reputation

Providing a seamless and easy experience creates a good impression and builds trust.

How to Design a User-Friendly Mobile Application

There are several key steps to creating an effective mobile application. Here are 7 steps businesses should consider.

Step 1 – Know your Target Audience

Firstly, research who will be using your application.

Find out what your target audience expect, what their common issues are, technical ability and how they use your application.

Some useful ways to research your audience are:

  • Interviews & Surveys
  • Competitor Applications
  • User Behaviour
  • Customer Feedback
  • User Requirements

Knowing your audience will allow designers to make informed decisions based on real user needs.

Step 2 – Define User Goals & Journey

Next, define what your users should be able to complete using your application.
For example, an e-commerce application may have the following user journey:

  • Browse Products
  • Open Application
  • Browse Products
  • Choose Product
  • Add to Basket
  • Complete Checkout
  • Receive Order Confirmation

As you can see, defining your users’ journey will help identify any unnecessary tasks, confusing navigation and potential user issues.

Step 3 – Keep Navigation Simple

Navigation should be easy to use so users can quickly find important features.
Complex navigation can cause frustration for users, especially on smaller screens.

Ensure your navigation is:

  • Simple & Easy to Understand
  • Easy to access important features
  • Information is grouped logically
  • Menu items are clearly labelled
  • Avoid too many layers

Overall, your users should be able to easily find where they want to go.

Step 4 – Create Wireframes & Prototypes

Wireframes will give you a simple layout of your application.

Designers will focus on where buttons, menus, images, forms and content will go. No detailed design at this stage.

Prototypes will show how users can interact with your application.

Creating wireframes and prototypes will help your team identify any issues early on.

Step 5 – Focus on Design & Accessibility

Once you have your application set-up, you can focus on design.

Things to consider are:

  • Consistent Colour Scheme & Fonts
  • Readable Font Sizes
  • Appropriate Spacing & Alignment
  • Clear Icons
  • Contrasting Colours
  • Touch Friendly Buttons
  • Responsive to all Screen Sizes

You should also consider accessibility. By following known guidelines for each platform and accessibility standards, your application will be accessible to a wider audience.

Step 6 – Test with Users

Before launching your application, test with real users.

Testing your application with users will help highlight any issues that may not have been obvious.

Ensure your users can:

  • Navigate between screens
  • Understand what features they have
  • Complete key tasks
  • Identify and recover from errors
  • Use your application easily on mobile devices

Gather feedback and prioritise which usability issues need to be resolved. Improve your design.

Repeat testing once your application has had major changes.

Step 7 – Work with Developers & Keep Improving

Once your design is complete, provide full details to developers.

This could include:

  • Layout of each screen
  • Reusable Components
  • How interactions behave
  • Assets
  • Different states e.g. loading, empty & error screens.

However, don’t stop improving your UX. Once your application is live, keep an eye on feedback from users, application analytics, navigation and task completion.

Improving your application will help keep it relevant.

Common Mistakes to Avoid
Despite having some advanced features, your application may struggle due to a poor user experience.

Some common mistakes are:

  • Too Many Menu Options – Users will struggle to find important features.
  • Too Much Information – This can cause confusion.
  • Small Buttons – Users will become frustrated trying to press buttons.
  • No Loading/ Error Screens – Users should know what is happening.
  • Not Consistent – Having different layouts, colours and behaviours can cause confusion.
  • No User Testing – You may miss important usability issues.

Avoid these mistakes to greatly improve your mobile application.

Final Thoughts

Creating a user-friendly mobile application requires you to understand your users, keep things simple, organise information and keep improving interactions.

Following a structured design process will help businesses create an easy to navigate, accessible application.

For more information on the process of UX design for mobile applications, best practice and considerations during development check out:

User-Friendly Mobile App UX Design – The Process, Step by Step from 4Labs Technologies

What do you feel is the most important thing to include in order to create a successful mobile application? Simple navigation, attractive UI, quick loading or accessibility? Let us know!.
