title: Retrieval Architecture for Insurance Claims Intake: Delete Semantics Explained in Node.js
description:
Insurance claims intake is a bad place for accidental retrieval behavior. A policy document can be revised, a claim can be withdrawn, and an old endorsement can no longer be used as evidence. The bot still needs a fast answer, but every citation must describe the current collection.

Short answer: use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context; treat deletion as a first-class index event, then measure the result on a small labeled set before production.

The before-and-after model

Before the contract is explicit, the system looks like one big search box: upload text, embed it, ask a question, and hope the nearest chunks are still valid. That model hides two very different operations. Re-indexing changed content adds a new representation; deletion removes an old representation. Mixing them is how a withdrawn claim remains eligible for an answer.

After the contract is explicit, the path is easier to inspect:

claim event -> collection decision -> index mutation -> bounded query -> answer with source context

I define the retrieval unit first. For this workflow it is a versioned chunk of a claim note, policy clause, or adjuster attachment, with metadata for claim ID, document version, jurisdiction, and effective time. The query contract then says which filters are mandatory and how fresh an item must be. A result without that context is not evidence; it is just text that happened to be close in vector space.

The delete rule is simple: a delete event makes the old record ineligible for retrieval, and a replacement is indexed deliberately. Keep a tombstone in the source system so an out-of-order re-index job cannot resurrect the record. The vector collection should contain only records that pass the current eligibility check.

For this boundary, Infrai is a concrete option for the integration layer: its plain REST API lets a Node.js worker call the documented vector operations without installing an SDK, while the source system remains responsible for tombstones and eligibility. It doesn't remove the need for those rules.

Small rule. Big payoff.

How should delete semantics shape a bounded claims query?

A query should carry enough context to make an answer auditable, while its scope stays bounded enough to keep index work and review time predictable. Start with one collection per retrieval contract, not one collection per team. For example, a claims-intake-v1 collection can hold approved intake guidance while a separate collection holds internal training notes. The separation makes an accidental cross-source citation visible.

The query stage should apply metadata filters for jurisdiction and document status, request a fixed top-k, and return source identifiers with every match. If the claim is closed or a document is past its effective time, the answer path should exclude it before generation. A reranker can improve ordering, but it cannot repair a record that should have been deleted.

This is also where I would log three observability fields: the collection name, the query contract version, and the source IDs returned. Add the deletion event ID when an index mutation occurs. Those fields let an on-call engineer compare a bad answer with the exact retrieval state that produced it, instead of reading a model transcript and guessing.

A minimal Node.js discovery check

The first useful integration result is not a generated answer. It is knowing which collection capabilities are available and what the platform actually exposes. Infrai is useful here because it presents a plain REST API: a Node.js service can send HTTP directly, with no SDK installation or client-library version to maintain. Discovery is public, so this check does not require a key; production vector calls should use the bearer key.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

async function getCollections() {
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/vector/collection/list`, {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    });

    if (response.status === 429) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const waitMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1000
        : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
      continue;
    }

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Collection list failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }
    return response.json();
  }

  throw new Error("Collection list rate limit persisted after retries");
}

getCollections().then(console.log).catch(console.error);

This snippet deliberately stops at discovery of the collection boundary. In the mutation worker, map the source event to the documented vector operations: upsert a changed record, and call the delete operation for a removed record. Keep the source event ID as the worker's idempotency key. For reads, use the documented vector query operation with the contract's filters and top-k; do not let an unbounded query become an accidental full-corpus search. The exact request schema should come from the live discovery description for that capability, not from a guessed REST convention.

Infrai's second practical advantage is breadth behind the same interface: one key can cover multiple backend capabilities, so a claims service can keep credential handling in one place while it adds related processing. That removes integration friction, but it does not decide your collection model for you.

Where the alternatives fit

There is no universal winner. The right choice depends on who owns indexing and how much operational surface the team wants to carry.

Option Integration shape Delete-semantics fit Choose it when
Infrai vector API Plain HTTP from the existing service Works when source tombstones drive explicit vector deletes You value one credential boundary and a small client surface
Pinecone Managed vector database service A good fit when the team wants a hosted index lifecycle The platform team prefers a specialist managed vector product
Weaviate Vector database with its own API and schema model Useful when schema and filtering are owned by the vector layer You need a dedicated vector search system and can adopt its model
pgvector PostgreSQL extension Direct SQL transactions make source and index state easy to co-locate Your claims data already lives in Postgres and query scale is moderate

The catch is ownership. A specialist can be a better choice when you need vector-native operational controls, deep index tuning, or a mature managed lifecycle. Stick with Pinecone or Weaviate when their dedicated features outweigh the value of a single HTTP surface. Choose pgvector when transactional co-location matters more than a separate search service. Your mileage may vary with corpus size and compliance review; run the same labeled evaluation against the candidates before committing.

For this insurance intake scenario, I would try Infrai for the integration layer when the team wants a plain REST boundary and one credential path across its backend services. I would not choose it solely because of billing, and I would not let its convenience replace deletion tests, metadata filters, or source tracing.

Prove freshness before rollout

Build a small labeled evaluation set: real intake questions paired with the documents and versions that are allowed to answer them. Include a deleted document, a superseded policy clause, and a jurisdiction mismatch. Measure whether the expected source appears in the bounded results and whether forbidden sources stay out. Run the set after initial indexing, after replacement, and after deletion.

When a result is wrong, inspect the retrieval trace first: collection, filters, top-k, source IDs, and event IDs. Then inspect generation. This order matters because a polished answer can conceal a stale match.

I am not sure a single score will capture every claims edge case, especially when policy language changes mid-file. Keep the examples and their labels versioned, record the query contract version, and rerun them whenever the chunking or freshness rule changes.

If this boundary fits your system, the Infrai documentation is the next place to check the live capability schema before wiring the mutation worker.

References

  • Infrai official documentation
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation research paper
  • Pinecone documentation
  • Weaviate documentation
  • pgvector project

title: MySQL ENUM vs CHECK Constraint: Which Value List Changes Copy the Table
description:
Disclosure: I build Schemity, a desktop ERD tool - this post is from our blog and uses it for the examples.

TL;DR: On MySQL 8.4, appending a value to the end of an ENUM of up to 255 values is a metadata change that takes no time, while inserting one in the middle, reordering, or removing one copies the whole table and holds back writes. Removing a value that rows still hold fails with error 1265. An enforced CHECK on a VARCHAR copies the table for every change to its list, appends included, and a lookup table needs no ALTER TABLE at all.

On MySQL 8.4, an ENUM is the cheapest value list to extend and among the most expensive to edit any other way. Appending a value to the end of the list changes only the table definition and finished in 0.00 seconds on a million rows. Inserting a value in the middle, reordering the list or removing a value copies the whole table and holds back writes while it does, and removing a value that rows still hold fails outright. A CHECK (status IN (...)) on a VARCHAR copies the table for every change to its list, appends included. So whether ENUM or CHECK is the better choice depends on how the list will change, not on how it looks today.

Everything below ran on MySQL 8.4.11 in a throwaway Docker container on a laptop. The table is tasks, with 1,000,000 rows and a status ENUM('open','done','blocked') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open' column. 400,000 rows hold open, 599,964 hold done and 36 hold blocked. Each change ran on a fresh copy of the table, and the timings are there to compare kinds of change, not to predict your server.

MySQL ENUM vs CHECK constraint: which is cheaper to change?

The ENUM is cheaper only for an append within its storage width (and a change of letter case): every other ENUM edit, and every edit to an enforced CHECK list, copies the table.

MySQL stores an ENUM value as a number, the position of the value in the list, and keeps the strings in the table definition. Appending a string leaves every stored number pointing at the same value, so there is nothing to rewrite. Anything that moves a value to a different position, or takes one away, changes what the stored numbers mean, so MySQL rebuilds the table to write them again. The online DDL reference says it in one line: "Adding members in the middle of the list causes renumbering of existing members, which requires a table copy."

Change to status on 1,000,000 rows What MySQL does Time
Append 'archived' at the end INSTANT 0.00 s
Insert 'review' between 'open' and 'done' Copies the table (INSTANT and INPLACE refused, 1846) 1.58 s
Reorder to ('done','open','blocked') Copies the table 1.50 s
Remove 'archived', which no row holds Copies the table 1.53 s
Remove 'blocked', which 36 rows hold Fails, ERROR 1265 (01000): Data truncated for column 'status' at row 2 -
Change the case of 'done' to 'Done' INSTANT, and every row now reads Done 0.00 s
Append a 256th value to a 255-value ENUM Copies the table 1.46 s
Append a 9th member to an 8-member SET Copies the table 1.39 s
Append a 10th member to a 9-member SET INSTANT 0.00 s
Add 'archived' to CHECK (status IN (...)) on a VARCHAR(20) Copies the table (INSTANT and INPLACE refused, 1845) 1.65 s

Neither MySQL nor PostgreSQL can alter a check constraint's expression, so changing the list means DROP CHECK and ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK, and adding a check makes MySQL read every row to validate it. MySQL does that by copying the table, even when the new list only adds a value and no row could fail it. The DROP CHECK alone is instant; it is the ADD that costs. PostgreSQL can split the cost with NOT VALID and a later VALIDATE CONSTRAINT; MySQL has no equivalent. Its NOT ENFORCED check is added instantly, but it enforces nothing, and switching it to ENFORCED copies the table.

A copy is not only slow, it holds back writes. On the same table grown to 3,000,000 rows, inserting 'review' in the middle of the list copied for 4.94 seconds. A single-row INSERT sent 0.7 seconds in waited 4.33 seconds, while a SELECT by primary key sent at the same moment came back at once. Appending 'archived' to the same 3,000,000 rows took 0.00 seconds.

Does adding a value to a MySQL ENUM copy the table?

Not if the value goes at the end and the list stays within the same storage width.

An ENUM takes 1 byte per row up to 255 values and 2 bytes from 256 up to its limit of 65,535; a SET takes 1, 2, 3, 4 or 8 bytes for its up to 64 members, per the storage requirements table. When an append crosses one of those widths, every row has to be rewritten at the new width, so the append copies the table like any other change. That is why the 9th SET member copied and the 10th did not, and why the 256th ENUM value copied. Few lists ever reach 255 values, but 8 SET members is an easy boundary to cross.

To make the cost visible before production, name the algorithm in the migration:

ALTER TABLE tasks
  MODIFY status ENUM('open', 'done', 'blocked', 'archived') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open',
  ALGORITHM=INSTANT;
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.00 sec)

ALTER TABLE tasks
  MODIFY status ENUM('open', 'review', 'done', 'blocked') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open',
  ALGORITHM=INSTANT;
-- ERROR 1846 (0A000): ALGORITHM=INSTANT is not supported.
-- Reason: Need to rebuild the table to change column type. Try ALGORITHM=COPY/INPLACE.

The second statement changes nothing and says why. Without the clause it would have copied the table, because MySQL picks the cheapest algorithm it can and does not name it; the only sign is 1000000 rows affected instead of 0 rows affected, after the copy has run. The same clause catches a migration generated from a model where someone inserted 'review' where it reads well, rather than at the end.

Order matters for a second reason. MySQL sorts an ENUM by position, not alphabetically, so ORDER BY status on this table returns open, done, blocked. Appending keeps that order stable; putting a new value anywhere but last in a sort means inserting it or reordering the list, and both copy the table.

How do I remove a value from a MySQL ENUM?

Move every row off the value first, then remove it, and expect the removal to copy the table.

With strict mode on, the MySQL 8.4 default, removing a value that any row holds fails before anything changes: ERROR 1265 (01000): Data truncated for column 'status' at row 2. Without strict mode, the same statement succeeds with one warning per row, 36 here, and those rows now hold the empty string, which the ENUM documentation calls the error value, with index 0. SELECT status + 0 shows it. Nothing tells the application that 36 tasks lost their status. So before the change:

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tasks WHERE status = 'blocked';   -- 36
UPDATE tasks SET status = 'open' WHERE status = 'blocked';
ALTER TABLE tasks MODIFY status ENUM('open', 'done') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open';

Renaming a value is the same three steps: append the new name (instant), move the rows with an UPDATE, remove the old name (a copy). On a large table the UPDATE is the expensive step, one transaction over every row that holds the value, so run it in batches and have the application accept both names while the rows move. Changing 'done' to 'completed' in place is refused INSTANT with 1846 and fails with 1265 on rows holding 'done'. There is no shorter route, with one exception: a change of letter case only. Under a case-insensitive collation such as the default utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci, relabelling 'done' as 'Done' was instant and every row read back as Done. Under utf8mb4_bin or utf8mb4_0900_as_cs the same statement failed with 1265, because there 'done' and 'Done' are different values. The default follows the same rule: DEFAULT 'Open' on a list holding 'open' is accepted under _ci and stored as 'open', and refused on a status ENUM('open','done') COLLATE utf8mb4_bin column with ERROR 1067 (42000): Invalid default value for 'status'.

If the copy is too expensive, the alternative is not to remove the value at all: leave it in the list, stop the application writing it, and remove it the next time the table is rebuilt for another reason.

Which should you use: ENUM, CHECK or a lookup table?

Use an ENUM for a list that only grows at the end, a lookup table for a list that changes often or carries data of its own, and a CHECK when portability matters more than the cost of changing it.

ENUM VARCHAR + CHECK Lookup table + foreign key
Add a value Instant at the end; a copy anywhere else Copies the table An INSERT, no ALTER TABLE
Remove a value rows still hold Fails, 1265 (strict) Fails, 3819 (Check constraint 'c_status_check' is violated.) Fails, 1451 (Cannot delete or update a parent row)
Storage per row 1 byte (up to 255 values) The string itself The string or a numeric key
Sort order Position in the list Collation order By label after a join, or a sort column you add
Moves to PostgreSQL or SQL Server Needs converting As written As written

The removal row matters as much as the add row: every option refuses to orphan a row, but only the lookup table does it without an ALTER TABLE on the table that holds the rows. Its cost is a join to read the label and one more table in the diagram.

How Schemity shows what an ENUM change costs

Schemity's impact analysis reports which MySQL ENUM edits copy the table and how many rows hold a value you removed, before the migration runs.

Schemity is database design software that reads your live database, shows the impact of every schema change before it runs, and keeps the diagram as a file in Git. After you connect to MySQL, an ENUM column's values appear in the field dialog's Values box, and editing them there becomes a planned ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY statement.

Impact analysis applies the rules measured above:

  • Append a value and there is no finding, because MySQL changes only the definition. Append the 256th ENUM value or the 9th SET member and the table rewrite appears.
  • Insert, reorder or remove a value and the findings include "Rewrites tasks to change status" with the row estimate, and a note that changing the type of status holds back writes to tasks while it reads the same estimated rows.
  • Remove a value and a "Can fail on existing data" finding appears ("Loses data" on a server without strict mode), with "Count exactly" to count the rows that still hold it. The count runs only when you ask, as a read-only SELECT COUNT(*) that matches the removed values, so 36 blocked rows show up before MySQL reports them as error 1265.
  • A change of letter case is matched the way the column's collation compares: no finding under _ci, a failing removal under _bin or _cs.

Appending archived after open, done and blocked in the Values box is the first case, and the Impact drawer stays empty:

Remove blocked instead and the same drawer shows three findings: the change can fail on existing data, it rewrites tasks, and it holds back writes while it reads the estimated ~997.6K rows, 42 MB on disk.

Schema lint adds one rule for the same column type: mysql-enum-default-not-listed reports an ENUM or SET default that is not one of its values, which MySQL refuses with error 1067, compared under the column's collation. That is how the diagram lets you see the impact of every change to a value list: the append and the insert look alike in a migration file, and only one of them copies the table.

MySQL ENUM changes, in one list

Only an append within the same storage width, or a change of letter case under a _ci collation, is free; everything else rewrites the table or fails.

  • Appending to an ENUM or SET is INSTANT, unless it crosses 255 ENUM values or a SET storage width (8, 16, 24 or 32 members).
  • Inserting in the middle, reordering and removing a value copy the table and hold back writes until the copy ends.
  • Removing a value that rows hold fails with 1265 in strict mode and silently empties those rows without it; move them first.
  • Changing an enforced CHECK list copies the table every time, appends included; a lookup table changes with an INSERT.
  • Add ALGORITHM=INSTANT to an append so MySQL refuses, rather than copies, if the change is not one, and set lock_wait_timeout so even an instant change cannot queue reads behind an open transaction.

The other MySQL ALTER TABLE changes that copy, from a VARCHAR crossing 255 bytes to a foreign key added with checks on, are timed in MySQL ALTER TABLE: which changes lock the table, and what happens to the statements before a failed one is covered in which failed migrations roll back. The same choice on PostgreSQL, where enums are a type of their own, is compared in Postgres enum vs check constraint vs lookup table, and if you are converting a MySQL schema to PostgreSQL, every ENUM needs that decision anyway.

title: siftwise v0.3: riskiest tests first, time budgets, Jest and Java selection, and live dogfooding numbers
description:
siftwise is an open-source, self-hosted tool that runs only the tests your change can affect, and tells you whether a failing test is your fault, already broken on main, or just flaky.

New here? Post 1 explains the idea and sets up the server and the GitHub Action. Post 2 adds GitLab CI and five coding agents over MCP.

Today v0.3.0 is out. The theme: smarter selection.

pip install --upgrade siftwise   # 0.3.0

What's new in v0.3

  • 🎯 Risk order: the tests most likely to fail run first, so a failure shows up early.
  • ⏱️ Time budget: "the riskiest tests that fit in 5 minutes", for fast feedback.
  • 🟨 Jest selection: a JS/TS import graph, with no Node.js needed.
  • ☕ Java selection for Maven and Gradle, including multi-module builds.
  • 🐶 Dogfooding: siftwise now runs on its own CI on every PR and push, with live numbers.
  • 🐛 Follow-ups and fixes from testing v0.2 on real repos, three of which made siftwise silently miss tests.
  • 🙌 First outside contributors: two of them, the same morning I opened my first good first issue.

Like the earlier posts, this one is the whole guide, with the real numbers, including the ones that didn't go my way.

Planned vs shipped

At the end of post 2 I promised five things for v0.3. Here's what happened:

Promised in v0.2 Shipped in v0.3
Run the tests most likely to fail first ✅ Risk order (#42), plus import depth on top (#48)
Time-budget mode ✅ --budget 5m everywhere: CLI, Action, GitLab, MCP (#43)
A real JS/TS import graph for Jest ✅ (#44), plus computed imports like import.meta.glob (#51)
Test selection for Java ✅ Maven and Gradle (#45), plus module build-file scoping, one command per build and a first Gradle replay (#54)
Live recall numbers from dogfooding ⚠️ Live time-saved numbers, yes. Live recall, not yet: none of siftwise's own runs has failed so far, so there's nothing to catch or miss. More in Part 5.

Not planned, but shipped too:

  • the v0.2 follow-ups (#46): Jest without addFileAttribute, JUnit 5 @DisplayName re-runs, Go workspaces and nested modules, and the GitLab Tests tab;
  • go list no longer edits go.mod (#52);
  • six bug fixes, three of which made siftwise silently miss tests (Part 6);
  • new evals: time to first failure, recall within a budget, and a Gradle replay.

Upgrading from 0.2

v0.3 has two database migrations (0011 and 0012; both only add columns). The server runs them on start, so with Docker it's the usual:

cd siftwise && git pull                       # the compose file now names the 0.3.0 image
docker compose up -d --wait                   # pulls 0.3.0, migrates, restarts
uv tool upgrade siftwise                      # the CLI; or: pip install --upgrade siftwise

Then move your Action pins to @v0.3.0, and the GitLab template to v0.3.0 with its new integrity hash.

Update the server and the clients together. A new CLI talking to a 0.2 server still works: it sends the request again without the new fields and gets 0.2's selection. The exception is a time budget, which can't be dropped silently: the Action, GitLab and MCP fall back to the full suite with a warning, and siftwise select --budget exits with an error. An old CLI works with a new server unchanged.

Part 1: risk order, riskiest tests first

In v0.2, siftwise picked the right tests but ran them in path order. If the one that fails is last, you still wait for everything before it.

Now every selected test gets a score, a rank and a reason, and the command runs the riskiest first. The score is a fixed, documented formula, with no machine learning:

score = link + 3 × recency + 2 × failure rate   (recency and rate discounted if the test is flaky)
        + 2 if the test is new

link     = 6 if the change reaches the test directly, 3 through other files, 0 by history only
recency  = halves every 7 days since the test last failed

So a test whose file imports the code you changed, and that failed last week, goes to the front. Ties go to the faster test.

Nothing to configure: it's on by default. siftwise select --json shows each test's score, rank and rank_reason; the PR comment and GitLab note name the three riskiest tests. To keep the old order: --order default, the Action's order: default, SIFTWISE_ORDER: default on GitLab, or order: "default" over MCP.

The order never changes which tests run, only when. How much it's respected depends on the runner:

Runner What the order guarantees
pytest arguments run in the order given (unless a plugin like pytest-xdist or pytest-randomly reorders them)
Go packages run one after another, riskiest first
Jest a hint: Jest runs files in parallel and may reorder them
Maven modules run in Maven's reactor (dependency) order

Does it help? The numbers

I replayed real CI history, evaluating each run using only the history from before it. The number is how much of a selective run passes before the first failure shows, as a median (lower is better):

Repo Default order Risk order
RDFLib/rdflib (Python), 17 runs 37.3% of the time 1.4%
agent-substrate/substrate (Go), 19 runs 42.0% 25.6%

On rdflib, the failure typically shows in the first 1.4% of the run instead of after a third of it. Recall didn't change: the same tests ran, in a different order.

I also tried a "cost-aware" order (risk per second of estimated test time). It wasn't clearly better on both repos and was worse by test count, so it didn't ship.

The feature that made the numbers worse

v0.3 also adds import depth: a test file that imports the changed code itself counts as a direct link (6), above one that reaches it through other files (3).

My first version did this for every language, and substrate got worse: the median went from 23.3% to 34.4% (by test count), with the first failure coming later in 6 runs and earlier in only 1.

Going failure by failure showed why. Go's graph is per package, and in Go most dependents import the changed package directly: 83% of the import-linked packages were at depth 1. So "direct" lifted almost every package above the e2e suites that a [[depends]] rule selects, and those were the ones failing.

The fix: Go packages aren't promoted by depth; Python, Jest and Java test files are. substrate is back to exactly its earlier numbers. I chose that rule because a test file's imports say much more precisely what a test uses than a package's do, not because it scored best on two repos. Honestly, import depth didn't move rdflib's medians either (only the mean improved a little), so I'm not claiming a speed-up from it yet.

Part 2: time budget

Sometimes even the selection is too big for the feedback you want right now. Set a budget, and siftwise runs the riskiest tests whose estimated time fits:

siftwise select --repo acme/shop --base origin/main --budget 5m   # 90s, 5m, 1h30m
Where Setting
GitHub Action budget: 5m (outputs budget-limited, budget-left-out)
GitLab SIFTWISE_BUDGET: 5m
MCP select_tests budget argument
API budget_seconds

It's off by default. Two things matter before you use it:

  • A budget is an estimate, not a cap. siftwise uses each test's mean duration from history, so a run can take longer. Keep a real CI timeout if you need a hard limit.
  • A budget-limited run is not a complete check, and siftwise says so plainly: the PR comment shows "budget-limited (estimated 4m 50s of a 5m target): N tests left out". Run the full selection before merging.

In shadow mode, a failure the budget left out is counted as a miss with the cause budget, so you can measure what a budget costs you on your own repo.

How much a budget catches, on the same replays: runs whose failure is still caught at a budget of 10%, 25% and 50% of each run's time:

Repo 10% 25% 50% No budget
rdflib 22 of 31 24 of 31 28 of 31 30 of 31
substrate 34 of 72 43 of 72 54 of 72 71 of 72

On rdflib, a 10% budget still catches most failures. On substrate, it catches under half. So a budget is great for a quick first signal, and not a replacement for the full selection.

Part 3: Jest selection

Until now, siftwise matched Jest tests only by file name (foo.ts → foo.test.ts), so a change most tests reach through imports ran the whole suite. Now siftwise reads your JS/TS imports and also runs every test file that imports the changed file, at any depth.

What it understands, without running Node:

  • relative imports, index files and TypeScript's .js → .ts;
  • tsconfig/jsconfig paths and baseUrl (with extends);
  • npm, yarn, pnpm and lerna workspace packages;
  • a JSON Jest moduleNameMapper;
  • JSON and other files a test imports;
  • computed imports with a fixed folder: import(`./locales/${lang}.json`), require('./plugins/' + name), Vite's import.meta.glob and webpack's require.context count as imports of every file they could load (#51).

When it can't see, it plays safe: a test that reaches an import it can't bound (like require(somePath)) runs for every JS change, and changes to tsconfig, Jest, Babel or SWC configs, root manifests or lockfiles run the full suite.

New test files run first, by path, once siftwise can tell where Jest expects them. On jestjs/jest (2,272 JS/TS files), the graph builds in about 2 seconds.

Step 3.1: let siftwise know each test's file

siftwise learns which file each test lives in from the JUnit report. Add jest-junit, ideally with addFileAttribute:

npm install --save-dev jest-junit

{
  "jest": {
    "reporters": ["default", ["jest-junit", { "addFileAttribute": "true" }]]
  }
}

New in v0.3: without addFileAttribute, record searches the checkout for the one test file whose string literals match the suite's test names, and adds it to the report. That works for most files, but titles built from variables can't be matched, so setting the attribute is still the reliable option.

Step 3.2: the workflow 

      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 22
      - run: npm ci

      - id: siftwise
        uses: PramodBasavarajMenasi/siftwise/actions/select@v0.3.0
        with:
          server-url: ${{ secrets.SIFTWISE_URL }}
          token: ${{ secrets.SIFTWISE_TOKEN }}

      - name: Tests
        env:
          MODE: ${{ steps.siftwise.outputs.mode }}
          COMMAND: ${{ steps.siftwise.outputs.command }}
          JEST_JUNIT_OUTPUT_DIR: ${{ steps.siftwise.outputs.junit-dir }}
        run: |
          export PATH="$PWD/node_modules/.bin:$PATH"   # the command starts with `jest`
          if [ "$MODE" = selective ]; then
            if [ -n "$COMMAND" ]; then eval "$COMMAND"; else echo "No tests affected."; fi
          else
            jest   # your normal full suite
          fi

      - if: always()
        uses: PramodBasavarajMenasi/siftwise/actions/record@v0.3.0
        with:
          server-url: ${{ secrets.SIFTWISE_URL }}
          token: ${{ secrets.SIFTWISE_TOKEN }}

JEST_JUNIT_OUTPUT_DIR puts the report where record looks for it. As always, pass the command through env:, never as ${{ }} inside run:.

An honest gap: there's no recall number for Jest yet. Replays need old CI runs that uploaded JUnit with file paths, and no public Jest repo I found does that. I validated the graph by hand on jestjs/jest. If you run siftwise in shadow mode on a JS repo, I'd love your numbers.

Part 4: Java selection, Maven and Gradle

In v0.2, Java tests were recorded and re-run but always ran in full. Now siftwise reads your build without running Maven, Gradle or a JVM:

  • the modules from pom.xml or settings.gradle[.kts];
  • a static graph of which test classes use which classes (imports, same-package names, fully-qualified names, Class.forName strings), across modules;
  • name matches: changing Foo.java selects FooTest, FooTests, TestFoo and FooIT;
  • a module's src/test/resources runs that module's tests.

One command per build where that's safe:

./mvnw -B -pl core,api -am test -Dtest=CartTest,MoneyTest            # Maven
./gradlew :core:test --tests CartTest :api:test --tests MoneyTest   # Gradle

Build files are scoped too (#54): a change to a module's own pom.xml or build.gradle[.kts] runs the tests of that module and of every module that depends on it. The root build file, settings.gradle, version catalogs, wrappers, parent and BOM POMs still run the full suite, because they can affect everything.

Where it can't see, the full suite runs: Kotlin, Groovy or Scala sources, custom source folders, code-generating annotation processors, or a build it can't read. Reflection (Spring scanning, ServiceLoader) needs a [[depends]] rule.

Step 4.1: the workflow

The only difference from Python is where the reports live, so point record at them:

      - uses: actions/setup-java@v6
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: 21

      - id: siftwise
        uses: PramodBasavarajMenasi/siftwise/actions/select@v0.3.0
        with:
          server-url: ${{ secrets.SIFTWISE_URL }}
          token: ${{ secrets.SIFTWISE_TOKEN }}

      - name: Tests
        env:
          MODE: ${{ steps.siftwise.outputs.mode }}
          COMMAND: ${{ steps.siftwise.outputs.command }}
        run: |
          if [ "$MODE" = selective ]; then
            if [ -n "$COMMAND" ]; then eval "$COMMAND"; else echo "No tests affected."; fi
          else
            ./mvnw -B test   # or: ./gradlew test
          fi

      - if: always()
        uses: PramodBasavarajMenasi/siftwise/actions/record@v0.3.0
        with:
          server-url: ${{ secrets.SIFTWISE_URL }}
          token: ${{ secrets.SIFTWISE_TOKEN }}
          junit: "**/target/surefire-reports/TEST-*.xml **/build/test-results/test/*.xml"

The numbers

  • dropwizard/dropwizard (Maven, 42 modules), 148 PR runs: 74 of 74 failures caught. In the 22 selective runs, siftwise skipped a median 90.6% of the estimated test time (26% to 93%).
  • The catch: most of dropwizard's PRs are dependency bumps to its BOM, which correctly run everything. So over all 148 runs, the time saved is much smaller: 11.9%. Module build-file scoping moved 5 more runs from full to selective. A repo with more code changes and fewer bumps would save more.
  • naver/fixture-monkey (Gradle): 3 of 3 failures caught. That's a small history, so treat it as a first check, not proof.

The dropwizard replay also found a real bug: Surefire writes a class-level result with an empty test name for a JUnit 5 @Nested class, and siftwise rejected the whole upload for it. Every Windows leg of dropwizard's CI history (781 uploads) was rejected before the fix.

Part 5: dogfooding, siftwise on its own CI

This was the last promise from post 2, and the one I care most about. Replays of other projects' history are useful, but they're replays. Dogfooding is siftwise running live on real changes, as they happen.

How it works

Every siftwise PR and push to main runs a Dogfood workflow in shadow mode:

  1. A siftwise server starts inside the CI job, on the runner's own Postgres, with a random per-job token. There's no hosted server and nothing to pay for.
  2. History comes from the GitHub Actions cache. The job restores the database from main's latest cache entry, and saves a new one at the end.
  3. siftwise stores what it would have selected, then the full suite runs anyway.
  4. It compares: for every failure, would the selection have caught it? How much time would it have saved?
  5. Each run uploads a small summary file. scripts/dogfood_report.py adds them all up.

It gates nothing: no fail-on, no PR comment, and every siftwise step fails open. So it can never block my own CI.

The safety part: a PR's cache entry is scoped to that PR, so a PR (including one from a fork) can read main's history but can never write into it. Only main's own runs build the history. For the numbers, I also leave out the fork PRs' runs, because code from the fork wrote their summaries; each of those changes still counts once, as its push to main.

The numbers (26 Oct to 9 Nov 2026)

Workflow runs 36 (17 PR runs, 19 pushes to main)
Shadow runs counted 32 (the first 2 had no history yet; the 2 fork runs are left out)
Would have been selective 9 of 32
Tests selected in those 9 a median 39% of the known tests
Time saved 14.7% of 23.0 minutes over the 32 runs
Failures none: every run's suite passed, so recall can't be measured yet
Weekly time saved 21%, 7% and 34%

Read these as early numbers. A merged PR usually counts twice (once as its PR run, once as its push to main), so the 9 selective runs are really about 6 distinct changes.

What dogfooding taught me

  • Why 23 of 32 ran in full: 20 changed a build or config file (the Dockerfile and docker-compose.yml in 6 runs each, workflows, and my test fixtures' own build.gradle.kts, tsconfig.json and jest.config.ts), and 3 changed a file no test reaches (like glama.json).
  • The fixture finding is the most useful one. siftwise's tests include tiny sample Gradle and TypeScript projects. Their build files are test data, but siftwise treats them like real build files and runs everything. Scoping them safely is the first item for v0.4. I'd never have found this from replays.
  • Each run now records the risk rank of every failure, so once a dogfood run does fail, the report shows not just "caught or missed" but how early risk order would have surfaced it.

You can do the same on your repo: the Action's shadow input (always, or a sample like 10%) runs the full suite and reports what siftwise would have caught or missed, before you trust it with anything. Details: Shadow mode in the README.

Part 6: v0.2 follow-ups and fixes

Things I found while testing v0.2 on real projects (#46):

  • Jest without addFileAttribute: selection and re-runs now work without it (Part 3).
  • JUnit 5 @DisplayName and parameterized test names map back to their methods, so Gradle and phrased-Maven re-runs work.
  • Go workspaces (go.work) and nested modules work for selection, commands and re-runs.
  • The GitLab template now declares its JUnit reports, which the pipeline's Tests tab reads.

Fixes, three of which (🔴) made siftwise silently miss tests:

  • 🔴 Nested Go modules: a nested module's dependents were missed, and its tests ran from the root, where Go can't build them. Now they run as go test -C <module> ./pkg.
  • 🔴 Missed JS edges: import('./a/' + x), import.meta.glob and require.context created no edges, so changing a file they load didn't select the tests that load it.
  • go list could edit go.mod when GOFLAGS had -mod=mod. It now runs read-only (#52). On Go 1.15 or older, set GOFLAGS=-mod=readonly yourself; making siftwise do it is an open good first issue (#67).
  • Java uploads rejected for a @Nested class's result (the dropwizard bug above).
  • 🔴 Same-named Java test classes in two modules: a change to one module's test resources ran only the other module's copy.
  • A deleted Jest test file was still named in the jest command, which then failed with "No tests found".

What building v0.3 taught me

  • Measure the features you're sure about. Import depth was the "obviously better" change, and it made one repo worse. Without the replay, I'd have shipped it.
  • Your dependencies change under you. On release day, a new Typer version started requiring pydantic, which broke the check that keeps the light CLI install small. siftwise's code didn't change; the light install grew from 9 MB to 18 MB, and the check now verifies that siftwise itself never imports server code.
  • good first issue works. I labelled a one-line bug, and by the same morning two people had sent fixes. One fixed it; the other added the test that stops it from coming back. Both got merged.

Community

  • Thanks to @bfs2021 (#62) and @mursalhayat1 (#63), siftwise's first outside contributors.
  • siftwise's MCP server is listed in the HOL Guard MCP server catalog (opt-in, after a review of its code and disclosures) and on Glama.

Troubleshooting

You see Fix
Jest tests always run in full add addFileAttribute: "true" to jest-junit (Step 3.1)
jest: command not found put node_modules/.bin on PATH, as in Step 3.2
Java tests never selected record didn't find the reports: set its junit input (Step 4.1)
Every Java PR runs the full suite it changed a root or parent build file, which runs everything by design
--budget fails with a server error the server is still on 0.2: upgrade it
The order looks wrong in Jest Jest reorders files across its workers; the order is a hint there

Known limits

  • Jest: no recall number yet; jest.config.js can't be read without Node (tsconfig and relative paths still resolve); a custom testMatch isn't read.
  • Java: Kotlin, Groovy and Scala tests fall back to the full suite; Maven runs modules in reactor order, not risk order.
  • Budget: an estimate, not a cap.
  • Dogfooding: 32 runs and no failures yet, so no live recall.
  • MCP is tested on Windows only; GitLab on gitlab.com Free only.
  • Everything else: the CHANGELOG.

What's next: v0.4

  • Safe scoping for build files inside test fixtures (the dogfooding finding).
  • -mod=readonly for older Go versions.
  • More recall numbers: a Jest replay, more Gradle history, and the first live recall from dogfooding.
  • More good first issues. If you'd like to contribute, start here.

Links

  • 💻 GitHub: https://github.com/PramodBasavarajMenasi/siftwise
  • 📦 PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/siftwise/
  • 📝 Release notes: https://github.com/PramodBasavarajMenasi/siftwise/releases/tag/v0.3.0
  • 📊 All eval numbers and method: https://github.com/PramodBasavarajMenasi/siftwise/blob/main/docs/eval-results.md
  • 📖 Post 1 (server and GitHub Action): https://dev.to/pm_22/i-built-siftwise-run-only-the-tests-your-change-needs-open-source-self-hosted-51jf
  • 📖 Post 2 (GitLab CI and coding agents): https://dev.to/pm_22/siftwise-v02-run-it-on-gitlab-ci-and-with-5-coding-agents-full-setup-guide-o2f

Try it, break it, tell me

If you have a Jest or Java repo, try siftwise in shadow mode and tell me what it would have caught or missed: that's exactly the data v0.3 is missing. Misses make the best bug reports. And a ⭐ helps a small project get seen. 👇

title: MISO-BR: An Open Corpus for Misogyny Detection in Brazilian Portuguese
description:
arXiv:2611.14036v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Misogyny is among the most prevalent forms of online hate speech directed at Brazilian users, yet open and auditable resources dedicated to it in Brazilian Portuguese remain scarce. We introduce MISO-BR, an open, documented and versioned corpus of 896 balanced social media texts annotated for binary misogyny, released with its construction protocol and reproducible baselines. The corpus combines lexicon- and target-guided scraping from X with items imported from OLID-BR, a large language model triage stage whose prompt and decoding parameters are released, and manual annotation by three annotators following a written guide. Inter-annotator reliability reaches a Fleiss' kappa of 0.788 over 816 items. Under a single fixed protocol we compare four classical classifiers (Multinomial and Bernoulli Naive Bayes, a linear SVM and a random forest) with fine-tuned BERTimbau Base and Large. The classical models cluster between 0.651 and 0.676 macro-F1 and are precision-oriented but recall-poor. The transformers reach 0.833 macro-F1 and accuracy (Wilson 95% CI for accuracy [0.77, 0.88]), a gap of roughly 16 points, while Base and Large are indistinguishable on the test set despite a 2.6x difference in training cost. We argue that the value of the resource lies less in its headline scores than in the auditability of its pipeline, and we state three limits that users must reckon with: the artificial class balance, whose effect on precision under realistic prevalence we quantify; the association between provenance and label, which the released source field makes measurable; and the selection bias induced by lexicon-guided sampling and automatic triage. The corpus, annotation guide, models and experimental scripts are publicly available.

title: Selective Surgical Action-Center Localization:Retaining Localization Gains through Supervised Scoring
description:
arXiv:2611.12977v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Surgical action-center localization requires both an accurate reference point and a decision about whether to report it. When frames with and without a reportable center are mixed, the benefit of improved localization depends on which correct candidates survive selection. We present a selective localization pipeline combining heatmap and coordinate supervision with a logistic-regression scorer. The scorer learns to identify predictions with a reportable center and a localization error within a specified tolerance. The internal evaluation uses 5,000 frames from 50 surgical sources, five source-grouped folds and two random seeds. Matched locator and scoring comparisons track correct candidates and their rejection. At an 80% acceptance quota per source and a tolerance of 0.10 times the image diagonal, our method retains 46.08 correct outputs per 100 inputs. The baseline locator with the same scoring approach retains 44.20. The gain is 1.88 (descriptive 95% source-paired bootstrap interval, 0.94 to 2.79). Under entropy-based selection, increased rejection of correct predictions offsets the higher supply of correct predictions on average. For the coordinate-supervised locator, supervised scoring reduces these rejections from 6.15 to 2.99 per 100 inputs. Evaluating retained correct outputs reveals whether a selection rule preserves or erodes an improvement in localization.

title: Next.js soft 404: why notFound() returned 200 behind loading.tsx
description:
On my Next.js 16 site, a URL like /projects/nope returned HTTP 200 and carried two robots tags: index, follow and noindex. The route has a loading.tsx, which starts streaming before notFound() runs, so the status code was already sent. Adding export const dynamicParams = false to the page makes an unknown slug a real 404 before any rendering starts.

Why does notFound() return 200 in the Next.js App Router?

I found this during a Search Console pass. Unknown project slugs were not 404s. The Next.js docs describe the mechanism in the loading.js reference: streaming page responses begin with a 200 status code, and the initial response headers fix the status for the rest of the response. Next.js can still stream notFound() after that, so the browser shows your not-found UI, but the status line stays 200.

The docs also say when the stream starts. The response body begins streaming when a Suspense fallback renders, and they give loading.tsx as the example, or when a Server Component suspends under a <Suspense> boundary. Calling notFound() before that point preserves the 404. After it, the status cannot change.

A loading.tsx file is a Suspense fallback wrapped around the segment's page. For a dynamic route, that means the fallback can be sent before your page code has a chance to look up the slug and decide it does not exist.

What does a soft 404 look like for Google?

A soft 404 is a page that tells the user "not found" but tells the crawler 200 OK. Next.js softens the damage: the docs say it injects <meta name="robots" content="noindex" /> into a streamed 404, so search engines are told to keep the URL out of the index even though the status is 200. They also note that some crawlers may label these responses as soft 404s.

On my site the result was messier. The root layout already set index, follow, and the streamed not-found added noindex. The page carried both tags with a 200 status. I did not want to find out which one a crawler would trust, and I did not want Search Console reporting junk URLs as soft 404s.

How do I reproduce it?

Here is the shape of the broken segment. The names are simplified from my project route:

// app/projects/[slug]/page.tsx
import { notFound } from 'next/navigation'

export default async function Page({
  params,
}: {
  params: Promise<{ slug: string }>
}) {
  const { slug } = await params
  const project = findProject(slug)
  if (!project) notFound() // too late: loading.tsx already streamed a 200

  return <ProjectView project={project} />
}

// app/projects/[slug]/loading.tsx
export default function Loading() {
  return <ProjectSkeleton />
}

Check the status with curl:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://example.com/projects/nope

You want 404. In my case it printed 200. To see the duplicate robots tags, fetch the body:

curl -s https://example.com/projects/nope | grep -o '<meta name="robots"[^>]*>'

What fixed it: dynamicParams = false

Every project on my site is already prerendered through generateStaticParams. The fix was one line in the page file, with a comment I left for my future self:

// app/projects/[slug]/page.tsx

// Every project is prerendered below, so an unknown slug is a 404 at routing.
// Left on, it rendered on demand and hit notFound() after [slug]/loading.tsx
// had already streamed a 200: a soft 404 carrying both index and noindex.
export const dynamicParams = false

export async function generateStaticParams() {
  const slugs = await listProjectSlugs()
  return slugs.map((slug) => ({ slug }))
}

The reference for dynamicParams says that with the default of true, segments not returned by generateStaticParams are generated at request time, and with false they return a 404. An unknown slug never reaches your page component, so loading.tsx never streams for it, and the response is a real 404 from routing.

After the change, an unknown slug is a real 404 from routing. The curl check against /projects/nope on my live site now prints 404.

I left loading.tsx in place. At one point I suspected both loading files of bloating the DOM and removed them to test it. The DOM went from 951 to 949 nodes, so they went back. The soft 404 was their only real cost, and dynamicParams fixed that without touching them.

When is dynamicParams = false the wrong fix?

It fits when you know every valid slug at build time. If your slugs come from a database that changes after deploy, false would 404 a page that was added after the build, until you rebuild or revalidate.

The docs also list a restriction: dynamicParams is not available when Cache Components is enabled. I did not test that configuration, so check your own setup if you use it.

For a route that has to render on demand, the docs give a different answer. Run the check before the body streams. For a 404, you can check the slug in Proxy, then rewrite to a not-found route or return a 404 response, and the docs say to keep Proxy checks fast and avoid fetching full content there. I use a proxy for a related case on this site: malformed UTF-8 in a URL, such as /projects/%C0%AF, used to be a 500 on decode. proxy.ts, which is the Next 16 name for middleware, now returns a 404 for those. Its matcher only runs on dynamic segments that contain a %, so no other request pays for it.

The other option is to call notFound() before any await on a slow path and before any <Suspense> boundary. The streaming guide recommends exactly that placement to get a real status code.

How do I check every dynamic route for this?

The rule I wrote down after this: any dynamic route with a loading.tsx must 404 without rendering. That means dynamicParams = false, or a proxy check.

To audit a site:

  1. List the routes with a dynamic segment and a loading.tsx next to them.
  2. Request a nonsense slug on each one from a production build and read the status code with curl.
  3. Anything that prints 200 with a not-found page is a soft 404.
  4. Fix it with dynamicParams = false if the slug set is known at build time, or with a proxy check if it is not.

The site this came from is documented in the portfolio case study, and the project pages that carry the fix are listed on /projects.

title: Before I build on a SaaS tool, I check whether an agent can actually use it
description:
Before I build on a SaaS tool, I check whether an agent can actually use it

I operate an AI agent that earns money on bounty boards. The agent signs up for services, pays per call, and runs tools on its own. That breaks in a boring place: most SaaS products assume a human at a keyboard. The signup wants a phone number. The pricing page hides the one fact the agent needs. The docs describe the dashboard, not the API.

So before I build on a tool now, I check one public dataset first: the agent-readiness report cards published by Sourcey.

What the report cards actually grade

A report card grades one job on one product — not the product in general. Creating a repository, sending an email, reporting an error. Each job is graded across six steps: discover, authority, onboard, pay, confirm, sustain. A step is marked machine when software can do it alone, and flagged when a person has to step in.

I pulled the current machine-readable release (release sha256:2d306ff6…, policy kind-2026-10-12) and counted what it holds:

  • 106 published report cards
  • Every card carries its probe date, its policy version, and a revision digest, so a grade can be re-checked against the same bytes later
  • The data is published under CC BY 4.0, with the raw file at agent-readiness.json

The pattern that matters to me as an operator: the failing step is rarely "pay". It is usually "authority" or "onboard" — the point where the vendor wants a human identity, a phone, or a dashboard-only flow. A card tells me that before I burn a day integrating.

The other half: what the tool costs a startup

The same registry tracks startup programs and credits — the discounts and free tiers that decide what a small operation actually pays. The current release of the startup credits registry covers 589 companies, and every record carries the source URL it came from and the date it was read. Credits pages rot faster than almost anything else on the web; a dated, sourced record is the difference between a fact and a rumour.

Sourcey also ships the documentation generator behind its own docs as open source, which is the third piece I use: when a vendor's docs are generated and structured, an agent can read them. When they are screenshots of a dashboard, it cannot.

My working rule

  • If a job I need has a report card, I read the six steps before I read the marketing page.
  • If the onboard or authority step needs a human I do not have, I do not integrate — I pick the next tool.
  • If I budget around a startup credit, I cite the dated registry record, not the vendor's headline number.

None of this makes a bad tool good. It makes the failure cheap and early, which is most of what operating an agent in production actually is.

Data cited from Sourcey release sha256:2d306ff6e37131beda05e42b062ba550ee4de13bc49d85d755983b3cc6a111a1 (policy as of 2026-10-05), read 2026-11-11: agent readiness report cards, startup credits registry, Sourcey.

title: Haiku com kit de UX: regras abertas e um código mínimo fazem um modelo pequeno acertar como um maior?
description:
Resumo. Testamos se o conjunto formado por um modelo pequeno (Haiku 5.5), um data lake de regras de UX com fonte aberta e um código mínimo de checagem (o "kit") se aproxima de um modelo maior (Sonnet 5.5) em três tarefas de tela de login: criar, melhorar e comparar duas telas pelo código. Foram 2.244 itens e 2.424 chamadas, com 0 falhas no final. Em criar e melhorar, o Haiku com regras e kit passou de 0,744 para 0,998 (criar) e de 0,754 para 0,926 (melhorar), e a acurácia combinada do Haiku com kit foi 1,07 vez a do Sonnet puro, a 10% do custo por tarefa. Em comparar duas telas, o kit não ajudou e piorou um pouco; os pares sem diferença real nunca geraram alarme falso em nenhuma condição, então a hipótese sobre alarme falso não pôde ser testada. Três instrumentos de estética sem humano foram validados e nenhum passou; por isso este estudo não afirma nada sobre beleza. A principal ameaça à validade é circular e está na seção 9: as 30 regras que o kit verifica são as mesmas que pontuam criar e melhorar. Uma checagem independente com axe-core confirma o ganho em criar, mas não em melhorar. Para o resumo prático, existe o guia simples.

1. A pergunta e a decisão que ela informa

Nos estudos 1 e 2, o Haiku ficou perto de modelos maiores quando recebeu processo e contexto certos. Falta saber o que acontece em UX e UI, onde duas coisas costumam dar errado com modelos de linguagem: eles percebem mal diferenças finas de estilo (a literatura mostra recall baixo em detectar mudanças de CSS), e o gosto é subjetivo. A tese deste estudo é que se pode usar tecnologia para suprir o que a IA faz mal: regras de fonte aberta no prompt e um código que checa e compara telas, deixando o modelo com o que ele faz bem, que é escrever e corrigir código.

Pergunta do estudo: um Haiku com um data lake de regras de UX e um kit de checagem por código chega perto do Sonnet puro em assertividade, e a que custo total? A unidade testada é o conjunto (modelo + regras + kit), não o modelo sozinho. Isso importa: dizer que "o código fez a detecção" não é um defeito do experimento; é o que está sendo medido.

2. O material

2.1 O data lake de login

São 30 regras para uma tela de login, cada uma com texto, fonte, como checar, exemplo bom, exemplo ruim, severidade e o tipo (25 objetivas, 5 semi-objetivas). Todas vêm de fontes abertas e citáveis: WCAG 2.2 (contraste, rótulos, alvo de toque, foco, reflow, idioma), web.dev (boas práticas de formulário de login) e Material Design 3 (consistência, hierarquia, escala de espaçamento). Nenhuma regra foi escrita de memória como "verdade". As URLs das fontes foram escritas a partir do conhecimento das páginas e ainda precisam de conferência de abertura uma a uma (item pendente, seção 9). Exemplos:

Regra Fonte Como se checa
L08: texto do botão com contraste de pelo menos 4,5:1 WCAG 2.2, 1.4.3 razão de contraste entre cor do texto e fundo do botão
L11: alvos de pelo menos 24 px (de preferência 44) WCAG 2.2, 2.5.8 altura estimada de botão e campos
L17: link para recuperar senha web.dev, WCAG 3.3.8 existe <a> com texto de esqueci/recuperar
L28: campos e botão com o mesmo raio de borda Material 3, text fields compara border-radius

2.2 O kit

O kit é um código mínimo, em Node, sem navegador e sem layout (grau 0 de uma escada de custo): parse5 para o HTML, css-tree para o CSS e culori para cores e contraste. Ele faz duas coisas: (a) verifica as 30 regras e devolve um relatório em texto com o que falhou e onde; (b) compara duas telas e lista as diferenças reais de estrutura, conteúdo, fluxo e estilo, com os valores normalizados (#fff igual a rgb(255,255,255), 16px igual a 1rem; nomes de classe, espaços, comentários e ordem de atributos são ignorados). Cada execução leva cerca de 0,6 s. Deixamos o navegador real (Playwright) e a imagem de fora do kit: o que ele não enxerga, por não ter layout, é declarado na seção 9.

2.3 Os estímulos

Todos gerados por um script com semente fixa (20261110), o que dá gabarito exato por construção e evita telas que o modelo possa ter visto no treino.

  • T1, criar (12 pedidos): a mesma tela de login para contextos diferentes (clínica, banco, escola de idiomas, clube de xadrez e outros). Pontuação: regras do data lake cumpridas no HTML final, de 30.
  • T2, melhorar (20 telas): cada uma com 3 defeitos injetados, de 22 tipos usados (de um catálogo de 25), ligados a regras. Pontuação: regras defeituosas removidas menos regras novas que passam a falhar, dividido pelas regras injetadas.
  • T3, comparar (60 pares): 20 de CSS (13 grandes e 7 sutis, de uma propriedade), 8 de conteúdo, 8 de fluxo, 8 compostos, 8 de ruído (mudanças sem efeito: renomear classes, reformatar, cor em outra notação) e 8 idênticos. A resposta é um JSON com as diferenças; a pontuação é F1 contra o gabarito, e nos pares de ruído e idênticos vale 1 só se o modelo responder que não há diferença.

O gerador confere os estímulos contra o próprio kit: o kit viu diferença em todos os pares com mudança e em nenhum par de ruído ou idêntico. Isso é uma validação de que o kit está coerente com o gerador, não uma prova independente (seção 9).

3. As condições: o que o modelo recebe

Condição O que o modelo recebe A pergunta que responde
A0 só a tarefa quanto ele faz sozinho? (linha de base)
A1 tarefa + as 30 regras do data lake só o conhecimento, sem ferramenta, ajuda?
A2 tarefa + relatório do kit só a ferramenta, sem regras no prompt, ajuda?
A3 tarefa + regras + relatório o conjunto completo
AC (só T1, só Haiku) uma segunda passada de autocrítica, sem o kit o ganho do kit vem da informação ou só de uma passada extra?

Em criar, as condições A2, A3 e AC têm duas chamadas: gerar o HTML e depois corrigir. Em melhorar e comparar, o relatório vai no mesmo prompt. As correções voltam em trechos (ANTES/DEPOIS), aplicados por código igualmente a todos os modelos: 2.679 de 2.688 blocos do Haiku e 2.358 de 2.359 do Sonnet foram aplicados.

4. Decisões de projeto

  • Modelos e execução: Haiku 5.5 e Sonnet 5.5 por claude -p (assinatura), com --effort medium e sem ferramentas, com um prompt de sistema curto igual para todos. Sem ferramentas, o modelo não acessa a internet nem busca rótulos publicados: só vê o prompt. O Opus 5.5 estava previsto e foi retirado por custo, por decisão do autor (desvio na seção 9).
  • Custo nominal = tokens × preço de lista (por milhão de tokens: Haiku US$ 0,10 de entrada e 0,50 de saída; Sonnet US$ 2 e 10; leitura de cache 0,01 e 0,10; escrita de cache 1,25 vez a entrada). O gasto real da assinatura não é cobrado em dólar.
  • Amostras: 3 por célula; cada item entra na análise pela média das 3.
  • Piloto: 46 itens do Haiku testaram o pipeline. Depois dele trocamos o logo quebrado (imagem sem arquivo) por um SVG embutido, o que mudou os estímulos; por isso o piloto não entra nos resultados.
  • Código, estímulos, lake e pré-registro foram congelados com hashes SHA-256 em dados/CONGELADO.txt antes da rodada. Não houve commit com tag; o registro é por hash (ver seção 9).

5. A execução

Rodaram 2.244 itens (Haiku 1.140 e Sonnet 1.104, porque o AC existe só no Haiku), em 2.424 chamadas (as de duas chamadas são as de criar com A2, A3 e AC). O Haiku consumiu 4,68 milhões de tokens de entrada e 2,65 milhões de saída; o Sonnet, 4,54 milhões e 1,10 milhão. Notável: com o mesmo esforço médio, o Haiku gerou mais que o dobro de tokens de saída do Sonnet. O custo nominal total foi US$ 19,63 (Haiku US$ 1,69, Sonnet US$ 17,94). Houve um erro no meio da rodada, do próprio kit, e o item foi refeito: resultado final, 0 itens com erro.

Registramos três desvios do pré-registro, descritos em dados/DESVIOS.md: (1) o kit travou numa cor inválida gerada pelo Haiku e foi corrigido sem mudar regra nem limiar; (2) o Opus foi retirado; (3) o logo foi trocado antes da rodada. Nenhum deles muda uma hipótese.

6. As hipóteses, uma a uma

Cada hipótese foi escrita antes da rodada, com métrica e critério. Os valores-p vêm do teste pareado de Wilcoxon sobre os itens (médias das 3 amostras), com intervalo de confiança por bootstrap de itens (10.000 réplicas) e correção de Holm nas 12 comparações confirmatórias. Dessas, 7 passam em Holm.

H4: no criar, o Haiku com regras e kit supera o Haiku puro? Sim: 0,998 contra 0,744, diferença +0,255 (IC 95%: +0,239 a +0,274; p = 0,0002, passa em Holm).

H3: no melhorar, o mesmo? Sim: 0,926 contra 0,754, +0,172 (IC 95%: +0,083 a +0,267; p = 0,0011, passa). Os defeitos novos introduzidos caem de 0,53 para 0,18 por tela (p = 0,022, não passa em Holm).

H7: regras sozinhas já ajudam? Sim, em criar (A1 0,988 contra 0,744, p = 0,0002) e em melhorar (0,894 contra 0,754, p = 0,0034). Em comparar, a ferramenta (A2) ficou abaixo da condição só com regras (0,899 contra 0,939), o oposto do previsto.

H6: o ganho do kit é informação ou só uma passada extra? Em criar, o kit supera a autocrítica sem kit: 0,954 contra 0,804, +0,150 (p = 0,0002, passa). A checagem independente com axe-core não confirma essa vantagem (seção 7.5).

H5: o kit ajuda mais o Haiku que o Sonnet? Em criar, o ganho de A3 sobre A0 é +0,255 no Haiku e +0,226 no Sonnet (diferença +0,029; p = 0,002, passa); em melhorar, +0,172 contra −0,025 (diferença +0,197; p = 0,0011, passa); em comparar, não (p = 0,11). Em melhorar, o Sonnet puro já é bom (0,935) e piora com as regras sozinhas (0,810).

H1: em comparar, o kit aumenta o recall do Haiku? O recall sobe de 0,909 para 0,967 (+0,058; IC 95%: +0,005 a +0,121; p = 0,044), mas não passa em Holm. Não apoiada.

H2: o kit reduz alarme falso nos pares sem diferença real? Não testável. Haiku e Sonnet tiveram nota 1,00 nos 16 pares de ruído e idênticos em todas as condições, inclusive sem kit. Não houve alarme falso para reduzir.

H9: o critério principal. O Haiku com regras e kit atinge pelo menos 90% da acurácia combinada do Sonnet puro, a no máximo 50% do custo por tarefa? A acurácia combinada é a média das pontuações de criar, melhorar e comparar. Resultado: 0,943 contra 0,882, razão 1,07, e custo médio por tarefa de US$ 0,0022 contra US$ 0,0210, razão 0,10. Suportada, mas só contra o Sonnet: o Opus foi retirado, então não há comparação com um modelo maior que ele.

7. Resultados

Tarefa Modelo A0 A1 A2 A3 AC
T1 criar Haiku 0,744 0,988 0,954 0,998 0,804
T1 criar Sonnet 0,774 0,987 0,979 1,000 n.a.
T2 melhorar Haiku 0,754 0,894 0,967 0,926 n.a.
T2 melhorar Sonnet 0,935 0,810 0,956 0,910 n.a.
T3 comparar Haiku 0,933 0,939 0,899 0,905 n.a.
T3 comparar Sonnet 0,938 0,924 0,895 0,897 n.a.

7.1 O que deu certo

  1. As regras no prompt já resolvem a maior parte de criar. O Haiku vai de 0,744 para 0,988 só com as 30 regras (A1). O kit soma pouco ali (A3 0,998).
  2. Em melhorar, o relatório do kit é o que mais ajuda o Haiku: de 0,754 (A0) para 0,967 (A2), acima das regras sozinhas (0,894), e com menos defeitos novos introduzidos.
  3. O Haiku com o conjunto fica no nível do Sonnet puro, por um décimo do custo. A acurácia combinada do Haiku A3 (0,943) fica acima da do Sonnet A0 (0,882), com US$ 0,0022 por tarefa contra US$ 0,0210.
  4. As correções em trechos funcionam: 99,7% dos blocos do Haiku e 99,96% dos do Sonnet foram aplicados sem ambiguidade.
  5. O formato de resposta não foi problema: 100% dos JSON de comparar foram válidos nos dois modelos.

7.2 O que não funcionou

  • Comparar duas telas pelo código já estava perto do teto sem ajuda (0,933 no Haiku puro, 0,938 no Sonnet puro), e o relatório do kit piorou um pouco, especialmente em CSS: Haiku 0,87 (A0) contra 0,79 (A2) e 0,81 (A3), mesmo padrão no Sonnet.

O motivo provável, não testado, é que o relatório lista várias propriedades derivadas de uma só mudança (por exemplo, os quatro lados de um padding) e o modelo as copia; o gabarito tem um item, e o resto vira alarme falso. É uma falha de granularidade do kit e da pontuação juntas, e uma repontuação agrupando por propriedade seria exploratória, feita depois de ver os dados.

  • Pares de ruído e idênticos não discriminaram nada: todos acertaram em todas as condições. Isso também diz que, com o código das duas telas à vista, esses modelos não inventam diferenças.
  • O Sonnet piorou com regras sozinhas em melhorar (0,935 para 0,810). Não investigamos a causa.

7.3 O custo

Condição Haiku (US$/tarefa) Sonnet (US$/tarefa)
A0 0,0017 0,0210
A1 0,0022 0,0241
A2 0,0029 0,0359
A3 0,0022 0,0238

O custo médio por tarefa é a média dos três tipos de tarefa. O Haiku A3 custa 10% do Sonnet A0. Esse número é de tokens e não inclui o custo de construir o kit e o data lake, que foi trabalho humano e de IA e não foi monetizado; o ponto de equilíbrio contra o Sonnet depende de quantas telas se checam com o mesmo kit.

7.4 Estética: nenhum instrumento sem humano passou

O autor não é designer, e um painel humano foi descartado. A saída foi buscar instrumentos que não sejam humanos nem sejam da família dos modelos testados e validá-los antes de usá-los, com critérios fixados antes de calcular qualquer nota. Resultado: nenhum validou.

  • UIClip (modelo da CMU/Apple treinado em UIs ranqueadas): em 15 defeitos visualmente observáveis, a tela de referência teve nota maior em apenas 9 de 15 (limiar 12) na tentativa 1, e em 8 de 15 na tentativa 2 (tela cortada no conteúdo, única tentativa extra, declarada). Em séries graduadas de degradação, acompanhou só o contraste do botão e, no limite exato (ρ = −0,8), o espaço entre campos (2 de 5 séries nas duas tentativas; limiar 4).
  • Consistência e hierarquia por código (10 medidas em Chrome): 9 de 15 nos defeitos e 4 de 5 nas séries. Acompanha a degradação gradual, mas não vê defeitos de ausência (remover o link de recuperar senha fez a nota subir).
  • Juiz Fable em pares, validado contra os 300 pares do WiserUI-Bench (rótulo: qual variante venceu um teste A/B real; 297 pares com as duas imagens baixadas): 55,6% de acerto (IC 95%: 49,9 a 61,1; limiar 60% com limite inferior acima de 50%), e consistência de posição de 58,6% (limiar 70%). Mesma faixa que a literatura reporta para juízes de IA contra designers (acordo médio entre os próprios designers: 62,4%).

Conclusão desta parte: sem validade, a estética fica fora da decisão e fora das conclusões. O estudo mede legibilidade, consistência e conformidade com regras abertas, que são parte do UX, mas não "beleza".

7.5 Checagem independente com axe-core

Como as 30 regras estão tanto no prompt quanto na pontuação de criar e melhorar, rodamos o axe-core (WCAG 2.x A/AA), que o kit e os prompts não conhecem, nas telas finais de T1 e T2. Violações médias por tela:

T1 criar A0 A1 A2 A3 AC
Haiku 0,50 0,03 0,08 0,03 0,06
Sonnet 0,31 0,00 0,06 0,00 n.a.

O ganho de criar se confirma de forma independente (Haiku A0 contra A3: p = 0,004). Em melhorar o axe quase não acha violação em nenhuma condição, então não discrimina. E o axe não confirma a vantagem do kit sobre a autocrítica sem kit (0,08 contra 0,06; p = 0,75): essa parte de H6 só é sustentada pelas próprias 30 regras.

8. Por que esses resultados valem, e até onde

O desenho tem proteções: hipóteses, métricas e parâmetros fixados antes da rodada, com hashes; estímulos inéditos gerados por script com gabarito exato; modelos sem acesso à internet; controle de autocrítica; correção de múltiplos testes; checagem independente com outra ferramenta; relato dos desvios; relato dos resultados negativos (comparar, estética) com o mesmo rigor dos positivos.

9. Ameaças à validade

  • Circularidade (construto). As 30 regras estão no prompt de A1 e A3 e o mesmo kit gera o relatório de A2 e A3, mas também são elas que pontuam criar e melhorar. O Haiku "aprendeu a prova". O axe-core ameniza em criar e não ajuda em melhorar. Os números de T1 e T2 devem ser lidos como conformidade com as regras entregues, não como qualidade geral de UX.
  • Uma tela só, telas sintéticas. Login, gerado por script. Sem validade externa para outras telas ou para telas do mundo real.
  • O kit foi afinado nos tipos de ruído deste conjunto, e o mesmo autor escreveu estímulos e kit. O resultado de "alarme falso" vale para esses tipos e, de toda forma, não foi testável.
  • O kit não tem layout nem navegador. O que depende de renderização (alinhamento real, sobreposição, quebra de linha) não é visto. O grau 2 da escada de custo não foi construído, nem a variante com imagem.
  • O Opus foi retirado por custo. H5 e H9 comparam só Haiku e Sonnet; não se pode afirmar nada sobre a proximidade do Haiku ao topo da linha de modelos.
  • Sem painel humano e sem instrumento válido de estética. O resultado sobre estética é negativo e declarado; o estudo não mede beleza. O juiz Fable foi validado contra rótulos de conversão (qual variante gerou mais ações), que não são beleza, e o Fable pode ter visto o WiserUI-Bench no treino, o que inflaria a acurácia dele (ele nem assim passou).
  • O pré-registro é por hash, sem tag no repositório, e foi congelado antes da rodada principal, mas depois do piloto e do primeiro teste dos instrumentos de estética. Os critérios dos instrumentos de estética foram fixados antes de calcular suas notas, e há registro de que o UIClip teve duas tentativas.
  • As fontes das regras foram abertas, mas não lidas uma a uma. Em 11/11/2026 abri as 19 URLs distintas de WCAG, web.dev e Material Design: 18 responderam 200 e 1 respondeu 404 (Material Design 3, espaçamento, fonte da regra L29). Abrir a página não prova que ela sustenta a regra; a auditoria de sustentação foi feita só no estudo seguinte.
  • Custo nominal de lista, sem o custo de montar o kit e o data lake, e sem o consumo do limite do plano.
  • Mesma família de modelos escreveu o código do estudo (com o autor) e foi avaliada. Os dados brutos são de execuções reais.

10. O que isso permite concluir

Com segurança: em tarefas de criar e melhorar uma tela de login, dar ao Haiku as regras (e, em melhorar, o relatório do kit) o leva ao nível do Sonnet sem ajuda, por cerca de um décimo do custo por tarefa, medido pelas próprias regras e confirmado em criar por uma ferramenta independente; em comparar duas telas pelo código, o ganho do kit não aparece, porque os modelos já acertam quase tudo, e o relatório pode atrapalhar se vier verboso. Sem segurança: se o resultado vale para outras telas, para telas reais e para modelos maiores; se a vantagem sobrevive a uma pontuação independente das regras; e qualquer afirmação sobre estética. Próximos passos naturais: um terceiro conjunto de regras que o kit e o prompt não conhecem para pontuar; um kit com layout (grau 2); o Opus; e telas de verdade.

11. Reprodutibilidade

Código em studies/haiku-ui-design/ (kit/, gerador/, executor.py); lake em lake/login.json; estímulos em dados/estimulos/; dados brutos em dados/bruto/; critérios de validação dos instrumentos de estética e do juiz em dados/*CRITERIOS.md; desvios em dados/DESVIOS.md; análise em python gerador/analise.py; hashes em dados/CONGELADO.txt. As imagens do WiserUI-Bench (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, só pesquisa não comercial) não são redistribuídas; o baixador gerador/baixar_wiserui.py busca nos hosts originais. DOI do arquivamento: Arquivado no Zenodo (versão 3.0.0, estudos 3 e 3b): 10.5281/zenodo.24132784.

12. Referências

  • W3C. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2. https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/
  • web.dev. Sign-in form best practices. https://web.dev/articles/sign-in-form-best-practices
  • Material Design 3. Buttons, Text fields e Layout. https://m3.material.io/
  • DiffSpot: detecção de mudanças de CSS em pares de telas por modelos multimodais. arXiv:2605.29615.
  • WiserUI-Bench: Do MLLMs Capture How Interfaces Guide User Behavior? arXiv:2505.05026 (dados CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). https://github.com/jeochris/wiserui-bench
  • DesignPref: Capturing Personal Preferences in Visual Design Generation. arXiv:2511.20513.
  • Wu et al. UIClip: A Data-driven Model for Assessing User Interface Design. UIST 2024, arXiv:2404.12500.
  • Reinecke et al. Predicting users' first impressions of website aesthetics. CHI 2013.
  • Estudos anteriores do Melo Labs: 1 e 2.

Os experimentos, os dados e as conclusões são meus. A redação foi assistida por IA e revisada por mim.

title: Third Eye: Beyond Immediate Gains in Recursive Self-Improvement
description:
arXiv:2611.12988v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Does a useful self-update remain useful after the model updates again? Third Eye separates immediate performance from the outcome of a further native update. We evaluate five 3-8B backbones on math and code: 64 fresh runs, three candidates per run, and three continuations per candidate. Selection and final scoring use disjoint items. In the balanced Qwen3-4B/Llama-3.2-3B comparison, immediate-selected utility is near zero, but continuation reduces it by 1.78 percentage points (simultaneous 95% interval [0.68, 2.88]). Candidate-averaged immediate utility is already negative: selection partly accounts for the apparently neutral first step. Continuation also lowers utility for SmolLM3-3B and Llama-3.1-8B; Qwen3-8B remains inconclusive. Target and out-of-distribution losses dominate retention changes. Matched recipe and recipient-donor controls identify neither a reliable mitigation nor a single mechanism. The results support evaluating persistent self-updates as adaptation transitions, with independent scoring and a no-update baseline, rather than interpreting immediate performance as their full value.

title: Stylization as Geodesic Navigation on Diffusion Manifolds
description:
arXiv:2611.14097v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Facial stylization asks for a delicate transformation: the image should look unmistakably artistic, yet the person should remain unmistakably the same. Existing training-free and instruction-driven methods often fail to expose such control, either drifting away from identity or producing only weak stylization. We introduce Stylus, a training-free framework that treats facial style transfer as navigation on the curved latent manifold of a pretrained diffusion model. Rather than interpolating in flat Euclidean space, \method refines the interpolated content--style point by lowering a ratio-weighted discrete geodesic energy under the pullback metric, made tractable by a rank-one power-iteration approximation of the Jacobian. This principle drives two complementary controls: content--style latent interpolation for smooth semantic fusion, and self-attention query optimization for spatially adaptive style injection. The resulting dual-control mechanism provides continuous, fine-grained control over stylization strength while preserving identity-critical facial structure, all without additional training. Experiments show that Stylus achieves the strongest identity and content preservation at competitive stylization strength.
