title: A 10K drone image dataset with component-level annotations for rooftop photovoltaic inspection
description:
arXiv:2611.13892v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Component-level information supports rooftop photovoltaic (PV) inspection, but recognizing individual components across complex scenes remains challenging. We present PVIS-10K, a dataset of 10,065 drone images with component-level annotations covering 63,632 physical PV modules across 22 rooftop installations. The high-resolution red-green-blue (RGB) images were acquired by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs, also known as drones) in Ningbo, Shaoxing and Shenzhen, China. Multi-angle oblique observations capture installation-height and scale variation, dense arrangements, occlusion, shadows and reflections. Three-dimensional delineation, reprojection and image-by-image review produced 3,516,675 image-level polygon annotations, stored in Common Objects in Context (COCO) format. Station-disjoint partitions support evaluation on unseen stations within and across cities. Four supervised models and text-prompted zero-shot Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) provide full-resolution benchmarks of instance matching and foreground coverage. PVIS-10K supports component localization, delineation and image-based counting for drone-based rooftop PV inspection research.

title: Example Of Web Design Proposal
description:
Executive Architectural Breakdown: The Web Design Proposal as a Conversion System

A web design proposal is not a document. It is a pre-negotiated architecture of trust, scope, and risk transfer. Most agencies treat it as a decorative estimate—a price list wrapped in a logo header. That is a structural failure. The proposal is the first working artifact of the project itself, and it must be engineered with the same precision as the final interface.

Standard off-the-shelf templates and generic proposal forms fail for a fundamental reason: they are built for the sender’s convenience, not the buyer’s decision-making psychology. A template assumes the client already understands your process, your value model, and your technical constraints. In reality, the client is evaluating you against three unspoken criteria: Can this team solve my problem? Will they protect me from unknown risk? Is the investment framed in terms of business outcomes, not hours? A generic form answers none of these. It lists deliverables, but not the logic behind them. It quotes a price, but not the cost of inaction. It describes phases, but not the decision gates where the client retains control. The result is a proposal that reads as a commodity—and is negotiated like one.

The most effective proposals are structured as a conversion funnel. They open with a diagnostic reframing of the client’s business problem, not a boilerplate introduction. They define the system architecture of the engagement: discovery, design, build, and validation—each phase with an explicit entry criterion, exit deliverable, and success metric. They include a risk register, not as legal padding, but as a shared map of what could go wrong and who owns each mitigation. And they close with a clear, singular call to action: a fixed-scope engagement with a defined start date, not an open-ended "let’s talk."

Three concrete engineering takeaways from Vareli’s analysis:

  1. Model the proposal as a state machine. Every section should transition the client from awareness to agreement to activation. If a section does not move the client closer to a signed decision, remove it. Generic templates are static; high-converting proposals are sequential and cumulative.

  2. Replace feature lists with outcome-based specifications. Instead of "responsive design," write "a layout system that maintains a 95% task completion rate across mobile and desktop viewports." This shifts the conversation from cost to performance, and it gives your engineering team a measurable target.

  3. Build in a risk-reversal mechanism. A generic form asks the client to accept all risk. A strong proposal includes a conditional guarantee—e.g., a free technical audit within 30 days post-launch, or a performance-based holdback. This is not a discount; it is an architectural trust signal that differentiates you from every template-based competitor.

Vareli breaks this down in the complete analysis:
https://vareli.info/blog/example-of-web-design-proposal

title: Domain-Routed Delta Optimization for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
description:
arXiv:2611.13249v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation assigns each sample a domain teacher but typically updates shared student parameters. We introduce Domain-Routed Delta Optimization (DRD-MOPD), which specifies which parameter components each domain's samples update. The student is the sum of a frozen base and trainable components initialized from expert-minus-base weights. All components participate in every forward pass; four update modes define the correspondence between sample domains and components, each with independent optimizer states. We analyze these update rules and measure retention of the original expert geometry through angles, projection coefficients, and energy. Prior work such as Open-MOPD distills directly from the base model; 97.02% of its released final checkpoint's increment energy lies outside the span of the original expert directions. In comparison, our Own checkpoint after 20 updates retains coefficients near one along each component's original direction and pairwise angles ranging from 88.04 to 92.41 degrees; its exported BF16 student's increment has 4.90% outside energy, versus 10.52% for the sum of saved FP32 components. The same checkpoint achieves a 32.72% macro score across six benchmarks, compared with 32.44% for its initial task-arithmetic merge. These measurements describe geometry and capability at the evaluated training stages and settings.

title: On the information rate of phones, syllables and words
description:
arXiv:2611.13990v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Which linguistic units minimise the bitrate required to encode speech content: phones, syllables, words, maybe larger units, or something in between? This question has implications for the development of speech and language systems and theories of human language processing. Using a transcribed corpus of 960 hours of English audiobooks, I compare the information rates of phones, syllables, words, multi-word combinations and intermediate tokenisations. While all units are equivalent under a perfect language model, it makes sense to compare these under limited modelling budgets; I use $n$-gram and transformer language models. The lowest bitrates are achieved using words, with slightly longer units sometimes performing best. The results show that, when modelling capacity is limited, units larger than syllables but smaller than long multi-word phrases provide the most efficient representation in terms of information rate.

title: A Cross-Scenario Survey and Analysis of Self-Evolving Multimodal Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.14256v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent work shows that multimodal agents increasingly self-improve without recurring human annotation. However, each self-improvement mechanism is designed and evaluated within a single scenario, leaving its preconditions unverified under cross-scenario transfer. This survey investigates the structural source of asymmetric mechanism transfer across four scenarios: multimodal reasoning, multimodal generation, GUI and Web navigation, and embodied manipulation. We first formalize the self-evolving multimodal agent by four criteria and a differentia of self-reference, and adopt the three-stage self-evolving loop of experience generation, feedback acquisition, and update consolidation as our analytical framework to position the scenarios along ceilings on rollout count and feedback fidelity. Comparing self-evolving with fixed loops within each scenario separates the limitations that the scenario imposes from those inherent in the self-evolving design. We then recast each mechanism as a trade-off that raises a scarce factor by presupposing a task-structural resource, such as output equivalence or checkable outcomes, and judge it portable, conditional, blocked, or redundant across scenarios. We attribute the asymmetry to divergent combinations of scarce factors and resources across opposite transfer directions, and identify the matched-budget measurements that could overturn these still untested verdicts.

title: Enforcing Maker-Checker Approvals in Financial AI Agents: A Hybrid Gateway-Orchestration Topology
description:
As enterprise core banking platforms integrate Large Language Model (LLM) agents to automate operational decisions, governing AI Tool-Calling (Function Calling) has emerged as a primary architectural challenge. When an AI agent generates tool calls to execute REST APIs—such as initiating wire transfers, adjusting credit limits, or waiving fees—the system must enforce strict regulatory controls.

A common design pitfall is confusing Structural Access Control with Stateful Business Process Logic. Attempting to force an Identity and Access Management (IAM) provider like Keycloak to evaluate stateful financial metrics (such as fetching database balances or evaluating $10,000 threshold routing) introduces tight coupling, database latency, and broken execution flows. Throwing a 403 Forbidden error at the gateway for a high-value transaction kills the request entirely, preventing the system from ever instantiating the required human supervisor approval task.

Under the Xenon Architecture Standards, modern core banking platforms govern AI tool-calling through a Hybrid Gateway-Orchestration Topology. Structural capability authorization ("Is this AI agent allowed to invoke the wire transfer tool?") is handled at the perimeter gateway via Keycloak. Stateful context evaluation ("Does a $10,000 transfer require a human supervisor sign-off?") is handled within the durable execution layer via Temporal Sagas and Flowable DMN Engines.

💡 Explore the Xenon Architecture Standard For comprehensive architectural blueprints, BIAN service domain mappings, and dual-orchestration integration patterns, visit the official Xenon Architecture Guide. To inspect reference code, infrastructure templates, and open-source banking modules, explore the VecPay-Tech GitHub Organization.

Architectural Taxonomy: Capability vs. Context Governance

Separating Identity Capability from Business Context establishes clear boundaries across the BIAN (Banking Industry Architecture Network) ecosystem.

Governance Layer Primary Component Evaluation Scope State Requirement System Action on Positive Match System Action on Failure / Boundary Match
Structural Capability (Gateway) Keycloak IAM Token OAuth2 scopes (wire:execute), role claims, identity validity Stateless (Evaluates JWT claims) Pass request to API Ingress Gateway 403 Forbidden (Hard stop; blocks malicious calls)
Stateful Context (Orchestration) Temporal + Flowable DMN Transaction amounts, stateful balance lookups, DTI ratios Stateful (Queries core databases & DMN tables) Execute automated transaction Saga Suspend & Route (Generate Flowable Checker task)

Mathematical Model: Risk-Driven Workflow Routing

To evaluate whether an AI agent's tool payload requires human intervention, the durable workflow layer calculates a Contextual Risk Index Rcontext​ by combining real-time database facts with agent execution metrics:

Rcontext​=w1​⋅(ThresholdmaxRequested-Amount​)+w2​⋅(1−Cagent)+w3​⋅(Current-LimitRequested-Limit​)

Where:

  • Requested-Amount is the transaction value normalized against the BIAN domain cap Thresholdmax​ .
  • Cagent​ is the LLM agent's reported confidence score ( 0.0≤Cagent​≤1.0 ).
  • Current-Limit is fetched statefully from the core database during activity execution.
  • w1​,w2​,w3​ are policy weight vectors such that ∑wi​=1.0 .

If Rcontext​ exceeds defined DMN thresholds, Temporal does not fail the execution. It suspends the workflow state, generates a cryptographic approval token, and creates a Flowable Human Checker User Task.

Hybrid System Topology

The system separates perimeter identity validation from stateful business process routing.

                           HYBRID GOVERNANCE ARCHITECTURE

  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | PERIMETER GATEWAY LAYER (Stateless Capability Enforcement)                     |
  |                                                                                 |
  |  AI Agent Tool Call ---> [ API Gateway + Keycloak Filter ]                       |
  |                           ├── Missing Scope `wire:write` ──► [ 403 Forbidden ]  |
  |                           └── Has Valid Scope ───────────────► [ PASS ]         |
  +-----------------------------------|---------------------------------------------+
                                      |
                           1. Dispatch Authorized Tool Call
                                      |
                                      v
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | DURABLE ORCHESTRATION LAYER (Stateful Context Execution - Temporal)             |
  |                                                                                 |
  |  [ Start PaymentExecutionWorkflow ]                                             |
  |    ├── Activity: Fetch Stateful DB Balances & Credit Limits                     |
  |    └── Activity: Evaluate Business Rules (Flowable DMN)                         |
  +-----------------------------------|---------------------------------------------+
                                      |
            ┌─────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────┐
            | DMN Decision: AUTO_APPROVE                        | DMN Decision: REQUIRES_CHECKER
            v                                                   v
  +-----------------------------------+               +-----------------------------------+
  | MICROSERVICE SETTLEMENT           |               | FLOWABLE HUMAN WORKFLOW           |
  |                                   |               |                                   |
  | [ Executes Ledger Mutation ]      |               | 1. Create Human Checker Task      |
  +-----------------------------------+               | 2. Temporal Suspends (Awaits Sig) |
                                                      | 3. Human Checker Signs Off        |
                                                      +-----------------+-----------------+
                                                                        |
                                                               4. Send Temporal Signal
                                                                        |
                                                                        v
                                                      +-----------------------------------+
                                                      | MICROSERVICE SETTLEMENT           |
                                                      | [ Executes Ledger Mutation ]      |
                                                      +-----------------------------------+

Technical Implementation

1. Keycloak Gateway Filter (Stateless Capability Check)

This gateway component validates that the calling AI agent possesses the required structural OAuth2 scope (wire:execute) before allowing the request to enter the orchestration mesh.

package com.xenon.banking.gateway.filter;

import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.web.server.ServerWebExchange;
import org.springframework.web.server.WebFilter;
import org.springframework.web.server.WebFilterChain;
import reactor.core.publisher.Mono;

import java.util.List;

@Component
public class KeycloakCapabilityGatewayFilter implements WebFilter {

    @Override
    public Mono<Void> filter(ServerWebExchange exchange, WebFilterChain chain) {
        String path = exchange.getRequest().getURI().getPath();

        // Target AI tool-calling execution endpoints
        if (path.startsWith("/api/v1/tools/wire-transfer")) {
            List<String> authHeaders = exchange.getRequest().getHeaders().get("Authorization");

            if (authHeaders == null || authHeaders.isEmpty()) {
                exchange.getResponse().setStatusCode(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED);
                return exchange.getResponse().setComplete();
            }

            // Extract JWT and verify structural capability scope
            String token = authHeaders.get(0).replace("Bearer ", "");
            boolean hasWireScope = extractScopesFromJwt(token).contains("wire:execute");

            if (!hasWireScope) {
                // Structural failure: Hard fast-fail at gateway
                exchange.getResponse().setStatusCode(HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN);
                return exchange.getResponse().setComplete();
            }
        }

        // Structural check passed: Forward request to Temporal Workflow trigger
        return chain.filter(exchange);
    }

    private List<String> extractScopesFromJwt(String jwtToken) {
        // Standard stateless JWT claims parsing logic
        return List.of("wire:execute", "account:read");
    }
}

2. Temporal Workflow (Stateful Business Process & Signal Gateway)

The workflow orchestrates stateful database reads, evaluates dynamic DMN rules, and handles asynchronous human checker approval signals without terminating execution.

package com.xenon.banking.workflow;

import com.xenon.banking.activity.AccountStateActivities;
import com.xenon.banking.activity.BusinessRuleActivities;
import com.xenon.banking.activity.PaymentSettlementActivities;
import com.xenon.banking.model.DmnEvaluationResult;
import com.xenon.banking.model.PaymentExecutionPayload;
import io.temporal.activity.ActivityOptions;
import io.temporal.workflow.Workflow;
import io.temporal.workflow.WorkflowInterface;
import io.temporal.workflow.WorkflowMethod;
import io.temporal.workflow.SignalMethod;

import java.time.Duration;

@WorkflowInterface
public interface PaymentExecutionWorkflow {

    @WorkflowMethod
    void executePayment(PaymentExecutionPayload payload);

    @SignalMethod
    void receiveCheckerApproval(String checkerUserId, String approvalSignature);
}

public class PaymentExecutionWorkflowImpl implements PaymentExecutionWorkflow {

    private final AccountStateActivities accountActivities = Workflow.newActivityStub(
            AccountStateActivities.class,
            ActivityOptions.newBuilder().setStartToCloseTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)).build()
    );

    private final BusinessRuleActivities ruleActivities = Workflow.newActivityStub(
            BusinessRuleActivities.class,
            ActivityOptions.newBuilder().setStartToCloseTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)).build()
    );

    private final PaymentSettlementActivities settlementActivities = Workflow.newActivityStub(
            PaymentSettlementActivities.class,
            ActivityOptions.newBuilder().setStartToCloseTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10)).build()
    );

    private boolean checkerApproved = false;
    private String approvingCheckerId;

    @Override
    public void executePayment(PaymentExecutionPayload payload) {

        // 1. Stateful Data Fetching via Temporal Activity (Core DB lookup)
        double currentAccountBalance = accountActivities.fetchCurrentBalance(payload.getSourceAccount());
        String customerRiskTier = accountActivities.fetchCustomerRiskTier(payload.getSourceAccount());

        // 2. Evaluate Dynamic Business Rules via Flowable DMN Engine
        DmnEvaluationResult dmnResult = ruleActivities.evaluatePaymentRules(
                payload.getAmount(),
                currentAccountBalance,
                customerRiskTier,
                payload.getAgentConfidenceScore()
        );

        // 3. Process Execution Path Based on Business Rules
        if ("REQUIRES_CHECKER".equals(dmnResult.getDecision())) {

            // Instantiates Flowable Human Task for Supervisor Review
            String taskId = ruleActivities.createFlowableCheckerTask(
                    payload.getPaymentId(),
                    payload.getAmount(),
                    dmnResult.getReasoning()
            );

            Workflow.getLogger(PaymentExecutionWorkflowImpl.class)
                    .info("Payment " + payload.getPaymentId() + " requires Maker-Checker sign-off. Created Task: " + taskId);

            // Suspend workflow execution and await external Human Approval Signal
            Workflow.await(() -> checkerApproved);

            Workflow.getLogger(PaymentExecutionWorkflowImpl.class)
                    .info("Human Sign-Off received from Checker: " + approvingCheckerId + ". Resuming settlement.");
        }

        // 4. Final Settlement Execution
        settlementActivities.executeSettlement(payload.getPaymentId(), payload.getAmount(), approvingCheckerId);
    }

    @Override
    public void receiveCheckerApproval(String checkerUserId, String approvalSignature) {
        this.checkerApproved = true;
        this.approvingCheckerId = checkerUserId;
    }
}

3. Flowable Human Checker Task Signaling Bridge

When a human supervisor approves the task within the operational dashboard, this service emits a Temporal signal to wake up the suspended workflow.

package com.xenon.banking.bridge;

import io.temporal.client.WorkflowClient;
import org.flowable.engine.TaskService;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class FlowableTemporalBridgeService {

    private final TaskService flowableTaskService;
    private final WorkflowClient temporalWorkflowClient;

    public FlowableTemporalBridgeService(TaskService flowableTaskService, WorkflowClient temporalWorkflowClient) {
        this.flowableTaskService = flowableTaskService;
        this.temporalWorkflowClient = temporalWorkflowClient;
    }

    public void approveCheckerTask(String taskId, String checkerUserId, String cryptographicSignature) {
        // 1. Complete Flowable Task
        var task = flowableTaskService.createTaskQuery().taskId(taskId).singleResult();
        String paymentId = (String) flowableTaskService.getVariable(taskId, "paymentId");

        flowableTaskService.complete(taskId);

        // 2. Signal Temporal Workflow to resume execution
        var workflowStub = temporalWorkflowClient.newWorkflowStub(
                com.xenon.banking.workflow.PaymentExecutionWorkflow.class,
                "PaymentWorkflow-" + paymentId
        );

        // Emit signal directly into Temporal's event history
        workflowStub.receiveCheckerApproval(checkerUserId, cryptographicSignature);
    }
}

Analysis of Architectural Trade-Offs

Analyzing the hybrid architecture highlights how responsibilities are balanced across the stack.

1. Separation of Concerns & System Governance

  • Keycloak manages IAM scopes, OAuth2 client identities, and role assignments.
  • Temporal & Flowable DMN handle business logic, stateful database queries, and workflow routing.
  • Outcome: Security policies remain clean and stateless, while business workflows retain full access to operational context.

2. Dynamic Rule Management

  • Business parameters (such as lowering an approval threshold from $10,000 to $5,000) are managed inside the Flowable DMN Engine or dynamic configuration services.
  • Outcome: Rule adjustments take effect instantly without re-deploying microservices or updating Temporal workflow code.

3. Fast-Fail Security Protection

  • Invalid requests (e.g., an AI agent attempting an unauthorized API call without proper scopes) are blocked at the API Gateway by Keycloak.
  • Outcome: Malicious or malformed requests fail fast at the perimeter, preventing invalid state entries from polluting Temporal's event store.

4. Enterprise Audit Trails & Compliance

  • Keycloak logs authentication and token issuance events for IAM auditing.
  • Temporal maintains an event history recording the complete execution lineage: AI Agent initiated -> DMN evaluated -> Flowable task generated -> Human Checker signed off -> Settlement executed.
  • Outcome: Provides financial regulators (OCC, EBA, BCBS 239) with proof of non-repudiation and process compliance.

Decoupling structural access control from stateful business process routing establishes a resilient architecture for financial AI agents. Assigning capability validation to Keycloak at the gateway while executing contextual Maker-Checker workflows within Temporal and Flowable DMN allows core banking systems to preserve security perimeter defenses, maintain sub-second operational execution, and meet stringent regulatory requirements across all BIAN service domains.

title: Discovering Structurally Plausible and Interpretable Cognitive Models with Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.13561v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Computational cognitive modeling has traditionally relied on manual model construction, which is a time-intensive process that requires substantial domain expertise. Although recent LLM-based approaches have begun to automate model generation, they often prioritize predictive accuracy at the expense of structural plausibility and parameter identifiability. We introduce DisCo, an LLM-guided framework that discovers interpretable symbolic cognitive models through evolutionary search with two structural components: a Validator that filters structurally invalid models, and a Cleaner that promotes parameter identifiability by removing redundant parameters. Across three behavioral tasks, DisCo consistently discovers models that achieve performance competitive with task-specific baselines. Ablation analyses show that the Validator is important for recovering psychologically meaningful structure. Without this component, models tend to violate behavioral constraints and show less consistent associations with external cognitive measures. These results suggest that LLM-driven model discovery, when coupled with appropriate structural constraints, can yield cognitively plausible models that go beyond predictive fit.

title: Sanity Checks for Attention Surgery: Null Models and Matched Interventions for Representation-Motivated Design
description:
arXiv:2611.13543v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Transformer architectural modifications frequently measure a statistic on internal representations, observe that it is large, remove it architecturally, and report an improvement. Interpreting that sequence requires evaluating whether the statistic exceeds its noise floor, whether it survives a geometric null, and whether the training gain requires the specific direction removed. We formulate these requirements as three reusable checks and apply them to self-attention removal, which deletes the component of an attention head's output aligned with its own value vector. Across nine multi-head pretrained models (5,408 heads, 124M to 6.9B parameters), an earlier-position causal null accounts for 48% to 63% of the head-value cosine alignment, with no monotone scale trend. Under grouped-query attention, this alignment is specific to each head's own key-value group and reverses across groups (+0.24 to +0.27 within-group, -0.11 to -0.19 across-group). Split-half reliability demonstrates that the per-head intervention effect is resolvable in GPT-2 ($r_\Delta = 0.80$) but attenuated in Pythia-160M (0.42) and Pythia-410M (0.53), whereas structural self-cosine reliability is near-perfect in all three ($r_{\text{stat}} > 0.99$); which statistic predicts its own intervention is model-dependent. In a pre-registered 3-arm by 8-seed paired factorial at $4.0 \times 10^8$ tokens per run (399,900,672 tokens), a fixed arbitrary rank-one direction does not differ from baseline (+0.0011 nats, $p = 0.197$), while self-directed removal lowers validation loss (-0.0029 nats, Holm-corrected $p = 0.0023$) and outperforms the fixed arbitrary control directly (-0.0040 nats, $p = 0.0018$). At 50.9M scale the training benefit requires the own-value direction rather than a fixed arbitrary one, but a large cosine alignment alone does not establish redundancy in frozen models.

title: Deterministic, Reproducible Inference in Exact Integer Arithmetic, and Verifiable Distributed Inference as Its Consequence
description:
arXiv:2611.13730v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Optimized floating-point inference is not reproducible across environments: the same model on different hardware, compilers or thread counts can produce different bits. We present tritify, an open-source runtime that executes the forward pass of real models -- decoder-only language models, Mixture-of-Experts decoders, and the Segment Anything 2.1 image/video stack -- with the entire run-time path in exact integer arithmetic; floating point is confined to offline quantization and the float reference used for verification. We make three separate claims and verify each. (1) Cross-hardware reproducibility: the integer path produces bit-identical output run to run, across CPU instruction-set architectures, and across CPU/GPU, carried by a reproducing SHA-256 of the output. (2) Decision fidelity: the integer path reproduces the float reference's decision on the models and inputs tested, with the numeric exceptions measured; per-layer fidelity through sixteen layers of OLMoE-1B-7B and of a 106-billion-parameter MoE shows no fidelity cliff. (3) Location independence: a model's computation can be split across instruction sets, CPU and GPU, and networked machines with zero effect on the output bits. GLM-4.5-Air (106,852,251,264 parameters, 427 GB of integer codes) generated its answer across three machines, none of which can hold its integer codes in RAM, bit-identically to a single-host reference. The consequence is verifiable distributed inference: an untrusted server or a fleet of devices runs the model while an open scalar oracle re-derives the exact bytes; a guarantee against a dishonest server is future work. We do not claim a per-device speed-up, bit-equality of floating-valued intermediates, or confidentiality. Code: https://github.com/pelloran-inc/tritify

title: Track 1-star reviews of your app (and your competitors') across App Store and Google Play
description:
Your users tell you exactly what's broken — in 1★ reviews. The problem is that they're split between App Store and Google Play, across countries, and nobody reads them every day.

Here's a 10-minute setup that sends you only the new 1–2★ reviews mentioning "crash" or "login" for your app and your top competitor, from both stores.

The data

I built App Store & Google Play Reviews Scraper for this (disclosure: it's my Apify Actor): App Store reviews come from Apple's public reviews feed and Google Play reviews from the store's public pages, normalized into the same fields (rating, title, text, version, date, developer reply).

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("fujiwaranosai/app-reviews-scraper").call(run_input={
    "apps": [
        "https://apps.apple.com/us/app/spotify/id324684580",
        "play:com.spotify.music",
    ],
    "countries": ["us", "gb"],
    "maxRating": 2,
    "keywords": ["crash", "login", "freez"],
    "onlyNew": True,
})
for r in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(r["store"], r["country"], r["rating"], r["app_version"], r["text"][:120])

Turning it into a weekly report

Group by app_version and you immediately see which release introduced a problem. Group competitors' complaints by keyword and you have a list of features to build better than them.

Tips

  • App Store's public feed returns up to 500 recent reviews per country; add countries to get more.
  • onlyNew: true + a daily schedule = an alert channel instead of a spreadsheet you never open.
  • With star or keyword filters, maxReviewsPerApp counts the reviews you get back, not the ones read.
  • The first 500 reviews of every account are free; after that it's $0.15 per 1,000.

More ready-to-run examples: https://github.com/novosai0day-a11y/public-data-apis

title: EJAI: Judgment-Preserving Civic AI for Data Center Environmental Justice
description:
arXiv:2611.13525v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Communities in the United States and around the world are contesting data centers, the physical infrastructure of AI. These disputes pose environmental justice issues: residents must weigh unevenly distributed burdens using evidence scattered across metrics, corporate claims, policy documents, and public testimony. A formative study with 10 users showed that dashboards and single-agent AI can settle questions before people examine that evidence. Here we present EJAI, a source-grounded system that links an interactive map, retrieved evidence, missing-data statements, and two stakeholder personas that allow people to inspect evidence and form their own policy recommendations. In a small functional benchmark of 21 queries, retrieved evidence supported 98.4% of factual claims and the system acknowledged missing evidence in 32 of 33 cases. Persona alignment carried a grounding cost: the Corporate Executive omitted some evidence that conflicted with its assigned priorities. In a within-subjects study, 15 participants acting as residents prepared for a simulated town hall. Some checked cited AI claims while treating map metrics as official, some made conditional recommendations with safeguards such as water-use disclosure, and some found the personas simplified or biased. Our results suggest that civic AI can support preparation for public reasoning when it makes evidence, gaps, and disagreement open to inspection, and that corpus imbalance and two-sided personas remain open justice concerns.

title: From Neural Networks to Creative AI Tools: How Ruvarashe Is Making Development More Accessible
description:
📝 DEV STORY
Ruvarashe S Nemaramba
•
Developer
Interviewed by: Mehadi Hasan

Developer: Ruvarashe S. Nemaramba

Role: Artificial Intelligence Student, Developer & Technical Writer

Location: Mutare, Zimbabwe

Website: ruva.dev

Some developers build tools because they identify a gap in the market. Others build them because they remember struggling with a problem themselves. For Ruvarashe S. Nemaramba, the motivation behind one of her most meaningful projects came from the experience of being a beginner who simply wanted to understand what her code was doing.

Today, Ruvarashe is an Artificial Intelligence student at Africa University, exploring machine learning, deep learning, and creative computing while developing tools that make programming more approachable. Her work includes Code Learner, an AI-powered Visual Studio Code extension designed to help beginners understand code directly inside their development environment.

But her journey into technology did not begin with programming. It started with an interest in statistics and data, a university recommendation, and an unexpected introduction to neural networks. Along the way, she has also challenged conventional ideas about developer tools, demonstrating that technical functionality and personal creativity can exist together.

Her story offers an interesting perspective on learning AI, building for beginners, and finding your own identity as a developer.

From Statistics and Data to Artificial Intelligence
Ruvarashe's journey into technology began in 2024, after completing her A-levels the previous year. At the time, she was considering which university to attend and what degree to pursue. Although she had no previous experience in technology, she knew that she enjoyed statistics and working with data.

During a visit to Africa University in January 2024, she met a lecturer who asked what she wanted to study. When she explained her interests, he encouraged her to apply for the Artificial Intelligence degree programme.

Initially, she was hesitant. Technology was unfamiliar territory, and she had very little knowledge of programming or computer science. Nevertheless, after thinking about the opportunity for a few days, she decided to follow the recommendation.

Seven months later, she began her university classes.

The early experience was a significant adjustment. She recalls that she did not even know what a command line was. Her existing knowledge was centred on statistics and data rather than using computers to work with them.

Then came an introduction to neural networks.

During one class, the lecturer divided students into groups, and Ruvarashe ended up in the neural networks group. Within three days, she had explored the fundamentals of neural networks and discovered something that would shape her interests in technology.

She had fallen in love with the subject.

That initial experience helped establish her interest in artificial intelligence, particularly deep learning and the possibilities of teaching machines to recognise patterns and learn from information.

Learning to Build Solutions, Not Just Software
Studying for a B.Sc. Hons in Artificial Intelligence at Africa University has influenced more than Ruvarashe's technical knowledge. It has also shaped how she thinks about software development and problem-solving.

One important aspect of her academic experience is learning to consider the African context when developing technological solutions.

For her, building software is not simply about completing an assignment or implementing a feature. Developers need to understand the problem, consider the environment in which their solution will be used, and determine whether the result genuinely addresses the need.

She illustrates this with a university database assignment. Creating the database is only one part of the task. It is equally important to understand the problem it is intended to solve, how it fits into the wider African context, and whether the proposed solution is effective.

This perspective has encouraged her to approach development more critically.

Rather than immediately selecting a programming language, framework, or model, she believes developers should first understand the problem and identify the tools that are appropriate for solving it.

It is an approach that also appears in her thinking about machine learning and deep learning.

Understanding When to Use Machine Learning and Deep Learning
Ruvarashe has explored both traditional machine learning and deep learning, including the differences between the two approaches in her CoderLegion article, Machine Learning VS Deep Learning: What's the Difference?

One misconception she identifies among beginners concerns feature engineering.

Traditional machine learning often requires developers to manually select and engineer useful features from a dataset. Deep learning, on the other hand, can learn features and representations automatically during training.

Understanding this distinction can help developers make better decisions when choosing an approach.

Ruvarashe believes the dataset and the intended outcome should guide that decision.

For relatively small, structured datasets where interpretability matters and meaningful features can be identified, traditional machine learning may be the more appropriate choice.

For complex or unstructured data, such as images, deep learning can be particularly useful because it can learn intricate patterns and representations directly from the data.

Her approach is not to assume that one technique is always superior.

She also enjoys experimenting with different approaches, including exploring traditional machine learning models for image-related tasks, even though deep learning is more commonly associated with computer vision.

Working with tools such as Python, TensorFlow, Keras, and scikit-learn has reinforced this mindset.

She sees TensorFlow and Keras as particularly useful for neural networks, while scikit-learn offers tools for traditional machine learning, preprocessing, and evaluation.

The important lesson is that choosing a tool should come after understanding the problem, the available data, and the results a developer wants to achieve.

Code Learner: Turning a Beginner's Frustration Into an AI Tool
One project that stands out in Ruvarashe's development journey is Code Learner, an AI-powered Visual Studio Code extension designed to help beginners understand code without the additional complexity of configuring API keys or setting up external tools.

The idea came from a problem she had personally experienced.

When she was learning programming, looking at an unfamiliar line of code could feel like trying to understand another language. To get an explanation, she would often copy the code, write a prompt describing what she needed, and paste everything into ChatGPT.

Although the process worked, it involved unnecessary steps, particularly for someone who was still learning the fundamentals.

She began thinking about how to make that experience easier.

Code Learner brings AI-powered code explanations directly into the development environment. It uses a Large Language Model (LLM) to interpret and explain code, allowing beginners to understand what they are working with without repeatedly moving between different applications.

One of its particularly interesting features is the ability to analyse an entire code file and generate a flowchart representing its logic and execution flow.

This offers an alternative way to understand how a program works. Instead of relying entirely on written explanations, users can explore a visual representation of the code's structure.

For beginners who are still developing their ability to read and interpret code, this kind of visual assistance can make unfamiliar logic easier to approach.

What makes the project especially meaningful to Ruvarashe is its personal motivation.

She did not begin with an abstract idea of what an AI-powered developer tool should look like. She started with a frustration she understood from experience and attempted to create something that could make the learning process easier for others.

As she puts it, Code Learner is essentially a tool she wishes she had when she was first learning to code.

The Engineering Challenge Behind Making AI Accessible
Building an AI-powered feature is one challenge. Making it accessible to the people who need it is another.

During Code Learner's development, Ruvarashe had to think carefully about how users would access the underlying AI functionality.

One initial option was to ask users to download Ollama and run a model locally. However, the size of the models and the computing resources required would introduce another barrier for beginners.

Requiring users to provide their own API keys was not an ideal alternative either. Many people who are just starting to learn programming are unfamiliar with managing API credentials.

She eventually decided to implement a serverless proxy, allowing users to access the AI functionality without configuring their own API keys.

This made the initial user experience simpler, but it introduced a different engineering constraint.

The proxy currently relies on her own API key, making the extension dependent on the API provider's usage limits. As more people use the extension, those limits can become a bottleneck. The current arrangement is not designed to support sustained usage from a growing number of users.

Rather than treating this as a problem that can be ignored until later, Ruvarashe has been exploring possible improvements.

Two approaches she is considering are:

Bring Your Own Key (BYOK): An optional setting that allows users who prefer it to provide their own API credentials.
Daily usage limits: A way to manage API consumption and make usage more sustainable.
She is also interested in exploring other approaches that could help the system remain sustainable as its user base grows.

This experience has taught her an important lesson about software development: getting a feature to work is only part of building an application.

Developers also need to understand the services their applications depend on, the limitations of those services, and how those dependencies affect the ability to scale.

A design decision that makes an application easier to use initially may introduce operational challenges later. Those decisions sometimes need to be revisited as a project evolves.

For Code Learner, balancing beginner accessibility with sustainable API usage remains an important part of the development process.

Building Developer Tools With a Creative Identity
Not all of Ruvarashe's projects are focused on artificial intelligence. She also enjoys creating developer tools that combine functionality with visual creativity.

Interestingly, her first developer tool was a Visual Studio Code colour theme.

The motivation was simple: she could not find a pink theme that looked the way she wanted it to.

She noticed that she was not coding as much as she would have liked because she did not particularly enjoy the appearance of her development environment.

Her first attempt at creating a theme was unsuccessful. However, she decided to try again a week later and eventually published it.

She downloaded the theme herself and was happy that her IDE finally looked the way she wanted.

Then something unexpected happened.

Just two days after publishing it, she discovered that the theme had already received 26 installs.

She was genuinely surprised that other developers wanted to use something she had created.

That small experience encouraged her to continue building developer-focused tools, including playful extensions such as Bunny Code Tracker and Code Orb.

Her creative process often begins with inspiration from something outside the conventional developer space. She might see an interesting visual idea and start thinking about how it could be incorporated into an IDE.

For Ruvarashe, developer tools do not have to follow the familiar dark backgrounds and neon colours often associated with programming environments.

They can be colourful, playful, and personal while still serving a practical purpose.

Her philosophy is straightforward: technology can be functional without being boring.

Choosing Technologies That Support Creativity
Ruvarashe also brings this creative mindset into her personal web projects.

Her technology choices are influenced by the type of experience she wants to build rather than simply following popular trends.

For example, she chose Next.js for ruva.dev, her personal portfolio, because she wanted to create something more ambitious and interactive.

She appreciates the flexibility Next.js provides when working with complex interfaces, routing, and different rendering approaches.

Her experience with JavaScript, TypeScript, React, and Next.js has given her opportunities to experiment with different layouts, colours, and interactive elements.

She believes frameworks should provide structure and capabilities without limiting a developer's creativity.

The tools may determine how certain things are implemented, but they should not dictate the personality of the finished product.

This idea connects her portfolio, VS Code themes, and extensions. Each reflects an interest in making technology more personal and enjoyable to use.

Technical Writing as Another Way to Learn
Alongside development, Ruvarashe has also discovered an interest in technical writing.

She initially approached writing as a side hobby, mainly as a way to share her projects and reach a wider audience.

However, after publishing her first article, she realised that she genuinely enjoyed explaining technical concepts in a way that other people could understand.

She describes the experience as learning alongside her readers.

As she develops her own knowledge and works on new projects, someone reading her articles can follow a similar learning journey.

Writing has also improved her confidence in expressing ideas and sharing her work publicly.

More importantly, explaining technical concepts has encouraged her to understand them more deeply. Communicating an idea clearly requires more than simply knowing how something works; it requires understanding it well enough to explain it to someone else.

Her CoderLegion contributions reflect this combination of learning and sharing. Among her published articles are:

The Birth of Artificial Intelligence
The New ML Perspective
Machine Learning VS Deep Learning: What's the Difference?
Five Internship Mistakes I Made
These topics span artificial intelligence, machine learning, and professional development, reflecting her interests as both a student and an emerging developer.

Looking Beyond the Current AI Landscape: NLP and African Languages
Although deep learning currently holds a special place in Ruvarashe's interests, Natural Language Processing (NLP) is one area she particularly wants to explore further.

She is interested in how machines can understand, interpret, and generate human language.

One area that stands out to her is the development of language technologies for African languages.

Many African languages remain underrepresented in language technology development, creating an opportunity to explore AI applications that are more relevant to different linguistic communities.

She is particularly interested in conversational AI and machine translation, as well as building systems that can understand language more effectively and make communication easier.

This interest also connects with her broader academic perspective.

Just as she believes software solutions should consider the African context, she sees opportunities for AI systems to become more accessible by supporting linguistic communities that are often overlooked.

Her ongoing exploration of PyTorch, computer vision, image processing, and NLP provides several directions for further learning, but language technology is an area she is especially excited about.

Learning to Adapt: Lessons From an Internship
Technical knowledge is only one part of professional development. Ruvarashe has also learned important lessons through her internship experience.

In her CoderLegion article Five Internship Mistakes I Made, she reflected on some of the challenges she encountered.

The lesson that had the biggest impact on her was learning not to have too many expectations.

Entering an opportunity with a fixed idea of what she should learn or how the experience should unfold sometimes made it easier to overlook the value of what was actually happening.

Her experience taught her that learning does not always take place in a structured or carefully guided environment.

Sometimes valuable lessons come from unexpected situations and experiences.

She has since adopted a more open approach to professional opportunities, allowing herself to learn, adapt, and make the most of what comes her way.

Her academic achievements have also encouraged her to continue developing.

She received Dean's List recognition at Africa University and completed the Matsuo-Iwasawa Lab's Global Consumer Intelligence course.

Rather than viewing these achievements as final destinations, she sees them as reminders that the time and effort invested in learning matter.

They motivate her to keep challenging herself, exploring new areas, and taking advantage of opportunities for academic and professional growth.

Building a Career Around Useful and Enjoyable Technology
Looking ahead, Ruvarashe wants to become a developer who creates projects that make a difference while remaining enjoyable and fun to use.

Artificial intelligence is an important part of that ambition, but she is also interested in exploring different areas of technology and finding creative ways to apply what she learns to real-world problems.

She wants to continue experimenting, building tools that reflect her personality, and exploring ideas that might otherwise seem unconventional.

Beyond the projects themselves, she hopes her work will encourage other people to explore technology and start building things of their own.

This ambition connects directly with her experience developing Code Learner. A tool created to help beginners understand code is also an example of how personal experiences can inspire solutions that may benefit others.

For her, meaningful development is not only about technical complexity. It is also about whether something is useful, accessible, and enjoyable for the people who use it.

Advice for Developers Starting Their AI Journey
For students and beginners who want to enter artificial intelligence, the number of programming languages, frameworks, libraries, and concepts can feel overwhelming.

Ruvarashe's advice is to take things day by day and remember that everyone learns at their own pace.

Comparing your progress with someone else's can create unnecessary pressure. Someone who appears to be further ahead is not necessarily an indication that you are falling behind.

Instead, she encourages beginners to:

Trust themselves and their ability to learn.
Stay curious and continue exploring.
Experiment with ideas, even when they seem unfamiliar.
Avoid being afraid of mistakes.
Put their work out there and learn from the experience.
Give themselves enough time to develop their skills.
She believes a lot of learning happens along the way, especially when developers are willing to explore things they do not fully understand yet.

Her own journey is a useful example. She entered university without knowing what a command line was, discovered neural networks within her first classes, and eventually began developing AI-powered tools of her own.

Progress does not always happen immediately, and the results of consistent effort may not be visible at first.

But as she reminds beginners, keep showing up. Eventually, you will look back and realise just how far you have come.

About Ruvarashe S. Nemaramba
Ruvarashe S. Nemaramba is an Artificial Intelligence student, developer, and technical writer at Africa University in Zimbabwe. Her interests include machine learning, deep learning, creative computing, computer vision, image processing, and Natural Language Processing.

She works with Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, SQL, React, Next.js, TensorFlow, Keras, and scikit-learn. Her projects include Code Learner, an AI-powered Visual Studio Code extension designed to make understanding code easier for beginners.

She also enjoys creating developer tools, VS Code themes, and playful extensions that combine practical functionality with creative design. Outside development, she enjoys crochet and designing cute, pink-themed developer tools.

title: Adaptive catalyst discovery emerges from composable scientific intelligence
description:
arXiv:2611.13536v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Catalysis underpins chemical manufacturing, yet knowledge for catalyst design remains dispersed across experimental observations, computational data and catalysis subdisciplines. To overcome this challenge, we present Composable Catalytic Intelligence (CatAI), a physics-grounded modular AI framework that learns 1.8 million structure-property relations and organizes them into 30 physicochemical encoders. This reusable intermediate layer enables task-specific models to guide catalyst discovery for targeted reactions and objectives. Across benchmark tasks, CatAI achieves a 7.8% lower task-averaged prediction error than the next-best models. In experimental validation, CatAI identified a new confined-passable pocket catalyst applicable in industrial homogeneous polymer synthesis with 9 times the activity of the commercial benchmark. In parallel, it guided autonomous closed-loop optimization of a highly active Cu-based geminal-atom photocatalyst for C-O coupling reactions surpassing the traditional Ni-based systems. This approach connects property-level data to catalytic objectives, supporting physicochemical knowledge reuse across mechanistically distinct systems through computational screening and iterative model-experiment feedback.

title: I rechecked 23 public MCP issues on GitHub. OAuth sign-in and docs mismatches came up most.
description:
On 10 November 2026 I went through public GitHub issues on MCP servers that were already in that week's research notes, and rechecked each issue the same day through the public GitHub Issues API. The set is 23 issues, and two classes came up more than any other: OAuth sign-in that fails before the server is usable, and docs that don't match the live server.

At the recheck, about 16:00 Europe/Sofia, 21 issues were open and 2 had been closed as completed earlier that day. 5 of the 23 are feature requests, and I list them separately near the end. Some of the open issues were opened in October.

I didn't file these issues and I didn't reproduce them, so everything below is what the issue itself says. I don't name the projects. Each section gives the failure class, then what to check on your own connector.

1. OAuth sign-in fails before the server is usable

Five open issues describe a client that can't finish sign-in, or that signs in and then gets an expired-session or invalid-client error.

  1. Dynamic client registration accepts a loopback redirect URI such as http://127.0.0.1:53682/, then the authorize endpoint answers invalid_redirect for that same URI. Repeating the flow with http://localhost:53682/ works, and registering with application_type: "native" doesn't change the result.
  2. A hosted server can't be connected from the Claude.ai connector because OAuth fails at dynamic client registration. The quoted error begins "Couldn't register with" and then names the vendor's sign-in service.
  3. A second server fails the same way when it's added as a remote connector in Claude Desktop with automatic registration. This issue was opened in October and was still open on 10 November.
  4. VS Code's MCP client registers through POST /register and persists the client_id it's issued. After the server evicts or expires that id, /authorize fails with "Invalid client_id".
  5. initialize succeeds, then every tools/call returns a session-expired message or a 401 for a dynamically registered client. The issue says a fresh authorization and a brand-new client registration still fail within two minutes of the token being issued, while the same account works at the same time through the Claude connector.

Check on your connector:

  1. Register a client dynamically, then send the redirect URI that registration accepted to the authorize endpoint. Do it once with 127.0.0.1 and once with localhost.
  2. Add the server as a connector in each client your users run, with automatic registration, and watch whether registration completes.
  3. Remove a registered client_id on the server, start sign-in again from the client that still holds it, and read the error the client gets.
  4. After initialize, call a tool with a token issued a few seconds earlier to a dynamically registered client.

2. Docs, skills or the listed schema don't match the live server

Five issues fall here. Two of them were closed as completed on 10 November, so I describe those two in the past tense.

Closed as completed:

  1. A documented Claude Desktop setup put a remote server in claude_desktop_config.json with only url and headers. The issue says that file only accepts local stdio servers, where each entry needs a command, so Claude Desktop rejected the entry and the server never loaded. The docs also said 6 or 7 tools depending on the page, while the server registers 8 core tools plus 6 more on API-key connections. The issue was closed 25 minutes after it was opened. A comment on it says the production docs were updated and verified live the same day: the Claude Desktop pages now give an mcp-remote command entry, and the API reference says 8 core tools.
  2. A config class had a fluent instructions() method, but filters was only a public property, so ->filters([]) threw an unknown-method error. The issue was closed as completed the same day.

Open on 10 November:

  1. A hosted tools/list marks a parameter as required on two tools. The issue says calls without it succeed, sending it doesn't change the output, and the main branch has no such parameter on either tool.
  2. A README's Claude Code install command uses npx -y @anthropic-ai/mcp-remote. The issue says that npm package doesn't exist and the registry returns 404.
  3. Two skills call MCP actions that the live tool reference doesn't list. The reporter checked the public tool reference on 9 November 2026.

Check on your connector:

  1. Run every documented install command, and paste every documented config block into the client it names, on a machine that has never had your server on it.
  2. Count the tools tools/list returns, then compare that number with every page that states one.
  3. Diff the hosted tools/list against the tool definitions on your main branch, required parameters included.
  4. For each skill you ship, look up every action it calls in the live tool list.

3. Tool annotations a directory checklist flags

One issue, opened in October and still open on 10 November, says none of a server's 39 registered tools passes a title. It states that Anthropic's Connectors Directory requires a title plus readOnlyHint or destructiveHint on every tool. It also says two tools that overwrite an existing object at the same key are marked destructiveHint: false.

Check on your connector:

  1. Confirm every tool has a title and carries readOnlyHint or destructiveHint.
  2. Call each write tool against a target that already exists. If the call replaces what was there, the tool modifies data and destructiveHint: false is the wrong annotation.

4. Install, runtime and argument coercion

Three open issues fall here.

  1. A fresh install exits on startup with ImportError: cannot import name 'eval_type_backport' from 'pydantic._internal._typing_extra'. The issue attributes it to a pin on mcp[cli]==1.6.0 with pydantic left unpinned, after pydantic 2.14.0 removed that private name.
  2. Number(null) and Number("") are both 0, so an optional max-age parameter sent as null becomes 0, and 0 forces a live crawl.
  3. A tool call ended with MCP call failed: TimeoutError: MCP call timed out after 300.0s (configured timeout: 300.0s) and no result. The issue records one attempt, so it says nothing about how often this happens or why.

Check on your connector:

  1. Install into an empty environment, with no lockfile and no cached image, and start the server.
  2. Send null and "" for every optional number, and compare the result with leaving the field out.
  3. Make the upstream API hang, then look at what the client receives and how long it waits.

5. The connection reports connected and the agent has zero tools

One open issue reports a regression after a version upgrade: tools/list returns 403 and the agent sees zero tools, while the connection is still reported as connected.

Check on your connector: after every upgrade, call tools/list with the credentials an agent uses and count the tools that come back. The connected status in that report didn't show the failure.

6. A cache keyed on the raw caller URL, with no size bound

One issue, opened in October and still open on 10 November, says a docs client keys its cache on the caller's raw URL, has no size bound and no eviction, and removes an expired entry only when the same key is read again. It adds that the live docs site returns 200 for query-variant URLs, so each variant is cacheable.

Check on your connector: for every cache in the server, write down the key, the size bound and the moment an expired entry is removed. If the key is caller input, count how many distinct keys one caller can create.

7. The documented remote URL doesn't accept the connection

One issue, opened in October and still open on 10 November, says adding the documented remote MCP URL as a Claude.ai custom connector fails at the first step with "Couldn't reach this address". After "Continue anyway" the connector saves, but it stays in a "needs reconnect" state with no tools exposed.

Check on your connector: add the URL from your docs as a custom connector in the client the docs name, and confirm the tools appear.

8. Link-formatted values that don't open

One open issue says link-formatted values in an MCP view don't open in Claude on the web, and that the view should use ui/open-link.

Check on your connector: click every link your views render, in the web client.

The five feature requests

Five of the 23 issues ask for something new, and I don't count them as failures:

  1. OAuth support in an MCP client toward MCP servers (RFC 9728 discovery and PKCE).
  2. Per-user SQL identity through JWT passthrough on a shared HTTP deployment.
  3. MCP management of public sharing.
  4. Create-environment and delete-variables tools on a hosted MCP server.
  5. Native Streamable HTTP and/or SSE transport, so a server can be hosted remotely instead of only as local stdio. This request was opened in October and was still open on 10 November.

MCP connector review

If you want an outside review before your connector goes to customers or the Claude directory, I do an MCP connector review: an independent review of your existing MCP connector against Anthropic's connector pre-submission checklist.

  1. Every tool goes through the MCP Inspector, and through Claude as a custom connector where hosting allows it.
  2. Every tool is tested with valid input, bad input, denied access and an upstream error.
  3. The permission boundary is checked with two users.
  4. You get a checklist report where each finding has severity, impact, reproduction steps and a proposed fix.
  5. You get one retest after you fix the findings.

I don't claim the review would have caught every class in this article. Anthropic doesn't run, approve or certify it, and it can't guarantee a Community or Verified listing.

The scope is on the MCP connector review page.

If the server isn't built yet, the MCP build is an MCP server over your existing API: four to six read-only tools, one sign-in flow and deployment to your infrastructure. Following the checklist doesn't mean Anthropic approves or certifies the connector.

title: Are Dense Rewards Worth Their Tokens in GRPO?
description:
arXiv:2611.13560v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: RLVR trains language models to reason by rewarding correct final answers. A widely used algorithm, group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), gives every token of a solution the same credit, so dense process rewards have been proposed to credit intermediate steps, for example with a Monte-Carlo reward that scores each step by sampling continuations from it. Comparing such a reward with GRPO per training update, or vetting it with a gradient test on a single batch, leaves out what it costs: in our setting, the continuations alone take 91% of all generated tokens. We introduce a matched-compute protocol that gives every training intervention the same budget, measured in generated tokens and training GPU-hours, and tests it in preregistered studies with controls for side effects. Across 1,668 runs on six models, matching compute reverses the ranking. On Qwen2.5-1.5B, the Monte-Carlo reward leads standard GRPO per update, yet ends 14.3 percentage points lower at equal tokens and 7.8 points lower at equal training time, and none of four dense-reward variants outperforms GRPO even with as much training time. A per-token gradient test orders these rewards as training does but overestimates each by one to two points, as much as the gains it is meant to detect. In contrast, training on the prompts whose predicted success is nearest 1/2 improves accuracy at matched compute, by 1.7 points on Qwen3-0.6B and 0.8 on Qwen2.5-1.5B. These gains replicate on fresh seeds and unseen problems, and a simple rule, that the candidate prompts are predicted to fail more often than not, predicted where they appear in five of six preregistered tests. Both gains come early in training, and standard GRPO with twice the initial learning rate comes within half a point of them. We argue that training interventions should be validated at matched compute, which overturns some apparent gains and confirms others.

title: Comparing SMM Panel Service Lists for the Philippine Market with Python and Pandas
description:
If you run or resell social media services in the Philippines, you eventually end up with three or four panel service lists open in different tabs, trying to compare TikTok views prices in pesos. Here's a small pandas workflow that makes that comparison sane.

Get the data into one shape

Most panels using the standard /api/v2 pattern return services as JSON with service, name, category, rate, min, max and sometimes refill. Save each panel's response to a file first, then load them together.

import json
import pandas as pd

def load(path, panel, currency, php_rate=1.0):
    rows = json.load(open(path, encoding="utf-8"))
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    df["panel"] = panel
    df["rate"] = pd.to_numeric(df["rate"], errors="coerce")
    # normalise everything to PHP per 1,000
    df["php_per_1k"] = df["rate"] * (php_rate if currency != "PHP" else 1.0)
    df["refill"] = df.get("refill", False).fillna(False).astype(bool)
    return df[["panel", "service", "name", "category", "php_per_1k", "min", "max", "refill"]]

frames = [
    load("panel_a.json", "panel_a", "PHP"),
    load("panel_b.json", "panel_b", "USD", php_rate=57.0),  # use today's rate
]
services = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)

Filter to what you actually sell 

mask = services["name"].str.contains("tiktok", case=False) & \
       services["name"].str.contains("view", case=False)
tiktok_views = services[mask].sort_values("php_per_1k")
print(tiktok_views.head(10).to_string(index=False))

Don't sort by price alone

The cheapest row is rarely the best buy. Add a column for your own test results, like the share delivered and the share still there after 7 days, then rank by effective cost.

tests = pd.read_csv("test_orders.csv")  # panel, service, kept_ratio
merged = tiktok_views.merge(tests, on=["panel", "service"], how="left")
merged["effective_php_per_1k"] = merged["php_per_1k"] / merged["kept_ratio"].fillna(0.5)
print(merged.sort_values("effective_php_per_1k").head(5))

A missing test defaults to a pessimistic 0.5 so untested services don't sneak to the top.

A note on currency

Exchange rates move. Keep the PHP rate as a parameter, not a hardcoded constant buried in the code, and refresh it before every comparison.

For the business side of picking suppliers in the Philippines, this boosting site social media growth guide explains what PH buyers expect. And BoostingPH publishes peso rates directly, which skips the conversion step above.

Mighil

Anelka Bagalane

Aoyue Design

📰 Classifieds

🔁 Your agent checks web work with a refresh. On mobile it needs a device. Expo Simulators gives it one in the cloud.

title: When Reasoning looks like Hidden Understanding: How Chain-of-Thought Fosters Anthropomorphism, Perceptions of Epistemic Superiority, and Cognitive Deference
description:
arXiv:2611.13456v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As AI-based products permeate society, specifically systems using generative models, a belief system is emerging about what these products are and what they can and cannot do. One common belief concerns the perception of the form of language as evidence of 'understanding' language. As these generative models reproduce linguistic patterns rather than understand meaning, interpreting these patterns as evidence of understanding is a misattribution. This misconception is extended by the notion that generative models can 'explain their reasoning.' Anecdotally, these misconceptions which mistake the form of language for its meaning are driving cognitive deference to AI systems in a way that displaces human agency. Such mistakes involve attributions of cognitive properties to the system, allowing them to be treated like intentional 'minds'. Importantly, perceived epistemic authority and superiority make that 'mind' worth deferring to. Anthropomorphism in tandem with epistemic authority and superiority, we argue, increases the risk that users generalise from narrow task performance to broader competencies, committing the "fallacy of composition". This paper explores misconceptions of Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning as sufficient transparent 'explanation'. We explore how anthropomorphism acts as a vehicle for cognitive deference of decision-making and perceptions of epistemic superiority in AI systems. Finally, we explore CoT's ramifications using medicine as an example. Taken together, we conclude that explainability operationalised through CoT is highly problematic and undercuts the very ethical principles it is intended to serve. While CoT may be valuable for improving output accuracy and moderation, we suggest that the practice of asking models to provide user facing reasons for their outputs should be actively discouraged, and AI literacy training should explicitly caution against its use.

title: Region-Wise Logit Fusion and Utility-Gated Refinement for Brain Metastasis Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2611.13884v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: BraTS-METS 2026 Task 1 evaluates segmentation of brain metastases and postoperative resection cavities on heterogeneous multiparametric MRI, requiring detection of small enhancing foci while preserving the geometry and hierarchy of enhancing tumor (ET), tumor core (TC), whole tumor (WT), and resection cavity (RC). We present COMPASS-METS (Component-Aware Multi-Trainer Probability Assembly with Structured Segmentation), which combines three five-fold nnU-Net configurations into aligned regional probability ensembles. A structured-probability anchor applies region-specific component decisions, TC boundary completion, RC filtering, and hierarchy-preserving conversion. Omitted ET candidates are recovered additively using learned component confidence and deterministic multi-trainer support for ET and its TC/WT parents; a final utility gate admits only disconnected candidates with sufficient lesion-existence and geometry-safety probabilities. On the reused 179-case challenge development cohort, COMPASS-METS (Team: MicroBT) achieved Small F1 0.354, lesion-wise DSC 0.712, NSD 0.714, All F1 0.779, and HD95 56.6 mm. Relative to ResEncXL, it improved DSC, NSD, and All F1 and reduced HD95, while Small F1 changed from 0.367 to 0.354. Stagewise analysis attributes the principal geometric gains to structured probability construction and shows that guarded ET refinement recovers most of the associated small-lesion detection loss. These 179-case results remain selection-aware development estimates. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/leonlou921/COMPASS-METS.

title: Obscured Wildfire Flame Detection by Spatio-temporal Analysis of Smoke Patterns Using Frame-wise Transformers
description:
arXiv:2611.14074v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this paper, we propose a new paradigm in wildfire management for detecting both visible and obscured fire using Deep Learning (DL). The essence of our method is the joint spatial and temporal analysis of RGB videos, embracing the fact that temporal patterns of smoke motions in consecutive video frames can indicate obscured fire flames. This perspective contrasts the traditional approach of independently analyzing images and individual video frames. To this end, we propose a frame-wise transformer architecture that applies an attention mechanism between the consecutive frames while preserving spatial information within frames as opposed to regular attention mechanisms like the non-local block, which combines spatial and temporal information into a single vector. We also optimize the temporal pattern lengths under different spatial resolutions to achieve the highest performance while reducing the computational cost. To investigate the applicability of our method in aerial image processing, we applied it to a curated version of the FLAME2 dataset that includes dual-mode RGB/IR videos. The IR video feed is used to extract ground truth, while the model is trained only on RGB videos to maintain applicability to lowcost commercial drones (which are equipped only with regular cameras) and facilitate processing existing RGB-only datasets. Our proposed method achieves a Segmentation Foreground Dice score of 92.61%, an Object Detection Precision and Recall rate of 93.21% and 91.73%, and clip-level classification accuracy of 98.02%, respectively. We also investigated the efficacy and generalizability of our method through ablation study
