title: Instance-preserving graded semantic reporting for surgical action triplets
description:
arXiv:2611.13009v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Complete-or-reject reporting of surgical action triplets can discard a correctly identified instrument and action when the target is uncertain. We introduce instance-preserving graded semantic reporting, which separates instance selection from the choice of semantic detail. Each selected instance retains its predicted mask and labels while hierarchical correctness scores guide instrument (I), instrument-verb (IV), or complete instrument-verb-target (IVT) reporting. The utility-increment rule DELTA weighs the expected gain from finer reporting against its error cost. We compare three decision rules on 5,641 test frames from eight surgical videos using fixed predictions and scores. At the 10% development calibration target, DELTA retains correct partial reports for 80.0% of candidates rejected by a matched complete-or-reject baseline (5,329/6,662). Adding IV increases source-normalized weighted correct-report yield by 19.13 to 23.13 per 100 frames across all three rules relative to separately recalibrated I/IVT controls. Weighted reporting risk changes by -0.77 to +1.01 percentage points, with complete correct-triplet counts unchanged or reduced. Graded reporting makes partial surgical predictions available as localized descriptions, with an explicit trade-off between report utility and completeness.

title: Applying ReAct Agents to Exception Recovery in Distributed Sagas
description:
The Saga pattern is the industry standard for maintaining eventual consistency across microservices without distributed two-phase commits (2PC). In a Saga, a sequence of local transactions executes across domain boundaries. If any step fails forward execution, the Saga orchestrator (such as Temporal) executes compensating transactions in reverse order to undo previously committed changes.

However, modern distributed systems face a critical failure mode: The Failed Compensation Paradox. What happens when a compensating action itself fails?

For instance, in a Payment Execution workflow, if a downstream ledger debit succeeds, but a subsequent sanctions check fails, the orchestrator triggers a compensating refund activity. If that refund API returns a 500 Internal Server Error, times out, or encounters an unexpected schema constraint, the Saga enters a stalled, indeterminate state.

Historically, core banking architectures handle failed compensations by halting the workflow and emitting an operational alert to a manual exception queue. In high-volume environments, this creates massive operational queues, inflates Recovery Time Objectives (RTO), and exposes customer balances to inconsistent holds.

Under the Xenon Architecture Standards, modern core banking platforms eliminate manual triage bottlenecks by deploying Autonomous ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) Agents as dynamic self-healing nodes. When a Temporal Saga compensation branch fails, an isolated ReAct agent analyzes the failure context, queries live microservice telemetry, executes corrective tool actions in real time, and either restores the compensation path or cleanly escalates to human operators.

💡 Explore the Xenon Architecture Standard For comprehensive architectural blueprints, BIAN service domain mappings, and dual-orchestration integration patterns, visit the official Xenon Architecture Guide. To inspect reference code, infrastructure templates, and open-source banking modules, explore the VecPay-Tech GitHub Organization.

BIAN Service Domain Exception Recovery Matrix

Within a Banking Industry Architecture Network (BIAN) topology, compensation failures vary in operational complexity. The ReAct agent exception recovery framework establishes clear toolsets and boundary limits mapped by domain criticality.

BIAN Service Domain Failed Compensation Scenario ReAct Agent Toolset Maximum Autonomy Bounds Fallback Action
Payment Execution Refund API returns 500 due to temporary ledger lock inspectLedgerLock(), retryWithBackoff(), forceReleaseLock() Retry count <= 3; Max amount <= $50,000 Escalate to Payment Ops Task
Position Keeping Reversing balance hold fails due to account status change getAccountState(), rerouteToSuspenseAccount(), logAudit() No direct balance overrides; Suspense routing only Route to Risk Officer Queue
Foreign Exchange (FX) Unwinding FX spot rate lock fails due to expired quote fetchCurrentFxRate(), negotiateSlippage(), rebookFxLock() Slippage tolerance <= 0.10% Freeze FX Position & Alert Desk
Consumer Loan Origination Reverting collateral reservation fails due to lock contention queryCollateralState(), clearLockKeys() Non-destructive database lock release Re-queue for Scheduled Batch Worker

Mathematical Model: Self-Healing Reliability & Unresolved Saga Risk

To quantify the risk reduction achieved by autonomous ReAct compensation repair, we model the overall unresolved Saga probability Punresolved-saga​ across distributed banking transactions.

Let Pforward-fail​ be the probability of a forward transaction step failing, and Pcomp-fail​ be the conditional probability that a registered compensating action fails due to transient infrastructure outages or state locks. The baseline unresolved Saga rate without AI self-healing is:

Pbaseline-risk​=Pforward-fail​×Pcomp-fail​

By introducing a ReAct agent to inspect and repair failed compensations across K reasoning iterations, the joint unresolved Saga probability becomes:

Punresolved-saga​=Pforward-fail​×Pcomp-fail​×i=1∏K​(1−Pagent-repair-i​)

Where Pagent-repair-i​ is the probability that the agent successfully diagnoses the root cause and executes an authorized corrective tool action during iteration i . Assuming Pagent-repair​≈0.85 over 2 reasoning loops, the manual operational exception queue footprint is reduced by over 97%.

Architectural Topology: The ReAct Saga Repair Engine

The architecture separates Deterministic Workflow Orchestration (Temporal) from Autonomous Reasoning (ReAct Agent). The workflow definition remains 100% deterministic, while non-deterministic AI reasoning executes inside a specialized Temporal Activity.

                       REACT SAGA COMPENSATION RECOVERY TOPOLOGY

  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | TEMPORAL SAGA WORKFLOW ENGINE                                                   |
  |                                                                                 |
  |  [ Forward Transaction Steps ] ───► ( Fail ) ───► [ Execute Compensation ]      |
  |                                                               │                 |
  |                                                      Compensation Fails         |
  |                                                               │                 |
  |                                                               v                 |
  |  [ Saga Suspended ] ◄── ( Return Final Status ) ─── [ Invoke ReAct Activity ]   |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------|------------------+
                                                                 |
                                       1. Pass Execution Trace & | Payload
                                                                 v
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | REACT AGENT REPAIR ACTIVITY (Non-Deterministic Reasoning Loop)                  |
  |                                                                                 |
  |  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
  |  | ReAct Execution Loop (Max 3 Iterations)                                  |  |
  |  |                                                                           |  |
  |  |  1. THOUGHT: "Refund failed with HTTP 500. Inspecting ledger locks..."   |  |
  |  |  2. ACTION:  Call tool `inspectLedgerLock(accountId)`                     |  |
  |  |  3. OBSERVE: "Stale optimistic lock found on row #9012."                  |  |
  |  |  4. THOUGHT: "Clearing stale lock key and retrying refund API..."         |  |
  |  |  5. ACTION:  Call tool `clearLockKey(accountId)` -> `retryRefund()`       |  |
  |  |  6. OBSERVE: "Refund API succeeded with Transaction ID TX-8812."          |  |
  |  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------|------------------+
                                                                 |
                                       2. Return Repaired Status | Payload
                                                                 v
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | IMMUTABLE COMPLIANCE AUDIT STORE                                                |
  |  [ Persists Complete ReAct Thought-Action-Observation Trace & Signatures ]      |
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Technical Implementation: Temporal Workflow & ReAct Engine

1. Temporal Workflow with Compensation Fallback (Java 21)

The workflow executes forward steps within a try-catch block. If a compensating activity throws an unrecoverable exception, control shifts to the ReActSagaRepairActivity.

package com.xenon.banking.saga.workflow;

import com.xenon.banking.saga.activity.PaymentActivities;
import com.xenon.banking.saga.activity.ReActRepairActivity;
import com.xenon.banking.saga.model.PaymentSagaInput;
import com.xenon.banking.saga.model.RepairResult;
import io.temporal.activity.ActivityOptions;
import io.temporal.workflow.Workflow;
import io.temporal.workflow.WorkflowInterface;
import io.temporal.workflow.WorkflowMethod;

import java.time.Duration;

@WorkflowInterface
public interface ResilientPaymentSagaWorkflow {
    @WorkflowMethod
    void processPaymentSaga(PaymentSagaInput input);
}

public class ResilientPaymentSagaWorkflowImpl implements ResilientPaymentSagaWorkflow {

    private final PaymentActivities paymentActivities = Workflow.newActivityStub(
            PaymentActivities.class,
            ActivityOptions.newBuilder().setStartToCloseTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10)).build()
    );

    private final ReActRepairActivity repairActivity = Workflow.newActivityStub(
            ReActRepairActivity.class,
            ActivityOptions.newBuilder().setStartToCloseTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(45)).build()
    );

    @Override
    public void processPaymentSaga(PaymentSagaInput input) {
        boolean ledgerDebited = false;

        try {
            // Step 1: Debit Source Ledger Account
            paymentActivities.debitSourceAccount(input.getPaymentId(), input.getSourceAccount(), input.getAmount());
            ledgerDebited = true;

            // Step 2: Perform Real-time Sanctions Screening (Fails intentionally for demonstration)
            paymentActivities.executeSanctionsScreening(input.getPaymentId(), input.getDebtorName());

        } catch (Exception forwardException) {
            Workflow.getLogger(ResilientPaymentSagaWorkflowImpl.class)
                    .warn("Forward execution failed. Starting compensation. Error: " + forwardException.getMessage());

            if (ledgerDebited) {
                try {
                    // Attempt Standard Compensation: Refund Source Account
                    paymentActivities.refundSourceAccount(input.getPaymentId(), input.getSourceAccount(), input.getAmount());
                    Workflow.getLogger(ResilientPaymentSagaWorkflowImpl.class).info("Compensation succeeded standard execution.");

                } catch (Exception compensationException) {
                    Workflow.getLogger(ResilientPaymentSagaWorkflowImpl.class)
                            .error("CRITICAL: Compensation failed! Invoking Autonomous ReAct Repair Agent...");

                    // Invoke ReAct Repair Activity to autonomously triage and repair state
                    RepairResult repairResult = repairActivity.repairFailedCompensation(
                            input.getPaymentId(),
                            input.getSourceAccount(),
                            input.getAmount(),
                            compensationException.getMessage()
                    );

                    if (!repairResult.isRepaired()) {
                        // ReAct agent failed or reached maximum safety limits -> Escalate to Human Queue
                        repairActivity.escalateToHumanQueue(input.getPaymentId(), repairResult.getReasoningTrace());
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

2. ReAct Engine Repair Activity Implementation (Java 21)

This Java activity executes the Thought-Action-Observation reasoning loop. It inspects diagnostic tools, analyzes exception context, and takes corrective action within strict safety bounds.

package com.xenon.banking.saga.activity;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import com.xenon.banking.saga.model.RepairResult;
import io.temporal.activity.Activity;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

@Component("reActRepairActivity")
public class ReActRepairActivityImpl implements ReActRepairActivity {

    private final MicroserviceDiagnosticToolSet toolSet;
    private final ObjectMapper objectMapper;

    public ReActRepairActivityImpl(MicroserviceDiagnosticToolSet toolSet, ObjectMapper objectMapper) {
        this.toolSet = toolSet;
        this.objectMapper = objectMapper;
    }

    @Override
    public RepairResult repairFailedCompensation(String paymentId, String accountId, double amount, String failureMessage) {
        var activityContext = Activity.getExecutionContext();
        String workflowId = activityContext.getInfo().getWorkflowId();

        List<String> reasoningTrace = new ArrayList<>();
        reasoningTrace.add("INITIAL OBSERVATION: Compensation failed for payment [" + paymentId + "]. Error: " + failureMessage);

        int iteration = 0;
        int maxIterations = 3;
        boolean repaired = false;

        while (iteration < maxIterations && !repaired) {
            iteration++;
            reasoningTrace.add("--- REACT ITERATION " + iteration + " ---");

            if (iteration == 1) {
                // THOUGHT 1: Inspect database locks and service availability
                reasoningTrace.add("THOUGHT 1: Inspecting if account [" + accountId + "] is currently locked by concurrent workers.");

                // ACTION 1: Invoke Diagnostic Tool
                String lockStatus = toolSet.inspectAccountLock(accountId);
                reasoningTrace.add("ACTION 1: Called tool inspectAccountLock(" + accountId + "). Result: " + lockStatus);

                if (lockStatus.contains("STALE_LOCK_FOUND")) {
                    // THOUGHT 2: Clear stale lock key
                    reasoningTrace.add("THOUGHT 2: Stale lock detected. Attempting non-destructive lock clearance.");

                    // ACTION 2: Clear stale lock
                    boolean lockCleared = toolSet.clearStaleLock(accountId);
                    reasoningTrace.add("ACTION 2: Called tool clearStaleLock(" + accountId + "). Success: " + lockCleared);
                }
            } 
            else if (iteration == 2) {
                // THOUGHT 3: Retry the refund transaction API after lock cleanup
                reasoningTrace.add("THOUGHT 3: Retrying compensating refund transaction API...");

                // ACTION 3: Retry Refund Execution
                Map<String, Object> refundResponse = toolSet.retryRefundApi(paymentId, accountId, amount);
                reasoningTrace.add("ACTION 3: Called tool retryRefundApi(). Response: " + refundResponse.get("status"));

                if ("SUCCESS".equals(refundResponse.get("status"))) {
                    repaired = true;
                    reasoningTrace.add("OBSERVATION: Compensation successfully repaired and executed!");
                } else {
                    reasoningTrace.add("OBSERVATION: Refund API failed again. Details: " + refundResponse.get("error"));
                }
            }
        }

        return new RepairResult(repaired, String.join("\n", reasoningTrace));
    }

    @Override
    public void escalateToHumanQueue(String paymentId, String reasoningTrace) {
        System.err.println("ESCALATING TO HUMAN OPS: Payment " + paymentId + "\nTrace:\n" + reasoningTrace);
        // Create Flowable Human User Task for operational staff review
    }
}

Bounded Autonomy & Deterministic Safety Guardrails

Allowing an autonomous agent to execute diagnostic tools over financial databases introduces operational risk if left unconstrained. ReAct repair activities must operate within strict Safety Guardrails:

                       REACT AGENT BOUNDED AUTONOMY MATRIX

  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | REACT AGENT REASONING ENGINE                                                    |
  +----------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+
                                           |
                                 Proposed Tool Execution
                                           |
                                           v
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | POLICY-AS-CODE GUARDRAIL INTERCEPTOR (OPA / DMN)                                |
  |                                                                                 |
  |  Check 1: Is Tool Permitted? ────► `clearStaleLock()` ──► [ ALLOWED ]          |
  |  Check 2: Is Action Destructive? ─► `deleteAccount()`   ──► [ BLOCKED ]          |
  |  Check 3: Max Monetary Value? ───► `overrideBalance()`  ──► [ BLOCKED > $10k ]   |
  +----------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+
                                           |
                                   Validated Tool Call
                                           |
                                           v
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | MICROSERVICE DIAGNOSTIC LAYER                                                   |
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Core Safety Rules

  1. Max Reasoning Iterations: The ReAct loop is strictly bounded (e.g., maximum 3 iterations). If the agent cannot diagnose and repair the issue within 3 cycles, it must halt and escalate.
  2. Forbidden Tool Actions: ReAct agents are strictly prohibited from invoking destructive API endpoints (e.g., deleteRecord(), truncateLedger(), or directBalanceCredit()). Agent tools must be read-only diagnostics or safe, idempotent retry handlers.
  3. Monetary Value Limits: If a failed compensation involves an amount exceeding a defined threshold (e.g., > $50,000), the ReAct activity bypasses autonomous repair entirely and routes the transaction directly to human underwriters.

Observability, Forensic Lineage, and Regulatory Audit

Financial regulators (such as OCC, EBA, and MAS) require full explainability for autonomous self-healing actions. System history must record not only the outcome, but the complete Thought-Action-Observation chain.

Audit Payload Structure (react-saga-audit.json)

For every self-healing execution, the ReAct activity logs an immutable audit event to the central compliance data lake (Elasticsearch / ClickHouse):

{
  "auditId": "AUDIT-REACT-2026-770192",
  "temporalWorkflowId": "PaymentSaga-PAY-90128",
  "temporalRunId": "c89f102a-331b-429a-b802-991204812a41",
  "bianDomain": "PaymentExecution",
  "paymentId": "PAY-90128",
  "failedCompensationActivity": "refundSourceAccount",
  "originalError": "HTTP 500 Internal Server Error: LockWaitTimeoutException",
  "reActExecutionTrace": [
    {
      "step": 1,
      "thought": "Inspecting account lock state to determine root cause of 500 error.",
      "action": "inspectAccountLock",
      "actionInput": {"accountId": "ACC-GB-40912"},
      "observation": "Found stale lock held by dead worker pod payment-worker-77b"
    },
    {
      "step": 2,
      "thought": "Lock is stale. Clearing lock key to allow compensation API to proceed.",
      "action": "clearStaleLock",
      "actionInput": {"accountId": "ACC-GB-40912"},
      "observation": "Lock key cleared successfully."
    },
    {
      "step": 3,
      "thought": "Retrying refund compensation activity now that lock is cleared.",
      "action": "retryRefundApi",
      "actionInput": {"paymentId": "PAY-90128", "amount": 1250.00},
      "observation": "Refund API responded HTTP 200 OK. Transaction ID: TX-88120"
    }
  ],
  "repairStatus": "SUCCESSFULLY_REPAIRED",
  "executionDurationMs": 1420,
  "timestamp": "2026-09-16T12:30:00Z"
}

Integrating autonomous ReAct agents into Temporal Saga exception workflows resolves the long-standing challenge of failed compensations in distributed core banking. By isolating non-deterministic reasoning inside bounded Temporal Activities, enforcing Policy-as-Code safety limits, and maintaining cryptographic auditability, modern financial architectures eliminate operational queue bloat, achieve sub-second self-healing, and protect end-to-end data integrity across all BIAN service domains.

title: From Process Models to Composable Agentic Workflows: Combining BPMN, Agents and Enterprise Knowledge
description:
arXiv:2611.13196v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-based agents can reason, use tools and collaborate. However, coordinating increasingly complex agentic applications becomes difficult to understand, monitor and improve. Decisions distributed across prompts, tool calls and application logic make workflows implicit. We introduce **Recursive Capability Composition**, enabling agents to execute business processes and expose them as reusable Agentic Tools.
  This paper presents a BPMN-based approach to Agentic Workflows, combining explicit orchestration with autonomous reasoning. SemTalk BPMN models are transformed into executable workflows using a LangGraph/Pregel runtime. Agentic Tasks introduce LLM reasoning at selected activities, while conventional BPMN controls process flows, deterministic decisions, system interactions and human approvals. Agentic Participants provide reusable interfaces for agent behavior or other executable processes.
  BPMN orchestration makes multi-agent systems more understandable and manageable. Explicit process models provide developers and operators with a shared view of workflow structures and execution progress, facilitating debugging, monitoring and optimization.
  Enterprise agents also need organization-specific context. Process Models and Knowledge Graphs describe activities, participants, information objects, decisions and relationships between processes. They provide structured knowledge of how an organization operates, supporting informed agent decisions and actions.
  Our contributions are threefold: 1. **Model-Driven Execution:** Transforming BPMN models into executable Agentic Workflows. 2. **Recursive Capability Composition:** Exposing agents and executable business processes as reusable tools for other agents. 3. **Enterprise Context:** Using Process Models and Ontologies to provide organization-specific knowledge for agent reasoning.

title: Vercel Flags starts 7x faster and no longer extends function duration
description:
On Vercel, the Vercel Flags SDK now initializes faster on cold starts, and usage reporting no longer keeps functions running after the response.

Faster cold starts

Two changes speed up SDK initialization on cold starts:

  • The SDK loads and parses the flags datafile bundled with your deployment as soon as the client is created, so it’s ready before your code evaluates its first flag.

  • Every function invocation now includes the current datafile revision, so the SDK can check whether the bundled datafile is up to date without a network request.

In internal testing, eliminating the network wait reduced p75 cold-start SDK initialization time from over 70 ms to 10 ms, roughly 7x faster.

After initialization, flag reads are effectively instant. Across cold and warm invocations, p99 flag-read latency is under 1 ms.

Usage reporting no longer extends function duration

The SDK previously used waitUntil for usage reporting, keeping functions running after the response was sent. It now passes usage events to the Vercel runtime, so reporting no longer adds to function duration.

title: Graph Visualizations in Prompts for Knowledge Graph Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2611.12938v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study when and how multimodal input improves knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) in large vision--language models. Using a controlled evaluation over 1,500 WebQSP and CWQ questions and six VLMs within a fixed KGQA pipeline, we compare text-only prompting against text-plus-graph visualization at the per-question level and analyze performance changes as a function of reasoning complexity, model size, and image layout. Adding a graph image yields an average gain of 1.85 F1 points, driven by strong precision improvements on low-complexity questions (+4.65 F1). Mixed-effects and regression analyses show that these multimodal gains do not depend strongly on model scale, but are highly sensitive to graph layout: image-only settings sharply degrade performance, hierarchical Graphviz layouts outperform less organized renderings, and decomposing large subgraphs into separated paths yields the largest improvements. Taken together, the results indicate that visual prompting primarily aids KGQA by enhancing prediction precision in low-complexity contexts, provided that visual design respects cognitive and perceptual constraints. To optimize both accuracy and inference efficiency, we argue for adaptive visual prompting policies that selectively append diagrams to small, visually sparse subgraphs with well-structured layouts, avoiding unnecessary visual clutter and token overhead on complex queries. We conclude by relating these findings to a visual notation design theory, outlining how principled diagram encoding can guide future multimodal VLM prompting.

title: Massive Activations Confound Sparse Autoencoders
description:
arXiv:2611.13548v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are commonly evaluated by variance explained and ablation damage. We show how massive activations undermine both evaluations, and propose a correction. Massive activations cause up to 99.9% of activation variance to lie along the first principal component (PC1). Because the PC1 component has no unique sparse decomposition, each SAE run rebuilds it from a different set of features. These features dominate importance rankings: an average of 47 of the 50 most important features are unmatched in a separate run, compared with about 27 of a random 50. A dictionary can also report 99.96% of variance explained while leaving 33% of the variance outside PC1 unexplained. We bypass PC1 by training the SAE on activations with PC1 removed, then adding PC1 to the reconstruction. In affected models, the top-50 feature sharing rate rises from 4-39.5% to 73-99.5%. At the same TopK sparsity, the resulting SAE degrades the model up to 44% less and reduces content reconstruction error by up to 33.9%.

title: G-STAR: Group-Scaled Token Capacity for Deeply Compressed Autoregressive Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.13004v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Discrete autoregressive models offer a scalable framework for image generation. However, they face a fundamental trade-off: long token sequences preserve representation quality but slow generation, while aggressive spatial compression reduces representation capacity. Based on product quantization, we show that, under a fixed nominal information budget, group size should scale quadratically with the per-axis spatial compression factor. Building on this principle, we propose GSTAR, a spatial--group co-scaling framework that enables \(32\times\) and even effective \(64\times\) compression while preserving strong reconstruction, understanding, and generation performance. Since larger groups introduce intra-group dependencies that must be modeled efficiently, we analyze their impact on inference latency and generation quality and introduce a semi-autoregressive decoder that combines parallel feature computation with lightweight causal modeling. With these designs, our highly compressed models perform competitively with leading models across five representative text-to-image benchmarks (GenEval, DPG-Bench, PRISM, LongText-Bench, and Qwen-Image-Bench). At \(1024\times1024\) resolution, our model delivers a \(20\times\) speedup over prior discrete autoregressive models, generating each image in 2.5 seconds on a single NVIDIA H200. Together, these results show that highly compressed discrete representations can enable high-quality autoregressive generation at low latency.

title: Measuring Definition Sensitivity in LLM Annotation of Social Science Concepts
description:
arXiv:2611.13339v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In social science research, text annotation is a fundamental task that is traditionally a costly, hard-to-scale manual process. Researchers have used large language models (LLMs) to perform annotation by writing a definition of a concept into a prompt - a rule that determines whether a label should be attributed to a text depending on its content. However, concepts such as hate speech, fake news, and terrorism typically have several theoretically defensible competing definitions. It is also unknown whether the model actually applied the definition to provide the label or the label was based on the model's pretrained notion of the concept. To test this, we have the model annotate the same texts twice, each time with a different definition. We call the disagreement between the two sets of annotations definition sensitivity. As a control, we paraphrase one definition but leave its requirements unchanged - the disagreement between the annotations with the two wordings becomes the paraphrase floor. Across six concepts and three LLMs, a swap of competing definitions always changes more annotations, on average, than a paraphrase. This shows that the annotations depend on the prompted definition, so any set of annotations should be interpreted together with the definition that produced it. The LLM annotator's definition sensitivity and its paraphrase floor should both be reported in such work.

title: AutoManifold: Agentic Design of Data Visualisation Algorithms via Manifold Embedding
description:
arXiv:2611.13710v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Manifold embedding for data visualisation is dominated by a small set of hand-designed state-of-the-art (SOTA) algorithms. Their design targets are fixed at development time, resulting in inflexible algorithmic behaviour that cannot be readily steered towards user-specified structural priorities. Hand-designing new embedding algorithms to address user priority requires highly specialised expertise and is time consuming. To address autonomous algorithm design tailored to user preference, we introduce an agentic algorithm generation pipeline AutoManifold. It composes new manifold embedding algorithms from a constrained vocabulary of affinity, cost, and optimisation primitives, supported by multi-agent large-language-model (LLM) orchestration. AutoManifold conditions every stage of its design on user-specified structural preservation preferences, and iteratively refines the algorithm configuration through an LLM-guided, metric-grounded iterative loop. We compare the generated algorithms against the three strongest and most frequently used SOTA methods (t-SNE, UMAP, and PaCMAP) on real-world datasets spanning different difficulty regimes under identical evaluation infrastructure. The results demonstrate that LLM-driven, priority-conditioned algorithm synthesis can move beyond hyperparameter tuning, producing genuinely new algorithms that outperform traditional hand-designed methods in their ability to steer towards user-specified properties without compromising the intrinsic structure in the original data. The code of AutoManifold is available at https://github.com/buraksusam/AutoManifold_NeurIPS2026.

title: Dyship: Leveraging Acoustic Features For Speaker Relationship Classification From Dyadic Conversations
description:
arXiv:2611.14241v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce DyShip, a framework for classifying speaker familiarity and kinship from dyadic conversations in the Seamless Interaction corpus. We compare five speech representations: spectrograms, MFCCs, self-supervised WavLM representations, x-vectors, and estimated articulatory movements. Spectral features perform best for familiarity classification, reaching an accuracy of 87.81%, while WavLM achieves the highest kinship accuracy of 85.17%. X-vectors and articulatory features yield weaker results on familiarity classifiaction, but shine for kinship classification, with an AUC of 0.909 for x-vectors. Most classifiers exceed previously reported human and audio language model scores on the same dataset. These findings highlight the potential of conventional acoustic features for relationship inference and motivate further investigation of the conversational cues captured by different representations.

title: 3 UX Design Courses Worth Taking If You’ve Already Mastered the Basics
description:
Go beyond the fundamentals with three courses that can help experienced product designers sharpen their skills.

After a few years working in product design, you likely reached a point where learning another prototyping trick or reviewing the basics of user research doesn’t bring much value.

That’s because challenges you face are different from the challenges you’ve faced at the beginning of your career journey: you need to design more complex systems and make sure the products your team builds will satisfy the growing expectations of your audience.

Interaction Design Foundation (IxDF) has three dedicated courses that could be particularly interesting for seasoned product design professionals like you. And you will find links to FREE trials to top 3 most interesting courses.

1. Object-Oriented UI Design: Build Interfaces Users Love

45 lessons | 9.25 hours in total

(Link to the course)

One of the biggest challenges in product design is managing complexity. As products grow, they accumulate new features, workflows, and navigation patterns. Without a proper design process, eventually, the product becomes a collection of disconnected screens.

Object-oriented UI design offers a different way to approach the problem of raising complexity: instead of starting with individual features or screens, you begin by identifying the objects users interact with and the relationships between them.

For example, imagine you’re designing a project management application. Rather than starting with a dashboard, task list, or settings page, you identify the core objects: projects, tasks, team members, and milestones. Then you define what users can do with these objects and how they relate to each other.

Object-Oriented UI Design course explores 3 important topics:

  • Key point #1: Turn requirements into structured interface models. You’ll learn how to translate user needs, use cases, and requirements into conceptual models. These models help define the underlying structure of a product before you begin designing individual screens.
  • Key point #2: Prioritize features based on user needs. The course introduces persona-based feature prioritization, including matrices that help designers evaluate which features matter most to different user groups. This can be particularly useful when stakeholders have conflicting priorities or when a product has accumulated too many features.
  • Key point #3: Create a better connection between design and development. Another interesting part of the curriculum is the use of design maps and different levels of design detail, from essential concepts to implementation specifications. The goal is to help you communicate not just what the interface looks like, but also how the product is structured and how it should behave.

Why I recommend it: I think this course is especially valuable for seasoned designers working on enterprise software, complex SaaS applications, and other products with complex information structures. It can help you move from designing individual screens to designing coherent product systems.

2. Game UX Design: The Ultimate Guide

83 lessons | 18.5 hours

(Link to the course)

You don’t need to be a game designer to learn something valuable from game UX. In fact, I think game design is one of the most interesting fields to study if you want to understand how people interact with digital products.

Traditional UX design typically focuses on reducing friction and helping users complete tasks efficiently. Game design introduces another dimension: How do you create experiences that people want to engage with?

Games are particularly interesting because they challenge the traditional assumption that every obstacle in the user journey is a usability problem. Sometimes, difficulty is part of the experience. The challenge is understanding the difference between intentional difficulty and unnecessary frustration.

The Game UX Design is taught by Celia Hodent, former UX Director for Fortnite and author of The Gamer’s Brain. The curriculum covers cognitive psychology, motivation, usability, and behavioural design.

Here are 3 important points you will learn:

  • Key point #1: Understand how attention and memory influence user experience. You’ll explore how the brain processes information, why people overlook important interface elements, and why users often forget instructions shortly after reading them.
  • Key point #2: Design for intrinsic motivation. Another important topic is Self-Determination Theory. The course explores three fundamental psychological needs: competence, autonomy, and relatedness. These concepts help explain why some experiences feel naturally engaging while others rely heavily on external rewards, notifications, or artificial incentives.
  • Key point #3: Understand the relationship between challenge, feedback, and flow. The course also explores flow states, emotional design, reward systems, and how games teach players through interaction. One particularly interesting idea is designing onboarding as part of the experience rather than forcing users through a separate tutorial.

Why I recommend it: This course is a great opportunity to explore UX from a different perspective. Even if you never plan to design a video game, studying cognitive psychology, feedback, and motivation can help you create more thoughtful interactive experiences.

3. Accessibility in Practice: Build Digital Experiences Everyone Can Use

38.75 hours | 63 lessons

(Link to the course)

Accessibility is often treated as a checklist that designers review near the end of a project. Teams check colour contrast, add labels to form fields, fix a few issues, and assume the product is accessible.

But accessibility is much more complex than that.

Creating a truly accessible product requires understanding how people with different abilities perceive, navigate, and interact with digital interfaces.

For experienced product designers, accessibility is not only about individual design decisions. It’s also about creating processes, patterns, and systems that help an entire organisation deliver inclusive experiences consistently.

Accessiblity in practice, taught by Frank Spillers, covers accessibility from fundamental standards to organisational implementation.

Here are 3 areas I find particularly valuable.

  • Key area #1: Go beyond basic WCAG compliance. The course explores accessible interaction patterns, keyboard navigation, focus management, semantic HTML, ARIA, forms, menus, and dynamic content. It also discusses the limitations of relying entirely on automated accessibility tools.
  • Key area #2: Learn how to test accessibility with real users.Accessibility cannot be fully evaluated by inspecting a design file. The course covers accessibility testing in context, working with assistive technologies, and involving users with disabilities in research and evaluation.
  • Key area #3: Scale accessibility across an organisation. This is probably the most interesting part of the course for senior designers and design leaders. The curriculum includes building accessibility roadmaps, creating organisational programs, defining responsibilities, and making the business case for accessible design.

Why I recommend it: Accessibility is an essential part of professional product design. This course is particularly valuable for designers who want to move beyond fixing individual accessibility issues and start influencing how their organisations build products.

Final Thoughts

What I like about 3 three courses is that they approach product design from different perspectives.

Object-Oriented UI Design course focuses on the structure of digital products. It’s particularly valuable when you need to manage complex requirements and design scalable interfaces.

Game UX Design focuses on human behaviour. It helps you understand the psychological principles behind attention, motivation, and engaging interactions.

Accessiblity in practice focuses on inclusive experiences and organisational maturity. It teaches you how to make accessibility an integral part of the design process rather than an afterthought.

3 UX Design Courses Worth Taking If You’ve Already Mastered the Basics was originally published in UX Planet on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: The Indic Token Tax in 2026: Measuring Tokenizer. Disparity and Its Cost for the Languages of India
description:
arXiv:2611.13058v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Commercial language model APIs bill per token, so a tokenizer that needs more tokens for the same content in one language makes that language more expensive, slower, and able to fit less text in a fixed context window. We measure this disparity for nine public tokenizers, including those of GPT-4, GPT-4o, Qwen2.5, DeepSeek-V3, Mistral-Nemo and four Sarvam models, on all 25 languages of India available in FLORES-200 (2,009 professionally translated sentences aligned with English) and on 13,732 human-translated Hinglish-English social media pairs from PHINC. On GPT-4o's tokenizer the same content needs between 1.57 times (Hindi) and 5.01 times (Odia) the tokens of English, and 13.7 times for Santali in Ol Chiki script; GPT-4's tokenizer needs up to 12.8 times. Sarvam-30B/105B is the only third-party tokenizer that stays below 2.6 times on every language (median 1.53). In an illustrative scenario using official list prices accessed on 5 November 2026 and stated assumptions, a support bot handling 100,000 chats a month on GPT-4o would cost about INR 56,640 in English and INR 102,829 in Marathi; these are estimates, not measured production costs. Against an openly licensed Hindi and Marathi morphological segmentation set, no tokenizer places more than 35% of its word-internal boundaries on morpheme boundaries (boundary F1 at most 0.48). In a companion paper we present a tokenizer that reduces this tax. Code, pinned artifacts and raw token counts are available at https://github.com/HavonAI/indic-token-tax.

title: How to Route Users to the Nearest Healthy Region Automatically (and How Fast Each Method Fails Over)
description:
Route users to the nearest healthy region with latency-based or geo-based DNS routing backed by health checks, an anycast global load balancer, or a platform that combines deployment and routing behind a global endpoint. How fast traffic moves away from a failed region depends on how quickly health checks detect the failure and how long clients hold onto the old DNS answer. Failover is often slower than expected when nobody has measured the full chain from detection to the last cached client. This guide compares the three methods, works out worst-case failover times from each provider’s documented defaults, and explains how to test the result.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

Three methods route each user to the nearest healthy region automatically:

  • Platforms with a built-in global endpoint. A platform like Control Plane deploys one workload definition to multiple locations and routes each user to the nearest location where the workload is healthy, using the workload’s own readiness probes, with no per-service DNS records or external health checks to configure.
  • DNS routing with health checks. Amazon Route 53, Azure Traffic Manager, and Google Cloud DNS answer each query with the closest healthy endpoint. Failover time is health check detection plus DNS TTL plus resolver and client caching.
  • Anycast global load balancers. AWS Global Accelerator, Google Cloud’s global external Application Load Balancer, and Azure Front Door announce anycast IP addresses from edge locations and forward traffic to healthy backends. Failover avoids DNS caching; with default health checks it ranges from about 10 to 30 seconds (Google Cloud) to about 90 seconds or more (Global Accelerator, and Azure Front Door with Microsoft’s example settings), and tuning brings it lower.

Failover time is detection (health check interval × failure threshold) plus propagation (DNS TTL and caching, near zero for anycast) plus the time long-lived connections take to close. Test by failing a health check on purpose and timing the shift with synthetic probes and with real clients that cache DNS.

How do I route users to the nearest healthy region automatically?

Automatic region routing rests on two building blocks: choosing the nearest region, and removing an unhealthy region from the pool.

Choosing the nearest region can be done by latency or by geography. Latency-based routing uses the provider’s latency measurements between the user’s network (identified by the resolver’s IP, or the client subnet when the resolver sends EDNS Client Subnet) and each region, then returns the lowest-latency region. Geolocation routing maps the user’s IP to a country or subdivision and returns a pre-assigned region. VPNs and mobile carriers can make a geographically close region slower than a distant one, and both methods see the resolver’s location instead of the user’s when the resolver does not send EDNS Client Subnet.

Removing an unhealthy region requires active health checks. The routing system probes each regional endpoint on a schedule. If a probe fails a configured number of times in a row, the region is marked unhealthy and excluded from routing answers. When it passes enough consecutive checks, it is added back.

DNS routing with health checks

DNS routing services answer each query by latency or geolocation policy and stop returning an endpoint’s IP once it fails its health check. Resolvers and clients cache answers for the TTL and sometimes longer, so some clients keep reaching the failed region until their cached answer expires. Weighted, geolocation, and failover policies give fine-grained control over which users reach which region.

Anycast global load balancers

Managed anycast load balancers announce the same anycast IP addresses from many edge locations. BGP delivers each client to a nearby edge, which forwards traffic to the closest healthy backend region. When a region fails its health checks, the edge stops sending it traffic. The anycast IP and BGP announcements stay the same, so failover waits on neither DNS TTL nor BGP convergence. Plain anycast setups that you run yourself fail over by withdrawing a region’s BGP route instead.

Platforms with a built-in global endpoint

Some platforms run one workload definition in multiple regions behind a global endpoint that handles health-aware routing, which removes much of the work of configuring DNS records, health checks, and failover policies separately for each service.

How fast each routing method fails over

Values are defaults and configurable ranges documented on each provider’s own pages. Detection time is roughly the health check interval multiplied by the failure threshold (Traffic Manager marks an endpoint unhealthy only after tolerated failures plus one consecutive failure; Front Door and Cloudflare use sample- and quorum-based rules). Propagation covers DNS TTL plus resolver and client caching for DNS methods, or the time the edge takes to stop sending to a failed backend for anycast methods. Totals are estimates from documented defaults.

Method How it picks a region Health check defaults Detection time (defaults) Propagation delay Worst-case switch time (estimate) Notes
Amazon Route 53 latency or geolocation routing with health checks Latency or geolocation DNS policy 30 s interval × 3 failures (default; threshold 1 to 10); fast checks: 10 s interval ~90 s (standard); ~30 s with fast checks TTL you set (AWS recommends 60 s or less with health checks) plus resolver and client caching ~2.5 minutes to several minutes Checkers run from multiple regions; the endpoint is marked unhealthy when 18% or fewer of checkers report it healthy.
Azure Traffic Manager (performance routing) Latency-based DNS 30 s interval; tolerated failures 3 (range 0 to 9); probe timeout 10 s ~2 min (marked degraded after the fourth consecutive failure) Profile TTL (Azure CLI default 30 s; can be set as low as 0 s) plus resolver and client caching ~2.5 minutes to several minutes Supports custom headers in probes. Microsoft says failover can complete under 10 s after an endpoint goes unhealthy with 10 s probes, 0 tolerated failures, and TTL 0.
Google Cloud DNS routing policies with health checks Geolocation, weighted round robin, or failover DNS policy External endpoints: 30 to 300 s interval × unhealthy threshold (Google Cloud default 2); internal load balancers: their own health check (default 5 s × 2) ~60 s at the 30 s minimum interval for external endpoints; ~10 s for internal load balancer targets TTL you set plus resolver and client caching ~1 minute plus TTL to several minutes Public zones health-check external IPs, including a global external Application Load Balancer VIP; private zones health-check internal load balancers.
AWS Global Accelerator Anycast; routes to the nearest healthy endpoint group 30 s interval × 3 (default; interval 10 or 30 s, threshold 1 to 10) ~90 s No DNS change; the anycast IPs stay advertised and the edge sends new connections to the next healthy endpoint group ~90 to 120 s These settings apply to EC2 and Elastic IP endpoints; ALB and NLB endpoints use Elastic Load Balancing target-group health checks.
Google Cloud global external Application Load Balancer Anycast; routes to the nearest healthy backend 5 s interval × 2 failures, 5 s timeout (defaults) ~10 to 15 s No DNS change; the anycast VIP stays advertised and Google’s front ends stop sending requests to unhealthy backends ~10 to 30 s Fastest defaults in this table. Each backend service can set its own health check.
Azure Front Door Anycast; routes to the nearest healthy origin 30 s probe interval in the health-probes doc (the CLI reference says 240 s); healthy if at least x of the last n probes succeed No documented default sample counts; ~90 s with Microsoft’s example (30 s, 5 samples, 3 required) No DNS change; the edge stops routing to unhealthy origins ~90 s or more with that example Every edge location probes origins independently. Latency sensitivity picks among healthy origins; it does not decide health.
Cloudflare Load Balancing Steering policy (failover, geo, proximity, dynamic latency, and others), DNS-only or proxied (anycast) 60 s interval, 5 s timeout, 2 immediate retries (defaults in Cloudflare’s API schema); minimum interval by plan ~15 to 75 s per failed check cycle, plus 60 s for each extra consecutive failure you require Proxied: no client DNS change. DNS-only: the load balancer TTL plus resolver caching ~75 s (proxied) to several minutes (DNS-only) Minimum interval is 60 s on Pro, 15 s on Business, and 10 s on Enterprise. Health is decided by a majority of data centers per region, then a majority of regions.

Shortening the health check interval, lowering the failure threshold, and reducing the DNS TTL improve every value in the table. After tuning, measure with real clients and real traffic, since detection times on paper leave out caching.

What decides how fast traffic moves to another region?

Failover time is the sum of several independent delays, so shortening one delay cuts the total only by that amount, and the slowest delay usually dominates.

Health check interval and failure threshold. Detection time follows from the interval and the threshold. A 30-second interval with a threshold of 3 means up to 90 seconds pass before the system acts. Lower values speed detection but raise the risk of flapping if probes are flaky.

What the health check actually tests. A TCP port check confirms the process is listening but says nothing about whether it can serve requests. An HTTP check on a path that exercises the request path catches failures a port check misses. Leave out dependencies every region shares: if a shared database fails, every region fails its check at once, and Route 53 then treats all endpoints as healthy. Set probe timeouts shorter than the interval.

DNS TTL and real-world caching. The TTL tells resolvers how long to cache an answer, but some recursive resolvers and client operating systems apply a minimum floor, and browsers and connection pools reuse addresses for the life of a connection. Measure how resolvers in your client population actually honor TTLs.

Connection reuse and long-lived connections. gRPC streams, WebSocket connections, and HTTP/2 pools can stay open for minutes or hours and are unaffected by DNS changes until they close or error out. Use reasonable idle timeouts and retry logic with backoff that re-resolves DNS on reconnect.

Warm capacity in the surviving region. If the surviving region cannot absorb the redirected traffic, failover succeeds at the routing layer and fails at the application layer. Autoscaling helps, but new instances take time to become ready. Running active-active with enough headroom in each region to absorb the largest region’s share of traffic avoids this gap. The guide on how to run an app across multiple regions with routing, databases, and failover covers the full architecture.

How do I deploy one application to multiple regions with a single configuration?

Routing works only if every region runs the same application version and has enough capacity to serve traffic.

  • Infrastructure as code modules. Terraform or Pulumi can parameterize a deployment module by region and apply it to several regions in one pipeline. Adding a region means adding an entry to a list.
  • Kubernetes with GitOps tooling. Argo CD ApplicationSets, or Flux bootstrapped on each cluster against the same repository, deploy to multiple clusters from one Git repository. Federating health signals across clusters needs additional tooling.
  • A platform that deploys one definition to many locations. A workload deployed to a Control Plane Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), a named set of locations across one or more clouds, runs in every location from one definition, with no per-region pipeline or cluster configuration to maintain.

Whichever method you use, the pipeline should verify that every region converges on the same version. Staged region-by-region rollouts are safe only when old and new versions are backward-compatible. The best multi-region and multi-cloud networking platforms compares platforms that handle multi-region deployment and networking.

How do I test that failover works?

Run this checklist at launch and on a regular schedule.

  • Fail a health check on purpose. Stop the application in one region or return an unhealthy response from the health check endpoint, and record when the routing system reacts.
  • Measure the shift with synthetic probes from several regions. Run HTTP probes from at least three locations, record when each starts reaching the new region, and compare it to the worst-case switch time in the table.
  • Test with real clients that cache DNS. Synthetic probes often resolve DNS fresh on every request, so use a browser, a mobile device, or a CLI with DNS caching enabled.
  • Check capacity in the surviving region. Watch CPU, memory, latency, and error rates, measure how long autoscaling takes to reach steady state, and confirm new instances pass readiness checks before they receive production traffic.
  • Test failback. Restore the failed region, confirm traffic rebalances, and watch for flapping if the healthy threshold is too low.
  • Run the test under load. A failover test on an idle system does not reveal capacity problems.
  • Document the results. Record detection time, propagation time, and total switch time, and adjust health check settings, TTLs, or capacity against your SLA targets.

Lessons from real regional outages are collected in how companies stay online during AWS us-east-1 outages.

How Control Plane routes users to the nearest healthy location

Control Plane is the unbreakable platform for running production workloads. It runs serverless, standard, stateful, and cron workloads natively on AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), VM workloads on locations joined through Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes, and workloads on Kubernetes clusters you already run or your own machines, including on premises, active-active across regions and clouds.

A workload runs in every location of its GVC, so routing always has a set of identical locations to choose from. Adding a location provisions it for every workload in the GVC; removing one drains its replicas and shifts traffic to the locations that remain, without touching a workload definition.

On Control Plane, every workload gets its own global endpoint (its canonical endpoint), and each custom domain you route to it gets one too. Control Plane DNS geo-routes clients to the nearest location where the workload is healthy, using the workload’s own readiness probes, so a location drops out of DNS answers when the workload there stops reporting ready. Each GVC also has an alias endpoint; by default it is health-checked only with a basic TCP probe, so point its alias workload link at a workload to make the alias follow that workload’s health.

Control Plane’s location routing options, set per location on the GVC, reshape that default for every endpoint in the GVC:

  • A priority tier per location. Lower tiers are preferred, and within a tier the lowest-latency location wins. If every location in the preferred tier is unavailable, traffic moves to the next tier, which lets you prefer one region and keep others as backup.
  • A latency offset that nudges a location up or down in the latency ranking.
  • A latency threshold past which a location is treated as unavailable. If every location exceeds its threshold, Control Plane ignores the thresholds so traffic is not dropped.

For TCP or UDP traffic that should bypass the HTTP ingress, you can enable a direct load balancer on a workload. Control Plane then creates a load balancer in each location and registers each one as a Geo DNS target with latency-based routing.

During the October 20, 2025 AWS us-east-1 outage, Control Plane customers with us-east-1 in their GVC had workloads active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds, with no customer downtime, according to Control Plane’s internal incident telemetry, as reported in Beyond Backups: Designing Systems That Survive the Inevitable. The guide to keeping your app online during an AWS region outage walks through the pattern.

The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations. Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

Control Plane’s global endpoints are DNS-based, so clients that cache DNS answers beyond their TTL can keep sending traffic to a withdrawn location for a short time. Teams that want an anycast IP or a specific CDN in front of their traffic can place a global load balancer or CDN ahead of Control Plane endpoints. Failover options beyond routing are compared in the best multi-cloud failover solutions in 2026.

FAQ

Short answers on deployment, DNS failover speed, TTLs, health checks, backup regions, and testing.

How do I route users to the nearest healthy region automatically?

Use latency- or geo-based DNS routing with health checks, an anycast global load balancer, or a platform with a built-in global endpoint such as Control Plane. Each method health-checks every region and sends users to the nearest one that is passing its checks.

How do I deploy one application to multiple regions with a single configuration?

Use infrastructure as code modules parameterized by region, Kubernetes GitOps tooling such as Argo CD ApplicationSets, or a platform like Control Plane, which runs one workload definition in every location of a GVC. Every region should run the same version and have spare capacity before it receives traffic.

Is DNS failover fast enough?

It depends on your tolerance. With default settings, worst-case failover on the DNS services in the table ranges from about a minute plus the TTL to several minutes, and resolver and client caching makes the tail unpredictable. If your SLA requires sub-30-second failover, use an anycast global load balancer with tuned health checks (Google Cloud’s defaults already detect in about 10 seconds), or tune DNS health checks to their fastest settings and keep TTLs very low, knowing some resolvers do not honor them, and confirm the result by testing.

What DNS TTL should I use for failover?

A TTL of 30 to 60 seconds is a common starting point for failover-critical records. Lower TTLs shorten the stale-answer window but raise query volume and cost, and some resolvers apply a minimum floor or ignore TTLs, so measure what your clients actually honor.

What is the difference between anycast and DNS-based routing?

DNS-based routing returns different IP addresses depending on policy, so failover waits for clients to look up DNS again after cached answers expire. A managed anycast load balancer gives every user the same IP, and its edge stops forwarding to a region once health checks mark it down, so DNS caching plays no part. Total failover time for both still depends on health check settings.

How do health checks decide a region is down?

A health check probes each endpoint over TCP, HTTP, or HTTPS at a fixed interval and marks the region unhealthy after a set number of consecutive failures, usually combining results from probers in several locations (Route 53 marks an endpoint unhealthy when 18% or fewer of its checkers report it healthy); Azure Front Door uses a sample-based rule instead. An HTTP check that exercises the region’s own request path and region-local dependencies catches failures a TCP port check misses.

Can I prefer one region and use others only as backup?

Yes. Most DNS routing services offer failover policies that send traffic to secondary endpoints only when the primary fails, and Azure Front Door supports origin priority. On Control Plane, assign each location in the GVC a priority tier; traffic moves to the next tier only when every location in the preferred tier is unavailable.

What happens to in-flight requests during failover?

Requests in flight to the failed region fail and need a retry. With DNS routing, existing connections keep pointing at the old IP until they close or error out; with a managed Layer 7 anycast load balancer such as Google Cloud’s global external Application Load Balancer or Azure Front Door, the client’s connection to the edge usually survives and new requests go to a healthy backend; with Global Accelerator, which works at Layer 4, clients reconnect and land on a healthy endpoint. Long-lived gRPC streams and WebSockets need idle timeouts and reconnect logic that re-resolves DNS.

How often should I test failover?

Test at least quarterly and after any change to regions, health check settings, or DNS TTLs. Automate the test in a pipeline, and measure detection time, propagation time, and surviving-region capacity under load each time.

title: Activation-Guided Graph Retrieval for Cognitive Memory Reconstruction in Language Model Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.13127v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented language model systems generally select context by query-conditioned relevance. We argue that long-lived AI systems require a second operator: activation-conditioned memory availability. We specify an architecture in which request and goal cues seed an authorized memory graph, activation and fan attenuation allocate a bounded traversal frontier, retrieved entities recursively emit cues, and a typed evidence graph is reconstructed before generation. The specification yields five architectural consequences about candidate selection, traversal control, graph regularization, evidence reconstruction, and reinforcement. We derive implementation-level cost estimates and define ablations, failure conditions, and a reproducible evaluation protocol. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if a simpler graph reranker matches full traversal on causal and temporal recovery under equal budgets. This architecture-and-analysis preprint reports no benchmark measurements. If the claim holds, retrieval returns the evidence path that makes a memory available, not only a ranked list.

title: BioMem: Agentic Memory for Biomedical LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.13426v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable potential in biomedical applications, while agentic memory systems have emerged as a promising approach to preserving and utilizing information across tasks and interactions. However, a fundamental question remains: how effectively and reliably do these systems retain, retrieve, update, and utilize biomedical information? In this study, we systematically investigate agentic memory in the biomedical domain, focusing on task effectiveness, retrieval quality, information fidelity, and long-term robustness. We evaluate five memory approaches across four LLMs in three representative settings: biomedical knowledge reasoning, clinical prediction, and long-term conversational memory. Our analyses reveal how memory construction, evidence relevance, and conversational history shape downstream biomedical performance, highlighting the distinct challenges of retrieving relevant information, preserving its fidelity, and effectively utilizing it for reasoning. Building on these findings, we introduce Hybrid Memory Retrieval and Utilization (HMRU), a training-free framework that jointly enhances evidence accessibility and task-aware utilization to improve biomedical reasoning and long-term conversational memory. HMRU achieves an average relative improvement of 8.6% across biomedical question-answering and conversational memory benchmarks, with additional gains in selected clinical prediction tasks. It further reduces conversational answer errors by 24.9% and closes 48.0% of the performance gap to full-context inference. Our findings provide a systematic characterization of biomedical agentic memory and practical insights into developing more effective and reliable memory-augmented LLM systems.

title: How Virtual DOM Diffing Algorithms Affect UI Responsiveness and Memory Usage
description:
You’ve probably been there: you make a tiny change to your React or Vue component, expecting the UI to update instantly and smoothly. Yet, the page stutters, or memory spikes unexpectedly. It’s frustrating because your code looks clean, minimal , so why is the app struggling?

Turns out, the culprit often lives deep under the hood, in how your framework decides what actually needs to change on the screen. The virtual DOM diffing algorithm.

The Familiar Developer Headache: When UI Updates Feel Sluggish Despite Small Changes

Imagine you have a big list of items rendered in React:

function ItemList({ items }) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {items.map(item => <li key={item.id}>{item.text}</li>)}
    </ul>
  );
}

You update just one item’s text. Intuitively, you expect React to update only that one <li> node. But in some cases, React’s diffing might touch more nodes or run more CPU cycles than you expect. Why?

The answer is in the diffing algorithm’s design , how it balances minimal DOM mutations against CPU overhead and memory usage.

Virtual DOM Diffing: The Core Idea

Virtual DOM (VDOM) is a lightweight JavaScript representation of the UI. When your data changes, the framework creates a new VDOM tree and compares it to the previous version to find what changed.

This "diffing" process produces a set of minimal DOM operations , insertions, updates, removals , to apply to the real DOM.

Sounds simple, right? But the challenge is that diffing large trees is expensive if done naively.

How Diffing Algorithms Work Under the Hood

At its core, diffing is a tree comparison problem. Naively comparing every node in the new tree to every node in the old tree is O(n²) and impractical for large UIs.

Frameworks use heuristics and constraints to keep diffing fast:

  • Keyed children: Using stable keys lets the algorithm quickly match elements between renders.
  • Same-type optimization: Nodes of different types are replaced wholesale.
  • List reordering heuristics: Algorithms try to find minimal moves to reorder lists rather than remove and re-insert.

For example, React’s reconciliation uses an algorithm that assumes children with different keys are different nodes, so it can quickly delete and create nodes when keys change.

Tradeoffs: Minimal Updates vs CPU Overhead

Here’s the rub: striving for the absolute minimal DOM update can cost a lot of CPU time.

Some frameworks use more aggressive heuristics that are faster but produce more DOM mutations. Others spend more CPU to find the minimal set of changes.

For instance, Vue 3’s diffing is optimized to minimize both CPU and DOM mutations, but under complex scenarios (like large lists with many moves), the cost can still spike.

Memory Usage: How Diffing Influences It

Diffing also impacts memory:

  • Frameworks keep two VDOM trees in memory during diffing.
  • Additional metadata like keys and patch flags increase memory footprint.
  • Complex heuristics might require auxiliary data structures (maps, sets) to track moves or matches.

In long-lived apps with frequent updates, this can lead to increased GC pressure or memory bloat.

Real-World Example: List Reorders in React vs Vue

I once debugged a React app rendering a sortable list. When items reordered rapidly, the app stuttered and memory usage grew.

React’s diffing replaced nodes aggressively when keys weren’t stable or missing, causing DOM thrashing and extra GC.

Switching to stable keys and reducing unnecessary re-renders cut CPU usage and memory spikes dramatically.

Meanwhile, Vue’s algorithm tries harder to patch moved nodes instead of replacing them, which reduced DOM operations but required more CPU upfront.

Practical Tips to Help Your UI Stay Responsive

  • Use stable, unique keys: This is the foundation for efficient diffing.
  • Avoid anonymous inline functions or objects as keys: They change every render.
  • Batch state updates: So the framework can diff less often.
  • Consider list virtualization: When dealing with huge lists, rendering only visible items avoids massive diffing.
  • Profile renders: Use React DevTools or Vue DevTools to see which components re-render excessively.

When You Might Need Custom Diffing or Memoization

Sometimes, default diffing isn’t enough for extreme performance needs.

React’s memo or Vue’s shallowReactive can help skip unnecessary diffs.

In rare cases, you might implement custom comparison logic or immutable data structures to simplify diffing.

Wrapping Up

Virtual DOM diffing algorithms are a balancing act. They juggle CPU time, memory usage, and DOM update minimalism to keep your UI responsive.

Next time your app feels sluggish despite small changes, dig into the diffing details. Understanding how your framework’s reconciliation works will help you spot subtle performance traps and write UI code that stays snappy and light.

If you want to dive deeper, try comparing React and Vue’s source diffing implementations, there’s a lot of clever engineering under the hood waiting to be appreciated.

Helpful learning resources

  • MDN Web Docs
  • web.dev performance guidance
  • React documentation Originally published at Under The Hood. Get the next deep dive in your inbox: subscribe to Under The Hood.

title: A Practical Speed Checklist for Shopify Product Pages
description:
When a Shopify product page feels slow on mobile, start by looking at what the browser loads and when. Here are three checks you can run before changing the theme.

1. Find the LCP element

Run a mobile performance test and identify the Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) element. On a product page it might be the featured image, but the report will tell you which element actually counted for that run.

If it’s the main product image, make sure it appears in the initial HTML and loads eagerly. Consider fetchpriority="high" for that image when it’s the main LCP candidate. Keep offscreen gallery images lazy-loaded.

2. Check which image mobile visitors download

Open DevTools, select a mobile viewport, and reload with the Network panel open. Find the product image request and compare the downloaded image width with the space it occupies on screen, accounting for device pixel ratio.

In Liquid, use Shopify CDN image widths in your responsive markup. Make sure sizes describes the image’s rendered slot at each breakpoint so the browser can choose an appropriate srcset candidate. Include intrinsic width and height so the browser can reserve space before the image loads.

3. Scope scripts to the pages that need them

Look for scripts loaded globally that support a feature used on only one template. Before moving a script, check for shared entry points. A product gallery script might also power a quick view on collection pages.

After changing script loading, test variant selection, gallery navigation, quick view where applicable, and add to cart.

Verify the change

Repeat the mobile test under the same conditions and compare the median LCP. If the theme change is shared, check the homepage and a collection page too. Review real-user data when it’s available.
