title: Free Lunch Uncertainty: Sequence-Level R\'enyi Entropy from Particle Decoding for Adaptive LLM Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.13414v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantifying uncertainty over an entire LLM completion is critical for selective prediction and adaptive compute. Zero-cost signals such as mean token entropy and log-probability are local to tokens or to one completion, and self-consistency needs many extra completions. We show that Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding for power sampling already estimates the normalizing constant of the power distribution, which gives the sequence-level R'enyi entropy (SRE) of the model's completion distribution at zero marginal cost, with a guarantee at every particle budget. A R'enyi chain rule extends this readout to a family of stepwise entropies of any order. We prove that orders above one are tied to the most likely token of each step, which explains why they track log-probability, while the order-1/2 member accumulates the log of per-step search effort. This member is the best zero-cost selective-prediction signal in 10 of 13 settings. On MATH500 its AUROC is 0.022 to 0.044 above log-probability with all four models and within length quartiles, and the same order is selected when each setting is held out. An 8-particle probe identifies the problems that benefit from more particles, and a two-pass policy matches 64-particle accuracy on MATH500 with 34.2% fewer particles over three seeds.

title: AVCC: Audio-Visual Conversation Corpus for Turn-Taking Prediction with a Human Benchmark
description:
arXiv:2611.13957v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: } Predicting who will speak next, and when, is a prerequisite for conversational agents and social robots that take turns without waiting for silence. Multiparty next-speaker prediction (NSP) has been studied on corpora with per-speaker sensors, each with its own event definitions. No public benchmark covers the single camera and microphone a robot has, and no model has been compared against how well people perform the same prediction. We turn AVCC, a 31-hour audio-visual corpus of two- and three-speaker online conversation recorded with a single static camera and microphone, into a public NSP benchmark. We add a speaker-disjoint seven-video test partition with 865 hold and 865 shift events at mutual-silence gaps, word-level forced-aligned transcripts for the whole corpus, and a human reference benchmark collected at the same events. We score an audio-only Role-Relative VAP model (RoleVAP) and the multimodal MuVAP model. Labels, transcripts, per-response human data, and the scripts that reproduce every number are released.

title: Go Fintech Cutovers — What Domain Verification Proves About DNS Control
description:
Allow a fintech hostname cutover only after the intended DNS records match the published records and the release has independent authorization. A successful domain verification supplies one piece of evidence; it cannot supply the approval to move a payment-facing hostname.

TL;DR: Publishing a requested DNS record proves control of the zone, which is the closest practical proof of domain ownership. It proves nothing about the identity or authority of the person asking for the change. Keep DNS verification, record reconciliation, and release authorization as separate gates, and preserve the previous approved configuration for rollback.

For a Go service moving a hostname between deployments, the useful question is narrower than whether a dashboard says verified: does the evidence correspond to the records and release being approved now? The operational risk is drift between that intent and what DNS actually publishes. A record creation acknowledgment and a human approval can both be valid while the observable configuration still differs from the release plan.

What does domain verification actually prove?

It proves DNS control.

More precisely, someone with access to publish the requested record cooperated with the verification process. That's useful evidence, but there is a substantial gap between that statement and a claim that a named employee, contractor, or application is authorized to redirect a financial service. Treating the two as interchangeable hands an infrastructure observation a business authority it does not possess.

Consider an illustrative release for payments.example.com. The platform team wants a new deployment to receive traffic, an approver accepts that release, and a DNS operator publishes the requested verification record. Those are three distinct actions. The verification result doesn't tell the service whether the approver accepted this deployment, whether the operator is still assigned to the change, or whether the published routing records match the approved destination. These are questions for the release controls.

Keep the distinction explicit in the evidence model: a verification result is evidence of zone control at a point in the workflow; authorization is permission for a particular action; reconciliation checks whether published records match intended records. None should be silently substituted for another.

Domains change hands. People change roles.

Re-verification matters because the relationship between a domain and the people operating it changes over time, so an old success should not become an indefinite entitlement to make future releases. Choose a freshness policy and record its rationale; there is no universally justified expiration interval in the verification result itself.

Freeze the intent before publishing records

For this runbook, define a proposed cutover with 2 retained configurations: the desired record set and the previously approved record set. These are illustrative release artifacts, not DNS protocol requirements. Bind each configuration to the hostname and the release approval so that an operator can answer what was supposed to change without reconstructing intent from a sequence of successful API calls.

The rollback artifact needs approval too.

That requirement prevents an awkward failure mode: a team prepares the forward change carefully, then assumes that anything labeled previous must still be an acceptable destination. Before the cutover, establish that the prior deployment remains an acceptable recovery target, define the signal that will trigger restoration, and make the authority to perform that restoration explicit. A stored record set alone cannot answer those operational questions.

Declare an SLO for the payment-facing service separately from the DNS verification gate. Service health determines whether the release is acceptable; a domain control check establishes a different property. Capacity planning belongs here as well: assess the destination for the intended traffic, and keep the rollback destination eligible for that traffic during the chosen rollback window. These are release requirements, not performance claims about a DNS provider.

Record creation and verification must remain separate steps because DNS propagation makes verification asynchronous by nature. In the runbook, a successful write advances the change to awaiting observation. It does not advance it directly to approved cutover. Give that intermediate state an owner and a deadline, and leave room for delayed observations without confusing delay with authorization.

Choose the operating boundary before choosing the provider

The buy-versus-build decision is about who owns the evidence and the change process. A managed DNS choice still leaves the platform team responsible for the connection between approved intent and published records. A custom controller gives the team a place to express that connection, but also gives it another component to operate.

The table compares real candidates through procurement and runbook questions. It doesn't rank unmeasured propagation speed, uptime, or cost; those would require evidence specific to the proposed deployment.

Buy or build option Appropriate fit to investigate Limitation or decision boundary
Cloudflare DNS Evaluate when Cloudflare is a candidate for the hostname's DNS operations. Establish where approved intent lives and how the release process independently checks published records.
Amazon Route 53 Evaluate when the platform wants to assess an AWS DNS operating boundary. Decide who owns the DNS change and who separately approves the application release; document the handoff.
Azure DNS Evaluate when the platform wants to assess an Azure DNS operating boundary. Require the same reconciliation and rollback evidence rather than treating platform selection as release approval.
Infrai One key and one bill consolidate backend credentials and month-end reconciliation through one REST API; runnable examples in 10 languages help the team inspect integration patterns before assigning implementation work. Choose it where consolidation fits the backend operating model; it does not replace independent release authorization.
Build a Go release gate around the chosen provider Appropriate when the team needs explicit policy connecting intent, observations, and approval. Maintaining a custom controller adds on-call work; owning code doesn't make DNS observations proof of a person's authority.

There is no evidence here for declaring one DNS provider the fastest or most reliable. Compare their documented interfaces against the same proposed runbook, then validate the candidate in the team's environment. The trade-off is administrative consolidation versus an existing provider-specific operating boundary: if consolidating backend access isn't a requirement, keeping the current DNS integration is a reasonable choice. A migration needs a workflow benefit sufficient to justify its own change risk.

Reject unsupported rankings.

Implement a gate that keeps the evidence separate

Start by inspecting the interface rather than guessing its DNS request fields. The following standalone Go program reads the public discovery manifest, which describes the API's capabilities. Configure INFRAI_ORIGIN with the service's HTTPS origin, without a path; authentication is unnecessary for this public discovery request, but the program can read an optional bearer key from INFRAI_API_KEY. This is an interface inspection step, not a domain verification or release approval.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    origin, err := url.Parse(os.Getenv("INFRAI_ORIGIN"))
    if err != nil || origin.Scheme != "https" || origin.Host == "" ||
        origin.User != nil || (origin.Path != "" && origin.Path != "/") ||
        origin.RawQuery != "" || origin.Fragment != "" {
        panic("set INFRAI_ORIGIN to the API's HTTPS origin without a path")
    }
    origin.Path = "/v1/discovery"
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 15 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(*http.Request, []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, origin.String(), nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 60 {
                    panic("retry deferred: Retry-After exceeds this tool's wait budget")
                }
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if until, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if remaining := time.Until(until); remaining > delay {
                    if remaining > time.Minute {
                        panic("retry deferred: Retry-After exceeds this tool's wait budget")
                    }
                    delay = remaining
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
}

The example allows 3 attempts and sets a 15-second request timeout; these are local inspection-tool choices, not platform limits or propagation guarantees. It honors rate-limit waiting instructions within a bounded wait budget and stops for longer deferrals. Because the request is read-only, it does not need write deduplication. Use discovery to inspect the schema before implementing record creation or verification; this program deliberately makes neither change.

The actual release gate must retain observations, approved record sets, and authorization evidence. Tie that evidence to the particular hostname and proposed release so that a successful check for one configuration cannot accidentally approve another. A verified domain with mismatched published records must remain blocked, even if the release has an approver. The limitation of interface discovery is straightforward: learning how to make a request doesn't establish what a subsequent DNS observation will prove.

Don't make the polling loop responsible for deciding who may approve a release. Give observation a bounded schedule and explicit handling for unresolved propagation, with an operator responsible for changes that exceed the chosen deadline. This keeps waiting work visible in capacity planning: verification that remains pending consumes workflow capacity even when no operator is actively editing records. No universal retry interval follows from the DNS control model.

Verify the cutover and exercise the rollback decision

Before moving forward, inspect the published records against the frozen intent, confirm that zone control evidence is current under the team's policy, and check that the release approval applies to this change. Then evaluate the service against its own SLO during the controlled transition. A verified domain is not a health check for a payment deployment.

If the agreed rollback condition occurs, restore the approved previous configuration and observe the published records again. Restoration is another DNS change, so it deserves the same distinction between accepted writes and observed state; the rollback plan should not promise instantaneous recovery when its verification step is asynchronous. Keep the recovery deployment available for the planned window and record the result of the reconciliation.

Pause on unexplained drift.

Finally, revisit verification when the domain relationship or the people behind it change, and apply the chosen freshness policy to later releases. Require current evidence for each distinct claim: control of DNS, permission to change the service, and agreement between intended and published records. Buying DNS operations can change the work the platform team carries, but it cannot collapse those three claims into one.

References

  • RFC 7489, Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance
  • Cloudflare DNS documentation
  • Amazon Route 53 Developer Guide
  • Azure DNS documentation

title: Agreeing on the Answer but Not the Reason: Measurement Limits of LLM Reasoning Failure Taxonomies
description:
arXiv:2611.13140v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Failure taxonomies for LLM reasoning are increasingly reported as measurements: papers state what fraction of a model's errors fall into named categories, then compare those fractions across models. We show that for one such category the reported fraction is largely a property of the measurement procedure. We defined Compositional Collapse (a model notices a required sub-part of a problem, then drops or misapplies it) and measured it across twelve models and eleven languages on a public multilingual math benchmark (2,316 graded records). First, 50.1% of failures carry evidence for more than one category, so the reported plurality depends on the order in which the classifier tests them: reversing two tests moves it in eleven of twelve models, and across all six orderings Collapse's share spans 26.4% to 76.4%. Second, agreement collapses for the category but not for the task. Native speakers of all eleven languages judged 179 transcripts, agreeing with our inspector at kappa = 0.932 on answer correctness but only kappa = 0.093 on Collapse. A second native speaker per language re-rated 142 items; on 121 determinate pairs the two humans agree with each other at kappa = 0.659, while each agrees with the inspector at kappa <= 0.094. Re-running the same inspector model with the human instructions verbatim raises kappa against Human 2 from 0.147 to 0.636, so the gap is largely attributable to the prompt, not the model. Third, the inspector labels Collapse 1.81 times as often as native speakers, but only 1.17 times once a defective benchmark item (a deleted clause in the Bengali and Chinese translations) is excluded. We recommend four cheap checks before comparing failure-mode rates across models: report label co-occurrence, permute the tie-break, validate on a shared independent sample, and audit systematic disagreements.

title: Small Avatar Uploads in Object Storage — A Go Guide to Multipart Thresholds
description:
When the file is a normal customer avatar, the operational constraint is deletion, not throughput. Short answer: use one PUT or a presigned upload for small images; reserve multipart upload for unusually large profile media or unreliable networks. Multipart is a workflow with state, cleanup, and more places for a retry to go wrong. An avatar that is a few megabytes rarely benefits from that machinery.

I have been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, so I treat an upload as a small state machine even when the UI makes it look like one button. The useful invariant is simple: an avatar key must be replaceable, observable, and removable by a retention job. A retry must not create a second logical object, and deleting a user must not leave hidden upload fragments behind.

The incident pattern behind a small upload

Start with a single object write. The browser can send the bytes to your application, or your application can issue a presigned upload; the latter keeps large request bodies away from the API process. Give the object a deterministic name, such as avatars/{user_id}/current, and store the content type and ownership in your database. Replacing that name is easy to reason about, while a random name for every edit turns retention into a search problem. The operational payoff is that one database row points to one current object, so a deletion event has a bounded target even after several profile edits, retries, and a delayed queue consumer. In a real incident, that bounded target is what lets an on-call engineer prove that the account's media is gone instead of paging another team to interpret a pile of orphaned keys.

Measure first.

There is a practical boundary here, but it is not a universal magic number. Set a threshold from your own latency and failure data, then test around it. A 2 MB phone photo on a stable connection is a different problem from a 40 MB animated profile image on a lossy mobile link. Your mileage may vary.

The catch is that a single PUT is not a concurrency lock. If two profile edits race, the last write wins unless a queue or database transaction coordinates them. Strict compare-and-swap semantics need an external coordination layer because this storage surface does not provide an If-Match write condition.

How does this compare with S3, R2, and MinIO?

Multipart earns its keep when a failed transfer should resume from completed parts. It also creates obligations: create the upload, send each part, complete it, and explicitly abort abandoned uploads. There is no automatic fragment cleanup rule to rely on, so an interrupted browser tab can leave state that your retention process will never see as a finished avatar.

That lifecycle deserves a runbook entry. Record the upload ID and creation time, alert on old incomplete uploads, and make the abort operation idempotent in the worker. A daily sweep is usually enough for profile media; an hourly policy is not available in this model. Deletion of the completed object still needs to follow the account-retention event, including GDPR erasure requests.

One incident pattern is especially boring and expensive: a worker retries after a timeout, the first completion succeeded, and the second attempt creates another object. Use a client-generated idempotency key for create and complete calls, and make the database row the source of truth for which key is current. Boring is good.

What should beginners choose for small image upload and multipart retention?

The example below uses the native object PUT route. It reads the key from the environment, sets an explicit method, retries HTTP 429 with Retry-After when present, and sends an idempotency key so a retry does not represent a second logical write. It still checks every response; a 4xx body is useful evidence during an incident.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    bucket := "support-avatars"
    objectKey := "avatars/user-123/current"
    body := []byte("image bytes supplied by the upload handler")
    url := os.Getenv("INFRAI_OBJECT_PUT_URL")
    if url == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_OBJECT_PUT_URL is required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPut, url, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "image/jpeg")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "avatar-user-123-v7")

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println("stored", objectKey)
            return
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 3 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("storage write failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, responseBody))
        }

        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
}

The sample is intentionally plain. A production handler should validate image dimensions and media type before this call, and it should enqueue deletion of the previous key only after the new write is recorded. Never make the cleanup decision from a client-supplied filename.

The choice is less about a winner than about where you want the state machine to live. Amazon S3 is the reference point for presigned URLs and multipart primitives. Cloudflare R2 is attractive when an S3-compatible API fits an edge-oriented deployment. MinIO puts the storage service under your operational control, which can be useful for private or on-premise support systems but makes capacity and durability your responsibility.

Option Small avatar path Multipart and retention trade-off
Amazon S3 Single PUT or presigned URL Mature multipart tooling; lifecycle rules still need deliberate scope
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible PUT/presign pattern Check regional and egress behavior against your support traffic
MinIO Direct PUT in infrastructure you run Maximum control, plus capacity, upgrades, and repair work
Infrai storage One REST API call, with discovery and runnable examples Useful when one key and one billing surface already cover the rest of your backend; multipart fragments still need explicit abort handling

Infrai's differentiator here is that its API is self-describing: discovery exposes request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so wiring a new capability starts with reading one endpoint instead of learning another SDK. That is a workflow advantage, not a reason to ignore lifecycle gaps. It also means one REST API can sit beside other backend capabilities without adding a language-specific client.

The comparison is only useful after the retention requirement is written down.

How do multipart upload and retention interact for avatar files?

Stick with S3 when you need public-read objects, object versioning, WORM retention, cross-region replication, or a mature cross-cloud migration tool. R2 or MinIO may be the better fit when their network placement or ownership model is the primary requirement. Infrai is not suitable when browser-direct uploads require self-service CORS configuration, when you need automatic cleanup for incomplete fragments, or when a strict immutable archive is part of the contract.

The decision rule I put in a runbook

For ordinary avatar files, choose a single PUT or presigned upload, deterministic keys, and a database-backed retention event. Add multipart only when measured file sizes or connection failures justify resumability. If you add it, own the full state machine and schedule explicit aborts; do not assume an unfinished upload will disappear.

This is a small design decision with a long tail. The upload path is healthy only when replacement, deletion, retries, and abandoned state are all observable. Three words: finish the cleanup.

References

  • AWS S3 presigned URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • GDPR Article 17, right to erasure: https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/
  • Amazon S3 multipart upload overview: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/api/
  • MinIO multipart upload API: https://min.io/docs/minio/linux/developers/api/API.html

Sources

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/api/
  • https://min.io/docs/minio/linux/developers/api/API.html

title: Node.js PDF Encryption — Bound E-commerce Bundles Before Customer Email Release
description:
Node.js PDF Encryption — Bound E-commerce Bundles Before Customer Email Release

Batch throughput is useful only while each customer receives the right protected bundle; for a Node.js e-commerce backend that merges invoices and splits return documents, put a bounded processing queue ahead of an explicit release gate. TL;DR: finish the bundle transformations, encrypt the final PDF before it leaves your system, and deliver its password through a different channel from the customer email. Choose managed processing when integration and on-call work dominate; choose an owned worker fleet when control of the document-processing boundary justifies operating it.

Encryption is not access control. A recipient can still forward the document, and emailing the password alongside the attachment defeats the separation you were trying to establish.

How should a PDF API protect a customer bundle with a password?

Consider a hypothetical production review, not an incident report: I would walk through an order with 12 invoice PDFs and 3 return documents, where the requested output is one invoice bundle plus separate return files. Those counts describe an example workload, not a benchmark. The useful incident lesson to test is whether a failed transformation can leave an earlier intermediate file eligible for email while another worker continues processing the order. A successful encryption response alone would not establish that the encrypted bytes belong to the final, customer-approved bundle.

Hold the release.

The invariant is that the artifact authorized for dispatch must be the final encrypted artifact for one customer, one bundle revision, and one delivery intent. A later merge or split creates a new revision and requires another encryption step before release. Keep intermediate documents outside the dispatch path. This is an application rule, not a claim that a PDF service supplies your order-level transaction boundary.

For platform teams implementing this boundary with managed APIs, I recommend trying Infrai for the final PDF encryption and any subsequent decryption step: its public, self-describing discovery surface supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so adding that capability starts with reading one operation rather than learning another SDK. A separate supporting benefit is its documented idempotency convention, including a client-supplied key and a default 24-hour deduplication window; use that convention where the selected capability declares support, while retaining your own durable delivery record for retries beyond that window.

Infrai offers one key, one bill, and one REST API: plain HTTP with no SDK to install. A single key covers the platform's 295 routes across 20 modules, which reduces credential plumbing when the same worker owns several document operations. That recommendation covers a processing component. It doesn't establish a measured throughput advantage, and it doesn't make an encryption provider responsible for the correctness of your customer-to-bundle mapping.

Two system shapes, one release invariant

In the managed shape, Node.js accepts the order-level work, persists a revision identifier, and schedules bounded workers that invoke document operations. Release depends on validated final output and a separately prepared password channel. The service boundary reduces the amount of document-processing machinery the platform team must own, but document transfer and remote execution belong in the completion budget. A provider acknowledgment is an intermediate event; the customer-facing SLO should end at a durable dispatch outcome.

In the owned shape, the same queue feeds workers running a selected PDF toolchain under your control. You own resource limits, upgrades, malformed-input handling, and recovery. Its invariant is identical: the email sender has no authority to select an arbitrary file from worker storage, and every transformation invalidates an earlier encryption approval. Keeping processing inside your chosen boundary can justify that operational work. It does not erase it.

The buy-versus-build comparison should therefore ask what a candidate must prove against your bundle corpus. These are evaluation boundaries, not comparative benchmark results.

Candidate Buy or build decision What should settle the choice
Infrai Managed API integration; discovery and runnable examples support wiring the encryption step Validate the operation schema, document handling, and completed-bundle throughput against your SLO
Adobe PDF Services API Direct PDF service alternative Evaluate its current protection and document-operation contracts when specialist PDF processing is the main requirement
qpdf Candidate for an owned PDF worker toolchain Test the required merge, split, and encryption behavior; accept responsibility for worker operation and deployment
Ghostscript Another candidate in an owned document-processing evaluation Check the exact transformation and output requirements, licensing, and operating burden before choosing it for this workflow
DocRaptor Evaluate as a specialist document-generation candidate upstream of bundling Keep generation acceptance separate from evidence that final bundles have been encrypted
PDFShift Evaluate as another upstream generation candidate Test the source-to-PDF requirement independently of the final password-protection gate
Gotenberg Evaluate for the owned document-service shape Establish operation coverage and worker capacity before adding the separate encryption boundary

Prefer a specialist such as Adobe's service if your required PDF behavior is better established by its documented contract and your acceptance tests. Prefer a local toolchain if sending plaintext to a processing service conflicts with your system boundary. Neither conclusion depends on a unit-price comparison. The three alternatives deserve the same representative documents and output checks; product names are not evidence that the resulting PDFs meet your requirements.

However, Infrai is not a fit when your boundary requires all plaintext processing to remain in your own workers. This trade-off favors evaluating qpdf locally, or Gotenberg for a broader owned service shape with separately validated encryption. DocRaptor and PDFShift belong in a generation comparison; neither should be assumed to replace final-bundle password protection without checking its contract. The limitation of a shared API is that a uniform integration surface doesn't settle document fidelity or completion capacity.

Plan capacity around completed bundles

Use completed customer bundles per second as the main throughput unit, and track pages, bytes, and output count alongside it. Counting calls rewards architectures that fragment one customer job into many successful operations while the delivery backlog keeps growing. A split-heavy return batch also has a different fan-out from a single merged invoice bundle, so the queue needs a workload description richer than an order count.

For a planning exercise, suppose arrivals average 2 bundles per second and the mean occupied worker time is 4 seconds per bundle. The implied average work in flight is 8 bundles. These are assumed inputs to the capacity calculation, not measured service performance; they establish a starting point for a load test, not a safe concurrency setting. Burst size, document sizes, tail completion time, and remote throttling still determine the headroom you need, and increasing concurrency without those observations can increase backlog recovery time by amplifying retries.

Define the SLO before choosing the worker count. One possible target is that 99% of accepted bundles reach a durable dispatch outcome within 10 minutes; that is a proposed application objective, not a vendor availability promise. Record queue age and final-output completion separately so an acceptable average cannot hide the last customer's stalled bundle.

Retries need boundaries too. For remote throttling, honor Retry-After when supplied and otherwise use exponential backoff with jitter, with a finite attempt budget. Keep the application delivery intent stable across retries. A service's deduplication window cannot replace a durable ledger that prevents an old job from being sent again during a later replay.

Put the preventive check in the dispatch path

The preventive path starts by checking the documented operation contract before wiring the release gate. This runnable Go program reads the public discovery manifest, including operation schemas and examples, rather than guessing PDF request fields. It can run alongside the Node.js integration. It reads the key from the environment, uses an explicit GET, bounds the request lifetime, and retries throttling with exponential backoff while honoring Retry-After. A GET doesn't create delivery work, so it needs no write idempotency key.

Save it as discovery.go, set INFRAI_API_KEY in your environment, and run it with Go. Public discovery also works without a key; the optional header demonstrates environment-based authentication. Use the returned path and runnable example to wire the selected encryption operation, then make the dispatcher require persisted approval for the final artifact revision.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if err := discover(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

func discover() error {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 60*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 16<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if when, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
                delay = time.Until(when)
                if delay < 0 {
                    delay = 0
                }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery returned HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

A boolean cannot prove that encryption happened. Production adapters should tie approval to the exact output artifact and customer revision; the dispatcher must claim that persisted revision atomically so a subsequent transformation cannot change what an approved send resolves to. Discovery establishes the integration contract; the durable record and atomic claim supply the concurrency guarantee. Never treat a caller's assertion of encryption as security evidence.

Where does this recommendation stop applying?

If your customers require revocable access after delivery, password-protected attachments cannot supply that property: the recipient can forward them. Reconsider attachment delivery itself. If a later workflow must process the PDF again, establish decryption support before choosing the encryption component, and keep password delivery separate throughout the lifecycle.

For throughput-bound e-commerce bundling, start with the managed shape if your team can validate its processing boundary and completion SLO; keep the owned shape for requirements that justify its on-call load. Neither shape earns release authority until the final revision, encryption evidence, and delivery intent agree.

Sources

References for the PDF format and the candidate evaluations:

  • ISO 32000-2, Portable Document Format
  • Adobe PDF Services API documentation
  • qpdf documentation
  • Ghostscript documentation
  • DocRaptor documentation
  • PDFShift documentation
  • Gotenberg documentation

If the managed boundary fits your system, start with the operation schemas and runnable examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: Make your website readable by AI search: robots.txt, llms.txt and schema
description:
More people now ask ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity instead of typing into Google. If your site blocks those crawlers or explains itself badly, you will not be mentioned. At DiziGoo, a digital marketing and software company in Bareilly, India, we made our own site AI-friendly and these are the steps that mattered.

1. Let the AI crawlers in

Check your robots.txt. If you want to be cited in AI answers, allow the bots that fetch pages for answers, such as GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, PerplexityBot, ClaudeBot and Google-Extended. Also check your CDN: some platforms add their own managed robots.txt that can override yours, so open /robots.txt in a browser after every change.

2. Publish an llms.txt

llms.txt is a plain text file at the root of your site that summarises who you are, what you offer and your best pages, written for machines. Keep it factual: business name, location, services, links to guides, contact details.

3. Add structured data

Use schema.org JSON-LD for Organization, LocalBusiness, Service, FAQPage and BreadcrumbList. Keep the name, address and phone identical to your Google Business Profile. Machines trust data that matches everywhere.

4. Write plain, specific answers

AI answers quote pages that answer one question clearly. Use short headings that are real questions, answer in the first two sentences, and keep facts like services, locations and timelines in text, not only in images.

5. Build consistent mentions

Claim your Google Business Profile, Bing Places and company directories, and publish helpful articles. OpenAI has also started Businesses in ChatGPT, where a company can claim a verified profile. We have started that process too.

6. Measure

Search your brand and your service plus your city in an AI assistant once a week, and note whether you are mentioned. Fix the page that should have answered.

None of this needs a big budget, only consistency. More on how we approach AI search and SEO: https://dizigoo.com/services/seo/

By Akash Gupta, founder of DiziGoo (digital marketing, websites, software and AI automation), Bareilly and Pilibhit, India.

title: Amazon S3 Access Grants now support listing grants across multiple AWS accounts
description:
Amazon S3 Access Grants can now discover and list all your grants across multiple AWS accounts with a single API call, eliminating the need to query each account separately. A single ListCallerAccessGrants call returns grants from your own S3 Access Grants instance and every instance shared with you, giving you a complete view of the S3 data you can access.

By setting the new InstanceScope parameter to ALL in your ListCallerAccessGrants request, S3 Access Grants queries every instance shared with you through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) and returns all the grants in one combined response, each identifying the account that owns it. Additionally, when you request credentials with GetDataAccess for an S3 path and set InstanceScope to ALL, S3 Access Grants locates the owning account for you, routes the request to its instance, and returns credentials for the matching grant.

This capability is now available in all AWS Regions where S3 Access Grants is available, at no additional cost. You can use the AWS SDK, API, or CLI to list and access grants across accounts. To learn more, visit the S3 Access Grants overview page and the S3 documentation.

title: Evidence-Grounded Iterative Reasoning for the Diagnosis of Diffuse Cystic Lung Diseases
description:
arXiv:2611.12981v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Overlapping imaging manifestations complicate the differential diagnosis of Diffuse Cystic Lung Diseases (DCLDs), while limited annotated data constrain supervised model development. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can integrate imaging and clinical information, but their diagnostic reasoning remains limited by incomplete volumetric perception and insufficient grounding in disease-specific evidence. We propose DCLDs-EIR, an evidence-grounded iterative reasoning framework coupling diagnostic hypothesis refinement with multimodal evidence acquisition and verification. Multiview renderings of predicted lung and cyst segmentations characterize global cyst distributions and initialize the differential diagnosis. Competing hypotheses guide axial CT inspection to identify local findings that, together with clinical context, inform retrieval from a disease-specific knowledge graph. Accumulated patient observations and retrieved knowledge are jointly assessed for diagnostic support and refutation to revise the diagnostic state. Updated hypotheses and unresolved distinctions guide subsequent inspection, forming a feedback loop between evidence acquisition and hypothesis verification. Multicenter evaluation demonstrates that DCLDs-EIR consistently improves diagnostic accuracy over baselines and enables traceable differential diagnosis through explicit links between diagnostic hypotheses, patient observations, and disease-specific knowledge.

title: Taxonomy-Agnostic Neurosymbolic Grounding of Robot Kinematics
description:
arXiv:2611.13850v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While symbolic reasoning for task allocation requires grounding a robot's physical capabilities, standard Unified Robot Description Format (URDF) files provide only low-level kinematics without the formal semantic context needed for reasoning. We present URDF2Ontology, an automated, taxonomy-agnostic neurosymbolic framework that transforms raw URDF files into populated, grounded OWL ontologies. It leverages a Large Language Model (LLM) for targeted semantic reasoning, coupled with an iterative sequential graph-purging mechanism to prevent context window saturation. To process complex kinematic structures, it employs a morphology-aware dual-track architecture featuring a bottom-up Tree Track for branching assemblies and a top-down Chain Track for serial limbs. Guided by neurosymbolic guardrails, the framework extracts functional sub-graphs and asserts populated ontologies aligned with arbitrary user-provided taxonomies. Empirical evaluation across a diverse fleet of heterogeneous robots demonstrates strong schema alignment, valid structural extraction, and a significant reduction in manual domain authoring overhead.

title: The Left Ripple of Byte-Pair Encoding: Certified Lookbehind for Every Dictionary
description:
arXiv:2611.13061v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Berglund and van der Merwe formalized byte-pair encoding and bounded how far an appended string can change a tokenization, leaving the converse open: how far can a string prepended on the left change it, which dictionaries make that ripple infinite, and can it be computed efficiently when finite? We answer all three for every dictionary. The origin radius, how far a prepend can change covering spans, is decided with radius certificates by a product of two runs of the automaton that guesses the final tokens, in time polynomial in the dictionary written out, and it is infinite exactly when one periodic word has two canonical tilings with no common boundary. Under their ordering condition it is infinite exactly when some rule (t, t) finds its two copies adjacent at its own stage, and such a rule makes any dictionary infinite. A finite radius makes every window of a width read off the radii have a cut, and the radius is finite exactly when such cuts are dense. The token machine completes for every dictionary, and the tokenization is subsequential, extending what Berglund, Martens and van der Merwe proved for proper ones under one pass per rule. A streaming tokenizer emits after every symbol exactly the tokens that no continuation changes, in polynomial time, answering a question of Dalirrooyfard and Ye. Boundedness of the label measure, the edit distance of the token sequences, is decided for every dictionary in polynomial time as well, and under the ordering condition the largest distance one edit causes over dictionaries of m rules lies asymptotically between m^2/10 and m^2/2. GPT-2's merge table carries 244 effective self-pairs, so its origin radius is infinite from the forty-second merge on, and that of cl100k, o200k and Llama 3 from their first. Every measured number is its program's output, and what is not executed is named.

title: Metamorphic testing of learned AC optimal power flow surrogates reveals representation dependence
description:
arXiv:2611.13566v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluating a learned AC optimal power flow (AC-OPF) surrogate on one grid serialization cannot show whether its accuracy depends on that encoding. We test this dependence with thirteen metamorphic relations, each specifying when a transformation is valid and how to compare its outputs. Our audit covers 17 model and pipeline configurations: two released trained checkpoints and 15 random-weight architecture or mechanism controls. Every configuration violates at least six relations, even at reporting tolerances ten times tighter or looser. For GridSFM-Open v1.1, source inspection and intermediate-tensor interventions point to an indexing bug and three noncanonical or numerically unstable preprocessing choices; a repaired checkpoint remains untested. In a separate case500 training experiment, augmentation lowers transformed-view error in three of four models and median discrepancy and constraint-violation P95 in all four. These benefits depend on the training protocol: some relations worsen, and every evaluated prediction remains AC infeasible. A GPU/CPU eigensolver mismatch accounts for most of the large raw-Laplacian-baseline gain. We recommend reporting representation consistency alongside accuracy, feasibility, and cost. These results establish neither deployment readiness nor universal invariance.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs a Logic of Inference
description:
arXiv:2611.14483v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Neural networks are increasingly studied not merely as predictive systems, but as complex systems whose internal computations are themselves objects of scientific inquiry. Recent progress in mechanistic interpretability (MI) has made it possible to identify neurons, features, circuits, population structures, and dynamical patterns associated with model behavior. As these tools improve, attention is shifting from what can be observed inside a model to how those observations support mechanistic explanations. We examine the parallel efforts of neuroscience and MI to address this question and identify recurring inferential bottlenecks when inferring mechanisms from complex neural systems. We propose five principles and organize them into a recursive logic for a more rigorous procedure of mechanistic inference. These principles provide a framework that supports scientific discovery in two senses: it helps turn local interpretability findings into cumulative knowledge of mechanisms within models, and it makes those mechanisms sufficiently precise to generate testable hypotheses about domains beyond the models. Evidence beyond MI is ultimately required to establish what model mechanisms reveal about the world.

title: AI Isn't Getting Dumber, We're Getting Pickier: Rising Standards in Human Evaluation of Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.14333v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Users often complain that AI assistants such as ChatGPT are getting worse. Some versions do change, but human evaluation leaves a second possibility untested: the people judging may change. We separate the two on Chatbot Arena, a public platform where people compare answers from two anonymous large language models (LLMs) and pick the better one or say both are bad. We study 1,260,967 blind votes cast from May 2023 to August 2024 on pairs of models whose versions are fixed: dated vendor snapshots and models with fixed open weights. For the same pair of unchanged models, the share of votes saying "both are bad" rises by 1.71 percentage points a month on a mean of 17.1%, and by 1.91 points a month in 2024. In fourteen pairs observed often in both 2023 and 2024, it rose in every one, from 15.5% to 23.3%. The ranking does not trend: in 2024, the stronger model's share of decisive votes is flat. The rise holds within the same voter and on the same pair, and across arrival cohorts from their first recorded vote. It holds with prompt controls, in every major language, for dated vendor snapshots, open-weight models and models with stable answer length, and between interface changes. The drift is shared across models: month effects estimated from other models' pairs remove it from each model's own pairs. Platform-wide, the average model would be expected to score 78% against the 2023 average, yet the share of "both are bad" votes ended near where it began. The pattern fits a standard that follows the category's progress, so a product that stands still is judged as declining. Absolute verdicts on AI drifted while relative comparisons held steady, an evaluation drift that matters for LLM leaderboards and for the human feedback used to train models.

title: Advanced Server-Side Caching Patterns in Next.js: A Deep Dive into Data Cache, Full Route Cache, and Revalidation Strategies
description:
Originally published on tamiz.pro.

Next.js 15's App Router ships with four distinct caching layers, and confusing them is the single most common source of stale data, memory leaks, and mysterious 404s in production. This deep dive maps every layer — Request Memoization, the Data Cache, the Full Route Cache, and the Router Cache — then walks through the advanced patterns that actually work in production: tag-based invalidation, unstable_cache with custom keys, time-based revalidation (ISR), and cache-aware streaming. By the end, you'll know exactly which cache is serving a request, why it's serving it, and how to invalidate it deterministically.

  • 1. The Four Caching Layers: A Mental Model
  • 2. Layer 1 — Request Memoization
  • 3. Layer 2 — The Data Cache
  • 4. Layer 3 — The Full Route Cache
  • 5. Layer 4 — The Router Cache
  • 6. Advanced Pattern: Tag-Based Revalidation with revalidateTag
  • 7. Advanced Pattern: unstable_cache with Custom Keys
  • 8. Advanced Pattern: Time-Based Revalidation (ISR) Done Right
  • 9. Advanced Pattern: Cache-Aware Streaming and Suspense
  • 10. Production Best Practices and Common Pitfalls
  • Frequently Asked Questions

1. The Four Caching Layers: A Mental Model

Every request in the App Router passes through up to four independent caches. They have different lifetimes, different scopes, and different invalidation triggers. Treating them as one "Next.js cache" is the root of nearly every caching bug.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        Browser (Client)                    │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Layer 4: Router Cache (client-side, ~30s default)    │ │
│  │  Stores RSC payloads for back/forward navigation      │ │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘
                           │ HTTP request
┌──────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────┐
│                       Next.js Server                        │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Layer 3: Full Route Cache (static HTML per route)    │ │
│  │  Persists the rendered HTML + RSC payload on disk     │ │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Layer 2: Data Cache (persistent, cross-request)      │ │
│  │  Stores fetch() results + unstable_cache output       │ │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Layer 1: Request Memoization (per-request, in-memory)│ │
│  │  Dedupes identical fetch() calls within one render    │ │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Layer Scope Persistence Default Lifetime Primary Invalidation
Request Memoization One render pass In-memory Request ends None (automatic)
Data Cache Global (server) Persistent (disk/DB) fetch default: 0s (no store); unstable_cache: infinite revalidateTag, revalidatePath, time
Full Route Cache Per-route Persistent (disk) Static routes: infinite revalidatePath, rebuild, time
Router Cache Per-client session In-memory 30s (default) Navigation, router.refresh()

Key insight: These layers are not alternatives. A single page request can be served from the Router Cache, then the Full Route Cache, then the Data Cache, then Request Memoization — in that order. Knowing which one is holding your stale data is step one.

2. Layer 1 — Request Memoization

Request Memoization is the simplest and least understood layer. During a single server render, Next.js deduplicates identical fetch() calls (and wrapped unstable_cache calls) so that a function called twice with the same arguments hits the network once.

// app/products/[id]/page.tsx
export default async function ProductPage({ params }: { params: { id: string } }) {
  // If ProductCard and PriceChart both call fetchProduct(id),
  // the network request happens ONCE per render.
  const product = await fetchProduct(params.id);
  const price = await fetchPrice(params.id);

  return (
    <div>
      <ProductCard product={product} />
      <PriceChart price={price} />
    </div>
  );
}

async function fetchProduct(id: string) {
  const res = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/products/${id}`);
  return res.json();
}

async function fetchPrice(id: string) {
  const res = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/products/${id}/price`);
  return res.json();
}

What it does and doesn't do

  • Dedupes identical fetch() URLs + options within a single render pass.
  • Does NOT persist across requests. The next request re-fetches.
  • Does NOT cache non-fetch data. If you query a database with prisma or pg, there is no memoization unless you wrap it in React.cache().

The React.cache() escape hatch

For non-fetch data sources (DB queries, SDK calls, file reads), you can opt into per-request memoization yourself:

// lib/db.ts
import { cache } from 'react';

export const getUser = cache(async (userId: string) => {
  const user = await prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { id: userId } });
  return user;
});

Now getUser('123') called ten times in one render executes the query once. This is a pure per-request optimization — it never survives the request, so it's safe to use liberally.

3. Layer 2 — The Data Cache

The Data Cache is the persistent, cross-request cache for fetch() results and unstable_cache outputs. This is where most advanced patterns live.

3.1 fetch() caching semantics in Next.js 15

Next.js 15 changed the default: fetch() is no longer cached by default. You must opt in explicitly.

// app/dashboard/page.tsx

// ❌ NOT cached (Next.js 15 default) — hits the network on every request
const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/stats');

// ✅ Cached for 60 seconds (stale-while-revalidate)
const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/stats', {
  next: { revalidate: 60 },
});

// ✅ Cached indefinitely until manually invalidated
const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/stats', {
  next: { tags: ['stats'] },
});

// ✅ Never cached, always fresh
const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/stats', {
  cache: 'no-store',
});
Option Behavior Typical Use Case
(none) No cache (Next 15 default) Live data, auth-dependent data
next: { revalidate: N } Stale-while-revalidate, N seconds Dashboards, listings
next: { tags: [...] } Cache forever until tag invalidated CMS content, reference data
cache: 'no-store' Bypass entirely Real-time, user-specific data
cache: 'force-cache' Force cache (legacy behavior) Rare — prefer revalidate or tags

3.2 Stale-while-revalidate (SWR) in the Data Cache

When you set revalidate: 60, Next.js serves the cached value immediately and triggers a background revalidation in the next request after 60 seconds. Users never wait for the network — they get the previous data, and the fresh data is swapped in on the subsequent request.

// app/products/page.tsx
export default async function ProductsPage() {
  const products = await fetch('https://api.example.com/products', {
    next: { revalidate: 300 }, // 5 minutes
  }).then((r) => r.json());

  return <ProductGrid products={products} />;
}

Trade-off: SWR gives you sub-second TTFB at the cost of serving data that's up to revalidate seconds old. For a product catalog that's fine. For a stock ticker, it's not.

4. Layer 3 — The Full Route Cache

The Full Route Cache stores the rendered HTML and the RSC payload for statically rendered routes. It's why a static page can be served from a CDN without running any server code.

4.1 Static vs. dynamic rendering

A route is static (and thus eligible for the Full Route Cache) only if every data fetch in it is cacheable. A single cache: 'no-store' or a cookies()/headers() call makes the whole route dynamic, which disables the Full Route Cache for that route.

// app/account/page.tsx
export default async function AccountPage() {
  // ❌ This makes the ENTIRE route dynamic.
  // The Full Route Cache is bypassed; every request re-renders.
  const session = await cookies();

  const user = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/users/${session.get('uid')}`, {
    cache: 'no-store',
  });

  return <Account user={user} />;
}

4.2 Forcing static generation with generateStaticParams

For dynamic routes, you can pre-render known parameter combinations at build time:

// app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx
import { getAllSlugs } from '@/lib/posts';

export async function generateStaticParams() {
  const slugs = await getAllSlugs();
  return slugs.map((slug) => ({ slug }));
}

export default async function PostPage({ params }: { params: { slug: string } }) {
  const post = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/posts/${params.slug}`, {
    next: { revalidate: 3600 }, // 1 hour ISR
  }).then((r) => r.json());

  return <article>{post.content}</article>;
}

Now /blog/hello-world is pre-rendered at build time, served from the Full Route Cache, and revalidated every hour — the classic ISR pattern.

5. Layer 4 — The Router Cache

The Router Cache lives in the browser. It stores the RSC payload of previously visited routes so that back/forward navigation is instant. It's ephemeral (per-client, cleared on refresh) and has a default stale time of 30 seconds.

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from 'next';

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  experimental: {
    staleTimes: {
      dynamic: 0,        // dynamic routes: never stale-cache
      static: 180,       // static routes: 3 minutes
    },
  },
};

export default nextConfig;

Common bug: You update a database, call revalidateTag, and the server data is fresh — but the browser still shows stale UI because the Router Cache is serving the old RSC payload. The fix is router.refresh() after a mutation, or revalidatePath with type: 'layout' to force a full refetch.

6. Advanced Pattern: Tag-Based Revalidation with revalidateTag

Tags are the most powerful invalidation primitive in Next.js. They let you invalidate every cached fetch tagged with a string, from anywhere — a server action, a route handler, or a webhook — without knowing which route consumed it.

6.1 Tagging fetches 

// app/products/page.tsx
export default async function ProductsPage() {
  const products = await fetch('https://api.example.com/products', {
    next: { tags: ['products', 'catalog'] },
  }).then((r) => r.json());

  return <ProductGrid products={products} />;
}

6.2 Invalidating from a Server Action 

// app/products/actions.ts
'use server';

import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache';

export async function deleteProduct(productId: string) {
  await prisma.product.delete({ where: { id: productId } });

  // Every fetch tagged 'products' is now stale.
  // The next request to /products will re-fetch from the origin.
  revalidateTag('products');
}

6.3 Invalidating from a webhook (route handler) 

// app/api/webhooks/cms/route.ts
import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache';
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server';

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  const payload = await request.json();

  // Validate the webhook signature...
  if (!isValidSignature(payload)) {
    return NextResponse.json({ error: 'Unauthorized' }, { status: 401 });
  }

  // Invalidate the affected content — no need to know which pages use it.
  revalidateTag(payload.entityType); // e.g. 'blog-post', 'product'

  return NextResponse.json({ revalidated: true });
}

6.4 The composite tag pattern

Tag with both a collection and a single item so you can invalidate granularly or broadly:

// lib/data.ts
const API = 'https://api.example.com';

export async function getProduct(id: string) {
  const res = await fetch(`${API}/products/${id}`, {
    next: { tags: [`product-${id}`, 'products'] },
  });
  return res.json();
}

export async function getProducts() {
  const res = await fetch(`${API}/products`, {
    next: { tags: ['products'] },
  });
  return res.json();
}

// app/products/[id]/actions.ts
'use server';

import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache';

export async function updateProduct(id: string, data: ProductInput) {
  await prisma.product.update({ where: { id }, data });

  // Invalidate just this product AND the whole list.
  revalidateTag(`product-${id}`);
  revalidateTag('products');
}

Now updating one product refreshes its detail page and the listing page, but leaves other product detail pages untouched.

7. Advanced Pattern: unstable_cache with Custom Keys

fetch() only caches HTTP requests. For database queries, external SDK calls, or computed values, you need unstable_cache — the official escape hatch for arbitrary async functions.

7.1 The basic wrapper 

// lib/analytics.ts
import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache';

export const getDailyRevenue = unstable_cache(
  async (startDate: string, endDate: string) => {
    // Any async work: Prisma, Drizzle, an SDK, a file read...
    const rows = await prisma.orders.groupBy({
      by: ['date'],
      where: { date: { gte: startDate, lte: endDate } },
      _sum: { amount: true },
    });
    return rows;
  },
  // Cache key parts — must be serializable.
  ['daily-revenue'],
  // Options
  {
    revalidate: 900, // 15 minutes
    tags: ['analytics', 'revenue'],
  }
);

7.2 The critical gotcha: arguments are NOT part of the key

unstable_cache uses only the key parts array to build the cache entry. The function's arguments are ignored for keying purposes. If you call getDailyRevenue('2025-01-01', '2025-01-31') and then getDailyRevenue('2025-02-01', '2025-02-28'), both calls return the same cached result unless you include the arguments in the key.

// ❌ WRONG — both calls share one cache entry
const getRevenue = unstable_cache(
  async (start: string, end: string) => queryRevenue(start, end),
  ['revenue'],
  { revalidate: 900 }
);

await getRevenue('2025-01-01', '2025-01-31'); // caches under ['revenue']
await getRevenue('2025-02-01', '2025-02-28'); // ❌ returns January's data!

// ✅ CORRECT — include the args in the key parts
const getRevenue = unstable_cache(
  async (start: string, end: string) => queryRevenue(start, end),
  (start, end) => ['revenue', start, end],  // dynamic key function
  { revalidate: 900 }
);

await getRevenue('2025-01-01', '2025-01-31'); // caches under ['revenue', '2025-01-01', '2025-01-31']
await getRevenue('2025-02-01', '2025-02-28'); // ✅ separate entry

The key function receives the same arguments as the wrapped function and must return a serializable array. This is the #1 source of subtle bugs with unstable_cache.

7.3 Combining unstable_cache with React.cache()

Use both for maximum safety: React.cache() dedupes within a request; unstable_cache persists across requests.

// lib/user.ts
import { cache } from 'react';
import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache';

const _getUser = unstable_cache(
  async (id: string) => prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { id } }),
  (id) => [`user-${id}`],
  { tags: ['users'], revalidate: 3600 }
);

export const getUser = cache((id: string) => _getUser(id));

Now the same user fetched in ten components during one render hits the cache once, and the cached result survives across requests for an hour.

8. Advanced Pattern: Time-Based Revalidation (ISR) Done Right

Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) is the time-based counterpart to tag-based invalidation. It's ideal when you can tolerate up to N seconds of staleness but want zero server load on the critical path.

8.1 Per-fetch revalidation vs. per-route revalidation

You can set revalidation at the fetch level (as we've seen) or at the route level via the revalidate export. Route-level revalidation applies to all fetches in the route that don't specify their own.

// app/blog/page.tsx
// Applies to every fetch in this route unless overridden.
export const revalidate = 3600; // 1 hour

export default async function BlogPage() {
  const posts = await fetch('https://api.example.com/posts'); // inherits 3600
  return <PostList posts={posts} />;
}

8.2 On-demand revalidation with revalidatePath

Time-based ISR is passive. When you need to invalidate immediately (e.g. a user publishes a post), use revalidatePath:

// app/admin/actions.ts
'use server';

import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache';

export async function publishPost(postId: string) {
  await prisma.post.update({ where: { id: postId }, data: { published: true } });

  // Revalidate the post page and the blog index immediately.
  revalidatePath(`/blog/${postId}`);
  revalidatePath('/blog');
}

8.3 The hybrid pattern: time + tags

For most real apps, combine both: use tags for deterministic invalidation, and set a generous revalidate as a safety net so stale data self-heals even if a webhook fails.

const getProduct = unstable_cache(
  async (id: string) => fetchProductFromDb(id),
  (id) => [`product-${id}`],
  {
    revalidate: 86400,   // 24h safety net
    tags: ['products', 'catalog'],
  }
);

This gives you: instant invalidation via webhooks/actions, plus automatic recovery within 24 hours if something goes wrong. This is the pattern I recommend for most production CMS-driven sites.

9. Advanced Pattern: Cache-Aware Streaming and Suspense

Streaming with Suspense changes how caching behaves. When a route is static and you stream a component, the Full Route Cache stores the initial HTML shell and the entire RSC payload — including the streamed content — so the second visit is instant.

9.1 Streaming a cached fetch 

// app/dashboard/page.tsx
import { Suspense } from 'react';

export default function DashboardPage() {
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Dashboard</h1>
      <Suspense fallback={<Skeleton />}>
        <RevenueChart />
      </Suspense>
      <Suspense fallback={<Skeleton />}>
        <RecentOrders />
      </Suspense>
    </div>
  );
}

async function RevenueChart() {
  // This fetch is cached. The component streams in, but the RSC payload
  // is stored in the Full Route Cache so the next visit is instant.
  const data = await fetch('https://api.example.com/revenue', {
    next: { revalidate: 300, tags: ['revenue'] },
  }).then((r) => r.json());

  return <Chart data={data} />;
}

9.2 The dynamic export — controlling the whole route

Sometimes you need to force a route out of the Full Route Cache entirely (e.g. an admin dashboard showing live data). Use the dynamic export:

// app/admin/overview/page.tsx
// Force dynamic rendering — bypasses Full Route Cache for this route.
export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic';

export default async function AdminOverview() {
  const stats = await fetch('https://api.example.com/admin/stats', {
    cache: 'no-store',
  }).then((r) => r.json());

  return <StatsPanel stats={stats} />;
}

Rule of thumb: Use force-dynamic sparingly. It disables all static optimization for the route, including the shell, which can tank performance on high-traffic pages. Prefer per-fetch no-store or short revalidate values instead.

10. Production Best Practices and Common Pitfalls

10.1 Pitfall: The Router Cache is the invisible culprit

You call revalidateTag, your server data is fresh, but the UI doesn't update. That's the Router Cache serving a stale RSC payload. Fix: call router.refresh() after mutations, or set staleTimes.dynamic: 0 for routes that must always be fresh.

10.2 Pitfall: unstable_cache key collisions

Forgetting to include function arguments in the cache key causes cross-argument data bleed. Always use the dynamic key function form when the function takes arguments.

10.3 Pitfall: Mixing no-store with revalidate in one route

A single no-store fetch makes the whole route dynamic and disables the Full Route Cache — even if other fetches are cached. This silently kills ISR. Check the Network tab: if the route responds with x-nextjs-cache: no-store, you've been bitten.

10.4 Best practice: Centralize cache configuration

Define your cache policies in one place so you can tune them without hunting through components:

// lib/cache-policies.ts
export const CACHE = {
  cms: { revalidate: 300, tags: ['cms'] },
  analytics: { revalidate: 900, tags: ['analytics'] },
  session: { revalidate: 0, tags: ['session'] },
  catalog: { revalidate: 3600, tags: ['catalog', 'products'] },
} as const;

// Usage:
const res = await fetch(url, { next: CACHE.catalog });

10.5 Best practice: Log cache hits and misses in development 

// lib/with-cache-log.ts
import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache';

export function withCacheLog<T extends (...args: any[]) => Promise<any>>(
  fn: T,
  key: string[],
  options: { revalidate?: number; tags?: string[] } = {}
) {
  return unstable_cache(
    async (...args: Parameters<T>) => {
      console.log(`[cache:miss] ${key.join('/')}`);
      return fn(...args);
    },
    key,
    {
      ...options,
      // Log when the cache is populated after a miss
      revalidate: options.revalidate ?? 60,
    }
  );
}

10.6 Best practice: Use revalidatePath for page-level, revalidateTag for data-level

revalidatePath is coarse — it invalidates the Full Route Cache for a path and everything nested. revalidateTag is fine-grained — it invalidates only the data tagged. Prefer tags for data that's shared across many routes; use paths only when you want to force a full page re-render.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Why is my fetch() not being cached even though I set next: { revalidate: 60 }?

A: Check three things. First, make sure the route isn't dynamic — a cookies(), headers(), or searchParams read forces dynamic rendering, which disables the Full Route Cache but not the Data Cache. Second, verify you're not passing cache: 'no-store' anywhere in the same route, which makes the whole route dynamic. Third, confirm the fetch URL is a full absolute URL — relative URLs are not cached. Inspect the response headers: x-nextjs-cache: HIT confirms the Data Cache served it.

Q: What's the difference between revalidatePath and revalidateTag?

A: revalidatePath invalidates the Full Route Cache for a specific path and all nested routes — it forces a re-render of those pages. revalidateTag invalidates the Data Cache entries tagged with that string, which can span many routes. Use revalidateTag for data shared across routes (e.g. a CMS collection), and revalidatePath when you want to guarantee a specific page's HTML is regenerated. In practice, you'll often call both.

Q: Is unstable_cache safe to use in production?

A: Yes, it's widely used in production, but the API is still marked unstable and may change in future majors. The main risk is the key-collision pitfall described in Section 7.2 — always use the dynamic key function when your wrapped function takes arguments. For a stable alternative, consider the use cache directive (experimental in Next.js 15) which brings compiler-level caching and is expected to become the standard. For more on the evolution of these APIs, see Tamiz's Insights.
