title: Decode Token Parallelism: Memory-Efficient Distributed Attention Parallelism for Scalable LLM Decoding
description:
arXiv:2611.13293v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Serving large language models at high concurrency with long contexts requires KV-cache capacity and attention bandwidth that grow with the decode pool. Existing parallelization strategies trade one against the other: data parallelism replicates model weights, limiting KV capacity; tensor parallelism stops scaling attention at the model's KV-head count and pushes dense collectives across nodes; and decode context parallelism (DCP) recovers capacity by sharding the sequence but adds cross-node aggregation of partial attention results. We observe that during decode, dense layers and attention scale differently: dense layers amortize weight reads across the batch and run efficiently within a single NVLink domain, whereas attention cost grows with every active request's KV cache. We present Decode Token Parallelism (TKNP), a decode-pool architecture that decouples weight placement from attention ownership. TKNP distributes a single model copy across nodes in balanced layer blocks. The active node holding a block executes its projections and MLP for the full batch using intra-node tensor parallelism, while every node computes attention for its own requests against locally resident KV cache. This extends request-local attention across nodes without replicating weights: only current-token activations cross the network, dense all-reduces remain within NVLink, and attention requires no cross-node merging of partial results. Implemented in vLLM and evaluated on Llama 3.1 405B and Nemotron-4 340B on up to 64 H100 GPUs, TKNP improves completion throughput for long-context, high-concurrency workloads by up to 1.7$\times$ over DCP and by up to 2.06$\times$ over data parallelism at matched GPU count.

title: X Marks the Spot: Diffusion for Image Geolocalization with Location Representations
description:
arXiv:2611.13180v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Image geolocalization predicts the location at which a photo was taken. Accurate geolocalization requires discriminating between both physically and semantically adjacent areas on Earth. However, prior diffusion-based approaches predict locations by generating coordinates, which are semantically unstable over space. We avoid this limitation by learning geolocalization behavior in the pretrained representation spaces of location encoders, which provide both positional and semantic understanding. To make this space usable for coordinate prediction, we introduce a Location Autoencoder (LAE), which pairs a frozen location encoder with a learned decoder mapping embeddings back to coordinates with kilometer-level accuracy worldwide. In the LAE space, we train DIG, a latent diffusion model that transports noise to location embeddings conditioned on image features. DIG consistently outperforms coordinate-based generative models and sets a new state of the art for parametric geolocalization on three benchmarks: OSV-5M, Im2GPS3k, and YFCC4k. Notably, DIG is the first generative model to outperform retrieval-based methods, and further improves retrieve-and-rerank systems when used as a prior. Code and models will be released.

title: AWS Billing and Cost Management now supports AWS Billing Conductor and AWS Billing Transfer views as source views for custom billing views
description:
Custom billing views now support AWS Billing Conductor and AWS Billing Transfer views as source views. These are the views AWS maintains per billing group and per billing transfer relationship. You can combine them into a single custom billing view, apply filters, and use that view in Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, and the Billing and Cost Management console. There are three source view types. Billing group views contain the cost of each Billing Conductor billing group, which you can combine for chargeback and showback across business units. Billing transfer views contain the cost transferred to you for each end customer, and transfer showback views contain the cost that end customer sees. Aggregating each type gives you your total transferred cost and the total bill your end customers see.

Your access does not change: you can use an AWS-managed view as a source only where you can already access it. Once created, you can share a custom billing view using AWS Resource Access Manager with accounts inside or outside your organization, so your finance team or a downstream seller works with the data in their own account. Whether you are an AWS Partner reselling AWS services or an organization using billing groups for pro forma billing, you get one consolidated view instead of one per customer or group.

This feature is available in all commercial AWS Regions at no additional cost. To get started, navigate to Billing Views in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console or view the user guide.

title: MICRO: A Surgery-Phase Retinal Image Rigid Registration Benchmark and One-Step Frequency-Structure Similarity Registration Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.13045v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Precise multimodal retinal image rigid registration (MRIRG) is essential for aligning cross-modal vessel structures, offering critical guidance for ophthalmic surgery. Despite its significance, the advancement of MRIRG is hindered by the lack of publicly available multimodal retinal image rigid registration datasets spanning various ophthalmic surgery phases (e.g., preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative). To address this issue, we introduce the MICRO dataset, a large-scale MRIRG benchmark, comprising 1,365 cross-modal retinal image pairs with standardized annotations across all ophthalmic surgery phases. Moreover, existing deep registration methods achieve competitive MRIRG results via a two-step segmentation-then-detection framework, but segmentation quality heavily constrains their performance. We argue that this dependency stems from an implicit need for keypoint topology constraints, which have not been exploited for MRIRG through a one-step registration framework. Inspired by the above analysis, we propose a novel One-step Frequency-Structure Similarity Registration (OFS2Reg) learning framework for MRIRG that leverages the potential of cross-modal vessel structure similarities to construct keypoint topology constraints under a shared detection network. To be specific, OFS2Reg applies a well-designed frequency-guided structure preservation descriptor to construct coarse keypoint topology constraints in descriptors by highlighting significant vessel structures. Additionally, we develop a new cross-modal vessel structure similarity learning method that refines cross-modal keypoint topology constraints to precisely align pixel-level cross-modal vessel structures by leveraging cross-modal vessel structure similarity priors.

title: Nepali-English Code-Mixed Speech Recognition: Data Preparation and Adaptation of a Speech Foundation Model
description:
arXiv:2611.13512v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Nepali speakers regularly mix English words into conversation, but multilingual speech recognisers often struggle with language switches and the writing script used for English words. We study how to adapt SraVaani, a 449M-parameter hybrid TDT-CTC model, using a 172.8-hour corpus covering six Nepali speech domains. Its pretrained tokenizer does not support digits and several common symbols. Rather than replace it or discard these recordings, we generate Nepali and English readings for numbers and use zero-shot ASR output to select a plausible form. Full fine-tuning reduces test word error rate (WER) from 48.6% to 17.1%; a 12-epoch run reaches 16.3%, compared with 16.4% for fine-tuned Whisper large-v3-turbo. Freezing the encoder increases WER to 25.5%, while excluding numeric clips raises WER on numeric test speech from 14.3% to 21.3%. We also evaluate on FLEURS using both its original references and mixed-script alternatives. The comparison shows that transcription conventions explain part, but not all, of the out-of-domain performance loss.

title: Multi-Stage Phase-Aware Self-Supervised Reconstruction for Multi-Echo Gradient-Echo MRI
description:
arXiv:2611.13352v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Purpose: To develop a phase-aware self-supervised framework for accelerated high-resolution multi-echo gradient-echo (mGRE) MRI that preserves anatomical detail and complex echo information for quantitative mapping. Methods: We developed multi-stage phase-aware self-supervised reconstruction (MSPR-GRE), integrating progressive k-space expansion with phase estimation and refinement. Sequential unrolled networks reconstruct complex multi-echo images and update echo-dependent phase priors. A relaxation-informed temporal subspace is used for acquisitions with at least four echoes, while shorter echo trains are reconstructed in the image domain. Training uses held-out acquired k-space samples without fully sampled targets. Evaluation included 9.4 T ex vivo mouse-brain data 30um eight-echo and 18um dual-echo) and retrospectively undersampled 7 T AHEAD human-brain data, with supervised ablations. Results:MSPR-GRE reduced artifacts in regions of rapid phase variation and preserved fine mouse-brain anatomy. Across five AHEAD test datasets at R = 4, 8, and 12, it generally improved magnitude-image, T2* map, and QSM metrics, particularly at higher acceleration. At R = 12, fourth-echo magnitude NRMSE was 12.09$\pm$0.60% versus 21.55$\pm$1.12% for SSDU. Ablations indicated benefits of phase refinement, while supervised experiments supported multi-stage phase-aware reconstruction. Conclusion: MSPR-GRE improves accelerated mGRE reconstruction and quantitative-map agreement without fully sampled training targets. Further validation of generalizability and phase-estimation accuracy is needed.

title: AWS Regions, Availability Zones and Edge Locations Explained (Beginner Guide)
description:
A simple beginner guide to AWS Global Infrastructure: what Regions, Availability Zones and Edge Locations are, how they differ, and how to choose between them."
tags: aws, beginners, cloud, tutorial

series: AWS Beginner Journey

When I started learning AWS, one thing confused me before I even launched my first server: Region, Availability Zone, Edge Location. What's the difference?

If you are preparing for the Cloud Practitioner exam or just starting your cloud journey, this is one of the most important concepts to get right. In this article, I explain it in simple words with real examples.

Why Does AWS Have a "Global Infrastructure"?

AWS doesn't run from one giant building. It runs from data centers spread across the world. This is done so that:

  • Your app stays available even if one data center fails
  • Your users get low latency (faster response) from nearby locations
  • You can follow data rules of your country or company
  • You get fault tolerance and disaster recovery options

AWS organizes this global network into three main building blocks: Regions, Availability Zones and Edge Locations.

1. AWS Region

A Region is a separate geographic area in the world where AWS has multiple data centers grouped together.

Each Region has a name and a code. Some examples:

Region Name Code
Asia Pacific (Mumbai) ap-south-1
Asia Pacific (Hyderabad) ap-south-2
US East (N. Virginia) us-east-1
Europe (Ireland) eu-west-1

Key points about Regions:

  • Regions are completely independent of each other
  • Your data stays in the Region you choose unless you move or replicate it yourself
  • Most services are Region-specific. An EC2 instance in Mumbai will not appear when you switch to N. Virginia
  • Pricing can differ from Region to Region
  • Not every service is available in every Region

How to choose a Region

  1. Latency: Choose a Region close to your users. For users in India, Mumbai (ap-south-1) is a natural choice.
  2. Compliance: Some businesses must keep data within a country.
  3. Service availability: New services often launch in a few Regions first.
  4. Cost: Prices vary between Regions.

2. Availability Zone (AZ)

An Availability Zone is one or more separate data centers inside a Region, each with its own power, cooling and networking.

AZs inside a Region are named like this:

  • ap-south-1a
  • ap-south-1b
  • ap-south-1c

Key points about AZs:

  • Every Region has multiple AZs (at least three in most Regions)
  • AZs are physically separated so that a fire, flood or power failure in one does not affect the others
  • AZs in the same Region are connected with high-speed, low-latency private networking
  • Some resources, like subnets and EC2 instances, live in a single AZ

Why AZs matter

If you run your whole application in a single AZ and that AZ has a problem, your app goes down. If you spread it across two or more AZs, your app keeps running.

This is exactly why services like Application Load Balancer, Auto Scaling Group and RDS Multi-AZ are built around AZs. They help you create a highly available architecture.

3. Edge Location

An Edge Location is a site that AWS uses to deliver content closer to users. It is not where you launch your servers. It is where content is cached and served.

Edge Locations are mainly used by:

  • Amazon CloudFront (CDN) to cache websites, images and videos
  • Amazon Route 53 (DNS) to answer DNS queries quickly
  • AWS Global Accelerator to route traffic over the AWS network

Simple example

Imagine your website's origin is an S3 bucket in the US, but your visitors are in India.

  • Without an Edge Location: every request travels all the way to the US and back, so it is slower.
  • With CloudFront: a copy of your content is cached at a nearby Edge Location, so users get it much faster.

Region vs AZ vs Edge Location: Quick Comparison

Feature Region Availability Zone Edge Location
What is it? Geographic area Data center(s) inside a Region Content delivery site
Purpose Host your resources High availability Low-latency delivery
You launch EC2/RDS here? Yes (you choose the Region) Yes (you choose the AZ) No
Example ap-south-1 (Mumbai) ap-south-1a CloudFront cache site

An Easy Real-Life Analogy

Think of AWS like a courier company:

  • Region = a city where the company operates
  • Availability Zone = separate warehouses inside that city. If one warehouse has a power cut, the others keep working
  • Edge Location = small pickup points in different neighborhoods so customers get parcels faster

Other Terms You May Hear

  • Local Zones: extend a Region closer to large cities for ultra-low latency
  • Wavelength Zones: bring AWS services to the edge of 5G networks
  • Outposts: AWS infrastructure installed in your own data center

You don't need these as a beginner, but it's good to know they exist.

Hands-On: See It Yourself in the AWS Console

  1. Log in to the AWS Management Console
  2. Click the Region selector at the top right and switch between Regions
  3. Open EC2 → Launch instance, then under Network settings choose a Subnet. Each subnet shows the AZ it belongs to (for example, ap-south-1a)
  4. Open CloudFront and notice that it is a global service and does not ask you to pick a Region

Try this once and the concept will stay in your mind for good.

Key Takeaways

  • A Region is a geographic area, and Regions are independent of each other
  • An Availability Zone is an isolated data center location inside a Region, and using multiple AZs gives you high availability
  • An Edge Location caches and delivers content closer to users, mainly through CloudFront
  • Choose your Region based on latency, compliance, service availability and cost
  • Design for failure: spread your resources across multiple AZs

Cloud Practitioner Exam Tip

A common exam question: "How can you make your application highly available on AWS?" The answer is usually deploy across multiple Availability Zones. And "Which service uses Edge Locations?" The answer is Amazon CloudFront.

Final Thoughts

Understanding AWS Global Infrastructure is the foundation for everything else you will learn, from EC2 and S3 to VPC and load balancing. Once you know where your resources live and why, designing reliable and fast applications becomes much easier.

I'm sharing what I learn step by step as part of my cloud journey. If this helped you, feel free to like, comment or share your own experience.

title: Use @layer + low-specificity selectors so site overrides don’t turn into selector wars
description:
Problem

Component libraries simplify UI work—until their styles start winning every time. Product tweaks become an arms race: nested selectors, extra classes, and the occasional !important to force a visual change. That creates brittle overrides and long-term maintenance pain.

Implementation (what to do)

1) Declare a stable @layer order and keep it explicit in your imports or build. Make sure the library layer is declared earlier and the site (product) layer declared later.
2) Wrap or import third-party library CSS into the earlier layer. Keep product/theme overrides and page-specific rules in the later layer.
3) When authoring site rules, prefer short, descriptive selectors (type, single class) or use :where() to scope matches without increasing specificity.

Expected behavior

For normal (non-!important) declarations, layer precedence is evaluated before selector specificity. That means a low-specificity selector in the later site layer can override a more-specific selector in the earlier library layer. The result: concise site overrides that don’t require escalating selector strength and clearer ownership in code.

What the included fixture proves

The article ships a minimal cascade evaluator plus tests demonstrating three points: (1) a site rule in a later layer wins even if the library selector is more specific; (2) :where() matches without adding specificity so site selectors stay easy to override later; (3) tests can assert selector specificity to detect accidental increases that would make future maintenance harder.

Limitations

Layers make ownership legible but don’t enforce it: teams must still agree which styles belong to the library versus the site. The included evaluator is intentionally simplified to demonstrate the migration contract; it does not replicate every browser quirk and should not replace cross-browser verification.

Why this is useful

The approach is incremental: wrap existing library CSS into a layer and migrate site overrides into the later layer gradually. Add a small test that asserts both the visual winner and the selector specificity to prevent silent drift back into selector wars. The article contains a compact, testable evaluator and concrete test cases you can adopt as guardrails during refactors.

(The server will append the verified implementation example below.)

Working example 

// Minimal CSS cascade evaluator focused on demonstrating @layer ordering and specificity
// Exports a pure function evaluateCascade(rules, element) with no side effects.
// rules: array of {layer: string, selector: string, declarations: {prop: value}}. The order of first appearance of layer names
// determines layer precedence: later-declared layers win over earlier ones for normal (non-!important) declarations.
// element: {tag: 'div', id: 'x', classes: ['a','b']}

function normalizeLayerOrder(rules) {
  // Determine first-seen order of layers
  const order = new Map();
  let idx = 0;
  for (const r of rules) {
    if (!order.has(r.layer)) order.set(r.layer, idx++);
  }
  return order; // map layer -> index (lower = declared earlier = lower precedence)
}

function splitCompound(compound) {
  // Split a compound like "div.btn#id" into tokens: ['div', '.btn', '#id']
  return compound.split(/(?=[.#])/g).filter(Boolean);
}

function matchesSelector(selector, element) {
  // Support simple selectors used in examples: tag, .class, #id, and :where(...)
  selector = selector.trim();
  // If selector contains descendant spaces (e.g. '.toolbar .btn'), the evaluator used in tests
  // models only the target element, not the ancestor chain. To match the intent of the tests,
  // consider a selector with spaces to match if its last compound (the rightmost sequence)
  // matches the element. This preserves counting of specificity across the full selector.

  // handle top-level :where() wrappers by delegating to inner selector for matching
  if (selector.startsWith(':where(') && selector.endsWith(')')) {
    const inner = selector.slice(7, -1).trim();
    return matchesSelector(inner, element);
  }

  // Split by whitespace to tokens (descendant combinator); we match only against the last token
  const tokens = selector.split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
  const last = tokens[tokens.length - 1];
  // If last is a :where() wrapper, test its inner selector(s)
  if (last.startsWith(':where(') && last.endsWith(')')) {
    const inner = last.slice(7, -1).trim();
    // inner may be a selector list, but tests use simple cases, so just test inner against element
    return matchesSelector(inner, element);
  }

  const parts = splitCompound(last);
  // first part might be tag (no prefix)
  let idx = 0;
  if (parts[0] && !parts[0].startsWith('.') && !parts[0].startsWith('#')) {
    const tag = parts[0].toLowerCase();
    if (element.tag && element.tag.toLowerCase() !== tag) return false;
    idx = 1;
  }
  for (; idx < parts.length; idx++) {
    const p = parts[idx];
    if (p.startsWith('.')) {
      const cls = p.slice(1);
      if (!element.classes || !element.classes.includes(cls)) return false;
    } else if (p.startsWith('#')) {
      const id = p.slice(1);
      if (!element.id || element.id !== id) return false;
    } else {
      // unsupported token, be conservative and return false
      return false;
    }
  }
  return true;
}

function specificityOf(selector) {
  // Return tuple [a,b,c] following MDN: a = #ids, b = classes/attrs/pseudo-classes, c = type/pseudo-elements
  selector = selector.trim();
  // We must account for selectors with descendant combinators and :where() which contributes 0
  let a = 0, b = 0, c = 0;
  const tokens = selector.split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
  for (const token of tokens) {
    // If token is :where(...), its parameters do NOT add specificity. Still, those parameters
    // are used for matching; here we intentionally skip adding any specificity for :where.
    if (token.startsWith(':where(') && token.endsWith(')')) {
      // skip adding specificity for :where(...) entirely
      continue;
    }
    // For other tokens, break into compound parts like "div.btn#id"
    const parts = splitCompound(token);
    if (parts[0] && !parts[0].startsWith('.') && !parts[0].startsWith('#')) {
      // type selector
      c += 1;
    }
    for (const p of parts) {
      if (p.startsWith('#')) a += 1;
      else if (p.startsWith('.')) b += 1;
      // else it's a type already counted
    }
  }
  return [a, b, c];
}

function compareSpecificity(s1, s2) {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    if (s1[i] > s2[i]) return 1;
    if (s1[i] < s2[i]) return -1;
  }
  return 0;
}

function evaluateCascade(rules, element) {
  // rules is an array where layer names' declaration order is the order of appearance.
  // For simplicity we only evaluate a single property key at a time in examples; here we return a map prop->value
  const layerOrder = normalizeLayerOrder(rules);
  // for each rule that matches the element, consider each declaration
  const wins = new Map(); // prop -> {value, layerIndex, specificity, ruleIndex}
  rules.forEach((r, idx) => {
    if (!matchesSelector(r.selector, element)) return;
    const layerIndex = layerOrder.get(r.layer);
    for (const [prop, value] of Object.entries(r.declarations)) {
      const spec = specificityOf(r.selector);
      const existing = wins.get(prop);
      if (!existing) {
        wins.set(prop, {value, layerIndex, specificity: spec, ruleIndex: idx});
        continue;
      }
      // Compare by layer precedence (higher layerIndex wins). If same layer index, compare specificity.
      if (layerIndex > existing.layerIndex) {
        wins.set(prop, {value, layerIndex, specificity: spec, ruleIndex: idx});
      } else if (layerIndex < existing.layerIndex) {
        // losing by layer order -> ignore
      } else {
        // same layer: compare specificity
        const cmp = compareSpecificity(spec, existing.specificity);
        if (cmp > 0) {
          wins.set(prop, {value, layerIndex, specificity: spec, ruleIndex: idx});
        } else if (cmp === 0) {
          // same specificity: later rule (higher ruleIndex) wins
          if (idx > existing.ruleIndex) {
            wins.set(prop, {value, layerIndex, specificity: spec, ruleIndex: idx});
          }
        }
      }
    }
  });
  // return plain object of properties to values
  const out = {};
  for (const [k, v] of wins.entries()) out[k] = v.value;
  return out;
}

export { evaluateCascade, matchesSelector, specificityOf };

title: URL-Sim: Unified and Regulated LiDAR Simulation for High-Fidelity Reconstruction of Dynamic Driving Scenes
description:
arXiv:2611.12932v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reconstructing high-fidelity LiDAR simulation scenes from real-world driving logs is essential for cost-effective safety validation of autonomous driving systems. While simulators based on Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) achieve realistic scene reconstruction, their large-scale adoption is limited by slow rendering speeds. Recent 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) approaches have improved rendering efficiency through explicit primitive representation and differentiable rasterization. However, existing 3DGS-based methods remain largely restricted to rigid vehicles and produce redundant primitives through unconstrained densification. To address these limitations, we propose URL-Sim, a unified and regulated dynamic LiDAR simulation framework. URL-Sim constructs a dynamic Gaussian scene graph that decouples the modeling of traffic participants, including vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists, enabling accurate reconstruction of heterogeneous dynamic objects within a single framework. It further introduces a regulated Gaussian densification strategy that ranks primitives with multi-dimensional importance scores and allocates Gaussians to the most critical regions while keeping the total primitive count bounded. Experiments on the Waymo and KITTI-360 datasets demonstrate that URL-Sim achieves higher quantitative accuracy and visual quality than existing baselines under comparable primitive budgets, and accurately recovers the geometry and poses of diverse dynamic traffic participants.

title: Postgres to Snowflake Replication Without Kafka or Airflow
description:
Postgres to Snowflake Replication Without Kafka or Airflow

Replicating data from PostgreSQL to Snowflake is a common requirement for teams building analytics platforms, reporting systems, and data warehouses. However, keeping the two systems synchronized can become complicated when data changes frequently.

Traditional data pipelines often rely on tools such as Kafka, Debezium, and Airflow to capture, transport, and orchestrate database changes. While these tools offer flexibility, they also introduce additional infrastructure, configuration, and operational overhead.

For teams that want to replicate an existing PostgreSQL database into Snowflake without managing a Kafka cluster or Airflow DAGs, managed Change Data Capture (CDC) services offer a simpler alternative.

In this guide, we'll compare seven tools for PostgreSQL-to-Snowflake replication, including Estuary, Fivetran, Airbyte, Striim, Artie, Snowflake Openflow, and Snowflake Postgres data mirroring. We'll examine their CDC capabilities, Snowflake write paths, delete handling, freshness, pricing models, and limitations.

Can You Replicate PostgreSQL to Snowflake Without Kafka or Airflow?

Yes. A managed CDC service can capture PostgreSQL changes and deliver them to Snowflake without requiring you to deploy and maintain Kafka, Debezium, or Airflow.

PostgreSQL supports logical replication through its Write-Ahead Log (WAL). CDC connectors use this mechanism to capture database changes, including inserts, updates, and deletes, and send them to a destination.

A typical managed replication pipeline looks like this:

PostgreSQL → CDC Connector → Managed Data Pipeline → Snowflake

The main advantage is that the replication service handles change capture and delivery, eliminating the need to maintain separate infrastructure for message streaming and workflow orchestration.

However, not every PostgreSQL-to-Snowflake integration works with an existing external PostgreSQL database. Snowflake's native data mirroring, for example, is designed specifically for Snowflake Postgres.

Understanding this distinction is important when selecting a tool.

How We Selected These PostgreSQL-to-Snowflake Tools

We compared seven tools based on six requirements relevant to teams that want to avoid Kafka and Airflow.

1. PostgreSQL source support

The tool must support an existing PostgreSQL database, whether self-hosted or running on a major cloud platform. Version requirements also matter. For example, Estuary supports PostgreSQL 10.0 and later, while Snowflake Openflow requires PostgreSQL 11 or later.

2. Managed operation

The objective is to reduce infrastructure management. We considered whether the service handles CDC and data delivery without requiring teams to operate their own Kafka cluster, connector deployment, or orchestration DAG.

3. Snowflake write path

We examined how each tool delivers data to Snowflake. Some use staged loads, others support Snowpipe Streaming, and some apply changes through SQL operations.

4. Delete handling

Capturing inserts and updates is not enough. We also considered how tools handle deleted records and whether they support soft deletes, hard deletes, or operations such as TRUNCATE.

5. Data freshness

Replication frequency directly affects how current the Snowflake data remains. We compared configurable sync schedules, advertised latency, and available low-latency ingestion options.

6. Pricing transparency

We considered whether vendors publish pricing and how they charge for replication, including data volume, monthly active rows, connector instances, or compute capacity.

7 Tools to Replicate PostgreSQL to Snowflake Without Kafka or Airflow

1. Estuary

https://estuary.dev/

Estuary is a strong option for replicating an existing PostgreSQL database into Snowflake without deploying Kafka or Airflow.

Its PostgreSQL capture connector continuously reads source changes using CDC and writes them into Estuary collections. The Snowflake materialization then delivers those collections to destination tables.

For standard updates, Estuary stages changes before applying them transactionally. For delta-update bindings, it also supports Snowpipe Streaming.

You can follow the PostgreSQL-to-Snowflake setup tutorial to configure the pipeline.

Key capabilities:

  • Continuous PostgreSQL CDC.
  • Automatic schema evolution.
  • One capture can feed multiple destinations without rereading the source.
  • Standard updates through staged transactional loads.
  • Snowpipe Streaming support for delta bindings.
  • Configurable Snowflake synchronization frequency.

For teams that need to balance data freshness and warehouse costs, Estuary allows the Snowflake materialization's Sync Frequency to be configured to 0s. This removes the scheduled waiting period. Snowpipe Streaming provides its lowest-latency Snowflake loading path for delta bindings.

Pricing:

As of October 2026, Estuary's Cloud plan charges:

  • $0.50 per GB of data moved.
  • $100 per connector instance per month for the first six instances.
  • $50 per month for each additional connector instance.

Its free Developer tier includes 10 GB of combined captured and delivered data per month and two connector instances.

Limitations:

Estuary's PostgreSQL connector supports PostgreSQL 10.0 and later. Teams running PostgreSQL 9.x or earlier will need to upgrade or consider another option.

Best for: Teams that need continuous CDC from an existing PostgreSQL database, configurable Snowflake delivery, and a managed alternative to Kafka and Airflow.

2. Fivetran

https://www.fivetran.com/

Fivetran provides a managed PostgreSQL connector that replicates database data into Snowflake.

Its PostgreSQL connector captures source data, while its Snowflake destination connector handles delivery to the warehouse.

Fivetran is a suitable option for teams that want managed database replication without operating their own CDC infrastructure.

Key capabilities:

  • Managed PostgreSQL replication.
  • Snowflake destination support.
  • SQL MERGE operations for applying changes to Snowflake tables.
  • Standard and Enterprise sync-frequency options.

Pricing:

Fivetran uses monthly active rows (MAR) for connection billing.

As of October 2026:

  • The free plan covers 500,000 monthly active rows for connections.
  • Standard connections between 1 and 1 million monthly active rows have a $5 base charge.
  • Standard includes 15-minute syncs.
  • Enterprise adds 1-minute syncs.

Enterprise database connectors are available through the Enterprise plan.

Limitations:

Teams requiring sub-15-minute freshness may need to move beyond the Standard plan to Enterprise or Business Critical.

Best for: Teams that prefer managed replication and whose freshness requirements and monthly active row volumes fit Fivetran's pricing structure.

3. Airbyte

https://airbyte.com/

Airbyte provides PostgreSQL source and Snowflake destination connectors for database replication.

Its PostgreSQL source supports CDC through logical replication and also supports replication using PostgreSQL's xmin system column.

For PostgreSQL databases larger than 500 GB, Airbyte recommends logical replication.

The Snowflake destination connector handles delivery to the warehouse. Starting with version 5.0.0, username-and-password authentication for the Snowflake destination is deprecated.

Airbyte also uses PostgreSQL WAL-based logical replication to capture delete operations.

Key capabilities:

  • PostgreSQL CDC support.
  • Logical replication and xmin-based replication.
  • Snowflake destination connector.
  • Managed Cloud deployment options.
  • Delete capture through logical replication.

Pricing:

Airbyte offers different Cloud pricing structures:

  • Standard uses a fully managed, volume-based pricing model.
  • Pro and Enterprise Flex plans use Data Worker capacity for pricing.

Limitations:

Airbyte's CDC caching layer is incompatible with certain Aurora configurations where that layer cannot be disabled. Teams using Aurora should verify compatibility before selecting this approach.

Best for: Teams looking for managed PostgreSQL-to-Snowflake replication with volume-based or capacity-based Cloud pricing.

4. Striim

https://www.striim.com/

Striim provides PostgreSQL CDC capabilities through its PostgreSQL Reader and supports Snowflake as a destination through its Snowflake Writer.

One notable capability is support for capturing PostgreSQL TRUNCATE operations when using wal2json version 2.

This can be useful for workloads where table truncation is part of the source database workflow.

Key capabilities:

  • PostgreSQL CDC through its Reader.
  • TRUNCATE capture with wal2json version 2.
  • Snowflake Writer support.
  • Snowpipe Streaming support.
  • Support for staging events to local storage, Amazon S3, or Azure Storage.

The Snowflake Writer stages events to local storage, S3, or Azure Storage unless Snowpipe Streaming is enabled. Teams should verify that their PostgreSQL Reader and Snowflake Writer configurations support the required event propagation.

Pricing:

  • Striim Developer is free for up to 25 million events per month.
  • Striim Cloud pricing is available through its sales team.

As of October 2026, Striim does not publish a standard Cloud pricing rate.

Limitations:

Teams looking for transparent, published Cloud pricing may find it difficult to estimate costs without requesting a quote. The Developer allowance is measured in events rather than bytes, so event volume needs to be estimated separately.

Best for: Teams that need PostgreSQL TRUNCATE capture and can use Striim's supported PostgreSQL Reader and Snowflake Writer configuration.

5. Artie

https://www.artie.com/

Artie is a CDC replication platform that supports PostgreSQL and Snowflake.

Its PostgreSQL connector list includes several managed database services, such as:

  • Amazon Aurora.
  • Amazon RDS.
  • Google Cloud SQL.
  • Supabase.

Snowflake is also included among its supported destinations.

Artie advertises sub-minute replication latency and exactly-once delivery, making it an option for teams that prioritize data freshness.

Key capabilities:

  • PostgreSQL CDC support.
  • Support for several managed PostgreSQL services.
  • Snowflake destination support.
  • Advertised sub-minute latency.
  • Advertised exactly-once delivery.

Pricing:

As of October 2026:

  • The free plan covers up to 1 million billable rows per month.
  • Growth starts at $500 per month with an annual contract.
  • Growth costs $600 per month on a month-to-month basis.
  • Enterprise pricing is available through a quote.

Limitations:

Teams that need paid Growth features, such as proactive monitoring or single sign-on, must account for the plan's minimum cost.

Best for: Teams that need sub-minute CDC replication and support for managed PostgreSQL services such as Aurora, RDS, Cloud SQL, or Supabase.

6. Snowflake Openflow

https://www.snowflake.com/

Snowflake Openflow provides a native integration option for replicating PostgreSQL data into Snowflake.

Its PostgreSQL connector supports near-real-time or scheduled replication of selected tables. It also maintains a log of data changes alongside the current table state.

Openflow is built on Apache NiFi and provides a Snowflake-managed integration option, although its deployment and infrastructure requirements differ from fully managed third-party services.

Key capabilities:

  • PostgreSQL-to-Snowflake replication.
  • Near-real-time or scheduled updates.
  • Change logs alongside current table state.
  • Native Snowflake integration.

Requirements and limitations:

  • Requires PostgreSQL 11 or later.
  • Supports only username-and-password authentication with PostgreSQL.
  • Tables without a supported identity key replicate inserts only.
  • Ignores source TRUNCATE statements.
  • BYOC deployments are limited to AWS Commercial Regions.

Before using Openflow for a production workload, confirm that the source tables have the required identity keys if updates and deletes need to be replicated.

Pricing:

Snowflake bills Openflow BYOC compute per second, with a 60-second minimum.

Best for: Teams that want a Snowflake-native integration for external PostgreSQL databases and can meet its version, authentication, and deployment requirements.

7. Snowflake Postgres Data Mirroring

https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-postgres/postgres-data-mirroring

Snowflake Postgres data mirroring is different from the other options in this comparison.

It is designed to replicate tables from Snowflake Postgres into a Snowflake analytics database. Snowflake Postgres is a service where customers create and manage PostgreSQL instances directly within Snowflake.

This means it is not a general-purpose replication solution for an existing PostgreSQL database hosted outside Snowflake.

Key capabilities:

  • Continuous replication from Snowflake Postgres.
  • No external CDC service to deploy.
  • Serverless apply.
  • A $live view containing changes that have not yet been merged.
  • A seven-day change feed for inserts, updates, and deletes.

The $live view has an approximately 30-second lag. The change feed can be queried from both Snowflake and Postgres.

Pricing:

Snowflake bills the apply using its standard serverless task rate.

Limitations:

  • Supports Snowflake Postgres as the source, not arbitrary external PostgreSQL databases.
  • Available in AWS and Azure regions where Snowflake Postgres is supported.
  • Mirrors cannot cross accounts, regions, or clouds.

Best for: Teams already using Snowflake Postgres that want continuous replication into a Snowflake analytics database without deploying an external CDC service.

PostgreSQL-to-Snowflake Replication Tools Compared

The following table summarizes the main differences between the seven options.

Tool PostgreSQL source support Snowflake write path Pricing model Key limitation
Estuary PostgreSQL 10.0+, self-hosted and major cloud platforms Staged transactional loads; Snowpipe Streaming for delta bindings Per GB moved + connector-instance fees Requires PostgreSQL 10.0+
Fivetran PostgreSQL SQL MERGE Monthly active rows 15-minute Standard syncs
Airbyte CDC and xmin replication Snowflake destination connector Volume-based or Data Worker capacity Aurora CDC caching-layer compatibility
Striim PostgreSQL 9.4.x–17, self-managed Staging or Snowpipe Streaming Data moved; Cloud by quote Cloud pricing not published
Artie PostgreSQL, Aurora, RDS, Cloud SQL, Supabase Snowflake destination Billable rows; Growth from $500/month annually Growth plan minimum
Snowflake Openflow PostgreSQL 11+ Near-real-time or scheduled replication BYOC compute Ignores TRUNCATE
Snowflake Postgres mirroring Snowflake Postgres only Serverless apply Serverless task compute Cannot mirror external PostgreSQL sources

Pricing and plan information is based on published vendor details as of October 2026. Actual costs depend on usage, configuration, and applicable plan terms.

How to Choose a PostgreSQL-to-Snowflake Replication Tool

The right tool depends primarily on where your PostgreSQL database runs, how frequently Snowflake needs to receive changes, and how you want to manage replication costs.

Here are a few practical considerations.

Choose Snowflake Postgres data mirroring if:

Your source database is already running on Snowflake Postgres and you want replication into a Snowflake analytics database without deploying an external CDC service.

Choose Estuary if:

You have an existing PostgreSQL database and want managed CDC with configurable Snowflake delivery, without operating Kafka or Airflow.

You can set the Snowflake materialization's Sync Frequency to 0s to remove scheduled waiting time. For delta-update bindings, Snowpipe Streaming provides the connector's lowest-latency loading option.

Choose Fivetran if:

Your workload fits its monthly active row pricing and the Standard plan's 15-minute sync frequency is sufficient.

Choose Airbyte if:

You want PostgreSQL CDC and Snowflake destination support with volume-based or capacity-based Cloud pricing.

Choose Striim if:

Your workflow needs PostgreSQL TRUNCATE capture and its supported Snowflake Writer configuration meets your requirements.

Choose Artie if:

You prioritize its advertised sub-minute latency and need support for managed PostgreSQL services such as Aurora, RDS, Cloud SQL, or Supabase.

Choose Snowflake Openflow if:

You want a Snowflake-native option for an external PostgreSQL database and your source meets its PostgreSQL version, authentication, and deployment requirements.

Before committing to a tool, document these four things:

  1. Source type: Self-hosted PostgreSQL, RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL, Supabase, or Snowflake Postgres.
  2. Freshness requirement: Scheduled replication, 15-minute syncs, or sub-minute delivery.
  3. Data volume: Expected monthly data captured and delivered.
  4. Change operations: Whether the pipeline must support inserts, updates, deletes, and TRUNCATE.

Also, test your largest source table and verify that all required changes reach Snowflake correctly. If your application uses TRUNCATE, test that operation separately rather than assuming it behaves like a series of individual deletes.

FAQ

1. Can you replicate PostgreSQL to Snowflake without Kafka?

Yes. Managed CDC services can capture PostgreSQL changes and deliver them to Snowflake without requiring a separately managed Kafka cluster.

For example, Estuary's PostgreSQL connector captures changes into collections, and its Snowflake materialization delivers those changes to destination tables.

Estuary supports PostgreSQL 10.0 and later on major cloud platforms and self-hosted instances.

2. Do you need Airflow for PostgreSQL-to-Snowflake replication?

No. Airflow is an orchestration tool, not a requirement for CDC-based replication.

Managed services such as Estuary handle change capture and delivery through their own pipeline configurations. Snowflake Openflow also supports near-real-time or scheduled replication, while Snowflake Postgres mirroring runs within Snowflake.

3. Is Snowflake data mirroring available for any PostgreSQL database?

No. Snowflake data mirroring is designed specifically for Snowflake Postgres.

It continuously replicates tables from Snowflake Postgres into a Snowflake analytics database. If your PostgreSQL database runs externally, such as on Amazon RDS, Aurora, or a self-hosted server, you need a compatible external CDC connector.

Snowflake Postgres mirroring is available in supported AWS and Azure regions, and mirrors cannot cross accounts, regions, or clouds.

4. What is the fastest way to replicate PostgreSQL to Snowflake?

The answer depends on where the source database runs.

For Snowflake Postgres, the $live view exposes pending changes with an approximately 30-second lag.

For an external PostgreSQL database, Estuary is an option. You can configure its Snowflake materialization's Sync Frequency to 0s to remove scheduled waiting time. For delta-update bindings, Snowpipe Streaming provides its lowest-latency Snowflake loading path.

Actual end-to-end latency depends on the workload, processing, and ingestion configuration, so validate performance against your own freshness requirements.

5. How much does PostgreSQL-to-Snowflake replication cost?

Costs vary depending on the tool's pricing model and the amount of data being replicated.

For example, Estuary's Cloud pricing as of October 2026 is $0.50 per GB of data moved, plus connector-instance fees.

Consider a workload that captures 100 GB from PostgreSQL and delivers 100 GB to Snowflake. That produces 200 billed GB, costing $100. Two connector instances running for a full month add $200, bringing the estimated recurring pipeline charge to approximately $300.

Artie's Growth plan starts at $500 per month with an annual contract or $600 month to month, as of October 2026.

These figures exclude Snowflake storage and compute, as well as other applicable charges. Confirm vendor pricing and usage allowances before comparing final costs.

6. Should you use Snowflake Openflow or PostgreSQL data mirroring?

Use Snowflake Openflow when replicating an external PostgreSQL database that meets its PostgreSQL 11 or later requirement and supports its username-and-password authentication requirement.

Use Snowflake Postgres data mirroring when your source is already running on Snowflake Postgres and you want to replicate its tables into a Snowflake analytics database.

The two options serve different source environments, so the choice depends on where your PostgreSQL database is hosted.

Conclusion

Replicating PostgreSQL to Snowflake no longer requires every team to maintain a separate Kafka cluster, Debezium deployment, and Airflow orchestration layer.

Managed CDC services provide an alternative by handling change capture and destination delivery within a managed pipeline.

Estuary is a strong choice for existing PostgreSQL databases that need continuous CDC and configurable Snowflake delivery. Fivetran, Airbyte, Striim, and Artie offer alternative managed approaches with different pricing models and operational capabilities. Snowflake Openflow provides a native integration option for external PostgreSQL databases, while Snowflake Postgres data mirroring is specifically designed for databases hosted within Snowflake.

The best choice ultimately depends on your source environment, freshness requirements, change-handling needs, and expected data volume. Evaluate those requirements before selecting a replication tool, and test inserts, updates, deletes, and any TRUNCATE operations your application relies on.

title: Distribution Shift Detection in Remote Sensing Imagery using Machine Learning Models
description:
arXiv:2611.13510v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Remote sensing imagery acquired by Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) supports wide range of applications; however, deploying machine learning (ML) models on resource-constrained aerial platforms introduces challenges beyond predictive accuracy, particularly when deployment data differ from the distributions observed during training. Such shifts are common in remote sensing due to geographic, sensor, seasonal, and other visual variations. A practical solution is to equip deployed models with mechanisms that detect emerging distribution shifts and support subsequent responsive actions. This paper presents an empirical case study of three open-source detection tools: (i) Alibi-Detect; (ii) NannyML; and (iii) PyTorch-OOD. Using cross-dataset remote-sensing shifts, we evaluate both detection effectiveness and computational latency of these tools. Our results reveal differences in detection behavior and processing cost across methods and implementations, highlighting trade-offs between detection capability and response-time. These findings motivate further work toward lightweight, and latency-aware monitoring mechanisms for resource-constrained systems.

title: 426 services, 0 humans: AWS's emulator is written by agents
description:
426 services, 0 humans: AWS's emulator is written by agents

AWS launched a local emulator of its own cloud today, covering 426 services — and says autonomous agents wrote every line of the code, with no human reviewing it. I downloaded the release's own fidelity file: 56.5% of its 42,937 test units pass.

What launched

AWS Emulator is a local program that serves the AWS APIs on your machine, announced today (November 11) in a guest post on All Things Distributed by Swami Sivasubramanian. The source is public on GitHub at aws/aws-emulator, released under CC0 — effectively public domain. It is free, runs offline, and needs no AWS account. Point the AWS CLI or an SDK at it and your code runs against emulated resources instead of real ones.

The numbers AWS puts on it: more than 400 API models covering more than 200 services, per the launch summary — InfoWorld reports 426 services supported. It ships as an RPM or Debian package on Linux (the x86_64 RPM is 159 MB) and as a Docker image you build yourself on macOS and Windows. It serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297 with a self-signed certificate.

The part that actually matters: nobody human wrote it

Every line of the emulator was written and tested by agents, according to Amazon. The loop works like this: agents derive fidelity tests and end-to-end scenarios from the public Smithy API models, correct them until they pass against real AWS, then build the emulator until it passes the same tests. Every change goes through a merge gate that includes security agents doing adversarial reviews. Matthew Goldberg, a senior principal engineer on the project, says the team has not written or reviewed any of the code.

The commit history backs up the "agents did this" framing in a way a press release can't. The repo was created September 11 — 61 days before launch — and by this morning it had 29,684 commits and 322 releases. That is roughly 490 commits and 5 releases a day, every day, for two months. No human team ships at that cadence on a 400-service surface. The release notes read like machine output too: the launch release, v1.0.322, is mostly a long list of fidelity fixes with names like dynamodb-validationexception-messages-diverge-from-the-wording-aws and s3-listobjectversions-omits-markers-owner-and-checksum-members.

I checked the fidelity file it ships

AWS publishes versioned fidelity scores with each release, and the launch release ships a scores.json.gz. I downloaded it and counted, rather than taking the launch copy at face value:

Measure Count Share
Test units, total 42,937 —
Units passing 24,243 56.5%
Units failing 18,614 43.4%
Units skipped 80 0.2%
Individual steps passing 49,810 / 68,007 73.2%
Services scored in the file 355 —

Two things fall out. First, the honest launch number is 56.5%, not "AWS, on your laptop." A bit over half the scenario tests pass; step-level fidelity is better at 73.2%, which is the more useful figure — most scenarios get most of the way there and fail on one step. Second, the scores file covers 355 services against the 426 AWS claims, so about 70 services have no published score yet. That gap is worth watching, not assuming away.

One design decision deserves credit: operations that are not implemented or verified return HTTP 503 instead of fake success. An emulator that silently returns plausible-but-wrong data is worse than no emulator; a 503 is a loud, greppable failure. AWS also publishes the gaps in the open — issues/things-that-do-not-work/ lists behaviors that don't match AWS yet.

The limits AWS lists itself

This is a test tool, not a cloud: one region and one account (it accepts any region and account ID but doesn't keep resources separate), no IAM policy evaluation the way AWS does it, all state in memory and deleted when it stops, behavior checked against us-west-2 only (global services in us-east-1), no throttling or outage simulation, no snapshot and restore, and not tested for long-running use or load testing. And one flag for the privacy-minded: telemetry is on by default. --telemetry off or EMULATOR_TELEMETRY=off turns it off, but "runs offline on your machine" and "phones home by default" sit awkwardly in the same README.

Why now, and who it threatens

The timing is not subtle. LocalStack's Community Edition — the default answer to "how do I test AWS code without touching AWS?" for years — was archived in March 2026, and the unified image now refuses to start without an auth token tied to a registered account. Floci filled that hole: an MIT-licensed emulator, 128 services, past 31,000 GitHub stars by early November. AWS launching its own free, no-account emulator with a claimed 426 services is the incumbent answering both of them at once — with three times Floci's service count and the one thing neither rival has, which is AWS's own fidelity measurements against real AWS.

I didn't boot the emulator for this piece — the RPM is 159 MB and the from-source build wants 100 GB of disk for its per-service crates, so the scores file was the check I could actually run and stand behind. The question the launch really asks is not whether the emulator works today at 56.5%. It is whether you trust test infrastructure whose code no human has read, where the quality argument is "security agents review it" and the evidence is a public score file. AWS's answer is to publish the scores and the failing-issue list in the open, which is the right move — and also the reason the 56.5% is on the record at all. I would run it in CI with the 503s treated as test failures. I would not yet treat a green run against it as proof my code works on AWS.

Sources: AWS Emulator repository and v1.0.322 release, github.com/aws/aws-emulator (release published 2026-11-11T00:32Z; scores file scored 2026-11-11T00:09:58Z, downloaded and counted by me — 42,937 units, 24,243 pass, 18,614 fail, 80 skipped, 49,810/68,007 steps pass, 355 services); ministack.org, "AWS launches AWS Emulator" (November 11, 2026); InfoWorld, "AWS unveils local emulator service to help enterprises accelerate app development and testing" (November 11, 2026); The Circuitry, "AWS releases a local emulator written entirely by AI agents" (November 11, 2026); Floci/LocalStack background from AI Frontier Post (November 2026). Commit, release, star, and package-size figures are my own checks against the GitHub API and the AWS downloads server on November 11, 2026.

title: When does text encoding matter for language modeling?
description:
arXiv:2611.14459v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: UTF-8's role as the de facto encoding standard in language models introduces cross-lingual inequities due to its variable-length design. However, the effect that this encoding choice has on model performance remains largely unexamined. In this work, we investigate how text encoding impacts the performance of byte-level language models, comparing UTF-8 with a wide range of other encoding strategies, including other Unicode-based approaches, language-specific encodings, and our own customized encodings. To facilitate our analysis, we propose Aether: a hybrid encoding scheme that uses script-specific encodings for our target setting while maintaining full Unicode coverage through UTF-8 fallbacks, using this framework to model four orthographically diverse languages. Surprisingly, we find that while languages with information-dense characters (Chinese, Korean) significantly benefit from compressive encodings, languages whose characters carry less information individually (Georgian, Tamil) are largely insensitive to encoding choice. In light of these findings, we argue that text encoding should be a language-specific design decision, rather than a universal default.

title: The project stops at 80% the moment you stop doubting you can finish it
description:
@csm18 answered the question at the end of my last post with something I have not seen written down before.

He starts a new project because the idea is big and he has never built anything like it. Maybe he will not be able to. That uncertainty is the fire. It gets him to start without asking whether the thing is practical.

Then comes the point where he can see the progress is real. If he keeps going, it will be finished. And at exactly that point:

once I know I can do it, I start to think if I can, then why should I worry about it. Whenever I want to I will, not now.

The fire goes out. The project sits at 40, 60, 80, sometimes 90 per cent.

I read that twice, because we usually tell this story backwards. The doubt is the problem, confidence is the cure, and if you are stuck it is because you do not believe in yourself enough.

His version is closer to the people I know who are good at starting. The doubt was never the obstacle. It was the engine. "Can I do this" is a question that produces work, and the moment you have your answer the question stops. So does the work.

Which is why "just believe in yourself" is such useless advice, and why it can make things worse. Certainty does not add fuel. It removes the thing that was generating it.

So what keeps a piece of work alive after the doubt is gone?

Not proof. Proof is what ends it.

Something has to change about what the work is for. While the question is "am I capable", the work is a test, and a test ends when you pass it. After that the work has to be for something outside the test: someone who needs it, a thing you want to exist, a standard you refuse to drop. Otherwise the 80 per cent version is the rational place to stop. You already got what you came for.

@josaphatstar said the other half of it in the same thread. He prepares for the fight he expects, the new framework, the unfamiliar syntax, the thing he has not learned yet. The real blocker is always smaller and less dramatic: a misunderstanding about what was actually being asked, an assumption he made early that quietly broke everything downstream.

I prepare for the fight I expect, and the one that actually shows up is always different.

Put the two answers together and the shape is the same. What ends a piece of work is almost never the thing you were afraid of. It is the thing you stopped needing.

That is why I keep the record I asked about last time: one line, written in the week something finally works, about what actually broke. Not the fear. The other thing.

So, a new question. If you have a project sitting at 80 per cent: what question were you asking when you started it, and did you get your answer?

title: Adapting a Vision Foundation Model for Fracture Characterization in Acoustic Image Logs
description:
arXiv:2611.13911v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Natural fractures (NFs) and drilling-induced tensile fractures (DITFs) in acoustic image logs provide insights into rock mass structure and in situ stress, but manual characterization is time-consuming. Deep learning can automate this task, although expert-labeled data are scarce. We investigate whether adapting a pretrained vision foundation model (VFM) outperforms task-specific models trained from scratch with limited annotations. Using 80 annotated acoustic image samples, we fine-tuned DINOv3, pretrained on satellite imagery, and evaluated it on four boreholes excluded from fine-tuning. The adapted model estimated NF and DITF parameters comparably to human interpretation. Relative to U-Net, YOLOv8, and Swin Transformer models trained from scratch, it yielded fewer false positives and negatives and more accurate fracture counts and orientations. However, its performance advantage generally narrowed as training sample size decreased. We also assessed decoder architecture, fine-tuning strategy, and image enhancement. A progressive upsampling decoder with full fine-tuning performed best among the DINOv3 configurations tested, while fracture-focused image enhancement did not consistently improve accuracy. These results demonstrate the potential of VFM adaptation for fracture characterization in acoustic image logs with limited labeled data and suggest a transferable workflow for other annotation-scarce geoscientific imaging tasks.

title: What drives the emergence of symbolic mechanisms in large language models?
description:
arXiv:2611.13270v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent work has identified a set of emergent symbolic mechanisms that support abstract reasoning in large language models, but it remains unclear what factors drive the emergence of these mechanisms. To address this question, we trained neural networks from scratch on abstract sequence tasks, varying both architectural and data distributional factors, and investigated the effects of these factors on the emergence of symbolic mechanisms. Using representational, attentional, and causal mediation analyses, we first confirmed that transformer-based language models trained from scratch on our task developed symbolic mechanisms. We then found that, across multiple axes of data diversity, greater diversity produced stronger symbolic signatures. Surprisingly, the same signatures emerged in modified transformer architectures and even multilayer perceptrons, indicating that architectural inductive biases are not necessary for the development of symbolic mechanisms. We also observed consistent patterns in an entity-attribute binding task. Together, these findings identify data diversity, not architecture, as the primary driver of emergent symbolic computation in neural networks.

title: Agent-Guided Discovery of Exchange-Correlation Functionals with Physics-based Validation
description:
arXiv:2611.13329v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate, compact exchange--correlation functionals are central to predictive density functional theory. Symbolic search and language-model agents can propose new functional forms, but it remains unclear whether their gains survive self-consistency and external evaluation, whether the new terms carry physical content, whether agents outperform evolutionary search, and how language-model backbones compare. We connect frontier LLM agents to a GPU evaluator through the Model Context Protocol, with training-only fitting, persistent memory, and self-consistent and external evaluation. Opus-5.5 agents passed the screening gate with about 40-fold fewer tokens than Codex (GPT-6-Astra) agents and found a candidate with lower validation and held-out errors; only this candidate advanced to self-consistent evaluation. The resulting 13-parameter functional, O159, multiplies same-spin correlation by a smooth density window. Refitted controls favor a window that scales the entire same-spin factor, reducing it by 15--30\% at its peak, and that acts on reaction energies mainly in near-iso-orbital regions; against a refitted no-window control, it lowers heavy-atom total-energy errors on GSCDB137 by 29\%. With about 400 fits each, SyFES evolution did not improve on its GAS22 seed, whereas the agents found forms 0.10--0.13 \kcal\ lower in validation error by adding an explicit density scale. Self-consistent O159 lowers the held-out MGCDB84 test error of $\omega$B97M-V by 11.7\%, and its mean normalized error ratio on 36 GSCDB137 datasets (1.139) is comparable to $\omega$B97M-V (1.144) and below GAS22 (1.190). Frontier-LLM agents thus produced O159, a compact functional whose improvement over $\omega$B97M-V survives self-consistent, physics-based validation.

title: A citation list is a flat file; the research is a graph
description:
I kept losing the shape of a literature review. I'd export forty references, read the abstracts in order, and end up with a folder of notes that told me what each paper said but not how the papers related. The thing I actually needed - which result depends on which earlier result, who cites whom, where a cluster stops - isn't in a flat list.

That's the problem I built LiteratureMap around. Not summarization. Structure.

A list hides the edges

A bibliography is an array. Each entry has authors, a year, a title, a venue. You can sort it, you can filter it, but nothing in that array encodes a relationship. The relationship is the interesting part: paper B extends paper A, paper C contradicts B, paper D is the survey that ties A, B, and C together.

Modeled properly, the literature is a directed graph. Nodes are papers. Edges are citations, with a direction - the citing paper points back to the cited one. Once you have that, questions that were painful become queries. Which papers are the common ancestors of a cluster? Which node has many incoming edges and few outgoing ones, meaning it's a foundation everyone builds on but nobody extends? Which pair of clusters has no connecting edge, which is a candidate gap?

The 'Citation relationship graph' feature is exactly that view. It draws what builds on what, who cites whom, and where the gaps are. I'm careful with the word 'gap' though.

'Gap finder' is a hint, not a verdict

A missing edge in a graph is not proof of an unanswered research question. It can mean the two clusters genuinely haven't been connected, or it can mean I didn't give the tool enough papers for the connection to show up, or that the connection exists in a paper outside the set. The gap finder surfaces a structural observation; it doesn't certify novelty.

That distinction matters because 'find a gap' is the kind of claim that sounds authoritative. I'd rather the tool say 'here is where the graph is sparse' and let a researcher decide whether that sparsity is meaningful. Combined with 'Theme clusters', which groups papers by shared subject, you get a readable overview of a field's shape. But it's a starting map. You still read the papers. I would not cite a gap from the map as evidence in a paper without checking the primary sources myself.

Why an exportable outline is the real output

A picture of a graph is pleasant but hard to write from. The 'Exportable outline' feature matters more than it sounds: it turns the structure back into text you can drop into a related-work section. Clusters become headings, the foundational nodes become the paragraphs you open with, and the sparse regions become the questions you pose at the end.

That round trip - papers in, graph, outline out - is the whole design. The input is a set of papers or a topic. The tool draws the relationship graph, groups themes, flags gaps, and hands back an outline. Nothing in that chain decides what's true about the field. It rearranges what you gave it so the structure is visible.

The limits I won't paper over

The map is only as complete as the set of papers you feed it. Feed it a narrow slice and the graph will look confident about a field it has barely seen. That's the failure mode I worry about most, because a clean diagram reads as thorough even when the input was thin.

It's also not a systematic review, a citation database, or a live audit of the literature. It doesn't fetch papers, verify citations, or tell you whether a result has been replicated. It's decision-support for organizing reading, closer to a whiteboard than to a reference manager. If you need completeness for a review article, this is a first pass, not the final word.

LiteratureMap is useful precisely because it makes a structure visible that a flat list hides. Just don't mistake a clean graph for a complete one.

FAQ

What do I actually put in?

A set of papers or a topic. The tool draws the relationship graph between them, groups themes, flags gaps, and returns an exportable outline.

Does the gap finder prove a research gap is real?

No. It flags where the graph is sparse. A missing edge might be a real opening or just a paper you didn't include. Check the primary sources.

Is this a citation database or a systematic review?

Neither. It's a way to see the shape of a set of papers. It doesn't fetch papers, verify citations, or claim completeness.

Can I use the output directly in a related-work section?

The exportable outline is a starting draft. I'd verify every claim against the papers before citing it.

title: Resize a screenshot in the tab when the README hero is oversized
description:
The README hero looks sharp on your 2× laptop display. GitHub (or your docs host) shows it about 800px wide. The file you committed is a 3200×2000 PNG from a retina capture. Every clone pays for pixels nobody renders.

I’ve started treating oversized README screenshots as a packaging bug, not a design flex. If the image displays at ~800px, committing a 3000px source is optional — and usually accidental.

How heroes get fat

Common paths:

  • OS screenshot at native retina resolution
  • Design export at “2× for safety”
  • Drag from Slack / Notion without checking dimensions
  • “We’ll compress later” that never happens

Markdown doesn’t downsample for your repo weight. The viewer might, but git clone and PR diffs still move the bytes.

A simple size policy for docs images

Boring rules beat debate:

  • Display width — pick a target (e.g. 1200px wide max for README heroes, 800px for inline steps)
  • Format — PNG for UI chrome with sharp text; JPEG/WebP for photo-like shots
  • Alpha — keep PNG when transparency matters; don’t flatten by accident
  • Name — readme-hero.png, not Screen Shot 2026-11-09 at 9.41.03 PM.png

If the screenshot is also used in a marketing site with a real image pipeline, store the master there and link a resized derivative from the README.

Check dimensions in ten seconds

Before the PR:

# macOS
sips -g pixelWidth -g pixelHeight docs/images/readme-hero.png

# or ImageMagick
identify -format "%wx%h\n" docs/images/readme-hero.png

If width is past your policy (say 1600px for a hero shown near 800–1200px), resize first. Reviewers shouldn’t need a binary diff to notice a 4× capture.

Resize before commit (not after the complaint)

You want:

  1. Exact pixel target or percent downscale
  2. Aspect ratio locked (unless you intentionally crop elsewhere)
  3. Transparency preserved for UI PNGs
  4. A preview of output dimensions before download
  5. No mandatory upload of an unreleased product UI to a stranger’s server

When you’re already in the browser and the file is on disk, an in-tab resizer is enough. Uwarp’s image resize tool scales PNG/JPEG (and similar) by pixels or percent, keeps PNG alpha, previews dimensions, and downloads locally — handy for the README one-off. For batches every release, use sips, ImageMagick, or sharp in a docs script instead of clicking through by hand.

Caveats: heavy upscales won’t invent detail; prefer downscaling screenshots. Very large sources may hit browser limits. Cropping to a new aspect ratio is a different job than scaling — don’t stretch a 16:9 capture into a square hero and call it done.

README markdown that matches the file

After resizing:

![Pricing page — filtered empty state](./docs/images/readme-hero.png)

Avoid huge HTML width hacks as a substitute for resizing the file. Width attributes can help layout; they don’t shrink the blob in git.

If your host supports it, pair with WebP as in the PNG→WebP workflow — but dimension discipline alone fixes most README weight problems.

Reject / send back (in docs PRs)

Reject

  • Multi‑megapixel screenshots for a hero displayed under ~1000px
  • Screen Shot … filenames in docs/
  • Stretched aspect ratios to “fill the banner”
  • Uploading unreleased UI to a random online compressor when a local/tab path exists

Accept

  • Hero near the display width (with modest 1.5×–2× headroom if you care about crispness on dense screens)
  • Predictable names under docs/images/
  • Alt text that states what the screen shows
  • Masters stored outside the README path when design will reopen them

Tiny habit

Before you drop a fresh capture into the README, check the pixel dimensions once. If it’s more than ~2× the width the page will show, downscale in the tab (or CLI), keep a master elsewhere if you need it, and commit the derivative. Smaller clones. Faster PR diffs. Same information in the hero.

title: MicroBT: Centroid-Guided Synergistic Learning for Multi-Modal Micro Brain Tumor Segmentation and Counting
description:
arXiv:2611.13912v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-modal brain tumor segmentation is essential for clinical diagnosis, radiotherapy planning, and longitudinal monitoring. While recent studies have achieved remarkable overall segmentation performance, they rely on overlap-based objectives that inherently favor large regions, causing sub-3 mm micro-lesions to be systematically suppressed during training. Moreover, existing pixel-level segmentation frameworks lack explicit instance-level modeling, leading to unreliable lesion counting that directly impacts clinical staging and therapeutic decisions. To address these challenges, we propose MicroBT, a unified multi-modal framework for micro brain tumor segmentation and counting. Our core insight is that a fundamental geometric property is inherently scale-invariant: regardless of size, each lesion possesses a well-defined centroid. Leveraging this, we first devise a centroid-anchored synergistic paradigm that utilizes predicted centroids as shared anchors to simultaneously condition dense segmentation and instance-level localization. To counteract the tumor size imbalance, we further devise a Volume-Calibrated Loss (VC-Loss) that adaptively amplifies the gradient contribution of micro-lesions, alongside a Size-Aware Curriculum Optimization (SACO) that stabilizes multi-task training by establishing global representations before progressively unlocking fine-grained localization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MicroBT outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly on metastases, where micro-lesion ($\leq 3$ mm) localization precision improves by approximately 7% and counting estimation errors decrease by approximately 26%. The code is available at https://github.com/leonlou921/MicroBT.

title: CASCADE: Constraint-Aware SCAffolded DEcomposition for Logical Anomaly Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.13820v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Logical Anomaly Detection (LAD) requires verifying whether all category-specific constraints, such as object counts, pairing relations, and measurement ranges, are satisfied by a query image given only a few normal references. Recent LAD methods based on Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) formulate this as checklist verification, decomposing the decision into independent textual checks. This decomposition, however, is text-only. Every item still reads the same unmodified query image, so the LVLM must extract different forms of visual evidence from one raw image. We identify this text-image mismatch as a constraint-specific perception gap, the source of two failure modes: instance conflation for binding constraints and scale drift for calibration constraints. To diagnose whether these failures stem from insufficient reasoning or insufficient perception, we compare textual reasoning guides and visual perception guides in a training-free setting. Our analysis shows that reasoning over the same image provides little benefit, whereas adapting the visual input to each constraint substantially improves verification accuracy. Based on this finding, we propose CASCADE, a training-free framework that extends checklist decomposition using constraint-specific visual scaffolds. We further introduce CASCADE++, which adapts these scaffolds at the object level by deriving their configurations from the constraint structure and reference distribution. Across MVTec-LOCO and VID-AD, CASCADE++ surpasses the full-shot state of the art by 3.9 AUROC points with only three references, and improves over the strongest VID-AD baseline by 11.4, transferring across multiple LVLM backbones without any training.
