title: DUO: Dual Readouts of Diffusion Models for OOD Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.13304v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion models are powerful generative methods for learning and sampling from complex data distributions. Safely deploying these models requires detecting inputs that fall outside their training distribution. Because diffusion models recover clean samples from noisy inputs, reconstruction error is often used for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection. This approach assumes that in-distribution (ID) inputs are reconstructed more accurately than OOD inputs. However, OOD inputs may be reconstructed equally well or even better, making this score unreliable. We therefore propose the leading sensitivity spectrum of intermediate denoising features as a complementary OOD signal and demonstrate that it remains informative when reconstruction error is misleading. We introduce DUal-readout of diffusion models for OOD detection (DUO), a fully unsupervised, training-free OOD detector that combines reconstruction error and feature sensitivity. DUO improves average AUROC by approximately 6% points over the strongest baselines while substantially reducing inference cost, and achieves SOTA on near-OOD and high-resolution benchmarks.

title: Reconstructing Boundary Layer Wind Profiles with Machine Learning: A Comparative Study on IGRA Radiosonde Data
description:
arXiv:2611.13359v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Wind profiles in the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) drive short-range forecasting and wind-energy siting, yet sparse radiosonde coverage forces practitioners to interpolate them from a handful of physical predictors. We benchmark modern tabular learners against analytical parameterizations on 158,097 IGRA soundings. CatBoost, TabM, and FT-Transformer reduce RMSE to 1.3-1.6 m/s, against approximately 3 m/s for power-law and Monin-Obukhov fits; once the predictor set is fixed the three architectures differ by less than 0.05 m/s, so accuracy is driven by predictors rather than architecture. A cohort analysis of within-bin profile dispersion places an empirical floor of approximately 1.77 m/s on any point-wise predictor that uses standard radiosonde features, consistent with prior eddy-viscosity inversions. A one-dimensional Fourier Neural Operator applied as a post-hoc corrector to frozen tabular predictions reduces near-surface RMSE on U.S. stations from 1.5 to 1.2 m/s, while leaving upper-layer error unchanged. Further gains should come from new predictors rather than larger models.

title: I Built a Bare-Metal Deep Learning Engine in C++20 and Rust (VeloGrad v1.0.0)
description:
Hey developers!

My name is Ayushman Singh Rathore, and over the past several months I have been building VeloGrad (v1.0.0), a native-first machine learning and autoregressive inference runtime written from scratch in modern C++20, Rust, and CUDA.

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/IDKLETSCODESOMETHIN/VeloGrad

Why I Built It: PyTorch is great for research, but running modern long-context LLMs in production usually requires duct-taping multiple heavy frameworks together (vLLM, DeepSpeed, TensorRT-LLM). This carries Python GIL stalls, massive multi-gigabyte dependencies, and severe memory fragmentation.

I wanted to explore how far we could push runtime efficiency by designing an engine from bare-metal primitives:

Static Arena Allocator: Instead of dynamic heap allocations during inference, memory is managed via a contiguous arena aligned to 64-byte hardware cache lines (alignas(64)), eliminating GC stalls and latency jitter.

Virtual Paged Attention: We break the KV-cache into discrete physical pages (similar to OS virtual memory paging), reducing KV-cache VRAM usage by ~60% on long contexts without memory fragmentation.

Universal 1-Command Converter (velograd-convert): A zero-dependency binary parser that translates between Hugging Face Safetensors, PyTorch checkpoints, and GGUF v3 (for Ollama / llama.cpp) with no external packages.

PyTorch Drop-in API: Familiar .forward(), .backward(), and autograd syntax with array exchange protocols for NumPy, JAX, and DLPack.

Try it on local hardware in 30 seconds: You can clone the repository, install it locally, and run our universal test suite in under a second:

git clone https://github.com/IDKLETSCODESOMETHIN/VeloGrad.git
cd VeloGrad pip install -e . python tests/test_velograd_universal_compat.py

The project is completely open source under AGPLv3: https://github.com/IDKLETSCODESOMETHIN/VeloGrad

title: How One Tiny Bit Flip Saved 99% of Compute on a 7‑Billion‑Parameter LLM
description:
Tree‑Ising: How Bit‑Level Ising Edits Are Turning Model Repair into a One‑Click Operation

Lead

Fixing a seven‑billion‑parameter model’s hallucination loop took just fifty forward passes. A senior engineer at OpenAI revealed this breakthrough in a Slack thread on 12 Nov 2026. The method—Tree‑Ising—flips bits in a model’s BF16 weight tensors the way a physicist flips spins in an Ising lattice. By treating every mantissa bit as a binary variable, the technique solves a tiny discrete‑optimization problem that excises a specific reasoning error without touching the rest of the network.

The result? A repair that costs a fraction of the compute, a fraction of the carbon, and a fraction of the time required by conventional gradient‑based fine‑tuning. The community calls it “the first weight‑space program that edits a model by solving a sparse discrete optimization over its BF16 parameters.” This article unpacks the technical core, walks through a concrete debugging session, crunches the numbers, flags the remaining hazards, and sketches where the approach could land in the next two years.

The Case Study: Debugging a Recurring Hallucination Loop

The symptom

A customer‑support chatbot built on Qwen‑3.5‑0.8B began repeating the phrase “I’m not able to answer that question” after three consecutive user prompts about loan eligibility. The dialogue log showed a recurrence metric—the probability that the model re‑enters the same hidden state after each turn—spike from a baseline of 0.08 to 0.62.

Traditional fix

The engineering team tried a classic LoRA patch: they froze the lower layers, added a rank‑8 adapter, and ran 20 k steps of gradient descent on a curated “loan‑policy” dataset (≈2 M tokens). The process burned ~10 B FLOPs, took 12 h on a single A100, and still left a 15 % drop in performance on unrelated QA benchmarks.

Tree‑Ising in action

  1. Spin‑mapping the weight lattice – The repair agent queried the model’s BF16 tensors, extracted the 10‑bit mantissa of each weight, and stored each bit as a spin variable (s_i \in {-1,+1}). The resulting lattice comprised roughly 4 × 10¹² spins for the 0.8 B‑parameter model.

  2. Energy definition – The agent ran 50 forward passes on a synthetic probe set that reproduced the hallucination loop. For each pass it recorded activation‑gradient proxies (the product of activation magnitude and gradient magnitude at every neuron). It then summed these proxies over all spins that contributed to the loop, forming an energy function

    [
    E(\mathbf{s}) = \sum_{i} w_i \, s_i \, \phi_i,
    ]

    where (w_i) is the BF16 scaling factor for spin (i) and (\phi_i) the proxy value. High energy indicates a spin that reinforces the loop.

  3. Sparse Ising optimization – Using a tree‑structured belief‑propagation algorithm, the agent searched for a minimal set of spins whose flips would lower the energy by at least 70 %. The tree structure mirrors the hierarchical connectivity of transformer layers (embedding → attention heads → feed‑forward blocks), allowing the optimizer to prune irrelevant branches early.

  4. Bit‑level edit – The algorithm returned 3 800 spin flips (≈0.0001 % of total spins). The agent wrote the new bits back into the BF16 tensors, recomputed the model’s checksum, and re‑ran the probe set. The recurrence metric collapsed back to 0.09, and the full‑suite benchmark showed < 0.5 % deviation from the pre‑bug baseline.

  5. Audit trail – The system logged every step: initial energy, candidate spin clusters, final spin map, and a SHA‑256 hash of the edited weight file. The log file occupies 2 MB, easily attachable to a compliance ticket.

Result: 90 M tokens of interaction (≈158 GPT‑6 “Astra” agent turns) and 0.3 B FLOPs of forward‑only compute repaired the loop. Compared with the LoRA attempt, Tree‑Ising saved ≈99 % of compute, ≈95 % of wall‑clock time, and ≈80 % of performance degradation.

The Meat: Hard Numbers Behind the Hype

Metric Gradient‑Based Fine‑Tuning Tree‑Ising (Bit‑Level)
Compute (FLOPs) ~10 B (full back‑prop) ~0.3 B (forward‑only)
Token budget 2 M (curated dataset) 90 M (agent‑generated probes)
Wall‑clock time (single A100) 12 h 35 min
Parameter change ratio 1.2 % of total weights 0.0001 % (bits)
Performance drop on unrelated tasks 10 % (average) < 0.5 %
Energy reduction on target loop N/A (gradient loss) 73 % (measured)
Human‑in‑the‑loop steps Data curation, hyper‑parameter sweep Prompt design, verification run

Compute‑to‑Repair Ratio

[
\text{CTR} = \frac{\text{FLOPs for repair}}{\text{FLOPs for full fine‑tune}} \approx \frac{0.3\text{B}}{10\text{B}} = 0.03.
]

A CTR of 3 % means that any organization that can afford a full fine‑tune now can afford ~30 × more repairs per month.

Energy‑Efficiency of the Search

The Ising optimizer explores a tree of depth 12 (one level per transformer block) and evaluates at most 10⁶ candidate spin clusters before converging. Each evaluation costs a single forward pass (≈0.5 ms on A100). The entire search therefore consumes ≈500 s of GPU time, well within the 35‑minute wall‑clock budget reported above.

Token‑Efficiency

Although the probe set uses more tokens than a typical fine‑tuning corpus, the tokens are generated on‑the‑fly by an autonomous agent (GPT‑6 “Astra”). The agent tailors each probe to expose the specific failure mode, eliminating the need for expensive data‑annotation pipelines.

The Pivot: Risks, Limitations, and Governance

Opaqueness of the Energy Function

The energy function aggregates activation‑gradient proxies across billions of neurons. While the optimizer reports a monotonic descent, interpreting why a particular spin flip matters remains difficult. Researchers can visualize edited spin clusters, but mapping them back to human‑readable concepts (e.g., “the word loan”) often fails.

“We can patch a model in minutes, but we still lack a clear story about what we changed,” warned an AI‑ethics officer at the EU AI Office in a public comment on 14 Nov 2026.

Safety of Hidden Patches

A bit‑flip that removes a hallucination loop could unintentionally open a different logical shortcut. The current workflow mitigates this risk by running a full regression suite after each edit, but the suite itself cannot guarantee the absence of emergent failures in the wild.

Hardware Compatibility

Tree‑Ising assumes BF16 mantissa bits are addressable individually. Some custom ASICs store weights in packed 8‑bit quantized formats, making direct spin access impossible without a conversion step that re‑introduces quantization error. NVIDIA’s upcoming TensorCore‑5 roadmap includes a “Ising‑Edit” kernel to accelerate the energy evaluation, but widespread adoption will take at least another year.

Legal and Auditing Concerns

Regulators demand traceability for any post‑deployment model change. The audit logs generated by Tree‑Ising satisfy the “what changed” requirement, but they do not yet provide a semantic justification. A forthcoming IEEE standard (IEEE 7012‑2027) proposes a repair justification schema that could be layered on top of the current logs.

Scaling to Larger Models

The Qwen‑3.5‑0.8B experiment flips 3 800 spins. Scaling the same technique to a GPT‑6 175 B model would increase the search space by two orders of magnitude. Preliminary tests on a 13 B‑parameter sub‑model show a linear increase in required forward passes (≈500 → 1 500) but still stay under 1 B FLOPs. Researchers attribute the scalability to the tree‑structured belief propagation, which prunes irrelevant branches early. Nevertheless, the absolute wall‑clock time could exceed a single workday for the largest models.

Outlook: From Debugging Tool to Core Infrastructure

  1. Standardizing the API – MIT’s “Weight‑Space Programming” project already publishes a Python library (weightspace) that abstracts spin queries and edit commands. Within six months we can expect Hugging Face Transformers to expose a model.edit(spin_mask, new_bits) method, making Tree‑Ising a first‑class operation alongside model.save_pretrained.

  2. Automated Repair Agents – The GPT‑6 “Astra” agent that generated the probe set demonstrates a closed‑loop repair pipeline: detect failure → synthesize probe → compute energy → edit → verify. OpenAI’s internal roadmap lists “self‑healing LLMs” as a 2027 milestone, implying that future agents will trigger Tree‑Ising automatically when a monitoring service flags a drift.

  3. Hybrid Editing – Some teams already blend low‑rank LoRA adapters with bit‑level Ising flips. The adapter handles broad domain shifts, while Tree‑Ising patches specific pathological loops that LoRA cannot isolate. Early benchmarks report < 0.2 % total parameter change for combined edits, a figure that satisfies both performance and auditability criteria.

  4. Hardware Acceleration – NVIDIA’s “Ising‑Edit” kernel promises 10× speedup for the belief‑propagation step by mapping spin interactions onto tensor cores. If the kernel ships with the next driver release (Q2 2027), the wall‑clock time for a 175 B model could drop below 3 h, making on‑demand repair viable for production services.

  5. Regulatory Frameworks – The EU’s AI Act amendment (drafted Nov 2026) explicitly mentions post‑deployment model edits and requires immutable logs. Tree‑Ising’s deterministic spin‑flip log already satisfies the immutability clause; the next regulatory step will likely demand human‑readable explanations. Researchers are experimenting with counterfactual attribution methods that trace a spin flip back to the most influential training token, a promising path toward compliant explanations.

Closing Thoughts

Tree‑Ising flips a handful of bits, but it flips the entire conversation about how we maintain massive language models. By reframing weight‑space repair as a sparse Ising optimization, the technique sidesteps gradients, slashes compute, and delivers a surgical fix that leaves the rest of the model untouched.

The community’s response—eager developers, cautious lab scientists, hardware vendors ready to accelerate, and regulators asking for transparency—maps a clear trajectory: from a research demo to a production‑grade repair primitive within the next 12‑18 months.

If the ecosystem builds robust APIs, audit standards, and hardware support, we will see LLM services that self‑heal with the same ease that developers push a bug‑fix to a web app. The real breakthrough lies not in raw speed but in the new workflow it enables: detect, probe, edit, verify, and log—all in a single, token‑efficient loop.

In a world where models evolve faster than regulations can codify, Tree‑Ising may become the most practical tool we have for keeping AI systems honest, safe, and compliant—one spin at a time.

title: Making every harness durable
description:
Developers are familiar with running coding agents locally through harnesses like Pi, Claude Code, and others. They are reliable daily drivers for generating code, but keeping agents running around the clock requires your computer to be on and awake, which led to the laptop lid memes and Mac mini demand spike.

Running harnesses in the cloud

Harness workloads are moving to the cloud. Individual developers are deploying always-on coding agent workflows, projects like OpenWork and HanaAgent use open-source harnesses as the engines behind the apps, and engineers are building their own harness products.

These harnesses are designed for long-lived processes that keep the session in memory, and agent tasks commonly run for minutes or hours. Locally, a harness has direct, continuous access to the workspace and session history on the same disk, so resuming interrupted work only requires a simple prompt.

In the cloud, you can replicate that setup with a VM and persistent storage, but the VM doesn't automatically record which model and tool calls completed or resume interrupted turns after a crash. A failed turn or network error means lost work.

Also, not every agent task executed through a harness needs a sandbox. Database queries and API calls can run securely in functions, and that also means required credentials never have to enter the sandbox.

Making every harness durable

We built eve and fx to run durably in the cloud out of the box, and today we are introducing durable-harness, which extends that durability to any harness, including Pi, OpenCode, Codex, and Claude Code. It uses the same machinery that powers Workflow SDK to survive crashes and function timeouts.

With durable-harness, you can:

  • Run any of these harnesses durably on Vercel

  • Self-host a harness with your own Postgres instance

  • Make your local harness workflow durable

  • Build your own durable harness

Sessions that survive a crash mid-turn

Take the example of a coding agent adding a pricing page to an existing app. The agent reads the existing page, writes a new one, opens a pull request, and waits for CI to finish before reporting back.

What happens if its function times out while CI is still running?

Kill the function or drop the connection in the demo below to compare how the two agents recover and which work is repeated.

Without durability, the agent stops work until it is manually restarted, and completed work is repeated unnecessarily.

With durable-harness, a new function reads completed results from the log and resumes the turn. If the browser disconnects, the agent keeps running, and reconnecting catches up from the log.

Logs and queues

durable-harness is the newest package in our open source portfolio. It’s a set of adapters and utilities that let the harnesses you already use keep their sessions in a World, the Workflow SDK’s durable backend.

It writes each step of a turn to a durable log. Before a model call or tool call runs, it records an intent, and when the call finishes, it records the outcome. The turn itself is backstopped with a queue message, so if its function dies, the queue hands the turn to a new function that reads the log and continues where it left off.

After a crash, the log says what finished, what was running, and what never started:

  • Completed calls never run again because their results are read from the log, so you’re never billed twice for a finished model call’s tokens.

  • Models remember their previous calls rather than repeating them.

  • Interrupted tools marked replay: 'safe' run again. Any other tool comes back to the model as possibly run, and the model decides whether to check.

Harnesses that keep their own session files, like Claude Code's transcript, Codex's rollout, and OpenCode's event store, have every record mirrored into the log, so a new function or Sandbox rebuilds them from it.

Pick your harness

fx and eve are durable on their own. For the rest, durable-harness adds durability from the outside, without changing the harness.

For the full setup guide for each harness, check the docs.

Runs everywhere

Durable agents need a log of each step, a way to resume a turn when its process dies, and a stream for whoever is watching.

Workflow SDK ships all three behind one interface, a World.

durable-harness writes to that interface, so you can move the same agent from one World to another without changing its code:

  • On Vercel, it uses the Vercel World.

  • In development, it uses files on your machine.

  • On your own servers, it uses Postgres, MongoDB, Redis, or Turso.

Two variables move every agent using durable-harness to Postgres.

For more control, such as setting a namespace or recovering sessions when your server starts, create the World in code and pass it to your agent:

Check the self-hosting docs for more details.

See every session in Agent Runs

Agent Runs on Vercel shows the trace for every session, including each model call and tool call. Turns that resumed after a crash appear in the same trace, so you can see exactly where a turn stopped and picked back up.

Tools

An agent has only the tools you give it, and they run in your function. Each tool says what should happen if a crash interrupts it. A 'safe' tool, such as a lookup, can run again. A 'never' tool, such as a refund, never runs twice: the model is told the call may have happened, so it can check before it tries again.

Here’s how the coding agent from the demo above might define its tools:

  • A tool that reads a file or checks CI status is marked as 'safe' so it can run again automatically.

  • A tool that posts a PR comment is marked as 'never' so that comments aren't posted twice.

The following example defines a tool for each policy using the example of an agent processing a refund:

For each harness’s built-in tools, like its shell and file editing, read on.

Files

When a harness needs a shell and files, it’s not safe to run them directly on a shared serverless function host. Many sessions can share the same function, and its filesystem isn’t guaranteed to persist between invocations.

To address this, durable-harness gives you a few options:

  • virtual() keeps the files in the session’s log, with a bash-compatible shell that can’t reach your function’s files or the network. It suits short tasks and small workspaces without starting an entire sandbox.

  • virtual({ durable: false }) keeps the files in memory for scratch work and clears them at the end of every turn.

  • sandbox() gives the session its own Vercel Sandbox, with /workspace on a Drive that outlives every sandbox and every function. It suits real projects and long-running work.

Compare the three side by side in the docs.

Each harness’s built-in tools run on the workspace you choose. With Pi, CodingTools installs Pi’s own read, write, edit, and bash, and virtualEnv() or sandboxEnv() gives them a workspace:

For OpenCode, pass the workspace as workspace, and for fx, pass it to fxTools(). Claude Code and Codex always run in a Vercel Sandbox, since they expect a real shell and filesystem, and aren’t safe for multi-tenant use. Their built-in tools work on the session’s Drive once you turn them on with builtins: true. Each harness guide lists its built-in tools.

Documents

Some state belongs with the session but isn’t part of the conversation, such as a to-do list, a plan, or a form the agent fills in. A document is typed JSON that lives in the session’s log, so it survives a crash and moves with the session.

Tools can edit documents through io.docs, and each edit commits to the log alongside the tool’s result, so the document’s durable state stays consistent with the tool calls themselves:

Your app can read and edit the same document without a database of its own, and the chat route can even stream every change to your UI:

In fact, the virtual() workspace from earlier is built on documents: its file tree is a document in the session’s log, and each tool call’s changes commit with its result.

Learn more about tools, files, and documents and how to keep your agent secure.

Wrapping up

Developers choose a harness for the choices it makes about prompts, tools, and context. How it survives a crash shouldn’t be one of them. With durable-harness, a turn that loses its function partway through continues from the log on a new one, without a manual retry and without repeating what already finished. Self-hosting and portability work out of the box by building on top of the Workflow SDK’s World interface.

durable-harness is open source on GitHub.

title: 11 继承
description:
一、继承解决什么问题

狗和猫都有名字、年龄，也都会吃饭、睡觉。如果分别在 Dog 和 Cat 中编写这些成员，就会出现重复代码。把共同成员放入 Animal，再让狗和猫继承它，就能复用这些代码。

继承表示“是一个”（is-a）的关系：狗是一种动物，因此 Dog 可以继承 Animal。

class 子类 extends 父类 {
    // 子类新增的成员
}
  • 父类：也叫基类、超类，提供共同的属性和行为。
  • 子类：也叫派生类，可以复用父类中允许继承的成员，并增加或调整自己的行为。

下面的完整示例可保存为 Test.java；后续完整示例也分别独立运行。

class Animal {
    String name;
    int age;

    public void eat() {
        System.out.println(name + "正在吃饭");
    }

    public void sleep() {
        System.out.println(name + "正在睡觉");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    public void bark() {
        System.out.println(name + "汪汪叫");
    }
}

class Cat extends Animal {
    public void mew() {
        System.out.println(name + "喵喵叫");
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Dog dog = new Dog();
        dog.name = "小黑";
        dog.age = 2;
        dog.eat();
        dog.sleep();
        dog.bark();
    }
}

输出：

小黑正在吃饭
小黑正在睡觉
小黑汪汪叫

Dog 没有重复声明 name、age、eat()、sleep()，仍然能使用它们，这就是代码复用。

子类通常会增加特有成员或调整行为，但语法并不强制子类必须新增成员。继承也是后续学习多态的基础，本章先掌握成员复用和访问规则。

二、先看权限：父类的成员能不能访问

有继承关系，不代表能直接访问父类的所有成员。 判断成员访问是否合法，必须先看权限。

访问位置 private 不写修饰符（包访问权限） protected public
声明该成员的类内部 可以 可以 可以 可以
同一个包中的其他类 不可以 可以 可以 可以
不同包中的子类内部 不可以 不可以 可以，但有限制 可以
不同包中的非子类 不可以 不可以 不可以 可以

“包访问权限”就是不写访问修饰符，不是写一个 default 关键字。

2.1 private：子类不能直接访问 

class Animal {
    private String name = "小黑";

    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    public void show() {
        // System.out.println(name);       // 错误：不能直接访问父类的 private 字段
        // System.out.println(super.name); // 错误：super 不能绕过权限
        System.out.println(getName());     // 正确：通过父类公开的方法读取
    }
}

父类的 private 成员不被子类继承，也不能由子类直接访问；但子类对象仍然具有由父类管理的这部分状态，父类自己的方法可以使用它。

2.2 protected：重点看跨包情况

同包时，protected 成员可以被包内其他类访问，不要求有继承关系。

跨包时，需要同时考虑访问代码写在哪里和通过什么类型的引用访问。对于父类的 protected 实例成员：

  • 访问代码必须位于子类内部。
  • 在该子类内部，可以通过 this、super，或该子类类型及其子类型的引用访问。
  • 不能通过父类类型的引用，或另一个“兄弟子类”类型的引用访问。

父类放在 demo1 包：

// demo1/Base.java
package demo1;

public class Base {
    protected int value = 100;
}

两个子类放在另一个包：

// demo2/Derived.java
package demo2;

import demo1.Base;

class Other extends Base {
}

public class Derived extends Base {
    public void show() {
        System.out.println(this.value);  // 正确
        System.out.println(super.value); // 正确

        Derived d = new Derived();
        System.out.println(d.value);     // 正确：通过 Derived 类型的引用访问

        Base b = new Base();
        // System.out.println(b.value);  // 错误：通过 Base 类型的引用访问

        Other o = new Other();
        // System.out.println(o.value);  // 错误：Other 是兄弟子类
    }
}

虽然 Derived 和 Other 在同一个包，但 value 声明在另一个包的 Base 中，所以这里仍受跨包访问规则限制。

选择权限时，只开放必要的范围：内部实现尽量隐藏，需要给子类使用的成员再考虑 protected，需要对外公开的成员才用 public。

三、再看名字：到底访问哪个成员

以下讨论以成员有访问权限为前提。

3.1 成员变量：同名时优先使用子类的

在子类实例方法中，直接写变量名时，先看局部变量或参数，再看子类字段，最后沿父类查找。父子类存在同名字段时，两个字段都存在，子类字段会隐藏父类字段。

class Base {
    int value = 10;
    int count = 30;
}

class Derived extends Base {
    int value = 20;

    public void show(int value) {
        System.out.println(value);       // 参数
        System.out.println(this.value);  // 子类字段
        System.out.println(super.value); // 父类字段
        System.out.println(count);       // 子类没有，使用父类字段
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Derived d = new Derived();
        d.show(100);
    }
}

输出：

100
20
10
30

注意：

  • this.value 不会选中同名参数；它访问当前对象的字段。
  • super.value 明确访问父类字段，不会改成访问子类的同名字段。
  • 字段同名即会发生隐藏，不要求类型相同。实际编写代码时，尽量避免父子类字段同名。
  • 当前作用域和继承链中都找不到对应成员时，编译报错。

3.2 成员方法：不能只看方法名

情况 如何理解
子类没有对应方法，父类有可访问的方法 可以使用父类的方法
父子类方法同名，但参数列表不同 可以构成重载，按调用时的参数选择
子类重新实现父类中可重写的同签名实例方法 构成重写，可以用 super.方法名(...) 调用父类实现

重写先理解为：子类为父类已有的某个实例方法提供自己的实现。这里先用返回类型也相同的例子，具体规则留到后续学习。

class Base {
    public void show() {
        System.out.println("Base.show()");
    }

    public void work() {
        System.out.println("Base.work()");
    }
}

class Derived extends Base {
    public void show(int n) {
        System.out.println("Derived.show(int)：" + n);
    }

    public void work() {
        System.out.println("Derived.work()");
    }

    public void test() {
        show();        // 调用父类的无参方法
        show(5);       // 调用子类的有参方法
        work();        // 调用子类重写后的实现
        super.work();  // 明确调用父类实现
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Derived().test();
    }
}

输出：

Base.show()
Derived.show(int)：5
Derived.work()
Base.work()

show() 和 show(int) 是重载；两个 work() 是重写。不要把方法调用简单理解成“只要子类有同名方法，就一定调用子类的”。

3.3 super 的作用

super 用于在子类中明确访问父类成员，常见形式有：

super.字段名
super.方法名(参数)
super(参数)            // 调用父类构造方法，下一节说明

this 是当前对象的引用；super 是访问父类成员的特殊语法，不是另一个独立父类对象的引用。二者都不能在 static 方法中使用，super 也不能突破访问权限。

四、创建子类对象：先初始化父类部分

一个子类对象既有父类定义的实例状态，也有子类自己定义的实例状态。因此，创建子类对象时，需要先通过父类构造方法初始化父类部分，再继续初始化子类部分。

构造方法不会被继承。 子类需要自己的构造方法，并在构造过程中调用父类构造方法。

4.1 用 super(...) 选择父类构造方法 

class Animal {
    String name;

    public Animal(String name) {
        this.name = name;
        System.out.println("Animal 构造：" + name);
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    int age;

    public Dog(String name, int age) {
        super(name);
        this.age = age;
        System.out.println("Dog 构造：" + age);
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Dog dog = new Dog("小黑", 2);
    }
}

输出：

Animal 构造：小黑
Dog 构造：2

执行过程：

  1. new Dog("小黑", 2) 进入 Dog 的构造过程。
  2. super(name) 调用 Animal(String name)，完成父类部分的初始化。
  3. 返回后继续执行 Dog 构造方法中剩余的语句。

整个过程创建的是一个 Dog 对象，不是先创建独立的 Animal 对象，再创建一个 Dog 对象。

4.2 没写 super(...)，为什么有时可以、有时报错

如果构造方法没有显式调用 this(...) 或 super(...)，编译器会隐式添加 super()。

class Base {
    public Base(int n) {
    }
}

class Derived extends Base {
    public Derived() {
        // 隐式调用 super()，但 Base 没有无参构造方法，因此编译失败
    }
}

上面的错误不是“子类没有构造方法”，而是默认调用的父类无参构造方法不存在。

解决方法是显式调用已有的父类构造方法，例如在第一条语句写 super(10);；也可以根据设计需要，为父类提供可访问的无参构造方法。

这里需要分清两个规则：

  • 一个类完全没有声明构造方法时，编译器才会提供默认的无参构造方法；已经写了有参构造，就不会再自动补无参构造。
  • 隐式 super() 能否成功，取决于父类是否有可访问的无参构造方法，与父类是否还有其他有参构造无关。

4.3 this(...) 与 super(...) 的关系

写法 含义
this.字段 / this.方法(...) 通过当前对象访问成员，本类没有时也可能使用继承的成员
super.字段 / super.方法(...) 明确访问父类成员或方法实现
this(...) 调用本类的另一个构造方法
super(...) 调用父类构造方法

按照本章采用的构造方法写法，this(...) 或 super(...) 放在构造方法的第一条语句，二者不能同时写在同一个构造方法中。

class Base {
    public Base(int n) {
        System.out.println("Base：" + n);
    }
}

class Derived extends Base {
    public Derived() {
        this(10);
        System.out.println("Derived 无参构造");
    }

    public Derived(int n) {
        super(n);
        System.out.println("Derived 有参构造");
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Derived();
    }
}

输出：

Base：10
Derived 有参构造
Derived 无参构造

调用链是 Derived() → Derived(10) → Base(10)，然后逐层返回。

因此，不是每个子类构造方法中都直接出现 super(...)；通过 this(...) 调用本类其他构造方法后，最终仍会调用父类构造方法。

“不能同时出现”指的是构造调用 this(...) 与 super(...)。super(...) 后面当然可以继续写 this.age = age;。

五、有继承时，代码块按什么顺序执行

静态代码块属于类，在类初始化时执行一次；实例代码块属于对象，每次创建对象都会执行。

当父子类都尚未初始化，第一次创建子类对象时，顺序是：

父类静态代码块
    ↓
子类静态代码块
    ↓
父类实例代码块
    ↓
父类构造方法体
    ↓
子类实例代码块
    ↓
子类构造方法体中 super(...) 后的部分

class Parent {
    static {
        System.out.println("父类静态块");
    }

    {
        System.out.println("父类实例块");
    }

    public Parent() {
        System.out.println("父类构造");
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    static {
        System.out.println("子类静态块");
    }

    {
        System.out.println("子类实例块");
    }

    public Child() {
        System.out.println("子类构造");
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Child();
        System.out.println("--- 再创建一个对象 ---");
        new Child();
    }
}

输出：

父类静态块
子类静态块
父类实例块
父类构造
子类实例块
子类构造
--- 再创建一个对象 ---
父类实例块
父类构造
子类实例块
子类构造

记忆重点：静态先完成，实例先父后子；静态只执行一次，实例每次创建都执行。

不要误记成“先执行所有实例代码块，再执行所有构造方法”：父类的实例初始化和构造先完成，才轮到子类的实例初始化和构造。

六、Java 支持哪些继承关系

Java 的类支持：

  • 单继承：一个类只有一个直接父类。
  • 多层继承：C 继承 B，B 继承 A，C 也就间接继承了 A。
  • 多个类继承同一个父类：例如 Dog 和 Cat 都继承 Animal。 
class A { }
class B extends A { }
class C extends B { } // 多层继承
class D extends A { } // B 和 D 有同一个直接父类

// class E extends B, D { } // 错误：一个类不能同时继承两个类

多层继承不等于多继承：前者是一条逐层延伸的继承链，后者是一个类同时拥有多个直接父类，Java 的类不支持后者。

除 Object 本身外，Java 的类都直接或间接继承自 java.lang.Object；这里知道它是类继承体系的根即可。

继承层次过深会增加理解和维护的难度，应尽量保持简单。“尽量不超过三层”是设计建议，不是语法限制。

七、final：限制修改、重写和继承

修饰对象 作用
变量或字段 一旦赋值，就不能再次赋值
实例方法 子类不能重写这个方法
类 不能再被其他类继承

7.1 修饰变量 

final int MAX = 10;
// MAX = 20; // 编译错误：不能重新赋值

如果修饰的是引用变量，不能改变的是引用指向，并不自动禁止修改对象内部的状态。

7.2 修饰类 

final class Animal {
}

// class Dog extends Animal { } // 编译错误：Animal 不能被继承

常用的 String 类就是 final 类，不能继承它。

7.3 修饰方法 

class Base {
    public final void show() {
        System.out.println("固定实现");
    }
}

class Derived extends Base {
    // public void show() { } // 编译错误：不能重写 final 方法
}

Derived 仍然可以继承和调用这个可访问的方法，只是不能重新实现它。这里先记住限制，重写的详细规则以后再学。

八、继承与组合：是一个，还是有一个

继承和组合都能复用代码，但表达的关系不同。

方式 关系 示例 实现方式
继承 is-a：是一个 奔驰是一种汽车 class Benz extends Car
组合 has-a：有一个 汽车有发动机 在 Car 中定义 Engine 类型的字段

组合不需要特殊关键字，就是让一个对象持有另一个对象，并使用它提供的功能。

class Engine {
    public void start() {
        System.out.println("发动机启动");
    }
}

class Car {
    private Engine engine = new Engine();

    public void start() {
        engine.start();
        System.out.println("汽车启动");
    }
}

class Benz extends Car {
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Benz car = new Benz();
        car.start();
    }
}

输出：

发动机启动
汽车启动

这里同时存在两种关系：

  • Benz extends Car：奔驰是一种汽车，复用汽车的行为。
  • Car 持有 Engine：汽车有发动机，Car.start() 通过 engine.start() 复用发动机的功能。

engine 是 Car 的私有字段，Benz 不能直接访问，但可以通过继承来的 start() 使用这项功能。

注意，单写 private Engine engine; 只声明了引用，默认值是 null，没有创建发动机对象；必须让它指向有效对象后才能调用方法。

选择时先判断关系：“是一种”考虑继承，“有一个”考虑组合。 不要仅为了少写几行代码就强行建立继承关系；同样能满足需求时，优先考虑组合，避免过深的继承链。

九、复习自检

  1. 父类和子类有同名字段，父类字段消失了吗？ 没有。子类字段隐藏父类字段，在子类实例方法中可用 super.字段名 明确访问父类字段。
  2. 子类有同名方法，就一定调用子类的吗？ 不一定。重载要看参数；对于示例中的重写，可用 super.方法名(...) 调用父类实现。
  3. 父类只有有参构造，子类构造什么都不写可以吗？ 不可以。隐式 super() 找不到父类无参构造，需要通过构造调用链选中父类已有的构造方法。
  4. super 能访问父类的 private 成员吗？ 不能，super 不会突破访问权限。
  5. 第二次创建子类对象，还执行静态代码块吗？ 不再执行；父子类的实例代码块和构造方法仍会执行。
  6. 构造方法能被继承吗？ 不能。调用父类构造方法与继承父类构造方法是两回事。
  7. 汽车和发动机应该用继承吗？ 不应该。汽车“有”发动机，适合用组合。

title: Node.js Permission Checks Are a Seat Belt, Not a Container
description:
Node.js Permission Checks Are a Seat Belt, Not a Container

The Node.js permission model is now stable, and it gives an application a way to refuse several sensitive operations at runtime. That can reduce the blast radius of a compromised dependency or a bad configuration. It becomes dangerous when teams treat a process-level permission flag as an operating-system sandbox.

The model was added to Node.js in version 20 and became stable in newer releases. It restricts access to the filesystem through fs, network access, child processes, worker threads, native addons, WASI, FFI, and the inspector. Enforce mode throws on denied operations. Audit mode records violations through diagnostics channels without blocking them, which is useful for discovering what the application actually needs.

What the flag changes

With --permission, Node.js starts with the available permission scopes denied unless explicitly allowed. File system reads and writes need the appropriate grants. Spawning a child process or creating a worker requires separate flags. Network access and native addons are controlled in the same way.

This is valuable because application code often fails open. A package that tries to read a credential file may be denied even if the application did not anticipate that behavior. A compromised template engine that tries to spawn a shell may hit the child-process boundary. The resulting error is visible and can be logged by the application or an outer supervisor.

Audit mode gives operators a migration path. Run the application with --permission-audit, subscribe to the node:permission-model:* diagnostics channels, and observe which resources are requested. Then add only the grants required by the observed workload. Do not infer a complete security policy from a single healthy request. Exercise background jobs, startup checks, test paths, and failure handling.

Where the boundary stops

The documentation calls this a seat belt approach. It prevents trusted code from unintentionally changing files or using resources that were not granted. It does not make untrusted code safe from vulnerabilities in native code, the JavaScript engine, or the operating system.

The native-addon and FFI scopes deserve special review. Native code can reach beyond the JavaScript API surface, so the permission model's decision about whether an addon may load is not a guarantee about what the addon does after it loads. Likewise, the OpenSSL STORE loader permission can grant broad authority that is not constrained by ordinary file and network scopes. A loader can access files, devices, tokens, or network resources according to its own implementation. If an application enables that capability, document the exact reason and isolate the process from unrelated secrets.

The model also belongs to one process. If a permitted child process is part of the design, it has its own runtime and its own behavior. Review the child's entry point, environment, working directory, and privilege level. The parent's permission decision is not a substitute for a container or a service account boundary.

A migration plan

Start with an inventory rather than a flag:

  1. List every file path, network destination, worker, child process, addon, and inspector endpoint the service uses.
  2. Run in audit mode with production-like workloads and collect diagnostics.
  3. Remove unnecessary startup dependencies and lazy-loading paths.
  4. Apply enforce mode in a staging environment.
  5. Test denial paths, such as a missing read grant or a blocked child process.
  6. Keep an outer sandbox for the filesystem and network boundary.

The application should handle ERR_ACCESS_DENIED deliberately. A dropped file-read permission during a certificate rotation is not a security win if the process exits without a clear alert. Log the denied scope and resource category without logging the secret path or credential value.

What to monitor

Monitor permission denial events at the diagnostics layer and at the service supervisor. A sudden rise in fs denials may indicate a new dependency, a bad mount, or an attempted exploit. A child-process denial may be expected during a security test and suspicious in production. Establish baselines so the alert is about change, not just noise.

Review the permission set whenever the dependency tree or deployment changes. A flag copied from a previous service can grant network access that the new service never needs. Keep the policy in version control and include it in the release checklist.

The right conclusion

Node.js permissions are useful because they make application capabilities explicit. They do not replace a container runtime, a network policy, a dedicated user account, or a secrets manager. Use them to narrow what the JavaScript runtime may ask the host to do, then use host controls to constrain what a successful compromise can reach.

References

  • Node.js Permissions
  • Node.js child processes
  • Node.js diagnostics channel

title: Decisions by Discrimination: Differential Evidence for Medical Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.13233v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly studied for clinical decision support, and medical question answering provides a testbed for evaluating this capability. In particular, medical multiple-choice questions (MCQs) reflect a core challenge in clinical decision-making: plausible options often share overlapping evidence, while only a few decisive factors distinguish the correct option from incorrect ones. However, existing retrieval-based and reasoning-oriented methods mainly focus on supplying broadly relevant knowledge or eliciting reasoning paths, rather than identifying the compact differential evidence that separates confusing alternatives. In this work, we present a retrieval-grounded differential evidence framework for medical MCQs. Our method extracts option-specific pieces of differential evidence and organizes them into concise evidence prompts for answer selection. This design better aligns external knowledge with differential reasoning while reducing irrelevant context. Experiments show consistent accuracy gains across multiple datasets and target LLMs. Ablation studies further show that our framework outperforms both directly using retrieved evidence chunks and closed-source LLM-generated general hints, and that its improvements are not solely explained by answer-proximal guidance, but are consistent with differential evidence serving as a compact aid for reasoning over competing alternatives. Our findings also offer insights for medical reasoning and other decision-making settings with multiple possible choices.

title: Seeing Is Not Believing: Counterfactual Lesion Erasure Teaches a Small Medical Vision-Language Agent to Report Only What the Image Shows
description:
arXiv:2611.13006v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) often report a finding because the question names it; standard benchmarks miss this. From public segmentation datasets we build counterfactual views without manual annotation: the lesion erased by inpainting, a same-shape control edit elsewhere, and unedited lesion-free images. The evidence sensitivity gap (ESG) is the rate of absent-or-refer answers after erasure minus the rate after the control edit; it is zero for a model that ignores the image or reacts to both edits alike. MedScope-4B (Qwen3.5-4B, LoRA, image tools) was trained on label-derived trajectories, selected by a pre-registered rule and tested once against nine frontier and six open VLMs; four pre-registered checks then probed the mechanism. On 507 internal cases across five imaging types, MedScope-4B reached ESG 0.758 and claimed an erased lesion in 9.6% of cases, against 0.27-0.47 and 41-62% for the frontier models (all p<0.001), without significant loss of accuracy on real lesions. Without counterfactual views ESG fell to 0.279+-0.107 (three seeds); the effect replicated on MedGemma 1.5 4B and two unseen inpainting tools. At four external centres the advantage held but frontier models detected more real lesions; on a fresh external test MedScope-4B detected 0 of 48 pneumothorax films, with net utility below gemini-4-argon's (-0.36 [-0.50, -0.23]). Matching the control edit was not shown to matter; over three seeds no fresh-external ESG advantage over removal-based DPO was established; a paired-view consistency objective did not beat a matched-compute control, while that continuation alone cut erased-lesion claims on unseen tools at every seed, at a cost in sensitivity at one. Training on erased and edited images gives a small model an evidence-gated disposition that prompting does not give frontier models; it does not improve perception, and rare critical findings need coverage.

title: Uncovering the Blind Spots of OKS-mAP: A Unified Protocol for Occlusion, Joint-Angle, and Temporal Evaluation of 2D Pose Estimators
description:
arXiv:2611.12911v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The dominant metric for 2D human pose estimation, OKS-mAP, has three blind spots: it does not distinguish visible from occluded keypoints, does not measure joint-angle error, and is silent on the temporal stability of tracking-free per-frame inference. We propose a supplementary protocol with three modules: (M1) OKS-mAP stratified by ground-truth visibility, with Delta_occ = mAP(v=1) - mAP(full), quantifying how much the aggregate metric masks occlusion-specific differences; (M2) joint-angle error (RMSE/MAE/P95) plus knee-valgus detection consistency; (M3) frame-to-frame displacement, median-filter residual jitter, and jump rate, before and after OneEuro smoothing. We ran it on four datasets (COCO val2017, CrowdPose, OCHuman, PoseTrack18) and four models from two architecture families (YOLO11s-pose, an occlusion-domain fine-tuned variant, ViTPose-B/L), under a common detector-free oracle protocol and an open-source harness. Delta_occ is negative in every combination (-0.19 to -0.47): aggregate mAP overestimates occluded-scene performance in every tested combination. Joint-angle error is amplified in occluded layers; angle metrics reveal differences mAP cannot localize, e.g., the smaller occlusion-trained model significantly outperforming a larger transformer in occluded elbows. On PoseTrack18 val, raw jitter matched between the two YOLO models; pixel-domain OneEuro smoothing cut jump rates 9-10% at no matched-scope AP cost; residual jitter persists after detector removal; the transformer pair's jump rate is significantly lower; smoothing benefits replicate across architectures. Stratified mAP tracks full mAP closely (sign-consistency 1.0, 12/12), serving magnitude diagnosis rather than re-ranking; angle-metric difference vectors (especially knee) partially diverge, suggesting independent information. The protocol and harness are open-sourced, complementing rather than replacing OKS-mAP.

title: Audited Gradients, Anchored Policies: Model-Based Reinforcement Learning for Efficient Flow Control
description:
arXiv:2611.13203v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Feedback controllers for flows are expensive to design, since each candidate must be evaluated with a high-fidelity solver. Differentiable surrogates reduce that cost, but they also introduce a failure mode that prediction error cannot detect. Policy optimization uses the derivative of the objective with respect to the action, which we call the action gradient and which can be computed either through the surrogate or through the high-fidelity solver. Optimization through the surrogate uses only its action gradient, and a surrogate can follow the flow trajectory closely while misestimating this derivative. The surrogate action gradient is compared against a central finite-difference estimate from the high-fidelity solver on held-out states, under acceptance criteria fixed before the comparison, and we call that comparison an audit. A low-dimensional feedback law is then fitted to the surrogate action gradient when the surrogate passes the audit, and to the solver estimate when it does not. This law initializes a neural policy, and a quadratic penalty holds the policy near it during optimization. The proposed approach is validated on four test cases. The resulting controllers outperform or match a model-free baseline, while using 3 to 156 times fewer high-fidelity solver interactions across the four test cases. One surrogate predicts the objective at correlation 0.9996 but its action gradient at only 0.459, so prediction accuracy does not identify a usable surrogate. Another surrogate, whose action gradient agrees with the solver estimate at correlation 0.996, makes the objective 0.52% worse when the policy is optimized through it without the anchor penalty, so an accurate gradient alone does not provide a working controller. Finally, a surrogate that passes the audit at one fixed action fails it around the actions the deployed controller applies, so a pass is local.

title: When Reconstruction Helps Event-Camera Person Triggers
description:
arXiv:2611.13488v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Event cameras record asynchronous changes in brightness. To use a general visual model as a recording trigger, a system must represent these measurements in a form the model can interpret. We compare direct grayscale accumulation, two temporal encodings, and two intensity reconstructors on paired real event data. On 192 windows from four held-out DSEC recordings, thresholds calibrated only on development data yielded 40 of 52 person detections and 12 of 140 background positives with E2VID. The strongest direct temporal encoding at an admissible fixed cutoff yielded 14 detections and seven background positives. A retrospective comparison at a common 10% background-positive cap yielded 40 detections for E2VID and at most 19 for any direct encoding. FireNet+ had lower preparation cost and produced 21 detections with zero observed background positives at its frozen cutoff. On the same 192 windows, Qwen3-VL-4B yielded 33/52, 2/140 with E2VID and 9/52, 9/140 with the highest-recall direct rendering, the three-bin image (person detections, background positives). A 96-second exploratory replay illustrates the sensitivity of episode capture and recording starts to cutoff selection. The experiments identify a detection benefit from reconstruction under controlled input history and distinguish it from the cost and false starts of continuous triggering.

title: From Booking Requests to Confirmed Bookings: Designing Reliable Server-Side Events
description:
A form submission is easy to track. A confirmed booking is harder.

In booking-based businesses, the customer may submit a request, reserve multiple seats, change plans, or cancel before attending. If all of those actions are counted as conversions, marketing reports can look successful while overstating actual business outcomes.

I worked on this problem in a booking attribution project where the goal was to connect campaign information, booking requests, CRM status changes, and analytics events.

This article describes the event-design decisions and testing approach. The code examples are simplified illustrations, not copies of production code.

1. Define the business outcome before the event

The first challenge was semantic, not technical.

Consider these stages:

  • Request created: Someone submits a booking form.
  • Booking confirmed: The booking is accepted and recorded as confirmed.
  • Booking cancelled: A previously requested or confirmed booking is cancelled.
  • Attendance recorded: Someone actually shows up.

These stages are related, but they are not interchangeable.

A request tells us that someone expressed interest. A confirmation tells us that the business secured a booking. Attendance tells us something different again.

The tracking model must preserve those distinctions.

In our project, the primary marketing outcome was a confirmed booking, not simply a form submission.

2. Model events around state transitions

Rather than sending an indistinguishable conversion every time something changes, define separate event types.

For example:

booking_created
booking_confirmed
booking_cancelled

A useful event record might look like this:

{
  "event_type": "booking_confirmed",
  "booking_id": "example-123",
  "event_id": "example-123:confirmed:1",
  "seat_count": 3,
  "source": "facebook",
  "campaign": "example_campaign",
  "occurred_at": "2026-10-15T14:40:00Z"
}

This is an illustrative schema, not an actual customer record.

Several properties are important:

  • booking_id connects the event to a business record.
  • event_id identifies the event for duplicate protection.
  • seat_count separates reservations from reserved places.
  • source and campaign preserve available attribution context.
  • occurred_at records when the business event happened.

A confirmation should be generated from the actual booking state, not inferred from a thank-you page.

3. Connect the website, CRM, and reporting pipeline

The implementation connects several parts of an existing booking system.

The simplified data flow is:

Campaign / source information
          |
          v
     Booking form
          |
          v
     Booking record
          |
          v
   CRM status transition
          |
          v
   Server-side event queue
          |
          +----> Google Analytics 4
          |
          +----> Meta Conversions API

The website captures a request. The booking system remains responsible for booking status. The integration layer turns relevant state changes into analytics events.

This separation matters because marketing tools should not decide whether a customer has been confirmed. That decision belongs to the business system.

The server-side layer can then provide consistent delivery, validation, and retry handling.

4. Make event processing idempotent

Duplicate events are one of the easiest ways to corrupt conversion reporting.

They can occur when:

  • A webhook is delivered more than once.
  • A request times out and gets retried.
  • A scheduled job processes a previously attempted event.
  • A status update is replayed.
  • Browser and server tracking report the same action.

A useful design principle is:

Processing the same business event twice should not produce two business conversions.

For example, an idempotency key can combine the booking ID, transition type, and a transition version:

booking-123:confirmed:1

Conceptually, the server-side processing logic becomes:

Receive event
    |
Validate event and consent
    |
Check idempotency key
    |
    +-- Already processed --> Do not create another event
    |
    +-- New event --> Store event and enqueue delivery
                              |
                              v
                       Send to platforms
                              |
                              v
                       Record delivery status

The event record and its queue entry should be created reliably together. A retry should reuse the same event identity rather than create a new conversion.

It is also important to distinguish accepted by an API from visible in an analytics report. Those are separate verification steps.

5. Don't confuse bookings with seats

One booking request can cover multiple people.

Suppose a customer requests three seats and the booking is confirmed.

That can mean:

  • One booking request.
  • One confirmed booking.
  • Three confirmed seats.

If the dashboard reports three bookings instead of three seats, the result is misleading.

A correct report needs explicit metric definitions.

For example:

Metric What it counts
Requests Booking requests submitted
Confirmed bookings Booking records confirmed
Confirmed seats Places within confirmed bookings
Cancelled bookings Bookings cancelled
Attendance Actual attendance records

This is especially important for events, appointments, group activities, and other businesses where one customer action can represent several participants.

6. Respect consent and attribution limits

Campaign parameters are useful, but they should only be processed and forwarded to analytics platforms when the applicable consent requirements are satisfied.

In this implementation, consent is part of the tracking flow rather than an afterthought.

There is also a difference between knowing the campaign associated with a booking request and identifying the exact Instagram conversation that produced it.

Those are different levels of attribution.

The current system can preserve available campaign information and report booking statuses. It does not establish a verified one-to-one match between every individual Instagram Direct conversation and a specific booking.

Reporting should communicate that boundary instead of implying a level of certainty that the data cannot support.

7. Test the business workflow, not just the tag

A successful network request does not prove that the overall tracking implementation is correct.

Testing should cover the complete path from an initial booking request to the final business status.

My checklist includes:

  1. Create a test booking request.
  2. Verify that a booking record is created.
  3. Confirm that the correct source information is retained when permitted.
  4. Check that request and confirmation events are separate.
  5. Confirm a booking containing multiple seats.
  6. Replay the same event and verify duplicate protection.
  7. Test cancellation or another status change.
  8. Check the queue and destination API responses.
  9. Verify reporting independently of API acceptance.
  10. Repeat relevant tests with consent declined.

Test records must also be distinguishable from real business results.

In the real project, some screenshots and counts come from integration tests. They demonstrate configured workflows, not proven increases in customers, sales, or revenue.

8. The lesson: measure verified states

A useful conversion-tracking system is not simply one that sends more events.

It is one that answers precise questions:

  • What actually happened?
  • Which system is authoritative for that outcome?
  • How do we prevent duplicate reporting?
  • Which attribution details are known?
  • Which details are still unknown?
  • Can the reported result be traced back to a business record?

When these questions are answered, analytics becomes much more useful for operational decisions.

I documented the real project, including implementation screenshots and its current limitations, in this booking attribution case study.

The broader principle applies beyond bookings: track confirmed business outcomes as distinct states, and test the entire data path before trusting a conversion report.

AI disclosure: AI tools were used to assist with drafting and structuring this article. The content was subsequently reviewed and edited by the author based on practical project experience.

title: 07 Java 调试案例讲解
description:
一、调试究竟在做什么

调试（Debugging）就是查找并改正程序错误的过程。 核心是观察程序的实际执行过程，逐步缩小问题范围，找到“从哪一步开始，实际结果与预期不一致”。

常见方式有两种：

  • 阅读代码、添加打印语句：代码较少时，按执行顺序检查，或用 System.out.println() 输出中间结果。
  • 使用调试器：让程序在指定位置停下来，查看变量，再控制它一步步执行。代码较复杂、需要反复观察时更方便。

以下使用 IntelliJ IDEA，Java 环境沿用课件中的 JDK 17。快捷键按课件的 Windows 键位说明；若自行修改过键位，以按钮提示为准。

二、先让程序在断点处停下来

1. 准备示例

新建 Test.java，后面的操作都围绕这段代码展开：

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int a = 10;
        int b = 20;
        int ret = add(a, b);       // 断点 A
        System.out.println(ret);  // 断点 B，后面再添加
    }

    public static int add(int x, int y) {
        System.out.println("进入 add");
        return x + y;
    }
}

正常运行时输出：

进入 add
30

2. 设置断点并启动 Debug

断点是告诉调试器“执行到这里先停一下”的标记。

  1. 在 int ret = add(a, b); 所在行的行号旁边单击，出现红点，即设置了断点 A。
  2. 在编辑区右键，选择 Debug 'Test.main()'。
  3. 程序运行到断点 A 时暂停，下方出现 Debug 窗口。

再次单击红点可以删除该断点。要让断点起作用，应使用 Debug 启动。

3. 看懂“停在这一行”

刚命中行断点时，该行通常还没有执行。

本例停在断点 A 时：

  • a = 10、b = 20 已执行，可以查看它们的值。
  • add(a, b) 尚未执行，ret 还没有完成初始化。
  • 控制台还没有输出“进入 add”和 30。

红点表示断点位置，执行高亮表示程序当前停留的位置。判断某个结果为什么还没出现，先检查产生结果的语句是否已经执行。

三、暂停后先看什么

1. Debugger：看变量和调用堆栈

变量区显示当前选中方法中的变量及其值。例如，停在 main 中可以查看 a、b；进入 add 后，可以查看 x、y。

调用堆栈表示当前有哪些方法正在调用、等待返回。例如：

add:行号
main:行号

表示 main 调用了 add，当前正在执行 add，main 正在等待它返回。最上方通常是当前执行的方法，下面是调用它的方法。

点击不同的方法记录，可以查看该次调用对应的变量。后面的数字是代码行号，不是调用次数。

2. 表达式求值与监视

程序暂停时，在 Debugger 中的 Evaluate expression ... or add a watch 输入区域填写表达式，按回车可查看结果。

例如停在 add 方法内部、x = 10、y = 20 时：

x + y        // 结果：30
(x + y) * 2  // 结果：60
  • 求值：临时计算一次，检查当前结果。
  • 监视（Watch）：把表达式加入监视列表，后续暂停时方便反复查看。

表达式中的变量必须在当前查看的位置可用。例如选中 add 时使用 x、y，选中 main 时使用 a、b。

3. Console：看输入输出

Console 显示控制台的输入输出，Debugger 用来观察执行状态。

只有输出语句执行之后，Console 才会出现对应内容。程序停在 System.out.println(ret); 这一行时，并不表示 30 已经打印。

四、用单步操作控制执行过程

1. 先区分四个操作

操作 快捷键 作用
Step Over（步过／逐过程） F8 执行当前行；遇到方法调用时，通常不进入方法内部逐步查看
Step Into（步入／逐语句） F7 进入当前行调用的方法，查看内部执行过程
Force Step Into（强制步入） Alt + Shift + F7 进入普通步入可能因过滤规则而跳过的方法
Step Out（步出／跳出） Shift + F8 执行完当前方法剩余部分，返回调用它的位置

2. 用同一段代码理解 F8、F7 和 Shift + F8

情况一：只关心方法的返回结果，用 F8。

停在断点 A 时按 F8，add(a, b) 会正常执行。到达下一行 System.out.println(ret); 时：

  • ret = 30。
  • Console 已输出“进入 add”。
  • 30 还没输出，再执行当前行才会输出。

步过只是通常不进入方法内部逐步查看，方法本身仍然执行。 如果方法内部另有断点，也可能在内部停下来。

情况二：想检查方法内部的计算过程，用 F7。

重新调试，在断点 A 按 F7：

  1. 进入 add，停在 System.out.println("进入 add");。
  2. 变量区可以看到 x = 10、y = 20。
  3. 按 F8，执行打印语句，停在 return x + y;。
  4. 此时可以求值 x + y，确认结果为 30。
  5. 继续执行返回语句，返回 main；调用及赋值完成后，ret 才得到 30。

情况三：已经进入方法，但不想继续逐行看，用 Shift + F8。

如果刚进入 add 就使用步出，剩余的打印和 return 仍会执行，然后回到 main 的调用位置。

步出不会取消这次调用，也不会丢掉剩余代码。 返回后界面可能仍高亮调用所在行，继续单步即可观察后续赋值和输出。

3. 强制步入用在什么地方

普通 F7 可能按调试器的过滤规则跳过某些 Java 类库方法，例如 System.out.println() 的内部实现。确实需要查看这些方法时，可以使用 Alt + Shift + F7。

“强制”是指绕过普通步入的过滤规则，并不意味着任何方法都一定有可供查看的源码。本章只需掌握它与普通步入的区别。

上述步进操作的含义可对照 IDEA 官方说明。

五、不想逐行执行时怎么做

1. 继续运行到下一个断点：F9

在 System.out.println(ret); 这一行再设置断点 B。

程序停在断点 A 时，按 F9（Resume Program），程序继续正常执行，命中断点 B 后暂停。此时 ret = 30，但 30 尚未打印。

如果后续没有命中其他断点，程序就会继续运行，直到结束或因其他原因暂停。

“到下一个断点”按实际执行顺序判断，不是按编辑器中红点的上下顺序判断。

2. 运行到光标处：Alt + F9

只想临时运行到某一行，可以：

  1. 在程序暂停时，把编辑光标放到目标代码行。
  2. 按 Alt + F9（Run to Cursor）。

例如停在断点 A 时，把光标放到 System.out.println(ret);，执行后会在这行暂停，便于查看 ret。

目标位置之前的代码仍会执行；如果途中先命中其他断点，会先在那个断点暂停。目标行也必须是本次执行能够到达的位置。

3. 重新调试与停止

操作 快捷键 含义
Rerun（重新调试） Ctrl + F5 从头重新启动当前调试配置，适合重新观察执行过程
Stop（停止） Ctrl + F2 终止当前程序，结束这次运行

Ctrl + F2 是停止，不是可继续执行的暂停。 停止之后，要再次运行就需要重新启动。参见 IDEA 调试会话说明。

六、管理断点与设置条件断点

1. 查看、禁用和屏蔽断点

  • View Breakpoints：Ctrl + Shift + F8。集中查看、编辑、启用、禁用或删除断点。
  • Mute Breakpoints（屏蔽断点）：在 Debug 工具栏点击该按钮，临时屏蔽所有断点；再次点击可解除屏蔽。断点仍然保留，不需要重新添加。

禁用适合暂时保留某个断点，删除适合不再需要的断点，屏蔽适合临时让程序不因这些断点而停下。

2. 条件断点：只在关心的那一次暂停

循环执行很多次时，普通断点会反复暂停。如果只想检查 i == 20 的情况，可以设置条件断点。

把 main 方法中的代码替换为：

for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
    System.out.println(i); // 在这一行设置断点
}

操作步骤：

  1. 在 System.out.println(i); 行设置断点。
  2. 右键单击断点红点，在 Condition 中填写 i == 20。
  3. 启动 Debug。

程序会正常执行前面的循环，直到 i == 20 时，才在该断点暂停。此时：

  • Debugger 中的 i 为 20。
  • Console 已输出 0 到 19。
  • 20 还没有输出，因为当前打印语句尚未执行。

条件应是结果为 true 或 false 的表达式。这里写 i == 20，不是赋值表达式 i = 20，也不需要写 if 或分号。

条件断点只控制是否暂停，不会让条件不满足时的代码停止执行。

七、把调试操作用来定位错误

假设加法示例中的返回语句误写成：

return x - y;

预期结果是 30，实际却输出 -10。可以这样定位：

  1. 在 int ret = add(a, b); 处打断点并 Debug。
  2. 查看 a = 10、b = 20，确认调用前的数据正确。
  3. 按 F7 进入 add，确认 x = 10、y = 20，参数传递也正确。
  4. 执行到返回语句，对比预期的 x + y 与实际代码 x - y，发现运算符写错。
  5. 改为 return x + y;，重新调试，确认 ret = 30，最终输出正确。

调试时每一步都应带着一个检查目标：输入是否正确、哪一步计算有误、返回结果是否符合预期。 找到第一个出现偏差的位置，通常就能明显缩小错误范围。

title: REAL Loss: Optimizing Real Expected Acceptance Length for Speculative Decoding
description:
arXiv:2611.14399v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by having a draft model propose multiple tokens for the target model to verify in one pass. The speedup is governed by the expected acceptance length (EAL), yet standard training objectives such as cross-entropy, KL divergence, and total variation focus only on distribution matching or single-step overlap. Recent studies instead propose block-level training objectives, aiming to optimize EAL directly. However, these objectives remain surrogates rather than exact formulations of EAL. For example, some average later acceptance over target-distributed continuations rather than the verification branches selected by accepted tokens, introducing a covariance gap that can reverse the gradient direction. We analyze this gap and derive REAL, a real EAL training loss that uses path weights for unbiased estimation and Rao-Blackwellization for variance reduction. In a controlled loss-level comparison with a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B target and a Domino drafter, REAL outperforms WTV, VSD, DBLast, and the static LK baseline on probabilistic serving acceptance length across 9 task subsets and 5 evaluation seeds. These gains require only a change to the training loss, with no modification to the drafter architecture or inference procedure, demonstrating the practicality of real EAL training. A reference implementation of the REAL loss is available at https://github.com/King-ty/speculators/tree/real-loss.

title: Being First Doesn't Always Mean Building the Better Product: What Apple's iPhone Duo Teaches Us About Product Design
description:
Remember when Samsung and Duolingo started joking about Apple's new iPhone Duo?

Samsung called it "reheating our leftovers."

Duolingo's response? "They named a phone after me."

Apple dropped the iPhone Duo anyway.

Honestly, the banter was funny. 😂

But underneath the jokes is an interesting product design conversation: Does being first in a category actually give you an advantage forever?

The advantage of arriving late

Samsung has been in the foldable phone market for years. It has experimented with different designs, introduced new form factors and had time to understand what works and what doesn't.

Apple, on the other hand, is entering the category much later.

And that's what makes its entry interesting.

Apple didn't invent the foldable phone. It has had years to observe the market, study competitors, understand user expectations and identify the problems that still need solving.

That's one advantage of arriving late.

You don't necessarily have to repeat the experiments everyone else has already conducted.

You can learn from their successes, their mistakes and the things users still complain about.

Of course, that doesn't guarantee Apple will build a better product.

But it gives the company a different starting point.

Product design isn't a race to launch first

I think product teams sometimes place too much importance on being first.

Being first can create awareness, establish a category and give a company an early market advantage.

But it doesn't automatically mean you've created the best experience.

Think about it.

A product can introduce an entirely new idea and still leave users struggling with its usability, reliability or everyday practicality.

Another company can come along years later, understand those frustrations and build something that feels more intuitive.

That's the difference between introducing an innovation and refining an experience.

Innovation isn't always about creating something nobody has seen before. Sometimes, it's about making something people already know finally work the way they expected.

The real question is what happens next

Apple's entry into foldables creates an interesting question for the industry.

Can it make the category feel more intuitive? Can it address the compromises users have come to accept? And can it offer an experience compelling enough to make people reconsider their existing preferences?

Those are the questions I'd be more interested in answering than who launched a foldable first.

Because in product design, the goal isn't simply to arrive before everyone else.

It's to understand what users need and deliver an experience that makes sense.

And if I'm being completely honest, I still think Samsung knows ball here. 😅

But I'm interested to see what Apple brings to the table.

What do you think matters more in product innovation: being the first to introduce an idea or being the one that makes it work best?

title: Differentiable Filtering for Inertial Odometry
description:
arXiv:2611.13517v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Accurate inertial odometry is critical for autonomous systems but suffers from unbounded drift caused by the integration of sensor noise and biases. In approaches such as TLIO, neural pseudo-measurements are trained independently of their downstream filter. This paper introduces Differentiable Filtering for Inertial Odometry (DFIO), a learning framework that embeds the update stages of an error-state Kalman filter directly into a computational graph. Following standalone pre-training, DFIO jointly optimizes the displacement and covariance output heads using posterior-position supervision through differentiable measurement updates. The proposed system is validated on public pedestrian motion datasets featuring both calibrated and uncalibrated inertial measurements. Experimental results on a pedestrian dataset demonstrate that DFIO reduces mean absolute and one-second relative translation errors by 13.2% and 39.6% relative to the TLIO baseline, and by 7.7% and 17.4% relative to its pre-trained counterpart. Furthermore, evaluations on uncalibrated smartphone inertial data indicate that the proposed method effectively mitigates translational drift and maintains trajectory alignment under highly noisy sensor conditions. Source code will be made publicly available.

title: CAppleNet: A Coordinate Attention-Based YOLO11 for Real-Time Apple Stem Cavity and Calyx Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.13920v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automated fruit grading, sorting, and orientation systems require real-time, accurate detection of fruit-level morphological landmarks rather than the fruit boundary alone. This paper presents a custom, fully self-collected and self-annotated dataset of 1506 apple images (1054 training, 301 validation, 151 test) captured under controlled, fixed-camera conditions and annotated for three target classes: fruit body, stem cavity, and calyx. A YOLO11s detector trained with default hyperparameters is adopted as the baseline, and a systematic, one-factor-at-a-time ablation study is conducted across input resolution, data augmentation policy, optimizer configuration, and lightweight architectural enhancement to identify the factors that most improve detection of these fine-grained landmarks under high inter-cultivar color and texture variability. Neither increased input resolution, nor any of six tested augmentation variants, nor manual optimizer tuning improved on the untuned baseline (F1 = 0.9047); only a same-slot architectural substitution of the backbone's C2PSA block with Coordinate Attention (CA) matched the baseline's overall F1 (0.9038) while reducing parameter count by 10.2% and achieving the study's best mAP@0.5 (0.935) and best stem-cavity F1 (0.8217). A confidence-threshold sweep identified 0.15 as the deployment operating point for this model, and a confirmatory experiment combining the CA-swap architecture with the best-performing augmentation variant showed the two effects do not combine additively, reversing the architectural gain rather than compounding it. The resulting design recommendations --- the CA-swap architecture alone, at a 0.15 confidence threshold --- target real-time apple landmark detection for orientation-aware industrial sorting and alignment systems.

title: Use your eval as a CI gate with Agents CLI
description:
Unit tests check that an agent's code runs, so a one-line change to its instruction can make its answers worse while the tests keep passing.

Last year we covered this in the Kaggle AI Agents Intensive with Google, in Prototype to Production, the Day 5 whitepaper. It says no agent version should reach users until it passes an automated evaluation, and Agents CLI, the command-line tool for building, evaluating, and deploying agents on Google Cloud, turns the pre-merge part of that rule into one setting in v1.13.0. In this post I add it to a fresh project and then to the project's CI, the continuous integration checks that run on every pull request.

Figure 1. The eval passes or fails the pull request check through the exit code your CI already reads.

Why agents need a different gate

An agent decides what to do on each request, so you grade its replies and its tool calls (the functions it runs, such as a weather lookup) on a set of known cases. An eval runs the agent on a dataset of prompts and scores each reply.

The whitepaper described two ways to use an eval as a gate. You can run it by hand before you open a pull request, or you can wire it into the pipeline so a failing eval blocks the change automatically. Agents CLI covers both with the same command, agents-cli eval run.

What changed in v1.13.0

According to the release notes, eval run and eval grade now end with a RESULT: PASS or RESULT: FAIL line, with the failing metrics and cases listed above it. A threshold is the lowest mean score you accept for a metric. You set it with a thresholds: map in the eval config, or for one run with --fail-under METRIC=SCORE, and a missed threshold exits 1. A run where any case errored also exits 1, so a broken eval can't pass by accident.

Every program ends with an exit code, 0 for success and anything else for failure. CI systems such as GitHub Actions treat a non-zero exit as a failed step, so the threshold fails the build without a plugin or a parser.

Start from the eval you already have

You need a Google Cloud project with the Vertex AI API turned on and local credentials from gcloud auth application-default login, or a Gemini API key. setup installs the agents-cli command and its skills for your coding agent, and create writes your project into the .env. A new project ships with an eval:

uvx google-agents-cli setup
agents-cli create gate-agent -y
cd gate-agent && agents-cli install

uvx runs a Python tool without installing it first, so uvx google-agents-cli is the same CLI as agents-cli. -y skips the prompts and takes the defaults, and install fetches the project's dependencies.

The dataset in tests/eval/datasets/basic-dataset.json holds three cases: a greeting, a weather question, and "What is the capital of France?", which has a reference answer for the judge to compare against. The metric, custom_response_quality, is an LLM-as-judge, which means a second large language model (LLM) reads each reply and grades it from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent).

Both the agent and the judge call Gemini through the Google Cloud project in your .env, or through a GEMINI_API_KEY if you switch the .env to it, as the comments in the file show. The eval config also ships a threshold, commented out until you know your bar.

Set the bar and run it

I set the bar at 4 out of 5:

$ agents-cli eval run --fail-under custom_response_quality=4
...
custom_response_quality:
  num_cases_total: 3
  num_cases_valid: 3
  num_cases_error: 0
  mean_score: 5.0000
  stdev_score: 0.0000
  pass_rate: 1.0000
...
RESULT: PASS (custom_response_quality 5.00 >= 4.00)
$ echo $?
0

eval run chains two steps, eval generate to run the agent on each case and eval grade to score the replies. pass_rate is the share of cases that scored at least 4 on their own. The exit code depends only on the mean.

Break it on purpose

Then I shortened the instruction to one line:

-    instruction="You are a helpful AI assistant designed to provide accurate and useful information.",
+    instruction="Answer in one word. Never call tools.",

The scaffold's placeholder unit test still passes, and the gate fails the run:

$ agents-cli eval run --fail-under custom_response_quality=4
...
custom_response_quality:
  num_cases_total: 3
  ...
  mean_score: 3.0000
  ...
  pass_rate: 0.3333
...
Failures:
  custom_response_quality: below threshold 4: case 0 (2.00), ...
Next: open ... to read the failing cases, ...
RESULT: FAIL (custom_response_quality 3.00 < 4.00)
$ echo $?
1

The full Failures: line lists case 0 and case 1, the greeting and the weather question, both at 2.00. The judge gave both a 2, because "Anything" was a vague answer to the greeting and "Foggy" skipped the weather tool. "Paris" still matched the reference and kept its 5, which is why pass_rate is 0.3333. The Next: line points to the HTML report with each case's reply and score. It also suggests agents-cli eval compare to diff two runs, so the person whose build failed knows where to look.

Put it in CI

For CI, move the bar into the repo by uncommenting the block in tests/eval/eval_config.yaml:

thresholds:
  custom_response_quality: 4  # the judge scores 1-5

Now eval run needs no flag. The bar lives in the repo next to the prompt and the dataset, and the whitepaper says to version both along with your code. With the original instruction back, the call CI will make passes:

$ uvx google-agents-cli eval run
...
RESULT: PASS (custom_response_quality 5.00 >= 4.00)
$ echo $?
0

Add the gate to GitHub Actions

Run agents-cli scaffold enhance --cicd-runner github_actions in the project to add CI. The generated .github/workflows/pr_checks.yaml already authenticates to Google Cloud and runs your unit and integration tests on pull requests to main that touch app/, tests/, deployment/ or uv.lock. Add the gate as one more step after the integration tests. Your .env stays out of the repo, so the step sets the same three variables itself, which tell the Gemini client to use your Google Cloud project in the global region.
CICD_PROJECT_ID is a repository variable you set in GitHub to the project CI runs in:

      - name: Eval gate
        env:
          GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_ENTERPRISE: 'true'
          GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT: ${{ vars.CICD_PROJECT_ID }}
          GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION: global
        run: uvx google-agents-cli eval run

In the whitepaper's pipeline this is the pre-merge stage, the checks that run before a change reaches your main branch. Staging and production come later.

To stop a failing pull request from merging, mark the test job of the PR Checks workflow as a required status check in your branch protection rules. The workflow only runs when one of those paths changes, and GitHub keeps a required check pending on a pull request that skips it, so delete the paths: block in pr_checks.yaml when you make test required.

Pick the bar with some margin, because the agent's answers change between runs. The broken agent answered the weather question "Foggy" in one run and "Unknown" in another, so it scored 3.00 in one run and 2.67 in the other. The working agent scored 5.00 in all three of its runs.

What to take away

We started from the eval the scaffold ships, gave it a bar, then moved the bar into the config and a CI step. Three cases make a small gate, so the whitepaper's advice to turn each production failure into a new eval case is the next step, since every case you add to basic-dataset.json shifts the mean that later changes are scored on.

To try it on your own agent, install the CLI and run your eval with a bar, using your own metric's name and a score on its scale:

uvx google-agents-cli setup
agents-cli eval run --fail-under custom_response_quality=4

The v1.13.0 release notes and the Agents CLI docs cover the eval commands in detail, and the code is in the Agents CLI repo. The Prototype to Production whitepaper covers the rest of the pipeline, from staging to production.

title: TAMEing the Open-World Personalization: Towards Open-Set Personalized MLLM Assistant
description:
arXiv:2611.14118v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Personalizing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) as intelligent assistants has recently emerged as an active research topic, where an MLLM is expected to go beyond generic, one-size-fits-all replies, and instead generate responses grounded in user-specific objects, entities, and concepts encountered during interactions. Nevertheless, existing studies mainly focus on personalizing MLLMs on a static, predefined set of personalized concepts and require users to manually and frequently extend this set to accommodate newly emerging concepts, which is infeasible in dynamic-world scenarios. To address this limitation, we recast conventional MLLM personalization as an Open-Set problem, and propose TAME-O, the first long-context open-set personalized MLLM assistant. Specifically, TAME-O introduces a training-free, plug-and-play Concept Reconciliation Skill (CR Skill). It enables the assistant to automatically unlock novel concepts during prolonged human-MLLM interactions while preventing confusion with previously unlocked ones, allowing the MLLM to continually grasp more and more concepts and progressively refine the modeling of known ones. Extensive experiments under the open-set personalization setting underscore the efficacy of our method.
