title: One Sequence Is Enough: Fingerprinting Language Models from Fixed-Length Integer Sequences
description:
arXiv:2611.14010v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Users of model APIs and third-party platforms often rely on the declared model name to identify the model responding to their requests. However, the actual model may differ from the declared one, motivating identity verification based on observable outputs. Previous studies have shown that preferences in simple numerical-choice tasks can serve as model fingerprints. We investigate whether a single fixed-length integer sequence can combine multiple numerical observations to identify its source model. For this task, we introduce NumPrint, a benchmark of 5,036 answers from 51 models, collected using Chinese, Japanese, and English prompts that request 294 integers between 1 and 355 in one response. We propose the Shallow MLP and Causal Transformer (SMCT) to capture aggregate numerical preferences and behavioral patterns in generated sequences. In 51-class closed-set evaluation, SMCT achieves 92.72% accuracy from a single sequence, outperforming all methods compared in this study. Using two and four answers increases accuracy to 96.06% and 97.12%, respectively. These results show that a single integer sequence contains useful model fingerprints and that additional answers further improve identification.

title: Exploring Synchrony for Communication in Modular Neural Networks
description:
arXiv:2611.13759v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: One motivation for modular neural networks is to divide computation across components that learn distinct, reusable functions, which could then be recombined to support compositional generalisation. In practice, modular structure alone does not guarantee that such roles develop, and unrestricted communication between modules can undermine any specialisation that does emerge. This raises the question of how modular communication should be organised. The problem can be viewed as an analogue of the perceptual binding problem, where synchrony has been proposed as a mechanism for coordinating distributed representations. We introduce SyncNet, a modular architecture that separates module content from a dynamical phase state: learnt Kuramoto dynamics evolve the phases, while phase alignment determines communication through a shared channel. We evaluate SyncNet on Sort-of-CLEVR for relational reasoning and on SQOOP for systematic generalisation, where lower pair variety demands more recombination at test time. SyncNet gives the best held-out accuracy of the models compared at the three lowest pair varieties, by 5.1 percentage points at the hardest, and is competitive on Sort-of-CLEVR though below the strongest attention baselines. Test-time overrides show that performance depends on phases that evolve: fixed phases cost as much as no addressing at all, and permuting which module holds which region is nearly as damaging. A content-addressed variant trained from scratch nonetheless matches it, so the benefit appears to come from the modular decomposition rather than synchrony itself.

title: Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) now supports post-quantum TLS, wildcard indexes, and $unionWith in version 8.0.3
description:
Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) 8.0.3 adds hybrid post-quantum key exchange for TLS, wildcard indexes, the $unionWith aggregation stage, and new change stream events. Post-quantum TLS protects data in transit from traffic that is recorded today and decrypted later with a quantum computer. The new MongoDB APIs let you move more MongoDB workloads to Amazon DocumentDB without changing application code.

What's new in 8.0.3:

  • Post-quantum TLS: TLS 1.3 connections use hybrid key exchange based on the Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM) when the client supports it. Other clients keep using classical key exchange. Two new Amazon CloudWatch metrics, TLSHandshakesClassical and TLSHandshakesPostQuantum, count the handshakes of each type.

  • Wildcard indexes: index every field, or every field under a path, to query documents with dynamic schemas.

  • Aggregation: $unionWith combines results from multiple collections in one pipeline. $lookup and $graphLookup work in views, and correlated $lookup sub-pipelines accept $unionWith and $facet.

  • Change streams: dropIndex() and dropIndexes() now emit dropIndexes events.

  • Compression metrics: collStats and stats() report per-collection input bytes, output bytes, and compression ratio.

Amazon DocumentDB 8.0.3 is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon DocumentDB is offered. To learn more, see the Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide.

title: Physics2Weight: Direct Neural Network Architecture and Weight Generation from Physical Laws Using Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.12954v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled weight-space programming (WSP), which directly generates neural network weights without gradient-based optimization. However, extending WSP to physical problems remains challenging, particularly in achieving both solution accuracy and physical consistency. In this paper, we propose Physics2Weight (PtW), a framework that extends WSP to solving partial differential equations by directly generating neural network weights and editing architectures based on governing equations and initial and boundary conditions. PtW introduces physics-constrained prompting and physics-guided architecture editing, combined with iterative weight refinement from WSP, to improve solution accuracy and physical consistency without gradient-based optimization. Experiments on four PDEs, namely the heat, advection, Burgers', and Allen--Cahn equations, demonstrate lower solution errors than conventional physics-informed neural networks, while revealing limitations in satisfying the governing equations for nonlinear PDEs.

title: An evidence-traceable benchmark of clinical reasoning in large language models
description:
arXiv:2611.13562v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Benchmark scores for medical large language models (LLMs) are difficult to interpret when scoring criteria cannot be traced to clinical evidence. Here we developed Med Evidence Bench (MEB; https://www.medevidencebench.org.cn/), comprising 1,536 physician-constructed items across three levels: guideline knowledge, standardized clinical scenarios and real-world laboratory scenarios. Each criterion stating a medical claim is linked to a versioned source-text span. Across ten LLMs, the Evidence Trace Score (ETS) was 0.975-0.997 for guideline knowledge, 0.292-0.658 for standardized scenarios and 0.182-0.447 for real-world scenarios, and rankings varied across levels. For real-world scenarios, scores for identifying clinical information (mean, 0.770) exceeded those for matching evidence (0.165) or formulating recommendations (0.160). On 1,296 criterion-level judgments, automated grading agreed with the majority vote of three physicians (macro-F1, 0.930; 95% confidence interval, 0.915-0.945), although agreement was lower for evidence application. These findings from Chinese-language materials indicate that guideline recall does not ensure patient-specific evidence use and do not establish clinical effectiveness.

title: EVAThink: Evidence Sufficiency-Guided Training for Adaptive Thinking in Video Understanding
description:
arXiv:2611.13907v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Under a fixed frame budget, video understanding with vision-language models (VLMs) depends on whether the sampled frames provide sufficient evidence for the question. Sufficient frame evidence supports direct answering, whereas less informative observations may benefit from reasoning that connects the available cues. We introduce EVAThink, which enhances video understanding through evidence sufficiency-guided training for adaptive thinking. First, Recoverable Evidence Gap Mining constructs evidence-dense and evidence-sparse video views that share the same question and answer under an identical frame budget. It retains pairs where sparse views yield lower direct-answer accuracy than dense views but benefit from explicit reasoning, providing supervision for response-mode selection. Second, Evidence-Guided Two-Stage Reinforcement Learning uses stage-specific rewards to guide training with evidence-based mode preferences and then refine response efficiency, while first-token advantage regularization mitigates mode collapse. Trained on only 6.7K curated samples, EVAThink consistently improves upon the base model across video understanding benchmarks under both 32- and 64-frame budgets, while outperforming strong baselines on average. The code, model, and datasets are available at \href{https://github.com/ChangtiWu/EVAThink}{EVAThink}.

title: LM-SimBench: A Unified Framework, Dataset, and Benchmark for Large Language Model Training Simulation
description:
arXiv:2611.14285v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluating candidate parallelization strategies through distributed training runs makes strategy selection prohibitively expensive at scale. Performance simulation offers a lower cost alternative, yet controlled comparisons among existing simulators remain difficult because they differ in the training stages they model and the workloads on which they are evaluated. We introduce LM-SimBench, a unified framework, profiling dataset, and benchmark for evaluating LLM training simulators. The framework decomposes simulation into functional stages from model compilation to schedule level aggregation, connecting execution representations and cost estimators to measurable evaluation targets. Following this framework, we profile 23 model settings from 10 dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLM families on an Ascend Neural Processing Unit (NPU) cluster. The resulting dataset contains 348 feasible configurations that jointly vary five parallelism dimensions and activation recomputation, with six views spanning configuration, rank, operator, event, and kernel granularity. Evaluations of representative training simulators demonstrate how LM-SimBench supports comparisons of prediction accuracy, assessment of configuration selection, and diagnosis of prediction errors. Matched GPU-NPU experiments validate the cross-platform applicability of the collection and evaluation protocol and demonstrate NPU-guided GPU configuration selection.

title: Quanto mais regras de UX o Haiku vê, melhor ele decide: mas busca simples não basta
description:
Versão simples do estudo "O quanto o data lake de UX ajuda um modelo pequeno em telas grandes?". Para o método completo e todos os números, leia o artigo técnico. Aqui está o que ele significa para quem quer usar isso amanhã.

Em uma frase

Quando o pedido é vago ("deixa isso pronto para produção"), o Haiku (o modelo pequeno) acertou 46% das correções sem regras, 70% com o conjunto inteiro de 148 regras de UX e 78% com as regras mais o relatório de um verificador. Com as regras, ele passou o Sonnet (o modelo maior) sem regras (61%), por cerca de 8% do custo por chamada.

O que a gente fez

Montamos 6 tipos de tela grande (painel, listagem, formulário, checkout, configurações e navegação, de 383 a 1.200 linhas) e um data lake de 200 regras de UX tiradas de fontes abertas (WCAG, GOV.UK, web.dev, Nielsen Norman e outras), conferidas uma a uma contra a fonte. Em cada tela, estragamos de propósito de 3 a 30 regras. Depois pedimos ao Haiku e ao Sonnet que consertassem, mostrando 0%, 25%, 50% ou 100% das regras, e medimos com um verificador em navegador real quantas regras passaram a ser cumpridas. Foram 2.640 chamadas, e as hipóteses foram escritas e congeladas antes de rodar.

O que a gente descobriu

  1. Cada 25% a mais de regras rendeu de 8 a 12 pontos a mais de acerto no Haiku (47%, 59%, 67% e 76% nas regras mostradas). Na prática: vale ampliar o lake, não há sinal de que ele já tenha chegado ao fim.
  2. Não é só volume de texto. Dar o mesmo tanto de regras de outros assuntos subiu o acerto só de 47% para 52%. A regra certa é o que importa.
  3. O lake ajudou até onde ele não cobria. Nas regras que o modelo nunca viu, o acerto foi até 11 pontos maior com o lake cheio: o modelo ficou mais cuidadoso no geral.
  4. O relatório do verificador evita quebrar o que já estava certo. Ele cortou as regras que passaram a falhar de 0,94 para 0,21 por tela, e somado ao lake inteiro subiu o acerto de 70% para 78% (e de 76% para 89% nas regras mostradas).
  5. Melhor e mais barato. O Haiku com regras passou o Sonnet sem regras (70% contra 61%) por US$ 0,0225 por chamada contra US$ 0,2728, cerca de 8% do custo. No conserto de telas com defeitos conhecidos, o Haiku com regras chegou a 81% (contra 63% do Sonnet sem regras) por 6% do custo.
  6. Mais regras, decisões mais ancoradas. A fração das decisões do Haiku que citava uma regra realmente recebida subiu de 59% (25% do lake) para 90% (lake inteiro).

O que o estudo comprovou

Escrevemos as perguntas antes de rodar, e as que mais importam para quem usa o lake foram confirmadas, com correção estatística para múltiplas comparações:

  • Completude melhora a decisão: 25%, 50% e 100% do lake deram, cada um, acerto maior que o degrau anterior.
  • A regra certa pesa mais que o volume: o lake inteiro (76% nas regras mostradas) ficou muito acima do mesmo tanto de regras de outros assuntos (52%).
  • O lake não prejudica onde não cobre, e o relatório do verificador soma ao lake inteiro e reduz as regressões.
  • Custo: o modelo pequeno com o lake passa o modelo maior sem ele, por 6% a 8% do custo por chamada.

Algumas coisas que testamos não deram certo ou não se aplicaram (por exemplo, o que uma busca simples recupera do lake). Elas estão na seção 6 do artigo técnico.

Ressalvas

  • As telas são sintéticas (seis tipos, geradas por script) e a tarefa é revisar um rascunho, não criar do zero. Isso não prova o mesmo comportamento em um projeto grande em produção.
  • Medimos conformidade com regras, não se o usuário final ficou melhor.
  • O verificador errou em cerca de 13% dos veredictos auditados, e o lake foi auditado por modelo, sem revisão humana.
  • Só testamos dois modelos e nada sobre estética.

Quer os dados e o método? Leia o artigo técnico.

Os experimentos, os dados e as conclusões são meus. A redação foi assistida por IA e revisada por mim.

title: ScaleBrain: A Scale-Consistent Framework for EEG Foundation Models
description:
arXiv:2611.14035v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Foundation models pre-trained on large unlabeled electroencephalography (EEG) corpora have emerged as a transformative paradigm for Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) applications. Recent EEG foundation models have shown that multi-scale representations derived from fixed-length patches can improve EEG representation learning. Existing frameworks commonly construct temporal scales through feature-level operations. However, these operations leave the correspondence between learned features and scale-specific characteristics of the original EEG signals implicit. Moreover, when the self-supervised objective is not aligned with the multi-scale input representations, information at some temporal scales may receive insufficient supervision during pre-training. In light of this, we propose ScaleBrain, a scale-consistent pre-training framework that explicitly coordinates multi-scale representations of EEG from both the model input and optimization objective sides. Specifically, ScaleBrain introduces multi-scale EEG tokenization to represent the same EEG segment through analysis windows with different temporal spans and shared temporal anchors, and pairs these representations with scale-specific reconstruction to align with the multi-scale input structure and provide supervision across temporal resolutions during self-supervised learning. We further develop an axial spatio-temporal attention mechanism to contextualize the fused multi-scale representation along spatial and temporal dimensions. Extensive evaluations on six public BCI benchmarks against 12 representative baselines show that ScaleBrain achieves the highest mean Balanced Accuracy on five datasets and ranks third on the remaining one, with only 5.0M parameters, demonstrating strong performance and favorable parameter efficiency.

title: Where to Approximate in Neurosymbolic Inference?
description:
arXiv:2611.13862v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Probabilistic neurosymbolic methods rely on weighted model counting (WMC) to combine neural predictors with symbolic constraints. Exact WMC is #P-hard and typically scales poorly, so many methods resort to approximations. By unifying existing approaches under a three-step bottom-up approximate compilation pipeline, we study where approximation budget is best allocated. Inspired by tensor networks, we instantiate two steps with tensor train decompositions and derive new pipelines that exactly multiply approximated factors and recompress their products via SVD- or interpolation-based schemes. Across six tasks in Sudoku, arithmetic reasoning, and scene understanding, and across increasing problem sizes, our pipelines produce WMC estimates orders-of-magnitude more accurate than prior methods. This translates into stronger downstream learning on tasks where reasoning relies on tight interactions between symbolic factors, where cruder approximations ignore these dependencies. Our pipelines open novel design space for effective approximate compilation of challenging probabilistic reasoning tasks.

title: Closing the BF16-FP16 Convergence Speed Gap in RL Post-Training with Stochastic Rounding
description:
arXiv:2611.13545v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: BF16 is widely used to pretrain large language models because it has the same dynamic range as FP32 and converges similarly to FP32 training. However, in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where learning rates are typically low, we find that standard mixed-precision BF16 training converges more slowly than FP16 training at the same learning rate. We attribute this gap to weight sticking: when FP32 shadow weights are quantized to BF16 using round-to-nearest, small updates often leave the BF16 weights used for rollout generation and training unchanged. Consequently, several optimizer steps may be needed before updates to the shadow weights are reflected in the BF16 weights. Raising the BF16 learning rate reduces weight sticking and matches FP16's convergence speed, but it also increases the KL divergence from the reference model. We instead apply stochastic rounding when quantizing the FP32 shadow weights to BF16. This approach matches FP16's convergence speed across different models and datasets while reducing the KL divergence relative to BF16 training with a larger learning rate. Unlike FP16, it keeps BF16's wider dynamic range and needs no loss scaling.

title: SVGO Deleted the ID My CSS Needed (and the One-Line Fix)
description:
This post was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by the PerfectVector team.

SVGO made our badge almost 40% smaller and broke the page it lived on. The file still rendered fine on its own. What disappeared was an id the surrounding HTML used to recolor one shape, and nothing in SVGO's output warns you about that. If your page, script or sprite reaches into an SVG, run the optimizer on a copy and test the copy where it's actually used.

Here's the fixture: a 437-byte hand-made badge whose sun is <circle id="badge-accent" ... fill="#ef8067"/>, inlined in a page with #badge-accent { fill: #f5bf42; } outside the SVG. With SVGO 4.1.0 in a clean folder (so no stray svgo.config.mjs is picked up), npx svgo input.svg -o default.svg writes 263 bytes, and the id is gone. The sun stays coral instead of turning gold. That's documented behaviour: cleanupIds "removes unused IDs", and an ID referenced only by CSS in another document looks unused from inside the file. (Its back-off for <style> and <script> only applies when those elements are inside the SVG itself.)

If you can name the hooks, keep the rest of the preset and protect just those IDs:

// svgo.config.mjs
export default {
  plugins: [
    {
      name: 'preset-default',
      params: {
        overrides: {
          cleanupIds: { preserve: ['badge-accent'] },
        },
      },
    },
  ],
};

npx svgo input.svg --config svgo.config.mjs -o preserved.svg
wc -c input.svg default.svg preserved.svg

We re-ran it on 2026-11-04 and read the computed fill of the inlined circle in headless Chrome:

File Bytes #badge-accent present Computed fill
Original 437 yes rgb(245, 191, 66) gold
Default preset 263 no rgb(239, 128, 103) coral
preserve: ['badge-accent'] 281 yes rgb(245, 191, 66) gold

Keeping the hook cost 18 bytes. Turning cleanupIds off entirely (cleanupIds: false) gave the same 281 bytes here, but preserve (or preservePrefixes for a naming scheme like icon-) still cleans IDs you didn't ask for, which helps once several SVGs are inlined on one page. These numbers are for this one fixture. Your byte counts will differ.

An ID is only one kind of dependency, though. After any optimizer run (SVGO directly, or one your bundler runs for you later), check what consumes the file: CSS selectors, JS queries, gradient, clip and mask references, sprite <symbol> IDs, and the viewBox your layout scales with. Then test every state that touches it, like hover, theme and animation, because a static preview won't exercise them. And keep the unoptimized master: SVGO is for delivery copies, not the file someone will edit next.

The full guide includes the copy-paste fixture, a dependency checklist table, notes on numeric precision, viewBox and SVGZ, and an FAQ: SVGO: Optimize an SVG Without Losing Needed Structure

title: Zero-Cost Types? The Fine Print on Kotlin Value Classes
description:
Compose’s own Dp, Color and TextUnit are value classes. Here's why.

@JvmInline value class ShipmentId(val raw: String) reads like a free upgrade: a real type in the source, a plain String at runtime. Most of the time that is exactly what you get. Sometimes the compiler quietly allocates a wrapper object anyway, and sometimes the erasure itself causes trouble in Room, Retrofit, Java callers or your logs. This post walks through both halves so you can decide where value classes earn their keep.

Compose layout and drawing code touches sizes and colors constantly, often many times per frame. Wrapping each one in a heap object would add up, so the toolkit wraps primitive-backed values instead and lets the compiler erase the wrapper. Dp wraps a Float and TextUnit wraps a Long. Color wraps a ULong, which is itself a value class that lowers to a plain long on the JVM. You can borrow the same trick in app code.

1. The primitive-obsession bug

Here is a bug that survives code review more often than anyone admits:

data class Tracking(val status: String)

suspend fun trackShipment(shipmentId: String, courierId: String): Tracking = TODO()

class TrackingViewModel(private val shipmentId: String, private val courierId: String) : ViewModel() {
    fun refresh() = viewModelScope.launch {
        val tracking = trackShipment(courierId, shipmentId)   // arguments swapped, compiles fine
    }
}

Both parameters are String, so the compiler has nothing to object to. The backend returns a 404 or an empty page, and you spend an afternoon staring at logs. Typed wrappers turn the same mistake into a build error:

@JvmInline value class ShipmentId(val raw: String)
@JvmInline value class CourierId(val raw: String)

suspend fun trackShipment(shipmentId: ShipmentId, courierId: CourierId): Tracking = TODO()

class TrackingViewModel(private val shipmentId: ShipmentId, private val courierId: CourierId) : ViewModel() {
    fun refresh() = viewModelScope.launch {
        val tracking = trackShipment(courierId, shipmentId)   // Type mismatch: does not compile
    }
}

A regular wrapper class (or a data class) would also fix this, but it costs an allocation per ID. Value classes aim to remove that cost.

2. Declaring one, and what the compiler generates 

@JvmInline
value class ShipmentId(val raw: String) {
    init {
        require(raw.isNotBlank()) { "ShipmentId must not be blank" }
    }

    val isLegacy: Boolean get() = raw.startsWith("SH-")

    fun shortCode(): String = raw.takeLast(6)
}

The rules that matter on the JVM:

  • The primary constructor takes exactly one val.
  • The class is final and cannot extend another class, though it may implement interfaces.
  • Other members must be computed. Anything with its own backing field is rejected.
  • init blocks and secondary constructors with bodies are allowed on Kotlin 1.9 and later.

The compiler does not simply delete the class. It emits a set of static helpers plus a wrapper that exists for the moments when a real object is unavoidable.

To see it for yourself, open Tools > Kotlin > Show Kotlin Bytecode > Decompile on any file that uses the class, or run javap -p on the compiled .class. You will find constructor-impl, equals-impl0, box-impl and friends. Learn to recognize box-impl in decompiled output, because that call is the allocation you are trying to avoid.

3. Unboxed versus boxed

The rule of thumb: when the static type at the use site is exactly the value class, the value stays raw. When the value must be treated as some other reference type, it gets wrapped.

@JvmInline value class Meters(val value: Double)

fun describe(distance: Meters): String = "${distance.value} m"   // double in, no box
fun parseDistance(text: String): Meters = Meters(text.toDouble()) // returns a raw double

class Route(val length: Meters)                                   // field is a plain double

Now the cases where the wrapper sneaks back in:

val ids: List<ShipmentId> = listOf(ShipmentId("SH-1"))   // generics: each element boxed
val anything: Any = ShipmentId("SH-2")                   // Any: boxed
val maybeLength: Meters? = Meters(12.0)                  // nullable over a primitive: boxed
val onClick: (ShipmentId) -> Unit = { println(it.raw) }  // function type: boxed at invoke()

Interfaces are the quiet one:

interface Labeled { fun label(): String }

@JvmInline
value class Sku(val raw: String) : Labeled {
    override fun label(): String = raw
}

fun printLabel(item: Labeled) = println(item.label())

printLabel(Sku("A-100"))   // Sku is boxed to satisfy the Labeled parameter

The nullable subtlety

A common claim is that “nullable always boxes”. It does not. It depends on what is wrapped:

@JvmInline value class Email(val value: String)   // wraps a non-null reference
@JvmInline value class Meters(val value: Double)  // wraps a primitive

val a: Email? = null      // stored as String?, no allocation
val b: Meters? = null     // needs a box, because a primitive double cannot hold null

When the wrapped type is a non-null reference, null can reuse the underlying reference's own null. Primitives have no spare "null" bit pattern, so the wrapper object is required.

This is why Compose exposes Dp.Unspecified, a sentinel built on NaN, instead of encouraging Dp? in hot paths. You can follow the same design:

@JvmInline
value class Meters(val value: Double) {
    val isSpecified: Boolean get() = !value.isNaN()

    companion object {
        val Unspecified = Meters(Double.NaN)
    }
}

Where boxing actually hurts

In real Android code the culprits tend to be the boring ones: a StateFlow<ShipmentId>, a Map<ShipmentId, Shipment> consulted in a loop, a LazyColumn key lambda returning a value class, or mutableStateOf(0.dp) updated every frame. Compose does ship primitive-specialized holders such as mutableFloatStateOf, but they take a raw Float, not a Dp, and there is no built-in Dp equivalent. Using one means unwrapping on write and re-wrapping on read, which gives up the type safety you adopted value classes for. If profiling shows the boxing matters, confine the conversion to one private boundary:

private val offsetPx = mutableFloatStateOf(0f)
val offset: Dp get() = offsetPx.floatValue.dp

For everything else, measure with the Android Studio allocation profiler before reorganizing code. A few boxed IDs per screen are rarely the bottleneck, and a cleaner type is often worth the allocation.

4. Name mangling and Java interop

Because ShipmentId and String are the same thing in a method signature, overloads like these would collide:

class ShipmentRepository {
    fun load(id: ShipmentId): Shipment? = TODO()
    fun load(id: String): Shipment? = TODO()
}

To keep both legal, the compiler appends a hash derived from the signature to any function that takes a value class, so you end up with load-<hash>(String) and plain load(String).

Consequences you will actually run into:

  • Java callers cannot reference the mangled name. A hyphen is legal in bytecode but not in Java source. If a Java module must call the function, pin a readable name with @JvmName: 
  @JvmName("loadShipment")
  fun load(id: ShipmentId): Shipment? = TODO()

Java then passes a raw String, so the compile-time safety stops at the language boundary. Recent Kotlin releases have also been experimenting with an opt-in annotation for generating boxed-friendly entry points, so check the release notes for your version.

  • Stack traces and logs show hashed names. Expect frames like load-3fK9a. It is cosmetic but confusing the first time.
  • Reflection, mocking and name-based tooling need care. Anything that looks up methods by name, such as older mocking setups, ProGuard or R8 keep rules, and reflection-based DI, must account for the suffix. Run your test suite on the real tooling rather than assuming.
  • Binary compatibility changes. If you publish a library, changing a parameter from String to a value class changes the JVM method name. Source-compatible, binary-incompatible.
  • Constructors of classes with value-class parameters gain a synthetic marker parameter, which makes them awkward to call from Java.

5. Room, Retrofit and serialization

Every library below sees the erased type in some places and the boxed type in others. That split causes most integration bugs.

Room

Value classes are supported in Room when you use KSP with Kotlin code generation. Under KAPT, the generated stubs only see the underlying type, so the processor cannot tell a value class from its wrapped type without reading metadata. Prefer KSP, and note that Room 3.0 is KSP-only anyway.

@JvmInline value class CourierId(val raw: String)
@JvmInline value class Grams(val value: Int)

@Entity(tableName = "shipments")
data class ShipmentEntity(
    @PrimaryKey val id: ShipmentId,
    val courier: CourierId?,
    val weight: Grams,
)

@Dao
interface ShipmentDao {
    @Query("SELECT * FROM shipments WHERE id = :id")
    suspend fun find(id: ShipmentId): ShipmentEntity?
}

Add a migration test that opens a database created before the change. The column type is the underlying type, so schemas should not shift, but verify it instead of trusting it.

Retrofit

A single @Path or @Query parameter of type ShipmentId reaches Retrofit as a String, because reflection sees the erased signature. The trap is collections:

interface TrackingApi {
    @GET("shipments/{id}")
    suspend fun shipment(@Path("id") id: ShipmentId): ShipmentDto

    @GET("shipments")
    suspend fun shipments(@Query("id") ids: List<ShipmentId>): List<ShipmentDto>
}

For the list, each element is boxed, and with no converter registered Retrofit falls back to toString(). The server receives ShipmentId(raw=SH-1). The same thing happens in string templates: "/shipments/$id" calls the generated toString, not raw. Register a string converter so every route behaves the same:

object IdStringConverters : Converter.Factory() {
    override fun stringConverter(
        type: Type,
        annotations: Array<Annotation>,
        retrofit: Retrofit,
    ): Converter<*, String>? = when (type) {
        ShipmentId::class.java -> Converter<ShipmentId, String> { it.raw }
        CourierId::class.java -> Converter<CourierId, String> { it.raw }
        else -> null
    }
}

Back this with a MockWebServer test that asserts the actual request URL.

kotlinx.serialization

This is the smoothest option. A @Serializable value class is encoded as its underlying value. Every value class that appears in a serializable model needs the annotation too, or the plugin fails the build:

@Serializable @JvmInline value class ShipmentId(val raw: String)
@Serializable @JvmInline value class CourierId(val raw: String)

@Serializable
data class ShipmentDto(val id: ShipmentId, val courier: CourierId? = null)

// {"id":"SH-1"}   not {"id":{"raw":"SH-1"}}

The failure mode is validation. If init throws, a malformed payload throws during decoding. That is usually what you want, but handle it at the network boundary so one bad record does not crash the screen.

Gson and other reflection-based codecs

Reflection reads a field typed ShipmentId as String, but reads a List<ShipmentId> element as the wrapper class. The same ID can serialize as "SH-1" in one place and as an object in another. If you cannot move to a codegen or Kotlin-aware library, register explicit adapters and write round-trip tests. Check your Moshi setup the same way.

6. Where to use them

Identifiers. The strongest case. IDs are passed everywhere, compared rarely, and swapped by accident constantly.

Units. Dp-style types prevent seconds-versus-milliseconds and meters-versus-feet bugs.

@JvmInline
value class Millis(val value: Long) : Comparable<Millis> {
    operator fun plus(other: Millis) = Millis(value + other.value)
    override fun compareTo(other: Millis): Int = value.compareTo(other.value)
}

val Int.seconds: Millis get() = Millis(this * 1_000L)

Calling compareTo or < directly on Millis stays unboxed. Sorting a List<Millis> boxes the elements, because the list is generic.

Validated strings. Parse once at the edge, then carry a value that is known to be valid.

@JvmInline
value class Email private constructor(val value: String) {
    companion object {
        private val pattern = Regex("^[^@\\s]+@[^@\\s]+\\.[^@\\s]+$")

        fun parseOrNull(raw: String): Email? {
            val cleaned = raw.trim().lowercase()
            return if (pattern.matches(cleaned)) Email(cleaned) else null
        }
    }
}

Email? wraps a non-null reference, so the nullable return costs nothing. Treat the private constructor as a compile-time guard only. Reflection and some decoders can still construct an invalid instance, so keep an init check if the invariant is critical.

7. Gotchas and limitations

  • One property. Multi-field value classes are not available on the JVM today. Reach for a data class when you need two fields.
  • No identity. === on a value class is rejected, and you should not rely on object identity for synchronization.
  • No inheritance, no extra state. No superclass, no delegated properties, no stored var.
  • Interfaces box. Implementing one is fine, but any use through the interface type allocates.
  • Generics box. List, Map, Flow, State, Result wrappers and your own generic classes all hold wrappers rather than raw values.
  • toString is the generated one. Logs, templates and URL building show ShipmentId(raw=...) unless you unwrap explicitly.
  • Tooling surprises. Mangled names affect reflection, mocking, serialization and keep rules. Test with your real stack.
  • Library ABI. Changing a public parameter to or from a value class breaks binary compatibility.
  • Platform scope. @JvmInline is a JVM concern. Elsewhere in a multiplatform project, the same declaration compiles differently, so do not copy performance assumptions across targets.

A quick decision checklist

  1. Is it one value with a domain meaning that is easy to mix up? Use a value class.
  2. Is it mostly passed as an argument or stored in a field? Great, it stays erased.
  3. Does it live in collections, flows or interface-typed code in a hot path? Measure first.
  4. Does it cross Java, Retrofit or a reflection-based codec? Add an explicit test at that boundary.

Value classes are not literally free, but the costs are predictable once you know where the wrapper reappears. Use them for the swap-prone, validated, frequently passed values in your domain, and keep an eye on the generic and interface boundaries.

🧵 Stop Treating Coroutines Like Magic Keywords

If “just add launch and hope” describes how your team handles concurrency, I’d recommend “Kotlin Coroutines Under the Hood” — a 25-chapter deep dive that goes past the syntax and down to the bytecode: the Continuation-Passing Style transform, the compiler-generated state machine, and exactly why a suspended coroutine costs a few dozen bytes while a blocked thread costs a megabyte.

It walks through structured concurrency and Job hierarchies, dispatcher internals (Default vs IO vs Unconfined), cooperative cancellation and exception aggregation, Flow’s cold-stream semantics and the full operator vocabulary, StateFlow/SharedFlow’s hot-broadcast model, Channels and fan-in/fan-out patterns, Mutex/Semaphore/actors for shared state, and a complete Android case study retrofitting a legacy callback-driven app onto coroutines and Flow — including a 100,000-coroutines-vs-100,000-threads benchmark lab you can run yourself.

title: FedVP: Federated Learning across Heterogeneous Models by Pooling Locally Trained Verifiers
description:
arXiv:2611.13708v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conventional federated learning relies on the shared model backbone to aggregate client updates, limiting collaboration among institutions that deploy large language models (LLMs) from different families and at different scales. We propose Federated Verifier Pool (FEDVP), a new federated learning paradigm that enables heterogeneous clients to collaborate through shared verification rather than parameter aggregation. Each client trains a verifier using local data and responses generated by its chosen LLM backbone. The server pools these independently trained verifiers and combines their judgments to select answers without merging model parameters. This allows both LLM backbones and verifiers to differ in architecture and size, while keeping the LLM backbones frozen and deriving collaborative gains from improved answer selection. We evaluate FEDVP across five public medical question-answering datasets treated as federated clients, using Qwen and LLaMA backbones ranging from 3B to 14B parameters. FEDVP consistently improves performance across all five clients and outperforms the strongest conventional federated baselines by 1.46-5.79 percentage points in mean accuracy.

title: Haiku with a UX kit: can open rules and minimal code make a small model as accurate as a larger one?
description:
Summary. We tested whether the combination of a small model (Haiku 5.5), a UX rules data lake with open sources and a minimal checking code (the "kit") gets close to a larger model (Sonnet 5.5) on three login-screen tasks: creating, improving and comparing two screens at code level. There were 2,244 items and 2,424 calls, with 0 failures in the end. On creating and improving, Haiku with rules and kit went from 0.744 to 0.998 (create) and from 0.754 to 0.926 (improve), and the combined accuracy of Haiku with the kit was 1.07 times that of plain Sonnet, at 10% of the cost per task. On comparing two screens, the kit did not help and made things slightly worse; pairs with no real difference never produced a false alarm in any condition, so the hypothesis about false alarms could not be tested. Three non-human aesthetics instruments were validated and none passed; for that reason this study claims nothing about beauty. The main threat to validity is circular and is in section 9: the 30 rules the kit checks are the same ones that score create and improve. An independent check with axe-core confirms the gain in create, but not in improve. For the practical summary, there is the simple guide.

1. The question and the decision it informs

In studies 1 and 2, Haiku stayed close to larger models when it received the right process and context. What remains unknown is what happens in UX and UI, where two things tend to go wrong with language models: they perceive fine style differences poorly (the literature shows low recall in detecting CSS changes), and taste is subjective. The thesis of this study is that one can use technology to cover what AI does poorly: open-source rules in the prompt and code that checks and compares screens, leaving the model with what it does well, which is writing and fixing code.

Study question: does a Haiku with a UX rules data lake and a code-based checking kit get close to plain Sonnet in accuracy, and at what total cost? The unit under test is the whole (model + rules + kit), not the model alone. This matters: saying that "the code did the detection" is not a defect of the experiment; it is what is being measured.

2. The material

2.1 The login data lake

There are 30 rules for a login screen, each with text, source, how to check it, a good example, a bad example, severity and type (25 objective, 5 semi-objective). All come from open, citable sources: WCAG 2.2 (contrast, labels, touch target, focus, reflow, language), web.dev (login form best practices) and Material Design 3 (consistency, hierarchy, spacing scale). No rule was written from memory as "truth". The source URLs were written from knowledge of the pages and still need to be checked one by one by opening them (pending item, section 9). Examples:

Rule Source How it is checked
L08: button text with a contrast of at least 4.5:1 WCAG 2.2, 1.4.3 contrast ratio between the text color and the button background
L11: targets of at least 24 px (preferably 44) WCAG 2.2, 2.5.8 estimated height of button and fields
L17: link to recover the password web.dev, WCAG 3.3.8 an <a> exists with forgot/recover text
L28: fields and button with the same border radius Material 3, text fields compares border-radius

2.2 The kit

The kit is minimal code, in Node, with no browser and no layout (degree 0 of a cost ladder): parse5 for the HTML, css-tree for the CSS and culori for colors and contrast. It does two things: (a) it checks the 30 rules and returns a text report with what failed and where; (b) it compares two screens and lists the real differences in structure, content, flow and style, with normalized values (#fff equals rgb(255,255,255), 16px equals 1rem; class names, whitespace, comments and attribute order are ignored). Each run takes about 0.6 s. We left the real browser (Playwright) and images out of the kit: what it does not see, for lack of layout, is declared in section 9.

2.3 The stimuli

All generated by a script with a fixed seed (20261110), which gives an exact answer key by construction and avoids screens the model may have seen in training.

  • T1, create (12 requests): the same login screen for different contexts (clinic, bank, language school, chess club and others). Score: data lake rules met in the final HTML, out of 30.
  • T2, improve (20 screens): each with 3 injected defects, from 22 types used (out of a catalog of 25), tied to rules. Score: defective rules removed minus new rules that start failing, divided by the injected rules.
  • T3, compare (60 pairs): 20 CSS (13 large and 7 subtle, one property each), 8 content, 8 flow, 8 compound, 8 noise (changes with no effect: renaming classes, reformatting, color in another notation) and 8 identical. The answer is a JSON with the differences; the score is F1 against the answer key, and on noise and identical pairs it is 1 only if the model answers that there is no difference.

The generator checks the stimuli against the kit itself: the kit saw a difference in every pair with a change and in no noise or identical pair. This validates that the kit is consistent with the generator, not independent proof (section 9).

3. The conditions: what the model receives

Condition What the model receives The question it answers
A0 only the task how much does it do alone? (baseline)
A1 task + the 30 data lake rules does knowledge alone, with no tool, help?
A2 task + kit report does the tool alone, with no rules in the prompt, help?
A3 task + rules + report the complete combination
AC (T1 only, Haiku only) a second self-critique pass, without the kit does the kit's gain come from information or only from an extra pass?

In create, conditions A2, A3 and AC have two calls: generate the HTML and then fix it. In improve and compare, the report goes in the same prompt. Corrections come back as patches (ANTES/DEPOIS), applied by code equally to all models: 2,679 of 2,688 Haiku blocks and 2,358 of 2,359 Sonnet blocks were applied.

4. Design decisions

  • Models and execution: Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 through claude -p (subscription), with --effort medium and no tools, with a short system prompt identical for all. Without tools, the model has no internet access and cannot look up published labels: it only sees the prompt. Opus 5.5 was planned and dropped for cost, by the author's decision (deviation in section 9).
  • Nominal cost = tokens × list price (per million tokens: Haiku US$ 0.10 input and 0.50 output; Sonnet US$ 2 and 10; cache read 0.01 and 0.10; cache write 1.25 times the input). The actual subscription spend is not billed in dollars.
  • Samples: 3 per cell; each item enters the analysis through the mean of the 3.
  • Pilot: 46 Haiku items tested the pipeline. After it we replaced the broken logo (an image with no file) with an embedded SVG, which changed the stimuli; for that reason the pilot is not included in the results.
  • Code, stimuli, lake and pre-registration were frozen with SHA-256 hashes in dados/CONGELADO.txt before the run. There was no commit with a tag; the record is by hash (see section 9).

5. The execution

2,244 items ran (Haiku 1,140 and Sonnet 1,104, because AC exists only for Haiku), in 2,424 calls (the two-call ones are create with A2, A3 and AC). Haiku consumed 4.68 million input tokens and 2.65 million output tokens; Sonnet, 4.54 million and 1.10 million. Notably, at the same medium effort, Haiku generated more than twice as many output tokens as Sonnet. The total nominal cost was US$ 19.63 (Haiku US$ 1.69, Sonnet US$ 17.94). There was one error in the middle of the run, from the kit itself, and the item was redone: final result, 0 items with errors.

We recorded three deviations from the pre-registration, described in dados/DESVIOS.md: (1) the kit crashed on an invalid color generated by Haiku and was fixed without changing any rule or threshold; (2) Opus was dropped; (3) the logo was replaced before the run. None of them changes a hypothesis.

6. The hypotheses, one by one

Each hypothesis was written before the run, with a metric and a criterion. The p-values come from the paired Wilcoxon test over the items (means of the 3 samples), with a confidence interval by bootstrap over items (10,000 replicates) and Holm correction across the 12 confirmatory comparisons. Of these, 7 pass Holm.

H4: in create, does Haiku with rules and kit beat plain Haiku? Yes: 0.998 versus 0.744, difference +0.255 (95% CI: +0.239 to +0.274; p = 0.0002, passes Holm).

H3: in improve, the same? Yes: 0.926 versus 0.754, +0.172 (95% CI: +0.083 to +0.267; p = 0.0011, passes). The new defects introduced fall from 0.53 to 0.18 per screen (p = 0.022, does not pass Holm).

H7: do the rules alone already help? Yes, in create (A1 0.988 versus 0.744, p = 0.0002) and in improve (0.894 versus 0.754, p = 0.0034). In compare, the tool (A2) came out below the rules-only condition (0.899 versus 0.939), the opposite of what was predicted.

H6: is the kit's gain information or just an extra pass? In create, the kit beats self-critique without the kit: 0.954 versus 0.804, +0.150 (p = 0.0002, passes). The independent check with axe-core does not confirm this advantage (section 7.5).

H5: does the kit help Haiku more than Sonnet? In create, the gain of A3 over A0 is +0.255 for Haiku and +0.226 for Sonnet (difference +0.029; p = 0.002, passes); in improve, +0.172 versus −0.025 (difference +0.197; p = 0.0011, passes); in compare, no (p = 0.11). In improve, plain Sonnet is already good (0.935) and gets worse with the rules alone (0.810).

H1: in compare, does the kit raise Haiku's recall? Recall rises from 0.909 to 0.967 (+0.058; 95% CI: +0.005 to +0.121; p = 0.044), but does not pass Holm. Not supported.

H2: does the kit reduce false alarms on pairs with no real difference? Not testable. Haiku and Sonnet scored 1.00 on the 16 noise and identical pairs in every condition, including without the kit. There was no false alarm to reduce.

H9: the main criterion. Does Haiku with rules and kit reach at least 90% of the combined accuracy of plain Sonnet, at no more than 50% of the cost per task? The combined accuracy is the mean of the create, improve and compare scores. Result: 0.943 versus 0.882, ratio 1.07, and mean cost per task of US$ 0.0022 versus US$ 0.0210, ratio 0.10. Supported, but only against Sonnet: Opus was dropped, so there is no comparison with a larger model than that.

7. Results

Task Model A0 A1 A2 A3 AC
T1 create Haiku 0.744 0.988 0.954 0.998 0.804
T1 create Sonnet 0.774 0.987 0.979 1.000 n.a.
T2 improve Haiku 0.754 0.894 0.967 0.926 n.a.
T2 improve Sonnet 0.935 0.810 0.956 0.910 n.a.
T3 compare Haiku 0.933 0.939 0.899 0.905 n.a.
T3 compare Sonnet 0.938 0.924 0.895 0.897 n.a.

7.1 What worked

  1. The rules in the prompt already solve most of create. Haiku goes from 0.744 to 0.988 with just the 30 rules (A1). The kit adds little there (A3 0.998).
  2. In improve, the kit report is what helps Haiku most: from 0.754 (A0) to 0.967 (A2), above the rules alone (0.894), and with fewer new defects introduced.
  3. Haiku with the combination reaches the level of plain Sonnet, for a tenth of the cost. The combined accuracy of Haiku A3 (0.943) is above that of Sonnet A0 (0.882), with US$ 0.0022 per task versus US$ 0.0210.
  4. Patch-based corrections work: 99.7% of the Haiku blocks and 99.96% of the Sonnet blocks were applied without ambiguity.
  5. The response format was not a problem: 100% of the compare JSONs were valid for both models.

7.2 What did not work

  • Comparing two screens at code level was already near the ceiling without help (0.933 for plain Haiku, 0.938 for plain Sonnet), and the kit report made things slightly worse, especially in CSS: Haiku 0.87 (A0) versus 0.79 (A2) and 0.81 (A3), same pattern for Sonnet.

The likely reason, not tested, is that the report lists several properties derived from a single change (for example, the four sides of a padding) and the model copies them; the answer key has one item, and the rest becomes a false alarm. It is a granularity failure of the kit and of the scoring together, and a rescoring that groups by property would be exploratory, done after seeing the data.

  • Noise and identical pairs discriminated nothing: all got it right in every condition. This also says that, with the code of both screens in view, these models do not invent differences.
  • Sonnet got worse with the rules alone in improve (0.935 to 0.810). We did not investigate the cause.

7.3 The cost

Condition Haiku (US$/task) Sonnet (US$/task)
A0 0.0017 0.0210
A1 0.0022 0.0241
A2 0.0029 0.0359
A3 0.0022 0.0238

The mean cost per task is the average of the three task types. Haiku A3 costs 10% of Sonnet A0. This figure is about tokens and does not include the cost of building the kit and the data lake, which was human and AI work and was not monetized; the break-even point against Sonnet depends on how many screens are checked with the same kit.

7.4 Aesthetics: no non-human instrument passed

The author is not a designer, and a human panel was ruled out. The way out was to look for instruments that are neither human nor from the family of the models under test and to validate them before using them, with criteria fixed before computing any score. Result: none validated.

  • UIClip (a CMU/Apple model trained on ranked UIs): on 15 visually observable defects, the reference screen scored higher in only 9 of 15 (threshold 12) in attempt 1, and in 8 of 15 in attempt 2 (screen cropped to the content, the only extra attempt, declared). On graded degradation series, it followed only the button contrast and, at the exact limit (ρ = −0.8), the spacing between fields (2 of 5 series in both attempts; threshold 4).
  • Consistency and hierarchy by code (10 measures in Chrome): 9 of 15 on the defects and 4 of 5 on the series. It follows gradual degradation, but does not see defects of absence (removing the password recovery link made the score go up).
  • Fable judge in pairs, validated against the 300 pairs of WiserUI-Bench (label: which variant won a real A/B test; 297 pairs with both images downloaded): 55.6% accuracy (95% CI: 49.9 to 61.1; threshold 60% with a lower bound above 50%), and position consistency of 58.6% (threshold 70%). The same range the literature reports for AI judges against designers (mean agreement among the designers themselves: 62.4%).

Conclusion of this part: without validity, aesthetics stays out of the decision and out of the conclusions. The study measures legibility, consistency and conformity with open rules, which are part of UX, but not "beauty".

7.5 Independent check with axe-core

Since the 30 rules are both in the prompt and in the scoring of create and improve, we ran axe-core (WCAG 2.x A/AA), which the kit and the prompts do not know, on the final screens of T1 and T2. Mean violations per screen:

T1 create A0 A1 A2 A3 AC
Haiku 0.50 0.03 0.08 0.03 0.06
Sonnet 0.31 0.00 0.06 0.00 n.a.

The gain in create is confirmed independently (Haiku A0 versus A3: p = 0.004). In improve, axe finds almost no violations in any condition, so it does not discriminate. And axe does not confirm the kit's advantage over self-critique without the kit (0.08 versus 0.06; p = 0.75): that part of H6 is supported only by the 30 rules themselves.

8. Why these results hold, and how far

The design has safeguards: hypotheses, metrics and parameters fixed before the run, with hashes; novel stimuli generated by script with an exact answer key; models without internet access; a self-critique control; multiple-testing correction; an independent check with another tool; reporting of deviations; reporting of negative results (compare, aesthetics) with the same rigor as the positive ones.

9. Threats to validity

  • Circularity (construct). The 30 rules are in the prompt of A1 and A3 and the same kit generates the report of A2 and A3, but they are also what score create and improve. Haiku "learned the test". axe-core mitigates this in create and does not help in improve. The T1 and T2 numbers should be read as conformity with the rules delivered, not as general UX quality.
  • A single screen, synthetic screens. Login, generated by script. No external validity for other screens or for real-world screens.
  • The kit was tuned on the noise types of this set, and the same author wrote the stimuli and the kit. The "false alarm" result holds for those types and, in any case, was not testable.
  • The kit has no layout and no browser. What depends on rendering (real alignment, overlap, line wrapping) is not seen. Degree 2 of the cost ladder was not built, nor was the image variant.
  • Opus was dropped for cost. H5 and H9 compare only Haiku and Sonnet; nothing can be claimed about how close Haiku gets to the top of the model line.
  • No human panel and no valid aesthetics instrument. The aesthetics result is negative and declared; the study does not measure beauty. The Fable judge was validated against conversion labels (which variant generated more actions), which are not beauty, and Fable may have seen WiserUI-Bench in training, which would inflate its accuracy (it did not pass even so).
  • The pre-registration is by hash, with no tag in the repository, and was frozen before the main run, but after the pilot and the first test of the aesthetics instruments. The criteria for the aesthetics instruments were fixed before computing their scores, and there is a record that UIClip had two attempts.
  • The rule sources were opened, but not read one by one. On 11/11/2026 I opened all 19 distinct WCAG, web.dev and Material Design URLs: 18 returned 200 and 1 returned 404 (Material Design 3, spacing, the source of rule L29). Opening a page does not prove it supports the rule; the support audit was done only in the following study.
  • Nominal cost at list price, without the cost of building the kit and the data lake, and without the consumption of the plan limit.
  • The same family of models wrote the study code (with the author) and was evaluated. The raw data are from real runs.

10. What this allows us to conclude

With confidence: on the tasks of creating and improving a login screen, giving Haiku the rules (and, in improve, the kit report) brings it to the level of unaided Sonnet, for about a tenth of the cost per task, as measured by the rules themselves and confirmed in create by an independent tool; on comparing two screens at code level, the kit's gain does not appear, because the models already get almost everything right, and the report can get in the way if it comes out verbose. Without confidence: whether the result holds for other screens, for real screens and for larger models; whether the advantage survives scoring that is independent of the rules; and any claim about aesthetics. Natural next steps: a third set of rules that the kit and the prompt do not know, to score with; a kit with layout (degree 2); Opus; and real screens.

11. Reproducibility

Code in studies/haiku-ui-design/ (kit/, gerador/, executor.py); lake in lake/login.json; stimuli in dados/estimulos/; raw data in dados/bruto/; validation criteria for the aesthetics instruments and the judge in dados/*CRITERIOS.md; deviations in dados/DESVIOS.md; analysis with python gerador/analise.py; hashes in dados/CONGELADO.txt. The WiserUI-Bench images (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, non-commercial research only) are not redistributed; the downloader gerador/baixar_wiserui.py fetches them from the original hosts. Archive DOI: Archived on Zenodo (version 3.0.0, studies 3 and 3b): 10.5281/zenodo.24132784.

12. References

  • W3C. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2. https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/
  • web.dev. Sign-in form best practices. https://web.dev/articles/sign-in-form-best-practices
  • Material Design 3. Buttons, Text fields and Layout. https://m3.material.io/
  • DiffSpot: detection of CSS changes in screen pairs by multimodal models. arXiv:2605.29615.
  • WiserUI-Bench: Do MLLMs Capture How Interfaces Guide User Behavior? arXiv:2505.05026 (data CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). https://github.com/jeochris/wiserui-bench
  • DesignPref: Capturing Personal Preferences in Visual Design Generation. arXiv:2511.20513.
  • Wu et al. UIClip: A Data-driven Model for Assessing User Interface Design. UIST 2024, arXiv:2404.12500.
  • Reinecke et al. Predicting users' first impressions of website aesthetics. CHI 2013.
  • Previous Melo Labs studies: 1 and 2.

The experiments, data and conclusions are mine. The writing was AI-assisted and reviewed by me.

title: SteerDistill: Quantizing LLM Agents via Closed-Loop Teacher Steering
description:
arXiv:2611.13410v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Low-bit quantization reduces the inference cost of LLM agents but can compromise task success. Examining failed rollouts, we find that quantized agents overlook task requirements or environmental conditions, producing environment transitions that diverge from successful full-precision references. Correcting these behavioral divergences remains difficult: offline data may miss the student's failure contexts, while its own rollouts may provide few correct responses in those contexts. We introduce SteerDistill, a quantization-aware distillation method in which a full-precision teacher guides the student to revise failed responses and iteratively refines its guidance using feedback from student execution. This closed-loop teacher steering produces locally verified behavioral corrections. We internalize these corrections by training the student without guidance to match the steered student's predictions at corrected turns and the full-precision teacher's at other turns, enabling unassisted inference. Across five agentic benchmarks and three models, SteerDistill exceeds the strongest quantized baseline by 1.67--2.18 points in average score under W4A16 and stays within one point of BF16. On $\tau^2$-Bench, it outperforms QeRL by 1.84 percentage points in success rate using 67% fewer training GPU hours and produces shorter successful trajectories than the quantized baselines.

title: When Your Users Have to Chase You on X for Help, Your Product Has a Problem
description:
Imagine paying for an app, building your business around it, and suddenly running into an account issue.

You try the help centre. Nothing.

You contact support. No useful response.

So you leave the app, open X, and tag the company, hoping someone finally responds.

At what point did getting help become this difficult? 😂

Something has gone wrong with the product experience.

Why Should Product Teams Care?

Think about LinkedIn.

For many freelancers, it's not just a social network. It's their:

  • Portfolio and professional identity.
  • Lead-generation channel.
  • Client communication tool.
  • Inbox for business opportunities.

When something goes wrong, they aren't just losing access to an app. They could be losing access to work.

That's why support shouldn't be treated as an afterthought.

What Does Good Support Look Like?

A good support experience should make it easy for users to:

  1. Find the right channel to get help.
  2. Explain their problem without jumping through hoops.
  3. Know what happens after submitting a request.
  4. Reach a human when automation isn't enough.

LinkedIn already has AI-assisted help and support channels, although what's available varies by account and product type.

But having support options isn't the same as making support accessible.

Here's my take:

Don't measure your support experience by how easy it is for your team to resolve a problem.

Measure it by how easy it is for a user who doesn't know anyone at your company to get help.

Because support isn't a department sitting outside the product.

It's part of the product experience.

And when someone's livelihood depends on your platform, it becomes part of your trust and security

A product isn't truly user-friendly if it only works well when nothing goes wrong.

title: One Byte, One Token: Byteifying a 27B Hybrid-Attention LLM with Self-Generated Data
description:
arXiv:2611.13607v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Byte-level BPE fragments Chinese text (for Qwen3.8 on Chinese Wikipedia, 3.84 bytes per token on average; 64% of tokens are single characters) and hides spelling from the model. We ask whether an already-trained 27B subword model can be converted directly into a pure byte-level model (one byte, one token), without a patching structure or a local encoder, while keeping most of its ability. Starting from Qwen3.8-27B (48 Gated DeltaNet layers + 16 full-attention layers), we shrink the vocabulary from 248,320 to 384 entries (the 256 byte symbols already in the BPE vocabulary plus special ids), leave every other weight untouched, and continue training in a two-stage curriculum (encoding first, then reading) on 4.77 GB of supervised bytes: all dialogue/behavioral supervision is generated on-policy by the original model itself (character dictionary, word dictionary, general dialogue, coding sessions), and knowledge reading uses encyclopedia text (54% of supervised bytes). Training takes 178.6 h on 8xH200. On the same GPU and serving stack, the byte model's gap to the original falls within the paired bootstrap interval on MATH-500, HumanEval+, MMLU-Pro and non-thinking GSM8K, and it loses 4-6 points on C-Eval, thinking-mode GSM8K and non-thinking IFEval. Without thinking it leads on every character-level task (CUTE 75.2 -> 84.0, EXECUTE-zho 81.6 -> 93.9, our Chinese character suite 54.4 -> 64.0), but lookup knowledge about Chinese characters such as pronunciation and stroke count drops, and thinking does not recover it. The cost is throughput: per-step speed is identical, but each step yields 3-5x less output; Chinese characters per second is about 1/4 of the original, and prefill at 64K bytes is 6.5x slower. We also document four byte-model failure modes (greedy runaway, sampling breaking UTF-8, ineffective penalty terms on a small vocabulary, repetition) and their fixes.

Announcement

Starting November 1, 2026, at 02:00 a.m. local time, unpatched Cloud SQL for MySQL instances that evaluate certain local Canadian time zones (across Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, and Northwest Territories) will lag by one hour because the instances still follow the autumn fall back schedule. Stored timestamp data isn't modified.

What should I do?

Before November 1, 2026, do one of the following fixes:

  • Apply self-service maintenance (Recommended): If your applications rely on database functions to calculate, schedule, or display times in these Canadian time zones (such as Calgary, Edmonton, Vancouver, or Winnipeg), then update your instances to the latest maintenance release using the Google Cloud console or the gcloud CLI.

    Updated time zone rules that reflect permanent standard daylight offsets across Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, and Northwest Territories are supported in Cloud SQL for MySQL maintenance release *.R20260726.00_36 or later.

    For more information, see Perform self-service maintenance.

  • Database configuration stopgap: If your organization can't restart instances before November 1, 2026, then you can set the time zone for your database session without causing downtime for your instance. Set the default_time_zone flag for the database session to your target fixed numeric offset (for example, '-06:00' for Alberta, '-07:00' for British Columbia, or '-05:00' for Manitoba).

    For more information about configuring database flags, see Configure database flags.

title: A pre-start version guard for self-hosted services (after the LNbits 1.7.0 advisory)
description:
On 8 November the LNbits team told operators to shut their servers down after attackers created unauthorized accounts and withdrew funds. One operator reported losing 2,285,545 sats. On 10 November, version 1.7.0 shipped as an urgent security update, with a clear instruction: upgrade before you restart.

That instruction is easy to break by accident. A systemd unit restarts after a reboot, a container comes back with an old image, and the vulnerable version is serving requests again before anyone checks.

Here is a small guard you can put in front of any self-hosted service: it reads the installed version, compares it with a minimum you set, and exits non-zero if the version is too old, so the service never starts.

The script 

// version-guard.mjs
// usage: node version-guard.mjs <path-to-pyproject.toml> <min-version>
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

const [file, min] = process.argv.slice(2);
if (!file || !min) {
  console.error('usage: node version-guard.mjs <pyproject.toml> <min-version>');
  process.exit(64);
}

const text = readFileSync(file, 'utf8');
const m = text.match(/^version\s*=\s*"([^"]+)"/m);
if (!m) {
  console.error(`no version line found in ${file}`);
  process.exit(65);
}

const parse = (v) => v.replace(/^v/, '').split(/[.-]/).slice(0, 3).map((n) => parseInt(n, 10) || 0);
const cmp = (a, b) => {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) if (a[i] !== b[i]) return a[i] - b[i];
  return 0;
};

const installed = m[1];
if (cmp(parse(installed), parse(min)) < 0) {
  console.error(`refusing to start: installed ${installed} < required ${min}`);
  process.exit(1);
}
console.log(`ok: installed ${installed} >= ${min}`);

Wire it into systemd 

[Service]
ExecStartPre=/usr/bin/node /opt/guards/version-guard.mjs /opt/lnbits/pyproject.toml 1.7.0
ExecStart=/opt/lnbits/start.sh

If ExecStartPre fails, systemd doesn't run ExecStart. The unit fails, and you see it in systemctl status and your alerts.

Check it against the latest upstream release

To get told when upstream moves past your pin, compare with the GitHub releases API:

// latest-release.mjs
const res = await fetch('https://api.github.com/repos/lnbits/lnbits/releases/latest', {
  headers: { 'User-Agent': 'version-guard' },
});
const { tag_name } = await res.json();
console.log(tag_name);

Run it from cron and diff the output against your pinned minimum. A change means it's time to read the release notes.

Notes

  • The version parser handles 1.7.0, v1.7.0 and 1.7.0-rc1 (pre-release tags compare equal to the release; tighten it if that matters to you).
  • Point the guard at whatever file your install uses as the source of truth for its version.
  • A guard can only stop a restart. It does nothing for a server that is already running. When a project says "shut down now", shut it down first.

Sources: Bitcoin Magazine on LNbits 1.7.0, Crypto Briefing, Bitcoin.com News.

title: Spatial-Spectral Coupling as Attention: Scaling Shape Correspondence to High-Resolution Surfaces
description:
arXiv:2611.13870v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Establishing dense correspondence between high-resolution 3D shapes remains challenging due to the spatial--spectral coupling at the core of many functional-map methods, which grows quadratically with mesh resolution. We observe that this coupling is equivalent to a scaled dot-product attention formulation, with learned descriptors serving as queries and keys and spectral basis functions as values. This connection makes efficient attention implementations directly applicable to shape matching and an effective mechanism for scaling spatial-spectral coupling. We show that optimized quadratic attention implementations can scale modern deep functional map pipelines to large mesh sizes, improving both runtime and memory consumption, while sub-quadratic methods introduce errors, particularly for non-isometric shape pairs, where an exact coupling proves most necessary. These insights motivate \textit{Geo-FlashAttention}, which restricts the exact softmax to geometry-selected surface patches and achieves near-linear empirical scaling while preserving correspondence accuracy of exact implementations. Across six standard benchmarks and three functional-map pipelines, rigorous analysis shows that efficient couplings preserve correspondence accuracy. At $60k$ vertices, these insights reduce peak training memory from 106.08 to 5.67\,GiB, with Geo-FlashAttention being $1.5\times$ faster per training step than FlashAttention. This enables end-to-end learning for correspondence problems on large meshes such as cortical surfaces, where high resolution is required to preserve disease-relevant intricacies of the surface geometry. Project page available https://spatial-spectral-attention.github.io/

title: Disentangling Multimodal Rotary Positional Embedding in Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.13334v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models widely adopt Multimodal Rotary Position Embedding (MRoPE), an extension of Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) that incorporates temporal, height, and width axes to encode the spatial structure of visual tokens. However, MRoPE also assigns height and width coordinates to text tokens that lack inherent spatial structure, introducing spatial positional effects into text-vision attention. Existing MRoPE variants explore different frequency allocations and coordinate layouts, with their designs suggesting different intuitions about these cross-modal effects: they may provide useful spatial references for associating language with visual regions, or introduce unnecessary positional preferences that hinder text-vision interactions. In this work, we disentangle intra-visual spatial structure from cross-modal spatial effects to investigate this question. We identify a constraint of shared coordinate layouts that prevents eliminating cross-modal spatial effects while preserving intra-visual spatial encoding, and develop controlled experiments to isolate their respective contributions. Our results across multiple model scales, MRoPE variants, and benchmarks show that cross-modal spatial effects provide little additional benefit as spatial references and can even impair model performance, while intra-visual spatial encoding remains useful for fine-grained grounding.
