title: The draw is 24% of the outcomes and 0.8% of the labels: auditing class collapse in a three-way model
description:
A three-class classifier that reports one label per row is not a three-class classifier. It is a ranking function collapsed to a decision, and the collapse is where the information dies. On our platform, 11,177 of 46,189 settled predictions ended in a draw; the label draw was emitted 360 times.

Every number below comes from the live production table, queried today, not estimated.

Two distributions that are required to match, and don't

The base table stores one row per model per match with the realised outcome attached. Two distributions matter: what happened, and what the model said would happen. If the second is a faithful compression of the first, they should be close.

-- D0: outcome distribution vs emitted-label distribution
WITH actual AS (
  SELECT actual_result AS cls, count(*) AS n
  FROM ai_predictions
  WHERE settled AND actual_result IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY 1
),
emitted AS (
  SELECT prediction_direction AS cls, count(*) AS n
  FROM ai_predictions
  WHERE settled
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT 'actual' AS side, cls, n,
       round(100.0 * n / sum(n) OVER (), 2) AS pct
FROM actual
UNION ALL
SELECT 'emitted', cls, n,
       round(100.0 * n / sum(n) OVER (), 2)
FROM emitted
ORDER BY side, n DESC;
side class rows share
actual home 20,445 44.26%
actual away 14,238 30.83%
actual draw 11,177 24.20%
actual NULL 329 —
emitted home 18,819 40.74%
emitted away/draw 10,997 23.81%
emitted away 10,085 21.83%
emitted home/draw 5,928 12.83%
emitted draw 360 0.78%

The draw happens 24.20% of the time and is named as the sole answer 0.78% of the time — a 31× under-representation. 16,925 rows name it as one of two outcomes; 27,647 rows chose strictly between home and away and could not be correct if the match finished level.

That last set is the interesting one. Of those 27,647 binary picks, 6,269 (22.68%) finished level. The ceiling was set by the label vocabulary, not the analysis.

Why the headline accuracy hides it

Reported accuracy by output arity on rows with a settled outcome:

arity rows hit rate
single 32,223 18,857 58.52%
double 13,608 7,385 54.27%

58.52% on single-label rows looks like a margin over chance. But chance for a 44/31/24 class split under a majority-class strategy is 44.26% — and the "single" bucket is not homogeneous: 4,490 of those rows had a compound single label (home/draw, away/draw) and 27,647 were strictly two-class. Averaging them reports neither.

This is a binary classifier wearing a three-class schema: any binary classifier over football outcomes pays a fixed 22.68% tax on the subset it is applied to. A genuine three-class system moves that tax into calibrated probability on the draw.

The audit query that should be a unit test

Aggregate accuracy is what lets this bug live for 46,000 rows. Per-class precision and recall make it visible in one screen:

-- D1: per-class precision / recall on the collapsed label set
WITH base AS (
  SELECT actual_result, string_to_array(prediction_direction, '/') AS picked
  FROM ai_predictions
  WHERE settled AND actual_result IS NOT NULL
),
exploded AS (
  -- a compound label is a set; a single label is a set of one
  SELECT actual_result, unnest(picked) AS cls FROM base
),
per_class AS (
  SELECT cls,
         count(*)                                    AS emitted_n,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE actual_result = cls) AS correct
  FROM exploded
  GROUP BY cls
),
totals AS (
  SELECT actual_result AS cls, count(*) AS actual_n FROM base GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT c.cls, c.emitted_n, c.correct,
       round(100.0 * c.correct / c.emitted_n, 2) AS precision_pct,
       round(100.0 * c.correct / t.actual_n,  2) AS recall_pct
FROM per_class c
JOIN totals t USING (cls)
ORDER BY c.emitted_n DESC;

Result on the 45,860 rows with a non-null outcome:

class times emitted correct precision recall
home 24,564 13,154 53.55% 64.34%
away 20,941 8,399 40.11% 58.99%
draw 17,159 4,601 26.81% 41.16%

Draw precision of 26.81% hides the shape of the failure: draw alone hit 78 of 360 (21.67%), while away/draw hit 5,920 of 10,997 (53.83%) and home/draw hit 3,272 of 5,928 (55.20%). The compound labels are not predicting a draw — they express uncertainty between two outcomes, and the draw is an escape hatch. Recall on the draw is 41.16%: 6,576 draws were named by no label at all.

The most damning row: 283 distinct models emitted draw at least once across 46,189 predictions, and the busiest did it 4 times. No model here has learned to identify draws. Some occasionally guess.

Scoring both systems on one yardstick

Accuracy cannot compare a one-hot label with a distribution. Log loss can. The emitted label is scored as a probability vector (1.0 on the named class, split evenly for compounds) against the market-implied probability from the quoted three-way price, normalised to sum to one. 45,110 of 46,189 rows survive the price sanity filter.

import math

def implied(prices):
    inv = [1.0 / p for p in prices]
    s = sum(inv)
    return [x / s for x in inv]

LL_MARKET = LL_MODEL = BRIER_DRAW = 0.0
n = 0
for actual, ph, pd, pa, direction, arity in rows:
    mh, md, ma = implied((ph, pd, pa))
    LL_MARKET += -math.log(max({"home": mh, "draw": md, "away": ma}[actual], 1e-12))
    BRIER_DRAW += (md - (1.0 if actual == "draw" else 0.0)) ** 2

    if arity == "single":
        q_true = 1.0 if direction == actual else 0.0
    else:
        parts = direction.split("/")
        q_true = 1.0 / len(parts) if actual in parts else 0.0
    LL_MODEL += -math.log(max(q_true, 1e-12))
    n += 1

print(n, round(LL_MARKET / n, 4), round(LL_MODEL / n, 4), round(BRIER_DRAW / n, 4))
# 45110  0.9683  13.4625  0.1812

Log loss 0.9683 for the market-implied probabilities, 13.4625 for the emitted label — a factor of 13.9. That is what a zero looks like inside a logarithm: every row where the model picked a compound and the outcome was the excluded class contributes -log(0), clamped at 1e-12, or 27.6 nats.

This is not a claim that market probabilities are a good model. It is a claim about representation: a probability vector can be scored and improved; a one-hot label can only be counted, and counting rewards the majority class. The draw Brier of 0.1812 is what a real three-class output would have to beat.

What actually carries draw information

If confidence carried draw-risk signal, high-confidence binary picks would convert to draws less often. They don't. Draw rate among single picks restricted to home or away (27,647 rows, 6,269 draws):

confidence rows ended in draw draw rate
3 5,340 1,247 23.35%
4 5,188 1,013 19.53%
5 5,870 1,343 22.88%
6 5,426 1,314 24.22%
7 2,852 667 23.39%
8 1,705 437 25.63%
9 400 86 21.50%

Flat, and mildly inverted at the top: a model that says 9 is no less likely to be level than one that says 4. That is the expected failure when confidence is attached to a binary comparison and the third class was pruned before scoring — the pruning discards the evidence.

The market-implied draw probability, on the same 45,110 rows, is calibrated in the ordinary sense:

implied draw probability rows observed draw rate
0.0 – 0.1 688 6.40%
0.1 – 0.2 6,851 16.09%
0.2 – 0.3 34,460 25.11%
0.3 – 0.4 3,111 38.89%

Mean implied 0.2423 against an observed 24.20%. The information is already in a column we store, and it is thrown away at the label step.

The imbalance is structural, not random

Draw rates are not uniform across competitions. On 78,553 finished matches the overall draw rate is 24.69% (19,392 draws), and competition buckets with at least 500 settled rows span 15.49% to 30.42%:

competition matches draw rate
Argentina reserve league 674 30.42%
Spain RFEF third tier 1,635 29.60%
Italy fourth tier 898 27.17%
German regional league 667 27.14%
Club friendlies 5,297 26.79%
Norway third tier 594 15.49%

A single global threshold for "is this a draw?" is therefore wrong by about 15 percentage points. A per-class correction must be conditioned on the competition, and that requires a calibrated probability rather than a relabelled decision — you cannot attach a competition prior to a one-hot output.

Six rules that would have prevented this

  1. Store the distribution, not the decision. A row should carry p_home, p_draw, p_away; the label is a rendering derived at read time. Ours stores prediction_direction and a 1–10 integer, so every metric above had to reconstruct intent from a string.
  2. Never score a three-class problem by accuracy. Log loss and per-class recall, in the same query as the headline number.
  3. Assert a per-class floor in CI. If the draw is emitted in under 10% of rows while the observed base rate is 24%, fail the build.
  4. Measure compound labels separately. home/draw at 55.20% precision is not three-class capability; it inflates the "single" hit rate whenever the draw lands.
  5. Condition on competition before claiming a threshold. A 15.49%–30.42% spread makes one global cut miscalibrated for every league it touches.
  6. Score against market-implied probability. It is the only genuine distribution in the schema and it is already calibrated on our own rows — without it, a 0.78% draw rate looks like a modelling choice rather than a defect.

Two integrity facts

The 46,189 settled predictions cover 16,724 distinct matches, and only 3,736 (8.09%) join to matches on id; the rest carry a match_id from an older identifier space. Every per-competition number above was computed from matches directly — joining predictions to competitions would have dropped 92% of rows and produced a confident, wrong table.

Second: 329 settled rows have actual_result IS NULL and 121 have hit IS NULL while settled is true. They are excluded explicitly with FILTER.

The point

A 24% versus 0.8% gap is not a dataset problem. Twenty-four percent is an ordinary share for the third class of a football outcome. The imbalance was manufactured by the output format: the model emitted a label, the vocabulary had three slots, and the scoring loop only rewarded the slot that appeared most. Fixing it needs no better model — three numbers instead of one string, and a refusal to ship a three-class system whose per-class recall is never measured for one of its classes.

The draw was never hard to predict. It was hard to record.

Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+

title: An Augmented Lagrangian Approach to Lifted Bellman Linear Programming
description:
arXiv:2611.14183v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Temporal-difference critics regress onto a bootstrapped target and usually need a target network. Lifted Bellman Linear Programming (LBLP) instead expresses the in-sample optimal values of offline RL as the solution to a linear program over the dataset. Its neural solver ALBUM relaxes the constraints into hinge penalties with fixed coefficients, and its guarantees are conditions on coefficients chosen in advance. We solve the same program with the method of multipliers: the coefficients become multipliers learned by dual ascent, with one penalty parameter $\rho$. In the convex case the fixed points are the KKT pairs of LBLP, and at every stationary point the applied constraint weights balance the objective exactly. The critic can serve a Gaussian actor, a flow actor, and best-of-N sampling, and for the Gaussian actor we propose an advantage-normalized DDPG+BC objective. With a single $Q$ and $V$ and no target network, our AL-LBLP with best-of-N reaches 60.1\% average success on the 50 state-based OGBench tasks. On long-horizon tasks, it reaches 81.5% on humanoidmaze-giant and 79.8% on antmaze-giant. It does not collapse up to batch size 8192.

title: Hand-Object Contact Transition Detection in Egocentric Video
description:
arXiv:2611.13486v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper tackles the task of hand-object contact transition detection in egocentric video, which aims to localize the two temporal boundaries of a contact episode: the moment a hand first establishes contact with an object (touch) and the moment contact is released (release). We propose a unified framework that jointly models the interacting hand and object to accurately localize both transition types. The proposed framework augments hand-centric spatiotemporal representations with object-aware features learned directly from the video and introduces a transition-aware event spotting formulation tailored to contact transitions, without relying on external object or hand-object interaction detectors during inference. To support this task, we present ContactTransition, a dataset comprising 4,021 egocentric videos with 8,498 touch and 8,077 release annotations, together with object-of-interest supervision. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms strong two-stage and end-to-end event-spotting baselines on both transition types. Finally, we show that detected contact transitions provide effective temporal anchors for downstream egocentric hand-object reasoning.

title: Plug-and-Play ADMM for Inverse Problems with Flow Matching Denoiser
description:
arXiv:2611.13742v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Plug-and-Play (PnP) methods with generative priors have achieved strong performance in inverse problems, with recent flow matching models enabling fast and scalable reconstruction. However, a key challenge in PnP methods is maintaining consistency between data fidelity updates and the learned generative prior, as data-consistency steps can move iterates away from the flow trajectory. We propose an ADMM-based PnP framework for flow matching priors that enforces stronger consistency between the measurement model and the prior through auxiliary variables and dual updates. In addition, we introduce a trajectory correction mechanism that restores consistency with the flow via a combination of deterministic and stochastic projections. Our method provides a more principled integration of flow priors within PnP frameworks, achieving high-quality reconstructions with reduced computational cost.

title: DepthGS: Depth-Guided Gaussian Splatting with Adaptive Regularization for High-Quality Surface Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2611.13628v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as an efficient representation for novel view synthesis, offering fast differentiable rendering and high visual fidelity, and has increasingly been extended to surface reconstruction. However, the relationship between depth information and reconstruction error remains insufficiently explored, limiting the principled design of geometric optimization strategies. To fill the above gap, we propose DepthGS, a depth-guided Gaussian splatting framework. We derive theoretical relations between depth discrepancies and reconstruction error under single-view and multi-view settings, and rigorously establish corresponding upper bounds on reconstruction error. The above analysis informs the design of adaptive regularization strategies in both single-view and multi-view optimization. More specifically, for single-view optimization, we propose a depth-difference-guided adaptive normal regularization strategy that modulates the normal constraint strength using a geometric reliability weight computed from local depth differences. For multi-view optimization, we introduce a cross-view depth consistency regularization strategy that promotes consistency between neighboring-view depth maps and the corresponding depth predictions obtained by transforming the current view's depth predictions into those neighboring views. Extensive experiments on DTU, Mip-NeRF360, and Tanks and Temples demonstrate that DepthGS achieves competitive performance in both surface reconstruction and novel view synthesis.

title: Past the Tap: Making Compose Screens Behave When the Mouse, Keyboard, and Stylus Show Up
description:
Your app was tested with a thumb. Then a user opens it on a Chromebook, docks a foldable to a keyboard, or scribbles in a notes screen with a stylus, and a dozen assumptions fail quietly. Nothing crashes at first. The right-click does nothing, Tab skips the primary button, and holding Ctrl+S writes the file nine times.

This post walks through how input actually flows in Jetpack Compose, the idiomatic Kotlin for handling each device, and the failure modes that tend to reach production because nobody had a mouse on their desk during QA.

The mental model: two lanes, not one

Touch handling trains us to think in “taps.” Compose does not. It routes pointer events and key events through different machinery, and mixing them up is the root of most bugs below.

Pointer events (touch, mouse, trackpad, stylus) are hit-tested against the nodes under the pointer, then delivered in passes: initial (parent to child, so a parent can intercept), main (child to parent, where most code lives), and final. Key events skip hit testing entirely. They are routed by focus. In the preview pass (onPreviewKeyEvent) the event travels from the root down to the focused node, so an ancestor can intercept it first. If nobody does, the regular pass (onKeyEvent) starts at the focused node and bubbles back up toward the root.

That one difference explains a large share of “my shortcut doesn’t fire” reports. A handler fires only when focus sits on its own node or on one of its descendants, so a handler on a subtree where nothing ever takes focus is dead code.

Pointer input that knows what kind of pointer it is

Every PointerInputChange carries a type. Use it. A single gesture detector that treats all pointers alike is how you end up with a stylus that scrolls instead of draws.

@Composable
fun Whiteboard(
    onStroke: (Offset, Float) -> Unit,
    onContextMenu: (Offset) -> Unit,
    onZoomStep: (Float) -> Unit,
    modifier: Modifier = Modifier,
) {
    // Always call the newest lambdas, even though pointerInput(Unit) never restarts.
    val latestStroke by rememberUpdatedState(onStroke)
    val latestMenu by rememberUpdatedState(onContextMenu)
    val latestZoom by rememberUpdatedState(onZoomStep)

    Box(
        modifier.pointerInput(Unit) {
            awaitPointerEventScope {
                while (true) {
                    // Initial pass: we want the wheel before a scrollable ancestor swallows it.
                    val event = awaitPointerEvent(PointerEventPass.Initial)
                    // Pick the pointer we care about; changes[0] is not always the stylus.
                    val change = event.changes.firstOrNull { it.type == PointerType.Stylus }
                        ?: event.changes.firstOrNull()
                        ?: continue

                    when {
                        event.type == PointerEventType.Scroll &&
                            event.keyboardModifiers.isCtrlPressed -> {
                            latestZoom(if (change.scrollDelta.y < 0f) 1.1f else 0.9f)
                            change.consume()
                        }
                        event.type == PointerEventType.Press &&
                            event.buttons.isSecondaryPressed -> {
                            latestMenu(change.position)
                            change.consume()
                        }
                        change.pressed &&
                            change.type == PointerType.Stylus &&
                            (event.type == PointerEventType.Press ||
                                event.type == PointerEventType.Move) -> {
                            latestStroke(change.position, change.pressure)
                            change.consume()
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    )
}

Imports note: isCtrlPressed here is the PointerKeyboardModifiers extension from androidx.compose.ui.input.pointer, not the KeyEvent one from androidx.compose.ui.input.key. On Android these flags come from the underlying MotionEvent's meta state, so verify them on your target devices. This sketch also draws on every stylus move; a production canvas would accumulate points into a path per stroke.

Three details are worth calling out. rememberUpdatedState lets the long-lived pointerInput(Unit) block see fresh callbacks. The initial pass is what lets Ctrl+wheel zoom win against a scrolling parent. And consume() is how you stop other handlers, such as a parent's gesture detector or a scrollable, from also reacting to the same event. Current clickable implementations respond only to the primary button, but that was not always true everywhere: Compose Multiplatform desktop reacted to any mouse button until a 2022 change restricted it. A custom right-click handler should therefore consume the press so parent pointer handlers don't also act on it, and you should confirm the behavior on the versions and platforms you ship.

Hover is state, so model it as state 

@Composable
fun ToolbarButton(label: String, onClick: () -> Unit) {
    val interaction = remember { MutableInteractionSource() }
    val hovered by interaction.collectIsHoveredAsState()

    Text(
        text = label,
        modifier = Modifier
            .hoverable(interaction)
            .clickable(
                interactionSource = interaction,
                onClick = onClick,
            )
            .background(if (hovered) Color(0xFFEFF1FA) else Color.Transparent)
            .padding(horizontal = 12.dp, vertical = 8.dp),
    )
}

On recent Foundation versions (1.7+) clickable picks up the default indication itself, so there's no need to pass LocalIndication.current; on older versions, pass an indication explicitly. Sharing one MutableInteractionSource between hoverable and clickable keeps hover, press, and focus visuals consistent instead of fighting each other.

Keyboard: focus first, shortcuts second

Shortcuts belong on a node that actually owns focus, or on an ancestor using the preview pass so it sees keys on the way down.

fun Modifier.shortcut(
    key: Key,
    ctrl: Boolean = true,
    action: () -> Unit,
): Modifier = onPreviewKeyEvent { e ->
    val isMatch = e.type == KeyEventType.KeyDown &&
        e.key == key &&
        e.isCtrlPressed == ctrl &&
        !e.isAltPressed && !e.isMetaPressed && !e.isShiftPressed &&
        e.nativeKeyEvent.repeatCount == 0   // Android-only: ignore auto-repeat
    if (isMatch) { action(); true } else false
}

@Composable
fun EditorScreen(onSave: () -> Unit) {
    val focus = remember { FocusRequester() }

    Box(
        Modifier
            .focusRequester(focus)
            .focusable()
            .shortcut(Key.S, action = onSave)
    ) { /* editor content */ }

    LaunchedEffect(Unit) { focus.requestFocus() }
}

Checking Alt, Meta and Shift matters: without it, ctrl = false would match every plain key press, and Ctrl+S would also trigger a Ctrl+Shift+S binding. nativeKeyEvent ties this helper to Android; a multiplatform codebase needs its own repeat tracking instead.

Returning true marks the event handled. Returning false lets it keep travelling, which is exactly what you want for keys you don't care about.

The timeline above is the bug the repeatCount == 0 check prevents. Operating systems send repeated key-down events while a key is held, and a naive KeyDown handler treats each as a fresh press.

For traversal order, don’t fight Tab. Describe the order you want with focusProperties:

Modifier.focusProperties {
    next = nextFieldRequester
    previous = previousFieldRequester
}

Stylus: pressure is data, palms are noise

A stylus reports pressure and can be an eraser. Treat both as first-class:

val strokeWidth = lerp(2f, 14f, change.pressure.coerceIn(0f, 1f))
val erasing = change.type == PointerType.Eraser

When a stylus is down, ignore PointerType.Touch pointers in the same surface. A resting palm is just another finger as far as your gesture code is concerned, and it will pan the canvas mid-stroke if you let it.

Six failure modes that reach production

1. Stale lambdas inside pointerInput. pointerInput(Unit) captures the lambdas from the first composition. Your gesture keeps invoking an old callback after state has moved on. Either key the modifier on what it reads, or wrap callbacks with rememberUpdatedState as shown earlier.

2. Requesting focus before the node exists. FocusRequester.requestFocus() throws an IllegalStateException ("FocusRequester is not initialized") if no node is attached to that requester yet. It typically bites when the target sits behind a condition or inside a lazy item, and the LaunchedEffect lives somewhere the modifier is not guaranteed to have been applied. Waiting a frame is a guess, not a guarantee. Co-locate the request with the modifier instead:

@Composable
fun EditorHost(isEditorVisible: Boolean) {
    if (isEditorVisible) Editor()      // the effect is inside, with the modifier
}

@Composable
private fun Editor() {
    val focus = remember { FocusRequester() }
    Box(Modifier.focusRequester(focus).focusable()) { /* content */ }
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) { focus.requestFocus() }   // normally runs once Editor is in the tree
}

This covers the common case, but effects and node attachment are not a hard contract. Reports exist of the same crash when focus is requested while an animation or a lazy subcomposition is still settling. If you hit that, request focus after the first layout instead, once, from a callback that only fires when the node is placed:

@Composable
private fun Editor() {
    val focus = remember { FocusRequester() }
    var requested by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }

    Box(
        Modifier
            .focusRequester(focus)
            .onGloballyPositioned {
                if (!requested) { requested = true; focus.requestFocus() }
            }
            .focusable()
    ) { /* content */ }
}

Don’t reach for focusRestorer() as a substitute here. It restores focus to a previously focused child; it doesn't guarantee a requester is attached.

Inside lazy lists, request focus in response to an event or a restored-focus callback rather than at first composition.

3. Key-repeat double fire. Covered above. Filter on repeatCount, and decide deliberately whether any shortcut (say, arrow-key nudging) should repeat.

4. Click-only affordances. If a control is built from pointerInput { detectTapGestures }, it has no focus, no hover, no semantics, and no keyboard activation. Prefer clickable, toggleable, or selectable, which wire all of that for you. Reserve raw pointer handling for the canvas-like surfaces that truly need it.

5. Activity recreation on device attach. Plugging in a keyboard or mouse is a configuration change. Unless the Activity opts out, it is recreated and any state held outside rememberSaveable or a ViewModel disappears mid-typing. Declare what you handle:

<activity
    android:name=".MainActivity"
    android:configChanges="keyboard|keyboardHidden|navigation|screenSize|smallestScreenSize|screenLayout|orientation" />

Opting out means you own the responsibility of reacting to the new configuration, so test it with real attach and detach, not just emulator defaults.

6. Gesture versus scroll fights. If your handler consumes a scroll event, the list behind it stops scrolling. If you never consume it, both react. Pick an owner per modifier combination: plain wheel scrolls, Ctrl+wheel zooms, and nothing else is consumed.

Test it without owning every device

Compose’s test APIs can simulate these inputs, so regressions get caught in CI:

@Test
fun ctrlS_savesOnce() {
    var saves = 0
    composeRule.setContent { EditorScreen(onSave = { saves++ }) }

    composeRule.onRoot().performKeyInput {
        keyDown(Key.CtrlLeft)
        pressKey(Key.S)
        keyUp(Key.CtrlLeft)
    }
    assertEquals(1, saves)
}

@Test
fun rightClick_opensMenu() {
    composeRule.setContent { /* screen under test */ }
    composeRule.onNodeWithTag("canvas").performMouseInput { rightClick() }
    composeRule.onNodeWithTag("context_menu").assertIsDisplayed()
}

Pair automated tests with one manual pass on a real desktop-class device. Emulated input will never feel like a worn-out trackpad.

A short checklist before you ship

  • Every interactive element is reachable and activatable with Tab and Enter or Space.
  • Hover has a visual response, and right-click has a defined meaning or is deliberately ignored.
  • Shortcuts use the preview pass, check key-down only, and ignore repeats.
  • Stylus pressure and eraser are read, and touch is ignored while the pen is down.
  • Attaching and detaching hardware never loses user input.

Input support is rarely one big feature. It is a pile of small contracts between your UI and a device you didn’t picture. Test each contract once, and the screen feels native on hardware you never owned.

📱 Crack Your Next Android Interview

If you’re targeting a senior Android role at a FAANG or top-tier MNC, syntax knowledge alone won’t get you through the loop. I highly recommend “Cracking Top MNC Android Interviews” — a senior-level playbook covering framework internals, Jetpack Compose, coroutines, Android-specific system design, and DSA reframed around real mobile constraints, to help you walk into bar-raiser rounds ready.

  • Kindle Edition: Available on Amazon

title: Zero-Downtime GraphQL Evolution in GitLab: Fixing Multi-Node Upgrades with @gl_introduced
description:
A deep dive into GraphQL schema evolution, rolling deployments, mixed-version infrastructure, and backward-compatible frontend queries.

Distributed applications rarely upgrade every server instance simultaneously.

In a multi-node deployment, different application versions can temporarily coexist while a rolling upgrade is in progress. This creates an important compatibility challenge: frontend assets served by a newer application version may send GraphQL requests to an older backend node that does not yet understand the updated schema.

This is not simply a deployment sequencing problem. It is a contract compatibility problem between independently deployed frontend and backend components.

While contributing to GitLab, I investigated and fixed this exact issue on the GitLab Credits user page in GitLab Merge Request !268111, addressing Issue #638245.

The fix uses GitLab's @gl_introduced directive to make newly introduced GraphQL fields and arguments compatible with mixed-version environments during rolling upgrades.

This article walks through the failure mode, the underlying schema compatibility problem, the implementation, and the verification process.

1. The Distributed Systems Problem: Mixed-Version Deployments

Consider a GitLab installation running multiple application nodes behind a load balancer.

Initially, all nodes run GitLab 19.5:

                 Load Balancer
                       |
              +--------+--------+
              |                 |
          Node A              Node B
          GitLab 19.5         GitLab 19.5

Now suppose the deployment begins upgrading to GitLab 19.6.

During a rolling upgrade, Node A is upgraded first while Node B continues running the previous version.

                 Load Balancer
                       |
              +--------+--------+
              |                 |
          Node A              Node B
          GitLab 19.6         GitLab 19.5
              |                 |
              +--------+--------+
                       |
               Shared Application

At this point, both versions are active.

This is an expected intermediate deployment state, not necessarily an infrastructure failure.

However, it introduces a compatibility boundary.

1.1 How the mismatch occurs

Consider the following sequence:

  1. A browser requests the GitLab Credits user page.
  2. The upgraded node serves frontend assets containing the GitLab 19.6 GraphQL queries.
  3. The browser executes one of those queries.
  4. The load balancer routes the GraphQL request to the older GitLab 19.5 node.
  5. The older node validates the query against its previous GraphQL schema.
  6. The schema does not recognize the newly introduced argument.

The frontend and backend are individually functioning, but their contracts are temporarily incompatible.

This is a classic mixed-version deployment problem.

2. Understanding the GraphQL Schema Compatibility Failure

The GitLab Credits user page retrieves usage and subscription information through GraphQL queries.

In GitLab 19.6, the includeNonBillable argument was introduced to the following fields:

  • usedFlowTypes
  • events

The updated frontend queries started supplying this argument.

For example:

usedFlowTypes(includeNonBillable: true) {
  id
  title
}

The newer GraphQL schema understands the argument.

The older schema does not.

2.1 What happens on the older node?

When the query reaches a GitLab 19.5 node, GraphQL validates it against the schema available on that node.

The older schema cannot recognize the newly introduced argument.

The resulting validation errors are:

Field 'usedFlowTypes' doesn't accept argument 'includeNonBillable'

Field 'events' doesn't accept argument 'includeNonBillable'

GraphQL performs schema validation before normal query execution.

Therefore, an unknown argument is not simply ignored as an unsupported optional parameter.

The query fails validation.

This can prevent the affected operation from returning the expected data and break the Credits user page during the upgrade window.

2.2 Why this is more than a frontend issue

The frontend query is valid against the new schema.

The backend query validator is also behaving correctly against its own schema.

The actual problem is that the two components are temporarily operating with different versions of the same API contract.

This distinction matters when debugging distributed applications.

A query can be completely valid in the newest application version while remaining invalid on an older node that is still serving production traffic.

3. GraphQL Schema Evolution During Rolling Upgrades

GraphQL APIs evolve over time.

New fields, arguments, enum values, and input types are introduced as application requirements change.

In a single-version environment, frontend and backend changes can often be deployed together without exposing compatibility problems.

Multi-node deployments are different.

During a rolling upgrade, the system must tolerate requests crossing version boundaries.

A useful way to reason about this is to separate three concepts:

  1. Schema availability: Does the backend version understand the requested field or argument?
  2. Client compatibility: Can the frontend safely communicate with older backend versions?
  3. Deployment compatibility: Can multiple application versions serve requests simultaneously?

A robust rolling deployment needs these properties to remain compatible throughout the transition.

3.1 The problem with introducing arguments directly

Suppose a frontend query changes from:

usedFlowTypes {
  id
  title
}

To:

usedFlowTypes(includeNonBillable: true) {
  id
  title
}

The new query depends on an argument that does not exist in the older schema.

If the browser sends this query to an older node, validation fails.

The important point is that the compatibility problem exists even though the new argument is meaningful and supported in the upgraded application.

The frontend needs a mechanism to account for the version of the backend receiving the request.

4. Understanding GitLab's @gl_introduced Directive

GitLab provides version-aware GraphQL compatibility support through the @gl_introduced directive.

It allows frontend GraphQL operations to declare when a field or selection was introduced.

For example:

usedFlowTypes(includeNonBillable: true)
  @gl_introduced(version: "19.6.0") {
  id
  title
}

The annotation communicates that this selection belongs to a schema capability introduced in GitLab 19.6.0.

GitLab's multi-version compatibility layer can use this version information to omit the annotated selection when communicating with an older backend version that does not support it.

This prevents the older backend from receiving an incompatible field or argument as part of the transformed query.

4.1 Why the directive matters

Without version metadata, the compatibility layer cannot reliably distinguish a newly introduced selection from one that is expected to exist across supported versions.

The directive provides that information explicitly.

Conceptually, the process looks like this:

             Frontend GraphQL Query
                       |
                       v
             Version Compatibility
                    Layer
                       |
             +---------+---------+
             |                   |
             v                   v
       GitLab 19.6           GitLab 19.5
       New Schema            Old Schema
             |                   |
             v                   v
       Keep New Field       Omit New Selection
             |                   |
             v                   v
       Execute Query        Execute Compatible
                            Query

The important distinction is that the directive is compatibility metadata used by GitLab's query-processing pipeline. It is not a native GraphQL mechanism that automatically changes server schemas.

4.2 Compatibility is based on introduction version

The version annotation must accurately reflect when the relevant schema capability became available.

For this contribution, the introduction version was:

@gl_introduced(version: "19.6.0")

Using the correct version allows the compatibility mechanism to distinguish GitLab 19.5 from GitLab 19.6.

This is particularly important during the transition period when both versions can serve requests.

5. Implementing the Fix

The fix was applied to two GraphQL query files in the GitLab Credits usage billing frontend.

5.1 Updating the subscription usage query

File:

ee/app/assets/javascripts/usage_quotas/usage_billing/users/show/graphql/get_user_subscription_usage.query.graphql

The usedFlowTypes selection was updated to include the introduction directive:

usedFlowTypes(includeNonBillable: true)
  @gl_introduced(version: "19.6.0") {
  id
  title
}

This marks the selection as introduced in GitLab 19.6.

When the compatibility layer communicates with an older supported node, it can omit the version-gated selection instead of sending an argument that the older schema does not recognize.

5.2 Updating the subscription usage events query

The second change was made in:

ee/app/assets/javascripts/usage_quotas/usage_billing/users/show/graphql/get_user_subscription_usage_events.query.graphql

The events selection was updated similarly:

events(
  after: $after
  before: $before
  includeNonBillable: true
) @gl_introduced(version: "19.6.0") {
  # Existing selected fields
}

This ensures that the newly introduced includeNonBillable argument is covered by the version compatibility annotation.

5.3 Why both locations needed changes

The issue involved two separate GraphQL selections.

Fixing only usedFlowTypes would leave the events query vulnerable to the same schema validation failure.

Likewise, annotating only events would not protect the subscription usage query.

Both selections needed the same introduction version because both depended on the GitLab 19.6 schema change.

The resulting implementation was deliberately focused:

  • No changes to the backend schema.
  • No changes to the underlying business logic.
  • No changes to the load-balancing strategy.
  • No need to introduce a separate frontend version-detection mechanism.

Instead, the existing GraphQL compatibility infrastructure was used to describe the version dependency directly at the query level.

6. Verification and Regression Testing

After updating both GraphQL queries, I ran the usage billing frontend Jest suite.

Command:

yarn jest ee/spec/frontend/usage_quotas/usage_billing/

Verified result:

10 test suites passed
165 tests passed
0 failures

This verified that the existing usage billing frontend tests continued to pass after the query updates.

6.1 Why regression testing matters

GraphQL query files are part of the frontend application's API contract.

Even a small annotation change can affect how query selections are processed.

Running the relevant test suite helps verify that the changes do not introduce regressions in the surrounding usage billing functionality.

The verification was focused on the affected frontend area rather than relying only on the visual behavior of the Credits user page.

7. Engineering Considerations for Multi-Node Deployments

This contribution highlights several broader principles that are important when evolving APIs in distributed applications.

7.1 Deployments are not always atomic

In multi-node systems, application versions can coexist temporarily.

Any frontend change that depends on a newly introduced backend capability should account for this transition period.

Assuming that every request reaches the newest server version is unsafe in a rolling deployment.

7.2 GraphQL validation happens before normal execution

An unknown argument can invalidate an operation before its resolver executes.

This is why an optional-looking argument is not automatically backward compatible.

Compatibility needs to be handled before the query reaches a schema that cannot validate it.

7.3 Version metadata makes compatibility explicit

The @gl_introduced directive provides a clear declaration of when a GraphQL selection became available.

This is more maintainable than scattering assumptions about backend versions across application code.

7.4 Fix compatibility at the correct layer

The underlying schema change was intentional.

The problem was not that GitLab 19.6 introduced a new argument.

The problem was that the frontend needed to communicate safely with older nodes during the upgrade process.

Using the existing version compatibility mechanism addressed the actual failure without introducing unnecessary backend or infrastructure changes.

8. Final Summary

In GitLab MR !268111, I fixed a GraphQL compatibility problem affecting the GitLab Credits user page during multi-node rolling upgrades.

The failure occurred because frontend assets from GitLab 19.6 could send queries containing the newly introduced includeNonBillable argument to GitLab 19.5 nodes.

Those older nodes rejected the queries during GraphQL schema validation.

I added:

@gl_introduced(version: "19.6.0")

to both affected selections:

  • usedFlowTypes
  • events

This allows GitLab's multi-version compatibility layer to handle the new selections appropriately when communicating with older application versions.

Verification results:

  • 10 Jest test suites passed.
  • 165 tests passed.
  • 0 failures.

The broader engineering takeaway is that API evolution in distributed systems must account for deployment topology, not just the latest application version.

A frontend query that works perfectly against the newest schema may still fail in production when requests are routed to older nodes.

Version-aware GraphQL compatibility is an important part of making rolling deployments reliable.

References and Implementation

  • Issue: gitlab-org/gitlab#638245
  • Merge Request: gitlab-org/gitlab!268111
  • Subscription Usage Query: get_user_subscription_usage.query.graphql
  • Subscription Usage Events Query: get_user_subscription_usage_events.query.graphql
  • Test Directory: ee/spec/frontend/usage_quotas/usage_billing/

Author: Manish Kumar

GitLab: @manishpatel00

Contributing to GitLab's GraphQL architecture, frontend infrastructure, and distributed application reliability.

title: Time zones are the bug: a price feed that is wrong at midnight
description:
A fee comparison showed a price that was wrong for about six minutes every night, and only for some exchanges. Not stale, not missing — wrong. The kind of wrong that makes a user screenshot it and ask why your numbers do not match the exchange's own page.

The cause was not the price feed. It was the day boundary.

Every exchange resets on its own midnight

Trading fee tiers are usually computed per rolling period, but several exchanges reset allowances and volume counters on a calendar day in the exchange's local time. So the question "what is my fee tier right now" depends on what time it is where the exchange's accounting lives, not where the user is and not where your server is.

An aggregator that normalises everything to UTC — which is the correct instinct for storage — quietly moves that boundary. For an exchange at UTC+8, the tier resets at 16:00 UTC. If your code resets at 00:00 UTC, then between 16:00 and 24:00 UTC you are computing today's tier against yesterday's volume, and the fee you display is off by whatever the tier step is.

Six minutes was not the error window. Six minutes was how long it took someone to notice.

Three timestamp shapes, one of them a trap

The same normalisation bug shows up in three forms, and only the third is obvious:

  1. Epoch milliseconds. Unambiguous. Convert and move on.
  2. ISO 8601 with an offset (2026-11-11T09:00:00+08:00). Unambiguous if you keep the offset.
  3. ISO 8601 without an offset (2026-11-11T09:00:00). This is the trap. Every parser will assume something — server local, UTC, or browser local — and all three assumptions are wrong for at least one exchange. The string looks like a timestamp and behaves like a guess.

If you parse shape 3 with a default timezone, you get a value that is correct in one environment and wrong in another. That is the worst failure mode available: it passes local tests and fails in production, or passes in production and fails after a deploy moves the container's TZ.

Store the exchange's clock, not just the instant

The fix that held up was to stop treating time as a single instant and store two things:

  • the instant, in UTC, for ordering and display;
  • the exchange's local date, as a plain YYYY-MM-DD string, for anything that resets on a day boundary.

The second field is what makes tier logic testable. You are no longer asking "what time is it", you are asking "which of the exchange's days does this belong to", and that question has one answer regardless of where the code runs.

def exchange_day(ts_utc: datetime, tz: ZoneInfo) -> date:
    """The calendar date the exchange would print on a statement."""
    return ts_utc.astimezone(tz).date()

Two lines, and it removes an entire class of bug — the one where the same input produces different output depending on the machine.

Test the boundary, not the middle

The test that would have caught this is not "does the fee match for a sample trade". It is:

  • freeze the clock at 23:59 exchange-local and assert tier A;
  • freeze it at 00:01 exchange-local and assert tier B;
  • run both with TZ=UTC, TZ=Asia/Shanghai and TZ=America/New_York.

If the answers differ between the three runs, you have a timezone dependency in business logic, and it will surface as a support ticket at the worst possible hour. If they agree, you have actually fixed it rather than moved it.

The same discipline applies to rounding, which has the same shape of problem — the value is fine, the rule about when to apply it is what breaks. Rounding is a business rule, not a formatting detail, and it fails in the same quiet way: correct on the happy path, wrong at the edge, invisible until someone adds up a month of trades.

Cache the answer, but not the boundary

One more thing worth saying, because it is how this bug survived a deploy: the tier was cached. The cache key was the exchange and the account, with a TTL of an hour. That is a perfectly reasonable cache — and it made the bug persist for up to an hour after the real value changed.

If a value has a day-boundary dependency, the boundary belongs in the cache key, not just the TTL. Otherwise the cache outlives the fact. The general case for rarely-changing data is the same problem in slower motion: a TTL is a guess about when data changes, and a guessed boundary is a bug waiting for the one day it matters.

None of this is exotic. It is the ordinary cost of aggregating numbers that other people computed under assumptions they never wrote down. The exchanges are not wrong to reset on their own day; we were wrong to assume they reset on ours.

If you want to see what the output looks like when the boundaries are handled correctly, the comparison this work feeds is at fipst.com — the tier figures there are computed in exchange-local time, and the timestamps carry the offset they were computed with.

title: Counting Under Disagreement: Dollar-Weighted Measurement, Selective Machine Labelling and Budgeted Human Review from Disagreeing AI Readers of Administrative Text
description:
arXiv:2611.13215v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study AI-assisted measurement when one text label applies to many administrative records, the target is a monetary total, and the human readings that anchor the machines disagree. The testbed is 121,070 grant-purpose texts from US tax filings (799,675 records, \$126.4B), labelled by a rule-based classifier and three language models, with a designed sample of 651 texts read independently by three people under one codebook. We state exact conditions for a fixed-predictor difference estimator and for a cross-fitted predictor whose folds are assigned to the whole frame before sampling, under Poisson sampling, and assess the implemented fixed-size procedures by simulation: 8 predictors whose own totals span \$11.2-15.0B agree to within \$0.4B once rectified. Two rules that accept machine labels at a stated dollar-weighted error, weighted conformal p-values under a dollar measure and Learn-then-Test on the design estimate of the error, are evaluated on nested held-out folds and on re-draws of the design with synthetic truths; their error control in deployment is not established, and the count-based rule accepts no text under a dollar-drawn sample. In a replay that charges every human label, a two-phase review policy whose calibrator is fitted on its own first phase reduces the RMSE of the total by 28% at a budget of 100 texts relative to dollar-proportional sampling, while pure Neyman allocation fails with an uncalibrated predictor. Independent readers shift the estimated total by \$3.93B, 2.2 times the within-reader sampling interval, and institution-level intervals under-cover at every size. Every headline result is re-run under each reader. The results identify both the benefits and the limits of using learned predictions to decide what a person should verify.

title: I Built a Passive Web Security & DNS Posture Scanner (with a Live REST API & Telegram Bot)
description:
When you ship web apps frequently, security posture tends to drift silently. A missing Strict-Transport-Security header, a permissive SPF record exceeding 10 DNS lookups, or an forgotten CNAME pointing to a deleted cloud instance usually stays invisible until someone flags it.

Invasive vulnerability scanners require strict authorization and can stress production servers. I wanted something fast, read-only, and actionable that works just like an external browser.

So I built SurfaceScan
.

What a Passive Scan Checks

Enter any domain at surfacescan.uk
(no signup required) and it runs external checks in a few seconds:

Cryptography & Transport: SSL/TLS certificate chain, TLS 1.2/1.3, expiration warnings, and HTTP → HTTPS redirects
HTTP Security Headers: HSTS, CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, COOP
Sessions & Integrity: HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite cookie flags, permissive CORS wildcards, mixed content, and third-party script Subresource Integrity (SRI)
Email & DNS Trust: SPF (including recursive DNS lookup counting), DKIM, DMARC, DNSSEC, and CAA
Attack Surface: Certificate Transparency subdomain discovery, dangling CNAME takeover detection, RDAP domain expiry, and exposed files (security.txt, robots.txt, leaked .git endpoints)
Actionable Fixes Across 10 Stacks

Every issue includes ready-to-use configuration snippets tailored to your stack:

Nginx · Apache · Caddy · Cloudflare · Vercel · Netlify · Next.js · Express · IIS · WordPress

Built-in Security Builders & Live REST API

Under surfacescan.uk/tools
, there are free client-side builders and a Live API Tester:

Content-Security-Policy (CSP) Builder
SPF & DMARC Builder (tracks the RFC 7208 10-DNS-lookup limit live)
RFC 9116 security.txt Generator
Public REST API & Live Tester

You can hit the scan API directly from your terminal or CI pipeline:

bash

Or pass an optional X-API-Key (generated from your profile) for higher quotas:

Compare two domains side-by-side:

Scan Directly in Telegram

Need a quick check from your phone? Send any domain to @surfacescan_bot
on Telegram to get the grade, breakdown, and monitoring alerts in chat.

Pricing Model

Pro ($5/month): Up to 50 monitored domains, automated email/Telegram/webhook drift alerts, and 120 req/min (10,000/day) API limits.

title: Train on prefill, monitor at decode: Using sparse autoencoders for topic monitoring
description:
arXiv:2611.12935v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Topic monitoring is the task of labelling the topic of each token in a model's response during generation. Activation-based monitors that run at generation time have so far been trained to detect harmful content and are limited to two or three classes. We introduce TopicScope, a framework for training causal topic classifiers on SAE features that assign a topic to every token, so that the label can change partway through a response. We train three detector architectures on synthetic multi-topic conversations covering seven topics. Across Gemma-3 1B and 4B, monitors trained on features extracted from prefill hidden states were able to generalise to decoding. We also found that the classifiers are robust to perturbations, losing at most 5 macro-F1 points when off-topic asides are inserted, topics are removed or sections are reordered. Ablations conducted to understand the contribution of the SAE revealed that classifiers reaching baseline performance without it were several times larger. Our findings show that compact topic monitors can be trained inexpensively in prefill and deployed during generation. More broadly, our work shows where SAEs are useful beyond safety classification. Our code, dataset and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/Mercity-AI/SAE-Guardrails and https://huggingface.co/collections/Mercity/online-guardrails-using-sparse-autoencoders-6ac602940468c62fefb2b9e8

title: Target Selection with a Disappearing-Stimulus Mixed-Reality P300 Interface: Feasibility and Object-Distinguishable Versus Uniform Cues
description:
arXiv:2611.13906v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mixed-reality (MR) P300 interfaces can register selectable destinations, such as wheelchair goals, directly in the user's surroundings. When the cues disappear between flashes, however, the user must retain an intended target that is no longer visible. We tested whether such an interface supports target selection and whether giving each cue a stable colour-shape identity improves it compared with visually uniform spheres. Six healthy adults completed four trials in each cue condition of a 5x5 row/column task on a head-mounted MR display, with EEG from Fz, Cz, and Pz. Shrinkage linear discriminant analysis was evaluated with nested validation in which complete trials were held out from class balancing, hyperparameter selection, and fitting. Both conditions evoked a parietal target-related positivity. The decoded cell was correct in 18 of 48 held-out trials, against 1.9 expected by chance (binomial p < 1e-12), and in three participants individually. Cue format made no detectable difference: complete-target accuracy was 9/24 in both conditions (paired difference 0.0 percentage points, 95% CI [-37, 37]), and held-out AUC was 0.609 for spheres and 0.585 for object cues. Disappearing-stimulus MR P300 selection is therefore feasible under strict trial-level evaluation, but the benefit of object identity, if any, is too small to resolve in a pilot of this size.

title: Go, from zero to a running service · 2. Setup, modules and the shape of a project
description:
Go, from zero to a running service · Chapter 2 of 12 · Languages · new chapter every Tuesday night

By the end of this chapter: Create, build and run a Go project laid out the way the ecosystem expects.

The problem

Emma is a junior backend engineer on a fintech startup that just landed its first B2B client. The client wants a new “transaction‑validation” service that will sit behind the existing Java monolith. The product manager has pushed the deadline to two weeks because the client’s contract starts next month.

Emma, eager to prove herself, decides to write the service in Go because the team’s senior engineer swore it would “just work faster”. She clones a starter repository, adds a single http.Handler that parses JSON, validates a few fields and returns a 200 OK. She runs the binary locally and everything looks fine.

However, when she tries to build the project using the command go build, she gets an error message: go: cannot find main module; see 'go help modules'. She is not sure what this means or how to fix it. The error is costing her time, and the deadline is looming. Emma needs to get her project set up correctly and build a working Go service.

Before you start

To follow along with this chapter, you need to have Go installed on your machine. You can verify this by running the command go version in your terminal. You should see a version number, such as go1.19. You also need to have a code editor or IDE set up. If you have completed the previous chapter, you should have a basic understanding of why Go exists and what it optimises for.

Understanding Go modules

To create a new Go project, we need to understand how Go modules work. Go modules are the package management system for Go. They allow us to manage dependencies and ensure that our project is reproducible. A Go module is a collection of Go packages stored in a directory with a go.mod file. The go.mod file contains the module path, which is the unique identifier for the module, and the dependencies required by the module.

Creating a new Go project

To create a new Go project, we need to create a new directory for our project and navigate to it in our terminal. We can then run the command go mod init to create a new Go module. The go mod init command will prompt us to enter the module path, which should be in the format of github.com/username/repository. Once we have created the module, we can start adding dependencies to our project using the go get command.

Working with dependencies

When working with dependencies in Go, it's essential to understand the concept of versions. Go modules use semantic versioning, which means that each version of a dependency is identified by a unique version number. We can specify the version of a dependency in our go.mod file using the require directive. For example, to require version 1.2.3 of the github.com/gorilla/mux package, we would add the following line to our go.mod file:

require github.com/gorilla/mux v1.2.3

We can also use the go get command to update the version of a dependency. For example, to update the github.com/gorilla/mux package to the latest version, we would run the following command:

go get github.com/gorilla/mux@latest

Build it

Here are the steps to create, build and run a Go project:

  1. Create a new directory for your project: Run the command mkdir transaction-validation to create a new directory for your project.
  2. Navigate to the new directory: Run the command cd transaction-validation to navigate to the new directory.
  3. Create a new Go module: Run the command go mod init transaction-validation to create a new Go module.
  4. Create a new Go file: Run the command touch main.go to create a new Go file.
  5. Add the http.Handler code: Add the following code to the main.go file: 
package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"
)

type Transaction struct {
    ID   string `json:"id"`
    Amount float64 `json:"amount"`
}

func main() {
    http.HandleFunc("/validate", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        var transaction Transaction
        err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&transaction)
        if err != nil {
            http.Error(w, err.Error(), http.StatusBadRequest)
            return
        }
        if transaction.Amount < 0 {
            http.Error(w, "Invalid transaction amount", http.StatusBadRequest)
            return
        }
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
    })
    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
}
  1. Build the project: Run the command go build to build the project. To confirm that the project has been built successfully, you should see a transaction-validation executable file in your project directory.
  2. Run the project: Run the command ./transaction-validation to run the project. To confirm that the project is running successfully, you should be able to access the /validate endpoint using a tool like curl. For example: 
curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"id": "123", "amount": 10.99}' http://localhost:8080/validate

This should return a 200 OK response.

When this breaks

One common issue that can occur when building a Go project is the go: cannot find main module error. This error occurs when the go build command cannot find the go.mod file. To fix this error, make sure that you are in the correct directory and that the go.mod file exists.

Another issue that can occur is the undefined: Transaction error. This error occurs when the Transaction struct is not defined. To fix this error, make sure that the Transaction struct is defined in the main.go file.

What it costs

Using Go modules has several benefits, including reproducibility and dependency management. However, it also has some costs, such as the need to manage the go.mod file and the potential for version conflicts. Additionally, Go modules can make it more difficult to work with local dependencies, as they require a go.mod file to be present in the dependency directory.

In the interview

In an interview, you may be asked to explain how Go modules work and how to create a new Go project. A weak answer might be: "Go modules are a way to manage dependencies, but I'm not really sure how they work." A strong answer would be: "Go modules are a package management system for Go that allows us to manage dependencies and ensure that our project is reproducible. To create a new Go project, we need to create a new directory, navigate to it in our terminal, and run the command go mod init to create a new Go module."

A follow-up question might be: "How do you handle version conflicts in a Go project?" A strong answer would be: "To handle version conflicts in a Go project, we can use the go mod tidy command to remove any unnecessary dependencies and the go mod vendor command to vendor our dependencies. We can also use the go mod verify command to verify that our dependencies are correct."

As a senior engineer, you may be asked more advanced questions, such as: "How do you optimize the performance of a Go project?" or "How do you handle errors in a Go project?" A strong answer would demonstrate a deep understanding of Go and its ecosystem, as well as the ability to apply best practices to real-world problems.

Your tasks

  1. Create a new Go project using the go mod init command. Verify that the project has been created successfully by checking for the presence of a go.mod file.
  2. Add a new dependency to your project using the go get command. Verify that the dependency has been added successfully by checking the go.mod file.
  3. Run the go mod tidy command to remove any unnecessary dependencies. Verify that the command has been run successfully by checking the go.mod file.
  4. Run the go mod vendor command to vendor your dependencies. Verify that the command has been run successfully by checking for the presence of a vendor directory.
  5. Create a new Go file and add a new http.Handler to it. Verify that the handler is working correctly by using a tool like curl to access the endpoint.
