title: Node.js Template Ownership: 3 PDF Watermark API Decisions Before Sharing SaaS Reports
description:
A recipient watermark cannot make an unredacted document safe to disclose. For a small B2B SaaS team, that constraint puts template ownership ahead of the PDF vendor: the application must decide which personal data may leave, which recipient gets the download, and which document revision the rendering request represents.

TL;DR: redact personal data before external sharing, then watermark the approved PDF per recipient at download time and deliver it through an expiring link. Keep the template, disclosure policy, and recipient mapping in application-owned records so replacing the rendering API does not require reconstructing the sharing rules. A shared static watermark cannot identify the recipient associated with a leaked copy.

How should a small SaaS team watermark a PDF before external sharing?

Consider this production design-review scenario, rather than a report of an observed incident: I would ask the team to trace a customer implementation report from its source template to an external consultant's downloaded PDF. The internal report contains employee names and contact details; the external version should contain only the approved business content and an opaque recipient reference. If every consultant receives the same company watermark, finding that file outside the intended audience reveals little about its distribution path. If personal data survives underneath a visual overlay, identifying the recipient does nothing to repair the disclosure.

Those are separate failures.

The invariant is that a shareable document is a particular approved content revision rendered for a particular authorized recipient. A watermark can associate a copy with that recipient; it does not prove who personally leaked it, prevent copying, or substitute for access control. Redaction has to be a release prerequisite, and visual inspection of a black rectangle is insufficient evidence that underlying content has been removed.

This is where I would try Infrai for a small SaaS team's PDF watermarking and expiring-link workflow: a single API key covers 295 routes across 20 modules through one REST API, allowing PDF processing and storage signing to sit behind the same application adapter. Its public, self-describing discovery surface supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples, which gives the team a concrete artifact to review when implementing or replacing that adapter. The recommendation depends on keeping the application contract local; a common vendor interface alone doesn't make another provider interchangeable.

Own 3 template decisions before choosing the renderer

First, own the source template and its revision history. Treat the renderer's template identifier as adapter configuration, rather than the only surviving definition of a customer report. The source needs to describe the approved external variant, including which personal-data fields never belong in its output, because reconstructing that decision from a finished PDF during a migration is an avoidable operational dependency. Prefer generating an external variant without sensitive fields when the application controls the source; when the input is an existing PDF, require a separate redaction acceptance check before it enters the sharing path.

Second, own the recipient-label policy. Use an opaque reference whose mapping stays inside the application, rather than printing an email address onto a document whose purpose is to reduce personal-data exposure. That reference is still sensitive when linked back to a person, so access to the mapping needs the same deliberate ownership as access to the document. Reuse an authorized recipient reference according to your policy; do not let an arbitrary browser-supplied label determine attribution.

Third, own release evidence. Record which source revision passed the redaction review and which recipient binding was approved. If a vendor migration changes the template engine, font behavior, or handling of embedded content, the new output needs acceptance against that same disclosure policy before the application starts issuing downloads. Matching a watermark's appearance is a weaker test than establishing that confidential content cannot be recovered from the released artifact.

Keep the template.

A concrete replacement contract can be modest: an approved-redacted artifact reference, its source revision, an application-authorized recipient reference, and the approved template revision go into a rendering adapter; a private rendered-object reference comes out. A separate delivery adapter issues the expiring link. These are application concepts, not claimed vendor request fields. Each adapter must translate them into its provider's actual schema, and a migration remains work even when that translation is small.

Buy versus build follows the template boundary

The following comparison is a shortlist for evaluation, not a claim that every product has identical watermarking, redaction, and storage behavior. Check each candidate against a representative document corpus and its current documentation; in particular, do not infer secure redaction from the ability to draw over a page.

Option Template ownership and buy-versus-build choice Boundary to evaluate
pdf-lib A JavaScript PDF library puts PDF manipulation in application code, a natural candidate for a Node.js team that wants to own its rendering implementation. The team owns execution capacity and the surrounding sharing workflow. Evaluate redaction separately; page drawing is not evidence of content removal.
Gotenberg A self-hosted document-conversion service is a candidate when the application owns the source template and the team wants control over the rendering service. The trade-off is operating the service. Evaluate the complete redaction and recipient-watermark path separately from conversion.
WeasyPrint An HTML/CSS-to-PDF engine is a candidate for application-owned templates rendered from approved external data. It is not a substitute for validating redaction of an arbitrary incoming PDF. The team owns runtime integration and capacity.
Adobe PDF Services API A managed PDF service is a candidate when the team wants to buy document processing while maintaining its own source templates and release policy. Validate the particular operations and input formats required by the corpus, then account for a separate private-delivery integration.
Nutrient A specialist document SDK is a candidate when detailed document behavior should drive the selection. Keep the application's template and disclosure rules outside SDK-specific objects. Evaluate deployment fit, redaction requirements, and rendering fidelity before choosing the SDK integration boundary.
Infrai One key, one bill: a unified API covers PDF capabilities and storage signing over plain REST, with no SDK required. This reduces separate integrations in the sharing path. Retain application-owned templates and translate the published schemas in an adapter. The common contract does not establish cross-provider output fidelity.

A specialist such as Nutrient or a direct service such as Adobe PDF Services API is the better candidate when document-specific acceptance requirements dominate the decision and its evaluation results justify that integration. pdf-lib deserves a close look when the team can own PDF execution and its existing Node.js code already contains the source-generation logic. Infrai is worth trying when the main operating burden is connecting the approved PDF transformation to private delivery while keeping the provider replaceable. None of those choices transfers ownership of disclosure policy.

The expensive mistake is allowing a provider template identifier to become the business rule. It makes a later replacement a policy-reconstruction project, even if the HTTP integration itself takes little code. The limitation of buying a broad API is that the application still owns acceptance testing; Infrai is not suitable as a replacement for a document-specific validation process. Prefer a specialist when its evaluated document behavior is the deciding requirement.

Put the release prerequisite in the preventative code path

Infrai's plain HTTP API has no SDK to install. This language-agnostic REST interface lets a Node.js application and a Go worker use the same published contract without introducing separate SDK dependencies; it doesn't remove the need to implement and test each adapter.

The preventative path starts before deployment: inspect the actual rendering contract, then implement its translation behind the application gate. This runnable Go program fetches Infrai's public discovery manifest and prints the watermark capability entry, including the identifier needed to inspect its full schema through discovery. It reads the key from INFRAI_API_KEY, although public discovery itself requires no key. Save it as main.go and run it with Go. It performs a read, not a document transformation, so it needs no write-idempotency key and sends no personal data.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(value string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        candidate := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        if candidate > delay {
            delay = candidate
        }
    } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        if candidate := time.Until(deadline); candidate > delay {
            delay = candidate
        }
    }
    return delay
}

func run() error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(res.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", res.StatusCode, body)
        }
        var manifest struct {
            Capabilities []json.RawMessage `json:"capabilities"`
        }
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &manifest); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        for _, raw := range manifest.Capabilities {
            var entry struct {
                Method string `json:"method"`
                Path   string `json:"path"`
            }
            if err := json.Unmarshal(raw, &entry); err != nil {
                return err
            }
            if entry.Method == http.MethodPost && entry.Path == "/v1/pdf/watermark" {
                fmt.Println(string(raw))
                return nil
            }
        }
        return fmt.Errorf("watermark capability missing from discovery")
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery attempts exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The client uses a 15-second per-request timeout and at most 4 attempts. HTTP 429 responses trigger exponential backoff that also honors Retry-After; unsuccessful final responses retain their status and body. These are example settings, not a provider SLO. Use the returned discovery path rather than constructing a transformation URL from descriptive prose, and inspect the capability's full request and response schemas before writing the adapter.

The runtime prerequisite is independent of that discovery check. For example, approval for source revision r2 must not authorize source revision r3. A production service must load authorization and review evidence from trusted application state; accepting approval booleans from a download request would defeat the gate. The adapter also needs the reviewed artifact reference, not merely the source document's name, so that rendering cannot silently reopen an unredacted original.

A rendering adapter has to apply the recipient watermark to the approved artifact, preserve the release binding, and return its private output reference; only then should delivery mint an expiring link. A failed or rejected transformation must never cause the original document to be served as a fallback. Keep storage private, use presigned delivery URLs, and never forward the API Authorization header to a returned presigned URL.

Capacity and migration both need a bounded acceptance rule

On-demand rendering avoids retaining a separate permanent copy for every recipient, but it moves document processing into the download path. For capacity planning, measure arrival rate and render time on the actual corpus, then use concurrent work approximately equal to arrival rate times service time as an initial sizing estimate. Bound concurrency and queue depth before opening external sharing, because a burst of legitimate downloads can otherwise consume the capacity needed for ordinary application traffic. These are planning rules, not measured throughput claims for any provider.

Define the download SLO around successful delivery of the correct approved revision to the correct authorized recipient within your chosen time budget. Track rendering and link issuance separately so the team can locate a budget overrun, and keep the privacy prerequisite outside that error budget: missing redaction evidence blocks a release even when availability is under pressure. An expiring link bounds its period of usability; it cannot recall a copy someone already downloaded.

For migration, render the same approved corpus through both adapters, check content removal and recipient labeling, and approve the replacement before routing real downloads to it. Retain the application-owned template revision and recipient mapping throughout. Rollback must still satisfy the same release rule.

This advice does not make watermarks suitable for preventing deliberate extraction, and it is insufficient when the requirement is to prevent an authorized reader from reproducing document content. It also needs adjustment when the application cannot establish that an incoming PDF has been safely redacted. In that case, specialist review and document processing come before any leak-deterrence feature.

Sources

References for evaluating the PDF format and the implementation choices:

  • ISO 32000-2, Portable Document Format
  • pdf-lib documentation
  • Gotenberg documentation
  • WeasyPrint documentation
  • Adobe PDF Services API documentation
  • Nutrient documentation

If an application-owned template and adapter fit your sharing workflow, start with the schemas and examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: Attribute-Evidence Learning with Multimodal Prompt for Generalized Category Discovery
description:
arXiv:2611.12975v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generalized category discovery (GCD) aims to discover novel categories from unlabeled data by leveraging limited labeled samples from old classes. Existing methods that rely solely on visual cues often neglect the multimodal nature of human perception, prompting recent approaches to incorporate textual information such as category tags and attributes. However, these approaches typically entangle global tags and local attributes within a shared global image representation, rendering attributes unreliable and potentially providing misleading cues that can drive the model toward incorrect predictions. To this end, we propose AptM-GCD, a novel multimodal framework that exploits apt textual guidance through attribute evidence learning and multimodal prompt reasoning. Specifically, we design an Attribute-Evidence Learning (AEL) mechanism that treats attributes as localized visual evidence rather than global category descriptors. By interacting attribute embeddings with patch-level visual tokens, AEL identifies reliable attribute-related regions and extracts discriminative local evidence, thereby reducing the impact of noisy or irrelevant attribute cues. Building upon the extracted evidence, we further develop a Multimodal Prompt Learning (MPL) mechanism to bridge local attribute semantics and global visual understanding. MPL converts fine-grained textual evidence into visual prompts and injects them into a multimodal prompt transformer, enabling attribute information to enhance category discrimination through contextual reasoning without enforcing direct global alignment between modalities. Extensive experiments on six datasets demonstrate that AptM-GCD consistently achieves SoTA performance across both fine-grained and generic benchmarks. Moreover, the proposed framework exhibits strong generalization ability, delivering consistent gains under unimodal and class-imbalanced GCD settings.

title: Chem World: A Large-Scale Benchmark and Physics-Aware Framework for Trustworthy Molecular Property Prediction
description:
arXiv:2611.13945v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Molecular property prediction is fundamental to computational chemistry and drug formulation research, yet existing benchmarks remain fragmented across datasets, properties, and evaluation protocols, limiting systematic evaluation of model generalization. We introduce Chem World, a large-scale benchmark integrating 17 public datasets with over 800,000 molecular and chemical-system instances across 10 property tracks, covering single-molecule and multi-component systems, including drug solubility. Chem World provides a unified testbed for evaluating molecular representations and compositional modeling across diverse chemical properties. Building on the benchmark, we propose PACM (Physics-Aware Compositional Modeling), which combines molecular representations with composition-aware modeling and domain-specific physical constraints. Extensive experiments show that molecular language models provide strong and transferable representations, while PACM consistently improves prediction across diverse chemical systems. Chem World and our PACM-powered drug-property prediction Agent support generalizable chemical modeling and offer a foundation for AI-assisted biomedical research and drug formulation development.

title: IC-GNN: Modeling Individualized Brain Community Organization for Disease Prediction
description:
arXiv:2611.13070v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Brain networks exhibit modular organization, where community structures vary substantially across individuals and diseases. Understanding these individual differences is crucial for advancing both basic neuroscience research and precision medicine. However, widely used predefined group-level brain atlases often overlook this heterogeneity. While individualized functional parcellations capture subject-specific variability in community boundaries, they often require lengthy scan times to achieve fine-grained resolution and complicate cross-subject comparisons. To address this trade-off and investigate how individualized community organization captures disease-associated changes across individuals, we propose IC-GNN, an atlas-anchored model that forms distinct, individualized functional communities directly over atlas-defined brain regions. IC-GNN derives discrete, individualized multiscale communities from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data, refines community-guided connections, and adapts shared regional weights to each subject's community context to enable both individualized modeling and group-level comparisons. Across more than 30,000 participants from ABIDE (autism spectrum disorder), ADNI (Alzheimer's disease), and the UK Biobank (depression), IC-GNN achieves the highest performance compared with 15 baseline methods. We further demonstrate that these individualized communities are reproducible within scans and across sessions, and carry predictive power on their own. Furthermore, IC-GNN identifies disease-related shifts in community organization that align with established literature, highlighting a promising approach for modeling individualized community structure for disease prediction and biomarker discovery.

title: MicroLens: Read, Trace, and Rewire the Residual Stream with Two Lenses
description:
arXiv:2611.13322v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Lenses that decode hidden states into words are a popular way to look inside language models, but a heatmap of decoded words only shows what a vector reads as and cannot distinguish whether, or how much, the model uses the information. We present an interactive viewer that puts reading, tracing and editing on the same layers-by-tokens grid of the residual stream. In the viewer, every cell can be decoded with two lenses, the logit lens and the Jacobian lens (J-lens), traced back to the tokens it drew from, and edited, with the rest of the model rerun on the spot. We demonstrate three usage scenarios on Gemma-3-4B-it, backed by sweeps over a few hundred prompts, to show what this tool can discover. First, the two lenses give different directions to write with, each suiting a different edit: the logit lens's word direction sets what a token outputs, while the J-lens's direction changes what later tokens read. Second, in two-hop trivia questions (the capital of the state or country containing a given city), the state or country is readable at the city token from as early as layer 7, and swapping it there can redirect the answer 92-98% of the time; however, at the answer position, the state or country information is not used. Third, when a chat model answers questions with a step-by-step reasoning prompt, the correct answer is often already the top word in the residual stream before any reasoning is written: for 89-92% of retrieval questions and 39-63% of multi-hop and serial ones, far above their respective distractors (at most 5%). However, ordering puzzles are an exception, as the model works them out only once it writes its final reasoning steps. Furthermore, for answers that are visible in the residual stream, the J-lens reads them a layer or two earlier than the logit lens across the different types of question.

title: FlashMotion: Ultra-Fast Long-Term 3D Motion Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.13626v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: 3D human motion generation plays a crucial role in game development, extended reality (XR), digital humans, and embodied simulation. Beyond motion generation, practical pipelines include rigging, retargeting, and rendering, making ultra-fast long-term 3D motion generation without compromising quality valuable for real-time interactive applications. Despite promising progress, high-quality long-horizon motion generation under tight inference budgets remains challenging, owing to 2 coupled bottlenecks: (1) generative strategies that require many sampling steps for high-quality 3D motion generation and (2) model architectures with substantial per-step computational and memory costs for long sequences. We present FlashMotion, a co-designed framework for high-quality long-horizon 3D motion generation under a strict inference budget, covering text-to-motion, music-to-dance, and speech-to-gesture tasks. To enhance trajectory-level efficiency, we introduce a 3D motion-space MeanFlow formulation with kinematic and dynamic consistency constraints for few-step generation, together with an Adaptive Soft masking mechanism for temporally coherent motion editing. To improve per-step efficiency, we design a lightweight non-autoregressive BiMamba architecture with condition-guided state selection and AdaIN-based condition fusion mechanism, enhancing cross-modal alignment and generalization to longer motion sequences. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FlashMotion achieves overall state-of-the-art performance in both quality and efficiency across text-to-motion, speech-to-gesture, and music-to-dance generation. Code is available at FlashMotion (https://github.com/Sun-Happy-YKX/FlashMotion).

title: Put a test message on a Kafka topic without writing a producer first
description:
You wrote a consumer and want to see it handle one message. Writing a throwaway producer app for that is slow. Here are three ways to do it, from fastest to most realistic.

1. One message with kcat

kcat reads from stdin and produces to a topic. -K: tells it the key and value are separated by a colon, and -H adds a header.

echo 'user_1001:{"eventId":"evt_001","userId":"user_1001","status":"ACTIVE"}' \
  | kcat -b localhost:9092 -t user.events -P -K: \
      -H "eventType=USER_CREATED" -H "version=v1"

Two things trip people up:

  • The delimiter splits at its first occurrence. With -K: a key such as user:1001 is cut at the first colon. Pick a delimiter that cannot appear in the key, for example -K'|'.
  • Quote the JSON with single quotes so the shell leaves the double quotes alone.

2. Several messages from a file

Put one key:value pair per line and pass the file with -l:

kcat -b localhost:9092 -t user.events -P -K: -l messages.txt

Messages with the same key go to the same partition, so if your consumer depends on per-key ordering, reuse a key across lines to test it.

3. From Java, when headers and types matter

When the consumer reads headers or you want the same serializer as production, a ProducerRecord is the honest test:

ProducerRecord<String, String> record = new ProducerRecord<>(
    "user.events", "user_1001", objectMapper.writeValueAsString(payload));
record.headers().add("eventType", "USER_CREATED".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
record.headers().add("version", "v1".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
producer.send(record).get();

Header values are bytes. If the consumer decodes them with a different charset than the producer used, the header looks corrupted, so state UTF-8 on both sides.

Check what landed

Read the last message of each partition back, including key and headers:

kcat -b localhost:9092 -t user.events -C -o -1 -e \
  -f 'key=%k headers=%h value=%s\n'

If the key is empty here, the -K delimiter did not match when you produced.

Getting a payload that matches the schema

The slow part is usually not the command but writing JSON that satisfies the schema: every required field, the right types, the nested records. I built a small browser tool for that step. You paste an Avro schema or a JSON Schema, set the topic, key field and headers, and it returns a matching sample payload, the full message, a ProducerRecord snippet and a kcat command:

  • Kafka message generator
  • Avro schema generator if you only have a sample JSON message and need the schema first

The values are fixed placeholders based on field type and name, not random data, and it makes up to 20 messages per run. That is enough to check that a consumer parses the message; it is not a load generator. Everything runs in the browser and the schema is not uploaded.

Summary

Need Use
One message, right now `echo ... \
A batch, or ordering per key {% raw %}kcat -P -K: -l file
Headers and production serializers ProducerRecord in a test
Confirm key, headers and value kcat -C -o -1 -e -f ...

title: Rethinking in Spikes: Mitigating Hallucinations in MDLMs with Step-Aware Decoding
description:
arXiv:2611.12901v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advancements in multimodal diffusion language models (MDLMs) have exhibited strong global modeling capabilities through iterative refinement. We observe that mask uncertainty follows an overall downward trend during iterative denoising, while a few denoising steps exhibit localized entropy spikes closely associated with hallucinations. We argue that anomalous steps can be identified by measuring the entropy deviation of each denoising step from its neighboring temporal window. We hypothesize that discrete token commitment discards the distributional information at masked positions, limiting the continued interaction between candidate semantics and the context during entropy spikes. With this goal, we present StepRefine, a plug-and-play decoding strategy that leverages semantic context to achieve reliable denoising. The core of our method lies in a step-aware switch between discrete denoising and latent refinement. The model employs probability-weighted embeddings at entropy spike steps to preserve diverse reasoning hypotheses and performs multiple rounds of continuous refinement. Meanwhile, a refinement controller monitors distributional stability to reduce unnecessary loops and switch the model back to standard discrete denoising. Through extensive experiments, StepRefine demonstrates significant hallucination mitigation across different MDLMs on multimodal benchmarks.

title: Go from idea to first paying customer with your coding agent and the Whop CLI
description:
I write the developer tutorials at Whop, and most of them are code. This one is mostly prompts, because the parts of starting a business that pull you out of your editor aren't code: creating a product, setting a price, forming an LLC, and verifying your identity so you can get paid.

The Whop CLI lets your coding agent, like Claude Code, Cursor, or Codex, do most of this from your terminal. We're going to go through it in five steps, and each step has a prompt you can paste into your agent. We ran every prompt through a coding agent before publishing, and the dialogues below are shortened from those runs, with made-up founders.

The original post has a one-minute video of an agent forming an LLC through the Whop CLI, and prompt cards that open straight in Claude Code, Cursor, or Codex. You can find it on the Whop blog.

Step 1: Prepare your tools

Throughout this tutorial, we're only going to use a single tool: the Whop CLI. It lets you take actions on Whop from your terminal, and it lets your agent do the same with the prompts you give it.

First, let's install the Whop CLI and log in to your Whop account:

npm install -g @whop/cli
whop login --method oauth

Keep in mind that once you log in, the CLI acts on your live Whop account. That's why every prompt in this tutorial asks the agent to show you what it's going to do before it does it.

There are also three things you'll do yourself on Whop.com: add apps to your whop if you're selling a membership to it, use the LLC formation wizard if any founder lives in the US (since it's the safe place to enter a Social Security number), and verify your identity.

Step 2: Create your product

Now, let's create a product. Products on Whop always have a name, a price, and what the buyer gets once the purchase is complete.

First, let's plan out what you want to sell:

I want to sell [what you're selling] to [who it's for]. Ask me what I still need to decide, one question at a time. Then write a product name, headline, description, price, and how the buyer receives it. Tell me if this may fall under Whop's prohibited businesses list. Don't invent facts.

Then, create the product and set its price:

Use the Whop CLI. On my Whop business [business name], or a new one if I don't have it, add a product called [product name] with the headline [headline] and description [description]. Add a [one-time or monthly] price of [price]. Show me the values first. Then tell me exactly what a buyer pays at checkout and give me the link.

If you're shipping a physical product, add "collect a shipping address at checkout" to the prompt above. It's easiest to set this when you create the product.

Step 3: Decide what the buyer gets

The product is ready, but buyers don't get anything in return yet. Depending on what you're selling, the setup is different:

How the buyer gets it Good for What you set up
Directly from you Physical products and e-commerce, in-store sales, events, client work If you ship, collect a shipping address at checkout. Whop takes the payment, and you deliver
In your own software SaaS and other tools An access check or license key in your app
On Whop Educational programs, paid groups, newsletters, files, coaching calls The relevant app on the product, from your dashboard

Your agent can read the Whop docs page that fits your setup and walk you through it, even if buyers get access inside your own app:

Use the Whop CLI. On my Whop business [business name], a buyer of [product name] should receive [what they get] after paying. Read the page below that fits, and check Whop's docs for anything it doesn't cover:
- Physical products: https://docs.whop.com/supported-business-models/dtc-ecommerce.md
- In-store sales: https://docs.whop.com/supported-business-models/brick-and-mortar.md
- Events: https://docs.whop.com/supported-business-models/events.md
- Client work: https://docs.whop.com/supported-business-models/agency-services.md
- In my own software: https://docs.whop.com/supported-business-models/saas.md
- On Whop: https://whop.com/blog/add-apps-to-whop.md
Then tell me whether they'll get it directly from me, in my own software, or on Whop. Show me what you'd change and wait for my OK. If any part needs code or happens outside Whop, tell me exactly what I have to do. Then tell me how to check a buyer receives it.

Step 4: Form the LLC

Choose a state and check the name

For most businesses, the most straightforward option is to form the LLC in the state where you live and do business. But you can also live in one state and form your LLC in another. Wyoming is the default on Whop, and Delaware is another popular option.

  • If you live in the US: Forming in your own state means one set of fees. If you form somewhere else and run the business from home, you usually have to register in your home state too, so you pay that state's annual fees and taxes on top. Our LLC guide covers this in more detail.
  • If you live outside the US: Your country's taxes still apply, and the LLC files a US tax form every year. Which form depends on how many owners it has. Our guide on starting an LLC outside the US covers this in more detail.

Let's choose a state and check the name:

I want a US LLC. I live in [country, plus state if in the US] and I'll run the business from [place]. Explain what forming in [state] means for me, including what I may owe at home. Say what you're unsure of and don't choose for me. Then give me the state's official name search so I can check [business name]. Don't say a name is free unless you saw it there.

Launch the LLC

After the prompt below, your agent asks for the founders' details. Then, based on where the founders live, it either asks for your OK to submit or sends you to the LLC formation wizard. It won't pay for anything.

Use the Whop CLI to help me form an LLC on my Whop business [business name]. Company name: [company name]. State: [state].
Ask me for each founder's details. Never ask for or accept a Social Security number in this chat.
If any founder has a US home address, stop. Look up my business ID. Give me https://whop.com/form-company/ followed by that ID, and a list of what to type there.
Otherwise, show me every value and wait for my OK before you send it. Then give me the checkout link and total.
Use a new idempotency key after any error. If you get a business type error, wait a minute and retry once, then stop and tell me.
Don't choose a state, split or add-on for me. Don't pay for anything.

What the agent won't do

This is the longest prompt in the tutorial because it's the step where a wrong guess costs the most. Each line is there for a reason:

  • It never takes a Social Security number. If any founder has a US home address, the agent stops and sends you to Whop's LLC formation wizard, where you type the number yourself. That way, it never ends up in your chat history.
  • It shows every value before sending. You confirm the founders, the ownership split, and the address before anything reaches Whop.
  • It doesn't choose for you. The state, the ownership split, and add-ons like expedited EIN processing are your decisions, so the agent asks instead of filling in defaults.
  • It doesn't pay. The agent stops at a checkout link and a total, and you pay yourself.
  • It stops instead of looping. After an error, the agent uses a new idempotency key (a unique ID that tells Whop whether a request is new or a repeat), so the retry isn't mixed up with the failed request. A new business can also return a business type error on its first try, so the agent waits a minute, retries once, and then stops and tells you.

If one of the founders lives in the US

When a founder lives in the US, the prompt tells your agent to send you to the wizard. In our run, it went like this:

You: Ana Reyes is primary. ana@example.com, +1 307 555 0142, 100 Example Ave, Cheyenne, WY 82001, USA. Born 1990-06-15. 60%. Ben Cole. ben@example.com, +44 20 7946 0123, 10 Test Street, London, SW1A 1AA, UK. Born 1988-03-02. 40%. Use the registered agent address. No expedited EIN. No website.

Agent: Ana's home address is in the US, so I stopped here. Nothing was sent through the CLI and nothing was paid, so I don't have a checkout link or total for you.

Finish the filing on this page: https://whop.com/form-company/biz_abc123

(A table of what to type for the company and each founder.)

Social Security numbers: if the page asks for Ana's, type it only on that page, never in this chat.

Nothing from your chat carries over to the wizard, so you fill in your details again there. The wizard asks for the SSN in its Founders section. Then, you review the documents Whop prepares and go to checkout.

If all founders live outside the US

When every founder lives outside the US, there's no SSN to enter, so the agent stays in the CLI. It shows you every value, waits for your OK, and gives you the checkout link. In our run, it also caught a mistake before sending anything:

You: Ana Reyes is primary. ana@example.com, +44 20 7946 0123, 10 Test Street, London, Greater London, SW1A 1AA, UK. Born 1990-06-15. 60%. Ben Cole. ben@example.com, +44 20 7946 0124, 22 Sample Road, Manchester, Greater Manchester, M1 1AA, UK. Born 1988-03-02. 30%. Use the registered agent address. No expedited EIN. No website.

Agent: The ownership shares add up to 90%, not 100% (Ana 60% + Ben 30%). An LLC needs exactly 100%, and I won't pick the split for you, so nothing has been sent.

Both home addresses are in the UK, so the US stop doesn't apply and we can stay with the CLI.

(Every value it plans to send.)

You: Ben has 40%. Everything else is right. OK, send it.

Agent: The Lantern Labs LLC formation went through, and it's ready for you to pay.

  • Checkout link: https://whop.com/checkout/ch_abc123/
  • Total: $500.00 USD

I didn't open the link or pay anything. The formation status on the business is draft, and the CLI's spec says the filing is submitted once payment completes. So Whop has accepted these details for checkout, but nothing has been filed yet.

A Wyoming LLC costs $500 on Whop. After you complete the checkout, you sign Form SS-4, the IRS application for your EIN (your company's US tax ID). It can take up to 8 weeks to get your EIN unless you chose expedited EIN processing.

After the payment

Once you pay, Whop submits the application to the state. The status, your documents, and any signing links are attached to your business, so your agent can read them later through the CLI:

Use the Whop CLI. Read my Whop business [business name], including its company_formation field. Tell me the formation status, which documents are ready and what needs my signature, with links. Don't change anything.

Step 5: Your first sale

Now, you have a product, an LLC, and a way to deliver what your customers pay for. Your first customer will likely come from your circle, your waitlist, a community you're part of, or a small paid test.

Let's find your first customer:

I sell [product] at [price] to [who it's for]. My link is [checkout link]. Help me list the first ten people to contact from my network, waitlist or communities, and write one short, honest message for each group. Don't make up results.

Once someone pays, you can see it on Whop.com under Dashboard > Payments, or you can ask your agent for a breakdown. To withdraw, you need to verify your identity and add a payout method on Whop.com.

Let's start your identity verification:

Use the Whop CLI. Start identity verification for my Whop business [business name] and give me the hosted link. Don't ask me for ID numbers in this chat.

What's next

Now that you know how to go from an idea to a business without leaving your development environment, you can keep running it from the same place. Our guides on running your business from Claude Code, Cursor, or Codex, adding free trials, and adding promo codes cover what comes after your first sale. For everything else, check out the Whop developer docs.

If you try these prompts, let me know in the comments where your agent got stuck.

title: You Can Stop Reading the Code. You Can't Stop Knowing What It Should Do
description:
A lot of people write that developers using AI no longer understand their own code. I barely read code myself, so here is what I have in place of reading it.

For the last few weeks I keep running into articles about the same thing. Developers with AI write code much faster, but they no longer understand what they ship.

There is even a name for it: comprehension debt. In simple words, it is the gap between how much code there is in a system and how much of it any person actually understands.

The worst part about this debt is that you can't see it. The tests are green, the code looks clean, and nobody can explain anymore why it works the way it does.

So, have I lost control too?

I have to be honest about one thing. For more than a year I've barely read the code my agents write. So on paper, I'm exactly the person these articles are about.

I thought about it for a while and came to the conclusion that no, I haven't. Not because I'm special, but because over these two years a system slowly grew around my agents, and it does what reading code used to do.

The real question is not whether you read the code. It's whether someone in the system knows what that code is supposed to do.

That system is what this post is about.

We have been here before

In the early 1950s almost all programs were written in machine code or assembler. When Fortran appeared, people met it with a lot of distrust.

John Backus, who created it, later remembered that programmers back then saw their work as an art that could not be automated.

The arguments against it sound very familiar today:

  • the code a compiler generates is worse than code written by hand
  • you don't understand what it actually does
  • so you won't be able to debug it

In the end a simple thing won. Programmers stopped thinking about registers and memory addresses and started thinking about the problem itself.

I think the same thing is happening now, just one level higher. Instead of functions and classes, I think about how payment should work, who is allowed to see what, and what happens if a client changes their mind.

But an agent is not a compiler

There is one important difference, and this is where the analogy breaks.

A compiler always turns the same code into the same result. Once it matures, you can simply trust it.

An agent doesn't work like that. It can do one thing today and another tomorrow. It fills gaps in the task with guesses, and sometimes it even bends a test to fit its code so the test goes green.

If a person no longer reads the code, someone else has to do what reading used to do. And that someone can't be the same agent that wrote it.

Here is what that someone looks like in my setup.

1. Write down the intent before the code

The first thing is to write down what should be built before a single line of code exists.

Why does it matter so much? The reason is simple. Understanding of a system used to live in the head of the developer who wrote it. Now the code is written by an agent that remembers nothing after its session ends.

If the intent isn't written down anywhere, in a month nobody will tell you why payment works the way it does. That's no longer a code problem, it's a memory problem for the whole team.

Planning starts with an interview

Every bigger task starts with an interview. A planner asks me questions one by one until nothing is left to guess.

What comes out of it is a plan split into phases. For every phase it says not only what to do, but also how to tell it was done right.

The tests are then written from these descriptions, from what the client does, and not from what the agent wrote. If a test is written after the code by the same agent, it will just confirm what the agent already believed.

Finished plans don't disappear

This is the part people rarely talk about. Every finished plan goes into an archive: the plan, its phases and the reports on how they were done.

When months later I need to understand why something was built a certain way, I don't dig into the code. I open the plan and see how the thinking went, what the options were and what was decided.

Understanding of the system now lives not in someone's head and not in the code, but in these records.

2. Separate who writes from who checks

The second solution grew out of a simple observation: an agent can't properly check itself.

Not because it lies. It checks with the same blind spots it had while writing the code.

Auditors came first

Funny enough, in my case this happened almost by itself, because auditors appeared before agents that write code.

At first I wrote everything by hand and asked AI to review it and point out weak spots. Then I started letting agents apply those suggestions. First small fixes, then whole features, and now I delegate parts of the business logic.

But the auditors always stayed separate from the ones who write.


My trust grew step by step, and the auditors came first, not the agents that write code.

How it works now

When an agent finishes its part, the work is checked by a separate agent that can't change anything, it can only read. It doesn't see the writer's reasoning, only the code changes and the plan.

It checks not only whether the code works, but whether it does what the plan says.

If something is wrong, the system creates a fix task by itself. But not forever: after three attempts it stops and waits for me. If it didn't work three times, the problem is most likely not in the code, but in the task.

On top of that there is a security auditor that looks for typical holes and thinks about how this specific product could be broken. And an agent that simply runs the build, the linter and the tests and honestly reports what ran and what it said.


The one who writes the code and the one who checks it are always different agents.

The numbers surprised me a bit. Over the last 30 days the agents that check ran almost as often as the agents that write, and checking cost about five times less.


Agent runs across all my projects over the last 30 days, data from Swarmery. Cost is approximate, estimated from tokens.

"Don't know" is a separate answer

One more detail I didn't get right away. If a check couldn't give an answer, for example it timed out or couldn't read the changes, that is neither a fail nor a pass. It's a separate state: "don't know".

I used to have "done", "not checked" and "the process just died" all showing the same green badge, and I was lying to myself a bit. When I split them, the dashboard got uglier, but honest.

One thing in the data I didn't expect: in 8 cases out of 100 reviews the checker, which is only allowed to read, changed files anyway. The system caught it and didn't accept that verdict.


Verdicts of the separate checker: 100 reviews of phases and plans, Oct 10 to Nov 4.

When you don't look at the code yourself anymore, an honest "don't know" is worth more than a pretty green badge.

3. Check the product, not only the code

For me this is probably the most important one. Tests have one problem: they only check what they were asked to check.

In one of my earlier runs, the agents marked five phases as done, and the separate checker found serious problems in three of them. All the tests were green. Nobody lied, the problems were just exactly where the tests didn't look.

And most often they don't look at the business logic: what happens when several people with different permissions use the product at the same time.

Agents as manual testers

So I have manual testing done by agents. Let me show it on one of my projects, a platform where clients bid on cars from auctions and an operator places those bids on the real auction.

There is a scenario for it that covers the whole path, from a client signing up to the invoice and delivery. Before a run, the system creates test people: an admin and three clients.

The agents log in as each of them and go through the steps in a browser, like a real tester. Then they check the database and the logs to see whether what should have happened actually happened.

They never touch real lots, the system makes copies just for the test. The real Telegram bot, email and payments are switched off during the run.

The rules for the tester matter more than the run

  • The tester doesn't fix bugs. It only finds and describes them, because the one who fixes shouldn't be the one who checks.
  • It doesn't stop at the first failure. It records it and moves on.
  • No step can be skipped silently. Every step must have a status.
  • Every failure needs proof. And a plain script checks that the proof exists, not another model.

At the end I get a report with the status of every step and a list of bugs with steps to reproduce them.

Checks only see what you show them

There is a limit here too, and I want to name it honestly. The run happens on a local environment, so it can't see how production is configured.

When I was writing a handbook for the operator of this project, it turned out that payments and deposit top-ups were built and tested, but simply not switched on in the production settings.

So the code was right, the tests were green, and the most important part of the business, money from the client, wouldn't have worked in production. It wasn't the tests that caught it. It was someone walking through the whole path with the eyes of the operator.

Checks only cover the part of the world you showed them. Production settings need to be shown too.

4. Check by risk, and fix the factory

A fair question: if all of this exists, how often does it run? A full manual run is expensive, it takes the test environment for hours, so running it after every small change makes no sense.

I ended up with two rhythms:

  • Sprints. Development is split into two-week sprints. After each one I sum up the results, run full audits and run the manual tests.
  • Risk. If important business logic changed, or a new process appeared that many others depend on, I run the checks right away, without waiting for the sprint to end.


Full checks follow two rhythms: the calendar and the risk.

I think the second rule matters more. How often you check should depend on how much a mistake costs, not on the calendar.

What I do with audit reports

I said I barely read code, but it's more accurate to say I don't read it line by line.

During an audit I skim the changes and carefully read what the auditor reports. If it found a problem, I go into the code on purpose, straight to that place, and try to trace the whole chain: not only where the bug is, but why it appeared at all.

Often it turns out the agent didn't simply make a mistake, it was set up the wrong way. For example, I had an agent that kept reaching into files outside its own working copy. It still finished its tasks, so I wouldn't have noticed for a long time.

The reason was simple: its instructions were written before agents started working in separate copies, and nobody ever updated them.

Fix the factory, not only the product

So after that kind of review I don't just fix the bug. I fix the skill or the agent that let it happen, and make a new plan so the same mistake doesn't come back.


When an audit finds a problem, I fix not only the bug, but also what allowed it to appear.

A regular developer fixes the product. I mostly fix the factory that makes it.

That, I think, is the answer to whether you lose control. Control just moves from individual lines of code to how the whole system works.

Where the limit is

It would be dishonest to say all this protects you from everything.

All these checks share one limit: they catch code that doesn't match the intent, but they won't save you if the intent itself is wrong.

If I write in the plan that the deposit is always returned to the client, and the business needs something else, the agents will honestly build it, the tests will honestly check it, and everything will be green.

So my responsibility didn't get smaller. It got bigger, it just moved to a different place.

I used to spend most of my time on code, and often there was no energy left for the details of the business. Now agents and auditors take the code, and I can calmly think about how payment should work, what to do with a client who won a lot and disappeared, or who exactly should see other people's bids.

So, are developers losing attention?

I think some are, and the articles about it are not written for nothing.

The problem is not that people stopped reading code. It's that they didn't replace that reading with anything.

When programmers moved from assembler to Fortran, attention didn't disappear, it moved one level up. The same is happening now. Only this time the compiler can make mistakes, so you have to build a system you can trust yourself.

That takes time. It took me two years, and it's still not perfect.

But I think this is now the main job of a developer: not writing code and not reading it, but knowing what it should do, and having a way to check that it does exactly that.

How does it work for you? Do you still read every line your agents write, or have you moved to checks too? I'd like to hear where you draw the line.

Sources

  • Comprehension Debt, Addy Osmani
  • From Technical Debt to Cognitive and Intent Debt, Margaret-Anne Storey
  • The History of FORTRAN I, II, and III, John Backus
  • Programming in America in the 1950s, John Backus

Originally published on Swarmery on Substack, where I write about building with Claude Code agents in public. Swarmery itself is open source: atretyak1985.github.io/swarmery.

title: Towards Text-Only Remote Sensing Scene Classification via Semantic Proxy
description:
arXiv:2611.13851v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Remote sensing scene classification (RSSC) is traditionally formulated as a vision-centric problem, where inference relies on rich visual representations extracted from images. In this work, we revisit this assumption by introducing text-only RSSC, a new problem setting that investigates whether remote sensing scenes can be recognized using only textual semantic representations. To enable this study, we propose SeProRS, which reformulates RSSC as a text-only classification task through semantic proxy generation. Specifically, a vision-language model (VLM) is first employed to convert remote sensing images into textual descriptions, termed semantic proxies, which are then encoded by a text embedding model for scene classification. This decoupled pipeline provides a unified and reproducible benchmark for evaluating text-only scene understanding. Furthermore, we investigate representative prompting strategies and proxy generators, and analyze their impact on classification performance, text embedding behavior, cross-generator transferability, and efficiency. Extensive experiments on three well-known RSSC datasets show that semantic proxies can preserve substantial discriminative information, while also revealing inherent limitations of purely text-based scene understanding. This paper does not aim to replace image-based RSSC, but instead establishes a new research direction by quantifying the feasibility and boundaries of semantic proxy-based scene recognition. The proposed benchmark and analysis provide a foundation for future research on efficient and modality-reduced remote sensing scene understanding. The source code and datasets will be accessible at https://github.com/sstary/SSRS.

title: The WoW: A Large-Scale World Knowledge Corpus for Full-Lifecycle LLM Training
description:
arXiv:2611.13487v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing Chinese educational corpora often suffer from fragmented coverage and a lack of systematic organization. In this paper, we propose WoW (\textbf{Wo}rld Kno\textbf{w}ledge), a large-scale dataset designed for the full-cycle training of foundation models. The construction of this dataset is driven by an Educational Knowledge Graph, which serves as a taxonomic backbone for the systematic collection and completion of missing educational modules across all levels. Compared to previous versions, this iteration provides enhanced systematicity, superior quality, and a larger scale, while incorporating multimodal signals and supporting every stage of model development. Experiments demonstrate that WoW significantly improves model performance across diverse benchmarks. To facilitate community research, we further provide an interactive platform for graph-based data selection and retrieval.

title: Pick your phone route before you pick a voice AI framework
description:
Here's a view we hold firmly: work out how calls will reach your agent before you choose the framework. SIP trunking is the reliable path for production phone traffic, and WebRTC belongs to calls that start in a browser. That one choice also decides, quietly, whether a caller who asks for a human can ever get one.

Pipelines and models matter, of course. But what bites teams a month in is usually the phone side, so that's the lens here.

The transfer that isn't there

Pipecat is a lovely piece of engineering. A call is a pipeline of processors passing frames along, and the quickstart chains transport input, Deepgram speech-to-text, Silero voice activity detection, an OpenAI model, Cartesia text-to-speech and transport output. The transport at each end is swappable, so the same agent logic can answer a browser over WebRTC or a phone call over a carrier WebSocket. If it's Twilio, set the input and output sample rates to 8000, since Twilio streams 8 kHz mono audio and you don't want to resample.

Here's the catch. Pipecat's telephony guide lists its WebSocket integrations for Twilio, Telnyx, Plivo and Exotel with "No advanced call center features like transfers or reconnects". The carrier WebSocket is the fastest way to get a bot on a phone number, and it's also a route where "let me put you through to someone" has nowhere to go.

Transfers in Pipecat come from Daily PSTN or a SIP connection, which Pipecat lists for transfers, forwarding and multi-party calls. None of that is hard to set up. It's just much nicer to choose it on day one than to discover it after the demo, when someone in support asks how a caller reaches them.

LiveKit starts from SIP

LiveKit Agents comes at it from the other end. Your agent is a participant in a room on the LiveKit media server, and phone callers join that room over SIP. An inbound trunk takes calls from your carrier and a dispatch rule sends each caller, and your agent, into a room. Dialling out is an outbound trunk plus a SIP participant.

Transfers are native here: cold transfers over SIP REFER, plus agent-assisted transfers. LiveKit Cloud also sells US local and toll-free numbers, so you can skip a separate carrier if all your callers are in the US.

Self-hosting is where the phone side gets heavier. LiveKit says plainly that "the SIP service needs to be deployed separately", and its SIP signalling port and media port range have to be open to the internet. Budget a bit of ops time for that.

LiveKit deserves real credit on testing, too. The Python starter ships simulations that play whole conversations against your agent, plus a debugger that steps through one text turn at a time.

TEN and Vocode, quickly

TEN Framework builds an agent as a graph of extensions, and its default real-time transport runs on Agora, so the voice assistant example wants an Agora App ID and App Certificate next to your model keys. There's a WebSocket example and a SIP call example in the repo. The part to read slowly is the licence file: Apache 2.0 with added conditions from Agora. You can't host the framework on end-user devices like mobile phones, and you can't deploy it in a way that competes with Agora's offerings. For an on-device product or a voice platform, those two lines can settle the decision before any code is written.

Vocode is an MIT Python library and one of the earliest open voice agent projects, with inbound and outbound phone calls and integrations for lots of speech and voice providers. If you have a Vocode codebase and you're weighing a move, Pipecat is the shortest hop, since both are Python pipelines.

Your browser demo is too kind

One more phone-side trap. Most phone calls still reach the agent as 8 kHz audio, while a browser demo runs at 16 kHz. An agent that sounds sharp in a web test can mishear names and numbers on a real line, and how much depends on the speech-to-text model and the phone path. Place actual calls from a mobile and a landline before you commit to anything.

What's still on your plate

Even with the right route, a framework gives you the real-time loop as code and stops there. Pipecat is an excellent base, and production deployment still needs significant plumbing around it. There's no screen where a support lead edits the greeting without a pull request, and no outbound dialler with calling hours. Reviewing finished calls is yours to build as well.

That gap is where Dograh, the open-source AI voice agent platform we build, sits. It runs its call pipeline on our own fork of Pipecat, and you can self-host it or run it on our cloud.

Transfer Call in our case works on Twilio, Telnyx, Plivo, Cloudonix and Asterisk ARI, so the hand-off question from earlier has an answer on each of those carriers.

After each call, a QA node scores every step separately with tags, a 1-10 score, sentiment and a summary, so call review isn't a side project.

Our rough rule for the frameworks themselves: if your developers want Python control and transport freedom, start with Pipecat and plan a Daily PSTN or SIP route for transfers before launch. If you'd rather have native SIP and a media server you can also use for video, LiveKit Agents fits better, and LiveKit Cloud saves you running the SIP service.

If you've shipped a phone agent on Pipecat or LiveKit, which route did you end up on for transfers, and did you find out before launch or after?

The licence terms, transports and remaining build work for all five projects sit side by side in our comparison of open-source voice agent frameworks for phone calls.

title: The 50-Millisecond Verdict: Why UI Design is the Single Most Critical Factor in Brand Survival
description:
Cognitive neuroscience research proves that a human user forms an emotional and credibility judgment of your digital presence within 50 milliseconds (0.05 seconds). That is less than the blink of an eye. In those first 50 milliseconds, visitors have not read a single sentence of your value proposition; they have not reviewed your client testimonials or inspected your pricing tiers.

Their subconscious brain has processed only one thing: the visual posture of your user interface.

The Anatomy of Instant Perceived Authority

If your typography is unrefined, your margins are inconsistent by 4 pixels, or your hero section stutters upon scroll, the user’s limbic system instantly registers amateurism and operational instability. Conversely, when an interface presents:

  • Flawless Typographic Hierarchy: Tightly tracked brutalist display type contrasted with surgical utilitarian monospace captions.
  • OLED Pure Black Contrast (#000000): Giving the interface infinite perceived depth on modern displays.
  • Micro-Pixel Alignment: Every card, button, and container snapping to an unyielding 8pt grid system.

The visitor immediately assumes that the engineering, security, and customer service behind the company are held to the same immaculate standard. User interface design is not decorative veneer; it is the ultimate proxy for operational competence.

Authored by *Behnia Amirimanesh, Founder & Creative Director of **Amiry Design.*

title: Lipschitz-Controlled Flow Matching for Robust Image Restoration
description:
arXiv:2611.13995v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Flow-matching models can produce high-quality image restorations, but their learned dynamics may amplify small input perturbations and make reconstructions unstable. We introduce LipsFlower to reduce this amplification. We derive stability bounds for Flow-from-$Y$, which initializes the ordinary differential equation from a noise-perturbed observation, as well as for observation-conditioned posterior sampling, which conditions the velocity field on the observation throughout integration. Based on this analysis, we develop LipHDiT, a Lipschitz-aware hourglass diffusion transformer that serves as the vector-field architecture of LipsFlower. LipHDiT incorporates stabilized approximate spectral normalization, bounded modulation, and convex residual mixing. We also use adversarial finite-radius gain regularization at sampled interpolation states to penalize excessive sensitivity to the state and, for conditional sampling, the observation. We test both formulations on blind face restoration, measuring adversarial robustness and the perceptual quality of the reconstructions. LipsFlower reduces perturbation amplification while keeping restoration quality competitive with the evaluated baselines. These results suggest that Lipschitz-aware flow matching can improve the stability of generative image restoration.

title: Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II: Unlocking the Memory Potential of Pre-trained File Operations for Long-Horizon Tasks via On-Policy Distillation
description:
arXiv:2611.14009v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Language-model agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks whose interaction histories exceed the model's active context. They must therefore decide what to write down and what to read back, and when to do either. Recent work has begun to use on-policy distillation (OPD) to make memory control part of the policy, relying on memory tools and compaction protocols that lie outside either model's pre-training. However, this weakens the distillation on both sides: the teacher cannot give useful guidance on an interface it has never used, and the student samples too few meaningful memory actions for that guidance to take effect. To study this problem, we introduce Coding Agent Memory Gym II (CAMG-II), a suite of long-horizon agentic-RL environments spanning Shop, Coding, AutoResearch, General, and Visual. Alongside each environment's native task interface, CAMG-II provides ordinary Bash access and an episode-persistent workspace, enabling the policy to create, revise, search, and reuse files as memory across context replacements. We also introduce Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II (CAMP-II), which trains a single policy jointly across all five environments with fully asynchronous OPD to learn this file-based memory behavior directly from a frozen teacher with a prior for file operations. On CAMG-II, CAMP-II obtains 2.97 times the gain of the strongest OPD baseline. The memory behavior CAMP-II learns generalizes to two external benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, with improved success rates.

title: Where should gradient clipping go in a mixed-precision LoRA training step?
description:
I work on CloudGPU. When you use PyTorch gradient scaling, clip after scaler.unscale_(optimizer) and before scaler.step(optimizer). Clipping scaled gradients changes the meaning of the threshold. During gradient accumulation, wait until the effective batch is complete before unscaling.

1. Identify who owns the training step

The function below is for a custom, single-optimizer PyTorch loop using CUDA autocast with float16. It is not an instruction to add a second scaler inside a trainer that already manages mixed precision. In a managed trainer, use its documented clipping hook instead.

Construct the optimizer from the adapter parameters you actually intend to train. Frozen parameters do not become trainable just because you include them in a clipping call.

2. Put the operations in an explicit order 

import torch


def adapter_step(model, optimizer, scaler, inputs, targets, loss_fn):
    # Inputs, targets and the prepared model already belong to CUDA.
    optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    trainable = [p for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad]
    if not trainable:
        raise ValueError("No trainable parameters")

    with torch.autocast(device_type="cuda", dtype=torch.float16):
        loss = loss_fn(model(inputs), targets)
    if loss.ndim != 0 or not torch.isfinite(loss.detach()).item():
        raise ValueError("Expected a finite scalar loss")

    scaler.scale(loss).backward()
    scaler.unscale_(optimizer)
    torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(
        trainable, max_norm=1.0, error_if_nonfinite=True,
    )
    scaler.step(optimizer)
    scaler.update()
    return loss.detach()

Create one torch.amp.GradScaler("cuda") for the training loop, outside this function, and pass it in. The clipping threshold is an illustrative setting, not a recommendation validated for your adapter. The function assumes one update per call and that the optimizer owns the intended trainable parameters.

The non-finite checks are a fail-fast diagnostic choice. A failed gradient check raises before the update; stop and investigate rather than catching it and silently continuing the same step. PyTorch's normal scaler-managed path can instead skip an update when gradients are non-finite. Choose the behavior deliberately.

3. Adjust the boundary for accumulation

If several microbatches form one update, zero once at the beginning of the accumulation group. Keep the scale unchanged while accumulating. Unscale and clip once after the final backward call, then step and update once. Weight each microbatch's loss according to the effective-batch reduction, including a shorter final group; do not paste this one-batch function unchanged into an accumulation loop.

Official PyTorch mixed-precision examples document unscaling, clipping and accumulation. Use your model's own forward/loss contract; the example assumes a tensor-returning model and a scalar loss.

For server-side task limits around a custom training job, see the CloudGPU integration guide.

Related CloudGPU video: This Video Was Made by AI. Now Run AI Yourself. It is remote-compute context, not a LoRA training demonstration.

This function was syntax-checked, not run as a training experiment. No convergence, memory or performance result is asserted.

title: Point-in-Time Encoders for Earnings Calls
description:
arXiv:2611.14325v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Text encoders turn earnings calls into vectors for search, for language models that answer from retrieved passages, and for forecasting models. A live retriever can use an encoder trained once on all available text, as finance retrievers are, but a backtest needs an encoder that read no text written after the date of each vector. To address this look-ahead bias, from 412,248 calls we train vintages under four pretraining recipes, with yearly cutoffs from 2010 to 2024, and each vintage reads only text dated on or before its cutoff. We then fine-tune each vintage on the question-answer pairs of the calls themselves. The vintages we train on calls alone, with 33.8M parameters, retrieve answers on held-out calls better than the general retrievers we tested in every test quarter. Their vectors also raise by about half the rank correlation between next-day returns and forecasts built from past returns and firm size. When each vintage continues the previous one, a later vintage retrieves better on earlier quarters than the vintage available at the time, and a point-in-time language model that answers from the passages the later vintage retrieves inherits the gain. The 2024 vintage of our families also forecasts earnings surprises better, although the interval of this gain includes zero on calls that no vintage read. It forecasts returns no better, so point-in-time vintages matter most for retrieval and little for forecasts of returns.
