title: AnchorMTS: Multi-View Signal Representation and Forecast-Anchored Fusion for Long-Term Time-Series Forecasting
description:
arXiv:2611.13794v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-term time-series forecasters typically optimize a single numerical representation, even though the same history exposes complementary geometry, recurrence, and semantic structure. We propose AnchorMTS, which derives self-aligned visual and textual views from each observed window and uses them only to refine a complete numerical forecast. A trainable evidence path produces a candidate forecast, while a parameter-free output projection enforces an exact per-variable bound on its displacement from the numerical anchor. Across six benchmarks and four horizons, AnchorMTS achieves the best macro MSE/MAE (0.336/0.367) among seven supervised baselines and wins 18 of 24 MSE settings against the cellwise baseline envelope; removing the auxiliary path raises macro MSE to 0.340. The projection leaves 95.8% of candidate refinements unchanged while yielding zero bound violations, showing that complementary multi-view evidence can improve forecasting while its final influence remains explicitly controlled.

title: ABRR: Transforming Temporal Sentence Grounding with Wasserstein-Adaptive Refinement and Precision Ranking
description:
arXiv:2611.13310v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Temporal Sentence Grounding (TSG) aims to localize temporal segments in untrimmed videos that correspond to natural language queries, a critical task for video understanding with applications in video retrieval, summarization, and human-computer interaction. Despite significant progress driven by transformer-based models, existing TSG methods suffer from two key limitations: quantization errors due to temporal downsampling, which misalign segment boundaries, and suboptimal ranking of predictions based on semantic matching rather than localization precision. To address these challenges, we propose the Adaptive Boundary Refinement and Ranking (ABRR) framework, a novel, model-agnostic post-processing approach that enhances the performance of any TSG model without retraining. ABRR integrates three innovative components: (1) Temporal Distribution Smoothing, which mitigates noise in predicted score distributions using Gaussian kernel convolution; (2) Boundary Refinement via Optimal Transport, which leverages the 2-Wasserstein distance and Sinkhorn iterations to align coarse segment boundaries with true temporal moments, grounded in Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport theory; and (3) Quality-Driven Re-Ranking, which reorders predictions using a composite score balancing localization precision and semantic relevance. By correcting quantization errors and prioritizing accurately localized segments, ABRR achieves substantial improvements over state-of-the-art TSG models. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, including Charades-STA, ActivityNet Captions, and QVHighlights, demonstrate consistent gains at stringent IoU thresholds (e.g., IoU=0.7), alongside enhanced ranking performance. The framework's computational efficiency and compatibility with existing models make it a versatile and impactful solution for real-world TSG applications.

title: Why a CSS rotate with will-change: transform makes images and text blurry
description:
If an element is rotated or scaled and has will-change: transform, the browser can rasterise it once and then resample that bitmap every time it moves. Text and thin UI edges come out soft, and no amount of image quality fixes it. On my site, app screenshots looked pixelated because every card had a 0.9deg rotation under will-change: transform and a hover scale. Removing the tilt, the scale and the will-change made them sharp.

The report that started this was short: the images on the Masareef, Rafiq and Nafis project pages looked pixelated and bad. The files on disk were fine. Every screenshot was 1200px wide and sharp. The browser was blurring them on the way to the screen.

Why does will-change: transform make things blurry?

will-change: transform tells the browser to promote the element to its own compositor layer. That layer is drawn into a bitmap, and from then on the compositor moves, rotates and scales the bitmap on the GPU without repainting the content.

That is fast, and it is also the problem. A layer that is rasterised once, upright, has to be resampled to be turned. A bitmap that is resampled at an angle cannot keep a one-pixel edge crisp, and small text is made of one-pixel edges. My notes from the fix put it plainly: a rotated raster of small type is never sharp at any angle, and the angle only decides how much.

Scaling has the same cost. In my case the hover state scaled the card by 1.045 on that same layer. The layer was not re-rasterised at the new size, so the card under the cursor was an upscaled copy of its own bitmap. The one card the visitor was looking at was the softest on the page.

How did I confirm the cause?

I read computed style straight from production in the browser the report came from, a 1512px wide window at a device pixel ratio of 2. One evaluation returned three things: the transform matrix matrix(0.999877, -0.0157…), will-change: transform, and an image request for w=640&q=75. That was the diagnosis before I changed a line.

The matrix is what a rotation of about 0.9 degrees looks like: the cosine is close to 1 and the sine is about 0.0157. It is easy to dismiss that as "almost not rotated". The raster does not care how small the angle is.

The screenshots were part of a fanned deck. I had added the tilt earlier with a comment that kept it under a degree, because past that the captions baked into the images read as crooked. That earlier work measured the caption tops to within 3px. Nobody zoomed into the pixels on a 2x screen, so the blur was designed in and defended by a comment.

What did the CSS look like before and after?

Before, every card was a fanned, overlapping layer:

.shot {
  flex: 0 0 clamp(11rem, 44vw, 15rem);
  margin: 0 -1.5rem 0 0; /* overlap */
  transition: transform 0.28s cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.7, 0.3, 1);
  will-change: transform;
}
.shot:nth-child(odd)  { transform: rotate(-0.9deg); }
.shot:nth-child(even) { transform: rotate(0.9deg); }

.shot:hover,
.shot:focus-within {
  transform: rotate(0deg) translateY(-0.6rem) scale(1.045);
}

After, the cards are flat. No tilt, no scale, no will-change, and the hover lift is a plain translate that lands on whole pixels:

.shot {
  flex: 0 0 clamp(12rem, 58vw, 16.5rem);
  margin: 0;
}

.shot a.image-zoom {
  transition: translate 0.32s cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1);
}

/* Lift, never scale: a whole-pixel translate is the one transform that does
   not resample the screenshot once it lands. */
.shot a.image-zoom:hover,
.shot a.image-zoom:focus-visible {
  translate: 0 -0.375rem;
}

The rule I wrote down afterwards: never rotate or scale raster content that carries small type, and never put will-change: transform on anything that scales. If a card needs to lift, translate it by a whole number of pixels.

Was it only the CSS?

No. There were three more causes, and the CSS was the biggest.

The images were AVIF at quality 75, which left ringing around small UI type. Quality 90 was clean for 6 KB more per card, 25 KB to 31 KB at 640px wide. The cards were also 240px wide, a phone screen shown at a fifth of its size, and clicking one opened the raw file in a new tab. I changed the cards to 264px on desktop and 58vw on a phone, cut the srcset to 384, 640 and 828 at quality 90, and opened a full-height viewer on click.

Because Next.js only serves widths and qualities listed in next.config.js, I added q=90 to images.qualities, and a test now reads that config and fails if any rendered image URL asks for a width or quality the optimizer would reject.

Why were the cover banners blurry as well?

A second report came the same day: "I meant this", with a screenshot of the cover banner at the top of the Masareef page, not the gallery. I had fixed the wrong images first. The lesson there was to look at the first viewport before deciding which images a report means.

The banner problem was about device pixels. The source art was a 1024x500 store graphic. The hero rendered 1086 CSS pixels wide, which is 2172 device pixels on a 2x screen, so the browser stretched the file by about 2.1 times. An earlier "hi-res" version at 2560px wide was an upscale of the same 1024 pixels, so it was soft too, only larger. The file size had been the clue: 75 KB for 2560 pixels of supposed detail.

The check I keep now is to compare a raster's intrinsic width with the rendered width multiplied by the device pixel ratio, in device pixels and not CSS pixels. I redrew the covers from SVG at 3x, which gave a 3072x1500 source, and fixed the sizes attribute, which had assumed a 768px column when the header was 1086px wide.

When should text be an image and when should it be live text?

Redrawing the banner at 3x fixed the 2x screen and exposed the next problem a few hours later. A screenshot of the hero at about 1x showed the wordmark and tagline soft next to the real text above them. At 1x the browser was shrinking 3072 pixels into 768, and shrunk type is filtered just like stretched type.

No file size fixes that, because the words were pixels. I had answered "pixelated" with more pixels twice. The question to ask on the first report is whether the thing is text.

The hero of the five mobile app pages is now live HTML in components/projects/app-banner.tsx: the name, the Arabic name, an accent rule and the tagline are real text over a CSS background of two radial glows and a light SVG grain to avoid banding. The app icon is the only image. The frame is a query container, so the type scales with its own width and one rule covers both the 768px column and a 310px phone column.

The rule that came out of it: text a reader has to read is live text. A raster of type belongs only where the page cannot draw text, such as link-preview cards and store listings. The same lesson says to check sharpness at the pixel density of the screenshot you were sent. My test rig had emulated a 2x laptop, where the 3x cover looked fine, and the report came from a screen at about 1x.

A checklist for blurry images and text in CSS

  1. Search the stylesheet for will-change: transform and for any rotate() or scale() on elements with images or text. Remove them from anything that carries small type.
  2. Read the computed transform in devtools. A matrix that is not the identity on a card you thought was flat is a lead.
  3. Compare the image's intrinsic width with rendered width times device pixel ratio.
  4. Test at 1x and at 2x. A fix that is sharp at one density can be soft at the other.
  5. If the blurry thing is text, make it text.

You can see the finished pages on the Masareef, Rafiq and Nafis case studies. The site they live on is described in the portfolio write-up.

title: Next.js metadata openGraph not inherited: why my subpages lost og:site_name
description:
If a page in the Next.js App Router sets its own openGraph, the openGraph object from your layout is gone for that page. Next.js merges metadata shallowly, so og:site_name, og:locale and any other field you only set in the layout disappear. The fix I use is one helper that builds the full openGraph and twitter objects for every subpage, plus a build check that fails when a tag is missing.

I found this on my own site, mohamedgado.com. /now, /projects and all 55 case studies were shipping without og:site_name, og:locale, twitter:site and twitter:creator. The root layout set all four. Nothing in the browser looked wrong, and nothing errored.

Does Next.js merge openGraph metadata from the layout?

No, not field by field. The Next.js 16 docs for generateMetadata say that metadata objects exported from several segments of one route are shallowly merged, and that duplicate keys are replaced by the segment closest to the page. They also say it directly for nested fields: openGraph defined in an earlier segment is overwritten by the last segment that defines it.

The docs give the example. The layout sets openGraph.title and openGraph.description. The blog page sets only openGraph.title. The output has the page's og:title and no og:description, because the page's whole openGraph object replaced the layout's.

The same page does inherit when it does not set openGraph at all. A subpage with only a title still gets every Open Graph tag from the layout. The trouble starts the moment a page adds openGraph to change one field, such as the title or the image. That is the normal thing to do on a case study or a blog post, so it hits most real sites.

What did the broken setup look like?

My root layout carried the full set:

// app/layout.tsx
export const metadata: Metadata = {
  openGraph: {
    locale: siteConfig.openGraph.locale,
    siteName: siteConfig.name,
    url: siteConfig.links.websiteUrl,
    type: 'website',
    title: `${siteConfig.name} — ${siteConfig.tagline}`,
    description: siteConfig.description,
  },
  twitter: {
    card: 'summary_large_image',
    creator: siteConfig.twitterTag,
    site: siteConfig.twitterTag,
  },
}

A subpage then set what it needed, which looks harmless. This is a simplified version of what the case-study page did before the helper:

// app/projects/[slug]/page.tsx (before)
return {
  title: project.title,
  openGraph: {
    title: `${project.title} | Mohamed Gado`,
    description,
    url: `/projects/${slug}`,
    images: [ogImage],
  },
  twitter: {
    card: 'summary_large_image',
    title: `${project.title} | Mohamed Gado`,
    description,
  },
}

This page's openGraph has no siteName and no locale, so neither tag is rendered. Its twitter has no site or creator, so those are gone too. The layout's values were replaced, not combined.

How do I check the rendered tags?

Read the HTML the server sends, not the code. A dev tool that shows the metadata object tells you what you wrote, and the question is what crawlers receive. I curl the page and grep for the tag:

curl -s https://www.mohamedgado.com/projects/masareef | grep -o '<meta[^>]*og:site_name[^>]*>'
curl -s https://www.mohamedgado.com/projects/masareef | grep -oE '<meta[^>]*(og:locale|twitter:site|twitter:creator)[^>]*>'

An empty result means the tag is missing. I ran this against production before writing any code, because I wanted to know the gap was real on every subpage and not something I had inferred from reading the merge docs. It was.

What is the fix for Next.js openGraph not inheriting?

The docs suggest pulling shared fields into a variable and spreading it into each page's openGraph. That works, but it leaves it to every page author to remember the spread. I had 55 case studies built from one template plus a few static pages, so I put the whole thing in a function in lib/social-meta.ts:

import type { Metadata } from 'next'
import { siteConfig } from '@/config/site'

type SocialMetaInput = {
  title: string
  description: string
  /** Root-relative path, resolved against the layout's `metadataBase`. */
  path: string
  images: NonNullable<Metadata['openGraph']>['images']
  /** Case studies are articles; set this and `og:type` becomes `article`. */
  article?: { modifiedTime?: string }
}

export function buildSocialMeta({
  title,
  description,
  path,
  images,
  article,
}: SocialMetaInput): Pick<Metadata, 'openGraph' | 'twitter'> {
  const shared = {
    siteName: siteConfig.name,
    locale: siteConfig.openGraph.locale,
    title,
    description,
    url: path,
    images,
  }
  const twitter: Metadata['twitter'] = {
    card: 'summary_large_image',
    site: siteConfig.twitterTag,
    creator: siteConfig.twitterTag,
    title,
    description,
  }
  if (!article) {
    return { openGraph: { ...shared, type: 'website' }, twitter }
  }
  return {
    openGraph: {
      ...shared,
      type: 'article',
      authors: [siteConfig.links.websiteUrl],
      ...(article.modifiedTime ? { modifiedTime: article.modifiedTime } : {}),
    },
    twitter,
  }
}

A page spreads the result into its metadata:

// app/projects/[slug]/page.tsx (after)
return {
  title: project.title,
  alternates: { canonical: `/projects/${slug}` },
  ...buildSocialMeta({
    title: `${project.title} | Mohamed Gado`,
    description,
    path: `/projects/${slug}`,
    images: [ogImage],
  }),
}

Because buildSocialMeta returns both objects complete, the shallow merge no longer matters: the page's openGraph replaces the layout's, and the replacement already contains everything the layout had. The site name, locale and handles come from siteConfig, the same source the layout reads, so they cannot drift apart.

The helper also gave me a single place to add article fields. Case studies now pass article, which sets og:type to article and adds article:modified_time and article:author.

One detail in the helper: I leave twitter.images unset on purpose. My code comment says Next falls back to the openGraph images, with alt text and dimensions included, so the image is declared once.

How do I stop it coming back?

A convention in a README does not survive the next new page. I added a check to the postbuild step. scripts/check-index-parity.ts reads every prerendered page and asserts that it carries og:site_name, og:locale and both Twitter handles. Before the fix it reported 57 failures. After, 0.

The rule written down in my lessons file is short: a page that sets openGraph or twitter goes through buildSocialMeta, and the build fails otherwise. Because the check runs on built HTML, it also catches pages I did not think of, such as a new route someone adds later and forgets to wire up.

What else should I check on pages that override metadata?

Other nested fields behave the same way. The docs name robots next to openGraph as a field that is overwritten wholesale. If a layout sets robots: { index: true, follow: true, googleBot: {...} } and one page sets robots: { index: false }, the page does not keep the googleBot block. Anything that is an object in the Metadata type is a candidate: alternates, icons, twitter, appLinks and so on.

For each one, ask whether the layout sets it and whether any page sets it again. If both are true, the page's version has to be complete. A helper function, a spread of a shared object, or a build-time check on the output are all workable. I picked the helper and the check together, since the helper prevents the mistake and the check proves it.

The change was small, and nothing on the site looked different afterwards. What changed was the HTML that link previews and search engines read for 57 pages. If you set openGraph on any page below your root layout, curl one of those pages today and look for og:site_name.

title: A computational framework for understanding embodied plans
description:
arXiv:2611.13669v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reasoning about people's plans and goals based on their actions is fundamental to human social interaction and essential for cooperative, embodied artificial intelligence. Formalizing this capacity in naturalistic, embodied settings has been a longstanding challenge. Here, we present GenEA, a novel agent representation capable of reasoning over multi-step, long-horizon embodied plans. At the heart of GenEA lies a multilevel state-space that couples the coarse biomechanics of an articulated body and its interactions with nearby objects by extending the task-and-motion planning framework from robotics with simulation-based intuitive physics. By embedding this state-space in a generative model, GenEA yields a joint probability distribution over goals and embodied plans. Across several experiments spanning the qualitatively distinct domains of object manipulation and navigation, featuring diverse tasks and multiple behavioral measures, we show that GenEA, through simple transformations of this joint distribution, recapitulates how humans reason about embodied plans. Crucially, GenEA consistently outperforms strong alternative models, including plausible heuristics, standard task-and-motion planning, and a state-of-the-art vision-language model. GenEA thereby offers a new perspective on the architecture of human reasoning and social cognition, suggesting that embodied artificial intelligence systems seeking to seamlessly interact with humans should adopt GenEA-like generative models of action planning.

title: Background Job Queue vs App Polling — Choose HTTP Workers for SaaS Digests
description:
A weekly customer digest has an awkward operational constraint: one logical send must happen once, even when its job is delivered more than once. Short answer: choose a queue that pushes jobs to an authenticated public HTTP worker, supports delayed retries and a dead-letter queue, and preserves a stable idempotency key; keep database polling when private networking or strict transaction coupling matters more than managed delivery.

For an e-commerce SaaS, the cron trigger is the easy part. The harder path begins after it selects active customers. A worker may time out after the email provider accepted a message, a rate limit may defer half the batch, or a deploy may overlap a redelivery. A simple queue is useful only if those cases have explicit outcomes that an eval harness can assert.

My choice for this workload is managed HTTP delivery over database polling. It keeps scheduling, delayed jobs, retry state, and exhausted work outside the application process while leaving the business handler as ordinary Python HTTP code. The catch is real: it requires a reachable endpoint and careful request authentication. If workers must remain on a private network, or enqueueing must commit in the exact same database transaction as an order update, stick with a transactional outbox plus polling.

How should a SaaS app queue HTTP workers, retries, delayed jobs, and cron?

Start with two records, not one. A schedule records when to plan a digest. A delivery records which customer and digest period to send. At the weekly boundary, the scheduler creates one delivery per eligible customer with a deterministic key such as digest:{customer_id}:{period_start}. The queue message carries that key, a delivery ID, and a schema version. It should not carry an ever-growing customer profile or generated email body.

That split prevents cron from becoming the unit of retry. If a run selects 18,000 customers and customer 417 is rate-limited, only that customer's delivery should wait. Re-running the entire weekly selection would create duplicate risk and make progress hard to see. Delayed jobs are therefore a delivery mechanism, not a second scheduler: cron creates the work; a delay controls when a specific attempt becomes eligible again.

Keep the public webhook thin. It authenticates the request, validates the schema, claims the idempotency key, performs the send, records a terminal result, and returns a status that matches the retry policy. The queue owns attempt timing. The application owns whether repeating the same logical command changes the world twice.

There are two useful idempotency layers. First, put a unique constraint on (customer_id, digest_period) so overlapping planner runs cannot create two logical deliveries. Second, store the provider result against the stable delivery ID before acknowledging success. Don't generate a fresh key on each attempt. That turns every retry into a new operation and defeats the whole design.

Exactly-once delivery is not the practical contract here. The practical contract is at-least-once transport plus an idempotent effect. A network timeout can hide whether the downstream side accepted a request, so the same command may need to be presented again. The handler must recognize it.

The focused Python handler

This example keeps the durable operations behind small interfaces so the same cases can run in a notebook, a unit-test fixture, or production. claim() must be an atomic insert-or-read operation backed by a unique key. complete() stores the accepted provider reference. The code deliberately returns success for an already completed delivery because redelivery has reached the desired state.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from enum import Enum
from typing import Protocol


class State(str, Enum):
    CLAIMED = "claimed"
    COMPLETE = "complete"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DigestJob:
    delivery_id: str
    customer_id: str
    period_start: str
    idempotency_key: str
    schema_version: int


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Claim:
    state: State
    provider_reference: str | None = None


class DeliveryStore(Protocol):
    def claim(self, job: DigestJob) -> Claim: ...

    def complete(self, delivery_id: str, provider_reference: str) -> None: ...


class Mailer(Protocol):
    def send_digest(self, job: DigestJob, idempotency_key: str) -> str: ...


def handle_digest(
    payload: dict,
    store: DeliveryStore,
    mailer: Mailer,
) -> tuple[int, dict]:
    job = DigestJob(**payload)
    expected_key = f"digest:{job.customer_id}:{job.period_start}"

    if job.schema_version != 1 or job.idempotency_key != expected_key:
        return 400, {"status": "invalid_job"}

    claim = store.claim(job)
    if claim.state == State.COMPLETE:
        return 200, {
            "status": "already_complete",
            "delivery_id": job.delivery_id,
        }

    provider_reference = mailer.send_digest(
        job,
        idempotency_key=job.idempotency_key,
    )
    store.complete(job.delivery_id, provider_reference)
    return 200, {
        "status": "complete",
        "delivery_id": job.delivery_id,
        "completed_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
    }

This is the happy path and the duplicate path, not a complete web framework. Authentication should happen before handle_digest, and logs should avoid the email address or rendered digest. The payload contains identifiers because identifiers are enough to load current policy and template data at execution time.

The subtle case is a process interruption between the provider accepting the message and complete() committing. The clean resolution depends on the provider supporting the same idempotency key. If it does, replaying send_digest returns the original logical result rather than sending twice. If it doesn't, I'm not sure a generic queue setting can close that ambiguity; the evidence needed is the email provider's documented duplicate-suppression contract. In that case, use a durable provider submission record and accept that the final boundary has an explicit uncertainty state for operator review.

Retry classes, DLQ policy, and regional boundaries

Retry policy should be a small classification table, not “retry every non-200 response.” HTTP 429 Too Many Requests means the client has sent too many requests in a period, and a response may include Retry-After. Honor that delay when present, add bounded jitter, and keep the original idempotency key. A connection timeout is also retryable because the result is unknown. Authentication failure and schema rejection are not improved by waiting.

Outcome Queue action Application record
200 already complete or complete Acknowledge Terminal success
429 with Retry-After Delay, then retry Attempt and next eligible time
Connection timeout Retry with bounded backoff Attempt with unknown remote result
400 invalid schema Send to DLQ Permanent validation failure
401 or 403 Stop automatic retries, alert Authentication failure
Attempt budget exhausted Send to DLQ Exhausted with last classification

A DLQ is quarantine, not storage and not a retry loop. AWS's SQS documentation, for example, describes a redrive policy with a maxReceiveCount that moves repeatedly unprocessed messages to a dead-letter queue. The general lesson is portable: keep the original payload, attempt metadata, and failure classification; inspect the cause; then redrive with the same logical identity after correction. Blindly moving every DLQ item back on a timer can recreate the same load and conceal a deterministic error. Keep the attempt budget tied to elapsed business value. A weekly digest delayed by minutes may still be useful, while one delayed beyond the next digest window probably is not. I wouldn't hard-code a universal retry count without the provider's rate-limit behavior, the digest expiry policy, and the team's on-call response time. Those inputs determine the cap. US and EU execution adds a separate boundary. Put each customer's delivery record, queue, worker, and DLQ in the region selected by the application's data policy; route the planner to that regional control plane rather than pulling all recipients into one global batch. The public endpoint can still be region-specific. Verify where payloads, logs, and backups reside before assuming the queue's region selector covers every downstream system.

Retries preserve identity.

Small payloads help here. They reduce the personal data crossing queue and log boundaries, make redrive inspection less sensitive, and avoid freezing prompt or merchandising data inside a delayed message. For an AI-generated summary, store the prompt version and model configuration with the delivery evaluation record, then generate under a token budget before the send step. That makes cost regressions visible without turning queue metadata into an experiment database.

What to measure before copying this choice?

The first eval is duplication. Enqueue the same (customer_id, digest_period) twice and assert one delivery row and one accepted provider operation. Then interrupt the handler after provider acceptance, redeliver the job, and assert the stable idempotency key produces the same logical result. This test is more valuable than a demo in which every request returns 200.

Measure queue age at the oldest ready job, attempt counts by failure class, time from cron fire to planner completion, delivery latency by region, DLQ depth, redrive outcomes, and duplicate-suppression hits. Track generated-token usage by prompt version if the digest contains an AI summary. Averages will hide a stuck tail, so use percentiles and explicit age thresholds.

Also run a rate-limit experiment: return 429 with a known Retry-After, then verify that the next attempt does not arrive early and retains the same delivery ID. Run a poison-message experiment with an unsupported schema version and verify that it reaches quarantine without consuming the full transient retry budget. Finally, redrive one corrected item and confirm its original identity and history remain queryable.

Choose managed HTTP delivery when those tests pass, the endpoint can be exposed and authenticated, and the team wants the queue to own retry timing. Choose database polling when private reachability, local transactional enqueue, or bespoke ordering is the dominant constraint. Neither choice removes idempotency work. It decides where the operational state lives.

Measure first. Copy second.

Sources

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429

title: Evidential Deep Learning with conditional entropy for glaucoma detection
description:
arXiv:2611.13513v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose a novel conditional entropy function as a basis for quantifying predictive uncertainty in Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) for glaucoma detection from retinal fundus images. Using the EyePACS-AIROGS-light-V2 and RIM-ONE-DL datasets for validation, we found that our proposed EDL model regularized by conditional entropy function produced uncertainty estimates with substantially lower calibration errors than Deep Ensembles, MC Dropout, post-hoc calibration and the conventional EDL framework based on Dempster uncertainty. To further probe our models' interpretability, we analyzed Grad-CAM heatmaps using a focus index representing spatial concentration. Compared with the other uncertainty quantification methods, EDL models exhibited greater separation between the index distributions of correctly and incorrectly classified fundus images. In particular, false negatives were associated with localized Grad-CAM activations that were displaced from the optic disc, consistent with its established clinical importance in glaucoma assessment. Overall, our findings suggest that our proposed EDL framework for glaucoma detection provides not only enhanced uncertainty calibration but also admits a more physiologically consistent interpretability.

title: Teaching the Harness: Student-Aware Skill Transfer for LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.13144v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Effective teaching requires reasoning about the learner as well as the task, a capacity that Theory of Mind describes as inferring another agent's latent state from its behavior. We ask whether a stronger LLM teaches a fixed student better when it applies this principle. The student is an LLM agent acting through a harness that fixes its tools, context, and action budget, so a procedure that helps one model can exhaust the budget of another. We introduce Student-Aware Teaching (SAT). The teacher builds a learner model that pairs an empirical profile with hypotheses about the student's limitations, tests these hypotheses with diagnostic probes, and writes reusable skills for the diagnosed failures. A skill enters the library only after it raises success on matched development tasks. With Claude-Sonnet-5 teaching DeepSeek-V4-Flash, SAT reaches 86.46% task success across four primary runs, leading both a profile-free teacher with the same framework (81.04%) and the untaught student (75.00%) in each run. Removing the analytical learner model lowers both prediction and success, and under misleading learner profiles none of the 48 candidate skills passes admission. When DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Gemini-3.8-Flash exchange libraries, each performs better with its own. Saved libraries keep average gains of up to 11.1 points after the teacher leaves. The benefit depends on a student that can follow instructions and a deployment route that delivers them.

title: IaaS ARTICLE
description:
Understanding Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): A Case Study of Amazon EC2
Introduction
Cloud computing has made it easier for people, students and businesses to access computing resources through the internet. In the past, an organisation that needed a server had to buy the equipment and take care of it. Today, it can get these resources from a cloud provider instead. One of the cloud computing service models that makes this possible is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS).
This article explains what IaaS means, how it works and how Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is an example of this service.
What is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?
Infrastructure as a Service, also called IaaS, is a cloud service that allows users to rent computing resources over the internet instead of buying physical equipment. These resources include virtual machines, storage, networking and processing power.
The cloud provider is responsible for the physical servers and data centres. The customer, however, manages things such as the operating system, applications and data. For example, someone who wants to create a website can rent a virtual server from an IaaS provider instead of buying a server.
How IaaS Works
IaaS providers have large data centres with servers, storage devices and networking equipment. Through a technology called virtualization, these physical resources can be shared and provided to users as virtual resources.
First, a user creates an account with a cloud provider and chooses the resources needed. The provider then creates a virtual machine or another requested resource. The user can choose an operating system, install the required software and deploy an application. If the application needs more or fewer resources later, the user can adjust them. This makes it possible to use computing resources without owning the physical equipment.
Case Study: Amazon EC2
Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is a service offered by Amazon Web Services (AWS). It allows users to create and run virtual servers called EC2 instances. These servers can be used for different tasks depending on what the user needs.
EC2 is an example of IaaS because AWS takes care of the physical hardware, while users manage their virtual servers and the software running on them. Users can choose the type of instance, operating system, storage, network settings and security options that suit their work.
For example, a small business that wants to create an online shopping website can use an EC2 instance to host it. The business does not have to buy a physical server. It can rent a virtual server from AWS, install the software it needs and manage the website from there.
Key Features of Amazon EC2

  1. Virtual servers: Users can create virtual servers without buying physical computers or server equipment.
  2. Scalability: Users can increase or reduce their computing resources when the needs of their application change.
  3. Flexible configuration: EC2 provides different server options, allowing users to choose resources that fit their applications.
  4. Security controls: Users can set access permissions and configure network and security settings for their resources.
  5. Different uses: EC2 can be used for hosting websites, testing applications, development and processing data.
  6. Flexible pricing: AWS provides different payment options, so users can choose what works for their needs and usage. Advantages of IaaS IaaS has many advantages. One of them is that it can reduce costs because businesses do not have to spend a lot of money buying physical servers and other equipment. It also makes it easier to increase or reduce resources when demand changes. Another advantage is that resources can be set up quickly, instead of waiting to buy and install hardware. Users can also access and manage their infrastructure remotely, while the cloud provider handles the maintenance of the physical equipment. Disadvantages of IaaS Even though IaaS is useful, it also has some disadvantages. Users need a reliable internet connection to access and manage their resources. They also need technical knowledge to manage operating systems, networks and security settings. If resources are not managed properly, the cost can become higher than expected. There is also a risk of depending too much on one cloud provider and its services. IaaS Compared with Traditional Infrastructure With traditional infrastructure, a business has to buy its own servers, storage devices and networking equipment. It is also responsible for installing, maintaining and upgrading them. With IaaS, the cloud provider owns and maintains the physical equipment, while the customer uses virtual resources and manages the parts assigned to them. This can make managing technology easier and reduce the need to handle physical hardware. Conclusion In conclusion, Infrastructure as a Service is an important part of cloud computing because it allows users to access computing resources over the internet without buying all the physical equipment. Amazon EC2 is a good example because it gives users the ability to create and manage virtual servers based on their needs. Although IaaS requires technical knowledge and a good internet connection, it offers flexibility, scalability and can help reduce hardware costs. It is therefore useful for businesses, developers and organisations that need computing resources. References Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). Amazon EC2. https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/ Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). What is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)? https://aws.amazon.com/what-is/iaas/ Mell, P., & Grance, T. (2011). The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-145

title: How Hyperbolic Are Hyperbolic Vision-Language Models?
description:
arXiv:2611.13384v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hyperbolic vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as a rapidly growing area of research, reporting strong zero-shot performance alongside an interpretable embedding space in which radius orders representations by generality. But how hyperbolic are hyperbolic VLMs in practice? We investigate this at the exponential map, the single operation through which curvature enters an otherwise Euclidean network. We show that across MERU, HyCoCLIP, ARGENT, and PHyCLIP, the exponential map is well approximated by the identity function, i.e., pairwise distances and angles in the pre-map Euclidean space barely change under projection, and removing the map at inference leaves evaluation scores unchanged. Motivated by this observation, we train Euclidean VLMs on CC3M from scratch under the same hierarchy losses. Over roughly the final 90% of the training steps, the training statistics are nearly indistinguishable from those of their hyperbolic counterparts, and the resulting models match the evaluation scores and recover the same radial distributions. Our findings establish Euclidean space as a sufficient substrate for hierarchical vision-language learning as it is currently practiced, and motivate new paradigms in which hyperbolic geometry can deliver on its theoretical promise. Code is available at https://github.com/fbyrman/hyperbolic-vlms.

title: An Analytical Model of Compute-limited Multistage Training Pipelines
description:
arXiv:2611.13276v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern foundation models are trained through multiple stages, yet how these stages interact and how compute should be allocated across them remain poorly understood. We introduce an analytically tractable high-dimensional model combining unsupervised pretraining with a linear autoencoder, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with noisy stepwise labels, and reinforcement learning (RL) with sparse episodic rewards. Using random matrix theory and an operator-projection closure, we derive approximate low-dimensional learning dynamics that closely match simulations. We show that finite pretraining data imposes a representation-dependent performance limit, with Bayes classification error scaling as the inverse square root of the pretraining sample ratio, and observe the same exponent in asymptotic SFT and RL errors. Better pretraining also reduces sensitivity to noisy supervision. SFT initialization shortens the initial RL plateau induced by sparse rewards, an effect we also observe in OLMo-2 1B on GSM8K. Longer SFT warm starts additionally improve asymptotic RL performance. Optimizing compute across all three stages reveals that the optimal allocation depends on supervision quality and total budget, with a non-monotonic dependence of the RL compute share on budget. Finally, a complementary compositional model shows how RL selectively strengthens task-relevant pretrained skills while largely preserving unused skills. Together, these results identify mechanisms linking representation quality, feedback structure, and compute allocation in multistage training.

title: HiCAP: Hierarchical Cultural Adaptation via Personality for Dialogue Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.13207v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cultural adaptation in dialogue systems refers to the ability to generate responses that conform to linguistic norms and social expectations across different cultures. However, existing dialogue generation approaches pay limited attention to the role of personality in shaping cultural expression and communication style. We therefore propose HiCAP, a novel framework that integrates personality traits into culturally adaptive dialogue generation. HiCAP employs a personality-conditioned control mechanism that hierarchically modulates response style by first aligning it with the cultural tone and then refining linguistic expression and content according to individual personality attributes. To embed these factors, the model combines supervised fine-tuning and instruction-based tuning, supported by dynamic instruction templates and multi-agent demonstrations to capture diverse combinations of culture and personality. Experiments on CulturalPersonas and CPED show that HiCAP achieves the strongest overall performance across various dialogue generation metrics, demonstrating effective cultural adaptability and personality modelling.

title: ORA-01000 Maximum Open Cursors Exceeded: Don't Raise the Limit, Find the Leak
description:
The application has been fine for days. Then one request fails, then a few more, all from the same app server:

ORA-01000: maximum open cursors exceeded

The usual reaction is to raise OPEN_CURSORS. It's one ALTER SYSTEM, it needs no restart, and the errors stop. Then they come back a week later.

ORA-01000 is almost never a limit that's too low. It's an application that opens cursors and doesn't close them: a cursor leak. The limit is just where the leak becomes visible. This post covers what the limit counts, how to find the leaking session and the exact statement, the query that makes a healthy session look like the culprit, and why raising the limit doesn't help the connections that are already failing. It ends with a lab that proves each step on Oracle Database Free 26ai.

What the limit counts

OPEN_CURSORS is the maximum number of cursors one session can have open at once. It is not a database-wide pool. A session at the limit gets ORA-01000; every other session carries on. On 26ai the message reads:

ORA-01000: maximum open cursors for session exceeded

A cursor is the server-side handle for a statement the client is still working with. In application code it's a Statement or ResultSet in JDBC, a cursor object in Python, a data reader in .NET. It stays open on the server until the client closes it, or the session ends. If the code never closes it, it stays open for as long as the connection lives. With a connection pool, that can be days.

That's why ORA-01000 shows up late. A code path that leaks one cursor per call is harmless on the first call. Each pooled connection collects its leaked cursors over hundreds or thousands of requests, and fails when it reaches the limit. The request that fails is just the one that needed the next cursor.

The parameter's documented default is 50. Many databases run with something higher; the container in this post's lab runs with 300.

What the error tells you on 26ai

On 26ai the first ORA-01000 in a session carries a clue:

ORA-01000: maximum open cursors for session exceeded Potential Leaked SQL_ID:
4cgc7syjwjw3y

In the lab, that SQL_ID was the statement the session held open the most, and not the statement that failed. A session leaked 298 result sets from one procedure and then called a different one. The different call failed, and the message named the leaked statement. In a second test the session leaked 200 result sets from one statement, then 98 from another, and the message still named the one with 200. That's what you want: the application log now points at the code that leaks, not the innocent request that happened to need the next cursor.

Two things to know:

  • Only the first error in the session names it. In the lab the next 21 errors in the same session said only "maximum open cursors for session exceeded". Find the first one in the application log.
  • It may be wrapped. When the failing statement needs internal SQL first (parsing a new statement, for example), the application sees ORA-00604: Error occurred at recursive SQL level 1 with ORA-01000 underneath. The lab got both forms.

Look the SQL_ID up in V$SQL (it stays in the shared pool after the session ends, until it ages out), then find that statement in the code.

The database itself logs nothing. After a run that raised ORA-01000 22 times, the lab found no ORA-01000 in the alert log. If the application swallows its errors, you won't see this one.

Find the session

If you don't have the SQL_ID, or want to confirm it, start with the session. The count that the limit applies to is the statistic opened cursors current:

SELECT s.sid, s.serial#, s.username, s.module, s.machine, st.value AS open_cursors
FROM   v$sesstat st
JOIN   v$statname n ON n.statistic# = st.statistic#
JOIN   v$session  s ON s.sid = st.sid
WHERE  n.name = 'opened cursors current'
AND    s.username IS NOT NULL
ORDER  BY st.value DESC
FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY;

A leaking session sits near OPEN_CURSORS. A healthy one holds a handful. MODULE and MACHINE tell you which application and which app server. Run this on a schedule and you'll see a leak as a number that grows with uptime long before it reaches the limit.

Find the statement, and don't count cached cursors

V$OPEN_CURSOR lists cursors per session with their SQL text. It also lists cursors that are closed and kept in the session cursor cache so the next parse of the same statement is cheap. Cached cursors don't count against OPEN_CURSORS. If you count rows in V$OPEN_CURSOR without filtering, a busy, healthy session can look like the problem.

The lab ran two sessions side by side. One leaked 250 result sets. The other ran 450 different queries four times each, closing every one, with SESSION_CACHED_CURSORS set to 1,000:

session      opened cursors current    rows in V$OPEN_CURSOR
leaky-app    252                       265
busy-app     2                         458

By raw row count, the healthy session has more "open cursors" than the leaking one, and more than the 300 limit. It had two open. 454 of its rows were SESSION CURSOR CACHED. (The lab set the cache to 1,000 to make the point; at the default of 50, expect a few dozen extra rows per session. Some shops set it much higher.)

The CURSOR_TYPE column separates them. Filter on the types that start with OPEN, and group by statement:

SELECT o.sql_id, MAX(o.sql_text) AS sql_text, COUNT(*) AS open_count
FROM   v$open_cursor o
WHERE  o.sid = :sid
AND    o.cursor_type LIKE 'OPEN%'
GROUP  BY o.sql_id
ORDER  BY open_count DESC;

In the lab that returned a single row:

SQL_ID         OPEN_COUNT  SQL_TEXT
4cgc7syjwjw3y  250         SELECT ID, CREATED FROM APP.ORDERS WHERE CUSTOMER_ID = :B1

One statement open 250 times in one session is a leak. Nothing legitimate holds the same query's result open 250 times at once. If instead you see many different statements, each open a few times, the session may genuinely need more cursors (see the sizing section below).

ORA-01000 is a per-session limit. Find the session by 'opened cursors current', then the statement by V$OPEN_CURSOR filtered to CURSOR_TYPE LIKE 'OPEN%'. One statement open hundreds of times is a leak to fix in code; many different statements may be a real need.

Raising OPEN_CURSORS: what it does and doesn't do

OPEN_CURSORS can be changed with ALTER SYSTEM, without a restart, and in a PDB. The lab raised it from 300 to 400 in the PDB while one session was stuck at the limit:

session                                         result after the raise
stuck at the limit before the raise             55 more calls, 55 x ORA-01000
connected before the raise, leaking after it    first ORA-01000 at call 299 (the old limit)
connected after the raise, same leak            first ORA-01000 at call 399

Two things went wrong with the "fix":

  1. It didn't reach the connections that were already open. On 26ai in the lab, every session connected before the change kept the old limit, stuck or not. Only new connections got 400. In a pooled application, that means the raise does nothing until the pool reconnects. When the errors stop after a raise, it's often the app restart that went with it.
  2. The leak failed again, just later. The new connection hit ORA-01000 at call 399 instead of 299. The leak rate didn't change.

So raising the limit is a way to buy time while the code is fixed, and it only buys it after the connections are recycled. Each open cursor also holds memory on the server, so a high limit on a leaking app means more memory held before it fails.

The fix

Right now: the leaked cursors belong to the session. Ending the session releases all of them. Recycle the affected pool's connections or restart that app server. Capture opened cursors current and the session's V$OPEN_CURSOR rows first, because they're gone when the session is.

In the code: close what you open, on every path, including the error path. That means try-with-resources in Java for every Statement, PreparedStatement, CallableStatement and ResultSet, including result sets returned as ref cursors from stored procedures. In Python, use with blocks for cursors; in .NET, using. In PL/SQL, close explicit cursors and DBMS_SQL cursors in the exception handler too. The leak in the lab is a stored procedure that returns a result set to the caller (a SYS_REFCURSOR). The caller owns that cursor, and the caller never closed it. The same 400 calls with each result set read and closed ran with no error, at the original limit of 300.

When the limit really is too low

Some sessions do need more than the default: an application that keeps many statements prepared at once, or a client-side statement cache. Oracle's JDBC driver, for example, can cache statements per connection, and each cached statement keeps its cursor open on the server. That's by design, and the cursors are spread over many different statements, not one.

Size OPEN_CURSORS from what the application uses at peak, not from the last error:

SELECT s.module, MAX(st.value) AS peak_open_now
FROM   v$sesstat st
JOIN   v$statname n ON n.statistic# = st.statistic#
JOIN   v$session  s ON s.sid = st.sid
WHERE  n.name = 'opened cursors current'
AND    s.username IS NOT NULL
GROUP  BY s.module
ORDER  BY peak_open_now DESC;

Run it over a normal business day. If the healthy peak is close to the limit, raise it with headroom and recycle the connections. If one module keeps climbing, it's a leak, and a higher limit only delays the next outage.

Prove it

The lab runs Oracle Database Free in a container. The "application" is SQL*Plus calling a procedure that returns a result set, and holding each result set in its own variable without closing it: the same thing a ResultSet that's never closed does on the server. Then it breaks and fixes things five ways:

drill   what happens                                             result
leak    320 calls, no result set closed (OPEN_CURSORS 300)       ORA-01000 from call 299; first error names the SQL_ID
blame   298 leaked, then a different call                        the other call fails, message names the leaker;
                                                                 another session runs that call fine
find    a leaking session next to a busy healthy one             raw V$OPEN_CURSOR rows: 265 vs 458;
                                                                 'OPEN%' filter finds the leak, 250 x one SQL
raise   OPEN_CURSORS 300 -> 400 during the outage                stuck and pre-existing sessions keep 300; new: call 399
fix     400 calls, each result set closed                        no ORA-01000

Why call 299 and not 301? The session already had two cursors open before the first call: SQL*Plus's own statement and one recursive cursor. 298 leaked plus those two is 300.

Don't take my word for it — run it. The open-cursors lab asserts every row: the failing call number from the limit; that the first error, and only the first, names the leaked statement's SQL_ID; nothing in the alert log; the leaked statement named even when a different call fails, and a second session unaffected; the healthy session's V$OPEN_CURSOR row count above the limit while it has almost nothing open; the leaked statement found 250 times by the OPEN% filter; both sessions opened before the raise keeping the old limit and a new one failing at 399; and no error once each result set is closed. If any of that doesn't reproduce, the run fails. Proven on every CI push.

What teams get wrong

  • Raising OPEN_CURSORS as the fix. It moves the failure, and only for new connections. Find the statement first.
  • Counting rows in V$OPEN_CURSOR. That includes cached cursors, which are closed. Use opened cursors current, or filter CURSOR_TYPE LIKE 'OPEN%'.
  • Blaming the statement that failed. It's whichever call needed the next cursor. On 26ai, read the SQL_ID in the first error; on any release, look at what the session holds open.
  • Closing the ResultSet on the happy path only. An exception between open and close leaks it just the same. Close in finally, or let try-with-resources do it.
  • Treating ORA-01000 as a database problem. It's per session, the database logs nothing, and every other session is fine. The fix is in the application.

Frequently asked questions

What does ORA-01000 maximum open cursors exceeded mean?

It means one database session tried to open more cursors at the same time than the OPEN_CURSORS parameter allows. The limit is per session, not for the whole database, so other sessions keep working. It is almost always caused by a cursor leak: the application opens statements or result sets and doesn't close them, so each connection accumulates open cursors until it reaches the limit. Less often, the application genuinely needs more cursors at once than the limit allows.

How do I find which SQL is causing ORA-01000?

On Oracle Database 26ai the first ORA-01000 in a session includes 'Potential Leaked SQL_ID' followed by the statement the session holds open most; look it up in V$SQL. On any release, find the session with the highest 'opened cursors current' in V$SESSTAT, then query V$OPEN_CURSOR for that SID with CURSOR_TYPE LIKE 'OPEN%', grouped by SQL_ID. One statement open hundreds of times is the leak. In the companion lab that returned one statement open 250 times.

Should I just increase OPEN_CURSORS?

Only if the application genuinely needs more cursors at once, which shows up as many different statements each open a few times. For a leak, raising the limit only delays the error: in the companion lab, raising it from 300 to 400 moved the first ORA-01000 from call 299 to call 399. And the new value applied only to new connections; sessions connected before the change kept the old limit, so a connection pool has to reconnect before a raise has any effect.

Why does V$OPEN_CURSOR show more cursors than OPEN_CURSORS without an error?

Because V$OPEN_CURSOR also lists cursors that are closed and kept in the session cursor cache (CURSOR_TYPE 'SESSION CURSOR CACHED'), and cached cursors don't count against OPEN_CURSORS. In the companion lab a healthy session with SESSION_CACHED_CURSORS set to 1,000 showed 458 rows in V$OPEN_CURSOR against a limit of 300, while its 'opened cursors current' was 2. Filter on CURSOR_TYPE LIKE 'OPEN%' or use the 'opened cursors current' statistic.

Does increasing OPEN_CURSORS require a restart?

No. OPEN_CURSORS can be changed with ALTER SYSTEM while the database is running, and in a PDB. But in the companion lab on 26ai the new value applied only to sessions that connected after the change; sessions that were already connected, including the one stuck at the limit, kept the old limit. Recycle the application's connections after changing it.

How do I fix a cursor leak in Java?

Close every Statement, PreparedStatement, CallableStatement and ResultSet on every path, including when an exception is thrown. try-with-resources does this automatically. Result sets returned from stored procedures as ref cursors are cursors too and must be closed by the caller. To release leaked cursors immediately, recycle the affected connections; ending a session closes all of its cursors.

ORA-01000 is a leak that took days to fill up, reported by whichever request came last. Before you raise anything, find the session by opened cursors current, find the statement by V$OPEN_CURSOR with the cached cursors filtered out, and fix the code that opens it. It's the same family of problem as the hard-parse storm: application habits showing up as a database error. Then prove it with the open-cursors lab, where one leaked result set per call takes a session down at call 299, and closing it runs 400 calls clean.

Originally published at uptimearchitect.com.

title: From Questions to Decisions: Benchmarking How LLM Agents Acquire Decision-Relevant Information from Human Beings
description:
arXiv:2611.13015v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly asked to make plans for people, such as scheduling drivers or assigning nurses. However, people's requests are often incomplete, and the supporting information for decision-making may be outdated, requiring agents to ask for clarification. Existing benchmarks typically provide fully specified problems or rely on uncalibrated LLM-simulated users, leaving this ability insufficiently tested. We introduce Ask2Decide, a benchmark of 43 planning tasks that evaluates whether agents ask for missing information that matters for their decisions. An operator holds facts absent from the agent's request and records, and optimization solvers determine which facts change the optimal plan. We also include similarly worded facts that leave the optimal plan unchanged to test whether agents distinguish useful information from irrelevant details. We collect 79 interaction sessions from 19 participants and find that, after an incorrect plan, human replies omit the correcting fact far more often than replies from an uncalibrated simulated user (43% versus 7%). Using these interactions, we calibrate a simulated operator that more closely matches human reply patterns. Evaluating four frontier LLMs, we find that their initial plans are infeasible on 58-98% of tasks when information is missing, compared with 5-28% when all facts are provided upfront. Agents uncover facts that change the optimal plan only slightly more often than facts that leave it unchanged (39-52% versus 32-41%). These results show that obtaining decision-relevant information through interaction remains a major bottleneck for LLM planning. This is ongoing work and will be updated. The date of this version is shown on the first page.
