title: Benchmarking Vendor-Guided Optimizations on Edge NPUs: From NPU Only to End-to-End Performance. Extended technical report
description:
arXiv:2611.13563v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Edge NPU performance depends not only on hardware capabilities, but also on model transformation and the overall deployment pipeline. We propose a benchmarking methodology that separates these effects by comparing three configurations: Baseline, Vendor Guided NPU Only (VG-NPU), and Vendor Guided End-to-End (VG-E2E), where VG-NPU preserves common model I/O and host-side processing while VG-E2E follows the vendor-native deployment pipeline. We apply this methodology to four edge NPUs and three vision workloads. VG-NPU improves both accuracy and Runtime-call latency in 10 of 12 NPU--workload combinations, whereas VG-E2E reduces System-level latency in all combinations but improves accuracy in only four. Moreover, NPU-level performance rankings do not always match End-to-End rankings, and VG-E2E provides an additional 10.4--70.7\% reduction in System-level latency over VG-NPU. These results demonstrate the importance of evaluating vendor-guided optimization separately at the controlled model-transformation and full deployment levels when comparing heterogeneous commercial Edge NPU platforms in practice.

title: The $5 Trillion Shift: Preparing Retail Backends for the Age of AI Agents
description:
Retail is entering the era of the multi-agent shopping assistant. Instead of a single, stateless chatbot following a rigid script, retailers are building systems where multiple agents collaborate behind the scenes, drawing on preferences and customer purchase history to deliver recommendations that improve with every interaction. More retailers are reconfiguring their backends to reflect the rise in agentic usage, as this is no small trend: McKinsey estimates AI agents could mediate $3 trillion to $5 trillion of global consumer commerce by 2030 (1).

The need is real, as the race is heating up to quickly respond to customer searches and take service to another level. A customer searching for a pair of running shoes for an upcoming marathon no longer triggers a keyword search. The query kicks off a coordinated reasoning process across multiple specialized agents. This has to happen rapidly and seamlessly to keep consumers' attention and needs met.

The promise of this shift is real, but the real architectural question has nothing to do with which LLM or orchestration framework a team chooses. It has everything to do with where the data lives and whether every agent can see the same version of the truth simultaneously. Increasingly, retailers are finding that solution in MongoDB.

The technology challenge behind multi-agent AI

Building a single AI agent is straightforward with modern LLMs and orchestration frameworks. Building a production multi-agent system is not. Why? Agentic AI has five distinct data needs:

  • Semantic search over vector embeddings 

  • Flexible user context 

  • Conversation state across sessions 

  • Long-term memory that evolves over time 

  • Observability through audit logs

Engineering teams pay a heavy ‘siloed database tax’ to meet these needs, standing up five distinct, single-purpose datastores: a vector store for product discovery, a session store for chat history, a short-term memory store for session context, a long-term memory store for accumulated preferences, and an audit log for compliance and debugging.

That fragmentation comes at a cost. Every additional datastore adds its own SDK, its own operational overhead, and its own failure mode. If the profile agent writes a new preference to one store while the product agent reads from another, the two are only as consistent as the ETL job connecting them. In a real-time conversation, that gap shows up as an agent recommending a product the customer already ruled out, or forgetting a preference captured moments earlier.

Retail makes the problem concrete. Carol asks for running shoes for a road marathon. Her profile has her static preference on file: She wears a size eight. Earlier in this conversation, she mentioned wanting maximum cushioning; that's short-term session context. John asks for running shoes, too. His profile puts him at a size 11, but long-term memory holds something neither his profile nor this conversation does: He needs a waterproof build, a fact learned from a past return after a pair let water soak in. Serving both well, consistently, and across every channel requires holding all three—static preferences, session context, and long-term memory—as one coherent view. This is what we’ve built to make this all happen fluidly

Giving every agent the same context

Retailers building a multi-agent system need specialized agents—including planner agents, profile agents, product agents, and eventually others—to discover and invoke each other's capabilities regardless of which team built them. This is what an open protocol like Agent2Agent (A2A) (2) provides. The Multi Agent Retail Advisor (MARA) is a reference implementation. Here, a planner agent delegates to a profile agent and a product agent, coordinating through A2A. The orchestration framework and LLM are both swappable; MongoDB, the data layer underneath every agent, is not.

Figure 1. Reference architecture for the MARA, showing how the planner, profile, and product agents interact through the A2A protocol, with MongoDB Atlas unifying operational and agentic data via Vector Search, text search, and auto-embeddings.

MongoDB Atlas handles all five agentic data needs natively in one platform, as shown in Figure 2 below. Atlas Vector Search stores product embeddings alongside the catalog data itself, so semantic search runs directly against operational data instead of a separate index to remain in sync. The same flexible document model holds customer context and preferences without a schema migration every time a field changes. Short-term memory lives as a nested array inside each session document, allowing the planner agent to fetch an entire conversation in one read. Long-term memory accumulates in its own collection, capturing facts an agent learns about a customer, like a preference for polyester base layers because they dry faster, independent of any single session. Observability runs through the same platform, too, logging every tool call's inputs, outputs, and latency so a request's full execution path can be reconstructed instantly.

Figure 2. MongoDB Atlas consolidates all single-purpose datastores to meet agentic AI’s data needs into one platform.

For product discovery, retailers build directly on Atlas Vector Search. They embed queries with Voyage AI and match them semantically against the catalog, falling back automatically to Atlas full-text search on the same collection when a query needs it, with no extra infrastructure. Because Voyage AI's newer models share a common embedding space, retailers can embed the catalog once with a larger, accurate model, and then run live queries with a smaller, faster model without ever re-indexing.

A simpler, more resilient stack for IT teams

For retailers, the payoff is architectural simplicity that compounds into speed and cost savings. Teams no longer manage four or five separate systems; they manage one. Schema flexibility, shown in Figure 3, lets agent state and user profiles, each varying by shopper or task, evolve without disruptive migrations. Because MongoDB Atlas scales horizontally, it supports the bursty, unpredictable request patterns of autonomous agents without becoming a bottleneck. Full observability works the same way: A single aggregation pipeline query joins the tool_invocations log, agent_state history, and session record for a request, reconstructing what each agent did, in what order, and how long each step took. That gives IT teams a queryable execution trace for every agent decision, shortening the path from a production issue to a root cause.

Figure 3. Two documents from the agent_state collection and two from the users collection. This shows the same collection, different shape, depending on which agent ran or which shopper it describes.

This consolidation also changes how fast a team can move. The product catalog, user profiles, session history, long-term memory, and tool-invocation logs all live as collections in one MongoDB cluster, not four separate systems linked together. That's the difference between a proof of concept shipping in weeks and one spending its first quarter wiring systems together before a single agent runs.  This setup lowers total cost of ownership the same way: one licensing agreement, one scaling model, and one team. Governance benefits too. Fine-grained access controls, encryption, and audit logging apply consistently across every agent's data, instead of system-by-system configuration. Because the architecture is not tied to a specific framework or model provider, retailers can add new agents, inventory, loyalty, and fulfillment onto the same data plane without replatforming. That matters most for agents no one can name yet. Any future agent built on the same document model plugs into the same unified context, turning what would otherwise be a multi-quarter integration effort into a schema extension.

An experience that feels seamless for customers

For customers, this translates into an experience that feels genuinely continuous. Because every agent reads from and writes to the same unified context, a preference shared in one conversation carries into the next. A question that starts in a chat can hand off cleanly to an inventory agent checking store stock or a loyalty agent applying a reward without the customer repeating themselves. This results in recommendations that get sharper the more a customer interacts with the system and a shopping experience that feels like one relationship rather than a series of disconnected sessions.

Figure 4. Any multi-agent retail architecture needs a swappable layer for orchestration and the LLM, but every agent still needs one constant data layer underneath it. Here, that's MongoDB Atlas beneath MARA's planner, profile, and product agents.

That continuity holds up across channels, not just across conversation turns. A preference a customer states while browsing on mobile is available the next time they open a chat window, walk into a store, or call support because it lives in the same unified profile every agent reads from rather than in a channel-specific cache. Customers also benefit from recommendations that account for their actual history rather than generic popularity signals. This happens since the product agent's semantic search runs against a catalog informed by what a shopper has already bought, browsed, and rejected. For the business, that precision compounds directly into commerce metrics: higher conversion, larger basket sizes, and fewer costly returns from recommendations that miss the mark.

Building for what comes next

The orchestration framework and LLM a retailer chooses today will likely change more than once. What shouldn't change is the data layer holding the system together. MongoDB gives retailers a single, flexible foundation for the knowledge, context, memory, and observability multi-agent retail experiences depend on, so the architecture underneath doesn't have to be rebuilt as frameworks and models evolve. Retailers that consolidate this layer now will be the ones ready to add the next agent—and the next protocol—without starting over.

References

  1. The automation curve in agentic commerce. McKinsey. January 28th, 2026. https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-automation-curve-in-agentic-commerce

  2. Getting Started with Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol https://codelabs.developers.google.com/intro-a2a-purchasing-concierge#0

title: Weighted-AoI-Driven UAV Trajectory and Reporting for Dynamic CKM Tracking
description:
arXiv:2611.13726v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing channel knowledge map (CKM) construction assumes quasi-static environments, failing when channels rapidly decorrelate. This paper investigates continuous online dynamic CKM tracking over an airborne 2D plane via a UAV fleet. We formulate a long-term error minimization problem under UAV mobility and reporting constraints. This problem, however, is intractable with unobservable errors for unmeasured cells. To tackle this, we propose a metric-driven scheduling approach featuring the Weighted-Age of Information (W-AoI). W-AoI evaluates cells by combining exact temporal staleness with spatial uncertainty predicted by a 2D U-Net. We prove that top-$K$ W-AoI selection maximizes the one-slot error reduction bound. Guided by this guarantee, we develop a lightweight greedy trajectory policy incorporating continuous along-path sensing. Simulations demonstrate our method reduces steady-state error by 3.8 dB$^2$ and 4.8 dB$^2$ over AoI-only and FIFO baselines, closely approaching an idealized oracle.

title: How to retry a paid Google SERP request safely
description:
A worker sends a paid search request. The connection drops before a reply arrives. On the next queue delivery, the worker creates a fresh UUID and sends the same body. If the first search completed, the second UUID can buy the same observation twice.

Now change one detail. The worker receives a confirmed 408 search_timeout from the API. Sending the same key can replay that failure. One retry policy has to handle both outcomes.

Keep the scheduled check and the API attempt in storage

Use a durable job ID for the scheduled observation. Persist the request body and a UUID for its current API attempt before sending it. If the worker restarts, the next worker can resume the same attempt. A later scheduled check gets its own job and attempt key, even if the query is identical.

In Serper.live, Idempotency-Key identifies an attempt. A replay can return the first attempt's result with Idempotent-Replayed: true. Sending a modified body with the same key can still return the original result. Save the key and body together. Serper.live retry contract

Outcome Next action
Reply missing or unreadable Back off and use the saved key and body
409 idempotency_in_progress Back off and use the saved key and body
Confirmed API 408, 424, or 503 Back off, persist a new attempt key, and retry the same body
409 idempotency_replay_unavailable Stop automatic retries and reconcile the attempt
Successful search Save the observation and finish the job
Other confirmed API error Record the failure for handling by the caller

The replay window is up to 15 minutes. Bound the retry budget accordingly. If the result is still unknown when the window expires, use the saved attempt details and any request ID to investigate before starting a fresh paid search. A new key starts a new search. Serper.live errors and replay behavior

Test the decision without making a search

Save this as retry.mjs and run node retry.mjs. The worker passes an HTTP status only when it can identify the response as coming from the API. A connection reset or a generic gateway reply leaves the outcome unknown. For a success, pass status 200 after decoding the result.

import assert from "node:assert/strict";

function retryAction({ status = null, code } = {}) {
  if (status === 200) return "store-result";

  if (status === null ||
      (status === 409 && code === "idempotency_in_progress")) {
    return "retry-same-key";
  }

  if (status === 409 && code === "idempotency_replay_unavailable") {
    return "reconcile";
  }

  if ([408, 424, 503].includes(status)) return "retry-new-key";
  return "record-failure";
}

assert.equal(retryAction(), "retry-same-key");
assert.equal(
  retryAction({ status: 409, code: "idempotency_in_progress" }),
  "retry-same-key",
);
assert.equal(
  retryAction({ status: 409, code: "idempotency_replay_unavailable" }),
  "reconcile",
);
for (const status of [408, 424, 503]) {
  assert.equal(retryAction({ status }), "retry-new-key");
}
assert.equal(retryAction({ status: 200 }), "store-result");
assert.equal(retryAction({ status: 422 }), "record-failure");
console.log("Retry decisions passed");

A real worker executes the decision. Claim the job before reading its current attempt so two deliveries cannot both rotate the key. For a same-key retry, keep the body byte-for-byte and schedule the next attempt with backoff. For a new-key retry, write the new key to storage before the next POST. An attempt counter and next-run time belong in that same write.

When the worker sends the request, the persisted key goes in the header. The API allows a search to run up to 90 seconds and documents a client timeout of at least 100 seconds. A short deadline can leave the outcome ambiguous while the search is still running. Serper.live client timeout guidance

curl --include --max-time 100 https://api.serper.live/v1/search \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SERPER_LIVE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: $SERPER_LIVE_ATTEMPT_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-binary @attempt-body.json

Use a stored JSON body such as {"query":"espresso scale","country":"US","language":"en","device":"mobile","limit":10}. On success, save the response and mark the job complete in one local transaction, or make the result write idempotent by job ID. That handles the other common crash window, when the worker gets the result and dies before acknowledging the queue message.

title: How an EV Charger Talks to Your Car: Building an EVSE State Machine in Rust
description:
When you plug an electric car into a charger, nothing happens for a moment. The charger isn't broken, it's doing a handshake. Before any real power flows, the charger (the EVSE, Electric Vehicle Supply Equipment) and the car agree over a single wire that it is safe to start.

That handshake is a classic state machine problem, and Rust handles it well. In this post I'll explain how the signalling works, show a firmware architecture that keeps the safety logic testable, and build the core in Rust.

Disclaimer: this is an educational example. Real chargers handle mains voltage and must be designed and certified to standards like IEC 61851 and UL 2594. Don't use this code as-is in a real product.

The control pilot signal

The connector has a signal wire called the Control Pilot (CP). The charger puts a 1 kHz square wave on it, and the car pulls the voltage level down with a resistor network. The charger reads the positive peak voltage to learn what the car is doing:

State CP voltage Meaning
A +12 V No vehicle connected
B +9 V Vehicle connected, not ready to charge
C +6 V Vehicle ready, charging
D +3 V Charging, ventilation required
E 0 V Error (short to ground)
F -12 V EVSE unavailable

The charger also uses the duty cycle of that square wave to tell the car the maximum current it may draw. For 6 to 51 A, the duty cycle in percent is amps / 0.6. For 32 A that's about 53.3%.

The handshake

  1. Idle: nothing plugged in. The charger outputs a steady +12 V and reads state A.
  2. Connected: the car is plugged in, and the pilot voltage drops to +9 V (state B). The charger starts the PWM to advertise how much current it can supply.
  3. Charging: the car accepts and pulls the voltage to +6 V (state C). Only now does the charger close the contactor and let power flow.
  4. Faulted: if anything looks wrong (ground fault, error states, ventilation required), the charger opens the contactor immediately and stays latched in the fault until the car is unplugged.

The most important design rule is that the contactor closes only in Charging, and Charging requires pilot state C with no ground fault. Everything else in the design exists to enforce that rule.

Firmware architecture

A good EVSE firmware separates concerns into layers:

  • Hardware: the pilot generator (+/-12 V, 1 kHz), an ADC to sample the pilot peak, the contactor driver, the ground fault (GFCI) detector, the proximity pilot (cable rating), and an energy meter.
  • Hardware abstraction layer: a Rust trait that hides the real peripherals. On the microcontroller it talks to ADC, PWM and GPIO. In tests it's a fake.
  • Pure Rust core: the part that decides things. It takes inputs (pilot voltage, ground fault flag) and returns the next state and the required outputs. No I/O, no globals, no heap, so it can be no_std.
  • Application / supervisor: authorization (RFID or app), load management, display and logging. It decides what max current to offer, and it can request a stop, but it can never force the contactor closed.
  • Backend: the charging station management system, usually reached over OCPP. DC fast chargers also talk to the car with higher-level protocols like ISO 15118, but the basic pilot handshake still comes first.

The key decision is keeping the core as pure functions. Pure functions are trivial to test exhaustively, and you can run the exact same code on your laptop and on the chip.

The Rust implementation

First, classify the measured voltage into a pilot state, and compute the PWM duty cycle for a given current limit:

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum PilotState { A, B, C, D, E, F }

/// Classify the positive peak of the control pilot signal.
fn classify_pilot(volts: f32) -> PilotState {
    match volts {
        v if v >= 10.5 => PilotState::A, // ~ +12 V
        v if v >= 7.5 => PilotState::B,  // ~ +9 V
        v if v >= 4.5 => PilotState::C,  // ~ +6 V
        v if v >= 1.5 => PilotState::D,  // ~ +3 V
        v if v >= -1.5 => PilotState::E, // ~ 0 V
        _ => PilotState::F,              // ~ -12 V
    }
}

/// Duty cycle (percent) that advertises `amps` to the vehicle.
fn duty_for_amps(amps: f32) -> f32 {
    let amps = amps.clamp(6.0, 80.0);
    if amps <= 51.0 {
        amps / 0.6
    } else {
        amps / 2.5 + 64.0
    }
}

Next, the state machine itself. States and faults are enums, so the compiler forces us to handle every combination:

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum Fault {
    PilotFault,
    VentilationRequired,
    GroundFault,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum EvseState {
    Idle,
    Connected,
    Charging,
    Faulted(Fault),
}

struct Inputs {
    pilot: PilotState,
    ground_fault: bool,
}

fn next_state(current: EvseState, input: Inputs) -> EvseState {
    use EvseState::*;
    use PilotState::*;

    // Safety checks override everything else.
    if input.ground_fault {
        return Faulted(Fault::GroundFault);
    }

    match (current, input.pilot) {
        // A fault only clears when the car is unplugged.
        (Faulted(_), A) => Idle,
        (Faulted(f), _) => Faulted(f),

        (_, E) | (_, F) => Faulted(Fault::PilotFault),
        (_, A) => Idle,
        (_, D) => Faulted(Fault::VentilationRequired),

        (Idle, B | C) => Connected,
        (Connected | Charging, B) => Connected,
        (Connected | Charging, C) => Charging,
    }
}

The match has no wildcard arm for the non-faulted cases. If you add a new state later, the compiler refuses to build until you've decided what happens in every combination. That is the main reason I like Rust for this kind of code.

Now the outputs. Notice that the contactor is a pure function of the state:

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
enum PilotOutput {
    Steady12V,
    Pwm { duty_pct: f32 },
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
struct Outputs {
    contactor_closed: bool,
    pilot: PilotOutput,
}

fn outputs(state: EvseState, max_amps: f32) -> Outputs {
    use EvseState::*;
    let pwm = PilotOutput::Pwm { duty_pct: duty_for_amps(max_amps) };

    match state {
        Idle => Outputs { contactor_closed: false, pilot: PilotOutput::Steady12V },
        Connected => Outputs { contactor_closed: false, pilot: pwm },
        Charging => Outputs { contactor_closed: true, pilot: pwm },
        // Contactor open, no PWM: the car sees "not ready".
        Faulted(_) => Outputs { contactor_closed: false, pilot: PilotOutput::Steady12V },
    }
}

Plugging in the hardware

The real hardware lives behind a trait, and the control loop is just glue:

trait EvseHardware {
    fn read_pilot_peak_volts(&mut self) -> f32;
    fn ground_fault(&mut self) -> bool;
    fn set_pilot(&mut self, out: PilotOutput);
    fn set_contactor(&mut self, closed: bool);
}

fn control_tick<H: EvseHardware>(hw: &mut H, state: &mut EvseState, max_amps: f32) {
    let pilot = classify_pilot(hw.read_pilot_peak_volts());
    let ground_fault = hw.ground_fault();

    *state = next_state(*state, Inputs { pilot, ground_fault });

    let out = outputs(*state, max_amps);
    hw.set_pilot(out.pilot);
    hw.set_contactor(out.contactor_closed);
}

Call control_tick from a timer interrupt or an async task and you have the full loop. On an STM32 or ESP32, EvseHardware would wrap embedded-hal peripherals.

Running a simulated session

Here's a small main that replays a scripted session, including a ground fault halfway through:

fn main() {
    let max_amps = 32.0;
    let mut state = EvseState::Idle;

    // (pilot voltage read by the EVSE, ground fault flag)
    let script = [
        (12.0, false), // nothing plugged in
        (9.0, false),  // car plugged in
        (6.0, false),  // car asks for power
        (6.0, false),  // charging
        (6.0, true),   // ground fault!
        (6.0, false),  // fault stays latched
        (12.0, false), // unplugged, fault clears
    ];

    for (volts, gf) in script {
        let pilot = classify_pilot(volts);
        state = next_state(state, Inputs { pilot, ground_fault: gf });
        let out = outputs(state, max_amps);

        let pilot_out = match out.pilot {
            PilotOutput::Steady12V => "steady +12 V".to_string(),
            PilotOutput::Pwm { duty_pct } => format!("PWM {duty_pct:.1}%"),
        };
        let contactor = if out.contactor_closed { "CLOSED" } else { "open" };

        println!("{volts:>5.1} V | {pilot:?} | {state:?} | contactor {contactor} | {pilot_out}");
    }
}

Expected output:

 12.0 V | A | Idle | contactor open | steady +12 V
  9.0 V | B | Connected | contactor open | PWM 53.3%
  6.0 V | C | Charging | contactor CLOSED | PWM 53.3%
  6.0 V | C | Charging | contactor CLOSED | PWM 53.3%
  6.0 V | C | Faulted(GroundFault) | contactor open | steady +12 V
  6.0 V | C | Faulted(GroundFault) | contactor open | steady +12 V
 12.0 V | A | Idle | contactor open | steady +12 V

Testing the safety rule

Because the core is pure, we can check the most important rule exhaustively. This test tries every state, every pilot reading and both ground fault values, and asserts that the contactor only ever closes when the pilot is C and there is no ground fault:

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn contactor_closes_only_in_state_c_without_fault() {
        use PilotState::*;
        let states = [
            EvseState::Idle,
            EvseState::Connected,
            EvseState::Charging,
            EvseState::Faulted(Fault::PilotFault),
        ];

        for s in states {
            for p in [A, B, C, D, E, F] {
                for gf in [false, true] {
                    let next = next_state(s, Inputs { pilot: p, ground_fault: gf });
                    if outputs(next, 32.0).contactor_closed {
                        assert_eq!(p, C);
                        assert!(!gf);
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn ground_fault_opens_contactor() {
        let s = next_state(
            EvseState::Charging,
            Inputs { pilot: PilotState::C, ground_fault: true },
        );
        assert_eq!(s, EvseState::Faulted(Fault::GroundFault));
        assert!(!outputs(s, 32.0).contactor_closed);
    }

    #[test]
    fn thirty_two_amps_is_about_53_percent_duty() {
        assert!((duty_for_amps(32.0) - 53.3).abs() < 0.1);
    }
}

Run it with cargo test. This is something you can't easily do with firmware that mixes I/O into the decision logic.

What this leaves out

A real charger needs much more than this:

  • Proximity Pilot (PP) to detect the cable's current rating, and the plug-latch button.
  • Diode check on the pilot's negative half, which proves the car's circuitry is intact.
  • Welded contactor detection, so the charger notices if the contactor didn't actually open.
  • Timing requirements from the standard for how quickly outputs must change after a state change.
  • Hysteresis and debounce on the ADC reading, so noise doesn't cause false transitions.
  • Watchdogs and redundant protection that work independently of the firmware.

Where to take it next

  • Move the core to no_std and run it on an ESP32 or STM32 with embedded-hal.
  • Add the proximity pilot and cap max_amps to the cable rating.
  • Add an OCPP client in the application layer for remote start/stop.
  • Write a fake EvseHardware and replay recorded sessions as integration tests.

Wrapping up

An EV charger handshake is a small problem with real safety stakes, which makes it a great fit for Rust. Enums make the states explicit, exhaustive match stops you from forgetting a case, and keeping the core pure lets you prove the safety rule with a test instead of hoping for it.

If you build on this, tell me in the comments.

title: One Turnstile or One Lane? Mutex vs. a Single-Thread Executor on Android
description:
Both give you “one at a time.” They protect different things, fail in different ways, and picking the wrong one produces bugs that only show up under load.


One Turnstile or One Lane? Mutex vs. a Single-Thread Executor on Android

The short version

  • A Mutex guards a region of code. Waiting coroutines suspend, no thread is blocked, and whoever wins may resume on any dispatcher thread.
  • A single-thread executor guards a thread. Work queues up and runs on one dedicated thread, always the same one.
  • If the code must live on a specific thread (a JNI handle, a thread-affine SDK), you want the executor. If you only need to keep a read-modify-write sequence from interleaving, you almost always want the Mutex.
  • Neither is a free lunch. The Mutex hangs silently when misused; the executor leaks or swallows errors silently. Most of this post is about those silences.

Two different promises

People reach for both tools with the same sentence in their head: “I need these calls to not overlap.” That sentence hides a real difference in what is being guaranteed.

A Mutex promises mutual exclusion over a block. Between lock() and unlock(), no other coroutine using the same mutex is inside that block. It says nothing about which thread runs the block, and a coroutine can hop threads inside it if it suspends and its dispatcher resumes it elsewhere.

A single-thread executor promises thread confinement. Every task runs on the same worker, one after another. It says nothing about whether two logical operations can interleave, because a coroutine that suspends gives the thread to the next task in the queue.

The side-by-side below is the reference I keep coming back to.

A single thread is not an atomic step

This is the misconception that causes the most damage, so it comes first.

Suppose a wallet class keeps a balance and records every deposit with a remote ledger:

class CreditsWallet(private val ledger: LedgerApi) {
    var balance = 100
        private set

    suspend fun deposit(amount: Int) {
        val before = balance           // 1. read
        ledger.record(amount)          // 2. suspension point
        balance = before + amount      // 3. write back a possibly stale total
    }
}

“I’ll run it on one thread, so there’s no race.” Here is a test that tries exactly that:

@Test
fun `one thread still loses a deposit`() = runBlocking {
    val single = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher()
    val wallet = CreditsWallet(FakeLedger(delayMs = 20))

    try {
        withContext(single) {
            listOf(30, 50).map { launch { wallet.deposit(it) } }.joinAll()
        }
        assertEquals(180, wallet.balance)   // fails: you get 130 or 150
    } finally {
        single.close()
    }
}

Both children inherit single, so everything runs on one thread. The assertion still fails, because the delay inside FakeLedger.record suspends the first coroutine, the thread picks up the second one, and both captured before = 100. Whichever finishes last wins, and one deposit disappears.

The thread guaranteed that no two statements ran simultaneously. It never promised that your three-step sequence would run contiguously. Suspension points are exactly where contiguity breaks.

There are two honest fixes. The first is to make the critical section a single non-suspending step, so the dispatcher cannot slip anything in:

suspend fun deposit(amount: Int) {
    ledger.record(amount)      // slow work first, outside any shared-state access
    balance += amount          // one non-suspending step; atomic on a single thread
}

That works only while everything stays on one thread. The moment someone injects Dispatchers.Default, balance += amount is a data race again. The second fix does not depend on where the code runs:

class CreditsWallet(private val ledger: LedgerApi) {
    private val mutex = Mutex()
    private var balance = 100

    suspend fun deposit(amount: Int) {
        ledger.record(amount)
        mutex.withLock { balance += amount }
    }

    suspend fun current(): Int = mutex.withLock { balance }
}

I prefer this one for shared state. It states its own invariant instead of borrowing it from a dispatcher choice made in another file.

Mutex, idiomatically

Three habits cover most of what goes right with Mutex.

Always use withLock. It wraps the body in try/finally, so an exception or a cancellation releases the lock. Bare lock() and unlock() pairs belong in library internals.

Keep the critical section small, except when atomicity demands otherwise. Sometimes check and act really must be one unit. A spend operation is the textbook case: checking the balance, asking the server to authorize, and deducting cannot be split, or two concurrent calls can both pass the check.

suspend fun spend(amount: Int): Boolean = mutex.withLock {
    if (balance < amount) return@withLock false

    // Lock held across a network call on purpose: check and deduct are one unit.
    val approved = withTimeout(3_000) { ledger.authorize(amount) }
    if (approved) balance -= amount
    approved
}

The withTimeout is not decoration. Every other caller is queued behind this one, so an unbounded call turns one slow request into a frozen feature. When the timeout fires, withLock still releases the lock on the way out.

Remember that Mutex is fair and cancellable. Waiters are served first come, first served, and a coroutine cancelled while waiting for lock() leaves the queue cleanly. That is why a screen that launches work in viewModelScope does not strand a lock when the user navigates away.

Single-thread executor, idiomatically

Reach for an executor when the thread is the constraint. A common Android case is a native engine, reached through JNI, that must be created, used, and released from the same thread:

class NativeRecorder(private val engine: RecorderEngine) {

    private val executor = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { task ->
        Thread(task, "native-recorder").apply { isDaemon = true }
    }
    private val dispatcher = executor.asCoroutineDispatcher()

    suspend fun start(sampleRate: Int) = withContext(dispatcher) {
        engine.open(sampleRate)
        engine.start()
    }

    suspend fun nextFrame(): ShortArray = withContext(dispatcher) { engine.pull() }

    suspend fun shutdown() {
        // Teardown must still run on the owning thread, even if the caller was cancelled.
        withContext(NonCancellable + dispatcher) { engine.release() }
        dispatcher.close()   // shuts the executor down
    }
}

A few choices here are deliberate.

  • Build the executor yourself. A custom ThreadFactory gives the thread a name that shows up in traces and lets you decide about the daemon flag. The convenience factory newSingleThreadContext is marked as a delicate API precisely because it makes leaking a thread easy.
  • Bridge with asCoroutineDispatcher(), then use withContext at the call sites. Callers stay in ordinary suspending code and never touch the executor directly.
  • Release on the owning thread. The engine.release() call runs through the same dispatcher, so the native side sees the same thread from open to close.
  • Use NonCancellable for teardown. If shutdown() is invoked from a scope that is already cancelled, a plain withContext throws before running its block, and the engine is never released.

If all you need is “no two of these run at once” and you do not need a particular thread, Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1) gives you serialized execution without owning a thread. Be clear about what it does not give you: it does not promise the same thread each time, so it is not a substitute for thread affinity.

Failure modes in production

The cheat sheet below summarizes the six I see most. The sections after it explain the ones that deserve code.

1. The lock that waits on itself

Mutex is not reentrant. A coroutine that holds the lock and calls another function that takes the same lock suspends forever, waiting for a release only it can perform. There is no exception, no log line, and the ANR (if this was on the main path) is the first symptom anyone sees.

class Ledger {
    private val mutex = Mutex()
    private val entries = mutableListOf<Entry>()

    suspend fun transfer(from: String, to: String, amount: Int) = mutex.withLock {
        entries += Entry(from, -amount)
        entries += Entry(to, amount)
        audit()                      // takes the same mutex: never returns
    }

    suspend fun audit() = mutex.withLock {
        check(entries.sumOf { it.delta } == 0) { "ledger out of balance" }
    }
}

The fix is structural, not clever. Public functions lock once; private helpers assume the lock is held and say so in their name.

suspend fun transfer(from: String, to: String, amount: Int) = mutex.withLock {
    entries += Entry(from, -amount)
    entries += Entry(to, amount)
    auditLocked()
}

suspend fun audit() = mutex.withLock { auditLocked() }

private fun auditLocked() {
    check(entries.sumOf { it.delta } == 0) { "ledger out of balance" }
}

A cheap test catches this class of bug: call every public method from every other public method inside a withTimeout, and fail on timeout.

2. Slow work inside the lock

Head-of-line blocking is the quiet cousin of the deadlock. The lock is correct, the code is correct, and the screen is still frozen because the one coroutine in the critical section is waiting on a slow endpoint. Where atomicity does not require holding the lock across I/O, split the work into three phases: snapshot under the lock, do the slow part outside, commit under the lock.

suspend fun refreshQuota() {
    val stamp = mutex.withLock { version }          // snapshot
    val fresh = api.fetchQuota()                    // slow, no lock held
    mutex.withLock {
        if (version == stamp) quota = fresh         // commit only if nothing changed
    }
}

3. Executors that swallow or crash

The two ways to hand work to an executor treat exceptions differently, and both surprise people.

executor.submit { error("lost forever") }    // failure is stored in the Future; nobody sees it
executor.execute { error("loud") }           // reaches the thread's uncaught-exception handler

With submit, the error sits inside a Future that nobody reads. With execute, the uncaught exception reaches the thread's handler, which on Android normally ends the process. Inside a coroutine dispatcher the picture changes again: the coroutine machinery catches the exception and routes it through the job hierarchy. The rule of thumb is to decide on purpose. Catch and report inside the task, or read the result, and never let the choice be an accident of which method you called.

4. The thread nobody shuts down

A thread from newSingleThreadExecutor stays alive while idle, and it holds references to everything its tasks captured. If the owner is a screen-scoped object and the executor is never shut down, the thread and those references live as long as the process. Pair every executor with an owner that closes it: shutdown() for the raw executor, close() for the coroutine dispatcher built on it.

5. Waiting on your own queue 

val worker = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()
worker.submit {
    val inner = worker.submit { compute() }   // queued behind the task that is running
    inner.get()                               // blocks the only worker: deadlock
}

The inner task cannot start until the outer one finishes, and the outer one will not finish until the inner one does. With a pool of one, every blocking get() on the same executor is a self-deadlock. Chain the work, or pass a callback.

Android-specific notes

  • The main thread. A suspended Mutex.withLock does not block the main thread, which is the point. A blocking primitive combined with runBlocking on the main thread absolutely does, and that is how lock bugs turn into ANRs.
  • Do not suspend inside synchronized. The compiler rejects it, and a ReentrantLock held across a suspension is worse, because the coroutine may resume on another thread and then fail to unlock a lock owned by the first.
  • Testing. A Mutex does not care which thread runs it, so StandardTestDispatcher and virtual time work fine. A thread-affine design cannot be faked that way. Inject the dispatcher, use a test dispatcher for logic, and add one integration test on the real single-thread dispatcher that asserts Thread.currentThread().name inside the guarded calls.
  • Lifecycle. Put the thing that owns a thread in a scope that outlives the screens using it, and run teardown with NonCancellable, as in shutdown() above. A ViewModel's scope is already cancelled by the time onCleared() runs.

Choosing

A few notes on that flow, since a diagram flattens the nuance.

  1. Thread first. If a library or native handle demands one thread, nothing else on the list can satisfy it. This is the only question where the executor is the only correct answer.
  2. Suspension second. If the guarded section suspends, a blocking lock is off the table. Mutex is the tool built for that.
  3. Single values third. A counter or flag does not need a lock object. AtomicInteger, or MutableStateFlow.update { } when observers care, is shorter and cannot deadlock.
  4. Otherwise, keep it boring. If nothing suspends and no thread is mandated, a plain synchronized block over a tiny section is the cheapest option. Use Mutex there only if you want one consistent tool across the codebase.

🔚 Closing

The two tools answer different questions. The executor answers where does this run? The Mutex answers who is inside this block right now? Confusing them is how a "thread-safe" wallet ends up with a missing deposit. Treat suspension points as the places where guarantees break, keep critical sections small, close what you open, and write the test that makes the silent failures loud.

Further reading

  • The Kotlin guide on shared mutable state and concurrency covers thread confinement and Mutex from the language's own perspective: https://kotlinlang.org/docs/shared-mutable-state-and-concurrency.html
  • The Mutex API reference documents fairness, reentrancy, and tryLock: https://kotlinlang.org/api/kotlinx.coroutines/kotlinx-coroutines-core/kotlinx.coroutines.sync/-mutex/

🔐 Master Android Architecture: Volume 1, Foundations and Core Architecture

Most Android architecture advice is a diagram and a list of rules. This book teaches the judgment behind them. You build NowReading from an empty project into an offline-first app, one decision at a time. It covers the principles behind Google’s layered architecture, then every layer in depth: Compose and state holders, MVI, navigation, the domain layer, Room and DataStore, networking, offline-first sync, Hilt, coroutines and Flow, background work and error handling. Every chapter opens with a realistic failure and ends with pitfalls, trade-offs, review questions and an exercise.

title: SafeRoute-MAS: Coverage-Aware and Risk-Calibrated Message Routing for Multi-Agent Scientific Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.13454v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce SafeRoute-MAS, a coverage-aware, risk-calibrated procedure that keeps all specialist messages or removes one using only pre-integration information. On a sealed cache of 5,328 committees, its source-compatible operating point gains +1.80 percentage points (95% CI [+1.13, +2.52]) while removing 12.76% of message tokens. We also run 4,580 controlled integrations over a stratified 458-committee sample on a public gpt-oss-120b endpoint. The sample estimate is -0.09 points; design weighting to the original workload gives +0.94 points (95% CI [-1.31, +3.50]) and 18.72% acted-input reduction. A weighted token-matched comparison likewise does not establish a selector advantage (+1.68 points, CI [-1.27, +5.10]). Only 13 of 88 cached non-neutral labels (14.8%) retain direction by repeated-call majority. Expected-corruption UCL is 4.60% after weighting, but only 2 of 11 prespecified marginals pass the support/risk rule. We therefore propose a numerical qualification with Keep-All fallback, applied here retrospectively rather than validated prospectively.

title: RadRef: A Reference-Free Metric for Radiology Report Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.13168v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI-generated radiology reports are usually evaluated by comparison with a radiologist-authored reference, leaving no way to score them when no reference exists. We introduce RadRef, a reference-free metric that scores report claims against image-derived beliefs over a clinical finding vocabulary, weighted by relevance to the clinical indication. On ReXVal, RadRef achieves 73.1% agreement on non-tied same-radiograph report pairs with radiologist rankings, comparable to leading reference-based metrics overall. It is also competitive on false findings and has its clearest relative result on omissions (missed findings). We further evaluate 100 model-generated and 100 radiologist-authored reports from 100 MIMIC-CXR studies, all independently annotated by two board-certified radiologists. On omissions, RadRef attains Kendall's tau-b = 0.295, against 0.386 between the two readers themselves, and no compared metric differs significantly from RadRef on this target. The same image-grounded representation provides a false-finding readout, RadRef-FF, with tau-b = 0.32 on ReXVal and 0.29 in the reader study, without requiring a reference. Controlled perturbations confirm that RadRef depends on the radiograph, report, and clinical indication. RadRef enables image-grounded evaluation before a radiologist-authored reference exists, supporting quality monitoring of report-generation systems in clinical settings, and complements reference-based metrics when one is available.

title: Backend Interview Question: Two Buyers Want the Last Seat. Who Gets It?
description:
A small PostgreSQL example, a deliberately broken timeline, and the follow ups that turn a working demo into a defensible answer.

Both buyers saw the same available seat. Both clicked the button and both received a confirmation, and now somebody has a very awkward email to write.

Nothing about this requires a million requests per second. Two requests arriving in the wrong order are enough.

That is why I like this backend practice problem. You can draw an impressive architecture around it, but eventually somebody has to explain which operation is allowed to say that seat A7 belongs to one buyer.

Let’s work through an original interview style exercise, without pretending it came from a particular company. We control the inventory, use one PostgreSQL database for claims, and start with a single seat for a single event. Payment and expiring holds come later because they add different promises.

Start with the promise, because available is only an observation

Our first rule is that a seat can have at most one committed owner. We also need the application to avoid telling two different buyers that each owns it.

Those are related, but they are not identical. A database row can end up with one owner even after the application has sent two contradictory success messages.

For this exercise, a claim is final once committed. We are not implementing cancellation, seat transfers, or checkout timeouts yet. Buyer identity comes from the authenticated request, and the seat is identified by both event and seat number.

I prefer making those assumptions visible before reaching for a lock. Otherwise, we can spend ten minutes solving a reservation problem when the interviewer meant a temporary hold.

Watch the version that looks perfectly reasonable in a demo

Imagine the application reads the row, sees no owner, and then sends a separate update that assigns the buyer. Its update identifies the seat but does not require the owner to remain empty.

Buyer A reads the empty owner. Before A writes anything, buyer B reads that same empty owner. A assigns the seat to A and receives a success response. B then assigns the seat to B and receives another success response.

The final row contains B. That does not rescue A’s confirmation.

Wrapping this exact read-then-unconditional-write sequence in transactions is not, by itself, the missing explanation. You still need to explain how competing transactions are prevented from acting on the same earlier observation.

Disabling the button in the browser cannot coordinate two buyers either. Neither can a lock inside just one application process when requests can land on different instances.

Put the condition where ownership changes

Here is a deliberately small schema for the exercise. Each event seat pair has exactly one row, and an empty owner means unclaimed.

CREATE TABLE seat_claims (
  event_id bigint NOT NULL,
  seat_no text NOT NULL,
  buyer_id bigint,
  PRIMARY KEY (event_id, seat_no)
);

INSERT INTO seat_claims (event_id, seat_no)
VALUES (42, 'A7');

Buyer 101 attempts this conditional update. Buyer 202 runs the same statement with their own authenticated identity.

UPDATE seat_claims
SET buyer_id = 101
WHERE event_id = 42
  AND seat_no = 'A7'
  AND buyer_id IS NULL
RETURNING event_id, seat_no, buyer_id;

Now the requirement that the seat is unclaimed belongs to the write itself. We have removed the gap between trusting an earlier check and assigning ownership.

Under PostgreSQL’s Read Committed behavior, competing updates to the same row coordinate through the database. If A holds the row while B attempts the update, B waits. When A commits, B checks its condition against the updated row. The owner is no longer empty, so B changes zero rows. PostgreSQL documents this rechecking behavior for concurrent updates.

One returned row means this statement assigned the seat in its transaction. Zero returned rows means it did not claim the seat. In our fixed fixture the seat exists, so zero means it is already claimed; a real endpoint must also decide how to handle missing or inaccessible seats.

This is a narrow solution for a narrow rule. Every ownership-changing path must respect the same rule. An administrative endpoint that blindly overwrites buyer_id would undo the guarantee we are trying to offer.

Also, concurrency safety does not promise fairness. We have not established that the person who clicked first will win. Either buyer can win depending on execution order.

Keep the celebration on the other side of COMMIT

Honestly, this is the part I want written beside the code in big letters.

If the statement runs inside an explicit transaction, receiving a returned row is not the same as committing that transaction. A later error can still cause a rollback. The application must not confirm ownership before it knows the commit succeeded.

Suppose a booking record must accompany the claim. Write both in one database transaction and roll back together if either operation fails. Our tiny example uses the seat row as the ownership record, so it intentionally leaves that extra table out.

Now let the commit succeed but lose the response on its way to the client. The buyer retries and the conditional update returns nothing because the seat is already owned. That does not necessarily mean their first attempt failed.

For a production contract, give the operation a durable identifier scoped to the authenticated buyer, persist its result with the claim, and let a retry recover that same result. Reusing an identifier with different intent needs a defined conflict response. The ownership predicate prevents competing claims; identifying the original operation resolves an ambiguous retry. Our short SQL statement implements the first part, not the entire retry contract.

Make the race happen deliberately in two terminals

Do this in a disposable local database with two independent connections, using Read Committed. The sequence below is a reproducible practice exercise with expected outcomes, not a claimed production benchmark.

  • In connection A, begin a transaction and run the conditional update as buyer 101. Leave the transaction open after it returns A7.
  • In connection B, begin another transaction and run the same update as buyer 202. It should wait while A holds the conflicting row lock.
  • Commit A. B should finish without returning a row, and you can then commit B. Inspect the stored owner and expect 101.
  • Reset the fixture after both transactions finish, then repeat with A rolling back instead. B should now be able to claim A7, and committing B should leave owner 202.

Keep the waiting transactions short, and clean up both connections if you interrupt the exercise. A lock timeout or another database error is an error path to handle, not evidence that somebody successfully acquired the seat.

Check what the database stores and what each caller is told. Two green HTTP responses are not a correctness test, and one final row is not proof that every earlier response was truthful.

Let the follow-up change the design instead of adding random boxes

An expiring hold changes our state model. Now we need a hold identity, an owner, an expiry rule, and a guarded transition to confirmed. An old timeout task must not release a newer buyer’s hold, so its update needs to identify the exact hold it is expiring.

Payment introduces another boundary. A database transaction cannot roll back a charge performed by an external payment provider. Avoid holding the seat’s database lock open while waiting for that network call. Design the hold, payment result, confirmation, and recovery rules explicitly, including what happens when payment succeeds after the hold expires.

For a useful variation, try this inventory design problem. Begin by deciding whether the service actually controls the stock. A reservation in your database cannot stop an unrelated shopper from taking an item off somebody else’s store shelf.

That is the habit I want this little seat example to build. Name the promise, find the exact write that protects it, and make two callers challenge it at the same time.

Before moving to your next problem, explain what changes when A rolls back and when A commits but loses the response. If those two stories sound different in your answer, you are practicing something much more useful than memorizing the word transaction.

~ Emily
