title: Pair-Merge Tokenisation Is Hard to Approximate on Binary Strings and Strongly NP-Hard on Unary Datasets
description:
arXiv:2611.13568v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Tokenisers such as Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) shorten text by repeatedly merging an adjacent pair of symbols into a new one; fewer tokens mean less computation. We ask whether an efficient algorithm can choose $k$ merges that leave a string of length $n$ almost as short as possible; doing nothing is already within a factor $n$. We prove that, unless P = NP, no polynomial-time algorithm comes within a factor $c\,n/\log n$, for some constant $c>0$, already for one binary string and for BPE-style merges that replace every occurrence. The key idea is that $k$ merges form a grammar with $k$ rules: a vertex-cover gap becomes a grammar-size gap, which we amplify with relabelled copies, encode in binary and realise with explicit merges. For merges that may skip occurrences, a simple algorithm achieves $O(n/\log\log n)$, and no Karp reduction can prove hardness beyond order $n/\log n$ unless coNP $\subseteq$ NP/poly. Over a one-letter alphabet, both tokenisation problems left open by Kastreva et al. are strongly NP-complete on datasets with repeated strings.

title: E-commerce Product Search Retrieval Architecture: Go Freshness Windows for Bounded Updates
description:
Short answer: for e-commerce product search, use a staged retrieval architecture with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that can be traced back to a product record.

At 3 a.m., the useful question is not “is the dashboard green?” It is “which page fired, and can I explain the result a shopper is seeing?” Product search makes that question concrete: price, inventory, and compliance fields change on different clocks, so one global freshness window quietly turns either into stale results or needless re-indexing.

The incident lesson: freshness is a retrieval contract

The production scenario is bounded rather than heroic. A catalog importer writes product documents, an embedding job chunks descriptions, and a vector index serves semantic candidates before a lexical or business-rules stage narrows them. When a price edit arrived during an embedding run, the system had two conflicting truths: the text chunk was recent, while the offer metadata was old. The alert told us indexing was healthy. It did not tell us the answer was explainable.

That was the page.

The invariant is simple: map the user-visible answer to a retrieval contract before choosing a database. The contract should name the collection, the fields allowed to participate, the maximum age for each change class, and the source URL or document identifier returned with every chunk. Tenant and access-control metadata travel with the item; they are filters, not optional annotations.

A practical policy uses separate windows. Inventory and price changes deserve minutes, editorial copy can tolerate hours, and rarely changing specifications can tolerate a day. Those are policy examples, not a benchmark. Your catalog may demand tighter bounds, and I’m not sure a single number can survive a seasonal sale without an explicit override.

How should an e-commerce product search query use freshness windows?

First retrieve narrowly from the collection whose freshness contract is satisfied. Apply a hard timeout, a result limit, and a retry budget at each stage. A slow source must not hold the shopper request open while a background refresh catches up. The response should carry the chunk’s product identifier, source URL, collection, and observed version so a reviewer can reconstruct why it was selected.

The second stage can rerank candidates with current offer data. If that data is outside its window, mark the candidate stale and exclude it from a purchase-critical answer; do not silently blend it with fresh text. This is where traceability pays for itself: a support engineer can compare the answer to the source record instead of trusting a score on a dashboard.

Here is a small Go client for the bounded query stage. It keeps the decision visible in code, reads the key from the environment, and backs off when the service asks for a retry.

package freshness

import (
    "bytes"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type ChangeClass string

const (
    Inventory ChangeClass = "inventory"
    Offer     ChangeClass = "offer"
    Content   ChangeClass = "content"
)

type Item struct {
    ProductID   string
    TenantID    string
    Class       ChangeClass
    UpdatedAt   time.Time
    Source      string
    AccessScope string
}

func window(class ChangeClass) time.Duration {
    switch class {
    case Inventory, Offer:
        return 10 * time.Minute
    case Content:
        return 6 * time.Hour
    default:
        return 24 * time.Hour
    }
}

func needsRefresh(item Item, now time.Time) bool {
    return now.Sub(item.UpdatedAt) >= window(item.Class)
}

func idempotencyKey(item Item) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(item.TenantID + ":" + item.ProductID + ":" + string(item.Class) + ":" + item.UpdatedAt.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339Nano)))
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

func query(vector []float64, collection string) ([]byte, error) {
    body, err := json.Marshal(map[string]any{"collection": collection, "vector": vector, "limit": 20})
    if err != nil { return nil, err }
    base := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if base == "" { return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required") }
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, base+"/v1/vector/query", bytes.NewReader(body))
    if err != nil { return nil, err }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            resp.Body.Close()
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 200 * time.Millisecond)
            continue
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("vector query: status %s: %s", resp.Status, data)
        }
        return data, readErr
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("vector query: rate limit after retries")
}

That request uses the verified vector query path and an explicit method; production code should also honor the server’s Retry-After value when present. The deterministic key is not a substitute for consumer idempotency; it is a stable identity for a refresh operation. A worker can upsert the item, attach its access metadata, and record the source identifier, then safely retry after a 429. Query handlers should fail closed when the timeout budget is exhausted, and they should log the collection, tenant, source identifier, and request ID together so a replay has enough context to prove which freshness window was applied.

What should you compare in an e-commerce retrieval backend?

The backend changes the operational shape of the contract, but it does not remove the contract.

Option Freshness and filtering fit Traceability work Good reason to choose it
Elasticsearch Rich lexical plus vector search; explicit filters and refresh controls Map _source and version fields carefully You already operate search clusters and need broad query DSL support
Typesense Simple collection model and fast typo-tolerant lexical search Store source identifiers in documents and verify update visibility A small team wants a focused search service with low operational surface
Weaviate Vector-first collections with metadata filters and modules Preserve tenant and source properties in every object Semantic retrieval is the center of the product and schema governance is acceptable
Infrai vector endpoints A plain HTTP path for collection, upsert, and bounded query stages Return your own product/source fields and keep the contract in the caller You want discovery plus runnable examples to wire capabilities without installing another SDK

Infrai’s useful distinction here is its self-describing API, where discovery exposes a capability’s request and response schema, billing metadata, and runnable examples, so connecting a new retrieval stage is reading one endpoint rather than learning a new client library, and Infrai uses one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules, which can reduce glue and secret rotation when web acquisition and vector operations belong to one service boundary. That breadth comes with consistent API conventions, although it does not make vector semantics identical to Elasticsearch, Typesense, or Weaviate; validate filtering, refresh visibility, and audit requirements against your contract.

The catch: when this design is the wrong fit

Do not use staged semantic retrieval as the primary path when inventory must be transactionally consistent with checkout, when strict faceting and aggregations dominate, or when your team already has a heavily tuned Elasticsearch cluster whose refresh and audit controls are proven. Stick with that system and put the freshness contract around it. A vector-first store is also a poor fit for a catalog whose queries are almost entirely exact SKU lookups.

Conversely, a single undifferentiated index is risky when tenants have different retention or access rules. Splitting collections by contract, keeping bounded limits, and returning source context costs some orchestration code, but it gives the on-call engineer a explainable failure mode: stale collection, timed-out source, or rejected access filter.

A runbook that survives the next page

Instrument each stage with collection name, freshness class, requested limit, timeout, retry count, and request identifier. Alert on contract violations, such as a result older than its class window or a missing source identifier, rather than on vector latency alone. During an incident, replay the exact query against the recorded collection and source version; that is more useful than a green aggregate metric.

Start with a small catalog slice, measure freshness at the user-visible answer, and widen windows only when the evidence supports it. The architecture is a decision rule, not a vendor badge: explicit contracts and bounded behavior matter more than where the vectors happen to live.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/knn-search.html
  • https://typesense.org/docs/guide/
  • https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate

title: Mapping Instructors' Attitudes Towards Cheating with AI: An Exploratory Analysis Using Forum Analysis
description:
arXiv:2611.13366v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In teaching and learning environments, cheating and the violation of academic integrity have always been one of the challenges, involving different levels of concerns such as administrative, personal knowledge, learning, and equity. The introduction of large language models has brought cheating in dialogue to the forefront, given the apparent capabilities of these models to complete students' academic assignments. This study aims to leverage recent dialogues among university professors about cheating with Generative AI to better understand their beliefs about academic honesty. In doing so, we analyze a corpus of 2.01 million posts (threads and comments) in the r/Professors subreddit discussing cheating after the release of ChatGPT, providing a better understanding of teachers' motivations to discourage cheating and the strategies they use to do so. We synthesize the why and how of addressing cheating to identify caveats about the future of AI and academic integration.

title: You're Still Optimizing Re-Renders Wrong: The Vue 3 Architecture That Outsmarted the Virtual DOM
description:
If you have built applications in modern frontend frameworks, you have almost certainly encountered the re-render nightmare.

In traditional Virtual DOM architectures, updating a single state variable often causes an entire component tree to re-execute from top to bottom. To prevent performance bottlenecks, developers must manually wrap calculations in memoization hooks, carefully manage dependency arrays, and worry about stale closures:

// The manual dependency tightrope
const userProfile = useMemo(() => {
  return calculateComplexMetrics(user, filters);
}, [user.id, filters.activeStatus]); // Miss a dependency, and your UI breaks

One missing dependency in that array creates subtle, agonizing bugs. One unnecessary dependency triggers expensive cascading re-renders across dozens of child components.

Then you look at Vue 3:

// In Vue 3: No dependency array. No manual memoization.
const userProfile = computed(() => {
  return calculateComplexMetrics(user.value, filters.activeStatus);
});

You mutate user.value.name, and only the exact paragraph rendering that name updates. The parent component does not re-render. Sibling components do not recalculate. There are no dependency arrays, no stale closures, and no manual memoization hooks.

To many developers, this behavior looks like magic or dangerous hidden reactivity.

In reality, Vue 3 is powered by one of the most sophisticated engineering architectures in modern software: a fine-grained Proxy dependency graph coordinated with a Compiler-Informed Block Tree.

Here is how Vue 3 actually tracks state, updates the DOM, and eliminates the re-render cascade.

1. The Reactivity Engine: Proxies, track(), and trigger()

In Vue 2, reactivity was implemented using Object.defineProperty(). The engine recursively traversed every property of your data object on initialization and converted them into getters and setters.

This approach suffered from notorious limitations:

  • Adding a new property (obj.newKey = 123) went undetected, requiring Vue.set().
  • Deleting a property went undetected, requiring Vue.delete().
  • Direct array index mutations (arr[0] = 'new') were unobservable without overriding prototype methods.
  • Deeply nested objects incurred heavy upfront performance costs during initialization.

Vue 3 replaced Object.defineProperty() entirely with modern JavaScript Proxy objects.

The Global Dependency Store (targetMap)

At the core of Vue 3 is a private, module-level data structure named targetMap.

targetMap is a nested multi-level registry that maps objects and their properties to the functions that depend on them:

targetMap (WeakMap)
 └── [target object] ──► depsMap (Map)
                          └── [property key] ──► dep (Set of ReactiveEffects)
  1. targetMap (WeakMap): Holds raw target objects as keys. Because it is a WeakMap, if your application discards the original object, the garbage collector cleans it up automatically, preventing memory leaks.
  2. depsMap (Map): Maps each specific property name of that object (e.g., 'count', 'username') to its dependency tracker.
  3. dep (Set): A Set containing all active ReactiveEffect instances (such as a component render function, a watch callback, or a computed value) that read that specific property.

How track() Registers Dependencies (The Getter Trap)

When you write:

const state = reactive({ count: 0 });

Vue wraps your raw object in a Proxy.

When a component renders, it executes inside a ReactiveEffect wrapper, setting a global pointer named activeEffect to point to that component's render function.

When your template evaluates state.count:

  1. The Proxy's get trap intercepts the property read.
  2. The proxy invokes Vue's internal track(target, 'count') function.
  3. track() checks: Is there currently an activeEffect running?
  4. If yes, it fetches or creates the dep Set for target.count inside targetMap and adds activeEffect to the Set.

You never declare dependency arrays because JavaScript's runtime call stack declares them for you. Any property read while activeEffect is running is automatically recorded as an exact subscriber.

How trigger() Fires Updates (The Setter Trap)

When you execute:

state.count = 42;
  1. The Proxy's set trap intercepts the mutation.
  2. The proxy assigns the new value to the raw underlying object using Reflect.set().
  3. It invokes Vue's internal trigger(target, 'count') function.
  4. trigger() looks up targetMap.get(target).get('count').
  5. It retrieves the Set of subscribed effects and schedules them for execution.

Only the exact components and computed properties subscribed to state.count are scheduled to run. Unrelated components are completely untouched.

2. The Compiler-Informed Virtual DOM: Block Trees and Patch Flags

Virtual DOMs earned a reputation for being heavy and resource-intensive because traditional implementations (like React's standard reconciler) operate on brute-force tree diffing.

In a traditional Virtual DOM:

  • When state changes, the component function executes again.
  • It allocates a brand-new tree of Virtual DOM nodes (VNodes) in memory.
  • The reconciler recursively compares every old VNode with every new VNode, checking tags, props, and children, even if 95% of those nodes are purely static HTML that can never change.

Vue 3 solved this through an architectural breakthrough: the Compiler-Informed Virtual DOM.

The Static Analysis Advantage

Because Vue templates have a deterministic structure, the Vue compiler analyzes your template at build time to identify which parts are dynamic and which parts are static.

Consider this template:

<div class="user-card">
  <header>
    <h1>User Profile</h1>
    <span class="badge">Verified</span>
  </header>
  <p class="bio">{{ user.bio }}</p>
  <button :class="{ active: isActive }">Follow</button>
</div>

In a traditional framework, updating user.bio requires diffing the <div class="user-card">, the <header>, the <h1>, the <span>, and the <button>.

The Vue 3 compiler does something radically different:

1. Static Hoisting

The <header> containing <h1>User Profile</h1> and <span class="badge"> contains zero dynamic bindings.

The compiler pulls those VNodes completely outside the component render function. They are created once when your application loads and reused across every future render. Their memory allocation during updates is zero.

2. Patch Flags (Bitwise Optimization)

For dynamic elements, the compiler attaches a numeric PatchFlag representing precisely what can change:

// Compiled output snippet
_createVNode("p", { class: "bio" }, _toDisplayString(_ctx.user.bio), 1 /* TEXT */)
_createVNode("button", { class: _normalizeClass({ active: _ctx.isActive }) }, "Follow", 2 /* CLASS */)

The number 1 is a bitmask for TEXT. The number 2 is a bitmask for CLASS.

When diffing the <p> tag, Vue performs a single bitwise check (patchFlag & PatchFlags.TEXT). If true, it updates node.textContent directly, skipping any checks for attributes, event listeners, or styles.

3. The Block Tree (dynamicChildren)

The root <div> is compiled into a Block.

A Block maintains a flat array called dynamicChildren. Instead of traversing the nested DOM tree recursively, the Block collects only the dynamic elements:

Block (div.user-card)
 └── dynamicChildren: [
       VNode (p.bio, PatchFlag: 1),
       VNode (button, PatchFlag: 2)
     ]

When user.bio updates, the diffing algorithm does not traverse the tree. It iterates over a flat array of two items!

The diffing cost becomes proportional to the number of dynamic bindings on the page, rather than the total size of your HTML tree.

3. ref() vs reactive(): The Destructuring Trap

One of the most frequent points of confusion for developers adopting Vue 3 is choosing between ref() and reactive().

Both create reactive state, but their underlying implementation mechanisms differ fundamentally.

The Mechanism of ref()

JavaScript primitive types (number, string, boolean, null, undefined) are passed by value, not by reference. You cannot wrap a primitive in a JavaScript Proxy.

To make primitives reactive, Vue introduces the RefImpl class:

class RefImpl {
  private _value;
  public dep = new Set();

  constructor(val) {
    this._value = val;
  }

  get value() {
    trackRefValue(this);
    return this._value;
  }

  set value(newVal) {
    this._value = newVal;
    triggerRefValue(this);
  }
}

A ref() is simply an object with a single property: .value.

Reading .value triggers the getter and tracks dependencies. Mutating .value triggers the setter and notifies subscribers.

Because it is wrapped in an object container, you can pass a ref across composable functions, return it from stores, and pass it as function arguments without losing reactivity.

The Mechanism of reactive()

reactive() accepts an object and wraps it directly in a Proxy.

It feels more natural to write because you do not need to append .value in your script code:

const user = reactive({
  name: "Emma",
  age: 26,
});

user.age++; // Natural syntax

The Destructuring Trap

Here is where thousands of developers run into unexpected silent failures:

// A common fatal mistake
const user = reactive({ name: "Emma", age: 26 });

// Destructuring breaks reactivity!
const { name, age } = user;

Why does destructuring destroy reactivity?

Remember: user is a Proxy intercepting property access on the user object.

When you write const { age } = user, JavaScript evaluates user.age, retrieves the raw primitive number 26, and assigns it to a new local variable named age.

The variable age is now just the plain number 26. It is completely disconnected from the Proxy. When the original user.age mutates later, age remains 26. The Proxy's getter and setter traps are never invoked.

The Solution: toRefs()

If you need to destructure a reactive object, you must convert its properties into individual ref objects using toRefs():

import { reactive, toRefs } from 'vue';

const user = reactive({ name: "Emma", age: 26 });

// toRefs wraps each property in a custom getter/setter proxy pointing back to user
const { name, age } = toRefs(user);

age.value++; // Reactivity is fully preserved!

4. The Batching Engine: Scheduler and nextTick()

What happens if you update a reactive variable fifty times inside a loop?

const count = ref(0);

function runStressTest() {
  for (let i = 0; i < 50; i++) {
    count.value++;
  }
}

Does Vue re-render the DOM fifty times in rapid succession, thrashing the browser layout engine?

No. Vue updates the DOM asynchronously using an internal Scheduler.

The Microtask Queue

When a reactive state change invokes trigger():

  1. Vue does not execute the component's render function immediately.
  2. It passes the render job to queueJob(job).
  3. The scheduler checks if this specific component's render job is already queued. If it is already in the queue, it ignores the duplicate call.
  4. The scheduler flushes the entire job queue in a single batch on the browser's next Microtask tick using Promise.resolve().then(flushJobs).

Regardless of how many times you mutate reactive state synchronously during a function execution, the component's render function runs exactly once.

Accessing Updated DOM via nextTick()

Because DOM updates are queued on a microtask, reading the physical DOM immediately after mutating state returns the old layout:

count.value = 5;
console.log(document.querySelector('.counter').textContent); // Still prints old value!

To wait until the scheduler has completed its microtask flush and committed the updates to the physical DOM, Vue provides nextTick():

import { nextTick } from 'vue';

count.value = 5;
await nextTick();
console.log(document.querySelector('.counter').textContent); // Now prints "5"

nextTick() simply attaches a callback to the exact same microtask promise chain, guaranteeing that your inspection logic runs immediately after the DOM update commits.

5. The Evolution: Vue 2, Vue 3, and Vapor Mode

Frontend framework design is moving away from heavyweight runtime Virtual DOM reconciliation toward compile-time direct DOM operations.

We have seen this trend through frameworks like Svelte and SolidJS.

Vue is uniquely positioned in this landscape because of its architectural progression across three distinct eras:

Era 1: Vue 2 (Runtime Virtual DOM + Object.defineProperty)

  • Relied on ES5 getters and setters.
  • Full-tree recursive Virtual DOM diffing.
  • Required manual workarounds for array mutations and dynamic properties.

Era 2: Vue 3 (Proxy Reactivity + Compiler-Informed Block Trees)

  • Native ES6 Proxies for complete reactivity coverage.
  • Build-time static hoisting, PatchFlags, and Block Trees.
  • Up to 300% faster VDOM reconciliation than traditional brute-force diffing engines.

Era 3: Vue Vapor Mode (Opt-In Direct DOM Compilation)

  • The next major leap in Vue's architecture.
  • For opted-in components, Vapor Mode completely eliminates the Virtual DOM.
  • The template compiler translates your template into fine-grained direct DOM creation and update calls tied directly to reactivity signals: 
// Conceptual Vapor Mode compilation output
import { renderEffect, setText } from 'vue/vapor';

const n0 = document.createElement('h1');
renderEffect(() => {
  setText(n0, count.value);
});

When count.value updates in Vapor Mode:

  • Zero VNodes are allocated in memory.
  • Zero diffing algorithms run.
  • The signal directly triggers setText(n0, count.value) to mutate the physical DOM node in place.

Best of all, Vapor Mode uses the exact same Single-File Component syntax (<template>, <script setup>). You do not need to learn a new templating language or rewrite existing components to benefit from zero-VDOM performance.

6. Three Common Vue Reactivity Traps

Understanding Vue's internal architecture immediately arms you against the three most frustrating pitfalls developers encounter:

Trap 1: Storing Heavy External Objects in reactive()

If you store non-primitive third-party objects (such as a Three.js scene, a Monaco Editor instance, a Chart.js canvas, or a Mapbox map) inside a standard reactive() or ref():

// DANGEROUS: Destroys performance
const editorInstance = ref(monaco.editor.create(...));

Vue will recursively wrap the thousands of internal properties, prototypes, and event listeners of that third-party library in reactive Proxies. This creates massive memory overhead and frequently causes third-party libraries to crash when their internal this contexts are proxied.

The Fix: Use shallowRef() or markRaw():

import { shallowRef } from 'vue';

// Safe: Only the .value pointer is reactive; inner properties are untouched
const editorInstance = shallowRef(monaco.editor.create(...));

Trap 2: Infinite Watch Loops

Because Vue tracks dependencies automatically during execution, creating circular reads and writes inside watchEffect() will crash your application:

// CRASHES: Maximum recursive update cycle exceeded
watchEffect(() => {
  total.value = items.value.length;
  // If reading total somewhere triggers items to update, an infinite loop ensues
});

The Fix: Prefer explicit computed() for derived state, and reserve watchEffect() strictly for side effects (such as making API calls or updating local storage).

Trap 3: Direct Mutation of Props

In Vue, data flow is strictly unidirectional. Passing a reactive object as a prop and mutating it directly in a child component bypasses parent state tracking and leads to unpredictable rendering inconsistencies.

The Fix: Emit events using defineEmits() or use v-model with defineModel() to maintain clear ownership over state mutations.

The Mental Shift

The difference between struggling with frontend performance and building scalable interfaces comes down to your mental model:

Stop thinking of reactive components as functions that need to re-execute repeatedly from top to bottom.

Vue 3 is an event-driven signal graph paired with an intelligent compiler.

  • State is a Proxy network, registering dependencies automatically on access.
  • Templates are Block Trees, diffing only the slots marked with PatchFlags.
  • DOM updates are batched asynchronously through microtask queues.
  • And with Vapor Mode, the Virtual DOM step disappears entirely, connecting state directly to DOM nodes.

Once you understand this architecture, the need for complex memoization hooks disappears, re-render cascades vanish, and building reactive user interfaces becomes natural, predictable, and exceptionally fast.

How has Vue's fine-grained reactivity model influenced how you design your frontend state? Have you experienced the performance shift between traditional re-render engines and Proxy-based tracking, or experimented with early Vapor Mode builds? Share your thoughts and architecture experiences in the comments below.

title: Understanding-First AI Engineering: Purposes, Reference Architecture, and Architectural Patterns for Human Understanding
description:
arXiv:2611.13022v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI systems can produce reliable results without developing human understanding. However, human understanding remains valuable for shaping subsequent AI-supported work, forming preferences, governing collective choices and satisfying curiosity, even when human participation is unnecessary for correcting errors. We propose understanding-first AI engineering, which treats purpose-specific human understanding as a first-class design principle guiding requirements, design and operation. The purposes of understanding are organised into four complementary rationales: reflective agency, effective action, collective governance and epistemic value. A reference architecture connects production, verification, use, and learning and exploration through shared records, supporting understanding through explanation and participation. Five candidate architectural patterns guide choices about parallel learning, explanatory models, goal exploration, audience-specific views and distributed expertise. Qualitative scenario analysis of two hypothetical use cases demonstrates how the purpose classification, reference architecture and selected patterns guide investigation, participation and decision processes while retaining operational controls. The cases illustrate design consequences and limitations rather than establish empirical effectiveness. The approach makes human understanding an explicit engineering commitment whose justification need not depend on improving the original AI task.

title: Lightweight Deep Learning Framework for Astrocyte-Centric 3D Reconstruction across Normal and Stress-associated Ultrastructural States
description:
arXiv:2611.13581v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The morphology of astrocytes is closely associated with their ability to support and modulate neural circuit functions; however, its reconstruction from volume electron microscopy (vEM) data remains labor-intensive and computationally resource-intensive, placing substantial barriers on its broader adoption and scalability despite the high spatial resolution of vEM. We present AstroSeg-vEM, a lightweight, astrocyte-centric framework for morphology-preserving astrocyte segmentation, 3D reconstruction, and quantitative morphological analysis in vEM images. AstroSeg-vEM combines transformer-based 2D segmentation with dedicated post-processing methods and operates directly on high-resolution EM sections, making it well suited to anisotropic vEM data and downstream proofreading workflows while preserving the full in-plane resolution of the original EM data. Across four mouse hippocampal datasets representing normal and morphologically defined stress-associated astrocyte ultrastructural states, AstroSeg-vEM demonstrates robust performance and generalization, achieving average Dice and weighted Dice values of 0.92 and 0.95, respectively, on a held-out test dataset. Its lightweight architecture enables efficient, high-fidelity reconstruction on consumer-grade hardware, providing a scalable and accessible platform for large-scale astrocyte ultrastructure analysis and future astrocyte-neuron interaction studies.

title: Musinator: A Music Player for the Terminal That Looks Good
description:
A free terminal music player for Omarchy and Linux. Real album covers, lyrics in time with the song, 22 themes, internet radio, podcasts, and your Navidrome or Jellyfin servers.

So here is the thing about music in the terminal. The players are fast, but most of them look like 1998.

I live in the terminal on Omarchy, and I wanted my music there too. cmus is fast. ncmpcpp is powerful, but you set up MPD first. None of them show me the album cover, the lyrics, or colors that match my desktop. So I built the player I wanted.

What it does

Two screens. Library on the left, your music on the right. Now Playing with a big cover, the lyrics and a visualizer. z switches between them.

Real album covers. In Ghostty, which Omarchy uses, the covers are real pictures. In other terminals they are block pictures. There is also an album grid, if you like to browse by cover.

Lyrics in time. From an .lrc file next to the song, from the song itself, or from LRCLIB when you press ctrl+l. f opens full-screen lyrics with the current line in big letters.

22 themes. Press t and they change live while you move through the list. Or pick "Match Omarchy", and Musinator follows when you switch your Omarchy theme.

Not only your files

This started as a player for my own music. Then it grew:

  • Internet radio from radio-browser.info: popular stations, genres, countries, search, and favorites. It shows the song that is on air.
  • Podcasts. Find a show, subscribe, stream or download. It remembers where you stopped in every episode.
  • Music servers. Navidrome, Jellyfin and other Subsonic servers. As many as you like, each in its own part of the sidebar.
  • Last.fm. Scrobbles, now playing, and your recent and top lists.

All in the same screens, and one search (/) finds songs, albums, stations and server songs together.

The details I cared about

  • Gapless. No gap between songs, in every format: FLAC, MP3, AAC, ALAC, Vorbis, Opus, WAV, AIFF.
  • Honest audio. It plays at the file's own sample rate. If the sound system changes it, the info line says so in orange.
  • Volume leveling. ReplayGain from the tags, or measured by Musinator for songs without it.
  • Tag editing. One song or a whole album. Fill tags from the file name, add a cover, or look the album up on MusicBrainz.
  • Light. Near 0% CPU when idle. The visualizer stays under 5% of one core.
  • Private. No account, no telemetry. It only goes online for the things you use.

Plus a 10-band equalizer, a sleep timer, mini mode with m, mouse support, and the Omarchy media keys.

What broke along the way

To be honest, a lot of it only showed up with real use:

  • The lyrics switched a little late. The sound needs a moment from the program to your ears, about 40 ms on my machine. Now the lyric clock counts that in, so the line changes when you hear it.
  • Album covers piled up in the terminal's memory while scrolling. Every new picture got a new number. Now each place on the screen reuses its number.
  • In tmux the first key press after starting got lost. Musinator asked the terminal a question at startup, and tmux never answered. Now it does not ask terminals that cannot answer.
  • With a new Navidrome, the artist list stayed empty and the server said "Library not found". It was still reading the music for the first time. Now Musinator tells you that, and how far it is.

Seventy automatic tests run on every change now.

Install

One line, no sudo:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/smanookian/musinator/main/install.sh | sh

It needs PipeWire and libopus. On Omarchy you have both. Then run musinator and press ? for all keys. An AUR package is coming.

Where to find it

  • App page, keys, and FAQ: stevinator.com/apps/musinator
  • Source: github.com/smanookian/musinator

Rust, MIT license. If something sounds wrong or looks wrong on your machine, open an issue. I would rather hear about it than not.

Most of the code was written with an AI coding assistant; I designed it, reviewed it and tested it on my machine.

First published on stevinator.com.

I hope to see you next time. Steve out. Tschau!

title: User Avatar Metadata Search: Content Types, Tags, and Prefix-Only Object Storage
description:
Short answer: keep avatar bytes under immutable, addressable keys; put content type, tags, ownership, and moderation state in a queryable catalog, and use bucket listing by prefix for repair and audit rather than interactive search.

That is a constraint decision, not a preference. Object storage is excellent at answering “give me this key” and “enumerate keys beginning with this string.” It is generally not a relational query engine for “find every active avatar whose detected type is PNG, whose labels include team-photo, and whose owner is in this tenant.” Treating those operations as equivalent creates a system that looks fine in a demo and becomes difficult to reconcile after retries, renames, or policy changes.

What can object storage actually tell you about avatar metadata?

An object key is the primary address. A prefix narrows a lexicographic range; it does not mean the service can evaluate arbitrary predicates over HTTP metadata, user-defined tags, image dimensions, or application state. Some platforms offer inventories or analytics exports, but their snapshot cadence and filtering semantics are separate contracts. They are useful only when their freshness matches the reader's need.

Content-Type is a representation hint in HTTP, not proof of the bytes' contents. An uploader can label arbitrary bytes image/png. Store the declared value for diagnostics, inspect the payload with a bounded decoder, and record a detected type separately. Authorization and moderation should never depend on the header alone.

Tags are similarly easy to overestimate. A tag attached to an object may be retrievable with that object, yet still have no index that answers intersections quickly. Encoding every future search dimension into a key is worse: tenant/user/type/status/date becomes an irreversible grammar, and changing one dimension forces a copy or a full scan. Keys should make retrieval and lifecycle operations predictable, not pretend to be a schema.

The important limitation is query shape. Prefix listing can support a known owner, a migration range, or an administrative sweep. It cannot, by itself, provide a bounded-latency search over content type and tags.

How should avatar metadata, content type, tags, and prefix listing fit together?

Start from the reads. The profile path usually needs one current avatar for (tenant_id, user_id). Moderation needs a queue filtered by state and detected media type. Support needs an audit trail by upload time. Those are catalog queries, so model them explicitly instead of asking the bucket to infer them.

Give each upload an immutable ID. Keep the object key stable, for example avatars/{tenant_id}/{upload_id}; mutable labels belong in a database row. That row can hold owner, key, declared and detected type, byte length, checksum, labels, moderation state, creation time, and lifecycle state. A uniqueness constraint can enforce one current avatar per owner while old versions remain addressable.

The trade-off is another stateful boundary. A catalog and a bucket cannot be committed atomically unless a service specifically provides that transaction. Define visible states instead: reserve the row, write the immutable object, validate its attributes, then mark the row ready. Readers select only ready rows. A sweeper can find old pending rows, while an inventory comparison can find unreferenced objects.

Failure modes are more useful than “eventual consistency”

Name the failures. An orphan object is a successful object write with no catalog row. A dangling row points at a missing key. A duplicate operation happens when a timeout is retried without an idempotency key. A stale current pointer serves an older version. A cross-tenant key leak is an authorization failure, not a storage consistency detail.

I once reproduced the duplicate case with 2 objects from one user action: the first upload completed, the response timed out, and the retry received a fresh upload ID. The fix was unglamorous: bind the request to an idempotency key, reserve the identity before writing, and make repeats return the existing operation state. A metric for pending-row age would have exposed the drift sooner than an upload-latency dashboard. I'm not sure why that metric is so often omitted; your mileage may vary.

Keep repair deterministic. For each pending row, check object existence and age. For each object found by a prefix sweep, check that exactly one authorized row references it. Reconcile by immutable ID, never by a display filename. Record checksum mismatches and validation rejections as separate counters so an operator can distinguish corruption, policy change, and a client retry.

How do exact-key reads complete an avatar metadata search?

The online request should query the catalog with tenant authorization, then issue an exact-key read or a short-lived read grant. Browser clients should not receive broad bucket credentials. Cursor pagination belongs to the catalog's ordering, such as (created_at, upload_id), rather than to a listing token that only knows about key order.

This Python sketch shows the boundary without tying it to a provider SDK:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AvatarUpload:
    tenant_id: str
    user_id: str
    idempotency_key: str
    declared_type: str


def publish_avatar(request, catalog, store, decoder, payload):
    row = catalog.reserve(request)
    if row.state == "ready":
        return row

    checksum = store.put(
        key=row.object_key,
        body=payload,
        content_type=request.declared_type,
    )
    detected_type, width, height = decoder.inspect(payload)
    return catalog.mark_ready(
        upload_id=row.upload_id,
        checksum=checksum,
        detected_type=detected_type,
        width=width,
        height=height,
    )


def search_avatars(catalog, tenant_id, detected_type, labels, cursor=None):
    return catalog.search_ready(
        tenant_id=tenant_id,
        detected_type=detected_type,
        labels=labels,
        cursor=cursor,
        limit=50,
    )

In a real worker, stream and decode with bounded memory, cap dimensions and encoded size, and scan uploads before publication. A checksum links the catalog fact to stored bytes; it does not replace image parsing or malware controls. Instrument query latency, result counts, validation reasons, duplicate idempotency attempts, pending age, and reconciliation drift. Those signals tell you whether the catalog is trustworthy.

Which discovery method matches the workload?

There is no universal winner. Choose against freshness, query shape, and repair cost.

Method Fits Limitation Check
Exact keys plus prefix listing Known owners and offline sweeps Metadata predicates require scanning Measure objects listed and scan duration
Transactional catalog Online filters and ownership rules Cross-system states need repair Track pending age and orphan count
Search index Many labels, text, or facets Asynchronous copies can be stale Measure ingestion lag
Periodic inventory Audits and migration planning Snapshot is too stale for profile reads Record snapshot age and coverage

Use prefix listing when discovery is an administrative batch job and delayed results are acceptable. Use a transactional catalog when identity, authorization, and uniqueness are already database concerns. Add a search index only when query volume or shape justifies another asynchronous copy. The recommended catalog is not suitable when the workload is strictly exact-key reads and occasional maintenance; in that case it adds failure modes without buying a useful capability.

Cost also includes list requests, attribute reads, index writes, replication, egress, reconciliation work, and abandoned-upload retention. A low byte price does not make a full-bucket scan an inexpensive search service. Conversely, a search cluster for a few filters over a small table is needless operational surface.

Roll out with a reversible read path

Measure the existing namespace first. Create the catalog schema, dual-write new uploads through the state machine, and backfill old objects in bounded prefix pages. A backfill cursor records progress, not completeness, so compare the result with an independent inventory and sample exact keys, checksums, owners, detected types, and lifecycle state.

Shadow representative searches before switching reads. Require zero cross-tenant mismatches, then move one read cohort at a time. Keep reconciliation running after cutover: migration code and steady-state code fail differently. Rollback should switch the read path, not delete newly indexed data.

Go slowly.

Keys locate bytes. Catalogs answer questions. Prefix listing proves what exists in a namespace, and reconciliation proves that the namespace and the catalog still agree.

References

  • RFC 9110, “HTTP Semantics”: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • Backblaze, “B2 Cloud Storage Pricing”: https://www.backblaze.com/cloud-storage/pricing

title: IFRS Compliance Verification: An Open Multi-LLM Benchmark and Content-Conditioned Ensemble Classifier
description:
arXiv:2611.13595v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Verifying corporate financial disclosures against the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) is a core auditing task in which experts cross-reference disclosures with hundreds of fine-grained regulatory paragraphs: a laborious, costly, and error-prone process that motivates growing interest in large language models (LLMs) as compliance assistants. Yet single-model accuracy remains insufficient for high-stakes use, and naive ensembling is vulnerable to systematic per-model biases that can drag aggregate accuracy below that of the strongest individual annotator. This gap is addressed with a multi-stage framework, supported by a new benchmark of 19,998 IFRS regulation-disclosure pairs comprising 11,161 unanimous multi-LLM labels and 8,837 human annotations on items where the LLMs disagreed. The framework couples a three-stage domain-adapted sentence embedding pipeline (BERT masked language modeling on SEC EDGAR filings, unsupervised TSDAE and SimCSE adaptation, and supervised contrastive alignment) with a learned ensemble classifier that fuses frozen embeddings and LLM probability features from GPT-4.1, Claude Sonnet 4, and Gemini 2.5 Pro via Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) optimized gradient-boosted trees. On the disagreement set, the ensemble achieves 81.7% weighted F1, exceeding the strongest single LLM by 10.4 points and majority voting by 14.6 points, and outperforms eleven unsupervised aggregation baselines; the retrieval pipeline attains Recall@15 of 45.3% on unseen regulations. The dataset, model checkpoints, annotation platform, and classifier implementation will be publicly released.

title: Multi-Future Drafting: Mixture Block Drafters for Tree-Verified Speculative Decoding
description:
arXiv:2611.13017v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Block drafters such as DFlash draft a block of future tokens in one forward pass, and draft trees such as DDTree verify the prefixes ranked highest by the product of the drafter's per-position distributions. Under tree verification, the expected number of accepted tokens is the probability mass the tree covers. We show that a product misallocates it: when the continuation can follow several futures, it splices them into chimeras, prefixes stitched together from different futures that the target never produces, and gives them as much budget as the futures themselves. Barring ties, no product-ranked tree can hold two futures that disagree in $m$ positions without $2^{m-1}-1$ chimeras, however well the drafter is trained, and in practice chimeras make up 27-33% of a 64-node tree. We propose Multi-Future Drafting (MFD), which restores the coupling with a latent variable instead of the chain rule: $K$ learned mode embeddings at the drafter's input draft $K$ coherent blocks in the same pass, and a mixture DDTree lets the verifier pick the future the target takes, losslessly and with $K+1$ extra vectors. On four Qwen targets from 4B to 27B parameters, at batch size 1, MFD reaches up to 7.8$\times$ speedup, 5-8% faster than the best single-mode tree trained identically and, on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, 9-16% faster than the released DARTree trained on the same prompts.

title: Understanding Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): A Case Study of Amazon Web Services (AWS)
description:
Introduction
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) is a cloud computing model that provides users with virtual computing resources over the internet. These resources include servers, storage and networking. It allows businesses to use IT infrastructure without purchasing or maintaining physical equipment.

Case Study: Amazon Web Services (AWS)
Amazon Web Services (AWS) is a cloud computing platform that provides IaaS solutions. One of its major services is Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud).
Amazon EC2 allows users to rent virtual servers to run applications, store data and host websites.
For example, a business can use Amazon EC2 to host its website without purchasing a physical server. If the number of website visitors increases, the business can increase its computing resources.

Other AWS infrastructure services include:
• Amazon EBS: Provides virtual storage.
• Amazon VPC: Provides virtual networking.
• Amazon EC2: Provides virtual computing servers.

Benefits of AWS IaaS

  1. Cost-effective: Reduces the need to purchase expensive hardware.
  2. Scalability: Resources can be increased or reduced when needed.
  3. Flexibility: Users can choose their preferred server configurations.
  4. Accessibility: Infrastructure can be managed remotely through the internet.
  5. Fast deployment: Virtual servers can be created within minutes.

Challenges of IaaS
• Security risks due to poor configurations.
• Dependence on a stable internet connection.
• Requires technical knowledge to manage.
• Unexpected costs from excessive resource usage.

Conclusion
Infrastructure as a Service makes computing resources more accessible, flexible and affordable. Amazon EC2 demonstrates how businesses can rent virtual servers instead of purchasing physical hardware. Despite some challenges, IaaS remains an important solution in modern cloud computing.

References

  1. https://aws.amazon.com/what-is/iaas/
  2. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/

title: Which Successes Make Good References? Action-Sequence Alignment for Multi-Turn On-Policy Distillation
description:
arXiv:2611.13135v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) reduces train-inference distribution mismatch by supervising a student on its own trajectories. For multi-turn tool-use agents, conditioning the teacher on a validated same-task successful trajectory as a reference can provide useful hindsight, but different successes may reach incompatible interaction states and offer misleading supervision. We cast successful-reference selection as a free-target optimal transport problem, which reduces to assigning each failed trajectory its most compatible successful reference. Because latent state paths are hidden, we use action-sequence alignment as an observable proxy for compatibility and instantiate it with longest common subsequence (LCS), which identifies a shared ordered backbone of actions while allowing recoverable detours. This perspective makes trajectory compatibility the central criterion for reference selection in multi-turn OPD. Experiments on ALFWorld and the airline domain of $\tau^3$-bench show that LCS is the only evaluated reference selector to improve over reference-free OPD on both ALFWorld overall scores and all three airline metrics. Without further optimization, the airline-trained models also transfer to the retail domain, where LCS improves all three metrics.

title: Game Cleanup Message Queue Timeout Issues: Delivering Delayed Webhooks
description:
A delayed webhook worker for game events should acknowledge the queue message only after the delivery attempt has a durable outcome. The deciding constraint is delivery guarantee: a timeout must produce a retryable state, not a lost cleanup job or an unbounded retry storm.

Short answer: separate the queue lease from the webhook request timeout, persist an attempt record before making the request, and make the receiver idempotent. A five-second HTTP timeout can be useful, but it is not a delivery guarantee. It only bounds one attempt.

That distinction matters.

For a periodic cleanup job, I use three explicit outcomes: delivered, retryable, and terminal. The worker owns the transition between them. That small state machine is more dependable than treating a queue timeout as proof that the remote game service did or did not receive the request.

How do message queue timeout issues affect delayed webhook delivery?

There are two different clocks. The queue lease controls how long one consumer may work before another consumer can receive the message. The HTTP timeout controls how long that consumer waits for a response. They can expire in either order.

Suppose a cleanup message targets expired match-room records. The worker sends the webhook, the remote endpoint commits the request, and the response is delayed. The HTTP client reports a timeout. If the worker immediately requeues the message, the same cleanup may run twice. If it marks the message complete, a timeout caused by a dropped response can hide a real delivery failure. Neither choice can infer the remote side's state from the local timer alone.

That is the first trap. A timeout is an observation about waiting, not an observation about side effects. The receiver needs an idempotency key such as cleanup:<roomId>:<periodStart>, and it must record that key before applying the cleanup again. The key belongs to the logical job, not to an individual retry.

The small state machine I would ship

Keep it explicit.

The queue payload should contain a stable job identifier, the game scope, and the scheduled period. It should not be the only record of progress. A database row or equivalent durable store can keep the current state, attempt count, next eligible time, and last error category.

The worker flow is deliberately boring:

  1. Claim the job under the queue's lease.
  2. Persist an attempt-start record with the same idempotency key used for the webhook.
  3. Send the request with a bounded timeout.
  4. Classify the result before acknowledging the queue message.
  5. Acknowledge only after the durable state says delivered or terminal.

Here is the boundary I want in a Node.js worker. The queue adapter is intentionally generic; the important contract is the classification, not a vendor-specific API.

type DeliveryResult =
  | { kind: 'delivered'; status: number }
  | { kind: 'retryable'; reason: string }
  | { kind: 'terminal'; reason: string };

async function deliverCleanup(
  job: { id: string; roomId: string; periodStart: string },
  send: (request: { idempotencyKey: string; body: unknown; signal: AbortSignal }) => Promise<{ status: number }>,
  persist: (state: { jobId: string; state: string; detail: string }) => Promise<void>
): Promise<DeliveryResult> {
  const idempotencyKey = `cleanup:${job.roomId}:${job.periodStart}`;
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const timeout = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 5000);

  await persist({ jobId: job.id, state: 'attempting', detail: idempotencyKey });

  try {
    const response = await send({
      idempotencyKey,
      body: { roomId: job.roomId, periodStart: job.periodStart },
      signal: controller.signal
    });

    if (response.status >= 200 && response.status < 300) {
      await persist({ jobId: job.id, state: 'delivered', detail: String(response.status) });
      return { kind: 'delivered', status: response.status };
    }

    if (response.status === 408 || response.status === 429 || response.status >= 500) {
      return { kind: 'retryable', reason: `remote status ${response.status}` };
    }

    await persist({ jobId: job.id, state: 'terminal', detail: String(response.status) });
    return { kind: 'terminal', reason: `remote status ${response.status}` };
  } catch (error) {
    const reason = error instanceof Error ? error.message : 'unknown delivery error';
    return { kind: 'retryable', reason };
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timeout);
  }
}

The caller still needs to persist a retryable result and release or extend the lease according to the queue contract. That choice matters. A retry scheduled for 30 seconds later is not helpful if the original lease remains held for 10 minutes, and a lease that expires during a live request invites concurrent workers.

A delayed request needs integrity protection as well as retry handling. HMAC authenticates a message with a shared secret and a cryptographic hash; RFC 2104 defines the construction using the inner and outer padding values. Sign the exact bytes the receiver will verify, and include the stable idempotency key and an expiration value in the signed representation.

The receiver should reject an expired timestamp and verify the signature before performing cleanup. It should then atomically check the idempotency key. A valid signature does not make a request safe to repeat by itself. Authentication and deduplication solve different failure modes. The trade-off is extra durable state and a little more work per delivery, but that cost buys an explainable retry boundary.

Keep the signing input explicit. JSON serialization can change if field order or whitespace changes, so the sender and receiver need one canonical representation. The key must stay outside the job payload and logs.

How do you test the timeout boundary?

A happy-path test proves very little here. I test the transition after each meaningful boundary: before the request leaves the process, after the receiver commits but before the response arrives, after the HTTP timeout, and after the queue lease expires. The useful assertion is that repeated delivery with the same key produces one cleanup effect.

I also force a slow receiver, a dropped response, a 429 response, a 500 response, malformed JSON, and a process stop during the attempt. Those cases should produce an intentional state, not a generic catch block that hides whether retrying is safe.

Metrics should separate queue age, lease extensions, request duration, retry count, terminal failures, and duplicate deliveries. One aggregate “webhook failed” counter cannot explain a timeout problem. Alert on jobs approaching their deadline and on retry age, because request latency alone misses work that is quietly cycling.

The decision rule

Use at-least-once delivery when the receiver can deduplicate by a stable key and the cleanup is safe to repeat. Use a terminal state for validation errors or other responses that retrying cannot repair. For an operation that cannot tolerate duplicates, the receiver needs an atomic idempotency record or a transactional handoff; increasing the client timeout does not create exactly-once behavior.

Before copying the five-second example, measure the receiver's normal and tail latency, the queue lease duration, the cleanup deadline, and the time needed to persist state. The timeout should leave room for durable bookkeeping and lease renewal. The number is a starting constraint, not a promise. The limitation is fundamental: a client timeout cannot prove whether the receiver committed the side effect.

This is the part I would review before choosing a queue implementation: can it make leases visible, schedule a retry without losing the job, and expose enough timing data to explain a duplicate? If those answers are unclear, the queue's feature list is less useful than a small, explicit state machine.

References

  • RFC 2104, HMAC: Keyed-Hashing for Message Authentication: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104
  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • MDN, AbortController: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController

title: How to scrape Twitter (x.com) without authentication using Gaffa
description:
This tutorial was written by John Fáwọlé and originally published on the Gaffa blog. I'm sharing it here with the DEV community.

Scraping a few tweets sounds simple until you hit a login prompt or your script returns a page without the posts you need. Because X (formerly Twitter) loads its content with JavaScript, a basic request often isn't enough, and you end up setting up a browser just to read a single post. With Gaffa's capture_dom action, you can load a public X profile in a real browser through one API call, with no login and no local browser. In this guide, you'll use Python and Gaffa's capture_dom to extract tweet text and engagement counts from real posts and save the results as JSON.

Can you scrape Twitter without an account?

Yes, you can scrape a public X post without logging in, but the page usually has to be rendered in a real browser first. A plain request may return a login page or incomplete content, whereas a browser runs the JavaScript needed to load the post.

X also offers an official API, but it requires an X account, developer credentials, and pay-per-use pricing with request limits, so it isn't an account-free option. Gaffa loads the public page for you without an X username, password, or saved session.

You're still limited to what X shows while signed out. A public profile may show only a few posts before asking you to log in, so the results may not include its full history.

Prerequisites

Before building the scraper, you'll need the following.

  • Python 3.10 or newer
  • A Gaffa API key
  • A terminal and code editor
  • The requests and beautifulsoup4 packages

You won't need to install Chrome, Selenium, or Playwright, since Gaffa handles the browser work for you.

How to scrape Twitter with Gaffa and Python

We'll build a scraper that loads a public X profile, finds the available tweet links, and saves each post's data as JSON. We'll use OpenAI's X account, but you can swap in any other public profile. You can follow along with the finished project in our GitHub repository.

Set up your Python project

Start by creating a project folder and a virtual environment to keep its packages separate from your other projects. On macOS or Linux, run the following.

mkdir twitter-scraper
cd twitter-scraper

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

On Windows PowerShell, use python instead of python3 and activate the environment with

.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

Next, install requests to make the API calls and beautifulsoup4 to read the HTML that Gaffa returns.

python -m pip install requests beautifulsoup4

Create a file named xscraper.py and add these imports and settings.

import getpass
import json
import os
import re
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path
from urllib.parse import urlsplit

import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

PROFILE = "https://x.com/OpenAI"
LIMIT = 3
OUTPUT = Path("twitter_data")
API_KEY = (os.getenv("GAFFA_API_KEY") or getpass.getpass("Gaffa API key: ")).strip()

if not API_KEY:
    raise SystemExit("A Gaffa API key is required.")

OUTPUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

PROFILE is the page we'll scrape, while LIMIT caps the number of tweets we process, and we're starting with three so the first run stays small. The script reads your key from GAFFA_API_KEY or asks you to enter it, so you never have to expose it in the code.

Load a public X profile with Gaffa

We'll use capture_dom to get the page's rendered HTML and pass it to BeautifulSoup for extraction. Add the following function, which we'll reuse for the profile and for each tweet page.

def fetch_page(url, label):
    response = requests.post(
        "https://api.gaffa.dev/v1/browser/requests",
        headers={"X-API-Key": API_KEY},
        json={
            "url": url,
            "async": False,
            "proxy_location": "us",
            "settings": {
                "max_media_bandwidth": 1,
                "actions": [
                    {"type": "wait", "selector": "article", "timeout": 15000},
                    {"type": "capture_dom"},
                ],
            },
        },
        timeout=90,
    )
    (OUTPUT / f"{label}.json").write_text(response.text, encoding="utf-8")
    response.raise_for_status()
    body = response.json()
    data = body.get("data") or body
    actions = data.get("actions") or []

    if data.get("error") or not actions or any(a.get("error") for a in actions):
        raise RuntimeError(f"Gaffa could not load {url}. Check {label}.json.")
    if not 200 <= (data.get("http_status_code") or 0) < 300:
        raise RuntimeError(f"X returned HTTP {data.get('http_status_code')}.")

    html = requests.get(actions[-1]["output"], timeout=30)
    html.raise_for_status()
    html.encoding = "utf-8"
    (OUTPUT / f"{label}.html").write_text(html.text, encoding="utf-8")
    return BeautifulSoup(html.text, "html.parser")

The wait action holds the request for up to 15 seconds until an article element appears, which gives the content a chance to load before capture_dom runs. Setting async to False makes the call wait for its result, and we also use a US proxy and cap media downloads at 1 MB, since we only need text.

The final action returns a file URL for the captured HTML, so the function downloads it, saves a local copy, and returns a BeautifulSoup object. It also saves the raw API response so you can inspect any errors.

Now call the function to load the profile.

profile = fetch_page(PROFILE, "profile")

On a successful request, this creates twitter_data/profile.json and twitter_data/profile.html.

Find the available tweet URLs

With the profile loaded, we can look through its articles for tweet links that belong to the selected account.

profile_path = urlsplit(PROFILE).path.rstrip("/")
pattern = re.compile(rf"^{re.escape(profile_path)}/status/\d+$", re.IGNORECASE)
urls = []

for article in profile.select("article"):
    link = article.find("a", href=pattern)
    if link:
        url = "https://x.com" + link["href"]
        if url not in urls:
            urls.append(url)

urls = urls[:LIMIT]
if not urls:
    raise RuntimeError("No tweet links found. Check twitter_data/profile.html.")

print(f"Found {len(urls)} tweet URLs.")

This works with the HTML we already downloaded, so it makes no additional API requests. Keep in mind that LIMIT only sets a maximum, so raising it won't reveal posts that aren't in the captured page.

Extract tweet text, timestamps, and engagement counts

Next, we'll define how to read an individual tweet page. We identify the requested post by its timestamp link, which stops us from accidentally collecting a reply beneath it. First, add a small helper for reading engagement counts.

def get_count(article, label):
    element = article.select_one(f'[aria-label="{label}"]')
    return (element.get_text(strip=True) or None) if element else None

It returns the count as displayed on the page, or None when no count is available, so a value like "6.9K" stays as displayed instead of becoming an assumed exact number. Now add the function that extracts the tweet.

def extract_post(soup, url):
    path = urlsplit(url).path
    stamp = soup.select_one(f'article a[href="{path}"]')
    if stamp is None:
        raise ValueError("The requested post's timestamp link is missing.")

    article = stamp.find_parent("article")
    body = article.select_one('div[dir="auto"]')
    handle = path.split("/")[1]
    author = None
    author_path = re.compile(rf"^/{re.escape(handle)}$", re.IGNORECASE)
    for link in article.find_all("a", href=author_path):
        if link.get_text(strip=True).lower() == f"@{handle}".lower():
            author = link.get_text(strip=True)
            break
    if author is None or body is None or not body.get_text(strip=True):
        raise ValueError("The expected author or tweet text is missing.")
    if any(b.get_text(strip=True) == "Show more" for b in body.select("button")):
        raise ValueError("The tweet text is still truncated.")

    post_id = path.rsplit("/", 1)[-1]
    published = datetime.fromtimestamp(((int(post_id) >> 22) + 1288834974657) / 1000, timezone.utc)
    return {
        "post_id": post_id,
        "url": url,
        "author": author,
        "published_at": published.isoformat(timespec="seconds"),
        "text": body.get_text(" ", strip=True),
        "links": [a["href"] for a in body.select('a[href^="https://"]')],
        "likes_display": get_count(article, "Like"),
        "reposts_display": get_count(article, "Repost"),
        "replies_display": get_count(article, "Reply"),
    }

The function returns the tweet's ID, URL, author, publication time, text, links, and engagement counts. It also checks for missing content and a "Show more" button, so a shortened preview is never saved as a complete post.

Rather than parsing the date shown on the page, which changes with language and time zone, the function reads the publish time from the tweet ID itself. X builds every post ID from the moment it was created, so shifting the ID right by 22 bits and adding X's epoch (1288834974657 ms) gives the exact UTC timestamp, down to the second. The parser still depends on the HTML structure reflected in its selectors, so if extraction fails, compare those selectors with the saved HTML before changing the code.

Save the tweets as JSON

Now add the block that opens each URL with fetch_page(), extracts its data with extract_post(), and collects the results.

posts = []
failures = []

for url in urls:
    post_id = url.rsplit("/", 1)[-1]
    try:
        soup = fetch_page(url, post_id)
        post = extract_post(soup, url)
        posts.append(post)
        print(f"Extracted tweet {post_id}.")
    except (requests.RequestException, ValueError, RuntimeError, KeyError) as error:
        failures.append({"url": url, "error": str(error)})
        print(f"Could not extract {url}: {error}")

Each tweet is processed separately, so if a request or extraction fails, the script records the URL and error and carries on with the remaining posts. Finally, sort the successful records by date and write both lists to disk.

posts.sort(key=lambda post: post["published_at"], reverse=True)

(OUTPUT / "posts.json").write_text(
    json.dumps(posts, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False), encoding="utf-8"
)
(OUTPUT / "failures.json").write_text(
    json.dumps(failures, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False), encoding="utf-8"
)

print(f"Saved {len(posts)} tweets; {len(failures)} failed.")
if not posts:
    raise SystemExit("No tweets extracted. Check twitter_data/failures.json.")

posts.json contains the extracted tweets with the newest first, while failures.json lists any URLs that couldn't be processed along with their error messages. You can find the full code on our GitHub repository.

Run the scraper and check the results

Run the script from your project folder.

python xscraper.py

If it prompts for your Gaffa API key, paste it and press Enter. The terminal will report how many tweet URLs it found and whether each post was extracted, and once it finishes, open twitter_data/posts.json in your code editor to see the results.


The extracted tweets in posts.json, sorted with the newest post first.

Why use Gaffa instead of the X API?

The official X API is the better fit when you need supported, structured access to X data, but it needs developer credentials, comes with its own authentication per endpoint, and enforces strict usage limits. For a workflow like this one, Gaffa is simpler because it works with the public web page itself, handling JavaScript rendering, browser infrastructure, and proxy routing behind one REST API.

Scraping public tweets doesn't have to mean fighting login walls or managing a browser yourself. With Gaffa's capture_dom action, you can load a real X page, extract the data you need, and save it as clean JSON in a few lines of Python. Sign up for free to grab your 500 free credits and run your first request in minutes, or see how to scrape a table with Python for another take on the same pattern.

Frequently asked questions

How do I scrape Twitter without an X account using Gaffa?

Use capture_dom to load a public profile or tweet in Gaffa's browser, then parse the returned HTML with BeautifulSoup. No X username, password, or saved session is needed for posts visible while signed out.

Do I need an X API key to scrape tweets with Gaffa?

No. This method uses Gaffa's browser API instead of the official X API, so you only need a Gaffa API key to make the requests.

How do I scrape a different public X profile?

Change the PROFILE URL in the script to the account you want. Make sure its posts are visible while logged out, and check that the captured HTML still matches the selectors in extract_post().

How do I scrape X without Selenium or Playwright?

Send your request to Gaffa's /v1/browser/requests endpoint with wait and capture_dom actions. Gaffa runs the browser for you, so there's no Selenium, ChromeDriver, or local headless browser to install.

How do I get more than a few tweets from a profile?

Raising LIMIT only helps if the captured page contains more links. Signed-out profiles often show just a few posts, so the results are limited to what X makes available without a login.
