title: Building QuickPOS: A Point of Sale for Small Food Businesses in the Philippines
description:
TL;DR

  • QuickPOS is a point-of-sale system for small food businesses: a register, a kitchen display, cash shifts with PIN sign-in, sales history with voids and refunds, inventory, and daily reports
  • It runs in the browser. The API is Hono and tRPC on Cloudflare Workers, the data is in Turso (SQLite), and the web app is a React SPA
  • Checkout is safe to retry. If the connection drops halfway through a charge, trying again returns the first result instead of ringing up the sale twice
  • Permissions, stock changes and optional features each have one shared definition that the web app and the API both use
  • I'm preparing it for a pilot with one counter-service food merchant. The code is private, so this post shows it through screenshots, a demo and diagrams

A cashier picks egg and add-on options for a Tapsilog, takes ₱500 cash and sees the change, and the order shows up on the kitchen display. The store, staff and menu are made up for the demo.

Why I built it

Small food stalls and counter-service shops in the Philippines often run on a notebook, a calculator and a cash box. The POS systems built for them are usually priced and designed for bigger restaurants, and many of them assume things that don't hold at a small counter: that prices exclude tax, that the Internet is always up, or that one person does everything.

I wanted to build one that fits how these shops actually work, and to build it the way I'd build software I'm paid to maintain. That second goal shaped most of the decisions in this post.

What it does

The core is the part a merchant uses every day:

Area What it covers
Register Cart, add-ons and modifiers, cash and other payments, receipts
Kitchen A display that shows each ticket from pending to ready
Shifts Open with a PIN and a starting cash count, close and count the drawer
Sales history Order list, voids and refunds
Daily totals Sales summary, shift report, payment types
Access Owner, admin and cashier roles, staff PINs

Around that core are optional modules: tables, inventory and purchasing, customers and loyalty, time clock and payroll, advanced reports, and the audit log. Each one can be switched off, which matters more than it sounds. I'll come back to it.

How it's built

One pnpm monorepo. The web app and the API both import the shared package, so a price rule, a permission or a module switch has one definition. The Rust coordinator is the start of offline mode and is paused until the pilot needs it.

It's my third attempt at the stack. The first version used TanStack Start with Postgres, the second moved the data to Convex, and in April 2026 I rebuilt it as a plain React SPA talking to a Hono and tRPC API on Cloudflare Workers, with Turso for storage. The SPA and tRPC split was the one that stuck: the API types flow into the web app, the Zod schemas live in one shared package, and Workers plus Turso cost close to nothing while there's one merchant.

The repository has about 975 unit and integration tests (Vitest) and 116 browser tests (Playwright) across the register, kitchen display, roles and module switches.

A charge must happen exactly once

The scariest bug a POS can have is charging twice, or losing a sale the customer already paid for. Both come from the same moment: the cashier taps Charge, the network is slow, nothing seems to happen, and they tap again.

The register makes one key per charge and keeps it until the charge succeeds or the cashier dismisses it. A retry with the same key gets the stored answer back, so a slow network can't ring up a sale twice.

Every money-moving call (creating an order, completing it, and refunding it) goes through one wrapper, withIdempotency. The register makes a key for the charge and reuses it on every retry. The server stores the response under that key the first time, and any repeat with the same key and the same cart gets the stored response back. A repeat with the same key and a different cart is refused, because that's a bug, not a retry.

Two smaller decisions back this up. The web app never retries a money mutation on its own; a retry is always the cashier pressing Retry in the checkout dialog. And the server checks whether an order is already finalized before completing it, which covers the rare case of two truly simultaneous requests.

Whose drawer is this money in?

At the end of a shift, the cashier counts the drawer and QuickPOS compares it with what it expected. That only means something if every sale lands in the right shift.

The client never says which shift a sale belongs to. The server works it out from the register and the device that activated it, so a browser that only knows a register id can't put money in someone else's drawer.

The rule I settled on is that the client never names a shift. It sends the register and the device, and the server works out the open shift from those. A register is activated on one browser by an owner, so knowing a register's id isn't enough to put money in it.

PINs get the care you'd give passwords, because a four-to-six-digit PIN is easy to guess. They're hashed with PBKDF2, failed attempts are rate-limited per store, and every attempt is logged. The rate limit lives in Workers KV rather than in memory: a Worker runs as many separate isolates, and an in-memory counter would let someone spread guesses across them.

Paid and cooked are different things

In a counter-service shop, customers usually pay first and wait for their food. My first version of orders had one status, so completing the payment also closed the order, and the ticket left the kitchen board before anyone had cooked it.

An order has two states that move on their own. Before the split, paying for an order took it off the kitchen board, so a counter that takes payment first lost the ticket before anyone cooked it.

The fix was to give the order two states that move on their own. The cashier moves payment; the kitchen moves fulfillment. The kitchen can only move a ticket forward, and only Cancel closes both, because cancelling also has to put the stock back. A migration closed the tickets for old paid orders so the kitchen board didn't fill up with history.

One rule, one place

By late 2026 the code had grown to about 85,000 lines of TypeScript, and I ran an architecture review over it. It found three rules that were each written in several places, and all three had already caused bugs.

Three rules that used to be written more than once. Each one now lives in a single module that both sides call, and the old way of doing it is the thing the docs tell you not to do.

Permissions. The web app decided what to show, and the API decided what to allow, each with its own checks. They disagreed: some screens showed buttons the API then refused, and some hid things the API would have allowed. Now there's one access policy in the shared package, with 25 named capabilities like products.edit and reports.export. The API enforces it and the web app reads the same rule. A misspelled capability is a type error.

Stock. More than a dozen API routes wrote stock levels directly. Some skipped the movement history, so the history didn't add up to the stock. Products could exist with no stock row at all, and replacing a product's variants deleted the product's own stock. Now one module, the stock ledger, is the only code that writes stock, and it writes the new count and the reason for the change in the same transaction.

Optional features. A pilot merchant should see only what they use, but switching a feature off used to mean finding its links, routes and API procedures by hand. Now each module has one switch in the shared package. Turning it off hides the menu entry, redirects its pages, and makes the API refuse the procedures it owns. Nothing is deleted, so turning it back on is a one-line change.

Decisions for a Philippine pilot

The module switches made the pilot scoping concrete. For a counter-service food merchant, I'm turning off tables, customers and loyalty, the time clock and payroll, and discounts for now. The kitchen display stays on.

Tax is off too, and the reason is specific to the Philippines. QuickPOS's tax rates add tax on top of the price, but prices here are shown VAT-inclusive, and most small merchants aren't VAT-registered. Adding tax at the register would charge customers more than the menu says.

I also wrote down the rules for while the pilot runs. New features are frozen, and only what blocks the merchant's day gets fixed. Correctness safeguards are never cut: accurate totals, authorization, duplicate-sale protection, and recovery from failed requests. And AI stays out of the checkout path, so a model outage can never stop a sale.

What about brownouts?

Power and Internet outages are common enough here that a POS needs an answer for them. I've designed offline mode and built its core, but I've paused it until the pilot shows how much it's needed.

The offline design, for brownouts and outages of up to eight hours. The cashier device keeps the record, the kitchen display follows it over the store's own Wi-Fi or a phone hotspot, and the cloud catches up later. The core and its tests exist; the Android shell doesn't yet.

The design has the cashier device act as the store's coordinator. It writes every sale to a local, signed, append-only event log before confirming it, and the kitchen display follows that log over the store's Wi-Fi or a phone hotspot. When the Internet comes back, the events sync to the cloud, and any conflict goes to a review list instead of overwriting data.

The core is a Rust crate of about 2,600 lines with 65 tests. It covers the event log in SQLite, Ed25519 signatures, the kitchen board rebuilt from events, QR pairing, and a LAN transport with TLS pinned to the cashier's certificate. The same test vectors run in Rust and TypeScript, so both sides agree on what a signed event looks like. The scope is deliberately narrow: no official receipts, no loyalty redemption and no menu changes while offline, and GCash or Maya payments are recorded as checked by the cashier but not confirmed.

What's next

The next step is the merchant visit. I'll watch how they work today and fill in the parts of the pilot plan I've left blank: which device they'll use, which modules they need, and what the first improvement should be. The goal is small on purpose: one merchant runs a normal day on QuickPOS, records sales, corrects mistakes, and reconciles the drawer at close.

If you run a small food business in the Philippines and want to try it, or you just want to talk about POS software, send me a message.

title: DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes: the AWS line that charges you for talking to yourself
description:
Some of the traffic on your AWS bill never leaves AWS and never leaves your region, and you still pay for it. It appears as DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes, and it is the line behind a lot of "my bill went up but my traffic did not" threads.

Prices here are US East (N. Virginia) list prices, checked on 2026-11-04 against AWS's public price list and the EC2 on-demand pricing page. Other regions differ. The example numbers are made up to show the arithmetic, not taken from a real account.

What the line is

AWS documents the rate as $0.01 per GB in each direction for data moving between availability zones in the same region. Because the sender and the receiver each pay one side, a gigabyte that crosses an AZ boundary costs $0.02 in total. The same page documents that traffic to or from a public or Elastic IPv4 address in the same region is charged at the same rate, even if both ends are in one AZ.

The line is easy to miss because the unit price is small and the quantity is huge, and nothing about it says "something is crossing zones".

A made-up month 

DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes   25,000 GB x $0.01 = $250.00

Now imagine one pair of chatty services where each side sends 3,000 GB a month to the other across zones: 6,000 GB crossing, and 6,000 x $0.02 = $120.00 a month. The line shows it as 12,000 GB, because each crossing is counted on the sending side and again on the receiving side. That is $120.00 from two services that look idle on a dashboard.

Where it comes from

The pattern is usually not one big mistake but good practice applied everywhere:

  • Multi-AZ everything. Calls between your own services that land on a target or node in a different zone (a client reaching a network load balancer node, service to service by IP, a cross-zone NLB) pay on both sides. At high call volume, that share is billed. Check how your load balancer type is billed before you blame it.
  • Replicas in another AZ. Databases and caches keep replicas in other zones for availability (worth keeping), and a client that reads from a replica in a different zone than the app pays on every read.
  • Message and log pipelines. Producers, consumers and log shippers that talk to a broker or node in another zone pay on every byte. Self-managed Kafka on EC2 also pays for its own cross-zone replication; check your managed service's pricing page before you count it, since MSK, for one, does not charge for replication between brokers.
  • One NAT gateway shared across zones. Private subnets in other AZs reach the single gateway across a zone boundary, so each byte pays regional transfer on top of the $0.045 per GB NAT processing charge.
  • Public or Elastic IPs used inside the region. Services calling each other by public address pay both sides even in the same AZ. Private IPs avoid that.

How to find which pair is responsible

You cannot fix this by looking at the bill alone, so do not change topology blind. Things to try, in order of cost:

  1. In Cost Explorer, daily granularity, usage type DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes. A line that steps on a deploy day points at a new call pattern; a slope that follows traffic points at general chatter.
  2. If you have the Cost and Usage Report with resource IDs, group by resource to see which instance, load balancer or NAT gateway is on the line.
  3. VPC Flow Logs for a day on the suspect subnets, with the AZ and the addresses, show which pairs talk the most across zones. They cost money themselves, so keep the window short.

What to change, and what to leave alone

Cross-AZ traffic is often the price of availability, so the goal is to remove the accidental share, not to put everything in one zone.

  • Use private IPs for in-region calls between your own services instead of public or Elastic ones.
  • Where your load balancer or client library supports zone-aware routing, keeping calls in the caller's zone removes most of the crossing for stateless services. Check how your stack does this and test it, because it changes load distribution.
  • Give each AZ its own NAT gateway route (one per zone) so private subnets do not cross a zone to reach it. That adds hourly charges ($0.045 per gateway-hour, $32.85 a month), so compare the two with your own numbers.
  • Keep read replicas in the same zone as the readers only if you accept the availability trade-off.

Make one change, watch the daily line for three days, then do the next.

The short version

DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes is $0.01 per GB each direction, so $0.02 per GB crossing a zone. Find the pair of services responsible with the daily view and flow logs, remove the accidental crossings (public IPs, a shared NAT, unaware load balancing), and keep the crossings that buy you availability.

The page for this line has the sources and the steps: DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes explained. It also has an upload box that reads your own Cost Explorer or CUR CSV in the browser and shows this line with the dollars for your account.

title: Vue Customer Reports: Node Grants, Private Objects, Axios Upload Metering
description:
Customer support reports have an awkward boundary: the browser should move bytes quickly, but it should never decide where a customer's file lives. Short answer: let a Node backend authorize a tenant-scoped key and presigned upload URL, let Vue/Axios upload directly with progress events, then issue a short-lived signed read URL only when an authenticated customer asks for the report.

That split keeps credentials and naming policy on the server while avoiding a second hop for the file itself. It also gives the UI an honest progress bar instead of pretending that a completed POST means the object is durable.

The constraint is authorization, not the progress bar

The tempting implementation is a browser POST to your Node server, followed by a server-side upload. It is easy to explain, and it is expensive in operational terms: your API process becomes a byte pump, request timeouts become file-size limits, and a support agent watching a report upload competes with ordinary API traffic.

The direct pattern has three explicit steps. First, the authenticated request asks Node for a key and a presigned URL. Second, Axios sends the file to that URL, with onUploadProgress driving the meter. Third, Node verifies the object (a HEAD check is enough for existence) and records the known key against the support case. The browser never chooses an arbitrary path such as another tenant's prefix.

Keep that boundary.

Use a namespace you can list without server-side metadata search:

tenant/{tenantId}/user/{userId}/reports/{reportId}/{filename}

I would also normalize the filename and generate the report ID on the server. A user-supplied filename is display data, not authorization data.

How should Vue, Axios, and a Node backend divide upload control?

Here is the small control-plane shape. The /upload-grant endpoint is your application endpoint; the storage call inside it uses the verified presign path. The presigned URL returned by storage is a different host, so it receives no Infrai authorization header.

type PresignResult = {
  url: string;
  method: "PUT";
  expires_at: string;
  headers: Record<string, string>;
  fields: Record<string, string>;
  max_bytes: number | null;
};

const key = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!key) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

const wait = (ms: number) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function createUploadGrant(bucket: string, objectKey: string): Promise<PresignResult> {
  const apiOrigin = ["https:/", "/api.infrai", ".cc"].join("");
  const path = "/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}"
    .replace("{bucket}", encodeURIComponent(bucket))
    .replace("{key}", encodeURIComponent(objectKey));

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${apiOrigin}${path}`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${key}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({ op: "put", expires_seconds: 3600 }),
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("Retry-After"));
      await wait(Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter * 1000 : 500 * 2 ** attempt);
      continue;
    }

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Presign failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }

    return (await response.json()) as PresignResult;
  }

  throw new Error("Presign rate limit persisted after four attempts");
}

Call createUploadGrant only after authenticating the session, deriving the tenant and user IDs from server-side claims, checking that the support report belongs to that tenant, and constructing the object key. Don't accept a complete key from the browser. Return only bucket, key, and the presign response's url to Vue.

import axios from "axios";

const api = axios.create({ baseURL: "/api" });

export async function uploadReport(file: File, reportId: string, onProgress: (n: number) => void) {
  const grant = await api.post("/upload-grant", {
    reportId,
    contentType: file.type,
    size: file.size,
  });

  const { bucket, key, uploadUrl } = grant.data as {
    bucket: string;
    key: string;
    uploadUrl: string;
  };

  await axios.put(uploadUrl, file, {
    method: "PUT",
    headers: { "Content-Type": file.type || "application/octet-stream" },
    onUploadProgress: (event) => {
      if (event.total) onProgress(Math.round((event.loaded / event.total) * 100));
    },
  });

  await api.post("/upload-complete", { reportId, bucket, key });
}

On the Node side, bind the authenticated user and tenant before constructing the key, then request a private presign. Persisting the key before returning success makes retries and page refreshes understandable. If the completion call is retried, make its database write idempotent on reportId; an upload should not attach the same report twice.

The progress number is transport progress, not processing progress. A 100% meter means Axios finished sending bytes to the presigned destination. The completion call and the HEAD verification still matter. A support console should show "uploaded, verifying" for that small gap.

What do private storage options trade off for support reports?

The storage choice changes how much control-plane code you own. This is the comparison I would put in an architecture review, before looking at a unit-price spreadsheet.

Option Direct browser upload Access model Operational trade-off
Amazon S3 Presigned PUT/POST IAM plus signed URLs Deep ecosystem; policy and CORS configuration are your responsibility
Cloudflare R2 Presigned requests S3-compatible credentials Useful at the edge; check region and egress assumptions for your customers
Google Cloud Storage Signed URLs IAM and signed URLs Strong Google integration; this workflow still needs a Node authorization layer
Infrai storage Presigned object URL through one REST API Private objects with signed access Self-describing discovery and runnable examples reduce SDK-specific glue; vendor coverage is r2/s3/oss/cos

Infrai's practical angle here is not a cheaper meter. Its public discovery describes request and response schemas and includes runnable examples, so wiring the presign capability is reading one endpoint rather than learning another SDK. The same key and REST convention can cover adjacent backend capabilities if the support product grows; that can reduce integration surface, though it does not remove the need for your own tenant authorization.

Where this pattern is a poor fit

The catch is that private, signed access is deliberately restrictive. There is no permanent public URL mode, so a public image host or static-site asset bucket is the wrong use case. Serve a report in the app with a backend-issued signed URL or a download proxy.

There is also no object versioning or WORM-style lock. If replacing a key must be recoverable or legally immutable, keep versions in your database and choose a storage system with those controls. Strict write races need coordination too: without an If-Match conditional write, use a queue or a database transaction around the report state.

Browser direct upload has one more boundary: CORS rules must be available on the bucket. If your provider does not expose a self-service CORS route, your platform team must configure it, or you should use a backend relay for that particular workflow. Lifecycle cleanup is another detail people miss; a one-day minimum expiry and no automatic multipart-fragment cleanup means abandoned uploads need a scheduled janitor.

Stick with S3 when you need its mature versioning, object lock, cross-region replication, or broad migration tooling. Choose R2 when its edge and egress model is the deciding factor. Choose Google Cloud Storage when your data and IAM already live there. Pick a unified REST layer such as Infrai when reducing SDK and credential sprawl matters more than those provider-specific controls.

Measure the handoff before shipping it

Track four events: grant issued, first byte sent, upload finished, and object verified. Record the key and report ID, never the presigned URL. Alert on grants that are not followed by a completion or HEAD check, then expire those records according to your retention policy.

The progress callback isn't the success signal. The useful invariant is "a customer can retrieve a verified private object through an authenticated decision," and the browser meter is only one observation along that path. Your mileage may vary with large files, mobile networks, and provider-specific CORS behavior, so test those cases with representative report sizes before standardizing the UI.

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs
  • https://aws.amazon.com/s3/features/presigned-urls/
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/

title: Scheduled Payment Cleanup Recovery: Postgres pg_cron, App Cron, or Webhook Scheduler?
description:
Short answer: for a nightly payment reconciliation cleanup, choose the least complex scheduler that can prove a run happened, retry it safely, and leave an audit trail. Use a database-native job for a small SQL-only deletion in one Postgres database. Use an app cron webhook when the cleanup policy belongs in Python or touches more than the database. Add a queue when recovery from a long or fanned-out run is the real problem.

The word “cheapest” is a trap here. A timer that costs little to start can cost much more to operate after a missed run, a duplicate request, or a partial deletion. The useful question is where recovery state lives.

This is the shape I use for an edtech payment system: a nightly trigger starts reconciliation, the application compares provider records with local records, and cleanup removes only artifacts that are both expired and safe to remove. The scheduler owns the clock. The application owns the policy. The database owns the transaction.

How should pg_cron, app cron, and webhook scheduling handle data cleanup recovery?

Start with a run record before choosing a timer. Give each scheduled attempt an identifier, a planned window, a status, and a cursor or batch marker. A successful HTTP response is not proof that every payment was reconciled; it only proves that the endpoint answered. Conversely, a timeout does not prove that no rows changed. The next attempt must be able to inspect the run record and safely continue.

For a small cleanup that affects one Postgres database, pg_cron can keep the schedule close to the data. A SQL statement can select expired reconciliation artifacts, delete a bounded set, and commit as one database transaction. This is attractive when the rule is genuinely relational and there are no external calls.

The boundary changes as soon as the rule includes provider state, tenant policy, legal holds, object storage, or application-level evaluation records. Those conditions are easier to test beside the Python application than inside a database scheduler. An app cron webhook can wake that code at a fixed time, while the handler records progress in the same system that owns the policy.

Neither choice removes recovery work. A database job can be triggered twice. A webhook can receive a retry after the first request already committed. Design for that fact.

Repeat it.

A small webhook with a bounded cleanup transaction

The example below is intentionally plain. It verifies an HMAC signature, creates a run identifier, claims one bounded batch, and records the result. The HMAC construction follows RFC 2104. In production, the endpoint would sit behind HTTPS and the run table would normally share the application database with the records it protects.

import hashlib
import hmac
import json
import os
import sqlite3
import uuid
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer


DATABASE = os.environ.get("CLEANUP_DATABASE", "cleanup.db")
SECRET = os.environ["CLEANUP_WEBHOOK_SECRET"].encode("utf-8")
BATCH_SIZE = 100


def utc_now():
    return datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()


def reconcile_cleanup():
    run_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
    now = utc_now()
    with sqlite3.connect(DATABASE) as connection:
        connection.execute(
            "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cleanup_runs "
            "(run_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, started_at TEXT NOT NULL, "
            "finished_at TEXT, deleted_count INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0)"
        )
        connection.execute(
            "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS payment_artifacts "
            "(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, expires_at TEXT NOT NULL, "
            "reconciled INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0)"
        )
        connection.execute(
            "INSERT INTO cleanup_runs (run_id, started_at) VALUES (?, ?)",
            (run_id, now),
        )
        rows = connection.execute(
            "SELECT id FROM payment_artifacts "
            "WHERE expires_at <= ? AND reconciled = 1 "
            "ORDER BY id LIMIT ?",
            (now, BATCH_SIZE),
        ).fetchall()
        ids = [row[0] for row in rows]
        if ids:
            marks = ",".join("?" for _ in ids)
            connection.execute(
                f"DELETE FROM payment_artifacts WHERE id IN ({marks})", ids
            )
        connection.execute(
            "UPDATE cleanup_runs SET finished_at = ?, deleted_count = ? "
            "WHERE run_id = ?",
            (utc_now(), len(ids), run_id),
        )
    return run_id, len(ids)


class CleanupHandler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_POST(self):
        if self.path != "/internal/payment-cleanup":
            self.send_error(404)
            return

        length = int(self.headers.get("Content-Length", "0"))
        body = self.rfile.read(length)
        supplied = self.headers.get("X-Cleanup-Signature", "")
        expected = hmac.new(SECRET, body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
        if not hmac.compare_digest(supplied, expected):
            self.send_error(401)
            return

        run_id, deleted = reconcile_cleanup()
        payload = json.dumps({"run_id": run_id, "deleted": deleted}).encode()
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(payload)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(payload)


ThreadingHTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", 8080), CleanupHandler).serve_forever()

The reconciled = 1 condition matters more than the timer. A payment artifact is eligible only after reconciliation has established that the local record is safe to remove. The deletion is bounded so a large backlog becomes several observable runs instead of one opaque request. I use 100 rows in this example because the limit is easy to inspect and change; it is an engineering parameter, not a universal setting.

Consider a school that retries a payment near midnight. The provider sends the record after the local reconciliation window has started, the first cleanup request selects the other expired artifacts, and the process is interrupted after its transaction commits. A retry must not infer that the missing record is safe to delete just because its expiry time has passed. The reconciliation flag is the gate: the later run sees the newly reconciled row only if it is eligible, while the run table shows that the earlier attempt finished with a bounded count. If two workers select overlapping batches, the transaction and stable ordering still need a claim strategy appropriate to the real database; the sample keeps that concern visible instead of pretending that a scheduler can solve row ownership. That is why recovery belongs in the data model, not in a dashboard label.

The code also shows what the endpoint must not claim. It returns the count for one transaction, not a promise that the whole dataset is clean. A follow-up run can inspect the remaining eligible rows. If the handler times out after committing, a repeated request creates another run but does not resurrect deleted rows. That is the basic idempotency property this workflow needs.

What belongs in the scheduler, application, and queue?

Keep the scheduler boring.

Its job is to fire at the agreed time and expose enough run history to detect a missing trigger. It should not contain tenant retention rules or payment-provider interpretation.

Put policy in the application: eligibility checks, reconciliation status, legal holds, and the decision to publish follow-up work. This keeps the notebook-to-prod path short. The same Python function can be exercised with fixtures before it is called by an HTTP handler, and an eval harness can assert that protected records never enter the deletion set.

Use a queue when one invocation cannot finish within a bounded transaction or when a school-by-school fan-out would make the webhook too slow. The webhook publishes small messages containing a run identifier, tenant identifier, and cursor. Workers perform idempotent batches and write their outcomes to the run record. A queue with at-least-once delivery requires consumers to tolerate duplicates; that is a normal delivery contract, not an exceptional event.

Pub/Sub is a useful reference model for this separation: publishers send messages, subscribers process them, and the application decides what completion means. The same design can be implemented with a self-hosted queue or another message system. The important part is the durable run state, acknowledgement policy, and replay decision.

There is a cost to every extra boundary. A webhook plus queue adds credentials, monitoring, worker deployment, and a way to reconcile messages with database rows. It is not suitable when the entire job is one local SQL statement and the team has no need for application policy. Stick with the database-native option in that case.

Failure modes worth testing before launch

Test the awkward cases, not only the happy nightly invocation. Send the same signed request twice. End the process after the delete but before the response. Run two workers against the same cursor. Mark a payment as unreconciled while a cleanup batch is being prepared. Then inspect whether the final state is safe and whether the run record explains what happened.

Authentication deserves an explicit test too. Compare the supplied signature with the expected digest using a constant-time comparison, as in the example, and reject a missing or invalid signature. The body being authenticated should be the exact bytes used to calculate the digest; parsing and re-serializing JSON first can change those bytes.

Watch for a different failure: a timer can keep returning success while the job does no useful work. Alert on stale run records, growing eligible-row counts, and a gap in expected run identifiers or windows. Logs should include the run identifier, batch bounds, tenant, row count, and final status. A scheduler’s execution history is a trigger log, not a deletion ledger.

I’m not sure a single retry policy fits every payment provider. Your mileage may vary with rate limits and reconciliation windows, so make backoff and retry ownership explicit in the run state. Never turn a transient response into an unbounded tight loop, and never treat a second invocation as permission to skip the eligibility check.

The decision rule for a nightly reconciliation

Choose pg_cron when the cleanup is local, SQL-only, short, and naturally transactional. Choose an app cron webhook when Python owns the rule or the job crosses service boundaries. Add a queue when the work needs fan-out, independent retries, or bounded worker batches.

The simplest option is the one with the fewest recovery states your team can actually observe. That might be one database transaction. It might be a signed webhook that records a run. It might be a scheduler feeding workers. The right answer is determined by the failure you can explain at 02:00, not by the timer’s label or an advertised price.

Before enabling the nightly schedule, verify the signature path, run-record transitions, bounded selection, duplicate delivery, process interruption, and alert for a missing run. Keep the retention rule under version control with the Python tests. Write down which component owns retry, acknowledgement, and final reconciliation. Then the operational choice remains reversible as the data flow grows.

References

  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104
  • https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/overview

Further reading

  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104
  • https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/overview

title: Structured Kernel Surrogate Models for Multimodal Attribution
description:
arXiv:2611.13198v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study the problem of cross-sample modality attribution, which involves measuring how one modality in one sample affects the learning outcome in other multimodal samples. This problem is crucial in a multimodal system because a data modality (such as a text description) may be redundant for one sample (a self-explanatory image), but the same data modality would otherwise be uniquely informative for another sample, or informative when combined with other modalities. Prior work focuses on influence estimation at the level of one sample, and it remains an open question how one should capture the interactions across both samples and modalities. To capture scenarios like the above, we propose structured kernel surrogate models, which are surrogate mappings from both samples and modalities to the prediction outcome when they are trained together. We design an algorithm, SKS, which applies kernel ridge regression with a structured, compositional kernel on the selection states of individual samples and modalities. Specifically, the kernel function multiplies kernel-based similarity scores between every pair of data modalities for one sample and a pair of two samples. Additionally, we design a gradient-based estimation algorithm to efficiently estimate the structured kernel surrogate model. We evaluate our approach on two multimodal benchmarks, spanning a range of data modalities including satellite images, road networks, text, audio, and tabular data. We find that SKS achieves $57.8$% higher correlation with the true prediction outcomes than existing methods. In downstream data selection, SKS improves the average accuracy by $1.93$% over baselines. Models with data selected by SKS have lower Hessian traces, indicating a flatter loss surface. Using SKS to select satellite images identifies road segments, where accident scenes commonly occur, as opposed to background images.

title: AWS Network Firewall launches next-generation firewall policy
description:
Today, AWS announces next-generation firewall (NGFW) policy for AWS Network Firewall, a new policy model that provides security teams with a simpler policy structure and increased rule capacity. AWS Network Firewall is a managed network security service that protects your Amazon VPCs with access control and threat detection.

The new policy model strengthens your security posture by layering firewall and IPS protections instead of combining them, which also makes policies easier to manage. You author firewall rules that enforce deny-by-default access control, such as allowing traffic only to approved domains. For IPS rules, you can use managed rule groups from AWS or AWS Marketplace partners, which update automatically as new threats emerge. You can also create your own custom IPS rule groups. Firewall and IPS rules each have their own capacity, so you no longer trade one off against the other. For rules you don't share across policies, you can create embedded rule groups that draw capacity on demand without pre-allocation. With NGFW policy, all rules are stateful and evaluate with full connection context, for consistent, predictable traffic handling. Your existing policies continue to operate without changes, and IPS rules remain backward compatible.

NGFW policy is available at no additional charge in all commercial AWS Regions and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. For a full list of supported regions, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page.

To learn more, see the AWS Network Firewall product page and documentation.

title: 7 Things to Check Before Buying a Full-Stack Website Template
description:
Buying a ready-made website can save weeks of development work. However, choosing the wrong template may introduce hidden costs, security problems, and unnecessary maintenance.

Whether you're a freelance developer or launching a startup, here are seven practical things to check before purchasing a full-stack website template.

1. Examine the Technology Stack

Start by identifying which technologies power the application.

A modern full-stack project might use Next.js, React, Node.js, TypeScript, and PostgreSQL. However, not every project needs the same stack.

Choose technologies your team understands and can maintain.

2. Review the Source Code Quality

Clean code matters more than impressive screenshots.

Before buying, look for:

  • A clear project structure
  • Reusable components
  • Environment variable documentation
  • Consistent naming conventions
  • Setup and deployment instructions

If a live demo is available, test its important features rather than judging the design alone.

3. Understand Authentication and Security

Security should never be an afterthought.

Check whether the project uses secure authentication, properly validates inputs, and protects sensitive routes.

For applications handling customer information, examine authorization rules, dependency updates, and data protection measures.

Remember that purchasing source code does not automatically make a website production-ready.

4. Evaluate Database Design

A full-stack application often depends on a database.

Review its schema, relationships, migration files, and configuration instructions.

A well-organized database makes future feature development easier.

Also check whether sample data is included and whether it can be safely removed before deployment.

5. Check Customization Options

Your business requirements may change after launch.

Therefore, select templates with reusable UI components, clear configuration files, and flexible styling.

For example, a React or Next.js template with organized components is often easier to customize than a project containing duplicated code.

However, actual flexibility depends on how the project was built.

6. Read the Licensing Terms

Licensing is an important part of buying website source code.

Before purchasing, clarify whether the license allows:

  • Commercial projects
  • Client work
  • Modifications
  • Multiple deployments
  • Redistribution or resale

Never assume that purchasing a template gives you exclusive ownership of its source code.

7. Test Deployment and Documentation

Finally, review how the application moves from development to production.

Check whether the seller provides environment setup instructions, build commands, required services, and deployment guidance.

If possible, test the project in a staging environment before going live.

Good documentation can reduce troubleshooting time and unnecessary expenses.

Final Thoughts

Full stack website templates can be a useful starting point for developers, agencies, and startups. Nevertheless, the best choice is not always the cheapest or most visually attractive option.

Focus on code quality, security, maintainability, licensing, and deployment requirements.

If you're exploring ready-made web applications or source code for your next project, you can browse SellOnBay, a marketplace for website templates and digital development resources.

Choose carefully, review the documentation, and build on a foundation that suits your project.

title: Inherited Weights: Measuring the Tokenization Premium and the Sovereignty Cost of Language Models for the Global South
description:
arXiv:2611.13441v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Most language models deployed outside the United States and China are fine-tuned descendants of a small number of pretrained families. We argue that fine-tuning leaves the decisive properties of a model inherited from its base: vocabulary, knowledge, cultural alignment, memorized data and license. We contribute (i) an updated, reproducible measurement of the tokenization premium across 31 languages and 7 tokenizers released in 2023-2024, on 27 articles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, with explicit correction for unknown-token collapse. Premiums reach 10x for Amharic in older tokenizers and remain at 6.8x in the newest commercial one; Indigenous South American languages pay between 1.6x and 2.7x under global tokenizers. A vocabulary built from Portuguese lowers the premium for 11 of 13 Latin-script Global South languages relative to every global tokenizer tested, by about 24% for Guarani and Quechua. (ii) An eight-test black-box sovereignty audit that a buyer can run without access to weights. (iii) A regime argument: under energy and liability constraints, accuracy per joule, calibration and selective risk should replace raw accuracy as design objectives, with metrics that abstention cannot inflate. We close with preliminary internal measurements from a proprietary architecture built around these objectives, reported with their limitations. Data and measurement code are included.

title: Links That Land Right: Type-Safe Deep Linking in Navigation 3, Failure Modes Included
description:
A field guide for teams who have already been paged at 2 a.m. because a marketing email opened the wrong screen.


Links That Land Right: Type-Safe Deep Linking in Navigation 3, Failure Modes Included

Deep links are the one part of your navigation graph you do not control. Every other route is typed by your own code, reviewed by your own teammates and exercised by your own tests. A deep link is a string that arrives from a browser, a push notification, a QR code, a partner app or a typo in a campaign spreadsheet, and your app is expected to turn it into a sensible screen with a sensible back stack.

Navigation 3 treats this as a first-class problem. Starting with 1.2.0, the library ships a deep link API built around DeepLinkRequest and DeepLinkMatcher, with kotlinx.serialization doing the argument decoding. This post follows the structure of the Android Dev Summit 2026 session on the topic (by Clara Fok and Ian Lake) and cross-checks everything against the official guide and the nav3-recipes repository. I will build one small, original example end to end and spend as much time on how it breaks as on how it works.

The example app is Fernwood, a cycling-route app. Its links look like https://links.fernwood.app/routes/42?tab=elevation.

1. The shape of the problem

Before any API, it helps to see the whole journey of a link. There are five steps, and every bug in this article lives in one of them.

Three design decisions in this pipeline are worth noticing, because they explain most of the API:

  1. Matching is separate from navigating. A matcher never touches your back stack. It answers one question: “is this request mine, and if so, which key does it map to?” That keeps matchers pure, testable and easy to spread across feature modules.
  2. Matches are comparable. Several matchers can say yes to the same link, and the library gives you a way to pick the most specific one instead of relying on registration order.
  3. The back stack is your output, not a side effect. You end up with a List<NavKey>. What you do with it (render it, persist it, log it) is your business.

Here are the keys we will use. Note they are plain @Serializable types, which matters later. The near property uses a documented pattern: to decode a repeated query parameter into a list of custom objects, you implement DeepLinkSerializer<T> for the element type and annotate the list's type argument with @Serializable(with = ...). The official Match URI deep links guide shows this same form under "Custom objects in repeated query parameters". No @Contextual or SerializersModule is needed.

@Serializable
data object HomeKey : NavKey

enum class RouteTab { OVERVIEW, ELEVATION, REVIEWS }

enum class Difficulty { ANY, EASY, MODERATE, HARD }

@Serializable
data class RouteKey(
    val routeId: Long,
    val tab: RouteTab = RouteTab.OVERVIEW,
) : NavKey

@Serializable
data class RouteListKey(
    val difficulty: Difficulty = Difficulty.ANY,
    val near: List<@Serializable(with = WaypointSerializer::class) Waypoint> = emptyList(),
) : NavKey

2. API design and URI pattern matching

Requests, matchers, results

A DeepLinkRequest is the incoming link: a DeepLinkUri plus optional extras such as the intent action or MIME type. On Android you build one straight from an Intent:

val request = DeepLinkRequest(intent = intent)

A DeepLinkMatcher binds a link shape to a navigation key. Calling match(request) returns a match result carrying the key, or null. Three matchers ship in the box: UriDeepLinkMatcher for hierarchical URIs, StaticKeyDeepLinkMatcher for fixed links (a launcher shortcut that always opens Home, say) and a back-stack-building matcher we will meet in section 5.

The workhorse is UriDeepLinkMatcher. You give it a pattern and the serializer of the key it should produce:

val routeMatcher = UriDeepLinkMatcher(
    DeepLinkUri("links.fernwood.app/routes/{routeId}?tab={tab}"),
    serializer<RouteKey>(),
)

Placeholder names map to property names on the key. That single convention is what makes the whole thing type-safe: rename routeId in the key and forget the pattern, and the argument is simply never found.

What a pattern actually compares

UriDeepLinkMatcher splits a URI into scheme, authority, path, query and fragment, and judges each part on its own rules. Knowing those rules cold is the difference between "it works on my emulator" and "it works for the link the campaign team actually sent".

The rules that bite in production:

  • The authority is an exact, case-insensitive match, and nothing else. No wildcards, no placeholders. fernwood.app and links.fernwood.app are different authorities, so a link pasted without the subdomain silently does not match.
  • A trailing slash is an extra, empty path segment. /routes/42/ is not /routes/42. URL builders, CMS plugins and email tools add slashes all the time.
  • Query order does not matter and unknown parameters are ignored. This is good news for utm_* noise, but it also means a typo in a parameter name is not an error; you just get the default.
  • Scheme handling is asymmetric. A pattern with no scheme accepts http and https. A pattern written with http accepts both. A pattern written with https rejects plain http. Pick on purpose.

When two matchers both say yes

Suppose Fernwood also supports links.fernwood.app/routes/saved for the user's bookmarks. The link /routes/saved now fits two patterns. The library ranks UriMatchResult instances by comparing, in order: whether the path is literal, how many path arguments were captured, whether any arguments were captured, and finally the total argument count.

In practice, the literal path wins, which is what you want. The failure mode is subtler. If routeId were a String instead of a Long, saved would be a perfectly valid route id as far as parsing goes, and you would rely entirely on ranking to avoid opening a route called "saved". With a Long, the placeholder match fails to parse and returns null before ranking even matters. Prefer the narrowest argument type you can, because the type system becomes your first disambiguation layer.

And one operational rule: if two different keys can produce identically ranked results for the same link, the winner is an accident of list order. Treat that as a bug and cover it in a test.

3. Type-safe deserialization and custom serializers

Every extracted argument starts as a String. What happens next depends on the property type, and it is worth knowing which of four lanes your property falls into.

Standard serialization covers primitives, strings, enums and single-dimension collections of those. A repeated query parameter such as ?id=10&id=20 becomes a List<Int> with no code from you. Enums match case-sensitively against the entry names, so ?tab=elevation fails for RouteTab.ELEVATION while ?tab=ELEVATION works. If you control the producers of the link, fine; if you do not, see section 4.

Flattening applies to nested @Serializable classes: each inner property gets its own placeholder in the same URI namespace. The trap is name collision. A parent id and a nested id fight over one parameter, and @SerialName is the way out.

Writing a DeepLinkSerializer

For anything that is one string in the URL but a richer type in your code, you extend DeepLinkSerializer<T>. It is a KSerializer that converts between a single String and T.

Fernwood passes map positions as lat,lng. First, the parsing logic, written once and kept free of serialization concerns so it can be reused (we will reuse it in section 4):

data class Waypoint(val lat: Double, val lng: Double)

fun parseWaypoint(raw: String): Waypoint? {
    val parts = raw.split(',')
    if (parts.size != 2) return null
    val lat = parts[0].trim().toDoubleOrNull() ?: return null
    val lng = parts[1].trim().toDoubleOrNull() ?: return null
    // Range checks also reject NaN, because every comparison with NaN is false.
    return if (lat in -90.0..90.0 && lng in -180.0..180.0) Waypoint(lat, lng) else null
}

That comment is a real failure mode, not decoration. "NaN".toDoubleOrNull() happily returns NaN, and so does "Infinity" for an infinite value. A coordinate that is not a number will sail through a naive parser and surface later as a map camera that never settles. The range check handles it because NaN in -90.0..90.0 is false.

Now the serializer, a thin wrapper that converts “could not parse” into the exception type the serialization layer expects:

object WaypointSerializer : DeepLinkSerializer<Waypoint>() {
    override val serialName: String = "app.fernwood.Waypoint"

    override fun deserialize(value: String): Waypoint =
        parseWaypoint(value)
            ?: throw SerializationException("Expected 'lat,lng' within valid ranges, got '$value'")

    override fun serialize(value: Waypoint): String = "${value.lat},${value.lng}"
}

Two details I want you to notice. The serializer is attached where it is used, using @Serializable(with = ...) on the type argument of the list in RouteListKey, which is how a repeated parameter like ?near=47.6,-122.3&near=47.7,-122.4 becomes a List<Waypoint>. And a custom serializer for a type like java.time.LocalDate has the same wrinkle as Waypoint: the platform's parse throws its own exception type, so wrap it:

object RideDateSerializer : DeepLinkSerializer<LocalDate>() {
    override val serialName: String = "app.fernwood.RideDate"

    override fun deserialize(value: String): LocalDate =
        try {
            LocalDate.parse(value)
        } catch (e: DateTimeParseException) {
            throw SerializationException("Expected ISO date, got '$value'", e)
        }

    override fun serialize(value: LocalDate): String = value.toString()
}

(java.time needs API 26 or core library desugaring on older devices.)

Null versus exception is the most important distinction in this API

The library separates two kinds of failure, and your error handling should too.

A mismatch returns null. Missing required parameter, a value that does not parse as the property type, an enum name that does not exist: all of these mean "this link is not for this matcher", and the next matcher gets its turn. Parameters with default values simply fall back to the default, including when the query parameter is present but empty.

A misconfiguration throws. A Map property, a nested collection, a List<Filter> with no serializer on the element type: these are mistakes in your key class, not in the link, and they blow up at match time.

That has a consequence people miss. The throwing case happens when a link arrives, not when the app starts. A broken key class can ship to production, sit quietly for weeks, and crash the front door the first time someone taps the right link. Instantiate and match every matcher against at least one sample URL in a unit test. One caveat on that advice: DeepLinkUri is a typealias for android.net.Uri on Android, so plain JVM tests hit the "not mocked" stub problem. Use Robolectric or run these as instrumented tests.

Also, test what your serializer does on malformed input in your library version. The official example throws SerializationException from deserialize, and the safe behavior for a bad value from outside is a mismatch, not a crash. I would not assume; write the test, and if your version propagates the exception, catch it at the router (section 5).

4. Preprocessing arguments with custom matchers

Sometimes the link is valid in spirit but wrong in shape. Fernwood has three real-world examples:

  • a legacy mobile site produced /v1/routes/42, and the QR codes on printed trail signs cannot be reprinted
  • an email tool appends a trailing slash
  • a maps app hands the app a geo: link, which is not hierarchical at all

UriDeepLinkMatcher is an open class for exactly this reason. You can override matchUri to normalize the incoming URI before the real matching runs, matchRequest to inspect extras first, and matchArguments to transform extracted values before the key is built.

Here is a normalizing matcher for the first two problems:

class TolerantUriMatcher<T : Any>(
    pattern: DeepLinkUri,
    serializer: KSerializer<T>,
) : UriDeepLinkMatcher<T>(pattern, serializer) {

    private val legacyPrefix = Regex("^/v1(?=/|$)")

    override fun matchUri(uri: DeepLinkUri): UriMatchResult<T>? {
        val path = uri.encodedPath ?: return super.matchUri(uri)
        val cleaned = path
            .replace(legacyPrefix, "")
            .trimEnd('/')
            .ifEmpty { "/" }
        if (cleaned == path) return super.matchUri(uri)

        // On Android DeepLinkUri is android.net.Uri, so buildUpon() is available.
        return super.matchUri(uri.buildUpon().encodedPath(cleaned).build())
    }
}

Two failure modes are baked into how I wrote that, on purpose:

  • Normalize the path, not the whole string. The tempting version is uri.toString().replace("/v1", ""). That also rewrites a query value containing /v1, and it corrupts any path segment that merely starts with those characters. Anchoring the regex and working on encodedPath avoids both.
  • Normalizing widens what you accept. Every normalization is a new input shape you now support forever. Keep this layer small and documented, and prefer fixing the producer when you can.

When the link is not a URI at all

The geo: scheme is opaque, so UriDeepLinkMatcher is the wrong tool and you extend DeepLinkMatcher directly. You supply the key type and the result type, and implement matchRequest:

class GeoLinkMatcher : DeepLinkMatcher<RouteListKey, DeepLinkMatcher.MatchResult<RouteListKey>>() {
    override fun matchRequest(request: DeepLinkRequest): MatchResult<RouteListKey>? {
        val uri = request.uri ?: return null
        if (uri.scheme != "geo") return null

        // schemeSpecificPart is Android-only, and may carry a "?z=12" suffix.
        val raw = uri.schemeSpecificPart?.substringBefore('?') ?: return null
        val center = parseWaypoint(raw) ?: return null
        return MatchResult(RouteListKey(near = listOf(center)))
    }
}

This is where factoring parseWaypoint out of the serializer pays off: one validation routine, two entry points. If you later need to rank this matcher against others, extend MatchResult and override compareTo, and remember to unwrap a wrapped result first when the matcher sits inside a back-stack matcher. Otherwise your precedence logic silently compares the wrapper instead of the thing inside it.

5. Synthetic back stacks

Here is the part that separates a deep link that works from one that feels right.

When a user taps a link to a route, you can resolve to listOf(RouteKey(42)) and call it done. The screen renders. Then the user presses Up, and there is nothing above it. Depending on how you wired things, they leave the app, or worse, land on a blank state. They came from a link, but they did not stop being a user of your app.

A synthetic back stack fixes this by constructing the history the user would have had. You attach it to a matcher with withBackStack:

private val hosts = listOf("links.fernwood.app", "fernwood.app")

private fun routeMatchers() = hosts.map { host ->
    TolerantUriMatcher(
        DeepLinkUri("$host/routes/{routeId}?tab={tab}"),
        serializer<RouteKey>(),
    ).withBackStack { result ->
        listOf(HomeKey, RouteListKey(), result.key)
    }
}

Look at what the back stack is not: it is not just [Home, Route]. Putting the route list in between means Up goes to "all routes", which is where a user browsing normally would have come from. The policy is a product decision, and it belongs in the matcher where it is declared and testable, not in a screen's LaunchedEffect.

Notice also the two hosts. Because authority matching is exact, the apex domain needs its own matcher. Generating them from a list keeps the two from drifting apart.

The router

The router is the only place that knows how to turn a request into a stack. It collates matchers, picks the best result, and always returns something renderable:

class DeepLinkRouter(
    private val matchers: List<DeepLinkMatcher<*, *>>,
    private val fallback: List<NavKey> = listOf(HomeKey),
) {
    fun resolve(request: DeepLinkRequest): List<NavKey> {
        val best = matchers.mapNotNull { it.match(request) }.maxOrNull()
        return when (best) {
            null -> fallback
            is BackStackMatchResult<*, *> -> best.backStack.filterIsInstance<NavKey>()
            else -> listOfNotNull(best.key as? NavKey).ifEmpty { fallback }
        }
    }

    /** Release-build wrapper: a bad link must never crash the front door. */
    fun resolveSafely(request: DeepLinkRequest, onError: (Throwable) -> Unit): List<NavKey> =
        try {
            resolve(request)
        } catch (e: SerializationException) {
            onError(e); fallback
        } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) {
            onError(e); fallback
        }
}

val fernwoodMatchers: List<DeepLinkMatcher<*, *>> =
    routeMatchers() + GeoLinkMatcher()

Two small idioms are doing real work. filterIsInstance<NavKey>() replaces the unchecked cast you would otherwise need after star projection, so a wrong type is dropped instead of crashing later. And resolveSafely exists because of section 3: a matcher that throws is a bug, but it should be reported and recovered from, not turned into a launch crash. In debug builds and tests, call resolve directly so the bug is loud.

Wiring it into an activity without breaking state

Now the failure modes that no amount of correct matching saves you from. The first one is the most common, and it is entirely about lifecycle.

class MainActivity : ComponentActivity() {
    private val router = DeepLinkRouter(fernwoodMatchers)

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        val initial = router.resolveSafely(DeepLinkRequest(intent = intent)) { Log.w("Deeplink", it) }
        setContent {
            FernwoodApp(activity = this, router = router, initialStack = initial)
        }
    }
}

@Composable
fun FernwoodApp(activity: ComponentActivity, router: DeepLinkRouter, initialStack: List<NavKey>) {
    // Initial elements apply only when there is no saved state.
    val backStack = rememberNavBackStack(*initialStack.toTypedArray())

    DisposableEffect(activity) {
        val listener = Consumer<Intent> { newIntent ->
            val stack = router.resolveSafely(DeepLinkRequest(intent = newIntent)) { Log.w("Deeplink", it) }
            Snapshot.withMutableSnapshot { backStack.clear(); backStack.addAll(stack) }
        }
        activity.addOnNewIntentListener(listener)
        onDispose { activity.removeOnNewIntentListener(listener) }
    }

    NavDisplay(
        backStack = backStack,
        onBack = { backStack.removeLastOrNull() },
        entryProvider = entryProvider {
            entry<HomeKey> { HomeScreen() }
            entry<RouteListKey> { RouteListScreen(it) }
            entry<RouteKey> { RouteScreen(it) }
        },
    )
}

What each line is protecting against:

  • Re-applying the link on every recreation. The original Intent is still attached to the activity after rotation or process death. If you rebuild the stack from it in every onCreate, the user's progress is replaced by the link's starting point. Passing the resolved stack as the initial value of rememberNavBackStack means it is used only when there is no saved state, so a restored session keeps its own history.
  • onNewIntent for already-running activities. With a single-top style launch mode, a second link does not create a new activity; it delivers a new intent to the existing one. If you only handle onCreate, the second link is ignored and the user sees whatever was already there. The listener above covers that.
  • The empty stack in the middle. Calling clear() and then addAll() as separate state changes can expose a momentary empty stack, and NavDisplay has nothing to render for it. Doing both inside one mutable snapshot makes the swap atomic.

Cross-app links and task stacks

Everything so far is about the in-app stack. Links from another app add a second dimension: which Android task your activity lands in. The official deeplinks-syntheticbackstack recipe simulates an "App A" linking into "App B" and demonstrates both options. With the link opened in the caller's existing task, Back returns to the calling app, and pressing Up moves you to your own app's parent screen in your own task. Opened in a new task, both Back and Up stay inside your app. Neither is universally right; what matters is that you decided, and that Up and Back behave consistently with that decision. Read the recipe's navigateUp helper before writing your own.

6. Lightning round: the things that will still get you

Verify your App Links, then verify the verification. An unverified HTTPS link shows a disambiguation dialog or opens the browser. After a release, check the state on a real device:

adb shell pm get-app-links com.fernwood.app
adb shell pm verify-app-links --re-verify com.fernwood.app
adb shell am start -W -a android.intent.action.VIEW \
  -d "https://links.fernwood.app/routes/42?tab=ELEVATION" com.fernwood.app

Intent filters and matchers must agree. The manifest decides whether your activity is offered the link at all, and the matchers decide what to do with it. Add a matcher for a new path without adding the filter and it works from adb and nowhere else. Keep one list of supported patterns and derive both from it, or at least have a test that compares them.

Treat every link as hostile input. A deep link is attacker-controllable. Never perform a destructive or irreversible action (delete, purchase, sign out) straight from a link; land on a confirmation screen. Do not put tokens in URLs. DeepLinkRequest(intent = ...) also copies the intent's extras into the request, so treat those as untrusted too, especially on exported activities.

Auth gates belong in the stack, not in a global. If a route needs a signed-in user, resolve to [Home, Login(next = RouteKey(42))], not "remember the link in a static variable and replay it later". The static variable is lost on process death; the stack is persisted.

Modularization can fail silently. If each feature module contributes its own matchers (the guide suggests multibindings for this), a module that is accidentally excluded from a build variant produces no error. Links just fall back to Home. Add a test asserting that every key that is meant to be linkable has at least one matcher in the final collated list.

Pin the version and read the changelog. This API is young, and the release notes show it moving: factory helpers such as fromAction and fromMimeType were removed in favor of the extras field, empty path segments and empty query values got fixes, and http versus https matching was corrected. Code copied from an older blog post (including a version of this one) may not compile against your resolved version.

Summary

The mental model fits in four sentences. A link becomes a DeepLinkRequest. Matchers turn requests into typed keys or null, ranked so the most specific one wins. Types decide whether a bad value is a harmless mismatch or a loud misconfiguration. And a synthetic back stack is what turns "the screen rendered" into "the app feels like it was already open".

A short checklist to take to your next code review:

  1. Does every linkable key have a unit or instrumented test that matches a real sample URL?
  2. Are apex and www hosts, trailing slashes and legacy prefixes handled deliberately?
  3. Is the narrowest possible type used for each argument, and does each custom serializer reject NaN, empty and out-of-range input?
  4. Does the initial stack apply only without saved state, and is onNewIntent handled?
  5. Does a thrown matcher exception degrade to a fallback instead of crashing launch?
  6. Do Up and Back behave correctly for links from both inside and outside your app?

  • Android Developers, Match URI deep links: https://developer.android.com/guide/navigation/navigation-3/deep-links/uri-matcher
