title: Walrus Technical Report
description:
arXiv:2611.13689v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We present Walrus, a unified 8B speech-and-audio foundation model handling speech recognition (including code-switching and multi-talker speech), speech-to-text and speech-to-speech translation, text-to-speech, emotion recognition, audio captioning, and general audio understanding. Our main contribution is not a new architecture but a data-centric training recipe; we use a standard decoder-only backbone initialized from Gemma 4, so that gains can be traced to the data. For speech generation, Walrus predicts low-bitrate discrete speech tokens, and a lightweight token-to-waveform decoder converts them into high-fidelity audio. The recipe is a three-stage data curriculum that moves from broad multilingual data to multi-talker, code-switching, and domain-specific data. At each stage, task-aware and dataset-aware weighting balances tasks with very different token budgets and protects core skills from forgetting. Trained on over 600M samples covering more than 20 tasks and 100 languages, Walrus leads on most multilingual, multi-talker, and code-switching ASR, speech translation, and audio understanding benchmarks, outperforming both open speech language models of comparable size and dedicated task-specific models. On most benchmarks, it even matches or surpasses the $4\times$ larger Qwen3-Omni's performance. Results suggest that data engineering is a primary driver of quality in multi-task speech and audio modeling.

title: One Temperature to Rule Them All?
description:
arXiv:2611.13077v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Inference-time sampling is a central mechanism for improving large language models, with temperature controlling the tradeoff between reliability and diversity. While recent work suggests that varying temperature across samples can improve multi-sample inference, simple fixed-temperature schemes remain the standard in practice. We investigate this discrepancy in the canonical pass@K setting, asking when temperature diversity is useful, and when a single tuned temperature suffices. To this end, we analyze per-question success probabilities across multiple models and datasets, tracking how they vary with sampling temperature. We identify several consistent properties of these profiles, including that harder questions are less likely to share efficient sampling temperatures, although this trend is only logarithmic in hardness. We then derive an efficient method for evaluating the theoretically optimal multi-temperature allocation scheme, and show that although such a scheme improves performance, its gains over single-temperature baselines are typically modest when temperature is tuned as a function of the sampling budget K. We explain this phenomenon through mathematical mechanisms that we call dulling effects, and show how they ensure the robustness of temperature choices across different question distributions. Our results clarify when multi-temperature sampling is useful, and how temperatures should ideally be chosen.

title: Fix Content Hash Mismatch in Publishing Pipelines
description:
Fix a content hash mismatch in publishing pipelines when a publishing worker and a static site validator disagree on the exact bytes covered by an integrity sidecar.

Quick solution:

const crypto = require('node:crypto');

function createCanonicalPayload(article) {
  const sortedFields = {
    body: article.body.replace(/\r\n/g, '\n').trim(),
    seo_description: article.seo_description.trim(),
    title: article.title.trim()
  };
  return JSON.stringify(sortedFields);
}

function computeQualityHash(article) {
  const payload = createCanonicalPayload(article);
  return crypto.createHash('sha256').update(payload).digest('hex');
}

module.exports = { computeQualityHash };

Prerequisites include Node.js runtime access and matching JSON serialization libraries on both the publishing worker and the static site build validator. Watch out for automatic line-ending conversions in different Git checkouts, which can silently invalidate hashes.

The Cross-System Quality Hash Challenge in Distributed Pipelines

A publishing worker can create an article and a quality sidecar, after which a separate static site build recomputes the sidecar hash before deployment. Both components may use SHA-256 correctly and still disagree because the serialized inputs are not identical. In production failures, the worker might include article topics or dynamic timestamps in its quality hash, while the site validator treats topic and taxonomy metadata as external and excludes them from editorial evidence. When the build rejects the sidecar, the article and its associated assets never reach their public paths. A cross-artifact audit often reveals that one sidecar followed a worker-only rule while the rest followed the site rule, leading to frustrating deployment bottlenecks.

This publication hash must remain entirely separate from the internal hash used to bind an AI review to draft text. Conflating those distinct hashes hides which system contract actually failed and weakens overall editorial safety checks. When maintaining complex publishing workflows, you also need to manage how content review hash changes after citation edits to ensure upstream inputs remain stable before generation begins. For instance, using Azure Devops For Product Managers can help streamline the process.

Defining a Canonical Field Contract Across Boundaries

To ensure deterministic equality, define the hash input once as a canonical payload. You must explicitly specify which frontmatter fields are included, which taxonomy and publication timestamps are ignored, how body text is normalized, and how object keys are ordered. Without this explicit boundary, slight variations in whitespace or property ordering across environments will break cryptographic validation.

Option / Pattern When to Use It Trade-off or Failure Mode Recommendation
Full Raw Frontmatter When every metadata property must influence the published output. Highly fragile; minor taxonomy updates or tag additions invalidate old hashes. Avoid for site quality sidecars.
Explicit Canonical Payload When separating core editorial content from transient build metadata. Requires strict maintenance when adding new required fields to articles. Recommended for multi-step publishing pipelines.
Post-Build Artifact Hash When hashing the final compiled HTML instead of source Markdown. Hides intermediate generation errors and ties validation too late in the cycle. Use only as a secondary sanity check.

Keeping the publisher implementation strictly aligned with the validator is far safer than relaxing the validator after a mismatch occurs. According to the official Node.js crypto.createHash documentation, cryptographic hashing requires consistent byte streams, meaning any string encoding discrepancy between systems will break validation.

Implementing the Repair and Versioned Markers

The repair strategy involves adding a shared helper to the worker that mirrors the site field exclusions and normalizes line endings prior to hashing. Unit tests should prove that changes to mutable metadata like topic or publication date do not alter the publication hash, while changes to core fields like the title do.

Furthermore, the worker should version its publication marker. A prior marker representing a failed build must not make a subsequent retry look complete. The new marker format causes one corrective site commit. After that write completes, a repeat attempt remains idempotent and does not create duplicate commits or redundant build runs.

Verification and Execution Checklist

  • Confirm that identical source Markdown files generate the exact same SHA-256 hash string on both the publishing worker and the site validator.
  • Verify that modifying an excluded field, such as a tag or taxonomy category, leaves the computed quality hash completely unchanged.
  • Check that modifying a core included field, such as the article title or body, successfully alters the hash and triggers a fresh build cycle.
  • Ensure that a failed deployment marker allows exactly one corrective write and remains idempotent on subsequent retry attempts.

title: CI/CD #01 - I finished my app locally. Now what?
description:
These days, what I see most often is people generating an entire app with AI and stopping the moment it runs on localhost. It works on my machine, and then what? This series covers what happens under the hood when an application has to go to a real server, and how I plan to improve that process step by step.

I’ll start from the most honest place possible: my process is raw today, and I’m going to show you what it looks like.

The context

S.O Manager is a service order management system I’m building with a colleague. He built the Android app in Kotlin, and I built the API with Java and Spring Boot, using PostgreSQL as the database and MinIO for file storage. Everything runs on a VPS that I set up from scratch, with Nginx, a firewall, and a domain.

Today, the system has two access levels: Administrator, who manages the creation and progress of service orders (SOs), and Technician, who sees the SOs assigned to them, fills in the relevant information, and collects the client’s signature and feedback. Everything is automated, removing bottlenecks in order management and in filling out manual spreadsheets.

How I deploy today

When I finish a feature, this is the process:

On my machine

  1. I bump the version in pom.xml to mark which version is going to production, and commit it.
  2. I build the Docker image with Google Jib, tagged with the current version.
  3. I docker push the image to the registry.

On the VPS, via SSH

  1. I run git pull on the repository to update docker-compose.prod.yml.
  2. I run docker pull to download the new image.
  3. I take the application down with docker container kill.
  4. I edit .env to point to the new version and bring everything up with docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml --env-file .env.prd up -d.

Compose starts three services together: Postgres, MinIO, and the application. Database migrations run with Flyway when the application starts. And if something breaks, the rollback is to edit .env back to the previous image and bring everything up again.

One note: I don’t build on the VPS. It only pulls a ready-made image, which keeps the server simple and guarantees that what ran on my machine is what goes to production.

Two environments

I just set up a staging subdomain. api.mydomain.com.br is production, with real data, and hml.api.mydomain.com.br is where I’ll validate versions before promoting them.

What hurts

The process works, but it has clear problems:

  • Too many steps, all manual. There are seven steps across two machines, and any slip becomes a bug in production.
  • Downtime. Since I take the container down before bringing the new one up, the API is offline for a few seconds.
  • Manual rollback. Reverting a version requires editing a file on the server.
  • Almost no automated tests, and none run before the deploy. Today, the only barrier between a bug and production is me.
  • I depend on memory. If I forget a step or the order, nobody notices until something goes wrong.

A concrete example: I once hit a conflict with an existing container when bringing up the new version. I thought docker container kill removed the container, but it only stops it. (This deserves its own post.)

What’s next

In the next posts of the series, I’ll evolve this process with GitHub Actions:

  1. A first pipeline that runs the build and tests on every push.
  2. Automatic deploy to the VPS, going through the staging environment first.
  3. How to handle secrets outside the repository.
  4. Rollback and reducing downtime.

The idea isn’t to show a perfect process, but to record the evolution of one that started raw. If you’ve been through this, tell me in the comments: what was the first step you automated?

title: Uni-Loc: Weakly Supervised 3D CT Pathology Localization via Spatially Grounded Vision-Language Classification
description:
arXiv:2611.13330v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate localization of abnormalities in three-dimensional (3D) CT scans is essential for linking automated predictions with clinically relevant pathological findings. We propose Uni-Loc, a vision-language framework that unifies pathology classification and 3D localization using scan-level supervision. Uni-Loc derives both predictions and localization maps from spatial similarities between pathology-conditioned queries and image features. A token-to-voxel upsampling module enables high-resolution localization, while gradient-guided thresholding identifies pathology regions without additional learned parameters. Evaluated on five localization tasks comprising 355 annotated CT scans, Uni-Loc achieves macro-averaged voxel-level AUROC/AUPR of 96.1\%/34.5\%, outperforming relevance propagation (80.7%/13.9%) and gradient saliency (88.7%/8.1%). Uni-Loc also achieves classification AUROC of 88.39% on CT-RATE and 78.03% on RAD-ChestCT, improving over a matched baseline. These results demonstrate effective 3D pathology localization without requiring pathology-specific voxel-level supervision.

title: Just Image Transformers with Late-Stage Pixel Refinement
description:
arXiv:2611.13120v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent work on latent-free diffusion transformers has demonstrated the feasibility of training image generators without a latent VAE. This avoids compression artifacts from the VAE and simplifies the training pipeline. In particular, JiT showed that even a standard transformer can be trained to generate images when the model is trained to predict the final image ($x$-prediction). Even though JiT unlocks training efficiency comparable to latent models, it still suffers from reduced image quality likely arising from modeling the image as a collection of large patches. In this work, we revisit JiT and show that adding simple convolutional pixel-pathway layers in a post-training phase significantly improves generation quality. Moreover, we show that the added pixel-pathway does not need to be active in the early denoising stages, and can be activated as late as in the last $20\%$ of the denoising process. Our experiments on ImageNet@256 show improvements compared to the original JiT results, achieving an FID of $1.78$ (from $2.34$ with corrected sampling), without using additional losses.

title: Sckwoky at SHROOM-Visions: Character-Level Hallucination-Span Detection in Image-Conditioned VLMs via Dual-Prompted LoRA Decoders
description:
arXiv:2611.14100v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present our system for the SHROOM-visions 2026 shared task on character-level hallucination span detection in image-conditioned vision-language model (VLM) responses, evaluated across English, French, Italian, and Chinese. The detector is built on a frozen Gemma-4-12B-it backbone with trainable LoRA adapters (approximately 10.7M parameters). Because the backbone is a causal decoder, hidden states read from a single copy of an answer cannot attend to subsequent tokens; we therefore repeat the candidate answer within one prompt and extract features from its second occurrence, giving every position approximate bidirectional context in a single non-autoregressive pass. A character-level locator combines intermediate hidden states to predict hallucination probabilities, BIO boundaries, and a response-level abstention score, while separate language-specific classifiers assign one of five hallucination types to each predicted span. On the closed test set, our system reaches a macro-averaged character IoU of 0.4404, more than doubling the official baseline (0.1854), and ranks 5th-6th on IoU across the four languages. On the English tuning split, controlled ablations attribute a gain to the repeated answer that is comparable to that of LoRA adaptation (its held-out gain is smaller and concentrated on hallucinated answers), and they show that the detector relies on the image-answer pairing: shuffling images across examples drives IoU down to the level of the predict-nothing floor or below it in every language. In deployments where the same Gemma-4-12B-it model also generates answers, its base weights can be reused, making the approach practical for local question-answering systems that cannot run a separate verifier.

title: Introducing Go++
description:
My dear fellow developers,

I’d like to take a moment of your time to announce that I’ve been working on an experimental project called Go++, a superset of Go that compiles to plain Go; the project is still in early stages and definitely not ready for production use but I was hoping to get some early feedback from the community that could help steer it in the right direction.

I love Go and its simplicity, but many a time I’ve wished it allowed me to express my intent a little more succinctly and Go++ is an attempt towards exactly that but while remaining firmly grounded to the Go runtime and its awesome and mature standard library and the ecosystem.

In a nutshell, Go++ currently offers things like:

  • Classes and polymorphism
  • Generics
  • Multiple inheritance
  • Function and method overloading
  • Named and default arguments
  • Enums and structural records
  • Extension methods
  • String interpolation
  • Safe nil walking and fallbacks
  • Exceptions
  • Annotations and introspection
  • and more!

One important project constraint driving the compiler has been to compile a Go project without any modifications thus letting developers incrementally adopt Go++ features as they see fit for the problem at hand.

The project has grown beyond the compiler itself and now includes a CLI, formatter, language server/VS Code extension, testing, and some opinionated built-in packages for HTTP routing, serialization, ORM and more.

Go developers can quickly try it with:

go install github.com/telgatech/gpp@main
gpp init hello
cd hello
gpp run

Detailed documentation including getting started guide and sources available at:
https://gpp.telga.in/
https://gpp.telga.in/guide/getting-started
https://github.com/telgatech/gpp

I’d love feedback from Go developers who are willing to give it a spin—particularly around the language design, Go interoperability, tooling, rough edges, and anything that feels surprising or inconsistent.

If you try it, let me know what works, what breaks, and what you’d like to see next.

title: Geometry-Dependent Approximation and Stability Properties of Shallow ReLU$^k$ Networks on Bounded Euclidean Domains
description:
arXiv:2611.13952v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On bounded Euclidean domains, we study how hidden-parameter geometry affects shallow ReLU$^k$ networks through results on approximation rates, saturation-type lower bounds, Gram and stiffness matrix spectra, Bernstein and Marcinkiewicz--Zygmund inequalities, discrete least-squares recovery, and inverse approximation.
  Our analysis uses smooth localization and dyadic Fourier estimates. We quantify parameter geometry by the fill distance $h$ and antipodal separation distance $\underline h$. For the prescribed network space $L_n^k$, representative approximation estimates take the form \begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} \inf_{g_n\in L_n^k}\|f-g_n\|_{\mathcal L^2(\Omega')}&\lesssim h^r\|f\|_{\mathcal H^r(\Omega)},\\ \inf_{g_n\in L_n^k}\|f-g_n\|_{\mathcal L^2(\Omega)}&\gtrsim \underline h^{\frac{d+2k+1}{2}}\|f\|_{\mathcal L^2(\Omega')}. \end{aligned} \end{equation*} The upper bound exploits target regularity up to the critical order $\frac{d+2k+1}{2}$, while the lower bound applies asymptotically to fixed targets smoother than this order. The upper estimate holds on an interior subdomain $\Omega'$, whereas the lower estimate concerns the larger domain $\Omega$.
  We also obtain geometry-dependent spectral estimates that quantify conditioning and coefficient stability. Further results establish norm discretization and regularized recovery from function values, and infer target regularity from approximation rates under coefficient or separation conditions. Altogether, these results describe how parameter geometry governs approximation accuracy, the stability of coefficient representations, discrete recovery, and the regularity information contained in convergence rates.

title: Compute the Interactions, Not the Attributes: What a Fact Layer Must Supply in the Chinese Sexagenary System
description:
arXiv:2611.13597v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language-model systems in rule-governed domains often pair the model with a deterministic fact layer, but which facts that layer should supply is rarely measured. We measure it in the Chinese sexagenary system underlying BaZi chart analysis, where every fact has one table-checkable value: 682 items over twelve fact categories and 160 transit--natal collision items, posed closed-book, with the reference table, and with computed facts at increasing levels. In eleven open-weight models answering directly, errors concentrate where attributes must be combined: none gets more than 4\% of sexagenary days or 1\% of collisions right. Static attributes have no consistent effect, and the complete relation list leaves most direct-answering models near zero although it contains the answer. A query-filtered layer (exploratory) raises Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B to 78--92\% and four further models to 96--100\%. Three proprietary reasoning models compute 68--95\% of collisions unaided. On chess positions, under predictions locked in advance, attributes again do not substitute for relations and listed distractors are misattributed. The fact layer must supply computed interactions; how they are presented depends on the model and the domain.

title: Integrating Action Prefix Prediction and Alignment Across Modalities for Multimodal Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.13782v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Learning representations from multimodal observations is difficult in reinforcement learning with limited interaction data. Multimodal Joint Predictive Representation combines multimodal latent prediction with contrastive learning across modalities, but its recursive rollout depends on earlier predictions and its pairwise alignment focuses on correspondence between modalities. We propose Improved Predictive Representation, which combines prediction from action prefixes with alignment at the observed anchor based on Contrastive Multimodal learning. At each horizon, it predicts future representations directly from the observed anchor and the corresponding sequence of actions. We evaluate two crop configurations: IPR-S with a minimum retained crop area of 10%, and IPR-H with 50%. Across five DeepMind Control Suite tasks, IPR-H achieves an average return across tasks that is 10.0% higher than the baseline with visual and depth images and 3.4% higher with visual images and position vectors. The relative performance of the two configurations varies across tasks. In Webots, both IPR configurations achieve higher mean final returns than the baseline without LiDAR, but not when LiDAR is available.

title: Leveraging Psychophysical Attentional Distribution for Gaze-Augmented Reward Modeling
description:
arXiv:2611.13477v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Integrating human feedback into language models has gained increasing attention as a means to align model outputs with human preferences, with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) serving as a prominent framework for preference-based alignment. Recent studies have incorporated eye-tracking (ET) data as an additional supervisory signal for reward model training, grounding reward learning in human reading behavior. Building on this approach, we extend prior fixation-centric models by leveraging established findings from cognitive psychology on human letter recognition. Specifically, we model visual attention as a spatially graded distribution centered on the current gaze location and incorporate this representation into reward model training. Our results show that the reward model trained with the proposed gaze distribution achieves higher preference prediction accuracy than a baseline model. Moreover, some results from our experiments are qualitatively consistent with established findings on human attention during reading, suggesting that they potentially capture cognitively meaningful aspects of human attention allocation.

title: Understanding Mixture-of-Experts Language Models Beyond Expert Boundaries
description:
arXiv:2611.13975v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, the nature of expert specialization remains controversial. Reports of domain-associated expert preferences contrast with analyses attributing routing primarily to token identity or syntactic patterns. To clarify these differing accounts, we look beyond expert-level routing to investigate the neuron-level organization of domain-specialized computation using Routing-Aware Magnitude Profiling (RAMP), a measure developed for this analysis. Using mixed-domain calibration data, we identify domain-specialized neuron sets with 58-74% overlap across multi-source samples of the same domain, compared with 15-24% across domains. To understand how this organization evolves during training, we trace neuron importance throughout pre-training and post-training across three fully open MoE families. Neuron importance continues to reorganize between pre-training checkpoints despite comparatively stable expert-level importance rankings, while post-training largely preserves neuron rankings. Building on these neuron-level perspectives, we further introduce RAMP-based Pruning (RAMPr) to select neurons across experts for balanced multi-domain capability preservation. At 75% neuron retention, RAMPr preserves average 91-98% of original full performance across six models. At 50% retention, our pruning method can reduce resident GPU memory by 36-43% and improves batched prefill throughput by 17-39% effectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/ydyjya/Neuron-Level-Specialization-in-MoE

title: AI Governance Should Prioritize Control and Knowledge Boundaries Over Limiting Intelligence
description:
arXiv:2611.12941v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The rapid proliferation of autonomously acting AI agents makes the governance of agentic systems urgent. We propose the competence circuit, summarized as IKC + KC + C, that decomposes an agent's real-world impact into three pathways: intelligence-mediated discovery, procedural know-how, and direct control. Using the canonical fast-takeoff debate as a stress test, we formalize the conditions for intelligence-mediated fast takeoff as a conjunction jointly sufficient for fast catastrophic supremacy, showing that most rely on rapid knowledge acquisition or control attainment rather than intelligence alone. We operationalize epistemic intelligence as hypothesis-selection efficiency and validate this framework via stochastic simulation on NK fitness landscapes across six scenarios spanning the conjunctive chain. An analytic bound supported by the simulations shows that intelligence-driven speedup is capped by the ratio of competing intelligence levels regardless of task difficulty. The simulations also expose a fast-takeoff dilemma: a large intelligence-driven speedup multiplier materializes only when the hypothesis space is noisy, but the absolute timescale remains constrained by the time required for capability-critical tests, so a large multiplier need not imply rapid progress. Simulations also indicate that institutional chokepoints disproportionately slow down superintelligent agents when mandatory authorization delays are large relative to the negligible time these agents spend on unproductive search. We argue that the dominant safety levers are restricting control and enforcing knowledge boundaries rather than limiting intelligence alone, and this applies to agentic systems at any capability level. Purely digital domains weaken these bottlenecks, strengthening the case for architectures that intentionally "put physics in the loop."

title: Few-Step Streaming Video Generation via Condition Shifting
description:
arXiv:2611.14033v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Few-step sampling reduces the cost of streaming video generation. Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) supervises few-step generators with a separate fake-score network, which adds training memory and computation and must track the evolving generator. We extend APEX to streaming video by using condition shifting to estimate the velocity field of the generated distribution within the generator. The original text condition selects generation, while a shifted condition selects fake estimation using the same parameters. This removes the independent fake network while retaining S2-Avatar's frozen reference teacher, Self-Replay Forcing, and perceptual regularization. We evaluate APEX on 180-second videos using three backbone evaluations per block and a one-step spatial Refiner, with a 70-case human study and a 320-case StreamAV-Bench comparison. Compared with S2-Avatar, APEX achieves higher video instruction fulfillment on the Progressive track (3.856 versus 3.831) and higher visual aesthetics across both tracks (0.641898 versus 0.632606). Human raters favor APEX most strongly on instruction following, with +30.0% net preference, followed by consistency and video quality at +4.3% each. Motion quality favors S2-Avatar, audiovisual synchronization is predominantly tied, and usability is unchanged. Separate measurements under matched training settings show 4.4% lower peak allocated GPU memory per GPU and 9.2% shorter mean iteration time than DMD.

title: PostgreSQL 14 Reaches End of Life on November 12: Three Ways to Upgrade
description:
PostgreSQL 14 gets its final release on November 12, 2026. After that, the community stops shipping fixes for it, security fixes included, so upgrade to PostgreSQL 18 with pg_upgrade, a dump and restore, or logical replication.

What ends on November 12, 2026

The PostgreSQL project supports each major version for 5 years after its first release, then ships one final minor release and stops (versioning policy). PostgreSQL 14 came out on September 30, 2021. Its final release is November 12, 2026, which is also the date of the next scheduled minor releases (release roadmap).

Minor releases are where bug fixes, security fixes and data corruption fixes ship. Once 14 stops getting them, anything found later stays unfixed on 14. Your database keeps running.

From the PostgreSQL versioning policy, as of Nov 4, 2026

Version First release Final release
18 September 25, 2025 November 14, 2030
17 September 26, 2024 November 8, 2029
16 September 14, 2023 November 9, 2028
15 October 13, 2022 November 11, 2027
14 September 30, 2021 November 12, 2026

PostgreSQL 19 reached its first release candidate on October 15, 2026 (announcement) and isn't on the supported list yet. Don't wait for it: 18 is the newest supported major and has the most years left.

Plenty of setups still run 14. About 72,000 public files on GitHub say image: postgres:14 (GitHub's code search count, November 2, 2026, approximate).

Where the version hides in your repo

Where PostgreSQL 14 is pinned

Place Look for Watch out for
docker-compose.yml image: postgres:14, 14-alpine or 14.x A volume that already holds 14 data. See the dump and restore steps below.
Dockerfiles FROM postgres:14 Extension packages built for 14, such as postgresql-14-*
CI workflows A service container with image: postgres:14 Tests that pass on 14 say little about 18
Helm values image.tag, or the chart's appVersion The chart's own version is not the PostgreSQL version
Terraform engine_version (RDS, Aurora), version (Azure), POSTGRES_14 (Cloud SQL) The provider's own end date, covered below

To find them, run these from the repository root:

git grep -nE "postgres(ql)?:14"
git grep -nE "engine_version|POSTGRES_14"
git grep -n "postgresql-14"

An untagged image: postgres pulls whatever the newest major is on the day the container is created. Pin the major you've tested.

Managed databases set their own dates

If a cloud provider runs your database, its date is the one that counts, and it often isn't the community date. Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, for example, keeps 14 in standard support until February 28, 2027, then charges for Extended Support until February 28, 2030 (AWS release calendar). Google Cloud SQL and the others set their own schedules too. We track these on the calendar:

  • Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL
  • Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL
  • Azure Database for PostgreSQL
  • Heroku
  • PostgreSQL itself

On a managed service, use the provider's major version upgrade instead of running the tools below yourself. The testing steps still apply.

Three ways to upgrade

You can go from 14 straight to 18 without stopping at 15, 16 or 17, but read the release notes for each version in between (versioning policy). The upgrading docs describe three methods:

Upgrade methods, from the PostgreSQL 18 docs

Method Downtime Good fit
pg_upgrade Minutes, especially in link mode Servers you run yourself
Dump and restore As long as the dump and restore take Small databases, local dev and CI
Logical replication Several seconds at switchover Large databases that can't go down

pg_upgrade

Install 18 next to 14, create the new cluster with initdb, then run a check first. -c checks both clusters and changes no data (pg_upgrade docs). The paths are placeholders:

pg_upgrade -c \
  -b /old/14/bin -B /new/18/bin \
  -d /old/14/data -D /new/18/data
  • Stop both servers and drop -c to run it for real. Add -k for link mode: it skips copying files, but once you start the new cluster you can't go back to the old one.
  • PostgreSQL 18's initdb turns data checksums on by default, and pg_upgrade needs both clusters to match. If your 14 cluster has no checksums, create the new one with checksums off; initdb has a new option for that (18 release notes).
  • Install the 18 build of every extension's shared library, such as pgcrypto, before you run it. Don't run CREATE EXTENSION in the new cluster: pg_upgrade copies those definitions over.
  • Upgrading to 18 keeps most planner statistics, but not ones made with CREATE STATISTICS. Afterwards, run vacuumdb -a -Z to analyze every database, as the docs recommend.

Dump and restore

The simplest and slowest path. For production, the upgrading docs recommend running pg_dumpall from the newer version, which can read servers back to 9.2. Don't just bump the image tag on a volume that holds 14 data: major versions change the data directory format, so 18 can't start on it (versioning policy). For a local Docker Compose database you can rebuild, this is enough:

docker compose exec db pg_dumpall -U postgres > dump.sql
docker compose down -v
docker compose up -d db
docker compose exec -T db psql -U postgres < dump.sql

down -v deletes the volume, so check dump.sql before you run it. Between the second and third commands, change the image to postgres:18. From 18 on, Docker's image docs say to mount the volume at /var/lib/postgresql, not /var/lib/postgresql/data (Docker image docs). Run vacuumdb -a -Z after the restore so the planner has statistics.

Logical replication

Logical replication works between major versions. Build an 18 server, let it catch up with 14, then switch your app over (upgrading docs). Set wal_level = logical on the 14 server, which needs a restart, then on 14:

CREATE PUBLICATION upgrade FOR ALL TABLES;

And on 18:

CREATE SUBSCRIPTION upgrade
  CONNECTION 'host=old-db dbname=app'
  PUBLICATION upgrade;

Know the limits first (restrictions):

  • The schema doesn't replicate. Copy it first with pg_dump -s and freeze schema changes until you switch.
  • Sequences don't replicate. Set them to current values on 18 right before you move writes over, or inserts will collide.
  • Large objects don't replicate.
  • Tables need a replica identity, the primary key by default, for UPDATE and DELETE to replicate. Without one, those statements fail on the 14 server, which is your production database (publication docs).

What to test before you switch

Point CI at 18 first. Change the service container image, run the full test suite, and fix what breaks before you touch production. Then check these:

  • Extensions. List them on 14 with SELECT extname, extversion FROM pg_extension; and confirm each one is available for 18. On a managed service, check the provider's extension list for 18.
  • Query plans. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on your slowest and most frequent queries on both versions and compare. pg_stat_statements helps you find them.
  • Connection drivers. Update your driver to a release that supports 18. PostgreSQL 18 deprecates MD5 passwords and warns when you set one (18 release notes), so move any MD5 roles to SCRAM and make sure your driver handles it.
  • Permissions on new databases. From 15 on, new databases don't let every user create objects in the public schema (15 release notes). An upgrade keeps your old permissions, but a fresh 18 database in CI or a new environment won't have them, so migrations run by a non-owner role can fail.
  • Backup scripts. 15 renamed pg_start_backup() and pg_stop_backup() to pg_backup_start() and pg_backup_stop().
  • The Migration section of each release note from 15 to 18. That's where the project lists every change that can break existing apps.

Where Since.dev fits

Since.dev tracks end-of-life dates like this one from the publisher's schedule. For a repository you scan or connect, it finds the exact file and line that pins PostgreSQL 14, with the days left and the version to move to.

  • Scan any public GitHub repo, no sign-in.
  • See every PostgreSQL date on the PostgreSQL calendar.
  • Your coding agent can ask check_code over MCP with the surface runtime:postgresql@14.
  • For public repositories on any plan, and private ones on Team and up, it opens a fix pull request for supported cases, ready for review. Nothing merges or deploys.

Questions

When is PostgreSQL 14 end of life?

Its final release is November 12, 2026, five years after it came out on September 30, 2021. After that, the PostgreSQL project ships no more fixes for 14, security fixes included.

Will PostgreSQL 14 stop working after November 12, 2026?

No. The server keeps running. It just gets no more bug or security fixes, so anything found later stays open until you upgrade.

Can I upgrade straight from PostgreSQL 14 to 18?

Yes. pg_upgrade and a dump and restore both go from 14 to 18 directly. Read the release notes of 15, 16 and 17 as well, since their changes apply to you too.

Does Amazon RDS end PostgreSQL 14 on the same day?

No. RDS keeps 14 in standard support until February 28, 2027. After that it runs under paid Extended Support until February 28, 2030. Other managed services set their own dates.

Which upgrade path are you taking, and what broke on the way? Tell me in the comments.

First published on since.dev.

title: The RSI Tax: When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost
description:
arXiv:2611.13524v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) seeks to improve an agent using its own task experience. Its practical value depends on whether performance gains justify the full cost of self-improvement and task execution. We evaluate this trade-off on continual task streams, scoring each task before its feedback is used for subsequent updates. We define the \emph{RSI Tax} as the token cost of the self-improvement process and include it alongside task-execution costs in end-to-end evaluation. Across six methods and two language models, a bounded-note baseline matches or exceeds the observed accuracy of Meta-Harness, EvoSkill, and RRSI, with mean total-token savings of 65.6-71.0\%. We decompose the RSI Tax into verification, exploration, and writing costs, and track subsequent use of the associated state or artifact. For these three RSI methods, verification accounts for 74.8--93.6% of the aggregate RSI Tax. A substantial share of the RSI Tax is also associated with states or artifacts that are not used later in the evaluated streams. These results expose a practical limitation of costly RSI procedures: improvements in the deployed agent need not justify the expense of the improvement process. They motivate RSI objectives that jointly optimize the RSI Tax and expected task-execution cost while ensuring continued growth in agent capabilities across the task stream.

title: Comparative Evaluation of Deep Learning Models for Geographic Atrophy Segmentation in En Face OCT Images
description:
arXiv:2611.13191v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Background: Geographic atrophy (GA) is an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD). It causes irreversible vision loss due to progressive degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptors. Accurate segmentation of GA in en-face image is crucial for early diagnosis, monitoring disease progression, and developing personalized treatment strategies. However, existing deep learning approaches are typically evaluated using single architectures and single-device datasets, limiting insight into relative performance and cross-device robustness. Methods: We trained and systematically compared five deep learning architectures for GA segmentation: Nested U-Net, ResU-Net, nnUnet, Swin-Unet and MedSegDiff model, together with a thresholding based classical baseline. The models were trained on a dataset of en-face OCT images derived from 269 OCT volumes from two different devices, following a three-step preprocessing technique involving normalization and inpainting to enhance the quality of the en-face images. Results: On the fixed held-out validation set comprising OCT scans from both Cirrus (R) (Carl Zeiss Meditec, Inc., USA) and Spectralis (R) (Heidelberg Engineering, Germany) devices, nnUnet achieved the highest mean Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.8882 +/- 0.0033. The other models yielded the following Dice scores: Nested U-Net (0.7932 +/- 0.0423), ResU-Net (0.8453 +/- 0.0074), Swin-Unet (0.6886 +/- 0.0294), and Diffusion model (0.7959 +/- 0.0242). Conclusions: nnUnet framework, demonstrated most reliable performance for GA segmentation in en-face OCT under limited data conditions. It offers the best balance of accuracy, stability, and efficiency for GA quantification.

title: Onboarding that ends with a workout you can start, not a feature tour
description:
I work on FightNome, so this post is about our own app.

FightNome is a pad-work trainer for boxing, Muay Thai, kickboxing and MMA. A recorded voice calls strikes on the beat of the music and you throw them on a bag, on pads or in the air. The app has a fair amount of depth: a combo editor, sections and rounds, tempo, conditioning between rounds. None of that helps someone who just installed it and wants to hit something tonight.

So onboarding doesn't explain the features. It asks a few questions and hands back workouts that are ready to play.

Five questions

The questions are goal, level, discipline, stance and music style. Each one exists because it changes what the coach says or how the session is put together.

Discipline is the obvious one. A boxing session and a Muay Thai session shouldn't call the same strikes, and a Muay Thai session that never says "teep" or "knee" would feel wrong in the first minute.

Stance matters more than I expected. Kicks, elbows and knees are called by name with lead or rear, so the app needs to know which side is which before the first call. Getting that wrong is the kind of thing a user notices right away and doesn't forgive.

Level and goal decide how much is asked of you. They're also where vocabulary comes in. Pad numbers (1 jab, 2 cross, 3 lead hook and so on) are normal in a lot of gyms, but to a beginner "one, two, three" means nothing. In FightNome only the amateur-fighter persona hears numbers. Everyone else hears the names of the strikes.

Music style is the soft one. It doesn't change the technique, but it's part of whether the session feels like yours.

What comes out

From those answers the app builds four starter workouts, with names like First Fight, Sharp Fundamentals and React & Fire. They're normal workouts, the same kind you'd build yourself in the editor: sections, rounds, rests, and conditioning parts like rope, shadow work and bodyweight between striking rounds. Nothing about them is a special tutorial mode.

That was a deliberate choice. If the starters were a separate thing, people would have to learn the real app later anyway. Because they're regular workouts, opening one and changing a combo is also the moment you learn how the editor works.

Why not a tour

A tour would have to show screens, and the main point of the app is that you don't look at the screen during a round. The phone goes in a pocket or a waistband and the voice runs the session. Explaining that with screenshots felt backwards. What actually explains it is pressing play and hearing the first round.

Every workout shows its full plan before you start (every section, every round, every rest), so that preview does the job a tour would do, just for the session you're about to do.

The part I keep going back and forth on

The paywall comes after onboarding, and the app doesn't have a free tier. That means the questions have to be worth answering before anyone has heard a single call. Five questions is about where I think patience runs out, but I don't have a clean way to test that without guessing.

If you've built an onboarding flow that generates content instead of explaining it, I'd like to hear how many questions you ended up with and which one you cut.

If you want to try it

FightNome is on the App Store (iOS 26 and up) and Google Play. It's a paid subscription, and only the yearly plan has a 3-day trial. More at https://fightnome.app.

I used AI assistance to draft this post and edited it myself.

Apigee X

Announcement

Apigee Emulator

Apigee Emulator v2.0.2

On October 21, 2026, we released Apigee Emulator version 2.0.2.

This release upgrades the Apigee Emulator runtime to Java 21 (Eclipse Temurin JRE 21) to align local proxy development and policy execution with the production Apigee runtime, while keeping the embedded Apache Cassandra datastore pinned to Java 8. It also addresses 46 security vulnerabilities across Netty, Jackson, Apache Log4j, BouncyCastle, Apache CXF, Eclipse Jetty, and the embedded Cassandra Go standard library health-check binary.

The emulator image is available at Artifact Registry.

To upgrade, update the emulator version in your Cloud Code for VS Code settings to 2.0.2. See Manage the Apigee Emulator for details.

Feature

Apigee Emulator

Changed in this release

  • Upgraded the Apigee Emulator runtime JVM to Eclipse Temurin JRE 21 (21.0.12.1.0+1-0, from JRE 11 11.0.31+11), adding JVM 21 compatibility flags (-Djava.security.manager=allow and --add-opens module flags) for JavaCallout, JavaScript (Rhino), and Python (Jython) policies while keeping the embedded Apache Cassandra 4.0.19 datastore pinned to Eclipse Temurin JRE 8.
  • Upgraded Netty to 4.1.137.Final (from 4.1.135.Final) and updated netty-tcnative-boringssl-static and netty-tcnative-classes to 2.0.81.Final (from 2.0.77.Final).
  • Upgraded Jackson (jackson-core, jackson-databind, and jackson-dataformat-yaml) to 2.21.7 (from 2.18.6 and 2.19.2) and jackson-annotations to 2.21.
  • Upgraded shaded Apache Log4j (log4j-api and log4j-core) in ConfigUtil.jar to 2.25.5 (from 2.17.1 and 2.25.4).
  • Upgraded BouncyCastle (bcprov-jdk18on, bcpkix-jdk18on, and bcutil-jdk18on) to 1.85 (from 1.84).
  • Upgraded Apache CXF (cxf-*) to 3.6.12 (from 3.5.11).
  • Upgraded gRPC to 1.82.3 (from 1.62.2), Protobuf (protobuf-java and protobuf-java-util) to 4.33.6 (from 3.25.5), and Guava to 33.5.0-jre (from 33.4.8-jre).
  • Removed unused org.eclipse.jetty:jetty-* (9.4.58.v20250814) and commons-collections:commons-collections (3.2.2) JARs from the emulator distribution.
  • Refreshed the Cassandra base image to pick up Go standard library 1.27.0 (from 1.25.11) in the embedded /opt/apigee/ready health-check binary.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.16.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Deep scan by default (cm find): cm find now runs a concurrent file-by-file deep scan (--deep) by default for higher vulnerability recall across repositories. To run a single-session quick scan instead, pass the --quick flag (cm find --quick). cm stats now breaks down scan usage by mode (--deep, --quick, and --diff).
  • Pre-flight health checks (cm health): Added the cm health command (with --json, --strict, and --timeout flags) to verify credentials, configuration, endpoint reachability, and project authorization before running scans.
  • Expanded file discovery: cm find now scans .hh, .hxx, .inl, and .ipp C++ headers, extensionless scripts with supported language shebangs (python, node, ruby, and php), nested build/, target/, obj/, and bin/ source directories, and production code under spec/, locale/, and i18n/.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Restricted cm verify file writes to .exploit/ inside the project root and skipped missing or out-of-scope session artifacts during workspace restore.
    • Capped single-turn file reads at 256 KiB with pagination hints, bounded unified diff generation on large files, and raised run_command default and maximum timeouts to 120 seconds and 300 seconds.

title: OpticalRAG: Pixel-Space Compression for Token-Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.13675v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is bottlenecked by the token budget of large language models: feeding long documents into the context window is expensive, while aggressive textual compression discards fine-grained information that is irreversibly lost in a one-dimensional token sequence. We argue that this bottleneck is not fundamental to information density but to the choice of compression \emph{modality}. Modern visual encoders can pack the contents of a rendered text page into roughly a hundred visual tokens with little semantic loss, opening a new compression-fidelity tradeoff that purely textual methods cannot reach. We present \textbf{OpticalRAG}, a framework that renders documents as page images, encodes them with a frozen vision encoder, and distills the retrieved visual tokens into as few as $16$ injected tokens before passing them to the LLM. Two ingredients make this work without expensive cross-modal training: (i) \emph{Encoder-Bridged Retrieval}, which projects text-query states into the visual feature space of the frozen encoder, through a projection shared with the compressor, to retrieve visual tokens from a text query, with no contrastive training; and (ii) \emph{Query-Driven Distillation}, a lightweight cross-attention compressor that condenses the retrieved visual tokens into a small set of query-conditioned prefix tokens. On LongBench-v2, BAMBOO, and LooGLE-v2, OpticalRAG achieves the best compression-aware accuracy (CAP) on all three benchmarks while injecting only $16$ tokens, and improves the closed-book Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbone by $5.17$ points on LongBench-v2.Code is available at https://github.com/brighterr/OpticalRAG.

title: Persistent Metric-Semantic Maritime Scene Memory from Open-Vocabulary 3D Scene Graphs
description:
arXiv:2611.13903v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Three-dimensional scene graphs (3DSGs) can provide robots with persistent metric-semantic representations for spatial reasoning, but the existing methods have primarily been developed for indoor and terrestrial environments. In this paper we investigate how a representative outdoor open-vocabulary method transfers to maritime environments and which adaptations are needed. Our experiments show that zero-shot representative outdoor 3DSG descriptions agree with our labeled ground truth for a majority of geometry-supported objects on our data, but the resulting map exhibits considerable physical-entity fragmentation, and its terrestrial higher-level assumptions don't capture maritime spatial organization needs. We therefore keep the underlying mapping method and post-process its accumulated evidence. We show a metric-semantic consolidation method followed by geometry-grounded multi-view vision-language model (VLM) reasoning that reconciles remaining fragments into physical entities and groups entities through observations into local places. In parallel, we construct maritime macro regions using map priors and onboard water and structure observations, and associate them with the local places. The resulting representation reduces physical-entity fragmentation beyond both the baseline and our geometry-semantic consolidation component alone, supports correspondence of fixed local places across repeated maritime traversals, and improves contextual retrieval on our reviewed queries over tested baselines. These results show how an outdoor open-vocabulary map can be adapted into persistent maritime scene memory with our methods for object/place identity and spatial abstractions.

title: W-ISA: Transactional Execution of Weight-Space Intervention Programs
description:
arXiv:2611.13232v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present W-ISA, a software instruction set and transactional runtime for executing weight-space intervention programs on pretrained language models. Shape-checked instructions express parameter updates, projections, ablations, and rank-one transformations. The runtime applies these programs within request-scoped execution contexts and restores saved parameters after completion or interruption. Activation-based match-action rules connect measured model states to intervention selection. We evaluate restoration and replay on SmolLM-135M-Instruct and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, and compare materialized rank-one updates with equivalent PyTorch hooks on the latter. In 45 timed requests, both intervention implementations produce identical greedy sequences at 32, 128, and 512 tokens; their maximum prompt-logit difference is 0.000184. On the complete WikiText-2 raw test split, the combined SmolLM attention-head ablation and MLP projection changes perplexity from 22.2353 to 22.3188, a relative increase of 0.3754%. W-ISA separates intervention specification, execution, and measurement, making parameter-level experiments reproducible and composable.

title: 4 AI privacy layers ranked by 2026 integration complexity.
description:
The most expensive enterprise suites often lag behind simple local-first layers in speed.

2026 compliance shifts from static checks to real-time data flow control.
The gap between regulation coverage and integration effort defines the tier.

  • Does it block data before it leaves the device?
  • Can it map findings to GDPR/CCPA controls?
  • Does it reduce manual review time?

🔴 S TIER
Local-First Redaction (Various)

  • Masks sensitive data on-device before any prompt is sent.
  • Highest leverage for organizations using AI day-to-day. Enterprise Prompt-Redaction APIs (Various)
  • Sits between your application and the model.
  • Best when customer data flows through your own apps. AI-Aware DLP / CASB Modules (Various)
  • Governs outbound AI traffic at the network or endpoint.
  • Uses ML detectors to identify PII and secrets with high precision. Automated Risk Scoring (Witness AI)
  • Assigns dynamic risk scores based on ToS and data handling.
  • Replaces lengthy manual reviews with data-driven decisions.

🟠 A TIER
OneTrust

  • Ensures responsible use via data discovery and classification.
  • Automates privacy rights and consent management. Nightfall AI
  • Scans data in motion and at rest for PII and health records.
  • Tuned to understand context, reducing false positives.

🟡 B TIER
Cycode

  • Maps security findings to SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, and FedRAMP.
  • Generates audit-ready compliance reports automatically. Black Duck
  • Best for open-source SCA and license management.
  • Part of the top 10 AI cybersecurity tools for 2026.

What this means for your team:

  1. Combine local redaction with enterprise contracts for maximum leverage.
  2. Add AI modules to existing CASB or DLP rather than buying new stacks.
  3. Use automated risk scoring to speed up new tool approvals.
  4. Ensure tools map findings to specific regulatory controls like GDPR.

Audit your current AI stack against these four categories today.

P.S. Local-first redaction is the highest-leverage move for most organizations in 2026.

title: Blurring the Block Boundaries: Overlapping Block Denoising for Efficient Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.14387v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have emerged as effective alternatives to autoregressive models for latency-critical tasks, enabling faster token generation. Recent advances employ block diffusion with self-editing capabilities, where each block refines tokens iteratively before advancing to the next one. Yet each block is only as fast as its slowest token, and the next block cannot start before it. We suggest Blurring the Block Boundaries (B3), a novel method with which two blocks are refined in parallel within a shared forward pass. B3 calibrates itself on the fly, opening the next block only once the model is ready to start generating it. It is a training-free and hyperparameter-free acceleration method which seamlessly integrates within any self-editing block diffusion model. Evaluated on state-of-the-art DLMs across 10 diverse datasets spanning varied tasks and difficulty levels, B3 results in on par generation quality and 11.5-14.5% speedup compared to the base model, pushing the Pareto frontier for latency-quality trade-offs in DLM inference.

title: GrapheneOS, LineageOS, /e/OS and Others Are Now Officially Supported
description:
This post is mostly about phones that don't have Google at all: GrapheneOS, LineageOS, CalyxOS, /e/OS and other Android builds. Codename One now supports them officially. After that, a shorter update on the Android compatibility layer, which runs existing Android apps on iPhone, desktop and the web.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

GrapheneOS, LineageOS, CalyxOS and /e/OS

I was a member of Team OS/2. I know what it's like to use an operating system the big vendors forgot, and to find that half the apps you need just don't start. People choose GrapheneOS, LineageOS and other AOSP builds for good reasons, usually privacy, and they deserve apps that work. There's a business case too: when you support a niche operating system its users have learned to live without, you get the most loyal advocates your product will ever have. They notice, they remember, and they tell each other.

Codename One apps mostly worked on these phones before. But mostly isn't support: call the wrong API and you could hit a failure, or behavior nobody could predict. Now it's official, with a clear boundary. One APK serves both kinds of phone: at run time it checks whether Google Play Services is there. No build hint, no flavor, no second build. The Android port never calls Play services, Play Core or Firebase without checking first, and CI enforces that, so a future change can't quietly break it.

Feature With Google Play Without Google Play
UI, storage, networking, SQLite, media Works Works
On device ML Kit models Works Works
Location and geofences Fused location Framework LocationManager
Maps Google Maps Vector MapView
Google sign in Native Browser OAuth flow
Push Firebase UnifiedPush (ntfy, NextPush, Sunup)
In-app purchase Play Billing Not available
Integrity attestation, in-app review Works Not available

The location fallback fixed something on Google phones too: builds without Play location now get proximity alerts and background location through the framework API.

Push, with one line

Push needs one line of configuration, because the phone has no Firebase to deliver it. UnifiedPush lets the user pick the app that holds the push connection, called a distributor. A UnifiedPush endpoint is a standard Web Push subscription, so the Codename One push service delivers to it with the Web Push credential your app already has. You copy its public key into a build hint:

codename1.arg.android.unifiedPush.vapidKey=<your 87 character VAPID public key>

Your app code doesn't change, and neither does your server. The registration order is automatic:

The one real gap is in-app purchase. Play Billing needs the Play Store. If selling on de-Googled phones matters to you, tell us; it's something we can add.

To test, use the Android emulator's AOSP system images, the default target, which have no Google apps. The Android without Google Play chapter has the details.

Also new: classic Android apps, on iPhone

Three weeks ago we showed that an Android Studio module's src/main can build unmodified as a Codename One app. There's no Android runtime inside it. Views are Codename One components, layouts follow Android's measure and layout rules, and resources compile to a binary table at build time. Nothing parses XML or uses reflection on the device. You import a project with one command:

mvn cn1:import-android-project -Dcn1.android.import=/path/to/MyAndroidApp
mvn cn1:build -Dcodename1.platform=ios

Material 3.
RecyclerView.
Kotlin activities.

Each pair shows Android on the left and Codename One on the right, from the same source.

What's new: the parts real apps lean on

Toy apps are mostly UI. Real apps store data, run work in the background and talk to the hardware. The layer now covers those:

  • Room. The build generates the _Impl classes, the way Android's annotation processor does. Features we don't support yet (@Relation, suspend DAOs, Flow, Rx, Paging, @AutoMigration and FTS) fail the build and name the member.
  • WorkManager. Chains, unique work, retries and LiveData status, persisted across app restarts.
  • Location and sensors. LocationManager and SensorManager.
  • Services. Manifest services, including startForeground() mapped to Codename One's ForegroundService. Notifications from NotificationManager and NotificationCompat show as local notifications.
  • Keystore. AES keys from AndroidKeyStore with GCM and CBC.
  • Document pickers. ACTION_OPEN_DOCUMENT, ACTION_CREATE_DOCUMENT and ACTION_GET_CONTENT, plus the ActivityResult contracts, open the platform's native open and save dialogs.

So this is ordinary Android code, and it now runs on an iPhone:

@Dao
public interface NoteDao {
    @Query("SELECT * FROM Note ORDER BY created DESC")
    List<Note> all();

    @Insert
    long insert(Note note);
}

Intent save = new Intent(Intent.ACTION_CREATE_DOCUMENT);
save.addCategory(Intent.CATEGORY_OPENABLE);
save.setType("text/plain");
save.putExtra(Intent.EXTRA_TITLE, "notes.txt");
startActivityForResult(save, SAVE_NOTES);

Where iOS says no

Some Android behavior has no iOS equivalent, and the Android chapter has a table for it. Location in a foreground service keeps running in the background when the manifest asks for background location. Other foreground service work gets only the short window iOS allows. Constrained WorkManager jobs go to iOS's background task scheduler, and iOS decides when they run. On iOS, ACTION_CREATE_DOCUMENT returns RESULT_OK right away and shows the save dialog when your app closes the output stream, so a cancel isn't reported back.

Other limits: Keystore keys aren't hardware backed there, Parcel is an in process container, SQLite uses a single connection, there are no system content providers or broadcasts, and reflection based libraries won't run on iOS.

Tomorrow, the last post of the week: Caches, Certificates, Streaming Uploads and a Simulator That Types.
