title: ASPIRE: An Agentic System-Identification Platform for Iterative Reasoning and Exploration
description:
arXiv:2611.13114v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: System identification requires expert decisions on the identification method, incorporation of prior physical knowledge, and model validation. We propose ASPIRE, a framework for nonlinear system identification in which a large language model agent selects and executes the identification method. ASPIRE constructs closed-form, nonlinear static or dynamic models from measured data, optionally supplemented by a system description, the intended use of the model, and physical requirements expressed formally or in natural language. Each model includes its parameters, an estimation record, an interpretation of its terms, and an error evaluated on test data inaccessible to the agent. Formal physical requirements are verified independently. ASPIRE operates autonomously or interactively, allowing the agent to ask questions and the user to request further analyses and identification rounds. We evaluate ASPIRE on three measured systems: a mobile robot, a rotational system with dry friction, and a laboratory fermenter. Each system is tested with and without a description, in five runs per task. All 30 runs delivered valid models, at a cost of 0.96 to 3.38 US dollars per run. An assessment by the authors found that, for the 30 models recommended by the agent, one per run, the interpretation of the model and the documentation of its structure selection and parameter estimation fully satisfied 132 of 150 assessed items and partly satisfied 18. The most frequent discrepancy, found in nine models, concerned inaccurate or unsupported claims about model structure selection.

title: One Kernel for 109 Cloud Services. Because It Specializes in the Right Place.
description:
✓ Human-authored analysis; AI used for formatting and proofreading.

The cloud security industry has a tool for every case. An S3 scanner. An IAM analyzer. A Lambda checker. A VPC auditor. A Kubernetes admission controller. A Terraform linter. A CloudFormation validator.

Each tool is specialized for its local domain. Each tool has its own engine, its own rule format, its own output schema, its own dashboard. The specialization is in the code. A different mechanism for every case.

The result: tool sprawl. Fifteen tools in the average organization. Hundreds of thousands of lines of mechanism across them. Adding support for a new AWS service means adding a new tool or a new module with its own parser, its own rules, its own integration.

There's a principle from innovation theory that says this is backwards. Specialize the outcomes, not the mechanisms. The mechanism stays uniform. The data varies by case. One kernel. 109 cloud services. The kernel doesn't grow when the catalog does.

The principle: Local Quality

Different parts of a system should not behave in a uniform way. Each part should adapt to its local purpose, conditions, and constraints — instead of enforcing global uniform behavior.

The principle seems to endorse the industry's approach: specialize each part. But there's a constraint that changes everything:

Local Quality must never introduce local MECHANISMS, only local OUTCOMES. Mechanisms remain generic. Only invariants and policies specialize.

The constraint separates scalable specialization from sprawl:

Localizing... What grows Result
Mechanisms (code per case) Code. Every new cloud service, compliance regime, or control type adds a new engine, parser, or module. Tool sprawl. Mechanism complexity grows linearly with cases.
Outcomes (data per case) Data. Every new cloud service, compliance regime, or control type adds a YAML file. One kernel. Data complexity grows. Mechanism doesn't.

The industry localizes mechanisms. The architecture localizes outcomes. Same specialization. Different place. Opposite scaling properties.

The industry's design vs the alternative

Dimension Industry default (local mechanisms) Local Quality (local outcomes)
Cloud service coverage Per-service scanner (S3 scanner, IAM scanner, Lambda scanner, ...) One kernel + 109 asset-type schemas
Compliance regime Per-regime engine (HIPAA tool, SOC 2 tool, PCI-DSS tool, ...) One kernel + 10 compliance profiles
Control time semantics One check type. Every condition treated the same. Two types: unsafe_state (instant) and unsafe_duration (threshold-based)
Compound risk scoping Uniform grouping (or none at all) Per-chain scope_field — each chain declares its own local scope
Threat taxonomy Per-taxonomy product Same catalog projected through different mappings (compliance OR threat taxonomy)
Observation contract Generic JSON for all cloud services 109 specialized schemas, each capturing its service's unique properties
Adding a new AWS service Add a new module: new parser, new rules, new tests, new integration Add a YAML file: new schema + new controls. Same kernel. Same tests. Same integration.

Every row on the right is the result of specializing outcomes while keeping the mechanism uniform. The left column grows mechanism complexity with every case. The right column grows data. Data is cheaper to maintain, cheaper to review, cheaper to test, and cheaper to add than mechanism.

Seven layers of specialization — all in data

1. 109 asset-type schemas — local observation contracts

An S3 bucket has properties IAM roles don't: encryption settings, public access blocks, lifecycle policies. An IAM role has properties S3 buckets don't: trust policies, attached policies, MFA requirements. Forcing them into one uniform schema wastes most fields on most assets.

Each of the 109 schemas captures exactly the properties its cloud service exposes. An S3 schema has 81 field paths. An IAM role schema has 64. A Bedrock agent schema has 31. Each is tuned to its local domain.

The kernel reads any of the 109 schemas through the same generic parser. One mechanism. 109 locally-specialized observation contracts.

2. 3,000+ controls — local security judgments

Each control is tuned to a specific unsafe state in a specific domain:

# S3-specific: public read access
id: CTL.S3.PUBLIC.001
unsafe_predicate:
  any:
    - field: properties.storage.access.public_read
      op: eq
      value: true

# IAM-specific: overprivileged role
id: CTL.IAM.ROLE.SCOPE.001
unsafe_predicate:
  any:
    - field: properties.identity.unused_services_pct
      op: gt
      value: 20

# Bedrock-specific: agent with broad Lambda invoke
id: CTL.BEDROCK.AGENT.ROLE.001
unsafe_predicate:
  any:
    - field: properties.agent.role.policies.statements.actions
      op: contains
      value: "lambda:InvokeFunction"

Three different domains, unsafe states and predicates. Same kernel evaluating all three. The specialization is in the YAML. The mechanism is uniform.

3. Two control types — local time semantics

Some conditions are unsafe instantly. A public S3 bucket is dangerous the moment it's created. Other conditions are unsafe only if they persist. An overprivileged role might be acceptable during a migration window but dangerous after 90 days.

# Instant: unsafe the moment it's observed
type: unsafe_state
predicate: properties.storage.access.public_read == true

# Durational: unsafe only after threshold exceeded
type: unsafe_duration
predicate: properties.identity.access_key_age_days > 90
max_unsafe: 168h

A uniform control type would either flag every transient condition (false positives) or miss every durational violation (low coverage). Two types let each control declare its local time semantics. The kernel handles both with the same evaluation loop.

4. 10 compliance profiles — local regulatory priorities

HIPAA prioritizes PHI protection and encryption. PCI-DSS prioritizes cardholder data protection. SOC 2 prioritizes availability and confidentiality. Each regime has different priorities with different subsets of the same controls.

stave apply --profile hipaa --observations ./snapshots      # HIPAA subset
stave apply --profile pci-dss --observations ./snapshots     # PCI-DSS subset
stave apply --profile nist-800-53 --observations ./snapshots # NIST subset

Same 3,000+ controls. Ten different projections. The operator names the regime. The profile selects the local invariant family. The mechanism doesn't change.

5. 700+ compound chains — local scope keys

A naive compound chain groups findings by some uniform criterion (asset type, or account). Stave's scope_field lets each chain declare its own local grouping:

  • An AI-agent chain groups by agent ID (which agent is the risk?)
  • A PHI-data chain groups by data-classification tag (which data is exposed?)
  • An IAM chain groups by role ARN (which identity is overprivileged?)

Each chain specifies what "this composition" means for THIS chain. The chain engine is uniform. It groups and evaluates. The scope key varies per chain.

6. OWASP NHI mapping — local threat taxonomy

The same 3,000+ controls projected through a threat-taxonomy lens (235 controls mapped to OWASP Non-Human Identity Top 10) vs a compliance lens (10 regulatory profiles). Two different axes of specialization. Same controls and kernel. Different local concerns.

7. The asymmetric interface — local granularity per audience

Each layer of the system has a different audience with different cognitive capacity:

Layer Granularity Audience
Operator interface Macro — one compliance profile name Humans
Control catalog Mid — predicate definitions in YAML Control authors
Observation schemas Micro — 81 field paths per S3 bucket Kernel
SIR export Sub-micro — raw Policy / ACL / IAM vectors External solvers (Z3, Soufflé)

Each layer is at the granularity appropriate to its local consumer. The operator doesn't see the 81 field paths. The solver doesn't see the compliance profile name. Each interface specializes its granularity. The mechanism connecting them is uniform.

Why this matters for scaling

The scaling property of data-local vs mechanism-local:

Day 1:     1,030-line kernel + 100 controls + 20 schemas
Day 180:   1,030-line kernel + 2,650 controls + 109 schemas
Day 360:   1,030-line kernel + 5,000 controls + 200 schemas
Year 2:    1,030-line kernel + 10,000 controls + 300+ schemas

Kernel: unchanged
Data: 100× growth
Operator cognitive load: unchanged (one command, one profile)
Maintainability: unchanged (one engine to test, debug, verify)

Compare to the industry's mechanism-local scaling:

Day 1:     50,000 lines across 5 tools
Day 180:   120,000 lines across 10 tools  
Day 360:   200,000 lines across 15 tools
Year 2:    500,000 lines across 20+ tools

Mechanism: grows with every case
Data: scattered across tool-specific formats
Operator cognitive load: grows with every new tool
Maintainability: degrades with every new tool

The mechanism-local approach can't escape linear growth. Every new cloud service, compliance regime, or control type adds mechanism. The data-local approach has constant mechanism cost. Every new case adds a YAML file.

This is the complexity-curve difference from the prior articles made concrete. The post-peak shape (function grows, complexity flat) is the Local Quality result. The pre-peak shape (function grows, complexity grows) is the Local Quality violation.

The pair that produces the architecture

Local Quality has a partner principle: Prior Action. Together they answer two questions:

Principle Question Answer
Prior Action WHEN should the work happen? Before the change ships — in the control author's YAML, the schema definition, the profile selection
Local Quality WHERE should specialization live? In the data, not the mechanism — controls, chains, profiles, schemas

Together they produce one commitment:

All cleverness happens earlier, in data appropriate to its local case.

Prior Action says: don't reason at runtime. Local Quality says: specialize via data, not via code. The combination produces a kernel that is both simple (no runtime derivation) AND generic (no per-case logic). 1,030 lines. 3,000+ controls. The literal result of applying both principles simultaneously.

Without Local Quality, Prior Action produces a uniform pre-bound system. Same controls for every case, no localization. Wrong for S3, IAM and Lambda. A universal tool that's universally mediocre.

Without Prior Action, Local Quality produces specialized runtime reasoning. Per-case logic running at decision time. Complex, non-deterministic, impossible to audit. A locally-correct tool that's globally unmaintainable.

Both principles together: a uniform kernel that runs locally-specialized data, all pre-bound before the runtime moment. Simple mechanism. Rich outcomes. Deterministic. Scalable.

The diagnostic for founders

When you add support for a new case in your product (a new customer type, a new cloud service, a new compliance regime, a new data format):

Are you adding code or data?

If code: you're localizing the mechanism. Your kernel grows with every case. Your test surface grows. Your maintenance cost grows. Your complexity curve is still ascending.

If data: you're localizing the outcome. Your kernel stays the same. A new case is a new file. Your test surface stays constant (the kernel tests cover every new file automatically). Your complexity curve is past the peak and descending.

The question is WHERE the specialization lives: in the mechanism (code) or in the outcome (data). The first produces sprawl. The second produces scale.

One kernel for 109 cloud services. Because the specialization is in the right place.

How this relates to existing compliance mods

Specialization in the right place cuts a specific way through the framework-mod ecosystem. turbot/steampipe-mod-aws-compliance
specializes along a different axis: per-framework benchmark hierarchies (CIS controls under CIS section IDs, PCI controls under PCI requirement numbers, HIPAA controls under HIPAA Security Rule citations). That specialization is in the data layer each control is a SQL query and a section ID and the mod's kernel is the Powerpipe runtime that renders the hierarchy. The specialization-in-data principle applies: Powerpipe stays small, framework content grows. Stave applies the same principle to a different specialization axis (asset types and compound shapes). Two specialization axes (framework-section + compound-shape), one specialization principle (data not code), both render in the same Powerpipe dashboard. Comparison: aws-compliance-mod.

Local Quality in 109 specialized schemas, 3,000+ specialized controls, 585 specialized chains, 10 specialized profiles, two control types, per-chain scope keys, asymmetric granularity per audience are all evaluated by one 1,030-line kernel that doesn't grow when the catalog does. Implemented in Stave, an open-source Risk Reasoner. Try it: bash examples/demo-ai-security/run.sh

title: TrustMod-SM: A Multi-Axis Benchmark for Evaluating Trustworthiness of LLMs in Social Media Content Moderation
description:
arXiv:2611.12970v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show strong potential for social media content moderation, but their trustworthiness beyond overall accuracy remains underexplored. We introduce TrustMod-SM, a benchmark of roughly 29,000 instances across eight datasets, to evaluate LLM moderators on five dimensions: trustfulness, fairness, safety, robustness, and context integrity. Evaluating 16 open-weight models (0.5B-284B parameters, spanning text-only and vision-language architectures) and one closed frontier model, we find persistent trustworthiness gaps. Higher detection accuracy often coincides with greater demographic disparity, and models frequently comply with concealment or exaggeration prompts, assign high confidence to wrong predictions, rarely escalate ambiguous cases, and struggle to separate hate speech from counter-speech or reclaimed language (especially below 8B parameters). Scaling does not uniformly resolve these issues, and no single model excels across all five dimensions.

title: AgenticConflictLens: From Long Traffic Videos to Verifiable Conflict Evidence
description:
arXiv:2611.13540v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Traffic cameras continuously record urban road-user behavior, providing proactive safety evidence beyond crash reports. Yet safety-critical events - conflicts, near misses, unsafe turns, sudden braking, and crosswalk interactions - are rare and brief, buried in hours of routine footage. Existing traffic-video pipelines extract detections, trajectories, and risk scores but process footage uniformly, without adapting to an analyst's query. Vision-language methods improve scene understanding but often lack traffic-specific verification of participant-level conflicts. We introduce AgenticConflictLens, an agentic, query-conditioned framework for efficient, auditable conflict extraction from long fixed-camera traffic videos. Given a natural-language safety query, a Traffic-Aware Controller combines structured traffic memory with specialized conflict-analysis tools to choose where to search, which road users to examine, and which evidence to verify or reject. A coarse-to-fine search retrieves candidate intervals and applies detailed verification selectively. The framework produces conflict records with refined time intervals, participant pairs, semantic regions, trajectories, motion evidence, uncertainty, rejection reasons, and supporting clips. On 96 annotated hours from Bellevue and NYC DOT, AgenticConflictLens achieves the highest conflict-existence F1 and temporal IoU on both datasets: 0.84 F1/0.77 tIoU on Bellevue and 0.80 F1/0.73 tIoU on NYC DOT, while inspecting only 8.7% and 11.9% of video, respectively. These results support scalable, evidence-grounded urban traffic-safety analysis.

title: UECA-React 3.2.2: two bugs that lost state without a word
description:
Part 5. Earlier: converting a vibe-coded MVP, the origin story, an AI agent testing the framework, UECA-React 3.2.

UECA-React 3.2.2 is a patch with no new API. It fixes two bugs that lost state without a word: no error, no warning, no failing test.

A new route kept the old screen

In UECA a component's id is its identity: DOM id, bus address and cache key. So a router can give each route its own screen through the id:

"/items/:itemId": (p) => (
    <ItemScreen
        id={"itemScreen-" + p?.itemId}
        routeParams={p}
    />
),

Going from item 1 to item 2 changes only the id, so React keeps the element. UECA kept its model too and renamed it: no init, and item 2 opened with item 1's state. It turned up while checking the shipped agent skills against 3.2.1, whose scaffold router had exactly this shape.

Now the id is the element's key. A new id gets its own model, and the old one waits in the cache until its id comes back.

An edit went nowhere 

editor: useNestedEditor({
    data: UECA.bind(() => model.entity, "nested"),
}),

The owner and the child share one object, so the child's edits land in the entity. When the owner reloaded the entity and the nested object came back equal but as a new instance, UECA treated it as no change. The child kept the old instance, and its edits went into an object the entity no longer held. This one was reported from a real application.

Now the child takes the new instance, without running onChange, since the value didn't change.

Also

  • React 16.14 is the minimum. Earlier 16.x versions could never load the package; the peer range now says so.
  • The programming guide, the agent skills and the app scaffold are corrected against the code. If you scaffolded an app from 3.2.1, compare your dialogs and REST client with the new scaffold.

Upgrading 

npm install ueca-react@3.2.2

npx ueca-react-skills

The second command refreshes the agent skills in your project. Details are in the changelog.

title: Parallel Broyden Methods for Efficiently Evaluating Nonlinear State Space Models
description:
arXiv:2611.13523v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Nonlinear state space models are typically evaluated sequentially, limiting their ability to exploit modern parallel hardware. Recent work has shown that state space models can be evaluated in parallel by reformulating evaluation as a root-finding problem, which can be solved with a parallel form of Newton's method. However, exact Newton methods require expensive multiplication of dense Jacobian matrices, and quasi-Newton methods based on diagonal approximations, while more scalable, are often slow to converge because they neglect interactions across state dimensions. We introduce a novel quasi-Newton approach based on Broyden's method, which captures coupling terms with diagonal-plus-low-rank approximations to blocks of the Jacobian. We construct the approximations from trajectory secants, avoiding automatic differentiation while retaining the favorable scaling of diagonal approximations and remaining compatible with parallel scan through rank compression. We prove finite-step recovery of the exact trajectory under the compressed scan, and show that convergence is tracked by the compression error and by the block approximation error along the current trajectory error, rather than in spectral norm. Empirically, we show that our method is advantageous when interactions are approximately low rank or when Jacobian evaluation is expensive: on low-rank RNNs, parallel MCMC algorithms, and denoising diffusion models, it converges in fewer iterations than other quasi-Newton methods and is the fastest parallel method when Jacobian evaluation is expensive or state dimensions are large.

title: Wrong the Same Way: Cross-Prompt Sharing Both Suppresses and Amplifies Reward Hacking in RLVR
description:
arXiv:2611.13218v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Two accounts of how reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) interacts with an imperfect verifier coexist: in one, reward hacking is inherited from the base model; in the other, RL amplifies it. We study both in a controlled environment small enough to compute the entire response distribution exactly. We vary the universality of a leak, or the fraction of prompts that accept the same wrong response, and the verifier's static false-positive rate. At its KL-regularized optimum, RLVR acts as a filter that reweights the accepted set without altering its composition, so the hack rate is inherited exactly. Taking that as a null model, a known decomposition writes the drift from it as a sum over prompts of covariances between reward and the empirical tangent kernel. The terms from other prompts vanish without parameter sharing. With sharing, every prompt that accepts a wrong answer pushes it up and every prompt that rejects it pushes it down through the baseline, in proportion to the model's probability of producing it there. A shared-parameter policy thus drives a leak that few prompts accept below the base rate and amplifies one that most prompts accept. At every convergent learning rate under Adam, SGD, and sampled GRPO, hacking ends higher at high universality than at low, but whether either end crosses the base rate depends on the step size. Independent per-prompt copies remove the dependence. The direction of this push depends on neither the verifier's error rate nor universality alone, but on how much of the model's kernel-weighted probability of a wrong answer falls on prompts that accept it, which frozen base model controls support. Verifier fixes should target the mistakes the model repeats across prompts: two patches that remove equally many errors differ by up to 38 points of true accuracy. We propose this alignment as a hypothesis for why earlier studies disagree.

title: Visual Similarity in Adult Word Extension and Artificial Word Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.14116v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When two objects share a name, how much does their visual similarity explain, and what do the teaching examples add? First, we reanalyzed trial-level data from a large adult word-extension study (Lewis & Frank, 2018), computing each test image's distance to the examples shown in the space of a frozen self-supervised visual encoder (DINOv2). Distance was associated with extension (log odds -3.23 per standard deviation; 520 people), and an exploratory post hoc analysis suggested that this association persisted within the taught domain after controlling for taxonomic level and teaching condition. Example composition also mattered: after three examples, adults extended a word to 1.1% of superordinate items when the examples were subordinate and to 77.5% when they were superordinate. Second, in an artificial learner using the same encoder, words joining two categories were learned less accurately the farther apart the categories were (84.7%, 65.4%, and 53.0% naming accuracy for near, mid, and far pairs). The encoder's distances correlated with human similarity and confusability measures from three datasets (rho = .501-.795), but this representational alignment did not translate into conclusive evidence that human-derived distances predict learner difficulty, and a second encoder trained on one child's experience reproduced the tier ordering but not the pair-level effect. The secondary human data were analyzed under an internal plan fixed before the confirmatory analyses (not externally preregistered). Visual similarity accounts for part of how generalization is organized in both systems, while the composition of examples contributes what the distance we used does not capture.

title: Explanation-Aware Fairness Beyond Output Parity: Joint Output-Attribution Regularization for Medical Image Classification
description:
arXiv:2611.13052v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Output-level fairness does not constrain whether demographic groups rely on similar predictive contributions in representation space. For a nonlinear encoder with a linear head, we show that outcome-conditioned output score disparity equals the signed sum of feature attribution differences across subgroups by allowing small prediction gaps to arise through cancellation effect. We test whether an attribution disparity penalty complements output-level equalized odds based fairness surrogates. Across 960 DINOv2-LoRA models on HAM10000 and Harvard-GF datasets for gender and race fairness, attribution augmentation increases utility-fairness trade-off performance for hypervolume in six different settings with paired 95% confidence intervals and relative gains of 1.49-10.57%. Under a predefined utility constraint, augmented model families also achieve 9.0-38.7% lower equalized odds difference, lower attribution disparity, and reduced cancellation ratio while preserving predictive utility. These results support attribution fairness as a complementary explanation-aware constraint on output fairness.

title: Camera3R: Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction from Heterogeneous Camera Models
description:
arXiv:2611.13453v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction (3R) from unconstrained multi-view images has recently emerged as a prominent research direction in 3D computer vision. Various foundational reconstruction models have been proposed with different architectures and reconstruction paradigms. Despite being trained on large-scale perspective datasets with substantial computational resources, these models generally struggle to generalize to non-perspective images. This limitation hinders their deployment in applications involving arbitrary, unknown, and potentially heterogeneous camera models. To build on the capabilities of existing reconstruction models with minimal retraining, we propose Camera3R, a low-rank adaptation framework that efficiently extends perspective-pretrained 3R networks to any other camera models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, with only 0.5% additional parameters and less than a day of training, Camera3R adapts a foundational 3D reconstruction model to non-perspective cameras while fully preserving its original performance on perspective inputs. Code is available at https://github.com/android-xr/camera3r.

title: Keeping AI-Generated SaaS Images Loading After Presigned URL Expiry
description:
Short answer: when a presigned download URL for a generated AI image has expired, keep the bucket and object key as durable metadata, then issue a fresh signed URL after each authorized read. This keeps a SaaS image loading path separate from credential age, cache behavior, object state, and browser policy; a longer lifetime only postpones the data-model mistake.

The constraint is easy to miss because the first demo works. A generation job writes bytes, an API returns a URL, and the browser displays a picture. Hours later, the same database row supplies an expired credential. The image identifier was never the URL; the query string was temporary authority attached to a transport request. Treating it as a permanent location makes expiry look mysterious when it is actually a predictable boundary.

Start with the record that must still make sense next month: tenant, image ID, bucket, object key, content type, byte length, creation time, and a publication state. The application can authorize a viewer against that record, check that the object is ready, and then mint a short-lived read credential. No stored credential needs to become the source of truth.

Small distinction. Large consequences.

How should a SaaS troubleshoot expired signed object-storage URLs for AI-generated images?

Do not regenerate the URL before collecting a narrow, non-secret trace of one failure. Capture the response status, request timestamp, credential age, object key, tenant-safe request ID, and whether the application returned the media metadata from a cache. Do not log the URL query string. A signed URL is credential material, even after it has expired, and OWASP's advice on limiting exposure of secrets applies to application logs, error trackers, browser telemetry, and support tickets alike.

The first branch is timing. If a newly issued URL succeeds and an old URL fails, inspect the expiration encoded by the signer, the server clock used to sign it, browser clock assumptions in client code, and the time spent in queues, retries, and cached API responses. If a newly issued URL fails too, expiration is probably not the immediate cause. Check the exact bucket and key, authorization policy, and the object's readiness state before changing a lifetime setting.

Then test delivery outside the page. A direct request that succeeds while the page remains broken points toward stale client state, a service worker, a cached JSON response, content-security policy, or markup that has escaped or transformed the URL. A direct request that fails consistently points back toward the credential or object record. HTTP status codes are clues, not a diagnosis: a 403 can represent expired authority or a policy mismatch, while a 404 can represent a wrong key or an object that was never published under the expected name.

This compact probe keeps credentials out of its output and bounds the transfer. It is useful as a temporary internal diagnostic; it does not prove that every viewer is correctly authorized.

from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


def probe_download(url: str) -> dict[str, object]:
    request = Request(url, headers={"Range": "bytes=0-1023"})
    try:
        with urlopen(request, timeout=5) as response:
            return {
                "status": response.status,
                "content_type": response.headers.get("Content-Type"),
                "bytes_read": len(response.read(1024)),
            }
    except HTTPError as error:
        return {"status": error.code, "content_type": None, "bytes_read": 0}

Use a sanitized host and key in diagnostic output, never the complete URL. A one-time refresh after an authorization failure is reasonable; an unbounded refresh loop is not. It can conceal a bad key, multiply requests, and turn a local rendering defect into load across the signing path.

Derive the image lifecycle from the storage constraint

An object becomes safe to advertise only after the upload is complete and its expected metadata has been recorded. That ordering matters more for generated media than for a static asset bundled at deployment, because generation, upload, database commit, and the browser's first fetch are separate events with independent retry behavior. A row marked ready before the object write has completed can yield a valid signed request for an absent object. The signer has followed instructions; the application published too early.

For large assets, multipart upload adds an explicit lifecycle: initiate, upload parts, complete, then expose the final key. The S3 multipart-upload documentation describes this sequence and notes that uploaded parts continue to incur storage charges until the multipart upload is completed or aborted. That is an operational concern rather than proof of an expired link, but it belongs in the same design review because abandoned work changes the cost and cleanup profile of an image pipeline.

The durable state machine can remain modest:

State Allowed reader behavior Operational concern
uploading Do not issue a download URL Retry or abort incomplete work
ready Authorize, then issue a fresh URL Track render and authorization outcomes
failed Return application-level media status Preserve a safe error reason for operators
deleted Do not sign the previous key Ensure metadata and object deletion converge

There is no need to put a credential in this state machine. The object key is stable enough to audit and migrate; access is deliberately perishable. Keep upload authority and download authority scoped separately where the storage system permits it, with a signer limited to the intended tenant namespace. That design also makes an accidental URL in a stale cache less consequential, although it never makes logging the credential acceptable.

One subtle failure mode sits between database and cache. Suppose media metadata is cached for ten minutes while the returned signed URL lasts five. The object can be healthy, the authorization policy can be correct, and every generated URL can be valid at issuance, yet a user who receives the cached response after minute six gets an expired credential. Cache media metadata that contains a URL for less than the URL's usable lifetime, or cache only durable metadata and mint the URL on the authorized read path. The latter costs a signing operation, but it gives the cache a clearer contract.

Your lifetime will vary with download size, page dwell time, retry policy, and the consequence of disclosure. I am not sure a universal number is defensible without those measurements. Boundary tests are more useful: issue a credential close to expiry, load it with and without a service worker, refresh metadata once after failure, and confirm that tenant A cannot request tenant B's key.

Which delivery boundary fits the application?

The comparison should be about authorization and failure containment, not convenience during the first sprint.

Pattern Durable record Strength Limit
Fresh signed URL after an authorized read Bucket, object key, image state Storage serves bytes directly Cached metadata can replay an aging credential
Authenticated application proxy Bucket and object key Policy is evaluated at the application boundary Application bandwidth and slow clients affect the service
Public, versioned object name Immutable object name and metadata Browser caching is straightforward Anyone with the address can retrieve the object

The catch is that direct signed delivery is not suitable when a document must render offline long after an application session, or when the application cannot perform a reliable authorization check for refresh. An application proxy is a poor fit for large, high-volume media when its compute and egress limits are smaller than the expected download load. Public object names are wrong for tenant-private generations regardless of cache efficiency. Choose the smallest disclosure boundary that satisfies the product requirement, then make its expiry and cache rules explicit.

Don't optimize the wrong layer. Persisted temporary URLs are a data-model bug, not a storage-throughput problem.

How can a SaaS roll out this signed-URL repair without losing legacy images?

Begin by adding nullable durable storage fields and a readiness state to the existing image record. Teach reads to prefer a ready bucket-and-key pair; only a controlled backfill job should derive a key from an old URL, and malformed rows should go to review instead of being guessed into another tenant's namespace. The job needs to be idempotent, rate-limited, and auditable. Its logs should record record IDs and sanitized keys, never signed queries.

Next, change the write path: create metadata in uploading, complete the object write, verify the expected content type and size against the recorded result, transition to ready, and issue access only on a subsequent authorized read. A feature flag by tenant or cohort can keep the application rollbackable while metrics compare issuance count, credential age at render, authorization failures, missing-object outcomes, and end-to-end image load latency. Avoid using a count of 403 responses alone as the launch signal; it cannot distinguish expiry from a policy mismatch.

Finally, test a deliberately expired credential, a ready object, an unfinished upload, a stale metadata cache, two tenant namespaces with similar keys, and a browser with its service worker enabled. Rotate any signing secret that may have reached a log system, following the organization's incident procedure. Once durable fields cover the remaining legacy records and the acceptance cases stay clean, remove the persisted URL field. The system should retain identities and states; it should create access credentials only when they are needed.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html

title: Cutting a Next.js page from 854 KB to 459 KB of HTML by weighing the RSC payload
description:
My /projects page in Next.js 16 shipped 854 KB of HTML for a list of 49 projects. Almost all of that weight was the same few strings repeated, and in the App Router every repeat ships twice: once as HTML and once more inside the inline React Server Components payload (the self.__next_f.push scripts at the bottom of the page). Three changes took it to 459 KB: an SVG sprite for the icon on every row, JSON-LD that links to detail pages instead of copying them, and named Tailwind utilities for the row classes. A fourth stopped the page from prefetching 36 routes it didn't need.

Why is my Next.js page HTML so large?

Open view-source on any App Router page and scroll to the bottom. After the HTML you will find self.__next_f.push([1,"..."]) scripts. That is the RSC payload, the serialized component tree React uses to hydrate the page and to navigate without a full reload. Every element a server component renders appears in it as data, props included.

So a server component that renders an inline <svg> 49 times puts that path in the document 98 times. On my page today the payload is 261 KB of the 460 KB document.

Compression hides this. The live page is 33 KB with brotli and 45 KB with gzip, because repeated strings are what compressors handle best. That is why the problem never showed up as a slow download. The phone still has to decompress, parse and hold every byte, and that cost lands on the main thread of the slowest device that opens the page.

How do I find what is making the page heavy?

Weigh it by parts before changing anything. My first guess was the usual one, large props passed into client components and duplicated into the payload. Every component on /projects was a server component, so that guess was wrong, and work planned around it would have saved nothing.

This script fetches a page and prints the HTML size, the RSC payload, the JSON-LD, and the long attribute values that repeat most:

// weigh.mjs: node weigh.mjs https://example.com/page
const html = await (await fetch(process.argv[2])).text()
const kb = (n) => `${(n / 1024).toFixed(0)} KB`

const flight = [...html.matchAll(/self\.__next_f\.push\(\[1,"([\s\S]*?)"\]\)<\/script>/g)]
  .reduce((sum, m) => sum + m[1].length, 0)
const jsonLd = [...html.matchAll(/<script type="application\/ld\+json">([\s\S]*?)<\/script>/g)]
  .reduce((sum, m) => sum + m[1].length, 0)
console.log(`HTML ${kb(html.length)}, RSC payload ${kb(flight)}, JSON-LD ${kb(jsonLd)}`)

// Long SVG paths and class strings, in the HTML (d="…") and the payload (\"d\":\"…\").
const counts = new Map()
for (const m of html.matchAll(/(?:\bd|class|className)\\?"?[=:]\\?"([^"\\]{80,})/g)) {
  counts.set(m[1], (counts.get(m[1]) ?? 0) + 1)
}
;[...counts]
  .map(([value, n]) => ({ n, bytes: n * value.length, value: value.slice(0, 50) }))
  .sort((a, b) => b.bytes - a.bytes)
  .slice(0, 5)
  .forEach((r) => console.log(`${kb(r.bytes).padStart(7)}  ${String(r.n).padStart(3)}x  ${r.value}…`))

On the 854 KB version the top line was a single 2,115-character path, the GitHub mark, 98 times.

Fix 1: draw repeated icons once with an SVG sprite

The GitHub link on each row rendered its own <svg> with the full path. I moved the paths into one hidden sprite rendered by the root layout, and every icon now points at it with <use>:

const SYMBOLS = {
  github: { viewBox: '0 0 438.549 438.549', d: 'M409.132 114.573c…' },
} as const

function symbolIcon(id: keyof typeof SYMBOLS) {
  return function SymbolIcon(props: React.SVGProps<SVGSVGElement>) {
    return (
      <svg viewBox={SYMBOLS[id].viewBox} fill="currentColor" {...props}>
        <use href={`#icon-${id}`} />
      </svg>
    )
  }
}

export function IconSprite() {
  return (
    <svg aria-hidden="true" width="0" height="0" style={{ position: 'absolute', overflow: 'hidden' }}>
      {Object.entries(SYMBOLS).map(([id, { viewBox, d }]) => (
        <symbol key={id} id={`icon-${id}`} viewBox={viewBox}>
          <path fill="currentColor" d={d} />
        </symbol>
      ))}
    </svg>
  )
}

<IconSprite /> goes once in app/layout.tsx. Each use is now under 200 bytes instead of 2.1 KB, and currentColor still follows the link's text colour. /projects went from 854 KB to 676 KB.

The sprite is not free. It adds about 3 KB to every page, so a page with one GitHub link got slightly heavier. That trade only pays off for icons that repeat. A single logo stays inline.

Fix 2: JSON-LD on a list page should link, not copy

The page's ItemList structured data held a full SoftwareApplication for each of the 49 projects: name, description, image, author, operating system. Each project's own page already publishes that same entity. The list was 40 KB of JSON-LD, shipped twice.

Google's carousel documentation describes this case as a summary page: list items that point at detail pages carry only position and url. The helper now returns the short form whenever a detail page exists:

export function projectListItem(position: number, detailUrl: string | undefined, item: object) {
  return detailUrl
    ? { '@type': 'ListItem', position, url: detailUrl }
    : { '@type': 'ListItem', position, item }
}

The JSON-LD went from 40 KB to 10 KB, and no entity is described in two places that could drift apart.

Fix 3: name the class strings every row repeats

Each row carried long Tailwind strings for its grid, thumbnail, title, counter, tag and links, and they shipped twice like everything else. In Tailwind v4 a string that repeats down a long list can become a named utility, variants included:

@utility feed-row {
  @apply relative flex flex-col gap-3 border-b border-slate-300/10 py-6 last:border-none
    sm:grid sm:grid-cols-[200px_1fr] sm:gap-6 sm:py-7 lg:grid-cols-[240px_1fr];
}

One catch: if the element's classes go through cn() (tailwind-merge), keep colours out of the utility. tailwind-merge can't see inside feed-link, so it won't know that a caller's text-teal-300 should replace the colour inside it. My feed-link holds layout only, and the colours stay on the element.

To prove nothing changed visually, I compared computed styles for every row part between a local next start build and production. They matched except for a rounding difference in one oklab channel.

Fixes 2 and 3 together took the page from 658 KB to 459 KB. (A rebuild between the two passes measured 658 KB, not the 676 KB from the sprite step.)

Fix 4: prefetch links on intent, not on scroll

This one doesn't change the HTML. Next.js prefetches every <Link> as it enters the viewport. On a page with a link per row, one visit to /projects fired 36 route prefetches, about 1 MB decoded, and on Vercel each one is a CDN request plus ISR reads.

The Next.js docs suggest a hover-only pattern for this. I added focus and touchstart so keyboard and phone users still get a head start:

'use client'
import Link from 'next/link'
import { useState } from 'react'

export function IntentLink(props: React.ComponentProps<typeof Link>) {
  const [intent, setIntent] = useState(false)
  return (
    <Link
      {...props}
      prefetch={intent ? null : false}
      onMouseEnter={() => setIntent(true)}
      onFocus={() => setIntent(true)}
      onTouchStart={() => setIntent(true)}
    />
  )
}

null is the default prefetch behaviour; false turns it off until there is intent. The <a href> in the HTML is identical, so crawlers see the same links.

How do I keep the page from growing back?

Set a budget that fails. My production check reads every URL in the sitemap and fails any page over 520 KB of uncompressed HTML:

const HTML_BUDGET_KB = 520
const kb = Math.round(html.length / 1024)
if (kb > HTML_BUDGET_KB) fail(`${url}: ${kb} KB of HTML, budget ${HTML_BUDGET_KB} KB`)

And pin each fix with a test. The sprite test renders each repeated icon and fails if one use is over 200 bytes or doesn't reference its symbol.

The budget alone wasn't enough. Writing this article, I ran the weighing script again and found a link arrow drawn inline 82 times on the page, about 11 KB, still under the budget and so never flagged. It is a symbol now too, and the page is 448 KB. So I re-run the weigh script whenever a list page changes, not only when the budget fails.

title: Permutation-Based Pre-trained Model Merging via Reciprocal Orthogonality
description:
arXiv:2611.13016v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ito et al. (2026) showed that sufficiently wide, independently trained neural networks can exhibit linear mode connectivity (LMC) with softmax temperature calibration, even without permutation. LMC means that a low-loss linear path connects the models' parameters. This behavior is explained by layerwise exponentially weighted connectivity (LEWC), whereby each merged layer outputs an exponentially weighted sum of the original models' corresponding representations, yielding ensemble-like predictions. However, prior work observed LEWC with substantial widening, such as 8192 units per hidden layer for MLPs and $16\times$ width for VGG-11, raising the question of whether such widths are necessary. We therefore search for permutations that encourage reciprocal orthogonality (RO), which suppresses interference between each model's weights and the other model's representations. This allows both models' computations to coexist in the merged network, promoting LEWC at smaller widths. We formulate the search as independent layerwise quadratic assignment problems and approximately solve their continuous relaxations using Frank--Wolfe. Experiments show that our method facilitates LMC with less width expansion. It also merges models trained on different data distributions, where weight matching, which maximizes weight similarity through permutations, struggles. The merged predictions approximate those of a logit ensemble of the original models.

title: Darmok: Championship Cryptic Crossword Solving via Constraint Tightening and Resilient Orchestration
description:
arXiv:2611.13557v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present Darmok, the first automated system to reach superhuman performance on British cryptic crosswords. Unlike American-style crosswords, cryptic clues disguise an unmarked definition and compositional wordplay beneath a misleading surface reading, sparse grids leave nearly half of each word's letters unchecked, and tournament rules rank a grid with even a single wrong or blank square behind all error-free solutions regardless of speed. Competing alongside an elite human field at the 55th Times Crossword Championship in London, Darmok solved all seven championship puzzles error-free and finished faster than every human competitor in every round. It solved the Final puzzle in 6m 52s, a full 3m 13s ahead of the human champion.
  Today's frontier AI models can on average solve a whole puzzle in a single try with comparable accuracy and speed. However, cloud API calls still stall, time out, trigger safety refusals, or get stuck in reasoning loops. To simultaneously achieve tournament-grade accuracy, speed, and reliability, Darmok cross-checks clues across three independent models in rounds; uses verified crossing letters to unlock harder clues; and uses a whole-puzzle model and dictionary lookups to fill any remaining gaps without overwriting confirmed words. This design maintained near-zero-error performance across a five-month daily evaluation period. Under normal benchmark conditions, removing backup models, fallback steps, or elaborate prompt instructions barely changes accuracy, making the architecture appear over-engineered. Yet during both the worst days of daily operation and a severe slowdown of our primary model in the live Championship Final, the backup paths carried the solve, showing that as foundation models master the average case, the central challenge in building complex AI systems shifts to resilience in the worst case.

title: I built 61 dev tools without a framework — here's what I learned about HTML tokenization
description:
The pitch is simple: tools4market.online is 61 browser-side dev tools — cron expression generator, JSON→CSV, HTML minifier, SVG optimizer, Markdown↔HTML, hash generator, text diff, email validator, robots.txt generator, and 50+ more. No login, no upload, no framework, no backend.

The interesting part is what I had to build to stay dependency-free:

1. A hand-written HTML tokenizer (~190 lines)

The HTML5 spec says

and <textarea> are RCDATA elements, but ONLY in the HTML namespace. Inside <svg>, they're normal elements. Get this wrong and a raw <title> inside an SVG silently swallows the rest of your page — which is exactly the bug I shipped and then spent a day finding.</p> <p>The fix is a namespace context stack (html / svg / math). When you enter <svg>, push svg onto the stack; RCDATA/RAWTEXT rules apply only when the stack top is html. This is what the HTML5 spec calls "foreign content" handling.</p> <p><strong>2. A multi-size favicon ICO encoder</strong></p> <p>Modern browsers (everything since 2015) accept embedded PNG inside ICO files. So I skipped BMP encoding entirely — the ICO is a 6-byte header, N×16-byte ICONDIR entries, then concatenated PNG bytes per size. Tested by reading the archive back and comparing every CRC with node:zlib.</p> <p>The PNGs themselves are rendered to canvas at 16/32/48/64/180/192/512, then toBlob'd. The ZIP is hand-encoded store-only (no DEFLATE) — favicons are tiny, no need for compression.</p> <p><strong>3. A conservative SVG optimizer</strong></p> <p>Strips comments, editor metadata (sodipodi/inkscape namespaces), unreferenced IDs, default attributes, collapses whitespace, shortens hex colors.</p> <p>The non-obvious part: before removing an ID, you have to scan for references — url(#id), href="#id", xlink:href="#id", marker-start/mid/end, clip-path, mask, filter. AND scan <style> text content for ID selectors (path#myId { ... }). AND scan SMIL begin="myId.click" attributes. I initially shipped without the <style> scan and called it a "documented limitation" — then went back and did it properly.</p> <p><strong>What I gave up staying dependency-free:</strong></p> <ul> <li>JS minifier (deferred — needs Acorn or Terser, ~50KB, not worth the cost until traffic justifies it)</li> <li>Full CommonMark (shipped a subset — tables, footnotes, GFM extensions all unsupported, documented on-page)</li> <li>Any client-side analytics beyond GTM</li> <li>A real test framework (using hand-rolled Node assertions)</li> </ul> <p><strong>The build:</strong></p> <p>Single Node script (build.mjs) reads tool definitions from src/data/<em>.js, inlines scripts from src/runtime/</em>.js, writes static HTML. Cloudflare Workers serves it. Desktop PageSpeed is 100/100/100/100 because there's nothing to slow it down — no framework hydration, no images on tool pages, no third-party JS.</p> <p>I'm shipping a new tool every few days. Looking for: what tool is missing from the set, what's broken in the ones I shipped, what tradeoffs you'd make differently.</p> <p>Site: <a href="https://tools4market.online">https://tools4market.online</a></p>

title: Hx2Dx: From Anamnesis to Diagnosis - A Multimodal Arena for Conversational Clinical Reasoning in LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.14122v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve expert-level diagnostic accuracy in static evaluations, where the model receives a curated vignette or case report that already condenses the diagnostically relevant findings. Such evaluations measure inference over already selected evidence; the evaluations do not account for the inquiry used to obtain it. In clinical practice, however, diagnosis is an iterative process of inquiry. Clinicians take the patient's history, or anamnesis (Hx), through targeted questioning, examine the patient, and request and interpret tests, progressively narrowing the differential until they reach a final diagnosis (Dx). We introduce Hx2Dx ARENA, an interactive benchmark of 1'000 clinical cases from the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM). Each case is a simulated encounter that proceeds from initial presentation through history taking and physical examination to diagnostic workup. We evaluate open- and closed-source LLMs under multiple configurations. Performance varies considerably across models in the interactive setting, and every model loses diagnostic accuracy relative to the static setting, where the full case is presented upfront. The ability to ask the right questions accounts for much of both the gap between models and the loss of accuracy: diagnosis improves as questions become more targeted and build a more complete clinical picture. LLMs thus reason well once the relevant data are available but remain limited in hypothesis-driven information gathering, in knowing what to ask in order to know. Closing this gap is a prerequisite for their safe integration into real-world diagnostic workflows.

title: You Don't Need Feature Learning to Do In-Context Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.13431v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How should we understand memorization vs. generalization in in-context learning (ICL) tasks, and when does one happen vs. the other? To investigate, we study how rotation-invariant kernel machines learn the ICL linear regression task proposed by Raventos et al. (2023). By decomposing the task in the kernel eigenbasis, we obtain a spectral picture of learning in this ICL setting. This picture reveals that as sample size grows, kernel machines learn successively-higher-degree components of the memorizing solution, which depend upon successively-higher-degree statistics of the training task set. The generalizing solution is approximately a low-degree truncation of the memorizing solution, and so the model first generalizes, then degrades into memorization as training proceeds.
  The takeaways are threefold. First, if this case is indicative, learning a "generalizing" solution on an ICL task is really just underfitting the memorizing solution! Second, the fact that kernel machines can generalize on this task means that feature learning is inessential to ICL. Third, transformers empirically trained to do ICL are shown to memorize tasks through the higher-order statistics of the training tasks that the kernel-based theory predicts, suggesting it applies even to models capable of feature learning.
