title: npm vs yarn: Choosing the Right Package Manager for Your Stack
description:
For most single-repository JavaScript and Node.js projects, npm is the sensible, zero-configuration default that provides universal ecosystem compatibility, robust security auditing, and frictionless onboarding. Yarn, specifically modern Yarn Berry v4+, excels in complex monorepos and enterprise codebases that demand strict dependency boundary enforcement, declarative workspace constraints, and custom CLI plugin workflows. However, the historic performance gap between npm and Yarn has largely closed, meaning the choice now rests entirely on your architectural requirements rather than raw speed.

Core Definitions, Ownership, and Ecosystem Trade-offs

To evaluate npm versus Yarn accurately, we must define what each tool is, examine their underlying architectures, and weigh their structural advantages and disadvantages.

1. npm (Node Package Manager)

  • Definition: npm is the default package manager for Node.js, consisting of a command-line client and a vast public registry hosting over two million packages.
  • Ownership: Maintained and developed by npm, Inc., which has been a wholly-owned subsidiary of GitHub (and thereby Microsoft) since 2020.
  • Benefits: Bundled directly into every standard Node.js installation with zero configuration required, ensuring universal compatibility across developer machines, CI runners, and Docker containers. It offers mature security auditing (npm audit) and broad community support.
  • Disadvantages: Historically prone to disk bloat via dependency hoisting, and default execution postures that run untrusted package lifecycle scripts (postinstall) during installation.

2. Yarn (Yet Another Resource Negotiator)

  • Definition: Yarn is an alternative package manager originally created by Facebook in 2016 to address early performance and security issues in npm. It exists in two vastly different eras: legacy Yarn Classic (v1), which is frozen in maintenance mode, and modern Yarn Berry (v4/v5), a ground-up TypeScript rewrite featuring pluggable architectures.
  • Ownership: Maintained as an open-source project driven by community contributors and core maintainers.
  • Benefits: Modern Yarn Berry introduces powerful workspace constraint enforcement (yarn constraints), parallel execution workflows across monorepo packages, and Plug'n'Play (PnP) architecture that eliminates the node_modules folder entirely. It also blocks untrusted lifecycle scripts by default to protect against supply chain attacks[cite: 4].
  • Disadvantages: Requires activation via Node's Corepack or manual setup, introduces a steeper learning curve for onboarding, and can occasionally cause compatibility friction with legacy native C++ build tools when running in PnP mode.

The Package Management Dilemma in Modern JavaScript

Every JavaScript and TypeScript developer relies on package managers daily, yet many treat them as invisible black boxes. You run an install command, dependencies materialize inside a folder, and your application compiles. But behind that simple developer experience lies a complex engineering trade-off regarding how software packages are fetched, resolved, verified, and stored.

Historically, package managers were treated as interchangeable utilities until scaling codebases introduced major performance bottlenecks and dependency conflicts. Teams running large CI/CD pipelines or multi-package monorepos began experiencing slow builds, bloated disk footprints, and mysterious runtime bugs caused by phantom dependencies where code could access unlisted packages. Selecting the right tool requires understanding what these package managers actually are, who maintains them, and what operational strengths and weaknesses they bring to your stack.

Core Architecture: Hoisting vs. Plug'n'Play

While modern npm (v10/v11) and modern Yarn (v4+) perform similarly on standard cached installs, their underlying dependency resolution mechanics differ fundamentally.


                   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
                   │  What is your project architecture?    │
                   └────────────────────┬────────────────────┘
                                        │
               ┌────────────────────────┴────────────────────────┐
               ▼                                                 ▼
    [ Single Repository / Standard App ]               [ Multi-Package Monorepo ]
               │                                                 │
  ┌────────────┴────────────┐                       ┌────────────┴────────────┐
  ▼                         ▼                       ▼                         ▼


[ Default Choice ]     [ Strict Security/PnP ]    [ Lightweight Workspaces ] [ Deep Monorepo Rules ]
npm 11                    Yarn 4                     pnpm / npm                Yarn 4 (Berry)
(Zero-Config,          (Plug'n'Play,             (Content-Addressable        (Workspaces, PnP,
Universal Support)     No node_modules)           Store, Fast CI)             Yarn Constraints)

Npm and legacy Yarn rely on hoisting, flattening the dependency tree by pulling nested dependencies up into the root node_modules directory. While this saves disk space and ensures compatibility, it creates the "phantom dependency" vulnerability where your code can accidentally import a package that is not explicitly declared in your package.json.

Conversely, modern Yarn Berry offers Plug'n'Play (PnP) mode, which completely avoids node_modules. Instead of writing files to disk, Yarn generates a single zero-install zip archive lookup map (.pnp.cjs). Node.js loads modules directly from this map via a virtual filesystem API. This eliminates disk I/O overhead and completely blocks phantom dependencies, though it requires strict adherence from third-party packages.

Step-by-Step Practical Framework: Implementation and Migration

Adopting or standardizing your package manager involves deliberate configuration choices to ensure deterministic builds.

Step 1: Analyze Project Scope and Choose Your Tool

  • Choose npm for standard single applications or libraries where zero-config onboarding and universal environment support are top priorities.
  • Choose Yarn 4 (Berry) for complex monorepos that require strict version constraints, parallel task execution across workspaces, or zero-install PnP pipelines.

Step 2: Pin the Package Manager Version

Prevent team version drift by explicitly declaring the tool version inside your manifest file:

{
  "name": "my-enterprise-app",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "packageManager": "yarn@4.12.0"
}

Step 3: Enforce Secure CI Execution Rules

  • For npm in CI: Run deterministic, secure installs: 
npm ci
npm audit --audit-level=high
  • For Yarn 4 in CI: Enable Corepack and execute immutable checks: 
corepack enable
yarn install --immutable

Step 4: Execute a Safe Migration

If switching tools across an existing codebase, delete your old lockfile and node_modules folder, initialize the target manager, generate a fresh lockfile, and thoroughly verify your test suites and build scripts.

Industry Scale, Security Postures, and Real-World Usage

Package managers operate at the absolute center of global software infrastructure. Because every modern web framework, cloud deployment, and CI pipeline relies on them, security and determinism have become critical concerns.

Supply chain security has shifted how package managers handle lifecycle scripts. Malicious packages frequently abuse postinstall scripts during installation to execute arbitrary code. Modern Yarn 4 blocks dependency lifecycle scripts by default to protect against these attacks, whereas npm continues to execute lifecycle scripts by default, requiring explicit opt-out flags.

Furthermore, multi-package monorepos managed by large enterprise engineering teams leverage Yarn's advanced workspace governance features, such as yarn constraints, to programmatically enforce uniform dependency versions across dozens of sub-packages and prevent version fragmentation.

Trade-offs, Counterpoints, and Limitations

While package manager tooling is mature, developers must navigate several real-world limitations:

  • PnP Compatibility Friction: While Yarn's PnP mode eliminates node_modules, some third-party packages with custom resolution logic or un-declared transitive dependencies struggle under PnP, forcing teams to fall back to nodeLinker: node-modules.
  • Corepack Uncertainty: Node.js introduced Corepack to manage package managers without global installations, but ongoing governance discussions regarding its long-term bundling status create minor operational ambiguity.
  • Migration Overhead: Switching an active commercial codebase from npm to Yarn is not merely cosmetic. Differences in lockfile resolution and peer dependency handling can introduce subtle runtime bugs if not audited carefully.

Summary Checklist and Next Steps

  • Match your package manager choice to your project architecture (npm for standard apps, Yarn 4 for complex monorepos).
  • Pin your exact tool version in package.json using the packageManager field.
  • Enforce deterministic and secure installs in CI pipelines using npm ci or yarn install --immutable.
  • Never commit multiple conflicting lockfiles to the same Git repository.

Sources

  • npm vs Yarn in 2026: Speed, Security, Workspaces (Mend.io)

  • npm vs Yarn vs pnpm Selection Guide (Tomoda Hinata)

  • Yarn Official Performance & Feature Documentation

title: How to Cut Cloud Costs Without Giving Up Multi-Region Redundancy: A Redundancy Cost Ledger
description:
To cut cloud costs without giving up multi-region redundancy, remove spend that does not buy recovery and keep spend that does. The right approach matches each workload tier to the cheapest architecture that still meets its recovery time objective (RTO) and recovery point objective (RPO), then verifies every cut with a failover drill. The redundancy cost ledger in this post itemizes multi-region spend and flags the cuts that quietly remove redundancy.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

  • Where redundancy spend goes. A second region adds compute, database replicas, cross-region data transfer, duplicated networking, duplicated observability ingestion, backup copies, DNS health checks, and capacity reservations. Itemize each one.
  • Spend that buys recovery versus spend that does not. Replicated critical state, failover-ready capacity, and tested routing buy recovery. Full-size idle standby VMs, replicated staging data, and a second region’s telemetry pipeline that nobody reads do not.
  • Tier workloads by criticality. Not every service needs multi-region. Revenue-critical APIs get active-active or hot standby. Internal batch jobs get backup-and-restore.
  • Standby capacity math. Active-active across N regions needs N/(N-1) times peak capacity: 200% for two regions, 150% for three, roughly 133% for four. Adding a third region can lower total provisioned capacity compared with two.
  • Cross-region data transfer. Selective replication and batched sync windows cut a cost that grows with every GB replicated. Replicate only the data you need to recover.
  • Storage and backup copies. Lifecycle policies move cold backups to cheaper tiers, but archive retrieval times must stay within your RTO.
  • Commitments. The discount from commitments that apply across regions, such as AWS Compute Savings Plans, follows a workload when it fails over. These commitments do not reserve capacity, so Tier 1 failover still needs a capacity reservation.
  • Cuts that quietly remove redundancy. Running standby on spot only, region-locked reservations, shrinking standby without load testing, and dropping the second region’s observability all look like savings until a real failure hits.
  • Drills. Follow every cost cut with a failover test. Revert any cut that fails the drill.
  • Where Control Plane fits. A Control Plane Global Virtual Cloud (GVC) runs a workload active-active across its locations from one definition, so redundancy runs without idle standby capacity.

How do I cut cloud costs without giving up multi-region redundancy?

Work through the steps in order. Skipping one risks cutting spend that was buying recovery.

1. Inventory the redundancy line items. Pull billing data and tag every resource that exists solely because you have a second region. Record each one in the redundancy cost ledger in the next section.

2. Tier workloads by RTO and RPO. Group services into three or four criticality tiers. A payment API that needs sub-minute RTO and a nightly analytics pipeline that tolerates hours of downtime belong in different tiers. Document the business impact of each tier’s failure so finance and engineering agree on what redundancy is worth paying for.

3. Pick the cheapest pattern per tier. Active-active or hot standby for Tier 1. Warm standby or pilot light for Tier 2. Backup-and-restore for Tier 3. Each step down the ladder keeps less compute running in the second region.

4. Shrink idle standby. If you run warm standby, right-size the standby instances to the minimum that can absorb traffic while new capacity scales out. Do not mirror production sizing one-to-one unless your RTO requires instant full-capacity failover.

5. Cut cross-region transfer and duplicated telemetry. Replicate only the data needed for recovery: transaction logs, user state, encryption keys, container images. Stop replicating intermediate build outputs, CI caches, staging databases, and cache warming data. Consolidate logs and metrics into a single multi-region observability backend instead of running parallel ingestion stacks. How to cut cloud compute costs covers compute spend in more depth.

6. Tier backup storage. Move backup copies older than your shortest recovery window to infrequent-access or cold storage. Keep the most recent backup in a standard tier so retrieval time stays within RTO.

7. Buy commitments that move with failover. AWS Compute Savings Plans, the Azure savings plan for compute, and Google Cloud compute flexible committed use discounts apply across regions. EC2 Instance Savings Plans, EC2 Reserved Instances, Azure reservations, and Google Cloud resource-based committed use discounts are tied to one region. Do not put all commitments into reservations locked to the primary region, because during a failover they go unused and the secondary region runs at on-demand rates. Savings Plans and regional Reserved Instances discount usage without reserving capacity, so Tier 1 failover capacity still needs a capacity reservation.

8. Drill after every cut. Run a failover test within days of any change to redundancy spend. Measure actual RTO, RPO, and throughput under load. If the drill fails, revert the cut.

What does a second region add to the bill?

Line item What drives the cost Lever that cuts it Resilience risk of the lever
Standby or second-region compute Instance hours for VMs or containers sitting idle or at reduced load Right-size standby, use pilot light, or run active-active with autoscaling so standby capacity also serves live traffic Medium: under-provisioned standby may not absorb traffic fast enough during failover
Standby database instances or clusters Per-hour cost of read replicas or hot-standby clusters in the second region Use a cross-region read replica instead of a full standby cluster; promote it on failover Medium: promotion adds about a minute (Aurora Global Database) to several minutes or longer (RDS read replica) of RTO; replication lag sets RPO
Cross-region replication data transfer Volume of data synchronized between regions, billed per GB by every major provider (AWS data transfer pricing, Azure bandwidth pricing, Google Cloud network pricing) Replicate selectively; batch non-urgent sync; compress payloads High if critical data is excluded from replication
Inter-region service-to-service calls Latency-driven retries and egress charges when services in one region call services in another Co-locate tightly coupled services in the same region; use async messaging Low if every region runs a full copy of the co-located services; High if co-location leaves a dependency in one region only
Duplicated load balancers, NAT gateways, and firewalls Per-hour and per-GB charges for networking infrastructure in each region Use one global load balancer or traffic manager in front of regional endpoints; remove NAT gateways in AZs that run no workloads; send Amazon S3 and DynamoDB traffic through gateway VPC endpoints Low if each active AZ keeps its own NAT gateway or a regional NAT gateway is used; Medium if consolidated to one zonal NAT gateway, since that AZ’s loss cuts outbound access for every AZ
Duplicated logs, metrics, and traces ingestion Per-GB ingestion and retention in a second observability stack Centralize observability into one multi-region backend Medium: losing regional telemetry delays diagnosis during a partial failure
Backup and snapshot copies in a second region Storage volume and cross-region copy transfer Lifecycle-tier older backups; replicate only the most recent recovery set Medium: if the latest set is corrupted, for example by ransomware, no older restore point exists in the second region; archive retrieval delays may exceed RTO
Global DNS and health checks Per-query and per-health-check fees for global traffic management Use standard 30-second health checks instead of fast 10-second checks, and drop optional health-check features, where faster detection is not required Low: slower failover detection, which adds to RTO
Capacity reservations for failover On-Demand rates charged for reserved capacity whether or not instances run in it Reserve capacity in the failover region, for example with AWS On-Demand Capacity Reservations, only for Tier 1 workloads; cover the discount with a commitment that applies across regions High if no reservation exists and on-demand capacity is unavailable during a regional event

No prices are listed because rates vary by provider, region, instance family, and negotiated discount. The point of the ledger is to ensure every line item is visible, owned, and justified.

How much extra capacity does multi-region redundancy need?

Active-active deployments must provision enough capacity in each region so that surviving regions can absorb a failed region’s traffic. The arithmetic is straightforward when traffic is evenly distributed.

Regions Capacity per region (share of total peak) Total provisioned capacity (share of peak)
2 100% 200%
3 50% 150%
4 ~33% ~133%

With two regions, each must handle 100 percent of peak load on its own, so you provision 200 percent of peak across both. With three regions, each needs only 50 percent of peak (each serves a third of peak normally and half of peak after one region fails), totaling 150 percent. A third region therefore lowers total provisioned compute compared with two. The saving covers compute only. A third region adds its own networking, observability, and a third copy of replicated data, and the 150 percent figure covers the loss of one region at a time. Active-active versus active-passive cost compares the two cost profiles.

This is arithmetic on peak load that assumes even traffic distribution and no headroom buffer. Real deployments add headroom for traffic spikes and uneven distribution. Warm standby keeps a scaled-down, working copy of production in the standby region. Pilot light keeps data replicated and core infrastructure running, with application compute off or minimal. Both accept a longer RTO because capacity must scale out before it absorbs full traffic. Running active-active across AWS and Azure without idle standby works through the capacity math for two clouds.

Which cost cuts quietly remove redundancy?

Each of these cuts looks safe on a spreadsheet and can remove the recovery capability you are paying for.

Cut Why it looks safe What it breaks Safer alternative
Running standby capacity only on spot or preemptible instances Spot prices are far below on-demand rates Spot capacity can be interrupted when the provider needs it back and is not guaranteed during regional demand spikes, which is exactly when you need failover capacity Mix spot with a baseline of on-demand or reserved instances for Tier 1 workloads
Region-locked reservations in the primary region only Maximizes discount on the region that handles most traffic Reservations become waste when you fail over; standby region runs at on-demand rates Use commitments that apply across regions, such as AWS Compute Savings Plans, the Azure savings plan for compute, or Google Cloud compute flexible committed use discounts, plus capacity reservations in the failover region for Tier 1
Shrinking standby without a load test Billing drops immediately and nobody notices in steady state Standby cannot absorb production traffic during failover; RTO blows past target Load-test the standby at expected failover traffic before shrinking
Replicating data but skipping its encryption keys, secrets, or container images Saves cross-region transfer and secrets management complexity Data is present but unusable; applications cannot decrypt, authenticate, or start Replicate secrets, keys, and images alongside the data they protect
Keeping control dependencies in one region (identity provider, DNS, CI/CD, secrets store) Simplifies operations and reduces cost A regional failure takes out the tooling needed to execute failover Distribute control dependencies or use providers with built-in multi-region resilience
Dropping the second region’s observability entirely Eliminates duplicated ingestion costs You cannot diagnose failures in the standby region during or after failover Centralize observability with a multi-region backend; keep minimal regional collection
Moving standby backups to an archive tier whose retrieval time exceeds the RTO Archive storage is the cheapest tier available S3 Glacier Deep Archive retrieval takes up to 12 hours with Standard retrieval or up to 48 hours with Bulk retrieval; if the latest standard-tier backup is also lost, recovery stalls Keep the most recent backup set in a standard or infrequent-access tier; archive only older copies
Consolidating to fewer availability zones in the surviving region Reduces per-AZ networking and compute costs If the surviving region runs in one AZ, an AZ failure there during a regional failover causes a full outage; with two AZs, it halves surviving capacity Maintain at least two AZs in every region that participates in failover

Which workloads need multi-region redundancy at all?

Not every service justifies the cost of a second region. Matching the redundancy pattern to the workload’s actual business impact is usually the largest cost lever.

Tier Example workloads Pattern Indicative RTO Indicative RPO
Tier 1: Revenue-critical, user-facing Payment processing, authentication, core API Active-active or hot standby Seconds to low minutes Near-zero to seconds
Tier 2: Important but tolerant of brief outage Order management, notification services, dashboards Warm standby or pilot light Minutes to tens of minutes Seconds to minutes
Tier 3: Internal or batch Analytics pipelines, dev/staging environments, batch ETL Backup-and-restore or single region with multi-AZ Hours Hours to a day

Multi-AZ deployments inside a single region protect against the failure of a data center or availability zone. Multi-region adds protection against region-wide failures, which are less frequent and higher impact. For Tier 3 workloads, multi-AZ with regular backups copied to a second region is usually sufficient and far cheaper than running live standby capacity. Cloud disaster recovery RTO and RPO targets covers target setting.

Backup-and-restore is enough when the business can tolerate hours of downtime and the data can be restored from a recent snapshot. If that matches the workload’s actual impact profile, spending on warm standby or active-active is waste.

How do you keep the savings without losing the failover?

Savings erode as infrastructure drifts and new services ship without a redundancy review. Four checks keep both the savings and the failover in place.

Drill on a schedule. Beyond the drill after each cut in step 8, run a failover drill at least quarterly so drift shows up before a real failure. Measure actual RTO, RPO, and throughput against targets.

Measure failover capacity continuously. Track the ratio of standby capacity to expected failover traffic. Alert when standby drops below the minimum needed to absorb a region loss. Autoscaling helps, but autoscaling from zero to full production load takes time that counts against your RTO.

Alert on replication lag. With asynchronous replication, current lag is the data you would lose if the primary failed now. If lag exceeds your RPO target, a failover at that moment would lose more data than the target allows. Alert before lag reaches the target, for example at half of it, so teams can investigate before a failure turns lag into data loss.

Review the ledger quarterly. Reassess every line item in the redundancy cost ledger. New services may have been deployed without replication. Old replication rules may cover data that is no longer critical. Assign ownership of each line item to a team or product so accountability is clear.

How does Control Plane fit?

Control Plane is the unbreakable platform for running production workloads. It runs serverless, standard, stateful, and cron workloads natively on AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), VM workloads on locations joined through Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes, and workloads on Kubernetes clusters you already run or your own machines, including on premises, active-active across regions and clouds.

A GVC is Control Plane’s named set of locations drawn from cloud regions, Kubernetes clusters you register, and your own hardware; a workload deployed to a GVC runs active-active in every location of that GVC from one definition, so redundancy runs without paying for idle standby capacity. Each workload’s canonical endpoint uses health-aware DNS geo-routing to send clients to the nearest location where the workload passes its readiness probes. Location routing options set a priority tier per location and latency offsets. A failover location can sit in a lower tier that receives traffic only when every higher-tier location is unavailable. Per-location overrides can give the workload a smaller replica range there than in the primary, for a warm standby layout on the same GVC.

During the October 20, 2025 AWS us-east-1 outage, Control Plane customers with us-east-1 in their GVC had workloads “active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds,” with no customer downtime, according to Control Plane’s internal incident telemetry.

Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security. Autoscaling sets each location’s replica count between minScale and maxScale, and maxScale caps each location separately, so a GVC spanning three locations at maxScale 5 can run 15 replicas. Capacity AI is Control Plane’s feature that right-sizes a workload’s CPU and memory reservation between a minimum and maximum based on historical usage. Built-in logs and metrics carry a location label, and logs, metrics, and traces from every location are queried in one place, so teams do not need a separate telemetry stack per region and still see each location’s health during a failover. A Cost & Usage view per org and per resource with a projected total, plus a monthly spend alert to billing admins, gives finance and engineering shared visibility into redundancy spend. The billing API breaks cost down by GVC, workload, or location, so each location’s workload and storage cost can be its own line in the redundancy cost ledger.

Control Plane customers typically see 30 to 50 percent lower compute costs compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure. You pay for the CPU and memory a workload reserves, billed per millicore and per MB, with no contracts or minimums. Egress, storage, observability, dedicated load balancers, and GPUs are billed too.

The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

Active-active removes idle standby, but each location still needs headroom to absorb a failed location’s traffic. minScale sets the capacity running at the moment of failover, and maxScale sets what autoscaling can add afterward. Adding a location to a GVC runs every workload there with no change to the workload definition. To move a two-location layout at 200 percent of peak to three locations at 150 percent, add the third location and lower each location’s minScale so it holds half of peak. Databases still set RPO based on replication lag, and that remains true regardless of the platform running the application tier.

FAQ

Short answers on cost, high availability, active-active, spot capacity, multi-AZ, hidden costs, and testing.

How do I cut cloud costs without giving up multi-region redundancy?

Remove spend that does not buy recovery, such as idle full-size standby compute, replicated non-critical data, and duplicated telemetry. Keep replicated critical state, obtainable failover capacity, and tested failover paths. Match each workload tier to the cheapest architecture that meets its RTO and RPO, then verify every cut with a failover drill.

How do I cut cloud costs without giving up high availability?

Use multi-AZ inside a region, with autoscaling and health-checked load balancing, for high availability. Reserve multi-region for Tier 1 workloads where regional outages are unacceptable.

How much does multi-region high availability cost compared with a single region?

Two-region active-active provisions about twice peak compute, warm standby adds a partial second copy plus data transfer, and pilot light keeps compute minimal but still pays for replication and storage. Itemize your own mix with the redundancy cost ledger.

Is active-active more expensive than active-passive?

It depends on standby size and region count. Two-region active-active and active-passive with a full-size standby both provision about 200 percent of peak. Active-passive with a scaled-down standby provisions less compute and accepts a longer RTO. Three-region active-active provisions about 150 percent of peak.

Are spot instances safe for a standby region?

Not as the only source of failover capacity for Tier 1 workloads. Providers can reclaim spot capacity, and it is scarcest during regional demand spikes. Use spot for non-critical standby and keep a baseline of on-demand or reserved capacity for critical services.

Does multi-AZ count as redundancy?

Yes, against the failure of a data center or availability zone within a region. It does not protect against region-wide outages. Multi-AZ alone is enough only when the business accepts the risk of a regional outage.

What is the biggest hidden cost of multi-region?

Cross-region data transfer is often the most underestimated cost. Replication traffic, inter-region API calls, and telemetry shipped across regions generate per-GB charges that grow with volume and frequency.

How often should I test failover after cutting costs?

Test within days of any change and run automated, non-destructive failover drills at least quarterly.

How does Control Plane reduce the cost of multi-region redundancy?

Control Plane runs a workload active-active in every location of its Control Plane Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), so redundancy runs without paying for idle standby capacity. Per-location autoscaling, Capacity AI right-sizing, built-in observability, and health-aware DNS geo-routing reduce the scaling, telemetry, and traffic-management tooling each extra region would otherwise duplicate. Each location still needs headroom to absorb a failed location’s traffic.

title: React error #418: fixing a matchMedia hydration mismatch with useSyncExternalStore
description:
Minified React error #418 means the HTML the server rendered did not match what the client rendered on its first pass. On my Next.js site the cause was a useMediaQuery hook that read window.matchMedia(query).matches inside a useState initializer. The server returned false, a desktop browser returned true, and React threw away the server HTML. Rewriting the hook on useSyncExternalStore with a getServerSnapshot of false made the first client render match the server by construction.

What does minified React error #418 mean?

React 19 reports it as "Hydration failed because the server rendered HTML didn't match the client." During hydration React walks the server HTML and the first client render side by side. If one has a node the other lacks, React cannot reuse the markup. It discards the server tree and renders the whole app again on the client.

In production the message is minified, so all you get is #418 and a link. It names no component and no node. On my site it fired on every production page load, and nothing looked broken, because the client re-render produced a correct page. The cost was invisible: the server HTML was thrown away, and every visitor paid for a full client render. I think this is what my earlier performance audit recorded as "mobile lab bound by react-dom hydration", but I have no before and after measurement to prove that link.

Why does reading matchMedia in useState cause a hydration mismatch?

The server has no window. A hook that wants to run on both sides has to pick a value for the server, and the natural choice is false. The mistake is reading the browser value during the first client render.

This is the shape of my broken hook. It is simplified, not the exact file I had:

import { useEffect, useState } from 'react'

// Broken: the first client render reads the browser, the server cannot.
export function useMediaQuery(query: string): boolean {
  const [matches, setMatches] = useState(() =>
    typeof window === 'undefined' ? false : window.matchMedia(query).matches
  )

  useEffect(() => {
    const mql = window.matchMedia(query)
    const onChange = () => setMatches(mql.matches)
    mql.addEventListener('change', onChange)
    return () => mql.removeEventListener('change', onChange)
  }, [query])

  return matches
}

On the server the initializer returns false. In a desktop browser the same initializer runs during the first client render and returns true. Hydration compares the two trees at that moment, so the value is already different before any effect runs.

The caller made it visible. My spotlight component draws a cursor-following overlay only when the device has a fine pointer:

const hasFinePointer = useMediaQuery('(pointer: fine)')

// ...
{hasFinePointer && (
  <div ref={overlay} className="pointer-events-none fixed inset-0 z-30 ..." />
)}

The server rendered no overlay. The desktop client rendered one extra child, so every sibling after it shifted position. That is enough for #418.

How do I find which component mismatches?

Production will not tell you. Run pnpm dev (or your package manager's dev command) and load the page. The development build of React prints the full, non-minified error, including a component stack with + and - lines that mark the exact mismatched node. The + side is what the client rendered and the - side is what the server sent. For my bug that diff pointed at the spotlight overlay div.

Two things to check once you have the component:

  1. Does it read window, document, localStorage, matchMedia or Date.now() while rendering, or in a useState initializer?
  2. Does it branch the JSX on that value?

If both are yes, you have found it. Other common causes of #418 are invalid HTML nesting and browser extensions that modify the DOM, but those did not apply here.

A second clue was sitting in my own code. A mounted guard already existed in a command palette trigger, with a comment explaining that the media query mismatched. The spotlight had no such guard. A per-caller workaround for a hook-level bug is the signal to fix the hook.

How do I fix it with useSyncExternalStore?

useSyncExternalStore takes three arguments: subscribe, getSnapshot and getServerSnapshot. From the React docs, getServerSnapshot is used during server rendering and during hydration on the client. That is the property that matters here. React does not call your client getSnapshot for the hydrating render, so the first client render sees the same false the server saw. Right after hydration finishes, React reads the real snapshot and re-renders if it differs. The docs describe this behaviour, and I did not trace it through React's source.

This is the hook as it is now in my repo:

import { useCallback, useMemo, useSyncExternalStore } from 'react'

export function useMediaQuery(query: string): boolean {
  // One MediaQueryList per query, reused by both subscribe and getSnapshot.
  const mql = useMemo(
    () => (typeof window === 'undefined' ? null : window.matchMedia(query)),
    [query]
  )

  const subscribe = useCallback(
    (onStoreChange: () => void) => {
      mql?.addEventListener('change', onStoreChange)
      return () => mql?.removeEventListener('change', onStoreChange)
    },
    [mql]
  )

  return useSyncExternalStore(
    subscribe,
    () => mql?.matches ?? false,
    () => false
  )
}

Three details in it are worth copying:

  • The MediaQueryList is created once per query in useMemo. getSnapshot runs on every render, so calling matchMedia inside it would repeat work for no reason.
  • subscribe is wrapped in useCallback keyed on the list. A new function identity each render would make React unsubscribe and resubscribe every time.
  • The server snapshot is a constant false. That is the contract for callers: the first paint always has false, and the real value arrives in the commit right after.

Do I still need a mounted guard?

No. Once the hook returns false on the first client render, a mounted state flag adds nothing. I deleted the guard in the palette trigger. That component now hides itself on desktop with the Tailwind class sm:hidden, which is CSS and needs no JavaScript value at all.

This points at the cheaper option for many cases. If a media query only changes layout or visibility, use CSS. Keep useMediaQuery for the cases where JavaScript has to act on the result, such as attaching a mouse handler, as my spotlight does.

The trade-off is a one-frame flash. With a false server snapshot, a desktop user gets the touch layout first and the desktop layout after hydration. For my overlay that is invisible, since it is a faint gradient. For a layout that changes the page structure, pick a server default that suits your most common visitor, or use CSS.

How do I confirm the fix worked?

In production, the console on a fresh page load no longer shows #418; the only errors left there come from browser extensions. If it ever comes back, pnpm dev is where to look, since it prints the full hydration warning with its component stack.

One trap while checking: counting JSON-LD tags with a bare grep for application/ld+json double-counts, because the RSC payload embeds the component tree as an escaped string. Count real tags with grep -o '<script type="application/ld+json"' instead, or document.querySelectorAll in the browser.

The rule I took from it: never read window, matchMedia or localStorage in a useState initializer in a component that renders on the server. Use useSyncExternalStore with a server snapshot, or use CSS.

The site this came from is described in the portfolio case study. Another rendering bug from the same site, a 200 status on unknown slugs, is covered in Next.js soft 404: why notFound() returned 200 behind loading.tsx.

title: Beyond the Log-Linear Frontier: Pre-Asymptotic Analysis of Finite-Budget Neural Scaling Laws
description:
arXiv:2611.13534v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Classical neural scaling laws model excess risk as a separable power law in model capacity $N$ and dataset size $D$. At finite budgets, however, empirical learning curves and compute-optimal allocations depart from this log-linear frontier. This paper analyzes how spectral and domain heterogeneity govern these finite-scale departures. Along the capacity axis, Mellin--Barnes analysis of covariance resolvents yields a three-term expansion where competing spectral and regularization modes produce finite-scale curvature and logarithmic transitions. Because fitting multiple power laws on narrow pilot grids is ill-conditioned, we eliminate the loss floor via first-order Aitken differencing to obtain a well-conditioned closed-form initializer. Along the data axis, KKT duality reduces $K$-domain mixing to scalar water-filling, yielding finite-budget bottleneck bounds, an online sampling curriculum, and a simplex Hessian metric for cross-domain transfer. Along the iso-compute frontier $C=6ND$, we prove that the optimal allocation exponent drifts in proportion to capacity and data exponent variances, while Schur-complement reduction separates intrinsic drift from frozen-hyperparameter bias. Across 45 operator spectra, Pythia (70M--12B), Chinchilla (245 runs), and RegMix (17 domains), our estimators achieve $5.89\%$ holdout MAPE, cut high-compute allocation regret by up to $76.4\%$, and reduce cross-scale mixture RMSE by $59.4\%$ with zero selection regret.

title: HiPFuse: Real-Time LiDAR Semantic Segmentation for Robotic Perception on Edge Devices
description:
arXiv:2611.14025v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real-time robotic perception requires accurate LiDAR semantics under limited resources. Bird's-eye-view (BEV) aggregation is efficient but can mix differently labeled surfaces in columns. We present HiPFuse, a point-BEV fusion framework that exchanges point and height-partitioned BEV features across horizontal scales, combining point-wise detail with 2D spatial context from one LiDAR scan. Fixed height assignments preserve separate vertical aggregation groups, with auxiliary supervision of initial BEV features using targets from the same 3D cells. A dual-scale BEV context module adds broader context from a coarser grid. On SemanticKITTI and MCD, HiPFuse achieves 63.7% and 62.5% mIoU at 14.2 and 22.4 FPS on Jetson AGX Orin, respectively, exceeding the 10 Hz scan rate. Separate training and evaluation show indoor applicability. Replacing only the baseline semantic front end with HiPFuse in fixed robotic systems reduces odometry absolute trajectory error RMSE by 10.6% on average across two outdoor sequences and increases accepted-loop recall by 8.7 percentage points on SemanticKITTI. Qualitative semantic maps show more continuous road labeling. Our code is available at https://github.com/haiyang2022/HiPFuse.

title: How to Retry 3 Tenant-Isolated Thumbnail Uploads — A Storage Decision Record
description:
Short answer: put each tenant's thumbnail under a deterministic tenant-scoped key, retry only transient failures with exponential backoff, and make every attempt carry the same idempotency key. This is the right boundary for a gaming image-resizing pipeline because a retry should repair a transport failure without creating a second artifact or crossing tenants.

The useful unit of analysis is not the storage request's unit price. It is the operating bill: implementation time, duplicate objects, rate-limit recovery, reconciliation work, and the cost of proving which thumbnail belongs to which tenant. I would start with a private object store and a small retrying writer, then choose among S3-compatible services, Cloudflare R2, Alibaba OSS, and an API surface such as Infrai according to the failure boundary the team can actually operate.

Decision Record: What Must Remain True

The system stores training artifacts produced while resizing game images. A source image may produce several thumbnails, so the object key should encode the tenant, source identity, rendition, and content version:

tenants/{tenantID}/thumbnails/{sourceID}/{variant}-{contentVersion}.webp

That key is an isolation rule, not a naming preference. The writer must reject an empty tenant ID, must never accept a caller-provided key outside that prefix, and must treat the object as private. A user-facing download should go through a signed URL; a permanent public URL is the wrong assumption for training artifacts.

Three invariants govern the retry loop:

  1. The same logical upload uses the same idempotency key across retries.
  2. A 429 or transient server failure increases the delay, while a client error is surfaced immediately.
  3. Every attempt is logged with tenant, object key, attempt number, status, and request ID when the service returns one.

The exactly-once mindset is useful here even though the network can deliver an operation more than once: make the write idempotent, then reconcile by deterministic identity. “Exactly once” is a storage property to design toward, not a promise that a client can observe from an unreliable connection.

Here is the option comparison I would put in the architecture record:

Option Good fit Boundary to verify
Amazon S3 A team already operating a direct object-storage integration and its surrounding controls Conditional concurrency, retention, replication, and audit requirements still belong in the design review
Cloudflare R2 An S3-compatible path is useful and the workload is close to the Cloudflare edge Confirm the required region, migration, and lifecycle behavior before treating compatibility as equivalence
Alibaba OSS A deployment already standardizes on OSS-compatible storage Verify the same private-access, retention, and recovery semantics for every tenant
Infrai storage A backend wants one REST surface and discovery with runnable examples while keeping the storage object private It has no public-read ACL, object versioning, object lock, cross-region automatic replication, or GCS/B2 vendor coverage

The table is intentionally unglamorous. S3, R2, and OSS are specialists with their own operational ecosystems. A common API can reduce integration surface, but it does not erase the need to evaluate retention, recovery, and concurrency separately.

Why Do Thumbnail Retries Fail in Practice?

A thumbnail upload is often retried because the first response is ambiguous: the connection closes, a gateway returns a 5xx, or the storage service applies a rate limit. The dangerous response is to retry every error at a fixed interval. Five workers can turn one transient event into a second outage, and a failed client can keep producing duplicate writes after the original request succeeded.

Backoff needs three controls: a cap, jitter, and a maximum attempt count. I use a full-jitter delay selected between zero and the exponential ceiling, because synchronized workers should not wake up together. The retry budget also belongs in the workload model. Three attempts per thumbnail may be reasonable for a small resize queue; it is not automatically reasonable for a burst of 10,000 source images.

The API's self-describing surface is useful during integration: discovery exposes a capability's request and response schema plus runnable examples, so an engineer can verify the actual storage contract before coding against an assumed SDK. That matters for this workflow because the retry policy is only correct when its status handling matches the documented response envelope. The discovery surface is public and does not require a key; the write still uses Bearer authentication. The broader platform currently exposes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, which can remove the recurring work of provisioning separate credentials as the thumbnail service grows into queues, notifications, and observability.

The Critical Path in Go

The function below is deliberately narrow. It writes one private object, uses the verified storage route, keeps the key tenant-scoped, and retries 429 plus 5xx responses. The caller supplies already-resized bytes, so image decoding and resizing remain separate concerns.

package thumbnail

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "math/rand"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func PutPrivateThumbnail(ctx context.Context, tenantID, sourceID, variant, version string, data []byte) error {
    if tenantID == "" || sourceID == "" || variant == "" || version == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("tenant, source, variant, and version are required")
    }
    if os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY") == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    key := fmt.Sprintf("tenants/%s/thumbnails/%s/%s-%s.webp", tenantID, sourceID, variant, version)
    // The bucket is private; reads must use a signed URL, never a public URL.
    if !strings.HasPrefix(key, "tenants/"+tenantID+"/") {
        return fmt.Errorf("object key escaped tenant prefix")
    }

    pathTemplate := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}"
    path := strings.Replace(pathTemplate, "{bucket}", url.PathEscape("game-thumbnails"), 1)
    path = strings.Replace(path, "{key}", url.PathEscape(key), 1)
    endpoint := path
    idempotencyKey := "thumbnail:" + tenantID + ":" + sourceID + ":" + variant + ":" + version
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}

    for attempt := 1; attempt <= 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPut, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(data))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "image/webp")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err == nil {
            body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
            resp.Body.Close()
            if readErr != nil {
                return readErr
            }
            if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
                return nil
            }
            if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests && resp.StatusCode < 500 {
                return fmt.Errorf("upload rejected: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
            }
            if attempt == 3 {
                return fmt.Errorf("upload failed after retries: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
            }
            wait := retryDelay(attempt, resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
            logRetry(tenantID, key, attempt, resp.StatusCode, wait)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-time.After(wait):
            }
            continue
        }

        if attempt == 3 {
            return fmt.Errorf("upload transport failed after retries: %w", err)
        }
        wait := retryDelay(attempt, "")
        logRetry(tenantID, key, attempt, 0, wait)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-time.After(wait):
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("unreachable retry state")
}

func retryDelay(attempt int, retryAfter string) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    ceiling := 250 * time.Millisecond * time.Duration(1<<(attempt-1))
    return time.Duration(rand.Int63n(int64(ceiling) + 1))
}

func logRetry(tenantID, key string, attempt, status int, wait time.Duration) {
    fmt.Printf("thumbnail retry tenant=%s key=%s attempt=%d status=%d wait=%s\n", tenantID, key, attempt, status, wait)
}

The sample intentionally does not attach the Infrai authorization header to any returned presigned URL. If the application needs to serve the thumbnail, the signing step should be a separate private-access operation, and the signed URL should be sent to the browser as-is. The write path has one route; it does not become a product-specific route catalogue.

One production adjustment is important: seed the jitter source once in the process rather than relying on the package default if the service has strict randomness requirements. The retry decision itself should be observable. Count attempts by status class, record the final outcome, and inspect whether 429s cluster after a deployment or a queue burst. Logs answer “what happened”; a reconciliation job answers “did the expected object exist afterward?”

The Effective Operating Bill

Suppose a game tenant emits three thumbnail variants per source image. The direct write count is three, but the effective workload includes rejected attempts, logs, queue executions, reconciliation reads, and occasional manual review. A retry policy that lowers visible failures while multiplying 429s is not reliability; it is deferred work.

This is where the alternatives diverge in practical cost. A direct S3 integration can be the best choice when the organization already has its controls and recovery procedures. R2 or OSS can fit an existing S3-compatible operating model, but “compatible” must be checked against the exact retention and isolation requirements. A unified backend API can remove SDK installation and key reconciliation across services; its benefit is strongest when that integration surface is a real recurring cost, not when storage alone is the whole system.

Infrai is a reasonable option for a team that wants a single REST surface for this private thumbnail workflow and values self-describing discovery with runnable examples when wiring the capability. Infrai also puts 295 routes across 20 modules behind one key, so the same credential and interface can cover the thumbnail writer, queue handoff, and operational signals as the service expands. Its second relevant advantage is the consistent platform convention around idempotency: documented idempotency behavior and request metadata make retry and audit instrumentation easier to standardize across a broader backend surface. I would try Infrai for the upload and adjacent backend integration, provided the team accepts the storage boundaries listed in the decision record. The trade-off is that one key and one consistent interface reduce integration toil, but they do not replace a specialist's storage controls.

The limitation is decisive when public delivery, immutable retention, object version recovery, strict conditional writes, automatic cross-region replication, or GCS/B2 coverage is a requirement. Infrai does not provide those storage capabilities in this snapshot; an external queue or database may be needed for strict concurrency, and an external recovery design is needed for financial-grade immutability. Those are architectural limits, not footnotes. Choose S3, R2, or OSS when its specialist controls are the requirement, and choose the unified surface only where its integration advantage is the real problem.

Rejected Option: Blind Fixed-Interval Retries

The rejected design was a three-line loop that sleeps one second and repeats the upload. It looked attractive because the code was short. It failed the decision record: it ignored Retry-After, synchronized workers, treated a completed-but-unacknowledged write as a new operation, and offered no useful evidence about recurrence.

There is a valid use for a simple retry, but it is narrower than this workload: a non-mutating read with a bounded timeout and no tenant-side effect can tolerate a simpler policy if its caller can safely repeat it. Thumbnail writes are different. They create durable artifacts, so the retry identity and the audit trail are part of the write contract.

The final test is operational. Force a transient response in a staging dependency, verify that attempts keep one idempotency key, confirm that 429 delays honor Retry-After, and check that the resulting object remains private and tenant-scoped. Then measure retry frequency by tenant rather than looking only at the global success rate; a global green dashboard can hide one tenant repeatedly exhausting its budget.

If this boundary fits the system, start with the storage capability's documented schema and examples at https://docs.infrai.cc. Recheck the live contract before production, especially for request fields and retention behavior.

  • Cloudflare Workers documentation
  • Amazon S3 API documentation
  • Google Cloud Storage documentation

title: Image Quality and the Reliability of Fabric-Density Measurement: Counting Threads from Smartphone Photos Through a Pick Glass
description:
arXiv:2611.13200v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Thread density, the threads per inch along and across a woven fabric, is a basic specification that buyers check whenever fabric is sold. Without laboratory instruments, inspectors count it slowly, by eye, through a pick glass, a folding 10$\times$ magnifier with a one-inch window. A smartphone photo through that glass could make the check faster and leave a record. We judge such a photo by what it is used for, as in task-based image quality: it is good if the thread count from it is within $\pm$5% of the true count, a common tolerance in fabric specifications. We introduce PickGlass-TPI: 76 factory scenes of 44 fabric patches, each counted in an open annotation tool by a textile-trained annotator, whose counts are the reference. On it we benchmark frontier and open vision-language models, CNNs, counting specialists and a training-free spectral counter (PG-Lattice). No method agrees with the reference within the tolerance. The best methods are off by about a quarter: a small open model that we tuned only on synthetic images (Molmo2-4B, 25%) is level with the best frontier model, GPT-6.1-sol (27% when asked directly, 25% given four magnified close-ups of the window). Both err less than a non-expert annotator (37%), but only the tuned model also beats, on both error measures, a baseline that guesses each scene's density as the average of the others. PG-Lattice most often repeats its count within 5% across two photos of the same patch, but its misses, like GPT-6.1-sol's errors, are often a factor of two. Even the reference repeats a count across such re-shoots only to a median 9%, so one photo cannot yet be shown to meet $\pm$5%; the image quality that matters is reliability across re-shoots. Generic no-reference quality scores chosen before labeling do not rank PG-Lattice's error, and generative enhancement raises perceptual scores but does not reliably improve the count.

title: CLADE: Category-Level Answering from Deficient Evidence in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.14355v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented systems often retrieve passages that are accurate and relevant but state the answer at a coarser level of granularity than the question requires. For example, a question may ask which specific disease a drug treats (familial hyperlipidemia), while the retrieved passage mentions the broader disease family (hyperlipidemia). Prior work on context sufficiency treats such coarse passages simply as insufficient. We argue that they form a distinct case, which we call resolvable insufficiency: text alone cannot settle the fine-grained answer, but the broader category it mentions maps to a short list of candidate answers in a domain ontology. When language models read these coarse, family-only passages, they exhibit a phenomenon we call Clade (Category-Level Answering from Deficient Evidence): they answer instead of abstaining or searching further. On biomedical questions from PrimeKG, family-only passages reduce abstention by 13.8 points compared to uninformative passages, and the resulting guesses are wrong about half the time. A counterfactual test confirms the cause: replacing an exact disease name with its broader family name lowers abstention by 17.4 points compared to deleting the sentence. Simple fixes like confidence filtering, scaling to a larger model, and explicitly instructing the model to abstain cannot resolve Clade, and this replicates on ecological species interactions in GloBI. Finally, we test whether an ontology can turn coarse passages into exact answers. Given the correct family, an ontology list includes the true answer in 98.5% of cases, but string matching finds that family on the page for only 19.8%. Letting the model choose the family raises this to 30.0% and end-to-end recovery from 10.0% to 26.8%. Overall, our results show when language models should stop guessing and consult an ontology, and highlight which steps of that process remain unsolved.

title: MouldIt: Data Efficiency of Multi-Task Temporal Representation Learning in Injection Moulding
description:
arXiv:2611.13646v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Smart industrial solutions that can address multiple tasks require models that understand the underlying processes. We examine representation learning for modeling the injection moulding process as an example of such solutions. We consider its data efficiency and multi-modal benefit compared to classical machine learning alternatives. To this end, we synthesize a process-informed dataset based on a real reference cycle of an Erlanger Tr\"ager part. We then introduce MouldIt, a temporal convolution and attention based variational autoencoder that reconstructs in-mould signals, while classifying parts as acceptable or as one of our synthetic failure modes. We evaluate MouldIt on two tasks, known-class classification and unknown-class detection, across nine dataset sizes in single-modal and multi-modal settings. We compare it with an accept-all baseline and the classical methods k-nearest neighbors, logistic regression, random forests, and principal component analysis, which we adapt to support both tasks. MouldIt outperforms classical methods across both tasks from 4000 cycles in the single-modal setting and from 2000 cycles in the multi-modal setting. It achieves part sorting losses of 6.0 $\pm$ 0.7% and 1.0 $\pm$ 0.3% in the single-modal and multi-modal settings respectively, ranking first across all baselines and a combination of principal component analysis and random forests.

title: Hint, Not Hole: Localization-Robust Video Overlay Removal
description:
arXiv:2611.13711v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Video overlay removal recovers the scene beneath burned-in subtitles, karaoke lyrics, titles, credits, logos and watermarks. Generative video models now fill a known region convincingly, but in practice the region comes from a detector or a segmenter, and it is wrong in both directions: it misses strokes, halos, whole frames and whole objects, and it covers background between characters, around boxes and on genuine scene text. Erasers that treat the mask as a hole, regenerating inside and copying outside, inherit every one of these errors. We present HintErase, which treats localization as a hint, not a hole. The model sees the full, unmasked video together with a hint channel; during training the hint is corrupted the way real localizers fail, while supervision follows the true overlay. The result is a single model that removes overlay the hint missed, keeps background the hint wrongly covered, and is trained to keep genuine scene text even when the hint lands on it. For full-length releases, a streaming pipeline handles interlaced sources, shot cuts, missed and jittering hints, paste-back and audio, with memory independent of the length of the video. This report describes the approach, the pipeline that turns it into full-length deliveries, and qualitative results; video results, with input, hint and output side by side, are on the project page.

title: BARS: Budget-Aware Sequential Sampling with Refusal for Majority Identification under Unknown Distributions
description:
arXiv:2611.14171v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Repeated sampling with majority selection is an effective means of enforcing self-consistency in large language models. Recently, a variant has also been introduced that terminates early to save costs when the output distribution is favorable. But it still cannot yield a correct confidence estimate from the answer distribution. For this issue, we formalize this as majority identification under an unknown distribution with a budget and a target error rate, and propose BARS, a sequential rule certifying the top-two gap and returning an early stop, a budgeted majority vote, or a refusal when feasibility cannot be established. A refusal is a statement about the rule and its budget, not a claim that a question is unanswerable, and it tells practitioners when to widen the budget or switch models. A certified mode carries proven bounds on the joint answering error and on refusing an instance the budget could handle, while a practical mode, used in our experiments, replaces them with empirical calibration. On synthetic instances drawn from known distributions over thousands of seeds, the difficulty-driven behavior is recovered and the price of the certified mode is measured.On GSM8K the practical mode draws 22.3\% fewer samples than fixed-8 sampling over the same pool, refused questions included, at the cost of declining 18.8\% of the questions. On MATH, it greatly improves the accuracy of its output answers into 82.5\% at the cost of honestly refusing to answer half of the difficult questions that the model itself is unable to solve.

title: picoEmergencyNet : Attention-Enhanced Ultra-Small Deep Learning Model for Aerial Image Classification in Emergency Monitoring
description:
arXiv:2611.13638v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real-time disaster recognition from aerial imagery requires deep learning models that operate under strict memory, compute, and latency constraints. While recent approaches achieve high accuracy, their computational cost limits deployment on resource-constrained UAV platforms. This work introduces picoEmergencyNet, an ultra-lightweight convolutional neural network designed for aerial image disaster classification. The proposed architecture combines depthwise dilated convolutions with efficient channel attention and channel shuffling to enable multi-scale feature extraction at minimal computational cost. picoEmergencyNet has 23k parameters and 7M FLOPs, requiring only 0.1 MB of model storage. Evaluated on the AIDER and AIDERv2 disaster datasets, it achieves up to 96.1% accuracy, matching or exceeding state-of-the-art lightweight models that are orders of magnitude larger. Deployment experiments on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin show that, without hardware-specific optimizations, picoEmergencyNet achieves 258 FPS on GPU and 46 FPS on CPU with a 7x lower activation memory footprint compared to competing models. These results demonstrate that careful architectural specialization, rather than model scaling, enables highly efficient and accurate TinyML-ready disaster recognition for real-time UAV-based emergency monitoring.

title: FaST: Factored Synthesis of Transitions for Offline Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.13013v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Synthetic data augmentation promises to scale offline reinforcement learning beyond fixed logged datasets, but leading diffusion-based generators model the transition tuple (state, action, next state, reward, terminal) as a monolith: no single factor can be natively redrawn in isolation. We present FaST (Factored Synthesis of Transitions), which factors transitions via the chain rule into state, action, dynamics, reward, and terminal stages, fitting each with an estimator matched to its statistical properties. Across twelve D4RL locomotion and maze benchmarks, TD3+BC and IQL agents trained on FaST transitions match the SynthER diffusion baseline while generating transitions over 90x faster. The explicit action-given-state conditional can also be re-queried for a fixed state, enabling targeted action synthesis: drawing N candidate actions per generated state and keeping the highest-advantage one under a value function fit to the same data, thereby synthesizing improved behavior during generation rather than filtering for it post-hoc. Best-of-10 synthesis beats training on real data on 11 of 12 medium and medium-replay settings (+8.9 D4RL points on average, up to +28.4), and is competitive with advantage-filtered SynthER at a fraction of its generation cost. On expert mixtures both mechanisms degrade identically, tracing the failure to the advantage estimate itself rather than to either targeting mechanism.

title: BuySideFlow: A Point-in-Time Benchmark for LLM Agents in Investment Research
description:
arXiv:2611.12966v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate SQL and SQL--Python workflows for investment research, but ensuring point-in-time (PIT) validity remains challenging. Agents must enforce disclosure cutoffs and select the appropriate historical states and record versions throughout data retrieval and financial analysis. We introduce \textsc{BuySideFlow}, a benchmark of 408 practitioner-derived Chinese-language tasks spanning equities, funds, fixed income, and macroeconomics over a fixed snapshot from a licensed production financial database. We provide executable references and a taxonomy of temporal errors, pairing result checks with expert audits of executed workflows. We evaluate nine agent configurations on all tasks, with result accuracy ranging from 16.2\% to 36.8\%. An audit of 900 runs on 100 shared tasks confirms PIT violations in 193 of the 380 runs that pass result checks (50.8\%), showing that output agreement alone does not establish temporal validity.

title: SSH Gives Too Much, Slurm Asks Too Much — and Both Leave Your Files to You
description:
You have a machine with a good GPU. It sits under a desk, or in a rack, or in a cloud account. Your laptop has the code. All you want is to send the work there, let it run, and get the results back.

So you do what everyone does.

scp -r ./src gpu-box:~/work
ssh gpu-box "cd ~/work && make -j8 linux"
scp -r gpu-box:~/work/out ./result

It works. But look at what you just did.

You moved the files in by hand, and you moved the results out by hand. You had to remember which folder to bring back, and ~/work is still sitting on the box. Every job, every time.

And to run one make, you needed a full shell. When a teammate needs the same build, you add their public key to authorized_keys. They only wanted to run make, but now they have a shell on your GPU box, and they can run anything there.

That was the easy version. 😅

Two ends, and nothing in the middle

When you look for a better way, you find two kinds of tools.

🔑 SSH and Ansible are too open. Whoever can send work can run anything. And the files are your problem: you copy them in, you copy them out, you clean up.

🏗️ Slurm is too heavy. It is powerful, but it needs a cluster, shared storage, and someone to keep it all alive. For "run this build on that machine", it is a lot.

Much of the real work sits between them: builds, tests, renders, conversions, model runs. Work that starts, runs, and ends.

SSH, Ansible GRID Slurm
What runs any command only the node's fixed cmds any batch script
Files you copy them in and out with the job a shared filesystem
To set up SSH access one binary per side a cluster

GRID (Generic Runtime Intent-Driven) is that middle column. It has two sides:

  • a hub takes your jobs, picks where each one runs, and keeps the results. It can be your laptop or a small server;
  • a node is a machine, container, or VM that offers some commands and runs jobs with them.

Narrower than a shell. Lighter than a cluster. And the files are part of the job.

Narrower than a shell

Remember the teammate in authorized_keys. With SSH, the person who sends the work decides what runs. With GRID, the machine decides.

A node names its commands, its cmds, in its own config:

# /etc/grid/node.toml
[cmds.build]
exec = ["make", "-j8"]

A job can only ask for a cmd by name. It can add args and env, nothing more:

[[steps]]
cmd = "build"
args = ["linux"]     # the node runs: make -j8 linux

A step that names a cmd the node does not offer is refused. There is no other way in.

SSH GRID
Who decides what runs whoever logs in whoever runs the node
What a job can send any command args and env for a known cmd
What a teammate gets a shell a way to ask

🛡️ So a teammate, a script, or another service can send work to your machines without getting the machines.

One honest note: a node is only as narrow as its cmds. If you offer exec = ["sh", "-c"], the args become a script, and you have given the shell back. Keep cmds specific. If you don't trust the work, run the node in a container or a VM.

A job is an intent, not a script. That is where the name comes from.

Lighter than a cluster

One binary, grid, runs either side, on macOS, Linux, and Windows. You don't need a scheduler, a shared filesystem, or certificates. Hub and node talk over one TCP port, 9420, encrypted end to end. Each side trusts only the other's public key, from a known IP.

Adding machines needs no script. Give each node tags, the kinds of work it does, and a job names the tag it needs. The hub sends it to a node with that tag and a free slot. If none is free, the job waits in the queue.

The cmd runs on the node, not inside your connection. Nodes report, and the hub decides:

When Then
a connection drops only that call is sent again; the cmd keeps running on the node
the node goes away the job starts over on another node, up to retries more times
the hub restarts its jobs are picked up again, from where they were
a step fails the rest are skipped and the job is failed; it is not retried

Light does not mean fragile.

Files in, files out — fully covered

This is the part SSH leaves to you, and a cluster hides behind shared storage. In GRID, the files are part of the job.

Every job runs in its own clean folder on the node, its space. The job file reads in the order it runs:

# build.toml
tag = "build"            # any node with the "build" tag
retries = 2

[[push]]                 # files in, before the steps
from = "./src"           # next to this file, on the hub's side
to = "src"               # in the space

[[steps]]                # the node's cmds, in order
cmd = "build"
args = ["linux"]
env = { CC = "clang" }

[[pull]]                 # files out, after the steps
path = "out"
Part Direction What happens
push hub → node your files are copied into the space
steps on node the node runs its cmds there, on those files
pull node → hub the files you named come back to the hub

Each part can repeat: several pushes, several steps, several pulls.

Now back to the first story:

By hand With GRID
you copy the files in push copies them in, before the steps
you copy the results out pull copies them out, after the steps
you remember which folder to bring back the job file names it, once
you clean up ~/work later when the job ends, its space is deleted

And a few things scp never did:

  • A broken push or pull resumes where it stopped, and a sha256 checks the whole.
  • The hub packs an input once, and knows it again by its files' names, sizes, and times. An unchanged input is not packed again.
  • The input is packed when you submit, so you can edit ./src right away. The job has its own copy.
  • When a step fails, the files are still pulled, so you can see what went wrong.
  • A path that would leave the space (../, absolute, a symlink out) is rejected.
  • Pulled files stay on the hub until grid hub drop, or for 30 days by default.

📦 Big inputs travel once. A model or a dataset that many jobs use can be a share:

[[push]]
from = "./model"
to = "model"
share = true

The node keeps it, read only, and links it into every job that pushes the same content. The first job sends it. The next jobs on that node send nothing for it. grid hub tail shows how each push went: hit (the node had it), installed (sent, and kept), or normal.

The share is off by default. A node turns it on with a size, like [share] limit = "10GB". A node without it takes the push as a normal one, and the job runs either way.

Push brings the inputs, the cmds work on them in place, and pull takes the outputs.

What GRID is not

To be honest about it: GRID does not try to be Slurm. Slurm shares a whole cluster among many users, with partitions, accounts, and fair-share scheduling. If you need that, use it.

Good fit Not a fit
builds, tests, renders, model runs: work that ends long-running services
sending work to machines you own, on any network an interactive shell, or arbitrary commands
a few to many workers, each offering what it is good at scheduling on its own: call submit from your cron
each job in its own clean folder splitting one job across many nodes

From nothing to the first result

Install it on both sides:

brew install diphyx/tap/grid

There is also a release archive, and Docker images: ghcr.io/diphyx/grid-hub and ghcr.io/diphyx/grid-node.

Each side makes its own key pair. Then copy hub.pub to the node and node.pub to the hub. A .key never leaves its machine.

grid key new /etc/grid/hub    # on the hub
grid key new /etc/grid/node   # on the node

The node says what it can do, and which hub it trusts:

# /etc/grid/node.toml
grid = 2
identity = "/etc/grid/node.key"
tags = ["build"]

[[hubs]]
ip = "10.0.0.1"
trust = "/etc/grid/hub.pub"

[cmds.build]
exec = ["make", "-j8"]

The hub knows its nodes:

# /etc/grid/hub.toml
grid = 2
identity = "/etc/grid/hub.key"

[[nodes]]
tags = ["build"]
ip = "10.0.0.2"
trust = "/etc/grid/node.pub"

Open TCP 9420 on the node to the hub's IP. Start both, then send the job from the hub:

grid node run                       # on the node
grid hub run                        # on the hub

grid hub submit build.toml --wait   # follow it; exits 0 only if it succeeds
grid hub pull <id> ./result         # copy the results out

grid hub tail <id> shows everything the job did, as it happens:

19:34:29.631     1 job  queued
19:34:29.633     3 hub  attempt 1 on 10.0.0.2:9420
19:34:29.640     6 cmd  running build
19:34:29.651     9 out  built linux
19:34:29.660    11 cmd  done build
19:34:29.663    13 job  done

🔌 Want your own hub or node, in any language? The protocol is written down byte for byte in spec/SPEC.md, with a test kit. If yours passes the kit, it works with every other GRID hub and node.

Give it a try

If you have ever typed scp, ssh, scp one more time and thought "there must be a better way", that is exactly what GRID is for.

The Get Started page goes from nothing to a first job's results in six steps. If it saves you time, share it with your team, your lab, or that colleague who still has an old ~/work folder on every box.

GitHub · Docs · Built by DiPhyx
