title: Designing Rolling-Deploy-Safe Async REST APIs: Returning Release Evidence IDs in GitLab
description:
An asynchronous API endpoint should give clients a way to identify and track the resource being created. Returning 202 Accepted with an empty response body makes that difficult: the server has accepted the work, but the client has no resource ID to use for subsequent requests.

That was the problem with GitLab's release evidence collection endpoint:

POST /projects/:id/releases/:tag_name/evidence

In GitLab MR !268983, addressing issue #214819, I worked on returning the newly created release evidence ID immediately while keeping the asynchronous workflow compatible with existing Sidekiq jobs and multi-node deployments.

The interesting part was not simply returning an ID. It was making the lifecycle of an asynchronously created database record safe across retries, deployments, and existing query paths.

The Problem: Accepted Work Without a Resource Handle

An endpoint that schedules background processing commonly returns HTTP 202 Accepted. This communicates that the request has been accepted, but processing is not necessarily complete.

For GitLab's release evidence endpoint, the response did not provide a handle to the evidence record being collected.

A more useful flow is:

  1. The API creates a placeholder evidence record.
  2. The API schedules background collection.
  3. The API returns the evidence resource, including its ID.
  4. The background worker fills in the collected evidence data.

This gives the caller an identifier immediately, without making the API request wait for the potentially expensive collection process.

However, introducing a placeholder record creates lifecycle and compatibility problems that need to be addressed explicitly.

The Architecture Challenges

Creating a Releases::Evidence record synchronously and passing its ID to a background worker introduces several production concerns.

1. In-flight Sidekiq jobs during rolling deployments

Before this change, existing jobs could have been enqueued with two arguments:

(release_id, pipeline_id)

The updated worker also needed to accept an evidence ID:

(release_id, pipeline_id, evidence_id)

During a rolling deployment, jobs enqueued by an older application version can still execute after newer code has been deployed. Changing the worker's argument contract without preserving compatibility could break those jobs.

2. Incomplete records becoming visible

The placeholder evidence record exists before collection finishes.

At that point, fields such as summary and summary_sha may not represent completed evidence. If existing GraphQL queries expose the record immediately, users can see an incomplete resource.

3. Orphaned records after permanent failure

Sidekiq retries failed jobs. But retries can eventually be exhausted.

If collection never succeeds, the placeholder record should not remain indefinitely as an uncollected database record.

The implementation needed to address all three concerns without making the API synchronous.

1. Create the Evidence Record Before Scheduling the Worker

The first part of the change was in:

ee/lib/ee/api/releases.rb

Instead of waiting for the background worker to create the evidence record, the endpoint creates a stub immediately:

evidence = release.evidences.create!(summary: {})

The evidence ID is then passed to the worker, and the endpoint returns the serialized resource:

present evidence, with: ::API::Entities::Releases::Evidence

The API entity was updated to expose id alongside the existing evidence attributes:

  • sha
  • filepath
  • collected_at

This changes the API contract in an important way: the caller receives an identifiable resource even though its evidence collection is still pending.

The API does not need to wait for the background job to finish.

2. Preserve Compatibility with Existing Sidekiq Jobs

The worker change had to account for jobs already present in the queue.

In:

app/workers/releases/create_evidence_worker.rb

The new evidence_id argument defaults to nil:

def perform(release_id, pipeline_id = nil, evidence_id = nil)
  release = Release.find_by_id(release_id)
  return unless release

  pipeline = Ci::Pipeline.find_by_id(pipeline_id)

  evidence = release.evidences.find_by_id(evidence_id) if evidence_id
  return if evidence_id && evidence.nil?

  kwargs = { pipeline: pipeline }
  kwargs[:evidence] = evidence if evidence

  ::Releases::CreateEvidenceService.new(release, **kwargs).execute
end

This preserves the older two-argument invocation:

perform(release_id, pipeline_id)

When evidence_id is absent, the worker continues through the existing service flow without requiring a pre-created evidence record.

When an ID is provided, the worker looks up the corresponding evidence record and passes it to CreateEvidenceService.

The additional guard:

return if evidence_id && evidence.nil?

prevents the worker from continuing with an explicitly supplied ID that no longer resolves to an evidence record.

This is an important rolling-deployment principle: when changing background job arguments, new code should account for jobs that were serialized by older code and are still waiting to execute.

3. Clean Up Placeholder Records When Retries Are Exhausted

Backward compatibility protects existing jobs, but it does not solve permanent collection failures.

For that, the worker uses Sidekiq's sidekiq_retries_exhausted callback:

sidekiq_retries_exhausted do |job, _exception|
  evidence_id = job['args'][2]

  if evidence_id
    evidence = Releases::Evidence.find_by_id(evidence_id)
    evidence.destroy if evidence && evidence.summary_sha.nil?
  end
end

The callback retrieves the third job argument, which is the evidence ID introduced by the change.

It then checks whether the record still exists and whether summary_sha is still nil.

Only an uncollected record is removed.

That condition matters because the callback should clean up an incomplete placeholder, not delete evidence that has already been successfully collected.

The result is a lifecycle with two possible outcomes:

  • Successful collection: the evidence record is populated and retained.
  • Permanently failed collection: the uncollected placeholder is cleaned up after retries are exhausted.

4. Keep Incomplete Evidence Out of Existing Queries

Creating a placeholder immediately means database records can exist before they are ready for normal consumption.

To keep incomplete records out of existing query paths, the change introduced a collected scope in:

app/models/releases/evidence.rb

scope :collected, -> { where.not(summary_sha: nil) }

It also added a collected? method to represent whether evidence collection has completed.

The GraphQL ReleaseType#evidences resolver was then filtered so that uncollected placeholders are not exposed as normal evidence records.

This separates two concepts that should not be conflated:

  • Existence: the evidence record has been created and has an ID.
  • Collection completion: the evidence data has been successfully collected.

The API can return the resource ID immediately, while existing GraphQL consumers continue to see only collected evidence.

That distinction is useful in asynchronous systems: a resource can exist before it is ready to be presented as completed data.

5. Roll Out the Change Safely

The new behavior was guarded behind the gitlab_com_derisk feature flag.

The corresponding configuration was added at:

config/feature_flags/gitlab_com_derisk/return_release_evidence_id.yml

The API documentation was also updated in:

doc/api/openapi/openapi_v3.yaml

The OpenAPI schema now reflects the 202 Accepted response using the API::Entities::Releases::Evidence response entity.

This keeps the implementation, feature rollout, and API contract aligned.

Feature flags are particularly useful for changes that affect API behavior and background processing. They provide a controlled way to introduce the new behavior rather than requiring every environment to adopt it at once.

The Complete Lifecycle

The resulting workflow can be understood as a sequence:

  1. A client sends a request to collect release evidence.
  2. The API creates an empty evidence record.
  3. The API enqueues CreateEvidenceWorker with the evidence ID.
  4. The API returns the serialized evidence resource, including its ID.
  5. The worker collects the evidence and updates the record.
  6. GraphQL exposes the record only after it has been collected.
  7. If the job permanently fails, the retry-exhaustion callback removes the uncollected placeholder.

Each part addresses a different failure mode: API usability, old queued jobs, incomplete data visibility, and permanent background-job failure.

Engineering Takeaways

This change illustrates several principles for building reliable asynchronous APIs.

Return a resource handle as early as possible. A 202 Accepted response becomes more useful when clients can identify the resource associated with the accepted operation.

Treat background job arguments as a compatibility contract. Sidekiq jobs can outlive the application version that enqueued them. Optional arguments and safe defaults help preserve compatibility during rolling deployments.

Separate record creation from readiness. A database record existing does not mean its asynchronous processing is complete. Explicit scopes and completion checks help prevent incomplete data from leaking into existing interfaces.

Design cleanup for permanent failure. Retry mechanisms improve resilience, but they do not eliminate the need to handle exhausted retries and orphaned intermediate state.

Keep API documentation synchronized with behavior. When a response changes from an empty accepted response to a serialized resource, the OpenAPI contract should reflect that change.

Conclusion

Returning a release evidence ID from an asynchronous endpoint sounds like a small API improvement. In a distributed application, however, it affects database lifecycle management, background job compatibility, query visibility, failure cleanup, feature rollout, and API documentation.

GitLab MR !268983 addressed these concerns together: creating the evidence record immediately, passing its ID to a backward-compatible Sidekiq worker, hiding incomplete records from GraphQL, and cleaning up placeholders after permanent failure.

The broader lesson is that asynchronous API design is not just about scheduling work. It is about making the resource lifecycle predictable before, during, and after that work executes.

  • Merge Request: gitlab-org/gitlab!268983

title: ExpertCrowd-SWE: Measuring Frontier Coding Agents on Expert-Authored Engineering Tasks in Unfamiliar Codebases
description:
arXiv:2611.13246v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: ExpertCrowd-SWE (EC-SWE) is a benchmark of 100 expert-authored, multi-file software engineering tasks for evaluating autonomous coding agents in large, unfamiliar codebases. Each task is a change request written by a practising engineer against a pinned commit of a real repository, paired with a sealed reference solution and a task-specific grader whose weighted, mostly executable criteria award partial credit; must-pass blockers and pass/fail gates encode what a maintainer would refuse to merge. The tasks span 87 open-source projects and 11 languages. The median ticket is 148 words, while the median reference solution changes 471 lines. Every task image is calibrated before release so that the reference solution scores 1.0 and both the untouched repository and an inert change score 0; nearly half of the tasks also ship alternative, lazy and adversarial control patches that the grader must classify correctly. The final 100 tasks were selected for difficulty against current frontier models. We evaluate seven frontier models, five runs each (3,495 scored runs), in a single platform harness that gives each model its provider-native tool interface. Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3%) and GPT-6 Astra (63.7%) lead without a statistically significant gap, followed by Claude Fable 5.1 (46.5%), Gemini 3.8 Flash (40.0%), and a statistically indistinguishable group of Qwen 3.8 Max, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Grok 4.6 (32-34%). No task is fully solved by every model, and on 80 tasks no model earns full credit on all five runs. Scores span 35 points. Depending on the model, agents take a median of 33 to 166 steps per run, with little relation to score. We release 24 tasks with their environments, graders and results, and hold out 76 to limit contamination.

title: Specify Privacy Yourself: Assessing Inference-Time Personalized Privacy Preservation Ability of Large Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.13997v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities but raise significant privacy concerns due to their abilities to infer sensitive personal information from images with high precision. While current LVLMs are relatively well aligned to protect universal privacy, e.g., credit card data, we argue that privacy is inherently personalized and context-dependent. This work pivots towards a novel task: can LVLMs achieve Inference-Time Personalized Privacy Protection (ITP$^3$), allowing users to dynamically specify privacy boundaries through language specifications? To this end, we present SPY-Bench, the first systematic assessment of ITP$^3$ ability, which comprises (1) 32,700 unique samples with image-question pairs and personalized privacy instructions across 67 categories and 24 real-world scenarios, and (2) novel metrics grounded in user specifications and context awareness. Benchmarking the ITP$^3$ ability of 21 SOTA LVLMs, we reveal that: (i) most models, even the top-performing o4-mini, perform poorly, with only $\sim$24% compliance accuracy; (ii) they show quite limited contextual privacy understanding capability. Therefore, we implemented initial ITP$^3$ alignment methods, including a novel Noise Contrastive Alignment variant which achieves 96.88% accuracy while maintaining reasonable general performance. These results mark an initial step towards the ethical deployment of more controllable LVLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/achernarwang/specify-privacy-yourself

description:
Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Announcement

On November 11, 2026, we began releasing Edge UI updates for Apigee Edge for Public Cloud.

Fixed

Bug ID Component Description
392653797, 399185014 Edge UI Fixed an issue where navigating to the App Details or New App pages in organizations with a large number of API products experienced slowness or UI freezing during the initial page load. The Edge UI now fetches API products on demand when you open the Add Product dialog, improving initial page load performance.

188163219 Edge UI Fixed a UI formatting issue in the Analytics Custom Reports list view so that dimensions display without overlapping.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.21.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Sandboxed build commands and patch refresh: When sandboxing is enabled, cm build and cm fix build validation now run build.command inside the sandbox, and cm fix refreshes stored patch diffs after build validation finishes.
  • Read-only host toolchains and isolated caches: Sandboxed cm build, cm fix, and cm verify runs now mount host toolchain and package-manager directories read-only and redirect supported compiler and package caches to session-scoped temporary directories.
  • Command environment isolation: Disabled repository Git hooks, isolated host Git configuration, and ignored repository Python bytecode caches (__pycache__) during command and build runs.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Added a 30-minute timeout for silent active turns so stalled sessions cancel and recover cleanly.
    • Preserved proof-of-concept execution output when reproducer errors occur, retaining stdout and stderr to help diagnose build failures, timeouts, and setup issues.
    • Fixed an issue where patch generation failed on mid-run sandbox failures by automatically retrying with a fresh sandbox environment.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Feature

Gemini 4 Carbon in CodeMender (Preview)

CodeMender now supports Gemini 4 Carbon. To use it, pass --model gemini-4-carbon to cm find, cm verify, or cm fix. Gemini 3.8 Flash remains the default model.

For more information, see Specifying the model.

Feature

Govern agents on any CNCF-conformant Kubernetes cluster with Agent Gateway for cross-cloud (Limited Preview)

Agent Gateway for cross-cloud is available in Limited Preview. It extends Agent Platform governance to agents that run on Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF)-conformant Kubernetes clusters outside of Google Cloud, such as Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), Red Hat OpenShift, and bare-metal clusters. Your agents keep running where they are, but you govern them from one place: give each agent a verifiable identity, register agents and MCP servers in Agent Registry, and route their LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic through local Agent Gateway proxies by using your existing service mesh or network stack. Those proxies enforce access and Model Armor safety policies, and send access logs and agent traces to Cloud Logging and Cloud Trace.

Agent Gateway for cross-cloud is available at no charge during Limited Preview. Other products that you configure with it, such as Model Armor, Cloud Logging, and Cloud Trace, are billed at their standard rates. To request access, complete the access request form.

For more information, see Set up Agent Gateway for cross-cloud.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal 1.34.1100-gke.125 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade clusters. Google Distributed Cloud for bare metal 1.34.1100-gke.125 runs on Kubernetes v1.34.12-gke.500.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for installations or upgrades with the GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

Feature

The following changes were added in 1.34.1100-gke.125:

  • Updated system components and container base images to remove the distrusted eMudhra (emSign) and AAA Certificate Services root CAs and reject compromised eMudhra intermediate CAs.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.34.1100-gke.125:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed an issue where deleting a user cluster left an orphaned k8s-health-check-reader-binding-<cluster-namespace> ClusterRoleBinding on the admin cluster. Health check permissions now use a namespaced RoleBinding, and legacy ClusterRoleBinding objects are automatically cleaned up.
  • Fixed a race condition where bmctl check cluster --snapshot could fail with a panic: send on closed channel error when taking Node Agent snapshots.
  • Fixed an issue where removing a node from a cluster left behind its local PersistentVolume resources instead of garbage collecting them. This fix applies to Google Distributed Cloud for bare metal local PersistentVolume resources created after upgrading to 1.34.1100-gke.125; existing orphaned PersistentVolume resources must be deleted manually.
  • Improved containerd resilience against state corruption if a node reboots while unpacking container images.
  • Fixed an issue where resetting or removing a control plane node could remove the wrong etcd or etcd-events member if another control plane node's IP address shared the same prefix (for example, 10.201.0.2 and 10.201.0.26), causing the affected node to become NotReady and stalling cluster upgrades.
  • Fixed an issue where the periodic configuration drift health check failed with a version not supported error while a cluster upgrade or rollback was in progress.
  • Fixed an issue where audit-proxy retried audit log exports indefinitely on permanent errors, generating excessive audit logging traffic.
  • Fixed an issue where the Kubernetes preflight health check scanned all namespaces in the admin cluster instead of the target cluster's namespace, causing cluster upgrades to fail if an unrelated cluster had stale reconciling resources.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Issue

On nodes that have Linux syscall auditing enabled, such as Container-Optimized OS nodes where you enabled Linux auditd logging, mounting Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver volumes can hang indefinitely. Pods that use these volumes don't start and remain in a status such as Init:0/1 or ContainerCreating. Pods that are being deleted remain in the Terminating state, and node drains, including drains during node pool upgrades, might not complete. Pod events show errors similar to the following:

MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "VOLUME_NAME" : rpc error: code = DeadlineExceeded desc = context deadline exceeded
MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "VOLUME_NAME" : rpc error: code = Aborted desc = An operation with the given volume key TARGET_PATH already exists

The following GKE versions are affected:

  • 1.31.14-gke.2963000 and later
  • 1.32.13-gke.2714000 and later
  • 1.33.13-gke.1973000 and later
  • 1.34.12-gke.1209000 and later
  • 1.35.8-gke.2014000 and later
  • 1.36.5-gke.1817000 and later
  • 1.37.1-gke.1777000 and later

In these versions, the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver uses a Debian 13 base image whose mount utility uses the newer Linux mount API. When syscall auditing is active, the mount operation can hang in the kernel before the FUSE file system is initialized. Restarting the gcsfusecsi-node Pod doesn't resolve the issue. Nodes that don't have syscall audit rules loaded aren't affected.

Workaround: Disable Linux auditd logging in clusters that use the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver, and then re-create the affected nodes to clear the audit rules that are loaded on them. If you must keep auditd logging enabled, contact Cloud Customer Care.

A fix is in progress.

Oracle Database@Google Cloud

Feature

For Exadata VM Clusters and Exascale VM Clusters, you can now choose to create a cluster without an Identity Connector, and enable or disable the Identity Connector after the cluster is created by using the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, or the API. For more information, see Enable and disable Identity Connector.

This feature is generally available (GA).

title: October 15, 2026
description:
Apigee Edge for Private Cloud

Announcement

Released Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Designated Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.00 a long-term support (LTS) release: 18 months of full support ending April 2028, then 18 months of maintenance ending October 2029. After October 2029, 4.54.00.00 receives no software updates, security mitigations, or technical support.

Installing a later 4.54 minor release or patch does not change those dates. To extend the support lifecycle, upgrade to the next LTS release.

For the support lifecycle phases, release cadences, and version numbering, see Apigee Edge for Private Cloud release and lifecycle policy.

Announcement

This release replaces Java 8 with Java 17 and Java 21, removes the Classic UI and the apigee-sso component, and updates the bundled Cassandra, Postgres, OpenLDAP, ZooKeeper, Qpid Broker-J, Nginx, and Consul versions. These changes are not backward-compatible.

For the 4.54.00 versions and the 4.53.01 versions they replace, see Supported software and supported versions.

Before upgrading, read Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00, then Update Apigee Edge 4.53.00 or 4.53.01 to 4.54.00 or New installation overview. For known issues, see Known issues with Edge for Private Cloud.

Announcement

Replaced the Classic UI (edge-ui) with the New Edge UI (edge-management-ui).

The New Edge UI is the only management UI in 4.54.00 and is installed by default. Deployments running the Classic UI must transition to it before upgrading. Custom Classic UI properties do not carry over automatically. The default port also changes from 9000 to 3001, configurable with conf_uebe_port, so firewall rules and load balancer target ports that point at 9000 fail until they are updated.

For the migration steps and the supported feature list, see Migrate to the New Edge UI and What features are supported?.

Breaking

In deployments with Apigee SSO enabled, an integrated OIDC identity broker in apigee-openldap replaces the standalone apigee-sso component and Apache Tomcat 9.0.x. Before upgrading, take a complete and validated LDAP backup; existing apigee-sso configurations do not migrate automatically. Deployments not using Apigee SSO require no action.

For migration prerequisites, validation checks, and rollback constraints, see Option 2: Upgrade UI (with Apigee SSO).

Breaking

4.54.00 runs Java in mixed mode: Java 17 for Cassandra and ZooKeeper, Java 21 for the Management Server, Message Processor, Router, and Qpid Broker-J. Both Oracle JDK and OpenJDK are supported at those versions.

Oracle JDK 8 and OpenJDK 8 are no longer supported.

API proxies with custom JavaCallout policies or custom resource JARs can break on Java 21. For details, see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Upgraded Nginx on the Edge Router to 1.30.0.

If you are upgrading from Nginx 1.20.x, see Nginx 1.30 changes in Apigee Edge 4.54.00 for the full list of changes.

Change

Changed the TLS defaults on Message Processors to the Java 21 cryptographic baseline.

Message Processors run on Java 21, which enables TLS 1.3 by default (JEP 332) and prefers it for outbound backend connections, falling back to TLS 1.2. No configuration change is required if your target servers and load balancers negotiate TLS 1.3, or negotiate TLS 1.2 with forward-secret (ECDHE) cipher suites.

Java 21 also disables the non-forward-secret static RSA key-exchange suites (TLS_RSA_*). If you have overridden conf_http_HTTPTransport.ssl.cipher.suites.whitelist or conf_message-processor-communication_local.http.ssl.ciphers with static RSA suites only, backend calls fail with no cipher suites in common and the Router cannot complete a TLS handshake with the Message Processor. Replace the TLS_RSA_* entries with modern cipher suites and restart the Message Processor.

For the remediation path, see Legacy backend requirements and remediation.

Feature

Added Basic authentication to the New Edge UI, which lets you sign in without configuring an identity provider.

The New Edge UI supports Basic authentication without additional configuration. You can also configure Apigee SSO, or an external identity provider such as SAML or OIDC. This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Feature

Added automated pre-flight validation checks to apigee-setup and apigee-service, which surface environment configuration problems before a component is installed.

This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Security

Fixed multiple security vulnerabilities in Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

These fixes ship as part of the component upgrades in this release; see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Changed the default garbage collector on Message Processors to the Garbage-First garbage collector.

Message Processors set useG1GC=true and useStringDeduplication=true by default in 4.54.00. In 4.53.01 neither was set by default. To configure garbage collection, see Configure the garbage collector for Message Processors.

The script does not change unrelated iptables NAT rules. Instances pick up the change the next time they are restarted or recreated.

You can now use reusable column aliases in GoogleSQL. This feature lets you define an alias for an expression in the SELECT clause of a SQL query and immediately reference that alias within the same SELECT list or in the WHERE clause of the same query block.

Reusable column aliases also streamline the migration of workloads from other data warehouses such as Snowflake and Teradata, by supporting their syntax.

Cloud Vision

Face detection model update

The emotion label response for face detection (FACE_DETECTION) in the Cloud Vision API is deprecated. Effective October 15, 2026, the joyLikelihood, sorrowLikelihood, angerLikelihood, and surpriseLikelihood fields in FaceAnnotation return UNKNOWN for new projects and projects without recent Face Detection usage. Beginning January 14, 2027, these fields will permanently return UNKNOWN for all projects.

Compute Engine

Feature

Preview: You can create regional disks, including Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability volumes, by cloning a zonal boot disk.

For more information, see Duplicate a disk with clones.

Change

If you try to create an on-demand reservation or increase the number of reserved Compute Engine instances in a reservation when the zone has reached its reservation capacity limit for your requested machine family, then the request fails with a RESERVATION_CAPACITY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED error. For more information, see Reservation capacity limit exceeded.

Feature

Generally available: The storage-optimized Z4M machine series is generally available for Compute Engine. Powered by fifth generation Intel Emerald Rapids Xeon Scalable processors and Titanium offload processors, Z4M instances are purpose-built for workloads that require larger storage capacity, such as:

  • Parallel file systems to support AI/ML workloads
  • I/O intensive workloads such as SQL, NoSQL, and vector databases
  • AI/ML training and inference workloads such as checkpointing and distributed Key-Value (KV) cache

The Z4M machine series delivers up to 1,536 GB of memory and 168,000 GiB of local Titanium SSD capacity. Z4M also supports up to 400 Gbps of network bandwidth using two physical NICs. Z4M instances use Titanium and Cloud RDMA to help enable higher levels of networking performance, isolation, and security.

For more information, see Storage-optimized machine family.

Dataflow

Feature

Dataflow Auto VM Selection now supports 4th generation Compute Engine machine series. When Auto VM Selection is enabled, the service prioritizes these newer generation VMs for improved performance. If 4th generation VMs are unavailable at startup, the service automatically falls back to widely available 2nd generation machine families to ensure that your jobs can start without unnecessary delays.

For more information, see Auto VM Selection.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Anthropic models are available in the Gemini Enterprise app

Administrators can make Anthropic models—Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5—available to users in the Gemini Enterprise app. After an administrator turns on a model in the Enable third-party models section of the Feature Management tab, users can select the model in the model selector. Claude models are available in the global location and the us and eu multi-regions, and are charged on a pay-as-you-go basis.

This feature is generally available. For more information, see Enable third-party models.

Looker

Announcement

The latest versions in the Looker (Google Cloud core) release channels are beginning deployment as follows:

  • Latest version in the Rapid channel: Looker 26.20
  • Latest version in the No Channel channel: Looker 26.20

The latest version in the Regular channel remains Looker 26.18.

Note: This item was added on October 23, 2026.

Feature

The Looker 26.18 features have begun to be enabled for Looker (Google Cloud core) instances.

NetApp Volumes

Announcement

Google Cloud NetApp Volumes now supports the Flex Unified service level, including custom performance, in the following region:

  • europe-west8 (Milan)

For more information about available regions, see Supported regions.

Security Command Center

Feature

To increase the precision of attack path analysis and provide attack exposure scores that help you prioritize confirmed internet exposures, Risk Engine attack path simulations support the EXTERNALLY_EXPOSED_VM_INSTANCE External Exposure finding category (Preview). This finding category identifies Compute Engine or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) resources with a direct public IP address that allows host OS access.

For more information, see Detect exposed resources, Risk Engine feature support, and Overview of attack exposure scores and attack paths.

Video Intelligence API

Deprecated

We are deprecating the emotion label response in the API. Going forward, the API will return UNKNOWN for all emotion related labels.

title: Making Strides in Symbolic Imitation Learning: Offline Demonstrations, Online Tuning
description:
arXiv:2611.13182v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) methods have been the dominant paradigm in continuous control tasks due to their efficacy in function approximation, while interpretable evolutionary methods have lagged largely behind for the opposite reason. In this work, we introduce Symbolic Imitation Learning, a framework for distilling an oracle policy through an offline dataset into a decision list with linear model motion primitives. We show that this, in conjunction, with online Augmented-Random Search (ARS) tuning of the constants and motion primitives approximates the performance of the oracle across 20 benchmark RL tasks and exceeds the oracle in 11 of those 20 tasks while simultaneously producing parsimonious, interpretable policies that domain experts can better understand.

title: Framing-Induced Vulnerability in Large Language Models: Evidence from Chinese News Headlines
description:
arXiv:2611.13531v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models increasingly evaluate, route, and moderate news, so a model's judgment of a headline has become a gatekeeping decision. We ask whether that judgment follows the fact being reported or the way the fact is framed. We combine an ecological audit of 63,926 Chinese news headlines with a controlled experiment. The experiment covers 30 real events, 30 synthetic events, and 29 natural headline pairs, tested on four Chinese models. Changing only the headline frame shifted both perceived misleadingness and event severity, and the direction and ordering of the shifts were the same for DeepSeek, MiMo, Dots, and LongCat. Emotionally intensified headlines raised severity ratings by 0.65 to 0.88 points, whereas positively reframed headlines lowered them by 0.34 to 0.52 points. Supplying the article body reduced this severity bias by 54 to 80 percent, and all four reductions were significant at p < .01. A small human reference study showed the same direction of effect. Headline-only LLM evaluation therefore carries a measurable robustness gap, and framing sensitivity belongs among the reliability properties that deployment and governance check.
