title: How to Analyse a Legacy Codebase Before Refactoring: A Developer's Guide
description:
Refactoring an existing application can be more challenging than building a new one.

When developers work with a legacy codebase, they often encounter outdated frameworks, undocumented business logic, tightly coupled modules and dependencies that are difficult to identify.

The biggest challenge is understanding how the application works before changing it.

A small modification in one module can affect several other components, particularly in enterprise applications with complex integrations.

In this guide, we will explore a practical approach to analyzing a legacy codebase before starting a refactoring project.

1. Start by Understanding the Project Structure

Before modifying any code, understand how the application is organized.

Start by examining:

  • Source code directories.
  • Application modules.
  • Configuration files.
  • Shared libraries.
  • Database connection settings.
  • API integrations.
  • Build and deployment files.

For example, a typical enterprise application might have the following structure:

banking-application/
│
├── src/
│   ├── authentication/
│   ├── customers/
│   ├── transactions/
│   └── payments/
│
├── config/
├── database/
├── integrations/
├── tests/
└── deployment/

Understanding this structure helps developers identify the main functional areas and locate important components.

2. Identify Dependencies Between Modules

One of the most important steps in legacy application analysis is dependency mapping.

A module rarely works independently. It may depend on shared services, databases, external APIs or other application components.

Start by examining:

  • Import statements and package dependencies.
  • API calls between services.
  • Database queries and stored procedures.
  • Shared libraries.
  • External integrations.
  • Background processing jobs.

Consider this simplified transaction workflow:

Customer Request
       |
       v
Authentication Service
       |
       v
Transaction Module
       |
       v
Payment Gateway
       |
       v
Transaction Database
       |
       v
Notification Service

Before modifying the transaction module, developers should understand how these components interact.

Dependency mapping helps identify the potential impact of changes.

3. Find Undocumented Business Logic

Legacy applications often contain business rules that are not properly documented.

These rules may exist inside:

  • Conditional statements.
  • Stored procedures.
  • Database triggers.
  • Configuration files.
  • Batch processing logic.
  • Custom application functions.

For example:

def calculate_transaction_fee(amount, customer_type):

    if customer_type == "premium":
        return amount * 0.01

    elif customer_type == "standard":
        return amount * 0.02

    return amount * 0.03

This simple example contains business logic that may affect other application workflows.

In larger applications, such rules may be distributed across multiple modules.

Before refactoring, developers should identify these rules and understand their expected behavior.

4. Assess Technical Debt

Technical debt accumulates as applications evolve.

Quick fixes, duplicated functionality, outdated dependencies and tightly coupled components can make applications difficult to maintain.

Look for common indicators:

Technical issue Potential impact
Duplicate code Difficult maintenance
Outdated libraries Compatibility and security concerns
Tight coupling Changes affect multiple modules
Complex functions Difficult debugging
Missing documentation Knowledge gaps
Unsupported frameworks Modernization challenges

Not every technical issue needs immediate attention.

Priorities issues based on application criticality, maintenance effort and business impact.

5. Analyze Application Behavior Before Making Changes

Source code does not always tell the complete story.

Runtime behavior, configurations, database interactions and scheduled processes may influence how an application operates.

Use a combination of:

  • Static code analysis.
  • Application logs.
  • Unit and integration tests.
  • Runtime dependency analysis.
  • Database inspection.
  • API monitoring.

This helps developers understand how the application behaves in real environments.

6. Use AI to Support Legacy Code Analysis

AI-assisted development tools can help developers understand unfamiliar codebases.

They can assist with:

  • Explaining complex functions.
  • Summarizing code modules.
  • Identifying potential dependencies.
  • Generating initial technical documentation.
  • Finding repeated code patterns.
  • Explaining unfamiliar programming constructs.

However, AI-generated explanations are not automatically accurate.

Developers should validate suggestions against the actual implementation, configuration, tests and runtime behavior.

AI should support engineering analysis, not replace engineering judgement.

7. Create a Refactoring Plan

Once the application has been analyzed, prepare a structured refactoring plan.

A practical checklist includes:

  • Identify critical application modules.
  • Document application dependencies.
  • Identify undocumented business rules.
  • Review third-party libraries.
  • Assess technical debt.
  • Identify high-risk components.
  • Establish regression test coverage.
  • Priorities refactoring activities.

This provides a clearer path for making changes without unnecessarily disrupting existing functionality.

8. Common Mistakes to Avoid

When working with legacy applications, avoid these common mistakes:

Rewriting without understanding: Replacing code before understanding existing functionality can introduce unexpected behavior.

Ignoring dependencies: A change in one component may affect several connected systems.

Trusting outdated documentation: Always validate documentation against the actual implementation.

Skipping regression testing: Existing functionality must be tested after refactoring.

Relying entirely on AI: AI-generated insights require technical validation and human oversight.

Conclusion

Legacy application refactoring requires more than improving code quality.

Developers need to understand application architecture, dependencies, business rules and technical debt before making significant changes.

A structured analysis approach helps reduce uncertainty, identify risks and establish a stronger foundation for application modernization.

title: Effects of Laser Beam Width and Measurement Noise on Tree Diameter Estimation in Laser Scanning
description:
arXiv:2611.13739v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Laser scanning has been utilized for decades to measure tree structure and geometry. Despite continuous advances in sensor technology, uncertainties arising from scanner characteristics and measurement conditions has remained relevant sources of error. In particular, factors such as laser beam diameter can introduce both systematic and random errors in the reconstructed tree geometry. This study investigates the main sources of these errors in mobile laser scanning (MLS) and quantifies their effects on stem curve (stem diameter) estimation. We discovered through simulations and experiments that the heteroscedasticity (difference in variance in ranging and scan angle) in the measurement noise is a key factor along with the beam width of the lidar, which cause the bias of the diameter estimates to depend not only on distance, but also on the tree diameter. We demonstrated that this bias can be reliably predicted and negated for trees with a diameter at the breast height greater than 10 cm using technical specifications of the sensor without any additional calibration. In experiments, the proposed bias compensation method reduced the root-mean-square error of stem diameter estimates to sub-centimeter level on boreal forest test sites. However, for small trees with diameter below 10 cm, the diameter bias becomes sensitive to the diameter of the tree$\unicode{x2013}$an unknown factor$\unicode{x2013}$and other factors, such as different bark and out-of-roundness of the stem, limiting the precision of lidar for measuring geometry of trees and applicability of the presented method.

title: Calcutta Hacks — Where Heritage Meets Technology
description:
1. Project Overview

Calcutta <Hacks/> is the official website developed for Apex Circle's 24-hour heritage hackathon in Kolkata. The event brought together technology enthusiasts, developers, designers, and innovators to explore the intersection of technology, creativity, and cultural heritage.

The goal was to create a digital platform that communicated the event's identity, presented essential information, and provided participants with a clear and engaging experience.

Rather than building another conventional hackathon landing page, the objective was to create a website that reflected Kolkata's cultural identity while maintaining a modern technology-focused visual language.

I contributed to the Web Team, focusing on frontend development, component architecture, responsive layouts, and the overall user experience.

2. The Problem

Hackathon websites are often treated as simple promotional landing pages. However, an event website needs to do more than look attractive.

Potential participants need to understand the event, discover its purpose, explore important information, and know how to participate without navigating through confusing sections.

The key challenges were:

  • Information Architecture: Presenting event details, schedules, speakers, themes, and participation information in an organized structure.
  • Visual Identity: Representing Kolkata's heritage and cultural identity without compromising the modern technology-focused appearance.
  • User Experience: Making important information easy to discover and understand.
  • Responsive Design: Delivering a consistent experience across mobile, tablet, and desktop devices.
  • Frontend Maintainability: Structuring the codebase so components and sections could be reused and maintained efficiently.

3. The Solution

I contributed to building a responsive, component-driven React website that served as the event's primary digital information platform.

The approach focused on three major areas:

A. Heritage Meets Technology

The visual direction balanced Kolkata's cultural identity with a modern hackathon aesthetic. The intention was to make the event recognizable and visually distinct rather than relying on a generic developer-event template.

B. Structured Information Experience

Event-related information was organized into clearly defined sections, helping visitors understand the event, explore its themes, discover schedules and speakers, and find participation information.

C. Responsive Frontend Architecture

The interface was developed using reusable React components and Tailwind CSS, with attention to consistent styling, responsive behavior, and maintainable code.

4. My Responsibilities

As part of the Apex Circle Web Team, my responsibilities focused on frontend engineering.

  • Developed frontend interfaces using React.js.
  • Implemented responsive layouts using Tailwind CSS.
  • Built reusable and modular UI components.
  • Organized website sections into a structured page architecture.
  • Worked on the visual presentation of event information.
  • Improved consistency across different screen sizes.
  • Focused on maintainable component structures and clean implementation.
  • Worked on translating the event's identity into a digital experience.

5. Key Features & Website Experience

Event Information

A structured presentation of the hackathon, its purpose, and essential event details.

Event Schedule

A dedicated information experience for communicating event activities and schedules.

Speakers & Themes

Organized sections for presenting speaker information and the event's central themes.

Participation Information

Clear presentation of participation-related details to help potential attendees understand how to get involved.

Responsive Interface

Layouts designed to adapt to mobile, tablet, and desktop screen sizes.

Reusable UI Components

A component-based approach to reduce duplication and maintain consistency across the website.

6. Technical Architecture

The project followed a frontend-only architecture.

Frontend Layer

  • React.js — Component-based UI development.
  • JavaScript — Application logic and interface behavior.
  • Tailwind CSS — Styling and responsive layouts.

Architecture Approach

  • Component-based development.
  • Reusable UI elements.
  • Separation of page sections and presentation components.
  • Responsive utility-based styling.

Backend: Not implemented.

Database: Not implemented.

Authentication: Not implemented.

API Integration: No custom backend API was implemented.

The project was intentionally limited to the frontend scope required for the hackathon website.

7. Design & User Experience Decisions

The primary design challenge was balancing two different identities:

  • Kolkata's cultural and historical heritage.
  • The innovation, experimentation, and energy of a technology hackathon.

The website needed to feel modern without losing its connection to the event's identity.

My frontend implementation prioritized:

  • Clear content hierarchy.
  • Consistent spacing and typography.
  • Responsive section layouts.
  • Reusable visual patterns.
  • Easy navigation through event information.
  • Consistent presentation across devices.

8. Challenges & How I Approached Them

Challenge 1: Balancing Heritage with a Modern Technology Identity

A conventional technology-event design would not communicate the cultural theme effectively.

Approach: The visual direction was designed around the relationship between Kolkata's heritage and modern innovation.

Challenge 2: Organizing Multiple Categories of Information

Hackathon websites contain different types of information, including event details, schedules, speakers, themes, and participation instructions.

Approach: I used a structured section-based layout to make information easier to discover.

Challenge 3: Responsive Layout Development

A website that looks good on desktop may not translate well to smaller screens.

Approach: I used Tailwind CSS responsive utilities and adaptable layouts to maintain usability across different screen sizes.

Challenge 4: Maintaining Reusable Code

Building every section independently can lead to duplicated markup and inconsistent styling.

Approach: I followed a reusable React component approach to improve consistency and maintainability.

9. Project Scope & Limitations

This project was developed as a frontend-only hackathon website.

The implementation focused on the visual interface, responsive layouts, component architecture, and event information presentation.

The following functionality was outside the project's implementation scope:

  • Backend services and server-side business logic.
  • Database storage and management.
  • User authentication and authorization.
  • Custom registration APIs.
  • Admin dashboard and content management.
  • Server-side participant data processing.

This distinction is important: the project demonstrates frontend development and UI engineering, not a complete full-stack event management platform.

10. What I Learned

Working on Calcutta <Hacks/> helped me understand that building a good event website requires more than writing React components.

Key takeaways:

  • Translating an event's identity into a consistent digital experience.
  • Organizing complex information into understandable sections.
  • Building reusable React components.
  • Developing responsive interfaces with Tailwind CSS.
  • Understanding the importance of frontend architecture and maintainability.
  • Working as part of a collaborative web development team.
  • Making implementation decisions within a defined project scope.

11. Project Outcome

The project delivered a dedicated frontend website for Apex Circle's Calcutta <Hacks/> 24-hour heritage hackathon.

It brought the event's identity, information, and participation experience into one digital platform while demonstrating my contribution to frontend engineering as part of the Web Team.

The biggest takeaway: A successful event website is not simply a collection of attractive sections. It is an organized digital experience that communicates the event's identity and helps its audience find the information they need.

Project Credits

Project: Calcutta <Hacks/>

Organization: Apex Circle

Contribution: Frontend Development — Web Team

Technologies: React.js, JavaScript, Tailwind CSS

Project URL: https://cuttahacks.abhishek-nexgen.xyz/

title: VIGOR: Benchmarking Visual Rationale Correctness in Multimodal Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.13150v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are typically evaluated by whether they produce correct answers, but correctness alone does not reveal whether their outputs are supported by the right visual evidence. We introduce VIGOR, a benchmark for evaluating VIsually GrOunded Rationales in MLLMs. VIGOR represents visual rationales as explicit concepts paired with pixel-level groundings, covering multiple abstraction levels including low-level visual properties, intermediate structures, objects, parts and high-level motion, relations. To construct VIGOR at scale, we develop an automatic annotation framework that reuses existing dense supervision when available and generates missing concept groundings through proposal-based annotation followed by conservative multimodal verification. Using VIGOR, we evaluate whether MLLMs "look at what they say" by comparing model-derived visual evidence for each expressed concept against annotated ground-truth rationales. Our results show that current MLLMs exhibit limited visual rationale correctness and reveal distinct grounding failures across concept levels. VIGOR provides a benchmark and scalable data construction pipeline for studying whether MLLM outputs are supported by appropriate visual evidence. Code is available at https://github.com/deep-real/VIGOR

title: Text-to-Image API Telemetry: A Backend Contract to Generate Marketing Images
description:
A media company's recruitment system has two different jobs: score candidates against a job rubric and produce marketing images for the campaign attracting those candidates. Provider portability matters to both, but an image-generation response must never become evidence of a candidate's suitability. The operational constraint is keeping enough telemetry to explain a provider change without retaining every prompt, image, and candidate identifier.

Short answer: put a simple text-to-image API behind a backend-owned contract: prompt in, image URL or base64 out. For a Node.js service using an OpenAI-compatible image interface, keep provider selection behind that boundary, check the available image models in the intended US or EU deployment, and bound telemetry before launch. HTTP compatibility reduces integration work; a rubric for acceptable campaign images determines whether switching providers is useful.

Keep scoring separate.

This design uses recruitment campaign artwork as its concrete image workload. Candidate scoring remains a separate consumer of the job rubric, with its own evidence and review requirements. Generating a newsroom recruitment banner does not score an applicant, and neither the banner prompt nor the resulting artwork should carry an applicant's private details.

How should a text-to-image API backend generate marketing images across providers?

The application should own the campaign brief, the approved image requirements, and the interpretation of a completed generation. A provider-specific model identifier belongs in the adapter configuration. It should not become a permanent field in every campaign record or a user-facing promise that a different model can reproduce identical artwork.

Consider a proposed brief: “An editorial illustration of a newsroom planning desk for a recruitment campaign; no applicant names, no candidate portraits, and no embedded hiring score.” This is example input, not a measured production request. The hiring team can relate it to the campaign's job rubric without asking an image model to infer qualifications. Keep actual applicant evidence outside this request.

The first backend endpoint needs little conceptual machinery. Accept the prompt, enforce the allowed image count and size, select an available model, and return the image result through an application-owned response. Support the URL or base64 form the selected image contract provides. Avoid promising that every provider accepts the same options or returns interchangeable artifacts merely because the transport looks familiar.

Check the catalogue first.

This curl example performs model discovery before configuring the image adapter. Set IMAGE_API_ORIGIN to the service origin, without a trailing slash or version path, and supply INFRAI_API_KEY through the environment. It deliberately prints the catalogue rather than guessing an image model identifier. Inspect capability and availability before selecting a model; a catalogue response for chat is not proof that an image model is available. The explicit GET is read-only. Curl checks HTTP errors, retries transient responses including HTTP 429 with backoff, and honors Retry-After when present; the retry budget is bounded to 90 seconds.

curl --request GET \
  --url "${IMAGE_API_ORIGIN:?Set the service origin}/v1/ai/models" \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${INFRAI_API_KEY:?Set the API key}" \
  --fail-with-body \
  --retry 4 \
  --retry-max-time 90

There is a useful distinction here: the HTTP request can be portable while the image specification still needs reevaluation. Prompt interpretation, approved dimensions, and campaign suitability belong in the acceptance process. An adapter cannot settle those questions.

Count dimensions before retaining events

Telemetry portability starts with a small vocabulary. Proposed metric dimensions might include deployment region, provider, operation, and outcome category. Campaign IDs, candidate IDs, complete prompts, and image URLs belong outside metric labels. A request identifier can help correlate a particular event without turning every request into another metric series.

The arithmetic is unforgiving. In a hypothetical configuration with 3 providers, 2 regions, and 4 outcome categories, one operation permits 24 label combinations. Adding 10,000 distinct campaign identifiers raises the possible combinations to 240,000. These are design calculations, not observed traffic or a prediction that every combination will appear. They explain why a seemingly convenient campaign label deserves scrutiny before instrumentation ships.

Count first. Store selectively.

Retention is a separate multiplier. Suppose an explicitly hypothetical workload produces 10,000 events per day at 800 bytes per event. Seven days retain 56,000,000 bytes; 30 days retain 240,000,000 bytes, before indexing, replication, or other storage overhead. Those figures describe event payload volume alone. Embedding image data would invalidate the assumption that events remain small, so the generation result should not be copied into routine request logs.

Bytes accumulate quietly.

The trade-off is real: a compact event cannot explain every detail of an unusual output. Preserve a deliberately bounded review record when image quality needs investigation, with access and expiration decided separately from metric retention. That choice keeps the explanation available without making every successful generation a permanent content archive. Don't use an applicant identifier as a convenient correlation label: each new applicant would expand the possible series count, while making operational telemetry a second repository of hiring data.

Sample outcomes without hiding the migration signal

Uniformly sampling all request events can erase the very cases needed to judge a provider transition. A proposed policy could retain operational failure records while sampling ordinary successes, subject to an explicit volume bound. Preserve aggregate request counts separately, and record the sampling policy with the retained events. Otherwise a reviewer may mistake a sample's provider distribution for the workload's distribution.

Sampling buys less retained detail at the cost of weaker reconstruction. That is acceptable for routine traffic only if the acceptance decision uses an intentional review set rather than whichever images happened to survive logging. Keep the same campaign briefs for a provider comparison and assess the returned images against the same requirements. Do not interpret an absence of sampled complaints as evidence of equivalent output.

Upscaling introduces another analytical trap. The available upscale operation uses Lanczos interpolation. Treat it as a resizing step, not a promise to generate missing semantic detail. A comparison that evaluates one provider's original output against another output after resizing has changed two variables at once; record the transformation in the review record and keep the image requirements fixed.

Before launch, estimate generation spend and cap prompt length, image count, and size. These bounds make workload behavior interpretable as well as predictable. They also prevent a campaign with unusually large requests from dominating a provider comparison that was intended to assess ordinary recruitment artwork.

Compare the integration boundary, then test the artwork

The options below are alternatives to evaluate, not a quality ranking. The primary documentation in References supplies the starting points for checking their current contracts. No comparative latency, output-quality, or savings measurement is implied.

Option Reason to include it in the evaluation Boundary to verify before selecting it
OpenAI image generation A direct-provider reference for a workflow framed around an OpenAI-compatible image request. Validate the chosen image model's request and response contract; compatibility alone does not establish equivalent artwork.
Google Cloud Vertex AI Imagen An alternative for a team considering a Google Cloud image-generation integration. Check the intended deployment and translate its documented contract into the application's accepted input and result forms.
Amazon Bedrock image generation An alternative for a team considering an AWS-hosted model integration. Evaluate the selected model's documented interface rather than assuming that the service name determines image behavior.
Shared REST platform described below A plain REST API with no SDK to install; anything that can send an HTTP request can call it, in any language. Check current image-model availability in the intended region and test the selected output contract against the campaign review set.

That public discovery surface gives the recruitment backend a second, distinct advantage: an engineer can inspect the image contract before distributing a production credential. Schema inspection helps establish which fields the adapter must validate and which response fields belong in a bounded telemetry record. It doesn't establish output quality; the campaign review set still does that. Documented capabilities also ship runnable examples in 10 languages, which gives teams maintaining different backend implementations a common starting point for contract checks.

Infrai combines a plain REST API with one key, one wallet, and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules. This single-key, single-bill model gives the recruitment backend one credential to administer across services and consolidated billing to reconcile as it adopts additional capabilities. The interface uses consistent conventions across those services. That breadth matters if the recruitment backend expands beyond image generation; for an image-only workload, it is a secondary benefit.

For a narrow workload with one accepted provider, a direct integration may be the more economical engineering choice because there is less adapter behavior to maintain. If the team expects provider changes across deployments, the shared application contract earns its maintenance cost. Neither choice removes the need to review generated artwork.

Specified per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request metadata can support a bounded operational event, but it is not evidence of measured service performance. Use it to attribute actual requests once the application runs. Keep vendor and outcome as bounded dimensions; retain detailed request correlation only where it supports an investigation.

Roll out one campaign before moving the workload

Start with one recruitment campaign and an approved set of image briefs. Confirm available image models, generate the review set, and compare results against the campaign requirements. Keep the candidate-scoring workflow outside this rollout. The release decision should depend on accepted artwork and a working application response contract, with measured operational behavior collected during that rollout.

Then inspect the telemetry itself: count emitted label combinations, calculate retained event bytes, and confirm that the sampling policy leaves enough evidence to assess the transition. Expand only after those checks hold. A provider change is easier to defend when the evidence is compact enough to inspect and explicit enough to challenge.

Sources

References for checking provider-specific image contracts and prompt design:

  • OpenAI, Image generation guide
  • Google Cloud, Generate images with Imagen
  • Amazon Bedrock, Model parameters
  • Prompt Engineering Guide

title: Safely Running Long-Running Index Operations in SQL Server
description:
Creating or rebuilding an index on a large, actively used table is not merely a schema change. It is a production operation that can consume significant CPU, I/O, transaction log, and storage resources, and it can introduce unexpected blocking even when the operation uses ONLINE = ON.

This article explains a particularly subtle failure mode: an online index operation holds a schema-stability lock while an automatic statistics update waits for a schema-modification lock. SQL Server's lock queue can then place otherwise compatible application queries behind the waiting schema-modification request, creating a lock convoy and widespread query timeouts.

This is one possible blocking pattern, not the only cause of blocking during an online index operation.

The broader lesson is simple:

Treat long-running index changes as controlled operational events. Estimate them, schedule them, monitor them, make them interruptible where possible, and define the recovery path before execution.

Why an Online Index Operation Can Still Block Queries

ONLINE = ON reduces blocking, but it does not mean "no locks." An online index operation still acquires locks during its lifecycle, including:

  • A long-lived schema-stability (Sch-S) lock during much of the build.
  • A short table-level shared (S) lock during preparation and a short schema-modification (Sch-M) lock during the final metadata switch.
  • Intent locks on the source and target structures while the new index is built and maintained.

Sch-S locks are compatible with other Sch-S locks. Under normal conditions, queries can compile and execute while the index is being built.

The problem begins when another operation requests an incompatible Sch-M lock.

The initial S lock can also wait behind an open transaction that modified the table. In that case, the waiting index operation can delay new writers before the build has fully started.

The Lock-Convoy Failure Mode

Consider this sequence:

Online index operation
  Holds: Sch-S on the target table
       |
       +-- blocks --> Statistics update
                       Wants: Sch-M
                            |
                            +-- queues ahead of --> New statements
                                                    Want: Sch-S

The new queries need Sch-S, which is compatible with the index operation's existing Sch-S. However, a waiting Sch-M request is already in the lock queue.

A lock request is generally not granted ahead of an earlier incompatible waiter, even when it is compatible with the locks currently granted. This behavior prevents an exclusive waiter from starving indefinitely, but it can create a convoy.

The result is a convoy:

  1. The index operation holds Sch-S for an extended period.
  2. A statistics update requests Sch-M and must wait.
  3. New statements touching the table request Sch-S.
  4. Those queries queue behind the pending Sch-M.
  5. Application requests accumulate and eventually reach their command timeout.

This behavior can make a database appear intermittently unavailable even though the index operation is running with ONLINE = ON.

Why Automatic Statistics Updates Can Trigger the Convoy

On an active table, inserts, updates, and deletes increase statistics modification counters. During a long index operation, one or more statistics objects may cross the automatic-update threshold.

When a compilation detects stale statistics, SQL Server may attempt to update them. In some engine versions and execution paths, the update can request Sch-M. If an online index operation is still holding Sch-S, the statistics update waits and can become the head waiter in the blocking queue.

This explains why problems may not begin immediately:

  1. The index operation starts and queries initially continue normally.
  2. Data modifications accumulate.
  3. A statistics object becomes stale.
  4. A query compilation triggers the statistics update.
  5. The waiting Sch-M request creates the convoy.

The delay between the start of the index operation and the first visible query failures can make the relationship difficult to identify. Confirm the mechanism rather than assuming it: look for an LCK_M_SCH_M waiter associated with statistics activity, blocked by the index session, followed by Sch-S waiters.

Why Recompilation Amplifies the Impact

Queries acquire schema-stability locks on referenced objects while compiling and executing. A queued Sch-M request can therefore delay all new statements touching the table, including statements that reuse cached plans.

Frequent recompilation can still amplify the impact because it adds compilation work and more lock requests during an already congested period.

Common causes include:

  • OPTION (RECOMPILE)
  • Stored procedures declared WITH RECOMPILE
  • Plan-cache eviction
  • Frequent ad hoc queries
  • Schema changes that invalidate plans
  • Statistics changes that trigger recompilation

A cached plan avoids repeated optimization work, but it does not allow execution to bypass the schema-lock queue. A query using OPTION (RECOMPILE) adds compilation on every execution, increasing pressure and the number of waiting requests during a convoy.

Recompilation is not inherently wrong, but it must be considered when planning maintenance against hot tables.

Why the Symptoms May Be Intermittent

Temporary relief can occur when the waiting Sch-M request is cancelled by a client timeout, a configured lock timeout, or an explicit operator action. Removing that request allows the queue to drain.

When that happens:

  1. The queued Sch-S requests can be granted.
  2. A burst of queries completes.
  3. A later compilation detects stale statistics again.
  4. Another statistics update requests Sch-M.
  5. The convoy returns.

This produces a repeating pattern:

Blocking -> temporary relief -> blocking -> temporary relief

Intermittent success does not prove that the index operation is healthy. It may indicate that the head waiter is repeatedly cancelled and requested again.

Risk Factors

The likelihood and impact of this pattern increase when several of the following are true:

Risk factor Why it matters
Very large table or index Extends the period during which schema locks and resource pressure exist
High write rate Makes statistics stale more quickly and increases index-maintenance overhead
Frequent recompilation Adds compilation work and more requests during the vulnerable window
Tight application timeouts Converts short blocking into visible request failures quickly
Limited transaction-log capacity Can slow or fail the operation
Insufficient free storage Online and resumable operations may temporarily require both old and new index structures
High CPU or I/O utilization Extends build duration and affects foreground workload
Fixed client or tool timeout May terminate the operation after hours of work
No tested abort procedure Increases recovery time when application health degrades

Plan the Change Before Running It

1. Measure the Target

Collect at least:

  • Table and index size
  • Row count
  • Current write rate
  • Peak and off-peak workload
  • Available database and temporary storage
  • Existing index definition
  • Edition and engine-version support for online and resumable operations
  • Temporary-database capacity when using options that require it
  • Planned MAXDOP and its effect on duration and resource use
  • Recovery model and transaction-log backup throughput
  • Replication, availability, or disaster-recovery constraints

Do not estimate duration solely from a development or staging database. Index build time does not scale linearly across different hardware, data distributions, workload levels, and log configurations.

2. Establish Success and Abort Thresholds

Define measurable thresholds before execution, such as:

  • Maximum acceptable blocked-query count
  • Maximum lock-wait duration
  • Maximum application error or timeout rate
  • CPU, I/O, and log-utilization limits
  • Maximum operation duration
  • Minimum free-storage reserve

3. Choose the Execution Model

Use the simplest model that provides enough safety:

Model Appropriate when
Application schema-migration step The operation is small, predictable, and the tool's command timeout exceeds the expected duration
Extended-timeout maintenance command The operation is long but can safely remain attached to its initiating tool
Separate maintenance job The operation must run independently or in a low-traffic window
Resumable index operation The work must be divided into bounded windows or survive process restarts
Scheduled maintenance framework Many databases require auditable, scheduled, retryable execution

Long-running data and index operations should generally be separated from fast schema changes. A routine application rollout should not depend on a multi-hour physical data operation finishing in the same execution window.

4. Test with Production-Like Conditions

A useful rehearsal should include:

  • Representative data volume and distribution
  • Concurrent reads and writes
  • Queries that commonly recompile
  • Monitoring of lock waits and blocking chains
  • An intentional pause or abort
  • Validation of retry or resume behavior

The goal is not only to prove that the index can be created. It is to prove that the system remains operable while it is being created.

Execution Safeguards

Run During the Lowest Practical Traffic Window

Lower traffic reduces:

  • Foreground workload contention
  • Data changes that must be reflected in the new index
  • Transaction-log generation
  • The probability of statistics becoming stale during the operation
  • The number of queries affected by an unexpected blocking chain

An online operation should still be scheduled thoughtfully. "Online" is a concurrency feature, not a maintenance-window substitute.

Use Low-Priority Lock Waiting

For supported operations, use WAIT_AT_LOW_PRIORITY so the index operation's own lock requests do not indefinitely block normal workload. Test all syntax against the deployed engine version and edition; support differs between CREATE INDEX and ALTER INDEX ... REBUILD.

ALTER INDEX [IX_Example]
ON [dbo].[LargeTable]
REBUILD
WITH
(
    ONLINE = ON
    (
        WAIT_AT_LOW_PRIORITY
        (
            MAX_DURATION = 5 MINUTES,
            ABORT_AFTER_WAIT = SELF
        )
    )
);

ABORT_AFTER_WAIT = SELF favors workload availability by cancelling the index operation if it cannot obtain the required lock within the specified period. For a non-resumable operation, cancellation discards completed build work and rollback can take time. ABORT_AFTER_WAIT = BLOCKERS can terminate user sessions and should be used only with explicit operational approval.

Choose the duration based on the workload's latency objectives. Do not copy a large value without understanding how long the operation may remain pending.

This option reduces blocking caused by the index operation's own lock requests. It does not prevent a separate statistics-update Sch-M request from queueing while the build holds Sch-S.

Consider Resumable Index Operations

Where supported, resumable operations reduce the cost of interruption:

CREATE INDEX [IX_Example]
ON [dbo].[LargeTable] ([KeyColumn])
WITH
(
    ONLINE = ON,
    RESUMABLE = ON,
    MAX_DURATION = 120 MINUTES
);

If the operation reaches MAX_DURATION, it pauses rather than discarding all progress. It can later be resumed:

ALTER INDEX [IX_Example]
ON [dbo].[LargeTable]
RESUME WITH (MAX_DURATION = 120 MINUTES);

Inspect resumable operations with:

SELECT
    object_id,
    index_id,
    name,
    state_desc,
    percent_complete,
    page_count
FROM sys.index_resumable_operations;

Resumability introduces operational responsibilities:

  • A paused operation consumes storage.
  • Writes may need to maintain both index structures.
  • Operations requiring a table-level exclusive lock, such as TRUNCATE TABLE, some ALTER TABLE statements, and offline index rebuilds, cannot proceed while the index is paused.
  • Automation must detect and resume, complete, or abort abandoned operations.

Resumability does not prevent the lock-convoy pattern while the operation is actively running. Enable it only when someone owns monitoring and cleanup for paused work.

Control Automatic Statistics Updates Deliberately

For a verified lock-convoy risk, temporarily disabling automatic statistics updates can prevent a statistics update from requesting Sch-M during the vulnerable period. Treat this as a last-resort mitigation after scheduling, low-priority waiting, resumability, and active monitoring have been considered.

Prefer the narrowest effective scope. Inspect the current table-level settings before changing them:

EXEC sys.sp_autostats N'dbo.LargeTable';

If testing confirms that table-scoped suppression addresses the risk, record the existing state, disable updates for the target table, and restore the recorded state afterward:

EXEC sys.sp_autostats N'dbo.LargeTable', N'OFF';

-- Run the controlled index operation here.

-- Restore each statistic to its previously recorded setting.

If a database-level change is required, first record is_auto_update_stats_on from sys.databases and restore that original value rather than hard-coding ON. A database-level change affects every table; stale statistics can accumulate and query quality can degrade. Switching to asynchronous automatic statistics does not eliminate this risk because the statistics update can still request the incompatible lock.

Use this mitigation only when:

  • The lock-convoy mechanism has been validated for the workload.
  • The maintenance window is bounded.
  • The setting change is monitored.
  • Re-enabling is part of the mandatory cleanup path.
  • Critical statistics are updated manually afterward when appropriate.

After the index operation has finished, update other affected statistics when appropriate. The newly created index already receives index statistics during creation.

UPDATE STATISTICS [dbo].[LargeTable];

The appropriate sampling level depends on table size, workload, and maintenance budget. A full scan can itself be expensive.

Ensure cleanup runs even after cancellation, timeout, or failure, and alert if any temporary statistics configuration remains in place.

Avoid Unnecessary Recompilation During the Window

If application behavior permits, reduce avoidable compilations during maintenance:

  • Reassess unconditional OPTION (RECOMPILE) usage.
  • Avoid unnecessary plan-cache clearing.
  • Do not combine unrelated schema changes with the index operation.

Do not remove recompilation hints blindly. They may exist to solve parameter-sensitivity or plan-quality problems. Any query change requires independent performance validation.

Monitoring During the Operation

Find Active Requests and Blockers 

SELECT
    r.session_id,
    r.status,
    r.command,
    r.wait_type,
    r.wait_time,
    r.wait_resource,
    r.blocking_session_id,
    r.percent_complete,
    r.cpu_time,
    r.total_elapsed_time
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests AS r
INNER JOIN sys.dm_exec_sessions AS s
    ON s.session_id = r.session_id
WHERE
    r.database_id = DB_ID()
    AND s.is_user_process = 1
    AND r.session_id <> @@SPID
ORDER BY r.total_elapsed_time DESC;

percent_complete is populated only for some commands and may remain zero for an index operation.

Look specifically for:

  • LCK_M_SCH_M
  • LCK_M_SCH_S
  • A growing number of blocked sessions
  • A head blocker associated with statistics or index maintenance
  • Increasing application timeout rates

Inspect Locks on the Target Object 

SELECT
    tl.request_session_id,
    tl.resource_type,
    tl.request_mode,
    tl.request_status,
    tl.resource_associated_entity_id
FROM sys.dm_tran_locks AS tl
WHERE
    tl.resource_database_id = DB_ID()
    AND tl.resource_type = N'OBJECT'
    AND tl.resource_associated_entity_id = OBJECT_ID(N'dbo.LargeTable')
ORDER BY
    tl.resource_associated_entity_id,
    tl.request_session_id;

This DMV does not expose queue order. Correlate it with sys.dm_exec_requests, sys.dm_os_waiting_tasks, and SQL text when deeper investigation is required. Capture evidence before terminating an operation, provided doing so does not delay recovery.

Monitor Resource Health

At minimum, track:

  • CPU
  • Data-file and log-file I/O latency
  • Transaction-log usage and growth
  • Database and temporary-storage free space
  • Query latency and timeout rate
  • Deadlocks
  • Blocking duration
  • Index-operation progress

Database health and application health must be observed together. A database command can be progressing normally while the application is already outside its service objectives.

Abort and Recovery

Stopping a non-resumable index operation can require a lengthy rollback. The database may remain under resource pressure while that rollback proceeds.

If a verified statistics-related LCK_M_SCH_M waiter is causing the convoy, cancelling that waiting session may drain the queue while preserving the index build. Confirm the session's identity and SQL text first; cancelling it also cancels the triggering query.

Before execution, document:

  1. How to identify the index session.
  2. The exact command used to stop or pause it.
  3. Whether progress will be preserved.
  4. How rollback progress will be monitored.
  5. Which temporary database settings must be restored.
  6. How statistics and index state will be validated afterward.
  7. When the operation may be retried.

For a resumable operation, prefer PAUSE when the goal is to preserve progress:

ALTER INDEX [IX_Example]
ON [dbo].[LargeTable]
PAUSE;

If the partial operation must be discarded:

ALTER INDEX [IX_Example]
ON [dbo].[LargeTable]
ABORT;

ABORT discards saved progress and may take time. Confirm the supported syntax and behavior for the deployed engine version before the maintenance window.

Post-Change Validation

Do not declare success when the DDL statement returns. Verify:

  • The intended index exists and is enabled.
  • The index definition matches the approved design.
  • No resumable operation remains paused unexpectedly.
  • Temporary database settings have been restored.
  • Statistics are sufficiently current.
  • Blocking and timeout rates have returned to baseline.
  • Query plans use the new index where expected.
  • Write latency has not regressed unexpectedly.
  • Data and log files have adequate free space.
  • The maintenance record reflects the final state.

Example checks:

SELECT
    i.name,
    i.type_desc,
    i.is_disabled,
    i.is_hypothetical,
    i.has_filter,
    i.filter_definition
FROM sys.indexes AS i
WHERE i.object_id = OBJECT_ID(N'dbo.LargeTable');

SELECT
    s.name AS statistic_name,
    sp.last_updated,
    sp.rows,
    sp.modification_counter
FROM sys.stats AS s
OUTER APPLY sys.dm_db_stats_properties(s.object_id, s.stats_id) AS sp
WHERE
    s.object_id = OBJECT_ID(N'dbo.LargeTable')
ORDER BY sp.last_updated;

Recommended Operational Checklist

Before

  • [ ] Measure table, index, log, and storage requirements.
  • [ ] Estimate duration using representative data and workload.
  • [ ] Confirm online and resumable feature support.
  • [ ] Identify queries that frequently compile or recompile.
  • [ ] Select a low-traffic window.
  • [ ] Define success, pause, and abort thresholds.
  • [ ] Prepare monitoring queries and dashboards.
  • [ ] Test pause, resume, abort, and cleanup behavior.

During

  • [ ] Monitor application latency and error rate.
  • [ ] Monitor Sch-S and Sch-M waits.
  • [ ] Watch the blocking chain, not only the index session.
  • [ ] Track CPU, I/O, storage, and transaction-log health.
  • [ ] Pause or abort when a predefined threshold is crossed.

After

  • [ ] Confirm the final index definition and state.
  • [ ] Restore temporary database settings.
  • [ ] Enable statistics auto update as needed.
  • [ ] Confirm no resumable operation remains paused.
  • [ ] Validate critical query performance.
  • [ ] Record actual duration, resource usage, and lessons learned.

Final Takeaways

  1. Online does not mean lock-free. Online index operations still interact with schema locks and can affect production traffic.
  2. A waiting Sch-M request can create a lock convoy. Later Sch-S requests may queue behind it even though they are compatible with the lock currently being held.
  3. Automatic statistics can create a head waiter, and recompilation can add pressure. All new statements need schema stability; frequent recompilation adds more work and requests during the convoy.
  4. Large index changes need an operational design. Maintenance windows, monitoring, abort criteria, and cleanup are part of the implementation.
  5. Resumable operations reduce interruption cost but require lifecycle management. Paused work must be visible, owned, and completed or aborted.
  6. Temporary configuration changes must be bounded and reversible. If automatic statistics are disabled, restoring them is a mandatory recovery action.
  7. Separate slow maintenance from routine application rollout when scale demands it. Fast schema changes and multi-hour physical data operations have different operational requirements.

The safest index change is not the one with the most options in its WITH clause. It is the one whose production behavior has been estimated, rehearsed, observed, and made recoverable.

title: Marrying Capacity and Precision for Efficient 2D Gaussian Image Representation
description:
arXiv:2611.13784v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: 2D Gaussian representations provide an explicit and efficient way to represent images, but their rate-distortion performance under limited budgets depends critically on how Gaussian capacity and parameter precision are allocated. Existing methods typically optimize these two resources separately, overlooking content-dependent capacity demands and heterogeneous quantization sensitivity. We present CP-GS, a capacity-precision coupled Gaussian splatting framework for budget-aware 2D Gaussian image representation that jointly optimizes capacity allocation and attribute precision under a shared rate constraint. CP-GS first constructs a content-adaptive Gaussian representation by dynamically reallocating a fixed Gaussian budget from redundant regions to areas with higher representation demand. It then introduces hierarchical distortion-aware representation quantization, using efficient rendering-based calibration to allocate precision across Gaussian attributes and further refine it within heterogeneous attribute groups. Finally, it jointly optimizes Gaussian capacity and attribute precision by constructing candidate representations with different Gaussian counts and precision configurations and selecting operating points according to decoded distortion and actual serialized size. Experiments on DIV2K and Kodak show that CP-GS achieves improved rate-distortion performance over representative 2D Gaussian and implicit neural representations across a range of budgets, while maintaining a fixed overall representation budget and low optimization cost. These results demonstrate the benefit of jointly optimizing spatial capacity and parameter precision for compact Gaussian image representation.

title: Ceci n'est pas une pipe -- Toward a Symbolic Solver for the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus Using Evolutionary Computation
description:
arXiv:2611.13831v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) is a benchmark designed to assess the capability of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems to generalize starting from a few samples, a task humans excel at. The ARC-AGI contests held since 2020 have been the focus of intense competition, with participants proposing approaches ranging from traditional symbolic AI to Transformer architectures. Despite a long history of successes, evolutionary algorithms (EAs) were notably absent from the approaches appearing in the main contest. As score-and-search program synthesis approaches, EAs suffer from issues related to choosing the proper representation in the Domain-Specific Language applied to the problem (for example, pixel-level or object-level), and distinguishing between two candidate solutions producing the same outputs. In this work, we present the first fully symbolic, evolutionary-based program synthesis approach submitted to the ARC-AGI-2 main contest. The main contributions are: evolving the grid parser and the output projector together with the program that transforms the grid, so that a task-specific language emerges during program synthesis; grounding the symbols the parser can extract in core knowledge theory from cognitive psychology; and an object-aware fitness that grades partially correct outputs beyond pixel-level discrepancies.

title: Why does ChatGPT keep giving me Godot 3 code? We tested 150 answers
description:
ChatGPT gives you Godot 3 code when the model behind it mixes up the two versions. Godot 4.0 shipped on 1 March 2023 and renamed or removed many Godot 3 classes, methods and keywords, so KinematicBody2D, export var and yield no longer work. A current model may not do this anymore: in November 2026 we asked GPT-6 Luna, a current OpenAI model, 10 beginner Godot questions in plain chat, with "Godot 4" in the prompt, without a version, and with web search on. In 150 answers it wrote 0 Godot 3 API errors. What did go wrong was different: a few parse errors, and a few runtime-only bugs that Godot's parser accepts. If you still get Godot 3 code, use a current model, say your Godot version, and check the code in Godot.

Ziva.sh makes Ziva, an AI agent for Godot, and ran this test. We captured every answer on 10 November 2026 (UTC) and checked the code on Godot 4.7.2. We called GPT-6 Luna through OpenAI's Codex endpoint with a ChatGPT account login, not through the ChatGPT app, which can behave differently. We also ran the same prompts through Ziva on the same model; results are below.

Where the complaints come from

  • In October 2024 a Godot forum user posted ChatGPT-written code with onready var and self.connect("input_event", self, "_on_input_event") that failed in Godot 4, and added the next day: "Even ChatGPT4.o failed".
  • In September 2025 a forum thread asked whether ChatGPT is a good way to learn Godot. One reply: "they confuse Godot 4 and Godot 3 functions". Another: "The Godot 3/4 mix up is real".
  • In September 2026 a forum user wrote that AI answers "are mixes from the syntax of Godot3 and Godot4. Even if i explicit say for Godot4..", without naming the AI.

Only the first names a specific model version, GPT-4o. We cannot tell which models the others used, and our result says nothing about those models.

How we tested

We wrote 10 beginner prompts from forum threads: a 2D platformer player, a third-person controller, spawning enemies on a timer, saving a high score, a Start button that changes scene, fading out a coin, placing tiles from code, a health bar that follows an exported variable, random numbers, and a trap that disappears after 2 seconds. None names an API that changed between Godot 3 and 4. Example: "I'm making my first 2D platformer in Godot 4. Can you write me a player script so my character can run left and right, jump, and fall with gravity?"

Plain chat got each prompt 3 times per setup, with no project and no system prompt apart from the web-search setup's short instruction to answer from web results. An AI agent read every code block and a script scanned it for a checklist of Godot 3 forms built from the official upgrade guide and Godot 4.7.2's own upgrade-tool rename map; the same agent did both, and the read was not blind to the scan. Every script also went through Godot 4.7.2's --check-only. Every runtime error below was confirmed by running the code headless on Godot 4.7.2.

Results

Setup Godot 3 API errors Other real errors
GPT-6 Luna plain chat, prompt says "Godot 4", default reasoning GPT-6 Luna plain chat: 0 in 30 answers GPT-6 Luna plain chat: 3 answers (2 parse errors, 1 runtime error)
GPT-6 Luna plain chat, prompt says "Godot 4", low reasoning GPT-6 Luna plain chat, low reasoning: 0 in 30 GPT-6 Luna plain chat, low reasoning: none
GPT-6 Luna plain chat, prompt says only "Godot" GPT-6 Luna plain chat, no version: 0 in 30 GPT-6 Luna plain chat, no version: 2 answers (1 runtime error, 1 told to connect a signal StaticBody2D does not have)
GPT-6 Luna with web search, prompt says "Godot 4" GPT-6 Luna with web search: 0 in 30 GPT-6 Luna with web search: 2 answers (1 runtime error, 1 wrong setup instruction)
GPT-6 Luna with web search, prompt says only "Godot" GPT-6 Luna with web search, no version: 0 in 30 GPT-6 Luna with web search, no version: 2 answers (both parse errors)
Ziva on GPT-6 Luna, question prompts as above Ziva on GPT-6 Luna: 0 in 10 chats Ziva on GPT-6 Luna: 2 chats (1 parse error in chat reply code, 1 runtime error)
Ziva on GPT-6 Luna, build-it prompts ("Add the script to my project.") Ziva on GPT-6 Luna: 0 in 10 chats Ziva on GPT-6 Luna: 1 chat (runtime error)
Ziva on GPT-6 Luna, build-it prompts, only "Godot" Ziva on GPT-6 Luna: 0 in 10 chats Ziva on GPT-6 Luna: 2 chats (1 runtime error, 1 instruction that breaks the script)

The code used Godot 4 forms throughout: @export, @onready, CharacterBody2D with the velocity property and move_and_slide() without arguments, instantiate(), pressed.connect(...), create_tween(), change_scene_to_file(), TileMapLayer.set_cell(), randi_range() and await ... .timeout.

Without a version in the prompt and without search, 18 of 30 plain-chat answers said they target Godot 4 and the rest named no version; none targeted Godot 3. With web search on, every search GPT-6 Luna ran started with site:docs.godotengine.org/en/stable, its own choice. Docs pages for Godot 3 or older came back in the search results of 23 of 60 answers, no answer cited one, and none of those answers had Godot 3 code.

Zero is not proof of never. If every answer were independent, 0 in 150 would put the rate below about 2% with 95% confidence; answers to the same prompt are not independent, so the real uncertainty is larger.

What went wrong instead

Seven of the 150 plain-chat answers had code that does not work in Godot 4.7.2: four fail to parse and three parse cleanly and break when they run. Two more gave wrong setup instructions. Three examples.

1. Turning off an Area2D inside its own signal. This line appeared in five places across plain chat and Ziva, in the coin and trap prompts:

func _on_body_entered(_body: Node2D) -> void:
    collected = true
    monitoring = false

--check-only accepts it. When the player touches the coin, Godot 4.7.2 prints this and monitoring stays true:

ERROR: Function blocked during in/out signal. Use set_deferred("monitoring", true/false).

Use set_deferred("monitoring", false), as several other answers did.

2. A setter that touches a node before it exists. One web-search answer wrote this health bar script:

@export var health: float = 100.0:
    set(value):
        health = clampf(value, 0.0, max_health)
        $ProgressBar.max_value = max_health
        $ProgressBar.value = health

It parses. Set Health to 50 in the Inspector and run the scene: the saved value is applied before the ProgressBar child is added, so the setter fails and the bar shows 0 until health changes again in code:

ERROR: Node not found: "ProgressBar" (relative to "Node").
SCRIPT ERROR: Invalid assignment of property or key 'max_value' with value of type 'float' on a base object of type 'null instance'.

Wrap the two $ProgressBar lines in if is_node_ready(): and update the bar once in _ready().

3. A type Godot cannot infer. Four answers failed to parse, three of them on an untyped loop variable in tile-placement code, like this:

for direction in [Vector2i.UP, Vector2i.DOWN, Vector2i.LEFT, Vector2i.RIGHT]:
    var neighbor := cell + direction

Parse Error: Cannot infer the type of "neighbor" variable because the value doesn't have a set type.

for direction: Vector2i in [...] fixes it. Unlike the first two, --check-only catches this one.

What Godot's parser catches, and what it does not

No answer used Godot 3 code, so this list comes from running each Godot 3 form through Godot 4.7.2 ourselves.

Godot 4.7.2's --check-only rejects these, so a parse check finds them:

  • export var, onready var, tool, setget, yield and remote func
  • button.connect("pressed", self, "_on_pressed"): "Invalid argument for "connect()" function: argument 2 should be "Callable" but is ..."
  • File.new(), Directory.new(), OS.get_ticks_msec(), rand_range(), update(), BUTTON_LEFT
  • .empty() on a typed Array
  • move_and_slide(velocity, Vector2.UP) and velocity = move_and_slide()
  • classes such as KinematicBody2D, Spatial, Position2D and PoolStringArray
  • rect_position and translation on the script's own node

These pass Godot 4.7.2's --check-only and fail only when the line runs:

  • scene.instance(): "Invalid call. Nonexistent function 'instance' in base 'PackedScene'."
  • get_tree().change_scene() and change_scene_to()
  • Tween.new() and the Tween node's interpolate_property(): "Tween can't be created directly. Use create_tween() method."
  • yield(get_tree(), "idle_frame") rewritten as await get_tree().idle_frame
  • TileMap set_cellv() and world_to_map()
  • rect_position and .empty() on an untyped variable

Check AI-written GDScript in one line

Parse and analyze one script without opening the editor:

godot --headless --path /path/to/your/project --check-only --script res://player.gd

It prints SCRIPT ERROR: Parse Error: ... with the line and exits with code 1. A clean script exits with 0. Replace godot with the path to your Godot 4 executable.

For the runtime-only list, run the scene. In the editor, press F6 and read the Output and Debugger panels. Headless:

godot --headless --path /path/to/your/project --quit-after 120 res://main.tscn

--quit-after 120 stops after 120 frames. Read the output for SCRIPT ERROR lines: in our run a scene calling change_scene() printed "Invalid call. Nonexistent function 'change_scene' in base 'SceneTree'." and Godot still exited with code 0.

If you still get Godot 3 code

  • Use a current model. The complaint above that names a model is about GPT-4o in 2024; GPT-6 Luna wrote none in our test. We did not test older models side by side.
  • Say your exact version, such as "Godot 4.7". It made no difference for GPT-6 Luna, but a chat model cannot see your project.
  • Check the code in Godot with the two commands above before you build on it.
  • Give your agent a rename table. Our free, MIT-licensed godot-skills pack includes a godot-4-api-pitfalls skill with a Godot 3 to 4 rewrite table and the list of Godot 3 lines that pass --check-only and fail at runtime. It works with agents that read the Agent Skills format; see Godot AI skills.

Where Ziva fits

Ziva is our AI agent inside the Godot editor. It is proprietary and has a free Hobby plan. We ran the same 10 prompts through Ziva on the same model, GPT-6 Luna, one chat per prompt, in three sets of 10. Ziva also wrote 0 Godot 3 API errors.

  • Asked a question, Ziva mostly answered in chat. With the prompts above ("How do I ...? Please write the script."), Ziva wrote a file in 1 of 10 chats and replied in chat in the other 9. Ziva does not check code in a chat reply.
  • Asked to build it, Ziva wrote the file and checked it. With the same prompts reworded as instructions ("Add the script to my project."), Ziva wrote a .gd file in all 20 chats. After each write, Ziva's check returned "No problems in this file or its callers." on all 21 writes in the build-it chats.
  • The check is a parse, not a run. It is Godot's GDScript language server plus the editor's script reload, the same kind of check as --check-only. Two of those files had the monitoring = false bug from example 1 and still got "No problems". In a separate probe, a script with instance(), change_scene(), Tween.new() and set_cellv() also got "No problems".

So this test did not show Ziva's check catching a Godot 3 error, because there were none to catch, and the check cannot see runtime-only errors. Running the scene and reading its output catches those. Ziva can run scenes too, but that was not part of this test.

Limits

  • One model, GPT-6 Luna, on one date. Older models, other providers and the ChatGPT app were not tested.
  • Plain chat used OpenAI's Codex endpoint, and web search used that endpoint's search tool with instructions to answer from web results. The model searched only the Godot docs, so old forum answers never came up.
  • 10 prompts that we wrote, 3 answers per prompt in each plain-chat setup and 1 chat per prompt in each Ziva set.
  • We added the "add the script to my project" Ziva prompts after seeing that Ziva answered the question prompts in chat, so the two Ziva sets are not a planned comparison. The no-version and web-search sets were also added after the first results, each written down before it ran.
  • Ziva ran with low reasoning effort and plain chat with the default; the low-reasoning plain chat set covers that gap. Ziva tells the model the Godot version in its own instructions, so its "only Godot" set still had a version.
  • An AI agent, not a person, read the code, and the same agent ran the checklist scan, so the read was not blind to the scan.
  • For the build-it Ziva runs we moved the second editor's language-server port, because two Godot editors were open on the test machine and Ziva's check otherwise queried the other editor, as it did for the one file written in the question set. We filed that as a Ziva bug.

Related reading

  • Claude Godot Code: Claude vs GPT-4o on Godot 4 APIs: training cutoffs and Godot versions
  • How do I generate GDScript with AI?: chat, AI code editors and agents inside Godot
  • Godot AI skills: skill packs for Godot and how to install one

FAQ

Why does ChatGPT keep giving me Godot 3 code when I'm using Godot 4?

Godot 4.0 (March 2023) renamed or removed many Godot 3 classes, methods and keywords, and a model that mixes up the two versions writes code Godot 4 rejects. The forum complaints are real; the one we found that names a specific model version is about GPT-4o, in October 2024. In our November 2026 test, GPT-6 Luna wrote 0 Godot 3 API errors in 150 plain-chat answers to 10 beginner Godot prompts, with Godot 4 in the prompt, without a version, and with web search on. If you still get Godot 3 code, use a current model, say your Godot version, and check the code in Godot.

Does it help to write "Godot 4" in the prompt?

Not measurably for GPT-6 Luna in our test: it wrote 0 Godot 3 API errors in 30 answers with Godot 4 in the prompt and 0 in 30 answers that said only Godot. Without a version, 18 of the 30 answers said they target Godot 4 and none targeted Godot 3. Stating the version still costs nothing, and a plain chat model has no other way to know which Godot you use.

Does web search make ChatGPT write Godot 3 code?

Not in our test. With web search on, GPT-6 Luna wrote 0 Godot 3 API errors in 60 answers. Every search it ran was restricted to the Godot docs site, and docs pages for Godot 3 or older came back in 23 of the 60 answers, but no answer cited one. We used the search tool on OpenAI's Codex endpoint, not the ChatGPT app, and no forum or Reddit page was ever returned, so this does not test old forum answers.

How do I check if AI-written GDScript is valid Godot 4?

Run godot --headless --path /path/to/project --check-only --script res://player.gd with Godot 4. It exits with code 1 and prints Parse Error lines for removed keywords such as export, onready and yield, renamed classes such as KinematicBody2D, and the old connect() form. Some Godot 3 code passes this check and only fails when the line runs, such as instance(), change_scene() and Tween.new(), so also run the scene and read the output.

Which Godot 3 code does Godot 4 only catch at runtime?

On Godot 4.7.2 these pass --check-only and fail when the line runs: PackedScene.instance(), get_tree().change_scene() and change_scene_to(), Tween.new() and the Tween node's interpolate_property, the idle_frame signal, TileMap set_cellv and world_to_map, and rect_position or .empty() on an untyped variable.

What mistakes did GPT-6 Luna make if not Godot 3 code?

Across 150 plain-chat answers, 4 had parse errors (for example var neighbor := cell + direction, where Godot 4.7.2 cannot infer the type) and 3 had runtime-only bugs that pass the parser: setting monitoring = false inside an Area2D body_entered handler, which Godot blocks, and a health setter that touches $ProgressBar before the node exists. Two more gave wrong setup instructions.

Does Ziva stop Godot 3 code?

This test cannot show that. Ziva, running the same GPT-6 Luna model, wrote 0 Godot 3 API errors in 30 chats, so there was nothing for its check to catch. In the build-it chats, its check (Godot's GDScript language server plus the editor's script reload) returned No problems on all 21 writes, including two scripts with a runtime-only bug, because the check parses and analyzes the script without running it.

title: PUMA: Probability-Constrained Sequential Interaction for Forensic Localization
description:
arXiv:2611.13621v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Image manipulation localization must jointly exploit semantic structure and noise-sensitive forensic evidence. However, the effects of spatial correspondence, matching quality, and interaction order are often conflated. Existing semantic-forensic fusion methods provide complementary representations, but do not explicitly preserve quality-mismatch information during spatial correspondence or adaptively select the order in which information is propagated across branches. We propose PUMA (Probability-constrained Unbalanced Matching and Aggregation), which combines spatially constrained unbalanced optimal transport with position-wise convex selection between two sequential operators through a shared positional interface. Before normalization, PUMA retains signed transport-mass residuals, constructs row-stochastic cross-branch and within-noise-branch operators, and updates noise features through a gated residual path. PUMA achieves strong localization results on four test sets, with scores on COVERAGE and NIST16 exceeding the published results of the representative methods listed in our comparison. The experiments support the utility of local matching states and adaptive sequential interaction for cross-source localization and several post-processing conditions.

title: PolyRoute: A Twelve-Language and Code-Mixed Benchmark for Typed-Decision Routing, with Baselines and a Leaderboard
description:
arXiv:2611.13843v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Typed-decision encoders answer a question about a text in one forward pass, but their behaviour outside English is rarely measured on a fixed yardstick. We release PolyRoute: 322 native-language support messages in 12 languages and 9 writing systems, 156 code-mixed or romanised messages (Hinglish, Spanglish, Arabizi), 967 optional native training rows, and a protocol for a three-way department-routing decision. Labels come from Qwen3.8-27B with a blind second pass (91% of candidates kept); an independent model, gemma4-31b, agrees on 97.2% of test items, and the largest character 5-gram similarity between any test text and any training text is 0.33. A leaderboard of 13 systems gives 61.2% for the English-root checkpoint, 77.3% for the shipped multilingual one and 96.6% for the best fine-tune; TF-IDF with logistic regression reaches 91.9%. On four withheld languages the three multilingual systems score 77%, 90% and 93%. On code-mixed text the English root (85%) is nominally ahead of the shipped multilingual checkpoint (79%; p=0.134). The split resolves differences only above about 4 points. All texts and labels are LLM-generated.
