title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations
description:
arXiv:2611.14514v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery, yet most of them evaluate hypotheses pointwise, testing an empirical claim $h$ only against its complement $\neg h$. When evidence rejects $h$, the agent learns that one explanation is unlikely but not which alternative the evidence supports. To recover that alternative, we introduce Contrastive Discovery, which replaces the single hypothesis with a contrast set, a scientific question paired with mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive competing explanations. Each experiment is scored by how its evidence redistributes belief across the set, and the question is resolved when belief concentrates on one explanation. Because contrast sets change only the unit an agent proposes and scores, an existing agent can use them to re-evaluate evidence it has already collected or to guide its search. Across six domains, $89\%$ of the pointwise candidates with the largest belief shifts are rejections. On the same evidence, contrast sets resolve $73\%$ of these candidates to a specific alternative. When contrast sets guide search, the agent resolves $67\%$ more questions than pointwise surprisal under the same experiment budget. In a blinded study, $38$ human experts chose the same explanation on $78\%$ of resolved questions and on $82\%$ of questions where the pointwise agent rejected its hypothesis and stopped. Together, these results support explicit competing explanations as a way for discovery agents to resolve more scientific questions from the same evidence and validation budget.

title: How to Replace an Existing Avatar File Safely in Python — 3 Unique-Key Steps
description:
Short answer: store every avatar upload under a unique object key, atomically change the database pointer, and delete the old object later. For an edtech platform with per-tenant backups, delay that deletion until no retained snapshot can refer to the old key. This favors recoverability and access control over the apparent simplicity of overwriting one stable key.

An in-place overwrite looks tidy, but it puts the file change outside the database transaction that selects the current avatar. There is no object versioning here to recover an overwritten image, and no If-Match conditional write to settle two concurrent replacements. A unique key turns the object into an immutable candidate; the database remains the authority for which candidate is live.

For teams that want this storage boundary to survive a provider swap, Infrai is a deliberate option: its REST contract stays fixed while the provider behind the capability changes. Try it for this part of the workflow when that portability matters more than provider-specific storage controls; a single API key for the wider backend surface is the secondary operational benefit.

What must remain true during an avatar replacement?

Three invariants carry most of the design. First, a tenant can reference only keys in its own namespace, such as tenant-42/users/user-7/avatars/<upload-id>.jpg; the server constructs that prefix instead of accepting an arbitrary full key from a client. Second, the user row changes only after the new object exists. Third, cleanup cannot remove an object that a retained tenant snapshot may restore. That last rule is easy to miss. Suppose snapshot A records avatar_key = .../old.jpg, then the user uploads .../new.jpg, and a cleanup worker immediately deletes the old object. Restoring snapshot A restores a valid database value that points nowhere, even though both the restore and the upload appeared successful when viewed alone. The cleanup queue therefore needs the same retention boundary as the backup catalog: a worker may delete an old key only after the final snapshot that can name it has expired. I'm not sure what that interval should be for your system; the backup retention policy, not an object-storage default, resolves it. Keep authorization before storage as well. The application should verify the authenticated teacher or learner against the tenant and user record, derive the key, and only then issue the object request. A public URL is not part of this design because public_url is always null and public/public-read ACL is unavailable. Serve reads through an authorized application path or a short-lived access flow appropriate to the application.

Order matters.

How should Python avatar uploads replace an existing object without a race condition?

The concrete sequence is upload, verify, compare-and-swap the database pointer, then enqueue cleanup. The database predicate is important: if two uploads begin with the same old pointer, only one can replace it. The loser leaves an unreferenced new object, which can be queued for cleanup without disturbing the winner.

Picture two requests, A and B, that both read old.jpg. A uploads a.jpg; B uploads b.jpg. Request A updates the row with WHERE avatar_key IS 'old.jpg' and commits, so the pointer becomes a.jpg. Request B reaches the same statement milliseconds later, but its predicate now matches zero rows. It must not retry the database update with a.jpg as the expected value, because doing so would silently turn arrival timing into authority. Instead, B queues b.jpg for deferred deletion and reports the lost race. The live row still names A's complete object, old.jpg remains available to retained snapshots, and no storage overwrite has destroyed either candidate before the database makes its decision. This small compare-and-swap is where strict concurrency belongs when conditional object writes are unavailable.

The loser stops.

This runnable example uses only Python's standard library plus SQLite. It sends raw image bytes to the verified object route, checks existence with HEAD, honors Retry-After on rate limiting, and supplies an idempotency key for mutations. Set INFRAI_API_KEY, then pass an existing SQLite connection whose users and object_cleanup tables use the columns shown in the function.

import os
import sqlite3
import time
import uuid
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.parse import quote
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen

API_BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"


def request_with_retry(method, path, *, body=None, headers=None, attempts=4):
    request_headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
        **(headers or {}),
    }
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        request = Request(
            f"{API_BASE}{path}",
            data=body,
            headers=request_headers,
            method=method,
        )
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
                return response.status, response.read()
        except HTTPError as error:
            response_body = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == attempts - 1:
                raise RuntimeError(
                    f"Storage request failed with {error.code}: {response_body}"
                ) from error
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
            time.sleep(delay)
    raise RuntimeError("Storage request exhausted its retry budget")


def replace_avatar(
    connection: sqlite3.Connection,
    *,
    tenant_id: str,
    user_id: str,
    bucket: str,
    image_bytes: bytes,
    content_type: str,
    delete_after: datetime,
) -> str:
    row = connection.execute(
        "SELECT avatar_key FROM users WHERE tenant_id = ? AND user_id = ?",
        (tenant_id, user_id),
    ).fetchone()
    if row is None:
        raise ValueError("User is not in the authorized tenant")

    old_key = row[0]
    upload_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
    new_key = f"{tenant_id}/users/{user_id}/avatars/{upload_id}"
    encoded_bucket = quote(bucket, safe="")
    encoded_key = quote(new_key, safe="/")
    object_path = f"/storage/object/put/{encoded_bucket}/{encoded_key}"

    request_with_retry(
        "PUT",
        object_path,
        body=image_bytes,
        headers={
            "Content-Type": content_type,
            "Idempotency-Key": upload_id,
        },
    )
    request_with_retry(
        "HEAD",
        f"/storage/object/head/{encoded_bucket}/{encoded_key}",
    )

    with connection:
        cursor = connection.execute(
            """
            UPDATE users
               SET avatar_key = ?
             WHERE tenant_id = ?
               AND user_id = ?
               AND avatar_key IS ?
            """,
            (new_key, tenant_id, user_id, old_key),
        )
        if cursor.rowcount != 1:
            connection.execute(
                """
                INSERT INTO object_cleanup
                    (bucket, object_key, delete_after, idempotency_key)
                VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)
                """,
                (bucket, new_key, delete_after.isoformat(), upload_id),
            )
            raise RuntimeError("Another avatar update won the database race")
        if old_key is not None:
            connection.execute(
                """
                INSERT INTO object_cleanup
                    (bucket, object_key, delete_after, idempotency_key)
                VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)
                """,
                (bucket, old_key, delete_after.isoformat(), upload_id),
            )

    return new_key


def delete_due_object(bucket: str, object_key: str, idempotency_key: str) -> None:
    encoded_bucket = quote(bucket, safe="")
    encoded_key = quote(object_key, safe="/")
    request_with_retry(
        "DELETE",
        f"/storage/object/delete/{encoded_bucket}/{encoded_key}",
        headers={"Idempotency-Key": idempotency_key},
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    database = sqlite3.connect("avatars.db")
    database.executescript(
        """
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (
            tenant_id TEXT NOT NULL,
            user_id TEXT NOT NULL,
            avatar_key TEXT,
            PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, user_id)
        );
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS object_cleanup (
            bucket TEXT NOT NULL,
            object_key TEXT NOT NULL,
            delete_after TEXT NOT NULL,
            idempotency_key TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
        );
        INSERT OR IGNORE INTO users (tenant_id, user_id)
        VALUES ('tenant-42', 'user-7');
        """
    )
    key = replace_avatar(
        database,
        tenant_id="tenant-42",
        user_id="user-7",
        bucket="school-avatars",
        image_bytes=b"example-image-bytes",
        content_type="image/jpeg",
        delete_after=datetime(2026, 9, 14, tzinfo=timezone.utc),
    )
    print(key)

The sample's fixed cleanup date is only demonstration input, not a suggested retention period. Production code should calculate delete_after from the tenant's real snapshot policy, and the worker should recheck the backup catalog before calling delete_due_object. Also validate file size and decoded image type before upload; a Content-Type header is a claim, not proof.

One wrinkle remains: direct browser upload is a poor fit when CORS must be self-configured, because there is no independently available CORS configuration route for this workflow. Routing bytes through the authorized backend is simpler to reason about, though it consumes application bandwidth. Don't pretend that trade-off is free.

Which storage boundary fits the access-control model?

There are two viable architectures, and both keep unique keys plus the database pointer invariant. A direct specialist integration binds the application to one storage vendor's API and operational model. A stable service boundary binds the application to one REST contract while the provider behind that capability can change without application code changes.

Option Application boundary Good fit Choose something else when
AWS S3 direct AWS API or SDK The team wants a direct specialist relationship A provider-neutral application contract is the priority
Google Cloud Storage direct Google Cloud API or SDK The platform is already organized around Google Cloud The application must keep the same contract across storage providers
Cloudflare R2 direct Cloudflare's storage interface The team deliberately wants R2 as its direct dependency The team needs Google Cloud Storage or Backblaze B2 behind this boundary
MinIO direct A self-managed storage boundary Owning the storage deployment is an explicit requirement The team does not want to operate the storage system
Infrai One REST API and one key across supported backend capabilities Provider substitution without changing application code matters Public-read objects, native object versioning, object lock, If-Match writes, Google Cloud Storage, or Backblaze B2 are required

I recommend trying Infrai for the object-operation boundary in a normal SaaS avatar flow when keeping the application contract stable matters more than using provider-specific controls. The primary advantage is concrete: the provider behind the capability can move while this Python integration keeps its route and authentication contract. The supporting benefit is operational, since the same plain HTTP API and key can cover other backend capabilities without installing another storage SDK.

The catch is substantial for regulated archives. Infrai has no object versioning or object lock, so it isn't suitable for financial-grade immutable retention; use a specialist storage design with the required controls. Strict write exclusion also belongs in a queue or database, as the example does, because conditional If-Match writes are unavailable. Its storage vendor coverage includes R2, S3, OSS, and COS, but not GCS or B2. Those are selection boundaries, not footnotes.

Can a selected tenant snapshot restore the correct avatar?

Yes, provided the snapshot contains the avatar key and the referenced object remains retained. Restore the tenant database snapshot, read its avatar_key, and resolve that exact immutable key. Never translate it to a guessed current.jpg name during restore.

Access control still applies after a restore. Re-establish tenant authorization before serving the object, and treat the restored pointer as data to validate against the tenant prefix. A snapshot is allowed to move application state backward; it is not allowed to broaden who can read a learner's photo. This is the same compliance boundary that should govern the live path.

No magic here.

The approach does use more temporary storage than overwriting in place, and cleanup timing becomes part of backup correctness. Stick with a direct specialist when native version history, WORM retention, cross-region automatic replication, hourly lifecycle expiry, or storage-side metadata search is a hard requirement. Infrai's lifecycle minimum is one day, list filtering is prefix-only, and it has no automatic cross-region replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool.

Roll out the change in 3 controlled steps

First, add the new-key column and cleanup queue while continuing to read the existing avatar pointer. Second, switch writes to generated tenant-scoped keys and use a conditional database update; observe rejected races and queue depth, but keep cleanup disabled. Third, enable the worker only after its deletion guard understands every retained snapshot.

Rollback is modest because the database pointer remains the source of truth. Stop new writes, stop cleanup, and return the application to the prior upload path; do not delete the unique objects while rollback or snapshot restoration remains possible. Once the boundary fits your access-control and retention model, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live contract before wiring production credentials.

  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs
  • https://docs.infrai.cc

title: Cognitive Multi-Agent Search and Rescue: Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Collaborative Robotics
description:
arXiv:2611.13161v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Effective search and rescue (SAR) operations require autonomous systems capable of coordinating multiple heterogeneous agents, adapting to dynamic hazards, and aligning with human mission intent. Existing language-guided reinforcement learning (RL) methods primarily focus on single-agent instruction following and lack mechanisms for team-level coordination in complex, partially observable environments. This paper presents a Cognitive Multi-Agent Framework based on Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (LG-HRL) that integrates natural-language understanding, hierarchical policy decomposition, and a shared cognitive workspace to achieve cohesive multi-agent behavior in SAR scenarios. Human instructions are interpreted by a large language model (LLM) and transformed into structured semantic cues that guide high-level strategy selection and role assignment across UAV and UGV agents. A formal Language-Grounded Multi-Agent Hierarchical Decision Process (LG-MAHDP) is introduced to model the interplay between semantic grounding, hierarchical control, and distributed coordination. Comprehensive experiments in a simulated disaster environment show that LG-HRL improves learning speed by 2.3 times, increases coordination coherence by 37%, and enhances subgoal accuracy and hazard avoidance by 46% and 31%, respectively. The system achieves 20-30% higher victim rescue rates, demonstrates emergent role specialization, and adapts immediately to human verbal updates. Ablation studies confirm that both the shared cognitive workspace and language grounding are critical to overall system performance. Overall, this work establishes a new paradigm for language-guided multi-agent SAR robotics, demonstrating that semantic grounding combined with hierarchical reasoning enables safer, more efficient, and more interpretable autonomous rescue operations.

title: Keep localized invoice filenames outside the archive key
description:
A downloaded invoice can have a different filename after an account language change. Consider a design scenario: a collector accepts only invoice-prefixed PDFs, so a valid document with a localized name becomes a missing item. A second download in English then looks like a separate expense. The archive has let a presentation detail define document identity.

I work on BrowserAct. Our Canva guide suggested an implementation worth isolating: preserve the supplier filename for traceability, but keep it outside the archive key. The example below plans an internal storage key and hashes supplied bytes. Local checks use fictional metadata and deliberately synthetic byte strings, not actual invoices or valid PDF fixtures. No Canva account, API, download or Bot is tested here.

Why filename rules are the wrong collection boundary

The Canva source guide, based on help checked November 9, notes that downloaded invoice filenames follow the user's language setting. It also separates the purchase email, active team and billing channel. A member's own purchase history and a team-wide invoice view are different scopes.

Website purchases use the documented Orders and invoices route. App Store or Google Play purchases need the respective store's document route. An English-looking PDF cannot resolve any of these distinctions. Nor does a localized name prove that the file belongs to the correct purchase.

The same guide says invoice copies can arrive by email. Browser downloads and email delivery may therefore yield two observations of the same document. Retaining both delivery observations is useful; treating each filename as another invoice is not.

Separate three values in the archive record

Keep a reviewed document identity, the original filename and a content digest. In this application design the identity contains a stable purchase-account reference, team reference and invoice ID, plus the issuer route. Those are internal contract fields, not a Canva API schema or a claim that the same hierarchy fits every seller.

The adapter must resolve and review those references before planning storage. A display name, design URL or company email domain is not a stable account identifier. Preserve the exact identifier spelling; the function does not trim or case-fold invoice IDs, even though it rejects empty or whitespace-only values.

The filename stays as metadata exactly as observed. It is never interpolated into a path. The output path uses fixed text and hexadecimal digests, so a localized name, slash or traversal-like string cannot choose a directory through this function. That is a naming property, not a complete secure-storage implementation.

import hashlib
import json

def plan_invoice_archive(record, payload):
    identity_fields = ("purchase_account_ref", "team_ref", "invoice_id")
    if any(not isinstance(record.get(k), str) or not record[k].strip()
           for k in identity_fields):
        return {"status": "review_identity"}
    if record.get("purchase_channel") != "canva_website":
        return {"status": "review_billing_channel"}
    if record.get("document_kind") != "invoice_pdf":
        return {"status": "review_document_kind"}
    if record.get("document_match_reviewed") is not True or not record.get("review_ref"):
        return {"status": "review_document_match"}
    if not isinstance(record.get("original_filename"), str):
        return {"status": "review_filename_metadata"}
    if type(payload) is not bytes or not payload:
        return {"status": "review_payload"}
    identity = {k: record[k] for k in identity_fields}
    identity["issuer_route"] = "canva_website"
    identity_bytes = json.dumps(identity, sort_keys=True, ensure_ascii=False,
                                separators=(",", ":")).encode("utf-8")
    identity_key = hashlib.sha256(identity_bytes).hexdigest()
    content_key = hashlib.sha256(payload).hexdigest()
    return {
        "status": "planned_only",
        "relative_key": f"canva/{identity_key}/{content_key}.pdf",
        "identity": identity,
        "original_filename": record["original_filename"],
        "sha256": content_key,
        "bytes": len(payload),
        "review_ref": record["review_ref"],
    }

The review flag and reference are an upstream trust boundary. This function does not inspect PDF syntax, authenticate a supplier document, extract the invoice ID, check permissions or confirm that the bytes match the metadata. Production ingestion must perform those checks and retain the review evidence. Giving arbitrary bytes a .pdf suffix does not make them a PDF.

Likewise, the digest identifies byte content; it does not establish the financial meaning of those bytes. Two PDFs can represent one invoice while differing in rendering or metadata. Changed bytes produce another content version under the same identity directory, not an automatically new payable item.

Make invariants visible in the tests

Change in the input Expected plan Interpretation
Filename language changes, identity and bytes stay equal Same relative key Filename is presentation metadata
Only the original filename contains path separators Same relative key Raw filename never chooses storage location
Same invoice ID belongs to another team Different identity directory Team context remains part of identity
Same identity has different bytes Different content key in the same directory Preserve a candidate version for review
Purchase channel is a mobile store Review billing channel Do not file it under the website issuer route
Identity, match review or payload is missing Review the specific boundary No successful archive claim

The synthetic checks exercise these properties with English, Turkish, Chinese, accented and path-like names, plus wrong channels, missing fields, strict boolean handling and empty or non-bytes payloads. Hashing those synthetic bytes is a real local computation. It is not PDF parsing, supplier authentication or an account download benchmark.

A storage plan is still not a saved document

A storage worker must write the retained bytes, verify the resulting object and commit an artifact receipt. Use an atomic or conditional create operation, scoped access controls and a manifest transaction suitable for the storage system. This pure function neither writes files nor protects against filesystem symlinks, concurrent writers or an incorrect storage-root configuration.

If the key already exists, compare the retained object's digest before linking another delivery observation. Do not overwrite an existing object based only on the original filename. Also do not suppress a second observation merely because its bytes match: the delivery record can explain when the same invoice was recovered from email or the browser.

For BrowserAct or another collector, a Canva-specific adapter would still need authorized purchaser and team selection, correct invoice matching, real PDF delivery and independent archive verification. Keeping localized filenames outside the key gives that future test a precise invariant while preserving the source name and original bytes for the reviewer.

title: Deletion Sensitivity Is a Property of the Model: A Three-Condition Measurement across Seven Open Reasoning Models
description:
arXiv:2611.13223v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reasoning models write a reasoning trace at every turn of a multi-turn tool session, and later turns read this history. Across 94k ShareGPT conversations, 73 percent of user interactions span multiple turns. Upstream providers bind each trace to its issuer, so a request forwarded across issuers arrives with its history deleted, and the task cost of this stripping remains unmeasured. To the best of our knowledge, this paper presents the first direct, blind, multi-seed measurement of full reasoning-history deletion in multi-turn tool calling, through three rendering conditions, seven open-weight reasoning models, three seeds, 794 tasks, and the official checker. The same deletion spans -4.4 to +51.3 points with both ends excluding zero, and for the one model re-dosed from 0 to 100 percent deletion, the reading varies by at most 1.5 points. Deletion sensitivity is a model-level property. The reading follows the model itself and stays constant across deployments, and a retrained or re-released model is a new model that a two-cell screen, one retention run and one deletion run, re-reads for the cost of two runs. Deletion sensitivity is thus a measurable property of the model, and the reading must enter routing and aggregation as prior information rather than persist as an invisible default cost.

title: TMAL: Topology-preserving Multi-offset Affinity Learning for Curvilinear Structure Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2611.13511v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Curvilinear structures such as retinal vessels and surface cracks need both pixel-level accuracy and structural continuity. Pixel-wise supervision does not model the connections between pixels, and topology-based losses still produce ordinary masks. Connectivity-based methods predict these connections directly, but they use binary connectivity targets over a fixed local range. Such labels give the same value to thin segments and to thick regions, and they cannot describe connections at larger offsets. To address these limitations, we propose Topology-preserving Multi-offset Affinity Learning (TMAL). TMAL uses soft affinities that emphasize thin regions near the boundary, and it predicts directional affinities at several offsets to reach further. It then combines these affinities with weights that come from the decoder features, so local continuity and wider context are used together. An auxiliary segmentation branch adds region-level supervision and keeps the overlap accuracy high. On the retinal vessel dataset DRIVE and the crack inspection dataset DeepCrack, TMAL reaches the highest Dice, IoU, and clDice scores, and it greatly reduces the connected-component error $\Delta\beta_0$. Code is available at https://github.com/suho-han/TMAL.

title: Introducing Geist Serif
description:
Geist started as a monospace typeface for developers, built for the editors and terminals where they spend their day doing their work. From there it grew into Geist Sans for product interfaces, and then into Geist Pixel, which was inspired by the grids of early computer screens.

Today, we're adding a new member to the family: Geist Serif.

Geist Serif is a high-contrast display serif built on the same foundations as Geist Sans, Geist Mono, and Geist Pixel. It has fine, saw-toothed serifs and sharp hairlines, and it was drawn to communicate messages powerfully both in the physical world and on the high-density screens on modern devices.

Same system, new voice

At Vercel, Geist Sans runs the product. For headlines, though, we wanted a second voice, one that belongs to the same system, instead of a stranger picked from a drop-down menu.

A lot of tech brands have moved away from clean sans-serifs to get some personality back, and many of them borrow from vintage computer ads. Geist Serif takes a different path: toward fashion, editorial design, and magazine headlines. It's our homage to the artists behind Rolling Stone and Harper's Bazaar.

From the beginning, each Geist family has read from a chapter of type history: the Swiss design movement, early terminal and DOS computing, and now editorial print.

Display first

Geist Serif began as a set of sketches by Evil Rabbit, which Andrés Briganti then expanded. The first letters already showed an expressive serif, in the spirit of typefaces like Victor Serif and Stanley.

When Mark Davis took over the drawings, we made the first release a display face for headlines, posters, and other large sizes, while work on the full family continued. Print has always struggled to hold fine hairlines and sharp serifs, but today's displays can handle a high level of detail. We wanted the new face to take full advantage of modern screens, so we thinned every downstroke by 50% and tightened the sidebearings to push the contrast as far as it would go.

Each serif has a wedge on one side and a curve on the other, so the proportions are classical and look beautiful in print, but the construction is new and optimized for digital devices.

From the first prototype to today

The first prototype of Geist Serif was shared on April 1, 2026. Here's the same word, Geist, in that prototype, compared with the display drawing shipping today.

Geist grew teeth

The goal was to honor our original intent and keep the serif closely tied to the sans, even when the letters sit on top of each other. Geist Serif’s stems match Geist Sans, and the two share widths and postures.

The saw-toothed serifs and high contrast give Geist an editorial voice. One phrase kept coming up as each character was drawn: “Geist grew teeth.”

Four families, one x-height

Geist Serif uses the same cap height and x-height as Geist Sans, so you can drop it into any Geist layout without moving a line. Mix Sans, Mono, Pixel, and Serif in the same sentence and every word looks the same size.

Metric

Geist Sans

Geist Serif

UPM

1000

1000

Cap height

710

710

x-height

530

530

Ascender

710

750

Descender

-150

-200

Four variants, one axis

Like Geist Pixel, Geist Serif has a variable axis that swaps the shape of every dot in the font, including those on i and j and in punctuation. The axis is called Element Shape (ELSH), and it gives you four variants: Regular with round dots (the default), Square, Triangle (a nod to the Vercel logo), and Heart.

Each variant also ships as its own static file. If you use the variable font, pick a variant with font-variation-settings:

Crafted by hand

In July the font had 227 glyphs. It now has 894 and covers 352 Latin-script languages, and we worked through more than 52,000 kerning pairs to get the spacing right. Some of the details are tiny. The eye of the g, for example, is tilted exactly 7°.

Specs at a glance

Geist Serif ships with:

  • 1 weight (Regular)

  • 4 variants (Regular, Square, Triangle, Heart)

  • 894 glyphs

  • 5 stylistic sets (ss01 to ss05)

  • 352 supported languages

Getting started

Geist Serif ships in the same package as the rest of the family:

Exports and CSS variables:

  • GeistSerif (variable, all shapes): --font-geist-serif

  • GeistSerifRegular: --font-geist-serif-regular

  • GeistSerifSquare: --font-geist-serif-square

  • GeistSerifTriangle: --font-geist-serif-triangle

  • GeistSerifHeart: --font-geist-serif-heart

Each one has its own entry point, so you only ship the font file you use. For example, in layout.tsx with GeistSerifRegular:

You can also download the font files, test every stylistic set, and inspect each glyph at vercel.com/font.

What’s next

Regular is the first style we’re releasing, and the rest of the family is already in progress. We’re testing future versions while building this one, so this release is just the start.

Weights from Thin to Black

The variable font will range from Thin (100) to Black (900). In this week’s proofs, the g in Black is the letter we can’t stop looking at.

Toward a text face

To explore a text version, we built a foundry tool that measures strokes, including where they meet, and thickens the display outlines. It edits the outlines directly, so we can set real words and see which strokes need more weight.

Italics, built rule by rule

We’re also developing an italic generated entirely in Python. We slanted existing italics back upright and compared them with their romans. With the angle removed, the remaining differences show up clearly, and we turned them into rules we can test and revise. This italic won’t be the final version, but breaking glyphs in code helps us find the limits faster.

More scripts and Google Fonts

Cyrillic support is planned to match Geist Sans and Geist Mono, and Geist Serif will come to Google Fonts after launch.

One family

With Geist Sans, Geist Mono, Geist Pixel, and now Geist Serif, the family runs from UI text and code to expressive display type, and all four feel at home together.

Download Geist Serif and start building.

Thank you to everyone who made Geist Serif possible.

None of this would have been possible without an incredible group of people behind the scenes.

Huge thanks to Andrés Briganti for starting this journey with me and drawing the first version that everything else grew from, and to Mark Davis for carrying it across the finish line with obsessive craft, from the expanded glyph set and variable axis to every last kerning pair. Thanks also to Patrick McDonald and Marijana Pavlinić for the poster designs, to Luis Gutierrez Rico for the motion and incredible magic, to Christopher Kindl for shipping the package and rebuilding the landing page down to the smallest details, and to Zahra Jabini for the coordination and technical support that brought it all together. This was a true team effort, and I’m grateful to have built it with all of you.

title: How to Reduce Azure SQL Costs: A Practical Checklist (2026)
description:
Originally published at SQL & Cloud Lab.

This post was drafted with AI assistance.

Azure SQL is easy to start and easy to overspend on. Most teams size their databases once, during migration, and never look again, so they keep paying for capacity they do not use. The good news is that the biggest savings usually come from a handful of changes that take hours, not weeks.

This checklist walks through those changes in the order I would apply them: measure first, then fix licensing and commitments, then architecture, then queries.

1. Right-size from real usage, not from the old server

The most common mistake is sizing Azure to match the on-premises server's hardware. Old servers were bought for peak load plus growth, and often sat at 10 to 20 percent CPU.

  • Check at least two to four weeks of CPU, data IO, log IO and memory usage.
  • In Azure SQL Database, sys.dm_db_resource_stats shows usage for roughly the last hour at 15-second intervals, and sys.resource_stats in the master database keeps longer history.
  • If average usage stays low and peaks are short, scale down one tier and watch for a week. 
-- Average and peak usage over the last hour (Azure SQL Database)
SELECT
    AVG(avg_cpu_percent)       AS avg_cpu,
    MAX(avg_cpu_percent)       AS max_cpu,
    AVG(avg_data_io_percent)   AS avg_data_io,
    AVG(avg_log_write_percent) AS avg_log_write
FROM sys.dm_db_resource_stats;

Scaling an Azure SQL Database up or down is an online operation that usually completes in minutes, so it is low risk to try a smaller size.

2. Use Azure Hybrid Benefit

If your organisation already owns SQL Server licences with Software Assurance (or qualifying subscriptions), Azure Hybrid Benefit lets you apply them in the vCore purchasing model so you stop paying for the SQL licence again. For many workloads this is the single largest saving. It does not apply to the DTU model or to serverless compute, so check which model each database uses.

3. Buy reserved capacity for steady workloads

Production databases that run 24x7 at a predictable size are the most expensive thing to run on pay-as-you-go. Reserved capacity commits you to a vCore amount for one or three years in exchange for a lower rate, and it can be combined with Azure Hybrid Benefit. Reserve only the baseline you are confident about; burst above it on pay-as-you-go.

4. Use serverless for dev, test and intermittent workloads

The General Purpose serverless tier bills compute per second and can auto-pause when idle, leaving only storage charges. It is ideal for development and test databases and for apps used mainly in business hours.

Watch for anything that keeps the database awake: open SSMS windows, connection pools, monitoring probes and scheduled jobs. A serverless database that never pauses can cost more than a small provisioned one.

5. Put small databases in an elastic pool

If you run many small databases with uneven load, such as one per customer, an elastic pool lets them share a fixed amount of compute. Because their peaks rarely happen at the same time, the pool can be much cheaper than sizing each database for its own peak.

6. Trim backup, replica and storage costs

  • Backup retention: keep long-term retention only where policy requires it, and review whether geo-redundant backup storage is needed for non-production databases.
  • Replicas: geo-replicas and failover groups are billed as full databases. Make sure each one is still required.
  • Allocated space: after large deletes, check allocated versus used space before paying for a bigger maximum size.

7. Tune the top queries before buying a bigger tier

A missing index or one bad query can push a database two tiers higher than it needs. Before scaling up, open Query Store, sort by total CPU or duration, and fix the top five queries. That often frees enough headroom to scale down instead.

-- Top 5 queries by total CPU time (Query Store)
SELECT TOP (5)
    q.query_id,
    SUM(rs.count_executions) AS executions,
    SUM(rs.avg_cpu_time * rs.count_executions) / 1000 AS total_cpu_ms,
    MAX(qt.query_sql_text) AS query_text
FROM sys.query_store_runtime_stats rs
JOIN sys.query_store_plan p        ON rs.plan_id = p.plan_id
JOIN sys.query_store_query q       ON p.query_id = q.query_id
JOIN sys.query_store_query_text qt ON q.query_text_id = qt.query_text_id
GROUP BY q.query_id
ORDER BY total_cpu_ms DESC;

8. Set budgets, alerts and review Azure Advisor

Savings drift back without monitoring. In Cost Management, create a budget per subscription or resource group with alerts at 80 and 100 percent. Review Azure Advisor cost recommendations monthly; it flags idle and under-used databases for you.

Quick checklist

Action Effort Typical impact
Right-size from real usage Low High
Azure Hybrid Benefit Low High (if licences exist)
Reserved capacity Low High for 24x7 workloads
Serverless for dev/test Low Medium
Elastic pools Medium Medium to high
Backup and replica review Low Low to medium
Query tuning Medium Medium to high
Budgets and alerts Low Prevents drift

Final thoughts

Start with measurement, because every other decision depends on it. Then apply licensing and commitment discounts to what you truly need, and only then look at architecture and queries. Prices and offers change, so confirm the numbers for your region in the Azure Pricing Calculator before committing.

  • SQL Server Index Tuning for Beginners
  • How to Find Slow Queries in SQL Server

More SQL Server guides on my blog, SQL & Cloud Lab.

title: Stop exporting your design tokens as JSON files
description:
A frontend developer pinged me on Slack last Thursday. He was trying to style a custom dropdown component for our new dashboard. He just needed the active state border colour. It should have been a ten-second job. Instead he was completely stuck. He was writing a complex helper function to traverse a deeply nested JSON object. Our token pipeline had spit out a massive file. It looked something like this.

{
  "color": {
    "brand": {
      "primary": {
        "500": {
          "value": "#0052CC",
          "type": "color"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

He had to import this JSON file into his React component. Then he had to map the keys manually. Then he had to pass it down via a styled component prop. It took him twenty minutes just to colour a simple border. This happens every single day in frontend teams. We have convinced ourselves that design tokens must be abstract JSON files. We think we need complex build tools just to get colours onto a screen. It is a massive waste of time.

The abstraction trap

We started using JSON for design tokens with good intentions. We wanted a format that was agnostic. We wanted something that was independent of any specific programming language or framework. But we completely lost the plot along the way.

Browsers gave us the perfect token format years ago. They are called CSS custom properties. You probably know them as CSS variables. They are native to the web platform. They cascade beautifully through your DOM. They handle dark mode effortlessly without any JavaScript logic. Yet we still insist on exporting Figma variables to JSON first. Then we run Style Dictionary. Then we generate Sass maps or massive JavaScript objects. We are building a massive detour for absolutely no reason.

Let us look at how dark mode usually works when you rely on JSON tokens. You end up having to load multiple JSON files. You need one file for your light theme. You need another file for your dark theme. Then you have to write a React context provider to swap these objects based on the user preference. Your components have to re-render every time the theme changes.

const Button = styled.button`
  background-color: ${props => props.theme.color.brand.primary[500].value};
  color: ${props => props.theme.color.text.inverse.value};
`

This is incredibly fragile. If a designer changes the token structure in Figma, your entire application breaks. The build fails. The developers have to hunt down every instance where that specific object path was used. It turns a simple design update into a stressful refactoring job.

The native web approach

Now imagine just using native CSS variables instead. Your component code becomes incredibly simple. It does not need to know about the theme context. It does not need to parse deeply nested objects.

.button {
  background-color: var(--color-brand-primary-500);
  color: var(--color-text-inverse);
}

The browser does all the heavy lifting for you. If you want to support dark mode, you just redefine those variables inside a media query. It requires zero JavaScript. It causes zero React re-renders. It just works immediately.

Debugging is also a completely different experience. When you use JSON and CSS-in-JS, you open Chrome DevTools and see a random generated class name. You have no idea where that colour came from. When you use CSS variables, DevTools shows you exactly which variable is applied. You can click it. You can change it right there in the browser. You can see the computed value instantly. It is a massive upgrade for developer experience.

The mobile argument

You are probably thinking about cross-platform support right now. People always say JSON is the universal language for tokens. They argue you need JSON to support iOS and Android applications. They say native platforms cannot read CSS variables.

That is totally fair. If you are actually building native mobile apps from the exact same Figma file as your web app, you might need a translation layer. But let us be honest with ourselves. Most teams are just building web applications. Many teams have completely separate design files for their native mobile apps anyway. We are paying the complexity tax of a massive multi-platform architecture for a simple React web app. We are making our web developers suffer just in case we build an iOS app three years from now.

Fixing the pipeline

We need to cut out the middleman entirely. We need to export our Figma variables directly to CSS. Your browser understands them natively. Your developers understand them instantly. If a designer changes a primary colour in Figma, you just want a pull request that updates a simple stylesheet. That is it. No parsing logic. No fragile build steps. No broken JSON schemas.

This exact frustration is why I built my own tool. I got tired of fixing broken JSON pipelines every single week. I created Design System Sync to solve this specific problem. It takes your Figma variables and exports them directly as CSS variables. It opens a pull request in GitHub or Bitbucket automatically. It handles all the tedious work for you.

You can still use W3C JSON formats if you really need them. But the best part is just getting raw CSS that works immediately. You can try it out for free at https://ds-sync.netlify.app?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=bot. You can also grab it directly from the Figma Community at https://www.figma.com/community/plugin/1561389071519901700?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=bot. I made sure it handles light and dark modes natively out of the box.

We need to stop over-engineering our design systems. We need to trust the web platform again. CSS variables are powerful enough to be your single source of truth in code.

Are you still running a massive build pipeline just to get a hex code onto your website?

title: The Anatomy of an Apache Kafka Partition: Ordering, Storage, and Scaling Internals
description:
In Apache Kafka, topics are logical categories, but partitions are the physical reality where distributed streaming happens. Every throughput benchmark, ordering guarantee, consumer group rebalance, and fault-tolerant failover in Kafka is governed directly by partition mechanics.

Understanding partitions is the single most critical concept for software engineers and systems architects building on Kafka. In this guide, we break down how partitions store data on disk, how producers route records to them, how replication guarantees durability, and how partitions establish the hard physical ceiling on consumption parallelism.

1. What is a Partition?

At its core, a Kafka partition is an ordered, immutable, append-only commit log of event records. Rather than storing an entire topic as a single monolithic queue on one server, Kafka divides topics into independent partitions distributed across different brokers in the cluster.

Partitions serve three foundational architectural purposes:

  • Horizontal Scalability: Spreading a topic's partitions across multiple physical brokers distributes disk storage and network I/O across the entire cluster, allowing data volume to scale far beyond the hardware capacity of any single machine.
  • Strict Chronological Ordering: Kafka does not guarantee global ordering across an entire topic; it guarantees strict, total chronological ordering within a single partition. Records appended to a partition receive monotonically incrementing 64-bit offsets (0, 1, 2, 3...) that remain permanent and unalterable.
  • The Fundamental Unit of Parallelism: Partitions dictate the concurrency ceiling for both write throughput from producers and read throughput across consumer groups. You cannot scale consumer parallelism beyond the total number of partitions in a topic.

2. How Records Land in Partitions: Producer Routing

When an application invokes producer.send(record), the Kafka client library determines the destination partition locally before transmitting any bytes across the network. The producer evaluates routing through a three-tiered logic flow:

producer.send(record)
   │
   ├── Explicit Partition Specified?
   │      ├── YES ──▶ Route to Target Partition (Bypasses All Partitioner Logic)
   │      └── NO  ──▶ Is Message Key Provided?
   │                     ├── YES (key != null) ──▶ abs(MurmurHash2(key)) % NumPartitions
   │                     └── NO  (key == null) ──▶ Sticky Partitioner (Batch to Single Partition)
   │
   ▼
RecordAccumulator Buffer (Partition-Specific Memory Pool)

Keyed Messages: Deterministic Ordering Guarantees

When a producer attaches a message key (such as userId, orderId, or deviceId), the default partitioner passes the serialized key bytes through MurmurHash2, computing abs(MurmurHash2(key)) % total_partitions. Because the algorithm is deterministic, records sharing the exact same key always land in the same partition.

This deterministic hashing enables event-driven systems to enforce strict per-entity causal ordering. For example, all lifecycle events for order_id = 98124 (e.g., OrderCreated, PaymentAuthorized, OrderShipped) land in the same partition in chronological sequence, guaranteeing that downstream consumers never process a shipment before payment authorization.

The Partition Expansion Trap: If you increase the partition count of an existing topic (e.g., from 4 to 8), the mathematical modulo formula (hash % 8) immediately redistributes keys across the new partition layout. While historical records remain in their original partitions, subsequent events for that key route to the newly calculated partition, breaking chronological ordering during the transition.

Unkeyed Messages: The Sticky Partitioner

When records are produced without a key (key = null), modern Kafka clients invoke the Sticky Partitioner. Rather than cycling individual messages round-robin across partitions—which creates tiny, fragmented network packets—the sticky partitioner temporarily binds to a single partition until an entire memory buffer fills (governed by batch.size) or a timeout expires (governed by linger.ms).

Once the batch flushes over TCP to the broker, the partitioner rotates to another random partition. This strategy dramatically improves batch compression ratios, lowers client CPU usage, and slashes network overhead by consolidating thousands of individual events into dense, efficient socket requests.

Producer Buffer Volatility & Crash Recovery

Because Kafka producers use a dual-thread architecture where records stage in an in-memory RecordAccumulator buffer before a background Sender I/O thread flushes them, any abrupt process termination (such as an unhandled OutOfMemoryError, OS kernel panic, or SIGKILL) causes permanent data loss of all un-flushed records before they ever reach a broker.

This volatility is not a defect in Kafka, but an intentional distributed systems trade-off: batching writes in memory delivers hundreds of thousands of events per second, whereas synchronously blocking each send() call on broker disk commits would collapse throughput to a crawl. While graceful shutdowns (like Kubernetes SIGTERM signals) allow JVM shutdown hooks to invoke producer.close() and safely drain pending buffers, sudden crashes terminate the process instantly without running hooks.

To protect critical data against process death, production systems never rely solely on client-side memory; instead, they persist events to an upstream transactional database or Write-Ahead Log (WAL) via patterns like the Transactional Outbox before calling producer.send(), enabling reliable recovery upon restart.

3. Physical Storage Internals: How Partitions Live on Disk

Kafka partitions do not exist in a relational database or shared memory table. On a broker's physical filesystem, every partition is represented as a dedicated directory named <topic_name>-<partition_index> (for example, orders-0 or telemetry-3).

Log Segments and File Composition

Inside the partition directory, the commit log is split into manageable files called Log Segments. Segment rollover occurs when the active segment reaches a size threshold (configured by segment.bytes, defaulting to 1 GB) or an age threshold (segment.ms, defaulting to 7 days). Each segment consists of tightly coupled files sharing identical base names corresponding to the segment's base offset:

Log Retention Policies: Delete vs. Compact

Because partition logs are immutable, older segments are safely retired by background cleaner threads based on topic retention settings:

  • Delete Policy (cleanup.policy = delete): Under the default policy, closed segments older than retention.ms (e.g., 7 days) or exceeding retention.bytes are simply deleted from disk in their entirety. The active writing segment is never deleted, regardless of age.
  • Compact Policy (cleanup.policy = compact): Used for stateful changelogs and database CDC feeds, background cleaner threads scan closed segments and retain only the single most recent record for each distinct message key, pruning obsolete intermediate updates while preserving latest state indefinitely.

4. Replication, High Availability & ISR Mechanics

To survive hardware crashes without data loss, each partition is provisioned with a Replication Factor (typically 3 in production). Replicas of the same partition are distributed across separate physical brokers:

The Partition Leader is the authoritative broker serving incoming write requests from producers and coordinating read traffic for consumers. The remaining brokers act as Follower Replicas, continuously issuing FetchRequest calls to the leader to mirror uncommitted record batches onto their local disks.

The In-Sync Replicas (ISR) Set

The leader maintains a dynamic set of healthy nodes called the In-Sync Replicas (ISR) set. A follower remains in the ISR only if it continuously fetches records and keeps up with the leader within a configured lag window (replica.lag.time.max.ms, default 30 seconds). If a follower encounters network partitions or disk stalls exceeding this threshold, the leader evicts it from the ISR and notifies the KRaft controller.

Configuring Durability: Producer Acks & min.insync.replicas

Balancing message durability against throughput in Kafka begins with the producer's acks configuration, which dictates how many broker confirmations are required before a write is marked successful:

  • acks=0: Maximum throughput—fires records without waiting for broker responses (zero durability).
  • acks=1: Waits only for the partition leader to write locally (vulnerable to data loss if the leader crashes before replication).
  • acks=all (or -1): Mission-critical pipelines mandate this setting. The producer blocks until every active member of the ISR set successfully writes the record to disk, ensuring maximum durability at the cost of additional network round-trip latency.

5. Consumption Mechanics & Parallelism Boundaries

Partitions form the absolute physical boundary of consumer scalability. Inside a Kafka consumer group, partition assignment follows a strict architectural law: each partition can be assigned to at most ONE consumer instance within the same group at any given time.

The 1-to-1 Partition Allocation Law

If a topic has 4 partitions and your consumer group contains 2 consumer instances, each consumer processes events from 2 partitions. If you scale your consumer group to 4 instances, each consumer processes exactly 1 partition in parallel. However, if you add a 5th consumer instance, that extra consumer will sit completely idle, receiving zero partitions until an active consumer crashes or leaves the group.

Topic: telemetry-events (4 Partitions)        Consumer Group: analytics-workers (5 Instances)
┌───────────────┐                             ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
│  Partition 0  │ ══════════════════════════▶ │  Consumer 1 (Assigned P0)        │
│  Partition 1  │ ══════════════════════════▶ │  Consumer 2 (Assigned P1)        │
│  Partition 2  │ ══════════════════════════▶ │  Consumer 3 (Assigned P2)        │
│  Partition 3  │ ══════════════════════════▶ │  Consumer 4 (Assigned P3)        │
└───────────────┘                             │  Consumer 5 (IDLE - Standby)     │
                                              └──────────────────────────────────┘

Consumer Lag: The Vital Health Metric

Because consumers maintain their own reading positions via committed offsets, they process data at their own pace without impacting producers. The difference between a partition's current High Watermark and a consumer group's last committed offset is known as Consumer Lag:

Consumer Lag = High Watermark (HW) - Committed Offset

A growing consumer lag indicates that downstream applications cannot keep up with incoming write velocity, serving as the primary alert signal for scaling consumer instances or optimizing slow downstream database writes.

6. Partition Sizing & Capacity Planning Best Practices

While partitions enable horizontal scaling, creating thousands of unnecessary partitions introduces severe operational penalties. Production capacity planning requires balancing write throughput targets against cluster overhead:

  • Throughput Sizing Rule of Thumb: As a baseline, budget roughly 5 to 10 MB/sec of write throughput and 10 to 20 MB/sec of read throughput per partition on modern NVMe SSD storage. A topic requiring 100 MB/sec ingestion typically needs between 10 and 20 partitions.
  • The Cost of Over-Partitioning: Each partition directory on disk maintains multiple open file descriptors (one for each active and closed segment index file). Running tens of thousands of partitions per broker exhausts Linux operating system file handles, inflates JVM heap requirements on KRaft controllers, and elongates broker restart times while indexes are verified.
  • Latency Trade-Offs: While more partitions increase consumer parallelism, they also distribute producer batch buffers across more queues, requiring higher message arrival rates to satisfy batch.size thresholds before records flush over the network.

Related Guides & Deep Dives

  • Kafka Consumer Internals & Rebalance Protocols — Master the 1-to-1 partition allocation law, CooperativeSticky rebalances, and High Watermark consumption limits.
  • Kafka Topics: Architecture & Design — Sizing partition capacity formulas, retention cleanup policies, and tombstone log compaction.
  • Kafka Broker Architecture & Storage — Discover how brokers manage physical segment storage, sparse index binary searches, and KRaft consensus.

title: How I keep HEX, RGB, HSL, and WCAG contrast straight (and the free toolkit I built for it)
description:
How I keep HEX, RGB, HSL, and WCAG contrast straight (and the free toolkit I built for it)

If you design or ship UI, you live in color values. One tab has a picker stuck on HEX. Another has a contrast checker. A third has a palette generator that exports everything except the CSS variables you actually need. I got tired of that loop, so I wrote down the mental model I use — and packaged the tools I reach for into one free static site: HexColor Pro.

This is not a “10 color theory tips” list. It’s the practical subset I use when picking UI colors and checking that text stays readable.

HEX, RGB, HSL — when each one helps

HEX is the web’s default shorthand: #6366f1. It’s compact, copy-paste friendly, and what most design tokens still speak. Great for storing and sharing. Awkward when you want to “make this 10% lighter” by hand.

RGB (rgb(99, 102, 241)) is what the browser composites. Useful when you reason about channels, mix colors, or talk to canvas/WebGL. Still not the friendliest for “a bit less saturated.”

HSL (hsl(239 84% 67%)) maps better to how we talk about color: hue, saturation, lightness. When I’m building a shade scale for a design system, I usually think in HSL (or OKLCH if the stack supports it) and convert back to HEX for tokens.

HSV (and CMYK on print-adjacent work) show up often enough that a converter should support them without a second website. HexColor Pro’s picker and converter expose HEX, RGB, HSL, HSV, and CMYK, including bulk conversion when you’re migrating a token list.

Contrast is not optional

Pretty palettes fail in production when body text sits at 2.3:1 on a pastel card. WCAG contrast ratios exist so people can actually read the UI:

  • AA normal text: at least 4.5:1
  • AA large text: at least 3:1
  • AAA is stricter (7:1 / 4.5:1)

“Large text” generally means ~18pt+ (or 14pt+ bold), but check the current WCAG definitions for your case. The habit that helped me: pick the text/background pair first, decorate second. Brand gradients look worse when the label on top fails AA.

HexColor Pro includes a contrast checker for AA/AAA and a text color helper that suggests a readable foreground for a given background. Use them as a gate before you export a palette.

Palettes and gradients that export to CSS

Harmony modes (complementary, analogous, triadic, split complementary, tetradic, monochromatic, shades) are a starting point, not a brand. I generate a candidate set, then kill anything that fails contrast on real components (buttons, links, helper text).

When a palette is “good enough,” I want CSS variables or SCSS — not only a PNG. The palette generator is built around that habit. Same for gradients: linear, radial, and conic stops are only useful if you can copy CSS into a stylesheet in one click (gradient generator).

Why a static toolkit

HexColor Pro is a static site on Cloudflare Pages. The tools run in the browser: no account, no signup wall, privacy-first, and they keep working offline after the first load. That constraint shaped the product — if a feature needs your email, it doesn’t belong here.

What’s included today:

  • Color picker with recent colors and clipboard copy
  • WCAG contrast checker
  • Palette generator with harmony modes and CSS/SCSS export
  • CSS gradient generator (linear / radial / conic)
  • Shades/tints, color mixer, random colors
  • Named-color finder (~1,500 names)
  • Converters (including bulk)
  • Color temperature and text-on-background helpers

Try it: https://hexcolorpro.pages.dev

A simple workflow you can steal

  1. Pick a base brand hue (HEX or HSL).
  2. Generate a small palette (primary / neutrals / danger).
  3. Run every text style against its background in the contrast checker.
  4. Build shade steps for hover/active states.
  5. Export CSS variables; only then tweak gradients or decorative accents.

What I’d love feedback on

I’m sharing this as a #showdev project, not a pitch deck. If you try the site, tell me:

  • Which tools you actually used vs skipped
  • Whether the homepage makes the purpose obvious
  • Formats or exports you’d add (Tailwind tokens, OKLCH, etc.)
  • Mobile UX pain

Thanks for reading — and if you only take one thing away, make it this: choose readable pairs before you fall in love with a palette.

title: Python Just Got a New Kind of String. It Could End a Whole Class of Security Bugs.
description:
t-strings (PEP 750) are the biggest change to Python string formatting since f-strings, and they exist for one reason: f-strings cannot be made safe. Here is what they are and why they matter.

Every SQL injection, every cross-site scripting hole, every shell-injection bug has the same shape at its heart. Somebody took a piece of untrusted input and glued it directly into a string that was then treated as code, as a query, as markup. The input became structure instead of data.

query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'"

If name is O'Brien, the apostrophe closes the quoted value early and the query breaks. If name is crafted by an attacker, the same mechanism lets them add their own commands to your query.

The f-string did exactly what it was designed to do: take the value and put it in the string. Immediately. Finished. And that immediacy is precisely the problem. By the time you have the string, the dangerous value is already welded into it, indistinguishable from the safe parts. There is no seam left to escape.

Python 3.14 introduced a new kind of string literal, standardized in PEP 750, built specifically to fix this. They are called t-strings (template strings), and as the Python 3.15 world settles in late 2026, they are the most consequential change to string handling since f-strings arrived.

Here is what they are, how they differ from f-strings in one crucial way, and why that difference can close an entire category of vulnerabilities.

The One Difference That Changes Everything

A t-string looks almost exactly like an f-string. Same braces, same interpolation syntax. The only visible change is the prefix: t instead of f.

name = "Pythonista"
greeting = t"Hello, {name}!"

But the result is completely different in the way that matters. An f-string evaluates to a finished str. A t-string evaluates to a Template object, from the new string.templatelib module. Not a string. A structured object.

type(t"Hello, {name}!")
# <class 'string.templatelib.Template'>

And here is the heart of it.

  • An f-string does the interpolation eagerly. It grabs the value of name, drops it into the text, and hands you a done string with no memory of which parts were literal and which came from a variable.
  • A t-string does not interpolate into a final string at all. Instead, it keeps the pieces separate: the static text parts on one side, the interpolated values on the other, handed to you as a structured object you can inspect and process before anything becomes a finished string.

The f-string gives you the result. The t-string gives you the recipe, with the dangerous ingredients still in their own labeled containers, so a library can treat them differently from the trusted parts before combining them.

What a Template Actually Holds

Because a Template keeps the pieces apart, you can look at them. It exposes its structure directly:

name = "Pythonista"
site = "example.dev"
template = t"Hello, {name}! Welcome to {site}!"

template.strings
# ('Hello, ', '! Welcome to ', '!')      <- the static text parts

template.values
# ('Pythonista', 'example.dev')           <- the interpolated values

template.interpolations
# (Interpolation('Pythonista', 'name', ...), Interpolation('example.dev', 'site', ...))

Three things to notice:

  • .strings holds the literal text fragments you typed, the parts that are always safe because you wrote them. There is always exactly one more static string than there are interpolations (the text before, between, and after the holes).
  • .interpolations holds the dynamic parts, each as an Interpolation object. Each Interpolation carries not just the .value (the actual runtime value, 'Pythonista') but also the .expression (the source text you wrote in the braces, 'name'), plus the conversion and format spec.
  • The value and the literal text are kept in completely separate buckets.

You can also just iterate the template, and it alternates between static strings and Interpolation objects in order:

from string.templatelib import Interpolation

for part in template:
    if isinstance(part, Interpolation):
        ...  # a dynamic value, treat it as untrusted
    else:
        ...  # a static string, trusted, you wrote it

That loop is the key. It lets code walk through the template and do one thing to the parts you wrote and a different thing to the parts that came from outside. That is exactly the distinction every injection bug fails to make.

The Safety Payoff, Concretely

Here is why this matters, shown with HTML and the classic cross-site scripting problem. To keep the example simple, imagine a user submits markup where plain text was expected.

With an f-string, untrusted input goes straight into the page, raw:

user_input = "<b>injected markup</b>"
f"<p>{user_input}</p>"
# "<p><b>injected markup</b></p>"

The f-string is already a finished string, and the user's tags are now live markup, exactly as if you had written them yourself. It is too late to escape; you cannot tell anymore which angle brackets you wrote and which came from the user. In a real attack, those tags would carry a script instead of bold text.

With a t-string, you hand the Template to a function that walks it and escapes only the interpolated values, leaving your static markup untouched:

from html import escape
from string.templatelib import Template, Interpolation

def to_safe_html(tpl: Template) -> str:
    out = []
    for part in tpl:
        if isinstance(part, Interpolation):
            out.append(escape(str(part.value), quote=True))   # untrusted: escape it
        else:
            out.append(part)                                   # trusted: your own text
    return "".join(out)

bad = "<script>alert('x')</script>"
to_safe_html(t"<p>{bad}</p>")
# '<p><script>alert('x')</script></p>'   <- neutralized

The interpolated value is treated as untrusted and escaped, while the static text is your own and passes through unchanged. The user's tags are now harmless visible text, while your <p> tags pass through intact.

One writer put the principle perfectly: the escaper "sees user input as user input, not as a string fragment."

Now generalize. The same pattern applies everywhere injection lives:

  • A SQL library can take a t-string and turn every interpolation into a bound parameter instead of concatenated text, which removes the main route for injection.
  • A shell library can quote every interpolated argument.
  • A logging library can redact.

In each case the library gets to decide how to handle the dynamic parts because they arrived separately, which is the one thing f-strings never allow.

The Deliberate Inconvenience: A Template Is Not a String

There is a design choice in t-strings that looks like a limitation and is actually the point. A Template does not render itself into a string by default. You cannot just use it where a string is expected.

  • Printing one shows its repr, not interpolated text.
  • You cannot add a plain string to a Template with + (that raises TypeError; only Template + Template is allowed).
  • It has no len().

It genuinely is not a string, and it refuses to pretend to be one.

print(t"Hello, {name}!")
# Template(strings=('Hello, ', '!'), interpolations=(Interpolation('Pythonista', 'name', None, ''),))

That is the structured object, not the text "Hello, Pythonista!".

This feels annoying until you see why. If a Template quietly turned itself into a string the moment you used it carelessly, it would reintroduce the exact danger it exists to prevent: an un-escaped interpolation sliding into output because someone forgot to process it.

By requiring that every template be run through a processing function before it becomes text, the design makes "forgot to escape" much harder. You cannot accidentally use the raw version, because the raw version is not usable as a string.

The inconvenience is a guardrail.

So t-strings do not escape anything on their own. They are the mechanism that lets a library escape safely. The t-string carries the pieces, apart and inspectable; the library does the right thing with them. What Python standardized is the shape, so every library can speak it.

The Rule I Take Away

Compressed to one line:

An f-string interpolates eagerly into a finished str, fusing trusted text and untrusted values together with no seam left to escape, which is why it is unsafe for SQL, HTML, and shell. A t-string produces a Template that keeps the static parts (.strings) and the interpolated values (.interpolations, each with .value) separate, so a library can escape or parameterize the untrusted parts before building the final string.

The deeper lesson, the one that outlasts this specific feature, is that safety against injection comes from preserving the boundary between structure and data for as long as possible.

Every injection vulnerability is a place where that boundary was erased too early, where a value became part of the sentence before anyone could treat it as a value. F-strings erase the boundary instantly, by design, because they were built for convenience, not safety. T-strings keep the boundary intact and hand it to you, which is what finally lets Python libraries offer "safe by construction" interpolation the way other ecosystems have with tagged templates.

And the practical reality as of today: t-strings are new (3.14, carried into the 3.15 world), and the libraries that consume them are still growing. You will not rewrite everything overnight. But the direction is set, and when a SQL, HTML, or shell library offers a t-string API, reaching for it instead of an f-string is one of the cheapest security upgrades you can make.

What to Actually Do With This

Concrete guidance for where t-strings are right now:

Situation Use Why
Logging a number, debug messages, formatting output you control f-strings Perfect there and not going anywhere. The problem is only ever untrusted input crossing into code, query, or markup.
SQL queries, HTML output, shell commands with values you didn't write t-strings + t-string-aware libraries That is the boundary t-strings were built to protect.

And two standing rules:

  • Never build SQL, HTML, or shell commands with f-strings and raw interpolation. This was always true; t-strings now give you a first-class, standard alternative instead of only "remember to use parameterized queries / escape manually."
  • Watch for t-string support in your libraries. As database drivers, template engines, and shell helpers add t-string APIs, prefer them. The whole value of PEP 750 is a single standard shape that every library can accept, so the ecosystem can make the safe path the easy path.

Python did not just add a nicer way to format strings. It added a way to hand libraries the raw ingredients of a string with the dangerous ones still labeled, so they can be made safe before serving. That is a small syntax change pointed at one of the oldest and most damaging categories of bug in software.

The 30-Second Takeaway

  • t-strings (PEP 750, Python 3.14+) look like f-strings but use a t prefix and evaluate to a Template object (string.templatelib), not a str.
  • The key difference: an f-string interpolates eagerly into a finished string, fusing your text and the values together with no way left to escape them. A t-string keeps the pieces separate for you to process first.
  • A Template exposes its structure: .strings (the static text you wrote, always one more than the values), .interpolations (each an Interpolation with .value the runtime value and .expression the source text), and .values. Iterating it alternates static strings and interpolations.
  • The security payoff: a library can walk the template and escape or parameterize only the interpolated (untrusted) values, leaving your static markup or query intact, before building the string. This removes the main route for SQL injection, XSS, and shell injection.
  • A Template is deliberately not a string: no default render, adding a plain string with + raises TypeError, no len(). This forces you to process it, so you cannot accidentally emit un-escaped output. The inconvenience is a guardrail.
  • t-strings do not escape by themselves; they are the standard mechanism that lets libraries escape safely. Use f-strings for safe internal formatting; use t-strings (and t-string-aware libraries) wherever untrusted input meets SQL, HTML, or shell.

Your Turn

Find one place in your code where you build SQL, HTML, or a shell command with an f-string and an interpolated value you did not write. That is an injection risk today. As your libraries add t-string support, that exact spot is where the t prefix becomes the cheapest security fix you will ever ship.

Have you tried t-strings yet? What's the first place you'd use them? Tell me in the comments 👇

title: AWS Marketplace SaaS free trials now convert automatically to paid subscriptions
description:
Today, AWS Marketplace announces that free trials of usage-based software as a service (SaaS) products can now convert automatically to paid subscriptions. When a free trial ends, the buyer's subscription continues at the seller's usage-based pricing, so buyers pay only for what they use after the trial. This helps sellers turn more trial users into paying customers. Buyers get a simple way to evaluate software before they buy, with no new subscription and no interruption in access.

Sellers can offer a free trial of 7 to 90 days that converts to a paid subscription at the price they set. For example, a data team can try an analytics product for 30 days and, if it meets their needs, keep using it after the trial ends. Buyers see the trial length, conversion date, and pricing before they subscribe. They receive reminder emails before the trial converts and can cancel at any time before conversion at no charge.

Sellers can create a free trial in AWS Partner Central, or update an existing free trial offer to convert automatically. This capability is available for public offers in all AWS Regions where AWS Marketplace is available.

To learn more, see the AWS Marketplace Seller Guide and the AWS Marketplace Buyer Guide.
