title: Why a Markdown scanner should blank code spans, not delete them
description:
A link into a repository is worth reading only if it names a commit that cannot move underneath it. Checking that is the easy half: read the file, find the links, print a file:line for every ref that is not forty lowercase hex characters. The hard half starts when the same tool has to turn a branch link into a pinned one. Now it needs to write forty characters into a byte range of the file it just read, and every shortcut the reader took with positions is a bug waiting in the writer.

That pressure is what shaped srcproof, a small Go tool I wrote to keep repository links in prose honest. Two subcommands sit on one extractor. check reports links whose ref is not a full commit. pin resolves the branch and tag links of an article against a local clone and, with --write, rewrites them in place and records what it resolved in srcproof.lock. Both commands read the same Markdown through the same code. Only one of them edits, so the shared extractor has to serve the stricter consumer.

Masking preserves length; deleting does not

A link inside a code span is not a link. `https://github.com/owner/name/blob/main/go.mod` is text you are being shown, not a reference you are expected to follow, and a tool that refuses branch links has to keep the right to print the form it refuses. So code spans must not be scanned.

The obvious way to not scan them is to cut them out of the line before looking for URLs. For a tool that only reports, that works perfectly. It also quietly destroys every column after the span: remove thirty bytes from the middle of a line and everything to the right of it now sits thirty bytes earlier than it does in the file. A rewriter that trusts those offsets writes into the wrong place.

So the span is overwritten instead of removed, with exactly as many spaces as it occupied:

// stripCodeSpans blanks out code spans without moving anything after them, so
// the column of a link is the column it has in the line as written.
func stripCodeSpans(line string) string {
    var out strings.Builder
    i := 0
    for i < len(line) {
        if line[i] != '`' {
            out.WriteByte(line[i])
            i++
            continue
        }
        open := run(line, i)
        close := -1
        for j := i + open; j < len(line); {
            if line[j] != '`' {
                j++
                continue
            }
            if length := run(line, j); length == open {
                close = j
                break
            } else {
                j += length
            }
        }
        if close < 0 {
            out.WriteString(line[i : i+open])
            i += open
            continue
        }
        out.WriteString(strings.Repeat(" ", close+open-i))
        i = close + open
    }
    return out.String()
}

func run(line string, start int) int {
    length := 0
    for start+length < len(line) && line[start+length] == line[start] {
        length++
    }
    return length
}

The opening run is measured, and the span closes only on a later run of exactly the same length. Three backticks do not close a single-backtick span, which is why the inner loop advances by length rather than by one when it finds a run of the wrong size. The replacement is close+open-i spaces, which is precisely the width of the span from its first backtick to its last. The output string has the same length as the input, byte for byte, and every offset to the right of the span is the offset it has in the file.

The unclosed case is the one I like most. A run of backticks with no matching partner is written back unchanged, because that is both what CommonMark says it is (literal backticks, not a span) and the only thing that keeps the length intact. The two requirements happen to agree, and when correctness and layout agree, you take it.

Fenced blocks are skipped whole, and that costs nothing

Fences are a different problem with an easier answer. A fenced block is a run of entire lines, so the extractor does not need to preserve anything inside it: it produces no links from those lines at all, and a line that yields no link has no column to protect.

func fenceMarker(line string) (byte, int, bool) {
    i := 0
    for i < 3 && i < len(line) && line[i] == ' ' {
        i++
    }
    if i >= len(line) {
        return 0, 0, false
    }
    char := line[i]
    if char != '`' && char != '~' {
        return 0, 0, false
    }
    length := run(line, i)
    if length < 3 {
        return 0, 0, false
    }
    return char, length, true
}

func closesFence(line string, char byte, length int) bool {
    start := strings.IndexByte(line, char)
    return strings.TrimSpace(line[start+length:]) == ""
}

A fence opens on a line that starts, after at most three spaces, with three or more backticks or tildes, and closes only on a run of the same character at least as long with nothing but whitespace after it. Everything in between is skipped. Notice that this fenceMarker returns the character and the run length and throws the indent away. It does not need the indent, because it is discarding the lines. The quoting side of the tool has its own fenceMarker that also returns the indent, because it keeps the body lines and has to strip that indentation off them. Same syntax, two readers, two signatures. Trying to share one was worse than writing both.

The practical payoff is that srcproof's own README passes srcproof's own check while containing a table of the refs it refuses (main, v1.4.0, refs/heads/main) and a worked example of a link it would reject. Documentation that cannot show the bad form is documentation that cannot teach.

From a column to a splice point

With the masked line in hand, finding URLs is unremarkable except for one detail:

func findURLs(line string) []candidate {
    locations := urlPattern.FindAllStringIndex(line, -1)
    candidates := make([]candidate, 0, len(locations))
    for _, at := range locations {
        url := strings.TrimRight(line[at[0]:at[1]], ".,;:!?")
        if url == "" {
            continue
        }
        candidates = append(candidates, candidate{url: url, col: at[0]})
    }
    return candidates
}

A URL at the end of a sentence swallows the full stop, so the match is trimmed, but trimmed from the right only, and the recorded column is at[0], the start of the match. Sentence punctuation can shorten a URL. It cannot move one. That is the kind of invariant worth being deliberate about, because the alternative spelling (trim both ends, record the trimmed start) looks identical in every test that does not involve a leading character.

That column lands in the Col field of the link. A second offset lands next to it: when the URL is parsed, the position of the ref within the URL is computed by walking the segments that precede it.

func segmentOffset(start int, segments []string, index int) int {
    for _, segment := range segments[:index] {
        start += len(segment) + 1
    }
    return start
}

For a github.com link the ref is the fourth segment, after owner, name and the blob, tree or commit keyword. For raw.githubusercontent.com it is the third segment, or three segments joined when that segment is refs, so that refs/heads/main is read as one ref rather than as refs. The parse drops the fragment and the query to decide these things, but the URL is kept exactly as it was written, and the offset is into that original string. Column plus ref offset is the byte range of the ref in the file.

The rewrite distrusts the position it was given

An offset computed earlier is a claim about a string that may since have changed, so both ends check it before they use it.

Pinning a link refuses outright unless the ref offset is positive and the URL really does hold the ref at that offset. Only then does it splice the commit in and leave the rest of the URL, fragment included, as written. And when the rewrites are applied to the file, the same suspicion shows up again:

// apply rewrites a line from its right edge inwards, so the column of a link
// is still the column it was read at after an earlier link on the same line
// has grown into a 40-character commit.
func apply(source string, rewrites []Rewrite) string {
    if len(rewrites) == 0 {
        return source
    }
    grouped := make(map[int][]Rewrite)
    for _, rewrite := range rewrites {
        grouped[rewrite.Line] = append(grouped[rewrite.Line], rewrite)
    }
    lines := strings.Split(source, "\n")
    for number, group := range grouped {
        line := lines[number-1]
        for i := len(group) - 1; i >= 0; i-- {
            rewrite := group[i]
            end := rewrite.Col + len(rewrite.From)
            if end > len(line) || line[rewrite.Col:end] != rewrite.From {
                continue
            }
            line = line[:rewrite.Col] + rewrite.To + line[end:]
        }
        lines[number-1] = line
    }
    return strings.Join(lines, "\n")
}

Two things are happening here. The loop runs backwards through the rewrites of a line, so replacing a nine-character branch name with a forty-character commit cannot invalidate the column of a link further right on the same line: the right edge is edited first, and the left-hand columns are still the columns they were read at. The bytes at the recorded column are also compared against what the rewrite expected to find there. If they do not match, or the range runs past the end of the line, the rewrite is skipped and the line stays as it is. A stale position produces a link that was not pinned, reported as unresolved. It does not produce forty hex characters spliced into the middle of a sentence.

It is also why no column ever reaches srcproof.lock. A link directive records the article, the repository, the commit and the ref it was resolved from, and nothing about where in the file that happened. A byte offset is valid against one exact revision of one file, so persisting it would mean persisting something that the next edit silently falsifies.

What I would do differently

The length-preservation contract lives in a comment above stripCodeSpans, which is probably the weakest place to put an invariant that three other packages depend on. It belongs in a test: for every line, the masked line and the original have the same length. That property is cheap to check, it fails loudly the first time someone replaces a span with the empty string, and it says the thing the comment only hints at.

The scanner is also line-by-line, and CommonMark lets a code span cross a newline. A URL inside such a span is read as a link today, which is wrong. The fix is not a different strategy but the same one at document scope: mask the span across the lines it covers, keeping the newlines, and offsets still hold. Indented code blocks have the same shape of gap and the same shape of answer.

The general lesson I keep relearning is that a position is not a diagnostic. The moment a tool grows from reporting to editing, every offset it computed becomes an address somebody will write to, and the transformations it performed on the way to finding that offset become part of its correctness. Masking rather than deleting is a one-line decision that keeps the two halves of the tool talking about the same file...

Originally published on polycratia.com — where I write about payment systems, crypto rails and marketplace backends.

title: Continuous Angular Control in Text-to-Image Generation via Geometric Token Encoding
description:
arXiv:2611.13172v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models can render a photorealistic analog clock but cannot control the time it displays. Across four pretrained models, fewer than 1% of generated clocks place both hands within 6 degrees of the requested time; the models instead collapse onto visually dominant configurations such as the canonical 10:10 pose. The same failure appears when a specific fraction of a circular object is requested, where models return complete or conventionally sliced objects. We observe that these two failures share a geometric structure: both target quantities can be parameterized by angular variables.
  We introduce a geometric token encoding framework that conditions generation directly on these angles. Each angular component is encoded as a periodic sine-cosine feature and projected into a role-specific token embedding that is injected into the prompt before a frozen text encoder. To spatially ground these tokens without requiring localization input at inference, we introduce Stochastic Localization Relaxation (SLR), which stochastically relaxes attention supervision from component-level to object-level to unconstrained localization during training. For clocks, we additionally introduce a hand-swap preference objective that discourages assigning the correct angles to the wrong hand roles. On analog clocks our method reaches 63-78% Acc@6 degrees across evaluation methods, compared with below 1% for the baselines. On circular-fraction generation, it achieves 89.5% Acc@0.10, while maintaining 88.8% on unseen object categories and 84.9% on unseen target values, compared with roughly 20% for pretrained baselines.

title: SpatialSR: Spatial Resolution-Centric Pipeline for Arbitrary-Scale Remote Sensing Super-Resolution
description:
arXiv:2611.13046v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Although remote sensing image arbitrary-scale super-resolution (RSI-ASSR) methods support reconstruction at arbitrary or continuous scales, they predominantly condition on the relative scale factor and have not sufficiently investigated the absolute spatial resolution itself as a reconstruction prior, thereby disregarding the inherent spatial context of objects, which frequently leads to spatial-related distortions and compromised performance in downstream remote sensing applications. To address these challenges, we introduce SpatialSR, a SRe-centric arbitrary-scale RSISR method that leverages the spatial resolution (SRe) of remote sensing images (RSI) as an essential prior for super-resolution reconstruction. Distinct from existing SR methods, SpatialSR aims to restore high-resolution remote sensing images with a target SRe (typically set to 0.1m/pixel to align with the metadata of commonly used downstream task datasets). Specifically, we design a Spatial Resolution Estimation Module (SREM) to estimate the SRe of low-resolution (LR) images, thereby dynamically determining the required arbitrary scaling factor. Next, we employ a pretrained SRe-to-image diffusion model to extract SRe-specified texture-style codes, which are further incorporated into a carefully designed Resolution-aware Style Consistency Module (RSCM) to constrain the SRe-aware texture consistency of reconstructed images. Furthermore, to overcome the high computational expense inherent in diffusion-based SR methods, we wrap the iterative diffusion process as a Trajectory Consistency (TC) loss, which enables comparable reconstructed texture quality of the generative model in SpatialSR within a single step. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed SpatialSR achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on commonly used RSISR and downstream (image classification and segmentation tasks) datasets.

title: grep can't check the numbers in a Japanese LLM summary. Here is why, and a small fix.
description:
Say your agent summarizes Japanese meeting transcripts. You want one cheap guardrail: every number in the summary must also appear in the transcript. In English you could almost do that with a regex over the digits. In Japanese you can't, because the same value is written in many ways.

The transcript says 三千五百万円. The model writes 3,500万円. Same amount (35 million yen), zero shared digits. A few more pairs that a digit search misses:

Transcript Summary Same value?
三千五百万円 3,500万円 yes
令和7年4月1日 (Japanese era date) 2025/4/1 yes
午後2時 ("2 o'clock p.m.") 14:00 yes
1割5分 (old-style rate) 15% yes
問い合わせ30件 (30 inquiries) 30人 (30 people) no, wrong counter

The last row is the dangerous kind. The digits match, so a naive check passes, but the unit changed.

Normalize first, then compare

I wrote JP Number Grounding for this. It pulls every quantity, date and time out of both texts, converts them to one form (kanji numerals, 万/億, full-width digits, era years, 午前/午後, counters), and then checks the summary against the source.

Here is a real run. The source:

来期の予算は三千五百万円とし、令和7年4月1日から開始する。説明会は午後2時から。問い合わせは30件あった。次回は5月18日。

A summary with two mistakes in it:

予算は3,500万円、2025/4/1開始。説明会は14:00。問い合わせ30人。期限は5月1日。

from jpnumground import check
r = check(source, summary)
r["ok"]  # False
Fact in summary Normalized Status
3,500万円 35000000円 supported
2025/4/1 2025-04-01 supported
14:00 14:00 supported
30人 30人 unit_mismatch
5月1日 ????-05-01 unsupported

It caught both: the counter swap and a deadline (May 1) that nobody said. The meeting said the next session is May 18.

How it compares with a digit search

The repo ships 30 test cases. On them the tool flags the right cases 30/30, and a plain "are these digits in the source?" check gets 14/30. I wrote the cases and the rules, so read that as a regression suite, not a benchmark.

Using it from an agent

It is an MCP server, a CLI and a Python library. Python standard library only, no network calls, MIT.

{"mcpServers": {"jp-number-grounding": {"command": "python", "args": ["-m", "jpnumground.server"], "cwd": "/path/to/jp-number-grounding"}}}

A rule that works well in a system prompt: after writing minutes or a summary from Japanese text, call jp_number_grounding_check and fix or drop every unsupported fact before sending.

What it does not do

It checks that values are present, not that they are used correctly. A summary can copy 15% from the source and attach it to the wrong item, and this tool will pass it. It only handles Japanese text, and it reports unknown number forms instead of guessing.

Code and the 30 cases: https://github.com/japan-ai-tools/jp-number-grounding

title: IaaS Explained: A Case Study ofAmazon Web Services
description:
By Queen Beri Kometa
A practical introduction to Infrastructure as a Service, and how AWS turned it into the
backbone of the modern internet.
Picture the early 2000s. You have a brilliant idea for a website, but first you must buy a
server, wait weeks for it to arrive, rent a cold, noisy room to keep it in, and pray you
guessed your traffic correctly. Guess too low and the site crashes on launch day. Guess
too high and you are broke. Today, a student with a laptop and a bank card can spin up a
powerful server in under a minute, from anywhere in the world, before their tea gets cold.
The idea that made this possible is called Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS).
So what exactly is IaaS, how does it work, and why did it change everything? Let's find out,
with Amazon Web Services (AWS) as our case study.
What Is IaaS?
IaaS is a cloud computing model in which a provider rents out the basic building blocks of
computing over the internet: virtual servers, storage, and networking. Instead of buying
and maintaining physical machines, you rent exactly what you need and pay only for what
you use.
It helps to compare the three main cloud service models:
IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): You get raw infrastructure. You manage the
operating system, software, and data. Examples: AWS EC2, Microsoft Azure Virtual
Machines, Google Compute Engine, DigitalOcean.
PaaS (Platform as a Service): The provider also manages the operating system and
runtime. You just deploy code. Examples: Heroku, Google App Engine.
SaaS (Software as a Service): You simply use finished software. Examples: Gmail,
Zoom, Salesforce.
Model You manage The provider manages Example
IaaS Operating system, apps, data Hardware, network, virtualization AWS EC2
PaaS Apps and data Everything under your code Heroku
IaaS Explained: A Case Study of Amazon Web Services
Page 1 of 5
Think of it like housing. IaaS is renting an empty plot with utilities connected: you build
whatever you want on it. PaaS is renting an unfurnished apartment. SaaS is checking into a
hotel.
The Core Components of IaaS
Most IaaS offerings are built from four pieces:

  1. Compute: Virtual machines (VMs) that run your applications.
  2. Storage: Block storage for disks, object storage for files and backups, and archival storage for long-term data.
  3. Networking: Virtual private networks, load balancers, firewalls, and IP addresses.
  4. Virtualization layer: Software (a hypervisor) that splits powerful physical servers into many isolated virtual ones. The provider owns and runs the data centers, power, cooling, and physical hardware. You interact with it all through a dashboard, a command line, or an API. Case Study: Amazon Web Services (AWS) How it started In 2006, Amazon launched two services that quietly changed the technology industry: S3 (Simple Storage Service) for storage and EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) for virtual servers. Amazon had spent years building internal systems to run its massive online store, and realized that other companies would pay to use the same kind of infrastructure without having to build it themselves. That decision turned what was basically an online bookshop into the world's largest cloud provider, and AWS remains the market leader in IaaS today. Not bad for a company people first knew for shipping paperbacks. Model You manage The provider manages Example SaaS Just how you use it Everything Gmail IaaS Explained: A Case Study of Amazon Web Services Page 2 of 5 AWS's IaaS building blocks Amazon EC2: Rentable virtual servers in many sizes, from tiny instances for a personal blog to machines with huge memory or GPUs for machine learning. Amazon EBS: Block storage volumes that act like hard drives attached to your EC2 instances. Amazon S3: Object storage for images, videos, backups, and static websites, designed for very high durability. Amazon VPC: A private, isolated network in the cloud where you control IP ranges, subnets, and security rules. Elastic Load Balancing and Auto Scaling: Tools that spread traffic across servers and automatically add or remove servers as demand changes. Global reach AWS organizes its infrastructure into Regions (geographic areas) and Availability Zones (separate data center clusters within a region). By deploying across multiple zones, a company can keep running even if one facility fails. It can also place servers close to its users to reduce delay. A real-world example: Netflix Netflix is the poster child ofAWS customers, and its story is a good one. After a major database corruption incident in 2008 disrupted its DVD shipping, the company decided to move away from running its own data centers and toward the cloud. Over several years it migrated its streaming platform to AWS, completing the move of its core services in 2016. The reasons are instructive: when millions of people press play on a Friday evening, Netflix needs a great deal of capacity, and on a Tuesday morning it needs far less. With IaaS, it scales up and down instead of owning hardware that sits idle. A simple scenario: a small startup Imagine a startup building a food-delivery app. With AWS they might:
  5. Launch two EC2 instances to run the app's backend.
  6. Store restaurant photos in S3.
  7. Place a load balancer in front of the servers to share traffic.
  8. Use Auto Scaling to add servers during the lunch and dinner rush, then remove them overnight. IaaS Explained: A Case Study of Amazon Web Services Page 3 of 5 They pay for what they actually run, with no up-front hardware purchase. Benefits of IaaS Cost efficiency: Pay-as-you-go pricing replaces large capital expenses with operating expenses. Scalability and elasticity: Capacity grows or shrinks with demand. Speed: Infrastructure that once took weeks to procure is available in minutes. Reliability: Providers invest heavily in redundancy, backups, and physical security. Global reach: You can deploy close to users around the world. Focus: Teams spend time on their product, not on racking servers. Challenges and Risks Before you get carried away: IaaS is not magic, and AWS shows the downsides as clearly as the upsides. Cost surprises: Pay-as-you-go also means pay-for-your-mistakes. Forget to switch off a server and the bill arrives like an unwelcome guest. Set budget alerts early. Shared responsibility: AWS secures the physical data centers and the underlying infrastructure, but customers are responsible for securing their own operating systems, applications, data, and access settings. Many cloud breaches come from misconfiguration, such as publicly exposed storage buckets. Complexity: AWS offers hundreds of services, and the learning curve is steep. Vendor lock-in: Heavy use of provider-specific tools can make moving to another provider difficult. Connectivity and latency: In regions with limited bandwidth or distant data centers, performance and internet costs can matter as much as the cloud price itself. Data residency and compliance: Some industries and countries require data to be stored in specific locations. When Should You Choose IaaS? IaaS is a strong fit when you: Need full control over your operating system and software stack. Have unpredictable or fast-changing workloads. IaaS Explained: A Case Study of Amazon Web Services Page 4 of 5 Are a startup that wants to avoid large upfront hardware spending. Need to run test and development environments that you can create and destroy on demand. Want disaster recovery or backup without building a second data center. If you would rather not manage servers at all, PaaS or serverless options may suit you better. Best Practices for Getting Started
  9. Start small and grow as you learn.
  10. Set budgets and billing alerts from day one.
  11. Follow the principle of least privilege when giving people and applications access.
  12. Use multiple Availability Zones for anything important.
  13. Automate your setup with infrastructure-as-code tools such as Terraform orAWS CloudFormation.
  14. Back up your data and test your recovery process. Conclusion IaaS turned infrastructure from something you must own into something you rent by the hour. AWS did not invent virtualization, but it packaged servers, storage and networking into on-demand services and showed the world what the model could do. Whether you are a student with a first virtual server or a company serving millions, IaaS is a flexible foundation, as long as you watch the costs and own your share of the security. So the next time you binge a series, order dinner from an app, or open your bank's website, spare a thought for the rented servers working hard behind the scenes. They never ask for a lunch break. IaaS Explained: A Case Study of Amazon Web Services Page 5 of 5

title: A database client that knows which connection is production
description:
DBCatz is a free, open-source client for MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, Redis, MongoDB and Elasticsearch with a Production mode that makes mistakes harmless.

Most of us have done it, or watched someone do it: a query meant for the local database, run in the tab that was connected to production. Same window, same colours, same confident Enter key.

DBCatz is built around one idea: the client should know which connection is production, and behave differently there. It is free and open source (GPL-3.0), for macOS, Windows and Linux.

Safety mode, per connection
Every connection has a safety mode:

Normal — what you would expect.
Production — a PROD chip on the tab, a confirmation before every write, and a destructive statement (a DELETE without a WHERE, a DROP, a TRUNCATE) needs the connection's name typed out before it runs.
Read-only — writes are refused, and the server session itself is set read-only, so nothing slips through.
Structure changes are checked before they run, too: a new primary key, foreign keys, values that would not fit a new type, duplicates before adding UNIQUE, and long table rebuilds are all named first. The client assumes you will make a mistake one day, and makes that mistake harmless.

Eight engines, one window
MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, SQLite, Redis, Valkey, MongoDB and Elasticsearch — a tab per connection, with an editor that speaks each one's language: SQL with suggestions, Redis commands, mongosh, and a Kibana-style console for Elasticsearch.

A data grid with filters (write a WHERE clause), editable cells and foreign keys you can click to jump to the row they point at
Structure, indexes, export and import, backups
A query editor with history; copy a result as CSV or JSON
Every way in
Local servers, a Unix socket, an SSH tunnel (key, password or ssh-agent, built in), AWS IAM for RDS (tokens signed locally and renewed every 10 minutes) and HashiCorp Vault (dynamic credentials or KV v2 secrets). No side scripts, no copied passwords.

Or just paste a URL — postgres://…, mysql://…, redis://…, mongodb+srv://…, even a whole DATABASE_URL= line from a .env — and DBCatz fills the form.

Passwords, SSH passphrases, AWS keys and Vault tokens are kept by your system: the macOS Keychain, Windows' protected storage, or your Linux keyring. Never in a plain config file.

AI that never touches your rows
Ask in plain words — "orders from last week that were paid but not shipped" — and the query lands formatted in the editor. It never runs on its own; you read it and press Run. Only structure is sent to the AI provider (tables, columns, types, keys, indexes, estimated row counts), never your data unless you switch on samples for a connection. Read-only connections only ever get SELECTs back. It is all off until you add your own key.

Better with DevCatz
If you use DevCatz for local development, every database it runs shows up in DBCatz by itself — no host, port or password to type. And from DialCatz, Check in DBCatz opens the table a request just touched.

The whole family working together, in two and a half minutes:

Try it
Download: catzoid.com/dbcatz/download — macOS (signed and notarized), Windows, Linux x64 and ARM64.
Homebrew:

brew tap catzoidhub/catz && brew trust catzoidhub/catz && brew install --cask dbcatz

Docs: catzoid.com/docs/dbcatz
Source: github.com/catzoidhub/DBCatz
Made in Indonesia by a small team, written with Claude. Tell me which engine or connection method you are missing — the issues on GitHub decide what comes next.

title: Beyond Interaction Scores: Selecting Feature Interactions via Independent Replication
description:
arXiv:2611.13765v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Learning feature interactions is essential for accurate prediction and interpretable modeling, yet a high interaction score may reflect fitting noise rather than a reproducible pattern. Ranking methods score feature pairs but leave the cutoff to the user; testing methods set the cutoff but rely on repeated model refits or a model of the joint feature distribution. We present LENS, a model-agnostic framework for selecting feature interactions through independent replication. LENS trains two models with the same learning algorithm on disjoint data and accesses them only through predictions. For each feature pair, it removes main effects from the joint-effect surface to isolate an interaction pattern, ranks pairs by its strength, and tests whether the second model reproduces it at a meaningful strength. A single multiple-testing correction determines which pairs to retain, using only two model fits regardless of the number of features. We prove that a replication ratio alone can retain arbitrarily weak patterns shared by both fits, whereas a strength floor restores selection consistency, and we characterize when normalization in Friedman's $H^2$ reverses interaction rankings. On 16 synthetic designs, LENS matches leading model-specific ranking methods (e.g., TreeSHAP) and recovers 91% of material interactions, against 45% for the knockoff-based DIAMOND, without selecting false pairs; with 1,225 candidate pairs and no interactions, it makes substantially fewer false discoveries. On large-scale French motor insurance data, it identifies interactions documented in the actuarial literature and recovers 90% of the deviance gain obtained using all pairs. On two credit datasets, LENS selects few pairs while maintaining or slightly improving predictive performance over the additive baseline.

title: Satellite Pretraining Is Not One Thing: A Matched-Pair Study of Generic and Earth-Observation Foundation Models for Scene Classification
description:
arXiv:2611.13849v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Geospatial foundation models are pretrained on satellite and aerial imagery, but whether such an encoder beats a strong generic one for few-label land-use/land-cover mapping remains unclear, as prior comparisons rarely isolate the pretraining data. We study five matched pairs of Earth-observation (EO) and generic encoders sharing objective and architecture (DINO/SatDINO, DINOv3/DINOv3-SAT, MAE/SatMAE, MAE/Scale-MAE, CLIP/RemoteCLIP) within a benchmark of 14 frozen encoders on five RGB scene-classification datasets (0.06-30 m GSD). With native preprocessing, we evaluate k-NN, linear and attentive probes and image retrieval over six low-label splits, using paired per-image significance tests. EO pretraining is not uniformly helpful: on most datasets and metrics, it significantly improves three pairs (SatDINO, Scale-MAE, RemoteCLIP, the latter evaluated only on unseen datasets) and significantly hurts two (linear probe: DINOv3-SAT by up to 22.5 points, SatMAE by up to 8.8), with opposite outcomes even for two MAEs pretrained on the same fMoW-RGB imagery. These effects are robust to patch-token pooling and attentive probing, concentrate on small man-made objects, and are largest with 1-5% labels. Across encoders, the silhouette score of frozen embeddings predicts k-NN accuracy and retrieval mAP almost perfectly (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.96$ on four of five datasets). Pretraining on satellite imagery is thus not a reliable selection criterion; candidate checkpoints must be validated on target data.

title: A Technique to Model Product Information and User Reviews (MPIUR)
description:
arXiv:2611.13361v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern e-commerce platforms naturally provide three complementary modalities: textual item descriptions, item images, and user reviews. However, existing multimodal recommendation methods often omit reviews or do not integrate all three modalities within a unified framework. In this paper, we propose MPIUR, a multimodal graph-based recommendation model that encodes reviews in heterogeneous graphs, aligns image and text representations, and adapts collaborative--semantic alignment to item interaction density. Experiments on the Amazon Reviews 2023 Musical Instruments and Baby categories show that MPIUR achieves the best global nDCG@10 and Recall@10 among the evaluated methods on both datasets. It also obtains the best nDCG@10 and Recall@10 on sparse items, indicating that jointly exploiting reviews and multimodal item content is particularly useful when interaction histories are limited.

title: Understanding Students' Rationales for AI-Mediated Cheating: An Instructor Perspective from Online Forums Analysis
description:
arXiv:2611.13358v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The extensive adoption of AI has precipitated a crisis in academic integrity. While studies attempt to quantify cheating, less is known about the motivations instructors believe students have for using AI in prohibited ways. We analyze 2.01 million posts on r/Professors to understand how instructors perceive students' justifications for AI-mediated cheating. Our qualitative analyses reveal four primary themes: (1) Academic System Gaming, (2) Digital-Academic Literacy Gap, (3) Performance Anxiety, and (4) Normalization of Dishonesty.

title: The Target Is a Predicate: Predicate-State Grounding for Semantic-Level Video Reasoning Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2611.13785v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this paper, we introduce Predicate-State Video Reasoning Segmentation (PS-VRS), where a query defines a dynamic predicate $P(o,t)$ over objects and time rather than a fixed object identity. Existing methods typically treat the target as permanently active once identified, leading to over-emission of masks during vacant intervals and failure to handle target switching. To address this, we construct PS-Bench, a large-scale benchmark with 2,077 videos and 16,250 queries annotated with explicit active/vacant predicate states, temporal intervals, and pixel masks. We further propose Predicate-State Grounding (PSG), a State-Bind-Emit pipeline that: (1) predicts [ACTIVE]/[VACANT] state tokens; (2) aligns them to video frames via dense cross-modal similarity; and (3) emits masks via SAM2 only for active states. Experiments show that PSG outperforms existing baselines by +9.32 J&F on PS-Bench and significantly reduces false-positive mask emissions. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of explicit predicate-state modeling for video reasoning segmentation with dynamic visual witnesses.

title: Nitori Breach: 37.6M Records Stolen via Network Compromise
description:
Originally published on satyamrastogi.com

Nitori, Japan's largest furniture retailer, confirmed attackers compromised network systems and exfiltrated 37.62 million customer records. Investigation ongoing.

Executive Summary

Nitori Holdings, operating Japan's largest furniture and home accessories retail network, disclosed a significant data breach affecting 37.62 million customer records. An attacker gained unauthorized access to systems on Nitori's network, successfully exfiltrating customer personal information. The company detected the intrusion during routine monitoring and initiated incident response procedures. No confirmation of data monetization or secondary sale has been reported, though the scale of exposure presents substantial regulatory and reputational risk under Japan's Act on Protection of Personal Information (APPI).

Attack Vector and Initial Compromise

Nitori's incident response timeline indicates network-level compromise, though specific attack vectors remain undisclosed pending investigation. Probable attack chains align with MITRE ATT&CK T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application) or T1199 (Trusted Relationship), given retail sector targeting patterns observed in 2023-2024 campaigns.

Common initial access vectors for Japanese retail operations include:

  • Vulnerable e-commerce platforms: Legacy retail infrastructure frequently runs outdated CMS or payment-processing plugins without security patches
  • Weak VPN/RDP exposure: Supply chain partners, contractors, and remote staff often maintain poorly segmented access
  • Phishing against administrative accounts: Social engineering targeting procurement or IT staff with access to customer databases
  • Supply chain compromise: Third-party service providers (payment processors, CRM vendors, logistics partners) may introduce initial foothold

Given Nitori's retail scale, the attacker likely achieved T1021 (Remote Services) access post-compromise, enabling lateral movement to customer data repositories.

Technical Deep Dive

Scope of Compromise

The 37.62 million records represent customer identifiable information (CII) stored across Nitori's e-commerce, loyalty program, and point-of-sale systems. Typical retail breach exposure includes:

  • Names, postal addresses, phone numbers
  • Email addresses
  • Purchase history and transaction metadata
  • Potentially encrypted or hashed payment card data (PCI DSS scope)

Dwell Time Assessment

Nitori's detection relied on "routine monitoring," suggesting Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) alerting identified anomalous access patterns or data exfiltration volumes. Japanese retail sector incidents typically show 30-180 day dwell times before detection, with this breach likely unfolding over weeks to months before discovery.

Data Exfiltration Method

Large-scale customer database theft in retail typically employs:

  • Bulk data export via SQL injection or compromised database credentials (T1020 - Automated Exfiltration)
  • Direct database replication to attacker-controlled storage
  • Incremental queries through legitimate API endpoints with stolen application credentials

The 37.6 million record size (~2-4 TB uncompressed) suggests automated exfiltration tools, likely consuming significant network bandwidth over days or weeks.

Detection Strategies

SIEM Signatures

  • Anomalous database query volume from non-standard source IPs or accounts
  • Large data transfer to external IPs on non-standard ports (SSH tunnels on 443, DNS exfiltration, HTTPS to unknown destinations)
  • Bulk SELECT queries returning entire customer tables without legitimate business context
  • Multiple failed authentication attempts followed by success (credential stuffing/spray)
  • Unexpected privilege escalation or role assumption on database systems

Network Indicators

  • Outbound connections to known bulletproof hosting providers, VPS resellers in high-risk jurisdictions
  • Large data transfers during off-business hours
  • DNS queries to data exfiltration services or anonymization infrastructure
  • Encrypted tunneling protocols (Wireguard, custom VPN) from internal systems

Application-Layer Indicators

  • Web application firewall (WAF) logs showing SQLi payloads, path traversal, or authentication bypass attempts
  • Unusually high query concurrency from single session
  • API abuse patterns (rate limiting bypass, token replay)

Mitigation Recommendations

Immediate Actions

  1. Credential Invalidation: Force password reset for all affected customers; invalidate any session tokens or API keys with customer data access
  2. Payment Card Reissuance: If PCI scope data was compromised (card numbers, CVC), coordinate with card networks for fraud prevention escalation
  3. Breach Notification Compliance: Submit mandatory reports to Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission; notify customers per APPI Section 34
  4. Forensic Lock-Down: Isolate affected database servers; preserve logs for 90+ days; engage third-party forensics for chain-of-custody

Short-Term Hardening

  • Implement database activity monitoring (DAM) with real-time alerting on bulk queries
  • Enable row-level security (RLS) and field-level encryption for PII columns
  • Deploy network segmentation isolating customer data repositories from internet-facing systems
  • Mandate multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all privileged database access
  • Rotate all service account credentials used by applications accessing customer data

Long-Term Controls

  • Establish zero-trust architecture for data access; require identity verification and session validation
  • Deploy data loss prevention (DLP) monitoring for PII exfiltration patterns
  • Conduct regular penetration testing on e-commerce and admin portals (quarterly minimum)
  • Implement security awareness training focused on credential hygiene and social engineering resistance
  • Establish customer data minimization policy; retain only necessary PII; archive historical data offline

Key Takeaways

  1. Scale Matters: 37.6 million records ranks among Japan's largest retail breaches, amplifying regulatory scrutiny and reputational damage
  2. Legacy Infrastructure Risk: Japanese retail sector heavily dependent on aging e-commerce platforms vulnerable to commodity exploit kits
  3. Supply Chain Exposure: Retail organizations must audit third-party access controls; contractor and partner compromise vectors are primary attack paths
  4. Detection Lag: Routine monitoring detected this breach; proactive threat hunting and continuous monitoring reduce dwell time
  5. Regulatory Precedent: APPI enforcement has shifted toward significant fines ($2M+ in recent cases); Nitori faces substantial compliance liability

Related Articles

title: Reliability of Claude Code as an Agentic AI Grading System for Handwritten University Exams
description:
arXiv:2611.13217v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This study examines the reliability of Claude Code, an agentic deployment of the Claude Opus 4.6 large language model, as a grading system for handwritten university exams. Four research questions addressed agreement with expert human grading on total scores (RQ1), agreement across five question types from multiple choice to evaluative judgement (RQ2), consistency across two independent grading sessions one week apart (RQ3), and the accuracy of AI-generated feedback (RQ4). Claude Code graded the 20-mark mid-term papers of 60 consenting students in a Saudi computer graphics course in a single agentic session, guided by three rubric files. Reliability was estimated on disjoint samples: 20 papers for RQ1, RQ2 and RQ4, and 15 papers for RQ3. Analyses used Pearson correlation, mean absolute error, Bland-Altman analysis, weighted Cohen kappa, intraclass correlation, and a four-category coding scheme separating diagnostic from confirmation feedback. The author, as the sole subject-matter expert for the course, provided the human benchmark, so the design assesses agreement with a domain-expert reference rather than inter-rater reliability. AI grading agreed strongly with human grading on totals (r = 0.97; MAE = 0.85 marks) with a small but significant AI-positive bias of 0.68 marks, showed excellent test-retest consistency (ICC = 0.96), and produced accurate feedback (92.8% diagnostic; 97.8% confirmation). Drawing items were the outlier on three of four measures. Three failure modes recurred: keyword matching without conceptual depth, selection-state ambiguity on corrected multiple-choice answers, and region-of-attention drift on hand-drawn diagrams. The findings suggest that AI grading at this capability level can assist instructors on objective and short-form items under structural safeguards but is not yet ready to replace instructor judgement at boundary cases or on drawing items.

title: CJRR-Net: A Candidate-Joint Reprojection Ranking for Future-View Selection in Human Pose Estimation
description:
arXiv:2611.13700v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-camera systems support performance recording, sports and human-movement analysis, where selecting an informative viewpoint is important for reliable human pose estimation. We propose the Candidate-Joint Reprojection Ranking Network (CJRR-Net) for future-view selection among eight calibrated cameras in MPI-INF-3DHP. The model combines current-view pose observations, camera configuration, and candidate-specific geometric features obtained by reprojecting the estimated 3D pose and its uncertainty into each candidate view. CJRR-Net achieves a selected-view 2D mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) of 105.18 pixels, compared with 114.64 pixels for the shared-input MLP and 117.56 pixels for adapted PoseErrNet. It also achieves the lowest mean error among the listed policies in each evaluated occlusion group. A blender rollout illustrates repeated camera selection. These findings support candidate-specific geometry for single-view selection in the evaluated fixed eight-camera setting.

title: Require the agent to leave existing test IDs alone unless the test changes in the same PR
description:
The component PR looks small. The bug is fixed. Then CI goes red in a file the agent never opened: checkout.spec.ts can’t find [data-testid="pay-cta"]. The agent renamed it to checkout-submit because the new name “was clearer.”

I’ve started treating silent test-id edits as a merge blocker, not a style nit. Selectors are a contract with tests you may not have in the same checkout.

Why agents rename them

Common reasons, all locally reasonable:

  • The id didn’t match the new label
  • A linter or the model’s taste prefers BEM, camelCase, or a longer name
  • The agent “cleaned up” inconsistent naming across a file
  • It moved a button into a child component and “updated the hook to match”

None of those are a reason to break a Playwright / Testing Library / Cypress suite that wasn’t in the PR.

A simple policy

Boring rules beat debate:

  • Existing data-testid, data-test, and stable aria-label hooks stay unless the test (or Storybook play function) that uses them is updated in the same PR
  • New elements may get new ids; don’t recycle or “improve” old ones in passing
  • If a rename is truly required (duplicate ids, the element went away), the PR must include the test diff and mention the rename in the description
  • Don’t replace a test id with a role+name query in application code “to be more semantic” unless the test migration is in the same change

The app code is not the only consumer. Visual tests, analytics event helpers, and QA snippets often key off the same attributes.

What to put in the prompt (or the PR template)

Give the agent the contract, not a vibe:

Do not rename, remove, or relocate existing data-testid / data-test
attributes unless you also update every test that references them
in this PR. If you need a new hook, add a new attribute. List any
test-id changes in the PR body.

Even better, paste the current ids for the files it may touch:

rg -o "data-testid=\"([^\"]+)\"" src/components/Checkout -N

A short allow-list in the prompt beats hoping the model notices pay-cta is load-bearing.

How to catch it in review

Before you approve:

  1. Diff only the test-id attributes: git diff -U0 -- '*.tsx' '*.jsx' | rg "data-testid|data-test"
  2. If any existing value disappeared or changed, search the repo for the old string
  3. If tests weren’t updated, request changes — don’t “fix CI later”
  4. If the agent added a second id “just in case,” delete the unused one or document why both exist

A one-line CI grep that fails when a test-id value disappears from src/ but still appears under e2e/ / tests/ is cheap insurance.

Reject / send back

Reject

  • Renames with no test diff
  • “Cleanup” that normalizes all ids in a file you asked to patch in one place
  • Removing a test id because the agent switched to getByRole in a story you didn’t ask to rewrite
  • Reusing an old id on a different element

Accept

  • Unchanged hooks on existing elements
  • New ids on new elements, with tests when those elements need them
  • A rename bundled with the test (and any docs/QA) update, called out in the PR body

Tiny habit

When you ask an agent to fix a button, tell it the test ids in that file are frozen. If a hook has to change, the test change ships in the same PR. Fewer mysterious red pipelines. Fewer “it worked on my story” merges.
