title: DailyWildfireCAN: A Dataset and Benchmark for Next-Day Wildfire Spread Prediction in Canada
description:
arXiv:2611.14207v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Wildfires represent a critical ecological and socio-economic challenge in Canada, where vast boreal forests and a warming climate have amplified the frequency and severity of extreme fire seasons. Predicting next-day wildfire spread can support fire management, but requires capturing complex interactions among weather, fuels, and terrain. Deep learning has emerged as a promising approach to learning these relationships from heterogeneous environmental data, yet its development and evaluation depend on representative datasets. Existing deep learning research on wildfire spread relies predominantly on US-focused datasets, leaving Canadian fire environments underrepresented. To address this gap, we present DailyWildfireCAN, a multi-modal, multi-temporal dataset and benchmark for predicting next-day wildfire spread across Canada. The dataset tracks continuous fire progression over multi-day events at a high spatial and temporal resolution of 90-m and 24-hour, respectively. This resolution preserves fine-scale information relevant to fire-edge geometry, local fuel variations, and terrain effects, supporting research toward improved daily wildfire spread forecasting. DailyWildfireCAN covers 2,440 wildfire events across eight fire seasons 2017-2024 and integrates 33 features across diverse modalities, including topography, meteorology, land cover, vegetation and forest structure, human influence indices, and satellite imagery. We establish a comprehensive benchmark comparing mono-temporal and multi-temporal prediction models, accompanied by a multi-dimensional evaluation framework assessing robustness across wildfire characteristics, geographic regions, and temporal conditions, spatial prediction quality, and sensitivity to reference label variations.

title: Day 18/90: Your AI Agent Has a Step Limit—But Does It Have a Budget?
description:
An AI agent can stay within its step limit and still exceed an acceptable response time or consume too many tokens.

A slow tool, growing conversation history, or repeated retries can make a short execution expensive.

Today’s challenge: define how much time and token usage an agent can spend—and what happens when either budget runs out.

Why a step limit is not enough

A step limit controls iterations. Individual steps can have very different costs.

One iteration might perform a quick lookup. Another might send a large context to a model and wait for a slow external service.

Anthropic recommends explicit stopping conditions for agents. Building on that guidance, this challenge adds two resource controls:

  • An end-to-end execution deadline
  • A cumulative token budget

These are engineering controls to evaluate, not universal settings.

1. Use one deadline for the entire run

A tool timeout limits an individual operation. A run deadline limits the total time available across model calls, tools, retries, and waiting.

For an illustrative configuration:

  • Total execution deadline: 30 seconds
  • Maximum timeout per tool call: 8 seconds

If only three seconds remain, the next operation should receive at most three seconds.

operation_timeout = min(tool_timeout, remaining_run_time)

Use a monotonic clock to measure elapsed time.

Checking the deadline between steps is insufficient if an operation can block indefinitely. Pass the remaining allowance into the client’s timeout controls as well.

AWS’s guidance on remote calls supports using timeouts and carefully controlling retries.

2. Track tokens across all model calls

An output limit applies to one generation. It does not automatically cap the full agent run.

Input tokens can grow as the agent carries forward conversation history, retrieved passages, and tool results.

Track cumulative usage:

total_run_tokens = sum(input_tokens + output_tokens)

Before each model request:

  1. Estimate the input tokens.
  2. Reserve an output allowance.
  3. Check whether both fit within the remaining budget.
  4. Reconcile the estimate with reported usage afterward.

Post-request accounting alone cannot prevent the current request from exceeding the intended budget.

A strict cap requires suitable provider controls and reliable input counting. Parallel requests also need shared reservations to prevent double spending.

Token usage is also not identical to monetary cost: pricing can differ by model, token category, and caching.

3. Keep retries inside the original budget

A retry should consume the remaining time and token allowance.

It should not receive a fresh execution budget.

Before retrying, check whether:

  • The failure is transient
  • Repeating the operation is safe
  • Enough time remains for backoff and another attempt
  • Another model request fits within the token allowance

For tools that change external state, a timeout can leave the outcome uncertain.

For example, a ticket might be created even though its confirmation never reaches the agent. Repeating the request could create a duplicate.

Use idempotency keys where supported and verify uncertain outcomes before retrying a write.

4. Return an explicit stop reason

Budget exhaustion should produce a clear application state, such as:

  • completed
  • deadline_exceeded
  • token_budget_exceeded
  • step_limit_exceeded
  • tool_failed

Keep verified intermediate results and explain what remains unfinished.

Example:

“I found the policy document, but the order lookup timed out. I could not confirm whether this order qualifies.”

Do not treat a local timeout as proof that a remote operation failed or was cancelled.

Today’s experiment

Test the agent against these conditions:

  • A normal successful request
  • A tool that responds slowly
  • Growing context across repeated model calls
  • A transient error requiring a retry
  • An external write whose confirmation is lost

Record task completion, elapsed time, token usage, retries, and the final stop reason.

Check whether any new operation starts after the budget is exhausted, and whether uncertain external outcomes are reported accurately.

These are proposed test cases—not measured results.

Key lesson

Reliable agent execution requires explicit resource limits and predictable behavior when those limits are reached.
The goal is to complete useful work within an agreed allowance and clearly report unfinished work when execution must stop.

Which limit would your agent reach first: time, tokens, or iterations?

title: SailPoint Developer Training: What a Course Should Cover (Rules, Workflows, Connectors)
description:
If you already write Java or support enterprise applications, SailPoint IdentityIQ (IIQ) development is one of the most direct routes into identity and access management. But "SailPoint developer training" means very different things on different course pages. Some teach the admin screens and call it development. This post lists what a developer-focused SailPoint course should actually cover, and how to check a syllabus before you pay.

What a SailPoint IIQ developer actually does

On a typical IIQ project, the developer:

  • Onboards applications: configures connectors, schemas, aggregation and correlation so identities and accounts match correctly.
  • Writes rules in BeanShell (Java syntax): correlation, customization, build-map, before/after provisioning and identity attribute rules.
  • Builds workflows: joiner, mover and leaver lifecycle events, access-request approvals and custom provisioning flows.
  • Debugs: reads logs, traces failed aggregations and provisioning, and fixes them without breaking production.
  • Deploys: moves configuration between DEV, TEST and PROD using XML exports and a build process.

A training course that skips any of these leaves you unprepared for the first week of a real project.

What SailPoint developer training should cover

Use this as a checklist against any syllabus:

  1. IIQ architecture and the object model: identities, links, entitlements, applications, rules and tasks, and how they relate in the database.
  2. Application onboarding: delimited file, JDBC and Active Directory connectors; schema design; aggregation tasks.
  3. Correlation: why accounts fail to correlate and how correlation rules fix it.
  4. BeanShell rules: writing, testing and debugging rules with the SailPoint API (SailPointContext, Identity, Link, QueryOptions).
  5. Roles and policies: business vs IT roles, assignment rules, separation-of-duties policies.
  6. Certifications: building access review campaigns and handling revocations.
  7. Lifecycle events and workflows: workflow XML, steps, transitions and variables; joiner-mover-leaver flows end to end.
  8. Provisioning: provisioning plans, before/after provisioning rules, handling failures.
  9. Reporting and quick links: custom reports and forms.
  10. Troubleshooting: log levels, common aggregation, correlation and provisioning errors, and how to read stack traces.

If troubleshooting and workflows are missing, the course is teaching screens, not development.

How to check a course before you enrol

  • Ask for the module list with hours per module. Rules and workflows need real time, not one session.
  • Ask how many years the trainer has spent implementing IIQ at clients.
  • Ask whether classes are live, and whether you can ask questions about your own code.
  • Ask how long you keep access to recordings. Most developers revise before interviews.
  • Be wary of "100% placement guarantee". Placement assistance (resume help, mock interviews, referrals) is the honest version.

How long it takes

For someone with basic Java and SQL, about 45 days of live evening classes plus regular practice is realistic to become comfortable with rules, workflows and troubleshooting. Recorded videos alone usually stop at configuration.

One option

IAM Careers runs a live online SailPoint IIQ course that covers all of the above across 15 modules in 45 days, including rules, workflows and a dedicated troubleshooting module. Classes run at 8 PM IST, Monday to Friday, in small batches, with recordings available for 2 years and a trainer with 15 years of IAM implementation experience. There is also a short guide on what a SailPoint developer course should cover.

This training is provided by IAM Careers and is not affiliated with, authorized by, sponsored by, or endorsed by SailPoint Technologies, Inc.

title: Lovable app not deploying or "Publishing failed"? Find the cause, then fix it
description:
Most of the "my Lovable app won't deploy" messages I see come down to one of a handful of causes. Some are inside Lovable (the change was never published, the build failed, a security scan or a workspace policy blocked it). The rest happen when you move the app to Vercel, Netlify or Cloudflare and the host is set up for the wrong kind of build.

Here is how I find which one it is, and the fix for each.

The messages you might see

  • Publishing failed
  • Fix security issues to publish
  • Publishing is blocked by workspace policy
  • You don't have permission to publish this project
  • Or no message at all: the deploy on Vercel or Netlify fails, or the live site still shows old changes.

Why it happens

  • The changes were never published. Lovable does not push edits to the live site by itself, and accepting a draft does not publish it. A small dot on the Publish button means there are unpublished changes.
  • The build fails. An error in the code stops the deploy. The Publish button turns into Try to fix, or a Publishing failed banner appears.
  • A security scan blocks it. The Publish dialog runs a quick security scan. Its findings don't block publishing by default, but with Block publishing with critical issues turned on, you get Fix security issues to publish until the critical findings are resolved.
  • A policy or a missing permission blocks it. By default editors and above can publish. On Enterprise workspaces a policy can require approval (Publish requires approval) or block publishing.
  • The outside host is set up for the wrong kind of app. A React and Vite project from Lovable builds static files into dist. A TanStack Start project needs a host that runs a server, and its build fails if nitro is missing from package.json.
  • Build-time values are missing. VITE_SUPABASE_URL and VITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY are written into the app when it builds. Set them after the build, or not at all, and the app loads but can't reach its backend.

Find the cause first

  1. Open the Publish dialog and read what it says. Publishing failed, Try to fix, Fix security issues to publish and a policy message each point to a different cause above.
  2. Look for the dot on the Publish button. If it's there, the live site is behind the editor.
  3. Visit the exact published address. Changing the URL subdomain moves the site to a new address, and a new custom domain serves the app only once it shows Live.
  4. On Vercel, Netlify or Cloudflare, open the failed deploy's build log and read the first error, not only the last line.
  5. Open package.json in the Code tab. @tanstack/react-start means a TanStack Start app that needs a server; otherwise it's a React and Vite app that builds to static files.

Fix 1: Publish from Lovable, then publish every change

  1. Click Publish (top right, next to Share), check the Website URL and who can see the site, then click Publish. The dialog says Your website is live when the deploy finishes.
  2. For every later change, open the Publish dialog again and click Publish changes.
  3. If a Publishing failed banner appears, use what it offers: Try again for a temporary problem, Try to fix for an error in the app or its configuration, and Ask the assistant to help for a database conflict. Internal errors go to Lovable support.

Fix 2: Clear a build error or a blocked publish

  1. Click Try to fix, or paste the exact error into the chat and ask Lovable to fix only that error.
  2. If the dialog says Fix security issues to publish, open the scan findings and fix the critical ones rather than turning the block off.
  3. For Publish requires approval or Publishing is blocked by workspace policy, ask a workspace admin. For You don't have permission to publish this project, ask for editor access.
  4. If the build keeps failing after each fix, open History, revert to the version marked Published (the last one that went live) and make the change again in smaller steps. Reverting restores code, not database data.

Fix 3: Deploy outside Lovable (Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare)

  1. Connect the project to GitHub with Git sync, then import that repository on the host.
  2. For a React and Vite app, use the build command npm run build, the output directory dist and Node 22.
  3. If npm ci fails because the repository has only bun.lock, build with Bun, or generate and commit a package-lock.json.
  4. Set the VITE_ values from the project's .env file on the host before the build, and redeploy after any change: they are fixed at build time.
  5. Add the fallback that serves index.html for app routes (a _redirects file on Netlify and Cloudflare, vercel.json on Vercel), and add the new domain to your sign-in provider's allowed redirect URLs.
  6. For a TanStack Start app, use a host that runs a server (Vercel, Netlify and Cloudflare Pages detect it automatically) and check that nitro is in package.json.

These are the settings for the common case:

React + Vite app from Lovable, on Vercel, Netlify or Cloudflare Pages

Build command     npm run build
Output directory  dist
Node version      22
Environment       VITE_SUPABASE_URL
                  VITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY
                  VITE_SUPABASE_PROJECT_ID
                  (values from the project's .env file, set before the build)

Check the fix worked

  • The Publish dialog says Your website is live, and the Publish button shows no dot.
  • Open the published address in a private window: your latest change is there.
  • On an outside host, open a deep link directly and refresh it: the page loads instead of a 404.
  • Sign in on the live domain: you come back to the app, not to the preview address or localhost.

Stop it coming back

  • Check the live address after you publish, not only the preview.
  • Ask a workspace admin or owner to turn on Block publishing with critical issues (Workspace settings > Security), so a change with critical findings can't go live unnoticed.
  • Keep the project in GitHub with Git sync, so an outside host builds every push and a failed build shows up at once.

Quick answers

Why does my Lovable app work in the preview but not on the live site? The preview shows the version you're editing; the live site is the snapshot you last published. Click Publish changes to update it, and check you're visiting the exact published address.

Can I deploy a Lovable app to Vercel or Netlify? Yes. Connect it to GitHub with Git sync and import the repository; a React and Vite app builds with npm run build into dist on Node 22. The frontend can move while the app keeps using its Lovable Cloud backend.

Do I need a paid plan to publish? No. Free and Pro projects can publish with public or invite-only access. Connecting a custom domain needs a paid plan.

Sources: Lovable: Publish your Lovable project, Lovable: Deploying and hosting outside Lovable, Lovable: Revert and restore your project with version history.

I keep the full checklist, with related fixes for 404s on refresh and undefined env variables, on our fix page. Once it's live, you can run the free Launch Check on the published address to catch exposed keys and missing security headers.

I wrote this with AI assistance and reviewed it myself.

title: Trending in self-hosting and Kubernetes: week of 10 November 2026
description:
Four things that picked up attention this week, with what we think of each. The originals are linked; read them. This page only tells you why they matter for a small self-hosted setup.

1. An empty resources: {} quietly downgrades your pods on Kubernetes 1.34 to 1.36

Original: An Empty resources: {} Makes Kubernetes 1.34 to 1.36 Pods BestEffort on devops-daily.com (also on dev.to).

The claim: if a pod sets spec.resources: {} at pod level, the kubelet classifies it as BestEffort even when every container has requests and limits. The authors measured it on k3s 1.34, 1.35 and 1.36: oom_score_adj jumped to 1000, and next to a busy neighbour a pod that requested half a CPU got 0.06 to 0.08 cores instead of about 0.57. A namespace quota that blocks BestEffort pods rejected it. On 1.37.1 the classes were correct. GitLab Runner's Kubernetes executor generates that empty block from version 18.10.0 to 19.4.3.

Our take: a useful correction to folklore as well. The article shows that the popular claim "these pods are evicted first" is wrong; the kubelet's eviction order did not change. Check your cluster in ten seconds:

kubectl get pods -A -o custom-columns=NS:.metadata.namespace,POD:.metadata.name,QOS:.status.qosClass | grep BestEffort

If a workload that has limits shows up there, you have found it. If you prefer to see QoS class in a UI, our Kubernetes GUI comparison covers the tools that show it at a glance.

2. A 10 USD OpenStick as a home server

Original: What I run on my $10 USD OpenStick homelab (825 points and 137 comments on Hacker News).

The hardware: four Cortex-A53 cores at 1 GHz, 512 MB of RAM (about 450 MB usable), 4 GB of eMMC, Debian with systemd and Podman, passively cooled. The author runs AdGuard Home (about 40 MB) and a handful of small utilities on it.

Our take: the interesting part is not the gadget, it is the budget discipline. Services measured in tens of megabytes are the right default for a DNS blocker, an uptime monitor or a notifier. When a service outgrows 512 MB, the next honest step is a small VPS rather than a bigger box under the desk; our VPS comparison shows what 4 to 6 EUR a month buys today.

3. HolyArrs: a 15 MB self-hosted media stack

Original: HolyArrs on GitHub, posted as "Show HN: A 15 MB self-hosted Netflix and Spotify for your media server" (about 160 points and 125 comments on Hacker News).

The project replaces six separate media apps with one binary: about 15 MB to download, about 140 MB of RAM idle with 10,000 titles, builds for amd64, arm64 and armv7, AGPL-3.0.

Our take: after the Plex exploitation earlier this season, a smaller attack surface is the selling point people are reacting to. One small binary is easier to audit than a stack of six apps, but a young project has no security track record yet. Note that 15 MB is the download, not the memory footprint: at 140 MB idle it would still fit on the OpenStick above, barely. Whatever you pick, keep it behind a reverse proxy with no directly published port; Docker bypasses ufw for published ports, which we measured in our Docker production gotchas.

4. NVIDIA publishes NVKE, a management plane for GPU Kubernetes

Original: dsx-ai-factory/nvke (124 points and 30 comments on Hacker News).

NVKE is a management plane in which every workload cluster gets its own control plane, etcd and node pools. The README labels it a preview and does not recommend it for production workloads. A local quickstart runs a management plane and a workload cluster on simulated machines, so you can try it without GPU hardware.

Our take: irrelevant for a single server, relevant as a signal that cluster-per-customer is turning into a packaged product. If you run one or two clusters, keep using k3s and revisit NVKE when the preview label is gone.

What we would do this week

  • Run the BestEffort check above on any 1.34 to 1.36 cluster.
  • If you use GitLab Runner's Kubernetes executor, upgrade it to 19.5.0 or later, as the original report recommends.
  • Do not move anything production-grade onto preview software.

Originally published at news.rozoom.app.

title: Rust is amazing, as long as I’m not the one writing it
description:
The creator of Ruby on Rails says reading Rust is like “pouring acid in my eyes.” Yet he loves it. I wanted to understand why.

I’m the JavaScript and PHP guy.

Web apps, full stack, a bit of infrastructure: Docker, servers, deploys.

Systems programming? Never needed it. Never wrote about it.

Then my timeline changed. Suddenly everybody is talking about Rust.

Rust this. Rewritten in Rust that. “Blazingly fast” under every other post.

I haven’t written a single line of Rust. So this is the view from outside the fence.

The picture we had of Rust

From where I sat, Rust was what you reach for when you write system code. The low-level stuff, close to the machine.

Same shelf as C and C++. The shelf you need a ladder for.

And the syntax. Here’s a function from the official Rust book:

fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if x.len() > y.len() {
        x
    } else {
        y
    }
}

It’s the simplest case in the book, and all it does is return the longer in bytes of two strings. Yes.

In JavaScript, that’s one line and nobody gets hurt.

That 'a? Not a typo. It's called a lifetime. I'll tell you what it is when I find out.

Even the Rails guy flinches

I’m not the only one squinting.

DHH, the creator of Ruby on Rails, at his Rails World 2026 keynote:

Rust to me is like pouring acid in my eyes when I have to look at the code.

He kept going:

It is, in my opinion, the ugliest programming language that has been invented in probably the last 40 years.

And going:

Absolutely inhumane to ask people of flesh and blood to subject their eyeballs to this.

He loves it. As long as he doesn’t have to look at it:

"If all I have to do is revel in applications being 30 or 100 times faster, compiling down to minuscule executables that start up in sub milliseconds. I love Rust."

Rust is amazing. As long as you never, ever have to read it yourself.

I think he was talking about a world where AI writes the low-level code.

So why the sudden outburst?

Did everybody get smarter overnight?

No. I checked. I didn’t.

My theory: AI does most of the typing now, and typing was the part of Rust that scared people off.

AI doesn’t make ownership and lifetimes any easier to understand. It just means you no longer have to type them from scratch. Once AI removed that bottleneck, what’s left is the part everyone wanted anyway: the speed and the safety.

Rust is also unusually friendly to AI.

Why Rust and AI get along

It’s statically typed. Every variable and every function call has a type, and the compiler knows it before the code runs. So do Go, Java and TypeScript. The difference is what Rust’s compiler does with that knowledge.

The compiler is strict. Most mistakes get caught before your code runs, not in production at 2am. For an AI, that’s a feedback loop: write, compile, read the error, fix, repeat. The compiler marks the AI’s homework.

No null. If a value might be missing, the type says so, and the compiler makes you handle it. No more Cannot read properties of undefined at the worst possible moment. Rust still panics, but at a line you can point to.

Rust’s compiler is just the strictest teacher in the room.

And when it finally compiles, you get the speed: same category as C and C++.

So the AI writes, the compiler checks and nobody’s eyes get hurt.

The rewrites are already on my timeline

Once the intimidation went, people started building. And rewriting. A lot.

  • PHP, reimplemented in Rust, mostly by AI (php-rust).
  • An experimental Rust port of the TypeScript compiler (ts-rust). Funny detail: Microsoft’s own native TypeScript compiler is written in Go. Someone ported that to Rust. With AI.
  • Your JavaScript build tools. More on this one below.

I went down the php-rust rabbit hole in an earlier post if you want the details.

You’re probably running Rust already

Vite 8 “ships with Rolldown as its single, unified, Rust-based bundler.”

And it’s not alone:

  • SWC: compiles and minifies JavaScript and TypeScript
  • Biome: linting and formatting
  • Oxc: parser, linter, transformer
  • Lightning CSS: parses, transforms and minifies CSS
  • Rspack: a webpack-compatible bundler

You npm install them like anything else. Under the hood it's a compiled Rust binary doing the heavy lifting, and that's much faster for CPU-heavy work: parsing, compiling, transforming code.

To be fair, a lot of these tools started before AI got good at writing code. The speed was always the selling point. AI didn’t put Rust in your build tools. It put Rust on your timeline.

You’ve been using Rust every day without having to look at it. DHH would approve.

Rust in the browser? Yes, really.

Rust also compiles to WebAssembly, which runs in the browser next to your JavaScript.

So the heavy part of a web app (image processing, parsing a huge file, anything that makes the tab freeze) can be Rust, while the rest stays JavaScript.

Will Rust replace JavaScript?

No.

JavaScript is still the language of the browser. Your web app is not getting rewritten in Rust. (Please don’t.)

But I think Rust will replace many of the JavaScript-based tools in the build pipeline, because it’s faster and it’s safer.

The future I see is Rust plus JavaScript, not Rust versus JavaScript.

If you’re a JavaScript developer feeling the FOMO

Don’t leave JavaScript. Add to it.

  1. Learn the basics of Rust: types, ownership, the borrow checker. Enough to read what the AI writes.
  2. Use AI to get your code right, and read the compiler errors with it.
  3. Keep reading. As you use AI to work, you get better at it too. Every error it fixes in front of you is a free lesson.

From outside the fence

I don’t know what the future of Rust looks like.

But from where I’m standing, it’s getting a lot less scary.

Keep building software someone can still read.

title: PhysMoE: Fast Spatial Grounding with Single-Token Coordinate Representation in Modality-Decoupled VLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.13000v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Embodied Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are backbones for robotic planning and manipulation. However, for coordinate prediction in grounding tasks, existing architectures suffer from two distinct bottlenecks: discrete tokenization disrupts spatial continuity with high decoding latency, while standard point regression fails on multi-contact affordances and irregularly shaped targets. To resolve these challenges, we propose PhysMoE, introducing three core contributions: (1) sharing lower layers for multimodal context while routing upper layers to specialized spatial (pixel) and linguistic (text) experts by physical modality, eliminating gradient interference; (2) encoding each coordinate as a single token by reusing the visual encoder's learned positional embeddings, injecting 2D spatial priors to natively align coordinates with visual features and ease training; and (3) differentiable Signed Distance Field (SDF) supervision on pointing, accommodating affordances and irregular geometries without costly mask decoders. Compared to the base model, PhysMoE achieves a 15.7% average gain and an 8.31x throughput speedup across 9 coordinate-based grounding benchmarks (trajectory, affordance, and localization), while preserving multimodal understanding and reasoning across 11 text-based embodied benchmarks.

title: SepsisFlow: an event-stream foundation model for continuous risk warning and trajectory modelling in ICU sepsis
description:
arXiv:2611.13661v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sepsis is a leading cause of ICU death with heterogeneous onset and course, yet most warning models predict only whether sepsis will occur, leaving clinicians uncertain of its onset context and early trajectory once an alarm sounds. To answer these questions on one hourly clock from ICU admission, we built SepsisFlow: before onset, it combines a Mamba model pretrained on 2.57 million EHRs with about 1,700 hourly features in gradient-boosted trees to predict 6/12/24-h risk; at onset, it fuses Mamba and tabular encoders via a gated network into continuous patient states defining onset contexts; after onset, it encodes 72-h organ-support and physiological trajectories via an attention bidirectional recurrent network into early courses. For pre-onset warning in MIMIC-IV, SepsisFlow detected more cases than NEWS2, qSOFA, and SIRS at equal alarms, gaining about 8 cases per 100 from hourly updating, while outperforming 16 retrained algorithms and maintaining risk ranking in eICU. At onset, its contexts separated 2% cardiovascular-ICU from 15%-17% other 28-day mortality, and within each context after onset, persistent support carried fivefold higher mortality than de-escalation. SepsisFlow establishes a foundation-model paradigm for continuous risk and trajectory stratification in critical care.

title: Pyrite benchmarks protein-ligand pose ranking where experts perform near chance
description:
Researchers introduce Pyrite, a pairwise pose-ranking benchmark with 1,500 pose pairs across diverse protein-ligand complexes. Expert chemists using 3D visualization and physics-based scores perform near chance, showing how hard ranking is. The work also introduces PyriteRep, a structured molecular representation for automated ranking agents.

Why it matters

Correct ligand pose ranking is central to drug discovery; reliable automated ranking could improve candidate selection from cofolding models.

Analysis

Drug discovery agents may combine cofolding generation with learned ranking, moving beyond human-interpretable chemical scores.

Source: arXiv

AI disclosure: this article was produced with AI assistance and reviewed for accuracy.

title: Representational Atoms in Neural Networks
description:
arXiv:2611.14168v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding the internal representations of neural networks and characterizing their relationship with human conceptual structure are two critical questions for elucidating model mechanisms. The former reveals how learned knowledge is organized in internal representations, whereas the latter provides a basis for interpreting these representations through human conceptual structure. Here, we formally define fundamental representational units (FRUs) and establish two evaluation criteria: fidelity and stability. We further prove that threshold-activated sparse autoencoders (TSAEs) can identify FRUs with high fidelity and stability under appropriate conditions, and validate this result through large-scale experiments. Further analyses reveal that FRUs with higher stability exhibit greater monosemanticity and can be composed across layers to recover semantic organization corresponding to human conceptual structure. These results provide a unified framework for defining, evaluating and identifying FRUs in neural networks, and establish a foundation for characterizing the relationship between neural network representations and human conceptual structure.

title: Exploration via Exploitation: The Blessing of Reward Diversity in Personalized Federated RL
description:
arXiv:2611.12964v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While federated reinforcement learning (RL) has traditionally guaranteed high efficiency in homogeneous environments, collaboration is often hindered when agents possess distinct goals. In this paper, we flip this paradigm, framing reward heterogeneity not as a hurdle to consensus, but as a structural asset that catalyzes exploration. We first propose Personalized Federated Upper Confidence Bound Value Iteration (PF-UCBVI), which achieves optimal linear speedup by decoupling shared dynamics from personalized objectives. To eliminate the risks of explicit exploration, we then introduce Personalized Federated Exploration-Free Value Iteration (PF-EFVI), a purely greedy algorithm that leverages reward diversity to ensure state-action coverage. We prove that PF-EFVI attains logarithmic regret without explicit exploration bonuses under sufficient reward diversity. Our results reveal that agent disagreement shifts the exploration burden from temporal complexity to spatial diversity, enabling efficient collective learning without explicit exploration.

title: Getting Started with Swift on Android: A Beginner's Guide to the Official SDK
description:
A beginner-friendly introduction to the official Swift SDK for Android

1. Introduction

For most of its life, Swift was known as the language for iPhone, iPad and Mac apps. That changed with Swift 6.3, which shipped the first official Swift SDK for Android. You can now compile Swift code for Android devices using official tools published on swift.org, instead of relying on unofficial community toolchains.

This tutorial walks you through the whole path from zero: what the pieces are, how to install them, how to build your first Swift program for Android, and how Swift fits into a real Android app. No previous Android experience is needed, but basic familiarity with Swift and the terminal will help.

What you will learn

  • What the Swift SDK for Android is, and what it is not
  • How to install the toolchain, the SDK and the Android NDK
  • How to cross-compile and run a "Hello, world" program on an emulator or device
  • How to share Swift code between an iOS app and an Android app

2. How it works: the three pieces

Building Swift for Android needs three components that work together:

Component What it does
Host toolchain The Swift compiler and tools running on your Mac or Linux machine.
Swift SDK for Android Libraries, headers and resources that let the compiler target Android (a cross-compilation SDK).
Android NDK Google's Native Development Kit, which provides the Android system libraries your Swift code links against.

Important: Xcode cannot build Android apps by itself. The Swift SDK for Android is used from the command line (Swift Package Manager) or from Android Studio via Gradle. SwiftUI and UIKit do not run on Android; for the user interface you typically use Kotlin with Jetpack Compose, or a third-party tool such as Skip.

3. Prerequisites

  • A Mac (macOS) or a Linux machine
  • Android Studio, with an emulator set up or a physical Android device with USB debugging enabled
  • Around 5 GB of free disk space for the toolchain, SDK and NDK
  • A terminal you are comfortable using

4. Step-by-step setup

Step 1: Install swiftly

swiftly is the official Swift toolchain manager. It lets you install and switch between Swift versions. On macOS:

curl -O https://download.swift.org/swiftly/darwin/swiftly.pkg && \
installer -pkg swiftly.pkg -target CurrentUserHomeDirectory && \
~/.swiftly/bin/swiftly init --quiet-shell-followup && \
. "${SWIFTLY_HOME_DIR:-$HOME/.swiftly}/env.sh" && \
hash -r

On Linux, follow the swiftly instructions at swift.org/install.

Step 2: Install a matching Swift toolchain

The host toolchain must be the same version as the Android SDK you install next. For example, for the latest release:

swiftly install latest
swiftly use latest
swift --version

Step 3: Install the Swift SDK for Android

Go to swift.org/install, open the Android section, and copy the install command for the SDK that matches your toolchain version. It looks like this:

swift sdk install <SDK-URL-FROM-SWIFT.ORG>.artifactbundle.tar.gz \
  --checksum <CHECKSUM-FROM-SWIFT.ORG>

Tip: Always copy the URL and checksum from swift.org rather than from a blog post. The checksum protects you from a corrupted or tampered download, and it changes with every release.

Check that it installed correctly:

swift sdk list
# Example output:
# swift-6.x-RELEASE_android

Step 4: Install the Android NDK and link it

In Android Studio, open Settings > Languages & Frameworks > Android SDK > SDK Tools, tick NDK (Side by side) and install the version recommended in the swift.org Android guide. Then point your shell at it (macOS paths shown; on Linux the SDK usually lives in ~/Android/Sdk):

export ANDROID_HOME=$HOME/Library/Android/sdk
export ANDROID_NDK_HOME=$ANDROID_HOME/ndk/<your-ndk-version>
export PATH=$PATH:$ANDROID_HOME/platform-tools

Finally, run the setup script that ships inside the SDK bundle. It links the NDK to the Swift SDK:

cd ~/Library/org.swift.swiftpm || cd ~/.swiftpm
./swift-sdks/<your-sdk-name>.artifactbundle/swift-android/scripts/setup-android-sdk.sh

You should see a success message saying the NDK sysroot was linked.

5. Your first Swift program on Android

Step 5: Create a package 

mkdir hello && cd hello
swift package init --type executable
swift build
.build/debug/hello      # prints: Hello, world!

This first build runs on your own machine. Now cross-compile the same code for Android.

Step 6: Cross-compile for Android 

# For the emulator (x86_64):
swift build --swift-sdk x86_64-unknown-linux-android28 --static-swift-stdlib

# For a real phone (arm64):
swift build --swift-sdk aarch64-unknown-linux-android28 --static-swift-stdlib

The number 28 is the minimum Android API level (Android 9). --static-swift-stdlib bundles the Swift standard library into the binary so you don't have to copy it separately.

Step 7: Run it on the emulator or device

Start your emulator (or connect your phone), then push the binary plus the C++ runtime from the NDK and run it:

adb push .build/x86_64-unknown-linux-android28/debug/hello /data/local/tmp/
adb push $ANDROID_NDK_HOME/toolchains/llvm/prebuilt/*/sysroot/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-android/libc++_shared.so /data/local/tmp/
adb shell "cd /data/local/tmp && LD_LIBRARY_PATH=. ./hello"
# Hello, world!

🎉 Congratulations! You just ran Swift code on Android. For a real phone, swap x86_64 for aarch64 in the first two paths.

6. Writing code that works on both platforms

The most practical use of Swift on Android today is sharing your app's core logic: models, validation, networking and business rules. You write it once in a Swift package and use it in both apps. When something needs to differ, use a compile-time platform check:

public struct Greeter {
    public init() {}

    public func greeting(for name: String) -> String {
        #if os(Android)
        let platform = "Android"
        #elseif os(iOS)
        let platform = "iOS"
        #else
        let platform = "another platform"
        #endif
        return "Hello, \(name)! Running Swift on \(platform)."
    }
}

Many existing packages already work: more than a quarter of the libraries on the Swift Package Index were marked as Android-compatible when the SDK launched. Check a package's page on swiftpackageindex.com before you depend on it.

7. From a program to a real Android app

Running a terminal program is the first milestone. To build an actual app with screens, you have two main options:

Option A: Kotlin UI + shared Swift logic

Build the user interface in Android Studio with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, and call your Swift package from Kotlin using swift-java, the official Java/Kotlin interoperability project. The official swift-android-examples repository on GitHub shows complete working setups. This is the best fit for teams that already have an Android app.

Option B: SwiftUI everywhere with Skip

Skip is a third-party tool that works inside Xcode. You write a SwiftUI app and Skip produces a native Android version, running on the iOS simulator and an Android emulator side by side. It is the closest thing to "Xcode for Android". Check its website for current features and pricing.

8. Common problems and fixes

Problem Fix
swift sdk list shows nothing The SDK install failed or ran with a different toolchain. Re-run the install command with the toolchain active.
Build errors about missing headers or sysroot The NDK isn't linked. Re-run setup-android-sdk.sh after setting ANDROID_NDK_HOME.
Version mismatch error Toolchain and SDK versions must match exactly. Check with swift --version.
libc++_shared.so not found on device Push it from the NDK sysroot (Step 7) and set LD_LIBRARY_PATH.
"Exec format error" on device Wrong architecture. Use x86_64 for most emulators and aarch64 for phones.

9. Resources

  • Official getting-started guide: Swift SDK for Android – Getting Started
  • Downloads and install commands: swift.org/install
  • Java/Kotlin interop: swiftlang/swift-java
  • Example apps: swiftlang/swift-android-examples
  • Community discussion: the Android category on forums.swift.org
  • Skip: skip.dev

10. Wrapping up

Swift on Android is young but official, and it is improving with every release. Start small: get "Hello, world" running, then move one piece of shared logic, such as a model or a validation rule, into a Swift package that both your iOS and Android apps use. Feedback and questions are welcome in the comments below!
