title: The 10-Minute Collision Window: Killing Duplicate Bank SMS Transactions
description:
When you build an automated transaction ingestion pipeline from banking SMS notifications, your biggest enemy is not malformed text.

Your biggest enemy is duplicate delivery.

Telecommunication networks and banking infrastructure duplicate messages regularly:

  1. Network Retransmission: If a phone travels through a weak cellular zone or hands off between cell towers, carrier SMS gateways frequently deliver the same message twice.
  2. Dual Bank Alerts: Many Indian banks send two distinct notifications for a single POS transaction: first an authorization alert from the card processor (e.g. Visa or Mastercard), followed minutes later by an SMS from the issuing bank confirming the debit.
  3. Inbox Re-Scanning: When a user runs a historical inbox scan, the scanner will encounter messages that were already captured in real-time by the application's background BroadcastReceiver days earlier.

If an expense tracker records both alerts, your account balance is deducted twice, ruining your ledger.

However, fixing this with naive deduplication is even more dangerous: it can cause silent data loss.

Here is how a subtle regression in FinLedger led to the discovery of the deduplication collision dilemma, and how we solved it with a calibrated four-factor matching engine.

The Flawed Query: When Deduplication Causes Silent Data Loss

In an early development sprint, FinLedger implemented a straightforward duplicate detection query in SQLite. The logic attempted to catch both identical timestamps and identical transactions:

-- The Flawed Early Query
SELECT * FROM transactions 
WHERE dateTimestamp = :timestamp 
   OR (amount = :amount AND accountId = :accountId);

Can you spot the catastrophic flaw in this logic?

Look closely at the OR condition:

flowchart TD
    subgraph SilentLoss["The Danger of Naive Deduplication"]
        MorningCoffee["9:00 AM: Buy Coffee for Rs. 150.00 at Starbucks"] --> Insert1["Inserted into Ledger:
        Amount: 150.00, Time: 9:00 AM"]

        LunchCoffee["1:30 PM: Buy Coffee for Rs. 150.00 at Starbucks"] --> Check["Deduplication Query:
        'Does a transaction exist with Amount = 150.00 on this account?'"]

        Check -->|YES: Matches Morning Coffee!| Drop["Catastrophic Bug:
        Lunch coffee dropped as 'Duplicate'!
        Rs. 150 quietly vanishes from ledger tracking."]
    end

Because the query used an over-broad OR clause:

  1. If you bought two coffees of the exact same price (Rs. 150.00) on the same day, the second coffee was rejected as a duplicate!
  2. Even worse, if you ran automated bills where two subscriptions (e.g., Spotify and iCloud) processed at the exact same second (dateTimestamp), the second subscription was discarded!

This was a severe accounting bug discovered during regression testing (documented under TASK-H4.4 in the FinLedger codebase). We were dropping genuine financial transactions to prevent duplicate SMS alerts.

The Four-Factor Matching Engine (DuplicateDetectionTest.kt)

To prevent duplicate bank alerts without dropping legitimate recurring transactions, we completely rewrote the deduplication predicate.

A candidate transaction is only classified as a duplicate if all four discriminating factors match simultaneously:

flowchart TD
    Candidate["Incoming SMS Candidate"] --> Factor1{"1. Amount Match:
    abs(a - b) < 0.005
    (Within half a paisa)"}

    Factor1 -->|No| Safe["Insert as Unique Transaction"]
    Factor1 -->|Yes| Factor2{"2. Time Window:
    abs(t1 - t2) <= 10 Minutes
    (600,000 ms)"}

    Factor2 -->|No| Safe
    Factor2 -->|Yes| Factor3{"3. Polarity Match:
    candidate.type == seen.type
    (DEBIT vs CREDIT)"}

    Factor3 -->|No| Safe
    Factor3 -->|Yes| Factor4{"4. Entity Match:
    candidate.merchant == seen.merchant"}

    Factor4 -->|No| Safe
    Factor4 -->|Yes| Duplicate["CONFIRMED DUPLICATE:
    Drop without corrupting balances"]

Let's examine why each factor is essential.

1. Amount Precision (Half a Paisa)

In financial math, floating-point numbers cannot be compared with direct equality (==). The engine verifies that:
abs(seen.amount - candidate.amount) < 0.005
This accounts for minuscule floating-point rounding quirks while strictly preserving distinct transactions.

2. The 10-Minute Collision Window (600,000 ms)

Why 10 minutes?

  • Cellular network retries and carrier message duplication almost always occur within 60 to 180 seconds.
  • Secondary bank authorization alerts for POS machines occasionally experience 5 to 7 minute delays during peak server loads.
  • However, it is virtually impossible for a human being to purchase the exact same item, for the exact same price, at the exact same merchant, within a 10-minute window without it being an accidental duplicate tap or double-charge.
  • If you buy coffee at 9:00 AM and another coffee at 1:30 PM, the delta is 270 minutes—well outside the collision window. Both are correctly preserved.

3. Transaction Polarity (Type Matching)

A debit followed immediately by a credit (such as an instant refund or reversed payment) carries the same amount, timestamp, and merchant. By verifying that candidate.type == seen.type, an incoming refund credit of Rs. 500 is never dropped because of the original Rs. 500 debit alert.

4. Counter-Party Normalization

The merchant name must match after string normalization (stripping trailing UPI reference numbers and whitespace). If you pay Rs. 500 for a taxi and Rs. 500 for groceries five minutes later, the distinct merchant identifiers ensure neither transaction is dropped.

Testing with Automated Regression Suites

To guarantee that future refactoring never reintroduces duplicate data loss, FinLedger maintains a comprehensive unit test suite in DuplicateDetectionTest.kt.

The test suite systematically asserts against real-world edge cases:

  • Two different transactions occurring at the exact same millisecond (e.g. simultaneous automated investments) are asserted as NOT duplicates.
  • Identical amounts at different merchants are asserted as NOT duplicates.
  • Identical amounts and merchants separated by 11 minutes (660,000 ms) are asserted as NOT duplicates.
  • Identical amounts, merchants, and accounts arriving within 3 minutes with matching transaction references are asserted as DUPLICATES and successfully consolidated.

Key Takeaway

Deduplication in financial software cannot be treated as a simple database uniqueness constraint.

Real-world banking alerts are messy, delayed, and asynchronous. By establishing a strict multi-factor collision window—spanning amount precision, time delta, transaction polarity, and merchant identity—FinLedger eliminates redundant SMS alerts without ever losing a penny of user data.

FinLedger is a privacy-first, offline-first personal finance application for Android that models bank accounts, credit cards, and cash without double-counting.

Explore FinLedger on Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.devanshufinance.app

title: NCP: Verifier-Guided Optimization of Weight-Space Control Policies
description:
arXiv:2611.13236v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present the Neural Control Plane (NCP), a closed-loop system that observes language-model execution, synthesizes candidate weight-space intervention rules, evaluates them, and maintains a versioned table of admitted policies. NCP separates a pretrained model's inference data plane from the control policy that selects temporary parameter interventions. W-ISA supplies transactional execution and parameter restoration; NCP supplies telemetry, candidate synthesis, admission criteria, priorities, and rule lifetime management. The optimization state consists of active rules and an archive of evaluated candidates, while base-model parameters are restored after each request. In a local SmolLM-135M-Instruct experiment, NCP generated three candidates from development telemetry and evaluated them on separate task examples and a 4,095-target WikiText-2 slice. One projection reduced validation token repetition from 0.4133 to 0.2191, with a perplexity change of -0.0574%. All candidates produced zero newly correct exact answers, so the configured admission gate archived all three and retained the original active policy. Fresh-process repetition and saved-table resumption reproduced the measured outcomes. NCP provides an executable framework for studying recursive self-improvement at the control-policy level through explicit synthesis, verification, and state transitions.

title: I gave a colleague a terminal into one Claude Code session
description:
I'm part of a small infrastructure team, and most days I have a handful of Claude Code sessions running on a few machines. sessionhub keeps track of them: one registry, one inbox, every machine.

Sooner or later someone asks: "can I look at that session with you?"

Until last week my honest answer was "sort of".

What I could offer before

A screen share. They watch, I type. Fine for five minutes.

An SSH account. This is the real answer most teams give, and it is the wrong size. An account on my machine shows every pane I have open, every other session, my shell history, and my files. They wanted one conversation. I would be handing over the building to show them one room.

The dashboard. sessionhub already had a web dashboard, so the first step was a guest link:

sessionhub login --name alice --session 3f2a9c10

That prints a one-time link. The browser that opens it sees that one session and nothing else. It can read it, reply to it, and answer its permission prompts and questions. It gets no other session, no tasks, no resume command, no Remote Control link. Every other route answers 403, and I take it back with sessionhub login rm alice.

That covered reading and answering. It was OK for a couple of days, then it wasn't. It did not cover the thing people ask for when they say "let me drive for a minute": the terminal.

sessionhub attach

So the same link now works in a terminal:

sessionhub attach https://hub.example.com/login/<code>

The guest's machine doesn't join anything. The command signs in with the link, shows that one session's terminal, and sends keystrokes to it. Ctrl-] detaches, and the session keeps running.

There is no SSH and no inbound port. The shape is the one the rest of sessionhub already uses: machines poll the server, and the server never connects out to them.

guest terminal ──HTTP──> sessionhub server <──HTTP── machine watcher ──> the pane

Each side holds one streaming GET for bytes coming toward it and makes small POSTs for bytes going away. The server relays between them in memory. I skipped WebSockets: Go's standard library has no WebSocket server, and sessionhub has four direct dependencies that I'd like to keep at four. Two chunked HTTP streams do the job with net/http alone.

The trade-off I took

The mirror is a snapshot, not a real terminal stream. The watcher reads the pane's screen every 250 ms and sends a fresh frame when it changed. That means:

  • The guest sees the host pane's size, not their own.
  • No scrollback on the guest's side.
  • A fast-scrolling build log looks choppy.

For a Claude Code session that is fine. The screen changes in bursts, and what the guest needs is the current state and a keyboard. A proper stream is a later change behind the same command.

One thing to be straight about: attaching gives the guest Claude's keyboard, and that includes ! shell commands. The link is scoped to one session, but that session runs as me. Hand it only to someone you would give a shell. The link is one-time, the sign-in expires, and an attach ends after 30 minutes without traffic.

A second terminal: Rex

Everything above first worked through herdr, the terminal multiplexer I run sessions in. This week I added Rex as a second backend, using only its rex CLI:

  • sessionhub start <machine> opens a new Rex session running Claude with Remote Control on.
  • sessionhub resume <id> focuses the block that runs a session.
  • sessionhub move <id> <machine> carries a session between machines, herdr or Rex on either side.
  • A watcher runs as a systemd unit on a machine with no herdr at all.

Status, plainly: start, resume, and Remote Control are tested live on Linux. Moves into Rex pass against a fake so far, and macOS is untested.

What I took from it

  • Scope the access to the question. "Can I see that session?" deserves one session, not a machine.
  • Reuse the direction of trust you already have. Machines polling the server made a relay possible with no new open port.
  • Ship the snapshot. The 250 ms mirror took a fraction of the work of a real stream, and it answers the request.

sessionhub is open source (MIT), a single Go binary with SQLite: github.com/abdallah/session-hub.

title: High Probability Risk Control for Online Policy Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.13163v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study risk control for online policy learning, where an agent adaptively collects data and aims to learn a new policy whose risk stays below a tolerance threshold at every round with high probability. Such policy updates and data collection induce feedback covariate shift (FCS): observed data depend on history through evolving policies and the data-collection process. FCS brings two substantive problems for risk control: 1) efficient risk evaluation for each candidate policy and 2) valid policy selection with high-probability risk control. To address these, we propose a permutation-based weighted risk evaluator with weights efficiently approximated by the Sinkhorn algorithm and select policies whose estimated risk upper confidence bounds (UCB) fall below the target threshold, with the UCB obtained through a proposed Gaussian bootstrap method. Theoretically, we prove that our risk evaluator has a no-larger variance upper bound than that of the standard importance-weighted evaluator. Our policy control method also yields an asymptotically valid simultaneous risk bound and provides asymptotic high-probability risk control for the selected policy. Empirically, we evaluate our method on the online contextual bandit problem, safe question answering benchmark, and Medical Claim Filtering tasks. Our method maintains the target risk level, achieves lower risk than baseline methods, has lower variance in risk estimation, and achieves reliable policy selection with high-probability risk control. Further ablation studies support our theoretical claims.

title: Using LLM Agents to Evaluate Prosocial Interventions on Social Media Platforms
description:
arXiv:2611.12922v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Social media platforms are a primary source of information for many users. Although research explores various interventions to promote prosocial content or demote harmful content on platforms, there are few systematic methods for evaluating competing intervention designs before conducting costly human-subject experiments. We develop a simulation-based evaluation pipeline built on the OASIS framework. We generate 13,835 LLM-based agents, each with a unique profile. Over 20 time steps, we expose them to real-world Twitter/X posts and let them comment, like, repost, or follow. We use those agents to systematically evaluate three interventions that increase exposure to verified news: adding content, upranking content, and celebrity source cues. All interventions significantly increase news engagement, with upranking news to prominent feed positions producing the largest effects. These effects hold across agents' gender, age, and education levels. We validate our injection treatment results against a comparable human-subject study and find strong directional alignment and similar dose-normalized efficiency. Our results suggest that LLM-based agent simulations can support early-stage evaluation of platform interventions before human-subject deployment, and upranking may be more effective than news volume or source.

title: Why AI PNG Uploads Fail: Node.js Buffer Boundaries in Compatible Object Storage
description:
Short answer: keep the generated image as bytes from the model boundary to the object-storage request, decode base64 exactly once only when the producer actually returned base64, and make retention state explicit before a delete job is allowed to run.

For a gaming service that keeps per-tenant image backups and restores a selected snapshot, the important design is not the upload call. It is the boundary around that call. A PNG must remain a PNG byte stream, a retry must address the same logical object, and deletion must be a deliberate state transition rather than a side effect of a failed restore.

Keep the object private.

I start with invariants. The stored object has the expected signature, media type, and byte length. The database names the snapshot only after verification. A tenant can ask for a restore while another snapshot is being deleted without turning the result into a race. Those checks are more useful than a successful-looking 200 response.

Decision record: define the storage boundaries

An image generator can return raw binary data, a base64 string, or a data URL containing a base64 string. These are different representations. A Node.js Buffer should go directly to the request body. A base64 value should be decoded once. A data URL needs its media-type prefix removed before that one decode. Calling toString() on binary data and later decoding the resulting text is a common way to turn valid bytes into a malformed payload.

The adapter should normalize all three cases into one internal value: bytes plus a declared media type. Reject an empty value, an unexpected PNG signature, and a media type that does not match the job before making a storage request. A 400-style “malformed base64” message is usually a representation error, not evidence that the object store damaged the image.

The object key is also an invariant. Include the tenant, generation job, and snapshot identity in it, for example tenant-17/snapshot-0042.png. Reuse that key on retries. Do not create a fresh random key inside retry code, because a timeout after a successful write would then leave an untracked duplicate behind. If two valid generations can intentionally target one key, serialize that operation in the application or queue; object storage alone should not be treated as the transaction coordinator.

After the write, read the object's metadata and compare its length and content type with the normalized input. Persist the database row only after that check. The verification is not a replacement for an end-to-end checksum, but it catches a truncated body and a missing media type close to the cause, where the failure is still diagnosable.

How should Node.js AI image generation handle malformed base64 before PNG storage?

The critical path is short. Keep it that way.

  1. Identify whether the provider returned bytes, base64, or a data URL.
  2. Normalize the result once and validate the PNG signature.
  3. Write the bytes to a deterministic tenant and snapshot key.
  4. Verify length and media type before committing the snapshot row.
  5. Return a time-limited read URL only after the snapshot is marked available.

The following Python example shows the protocol boundary without coupling the design to a particular SDK. The same ordering applies in a Node.js service: its Buffer is the png_bytes value, and its HTTP client must send those bytes as the request body rather than JSON text.

import base64
import binascii
import json
import urllib.parse
import urllib.request

PNG_SIGNATURE = b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n"


def normalize_png(value, representation):
    if representation == "bytes":
        png_bytes = value
    elif representation == "base64":
        try:
            png_bytes = base64.b64decode(value, validate=True)
        except (binascii.Error, ValueError) as exc:
            raise ValueError("image payload is not valid base64") from exc
    elif representation == "data-url":
        prefix, separator, payload = value.partition(",")
        if not separator or ";base64" not in prefix:
            raise ValueError("image data URL is not base64")
        try:
            png_bytes = base64.b64decode(payload, validate=True)
        except (binascii.Error, ValueError) as exc:
            raise ValueError("image data URL has malformed base64") from exc
    else:
        raise ValueError("unknown image representation")

    if not png_bytes.startswith(PNG_SIGNATURE):
        raise ValueError("normalized payload is not a PNG")
    return png_bytes


def put_and_verify(endpoint, token, bucket, object_key, png_bytes):
    path = "/objects/" + urllib.parse.quote(bucket, safe="")
    path += "/" + urllib.parse.quote(object_key, safe="/")
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        endpoint + path,
        data=png_bytes,
        headers={
            "Authorization": "Bearer " + token,
            "Content-Type": "image/png",
        },
        method="PUT",
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
        if response.status not in (200, 201, 204):
            raise RuntimeError("object write was not accepted")

    # The metadata read must target the same deterministic key.
    check = urllib.request.Request(
        endpoint + path,
        headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + token},
        method="HEAD",
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(check, timeout=30) as response:
        length = int(response.headers["Content-Length"])
        media_type = response.headers.get_content_type()
    if length != len(png_bytes) or media_type != "image/png":
        raise RuntimeError("stored object failed verification")

    return {"key": object_key, "length": length, "media_type": media_type}

The example deliberately does not retry every exception. Retrying a request after an unknown outcome is safe only when the key and write semantics are understood, and a retry policy should distinguish rate limiting, a transport timeout, and a validation failure. I would log the tenant, snapshot ID, byte length, and a request correlation ID, but never the image bytes or an access token. Your mileage may vary on the exact retry budget; it should follow the queue's delivery contract and the storage service's documented behavior.

Retention and deletion are part of restore correctness

Generated images become backups the moment a restore workflow can select them. That changes the deletion question. A cleanup process must know whether a snapshot is pending, available, restore_requested, restored, or delete_eligible; it should never infer eligibility from object age alone.

For each tenant, keep the retention decision in durable metadata: snapshot creation time, expiration time, generation status, and the policy version that produced the deadline. A lifecycle rule can remove old objects automatically, but the application still needs a way to stop a restore from selecting an object that policy has marked for deletion. The database and object store are separate systems, so deletion needs an observable transition: mark the row, enqueue the object deletion, record the result, and reconcile orphaned rows and orphaned objects.

The difficult case is a restore racing with cleanup. Claim the snapshot before reading it, or use a lease whose expiry is longer than the expected restore. Cleanup should skip claimed snapshots and should be safe to run again. If a delete request succeeds but the database update times out, reconciliation must converge on the same state; otherwise a later retry can either resurrect a supposedly deleted image or report a snapshot that no longer exists. That needs more than a timestamp check: the worker should load the current row, verify that the policy version still permits deletion, record an attempt ID, issue the object delete, and then compare the resulting state with the row it originally claimed. A restore request arriving between those steps should either inherit the claim or receive a clear “snapshot is being retained” decision. Silent last-writer-wins behavior is the failure mode to design out.

Which storage strategy fits this backup workflow?

The answer depends on the guarantee the team needs, not on whether an upload example is convenient.

Strategy Good fit Boundary or cost to accept
S3-compatible object storage with application metadata Private tenant snapshots, large PNGs, and time-based retention The database must coordinate restore claims, deletion, and orphan reconciliation
Object storage with native lifecycle rules Predictable age-based cleanup with low application traffic Lifecycle expiration is asynchronous; it is not a restore lock or an audit record
Database binary or base64 storage Very small artifacts that must commit atomically with relational state Payload size, encoding overhead, and database backup growth become the bottleneck
Content-addressed immutable storage Deduplication and strong snapshot identity matter more than simple expiry Deletion becomes a garbage-collection problem and requires a clear legal-retention policy

The catch is that the first option is not suitable when the product needs native immutable retention, cross-region disaster recovery, server-side image search, or a provider-specific conditional-write guarantee that the abstraction does not expose. Choose a storage system with those controls, or add a coordination layer that can enforce them. Stick with database storage when the files are genuinely small and atomic row-plus-payload commits are the dominant requirement.

Do not make price the decision rule. The operational questions are sharper: who owns the retention policy, how is a failed delete detected, how is a selected snapshot protected during restore, and which evidence proves that the bytes read are the bytes written? Those answers determine the architecture.

Rejected option: decode at every boundary

Repeatedly converting an image between bytes, base64, JSON, and bytes creates more failure points without improving durability. It also makes logs tempting to inspect, which can expose user-generated content. Normalize once at the edge, keep binary data binary, and pass a small metadata record between the image job, storage worker, and restore coordinator.

A public URL as the database's permanent representation is another poor fit for private tenant backups. Authorization belongs in the application workflow; a short-lived read URL can be produced after the snapshot claim is checked. For browser upload progress, the client can observe upload events, but progress is not proof of durable storage. The server-side verification and state transition still decide whether a snapshot is available.

This is the decision I would record: bytes are validated once, object identity is deterministic, retention is explicit, and deletion is reconciled. The upload endpoint is only one boundary in that system.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/XMLHttpRequest_API/Using_XMLHttpRequest

title: Broad-Persistent Advising in Interactive Reinforcement Learning via Latent State Encoding
description:
arXiv:2611.13712v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep Interactive Reinforcement Learning (Deep IntRL) accelerates reinforcement learning training by incorporating external advice. However, conventional Deep IntRL uses each piece of advice only in the current step and discards it after a single interaction. Persistent Advising and Broad-Persistent Advising (BPA) extend this process by storing advice in persistent memory and reusing it in similar states through state generalisation based on K-means clustering. This research proposes Encoder BPA, which employs a latent encoder to retrieve and reuse advice. In this framework, a trained encoder is used to map a state sequence into a latent representation at every time step. Advice can be retrieved through latent comparison, together with a top-(k) aggregation and a consistency condition to improve reuse stability. Experimental results show that Encoder BPA improves learning efficiency and advice utilisation at an early stage of training compared with different Deep IntRL approaches, especially in complex and partially observable environments.

title: How Do You Make a Bama Bound AI Clip Loop Without a Visible Jump? A Tail-to-Head Crossfade in ffmpeg, With a Seam Score
description:
Checked November 11, 2026. I build bamabound.app, which turns one photo of one person into a vertical clip of them holding a red I'M BAMA BOUND banner. The test clip in this post is synthetic (a red box swaying over a green field, with beeps), not a real person.

People ask some version of this a lot: "How do I make my Bama Bound video loop smoothly on my story / on a website / on a screen at a grad party?"

Players already repeat short videos. The problem is the moment where they do. A Bama Bound clip follows the reference timing of about eight seconds in a 9:16 frame, with the original soundtrack attached (FAQ). The last frame and the first frame were never meant to meet, so every repeat has a visible jump: the banner snaps from one side to the other, and the audio clicks.

This post fixes that with one ffmpeg graph and gives you a number to check the result instead of squinting.

The idea: crossfade the tail into the head

Split the clip into three parts:

| head (0..F) |          mid (F..D-F)          | tail (D-F..D) |

Then build a new clip: mid, followed by tail with head fading in on top of it. The output ends on the head's last frame, which is exactly where mid begins. So when the player jumps back to the start, frame N flows into frame N+1 of the original motion. No snap.

The cost is length: the output is D - F seconds. With F = 0.5, an 8 s clip becomes 7.5 s.

Audio gets the same treatment with acrossfade, so the beat doesn't click at the seam.

The script

Full file: loop_clip.py (Python 3, numpy, ffmpeg/ffprobe on PATH).

def make_loop(src, dst, fade):
    w, h, fps, dur = probe(src)
    body = dur - fade
    v = (f"[0:v]split=3[a][b][c];"
         f"[a]trim=0:{fade},setpts=PTS-STARTPTS[head];"
         f"[b]trim={fade}:{body},setpts=PTS-STARTPTS[mid];"
         f"[c]trim={body}:{dur},setpts=PTS-STARTPTS[tail];"
         f"[head]format=yuva420p,fade=t=in:st=0:d={fade}:alpha=1[hf];"
         f"[tail][hf]overlay=shortest=1[seam];"
         f"[mid][seam]concat=n=2:v=1:a=0,format=yuv420p[v]")
    if has_audio(src):
        v += (f";[0:a]asplit=3[x][y][z];"
              f"[x]atrim=0:{fade},asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS[ah];"
              f"[y]atrim={fade}:{body},asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS[am];"
              f"[z]atrim={body}:{dur},asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS[at];"
              f"[at][ah]acrossfade=d={fade}:c1=tri:c2=tri[as];"
              f"[am][as]concat=n=2:v=0:a=1[aout]")
    # then: ffmpeg -i src -filter_complex v -map [v] -map [aout] ... dst

Why not xfade?

My first version used xfade=transition=fade. It failed with:

The inputs needs to be a constant frame rate; current rate of 1/0 is invalid

After trim + setpts, the branches lose their frame-rate metadata, and xfade refuses them. Adding fps= up front didn't fix it either. Fading the head's alpha channel in and overlaying it on the tail does the same blend and doesn't care about frame-rate metadata. If you control your input, xfade works too, but the alpha version has been less fussy for me.

Measuring the seam

"Looks smooth to me" isn't a test. The script grabs the last frame and the first frame as grayscale arrays and reports the mean absolute pixel difference (0 = identical, 255 = opposite). It also reports the difference between two neighbouring frames in the middle of the clip, because that's the honest target: a good seam should look like any other frame step, not like a freeze.

def seam(path):
    w, h, fps, dur = probe(path)
    last = frame(path, max(dur - 1.5 / fps, 0), w, h)
    first = frame(path, 0, w, h)
    return float(np.abs(last - first).mean())

Results on a test clip

I ran it on two synthetic 480x854, 30 fps, 8 s clips: one with heavy film grain on the grass, one with no grain.

Clip Seam before Seam after (F=0.5 s) Normal frame step Length
grainy field 7.5 5.2 5.1 8.00 → 7.50 s
clean field 2.0 0.9 0.7 8.00 → 7.50 s

With F = 1.0 on the grainy clip, the seam was 4.5 and the clip 7.0 s.

Two things to notice:

  • The grainy "before" seam looks small (7.5) but the jump is real. Grain makes every frame differ by about 5, so the number only means something next to the normal frame step. That's why the script prints both.
  • After the crossfade, the seam lands right at the normal frame step (5.2 vs 5.1, 0.9 vs 0.7). That's the goal: the loop point stops being special.

Picking the fade length

  • 0.3 to 0.5 s is enough when the banner moves slowly at the start and end. You lose little length.
  • 1 s helps when the start and end poses are very different, but you'll see a soft double image of the banner for that second. For text that has to stay readable, that ghosting is worse than a tiny jump.
  • Don't go past about a quarter of the clip. You'd be cutting the part people came for.

Where a loop-ready file helps

  • A TV or laptop at a grad party, where a media player repeats the clip all night.
  • A website hero or a <video loop muted playsinline> embed.
  • A story that auto-replays while people read the caption.

TikTok, Reels and Shorts loop on their own. A seamless file just stops the repeat from looking like an edit.

What this doesn't do

  • It doesn't change the soundtrack's musical phrase. If the song is mid-word at 7.5 s, the crossfade blends two words. Listen once before posting.
  • It re-encodes (libx264 -crf 18). Keep your original download too.
  • It can't fix a clip that has a frozen or black lead-in from screen recording. Trim that first, then loop.

Prices, if you're making the clip itself

On the live pricing page today, one Bama Bound generation is $7.98 at 480p, $9.98 at 720p, $16.98 at 1080p and $24.98 at 4k, with tax added at checkout (pricing). There's no free tier and no subscription. Loop-ready output isn't a product feature, which is why this script exists.

And as always with this meme: it's a joke format, not an admission letter. The real Bama Bound is the University of Alabama's orientation program, which has nothing to do with it (about the meme).

title: Relaxing Cross-Modal Correspondence for Multimodal Remote Sensing Pretraining
description:
arXiv:2611.13807v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal remote sensing pretraining commonly relies on exact instance-level correspondence across modalities, implicitly treating strictly paired observations as a prerequisite for learning transferable representations. In this work, we revisit this assumption by relaxing cross-modal correspondence from the instance level to the semantic level. We introduce Semantic Pairing (SemPair), a pairing-relaxed pretraining strategy that replaces exact instance pairs with class-consistent cross-instance pairs. To characterize the effect of correspondence relaxation, we formulate a latent-factor model that separates cross-modal dependence into shared semantic structure and instance-specific correlation, showing that SemPair preserves the former while marginalizing instance-specific cross-modal correlations in expectation. We further introduce Mixed Pairing (MixPair) as a controlled interpolation between semantic and exact pairing to study correspondence granularity along a continuous spectrum. Extensive experiments consistently show that SemPair achieves transfer performance comparable to exact pairing (ExaPair), while MixPair reveals a non-monotonic relationship between downstream transfer and the instance-pairing ratio. These results demonstrate that exact instance correspondence is not a prerequisite for effective multimodal remote sensing pretraining and establish cross-modal correspondence granularity as an important design dimension for transferable multimodal representation learning. More broadly, this finding suggests a practical route toward scaling multimodal pretraining with reduced dependence on costly instance-aligned data.

title: Solving Trapped Escape Keys in Vue: Conditional Event Propagation in GitLab UI's GlTokenSelector
description:
Pressing Escape is one of the most familiar keyboard interactions in a web application. It should dismiss the active dropdown, close a dialog, or cancel the current interaction.

But what happens when an input component prevents that keyboard event from reaching the modal that contains it?

That was the problem in GitLab UI's GlTokenSelector when used inside GlModal. Pressing Escape while the input had focus could fail to close the modal because the component stopped keyboard event propagation unconditionally.

In Pajamas MR !6678, addressing work item #3762, I fixed this behavior while preserving the expected two-step Escape interaction.

The Problem: Escape Never Reached the Modal

The issue was in:

packages/gitlab-ui/src/components/base/token_selector/token_selector.vue

The input used Vue's .stop event modifier:

@keydown.stop="$emit('keydown', $event)"

Vue's .stop modifier calls event.stopPropagation() for every keydown event.

That means the component stopped not only ordinary keyboard events, but also Escape.

When GlTokenSelector was rendered inside GlModal, the event could not bubble to the parent modal's keyboard handler. As a result, the modal did not receive the Escape event it needed to close.

This created a keyboard accessibility problem: the expected keyboard interaction was blocked by an inner component.

Why Removing .stop Wasn't Enough

One possible fix would have been to remove .stop entirely:

@keydown="$emit('keydown', $event)"

But that would introduce another problem.

GlTokenSelector has its own suggestions dropdown. When that dropdown is open, pressing Escape should dismiss the dropdown first—not close the entire modal behind it.

The expected interaction is:

  1. First Escape: close the token suggestions dropdown.
  2. Second Escape: allow the event to reach the modal so it can close.

This is a small but important interaction detail. Nested UI components need to handle keyboard events according to which layer is currently active.

The solution therefore needed conditional event propagation rather than simply removing event isolation.

The Fix: Conditional Event Propagation

I separated the handling into two methods: handleEscape and handleKeydown.

1. Handle Escape According to Dropdown State 

handleEscape(event) {
  if (this.dropdownIsOpen) {
    event?.stopPropagation?.();
  }

  this.inputText = '';
  this.closeDropdown();
},

The important condition is:

if (this.dropdownIsOpen) {
  event?.stopPropagation?.();
}

When the suggestions dropdown is open, the component stops the Escape event from reaching the parent modal.

It then clears the input text and closes the dropdown.

When the dropdown is already closed, the method does not stop propagation. The event can continue upward to the modal.

2. Preserve Isolation for Other Keyboard Events

The general keydown handler now treats Escape differently from other keys:

handleKeydown(event) {
  if (event.key !== 'Escape' && event.key !== 'Esc') {
    event.stopPropagation?.();
  }

  this.$emit('keydown', event);
},

The input template uses the handler directly:

@keydown="handleKeydown"

This preserves the previous event-isolation behavior for non-Escape keys while allowing Escape to propagate when the dropdown is closed.

The optional chaining also makes the calls defensive when the event or method is unavailable.

Understanding the Two-Step Escape Behavior

The resulting behavior can be summarized as follows:

Current state Key pressed Event propagation Expected result
Dropdown open Escape Stopped by the token selector Dropdown closes; modal stays open
Dropdown closed Escape Allowed to bubble Parent modal can close
Either state Other key Stopped by the token selector Existing keyboard-event isolation is preserved

This is the central idea behind the fix: the component should intercept Escape only when it has something of its own to dismiss.

Once the dropdown is closed, the parent component should be allowed to handle the same keyboard interaction.

Regression Tests

I updated:

packages/gitlab-ui/src/components/base/token_selector/token_selector.spec.js

The tests verify the conditional propagation behavior:

  • stopPropagation is called when the dropdown is open and Escape is handled.
  • stopPropagation is not called when the dropdown is closed and Escape is handled.
  • stopPropagation continues to be called for non-Escape keys.

These cases protect both sides of the interaction: the dropdown must remain independently dismissible, and the modal must still receive Escape when the dropdown is no longer open.

Changeset

I also added a patch changeset:

.changeset/token-selector-escape-propagation.md

This records the fix as a patch-level change for the GitLab UI package.

Engineering Takeaways

Event propagation is part of component behavior. Calling stopPropagation() unconditionally can unintentionally break keyboard interactions in parent components.

Nested overlays need predictable dismissal order. A dropdown inside a modal should generally handle its own dismissal before allowing the modal to close.

Removing event isolation is not always the right fix. Other keyboard events may still need to remain isolated. Conditional propagation is more precise than removing .stop everywhere.

Test both propagation and non-propagation paths. Testing only that Escape closes the dropdown would miss the modal regression. The closed-dropdown case is equally important.

Conclusion

The GlTokenSelector issue was caused by a small event modifier with a wider effect: unconditional propagation stopping prevented a parent modal from receiving Escape.

The fix introduced conditional handling so that an open dropdown consumes Escape, while a closed dropdown allows the event to reach its parent. Other keyboard events retain their existing isolation behavior.

This is a useful lesson when building reusable Vue components: keyboard events do not belong to only one layer of the UI. Their propagation behavior must account for the complete component hierarchy.

References

  • Work item: design.gitlab.com#3762
  • Merge Request: design.gitlab.com!6678

Author: Manish Kumar

title: A Stage-Wise Explainable Pipeline for Arteriolar-to-Venular Ratio Estimation and Retinopathy Screening
description:
arXiv:2611.14013v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The arteriolar-to-venular diameter ratio (AVR) is a clinically motivated marker of retinal vascular health. We present a five-stage pipeline for AVR estimation and exploratory retinopathy screening from fundus images, with inspectable intermediate outputs at each stage. The pipeline combines vessel and artery-vein masks, optic-disc localization, vessel-calibre estimation using a minimal-chord boundary walk, and AVR computation from dominant arterial and venular branches. An explicit threshold-based rule produces the screening decision, enabling errors to be traced to individual processing stages. On an exploratory cohort of 30 HRF images, we report 96.7% accuracy, an F1-score of 0.968 and ROC-AUC of 0.978. Ablation studies and an exploratory comparison with VascX examine the effects of vessel pairing, calibre measurement and aggregation. Interpretation is limited by the small cohort, proxy disease labels and absence of independent reference calibre measurements. The pipeline provides a transparent framework for investigating retinal vascular biomarkers, with further validation needed on larger, clinically graded cohorts.

title: Introducing spec-desk – A Visual Workspace for AI-Powered Spec-Driven Development
description:
🚀 Introducing spec-desk – A Visual Workspace for AI-Powered Spec-Driven Development

AI coding tools are making software development faster. But there is another challenge that developers are beginning to face.

How do we manage requirements, specifications, architecture, tasks and implementation in a structured way when AI agents are doing much of the coding?

I started exploring this problem and decided to build SpecDesk.

What is spec-desk?

spec-desk is a visual workspace that brings structure to AI-assisted software development.

The idea is simple:

  1. Start with a software requirement or idea.
  2. Convert it into structured specifications.
  3. Organize development artifacts visually.
  4. Break requirements into actionable tasks.
  5. Use AI coding agents to implement the specifications.

I'm starting with Claude Code integration and building towards a more flexible agent-driven development workflow.

Why am I building this?

I believe the future of software development is not just about generating code with AI. It is about giving AI agents the right context, specifications and development structure.

spec-desk is my attempt to make that workflow simpler.

I'm opening this up to the developer community and looking for early adopters, contributors and honest feedback.

GitHub: https://github.com/srihari1247/spec-desk

Would love to hear how you're managing spec-driven development with AI coding agents today.

OpenSource #AI #DeveloperTools #SpecDrivenDevelopment #ClaudeCode

title: One Table, Many Queries: Benchmarking Generalist Tabular Models Across Generation, Imputation, and Prediction
description:
arXiv:2611.13001v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generation, imputation, and prediction query different aspects of the same tabular distribution, but are usually evaluated separately. This leaves unclear which capabilities they share, how their training objectives interact, and whether one model can perform all three well. We introduce the One Table Benchmark (\ours{}), spanning 56 datasets, 46 registered methods, and 20 capability axes under aligned data splits and explicit task contracts. We compare task ranks on aligned support, train five backbones under all seven non-empty objective combinations on five datasets with three seeds, and contrast fixed-model profiles with specialist portfolios. Rank comparisons connect imputation and prediction through numerical recovery and dependence preservation, and link generation to both through predictive utility; distributional fidelity follows different, sometimes opposing, rankings. Objective interventions show the largest pooled gains from including the recipient's own objective. Generation has the broadest coverage of positive pooled auxiliary effects, while prediction shows potential to improve imputation and synthetic-data utility, with responses that vary across backbones. Cross-addition effects reveal that objective benefits need not add and depend on the objectives already present. Fixed-model comparisons expose corresponding utility--fidelity trade-offs: some generalists surpass specialist portfolios on utility, while fidelity continues to favor specialization. Frozen foundation models show strong prediction and numerical point imputation, together with promising synthetic-data utility, highlighting their potential across all three tasks. These findings motivate unified tabular models that share useful conditional information while improving categorical reconstruction and faithful joint sampling.

title: Capacity Allocation at the Source: Sparse Target Optimization for LLM Knowledge Editing
description:
arXiv:2611.12995v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Knowledge editing has emerged as a promising approach for efficiently updating embedded knowledge in large language models (LLMs). It first computes an ideal target hidden state that steers the LLM toward the new output, and then edits the model parameters so that the original hidden state is mapped to this target. While most existing methods focus on the second stage of parameter editing in preserving other knowledge, we find that the upstream construction of the target hidden state also plays an important role in allocating the model's limited capacity space. We first establish a theoretical connection between interference in the parameter space and interference between target hidden states, showing that the two are positively correlated. Building on this insight, we propose a simple yet effective $\ell_1$ regularization method that prunes away unnecessary ``tentacles'' of each knowledge vector, retaining only the essential components. With fewer extraneous tentacles, each edit affects less other knowledge, enabling better coexistence. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmark datasets verify the effectiveness of our method. Code: https://github.com/wintersdragon-c/STO.

title: Pulse or Provenance? What rPPG-Based Deepfake Detectors Learn
description:
arXiv:2611.13992v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) has been proposed as a physiological cue for deepfake detection, based on the premise that synthesized faces lack a genuine cardiac signal. We examine what rPPG-style detectors learn on Celeb-DF++ (22 forgery methods) and FaceForensics++ (FF++), using one identically sampled window per real and fake video. On talking-face forgeries, simple chrominance traces reach an AUC of 0.998, exceeding a dedicated rPPG extractor (0.87). Controlled experiments indicate that this signal is not physiological in origin. On fully synthesized forgeries, it is equally discriminative when extracted from background regions or from full frames without face detection, and it is concentrated above the 0.7 to 4 Hz heart-rate band. It is largely removed by shuffling frame order but persists after normalizing resolution, frame rate and encoding, and an independent reimplementation reproduces these findings. Removing high-frequency content makes most synthesized videos appear real, adding it makes real videos appear fake, and injecting a synthetic pulse has little effect. In controlled self-reenactment experiments with two generators, animating a face from a single frame introduces the same high-frequency signal, whereas reconstructing each frame from its own source does not. Face-based chrominance detectors trained on Celeb-DF++ classify over 99% of real FF++ videos as fake, indicating that they largely encode video source rather than manipulation, and a CLIP-based detector exhibits the same behavior. A frozen CLIP backbone matches or exceeds fusions of CLIP with rPPG and frequency features. Finally, we show that the official Celeb-DF and Celeb-DF++ splits share identities and source-video content between training and test, and that custom protocols reusing test videos and identities in training inflate weaker detectors by up to 0.30 AUC.

title: WCAG Levels A, AA and AAA: What's the Difference?
description:
The short answer
A, AA and AAA are the three conformance levels in the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG). Level A is the minimum. Level AA is the standard most laws and policies require. Level AAA is the highest level.

Each level is a set of specific success criteria, and each higher level includes everything below it.

How the levels fit together
First, we must acknowledge that the levels stack. To claim AA, a page must meet every Level A criterion as well as every Level AA criterion. To claim AAA, it must meet all three sets, this means the website must meet Level A, Level AA and Level AAA.

WCAG 2.2 has 86 active success criteria:

Level A: 31 criteria
Level AA: 24 more (55 total for an AA claim)
Level AAA: 31 more (86 total for an AAA claim)
A few rules decide whether a claim holds up:

It's all or nothing. Missing one AA criterion means the page doesn't conform at AA. There's no "mostly AA."
Whole pages only. You can't claim conformance for part of a page.
Levels are about impact, not difficulty. Level A covers barriers that block some people completely. AA covers barriers that make content hard to use. AAA adds extra support for specific needs.
Level A: the baseline
Level A removes the barriers that lock people out entirely. If a site fails Level A, some people can't use it at all.

Examples of Level A criteria:

Text alternatives (1.1.1). Images that carry meaning have alt text. A screen reader user can't learn what a chart shows without it.
Keyboard (2.1.1). Everything works with a keyboard alone. Someone who can't use a mouse can still open menus and submit forms.
Info and relationships (1.3.1). Headings, lists, tables and form labels are coded, not just styled. Assistive tech can then announce the structure.
Use of color (1.4.1). Color isn't the only way to show meaning. An error field also gets an icon or a message, not just a red border.
Page titled (2.4.2). Each page has a title that says what it is.
Level A alone isn't enough for most real-world users. It's the floor, not the target.

Level AA: the practical target
Level AA is the level nearly every law, policy and contract asks for. It removes barriers that don't fully block people but make content hard or tiring to use.

Examples of Level AA criteria:

Contrast (1.4.3). Regular text has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background. Large text needs 3:1.
Non-text contrast (1.4.11). Buttons, input borders and focus indicators have at least 3:1 contrast.
Resize text (1.4.4). Text can zoom to 200% without breaking the page.
Reflow (1.4.10). Content fits a 320-pixel-wide screen without scrolling sideways.
Focus visible (2.4.7). Keyboard users can always see where they are on the page.
Captions, live (1.2.4). Live video and audio have captions.
Target size, minimum (2.5.8). Click and tap targets are at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or have enough space around them. New in WCAG 2.2.
Accessible authentication, minimum (3.3.8). Logging in doesn't depend on remembering or solving a puzzle unless there's a way around it, like allowing paste or a password manager. New in WCAG 2.2.
AA is achievable for almost any site with good design and development habits. That's why it's the standard.

Level AAA: enhanced support
Level AAA adds the highest level of support for specific needs. The W3C itself doesn't recommend requiring AAA for entire sites. Some content simply can't meet every AAA criterion.

Examples of Level AAA criteria:

Enhanced contrast (1.4.6). Regular text has at least 7:1 contrast. Large text needs 4.5:1.
Sign language (1.2.6). Prerecorded video includes sign language interpretation.
Reading level (3.1.5). When text needs more than a lower-secondary reading level, a simpler version or summary is available.
Unusual words (3.1.3). Jargon and idioms are defined.
No timing (2.2.3). Nothing has a time limit, except live events.
Target size, enhanced (2.5.5). Targets are at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels.
Here's why AAA site-wide isn't realistic. A live auction must have time limits, which fails 2.2.3. A medical research article can't always be rewritten at a lower-secondary reading level without losing meaning.

Still, AAA criteria are worth meeting where you can. Plain language, extra contrast and bigger targets help many people, including people with learning and thinking differences.

What to aim for
Target WCAG 2.2 Level AA across your whole site, then add AAA criteria where they help your audience most.

Fix Level A failures first. They block people completely.
Work through Level AA until every page and process conforms.
Test with automated tools, manual checks, assistive tech and real users.
Publish an accessibility statement that names the WCAG version and level, and lists known gaps honestly.

title: Turning a Home Care Audit Evidence List into Data: An Outcome Coverage Index for Support at Home Providers
description:
Originally based on our article the 7 strengthened Aged Care Quality Standards explained for home care on rostery.com.au. This version is rewritten for developers, data people and operations staff who look after the systems behind a Support at Home provider.

When a Category 4 home care provider renews its registration, the Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission asks for evidence in a fairly structured way. Its Care Delivery Evidence Collection Tool for Categories 4 and 5 (the CDECT, last updated 17 July 2026) lists 31 numbered documents and records to send before the audit opening meeting. Each row names the evidence, the outcomes it relates to and the time period it should cover. A second, shorter list sets out what the audit team may ask for while it's on site.

That's a schema, even if it arrives as a Word document. If you treat it as one, you can answer useful questions weeks before an audit letter: which outcomes have nothing behind them, which registers are stale for the window being asked about, and which older people are likely to end up in the sample.

This post builds a small Python model for each of those questions. It's deliberately plain: dataclasses, sets and a few pure functions. You can port it to SQL or whatever your reporting layer uses.

General information only, not legal advice. The outcome list comes from the Commission's Strengthened Quality Standards guidance pages and the evidence list from the CDECT for Categories 4 and 5, both read on 11 November 2026. Check the current versions before relying on any of this.

Start with the outcomes that apply to you

The strengthened standards have 7 standards and 33 outcomes. Three outcomes are written in two parts (2.2a and 2.2b, 2.6a and 2.6b, 4.1a and 4.1b), so in practice you work with outcome statements rather than outcome numbers.

Which statements apply depends on registration category. A Support at Home provider is registered in Category 4 with the service type "Care management", which brings in Standards 1 to 4 plus Outcome 5.1, clinical governance. The CDECT itself carries a footnote saying Outcome 5.1 applies only to the care management and restorative care management service types. A provider that also delivers nursing is in Category 5 and meets all of Standard 5.

Put that in a table rather than in someone's head:

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Outcome:
    code: str        # "2.6a"
    title: str
    standard: int

OUTCOMES = [
    Outcome("1.1", "Person-centred care", 1),
    Outcome("1.2", "Dignity, respect and privacy", 1),
    Outcome("1.3", "Choice, independence and quality of life", 1),
    Outcome("1.4", "Transparency and agreements", 1),
    Outcome("2.1", "Partnering with individuals", 2),
    Outcome("2.2a", "Culture that supports aged care workers", 2),
    Outcome("2.2b", "Culture that supports individuals", 2),
    Outcome("2.3", "Accountability, quality system, policies", 2),
    Outcome("2.4", "Risk management", 2),
    Outcome("2.5", "Incident management", 2),
    Outcome("2.6a", "Complaints and feedback: workers", 2),
    Outcome("2.6b", "Complaints and feedback: individuals", 2),
    Outcome("2.7", "Information management", 2),
    Outcome("2.8", "Workforce planning", 2),
    Outcome("2.9", "Human resource management", 2),
    Outcome("2.10", "Emergency and disaster management", 2),
    Outcome("3.1", "Assessment and planning", 3),
    Outcome("3.2", "Delivery of funded aged care services", 3),
    Outcome("3.3", "Communicating for safety and quality", 3),
    Outcome("3.4", "Planning and coordination", 3),
    Outcome("4.1a", "Environment: services in the person's home", 4),
    Outcome("4.1b", "Environment: services elsewhere", 4),
    Outcome("4.2", "Infection prevention and control", 4),
    Outcome("5.1", "Clinical governance", 5),
    # 5.2 to 5.7 omitted here: they apply in full to Category 5 and 6
]

def applicable(categories: set[int], service_types: set[str]) -> list[Outcome]:
    out = []
    for o in OUTCOMES:
        if o.standard <= 4 and categories & {4, 5, 6}:
            out.append(o)
        elif o.code == "5.1" and (
            categories & {5, 6}
            or (4 in categories and service_types & {"care management", "restorative care management"})
        ):
            out.append(o)
    return out

sah = applicable({4}, {"care management", "personal care"})
assert len(sah) == 24

That assert is worth keeping in your test suite. Twenty-three statements from Standards 1 to 4 plus 5.1 gives the 24 a Support at Home provider is assessed against, and if a refactor ever changes the count you want to know straight away.

Encode the evidence list as rows

Each CDECT row has four fields that matter to us: a number, a description, the outcomes it relates to, and a time period. Some rows say "Various" instead of listing outcomes. Keep that as its own value, because "Various" is not the same as "none".

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class EvidenceRequest:
    no: int
    title: str
    outcomes: frozenset[str] = field(default_factory=frozenset)
    various: bool = False
    window: str = "Current"

CDECT = [
    EvidenceRequest(1, "List of current management and workers", frozenset({"2.2a", "2.6a", "2.8", "2.9"}), window="Latest"),
    EvidenceRequest(5, "Worker roster or shift allocation sheet", frozenset({"2.8", "2.9"}), window="Last 4 weeks"),
    EvidenceRequest(8, "Training and induction register", frozenset({"2.8", "2.9"}), window="Last 12 months"),
    EvidenceRequest(11, "Data on unfilled shifts", frozenset({"2.2a", "2.8", "2.9"}), window="Last 4 weeks"),
    EvidenceRequest(12, "List of older people with risk factors", various=True),
    EvidenceRequest(17, "Risk register", frozenset({"1.3", "2.4", "2.10", "3.1", "3.2", "4.1b", "4.2", "5.3", "5.5"})),
    EvidenceRequest(18, "Complaints and feedback register", frozenset({"2.6a", "2.6b"}), window="Past 12 months"),
    EvidenceRequest(19, "Incident registers incl. SIRS notifications", frozenset({"2.5", "3.1", "3.3"}), window="Past 3 months"),
    EvidenceRequest(20, "Trend analysis of incidents and complaints", frozenset({"2.3", "2.5", "2.6a", "2.6b"}), window="Past 12 months"),
    EvidenceRequest(27, "Clinical meeting minutes", frozenset({"5.1"}), window="Last 4 meetings"),
    EvidenceRequest(29, "Older people and supporter meeting minutes", frozenset({"1.1", "1.3", "2.1", "3.3"}), window="Last 4 meetings"),
    # ...the full list has 31 rows; copy them from the current CDECT
]

Notice that outcomes from Standard 5 beyond 5.1 turn up in some rows (the risk register is tagged 5.3 and 5.5). The tool covers Category 4 and 5 together, so filter the tags against your own applicable set rather than trusting the row.

Check coverage, and read the gaps carefully

Now the first useful report: which of your applicable outcomes has no numbered pre-audit request tagged against it?

def coverage(requests, outcomes):
    codes = {o.code for o in outcomes}
    tagged = set().union(*(r.outcomes for r in requests)) & codes
    return sorted(codes - tagged)

print(coverage(CDECT, sah))   # with all 31 rows loaded
# ['1.2', '1.4', '2.2b', '2.7', '3.4']

We ran this over all 31 rows of the July 2026 version. Five Support at Home outcomes aren't tagged on any numbered pre-audit document: dignity, respect and privacy (1.2), transparency and agreements (1.4), the culture that supports individuals (2.2b), information management (2.7), and planning and coordination (3.4).

That doesn't mean the Commission ignores them. It means the evidence for them comes from somewhere else: the "Various" rows, interviews with older people and workers, observation, and the second list of records the audit team may ask for during the audit. That list includes agreements with older people, budgets and monthly statements, consent and dignity of risk forms, the tools used to share information with older people and workers, and progress or file notes for the previous 60 days. It carries no outcome tags, so map it yourself. Our own mapping, not the Commission's, looks like this:

DURING_AUDIT = {
    "Agreements with older people": {"1.4"},
    "Budget and monthly statements": {"1.4"},
    "Consent and dignity of risk forms": {"1.3"},
    "Communication tools, interpreters, other formats": {"2.7", "3.3"},
    "Progress or file notes, previous 60 days": {"3.2", "3.3"},
    "Current care and services plans": {"1.1", "3.1"},
}

The practical point is that outcome 1.4 sits almost entirely on records the auditors may ask for on the day. Those are exactly the records where home care has been weakest. The Department's first Support at Home payment integrity review found only 21% of the 262 monthly statements it reviewed had every required item, and the Commission's April to June 2026 data counted 1,011 home care concerns about fees and charges, or how they were communicated. Your coverage report should flag 1.4 for a manual check even though nothing is "missing" from the pre-audit list.

Normalise the time windows

The "Time period" column mixes three kinds of window:

  • Point in time: "Latest" and "Current".
  • Rolling date ranges: "Last 4 weeks", "Past 3 months", "Past 12 months", and "previous 60 days" for progress notes.
  • Counts: "Last 4 meetings".

The count-based one catches people out. If a team meets every quarter, the last four meetings reach back a year. If it met twice and then stopped, no date filter will tell you; you need the count.

from datetime import date, timedelta

def window_ok(records: list[date], window: str, today: date) -> bool:
    if window in ("Latest", "Current"):
        return bool(records)                      # plus a "still in force" check elsewhere
    if window == "Last 4 meetings":
        return len(records) >= 4
    days = {"Last 4 weeks": 28, "Past 3 months": 92,
            "Past 12 months": 366, "Previous 60 days": 60}[window]
    since = today - timedelta(days=days)
    return any(d >= since for d in records)

A rolling window passing doesn't prove much on its own. An incident register with one entry in three months passes the check but may tell an auditor something about reporting culture. Report the count alongside the pass, and let a person decide what's normal for the service.

"Current" also needs its own rule per record type. For care plans it means a plan in force with a review date in the future. For worker checks it means not expired. For an emergency plan it means reviewed on the cycle your own policy sets. Keep those rules next to the request, not buried in a report query.

Build the sample list before you're asked for it

Row 12 asks for a complete list of older people receiving care, and a list of those with particular risk factors. The factors include palliative and end of life care needs, specialised nursing needs, communication difficulties (cognitive or sensory impairment, disability, culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds), high-risk medications such as psychotropics or insulin, any restraint or seclusion, a recent history of falls, a transition to or from hospital or another provider in the last 3 months, living alone with limited outside contact, oxygen, a stoma, enteral feeding, a catheter, needing a higher level of care than they currently receive, greater than expected unspent funds, self-managing Support at Home funding, and being represented by a public guardian.

Most of these can be derived from data you already hold. A few can't, and the honest design is to say so:

from enum import Enum

class Source(Enum):
    DERIVED = "derived from records"
    CONFIRM = "needs a care manager to confirm"

RISK_FLAGS = {
    "recent_falls":        (Source.DERIVED, "incident type = fall, last 90 days"),
    "hospital_transition": (Source.DERIVED, "hospital or transfer record, last 3 months"),
    "high_risk_meds":      (Source.DERIVED, "active medication in a high-risk class list"),
    "restraint":           (Source.DERIVED, "restrictive practice recorded"),
    "unspent_funds_high":  (Source.DERIVED, "unspent balance above your own threshold"),
    "self_manages":        (Source.DERIVED, "funding management flag"),
    "lives_alone_limited": (Source.CONFIRM, "living situation plus contact pattern"),
    "needs_higher_care":   (Source.CONFIRM, "care manager judgement or pending reassessment"),
    "communication":       (Source.CONFIRM, "cognitive, sensory, disability or language needs"),
}

"Greater than expected" unspent funds has no number in the tool, so the threshold is yours to set and to explain. Write it down. The same goes for "limited contact outside of the provider".

This list does more than satisfy row 12. The people on it are the ones whose records an auditor is most likely to read closely, so it's also a good list for your own file reviews in the months before an audit.

Map each request to its system of record

Last step: for every request, record where the evidence lives and who owns it. In most small providers the answer is spread across a rostering tool, an HR folder, spreadsheets for registers and an accounting package for statements. A short table makes the gaps obvious:

Request System of record Owner Window
Worker list, roster, unfilled shifts Rostering system Rostering lead Latest / 4 weeks
Worker checks, training register HR or worker compliance HR Current / 12 months
Incident register, SIRS notifications Incident system Quality manager 3 months
Complaints register Complaints system Quality manager 12 months
Care and services plans Care management Care partners Current
Agreements, budgets, monthly statements Billing and statements Finance Current
Meeting minutes Shared drive Each meeting's chair Last 4 meetings

If a row has two systems in the owner column, expect a reconciliation problem at audit time.

In Rostery, a few of these joins are built in. The aged care complaints register has a Linked Quality Standard field on each complaint, so the register can be filtered by the standard it's evidence against. Aged care care plans carry a Review due date that turns amber within 30 days and red once it has passed, which maps neatly onto a "Current" rule. Support at Home statements and claims are generated for each participant's plan every month, including months with no services. None of that replaces the mapping exercise; it just means fewer columns of the table point at spreadsheets.

For a plain-language refresher on the standards themselves, the Aged Care Quality Standards glossary entry is a quick read, and our Blogger post on which Aged Care Quality Standards a home care provider actually meets walks through the registration categories. If incidents are your next build, our earlier dev.to post on a SIRS triage workflow for aged care compliance teams covers reportability and deadlines.

A short checklist for your own build

  • Derive the applicable outcome list from registration category and service types, and test the count.
  • Store evidence requests as rows with outcomes, a "various" flag and a window.
  • Run coverage against applicable outcomes only, and treat untagged outcomes as manual checks, not gaps.
  • Map the during-audit records yourself, and label that mapping as yours.
  • Normalise windows into point-in-time, rolling and count-based rules, and report counts next to passes.
  • Build the risk-factor sample list from data, and mark the flags that need human judgement.
  • Give every request one system of record and one owner.

Sources: Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission, Strengthened Quality Standards guidance (outcome pages for Standards 1 to 4 and Outcome 5.1); Strengthened Aged Care Quality Standards page (audit types and ratings); Support at Home provider requirements (Category 4 with care management, Outcome 5.1); Care Delivery Evidence Collection Tool, Categories 4 and 5 (last updated 17 July 2026); Sector performance data, April to June 2026. Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Support at Home Payment Integrity Rolling Review, cycle 1 summary report. Rostery help and feature pages read 11 November 2026.

Written by the Rostery team in Sydney. Rostery makes rostering, care and billing software for NDIS and aged care providers.

title: RF3DGS: Reflection-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting with Self-Priors
description:
arXiv:2611.13772v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: 3D reflection removal is crucial in applications demanding high-fidelity visualization, such as museum exhibitions. In this work, we propose Reflection-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting (RF3DGS), a novel method for superior reflection removal. RF3DGS exclusively leverages a widely-adopted photometric prior for reflection removal: that the minimum pixel intensity across multi-view images corresponding to the same 3D point strongly correlates with reflection-free information. However, generalizing this principle to a 3D Gaussian Splatting within a multi-view context is non-trivial. To address this, RF3DGS first optimizes a vanilla 3DGS model using a geometric prior to estimate a coarse, reflection-free depth map for each view. Leveraging these depth maps and photometric prior, a 3D warping process aggregates reflection-free information from auxiliary views to construct a clean transmission pseudo-label for a given reference view. This pseudo-label provides a robust self-supervised signal for optimization. We further introduce an Adaptive Twin Rendering (ATR) loss to synergistically utilize this pseudo-label while preserving high-frequency details from the original, reflection-degraded images. By adeptly fusing these internal 3D self-priors with the ATR loss, RF3DGS demonstrates state-of-the-art reflection removal performance across both synthetic and real-world scenarios. Furthermore, we establish the first 3D reflection removal benchmark, based on the Unity rendering engine, for rigorous quantitative evaluation.

title: XAI-Driven Confidence Estimation for OOD-Resilient Runtime Prediction
description:
arXiv:2611.13199v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Machine learning-based resource management (RM) models degrade under out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs at runtime, yet existing approaches in the literature rely on a single global error margin that is overly conservative and fails to distinguish reliablepredictions from catastrophic failures. We propose Lightweight Runtime EXplainability (LEX), the first post-hoc XAI framework for input-specific runtime confidence estimation in ML-based RM. LEX clusters the embeddings of the training input space using a Gaussian Mixture Model and associates per-cluster prediction error bounds to input samples, enabling fine-grained runtime confidence signals without retraining. Evaluated on a state-of-the-art LSTM-based IPS forecasting model on Intel Alder Lake, across 34 benchmark applications, LEX achieves ~94% containment on unseen workloads and produces ~17% tighter per-input confidence bounds than global baselines. With its negligible runtime overhead, LEX advances the field by providing explainable and reliable input-specific confidence signals of ML predictions, thereby making ML-based resource management resilient to OOD at runtime.
