title: How our open source coding agent scored 84.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 for $27
description:
AgenC Core is an open source (MIT) coding agent for the terminal. Our goal is to multiply model capability per dollar of inference: to get more verified work out of a model for every dollar spent on it.

To test that goal, we ran Terminal-Bench 2.1 with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. AgenC Core scored 84.5%, and the whole run cost $27. Every entry on the official leaderboard spent at least $134. All 445 trials are public, with full trajectories.

This post covers how we ran it, what the number does and does not mean, and what the benchmark taught us about our own harness.

Why the harness matters

Terminal-Bench measures how well an agent completes real tasks in a terminal: building software, repairing a git history, configuring servers, recovering data. Each trial gives the agent one instruction inside a container, and the task's own tests grade the result.

A leaderboard row is always an agent and a model together. The model supplies the reasoning. The harness around it decides how that reasoning turns into finished work: how the task is planned, which tools exist, how progress is kept, and how results are checked before the agent says it is done. With the same model, a better harness finishes more of the work for the same money.

How we ran it

  • The official Terminal-Bench 2.1 package, pinned to the leaderboard's dataset revision: 89 tasks, 5 trials per task, 445 trials.
  • The official timeouts and resources. No task timeout was changed.
  • AgenC Core 0.19.24 with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at max reasoning effort, run through Harbor, the benchmark's runner.
  • Contamination handling. An egress filter refused known routes to benchmark answers, and a local gateway held the API key and logged every call. In 5 passing trials the agent had still seen a task's solution or tests. We counted those as failures, which lowered the score from 85.6% to 84.5%. Late finishes also count as failures, and there were none.
  • Cost. $27 is the figure Harbor Hub lists for the run, the same basis as every leaderboard entry. At DeepSeek's list prices for the recorded request times it came to $27.21, across about 1.2 billion tokens with a 97% cache hit rate.

The run is public on Harbor Hub: job 2bf2c84d.

The results

Agent and model Score Cost
AgenC Core, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max) 84.5% $27
Codex, GPT-6 Astra (high) 87.4% $774
Claude Code, Fable 5 (xhigh) 83.8% $553
Cursor CLI, Grok 4.5 (high) 79.3% $134

The AgenC Core row is our public run. The other rows are entries on the official Terminal-Bench 2.1 leaderboard as of October 31, 2026, and Cursor CLI's is the cheapest of them. The top entry scored 2.9 percentage points more and cost more than 28 times as much.

Two caveats. Each row pairs an agent with a model, so this compares combinations, not agents alone. And our run is not on the official leaderboard: community submissions for 2.1 are closed, and only runs done by the maintainers are added. We have asked them to run AgenC Core (issue #253), and the adapter they would need is public.

What the benchmark found in our harness

The most useful part of running the benchmark was reading the transcripts. Across our runs, they exposed problems that had nothing to do with the model:

  • Services died when a command returned. The shell tool stopped every process the agent had started once the command finished, so a server the agent set up was gone by the time the grader ran. Three of the four failures in each of our early runs were tasks of that shape: nginx, a git server with a deploy hook, an sshd server. The tool result now says when leftover processes were stopped, and exec_command takes detach: true to start a service that outlives the session.
  • A safety policy blocked ordinary commands. Even with approvals bypassed, the shell write policy refused any command it could not analyse, which included everything containing $(...): 51 of 459 shell calls in one run. Under a full bypass with no sandbox those guards are now lifted, and protected paths stay protected.
  • The agent declared success without checking. Once the harness bugs were fixed, the remaining failures were tasks the agent had called done: sessions that ended early, with final messages claiming checks the transcript did not contain. Non-interactive sessions now carry a completion contract: restate the task as checkable requirements, run the checks before the final message, report what was verified. A completion gate enforces it in code: a final answer is held until it is backed by checks that ran after the last change.
  • Long sessions broke compaction. A 55-minute session with 191 tool calls reached the auto-compaction threshold and failed. Our planner assumed 4 bytes per token, the provider counted 2.29, and the summary request was rejected as too large. The planner now bounds its input at 2 bytes per token and splits large histories.
  • A dropped connection ended a trial. A truncated stream came back as a generic provider error that no retry rule recognized. It is now a typed error, retried like any stalled stream.

None of these were model problems, and each fix applies to every model the harness runs. That is what "multiply model capability" means in practice.

Reproduce it

The Harbor adapter is in the repository at runtime/eval/harbor/agenc_agent.py. It installs the pinned release through the public installer and checks its SHA-256, answers the project trust prompt in the real terminal UI, never changes task timeouts, and writes an ATIF trajectory for every trial.

uv tool install harbor
git clone https://github.com/tetsuo-ai/agenc-core
cd agenc-core
export PYTHONPATH=$PWD/runtime/eval/harbor
DEEPSEEK_API_KEY=... harbor run \
  -d terminal-bench/terminal-bench-2-1@sha256:7d7bdc1cbedad549fc1140404bd4dc45e5fd0ea7c4186773687d177ad3a0699a \
  -a agenc_agent:Agenc -m deepseek/deepseek-flash \
  --ak version=0.19.24 --ak reasoning_effort=max \
  -k 5 -n 4 -o ./jobs/agenc-tb21

Our published run also had the egress filter and the logging gateway described above, which are not part of the adapter. The full method is in docs/eval/terminal-bench.md.

Try AgenC Core

AgenC Core works with OpenAI, Anthropic, Grok, Gemini, DeepSeek, OpenRouter and other providers, or with local models through Ollama and LM Studio. It runs in the terminal or headless in scripts and CI with agenc -p, and its Goal mode takes a project through implementation, testing and an independent review.

macOS and Linux:

curl -fsSL https://get.agenc.ag/install.sh | sh

Windows (PowerShell):

iwr -useb https://get.agenc.ag/install.ps1 | iex

Then run agenc onboard to choose a provider.

  • Install and docs: get.agenc.ag
  • Full results and every leaderboard entry: get.agenc.ag/terminal-bench

title: StaRSE: Compact Russian Sentence Embeddings with a Sign-Coded Static Encoder
description:
arXiv:2611.14236v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Transformer sentence encoders provide strong retrieval quality, but their inference cost becomes a bottleneck when embeddings must be produced on CPUs or refreshed frequently. We introduce StaRSE, a compact Russian static sentence encoder that removes Transformer inference at deployment time: token directions are stored as sign bits, token norms are stored separately, and sentences are encoded by mean pooling over norm-scaled sign directions. StaRSE is initialized from ruBERT-base, fine-tuned on Russian adjacent-sentence and task-shaped pairs, and post-trained with a contrastive stage that directly optimizes the sign-projected token table. On RuMTEB, StaRSE reaches a task mean of $51.16$, $7.98$ points above the strongest included static baseline. The packaged model occupies $11.3$ MiB and has a mean CPU latency of $0.08$ ms per sentence, compared with an estimated $55.7$ MiB 16-bit parameter footprint and $1.43$ ms mean CPU latency for the closest-quality contextual encoder. Ablations examine adjacent-sentence supervision, token norms, and direct sign-projected post-training.

title: Race, Queue, or Cancel: Choosing the Right flatMap for Your Kotlin Flow
description:
Every Android codebase that uses Flow eventually grows a flatMap something. A map viewport triggers a trail query, a photo grid triggers thumbnail loads, a sync queue triggers uploads. The three flattening operators look interchangeable in a code review, and they are not. Swapping one for another changes what runs in parallel, what gets thrown away, what order the UI sees, and which bug you will be paged for.

This post puts flatMapMerge, flatMapConcat and flatMapLatest through the same input, shows exactly where the timelines diverge, and then walks through the failure modes that tend to survive code review. Examples come from a fictional hiking app called Trailhead.

The short version, as three mental models:

  • flatMapMerge races. Every item starts work right away, and results are emitted in the order they finish, not the order they arrived.
  • flatMapConcat queues. One inner flow runs at a time, in arrival order. Everything behind it waits, including the upstream producer.
  • flatMapLatest cancels. A new item kills the running inner flow. Only the freshest work gets to finish.

One input, three timelines

Instead of arguing in prose, let’s run the same upstream through all three. The upstream emits A, B, C, pausing 100 ms after each emit. Each item's inner work costs a different amount of time: 300, 150 and 200 ms.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*
import org.junit.Test

private data class Probe(val id: String, val costMs: Long)

private fun source(): Flow<Probe> = flow {
    emit(Probe("A", 300)); delay(100)
    emit(Probe("B", 150)); delay(100)
    emit(Probe("C", 200))
}

private fun work(probe: Probe): Flow<String> = flow {
    delay(probe.costMs)
    emit(probe.id)
}

private suspend fun TestScope.trace(label: String, results: Flow<String>) {
    val start = testScheduler.currentTime
    results.collect {
        println("${label.padEnd(6)} @ ${testScheduler.currentTime - start} ms -> $it")
    }
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
class FlattenLab {
    @Test
    fun sameInputThreeStrategies() = runTest {
        trace("merge", source().flatMapMerge { work(it) })
        trace("concat", source().flatMapConcat { work(it) })
        trace("latest", source().flatMapLatest { work(it) })
    }
}

Because runTest uses virtual time, there is no wall-clock jitter, and the timings follow directly from the delays. This is the expected output:

merge  @ 250 ms -> B
merge  @ 300 ms -> A
merge  @ 400 ms -> C
concat @ 300 ms -> A
concat @ 550 ms -> B
concat @ 850 ms -> C
latest @ 400 ms -> C

Each trace call is an independent run. The helper rebases the virtual clock to zero before collecting, so the three strategies are deliberately executed one after another and still line up at t = 0 in the diagram. The concurrency being compared lives inside each operator, not between the runs.

Snippets in this post omit most imports. Duration literals such as 150.milliseconds or 400.milliseconds need kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.milliseconds.

Three things in that picture deserve a second look.

Merge reorders. B arrived second and finished first. If your downstream code assumes arrival order, it is already wrong.

Concat is slower than the sum of its parts suggests. The pure work adds up to 650 ms, yet the last result lands at 850 ms. The reason is that flatMapConcat collects each inner flow inline, inside the upstream collector. While A runs, the producer is suspended in its emit call, so the 100 ms pause after A starts only after A finishes. Concat does not just serialize the work, it serializes the producer. With a cold flow that is harmless. With a hot source, it becomes a failure mode we will get to.

Latest throws work away. A and B were cancelled before producing anything, and the dashed outlines show the work that never happened. That is the entire value proposition: if nobody wants those results, not computing them is a feature.

flatMapLatest: when only the newest answer matters

Trailhead’s map screen reloads trails whenever the camera settles on a new viewport. Results for a viewport the user has already panned away from are worthless, which is the textbook case for cancel-and-restart.

import androidx.lifecycle.ViewModel
import androidx.lifecycle.viewModelScope
import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi
import kotlinx.coroutines.FlowPreview
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.milliseconds

sealed interface MapState {
    data object Idle : MapState
    data class Loading(val box: BoundingBox) : MapState
    data class Ready(val box: BoundingBox, val trails: List<Trail>) : MapState
    data class Failed(val box: BoundingBox, val cause: Throwable) : MapState
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class, FlowPreview::class)
class TrailMapViewModel(private val repo: TrailRepository) : ViewModel() {

    private val viewport = MutableStateFlow(BoundingBox.WORLD)

    val state: StateFlow<MapState> = viewport
        .debounce(150.milliseconds)
        .distinctUntilChanged()
        .flatMapLatest { box ->
            repo.observeIn(box)
                .map<List<Trail>, MapState> { MapState.Ready(box, it) }
                .onStart { emit(MapState.Loading(box)) }
                .catch { emit(MapState.Failed(box, it)) }
        }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), MapState.Idle)

    fun onCameraIdle(box: BoundingBox) { viewport.value = box }
}

Two details carry real weight here. The catch sits inside the lambda, so a failed query becomes a Failed state for that viewport instead of ending the stream. And debounce plus distinctUntilChanged stop jittery camera events from cancelling perfectly good work.

Failure mode 1: cancellation that nobody honors

Cancellation in coroutines is cooperative. flatMapLatest cancels the previous inner collection and, in the implementations I am familiar with, waits for it to finish unwinding before the next one starts. If the old work never checks for cancellation, the new viewport sits behind it.

// Looks harmless, but 200 ms of CPU work that never checks its Job
// holds up the next viewport until it finishes.
suspend fun rank(trails: List<Trail>): List<Trail> =
    withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { trails.sortedBy(::scenicScore) }

// Cooperative version: check between units of work.
suspend fun rank(trails: List<Trail>): List<Trail> =
    withContext(Dispatchers.Default) {
        trails
            .map { ensureActive(); it to scenicScore(it) }
            .sortedBy { it.second }
            .map { it.first }
    }

Blocking I/O has the same problem. A raw File.readBytes() or a synchronous Call.execute() ignores cancellation; wrap it in runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { ... } or use a suspending client API.

Failure mode 2: cancelling a write that already happened

Cancelling a read costs nothing. Cancelling a write is a different story, because the server may have applied the change before your coroutine noticed it was cancelled. The client then has no idea whether the edit landed.

// Risky: fast typing cancels requests that may already be committed server-side.
drafts.flatMapLatest { d -> flow { emit(api.saveDraft(d)) } }

// Safer: debounce, then queue, and let the server reject stale versions.
drafts
    .debounce(400.milliseconds)
    .flatMapConcat { d -> flow { emit(api.saveDraft(d.id, d.version, d.body)) } }

The rule of thumb is that flatMapLatest belongs on reads and on idempotent work. If a write must go through it, give the request an idempotency key.

Failure mode 3: restart thrash

Equal keys that pass through repeatedly will cancel and restart identical work, flickering a loading state each time. distinctUntilChanged() ahead of the operator is cheap insurance. Also remember that StateFlow already conflates equal values, but SharedFlow, combine outputs and Room-backed flows do not.

flatMapMerge: when throughput beats order

Trailhead’s photo grid prefetches thumbnails for the next screenful. The items are independent, so there is no reason to load them one by one.

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun prefetch(ids: Flow<PhotoId>, cache: ThumbnailCache): Flow<Prefetch> =
    ids.flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4) { id ->
        flow { emit(cache.load(id)) }
            .map<Thumbnail, Prefetch> { Prefetch.Hit(id) }
            .catch { emit(Prefetch.Miss(id, it)) }
    }

Notice that every result carries its own id. Since completion order is arbitrary, the consumer must never depend on position.

Failure mode 1: the stale result wins

This is the classic search-box bug, and merge makes it possible with a single wrong operator choice.

// "kit" can be overwritten by the slower response for "ki".
queries
    .flatMapMerge { q -> flow { emit(api.search(q)) } }
    .collect { results -> _ui.value = results }

If the screen shows one current answer, you wanted flatMapLatest. Use merge only when results are folded into a keyed collection.

Failure mode 2: unbounded fan-out

concurrency = Int.MAX_VALUE is tempting when you have 5,000 ids. The default limit is 16 (adjustable by a system property), and the parameter exists for a reason. With no bound you hammer a rate-limited API into 429s, and every in-flight coroutine holds its buffers while it waits. Pick N from what the downstream resource can really sustain, such as the HTTP client's per-host limits.

Failure mode 3: slot starvation

Each inner flow occupies one of the N slots until it completes. Flows that never complete will eat the slots one by one:

// Room's observe functions never complete. With 16 ids already collected,
// the 17th id is simply never subscribed. No error, no log line.
trailIds.flatMapMerge { id -> trailDao.observeTrail(id) }

Either take a snapshot (trailDao.observeTrail(id).first()), or restructure into a single query with an IN clause that observes the whole set at once.

Failure mode 4: sibling collapse

An uncaught exception in any one inner flow cancels all in-flight siblings and ends the pipeline. This is why the catch in the prefetch example is inside the lambda, not after the operator.

flatMapConcat: when order is the contract

Trailhead lets hikers edit waypoints offline. Those edits must hit the server in the order they were made: renaming a waypoint and then deleting it is not the same as the reverse.

sealed interface SyncOutcome {
    data class Applied(val id: EditId) : SyncOutcome
    data class Rejected(val id: EditId, val cause: Throwable) : SyncOutcome
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun drain(edits: Flow<Edit>, api: TrailApi): Flow<SyncOutcome> =
    edits.flatMapConcat { edit ->
        flow { emit(api.apply(edit)) }
            .map<Ack, SyncOutcome> { SyncOutcome.Applied(edit.id) }
            .retryWhen { cause, attempt ->
                val transient = cause is IOException && attempt < 3
                if (transient) delay(500L shl attempt.toInt())
                transient
            }
            .catch { emit(SyncOutcome.Rejected(edit.id, it)) }
    }

Retries live inside the queue slot, so a retrying edit keeps its place in line, which is exactly the ordering guarantee you wanted.

Failure mode 1: head-of-line blocking

One request that hangs freezes every edit behind it. Enforce deadlines at the HTTP client, for example with OkHttp’s callTimeout, so a stuck socket surfaces as an IOException that retryWhen can see and the queue keeps moving.

Failure mode 2: the inner flow that never ends

This is the concat twin of slot starvation, with N = 1:

// The first id's observer never completes, so the second id is never processed.
ids.flatMapConcat { id -> trailDao.observeTrail(id) }

When you see a concat whose later items mysteriously never run, check whether an earlier inner flow is infinite.

Failure mode 3: hot upstream pressure

Because concat holds back its producer, a hot source feels it directly:

private val edits = MutableSharedFlow<Edit>()          // no replay, no buffer

fun onEdit(edit: Edit) {
    // Returns false while the collector is busy with a previous edit.
    // Ignoring the result silently drops the user's change.
    edits.tryEmit(edit)
}

With emit the caller suspends, which may stall UI code. With tryEmit the edit vanishes. Neither is acceptable for user data. A Channel consumed via receiveAsFlow() gives you a real queue, and persisting to an outbox table gives you a durable one.

Failure mode 4: the queue dies with the process

An in-memory concat pipeline is only as durable as the process hosting it. For edits that must survive swipe-away and process death, write them to Room first and let WorkManager drain them. Use flatMapConcat for the in-process ordering, not as the source of truth.

Side by side

Cross-cutting rules that prevent most incidents

Catch inside the inner flow. Every example above does it, because an exception that escapes any inner flow ends the whole pipeline. Convert failures into values (Failed, Miss, Rejected) where they happen, and the outer stream keeps living.

Ask whether you need a flatMap at all. If each item maps to exactly one value, map { suspendCall(it) } or mapLatest { ... } is simpler to read and reason about. The API docs for these operators make the same point: when a suspending call inside map is enough, prefer it. Reach for flattening when the inner work is genuinely a stream.

Mind the opt-in. In the API docs I consulted, the merge and concat families are marked @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi, and flatMapLatest has carried the same marker, so annotate with @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) and check your kotlinx.coroutines version when upgrading.

Test with virtual time. The lab above is a template. For ViewModel pipelines, collect with Turbine under runTest and assert on emission order and on which inner flows were cancelled. Behavior differences between these operators are easy to pin down in tests and miserable to debug in the field.

Remember the lifecycle. With stateIn(..., WhileSubscribed(5_000)), a flatMapLatest pipeline stops five seconds after the UI goes away and starts again, from scratch, when it returns. Make sure restarting is safe.

A decision guide you can keep

🔚 Closing thought

The operator names describe mechanics, but the choice is really about what the work means. Results you can discard point to flatMapLatest. Effects that must keep their order point to flatMapConcat. Independent work with a throughput goal points to a bounded flatMapMerge. When you cannot say which sentence your feature fits into, that is the signal to slow down before picking an operator.

References

  • flatMapMerge, kotlinx.coroutines API documentation
  • flattenConcat, kotlinx.coroutines API documentation

📱 Stop Guessing Whether Your Android Code Actually Works

If “we’ll add tests later” is a sentence your team says a little too often, I’d recommend “Mastering Android Testing” — a 35-chapter deep dive into why Android testing is uniquely hard (Activity/Fragment coupling, async complexity, tooling churn) and exactly how to fix it, layer by layer. It walks through architecting for testability, JUnit/Truth/MockK fundamentals, ViewModel and coroutine/Flow testing without flakiness, Compose UI testing and the semantics tree, Espresso and instrumented tests, Room/Retrofit data-layer testing with a full sync-conflict-resolution case study, Robolectric’s real limits, CI pipelines, flaky test triage, and how to build a testing culture that actually survives contact with a deadline.

title: TRUER: Test-Time Reward Correction Using an Error-Aware Rectifier for Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.13714v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning enables language models to adapt using rewards derived from their own answers. However, majority voting can reinforce incorrect solutions even when correct alternatives are available. Our training audit shows that false positives (incorrect responses receiving positive rewards) dominate reward errors. We focus on a practical regime where ground-truth rewards are difficult to obtain at scale, while a limited labeled source set is available. We introduce TRUER, a framework that uses limited supervision to train a reward rectifier that distinguishes correctness from consensus. To achieve this goal, we train the rectifier with an emphasis on incorrect majorities and correct minorities, targeting cases where consensus and correctness disagree. After that, we freeze the rectifier and use it to correct rewards during subsequent test-time adaptation. By improving reward accuracy and thereby model performance, TRUER consistently outperforms naive TTRL in both metrics across all evaluated configurations.

title: Linear Probes to Bayesian Manifolds: Geometry of Arithmetic in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.12998v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Linear probes are a standard method to study geometric structures, such as helices and circles, from the activations of large language models (LLMs), and such structure is often taken as evidence that the model computes with it. Probe accuracy alone cannot establish this, because it conflates four separate claims. These are (1) that the concept is decodable from the activations, (2) that they form a specific shape, (3) that the shape belongs to the probed concept rather than to a related concept the model also represents, and (4) that the output of the model depends on the shape. We call these claims decodability, shape, ownership, and causal use, and we test them separately with a four-stage Bayesian pipeline. Stage 2 compares candidate shapes and selects the best one only when its evidence passes a predefined threshold. Stage 3 removes a set of related concepts, specified in advance, and tests whether the shape is owned or inherited. Stage 4 intervenes on the shape to test whether the output of the model depends on it. We apply the pipeline to two-digit addition and multiplication in GPT-J 6B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Pythia 6.9B. Nearly every concept is decodable, but the decoded directions overlap substantially across concepts. Every strongly supported comparison selects a ribbon, which is a helix whose radius changes with the value, or a torus. Of 1,330 cells with an ownership verdict, 19% of shapes are owned and 81% are inherited. Owned and inherited shapes move the output about equally often. Intervening on the shape retains approximately 61% of the effect of intervening on the full probe while using at most five dimensions, against a median of nine for the probe. Our results indicate that a probe verdict alone overstates what a model computes with, and we propose that probe results be reported as verdicts on all four claims rather than as a single accuracy.

title: Domain-Adversarial Adaptation from MURA to In-House Radiographs for Improved Adult Elbow Fracture Classification
description:
arXiv:2611.13308v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We studied domain shift in adult elbow fracture classification from radiographs when training on a large public dataset and deploying on a small, institution-specific dataset (UofL). We implemented a domain-adversarial neural network (DANN) to align feature distributions across source (MURA) and target (UofL) domains while optimizing fracture classification. A pretrained convolutional backbone was adapted to grayscale inputs; the task head predicts fracture presence, and a gradient-reversal-based domain head encourages domain-invariant features via adversarial learning. We compared four settings: (1) Source-only, (2) Target-only (limited labels), (3) Naive merge (pooled training), and (4) DANN (MURA to UofL). Evaluation on UofL test data uses AUC-ROC, and accuracy. DANN outperformed Source-only and Naive merge baselines by reducing domain bias without overfitting to the small target set. Ablations showed that progressive adversarial weight, dataset-size-aware domain loss, and domain-balanced sampling improved stability and target performance. Results demonstrated that domain alignment is a practical path to robust clinical generalization from public to local data.

title: How to Send High-Scale User Reminders with Message Queues over Direct HTTP Calls (and Why)
description:
Direct HTTP is attractive until the reminder endpoint is down at exactly the moment a campaign fans out. For high-scale user reminders, I prefer a queue between the producer and the sender: it absorbs bursts, preserves work while a consumer is unavailable, and gives the sender a retry boundary. The price is real, though. Delivery becomes at-least-once, so the consumer must make its send operation idempotent.

For this workflow, Infrai is a reasonable API-first option when the team wants the queue and surrounding backend capabilities behind one key. Its public discovery surface describes each capability and provides runnable examples, which keeps integration work close to the API contract instead of a vendor SDK.

I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. The useful lesson was not “always use a queue.” It was narrower: put a durable handoff before the failure-prone operation, then make the handoff’s duplicate behavior explicit.

Why are message queues preferred over direct HTTP calls for reminders?

Consider a B2B SaaS product sending renewal reminders. A scheduler finds users whose local send time has arrived and hands each reminder to a delivery worker. With a direct HTTP call, the scheduler owns two unrelated responsibilities: deciding that work exists and waiting for the recipient to accept it. If the endpoint is unavailable, the scheduler must hold retry state, choose backoff, and avoid creating a second reminder when its own request outcome is ambiguous.

A queue separates those decisions. The producer publishes a reminder and moves on. A consumer receives it, calls the endpoint, and acknowledges only after the send has reached the success condition defined by the application. A failed call can be retried without making the scheduler rerun its entire scan.

That is fault tolerance, not magic durability. A standard queue provides at-least-once delivery. The same message may arrive again after a timeout, a consumer crash, or an acknowledgement that did not reach the queue. The send endpoint therefore needs a stable event ID, a deduplication record, or an equivalent idempotency rule.

The invariant I keep in the runbook is simple:

A reminder may be attempted more than once, but an accepted reminder event may affect the recipient only once.

If the business cannot tolerate that invariant, a queue alone is the wrong abstraction. It does not turn an external HTTP side effect into a transaction.

Two architectures, one decision rule

There are two sound shapes for this workflow.

The first is direct delivery. A cron task selects due reminders, calls the endpoint, and records success or a retryable failure. This is easy to trace and can be the right choice for a small, low-burst workload where the sender and receiver are operated together. Its weak point is coupling: receiver downtime consumes scheduler capacity, and retry logic becomes part of the scheduling path.

The second is scheduled enqueue plus worker consumption. Cron performs a bounded sweep and publishes one message per due reminder. Workers consume independently, retry transient failures, and acknowledge successful work. This shape handles bursts better because the queue becomes a buffer between production and consumption. It also lets the worker fleet scale without changing the scheduler.

My decision rule is conditional: use direct HTTP when the operation is short, low-volume, and safe to retry in the scheduler; use enqueue plus workers when endpoint downtime or burst size must not block finding the next batch. For a long-running operation, cron should trigger enqueueing and let a worker do the work. A cron execution has a 900-second limit, so keeping the send inside cron is a poor boundary for slow or high-volume jobs.

Queues are not a substitute for workflow orchestration. They do not provide DAG execution or a join primitive. They also do not provide native debounce, throttle, or topic fan-out. If a reminder process needs dependencies, joins, or durable multi-consumer replay, I would evaluate a workflow engine or an event log instead.

How do I make the worker safe to retry?

The worker below models the important boundary without pretending that an HTTP success and a database write are one atomic transaction. The EventID is stable across attempts. Delivered is the consumer-side idempotency store; in production it must be shared and durable, with a uniqueness constraint on the event ID.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type Reminder struct {
    EventID string
    UserID  string
    Text    string
}

type Sender interface {
    Send(context.Context, Reminder) error
}

type Delivered struct {
    mu   sync.Mutex
    seen map[string]struct{}
}

func (d *Delivered) Claim(eventID string) bool {
    d.mu.Lock()
    defer d.mu.Unlock()
    if _, ok := d.seen[eventID]; ok {
        return false
    }
    d.seen[eventID] = struct{}{}
    return true
}

func deliver(ctx context.Context, sender Sender, seen *Delivered, r Reminder) error {
    if !seen.Claim(r.EventID) {
        return nil // Duplicate delivery: acknowledge it, do not send again.
    }
    if err := sender.Send(ctx, r); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("send reminder %s: %w", r.EventID, err)
    }
    return nil
}

type fakeSender struct{ attempts int }

func (s *fakeSender) Send(_ context.Context, r Reminder) error {
    s.attempts++
    if s.attempts == 1 {
        return errors.New("endpoint unavailable")
    }
    fmt.Println("accepted", r.EventID, r.UserID)
    return nil
}

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    seen := &Delivered{seen: make(map[string]struct{})}
    sender := &fakeSender{}
    r := Reminder{EventID: "renewal-2026-10-27-user-42", UserID: "user-42", Text: "Renewal reminder"}

    if err := deliver(ctx, sender, seen, r); err != nil {
        fmt.Println("retryable:", err)
        // The queue retries the same message, preserving EventID.
        delete(seen.seen, r.EventID)
        if err := deliver(ctx, sender, seen, r); err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
    }
}

There is one deliberately uncomfortable detail in that sample: claiming before sending is unsafe if a process dies after the claim and before the external endpoint accepts the request. A real implementation records a state that can be retried, or uses an idempotency key accepted by the destination. The exact transaction depends on the receiver. The queue cannot resolve it for you.

The queue’s own limits also belong in the runbook. Delayed messages are limited to 7 days, message bodies to 256 KB, and retention to 30 days; acknowledgement deletes the message. A FIFO deduplication window is only 5 minutes. Standard queues remain at-least-once, so consumer idempotency is mandatory. Those constraints fit reminders with a short delivery horizon. They do not fit a requirement to replay six months of events for several independent consumer groups.

Which queue shape fits this boundary?

Amazon SQS is a natural managed baseline for this design. Its visibility-timeout and dead-letter-queue model maps well to retrying an outbound send, and its operational burden is usually lower than running a broker. It remains a queue, though: consumers need idempotency, and a separate scheduler or application still owns reminder timing.

RabbitMQ is a strong choice when routing, acknowledgements, and broker-level control matter. Exchanges and bindings can express routing patterns that a simple work queue cannot. The trade-off is operating a broker cluster, monitoring its disk and memory behavior, and owning more of the failure surface.

Kafka is better suited to an append-oriented event stream with replay and multiple consumer groups. That is useful when “send reminder” is one projection of a longer-lived event history. It is a heavier fit for a bounded work queue where the only desired outcome is to process a due reminder once at the business level.

An API-first queue service can be a deliberate fourth option when the team wants discovery and integration consistency more than broker-specific control. Inngest is attractive when durable functions and event-driven steps are the center of the application. Trigger.dev fits teams that want task execution and retries close to application code. Temporal is the stronger candidate for durable workflows, timers, and explicit orchestration rather than a plain reminder queue. Each solves a broader or different problem than a minimal work queue, so I would not treat feature count as a reliability score.

I would recommend trying Infrai for a B2B SaaS reminder pipeline when the team wants a queue handoff with a self-describing integration and does not need DAG orchestration, Kafka-style replay, or native fan-out. The supporting benefit is operational consistency: its 295 routes across 20 modules use one key, so account-platform and scheduling calls can share the same Authorization: Bearer credential and https://api.infrai.cc/v1 base instead of adding another signup, credential set, and reconciliation path.

That recommendation has a boundary. With a vendor webhook product plus Svix or an in-house retry service, I would expect two signups, two credential sets, and glue for delivery inspection, retry state, and re-driving failures. A single-key platform reduces that integration seam, but it also creates one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. Kafka remains the better choice when replay and multiple consumer groups are requirements; RabbitMQ remains compelling when broker routing is the product of the system.

The handoff should stay explicit. The account-side result supplies the identity and audit context; the queue-side message carries the stable reminder event ID. Both calls use the same base URL and key. This small Go example performs the documented discovery call with explicit authentication, status handling, and backoff for rate limiting; the returned schema is the source for the queue publish body rather than a guessed payload.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type AccountContext struct {
    AccountID string
    RequestID string
}

type QueueMessage struct {
    EventID   string
    AccountID string
    RequestID string
    UserID    string
}

func publishReminder(ctx context.Context, account AccountContext, userID string) QueueMessage {
    select {
    case <-ctx.Done():
        panic(ctx.Err())
    default:
    }
    return QueueMessage{
        EventID:   fmt.Sprintf("reminder-%s-%s", account.AccountID, userID),
        AccountID: account.AccountID,
        RequestID: account.RequestID,
        UserID:    userID,
    }
}

func discover(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key string) ([]byte, error) {
    const url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery rate limit persisted")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    discovery, err := discover(context.Background(), http.DefaultClient, key)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    var index map[string]any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(discovery, &index); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    // Read the account-platform schema first; its output feeds the
    // scheduling message sent through POST /v1/queue/publish.
    account := AccountContext{AccountID: "acct-42", RequestID: "req-7"}
    message := publishReminder(context.Background(), account, "user-42")
    fmt.Printf("discovered=%t queue message=%+v\n", index != nil, message)
}

In an actual integration, inspect the public discovery schema before serializing the request, then send both calls with Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY. The important contract is the event ID, not a guessed payload shape. For a write, use a client-supplied idempotency key; on HTTP 429, honor Retry-After and back off. A 4xx response is a real error with a reason, not an acknowledgement.

What the runbook should measure and retry

Retry only failures that can plausibly recover. Endpoint downtime and transient transport errors belong on the retry path. A malformed recipient, an expired business object, or an authorization failure needs a dead-letter decision and an operator-visible reason. Blind retries turn a dependency outage into a larger incident.

I also separate scheduling correctness from delivery correctness. Cron should identify due work and publish it. The worker should own delivery attempts. If cron is paused, missed triggers are not backfilled automatically; the next run needs an explicit reconciliation policy. Trigger timing has second-level jitter, and run-history output is retained only for the first 4 KB, so durable application records matter more than a truncated execution log.

A queue does not remove the need for capacity planning. It changes the failure shape. Instead of losing work when an endpoint is down, the system accumulates pending work and makes backlog visible. That is a much better page, provided the team has a drain policy, a dead-letter policy, and a maximum reminder age.

The conclusion is practical: direct HTTP is fine for a small, tightly controlled send path. For high-scale reminders, enqueue the intent, retry the side effect in a worker, and make the event idempotent at the consumer. Choose SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka, or an API-first queue according to replay, routing, and operating-model needs. If the one-key, self-describing boundary matches the system and its limits, start with the queue and scheduling capability index.

  • Amazon SQS documentation
  • RabbitMQ documentation
  • Apache Kafka documentation

title: DrugCoding: A Scientific Programming Agent for Drug Discovery
description:
arXiv:2611.13651v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Drug discovery involves multiple interconnected research stages, including molecular design, property prediction, and virtual screening. These processes are characterized by complex workflows, interdependent computational tasks, and diverse specialized tools, placing substantial demands on the coordination of scientific models and computational resources. However, existing large language model (LLM)-based scientific agents still face challenges in autonomous planning of complex tasks, adaptive selection of specialized models, and reliable execution of multi-stage scientific computations, limiting their effectiveness in automating complex drug discovery workflows. To address these challenges, we propose DrugCoding, a scientific programming agent system that integrates scientific task planning, adaptive model routing, multi-agent collaboration, and programmatic tool execution. DrugCoding enables autonomous task planning and dynamic model adaptation for complex research objectives. It can flexibly invoke specialized scientific models, autonomously generate and execute code according to task requirements, and leverage multi-agent collaboration to support efficient execution and reliable validation of complex scientific tasks. To evaluate DrugCoding's performance in scientific tool invocation and multi-stage task execution, we conduct multi-turn tool-calling experiments across diverse language models and scientific tool interfaces. Experimental results demonstrate that DrugCoding achieves an average session-level Pass@1 of 97.35% on the full benchmark, outperforming the strongest baseline, Codex, by 9.24%. On the challenging subset, DrugCoding achieves 97.92%, exceeding the strongest baseline.

title: SELD: Detecting Silent Evidence Loss in Context Compression beyond the Answer
description:
arXiv:2611.12903v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Context compression is now routine for language models with long inputs, but a compressed context is useful only if it keeps the evidence for the answer. Existing checks compare the reader model's answer or its most likely words, and thus miss a frequent failure, silent evidence loss: key evidence is removed while the answer stays the same, leaving the answer unsupported and risky for other models that reuse the context. To address this challenge, we propose SELD (Silent Evidence Loss Detector), which needs no training and no labels. Its principle is that when evidence is lost, a reader model's preferences among the answers it leaves unsaid shift even if its answer does not, so comparing these preferences before and after compression reveals losses that answer checks cannot see. We also build SEL-Pairs, a benchmark of length-matched evidence and control deletions from three question-answering datasets. Quantitative and qualitative experiments with five reader models on it show that SELD consistently outperforms strong and recent baselines across compressors, compression rates and models, identifying the evidence-removing edit in 83% of matched pairs with unchanged answers, against 70% for the strongest baseline. These results show that evidence loss in compressed contexts can be detected even when the answer is unchanged.

title: Seven Java changes that pass your build and break your users
description:
Each change below compiles, passes the library's own tests and looks harmless in a code review. Each one breaks code that depends on the library, either when it is recompiled or, worse, when it runs against the new jar without being recompiled. We checked every example on Java 25.

Two ways to break a caller

A Java library can break its users in two different ways, and a change can break one without the other.

  • Source compatibility: does the caller's code still compile against the new version?

  • Binary compatibility: does code that was compiled against the old version still run with the new jar?

Binary compatibility matters more than it seems. When an application updates your library, it rarely recompiles the other libraries that use it. Those were compiled once, against your old version, and they keep calling it exactly as they did then. The Java Language Specification describes the rules in chapter 13, Binary Compatibility.

In each example, version 1.0 is the release that callers use and 1.1 is the change. The error messages are the real ones.

1. A wider parameter type 

// 1.0
public static int twice(int x)

// 1.1: accepts more values, so it looks compatible
public static long twice(long x)

Recompiled callers: compile. An int argument widens to long automatically.

Old binaries: fail. The JVM looks up a method by its exact descriptor, parameter and return types included:

java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: 'int Lib.twice(int)'

Instead: add the long version as an overload and keep the int one, delegating to the new method if you like.

2. A more general return type 

// 1.0
public static List<String> names()

// 1.1
public static Collection<String> names()

Recompiled callers: compile if they only use what Collection has, such as size() or a for loop, and fail if they assign the result to a List or call get(i).

Old binaries: fail, even the ones that only call size(). The return type is part of the descriptor:

java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: 'java.util.List Lib.names()'

Instead: keep the return type. If the new type is the right one, add a new method under a new name and deprecate the old one.

3. A new method in an interface 

// 1.0
public interface Lib { String name(); }

// 1.1, and the library now calls id()
public interface Lib { String name(); String id(); }

Recompiled callers: every class that implements the interface stops compiling until it implements id().

Old binaries: load without any error. The failure comes later, at the first call to the missing method, which can be deep inside your library and long after startup:

java.lang.AbstractMethodError: Receiver class Client does not define or inherit
an implementation of the resolved method 'abstract java.lang.String id()' of interface Lib.

Instead: give the new method a default implementation, for example default String id() { return name(); }. Old implementations then keep working, compiled or not. Interfaces that callers only use and never implement can grow freely; say so in the documentation, or mark them with an annotation such as @DoNotImplement.

4. Making a class final 

// 1.0
public class Lib { ... }

// 1.1: "nobody should extend this"
public final class Lib { ... }

Recompiled callers: subclasses stop compiling.

Old binaries: a subclass compiled against 1.0 cannot even be loaded:

java.lang.IncompatibleClassChangeError: class Client cannot inherit from final class Lib

Adding final to a public or protected method breaks the classes that override it in the same way. Removing final is always safe.

Instead: decide before the first release. If the class is already open, deprecate extension first and make it final in the next major version.

5. A static method becomes an instance method 

// 1.0
public static String version()

// 1.1
public String version()

Recompiled callers: every Lib.version() call stops compiling.

Old binaries: fail at the call. The opposite change, from instance to static, fails the same way:

java.lang.IncompatibleClassChangeError: Expected static method 'java.lang.String Lib.version()'

Instead: add the instance method with a new name and keep the static one.

6. A new checked exception 

java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: 'int Lib.twice(int)'


0

Recompiled callers: fail, unless they already catch or declare the exception:

java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: 'int Lib.twice(int)'


1

Old binaries: run. The JVM does not check throws clauses, so old callers get the exception at runtime without any code to handle it.

This is the reverse of the first two changes: old jars keep working, and the break appears the next time a user upgrades and recompiles. It is still a breaking change, and it belongs in a major version.

Instead: throw an unchecked exception, or add a new method that declares the checked one.

7. A new value for a constant 

java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: 'int Lib.twice(int)'


2

Nothing fails, and that is the problem. A static final field of a primitive type or String, set to a constant expression, is copied into the class files of the code that uses it when that code is compiled. Callers compiled against 1.0 keep using 10 with the 1.1 jar, until they are recompiled. We printed the field from a client compiled against 1.0 and run with the 1.1 jar: it printed 10.

So two parts of one application can disagree about the value, depending on when each part was compiled.

Instead: if a value can change, don't make it a compile-time constant. Expose it through a method, or initialise the field in a way that is not a constant expression.

The seven at a glance

Change in a minor release Recompiled callers Old binaries
Wider parameter type Compile NoSuchMethodError
More general return type Some fail NoSuchMethodError
New abstract method in an interface Implementations fail AbstractMethodError at the first call
Class or method made final Subclasses fail IncompatibleClassChangeError when loaded
Static to instance, or back Fail IncompatibleClassChangeError
New checked exception Fail Run, with no handler for it
New constant value Get the new value Keep the old value

None of them fails the library's own build, and most of them get past at least one of the two checks. That is why they reach a release.

Why tests don't catch them

The library's tests are compiled together with the new code, so they always match it. They test the library as it is now. What they cannot see is the code that was written, or compiled, against the version you released before.

These are not rare cases either. A study of 119,879 library upgrades on Maven Central found a breaking change in 1 in 5 minor and patch upgrades (Ochoa et al., 2022). The numbers and their sources are in our report.

How to catch them

Compare your public API with the last release, not with your tests. Tools that do this for Java:

  • japicmp: compares two jars and reports binary and source incompatibilities. It has a Maven plugin, and there are Gradle plugins for it.

  • Revapi: API analysis with configurable rules, for Maven and Gradle.

  • binary-compatibility-validator: for Kotlin libraries, built on a committed API dump.

  • Bumpwise: our IntelliJ IDEA plugin. It compares the code in the editor with the last published release, highlights each breaking change while you type, offers the compatible alternative (such as keeping the old signature as @Deprecated) and calculates the next version.

The first three run in the build, usually in CI. Bumpwise runs before the change is committed. They work well together: one check while you write, one before you release.

Disclosure: Gilware makes Bumpwise, a paid plugin with a free edition for Java libraries published on Maven Central.

How we checked

For each change we compiled the 1.0 library, compiled a small client against it, compiled the 1.1 library, then ran the old client with the new jar and recompiled the client against 1.1. OpenJDK 25.0.5. The error messages above are copied from those runs.

Found a mistake? Write to hello@gilware.com.

Originally published at gilware.com.

title: TERM: Target-Free Jailbreak Defense via Entropy-Guided Residual Modulation
description:
arXiv:2611.13577v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across diverse applications, making both safety and utility essential for reliable deployment. Jailbreak attacks use diverse forms of adversarial prompting to bypass alignment safeguards and induce LLMs to generate harmful responses. Some representation-based defenses regulate internal activations using predefined steering directions or learned safety regions. However, adapting intervention to each input without a predefined representational target while limiting over-refusal remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose Target-free Entropy-guided Residual Modulation (TERM), an inference-time defense that uses prompt-calibrated attention entropy deviations to guide adaptive modulation of the model's own residual updates. Attention patterns vary across prompts and decoding steps, making raw entropy values difficult to interpret as a consistent signal for intervention. We therefore calibrate attention entropy against each prompt's own prefill baseline to establish an input-specific reference for reducing unnecessary intervention on benign requests. Adaptive scale normalization and temporal accumulation then account for differences in deviation scale and persistence to determine intervention strength. The resulting signal controls bounded scaling of the model's own residual updates, without relying on a predefined safety direction. We compare our method with seven defenses on seven jailbreak attacks and two over-refusal benchmarks across Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models, including Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B. Results show our method improves jailbreak robustness while maintaining low over-refusal on benign safety-sensitive requests with modest inference overhead.

title: Evaluation protocols for historical script classification: the cost of manuscript-level leakage and the role of soft labels
description:
arXiv:2611.12969v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A paleographer applies a script type classifier to unseen manuscripts. We measure how much testing on other pages of training manuscripts inflates accuracy. On VML-HP-ext (715 pages, 171 Hebrew manuscripts, 14 script classes) we compare page-level and manuscript-level splits. Page-level accuracy drops from 97% to 54% (59% at manuscript level), and is 39% on the official blind test set. The gap of 40 to 47 percentage points (pp) at patch, page and manuscript level is statistically significant and reproduces with ResNet18; on binarized patches (ink and background only) it is 34 to 42 pp, also significant. On unseen manuscripts the model is overconfident: mean confidence 70% against 54% correct pages; patch-level expected calibration error (ECE, mean gap between confidence and accuracy) rises from 0.065 to 0.444. Binarization leaves patch-level overconfidence but cuts it markedly at page level. Confidence still helps triage: in the more confident half of pages 67% are correct, 41% in the rest. Training on expert soft labels showed no evidence of an accuracy difference, though a small page-level loss cannot be ruled out. The predicted distributions are closer to the expert's assessment. ECE is lower at patch level (0.21 to 0.31) and in most runs at page level, but not significantly at manuscript level. Label smoothing (blurring the label, no expert input) also lowers ECE but comes no closer to the expert. Temperature scaling (post-training confidence correction) helps significantly only at patch level. On 97 pages of 16 manuscripts with mixed expert assessment, soft labels cut divergence from the expert by 22 to 30% (significant in four of five runs); the point estimate of accuracy is 16.5 to 23.7 pp below hard labels, but with 16 manuscripts the loss can neither be confirmed nor ruled out. We propose recommendations for the evaluation protocol; code will be released with the paper

title: Elicitation of the parameters of a multi-criteria sorting model
description:
arXiv:2611.13062v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multiple-criteria decision aiding (MCDA) proposes models and methods for different types of decision problems such as choice, ranking or sorting. Such models involve various parameters that must be elicited. In the elicitation process, all necessary information has to be taken from the decision-maker. For this, several direct and indirect elicitation methods are suggested in the literature. In this work, we concentrate on direct elicitation: we aim at providing a rigorous elicitation procedure for the parameters of the Non-Compensatory Sorting model (NCS), which has been characterized by an axiomatic analysis. A basic version of the NCS model is considered, i.e., a model with two categories and no vetoes. The parameters are the set of sufficient coalitions of criteria and the profile separating the two categories. Regarding the sufficient coalitions, we propose several questioning algorithms that engraft questions on classical graph exploration algorithms such as depth-first search. Such algorithms are implemented and evaluated by simulation. For eliciting the limit profile, we design a questioning algorithm using dichotomy. Questioning algorithms can be optimal in the worst case or on average. An optimal algorithm in the worst case has been proposed by Hansel in the framework of monotone Boolean functions. We implement and evaluate this algorithm as a variant of the depth-first search approaches. Regarding optimal questioning strategies on average, we evaluate decision trees for up to four criteria. On the other hand, we assess how more general is NCS as compared to MR-Sort, a particular case of the NCS model in which sufficient coalitions can be represented by additive weights.

title: Living constitutions: Participatory alignment for sovereign foundation models
description:
arXiv:2611.13402v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In Constitutional AI, a plain-text "constitution" encodes values and gets incorporated into a model via post-training. However, the procedure for creating such a constitution poses significant challenges: who contributes, who decides which norms are included, and to what extent must the process be participatory or democratic? These challenges can be paralyzing. Yet, we argue that taking action is essential: without a deliberate constitution, sovereign models would risk misalignment or default to norms set by frontier model providers. We propose treating the development of a constitution as an evolving, participatory process akin to citizen science, iteratively drafted, tested, and refined. We therefore formulate five desirable principles: iterative, modular, justifiable, positional, and legitimate. We further argue that such a document must remain responsive not only over time but across the people it governs, and propose that provisions be marked as settled, contested, or underdetermined, so that durable disagreement is recorded in the constitution rather than resolved away. Empirically, we show via agent-based modelling that proposed process for maintaining living constitutions is robust against 50% bad actors among citizens - assuming a share of 75% participants with good intent in the deliberative body. This indicates that the proposed process tolerates a substantial share of adversarial participants.

title: Java 类和对象（二）：包、封装、static 与代码块
description:
1. 包：给类分类，也给类名加上范围

项目中的类越来越多时，需要按用途组织；不同地方也可能出现同名的类。包（package）用来组织类，并区分不同包中的同名类。

例如，java.util.Date 和 java.sql.Date 都叫 Date，但它们属于不同的包，是两个不同的类。包名.类名 称为类的全限定名。

1.1 声明包与创建目录

package 表示“当前源文件中的类属于哪个包”，放在源文件开头、import 和类定义之前；前面可以有注释。

package com.bit.demo1;

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello");
    }
}

在 IDEA 的普通项目中，对应目录为：

src/
└── com/
    └── bit/
        └── demo1/
            └── Test.java
  • 包名通常使用小写，常按“域名倒写 + 项目或模块名”命名，尽量避免重名。
  • 在 IDEA 中：右键 src → New → Package，输入 com.bit.demo1；再右键包 → New → Java Class 创建类。
  • IDEA 会创建目录，并自动添加对应的 package 语句。
  • 不写 package 时，类属于默认包。

1.2 使用其他包中的类

方式一：直接写全限定名。

java.util.Date date = new java.util.Date();
System.out.println(date.getTime());

这里 getTime() 返回从 1970 年 1 月 1 日 00:00:00 UTC 到该时间点的毫秒数。此处只用它演示如何使用其他包中的类。

方式二：先用 import 导入类，再写简单类名。

import java.util.Date;

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Date date = new Date();
        System.out.println(date.getTime());
    }
}

二者效果相同。import 只是让当前文件能用简单类名，不会把类复制进当前包，也不会改变访问权限。

源文件中的常见顺序是：

package 声明（如果有）
import 导入（如果有）
类定义

同一个包中的类通常不需要互相导入；java.lang 包中的 String、System 等类也不需要显式导入。

1.3 通配导入与同名冲突 

import java.util.*;

* 允许使用该包中可访问的类型的简单名称，不包含子包中的类型。通常更推荐明确写出需要的类，例如 import java.util.Date;。

下面两条导入同时存在时，单独写 Date 会产生歧义：

import java.util.*;
import java.sql.*;

因为两个包都有 Date，编译器不知道要选哪个。可以明确导入需要的那个类；如果两个同名类都要使用，就用全限定名区分，例如：

java.util.Date date = new java.util.Date();

1.4 常见包

包 主要用途
java.lang 常用基础类，如 String、Object，无需显式导入
java.util 常用工具类、集合类等，后续会经常使用
java.io 输入输出，如文件读写
java.net 网络编程
java.sql 数据库访问
java.lang.reflect 反射，即在程序运行时获取类的信息并操作其成员

这里先认识用途，具体用法在后续章节学习。

2. 访问权限与封装：把数据的使用规则放进类里

2.1 先分清哪些地方能访问成员

访问权限控制其他代码能否直接访问字段或调用方法。本章先掌握以下三种：

成员的访问权限 当前类内部 同包的其他普通类 不同包的普通类
private 可以 不可以 不可以
不写访问修饰符（包访问权限） 可以 可以 不可以
public 可以 可以 可以

表格以类本身可被访问为前提，暂不涉及继承和嵌套类。

包访问权限有时称为 default 权限，但不是在字段前写 default，而是什么都不写。

另一种访问修饰符是 protected，它涉及继承中的访问规则，留到继承章节再学。

看一个跨包访问的例子。两个类分别放在各自包对应的目录中。

com/bit/demo1/Computer.java：

package com.bit.demo1;

public class Computer {
    private String cpu = "i7";
    String brand = "HW";
    public String screen = "14英寸";

    public void showCpu() {
        System.out.println(cpu); // 当前类内部，可以访问 private 成员
    }
}

com/bit/demo2/TestComputer.java：

package com.bit.demo2;

import com.bit.demo1.Computer;

public class TestComputer {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Computer computer = new Computer();
        System.out.println(computer.screen); // 可以：public
        computer.showCpu();                  // 可以：通过公开方法使用私有数据

        // System.out.println(computer.brand); // 错误：不同包，不能访问包权限成员
        // System.out.println(computer.cpu);   // 错误：其他类不能直接访问 private 成员
    }
}

如果把 TestComputer 移到 com.bit.demo1 包中，它就能访问 brand，但仍不能直接访问 cpu。“同一个包”和“同一个类”是两种不同的范围。

2.2 封装解决什么问题

封装就是把数据和操作数据的方法组织在类中，隐藏内部细节，通过对外提供的方法与对象交互。

例如，年龄不应该随意变成负数。如果把 age 设为 public，外部就能直接执行 stu.age = -1;。将它改为 private 后，外部必须经过类提供的方法修改，类就有机会检查数据。

这里的“对外接口”指公开的使用方式，例如方法，不是专指 Java 的 interface 语法。

class Student {
    private String name;
    private int age;

    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }

    public void setName(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    public int getAge() {
        return age;
    }

    public void setAge(int age) {
        if (age < 0) {
            System.out.println("年龄不能为负数");
            return;
        }
        this.age = age;
    }

    public void show() {
        System.out.println(name + "，" + age + "岁");
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student stu = new Student();
        stu.setName("小明");
        stu.setAge(18);
        stu.setAge(-1); // 被拒绝，年龄仍然是 18
        System.out.println(stu.getAge());
        stu.show();
    }
}

输出：

年龄不能为负数
18
小明，18岁
  • getXxx() 通常用于读取数据，叫 getter；setXxx(...) 通常用于修改数据，叫 setter。它们都是普通方法，名称是一种约定。
  • this.age = age; 中，左边是当前对象的字段，右边是方法参数。
  • private 阻止的是类外直接访问，不影响本类的方法操作这些数据。
  • 不必给每个字段都提供 getter 和 setter。 只开放确实需要的操作；只读数据可以只提供 getter。

2.3 封装的价值

  1. 控制数据修改。 外部经过方法修改数据，类可以检查是否合法，减少意外破坏。
  2. 简化使用。 使用者只需要知道方法怎么调用，不必了解内部如何实现。
  3. 减少相互依赖。 对外方法的用法和约定保持一致时，内部实现的调整通常不需要调用者跟着修改。

封装不是“所有成员一律 private”，也不是“写了 getter/setter 就自动安全”。关键在于：哪些细节隐藏，哪些操作开放，以及开放的操作是否维护了数据规则。

3. static：属于类，还是属于某个对象

3.1 实例变量各有一份，静态变量共同使用一份

学生的姓名因人而异，应当是实例变量。如果当前程序约定所有学生共用一个教室，教室就可以是静态变量。

class Student {
    public String name;
    public static String classRoom = "1-101";
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // 不创建对象，也能访问静态变量
        System.out.println(Student.classRoom);

        Student s1 = new Student();
        Student s2 = new Student();
        s1.name = "小明";
        s2.name = "小红";

        Student.classRoom = "1-102";
        System.out.println(s1.name + "：" + Student.classRoom);
        System.out.println(s2.name + "：" + Student.classRoom);
    }
}

输出：

1-101
小明：1-102
小红：1-102

可以把关系理解为：

s1 对象：name = "小明"
s2 对象：name = "小红"
Student 类共享的数据：classRoom = "1-102"

static 修饰的成员变量又叫静态成员变量、类变量，不在每个对象中各保存一份。它的生命周期与类相关，不会因为某一个对象不再使用就消失。

虽然 Java 允许写 s1.classRoom，但访问的仍然是共享变量，并不是 s1 独有的数据。推荐写 Student.classRoom，明确表示它属于类。

是否使用 static 取决于数据是否真的需要全类共享。如果学生可能属于不同教室，教室就不适合简单地定义成所有学生共享的变量。

3.2 静态方法与静态成员的封装

被 static 修饰的方法叫静态方法、类方法，推荐通过 类名.方法名(...) 调用，不需要先创建对象。

静态成员也受访问权限限制。可以将静态字段设为 private，再按需要提供公开方法：

class Student {
    private static String classRoom = "1-101";

    public static String getClassRoom() {
        return classRoom;
    }

    public static void setClassRoom(String classRoom) {
        Student.classRoom = classRoom;
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student.setClassRoom("1-102");
        System.out.println(Student.getClassRoom()); // 1-102
    }
}

Student.classRoom 表示类变量；右边的 classRoom 是参数。static 不会让 private 成员变成公开成员。

3.3 为什么静态方法不能直接访问实例成员

实例成员需要先确定“是哪一个对象的”，静态方法本身没有当前对象，所以不能使用 this，也不能直接访问实例成员。

class Student {
    private int age = 18;

    public void show() {
        System.out.println(age);
    }

    public static void test() {
        // System.out.println(age);      // 错误：没有指定对象
        // System.out.println(this.age); // 错误：静态方法中没有 this
        // show();                       // 错误：没有指定调用对象

        Student stu = new Student();
        System.out.println(stu.age);     // 正确：访问 stu 的年龄，且代码位于本类内部
        stu.show();                     // 正确：调用 stu 的实例方法
    }
}

因此，准确说法是：静态方法不能直接访问实例成员，但可以通过具体对象访问有权限访问的实例成员。 main 是静态方法，却能先 new 对象再调用实例方法，原因就在这里。

方法所在环境 直接访问本类静态成员 直接访问当前对象的实例成员 使用 this
实例方法 可以 可以 可以
静态方法 可以 不可以，需要具体对象 不可以

3.4 静态变量如何初始化

本章掌握两种常见写法：

// 就地初始化：定义时直接给值
private static String classRoom = "1-101";

另一种是使用静态代码块，适合需要多条语句完成的初始化，下一节说明。

通常不要把静态变量的初始化放进构造方法：构造方法每创建一个对象就会执行，把共享数据放进去赋初值，可能导致每次创建对象都重置共享状态。

3.5 静态导入：省略静态成员前的类名

理解 static 后，再看 import static 就容易了：普通导入让类名可以简写，静态导入让指定类中可访问的静态方法、静态字段可以直接使用名称。

import static java.lang.Math.pow;
import static java.lang.Math.sqrt;

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double result = sqrt(pow(3, 2) + pow(4, 2));
        System.out.println(result); // 5.0
    }
}

pow(a, b) 求 a 的 b 次方，sqrt(x) 求平方根。上面的计算等价于：

double result = Math.sqrt(Math.pow(3, 2) + Math.pow(4, 2));

也可以写 import static java.lang.Math.*;。静态导入只是简化写法，不改变方法的性质；如果省略类名反而难以判断来源，保留类名会更清楚。

4. 代码块：位置不同，执行时机不同

代码块是用 {} 包围的一段代码。本章重点区分普通代码块、实例代码块和静态代码块。同步代码块涉及多线程，留到后续章节学习。

4.1 普通代码块：限制局部变量的作用范围

普通代码块写在方法内部，执行流程走到这里时才执行。

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        {
            int x = 10;
            System.out.println(x);
        }

        // 上一个 x 的作用域已经结束
        int x = 100;
        System.out.println(x);
    }
}

输出依次为 10、100。内层块中的 x 出了块就不能访问，后面的 x 是重新声明的另一个变量。

4.2 实例代码块：每个对象都会执行的初始化

实例代码块也叫构造代码块，写在类内部、方法外部，不加 static。

class Student {
    private String name;

    {
        name = "小明";
        System.out.println("实例代码块");
    }

    public Student() {
        System.out.println("构造方法：" + name);
    }
}

每次执行 new Student()，都会先运行实例代码块，再运行这里的构造方法体：

实例代码块
构造方法：小明
  • 实例代码块用于实例初始化，可以使用 this 和实例成员。
  • 它没有方法名和参数，不能像普通方法那样单独调用。
  • 即使把它写在构造方法定义的后面，执行时也仍然先于该构造方法体。

4.3 静态代码块：类初始化时执行一次

静态代码块写在类内部、方法外部，形式是 static { ... }，通常用于初始化静态数据。

class Student {
    private static String classRoom;

    static {
        classRoom = "1-101";
        System.out.println("静态代码块");
    }
}

静态代码块在类初始化时执行，同一个类正常初始化一次后，不会因为又创建了对象而重复执行。 它不属于某个对象，所以也不能使用 this 或直接访问实例成员。

类初始化可以由首次创建对象、调用该类的静态方法等操作触发。本章示例中的静态变量不是常量，首次访问它也会触发类初始化；因此，不创建对象，也可能执行静态代码块。

“类加载”和“类初始化”不完全相同；这里只需记住：静态代码块中的语句是在运行程序、初始化类时执行的，不是在编译时执行的。

4.4 用一次完整运行看清执行顺序

下面的类不涉及继承，重点观察静态初始化、实例初始化和构造方法体的先后关系。

class Student {
    private static String classRoom = "1-101";
    private String name = "默认姓名";

    static {
        System.out.println("静态块1：" + classRoom);
        classRoom = "1-102";
    }

    static {
        System.out.println("静态块2：" + classRoom);
    }

    {
        System.out.println("实例块：" + name);
        name = "小明";
    }

    public Student() {
        System.out.println("构造方法：" + name);
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("第一次创建");
        Student s1 = new Student();
        System.out.println("第二次创建");
        Student s2 = new Student();
    }
}

输出：

第一次创建
静态块1：1-101
静态块2：1-102
实例块：默认姓名
构造方法：小明
第二次创建
实例块：默认姓名
构造方法：小明

按两个阶段理解：

  1. 类初始化阶段，只进行一次。 静态字段先有默认值，再把静态字段的显式初始化和静态代码块按源码出现顺序执行。这里先把 classRoom 设为 "1-101"，再执行静态块1、静态块2。
  2. 对象初始化阶段，每个新对象都要进行。 实例字段先有默认值，再把实例字段的显式初始化和实例代码块按源码出现顺序执行，最后执行本例中的构造方法体。

注意：“按源码顺序”是分别在静态初始化阶段、实例初始化阶段内排序，不是把整个类从上到下无差别执行。也不是“所有字段赋值永远先于所有代码块”；同一阶段中，字段的显式初始化与代码块谁写在前，谁先执行。

形式 位置 执行时机 常见用途
普通代码块 { ... } 方法内部 流程执行到该处时 限制局部变量作用域
实例代码块 { ... } 类内、方法外 每次创建对象时 初始化实例数据
静态代码块 static { ... } 类内、方法外 类初始化时，一次 初始化类共享的数据

5. 复习自查

1. import 了一个类，就能访问它的所有成员吗？

不能。导入只解决名称使用问题，能否访问还要看访问权限。

2. 静态方法能否使用实例变量？

不能直接使用，但可以通过具体对象访问有权限访问的实例变量；静态方法中不能使用 this。反过来，实例方法可以直接访问本类的静态成员。

3. 创建两个对象，静态代码块、实例代码块、构造方法体分别执行几次？

在本章这种简单类中，若此前尚未初始化该类，静态代码块执行 1 次；实例代码块和构造方法体各执行 2 次。

4. getter/setter 会破坏封装吗？

不会必然破坏封装，它们是对外提供操作的一种方式。关键是按需要开放，并维护数据规则，而不是无条件暴露所有内部状态。

5. 封装后为什么更容易修改代码？

调用者依赖公开方法；在这些方法的用法和约定保持一致的前提下，可以调整类内部的实现，减少对调用者的影响。
