title: Continuous 3D Spatial Transcriptomics Reconstruction via Histology-Informed Implicit Neural Representations
description:
arXiv:2611.14129v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Three-dimensional spatial transcriptomics (3D ST) enables the analysis of gene-expression patterns across tissue depths. However, 3D ST measurements are acquired from discrete 2D tissue sections, which are often sparsely sampled due to high acquisition costs. To address this limitation, we propose a histology-informed multi-task implicit neural representation (HIM-INR) for continuous 3D gene-expression reconstruction from sparse ST observations. HIM-INR jointly reconstructs gene-expression profiles and histological representations using an INR with a shared backbone, leveraging densely sampled histological images as auxiliary spatial supervision. Once trained, HIM-INR predicts gene expression at arbitrary 3D coordinates without requiring histological images. Experiments on two 3D ST datasets demonstrate improved reconstruction over existing methods, particularly as the number of missing ST sections increases.

title: When the Window Lies: Compose Apps That Survive Resizing, Folding, and Docking
description:
Most adaptive-UI bugs are not layout bugs. They are assumptions that were true on the device you developed on: the screen is about 400dp wide, it stays portrait, it never changes while a screen is open, and a back press always means “go up one level”. Resizable windows, foldables, desktop windowing, and connected displays break every one of those assumptions at the same time.

This post walks through the session’s chapters in order and pairs each with the failure mode that tends to show up in production first. Code is idiomatic Kotlin. Where an API is still experimental, I say so, because pinning that down early saves a painful upgrade later. The mediaQuery, Grid, and FlexBox APIs are experimental, so confirm the exact artifact versions and import paths against the release notes for the Compose version you depend on before copying any snippet.

FieldNotes has three screens: a list of survey sites, a detail screen with a photo and notes, and a small dashboard. Nothing exotic, which is exactly why it makes a good test subject.

1. The assumption that breaks: device versus window

The mental shift is small to state and large to apply. The OS reports a window, and the window is what your UI actually lives in. A tablet can host your app in a one-third split-screen. A phone can unfold into something nearly square. A desktop session can drag your window to any size and keep changing it.

Two practical rules follow from this:

  • Derive layout from the window’s size and posture, never from a device category. A boolean like isTablet is wrong the moment someone splits the screen.
  • Treat any window property as something that can change while a screen is visible.

If your codebase has a DeviceType enum, search for every read of it. Each one is a future bug report.

2. Configuration changes and the state that disappears

Resizing a window can recreate the Activity, and it can also restructure your composition without recreating anything. Both look identical to the user: the text they were typing is gone.

Failure mode: state declared inside a branch

This is the subtle one. When a window crosses a breakpoint, the composable that was in the “narrow” branch leaves the composition, and its remember state goes with it, even though the Activity never restarted.

// Looks fine, loses scroll position every time the window crosses the breakpoint.
@Composable
fun SitesPane(isWide: Boolean, sites: List<Site>) {
    if (isWide) {
        Row {
            SiteList(sites, rememberLazyListState())
            DetailPlaceholder()
        }
    } else {
        SiteList(sites, rememberLazyListState())
    }
}

The fix is to hoist the state above the branch so both layouts share one instance:

@Composable
fun SitesPane(isWide: Boolean, sites: List<Site>) {
    val listState = rememberLazyListState() // lives above the branch

    if (isWide) {
        Row {
            SiteList(sites, listState, Modifier.weight(1f))
            DetailPlaceholder(Modifier.weight(1f))
        }
    } else {
        SiteList(sites, listState)
    }
}

Failure mode: durable state parked in remember

User input and filters need to survive recreation, and sometimes process death. Two tools cover most cases. For text, the state-based text field holder is saveable out of the box:

@Composable
fun NoteEditor(modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
    val note = rememberTextFieldState()
    BasicTextField(state = note, modifier = modifier)
}

For screen-level state that outlives a composable, use a ViewModel backed by SavedStateHandle, so it also survives process death:

class SiteFilterViewModel(private val handle: SavedStateHandle) : ViewModel() {

    val onlyUnsynced: StateFlow<Boolean> =
        handle.getStateFlow(KEY_ONLY_UNSYNCED, false)

    fun setOnlyUnsynced(value: Boolean) {
        handle[KEY_ONLY_UNSYNCED] = value
    }

    private companion object {
        const val KEY_ONLY_UNSYNCED = "only_unsynced"
    }
}

Failure mode: the configChanges escape hatch

Declaring configChanges in the manifest stops the Activity from being recreated on resize, and the missing-state bugs go quiet. They have not been fixed. Process death still wipes whatever you only kept in memory, and your layout code still has to react to the new size. Use the flag only when you have deliberately designed for it.

3. Detecting postures with the mediaQuery API

For years, reacting to a half-folded device meant wiring up a window-layout flow, collecting it, mapping it, and threading the result down. The mediaQuery API, introduced as experimental in the Compose April '26 release, collapses that into a condition evaluated against a UiMediaScope. It exposes window size and posture, plus input signals such as pointer precision and keyboard kind, and capability signals such as camera and microphone.

The important detail, easy to miss: posture describes the window, not the hardware. A phone that is half-folded but showing your app in single-panel split-screen reports Flat.

Turning it on

The feature sits behind a flag you set once, before the first composition. The documentation sets it in Application:

class FieldNotesApp : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        ComposeUiFlags.isMediaQueryIntegrationEnabled = true
        super.onCreate()
    }
}

Centralize the decision

The temptation is to sprinkle mediaQuery { ... } through leaf composables. Resist it. Turn the signals into one explicit model and let screens consume that:

sealed interface DetailLayout {
    data object Stacked : DetailLayout
    data object SideBySide : DetailLayout
    data object TabletopSplit : DetailLayout
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalMediaQueryApi::class)
@Composable
fun rememberDetailLayout(): DetailLayout {
    // Size changes arrive at high frequency while a window edge is dragged,
    // so read them through the derived variant.
    val narrow by derivedMediaQuery {
        windowWidth < WindowSizeClass.WIDTH_DP_MEDIUM_LOWER_BOUND.dp
    }

    return when {
        mediaQuery { windowPosture == UiMediaScope.Posture.Tabletop } -> DetailLayout.TabletopSplit
        mediaQuery { windowPosture == UiMediaScope.Posture.Book } -> DetailLayout.SideBySide
        narrow -> DetailLayout.Stacked
        else -> DetailLayout.SideBySide
    }
}

The same pattern works for input. Touch targets and shortcut hints depend on what the user is actually holding:

@OptIn(ExperimentalMediaQueryApi::class)
@Composable
fun SaveButton(onSave: () -> Unit) {
    val imprecisePointer = mediaQuery {
        pointerPrecision == UiMediaScope.PointerPrecision.Blunt
    }
    val hasPhysicalKeyboard = mediaQuery {
        keyboardKind == UiMediaScope.KeyboardKind.Physical
    }

    Button(
        onClick = onSave,
        modifier = Modifier.heightIn(min = if (imprecisePointer) 56.dp else 40.dp),
    ) {
        Text(if (hasPhysicalKeyboard) "Save  (Ctrl+S)" else "Save")
    }
}

Failure mode: previews that never show the interesting state

You will not have a folded device attached to every code review. The scope is provided through a composition local, so a preview can substitute its own. A small helper keeps this honest:

@OptIn(ExperimentalMediaQueryApi::class)
@Composable
fun PreviewWithPosture(
    posture: UiMediaScope.Posture,
    content: @Composable () -> Unit,
) {
    val base = LocalUiMediaScope.current
    val overridden = remember(base, posture) {
        object : UiMediaScope by base {
            override val windowPosture: UiMediaScope.Posture = posture
        }
    }
    CompositionLocalProvider(LocalUiMediaScope provides overridden, content = content)
}

Class delegation means everything you did not override still comes from the real scope, so the preview stays realistic for width, input, and the rest.

Notice what the helper does not do: it never touches ComposeUiFlags. The flag is global state that has to be set before the first composition, so it belongs at startup (Application.onCreate() in the app, test setup in instrumented or Robolectric tests), not inside a composable where it would run as a side effect on every composition. Studio previews do not run your Application, so check how your tooling version handles the flag for previews rather than assuming it carries over.

Failure mode: building on an experimental surface with no seam

mediaQuery is explicitly experimental and the team asks for feedback. That is a reason to adopt it behind your own function like rememberDetailLayout() above, not a reason to avoid it. When names or shapes change, you edit one file.

4. Responsive layouts with Grid and FlexBox

Compose has long had good tools for one dimension (Row, Column) and for large scrolling collections (the lazy grids). What was awkward was the middle: the structural, all-on-screen, two-dimensional layout of a dashboard, which people built from nested rows and columns and then fought every time the screen changed shape.

Grid is the new answer for two-dimensional structure. You describe tracks and named areas in a config lambda and place items into them. The big win for adaptivity is that you change the config, not the tree, so composables keep their identity when the window changes shape:

enum class DashArea { Map, Conditions, Notes }

@Composable
fun SiteDashboard(expanded: Boolean, modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
    Grid(
        config = {
            if (expanded) {
                column(2.fr)
                column(1.fr)
                row(1.fr)
                row(1.fr)
                area(areaId = DashArea.Map, rows = 1..2, columns = 1..1)
                area(areaId = DashArea.Conditions, row = 1, column = 2)
                area(areaId = DashArea.Notes, row = 2, column = 2)
            } else {
                column(1.fr)
                repeat(3) { row(GridTrackSize.Auto) }
                area(areaId = DashArea.Map, row = 1, column = 1)
                area(areaId = DashArea.Conditions, row = 2, column = 1)
                area(areaId = DashArea.Notes, row = 3, column = 1)
            }
            gap(12.dp)
        },
        modifier = modifier,
    ) {
        MapCard(Modifier.gridItem(areaId = DashArea.Map))
        ConditionsCard(Modifier.gridItem(areaId = DashArea.Conditions))
        NotesCard(Modifier.gridItem(areaId = DashArea.Notes))
    }
}

FlexBox covers the one-dimensional case that Row and Column cannot: items that wrap, grow into spare space, shrink under pressure, start from their own preferred size, change visual order, or align themselves individually. The official container guide lists it as superseding FlowRow and FlowColumn for these jobs. A tag chip strip or a toolbar that collapses gracefully is the textbook fit. I am deliberately not printing a FlexBox sample here: its configuration surface was still moving when I wrote this, so check the reference for the exact artifact version you depend on.

Failure mode: treating Grid like a lazy list

Grid does not lazy-load. Put five hundred items in it and you compose five hundred items. Use it for structure, and keep the lazy containers for data.

Failure mode: a scrolling child in a flexible track

If a LazyColumn sits inside a Grid cell, give its track a minimum of zero and a flexible maximum so the list can shrink and scroll, for example row(GridTrackSize.MinMax(0.dp, 1.fr)). An Auto track sizes to content, which a long list will happily inflate.

Failure mode: fractional tracks with nothing to divide

Flexible (fr) tracks divide available space. If the grid is measured with unbounded height, such as directly inside a vertically scrolling parent, there is nothing to divide. Prefer Auto tracks in that situation, and verify the behavior on your Compose version rather than trusting memory.

5. App-level layout architecture and Navigation 3

Per-screen adaptivity gets you far, but the biggest structural question is navigation. On a compact window, “list then detail” is two destinations on a stack. On an expanded window, it is one screen with two panes. If those are different navigation graphs, you will spend your life keeping them in sync.

Navigation 3 resolves this by keeping the back stack as plain data (your own keys) and delegating presentation to a SceneStrategy. The strategy looks at the entries and decides what to render: one pane, two panes, or something else. Strategies can be chained, and the first one that returns a scene wins.


@Serializable data object ListKey : NavKey
@Serializable data class DetailKey(val siteId: String) : NavKey

@Composable
fun FieldNotesNav(modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
    val backStack = rememberNavBackStack(ListKey)
    val sceneStrategy = rememberListDetailSceneStrategy<NavKey>()

    NavDisplay(
        backStack = backStack,
        modifier = modifier,
        sceneStrategy = sceneStrategy,
        entryProvider = entryProvider {
            entry<ListKey>(
                metadata = ListDetailSceneStrategy.listPane(
                    detailPlaceholder = { Text("Pick a site to see its notes") },
                ),
            ) {
                SiteListScreen(onOpen = { id -> backStack.showDetail(id) })
            }
            entry<DetailKey>(metadata = ListDetailSceneStrategy.detailPane()) { key ->
                SiteDetailScreen(siteId = key.siteId)
            }
        },
    )
}

Failure mode: stacking detail on detail

In a two-pane layout, tapping a different list row should swap the detail pane, not push another entry. Otherwise back has to unwind every row the user touched. One small extension keeps that rule in a single place:

fun MutableList<NavKey>.showDetail(siteId: String) {
    val target = DetailKey(siteId)
    if (lastOrNull() is DetailKey) removeLastOrNull() // replace, do not stack
    if (lastOrNull() != target) add(target)
}

Failure mode: deep links that skip the list

A notification that opens a site directly can leave a back stack of just DetailKey. On a phone, back then exits the app instead of showing the list. When handling an external entry point, seed the stack with ListKey underneath.

Failure mode: keys that carry payloads

Back-stack entries get saved and restored, so keep keys small and serializable: ids, not objects. Load the data in the destination.

6. Agentic development and automation

The session closes its technical section with a demonstration of using Gemini and Android’s skills, including an adaptive skill, to refactor legacy code for larger screens. I am working from the session description rather than reproducing the demo, so treat the following as my own workflow rather than a summary of theirs.

An agent is good at the mechanical part: replacing device checks, hoisting state, converting nested rows into a Grid. It is poor at knowing whether the result still behaves. So the safety net has to exist before the refactor, and the cheapest version is a resize matrix test that renders your screen at several fixed sizes and asserts the structure you expect:

@RunWith(Parameterized::class)
class SitesPaneResizeTest(private val width: Dp, private val expectDetailPane: Boolean) {

    @get:Rule val rule = createComposeRule()

    @Test
    fun showsDetailPaneOnlyWhenWide() {
        rule.setContent {
            Box(Modifier.size(width, 800.dp)) {
                SitesPane(isWide = width >= 600.dp, sites = sampleSites)
            }
        }
        val detail = rule.onAllNodesWithTag("detail_pane")
        if (expectDetailPane) detail.onFirst().assertExists() else detail.assertCountEquals(0)
    }

    companion object {
        @JvmStatic @Parameterized.Parameters
        fun sizes() = listOf(
            arrayOf(360.dp, false),
            arrayOf(600.dp, true),
            arrayOf(900.dp, true),
        )
    }
}

Review agent diffs against the failure list in this post: any new remember inside a conditional, any fresh device-type check, any configChanges addition. Those are the three regressions I would watch for first.

7. The return on investing in adaptive

I will not quote numbers I cannot source. The qualitative argument is strong enough on its own.

  • One layout model serves phones, foldables, tablets, and desktop windows, so a new form factor is a configuration change rather than a project.
  • Whole bug classes disappear: lost drafts, stretched content, stuck back stacks.
  • The test surface becomes explicit. Sizes and postures are inputs you can enumerate.

Takeaways

  1. Start from the window. Remove device-type checks and let size and posture drive layout.
  2. Hoist state above any branch that changes with window size, and put durable state in saveable holders.
  3. Route mediaQuery through one function that returns your own layout model, and use the derived variant for size.
  4. Use Grid for structure and change its config per window; use lazy containers for data.
  5. Keep navigation as plain keys and let a scene strategy decide pane count.
  6. Wrap every experimental API behind a seam you own.
  7. Build the resize test matrix before letting any tool refactor your screens.

title: TIB: Sample-wise Tempered Information Bottleneck for Multimodal Attribution beyond Alignment Assumption
description:
arXiv:2611.12997v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal (e.g. vision-language, in this work) attribution aims to interpret the models without access to ground-truth explanatory supervision. Existing multimodal attribution methods typically rely on paired modalities as proxy supervision, implicitly assuming that image-text pairs are semantically aligned. Information bottleneck (IB)-based attribution methods follow this general paradigm and instantiate it through a global sufficiency-compression objective. In realistic multimodal datasets, however, this assumption is frequently violated due to partial semantic misalignment and unreliable cross-modal correspondences. Through theoretical analysis, we show that, under such misalignment, information-bottleneck-based attribution objectives exhibit a structural limitation: by assuming equal reliability across all proxy supervision signals, they induce posterior over-contraction and forced explanations. To address this issue, we propose TIB, a sample-wise Tempered Information Bottleneck framework that adaptively modulates attribution strength according to cross-modal reliability, without assuming semantic alignment. Extensive experiments on controlled benchmarks and large-scale datasets show the effectiveness of the proposed approach, while also validating the identified failure mode.

title: APS-VLA: Action-Guided and Future-Aware Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
description:
arXiv:2611.13030v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have demonstrated strong generalization in robotic manipulation, yet processing dense visual tokens often incurs high inference latency. Visual token pruning offers a practical way to reduce this cost, but identifying a compact set of tokens that preserves reliable action generation remains challenging. Existing methods largely rely on static or immediate heuristic cues to estimate token importance. We introduce APS-VLA, a framework that learns visual token selection from robot demonstrations while keeping the pretrained VLA backbone frozen. A lightweight Decision Influence Estimator scores tokens conditioned on current visual observations, language instructions, and robot proprioception. Its training combines two complementary signals: action supervision matches both the full-input policy predictions and demonstrated actions, while an auxiliary visual transition objective uses demonstrated actions to predict subsequent visual features from the selected representation. At deployment, the estimator performs a single hard selection and packing step before the policy's native action-generation procedure; the auxiliary predictor is removed. Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO and with $\pi_{0.5}$ and XR-1 on RoboCasa365 demonstrate inference acceleration with modest changes in task success. Across five real-world tasks on two dual-arm platforms, APS-VLA reduces mean policy inference latency from 137.25 to 93.25 ms, achieving a $1.47\times$ speedup with an average success rate of 61%, compared with 60% for the unpruned baseline. Together, these results support APS-VLA as a modular, plug-in framework for efficient robotic control across VLA architectures, preserving the underlying policy parameters and native action-generation procedure.

title: Should you learn Node.js, Django or Laravel first in Nepal?
description:
For most beginners in Nepal, learn Node.js first. JavaScript shows up in Kathmandu job posts for all three stacks, and SQL matters more than whichever framework you pick.

That is our answer, and we should say up front that Saarathi Academy in Old Baneshwor, Kathmandu teaches Node.js in its Backend Engineering course. So check the reasons below yourself. We also say when Django or Laravel is the better first pick.

Why do Laravel jobs in Kathmandu still ask for JavaScript?

Many Kathmandu companies use PHP and Laravel. That is true, and our own course page says so. But look at what those jobs ask for.

A Tekkon Nepal post on merojob for a Full Stack Developer (PHP/Laravel) listed PHP, MySQL, Laravel, Vue.js and CSS. Its requirements also named JavaScript and jQuery. Vue.js is a JavaScript framework.

Laravel itself needs JavaScript tools. The Laravel installation guide says you should install Node and npm, or Bun, to build your app's frontend files. So a Laravel developer uses Node tools on the first day.

The reverse is not true. A Node.js developer never needs PHP. If you learn JavaScript first, it stays useful in whichever job you take. If you learn PHP first and later join a Node team, you start a new language.

What do backend job posts in Nepal ask for in every stack?

We read four Kathmandu backend posts on merojob from 2024 and 2025. Two asked for Laravel and two asked for Node.js.

Every one of them asked for SQL, through MySQL, PostgreSQL or both. A backend post from a financial institution listed Laravel next to MySQL and PostgreSQL. A NodeJS Developer post from Citizen Infotech listed JavaScript, Git, RESTful API, SQL and PostgreSQL. A Node.js and NestJS post from GCG International asked for PostgreSQL and TypeScript.

Three of the four also asked for Git or REST API design. The framework was one line in each post. The rest was the same in every stack: how a request travels, how to design tables, how to write a JOIN, how to work with Git.

The tests look the same too. Mid-sized companies are most of the market here, and they usually start with a written test at their office. The questions are string and array problems by hand, plus SQL joins and normalisation, which means organising database tables well. No framework question decides that round.

So spend more of your first months on SQL than on any framework. Many beginners do the opposite.

When is Django the better first backend?

Pick Django if you already write Python with ease. Maybe you used it in college, or you want to move toward data or AI work later.

Django gives you a lot from the start, including an admin site to add, change and delete data. But the official Django tutorial expects you to know Python already. It uses functions and imports without teaching them. If Python is new to you, you learn two hard things at once, and that is slow.

Don't pick Django because a video called it easy. Pick it because you already know Python.

When is Laravel the better first backend?

Pick Laravel if you already have a job offer, an internship or a family business that runs on PHP. Then the fastest way to useful work is the stack in front of you.

Laravel has clear rules about where each file goes, and its documentation is friendly to beginners. Those are real strengths. They do not change our pick for someone who starts from zero with no employer yet.

Why Node.js for a beginner with no stack yet?

The first reason is one language. The Node.js introduction says frontend developers can write server code "without the need to learn a completely different language". You learn JavaScript once and use it on the server, in the browser, and in the Vue.js part of a Laravel job.

The second reason is a small first step. A Node server can be one short file, built with the node:http module that comes with Node. You see the raw request and response before any framework hides them. Express, Django and Laravel all wrap that same request, so the lesson carries over.

Our course follows this order. JavaScript and TypeScript are taught from zero in Weeks 2 and 3. Your first HTTP server uses Node's built-in http module in Week 3, before any framework. Express comes in Week 4 and NestJS in Week 5. Weeks 6 and 7 are about databases: SQL, PostgreSQL, data modeling, indexes and transactions. MySQL is covered only at awareness level, but the SQL you write carries over to it.

What can you try tonight?

Install the LTS version of Node.js from nodejs.org. Copy the example server from the Node.js introduction page into a file named server.js. Run node server.js and open http://127.0.0.1:3000 in your browser.

Now change res.statusCode = 200 to 404, save, and stop the server with Ctrl+C. Start it again and open your browser's developer tools on the Network tab. Reload and find the 404 there. You will read status codes like this in Node, Django and Laravel alike.

If you want the full order of topics, the Backend Engineering syllabus is public, week by week, and the course page has the rest.

title: Conformal Risk Control for QoT-Aware Lightpath Feasibility Under Technology-Driven Domain Shift
description:
arXiv:2611.13893v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML)-based regression models support operational decision-making in optical networks but typically expose only point predictions, which carry no statistically controlled information about their reliability. This paper proposes a post-hoc conformal risk control (CRC) framework that keeps a pretrained AI/ML regressor fixed, provides a finite-sample guarantee on uncertainty band miscoverage, and maps the band to operational decisions through policy rules. The guarantee applies to interval miscoverage, while decision-error rates are evaluated empirically. We instantiate the framework for quality of transmission (QoT)-aware lightpath (LP) feasibility assessment, in which a regressor predicts optical signal-to-noise ratio (OSNR) under domain shifts caused by fiber, amplifier, and switching upgrades. Feature shift contribution scores identify the LP features whose relation to QoT changes the most across a technology transition, and two policies translate the bands into feasibility decisions, allowing operators to tune the trade-off between conservatively rejecting or aggressively accepting LP realizations. Experiments on open space-division multiplexing (SDM) QoT datasets over the CONUS topology show that, for a target coverage of 90%, the uncertainty bands meet the target in all 170 trials spanning 17 domain shifts and ten calibration-test partitions, whereas a source-only quantile regression (QR) baseline meets it in none. Under severe shifts, the efficiency-oriented (EO) policy empirically improves zero-shot (ZS) feasibility-decision accuracy from about 85% to above 99%, approaching a transfer learning (TL) policy while avoiding retraining. The framework provides finite-sample control of uncertainty band miscoverage for regression-based optical network decision support, with potential applications beyond QoT-aware LP feasibility assessment.

title: RetinexGS: Retinex-Inspired Gaussian Splatting for Low-Light RAW Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2611.13280v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pipelines struggle with severely underexposed images, producing unstable colors, floating artifacts, and incomplete reconstructions in dark regions. To better account for noise in these low-light observations, RAW images offer a natural basis for noise-aware reconstruction by preserving linear sensor measurements and providing access to noise metadata. We present RetinexGS, a RAW-domain 3DGS framework that combines Retinex-inspired appearance modeling with sensor-informed optimization for low-light novel-view synthesis. We factorize each Gaussian's color into a view-independent base color and a shared, position- and view-dependent modulation field, regularizing the two components separately to constrain appearance learning from noisy observations. We use DNG noise metadata to weight the reconstruction loss for signal-dependent noise, while distortion-aware rendering avoids spatially resampling RAW targets. To address sparse geometry in dark regions, we introduce depth-guided initialization. We evaluate RetinexGS on three public RawNeRF scenes and two custom-captured low-light RAW scenes. With all methods trained on the same RAW inputs for each scene, RetinexGS outperforms LE3D and RawNeRF in mean sRGB PSNR by 2.18 dB and 2.71 dB respectively, across the five scenes, while supporting real-time novel-view rendering.

title: AgenteDSH de DeepSeek Harness: mi experiencia migrando una app legacy
description:
tags: deepseek, javascript, java, ai

Durante algún tiempo he usado varias herramientas en mis desarrollos: Pool, Hermes, OpenCode y, de forma ocasional, Claude, OpenAI y DeepSeek. Estas últimas más que todo para verificación, consultas puntuales y, de vez en cuando, para alguna propuesta de desarrollo. En general, la cosa me ha funcionado bastante bien.

El problema

Se presentó la necesidad de migrar una aplicación que tenía. Usaba DWR como API y Tomcat como contenedor. El problema es que DWR ya no está soportado, así que tocaba migrarlo sí o sí.

Mi nuevo stack es Nginx, JavaScript vanilla ES6 y, ocasionalmente, Font Awesome y Bootstrap. La aplicación tiene bastantes archivos. En otras ocasiones he hecho migraciones puntuales o reescrito el código desde cero, pero esta vez eso era complicado.

Después de intentarlo con varias de mis herramientas usuales, me encontré con que se agotaban los tokens y se demoraban una eternidad; es decir, no podía por ese medio.

Plan B: entidad por entidad

Así que me di al dolor y empecé a cambiar los archivos con DeepSeek, entidad por entidad. Muy dispendioso, pero funcionaba.

El principal problema: DeepSeek normal no acepta archivos .rar, .tar, .zip ni ningún tipo de empaquetamiento. Al preguntar por qué, la respuesta fue sencilla:

"Porque DeepSeek no es un sistema operativo ni pretende reemplazarlo".

La sugerencia fue clara: si quieres hacerlo, usa DSH y descarga los plugins que permiten hacerlo.

Lo hice, y me di cuenta de que DSH no es una utilidad de DeepSeek: es un agente, bastante bueno por cierto, que puede intervenir tus archivos de forma local, en un ambiente gráfico.

El resultado fue impresionante. Lo que pensé que me iba a tomar días, semanas incluso, lo hice básicamente en 2 días, con DeepSeek como asistente general para temas gruesos y DSH para afinación y puesta a punto.

¿Qué es DSH?

DeepSeek Harness (DSH) es un agente de código open-source construido sobre el SDK de DeepSeek Harness. Su arquitectura se basa en que "todo es un plugin". No es solo un chat: es un entorno de ejecución que puede leer, escribir y ejecutar comandos en tu máquina, siempre bajo un modelo de permisos (sandbox).

Guía de instalación en Linux

Requisitos previos

  • Node.js ^22.19 o >= 24
  • pnpm (recomendado 11 o superior). DSH lo necesita para gestionar los plugins.

Paso 1: Instalar pnpm 

curl -fsSL https://get.pnpm.io/install.sh | sh -
source ~/.bashrc
pnpm --version

Paso 2: Lanzar DSH

El comando más rápido para empezar:

npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web

Esto descargará y ejecutará DSH, abriendo la interfaz web en http://127.0.0.1:3080.

Si npx da problemas, puedes forzar una versión específica (por ejemplo, la 0.2.2-rc.1 que usamos):

npx @deepseek-ai/dsh@0.2.2-rc.1 web

Paso 3: Configurar la API Key

La primera vez que intentes usar el agente, verás un error como:

llm-deepseek: no API key for provider route "deepseek-official"

Se soluciona de dos formas:

  1. Desde la interfaz web: ve a Settings → Models, pega tu API Key de DeepSeek (sk-...) y guarda.
  2. Desde la terminal: exporta la variable antes de lanzar DSH: 
export DEEPSEEK_API_KEY="sk-tu-clave-aqui"
npx @deepseek-ai/dsh@0.2.2-rc.1 web

Instalando plugins para leer ZIPs

DSH por sí solo no lee ZIPs. Necesitas un plugin. El que usamos fue dsh-dragndrop-attachments, que permite arrastrar un .zip a la interfaz y que el agente liste su contenido y lea archivos internos sin descomprimirlo.

Paso 1: Autorizar la compilación del plugin

Antes de instalar plugins desde GitHub, DSH (a través de pnpm) bloquea los scripts de compilación por seguridad. Hay que autorizarlo en el archivo de configuración del perfil web:

nano ~/.dsh/profiles/web/pnpm-workspace.yaml

Añade (o fusiona) al final:

allowBuilds:
  dsh-dragndrop-attachments: true

Nota: la clave debe ser el nombre exacto del paquete. Si pnpm se queja, revisa el mensaje de error para ver la clave correcta.

Paso 2: Instalar el plugin 

npx @deepseek-ai/dsh@0.2.2-rc.1 plugin --profile web add github:aa2246740/dsh-dragndrop-attachments

Paso 3: Reiniciar DSH

Detén DSH (Ctrl+C en la terminal donde corre) y vuelve a lanzarlo:

npx @deepseek-ai/dsh@0.2.2-rc.1 web

Refresca el navegador (F5). Ahora deberías poder arrastrar un .zip a la ventana del chat y pedirle al agente que liste su contenido.

Alternativa: un gestor de archivos visual

Si prefieres una experiencia más parecida a VS Code (árbol de archivos, editor con resaltado de sintaxis), el plugin @rose43/dsh-file es muy completo:

npx @deepseek-ai/dsh@0.2.2-rc.1 plugin --profile web add @rose43/dsh-file

Reinicia DSH y busca el botón Files en la barra lateral.

Conclusión

DSH ha sido un descubrimiento. No es solo un chat con plugins: es un agente de código que puede intervenir tus archivos localmente, con un sistema de permisos que te da control. Para migraciones grandes, la combinación de DeepSeek (para el análisis grueso) + DSH (para la afinación y la lectura/escritura de archivos) es muy potente.

Si estás en una situación similar, con un legacy que migrar y herramientas que se quedan cortas, vale la pena explorar DSH. La curva de instalación es baja y el retorno es alto.

¿Has usado DSH? ¿Qué plugins te han sido útiles? Cuéntamelo en los comentarios.


`

title: Temporal Behavior Trees for Reinforcement Learning: Specifications as Rewards, Curricula, and Diagnostics
description:
arXiv:2611.13993v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning from formal specifications often separates task definition, reward shaping, curriculum design, and policy diagnostics into different mathematical objects. This fragmentation requires additional conversion steps and discards structure already present in the specification, such as subtask boundaries, ordering constraints, and quantitative measures. We introduce TBTCL (Temporal Behavior Tree Centric Learning), a framework that uses Temporal Behavior Trees (TBTs) as a unified interface for specification-guided reinforcement learning. A single TBT specifies the task, induces dense robustness-based rewards, defines a curriculum, and supports better understanding of learned policies. By adapting TBT syntax and semantics for specification-guided reinforcement learning, we provide a formalism that is more expressive than popular specification languages such as LTL and inherently hierarchical. We present algorithms to automatically extract a curriculum DAG and derive dense, robustness-based rewards directly from TBT semantics. Furthermore, we utilize TBT trace segmentation to build understandable competence profiles and automatically adapt the reward toward bottlenecks. We evaluate TBTCL on six specifications across discrete and continuous domains and show that Temporal Behavior Trees can serve as a specification, a reward, a curriculum, and a diagnostic.

title: Японское ударение в одной цифре: генерируем рисунок тона из словарной записи
description:
Японское ударение в одной цифре: генерируем рисунок тона из словарной записи

Если вы делаете карточки для Anki, словарь или тренажёр японского, рано или поздно захочется показывать ударение. В японском оно тональное: слоги различаются не громкостью, а высотой — высоко (H) или низко (L). Хорошая новость для разработчика: хранить для каждого слова таблицу H/L не нужно. В словарях ударение записывают одним числом, а рисунок из него восстанавливается в несколько строк кода.

Что означает число

Число — это номер моры, после которой тон падает:

  • 0 — хэйбан: тон поднимается после первой моры и не падает, даже на частице после слова;
  • 1 — атамадака: высокая только первая мора;
  • от 2 до n−1 — накадака: тон падает внутри слова;
  • n — одака (n — число мор): тон высокий до конца слова и падает на частице.

Классический пример — три слова «хаси»: 箸 (палочки) — [1], 橋 (мост) — [2], 端 (край) — [0]. Внутри слова 橋 и 端 звучат одинаково, LH, а различаются только тоном частицы: はしが.

Шаг 1: делим слово на моры

Мора — единица японского ритма. Каждый знак каны — одна мора, кроме маленьких ゃ, ゅ, ょ (и катаканных ャ, ュ, ョ, ァ, ィ, ゥ, ェ, ォ): они прилипают к предыдущему знаку. При этом っ, ん и ー — полноценные отдельные моры.

const toMoras = kana => kana.match(/.[ゃゅょャュョァィゥェォ]?/g) ?? [];

toMoras('きょう');   // ['きょ', 'う'] — 2 моры
toMoras('がっこう'); // ['が', 'っ', 'こ', 'う'] — 4 моры

Шаг 2: рисунок по числу 

// accent: 0 — хэйбан, 1 — атамадака, 2…n−1 — накадака, n — одака
function pitchPattern(kana, accent) {
  const moras = toMoras(kana);
  const word = moras.map((_, i) => {
    if (accent === 1) return i === 0 ? 'H' : 'L';
    if (i === 0) return 'L';                       // первая мора низкая
    return accent === 0 || i < accent ? 'H' : 'L'; // высоко до места падения
  });
  return { moras, word: word.join(''), particle: accent === 0 ? 'H' : 'L' };
}

pitchPattern('はし', 1);   // { word: 'HL',  particle: 'L' } — 箸, палочки
pitchPattern('はし', 2);   // { word: 'LH',  particle: 'L' } — 橋, мост
pitchPattern('はし', 0);   // { word: 'LH',  particle: 'H' } — 端, край
pitchPattern('こころ', 2); // { word: 'LHL', particle: 'L' } — 心, сердце

Отсюда уже легко нарисовать линию тона над словом в интерфейсе — так, как это делают словари ударений.

Где брать числа

  • OJAD (Online Japanese Accent Dictionary) — показывает рисунок тона для слов и целых фраз.
  • Словарь ударений NHK — стандарт для токийского произношения.
  • Викисловарь — в японских статьях часто указан номер ударения.

Ограничения

  • Это токийская норма. Кансайское произношение устроено иначе.
  • При спряжении глаголов и в сложных словах ударение смещается — одного числа из словаря для каждой формы недостаточно.
  • В живой речи подъём после первой моры бывает сглажен, особенно если вторая мора — ん, ー или っ.

Для учебного приложения этого обычно хватает: показать рисунок, дать послушать и повторить. Примеры с аудио и тренажёр, где ИИ оценивает произношение, собраны в разделе японское ударение на Japanese Zen.

title: From Counterfactual Edits to Human Narratives: LLM-Driven Interpretations for Recommender System Explanations
description:
arXiv:2611.13914v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recommender systems increasingly influence what users discover and consume online, yet the decision logic behind their outputs often remains opaque. Counterfactual explanation (CFX) methods provide an effective way to show which changes to a user's interaction history would alter a recommendation. In recommendation settings, however, CFXs often require many edits, producing long, low-level lists that are hard for users to interpret. Moreover, most evaluations emphasize edit counts while largely overlooking whether the resulting CFXs are coherent and actionable for users. We argue that this gap between generating valid CFXs and communicating model behavior stems from the lack of user-centered abstraction and limited qualitative evaluation. To bridge this gap, we investigate large language models as mediators that summarize raw CFX interaction edit lists into concise natural language explanations describing higher-level preference patterns. We optimize these mediators for correctness, informativeness, and linguistic quality through preference optimization, and evaluate the resulting explanations with human-calibrated metrics derived from separate human-labeled datasets. On the MovieLens-1M dataset, across multiple counterfactual generators and language models, the resulting summaries achieve high overall linguistic quality, while the strongest semantic results are obtained with high-success CFX methods such as ACCENT and SPINRec. Direct Preference Optimization improves the semantic metrics in almost all evaluated settings.

title: SQLite foreign keys do not create child indexes: inspect a parent deletion plan
description:
Writing REFERENCES parent(id) in SQLite did not automatically create an index on the child's reference column. Referential-integrity checks still worked, but finding children during a parent deletion used a SCAN.

The existence of a foreign key and the access path used to find referencing children need separate checks. This experiment compared index lists and an actual DELETE plan in SQLite 3.53.1.

Enable foreign keys and inspect the index lists

Each condition used a fresh in-memory database through Python's sqlite3 module. The connection enabled autocommit, and foreign_keys was turned ON outside a transaction.

PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
CREATE TABLE parent (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE child (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  parent_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES parent(id)
);

The fixture contains 101 parents and 10000 children. Children reference parents 1 through 100 evenly; parent 101 has no children. Parent 1 therefore has 100 referencing children.

PRAGMA foreign_keys;
PRAGMA index_list(parent);
PRAGMA index_list(child);

With only the foreign key, foreign_keys returned 1, while both parent and child index lists were empty. Inserting a child referencing missing parent 999 and deleting referenced parent 1 both failed with FOREIGN KEY constraint failed.

An absent index did not mean an inactive constraint. The parent's INTEGER PRIMARY KEY also has a rowid access path. An empty index list should not be interpreted as the absence of that access path.

Deleting a parent searches the child table too

These two query plans were collected over the same data:

EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT rowid FROM child WHERE parent_id = 1;
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN DELETE FROM parent WHERE id = 101;

The DELETE targets parent 101, which has no children. Determining that deletion is allowed still requires checking for referencing rows.

Statement Child-side operation with only the foreign key
SELECT rowid FROM child WHERE parent_id = 1 SCAN child
DELETE FROM parent WHERE id = 101 SCAN child

The DELETE plan separately included SEARCH parent USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?). An efficient parent-key lookup did not automatically supply an access path for the child's reference column.

The SQLite foreign-key documentation explains the child lookup involved in parent deletion and why child indexes are useful even though they are not required. The recorded DELETE plan exposed that child-side operation.

Add an explicit child index

A separate comparison database used the same schema and data, plus this index:

CREATE INDEX child_parent_idx ON child(parent_id);
Check Foreign key only With child index
Number of child indexes 0 1
Child SELECT SCAN child SEARCH child USING COVERING INDEX child_parent_idx (parent_id=?)
Child lookup inside parent DELETE SCAN child SEARCH child USING COVERING INDEX child_parent_idx (parent_id=?)
DELETE referenced parent 1 Constraint violation Constraint violation
INSERT referencing a missing parent Constraint violation Constraint violation
DELETE unreferenced parent 101 Success Success

The index changed the plan used to find children. It did not change which INSERTs and DELETEs were allowed.

This comparison did not measure execution time. A change from SCAN to SEARCH does not establish a speedup ratio. Index maintenance during writes and selectivity in real data also need separate evaluation before adoption.

Do not confuse a parent's automatic index with a child index

Another condition declared the parent as code TEXT UNIQUE and the child as code TEXT REFERENCES parent(code). The parent gained sqlite_autoindex_parent_1, with index origin u; the child's index list remained empty. An index created for the parent's UNIQUE constraint is not an index on the child's foreign-key column.

A final condition retained the child index but turned foreign_keys OFF. It allowed an orphan row to be inserted. PRAGMA foreign_key_check then reported that one violation. Check the connection's foreign_keys setting separately from its index list.

The tests ran on September 11, 2026, with Python 3.14.5, SQLite 3.53.1, in-memory databases, and synthetic data. The reproduction code and four-condition results are available. No remote D1 database or ORM migration was run.

The official EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN documentation states that its output format can change between versions. The strings here are records from the tested version. In another environment, inspect the connection's enforcement setting, the child's index list, and the target DELETE plan together.

title: Parsing a whole PDF in one request with Unlimited OCR 2: the crop_mode setting and a silent cut
description:
The usual PDF pipeline is a loop: split the file, run OCR (optical character recognition, turning page images into text) on each page, concatenate the strings. When a table starts on one page and ends on another, every later page returns a headless fragment, and your code cannot tell they belong together.

Unlimited OCR 2, a document parser Baidu's team released under the MIT license, drops the loop: you send the whole PDF in one request. We served it on one RTX 4090 with the 59-page IRS employer's tax guide, where one table spans pages 46 to 52. It worked once we flipped one setting. One failed run raised no error. The full test of Unlimited OCR 2 on the 59-page tax guide has every table, flag and timing.

The setting that decides the result: crop_mode

By default the model sees each page twice over: one overview image plus a grid of zoomed-in tiles, meant to help with small print. Set crop_mode=false and it gets the overview alone.

For this guide, the overview alone won on speed and accuracy:

59 pages, one request, RTX 4090 Tiles (default) crop_mode=false
Whole document 6 min 45 s 3 min 44 s
Distance to the PDF's own text 38.1% 4.2%

The errors are not spread evenly. Drop pages 46 to 54 and both modes sit near 2.4% on ordinary prose. The table did the damage. With tiles on, page 46 came back with eight rows crammed into one cell, followed by "Taxable if wages subject to social security tax and Medicare tax" written 1,508 times. Only the per-page cap of 20,000 tokens stopped it (a token is a word piece, the unit a model reads and writes). Pages 47, 50 and 52 were blank. The authors' anti-repetition guard was on, and resending pages 46 to 54 alone looped again.

With long tables, start with tiles off and spot-check the figures on the table pages.

The trap: a context limit that truncates instead of failing

Baidu ships the model with its own patched build of SGLang, an open source inference server (the program that loads the weights and answers HTTP requests). By default it reads in windows of 10 pages, freeing memory for pages that leave the window. A switch turns windowing off so the model sees all 59 pages together. The context, meaning everything the model can hold at once, is 131,072 tokens, and the page images alone used about 89,000 of it. Output ended halfway through page 27, and the server only wrote this to its log:

Requested token count (89331 input + 472000 new) exceeds the model's
context length (131072 tokens). Truncating max_new_tokens.

The cause is the --allow-auto-truncate server flag. From the client side the stream simply finishes. Your only defence is to count pages in the output, which is cheap because every page opens with a <PAGE> tag. Assert on it in every mode.

One window with crop_mode=false might fit (an 18,277-token prompt); untested.

What to measure, and how to get a free reference

A born-digital PDF grades its own OCR: the embedded text layer, the selectable text you can copy out, is an exact answer key. Our score was the share of characters you would need to edit to turn the model's text into that layer, so 0% is a perfect match. Two caveats. It punishes reading order, so a sidebar placed before its paragraph loses points with every word correct. And it needs a text layer, which scans lack; we tested no scans.

Why run a model when the text is already in the file? The layer has no reading order, no block positions, no HTML tables and no markers across page breaks. Those come from the model, and they need their own checks. Each run flagged 31 to 34 paragraphs as continuing on the next page. The big table still arrived as seven per-page pieces, but five of its six joins carried an append_table tag; the page 49 join was untagged. We never merged the pieces, so stitching is your code and your test.

Sizing the GPU: read the share, not the peak

SGLang reserves a fixed fraction of whatever GPU it lands on (70% unless told otherwise) and fills it with working memory. So the 19.4 GB peak on the 4090 measures that reservation, not the model's needs. A real 16 GB RTX 2000 Ada, a 70-watt workstation card, parsed the full guide with tiles off at a 13.8 GB peak and 5.6 pages per minute, 4.23% off the text layer, the same quality as the bigger card.

Scope: one 59-page English document, one request at a time. Baidu aims at hundreds of pages; its 100 to 300-page benchmark is its claim, not our measurement.

Credit

The model and paper are the work of Baidu's ERNIE team. Shu Wei, Jingjing Wu and Qunyi Xie are the core contributors, with Lingshu Zhang, Xiangcheng Du, Yannian Fu, Mengjie Wang, Zuyi Wang, Zhichao Liu, Yangliu Xu, Youyang Yin, Huanhuan Liu, YY and Yi Yang as contributors. It builds on their first Unlimited OCR and on DeepSeek-OCR, so the DeepSeek-OCR team shares the credit. The server is the SGLang project's, patched by Baidu and shipped in the Unlimited OCR 2 model card repository. We spotted it in the AI Search channel's 1 November news video, then wrapped that server in an API and checked what it returned on a real document.

The write-up with the VRAM ladder, server flags and the two open rough edges links an SDK example for your own NVIDIA card.

To compare your numbers with ours, start from the Unlimited OCR 2 whole-document parsing results on inferencekey.com.

title: CP-MLPs: A Tensor-Rank Theory of Tied and Untied MLP Blocks
description:
arXiv:2611.13647v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Transformer feed-forward blocks combine several design choices: squared activations, gating, and tied versus untied parameter sharing, whose separate contributions to expressivity remain poorly understood. We introduce CP-MLPs, a tensor framework in which each multiplicative unit contributes a rank-1 interaction with three roles: detecting an input feature, reading a value, and writing to the output. Tied gated blocks such as ReLU$^2$ force the detector and value roles to share the same direction; untied gated blocks such as ReGLU and SwiGLU let them differ. We show that this distinction yields exact, degree-wise tensor-rank separations: untied detector-value units are strictly more width-efficient for indefinite quadratic interactions and role-asymmetric monomials, while tied units are structurally matched to symmetric pure-power targets. The width advantage of untying therefore depends on the target structure. Experiments show loss plateaus below the exact-representation width, but these plateaus alone do not establish a positive approximation gap: arbitrarily accurate approximation is governed by border rank. In trained gated MLPs, untied blocks retain an advantage in selected comparisons at matched input-projection budget. Code is available at https://github.com/rarefin/CP-MLPs.

title: I got tired of babysitting Playwright, so I turned it into a small render API
description:
Every small product I ship ends up needing one of two things: an Open Graph image, or a PDF of some HTML I already have.

Self-hosting Playwright or Puppeteer works. It also:

  • creeps up in memory until the box runs out
  • leaves Chrome hanging when a page never finishes loading
  • captures a GDPR banner over the thing you actually wanted
  • turns a weekend feature into an ops job

So I put it behind one endpoint, and it's now live as FrameForge: HTML or a URL in, PNG, JPEG or PDF out.

The request 

curl -X POST https://95-217-220-34.sslip.io/render \
  -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"html":"<!doctype html><h1>Invoice 1042</h1>","format":"pdf"}' \
  -o invoice.pdf

Swap html for url, or pdf for png / jpeg. width and height go up to 3840 and fullPage captures the whole page.

Design choices I made on purpose

  • One browser, a new context per request. Sharing tabs is how cookies and memory leaks spread between jobs. Each render gets a clean context that is closed afterwards.
  • Hard timeouts. 20 seconds to navigate, 30 for the whole render. A hung page must not hold one of only two slots.
  • Cap concurrency at 2 on a 2 vCPU / 4 GB box. Chromium contexts aren't free. A queue of 8 is better than an OOM kill.
  • Cache by hash. The request body is SHA-256 hashed. An identical request is served from disk in well under a second, which makes retries fast.
  • Hide banners with CSS rather than clicking "Accept". Clicking consent on other people's sites is messy and fragile. Hiding the common OneTrust / Cookiebot / Quantcast / generic cookie nodes covers most cases. It's best effort, and shadow-DOM banners still get through.
  • Treat every URL as hostile. Private and link-local addresses are refused, and the check runs again on every redirect and every subresource the page loads, so the renderer can't be used to probe internal networks.

What it runs on

Node, Playwright 1.56, Docker and Caddy for HTTPS on a single Hetzner CPX22 in Helsinki. The box costs about €17 a month, so one Starter customer pays for it.

Trying it

  • Free trial: 100 renders over 14 days. Email service+frameforge@rightemp.co.uk and I'll send you a key.
  • Starter £9/month for 3,000 renders, Studio £29/month for 20,000.
  • Founding Member: £49 once for 12 months of Studio, limited to the first 100 people.
  • 30-day refund on all of them.

Details and checkout: https://frameforge-efg.pages.dev (disclosure: this is my project).

What I'm still unsure about

Is a 100-render trial enough, or does an API like this need a permanent free tier? And is banner hiding a must-have or a nice-to-have for you?

If you've run Chrome in production, I'd like to hear what broke first.

title: Word-Level Alignment of OCR and Ground Truth under Zoning and Reading-Order Errors
description:
arXiv:2611.13752v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: OCR post-processing needs OCR text aligned word by word with its ground truth. Data sets rarely provide that mapping, and a monotone aligner can lose its place when zoning errors permute the reading order. We revisit this problem, the Zoning Problem of our 2019 paper, with a protocol that tests correctness under such permutations. We apply OCR-side reading-order permutations with construction-time word-level gold and score correct-match F1, cascade length and recovery. We compare the 2019 location-aware aligner, a re-anchoring extension of it, a RETAS-style baseline (RETAS-lite), a multi-region aligner that combines unique-word and unique n-gram anchors with chunk-to-window assignment, genalog's RETAS and the original Java RETAS. Experiments use synthetic character noise with block moves, paragraph swaps and column interleaving, historical newspaper reading-order permutations, geometry-derived gold for Tesseract OCR, and a small word-box set. Synthetic tests show where local tracking fails after large displacements and where unique-anchor methods collapse when unique anchors are scarce. On our synthetic boilerplate page the 2019 method had the highest F1 among those tested. Historical newspaper and geometry-derived evaluations carry the limitations of approximate gold and the article-order convention. The first multi-region version has a quadratic scaling cost. Local tracking remains fragile under large reading-order changes; the tested anchor-based methods handle many of those cases but fail when unique anchors are scarce. Approximate gold, the article-order convention, missing residual annotation, and the lack of modern multi-column word-level ground truth remain limitations.

title: Dê ao Haiku as regras de UX e um checador, não só o pedido
description:
Versão simples do estudo "Haiku com kit de UX". Para o método completo e todos os números, leia o artigo técnico. Aqui está o que ele significa para quem quer usar isso amanhã.

Em uma frase

Quando o Haiku (o modelo pequeno) recebe regras de UX com fonte aberta e um código simples que confere a tela, ele cria e melhora telas de login no nível do Sonnet (o modelo maior) sem ajuda, por cerca de 10% do custo por tarefa. Em comparar duas telas, o código não ajudou. E não conseguimos medir estética de forma confiável sem uma pessoa.

O que a gente fez

Escolhemos uma tela pequena, a de login, e criamos três tarefas: criar a tela do zero, melhorar uma tela com defeitos escondidos e comparar duas telas lendo o código. Para ajudar o Haiku, montamos:

  • um data lake de 30 regras (contraste, rótulo nos campos, tamanho de botão, link de recuperar senha e outras), todas tiradas de fontes abertas (WCAG, web.dev, Material Design), nenhuma de cabeça;
  • um checador de código pequeno, sem navegador, que lê o HTML e o CSS, diz quais regras falham e lista as diferenças reais entre duas telas.

Rodamos 2.244 tarefas com Haiku e Sonnet, cada uma 3 vezes, sem nenhuma falha no final. Antes de rodar, escrevemos as hipóteses e os critérios.

O que a gente descobriu

1. As regras no prompt já mudam muito. Ao criar uma tela, o Haiku sozinho cumpriu 74% das regras; com as regras no prompt, 99%. Ao melhorar uma tela com defeitos, de 75% para 89% só com regras, e para 97% com o relatório do checador.

2. O checador ajuda a melhorar e a criar, e mais o modelo pequeno. O ganho foi maior no Haiku que no Sonnet em criar e em melhorar. O Sonnet sozinho já melhora bem uma tela (94%) e até piorou quando recebeu só as regras (81%).

3. O conjunto custa um décimo. Em média por tarefa, o Haiku com regras e checador custou US$ 0,0022 e o Sonnet sozinho US$ 0,0210, com acurácia do Haiku 1,07 vez a do Sonnet.

4. Uma ferramenta independente confirmou em parte. Passamos as telas criadas pelo axe-core, um verificador de acessibilidade que o checador e os prompts não conhecem: as violações caíram de 0,50 por tela (Haiku sozinho) para 0,03 (com regras e checador).

5. Comparar duas telas não precisou de ajuda. Com o código das duas telas, Haiku e Sonnet já acertam cerca de 93%, e o relatório do checador piorou um pouco (para cerca de 90%), principalmente em mudanças de CSS. Nenhum dos dois inventou diferença onde não havia.

O que as hipóteses queriam dizer

Antes de rodar, fixamos hipóteses e quanto de resultado bastaria. Das comparações confirmatórias, 7 de 12 passaram na correção de múltiplos testes:

  • Criar e melhorar com regras e checador: sim, bem acima da linha de base.
  • O checador ajuda mais o Haiku que o Sonnet: sim em criar e em melhorar; não em comparar.
  • O checador vale mais que só uma segunda passada de autocrítica (criar): sim pelas nossas regras, mas o axe-core não viu essa diferença.
  • O checador reduz alarme falso ao comparar: não deu para testar, porque ninguém errou nesses pares.
  • O critério principal (Haiku com o conjunto chega a 90% do Sonnet por até metade do custo): suportada, mas só contra o Sonnet. O Opus ficou fora do estudo por custo.

O que não funcionou, e o que fica de cuidado

  • Estética: nenhum instrumento sem humano passou na validação. Testamos um modelo treinado em notas de design (UIClip), um conjunto de medidas por código e um juiz Fable em pares contra testes A/B reais. O Fable acertou 55,6% (precisávamos de 60%) e mudou de resposta ao trocar a ordem das telas em 4 de cada 10 vezes. Por isso, este estudo não diz nada sobre beleza.

  • A régua é a das regras. Criar e melhorar são pontuados pelas mesmas 30 regras que ajudamos o modelo a cumprir. O axe-core ameniza isso em criar, mas não em melhorar. Leia como "o Haiku cumpre as regras dadas", não como "o Haiku faz bom UX".
  • Uma tela só, telas geradas por script, sem Opus, sem navegador real no checador. Não sabemos se vale para telas reais.

A receita

  1. Escolha uma tela pequena e liste as regras que importam, só de fontes abertas (WCAG, guias oficiais), nunca de cabeça.
  2. Ponha as regras no prompt do modelo pequeno. Só isso já resolve boa parte de criar.
  3. Escreva um checador mínimo (ler HTML e CSS basta para muitas regras) e entregue o relatório ao modelo, pedindo correções em trechos.
  4. Meça com uma ferramenta que o modelo e o checador não conhecem, como o axe-core, e desconfie de pontuar com as mesmas regras que você entregou.
  5. Não meça estética sem uma pessoa. Se não tiver um designer, diga que não mediu.

Todo o código, os estímulos e os dados brutos estão no repositório do estudo, para você conferir ou repetir.

Os experimentos, os dados e as conclusões são meus. A redação foi assistida por IA e revisada por mim.
