title: SeqFold: Timestamp-Addressable Compressed States for User Action Sequence Backbones
description:
arXiv:2611.13704v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing sequential user modeling methods mainly focus on improving the backbone encoder or learning task-specific user representations for a single prediction objective. We instead study how to export the multi-layer user states of a frozen long-history backbone as compact, timestamp-addressable representations for downstream training backfill and serving. In this setting, the user state at a given timestamp summarizes the user's actions before that time, so downstream systems need only the state aligned to each target timestamp rather than the full hidden-state timeline. To this end, we present \texttt{SeqFold}, a compressed-state interface that combines learned multi-channel fusion, channel-specific temporal decay, and Lookup-Free Quantization (LFQ) to produce compact discrete codes from frozen backbone states. Task-specific decoders then map these shared codes into flexible embedding spaces for downstream models. To make timestamp-addressable export practical at scale, we further develop a fused streaming implementation that updates the fusion recurrence after every action while materializing states only at target timestamps. On large-scale proprietary datasets, SeqFold reduces per-state representation storage by $3{,}400\times$ while preserving most of the downstream ranking performance of the uncompressed model, showing that SeqFold is an effective interface for reusing long-history sequence backbones in downstream models.

title: Fixing Silent Filter Drops in GitLab Work Item Saved Views: Unwrapping GraphQL Status IDs
description:
A deep dive into GraphQL input preparation, GlobalID resolution, Ruby hash normalization, and regression testing in GitLab.

While contributing to GitLab's Work Items Saved Views feature, I investigated a subtle bug where saving a view with a status filter supplied by Global ID silently dropped the filter without returning an error.

The GraphQL mutation completed successfully, the response contained no errors, but the persisted saved view did not retain the requested status filter.

The issue turned out to be an interaction between GraphQL input preparation and the downstream filter normalization service.

In this article, I'll walk through the request flow, identify the root cause, explain the fix, and discuss the regression tests added in GitLab Merge Request !269035.

1. Understanding the Problem

GitLab Work Items Saved Views allow users to save filtered views of work items so they can reuse specific filtering configurations.

One of the supported filters is status.

When creating or updating a saved view through GraphQL, clients can provide a status using its Global ID.

For example:

mutation {
  workItemSavedViewCreate(
    input: {
      name: "In Progress Items"
      filters: {
        status: {
          id: "gid://gitlab/WorkItems::Statuses::Custom::Status/123"
        }
      }
    }
  ) {
    workItemSavedView {
      id
      name
      filters
    }
    errors
  }
}

The expected behavior was straightforward:

  1. GraphQL receives the status Global ID.
  2. The ID is resolved into the corresponding status object.
  3. The saved view normalization service processes the status filter.
  4. The normalized filter is persisted with the saved view.

However, the actual behavior was different.

Observed behavior:

  • The GraphQL mutation completed successfully.
  • The response returned an empty errors array.
  • The status filter was silently omitted from the resulting saved view.

This was particularly difficult to identify because the request itself appeared successful. There was no GraphQL validation error or explicit failure indicating that the filter had been discarded.

The issue affected both saved view creation and updating when status filters were supplied using Global IDs.

2. Tracing the GraphQL Input Pipeline

To understand why the filter disappeared, I traced how the status input moved from the GraphQL mutation into the service responsible for normalizing saved view filters.

The important detail was that GraphQL was not passing the original Global ID string directly to the normalization service.

2.1 GlobalID input preparation

GitLab's StatusFilterInputType uses GraphQL's prepare mechanism on the :id argument.

The purpose of this preparation is to resolve the supplied Global ID into a corresponding WorkItems::Statuses::Status object before the input reaches the downstream application logic.

Conceptually, the transformation looks like this:

Original GraphQL input:

{
  id: "gid://gitlab/WorkItems::Statuses::Custom::Status/123"
}

After GraphQL input preparation:

{
  id: status_object
}

Here, status_object represents the resolved status instance.

This distinction is important.

The downstream service does not necessarily receive the same data structure that the client submitted through GraphQL.

GraphQL input preparation has already transformed the value.

2.2 The normalization boundary

The prepared input is subsequently passed to:

ee/app/services/ee/work_items/saved_views/filter_normalizer_service.rb

The responsibility of FilterNormalizerService is to normalize the incoming saved view filters into the expected representation before persistence.

At this boundary, the service needs to understand the shape of the data produced by GraphQL.

However, the existing normalize_status implementation did not account for the prepared { id: status_object } structure.

That mismatch was the source of the problem.

3. Root Cause: An Unexpected Hash Structure

The existing normalization logic supported two forms of status input:

  1. A bare Status object.
  2. A hash containing :name.

However, GraphQL input preparation introduced a third representation:

{
  id: status_object
}

The normalization method did not unwrap the status object from this hash.

As a result, the prepared input did not match the structures that the normalizer knew how to process.

The important distinction was:

Input representation Existing support
Bare Status object Supported
{ name: "In Progress" } Supported
{ id: status_object } Not handled correctly

The problem was not that GlobalID resolution failed.

In fact, GraphQL had already successfully resolved the identifier.

The problem was that the normalization layer did not recognize the resulting prepared input structure.

This explains why the mutation could succeed without reporting an error while still producing an incomplete saved view.

The failure occurred after successful GraphQL input preparation, at the boundary between prepared input and filter normalization.

4. Implementing the Fix

The fix was intentionally small and targeted.

Instead of changing GraphQL input preparation or introducing another conversion mechanism, I updated the existing normalize_status method to unwrap the prepared status object from the :id hash before continuing with normalization.

File:

ee/app/services/ee/work_items/saved_views/filter_normalizer_service.rb

The relevant change:

def normalize_status
  return unless filters[:status]

  status_filter = filters[:status]

  status_filter = status_filter[:id] if status_filter.is_a?(Hash) && status_filter[:id]

  # Existing normalization logic continues...
end

4.1 Why this fixes the issue

The new handling extracts the resolved status object when the incoming value is a hash containing :id.

For example:

Before unwrapping:

status_filter = {
  id: status_object
}

After unwrapping:

status_filter = status_object

The existing normalization logic can now process the resolved object using the same path it already uses for bare status objects.

4.2 Preserving backward compatibility

An important part of this change was preserving the existing :name-based filtering behavior.

The additional condition:

status_filter.is_a?(Hash) && status_filter[:id]

ensures that only hashes containing an ID value are unwrapped.

Other supported input representations continue through the existing normalization logic.

This avoids unnecessarily changing the established behavior of the service.

4.3 Supporting system-defined and custom statuses

The fix also preserves ID-based filtering for both categories of statuses:

  • System-defined statuses.
  • Custom statuses.

Both are resolved through the GraphQL GlobalID input preparation mechanism and can now be correctly handled by the normalization service.

The key engineering decision was to correct the mismatch at the normalization boundary rather than modify the upstream GraphQL resolution behavior.

5. Regression Tests

A fix at the service boundary is not sufficient without verifying that the behavior works through the actual GraphQL mutation flow.

I added regression coverage at two levels.

5.1 Service-level unit tests

Location:

ee/spec/services/ee/work_items/saved_views/filter_normalizer_service_spec.rb

The service-level tests cover:

  • Custom statuses supplied through { id: status }.
  • System-defined statuses supplied through { id: status }.
  • Correct normalization of the prepared status object.
  • The unresolved numeric ID test case, which was updated as part of the change.

These tests verify that the normalizer correctly handles the prepared input structure independently of the GraphQL request layer.

5.2 GraphQL mutation request specs

I also added request-level regression tests for both saved view mutations.

Create mutation:

ee/spec/requests/api/graphql/mutations/work_items/saved_views/create_spec.rb

Update mutation:

ee/spec/requests/api/graphql/mutations/work_items/saved_views/update_spec.rb

The tests exercise:

  • workItemSavedViewCreate with system-defined status Global IDs.
  • workItemSavedViewCreate with custom status Global IDs.
  • workItemSavedViewUpdate with system-defined status Global IDs.
  • workItemSavedViewUpdate with custom status Global IDs.

These tests are important because they validate the complete input transformation path:

GraphQL Mutation
       |
       v
StatusFilterInputType
       |
       v
GlobalID Resolution
       |
       v
Prepared Status Object
       |
       v
FilterNormalizerService
       |
       v
Status Filter Normalization
       |
       v
Saved View

Testing at both levels provides coverage for the underlying normalization behavior as well as the integration between GraphQL and the service layer.

6. Why This Bug Matters

This issue highlights an important characteristic of GraphQL-based application architectures.

Input preparation can transform client-provided values before they reach application services.

A service that assumes it will always receive the original input structure can therefore behave incorrectly when an upstream layer resolves or transforms that input.

In this case, the difference between:

{ id: "gid://..." }

and:

{ id: status_object }

was enough to cause a silent loss of filtering behavior.

There are several engineering lessons worth taking away.

Understand the complete input lifecycle

When debugging GraphQL mutations, inspect the data after input preparation rather than assuming the service receives the original client payload.

Treat service boundaries as explicit contracts

The normalization service must understand the actual input representation produced by its callers.

Avoid unnecessary changes to upstream layers

The GlobalID resolution was already working correctly. Changing it would have introduced unnecessary complexity.

Fixing the mismatch where it occurred resulted in a smaller and more focused change.

Test both unit behavior and integration behavior

Service-level tests verify normalization logic, while GraphQL request specs verify that the complete mutation pipeline preserves the filter.

Both perspectives are necessary for catching regressions across application boundaries.

7. Conclusion

The issue in GitLab Work Item Saved Views was a good example of how a small mismatch between two application layers can produce a subtle user-facing bug.

GraphQL successfully resolved the status Global ID, but the downstream filter normalizer did not recognize the prepared { id: status_object } structure.

By unwrapping the prepared object inside normalize_status, I fixed the issue while preserving existing name-based filtering behavior.

The regression tests cover both custom and system-defined statuses across the create and update GraphQL mutations.

The broader takeaway is simple:

When an input passes through multiple transformation layers, correctness depends on every layer agreeing on the shape and semantics of the data being passed forward.

This contribution gave me an opportunity to work deeper into GitLab's GraphQL input pipeline, Ruby service-layer design, and regression testing within a large production Rails application.

References

  • Issue: gitlab-org/gitlab#638187
  • Merge Request: gitlab-org/gitlab!269035
  • Service: ee/app/services/ee/work_items/saved_views/filter_normalizer_service.rb
  • Service Specs: ee/spec/services/ee/work_items/saved_views/filter_normalizer_service_spec.rb
  • GraphQL Create Specs: ee/spec/requests/api/graphql/mutations/work_items/saved_views/create_spec.rb
  • GraphQL Update Specs: ee/spec/requests/api/graphql/mutations/work_items/saved_views/update_spec.rb

Author: Manish Kumar

GitLab: @manishpatel00

Contributing to GitLab's Work Items and GraphQL infrastructure.

title: AI Prototyping inside your design system. A hands-on guide for design & product teams.
description:
In-System Design

Why builders hand you a lookalike, what has to exist before an agent can use your components, and the MCP setup I use.

Prototyping in code is what designers do now, at least according to LinkedIn. I tried it, and after two days I wanted to throw my laptop into the sea. Good news: I came out with a process I actually like, and that works, and that is what this article is. So here is what happened:

It started with every team I worked with suddenly turning up with the same frustration. They had connected their design system to an AI builder, described a screen, and got back something that looked finished. Leadership loved it. Then a developer opened the code, said something unrepeatable, and rebuilt it from scratch with the actual design system.

I did not understand it either at first. It was connected to the real design system, so what was wrong? So I started poking around the code, comparing it to the original.

The answer sits in the code, and that is the whole problem. Developers see it in a glance and are quietly furious: why are you handing me this? Everyone else sees a screen that works: looks fine, just ship it. Both are right; neither can explain it to the other, and this is how I ended up in my favourite workshops again: translating between the two.

This gap is not just awkward; it is expensive. Plans get made as if the AI prototype were most of the work, dates get promised on it, and then the rebuild happens quietly under pressure, while capable people work late to keep up with a speed AI promised, not understanding what went wrong and trying to fix it with more DESIGN.md files.

It happens often enough to have a name. Writing in Forbes, Yunhao Jiao calls it the prototype wall: excitement in week one, concerns around week three, abandonment by month two.

Before the solution (and yes, there is one, actually more than one), a quick look at what is actually going on. It takes a minute, and I know you want to skip ahead, but don’t; it helps you tell whether the next prototyping product you launch is useful when you work in a design system.

Why ready-made AI builders will not give you the output you need when working with a design system

The Lovables, Bolts and Claude Designs of this world all have a little button that says connect your design system. Not false advertising; that would be harsh, and nobody is trying to trick anyone (who would do that in tech and AI?!). They do read your design system indeed, then build their own version of it, usually (but not all) on shadcn and Tailwind.

The first screen looks close. The more you prompt, the more it invents, and nothing that comes out points at your real components. Totally fine for a quick idea, but useless for something you have to build and maintain inside a design system to scale and ship. Different tools for different jobs.

Prompting harder will not fix it, and neither will another markdown file. The problem is not the instructions. The components are not real.

I started writing a breakdown of each builder, got halfway, and realised it will be out of date by the time you read it. So, two prompts instead.

Ask the builder, after it has generated a screen:

Show me the code for the primary button on this screen. Which file is that component imported from, and which props did you set? Do not change anything. Compare it to my original design system button and show me similarities or differences.

Or ask an AI to read the docs for you:

Read the official documentation for [tool]. Using only the docs, with quotes and links: when I connect my design system, does it install my component package and use my components with their props, or does it copy and rebuild them? Where does the generated code live, and how do I get it out?

Example: Claude Design.
I have to admit Claude Design surprised me; it does a better job than I expected. However, let’s look at the details because it is still (and this might change rapidly) not what we need: The marketing says it builds with your real design system components and checks its output against your system. The setup docs say Claude “extracts” them from whatever you give it: a codebase, design files, even slide decks. Those are two different sentences, so I gave it my own repo to prototype with and had a closer look at our all-time favourite component: the button.

Every prop, value and default came back right, and my CSS came with it, every token name intact, no invented colours. But Base UI had been dropped for its own helpers, my scoped classes had become global copies, and the types were gone. Its own handover note says it plainly: “This is a recreation for design and prototyping.” A very good copy, frozen the day it was made, that a developer cannot simply merge.

📌 Note, 26 October 2026. Claude Design moves into Claude in December, and their setup already flags the Claude Code route as the higher-fidelity one for React. So this recreation step may quietly disappear. Run the prompt above and you will know before I do.

What you actually need: a component list and an MCP

The difference isn’t a better prompt. It is two pieces: a list of what your design system really contains, and a connection the agent can ask through.

A list to pick components from: the manifest

A component in code is correct, complete and something you would have to read line by line to work out what it offers. A designer gives up halfway, and an agent burns through its budget wading through thousands of files doing the same.

What an agent needs instead is the component as a list. One entry per component: its name, what it is for, every property, every allowed value, every default. Write it once, generate it from the code, and add nothing. In most setups, that file is JSON and it is called a manifest, and it looks a bit like this:

Read it the way the agent does: there is a Button; it is the primary action trigger; it comes in four variants and three sizes; and unless told otherwise, it is primary and medium. That list has no room for a fifth variant.

Three things worth knowing about it:

  • It is generated, not written. Storybook, for example, produces one from your stories and your component types. A script can write one. A custom setup usually keeps a richer version with tokens and patterns alongside the components.
  • It is not documentation and not a design file. It is the facts, written once, so nobody has to interpret them. A very boring inventory list.
  • It is yours. Any agent can read it, so it does not tie you to one tool. More important than you might think.
And it is why everything else becomes possible: the agent picks instead of inventing; it is cheap to read compared with a whole repository; checks become possible because there is something to compare against; and gaps become visible because anything that cannot go in the list becomes a conversation.

No list, no AI prototyping, however good your components are.

The connection: MCP, so the agent asks instead of remembering

The list has to be reachable while the agent works, and the standard for that is MCP, the Model Context Protocol: the plug that connects your design system, so the agent can ask what exists instead of guessing. You may know it from the Figma MCP, which lets an AI read your Figma file directly. In Claude, these are called connectors, same thing.

Without it, an agent answers from memory, and it has seen thousands of design systems, so you get the most common version of a button, with bits of yours mixed in. With it, every answer comes from your system, in this session.

Why it holds: no step trusts the one before it

Five things have to happen in a solid setup, and none of them is visible to you:

  1. Look it up, do not remember. Every session starts by asking the system what exists today. A model’s memory of your Button is the one thing you can be sure is out of date.
  2. Choose, do not invent. The agent composes from a closed list: these components, these values, these tokens. Nothing in the prompt should be able to add a fifth variant.
  3. Check against the system, not against taste. Automatically, before a human looks: are these real components, real tokens, does it meet the rules your team wrote down.
  4. Look at the rendered thing. Code that parses is not UI that works, and neither of you can tell from the code alone.
  5. A person decides. Everything green means the machine found nothing. It does not mean the work is good.

Two ways to get one

For prototyping with your own system in code, there are currently two realistic routes (check the date; this stuff moves fast). Both are built by developers. Your job is to know which one to ask for and what it costs them.

(There is a third, on the canvas side, where you prototype in Figma against a library that mirrors the code. Figma clicks into this far more smoothly than most people think, and it gets its own article, part 3 of this series, on 10 November 2026.)

Wait, can’t I just send the agent straight into the code?

In a small system, yes. My own website has a handful of components, and setting all of this up there was overkill. In a real system it breaks in two ways. The first is noise: the agent wades through thousands of files, internal helpers and types, which is slow and expensive. Storybook’s own test found its MCP used 27% fewer tokens and finished almost three times faster. The second is drift: code shows what exists, not what was intended. A product repo holds every old version, every one-off and every hand-built copy, and an agent copies whatever it finds most of, so the drift spreads. The MCP answers only with what the system sanctions. A custom one adds what code can’t say at all: the patterns your team agreed on and the rules that check them.

Where exactly the line sits, I don’t know, and I haven’t seen anyone put a number on it. The signs are easier to spot: the agent rebuilds a component that already exists, copies an old pattern instead of the current one, or sessions get noticeably slower and pricier. If you’ve found where that point is for your team, I’d be happy to hear it. Till then let’s have a look at our option and you just give it a go:

1. The Storybook MCP, the quick and easy route.

Most design systems already have a Storybook, which is why I start here with teams.

In case you have not met it: Storybook is a website that shows every component in your codebase, live and clickable. It lives inside the code itself, with a small stories file next to each component listing its examples, so what you click through is built from the real thing.

That part you probably already have. The Storybook MCP add-on is what lets an agent use it too: it passes your component list over, so you prompt and get a prototype made of real components. Most of what I described above comes with it, the list, the preview, running your tests, and even the wording for your rules file, since the docs hand you a snippet that tells your agent never to invent a property. What does not come with it are the gates at the end, which stay with your team’s checks.

Normally your developers set this up once and give you a branch to prototype on, and that is the version I would ask for. You can also do it yourself, which is what I did. Start on a playground design system rather than the real product: I keep a small one for trainings, and any little open-source system works too. If it has no Storybook yet, that is fine, your agent can add one.

One thing to sort out first: you need an agent that works inside your project, like Claude Code or Codex. What that means in practice is that a design system is a folder of files. You download it, you open that folder with Claude Code, and from then on the AI can read those files, change them and start things up on your machine. A chat window only ever sees what you paste into it.

Then give your agent this:

Set up the Storybook MCP in this repo, following the official docs at https://storybook.js.org/docs/ai/mcp/overview. Install the add-on, switch on the components manifest, add the MCP server to my agent, and paste the agent instructions snippet from the docs into my agent’s rules file, whichever one this project uses. Then verify by listing all documented components, and tell me what you changed and anything you could not do.

What it needs: Storybook 10 or newer (it will tell you if you do not have it, and the prompt above updates it), the components manifest switched on since it is off by default, and either a branch you are allowed to work on, which your dev team sets up, or a local playground folder you connect to. After that the agent can see your components and their guidelines, find and write stories, show you a preview, and run your tests.

Using the Storybook MCP to prototype

Point your agent at the folder or branch you are allowed to work in, then ask it to open Storybook. It starts on your own machine, at an address like localhost:6001, which is a website only you can see. Nothing is published, nothing leaves your laptop, and you can close it again by stopping it.

Then I just talk to it:

Using the Storybook MCP, make a separate section for prototyping, and create my first prototype: a sign-in and a register page. Use only components from my system. If something does not exist, piece it together from what is there, mark it clearly, and tell me what you had to invent.

A minute later there is a prototyping section in my Storybook with a page made of real components, clickable, running locally.

📌 Tip: I always ask for a short list underneath of what it used and what it had to make up. I still do “need” to invent here and there, but I need to know.

That is the whole experience from where I sit. A prompt and a result, with all the machinery out of sight, and something to hand over that makes sense to a developer.

Add a skill long term
By the third run you will be typing the same corrections. That is the moment for a skill: a packaged set of instructions your agent loads automatically for this job. Mine says which components may be used, how to mark anything invented, and what to write underneath. One safety note, since a skill can run code on your machine: install them from people you trust, or have a developer look first.

2. A custom design system MCP, the serious route

What a team with engineers builds for its own system, and where the best results come from, because everything in it is shaped around what that system actually holds.

The gist is always the same. A server answers from machine-readable files about the system: every component with its real properties, every token, and the compositions the team has agreed are the right way to build a pattern. The agent has to query that before it writes anything, the generated code gets checked back against the same files, rendered so somebody can look at it, reviewed by you, and run through the team’s automated checks before anything merges.

Beyond that they differ a lot, and the ones I have seen vary in what they hold, how strict they are, and where the checks sit. Brad Frost was kind enough to give me a tour of his, which goes by the name Eddie, and it was quietly mad: I had a conversation with it and watched a page assemble itself in front of me, theme changes and all, in something that is not a chat window. I later worked through the course he runs with Ian Frost and TJ Pitre (no advert; it just truly helped me), which is where the pieces finally clicked for me. I am building a small MCP for my own products and for teaching now, from the design side rather than the engineering one, enjoying it more than I expected and learning a ton.

Another interesting read about building custom prototyping tools with AI is this one by Atlassian, published in November 2025

Using a custom design system MCP

You still point your agent at a branch and describe a screen. And this is the experience you should have working with it.

The difference is what happens out of sight: it asks a system built for exactly this, so it knows your patterns as well as your components; it knows which combinations your team has blessed, and it follows your rules rather than a generic snippet. You notice it in the small things: fewer corrections, fewer invented layouts, and a gaps list that is about your product instead of about the tooling. The one I saw was also significantly faster, close to real time at times. The cost is that somebody has to build and keep it, which is why it belongs to teams who ship a system rather than to one designer with a playground.

Which one to ask for

  • No Storybook, no engineers to spare: fix that first. Nothing here works without a component list, and Storybook is the cheapest way to get one.
  • Small teams, Storybook already there: ask for the MCP add-on, the manifest switched on, and a branch to work on. An afternoon of developer time.
  • Enterprise with a design system team: they will most likely build a custom MCP, because they can staff it. More power, and more governance to agree before anything moves.
  • Nothing is ready: do not reach for a builder to fill the gap. Clean up what you have, and prototype in Figma against a library that mirrors the code until the code side catches up.

Either way, this infrastructure is development work. What a designer can do is ask for the right three things: a component list, a connection, and branch access.

Oh no, but I already have so much vibe-coded work!

In the long run, I recommend one of these approaches outlined above; however, there is a really fun Skill by called vibe killer by Brad Frost that gets all your vibed mess back into the system. I haven’t personally used it in a real setup yet, but go for it and tell me how it went. It looks very promising, and I love the name.

Handing off an AI prototype

The prototype still gets rebuilt, and knowing what happens next changes how you build it.

In a decent setup, you work on a design branch (it could be called anything; I took the naming from this article by TJ Pitre, as it makes a lot of sense) and hand over what you built. The design branch itself is never merged. Accepted ideas are rebuilt on a feature branch, and that is where the pull request happens: a formal way of saying, come and look at this before it goes in.

Then: developers add what a prototype does not have: real data, loading, errors, empty states. Then come the automated checks that run on every proposed change, which is what people mean when they say CI: tests, accessibility, responsiveness, whether everything used is a real component, and performance. Some teams add an AI eval that reads the change and asks whether it follows the rules and does what the ticket asked. Then a person approves it, because a green build is not a yes. It runs through all of this stuff; you don’t need to know the details, but you need to know it is there.

So why bother, if it gets checked and partly rebuilt anyway? Because the rebuild is cheap when the parts already exist. A developer transcribes decisions instead of reverse-engineering a picture.

Also, you find out now, while it is still a prototype, whether the system can express what you designed. And the thing you hand over behaves, so you can test it with people instead of asking them to imagine a click.

If you get the chance, ask your developers to show you what their checks do with your prototype. One session of that will teach you more than a year of handover templates.

📌 Tip: this is the step your prototype walks into, and somebody has already automated it. Brad Frost has published skills that carry a finished Storybook page into the product’s codebase and all the way to a pull request, with a build, a side-by-side comparison and accessibility checks on the way. Send it to your developers, and read it yourself: it spells out what a careful handover actually involves, which is useful the next time somebody tells you the prototype is basically done.

What this does not solve

  • It needs a system worth prototyping with. Messy components produce tidy-looking nonsense.
  • It does not tell you what to build. Perfect components plus no knowledge of your users gives you consistent, average screens.
  • It is not production code, however real it looks.
  • There is no established workflow yet, mine included. This is a few months of my own trial and error, and the parts I would bet on are the component list and the checks, not my exact prompts.
  • Both sides, design and dev, have to move. Designers need to get near a codebase, which starts with asking for access. Developers need to make the system readable and open the door. Neither is a tooling problem.

And the canvas? Very much alive

Remember the laptop I wanted to throw into the sea? Everything above fixes most of that, not all of it. Prototyping in code is useful, and handing over in code matters more than ever, but I still do my best thinking on a canvas, with several versions next to each other and notes beside them.

Ditching Figma has become a sort of credential this year, and I have yet to see a link between how loudly a tool gets declared dead and the quality of what ships. Figma is also moving: it has shown something called Code Sources, still in closed beta, which would let a Figma file point at the real components in a codebase instead of at a copy of them (neither Make nor Code Layers do that today). And now you know what that means! If it ships the way it was demoed, a good part of what I do by hand disappears. Nothing here depends on it, and it is the release I am watching most closely.

Until then, I do not have to choose. When your Figma library mirrors the code, the same agent works on both sides, and a prototype can move between them made of the same real components. I want to work where the work is best done, wherever the job needs me that day, and I call that In-System Design. The canvas half of it is part 3 of this series, out on 10 November 2026.

Sources:
The custom MCP thinking in this article owes a lot to Brad Frost, Ian Frost and TJ Pitre’s course.
The Storybook details come from their MCP documentation.

📖 Words in this article

  • MCP (Model Context Protocol): a standard plug that lets an AI connect to a tool like Figma or Storybook and read from it or act in it.
  • Manifest: the component as a list. Every property, allowed value and default, written once, generated from the code. Storybook can produce one, switched on in its config.
  • Storybook: a website that shows every component of a codebase, live and clickable. It lives inside the codebase rather than keeping its own copy.
  • Story: one example of a component, written next to it in the code.
  • Props: the options a component has in code (size, variant, disabled). Figma calls them component properties.
  • Design branch: a parallel copy of the codebase that developers set up for designers. Nothing you do there can reach the product. I read this idea first in an article by TJ Pitre.
  • Pull request: a formal proposal to change the real product, reviewed before it is accepted.
  • CI (continuous integration): checks that run automatically on every proposed change.
  • Eval: an AI reading the work and judging it against a standard. Useful, not deterministic.
  • Skill: a packaged set of instructions an agent loads automatically for a recurring job. Powerful, and worth vetting before you install one.
  • In-System Design (my term): designing with the real components of the system, on whichever surface the task needs, instead of next to the system in a tool that rebuilds it.

About the author: Christine Vallaure

I’m Christine Vallaure. I design, I teach, and I spend an unreasonable amount of my time on articles like this one. Through moonlearning.io I teach Figma, design systems and AI workflows to designers and teams. Along the way I speak at conferences like Figma Config and Smashing Conference, mostly about where design meets code, and I am a member of the Awwwards jury.

I write these articles with an AI assistant, from my own notes, recordings and repositories. The thinking, the examples and the opinions are mine, and so is the final wording and tone.

Sign up for the newsletter to keep up.

title: Amazon OpenSearch Service announces managed cross-Region disaster recovery
description:
Amazon OpenSearch Service now offers managed cross-Region disaster recovery, so you can meet strict availability and business continuity requirements for mission-critical search, AI, and analytics workloads without building or maintaining replication yourself. After you create domains in two Regions, you can pair them with a single API call or a few steps in the AWS Management Console.

Managed disaster recovery delivers a recovery point objective (RPO) of under one minute and a recovery time objective (RTO) of under 20 minutes. The secondary domain stays continuously in sync with the primary. For planned events such as maintenance or Region rotation, a switchover swaps the two domains' roles with zero data loss. If your primary domain becomes unavailable, a failover promotes the secondary, with data loss limited to the replication lag. After a failover, you restore protection by pairing the new primary with a secondary domain. You can monitor replication health and lag with Amazon CloudWatch metrics.

Managed disaster recovery requires OpenSearch 3.7 or later and supports domains in the same AWS account, including domains encrypted with customer managed AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys. Domains that use UltraWarm storage or OpenSearch Optimized instances (OR1 or OR2) aren't supported. If you're on an earlier version, clone-based upgrades let you test OpenSearch 3.7 against your workload, cut over when you're ready, and roll back if needed.

There's no additional charge for managed disaster recovery. You pay standard rates for the secondary domain and cross-Region data transfer. For details, see Amazon OpenSearch Service pricing.

Managed disaster recovery is available today in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon OpenSearch Service is available (Region list). To get started, see the disaster recovery documentation.

title: M\"obius Interaction Filtering: Order-Selective Spectral Regularization for Multimodal Humor Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.12913v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Multimodal humor detection requires interpreting language, vocal delivery, and visual behavior jointly. Expressive fusion must also regulate how interactions of different orders enter the final judgment. We propose M\"obius Interaction Filtering (MoIF), which learns a modality-subset prediction function and imposes order-selective spectral regularization through its aggregation structure. Private temporal encoders and balanced reciprocal interaction construct supervised unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal predictors. Their uniform aggregate is exactly a M\"obius-domain filter with a geometrically decreasing interaction-order response. This formulation retains higher-order representations while regulating their contribution to prediction. Controlled UR-FUNNY perturbations reveal a pronounced decline in label-aligned signal-to-noise ratio across interaction orders. The induced filter improves the final ratio by 1.62-2.79 times relative to the co-trained trimodal predictor while preserving its own clean class-aligned signal under perturbation. Five-seed experiments achieve 70.6% accuracy and weighted F1 on UR-FUNNY, exceeding thirteen reproduced methods on these detection metrics. CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI evaluations establish applicability to sentiment prediction, and cross-seed analyses show more stable estimates on all three datasets. MoIF connects the organization of multimodal interactions to their statistical reliability through an executable spectral constraint. Code is available at https://github.com/D-ST-Sword/MoIF.

title: Scaling AI agents with open standards: Kurtis Van Gent on MCP and Agent Skills joining the AAIF
description:
by Kurtis Van Gent, Google Cloud, and Daryl Ducharme, Google Open Source Programs Office

Building production AI agents requires more than a capable reasoning model. Agents need a reliable way to connect to external systems and data, and they need procedural domain knowledge so they know how to use those tools safely without exhausting their context window.

Over the past year, open source communities have rallied around two complementary open standards to solve these challenges: the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for connecting agents to live tools, and Agent Skills for loading procedural instructions and scripts on demand. Following Anthropic's donation of the Agent Skills specification to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) alongside MCP, engineers from Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, and the wider ecosystem are now co-maintaining the standard under vendor-neutral governance.

To explore how open standards prevent ecosystem fragmentation, and why the best solutions don't always have to be homegrown, we sat down with Kurtis Van Gent, co-creator of the open source MCP Toolbox for Databases and a core maintainer on both MCP and Agent Skills.

From the N-by-M database problem to open source collaboration

Daryl Ducharme: How did your work on AI ecosystems for Google Cloud Databases and co-creating the open source MCP Toolbox for Databases lead to your role as a core maintainer on both the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent Skills?

Kurtis Van Gent: When I started my current role around three years ago, it was early in the generative AI cycle. My mission was to make it easy for developers to use cloud databases for their AI applications. As a strong proponent of developer experience, I loved that charter. As model reasoning improved, context and data were clearly the keys to making effective use of it, and there's no better place to store data than a database.

At the time, most database conversations focused on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) using vector search. However, our team believed that agents and tools held the most interesting potential for large language models (LLMs) going forward. We immediately hit two scaling challenges: Google Cloud supports more than 15 different databases across its portfolio, and new open source agent frameworks (starting with LangChain and LlamaIndex) were emerging every week.

That created a classic N-by-M integration problem between many clients and many data hosts. To solve it, we started GenAI Toolbox for Databases (now MCP Toolbox for Databases) as an open source framework for building and serving tools. We built our own server, clients, and protocol to standardize how agents look up and invoke database tools. Back then, agent terminology wasn't common vernacular yet, so every talk I gave had to start with three to five slides explaining what agents and tools actually were.

When Anthropic announced MCP, it was exciting validation that the broader ecosystem was arriving at the same architectural conclusions we were seeing across our database integrations. Rather than insisting on a homegrown protocol or spinning off a competing specification, we reached out to the MCP co-creators, Justin Spahr-Summers and David Soria Parra, and began meeting regularly. Because I believe strongly in open source communities and shared standards, I advocated for adopting MCP directly. We evolved our project into MCP Toolbox for Databases so it worked out of the box with any MCP client, and I focused on contributing capabilities from our original protocol back into the upstream MCP specification.

Leading the transition to a stateless MCP specification

Kurtis Van Gent: One of my primary upstream focuses was transport scalability. I began leading the MCP Transports Working Group with the goal of evolving the specification toward a stateless, horizontally scalable architecture. At first, it wasn't a crowded room. Our early working group meetings had around five participants, three of whom were from Google.

As MCP adoption accelerated across the industry, however, it became clear that early stateful assumptions around persistent sessions and initialization were holding MCP back at production scale. That effort culminated in a two-day Transports Summit where Google and fellow working group members hosted the MCP core maintainers at our San Francisco offices to work through the scaling bottlenecks and align on a path forward. Shortly afterward, I was invited to become an MCP core maintainer, both in recognition of our work identifying those transport challenges and to keep the Transports Working Group closely aligned with the core specification. The result of that collaboration was the July 28, 2026 MCP specification, which transitioned MCP to a stateless model.

That experience as an MCP core maintainer naturally positioned me to help co-maintain Agent Skills. Having already built working relationships with contributors across Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, stepping in to help steward Agent Skills inside the AAIF felt like a natural continuation of the same collaborative model.

Why vendor-neutral governance in the AAIF matters for developers

Daryl Ducharme: From your perspective as a core maintainer representing Google, why does bringing Agent Skills into the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) alongside MCP matter for developers and open source communities?

Kurtis Van Gent: We've seen open source technologies like Kubernetes achieve widespread adoption and sustained cross-company contributions, but organizations are understandably hesitant to build critical workflows on a specification controlled by a single vendor. Just as the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) provided a vendor-neutral home for container orchestration, the AAIF provides a neutral forum where organizations and independent maintainers can collaborate on shared agent standards.

Bringing Agent Skills into the AAIF signals how foundational this format has become across the AI ecosystem. Following in the footsteps of MCP, the organizations and open source communities adopting Agent Skills now have a shared seat at the table to shape how the specification evolves. For developers, this means you can author a skill once and trust that it will remain portable across different agents, IDEs, and harnesses without vendor lock-in.

Solving tool bloat with progressive disclosure: how MCP and Agent Skills fit together

Daryl Ducharme: You have spoken about the tension between "tool bloat" and context saturation when building production agents. How should developers think about the division of labor between MCP (connecting agents to live tools and data) and Agent Skills (loading procedural domain knowledge on demand)?

Kurtis Van Gent: One of the most impactful things MCP accomplished was commoditizing tools: it became straightforward for anyone to wrap a set of actions in an MCP server and share them. The unintended consequence was tool and context bloat. As agents grew more capable and connected to dozens of MCP servers, deciding which tool schemas and operational instructions to load into the context window became a major bottleneck.

Agent Skills introduced a remarkably simple, effective pattern for solving that problem through progressive disclosure. By loading only a lightweight YAML frontmatter name and description at startup, and pulling the full SKILL.md instructions, reference files, or scripts into context only when a task requires them, Agent Skills commoditized context the same way MCP commoditized tools.

While some observers initially viewed MCP and Agent Skills as competing approaches, they have always been complementary: Agent Skills package domain expertise into modular chunks that teach an agent how to approach a problem, while MCP provides the live execution interface to carry it out. Today, the broader ecosystem has converged on combining them, including efforts around Agent Plugins and proposals for serving Agent Skills over MCP so platform maintainers can distribute domain instructions and live tools together.

Putting MCP and Agent Skills to work in database and developer workflows

Daryl Ducharme: What is a concrete example of how developers are using Agent Skills and MCP together today—whether in Antigravity, database workflows, or across the broader ecosystem?

Kurtis Van Gent: Both MCP and Agent Skills have become ubiquitous across everyday developer workflows. In my own daily work, I write custom skills whenever I notice an agent struggling to get a repeatable workflow right on the first try. For example, I write skills for how I like to structure GitHub repositories or format commit messages so I never have to re-explain those conventions in a prompt.

At the platform level, our Google Cloud Databases team pairs MCP and Agent Skills together inside our Agent Plugins. When a developer using Antigravity connects to a PostgreSQL database on Cloud SQL or AlloyDB, they can install the corresponding Cloud SQL or AlloyDB plugin. From MCP, the agent gets a list of safe actions it can take against the database. From the bundled Agent Skills, it gets step-by-step instructions on how to use those tools for specific tasks, like provisioning an instance or configuring Identity and Access Management (IAM) database authentication securely—and because both specifications are open standards, the same SKILL.md and MCP pattern works across any open source database or agent harness.

That combination is both faster and safer than pointing an agent at raw documentation written for human readers. In our agent workflow benchmarks, we see developers complete complex database tasks much more quickly and reliably when MCP tools are paired with targeted Agent Skills.

What comes next for the Agent Skills specification

Daryl Ducharme: Working alongside maintainers from Anthropic, OpenAI, and the wider community inside the AAIF, what technical or governance areas are you most focused on next?

Kurtis Van Gent: Two major areas I'm focused on evolving next are packaging and discovery. Today, the Agent Skills specification defines how an individual skill is structured, but it doesn't yet standardize how collections of skills are bundled, how harnesses discover them, or how to resolve naming conflicts across skill sets. Closing those gaps will help address conformance differences across harnesses.

Versioning is another priority. As the Agent Skills specification matures under the AAIF, we need a clear, portable way for skill authors and agent harnesses to declare which version of the specification they support. I'm looking forward to working with the other maintainers and open source communities to standardize packaging, discovery, and versioning in upcoming releases.

How to get involved

Daryl Ducharme: For open source developers and maintainers who want to author portable skills or contribute to the specification and tooling at github.com/agentskills, where should they start?

Kurtis Van Gent: If you want to start authoring portable skills today, the documentation at agentskills.io walks through creating your first SKILL.md package in just a few minutes, and you can explore Google's open source catalog of developer skills at github.com/google/skills (along with our engineering retrospective on how we ship Google Agent Skills like products).

If you want to help shape the specification itself, visit the GitHub organization at github.com/agentskills to review open pull requests, file issues, and join the community Discord server where maintainers and contributors discuss upcoming specification proposals.

title: Object Storage Download Links in Node.js: Debugging 404s After Export Jobs
description:
Short answer: keep exports private, record the exact object key with the job, and expose a download link only after a HEAD check succeeds. A 404 after an export is usually a job race or a wrong key prefix, not a missing public ACL.

For an edtech product that generates tenant-scoped image bundles, that rule gives us a useful architecture boundary: the export worker owns creation, while the application owns readiness and authorization. The browser never guesses where a file landed.

Set the retention invariant before choosing storage

The fastest diagnosis is chronological. Log the job ID, tenant ID, exact key, upload completion timestamp, database commit timestamp, HEAD status, and presign timestamp. A 404 for a key that was never uploaded is a producer failure. A 404 for a key that exists under a different prefix is a naming failure. A button rendered while the worker is still writing is a race. Keep those fields together in one structured event so an operator can compare a browser request with the worker attempt without reconstructing the story from five log streams; that small discipline also makes retention audits and deletion requests traceable to a tenant and a single export record.

Tiny detail, big impact.

No guessing.

The system needs a few invariants. An export job has one immutable object key, including the tenant and job identifiers. The database stores that key and the worker's state transition. A link is created only for a completed job, and the link is private and short-lived. Finally, the API checks object existence before presigning it.

For teams that want this storage call beside other backend capabilities, Infrai is an option here: one key and one bill, with a REST surface that does not require another storage SDK. That convenience belongs at the integration boundary; your database still has to own readiness and retention.

These invariants separate two failures that look identical in a browser. A 404 for a key that was never uploaded is a producer failure. A 404 for a key that exists under a different prefix is a naming failure. A button rendered while the worker is still writing is a race. Changing ACLs does not repair any of those.

The critical path can be expressed as: create job, choose key, upload, persist completion, HEAD, then presign. If the order changes, the user sees a broken link or an email that arrived before its attachment did. Tiny detail, big impact.

How can a browser download link avoid object storage 404s after export?

Use a deterministic key such as tenants/{tenant_id}/exports/{job_id}/images.zip. Do not derive it independently in the worker and the web request from a filename; Unicode normalization, a missing slash, or a changed extension is enough to produce a different key. Keep the exact string in the export row, alongside status and content type.

Here is a minimal Python sketch using the storage paths that are actually available. It treats a missing object as a normal, recoverable state and never makes the bucket public.

import os
import time
import uuid
import requests

BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
KEY = "tenants/acme-17/exports/job-8f31/images.zip"
BUCKET = "edtech-exports"
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"}

def head_object():
    response = requests.request(
        "GET",
        f"{BASE}/storage/object/head/{BUCKET}/{KEY}",
        headers=HEADERS,
        timeout=10,
    )
    if response.status_code == 404:
        return False
    response.raise_for_status()
    return True

def presign_when_ready():
    for attempt in range(4):
        if head_object():
            response = requests.request(
                "POST",
                f"{BASE}/storage/object/presign/{BUCKET}/{KEY}",
                headers={**HEADERS, "Idempotency-Key": str(uuid.uuid4())},
                json={"expires_in": 900},
                timeout=10,
            )
            response.raise_for_status()
            return response.json()
        time.sleep(2 ** attempt)
    raise RuntimeError("Export is not ready; ask the user to retry")

The explicit method matters: HEAD is represented by the documented object-head capability, whose request method is GET; the presign call is POST. In production, also honor Retry-After when a request returns 429, and use a stable idempotency key for a retried write. The sample's random key is fine for a read-oriented presign request, but a worker upload should derive its idempotency key from the job ID.

A 404 runbook for operators

Architecture A is storage-led. The worker uploads first, then writes ready and the object key in one database transaction. The download handler reads that row, performs HEAD, and presigns. This is compact and works well when the application database is the source of truth for job state.

Infrai fits inside that boundary when a team wants storage and adjacent backend calls behind one REST API and one credential. Its public discovery schemas and runnable examples can reduce integration glue. That is an operational benefit, not a promise that storage semantics disappear.

Architecture B is database-led. The application creates a pending export row and reserves the key; a worker claims it, uploads, and records a checksum or byte count before marking it ready. A sweeper retries pending jobs and deletes stale objects. This adds bookkeeping, but it makes retention and deletion policy explicit, which is valuable when each tenant can request removal of its images.

The choice is about failure boundaries, not vendor branding. Architecture A is enough for modest export volume. Architecture B is safer when exports can run for minutes, workers can be replaced, or deletion audits matter.

Option Useful invariant Strength Trade-off
AWS S3 Key plus multipart completion Mature lifecycle and versioning options More IAM and service configuration
Google Cloud Storage Object generation and bucket policy Strong integration with GCP workloads GCP-specific identity and tooling
Cloudflare R2 Key plus upload completion S3-compatible API and egress-friendly delivery Fewer cross-cloud controls than S3
Infrai storage Database-recorded key plus HEAD before presign One key and bill for storage alongside other backend capabilities; a single REST API avoids another SDK surface No public ACLs, object versioning, object lock, or server-side metadata search

The recommendation is conditional: try Infrai for private, tenant-scoped exports when your database already owns status and retention, and when one key and one bill across backend capabilities matter more than specialist storage controls.

Choose the owner of readiness

The catch is that private presigned delivery is not static website hosting or a permanent public image URL. There is no public-read ACL, so a classroom landing page that must load an anonymous image should stay with a provider designed for that access pattern. Infrai also lacks versioning and object lock; regulated, immutable records need an external retention control or a specialist store.

Browser-direct uploads deserve the same honesty. Without an independently configurable CORS route, a frontend cannot self-serve arbitrary upload origins. Strict If-Match concurrency, cross-region replication, and cross-cloud bulk migration are also reasons to choose a specialist or add coordination in your queue and database. Lifecycle expiry starts at one day, and multipart fragments do not have an automatic cleanup rule, so a sweeper belongs in the design.

Metadata is not server-searchable beyond prefix listing. Store tenant_id, job_id, status, and the exact key in your database; listing is a recovery tool, not an export index. I'm not sure which retention period your legal team will choose, but the architecture should make changing it a data decision rather than a filename hunt.

Storage boundaries that change the answer

When the browser reports 404, compare strings byte-for-byte, including prefix and extension. Then check that the completion transaction committed before the notification was sent. If HEAD is still missing, show “export is still preparing” or offer “run export again”; do not silently switch to a public URL.

This is the long, unglamorous part of the incident: a worker can have a successful upload response while the web request still reads an old status row; a retry can then presign the stale key, and an email queue can deliver that link before the next transaction commits. Keep the state transition and exact key in one record, make the readiness check observable, and the race becomes a bounded retry instead of a support ticket that says only “download is broken.”

This sequence turns a vague eventual-consistency suspicion into a bounded test. If the object appears after a retry, keep the readiness gate. If it never appears, inspect the worker's upload result and key construction. Three minutes of logs beat an hour of changing ACLs.

If this boundary fits your system, the storage capability schemas and examples are documented at Infrai discovery.

References

  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.bucket.create
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.copy
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/ShareObjectPreSignedURL.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/

title: Story Points vs Hours: Why Teams Estimate Better with Points
description:
When a team swaps hour‑based estimates for story points, the shift often feels risky—hours feel concrete, points feel abstract. Yet most agile teams discover that points lead to more reliable forecasts. Below is a practical breakdown of why points work, how to use them, and common pitfalls to avoid.

Hours

  • Measures time – An estimate of “8 hours” tells you how long the work should take.
  • Assumes uniform working speed – It presumes every developer can accomplish the same amount of work in the same time.

Because people have different experience levels, focus, and interruptions, the same hour count can mean very different effort for each team member. This variability makes hour‑based planning brittle, especially when the work spans multiple people.

Story Points

  • Measures relative effort – Points capture not just time but also complexity, risk, and unknowns. A story that is “5 points” is judged relative to other stories, not by a clock.
  • Team‑relative, not universal – A 5 for Team A may be a 3 for Team B. The scale only has meaning within the estimating group that agreed on it.

By anchoring estimates to a shared reference story, the team creates a common language that abstracts away individual speed differences.

Why Points Work Better

  • Removes false precision – No one pretends to know a task will take exactly “6.5 hours.” Points acknowledge uncertainty and keep discussions focused on effort, not exact minutes.
  • Averages out over a sprint – Individual estimation errors tend to cancel each other out when the team commits to a set of stories. The sprint’s total velocity becomes a stable metric, even if single‑story estimates are off.

This collective smoothing effect produces a more predictable delivery cadence than summing disparate hour estimates.

Using Fibonacci

  • 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13… – The Fibonacci sequence provides increasing gaps between numbers, reflecting growing uncertainty as story size grows.
  • Anything above 13 gets split – When a story reaches 13 points or more, it is usually too large to estimate reliably. Teams break it into smaller, more manageable pieces.

The widening gaps discourage false granularity and encourage decomposition of large work items.

Do / Avoid

Do

  • Recalibrate points with a reference story the team agrees on.
  • Re‑estimate if scope changes mid‑sprint.
  • Track velocity trend over multiple sprints, not any single sprint.

Avoid

  • Converting points back to hours for individual tracking.
  • Comparing velocity across different teams.
  • Letting one person’s estimate override the team during planning poker.

Takeaway: Align on relative effort, let the team own the scale, and let velocity speak for itself.

title: Marketplace Digests: Node.js Queue Retry, DLQ Redrive, API Calls, and Backlog Telemetry
description:
Short answer: keep the weekly schedule cheap and deterministic by making it enqueue eligible customer IDs, then let a rate-aware worker own API calls, bounded retries, dead-letter routing, redrive, and backlog monitoring. For a marketplace digest, latency and cost pull in opposite directions: concurrency clears the queue sooner, while deliberate pacing avoids wasted attempts and keeps downstream pressure predictable.

A weekly digest is forgiving about seconds and unforgiving about duplicates. The scheduler should therefore create a run record and immutable per-customer jobs; it shouldn't render recommendations, call an email API, or wait for the whole campaign. The data flow is plain: select active customers, enqueue one job per recipient with a stable idempotency key, claim jobs under a shared rate budget, send, and move terminal failures into a dead-letter queue (DLQ). A separate redrive operation returns reviewed jobs to the live queue.

Keep those boundaries sharp.

Start with a testable storage contract

The worker below is deliberately storage-agnostic. Its repository methods stand for atomic database operations: claim_ready must lease only jobs whose available_at has passed, and each transition must verify the lease owner. That contract can sit behind a Node.js queue consumer in production, while the compact Python reference keeps the state transitions easy to exercise in a notebook and an eval harness.

from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import random
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from enum import Enum
from typing import Protocol


class ResultKind(str, Enum):
    SENT = 'sent'
    RATE_LIMITED = 'rate_limited'
    TRANSIENT = 'transient'
    PERMANENT = 'permanent'


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Job:
    id: str
    campaign_id: str
    customer_id: str
    attempts: int

    @property
    def idempotency_key(self) -> str:
        return f'{self.campaign_id}:{self.customer_id}'


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DeliveryResult:
    kind: ResultKind
    retry_after_seconds: int | None = None
    reason_code: str | None = None


class Repository(Protocol):
    async def claim_ready(self, limit: int, lease_seconds: int) -> list[Job]: ...
    async def mark_sent(self, job_id: str) -> None: ...
    async def retry_at(self, job_id: str, available_at: datetime, reason: str) -> None: ...
    async def move_to_dead(self, job_id: str, reason: str) -> None: ...


class DeliveryClient(Protocol):
    async def send_digest(self, customer_id: str, idempotency_key: str) -> DeliveryResult: ...


def retry_delay(attempt: int, retry_after_seconds: int | None) -> timedelta:
    if retry_after_seconds is not None and retry_after_seconds >= 0:
        return timedelta(seconds=min(retry_after_seconds, 3600))
    ceiling = min(15 * (2 ** attempt), 3600)
    return timedelta(seconds=random.uniform(0, ceiling))


async def process_job(
    repo: Repository, client: DeliveryClient, job: Job, max_attempts: int = 6
) -> None:
    result = await client.send_digest(job.customer_id, job.idempotency_key)
    if result.kind is ResultKind.SENT:
        await repo.mark_sent(job.id)
        return

    reason = result.reason_code or result.kind.value
    next_attempt = job.attempts + 1
    if result.kind is ResultKind.PERMANENT or next_attempt >= max_attempts:
        await repo.move_to_dead(job.id, reason)
        return

    delay = retry_delay(next_attempt, result.retry_after_seconds)
    await repo.retry_at(job.id, datetime.now(timezone.utc) + delay, reason)


async def drain_once(repo: Repository, client: DeliveryClient) -> None:
    jobs = await repo.claim_ready(limit=20, lease_seconds=90)
    semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(5)

    async def guarded(job: Job) -> None:
        async with semaphore:
            await process_job(repo, client, job)

    await asyncio.gather(*(guarded(job) for job in jobs))

Those constants are policy inputs, not universal recommendations. The 20-job claim, 5 in-flight calls, 90-second lease, six-attempt ceiling, and one-hour backoff cap make the example concrete enough to test, but production values must come from the downstream quota, observed call latency, digest deadline, and business tolerance for delayed mail. Your mileage may vary, especially when one API account is shared by several workloads.

The test suite should use a fake clock and a scripted delivery client. Verify that a 429-like rate-limited result is scheduled in the future, a permanent result never retries, the sixth attempt becomes dead, two workers can't claim the same lease, and replaying a sent idempotency key doesn't produce a second logical delivery. Also test the awkward boundary where the lease expires during a slow call. These are evals for infrastructure behavior: fixed inputs, explicit state transitions, and assertions over both the job row and emitted metrics.

Notebook-to-prod is useful here. First explore delay distributions and state transitions with an in-memory repository; then run the identical tests against the transactional repository used by workers. The notebook is for understanding the policy. The database is the authority.

How should a Node.js queue retry failed rate-limited API calls?

Treat delivery as a state machine rather than a loop around an API client. A job starts as queued, becomes leased while one worker owns it, and ends as sent, retry_wait, or dead. Only a confirmed delivery becomes sent. A rate-limited response belongs in retry_wait with a future availability time; a permanent failure or a job that exhausts its attempt budget belongs in dead. That distinction prevents a bad address from consuming the same capacity as temporary throttling.

Observed outcome Next state Operator meaning
Confirmed delivery sent No more queue work
Rate limit or transient response retry_wait Reappears after a bounded delay
Permanent response or exhausted budget dead Review before redrive

The retry delay should respect a valid server-provided delay when the downstream API supplies one. Otherwise, use capped exponential backoff with jitter. The cap matters because a campaign delayed by hours shouldn't create absurd multi-day retry times, and jitter matters because thousands of jobs becoming eligible on the same second can recreate the overload. Don't retry every failure: authentication and invalid-recipient failures require correction, not patience. Keep the classification table close to the adapter for the downstream API, since response semantics vary.

For the weekly marketplace run, use two independent controls. A token bucket or equivalent limiter controls request starts per time window. A smaller concurrency limit controls simultaneous in-flight requests. They answer different questions. The rate limit protects the provider quota; concurrency controls sockets, memory, and how many ambiguous outcomes exist when a worker stops. Increasing concurrency above the allowed request rate can raise cost through failed attempts without improving useful throughput.

Idempotency closes the most dangerous gap — the worker may lose its lease after the downstream service accepts a message but before local state records success. Build a stable key from the campaign and customer, such as weekly-2026-W32:customer-1842, and pass it through whenever the delivery API supports idempotency. Locally, enforce uniqueness on that key. If the remote API doesn't provide an idempotency contract, the honest limitation is that exactly-once delivery can't be guaranteed across the network; choose an application policy that tolerates a rare duplicate or add a reconciliation step based on provider delivery records.

One key. One logical send.

Treat the DLQ as a forensic dataset

A dead-letter queue is evidence, not a trash can. Store the original payload or a durable reference, campaign ID, customer ID, attempt count, first and last failure timestamps, a normalized reason code, and the worker version that made the decision. Avoid secrets in payloads and logs. API credentials should be loaded through the deployment's secret-management path, scoped to the required operation, rotated according to policy, and never copied into a job body; the OWASP key-management guidance is a useful baseline for the lifecycle around those keys.

Redrive should be explicit and auditable. Select jobs by a narrow predicate such as campaign plus normalized reason, record a redrive batch ID and operator or automation identity, reset only the fields required by policy, and enqueue them at a controlled rate. Preserve prior attempts and failure history. If 18,000 jobs failed because recipient data was invalid, putting all 18,000 straight back into the live queue after a data fix can starve current work and hit the same downstream limit again. Canary a small batch, compare its terminal outcomes with the pre-redrive reason, and expand only when the signal is clean.

Never make redrive mean infinite retry.

The catch is that a DLQ adds operational surface: retention rules, sensitive-data review, access control, tooling, and an ownership rota. It isn't suitable as the primary mechanism for expected long delays or routine quota smoothing; use scheduled availability in the live queue for those. Stick with a simpler retry table when volume is low, one team owns the entire path, and the database can provide atomic claims without turning cleanup into a second platform. Choose a dedicated broker when multiple consumers, high sustained throughput, or independent retention and replay controls justify the extra moving parts.

Let the campaign deadline set the worker budget

Queue depth alone is ambiguous. Ten thousand jobs can be healthy early in a weekly campaign and alarming near its deadline. The leading service-level signal is oldest eligible job age, split by campaign and priority. Pair it with ready depth, retry-wait depth, lease count, completion rate, dead-letter rate, attempt distribution, and downstream outcome classes. For cost, track API attempts per successful digest and rendering work per terminal delivery; retries that never create value are the first place latency tuning becomes a spend problem.

A practical forecast uses remaining eligible jobs divided by the recent successful completion rate, with a safety margin for retries. Compare the projected drain time with the campaign deadline. If the estimate crosses the deadline, first confirm the bottleneck: a rate budget, concurrency, slow rendering, or a growing permanent-failure class. Raising worker count helps only some of those. If the downstream limit is binding, more workers mostly compete for the same tokens.

Alert on trends that demand an action. Oldest-job age approaching the digest deadline deserves a page; a small DLQ increase with one stable reason may deserve a ticket; zero throughput while ready jobs exist deserves immediate investigation. Dashboards should expose each retry reason separately, because a combined failed counter hides whether the remedy is waiting, correcting customer data, rotating credentials, or pausing a campaign. I'm not sure a universal alert percentage is defensible without the campaign window and normal traffic curve. Establish thresholds from load tests and several observed runs, then reevaluate them when the customer population or downstream contract changes.

Deployment follows the same logic. Ship the scheduler, worker, and redrive command as separately controllable units. Before enabling a campaign, verify the unique idempotency constraint, lease recovery, credential scope, rate budget, retry classifier, DLQ retention, and dashboard dimensions in a staging run with a fake delivery client. Roll out with a small customer cohort, inspect completion and attempts-per-success, then increase the cohort. The weekly scheduler remains a thin trigger throughout; hosted cron documentation is useful for understanding trigger behavior, but durable campaign progress belongs in application state rather than in one scheduler invocation.

The final decision rule is compact.

Favor lower concurrency and predictable cost when the projected drain time remains inside the digest deadline; spend additional concurrency only when measurements show local capacity, rather than the downstream API limit, is the constraint. Keep dead letters reviewable, redrive them in canaries, and make oldest-job age the clock everyone watches.

title: Looking One Step Ahead: An Anticipation-guided Agent for Object State Readout in Videos
description:
arXiv:2611.14113v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding the progress of an activity requires tracking how the objects involved change over time. Object state readout provides this information by describing a target object's states and transitions across video frames. Although multimodal large language models (MLLMs) generate detailed visual descriptions, these descriptions may leave the attributes needed to distinguish successive states insufficiently specified. In this paper, we propose look-ahead state readout (LASER), an anticipation-guided agent for object state readout that uses possible next-step changes to determine which attributes to inspect in the present. Given temporally ordered frames and a target object, LASER converts anticipated changes into targeted visual questions and inspects the current frame to establish attribute values. It then checks state readouts and forecasts against independent observations of subsequent frames, refining a state record used to generate the final description. Reusable textual observation skills guide this process and are refined by tracing discrepancies with reference captions to the responsible instructions. Candidate revisions are selected on separate videos based on improved caption quality without increased contradictions with reference facts. Model parameters remain frozen throughout adaptation and inference, and the revised skills remain fixed during evaluation. Experiment results and further analysis on OSCaR and PLM RCap show consistent improvements of LASER over strong baselines and existing approaches, which demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach.
