title: Storage Object API Returned Malformed Responses During 3 Resized Image Upload Checks
description:
Large media uploads change the storage decision: the application should coordinate bytes, not become their transport path. For a thumbnail or resizing pipeline, the durable boundary is a private object plus a verified upload result, with the client or worker sending the payload directly to storage. That design keeps the API contract replaceable while making a malformed response an explicit failure rather than a misleading success.

The short answer is to separate the upload protocol from image processing. Create or obtain a signed upload target, upload the resized object with private access, validate the storage response before recording the object as ready, and retain enough request and response context to reconcile a retry. Infrai is a reasonable option when a plain REST contract and discovery metadata reduce migration work across storage providers; S3, Cloudflare R2, and Alibaba Cloud OSS remain better fits when their surrounding ecosystem or specific storage controls are requirements.

What should the application own?

A useful pipeline has three steps: produce the thumbnail, transfer it without proxying the bytes through the application, and commit a small record that says which object is available. The record should contain an object key, content type, expected size, a digest if the producer can provide one, and the upload request identifier. It should not be written merely because a client received an HTTP response.

That last distinction matters for the reported failure mode. A response can have an unexpected status, a body that is not valid JSON, fields with the wrong types, or an empty body where the client expected confirmation. A client that decodes whatever arrives and immediately marks the thumbnail ready has turned a transport or service problem into corrupted application state. Validate the status first, validate the content type and body shape second, and only then advance the state machine.

Reject it.

That is the boundary.

There is a more expensive case worth spelling out because it is easy to misdiagnose. Suppose the resize worker sends a 1,920 by 1,080 WebP, receives a 502 with an HTML body, and retries against the same key. The retry may succeed, while the first request may also have reached storage before the intermediary produced its error page. A database row written after the second response cannot prove which write won, and a raw response log cannot prove object contents. The adapter therefore needs a deterministic key, an idempotency record, and a post-write verification step; the reconciliation worker can compare the object metadata with the expected content type and size before moving the row from uploaded to verified. That is slower than trusting a 2xx response, but the alternative is an audit trail that says a thumbnail is ready when no consumer can safely establish what bytes it contains.

I initially treated a malformed response as an upload problem. The more useful diagnosis is narrower: it is a contract problem at the boundary. Inspect the request and response logs together, including method, target host, object key, status, content type, request ID, and body length. Redact credentials and image bytes. The comparison between a successful thumbnail and the malformed attempt often exposes a wrongly formatted request, an intermediary returning an HTML error page, or a service-side issue without requiring a second write.

For large media, this ownership model also avoids a common architectural trap: the API server has to hold open a connection while doing work that object storage is designed to handle. Resize workers should produce bounded objects and hand off the transfer. The application should coordinate state and retries. That is a much smaller blast radius.

Why did the storage object API return a malformed response?

Only if the application contract is narrower than the provider API. Define an internal operation such as putPrivateObject(bucket, key, contentType, body) and map it to a provider adapter. The adapter owns signed URLs, provider headers, multipart details, response parsing, and request IDs. The rest of the system sees states such as created, uploading, uploaded, verified, and failed; it does not see vendor-specific response fields.

The retry rule should be written down before production traffic arrives. A retry after an ambiguous response must use the same object key and an idempotency key or an equivalent deduplication record. Otherwise, a timeout can create two objects or cause a later worker to overwrite a newer thumbnail. Exactly-once delivery is not something an HTTP client can assume; it is a system property assembled from idempotent writes, durable state transitions, and reconciliation.

A small Go boundary makes the important dependency visible, even when the concrete provider adapter differs. This example uses the verified object-write route against a private bucket; the adapter should use a signed target when the workflow delegates the byte transfer to a client or worker.

func putThumbnail(ctx context.Context, bucket, key string, data []byte) error {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        return errors.New("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    baseURL := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
    path := "/storage/object/put" + "/" + url.PathEscape(bucket) + "/" + url.PathEscape(key)
    uploadURL := baseURL + path
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPut, uploadURL, bytes.NewReader(data))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "image/webp")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "thumbnail-"+key)
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("upload failed: status=%d body=%q", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        if len(body) == 0 || !strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(resp.Header.Get("Content-Type")), "application/json") {
            return errors.New("upload response has unexpected format")
        }
        return nil
    }
    return errors.New("upload retry limit reached")
}

This deliberately does not pretend that status success proves the object is usable. A production adapter should decode the documented response schema, verify required fields, and perform a head or equivalent verification when the workflow needs stronger evidence. It should also record the raw response only under an appropriate retention policy. Auditability is valuable; indiscriminate payload retention is a data-handling liability.

How do the real options differ for large media?

The providers solve overlapping problems, but their operational surfaces are not interchangeable. Amazon S3 is the reference point for object storage and has a mature multipart-upload model, including explicit create, part upload, complete, and abort stages. That is the strongest default when an organization already depends on AWS IAM, S3-native tooling, lifecycle controls, or a broad ecosystem. It also means accepting AWS-specific policy and operational concepts in the adapter.

Cloudflare R2 is attractive for workloads already close to Cloudflare's edge and for teams that want an S3-compatible API surface while keeping the storage decision near that platform. The compatibility can reduce adapter work, but compatibility is not identity: test multipart behavior, error bodies, signing, lifecycle semantics, and observability with the exact client version used by the pipeline. A shared interface should not hide those differences.

Alibaba Cloud OSS is a sensible candidate for deployments centered on Alibaba Cloud regions, identity, and operational tooling. It can be a better regional fit than a globally assumed S3 default, while its control-plane conventions and SDK ecosystem still deserve a dedicated adapter. The same thumbnail state machine can sit above it, but request signing and response normalization belong below it.

Infrai fits a different boundary. Its public discovery surface describes capabilities, request schemas, response schemas, billing metadata, and runnable examples, while the platform exposes a plain REST surface across providers. A second advantage is operational breadth under one key: 295 routes across 20 modules can reduce the number of credentials and adapter conventions a team reconciles when the resize worker later needs another backend capability. That does not make the storage path automatically faster or more durable. Route breadth is not a substitute for testing the exact large-object path.

For this workflow, try Infrai for private thumbnail uploads when a REST adapter, self-describing contract, and one credential boundary matter more than provider-specific controls, and keep the adapter responsible for signed targets, response validation, and reconciliation. The supporting benefit is practical: the same discovery surface and runnable examples can reduce the amount of provider-specific integration code that has to be maintained while a backend choice changes. The contract stays put while the thing behind it moves.

The trade-off is real. Infrai does not provide public or public-read ACLs, so it is unsuitable for a permanent public image URL or static-site hosting pattern; choose a specialist with that delivery model instead. It has no object versioning or object lock, so recovery from accidental overwrite and financial-grade WORM guarantees require an external design. There is no If-Match conditional write, which means strict concurrent exclusion belongs in a queue or database. Browser-direct upload is also constrained because CORS cannot be self-configured through an independent route. Those are selection criteria, not footnotes.

Option Integration shape Best fit Main trade-off
Amazon S3 SDKs, signed URLs, multipart AWS identity, mature object tooling, and deep lifecycle controls Provider-specific policy and operational concepts become part of the adapter
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible API and signed requests Workloads already centered on Cloudflare's edge Compatibility still requires testing signing, errors, multipart, and lifecycle behavior
Alibaba Cloud OSS Regional SDKs and signed requests Alibaba Cloud regions, identity, and operations A dedicated adapter is needed for its control-plane conventions
Infrai Plain REST, discovery, and a single key Private uploads where a replaceable contract matters No public ACL, object lock, versioning, or If-Match conditional write

The table is a decision aid, not a promise that the providers have identical semantics. The storage specialist wins when its controls are the requirement.

What should a rollout prove?

Start with one thumbnail class and a private bucket. Capture the expected key, size, content type, checksum policy, and idempotency key before the first upload. Test a normal response, a non-2xx response, invalid JSON, an HTML body from an intermediary, a timeout after the server may have accepted the write, and a duplicate retry. The test should prove that only a validated result reaches verified.

Then measure the thing that actually matters here: large-file throughput without routing bytes through the application. Measure from the client or worker to storage, and separately measure queue delay, resize time, and commit latency. Do not infer throughput from the application request time. A fast metadata response can coexist with a slow transfer, and a successful transfer can coexist with an unusable response.

Keep migration reversible by storing provider-independent metadata and retaining an adapter-specific diagnostic envelope outside the core object record. If a provider is replaced, re-run the same response-validation and reconciliation tests against the new adapter. Existing consumers should continue to understand verified and failed; they should not need to learn a new vendor's success vocabulary.

If this private, signed-only boundary fits the system, the storage object discovery documentation is the appropriate next check for the exact request and response schema.

Sources

  • AWS S3 multipart upload overview
  • Amazon S3 PUT Object API
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility
  • Alibaba Cloud OSS multipart upload
  • Infrai storage object discovery

title: Beyond Fluent Responses: Finding User Dissatisfaction in Human-AI Interactions
description:
arXiv:2611.13894v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As large language models generate increasingly high-quality responses, recent work on response evaluation has moved beyond response-centered criteria, such as correctness and coherence, toward user-centered criteria, including user preferences and perceived usefulness. This shift is fundamentally important for developing technologies that are truly useful to real-world users. While conventional response evaluation quantifies the quality of the response itself, users' satisfaction in real conversations also depends on their subjective preferences and perceptions of usefulness, which do not necessarily align with response quality. This study investigates whether such user-centered signals can be detected from conversational text. Specifically, we analyze user utterances with self-reported dissatisfaction labels to examine whether user dissatisfaction in text can be detected. In English interaction, models using user utterances exceeded the 17.8% dissatisfaction label prevalence in AUPRC by up to 15 percentage points. These results suggest that user utterances reveal cues to implicit dissatisfaction. Furthermore, changes from the immediately preceding user utterance may improve dissatisfaction detection, with anomaly detection methods appearing particularly effective.

title: Why Developer Experience Needs Continuous Improvement?
description:
What I Learned From My Open-Source Journey

When I started working on open-source projects such as Kubernetes SIG-Multicluster and KServe in the cloud-native community, I began to understand the importance of user experience (UX) in developer tools.

Today, many organizations and open-source communities are focusing on building new products, introducing AI features, and improving existing technologies. Engineers are busy developing new features, fixing technical issues, and releasing new versions of their software.

During my journey, I noticed that developer experience (DevEx) is important, but it does not always receive the same attention as product development.

Many engineers understand the value of UX, but they often do not have enough time to focus on improving the developer experience. Some engineers are interested in participating in UX research, but their busy schedules make it difficult to attend interviews or contribute to UX-related activities.

I also noticed that some engineers try to apply UX research methods themselves. However, without enough knowledge of UX research, they may choose methods or solutions based on what they personally feel is appropriate rather than following a structured research process.

At the same time, UX designers also face challenges when entering the developer experience field.

Unlike designing everyday applications, working on developer tools requires technical and domain knowledge. Designers need to understand how developers work, what tools they use, and what challenges they face.

For example, I have been learning about Kubernetes and the cloud-native ecosystem for almost two years. Even today, I feel there is still a lot to learn before I can fully understand the technical challenges developers experience.

Developer experience requires both UX knowledge and an understanding of the developer's technical environment.

These experiences made me think about an important question:

How can organizations improve developer experience without spending too much time, money, and effort?

1. Why Improving Developer Experience Can Be Challenging

During my open-source journey, I interacted with people from different organizations and learned how they approach developer experience.

I noticed that some large organizations have dedicated UX teams, budgets, and resources to improve their products. However, smaller organizations and open-source projects may not have enough time, money, or people to focus on UX improvements.

This does not necessarily mean they do not care about user experience. In many cases, they are already busy maintaining their products, developing new features, and supporting their users.

The challenge is not always a lack of interest in UX. Sometimes, it is a lack of time, resources, and a clear process for making improvements.

Another challenge is finding UX professionals who are interested in developer tools and have enough technical knowledge to work in this field.

As a result, even when engineers experience difficulties using a product, those challenges may not receive immediate attention.

2. Why UX Should Be a Continuous Improvement Process

One of the most important lessons I learned is that user experience is not a one-time activity. It is a continuous process of learning, testing, and improving.

Imagine an organization develops an application, tests it, and launches the first version.

During the first few months, users start exploring the application and using its features. After six months or one year, they may begin to experience challenges that were not identified during the initial development and testing stages.

These challenges may include confusing workflows, difficult navigation, unclear documentation, or features that do not work as users expected.

Even if the organization improves these issues and releases another version, users may discover new challenges as the product continues to grow.

This means UX improvements should not stop after a product is launched.

Every new version, feature, or workflow can create new opportunities to understand users and improve their experience.

In simple terms:

Build the product → Release it → Listen to users → Identify challenges → Improve the experience → Release the next version → Continue learning.

This cycle should continue throughout the product's life.

3. The Time, Cost, and Effort Behind UX Improvements

From my experience working as a Senior UX Designer at Super Purposes, I learned that even small UX improvements can require significant time, money, and organizational effort.

For example, imagine an organization decides to improve the user experience of an existing application.

The first step may be to hire a UX designer or build a UX team.

At Super Purposes, I was involved in hiring UX talent, assigning tasks, managing UX activities, and reviewing design work.

From this experience, I learned that hiring suitable UX talent can take approximately two to three months(For immediate hire, many be different time line for regular hiring talent), depending on the organization's requirements, candidate availability, interviews, and evaluation process.

During this period, the organization is already spending time and money on recruitment, hiring teams, and tools.

Once the UX designer joins the organization, the next stage involves understanding the existing product, discussing improvement opportunities with managers and developers, and identifying user challenges.

The UX improvement process may include:

  • Understanding the existing application: Learning how the product works and identifying its current limitations.

  • Conducting UX research: Interviewing users, running usability studies, and collecting feedback.

  • Analyzing research findings: Identifying common challenges, patterns, and opportunities for improvement.

  • Designing solutions: Creating design improvements and exploring multiple iterations.

  • Testing improvements: Evaluating whether the proposed solutions actually solve users' problems.

  • Collaborating with teams: Working with developers, managers, and stakeholders to review and approve changes.

  • Documenting the research: Recording findings, decisions, and improvements for future reference.

Depending on the size and complexity of the project, this entire process can take several months. In some cases, a major one feature UX improvement initiative may take nine to twelve months or longer.

For a solo UX designer, managing all these activities can be especially challenging, so it leads the organization to hire multiple talents.

Before AI tools became widely available, completing these activities often required more manual effort. Today, AI can help designers with tasks such as organizing research findings, preparing documentation, analyzing feedback, and exploring design ideas.

However, AI cannot completely replace the need to understand users, validate findings, and make thoughtful design decisions.

Even with AI assistance, a solo designer may need many months to complete a large UX improvement project (Start working on improvements and deliver the results and then documenting the project).

This helped me understand that UX improvements are not only about design. They also involve organizational time, money, people, collaboration, and long-term planning.

Why UX documentation is equally important

Another important lesson from my experience is the value of UX documentation.

Imagine a company completes user research and makes several improvements but does not document the findings or decisions.

After a year, the company decides to improve the same application again. If the previous research findings are unavailable, the new team may need to repeat some of the earlier work.

This can increase the time and cost of future improvements.

Good UX documentation helps organizations preserve knowledge, avoid repeating research unnecessarily, and make better decisions in future product versions.

4. New Features vs. Better Developer Experience

In software development, organizations often follow planned release cycles to introduce new features, fix bugs, and improve product capabilities.

For example, while working with the KServe project, I observed how the project continues to evolve with new releases and capabilities.

KServe has supported traditional predictive model serving, while its development has also expanded toward generative AI and large language model (LLM) workloads.

This is an example of how developer tools continue to evolve as technology and user requirements change.

However, releasing new features does not automatically mean the developer experience is improving.

A product may offer powerful technical capabilities while developers still face challenges understanding documentation, configuring the system, deploying applications, or troubleshooting errors.

In many organizations, engineering teams are already focused on delivering new releases. Conducting UX research and improving existing workflows may require separate planning, resources, and approval.

As a result, new feature development may move faster than UX improvements.

This creates an important question:

What if organizations could collect developer feedback continuously instead of waiting until they have enough time and resources to start a large UX research project?

I believe this approach could help organizations identify problems earlier and make improvements more regularly.

5. How Can We Improve Developer Experience With Less Time and Effort?

Based on my experience with Kubernetes SIG-Multicluster and KServe, I started thinking about practical ways to improve developer experience without always depending on large UX research projects.

I believe small, consistent UX activities can help organizations understand developers' challenges and make meaningful improvements over time.

Here are three approaches that I believe can help.

Approach 1: Collect Feedback Directly From Developers

One of the simplest ways to understand user challenges is to ask users for feedback while they are using the product.

For example, after a developer completes an important workflow, the application could invite them to share their experience through a short feedback form.

The form should take only two to three minutes to complete.

It could include simple questions such as:

  • What were you trying to accomplish?
  • Did you experience any difficulties?
  • What could we improve to make this task easier?

This approach allows organizations to collect feedback regularly without requiring every user to participate in a long interview.

Over time, the organization can build a useful collection of feedback that helps identify common problems and prioritize improvements.

Many organizations already use feedback surveys in their applications.

I believe developer tools and open-source projects can also benefit from making short feedback activities part of their regular workflows.

The important point is to collect feedback at the right moment without interrupting developers' work.

Approach 2: Use Existing GitHub Issues as a UX Research Resource

Sometimes, organizations may not receive enough responses from surveys or may struggle to recruit developers for interviews.

In these situations, valuable user feedback may already exist in the project's GitHub repository.

Developers regularly create GitHub issues to report bugs, ask questions, describe technical difficulties, and request new features.

These issues can provide useful information about the challenges developers experience while using a product.

For example, instead of starting a completely new research study, a UX designer or engineer can review existing GitHub issues and identify patterns such as:

  • Repeated deployment and configuration difficulties.
  • Confusing error messages or troubleshooting processes.
  • Missing or unclear documentation.
  • Challenges with maintenance and observability.
  • Feature requests that reveal unmet developer needs.

By organizing these issues into common themes, teams can identify areas that may need UX improvements.

During my KServe research, I explored GitHub issues to understand the challenges developers experience while working with the project.

This experience helped me recognize that GitHub repositories can be a valuable source of existing user feedback for developer experience research.

However, GitHub issues do not always explain the complete user journey or the reasons behind a problem. When possible, teams should validate their findings through interviews, usability testing, or additional feedback.

Approach 3: Use Developer Conferences to Collect Quick Feedback

Another opportunity I noticed during my open-source journey is the value of developer-focused conferences and community events.

Many open-source projects participate in conferences, organize booths, and introduce their technologies to developers.

For example, KServe participates in cloud-native community events where engineers can learn about the project and interact with contributors.

These events are already bringing developers and project teams together.

Why not use a few minutes of these conversations to understand developers' challenges?

Instead of only explaining the product or introducing new features, project contributors could ask developers a simple question:

"What is the biggest challenge you face while using our project?"

A developer may need less than five minutes to explain a challenge they recently experienced.

Even a short conversation can help the team discover a problem, understand a confusing workflow, or identify an opportunity for improvement.

Imagine speaking with ten developers during a conference. Their feedback may reveal common challenges that deserve further investigation.

These conversations do not replace formal UX research, but they can help teams identify important questions and decide where to focus their research efforts.

Sometimes, a five-minute conversation can be the starting point for a meaningful developer experience improvement.

6. Small UX Activities Can Create Long-Term Value

From my experience, I believe organizations do not always need to wait until they have a dedicated UX team or a large research budget to start improving developer experience.

They can begin with activities that fit into their existing development and community workflows.

For example, collecting short feedback surveys, reviewing GitHub issues, and talking to developers during community events can help teams understand user challenges continuously.

However, collecting feedback is only the beginning.

The real value comes from reviewing the feedback, identifying common patterns, prioritizing problems, making improvements, and checking whether those improvements actually help developers.

Over time, these small activities can build a stronger understanding of users and help teams make better product decisions.

They can also create useful research documentation that supports future improvements.

For smaller organizations and open-source communities, this approach may be more practical than waiting to launch a large UX initiative.

Conclusion: Developer Experience Is Everyone's Responsibility

My journey with Kubernetes SIG-Multicluster and KServe has helped me understand that improving developer experience is not always easy.

Engineers are busy building and maintaining products. UX designers need time to understand complex developer tools. Organizations must balance product development, budgets, and available resources.

But I also learned that improving developer experience does not always require a large team, a big budget, or a lengthy research project.

Sometimes, meaningful improvements can begin with simple activities:

Ask developers for feedback. Listen to their challenges. Learn from existing GitHub issues. Have short conversations at community events. Document what you discover.

These small efforts can help organizations understand their users and make better decisions.

As technology continues to evolve, especially with AI and cloud-native tools, I believe developer experience should receive continuous attention alongside new feature development.

Building powerful developer tools is important, but making those tools easier to understand, use, and maintain is equally important.

And most importantly, developer experience is not a one-time improvement. It is a continuous journey of listening, learning, and making things better for developers.

These are my personal observations and lessons from working on UX research in the cloud-native open-source community. I would love to hear how other engineers, maintainers, and UX designers approach developer experience improvements in their projects.

What small UX activities have helped your team improve developer experience?

title: A Multi-Word Tokenizer for 204 Languages That Needs Fewer Tokens Than GPT-4o's, Including on English
description:
arXiv:2611.13059v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Languages of India need 1.6 to 14 times as many tokens as English on GPT-4o's tokenizer for the same content, which makes them more expensive and slower to serve. We train tokenizers from scratch on human-written text in about 200 languages. Havon v3 is a byte-level BPE tokenizer with 262,144 tokens and a pre-tokenizer that keeps combining marks with their letters and chunks scripts written without spaces. On FLORES-200 devtest it needs fewer tokens than GPT-4o's o200k_base on all 25 languages of India (median 0.74 of GPT-4o's count) and on 172 of 204 languages, but 7% more on English. Havon v4 adds a second, multi-word training stage (SuperBPE) to v3. At exactly GPT-4o's vocabulary size of 200,019 tokens, v4 needs 6.1% fewer tokens than GPT-4o on English and fewer on 161 of 204 languages and all 25 languages of India (median 0.74); at the same size, v3 needs 9.4% more on English and wins on 133. With 262,144 tokens, v4 needs 9.6% fewer tokens on English and fewer on 182 of 204 languages, and with 524,288 tokens it needs fewer on 203 of 204. The gains are largest for English, Hindi and the Romance languages; scripts without spaces, such as Khmer, Burmese and Tibetan, gain little and lose subword merges. Havon v5 replaces v4's Python-only code sample with permissively licensed code in 15 languages: on code it needs 1.03 to 1.22 times GPT-4o's tokens, against 1.11 to 1.29 for v4, while keeping all 25 languages of India (median 0.74, all significant under a sentence-level bootstrap) and English (0.94). These are compression results only: we have not yet evaluated a model trained with v4 or v5.

title: Embodied Science Agents: Making Embodied Experimental Design Learnable
description:
arXiv:2611.12958v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advances in large models have accelerated AI for Science toward agentic science, where AI agents autonomously conduct scientific discovery. Realising this vision requires closing the loop between computational reasoning and physical experimentation, positioning self-driving laboratories (SDLs) as critical enablers. However, existing SDLs exhibit a fundamental paradox: foundation model integration has increased linguistic sophistication while severing physical grounding. By treating models as disembodied planners that output symbolic workflows for separate robotic systems, current architectures inherently block the development of embodied experimental intuition. We argue that overcoming this paradox requires embedding \emph{learnability} along three interdependent axes: cognitive learnability (learning what to investigate), experimental learnability (learning where to search), and embodied learnability (learning how to act). Building on this view, we introduce the Embodied Science Agent (ESA), which unifies digital intelligence with physical embodiment through three synergistic components: a Digital Agent that provides cognitive and experimental learnability via memory-based reasoning and Bayesian optimisation, an Embodied Agent that provides embodied learnability via generalisable instrument control, and an Embodied Unified Interface for seamless coordination. We validated ESA in autonomous wastewater treatment experiments, navigating over 200 million possible conditions. Through 15 continuous rounds, ESA raised the final solution transmittance from 82\% to 99.7\%, corresponding to a 98.5\% reduction in residual dye concentration and near-complete decolourisation, while its learned visuomotor policies generalised across varying instrument placements, a promising step toward next-generation SDLs for autonomous scientific discovery.

title: Earlybird: Predictive Streaming Speech Recognition in 29M Parameters
description:
arXiv:2611.14421v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Streaming speech recognizers output a word only after the speaker has finished it, typically 90-400 ms later. For a voice agent every millisecond counts: the sooner the words are outputted, the sooner the agent can start a search or plan its reply. We present Earlybird, a 29M-parameter streaming recognizer (16.8 MB at 4 bits). Earlybird learns from audio cut off at random points, including partway through a word, and is asked to predict every word that is due by then in full, plus a guess of the next two words. Its raw token probabilities give a confidence for every word including the one still being spoken. On clean audiobook speech (LibriSpeech test-clean), the median word is predicted correctly 90 ms before the speaker finishes it, while released streaming models get it 90 to 400 ms after it ends. Earlybird is the earliest on all six test sets we time, covering audiobooks, TED talks, public speech, earnings calls, and synthetic speech. On the same audiobooks, 69% of words are predicted correctly before they end, against 3-25% for the other models. For words still being spoken, confidence is calibrated, with an expected calibration error (ECE) of 3.7 to 5.5. On the eight English Open ASR Leaderboard sets, it is more accurate than Moonshine Tiny on every set and roughly ties Whistle, a model of the same size.

title: A Test Run I Aborted Came Back and Corrupted My Evidence
description:
A Test Run I Aborted Came Back and Corrupted My Evidence

From the agentdrill v0.1.0 release, part of agentic-suite: open-source, harness-agnostic security tools for AI-agent defenses.

The case finished at 12:09 with complete evidence. At 12:49 its assertions file was empty. Nothing was running. Or so I believed.

Somewhere in the background, a sweep I had aborted hours earlier was still alive, patiently re-running cases. Between 12:45 and 12:49 it wrote over the crew results and truncated an assertions file mid-case. The process I thought I had killed had killed my evidence instead.

This is the kind of thing that only happens to test data, because we treat test data as if it were not data. The full forensics are in the agentdrill v0.1.0 field test report, issues I-10 and I-11.

Two writers, one directory, no locks

The harness truncates a case's logs at the start of each run. That is correct behavior for a fresh run. It is catastrophic behavior when two runs touch the same case directory. The orphaned sweep started cases fresh, which wiped the assertions files, then got torn down partway, which left some of them empty.

The case it hit, FT-B-CREW-EXAMPLES, had a healthy verdict from 12:09 with all five assertions embedded in it. At 12:49 the backing file was blank. A pass verdict with no assertions behind it is a claim without proof, and it sat there looking exactly like every other green row.

The only reason it got caught: a grounding gate. The harness re-derives the report from disk, and a PASS with zero grounded assertions is flagged as over-claimed. It flagged exactly one case. That is the entire safety net between "corrupted evidence" and "shipped as proof", and it worked because it reads the raw files instead of trusting the summary.

The second landmine was a default

The same day, a different foot-gun surfaced. Running a single case directly defaulted its results to a directory called results/all/, next to the per-suite directories. So a quick one-case re-run created a duplicate case directory, a second copy of the truth that would drift from the first with every subsequent run.

Defaults that write files are quiet landmines. The second run does not fail. It forks the record. And a forked record is worse than a lost one, because now there are two answers and no marker saying which is canonical.

The fix in lib.sh is my favorite change of the whole run, mostly because of its tone. There is no default run ID anymore. If a runner starts without an explicit destination, the harness dies before writing anything, announcing FATAL: FT_RUN_ID is not set and refusing to write to a default results dir. A stray all/ directory can never be created silently again. run-case.sh now derives the correct suite directory from the case registry before anything else happens.

What recovery looked like

Three things made this recoverable instead of fatal:

  1. The verdict carried embedded evidence. The 12:09 verdict listed its assertions inline, so the proof existed in two places. When one was truncated, the other still testified.
  2. Git held the pre-corruption state. The evidence was committed, so recovery meant regenerating from source, not mourning.
  3. The grounding gate pointed at the wound. One over-claimed PASS was the signal, and it was precise. No scanning, no guessing. The gate named the case.

The evidence was regenerated in place, inside the correct suite directory, and the grounding gate went back to green with zero over-claims across all 73 units.

The lesson is about data, not tests

I keep re-deriving the same conclusion from this run: test evidence is production data. It needs the same engineering we would never skip for a database:

  • Unique write namespaces. No two writers in one directory, ever. Parallel runners get their own branches of the results tree.
  • No default write paths. If the destination is ambiguous, refuse to start. A hard failure at launch is infinitely cheaper than a silent fork at 12:49.
  • Re-derive conclusions from raw files. The summary is a cache. The grounding gate reads what actually happened and compares.
  • Abort must mean abort. A killed parent with living children is a ghost, and ghosts write files.

Tip: if two processes can write your results directory, make the second one crash at launch, not at 12:49.

What did not work: process hygiene, full stop. The sweep should have died with the tool call that started it. Process groups exist for exactly this, and we were not using them. Every other control was a net that caught the failure after it happened. This one was the only control that could have prevented it.

If two processes wrote your test results directory tonight, would tomorrow's report know? For us the answer was "only because a gate re-reads the raw files", which is a good answer but an accidental one. I would rather have the answer be "impossible by construction", which is what the FATAL guard now gives us.

Code and receipts: agentdrill · field test report · the guard that refuses a default results dir · the grounding gate

About agentdrill

This story is one of seven from the agentdrill v0.1.0 field test. agentdrill is the adversarial-testing engine in agentic-suite: open-source, harness-agnostic security tools for AI-agent defenses. It runs versioned attack packs against your deployed stack in CI and publishes honest results, misses included.

pip install agentsec-agentdrill   # v0.1.0 is live on PyPI
agentdrill quickstart             # first honest result in ~15 minutes, bundled demo

Dig deeper: the v0.1.0 field test report (73/73 units, every pass grounded), the release notes, and the rest of the suite at github.com/agentic-suite: agentdrill drills the defenses, agentwatch records the evidence.
